translation: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.
interpretation: The opening formula invokes Allah by His two names of mercy, al-Rahman and al-Rahim, teaching that every action a believer begins should be undertaken seeking divine help and blessing. The repetition of mercy frames the whole Qur'an as a revelation rooted in God's boundless compassion: al-Rahman points to a mercy that embraces all creation in this world, while al-Rahim points to a mercy specially bestowed upon the faithful. By starting with this phrase, the believer is reminded that they approach every task, and the reading of scripture itself, from a posture of humility, dependence, and hope in God's grace.

translation: All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The opening verse of the Qur'an establishes that all praise, in its fullest and most complete sense, belongs exclusively to Allah. The word 'alhamdu' encompasses gratitude for blessings received as well as admiration for perfect attributes, and by declaring that praise belongs to Him, the believer acknowledges that every good thing in existence ultimately traces back to its divine source. The title 'Lord of the worlds' (Rabb al-'alamin) points to Allah's sovereign nurturing, sustaining, and governing of all creation, seen and unseen, so that gratitude becomes the natural orientation of a servant who recognizes that he is continually sustained by a Lord who owns and directs every realm of existence.

translation: Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Raheem: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The phrase opens with the invocation of Allah by two of His divine names, ar-Rahman and ar-Raheem, both derived from the root r-h-m (mercy). Ar-Rahman points to a mercy that is vast and encompassing, extended to all creation without distinction, while ar-Raheem points to a mercy that is specific and enduring, bestowed particularly upon the believers. By beginning every action with this formula, the believer places the act under the protection and blessing of Allah and acknowledges that all capacity and success come from His mercy alone.

translation: Master of the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: The verse declares that Allah alone holds absolute sovereignty and ownership over the Day of Judgment, the day when all deeds are reckoned and every soul is recompensed. On that day no one will possess authority, intercession, or power except by His permission, so the believer is reminded that ultimate accountability belongs to God, which calls for sincere awe, humility, and righteous conduct in this life.

translation: You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.
interpretation: This verse stands at the heart of the Fatiha and expresses the core of tawhid in both worship and reliance. By placing 'You' before the verbs, the verse emphasizes exclusivity: worship is directed to God alone, not divided among any other object of devotion. The shift from third person in the preceding verses to direct address marks the believer's turn from describing God to standing before Him in personal speech. The second clause, seeking help, pairs with the first to show that true servanthood requires both sincere devotion in action and humble dependence on God for the strength to fulfill it. Worship without reliance can become self-sufficiency, and reliance without worship can become passivity; the verse joins the two into a single stance of the servant before the Lord.

translation: Guide us to the straight path.
interpretation: This verse, the opening supplication of Surah Al-Fatiha, is a prayer for continual divine guidance. The believer asks Allah to keep them firmly upon the path of truth, moderation, and right conduct, recognizing that guidance is not a one-time achievement but a need renewed at every moment. The 'straight path' is understood as the way of submission to Allah's commands, the path of those He has blessed, distinct from the ways of those who went astray through arrogance or ignorance. By repeating this request in every prayer, the worshipper continually reaffirms their dependence on God and their commitment to sincerely seeking the truth.

translation: The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor, not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray.
interpretation: The verse defines the straight path by its people rather than by abstract doctrine alone: it is the way of those whom God has blessed with guidance and right action, the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous, as described elsewhere in the Qur'an. Its two negations mark the twin ways of deviation. Those who 'have earned anger' are understood by many classical commentators to be those who knew the truth and rejected or neglected it, while 'those who are astray' are those who sought the truth without proper knowledge and wandered from it. Thus the prayer asks for a path that joins sound knowledge with sincere practice, guarding the believer against both willful rejection and ignorant error.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Alif, Lam, Meem.
interpretation: The verse opens with the basmala, anchoring the recitation in God's mercy, and then presents the disjointed letters Alif, Lam, Meem, which belong to the mysterious opening letters (muqatta'at) of certain surahs. Classical scholars held that these letters are God's own knowledge, not fully disclosed to humans, and that they signal the Qur'an's inimitable character: it is composed of the very same letters the Arabs used in speech, yet they cannot produce its like. The mystery invites the listener to humility before revelation, recognizing that the book's meaning reaches beyond what ordinary speech can fully unlock, while its opening in mercy assures that the guidance it brings flows from divine compassion.

translation: This is the Book about which there is no doubt, a guidance for those who are conscious of God.
interpretation: The verse opens by affirming that the Qur'an is beyond all doubt, not because of any external proof alone but because its truth is self-evident to the one who opens the heart to it. Its guidance is not given indiscriminately to all; it is received by those who have taken on taqwa, a conscious awareness of God that makes them vigilant over their conduct and sincerely receptive. The Book is thus a light that illuminates the path, yet the light is perceived only by eyes willing to see, which shows that revelation and the inner disposition of the seeker work together toward guidance.

translation: Those who believe in the unseen, establish the prayer, and spend out of what We have provided for them.
interpretation: The verse defines the core of true faith as a combined inner and outer discipline: belief in what lies beyond the senses (the unseen, such as God, the angels, the Last Day, and revelation) forms the foundation, while the establishment of prayer ties that belief to continuous worship and conscious remembrance of God. Spending from what God has provided shows that faith must also be carried into social responsibility, so that wealth is understood as a trust received from God and shared with others. Thus the verse presents the faithful as those whose conviction in the unseen shapes their devotion to God and their generosity toward people.

translation: And those who believe in what has been revealed to you, and in what was revealed before you, and in the Hereafter, they are certain of it.
interpretation: The verse defines true faith as a unified commitment: belief in the revelation given to the Prophet Muhammad and in the earlier revelations sent to previous messengers, joined with certainty about the Hereafter. The word yuqinun (certainty) signals that this faith is not mere assumption or inherited custom but firm conviction, which is why the verse places the Hereafter alongside revelation as a pillar of belief. It also implies that the message of the Qur'an continues the same divine guidance given through earlier prophets, so that acceptance of one revelation entails respect for the whole chain of prophetic guidance.

translation: Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful.
interpretation: The verse presents guidance from the Lord as the foundation of true success: those who are rightly guided are not merely upright in their conduct but are established on a firm path that comes from God, and it is this divine guidance that makes their success genuine, since worldly gain or apparent triumph without it cannot be called salvation. The repetition of the demonstrative 'those' emphasizes their distinction and elevated standing, and their being described as 'the successful' (al-mufliḥūn) signals that their reward is both in this life and the next, for the success the Qur'an affirms is the attainment of what is good and lasting, achieved through hearing the guidance and acting upon it.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe.
interpretation: This verse (2:6) describes a settled state of those whose hearts have closed to guidance after persistent rejection of the truth. Their refusal is not caused by a lack of warning but by their own inner choice to turn away, so the Prophet's effort to warn them yields no change in their condition. It consoles the Prophet by showing that the outcome of his mission is not in his hands alone, and it highlights that guidance requires a receptive heart, which these individuals have lost through obstinate denial.

translation: Allah has set a seal upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and over their sight is a veil; and for them is a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse describes a state in which persistent rejection of the truth gradually closes the faculties through which guidance reaches a person. The heart, hearing, and sight are the three channels of understanding, reception, and perception, and when they are sealed or veiled, the person can no longer grasp what is clearly set before them. This is not presented as arbitrary: it is the consequence of their own repeated choosing to turn away, so that Allah's sealing confirms and fixes a condition they had already chosen. The mention of a great punishment following this condition shows that such spiritual blindness carries its own weighty consequence, and it serves as a warning that the door to guidance remains open only as long as a person sincerely seeks it.

translation: And among the people are those who say, "We believe in Allah and in the Last Day," but they are not believers.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites (munafiqun) who profess faith with their tongues while their hearts reject it. Their claim is hollow because true belief is not merely verbal assertion but a conviction of the heart that is confirmed by sincere action and obedience. By stating "and they are not believers" immediately after their declaration, the verse teaches that outward confession alone does not make a person a believer, and it warns that Allah knows what is concealed within hearts, so a people cannot be deceived about their true state before Him.

translation: They seek to deceive Allah and those who believe, but they deceive none but themselves, and they perceive it not.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites' self-delusion: their attempt to deceive God and the believers is in truth a deception of their own souls, because their scheme rebounds upon them while they remain unaware of it. Their inability to perceive this reality shows that the deepest harm of hypocrisy is the blindness it inflicts on the heart, which cuts a person off from the truth about themselves and their condition before God.

translation: In their hearts is a disease, so Allah has increased them in disease. And for them is a painful punishment because they used to lie.
interpretation: The verse describes a condition of the heart that worsens in a cycle: those who harbor hypocrisy, doubt, and hostility toward the truth find that each refusal to accept guidance hardens them further, so that Allah leaves them to what they have chosen and their spiritual sickness grows. The increase in disease is thus presented as a consequence of their own persistent choices, which Allah confirms by giving them over to it. Their painful punishment is tied directly to their lying, indicating that the root of their spiritual illness is the gap between what they profess with their tongues and what they actually believe in their hearts.

translation: And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth," they say, "We are only reformers."
interpretation: The verse exposes a self-deceptive hypocrisy in which corruption is committed while the corrupter sincerely believes himself to be doing good. Those described here do not recognize their own harm, so when admonished they respond with self-justification rather than reflection. The phrase "we are only" (innama) signals an exclusive claim that closes the door to correction, since a person who regards his own actions as reform will resist any reproach. The verse thus warns that the greatest danger is not open wrongdoing alone but the moral blindness that disguises corruption as righteousness, and it calls the believer to examine his intentions and actions honestly, accepting counsel and measuring deeds by their actual effects on the earth and its people rather than by his own assurances.

translation: Unquestionably, it is they who are the corrupters, but they do not perceive it.
interpretation: The verse exposes a deep form of self-deception: those who spread corruption on earth often believe they are reforming and acting rightly, so their wrongdoing is veiled from their own awareness. Their inability to perceive their corruption is itself a symptom of the disease, since a heart that has grown accustomed to harm loses the capacity to recognize harm as harm. The emphatic opening "Unquestionably" (alā) and the doubled pronoun "they, they" (hum hum) assert the truth against their self-image, calling the believer to examine the true nature of their actions rather than trusting their own justifications.

translation: And when it is said to them, "Believe as the people have believed," they say, "Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?" Unquestionably, it is they who are the foolish, but they do not know.
interpretation: The verse exposes a mindset that treats sound faith as something beneath dignity, dismissing the conviction of the sincere believers as the folly of simpletons while claiming for itself the mantle of wisdom. God turns the accusation back on its makers: the true foolishness lies in rejecting guidance and in pride that refuses to follow the righteous, and the tragedy is that such people cannot perceive their own error. Their deficiency is not of intellect alone but of knowledge rooted in humility and in recognizing where truth actually lies.

translation: And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"; but when they are alone with their devils, they say, "Indeed, we are with you; we were only mocking."
interpretation: The verse exposes the duplicity of the hypocrites (munafiqun) who display a false faith before the believers to protect themselves and their standing, while privately reassuring their own leaders and companions of their true allegiance and contempt for the believers. Their words of faith are a mask rather than a reflection of the heart, and their claim that they were merely jesting reveals a double standard: they treat the religion of God as an object of mockery while hiding behind a pretext of playfulness. The verse thus warns that outward profession without sincere conviction is not only worthless before God but also a corruption of the self, since it fosters a divided character that is at ease in deception and scornful of truth.

translation: Allah mocks them and extends for them in their transgression, wandering blindly.
interpretation: The verse describes God's response to those who persist in hypocrisy and deceit: their mockery of the believers and their pretense are turned back upon them, as God leaves them free to continue in their rebellion. The phrase "Allah mocks them" (yastahzi'u bihim) is a figurative expression of divine requital, meaning that God gives them the rope they seek, allowing their own choices to deepen their error. Their extension in transgression is thus not a sign of favor but of a gradual abandonment that lets them wander in confusion, unable to see the consequences of their own self-deception. The verse thus warns that prolonged persistence in falsehood can itself become a form of divine test, in which the heart becomes ever more blind to its own condition.

translation: Those are the ones who have purchased error in exchange for guidance, so their transaction has not profited them, and they were not [rightly] guided.
interpretation: The verse uses the image of commerce to expose a moral reversal: people who had the means of guidance within reach but chose misguidance have made a losing bargain, as if they traded the valuable for the worthless. Their loss is not merely the absence of gain but the failure of the very purpose for which they were given the capacity to be guided, since a deliberate preference for error over the light they were offered leaves them outside the path of right direction.

translation: Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire, and when it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light and left them in darkness, unable to see.
interpretation: The verse presents a parable of hypocrites who, like one who lights a fire that briefly brightens his surroundings, enjoy a fleeting benefit from the outward light of faith and its worldly security. Yet because their faith was never rooted in sincere conviction, that light is suddenly extinguished, leaving them in a darkness of confusion and blindness to the truth. The image warns that light which is not sustained by genuine inner belief is temporary, and that a person may lose guidance after having briefly seen it, so one should seek a lasting light grounded in sincerity.

translation: Deaf, dumb, and blind, so they will not return (to the right path).
interpretation: The verse describes those who have closed their hearing, speech, and sight to the truth despite having the faculties to perceive it. Having persistently refused guidance, they have lost the very capacities through which return to faith would become possible, so their condition is one of spiritual impairment that is self-chosen rather than merely physical. The words "they do not return" point to a hardened state in which they neither hear the call, nor speak the truth, nor see the signs of God, and therefore remain in their error. It is a warning that persistent denial gradually strips a person of the ability to recognize guidance.

translation: Or like a rainstorm from the sky, within which are darkness, thunder, and lightning. They put their fingers in their ears against the thunderbolts, for fear of death. And Allah is encompassing of the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse presents a parable for the hypocrites of Madinah, whose condition is likened to a person caught in a violent storm at night. The darkness, thunder, and lightning represent the fearful and confusing circumstances that the hypocrites encounter when the truth of the Qur'an is presented: its warnings and clear signs strike their hearts with dread, so they stop their ears, as if refusing to hear will spare them what they fear. Yet their attempt to escape the reality they fear is futile, because Allah surrounds them in knowledge and power and cannot be evaded. The image thus conveys that fear of death and of exposure does not protect a person who rejects the truth, since the disbelievers remain fully within the reach of Allah's encompassing control.

translation: The lightning nearly snatches away their sight. Every time it lights up for them, they walk on in it; but when darkness falls over them, they stand still. And if Allah had willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse uses the image of a storm at night to portray the hypocrites, whose faith wavers according to circumstance: when the truth shines and brings them worldly benefit or ease, they move forward with it, but when hardship or doubt descends, they halt and hesitate. The lightning that nearly blinds them reflects how the clarity of the message dazzles and overwhelms them, yet they cannot bear its full light. The closing reminder that Allah could strip away their hearing and sight shows that their faculties are entirely under His power, and that every person's perception and guidance rest on His will and capability over all things.

translation: O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may attain righteousness.
interpretation: The verse opens with a universal address to all of humanity, calling people to the worship of their Lord on the basis of a single fact: that He is the Creator who brought them into existence, just as He brought into being those who came before them. Creation is thus presented as the ground of obligation, since the one who gives life is the one who alone deserves to be served. The phrase 'that you may attain righteousness' (la'allakum tattaqun) indicates that worship is the path to taqwa, a conscious God-consciousness that guards a person from wrongdoing. The verse thereby links the foundational theology of divine creation with the ethical purpose of worship, showing that true devotion shapes the believer's conduct and character.

translation: Who made the earth a resting place for you and the sky a canopy, and sent down from the sky water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you. So do not set up rivals to God while you know.
interpretation: The verse grounds the call to monotheism in observable creation: the same Lord who spread the earth as a bed and raised the heavens as a structure, and who sends rain that yields sustenance, is the only one deserving worship. Because the favors are evident and the people themselves know this, assigning partners to God is not merely mistaken but a contradiction of their own knowledge. Divine provision through rain and fruit thus becomes a sign that calls the heart from gratitude to exclusive devotion.

translation: And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it, and call upon your witnesses other than Allah, if you are truthful.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an as a challenge (tahaddi) directed at those who doubted its divine origin, meaning that if they suspected it was human composition, they should attempt to produce even a single chapter of comparable eloquence and wisdom, enlisting whatever helpers or witnesses they could muster apart from God. By framing the challenge conditionally, it places the burden of proof on the skeptics and implicitly establishes that the Qur'an's inimitable literary and moral excellence is itself the evidence of its revelation, a miracle that its contemporaries, masters of Arabic eloquence, were unable to match.

translation: But if you do not do it, and you will never do it, then fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones; it has been prepared for the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse is addressed to those who doubt the divine origin of the Qur'an, after a challenge to produce a chapter like it has been issued. Its phrasing 'and you will never do it' carries a note of certainty that no human effort can match the Qur'an, turning the challenge into a decisive proof of its revelation. Having established this, the verse shifts from argument to warning: the rejection of the message leads to the Fire, described with dreadful specificity as fueled by men and stones, a image that conveys both its intensity and the gravity of persisting in disbelief. The Fire is said to be 'prepared' for the disbelievers, signifying that it is not an accident of fate but an ordained consequence of a conscious choice to reject the truth after it has been made clear. The verse thus binds the intellectual challenge to a moral choice, urging the listener to take the warning seriously and turn toward God-consciousness, taqwa, as the protection against that Fire.

translation: And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds, that theirs are gardens beneath which rivers flow. Whenever they are provided with a fruit therefrom as provision, they will say, "This is what we were provided with before," and they will be given it in resemblance. And for them therein are purified spouses, and they will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: The verse joins faith and righteous action as the two conditions for the good tidings of Paradise, and it presents the reward as a fulfilment that begins in recognition: the believers, tasting fruits of the Garden, feel they have tasted them before, because the outward forms resemble the provisions of the world while their inner reality far surpasses them. This resemblance in form, with difference in essence, reminds the believer that the blessings of the Hereafter are continuous with the good deeds of this life yet exceed all they knew. The mention of purified spouses and of eternal abiding completes the picture, assuring the believer that what is promised is free from the defilements and the impermanence of the worldly state.

translation: Indeed, Allah is not shy to strike an example, even of a mosquito or something above it. As for those who believe, they know that it is the truth from their Lord; but as for those who disbelieve, they say, "What did Allah intend by this as an example?" He misleads many by it and guides many by it, and He misleads by it none except the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse shows that God's wisdom does not avoid even the humblest of comparisons, such as a gnat, because the purpose of a parable is to make truth clear to the sincere seeker. The same divine words produce opposite effects depending on the heart receiving them: faith recognizes in the example a truth from the Lord and is strengthened, while disbelief, looking for mockery or a pretext, is confused and turned further away. Thus the Qur'an's guidance is not a mechanical cause of misguidance; rather, misguidance falls upon those who have already chosen defiance, and the 'fasiqun' are those who have deliberately gone beyond obedience.

translation: Those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification, and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined, and cause corruption on the earth - it is those who are the losers.
interpretation: The verse identifies a chain of moral corruption that begins with breaking a sacred pledge to God, extends to severing the ties that God has ordered to be maintained, and culminates in corruption across society and the earth. The 'covenant of Allah' is best understood as the binding commitment humans made through their acknowledgment of God and the guidance given through revelation, which is confirmed by the natural disposition and the messengers' call. Severing what is to be joined most plainly refers to the bonds of kinship and the wider web of relationships that uphold social harmony, though it also reaches to any tie of faith, justice, and mutual obligation. The verse shows that spiritual betrayal and social breakdown are inseparable: whoever violates the bond with God inevitably ruptures the bonds with people, and the resulting disorder harms the earth itself. The final declaration that such people are 'the losers' frames true loss not as worldly failure but as the forfeiture of one's own well-being, both in this life and in the hereafter, since the one who abandons God's covenant has abandoned the very source of his salvation.

translation: How can you disbelieve in God when you were dead and He gave you life? Then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you back to life, and then to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: The verse opens with a rhetorical astonishment at disbelief, grounding the call to faith in the most undeniable evidence: the human being's own journey from non-existence to existence. Having been lifeless and then brought into life by God, the listener is confronted with a pattern that repeats across the whole span of human existence, with death followed by a second raising and finally a return to the Lord. The argument moves from the familiar experience of creation and mortality to the certainty of the afterlife, so that the one who recognizes the first gift of life has no rational ground for denying the final accounting. The verse thus unites the proof of divine power with the reality of accountability, presenting the return to God not as a distant abstraction but as the inevitable conclusion of the life that God has granted.

translation: It is He who created for you all that is on the earth; then He turned to the heaven and made it into seven heavens, and He is Knower of all things.
interpretation: The verse presents creation as a gift and a trust: the earth and all it contains were brought into being for the benefit of humankind, which should prompt gratitude and reflection rather than heedlessness. The order it mentions, first the earth and then the heavens, is a sign of the orderly, purposeful design of the cosmos under a Creator whose power is complete. Its closing words, that He is Knower of all things, link the vastness of creation to the perfect knowledge of its Maker, reminding the believer that nothing in the heavens or the earth is hidden from Him and that every act of creation reflects His wisdom.

translation: And [remember] when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a successive authority (khalifah)." They said, "Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?" He said, "Indeed, I know that which you do not know."
interpretation: The verse reveals that humanity's role on earth was determined by divine wisdom before the angels were told of it, and the angels' question reflects their understanding of earthly life through what they knew of prior creation, which was marked by disorder and bloodshed, while their own worship was constant glorification. God's reply, "I know what you do not know," points to a hidden capacity in the human being, one that includes the potential for corruption but also for knowledge, moral responsibility, and the stewardship of the earth, so that the khilafah is a trust that reflects God's own knowledge and authority exercised through a creature who can choose obedience.

translation: And He taught Adam the names, all of them; then He presented them to the angels and said, "Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful."
interpretation: The verse points to the distinctive station of humankind: Adam was given a capacity for knowledge, specifically the knowledge of names, which signifies the ability to name, categorize, and comprehend the nature of things. The angels, though devoted in worship, lacked this specific knowledge, and their humble confession that they have no knowledge beyond what they were taught reveals that true knowledge is a gift from God. The test thus exposes the limits of created beings' knowledge and establishes Adam's unique role as one entrusted with understanding and stewardship on earth.

translation: They said, "Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed, You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."
interpretation: The verse presents the humble admission of the angels before the Creator when they were asked to name what He had made known to Adam. Their words "Glory be to You" affirm God's absolute perfection and freedom from any deficiency, and their confession that they have no knowledge beyond what He has taught them reveals that all true knowledge originates with God and is granted by Him alone. The closing divine attributes, "the All-Knowing" and "the All-Wise," suggest that true wisdom lies in recognizing one's limits and in trusting the perfect knowledge and purpose of the One who teaches. The verse thus teaches that humility before God's knowledge is the proper stance of every creature, and that any ability we have to know or understand is a gift from Him.

translation: He said, "O Adam, inform them of their names." And when he had informed them of their names, He said, "Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?"
interpretation: The verse shows that Adam's knowledge of the names was a sign of the honor God gave him over the angels, who had professed ignorance and were humbled by the demonstration. God's question reminds them that His knowledge encompasses all that is hidden in creation and all that is apparent or concealed in the hearts of beings, so that submission to His wisdom, rather than presumption about one's own knowledge, is the proper response.

translation: And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis. He refused and was arrogant, and he was among the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse exposes the root of disobedience as pride rather than ignorance. Iblis was not unaware of God's command; he refused it out of arrogance, placing his own sense of superiority, derived from his origin of fire, above the divine will. His refusal shows that the sin of arrogance can lead a created being from obedience to outright disbelief, and it warns that self-regard which resists humble submission to God is the gateway to ruin. The verse also honors the human being Adam by making his station the occasion of a command to the angels, and it presents the human struggle as one between submission and the ego that claims superiority.

translation: And We said, "O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in Paradise, and eat from it in abundance wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, lest you be among the wrongdoers."
interpretation: The verse presents Adam's dwelling in Paradise as a state of abundant provision and freedom, bounded by a single prohibition. The tree serves as a test of obedience within an otherwise generous environment, showing that the human being is granted broad liberty yet must recognize limits set by the Creator. The warning that transgression makes one a wrongdoer frames sin as an act of injustice, first against oneself, since it deprives the soul of the blessing it was given. The address to Adam and his wife together emphasizes that the moral responsibility and the shared fate of the human pair are equal before God.

translation: But Satan caused them both to slip from it and removed them from the state they had been in. And We said, "Go down, some of you enemies to others, and for you on earth is a dwelling place and provision for a time."
interpretation: The verse marks the turning point of the human story in the garden: Satan's whisper succeeded in making Adam and his spouse slip from obedience, so that they lost the state of ease and closeness in which they had been. The command to descend is not merely a punishment but a shift in the human condition into a world of enmity, struggle, and mutual conflict, where the relationship between humans is tested by rivalry. Yet the verse immediately balances this with God's mercy: the earth is given as a settled place of stability and a temporary portion of provision, a reminder that human life is a trial with a set term, in which the believer is to recognize both the reality of the adversary and the sufficiency of divine guidance.

translation: Then Adam received from his Lord some words, and He turned to him in forgiveness. Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.
interpretation: The verse shows that repentance begins with God's grace: Adam is first given words of guidance from his Lord, meaning he is taught the proper way to seek forgiveness, and only then does God turn to him. Human turning back is thus met by divine turning toward the servant, and the closing names affirm that God's acceptance of repentance flows from His mercy. It teaches that the door of return is always open, and that the sincere penitent is not left in despair after a lapse.

translation: We said: "Descend from it, all of you. And when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance—there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve."
interpretation: The verse marks the descent of humanity from the state of paradise into the test of earthly life, and it frames that descent not as a curse but as the setting in which divine guidance is sent down repeatedly. The conditional phrasing ("whenever" guidance comes) signals that revelation is a continuing mercy rather than a single event, and human freedom lies in responding to it. Fear and grief, the two anxieties that attend every uncertain journey, are lifted from those who follow, so that the promise of security is tied directly to inner submission to God's guidance rather than to any worldly condition.

translation: And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs - those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: The verse draws a sharp line between two destinies based on a single root cause: rejecting the divine signs both through inward disbelief (kufr) and outward denial (takdhib). Denial of the signs is presented as more than a private doubt; it is an active refusal to acknowledge the evidence God has placed in creation and revelation. The phrase 'companions of the Fire' (ashab al-nar) conveys an intimate, enduring bond with the consequence of one's own choices, and the closing statement that they 'abide therein forever' underscores the finality of this outcome for those who persist in such rejection. The passage thus functions as both warning and moral clarification, urging the listener to recognize that sincere engagement with God's signs is the decisive matter of one's ultimate fate.

translation: O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you, and fulfill My covenant, I will fulfill your covenant, and fear only Me.
interpretation: The verse opens a call to the Children of Israel that rests on remembrance of God's favors as the basis for moral responsibility. Gratitude is presented as an active recollection that should move the one who remembers to keep faith with the divine covenant. The reciprocal structure, that God fulfills His covenant with those who fulfill theirs, shows that trust and obligation run in both directions and that divine faithfulness is not in question. The closing command to fear God alone places reverence at the center: awe of God, not of rivals or of human power, is what sustains covenantal faithfulness, so that remembering blessings, honoring commitments, and holding God alone in awe form a single inward and outward discipline.

translation: And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you, and do not be the first to disbelieve in it. And do not exchange My verses for a small price, and fear only Me.
interpretation: The verse calls the People of the Book to faith in the Qur'an as a confirmation of the revelation already in their hands, so that their own scripture is not rendered meaningless by their rejection. Being 'the first to disbelieve' warns that they must not become the leaders of rejection whose example others follow, since their early knowledge of the message makes their denial weightier. The prohibition on trading God's signs for a paltry price targets the worldly gains, status, and remuneration that led scholars to conceal or distort the truth for the sake of their positions and livelihoods. The closing command to fear God alone ties the whole admonition together: fidelity to revelation and honesty about its contents are the fruits of God-consciousness, and no worldly advantage is worth forfeiting it.

translation: And do not mix the truth with falsehood, nor conceal the truth while you know it.
interpretation: The verse addresses the People of the Book and holds them accountable for a twofold moral failure: corrupting truth by blending it with falsehood, and deliberately hiding what they know to be true. Their sin is not ignorance but knowing concealment, which makes it graver. The lesson extends beyond any single community: sincere knowledge demands that truth be kept distinct and openly stated, and that a person who recognizes the truth bears responsibility for not obscuring it through confusion, distortion, or silence for the sake of worldly interest or social comfort.

translation: And establish prayer, and give zakat, and bow along with those who bow.
interpretation: The verse joins the establishment of prayer with the giving of zakat, showing that worship of the heart and body is inseparable from social responsibility toward others. The command to bow with those who bow directs the believer toward the congregation: to pray together with the community of believers rather than in isolation, so that faith becomes a shared, visible practice that binds the individual to the wider community of worshippers.

translation: Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves, and you recite the Scripture? Will you not then use your reason?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who command others to goodness and piety while neglecting to practice it themselves, despite their knowledge of the Book they recite. Its sharp question exposes the contradiction between speech and conduct, and it implies that true knowledge of revelation must be reflected in one's own character and deeds. The closing question calls the hearer to exercise reason, for a person who knows the truth and yet fails to live by it has abandoned the very understanding that the Scripture was sent to cultivate. Thus the verse establishes that moral instruction is credible only when it is embodied in the instructor's own life, and that self-examination must accompany the exhortation of others.

translation: And seek help through patience and prayer, and indeed it is difficult except for the humbly submissive (khāshi'īn).
interpretation: The verse presents patience (sabr) and prayer (ṣalāh) as the two pillars of spiritual endurance: patience steadies the soul against hardship and temptation, while prayer reconnects it to God and renews its strength. The verse acknowledges honestly that this discipline is heavy upon the self, yet it is made light for those whose hearts are humble (khushūʿ), because the humble heart feels the presence of its Lord in prayer, finds its burden eased, and turns to God as the true source of help.

translation: Those who are certain that they will meet their Lord, and that they will return to Him.
interpretation: The verse describes the true believers by the quality of their conviction in the Hereafter: the word yazunnuna, which here carries the sense of firm certainty rather than mere suspicion, shows that their faith in the encounter with God and the return to Him is so settled that it shapes their conduct, their humility, and their patience. Their awareness that every deed will be presented before the Lord is what makes them steadfast in prayer and sincere in devotion, in contrast to those who are heedless of the Hereafter. The verse thus ties inner certainty about the meeting with God to the outward discipline of a righteous life.

translation: O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds.
interpretation: The verse calls the Children of Israel to active remembrance of God's blessings, which is more than recollection: it is gratitude expressed through recognizing the source of favor and living in accordance with it. The phrase "preferred you over the worlds" is best understood in its context as a distinction of guidance and prophethood entrusted to them in their era, not as an unconditional superiority, since that distinction carried a corresponding responsibility. The verse thus establishes a principle that privilege before God is tied to faithful response, and that forgetfulness of blessings is the root of moral failure, which the subsequent verses address at length.

translation: And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another soul in anything, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any compensation be taken from it, nor will they be helped.
interpretation: The verse places human accountability at the center of the Day of Judgment by stripping away every external means of escape that people commonly rely on in worldly life. Kinship, friendship, intercession, and ransom, the familiar supports of the worldly order, are shown to be useless when each soul stands alone before its Lord. The command to guard oneself against that Day is therefore a call to act now, through faith and righteous deeds, since the only real protection is what a person has prepared for himself before it arrives, and no one can rely on the merit or influence of another.

translation: And [remember] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who were inflicting upon you the worst torment: slaughtering your sons and keeping your women alive. And in that was a tremendous trial from your Lord.
interpretation: The verse recalls the Children of Israel's deliverance as a reminder that Pharaoh's oppression was not merely cruelty but a test from God, and that salvation comes from Him alone. By naming the specific horrors, the slaughter of sons and the sparing of women for humiliation and servitude, it shows that a community's extreme suffering can be a crucible through which faith is tested and tried. The word 'bala' carries the dual sense of affliction and trial, so the verse invites the believer to see hardship as something that reveals the sincerity of his reliance on God, and to remember that rescue after such trial is itself an act of divine favor that demands gratitude rather than forgetfulness.

translation: And [recall] when We parted the sea for you and saved you, and drowned the people of Pharaoh while you were watching.
interpretation: The verse recalls for the Children of Israel a tangible sign of God's deliverance: the sea was split before their eyes, granting them safe passage, while their enemies were destroyed in the very same waters. Its phrasing, 'while you were watching,' makes the witnesses of this event accountable for having seen with their own eyes the justice of God and the reality of His power, so that the favor of rescue and the warning of punishment are both made vivid. It teaches that divine help and divine judgment are often shown in the same moment, and that the believer should reflect on such signs rather than merely recount them as history.

translation: And [recall] when We appointed forty nights for Moses, then you took the calf [for worship] after him, while you were wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse recalls the covenant of Sinai, where Moses was set apart for forty nights of communion and receiving the law, and it exposes how quickly the Children of Israel abandoned their commitment in his absence by making a golden calf to worship. Its point is that the people's wrong was not merely a lapse of the moment but a betrayal of God's favor, and that their self-inflicted harm, the wrongdoing of worshipping an image instead of the One who had delivered them, is the core reproach: a warning that spiritual weakness appears most clearly when the guiding figure seems absent and that persistent reliance on the visible over the unseen leads a community into injustice against its own soul.

translation: Then We pardoned you after that, so that you might be grateful.
interpretation: The verse points to the mercy of God that follows a grave lapse. After the people of Moses had worshipped the calf, God did not abandon them to their fate but forgave them, and this forgiveness was meant to awaken gratitude in their hearts. The pardon is not only an erasure of guilt but an opening toward a renewed relationship in which the forgiven person recognizes the blessing received and responds with thankfulness expressed in belief, obedience, and righteous conduct. Divine forgiveness thus carries an obligation: the one who has been spared must become one who gives thanks.

translation: And [recall] when We gave Moses the Scripture and the criterion, that you might be guided.
interpretation: The verse places the revelation given to Moses within a single divine bestowal: the Book and the Furqan. The Book denotes the written scripture, while the Furqan, the criterion that distinguishes truth from falsehood and right from wrong, points to the clarity of judgment that such revelation confers. The closing phrase, 'that you might be guided,' shows the purpose of this gift: scripture and its discerning criterion are not ends in themselves but means by which a people may find the straight path. The address to the community reminds the listeners that the same mercy of guidance extended to earlier prophets is offered to them, and that the benefit of revelation depends on their willingness to follow the clarity it provides.

translation: And [mention] when Moses said to his people, "O my people, you have wronged yourselves by your taking of the calf [for worship], so turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves. That is better for you in the sight of your Creator." Then He accepted your repentance. Indeed, it is He who is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.
interpretation: The verse shows that sin against God is ultimately a wrong done to oneself, since idolatry corrupts the soul and cuts it off from its true good. Genuine repentance demands a decisive and painful break with the sin, even at great cost to one's own desires and attachments, and it is this sincerity that makes repentance acceptable. God's acceptance of the repentance of the Israelites, after such a severe trial, reveals that His mercy is greater than the gravity of the offense whenever the penitent turns back to Him wholeheartedly.

translation: And [recall] when you said, "O Moses, we will never believe you until we see Allah plainly," so the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on.
interpretation: The verse recalls the stubbornness of the Children of Israel toward their prophet: after witnessing signs, they demanded a direct, open vision of God as the condition for their faith, thereby placing their own terms upon belief rather than accepting guidance on the basis of trust in the messenger. Their request reveals a tendency to seek sensory proof beyond what is fitting for the limits of human perception in this world, and the sudden seizing by the thunderbolt, which came while they stood watching, shows that their insolence brought an immediate consequence. The lesson concerns the proper posture of the believer, who approaches the unseen with humility and reverence instead of demanding that God be made visible on human terms, and who recognizes that the arrogance of impudent demands can itself become a cause of ruin.

translation: Then We resurrected you after your death, so that perhaps you would be grateful.
interpretation: The verse presents resurrection as a mercy that follows the apparent finality of death, so that the one who was brought back to life is led to recognize the favor of the One who gave life and to respond with gratitude. Its ordering matters: after the stupor of death and the shock of being raised, the purpose stated is thankfulness, meaning that the very experience of being restored is meant to turn the heart toward acknowledging God's bounty and living in accordance with it. The verse thus links the doctrine of resurrection not merely to future accountability but to the present duty of shukr, which is gratitude expressed in belief, humility, and obedience.

translation: And We shaded you with clouds and sent down to you manna and quail, [saying], "Eat from the good things We have provided for you." And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.
interpretation: The verse recalls God's favors upon the Children of Israel in the wilderness: shade from the clouds, and food provided without toil in the form of manna and quail. Yet the blessing was given with a command to consume only what is pure and wholesome, a reminder that gratitude is shown through using provision rightly. The closing statement shifts the focus from divine ingratitude to human harm: their disobedience could never diminish God, since the injury fell upon their own souls. Sin, in this reading, is ultimately self-directed, for it deprives the person of the very goodness that was meant to sustain them.

translation: And [recall] when We said: "Enter this town and eat from it wherever you wish, in abundance, and enter the gate prostrating, and say, 'Relieve us of our burden [hittah],' and We will forgive you your sins. And We will increase the reward of the doers of good."
interpretation: The verse presents a covenant of forgiveness conditioned on humble obedience: the Children of Israel are commanded to enter the town with humility, symbolized by entering its gate in prostration and by seeking forgiveness through the word "hittah," which acknowledges their need for God's relief from their burdens. The blessings of provision are given freely, while forgiveness depends on sincere submission and repentance. The closing promise that God will increase the reward of the good-doers shows that sincere righteousness is rewarded beyond what is merely due, and that the path to divine mercy lies in humility joined with good conduct rather than in arrogance or disobedience.

translation: So those who did wrong substituted a saying other than that which had been told to them, so We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment from the sky because they had been defiantly disobeying.
interpretation: The verse shows that the wrongdoers did not merely disobey but deliberately altered the divine command, replacing what God had revealed with words of their own choosing. Their corruption of the message is presented as the root of their transgression, and the punishment that follows is the consequence of persistent defiance against God's explicit instruction. The repetition of 'those who did wrong' emphasizes that the sin of distorting the word of God brings a decisive and just retribution from heaven, a reminder that tampering with revelation is among the gravest forms of injustice.

translation: And [recall] when Moses asked for water for his people, so We said, "Strike the rock with your staff." And from it gushed forth twelve springs. Every people knew their drinking place. [We said], "Eat and drink from the provision of Allah, and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief."
interpretation: The verse presents the miracle of water from the rock as a sign of divine care that answers human need once it is sought sincerely, with the twelve springs reflecting the orderly distribution of provision among the tribes, each knowing its own place, so that no group is left without. The closing command links this bounty to moral responsibility: the sustenance of Allah is to be consumed with gratitude and not turned into a means of oppression, waste, or disorder on earth, since misuse of blessings is itself a form of corruption against the just order God established.

translation: And [recall] when you said, "O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food, so call upon your Lord to bring forth for us from what the earth grows: its herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic, its lentils, and its onions." He said, "Would you exchange that which is inferior for that which is better? Go down to a city, for indeed you will have what you asked." And they were struck with humiliation and poverty, and they returned with anger from Allah. That is because they used to disbelieve in the verses of Allah and kill the prophets without right. That is because they disobeyed and were transgressing.
interpretation: The verse exposes the Children of Israel's chronic ingratitude and their preference for the lowly over the noble: having been granted miraculous provision in the wilderness, they grew impatient with it and craved the earthly fare they had known, thereby trading what is better for what is worse. Their rejection of divine blessing is shown to be the root of their deeper moral corruption, culminating in their rejection of God's signs and their murder of His prophets, which brought upon them the lasting marks of humiliation, dependency, and divine wrath. The verse thus teaches that persistent disobedience and transgression gradually hollow out a people's dignity and self-sufficiency, and that a heart content with what is worse will eventually come to violate what is sacred.

translation: Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jewish, and the Christians, and the Sabians, whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds—they will have their reward with their Lord, and no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: The verse establishes that salvation and divine reward are tied to genuine faith in God and the Last Day together with righteous action, not to belonging to a particular community or label. By naming the believers, Jews, Christians and Sabians side by side and making the same condition apply to each, it directs the reader away from exclusive group identity toward sincere belief and good conduct as the true measure before God. The closing promise of freedom from fear and grief underscores that such a person's reward is secure with the Lord.

translation: And [recall] when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you, [saying], "Take what We have given you with determination and remember what is in it, that you may become righteous."
interpretation: The verse recalls the covenant God made with the Children of Israel at Mount Sinai, where the mountain was lifted over them as a reminder of the seriousness of their commitment. The command to hold fast to the revealed Book with real resolve, rather than in mere outward form, shows that faith is a living, active discipline. Remembering its contents continually keeps the heart attentive to God, and this sustained mindfulness is the path through which taqwa, God-consciousness and piety, is cultivated. The passage thus teaches that a covenant with God is not complete by declaration alone but must be carried out through steadfast engagement with the guidance received.

translation: Then you turned away after that, and were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have been among the losers.
interpretation: This verse, addressed to the people of Moses after their ordeal at Mount Sinai, shows that turning away from a covenant after having received clear signs is a grave failing that would place a person among the lost. Yet the verse turns the reader's gaze from human failure to divine mercy: it is Allah's grace, not human merit, that keeps a heedless soul from ruin. The lesson is twofold, a warning against complacency in faith and a reminder that one's continued standing before God rests on His bounty, which calls for humility, gratitude, and a renewed return to Him.

translation: And you have certainly known those among you who transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath, so We said to them: "Be apes, despised and driven away."
interpretation: The verse recalls the people who broke the sanctity of the Sabbath day by exploiting a prohibition meant to be observed in rest and devotion, and it presents their punishment as a transformation that mirrors their spiritual condition: having distorted their obedience, they were made into a debased form, cast away from mercy. Its purpose is to warn the community addressed in the Qur'an that familiarity with divine guidance does not protect against the same kind of deliberate evasion of God's commands, and that the outcome of such transgression is spiritual abasement and distance from God.

translation: So We made it an example (a deterrent punishment) for what was before it and what was after it, and an admonition for those who are mindful of God.
interpretation: The verse refers to the story of the cow in Surah Al-Baqarah, where a murder was committed and the Israelites were ordered to slaughter a cow as a means of uncovering the truth. God made this event a lesson for its own time and for later generations: the sinful deed and its consequence are a warning against hypocrisy, stubbornness and evasion of divine command. Its benefit is reserved for the God-conscious, who take the lesson to heart and act on it, because they are the ones whose hearts are open to admonition.

translation: And [recall] when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow." They said, "Do you take us in ridicule?" He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant."
interpretation: The verse shows that the people's mockery of a clear divine command stemmed from their reluctance to obey and their habit of questioning the prophet's seriousness rather than accepting what was commanded. Moses's response, seeking refuge in God, reveals that to treat revelation as a joke is a form of ignorance, and that a prophet must be guarded from such conduct. It teaches that ridiculing sincere guidance, or responding to a plain command with suspicion, is a mark of the ignorant, and that the believer should answer such mockery with patience, humility, and reliance on God.

translation: They said: "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is." He said: "Indeed, He says it is a cow neither old nor young, but of middle age between that. So do what you are commanded."
interpretation: The verse portrays the Children of Israel's tendency to over-question and seek excessive detail after a divine command, which made their obedience more burdensome. Their request for further clarification about the cow reveals a reluctance to act promptly on what was simply asked of them. Moses' answer places the emphasis back on straightforward compliance: the specification of a moderate, middle-aged cow is itself sufficient guidance, and the believer's duty is to carry out what is commanded without endless questioning. The lesson concerns the wisdom of accepting divine instruction with readiness, since needless inquiry can lead to added hardship.

translation: They said: 'Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is.' He said: 'Indeed, He says it is a cow, yellow in color, bright and pure in its hue, pleasing to those who look upon it.'
interpretation: This verse belongs to the story of the Children of Israel and the cow (Surah al-Baqarah 2:68-69). Their repeated questioning about the cow, after having been commanded to sacrifice one, reveals a tendency to over-scrutinize divine commands, which made the matter harder for themselves. The emphasis on a bright, vivid yellow that delights the beholder suggests that the specificity they demanded was granted as a trial, and that excessive questioning of what is clearly commanded can narrow one's own path to obedience.

translation: They said: "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is, for indeed the cattle have become confused to us, and indeed we, if Allah wills, will be guided."
interpretation: This verse, from the story of the cow in Surah Al-Baqarah, shows the Children of Israel repeatedly questioning Moses about a command that was already clear, and the more they asked, the more difficult it became for them. Their request for a precise description reflects a tendency to over-question divine instructions, which made the obligation harder to fulfil. Their added phrase "if Allah wills" shows that they sought guidance only by God's permission, yet their words also betray hesitation and a reluctance to comply promptly. The lesson is that sincere obedience is best served by acting on what God has made plain, rather than by seeking excessive detail that burdens oneself.

translation: He said: Indeed, He says it is a cow neither trained to plow the earth nor to water the tilled field, sound and without blemish. They said: Now you have brought the truth. So they slaughtered it, though they had almost not done so.
interpretation: The verse shows the Israelites' persistent tendency to question and over-specify what God commanded. After they were told to slaughter a cow, they kept asking for further description, and each added condition narrowed the choice until it became costly and difficult to fulfil. Their reluctance, which the phrase 'though they had almost not done so' conveys, reflects how excessive questioning and hesitation in obeying a clear command can make the obedience itself harder. The passage thus implicitly warns believers to accept divine directives with readiness rather than seeking to multiply their conditions.

translation: And [recall] when you killed a soul and then disputed among yourselves about it, but Allah was to bring forth that which you were concealing.
interpretation: The verse recalls the episode of the murder in the time of Moses, where a killing occurred and each party tried to shift blame onto the other, so that the matter became a dispute. It points to the truth that concealment before God is futile: whatever people hide in their hearts and deeds will inevitably be exposed. Its lesson is that human attempts to evade responsibility through denial and deflection cannot defeat the knowledge and justice of Allah, who will disclose what was secretly kept, and so one should act with honesty rather than trusting in concealment.

translation: So We said, "Strike him with part of it." Thus does Allah bring the dead to life, and He shows you His signs that you may understand.
interpretation: The verse belongs to the story of the cow (Surat al-Baqarah 2:73), where a murder had gone unsolved and the Israelites were ordered to slaughter a cow and strike the slain man with a piece of it, whereupon he came back to life and named his killer. The act is presented as a visible sign that the same power which revives the dead on the Day of Resurrection is in God's hands alone. Through such a sign God invites the human mind to reflect on how life and death are governed, and to draw from the miracle the lesson that the Creator who restores life to the dead can also bring justice to light and reveal what is hidden, so that people may reason and grasp His guidance.

translation: Then your hearts hardened after that, so they became like stones, or even harder. For indeed, among stones are those from which rivers gush forth, and among them are those that split open so water comes out of them, and among them are those that fall down out of fear of Allah. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse uses the image of stones to confront the hardness of the human heart: stones, though lifeless and inert, sometimes yield rivers, springs, and water, and even descend in awe before God, while the hearts of the people who witnessed the signs remained harder still. The contrast invites the reader to see that a heart which is not moved by clear signs and reminders has become more insensitive than inanimate matter, and that the proper response to God is softness, humility, and reverent submission. The closing reminder that God is not heedless of their deeds turns this observation into a warning of accountability.

translation: Do you then hope that they will believe you, when a group of them used to hear the words of Allah and then distort them after they had understood them, while they knew?
interpretation: The verse addresses the believers with a sharp question that exposes the gap between hope and reality: the community of Madinah had long been hoping that the Jews of the tribes, who had received scripture, would accept the message of Islam. Yet their own history showed a deliberate pattern: some of them heard God's speech, grasped its meaning with full understanding, and still altered it, and they did so consciously. The point is that corruption of revelation was not an innocent error of comprehension but a willful betrayal of known truth. Hence the believers should not expect sincere faith from people whose ancestors and factions had shown such deliberate distortion, and the verse teaches realism about the moral condition of those who knowingly bend divine guidance to suit their interests, while also warning the believers against the same tendency within themselves.

translation: And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"; but when they are alone with one another, they say, "Will you tell them what Allah has revealed to you, so that they may argue with you about it before your Lord? Do you not then use your reason?"
interpretation: The verse exposes the duplicity of a group among the People of the Book who outwardly professed faith before the believers while, in private, they rebuked one another for disclosing to the Muslims what Allah had revealed in the Scriptures, fearing that the believers would use those very revelations, which confirm the Prophet's message, as evidence against them before God. Their question is rhetorical and ironic: the believers are not to be shamed for sharing truths that the Muslims would recognize from their own books, and the verse calls such people to use their intellect, since concealing divine guidance out of worldly fear and the desire to preserve their standing is itself a failure of reason.

translation: Do they not know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal?
interpretation: The verse turns the reader's attention from the outward conduct of people to the inner reality of their hearts and intentions. Its opening question, 'Do they not know?', is a rebuke as much as an inquiry: the knowledge that God encompasses both the hidden thoughts and the spoken declarations of humans is already within reach of their reason and their own awareness, so their continued deception or heedlessness is shown to be unreasonable. Secret resolutions, concealed grudges, and hypocritical postures cannot escape the One whose knowledge is complete, and so the verse calls for sincerity between the inner self and the outer deed, making the believer's accountability begin in the heart rather than only in visible action.

translation: And among them are unlettered people who do not know the Scripture except for wishful fancies, and they do not have but assumption.
interpretation: The verse describes a segment of the People of the Book who, though they possess a revealed text, are unlettered in its true understanding: they do not truly know the Scripture, but rely on wishful thinking and baseless hopes, such as the claim that they are assured of salvation regardless of their conduct. Their reliance is on desire and conjecture rather than on knowledge and sincere engagement with what God has revealed, and the verse exposes the gap between possessing a book and actually comprehending and living by it.

translation: So woe to those who write the scripture with their own hands and then say, "This is from Allah," in order to exchange it for a small price. Woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they earn.
interpretation: The verse exposes a grave form of religious deception: people who fabricate or distort revealed teaching, attributing their own writing to God in order to gain worldly profit. By tying the punishment to "what their hands have written" and "what they earn," it teaches that falsifying the message of God is a personal act of responsibility, and that the material gain sought through it is trivial compared to the ruin it brings. It serves as a warning to scholars and believers alike that religious authority must never be used as a means of worldly advantage, and that the words attributed to God must be guarded with honesty and fear of Him.

translation: And they said, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days." Say, "Have you taken a covenant from Allah, so that Allah will not break His covenant? Or do you say about Allah what you do not know?"
interpretation: The verse exposes the false assurance of the Children of Israel, who believed their privileged descent and claimed status would shield them from punishment, allowing only a brief, countable period of torment. The Prophet is commanded to confront this claim with a decisive challenge: if they hold an explicit pledge from God, then His promise cannot be broken, but if no such pledge exists, they are merely fabricating religious claims about God without knowledge. The lesson is that salvation cannot be secured by wishful belief, lineage, or self-assigned privilege, and that attributing rulings or guarantees to God without a genuine basis is a grave form of falsehood. Accountability rests on verifiable divine truth, not on comfortable assumptions.

translation: Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him — those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: The verse teaches that sin is not merely an isolated act but something that can surround and overtake a person until it defines his whole state, so that he is wholly enveloped by the consequences of his persistent wrongdoing. The phrase "his sin encompasses him" suggests a condition in which a person has become so immersed in wrongdoing, unrepentant and unchecked, that no way out remains visible to him. The verse answers a claim made in the preceding context that only one particular community would enter Paradise: the criterion is not lineage or affiliation but the moral reality of one's own deeds and the state of the heart that those deeds have shaped. The word "Yes" (bala) affirms against that claim that the reckoning is universal and personal, and that eternal consequences follow from a life that has become enclosed in sin without repentance.

translation: And those who believed and did righteous deeds - those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: The verse binds faith and action together as inseparable: belief in the heart is meant to be proven and completed through good works, and it is this union that earns the rank of 'companions of the Garden.' The word 'companions' (ashab) signals a deep, intimate belonging rather than mere entry, suggesting that Paradise is a home to which one is joined by one's inner conviction made visible in conduct. The closing phrase 'abiding therein forever' emphasizes that the reward is not temporary or subject to loss, so the believer's hope is anchored in an eternal and unbroken state of nearness to God.

translation: And [recall] when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: Do not worship except Allah, and be good to parents, relatives, orphans, and the needy, and speak to people kindly, and establish prayer, and give zakat. Then you turned away, except for a few of you, and you were ignoring [it].
interpretation: The verse presents the covenant as a single comprehensive charter whose parts are inseparable: pure devotion to God is joined immediately to social responsibility toward parents, kin, the vulnerable, and all people in speech and conduct, and to the ritual and charitable acts of worship. Faith is thus shown to be tested in how one treats others, not only in ritual. The reproach that follows, that they turned away and only a few kept faith, is directed at a community that had accepted the terms yet neglected them, warning that breaking the covenant of compassion and justice is itself a betrayal of God's commitment.

translation: And [recall] when We took your covenant: that you shall not shed your blood, nor expel one another from your homes. Then you acknowledged it, and you were witnesses to it.
interpretation: The verse presents a foundational social covenant binding a community to two prohibitions that protect the sanctity of human life and the sanctity of dwelling and belonging. Shedding one another's blood and expelling one another from home are framed as the gravest breaches of communal bond, so the verse ties ethics to the security of persons and their place in the community. The shift from the covenant taken to the acknowledgment given, with the people as witnesses to their own commitment, emphasizes that moral obligation rests on conscious, public acceptance rather than mere inheritance. The address reminds the listeners that having affirmed the covenant, they are answerable for whether they honor it, so their later conduct is measured against a pledge they themselves made.

translation: Then you are these people: you kill your own selves, and you expel a group of you from their homes, backing one another against them in sin and aggression. And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them, while their expulsion was itself forbidden to you. Do you then believe in part of the Scripture and disbelieve in part? So what is the recompense of those among you who do that except disgrace in the worldly life; and on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the most severe punishment. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the Children of Israel for a glaring contradiction in their conduct: they treated the covenant selectively, fighting and expelling their own kinsmen and allies out of tribal loyalty and worldly interest, while at the same time ransoming captives from those same groups, as though the law applied only when it suited them. The deeper lesson is that faith cannot be divided into what one finds convenient and what one rejects; a person who honors God's commands in some matters but sets them aside in others, when they are costly to his desires or alliances, has in effect betrayed the whole of his commitment. The disgrace in this world and the severe punishment in the Hereafter show that selective obedience is not a neutral compromise but a moral corruption that undermines both social justice and the sincerity of faith, and the closing reminder that Allah is never heedless of what people do calls the believer to examine whether his own actions are consistent with what he professes.

translation: Those are the ones who have traded the worldly life for the Hereafter; so their punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be helped.
interpretation: The verse describes a deliberate exchange in which people choose the fleeting pleasures of this world over the eternal reward of the Hereafter, as if they had sold the greater for the lesser. Because they made this choice with full awareness, the consequence is not merely loss but a punishment that is neither eased nor interrupted, and they are left without any helper to rescue them. It teaches that the true cost of worldly preference is measured in the everlasting outcome, and that no intercession or worldly support can avert the reckoning for those who consciously exchanged their eternal destiny for transient gain.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture and followed up after him with messengers. And We gave Jesus, the son of Mary, clear proofs and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit. Is it then that whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you were arrogant? So a group you denied and a group you killed.
