interpretation: The verse exposes a recurring pattern in the history of the Children of Israel: their readiness to reject divine guidance whenever it conflicted with their own desires and pride. God reminds them that He sent Moses the Book and a long succession of prophets, and gave Jesus clear signs and the support of the Holy Spirit, yet they responded with arrogance, denying some messengers and even killing others. The rhetorical question shows that their conduct was not an isolated lapse but a consistent habit, in which the test of a prophet was whether his message suited their inclinations rather than whether it was true. The verse thus warns that rejecting truth because it is uncomfortable, and then turning on its bearers, is a grave spiritual disease that the listener must avoid.

translation: And they say, "Our hearts are wrapped (sealed away)!" Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief, so little is it that they believe.
interpretation: The verse exposes a self-serving posture: those who reject the message claim their hearts are naturally enclosed, beyond reach of guidance, thereby placing the blame for their unbelief on their own constitution rather than on their choice. God refutes this by stating that their rejection is the consequence of their persistent disbelief, which has drawn down a curse upon them, closing them off further. The phrase "so little is it that they believe" can be read both as a statement that faith is rare among them and as a reproach that their capacity to believe has been diminished by their habitual refusal. The verse thus affirms human responsibility: an excuse of inherent incapacity is dismissed, and the real cause of spiritual hardening is shown to be the people's own disbelief, which God then answers with a just consequence.

translation: And when there came to them a Book from Allah confirming what was with them, although previously they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved, yet when there came to them that which they recognized, they disbelieved in it. So the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse exposes a painful contradiction in the attitude of those who had received earlier revelation. They had long prayed for divine help against the pagans, announcing that a prophet was about to come, and they expected the truth to be on their side. Yet when the promised messenger and the Book confirming their own scripture actually arrived, and they recognized it as the very thing they had described, their recognition turned into rejection. The lesson is that knowing the truth is not enough; it is the pride, envy, or attachment to worldly status that prevents acceptance. Such a refusal after clear recognition is the most blameworthy form of disbelief, and it is why the verse closes by declaring Allah's curse upon those who persist in denying the truth.

translation: Wretched is that for which they have sold their souls: that they deny what God has sent down, out of resentment that God should send down His bounty upon whom He wills of His servants. So they have incurred anger upon anger, and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse exposes the root of the sin of the People of the Book: it is not ignorance of the truth but envy and spite. They knew the revelation was from God, yet they rejected it because it came through someone outside their own community, as though divine favor were theirs to grant or withhold. Their self-sale is thus a trade of their own spiritual wellbeing for the sake of pride and jealousy. The repeated wrath signifies the compounding consequences of persisting in such denial, and the humiliating punishment reflects that arrogance is answered with abasement.

translation: And when it is said to them, "Believe in what Allah has sent down," they say, "We believe in what was sent down to us," and they reject what is beyond it, while it is the truth confirming what is with them. Say, "Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah before, if you were believers?"
interpretation: The verse exposes a selective faith: the people of the Book claimed loyalty to their own revelation while rejecting the later revelation that confirms and completes it, showing that true belief in God's word cannot be partial or tribal. The Prophet is then told to confront their hypocrisy with a pointed question: if their scripture truly bound them, why did their ancestors kill the messengers God sent to them? Their own history of violence against the prophets contradicts their claim to be believers, so the verse teaches that faith is measured by acceptance of the truth God sends and by conduct consistent with it, not by inherited identity or selective adherence.

translation: And certainly Moses came to you with clear proofs, then you took the calf [for worship] after him, while you were wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse confronts the Children of Israel with the gravity of their apostasy: after witnessing the clear signs brought by Moses, they nonetheless turned to worshipping the golden calf in his absence, and this was a wrong done against their own souls. It reveals that clarity of evidence does not by itself guarantee faithfulness, since the heart can still be swayed by desire, fear, or impatience. The phrase 'after him' points to how quickly the people abandoned the truth once their prophet was out of sight, a warning that devotion must rest on conviction rather than on the presence of a guide. Finally, the closing words 'while you were wrongdoers' frame idolatry as zulm, an injustice that first and foremost harms the one who commits it.

translation: And [recall] when We took your covenant and raised above you the mount: "Hold firmly to what We have given you and listen." They said, "We hear and we disobey." And they were made to drink the calf into their hearts because of their disbelief. Say, "Evil is that which your faith commands you, if you are [truly] believers."
interpretation: This verse recalls the Children of Israel's broken covenant at Mount Sinai, where they were commanded to grasp the Torah with determination and to listen attentively. Their reply, "we hear and we disobey," exposes a gap between outward words and inward response: hearing without obeying. Their hearts became so saturated with love of the golden calf that it is described as having been absorbed into them, a vivid image of idolatry settling into the heart through disbelief. The closing rebuke turns their own claim against them: if their professed faith were genuine, it would never command such disobedience, so true belief must be shown in faithful action upon revelation rather than in mere profession.

translation: Say: If the Last Abode with God is exclusively yours, apart from the rest of mankind, then wish for death, if you are truthful.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hollowness of the claim that the Hereafter belongs exclusively to one's own group. Anyone who sincerely believed that paradise was theirs alone, with God's favor secured for them, would naturally long to pass into it, since death would be the gateway to what they claim is rightfully theirs. Their reluctance to wish for death betrays an inner doubt about their own claim, and so their refusal becomes a silent witness against their own assertion. The challenge thus turns a boast of spiritual privilege into a test of sincerity, showing that true confidence in God's mercy is measured by the readiness to meet Him, not by the pride of exclusive ownership of salvation.

translation: But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have put forward. And Allah is All-Knowing of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse refers to the Jews, who claimed that the abode of the Hereafter with Allah belongs exclusively to them (2:94). Allah tells them that they will never truly wish for death, because their own deeds, the corruptions and transgressions their hands have committed, stand as proof against them and as the reason they dread what awaits them. Their outward claim to be the beloved of Allah is thus exposed by their inner reluctance to face Him. The closing phrase, that Allah has full knowledge of the wrongdoers, warns that nothing of their injustice is hidden from Him, and that their false claims will not shield them from the consequences of their own conduct.

translation: And you will surely find them the most eager of people for life—even more eager than those who associate others with Allah. One of them wishes he could be granted a life of a thousand years, but his being granted long life will not remove him from the punishment. And Allah is Seeing of what they do.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrisy and cowardice of the Jews, who, despite their claim to be the chosen people and their belief in the afterlife, cling to worldly life with greater desperation than even the polytheists who have no such hope in an afterlife. Their intense craving for a long life reveals that their attachment to this world is driven by a guilty conscience concerning what they have done, since they know the punishment awaiting them. Yet no extension of years can shield them from the consequence of their deeds, for life's length is no protection against divine judgment. The closing reminder that Allah is All-Seeing of their actions serves as a warning that their concealed motives and conduct are fully known to Him.

translation: Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, then indeed he has brought it down upon your heart by the permission of Allah, confirming what came before it, and as guidance and good tidings for the believers.
interpretation: The verse answers those who opposed Gabriel as the bearer of revelation: their hostility is misplaced, since Gabriel merely delivered the Qur'an to the Prophet's heart by God's will. The Qur'an is presented as a confirmation of earlier scripture, which shows its continuity with the prior message, and its function is twofold: guidance that directs the mind and heart, and good news reserved for those who believe. The verse thus locates the authority of revelation in God's permission rather than in the messenger, and ties the believer's relationship to the Qur'an to hope and assurance.

translation: Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers, and Jibreel and Mikaal, then indeed Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse establishes that hostility toward Allah is hostility toward everything that is connected to His revelation and His messengers, so enmity toward any of His angels or prophets is itself an act of disbelief. The specific naming of Jibreel and Mikaal, after the general mention of the angels, highlights their particular honor and their role in conveying revelation and sustaining creation, so that opposing them is singled out as a grave matter. The closing statement shows that Allah's enmity toward such people is the natural consequence of their rejection: whoever opposes the sources of guidance places himself in opposition to the One who sent them, and so the disbelievers stand under the displeasure of their Lord.

translation: And We have certainly sent down to you clear revelations, and none disbelieves in them except the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the revelation given to the Prophet Muhammad is itself self-evidently clear, so that rejecting it is not the result of ambiguity or lack of proof but of a deliberate turning away by those who have abandoned obedience to God. Disbelief here is traced not to the evidence but to the character of the one who refuses it: the 'fāsiqūn' are those who have stepped outside the bounds of truth and righteousness by choice. The clarity of the signs thus places responsibility on the human heart, and it consoles the believer by showing that the failure to accept the message reflects the disposition of the rejecter rather than any deficiency in the message.

translation: Is it not that every time they make a covenant, a party of them casts it aside? Rather, most of them do not believe.
interpretation: The verse exposes a recurring pattern of the Children of Israel: their commitments were not anchored in steadfast faith, so whenever they bound themselves by a pact, a faction among them would discard it at the first opportunity. The rhetorical question, followed by the turn 'bal' (rather), locates the root of this treachery in their disbelief; most of them lacked genuine conviction, and that absence of inner faith is what made breaking covenants easy. The verse thus teaches that the sanctity of a promise depends on the faith that undergirds it, and it warns the believers not to imitate such inconsistency.

translation: And when there came to them a messenger from Allah confirming what was with them, a party of those who were given the Scripture threw the Book of Allah behind their backs, as if they did not know.
interpretation: The verse exposes a paradox of religious conduct: those who already possessed revelation, when the promised messenger arrived confirming their own scripture, did not embrace the truth but cast aside the very Book they claimed to revere, behaving as though they were ignorant. The sin lies not in lack of knowledge but in deliberately ignoring knowledge already in their hands, showing that true faith requires acting on what one knows, and that the rejection of a confirmation of one's own tradition is a form of wilful blindness.

translation: And they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon. Solomon did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic and that which was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut. Yet they did not teach anyone until they had said, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve." And people learned from them by which they caused separation between a man and his wife, but they could not harm anyone with it except by permission of Allah. And they learned what harmed them and did not benefit them. And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter. And wretched is that for which they sold themselves, if only they knew.
interpretation: The verse exposes the corruption of a people who abandoned the revelation they had been given and turned instead to what the devils fabricated under Solomon's name, thereby attributing unbelief to Solomon, who was innocent of it. Its deeper lesson is that knowledge which harms its possessor and others is no knowledge at all: these people knew the consequences of their bargain yet traded their own souls for a worthless and destructive craft, and their tragedy lies precisely in that the knowledge they possessed should have restrained them. The mention of Harut and Marut as a trial shows that God tests humanity by setting before it powers that tempt toward disbelief, so that the sincere are distinguished from the deluded, while the statement that no harm occurs except by Allah's permission affirms that all causation rests ultimately in His will.

translation: And if they had believed and feared God, a reward from God would have been far better for them, if only they knew.
interpretation: The verse contrasts the fleeting worldly gains that some people chase through deceit and sin with the enduring reward that comes from God. Faith joined with taqwa, the conscious awareness of God that restrains one from wrongdoing, is presented as the true path to a recompense far superior to anything this world offers. The closing phrase, 'if only they knew,' points to the root of the problem: people turn away from the greater good not because it is unavailable, but because they lack the knowledge and insight to recognize its value, and so they settle for what is lesser.

translation: O you who have believed, do not say "Raina" but say "Unzurna" and listen. And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse teaches believers to guard the courtesy and sincerity of their speech toward the Prophet. The word "Raina" (roughly "our shepherd" or "pay attention to us") could be twisted by the hostile into a derogatory pun, so the believers are directed to a clear and respectful alternative, "Unzurna" (look at us), and to attentive listening. The lesson extends beyond that occasion: the faithful must avoid any ambiguous or demeaning expression, even one harmless in intent, that opens a door to mockery or disrespect toward what is sacred, and must cultivate careful, humble attentiveness. Those who deliberately mock and deride the truth, by contrast, face a painful reckoning.

translation: Those who disbelieve among the People of the Scripture, and the polytheists, do not wish that any good should be sent down upon you from your Lord. But Allah singles out for His mercy whom He wills, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.
interpretation: The verse exposes the envy harbored by disbelievers, both from the People of the Book and the polytheists, toward the believers, whom they begrudge the blessing of divine revelation and guidance. Their hostility is not born of reasoned rejection alone but of resentment at seeing good bestowed on others. The verse then reassures the believers that the distribution of divine mercy is entirely in God's hands: He grants it to whom He wills according to His wisdom, and no one can withhold what He gives or grant what He withholds. Its closing reminder that God is the Possessor of immense bounty teaches that the believers should not fear loss from the envy of others, since God's favor is boundless and not diminished by being shared.

translation: Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring forth one better than it or similar to it. Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?
interpretation: The verse affirms Allah's absolute sovereignty over revelation: when He abrogates a ruling or removes a verse from recitation, it is never a loss or a mistake, but a wise act that is followed by something better for the believers, either in ease and benefit or in its equal in guidance. The question "Do you not know" rebukes doubt about this divine prerogative, reminding the listener that the One who has power over all things governs the progression of the law according to what suits human welfare and the gradual education of the community. It thus calls the believer to submit to the changing rulings with trust, recognizing that the divine wisdom is perfect even when its outward form changes.

translation: Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth? And you have not, besides Allah, any protector or any helper.
interpretation: The verse turns the believer's attention from the questions of the heart to the foundation of tawhid: since all sovereignty over the heavens and earth belongs to Allah alone, every created thing is under His authority, and therefore no one can shield a person from His decree or give them support that stands independent of Him. Recognizing this truth should lead a person to place reliance and loyalty solely in God, rather than in creatures who themselves possess no power to protect or to help.

translation: Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before? And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith has certainly strayed from the right way.
interpretation: The verse warns the believers against the habit of demanding excessive and presumptuous questions from their Prophet, as the Children of Israel did with Moses, whose people asked him to show them God openly and kept challenging his commands, which led them into hardship and disobedience. Its wider lesson is that a community which, instead of humbly accepting guidance, persists in such challenging and doubting inquiry is effectively trading the faith it has been given for a posture of unbelief, and this exchange is a clear departure from the straight path. The verse therefore links the proper manner of seeking knowledge from the Messenger with the preservation of true faith, showing that respectful submission to revealed guidance is the safeguard against going astray.

translation: Many of the People of the Scripture wish they could turn you back into disbelievers after your belief, out of envy from themselves, after the truth has become clear to them. So pardon and overlook until Allah brings His command. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse exposes the inner motive behind the hostility of some People of the Scripture toward the believing community: it is not a lack of evidence but envy rooted in their own souls, since the truth had already become manifest to them. Against such hostility, the believers are commanded to adopt forbearance and forgiveness rather than retaliation, entrusting the outcome to God's decree and reminding them that His power is absolute, so that their steadfastness rests on reliance upon Him rather than on the opponents' conduct.

translation: And establish prayer and give zakat, and whatever good you put forward for yourselves you will find it with Allah. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse binds the outward acts of worship, prayer and zakat, to an inward accountability: every good deed a person sends ahead is not lost but is stored with Allah as a treasure to be found on the Day of Reckoning, when it will be returned in its full worth. The closing phrase, that Allah is Seeing of what you do, reminds the believer that no charity given in secret and no devotion performed in private escapes His knowledge, so that the believer's motive and sincerity are what give these acts their lasting value.

translation: And they say, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians." That is their wishful thinking. Say, "Produce your proof, if you are truthful."
interpretation: The verse exposes a recurring pattern among the People of the Book: the monopolizing of salvation by one's own community, as though entry into Paradise were a matter of group identity or inherited affiliation rather than sincere faith and righteous conduct. By calling their claim mere 'wishful desires' (amani), the Qur'an reduces it to fantasy unsupported by evidence. The challenge to 'produce your proof' establishes the principle that religious assertions about God's judgment must rest on clear demonstration, not on assumption or ethnic and sectarian pride. The broader implication, drawn in the surrounding verses, is that salvation belongs to whoever submits their face to God and does good, so exclusivist claims are measured against the standard of genuine piety.

translation: Yes, whoever submits his whole self to God while being a doer of good, for him is his reward with his Lord, and no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: The verse establishes that salvation is not bound to any community label or outward claim but to a comprehensive inner and outer surrender to God (aslama wajhahu), joined with genuine excellence in conduct (ihsan). The phrase 'bala' (yes, indeed) answers the preceding claims of exclusivity by affirming that whoever fulfills this two-fold condition earns a reward secured with their Lord. The promise that there is no fear or grief for them points to a state of inner security and contentment that arises from a sound relationship with God and from righteous action, rather than from ritual identity alone.

translation: And the Jews said, "The Christians are not founded upon anything," and the Christians said, "The Jews are not founded upon anything," while they both recite the Scripture. Thus said those who have no knowledge, something similar to their saying. So Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ.
interpretation: The verse exposes the sectarian arrogance that arises when people possess revelation yet reduce it to a tool for mutual condemnation. Both communities recite the same Scripture, which affirms one God and calls for justice and humility, but their attachment to their own group made them blind to the common source they shared. Their claim that the other side has no standing is presented as the speech of those without true knowledge, because genuine knowledge of the Book would have restrained them from denying the truth in the other. The verse thus warns believers against exclusivist certainty that disowns others, and it reminds them that the final resolution of such disputes belongs to God alone on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned therein and strives toward their ruin? Those would not have entered them except in fear. For them in this world is disgrace, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse condemns in the strongest terms those who obstruct the worship of God in His houses and work to destroy them, placing them among the greatest wrongdoers. Its wording shows that such people forfeit the right to enter the sacred precincts, and that they should enter them only in fear, as a sign of their own transgression. Their punishment is twofold: disgrace in this life, through humiliation and loss of standing, and severe torment in the Hereafter. The principle extends beyond the literal case of the ancient sanctuaries to any act that bars people from remembering God in places of worship or that wrongfully tears down the spaces dedicated to His remembrance.

translation: And to Allah belong the east and the west; so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah. Indeed, Allah is All-Encompassing and All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse dissolves the idea that God is bound to a particular direction or place. Since the east and west, and every direction between them, belong to Allah, turning in worship is not confined to one spot on the earth; Allah's presence and knowledge encompass all places. Its broader meaning is that sincerity of intention and the orientation of the heart toward God matter more than the outward direction of the body. The phrase 'the Face of Allah' points to His self-manifestation and nearness to His servants, not to a physical form. The closing attributes, 'Wasi' (All-Encompassing) and 'Alim' (All-Knowing), reassure the believer that wherever he turns in devotion, his prayer is seen and accepted by a God whose mercy and knowledge reach everywhere.

translation: And they say, "God has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him.
interpretation: The verse refutes the claim that God has begotten or adopted a child by pointing to the nature of divine ownership and dominion. Since everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him as its creator and sustainer, and all of it stands in devoted submission before Him, there can be no kinship between the Creator and any part of His creation. The word "subhanahu" affirms that He is exalted above such attributions, and the phrase "kull lahu qanitun" shows that even the beings honored as sons by some are themselves servants bound in obedience. Sonship implies a shared nature and need, which is incompatible with the absolute self-sufficiency and unity of God.

translation: The Originator of the heavens and the earth. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.
interpretation: The verse presents God's creative power as absolute and effortless: He is the one who originates the heavens and the earth without precedent or model, and whatever He determines comes into being through the simple word "Be." This is not a description of a process requiring time, tools, or resistance, but an affirmation that the existence of all things depends entirely on His will. It invites the believer to recognize that the cosmos, in all its vastness, is a continual expression of a sovereign command, and therefore to place trust in the One whose decree no created thing can resist or delay.

translation: And those who do not know said, "Why does Allah not speak to us, or why does a sign not come to us?" Likewise said those before them the same as their words. Their hearts are alike. We have certainly made the signs clear for a people who are certain.
interpretation: The verse exposes a recurring pattern of stubborn disbelief: those who lack knowledge demand direct divine speech or a miraculous sign on their own terms, as though faith should depend on their preferred form of proof. Their request mirrors that of earlier generations, showing that the underlying obstinacy, rather than a shortage of evidence, is what drives such demands. The phrase "their hearts are alike" indicates that a shared inner disposition, not the lack of signs, produces this uniform refusal. The closing statement affirms that the signs have already been made clear, and that certainty of heart is what allows a person to perceive them.

translation: Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good news and a warner. And you will not be questioned about the companions of Hellfire.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet and clarifies the limits of his mission: he is sent with the truth, not as a guardian over people's destinies. His duty is to deliver glad tidings to those who believe and to warn those who persist in denial, and the outcome of those who choose the Fire rests with their own choices and with God's judgment. By saying he will not be asked about the companions of Hellfire, the verse lifts from him the burden of grief and self-blame over those who reject faith, and reminds him that accountability is individual and that delivering the message faithfully is what is required of him.

translation: And the Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion. Say, "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [only] guidance." And if you were to follow their desires after what has come to you of knowledge, you would have against Allah no protector or helper.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad directly and exposes a fundamental truth about the relationship between revelation and the People of the Book: their approval cannot be purchased by compromising the message, because their aim is not mutual accommodation but the dissolution of the prophetic mission into their own traditions. The command to say that Allah's guidance is the true guidance establishes that divine guidance is not a matter of negotiated consensus or communal preference, but is fixed by its source. The warning that following their desires after knowledge has arrived is a grave matter, is addressed to the Prophet himself to show that no one, however close to God, is exempt from the consequences of compromising revealed truth, and it teaches that the standard for the believer is loyalty to revelation rather than the pursuit of others' approval.

translation: Those to whom We have given the Scripture recite it as it should be recited; those believe in it. And whoever disbelieves in it, it is those who are the losers.
interpretation: The verse distinguishes between two kinds of people who have received the Book. Those who recite it with its true recitation, meaning they read it with proper care, understanding, and sincere attention to its meaning and commands, are precisely the ones who truly believe in it, since genuine belief is shown through engagement with its words and acting upon them. By contrast, the one who rejects it, despite having it within reach, forfeits the greatest benefit it offers and thereby bears the loss of his own soul. The phrase 'recite it as it should be recited' points to the inseparable bond between reading the divine word and faith in it: mere possession of the Scripture or superficial recitation does not suffice, while faithful, thoughtful recitation is the mark of true belief and salvation.

translation: O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds.
interpretation: The verse calls the Children of Israel to active remembrance of God's favors, which is more than nostalgic recollection: it is a summons to recognize those blessings, feel gratitude for them, and let that gratitude shape obedience. Their distinction over the worlds is read as a trust rather than a privilege owed by right, since it was granted with a responsibility to live up to the guidance they were given. By placing this reminder at the opening of the lengthy address to the Children of Israel, the verse establishes that remembering divine favor is the foundation for everything that follows, including the call to fulfill the covenant and to avoid complacency toward God's grace.

translation: And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another soul in the least, nor will any compensation be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it, nor will they be helped.
interpretation: The verse calls the listener to taqwa by fixing the mind on a Day on which the usual supports of this world fail entirely. Each soul stands alone: no one can pay for another, no ransom or equivalent can be taken, no intercession avails except by permission, and no outside help arrives. The repeated negations strip away every means by which a person might hope to escape accountability through kinship, wealth, or influential friends. The lesson is that the only real protection is the deeds one sends ahead, so awareness of that Day should drive a person to sincere righteousness now, while such action is still possible.

translation: And [mention] when Abraham was tested by his Lord with words, and he fulfilled them. He said, "Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people." [Abraham] said, "And from my descendants?" He said, "My covenant does not include the wrongdoers."
interpretation: The verse shows that divine leadership is a trust (ʿahd) granted by God and conditioned on righteousness rather than on lineage alone. Abraham's successful completion of the trials qualified him for the imamate, and his request for it to extend to his descendants is answered by a principle of justice: those who persist in wrongdoing (ẓulm, which at its root is placing things in other than their proper place, including the worship of others besides God) cannot inherit the covenant of leadership. Thus spiritual and moral authority passes through merit and faithfulness, not through mere biological descent.

translation: And [mention] when We made the House a place of return and security for the people, and [said], "Take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer." And We entrusted to Abraham and Ishmael [the command]: "Purify My House for those who circumambulate, those who stay in devotion, and those who bow and prostrate."
interpretation: The verse presents the Sacred House as a center to which people repeatedly return, a sanctuary where safety is established, and it ties its sanctity to the covenant made with Abraham and Ishmael to keep it clean of everything that contradicts its purpose. By naming the circling worshippers, the devoted dwellers, and those who bow and prostrate, it shows that the House is meant for sincere acts of worship of God alone, and that the station of Abraham, the place where he stood while building it, is singled out as a site of prayer, linking the legacy of the prophets to the continuing practice of devotion.

translation: And [mention] when Abraham said, "My Lord, make this city secure and provide its people with fruits, those of them who believe in Allah and the Last Day." He said, "And whoever disbelieves - I will grant him enjoyment for a little, then I will compel him toward the punishment of the Fire, and wretched is the destination."
interpretation: The verse shows that Abraham's prayer for provision was limited to the believers, and God's reply extends worldly provision to all, including disbelievers, as a temporary enjoyment, while placing the true consequence in the Hereafter. Divine generosity in this life is thus not a sign of approval, and the brevity of worldly pleasure is set against the lasting torment that awaits those who reject faith. Abraham's request thus joins material blessing with faith, teaching that a secure and prosperous community is ultimately measured by its belief in God and the Last Day.

translation: And [mention] when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House, and Ishmael [with him, saying]: "Our Lord, accept [this] from us. Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing."
interpretation: The verse presents the building of the Sacred House as an act of worship joined in humility and partnership between father and son. Abraham and Ishmael raise its foundations not for personal glory but while turning to God with a plea for acceptance, showing that the true value of any righteous deed lies in whether God accepts it, and that sincere effort must be accompanied by a heart that fears it may fall short. The closing divine names, the All-Hearing and the All-Knowing, convey that God hears the supplication and knows the intention behind the labor, so the believer should combine diligent action with trust in God's knowledge of his sincerity.

translation: "Our Lord, and make us [submitting] to You, and of our descendants a nation submitting to You, and show us our rites and accept our repentance. Indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful." (Al-Baqarah 2:128)
interpretation: This supplication, uttered by Abraham and Ismail as they raised the foundations of the Kaaba, reveals that true submission to God (islam) is not merely an individual achievement but a covenantal aspiration that extends to one's offspring, so that faith becomes a living inheritance across generations. The request to be shown "our rites" expresses a humble recognition that worship cannot be invented by human will but must be received from God, and the plea for forgiveness that follows teaches that even the most devoted builders of the House stand in need of divine mercy. The verse thus joins sincere striving, the transmission of faith to one's descendants, and continual turning back to God in repentance as the complete shape of a believer's relationship with the Lord.

translation: "Our Lord, raise up among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses, and teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise."
interpretation: This is the supplication of Abraham and Ishmael, peace be upon them, as they finished raising the foundations of the Kaaba, asking God to send to their descendants a prophet drawn from among them. The verse reveals that the purpose of the prophetic mission is fourfold: reciting God's signs so that hearts are awakened to the truth, teaching the Book so that its meaning is understood, imparting wisdom so that its application is sound, and purifying the soul from shirk, ignorance and moral corruption. The mission is thus not merely informational but transformative, shaping both the mind and the character. The closing names, the Mighty and the Wise, indicate that such a messenger is granted by a power that can accomplish its will and by a wisdom that chooses what is fitting for every people.

translation: And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself? And We had chosen him in this world, and indeed he, in the Hereafter, is among the righteous.
interpretation: The verse poses a rhetorical rebuke: no sound intellect would abandon the creed of Abraham, since to reject it is to degrade one's own soul through folly. The divine choosing of Abraham in this life and his place among the righteous in the next establish that his path is the model of guidance, so turning away from it is self-harm. The verse thus calls the reader to reflect on the reasonableness of monotheistic submission to God as the heritage of the prophet Abraham, whom the people of the Book claimed as their own, and it implicitly exposes the emptiness of those who reject it.

translation: When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: The verse presents submission (islam) as the essential posture of the believer, shown in Abraham's immediate and wholehearted response to his Lord's call. His answer is not a reluctant concession but a total surrender of the self to the one who creates and sustains all worlds. The brevity of the exchange is itself meaningful: a command is given and it is met at once, without hesitation or demand for proof. Islam here is understood not merely as a label for a later religious community but as the inner reality of turning the whole being toward God, a reality that the prophets before Muhammad also embodied.

translation: And Abraham instructed his sons to do the same, and [so did] Jacob: "O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims."
interpretation: The verse presents submission to God as a covenant inherited across generations: Abraham and Jacob bequeath to their children not merely a family tradition but the religion of surrender to the One God, chosen by Allah for them. The final injunction ties the whole of life to its end, so that a person's faith is to be held steadfastly until the moment of death. Islam here is understood in its root sense of submission, the shared prophetic message that unites the line of prophets, and the verse calls the listener to make this inheritance a living, unbroken commitment rather than a received label.

translation: Or were you witnesses when death approached Jacob? When he said to his sons, "What will you worship after me?" They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your forefathers, Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac, one God. And to Him we are submitting."
interpretation: The verse confronts the people of the Scripture with a question they cannot honestly answer in the affirmative: they were not present at Jacob's deathbed, so they cannot claim that he bequeathed to his sons a creed other than pure monotheism. Jacob's final concern was his children's faithfulness after him, and their unhesitating reply, affirming the one God worshipped by their fathers Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac and declaring their submission to Him, shows that the core of the prophetic message across generations is tawhid and islam (submission). The passage thereby refutes the claim that Jacob and his lineage were Jews or Christians in the later sectarian sense, and presents the faith of the prophets as a single, unbroken inheritance of devotion to the one God.

translation: That was a community that has passed away; for them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn, and you will not be asked about what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse closes the discussion of the prophets and their peoples by making accountability strictly personal: every soul bears the weight of its own deeds and reaps their fruit, so the merit of earlier generations cannot be claimed by descendants, nor their faults imposed upon them. The repeated warning against inheriting the past by lineage or pride turns the believer's attention from genealogical or communal prestige toward present conduct. By saying that no one will be questioned about what the bygone people did, it also reminds the listener that the Day of Reckoning will examine each person's own choices, so one should focus on reforming oneself rather than debating the actions of others.

translation: And they say, "Be Jews or Christians, [then] you will be guided." Say, "Rather, [we follow] the religion of Abraham, inclining toward truth, and he was not of those who associate others with Allah."
interpretation: The verse exposes the exclusivist claim of the Jews and Christians, each insisting that guidance belongs only to their own community, and it answers this by redirecting the believer to the pure monotheism of Abraham, who was upright (hanif) and free of any association of partners with God. By making Abraham the reference point rather than a later sectarian label, the verse shifts the criterion of guidance from group affiliation to sincere, undivided devotion to the One God, a standard that transcends the Jewish and Christian identities being contested in the passage.

translation: Say: "We believe in God, and in what has been revealed to us, and in what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes, and in what was given to Moses and Jesus, and in what was given to the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submitting."
interpretation: The verse instructs believers to affirm a comprehensive faith that embraces the revelations given to all the prophets from the same divine source, rather than selectively accepting some and rejecting others. By refusing to separate among the messengers, the believer acknowledges the unity of their message and the single God who sent it, and makes this unity the basis of an inclusive submission (islam) to Him. The phrase "we are submitting" ties the affirmation of faith to complete surrender, showing that true belief in the prophets is expressed through sincere devotion to the one Lord they all called people to.

translation: So if they believe in the same as you have believed in, then they have been guided. But if they turn away, then they are only in dissension, and Allah will suffice you against them. And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse establishes a standard of true guidance: faith that mirrors the faith of the believers, rooted in the same revealed truth, is the measure by which guidance is recognized, so that guidance is not defined by sectarian claims but by genuine conformity to what was revealed. Turning away is described not merely as error but as a state of schism (shiqaq), a deliberate opposition that splits the community of truth. To the Prophet and believers, the verse offers reassurance that their opponents' hostility need not be feared, since God alone is sufficient protector; His hearing and knowledge encompass every plot and speech, so the believers' trust should rest in Him rather than in their own strength or in the approval of others.

translation: Sibghat Allah (the baptism/coloring of God). And who is better than Allah in coloring? And we are worshippers of Him.
interpretation: The verse uses the image of dyeing: just as a dye gives cloth its distinctive color and identity, the religion of God marks the believer with a character that is wholly God's. The expression 'sibghat Allah' is thus a call to take on a faith that permeates one's whole being, in contrast to the baptismal or sectarian identities of the People of the Book. No dye is finer than God's, and the believer's response is sincere worship of Him alone, so that devotion, conduct, and inner disposition all bear the mark of God's guidance.

translation: Say: Do you argue with us about God, when He is our Lord and your Lord? For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds, and we are sincerely devoted to Him alone.
interpretation: The verse sets out a principled boundary for interfaith and inter-community debate: the Prophet is commanded to confront those who dispute with believers over God by pointing out that God is the common Lord of all, so the dispute is not really about who owns God but about the accountability each person bears for his own works. By affirming that each party answers for its own deeds, the verse shifts the focus from tribal claims and contentious argument to individual responsibility before God, and it closes by defining the believer's core stance as sincere devotion (ikhlas) to God alone, which is the inward ground from which all righteous action must spring.

translation: Or do you say that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Descendants were Jews or Christians? Say, "Are you more knowing, or is God?" And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God? And God is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse confronts the People of the Book who claimed the prophets before the revelation of the Torah and the Gospel as adherents of their own religions, when those figures lived before these scriptures were revealed. By asking whether they know better than God, it exposes the contradiction between their claim and the divine knowledge of the matter. The phrase "conceals a testimony from God" points to their concealment of what their own scriptures attest, namely the true, pure monotheism (hanifiyya) of Abraham and his line, which was neither Judaism nor Christianity. The closing warning that God is not unaware of their deeds makes concealment of truth a matter of moral accountability before Him.

translation: That was a community that has passed away; theirs is what they earned, and yours is what you have earned, and you will not be questioned about what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse closes a passage addressing the Children of Israel and their forefathers by drawing a firm boundary of personal moral accountability: each generation stands before God for its own deeds and not for the deeds of its predecessors. This dismisses the reliance on ancestral merit (as the Jews and Christians of Medina claimed to be heirs of the prophets) and equally dismisses the notion that later believers bear the sins of earlier ones. The repetition of 'what they earned' and 'what you earned' turns the verse into a call to self-examination, directing the listener's attention away from genealogy and toward his or her own conduct, which alone will be weighed.

translation: The foolish among the people will say: "What has turned them away from their qiblah, which they had been facing?" Say: "To Allah belong the east and the west. He guides whomever He wills to a straight path."
interpretation: This verse, revealed around the change of the qiblah from Jerusalem to the Ka'bah in Makkah, shows that God's command is not bound to a particular direction, since east and west belong to Him alone. The objection of the foolish reflects a shallow view that confuses the outward form of worship with its essence, which is turning the heart and the whole self toward God. The verse teaches believers to be steadfast when faced with criticism and to recognize that divine guidance to the straight path is a matter of God's wisdom and choice, not of human expectations or the orientation of the body.

translation: And thus We have made you a justly balanced community, that you may be witnesses over the people and the Messenger may be a witness over you. And We did not make the qibla which you used to face except that We might make evident who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels. And indeed, it was a great matter except for those whom Allah has guided. And Allah would never make your faith ineffective. Indeed Allah is to the people Kind and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the change of the qibla from Jerusalem to the Ka'bah was a test that distinguished sincere believers from those who would abandon the Prophet's guidance under pressure, and it frames the Muslim community's role as a moderate, balanced witness over humanity, a status grounded in its faithful adherence to the Messenger. By affirming that their prior prayers toward Jerusalem would not be lost, God reassures the believers that their faith remains valued, showing that divine mercy encompasses sincere devotion even when the outward direction of worship is redirected.

translation: We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven, so We will surely turn you to a qibla that you will be pleased with. So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it. Indeed, those who were given the Scripture know that it is the truth from their Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what they do.
interpretation: The verse records the change of the prayer direction from Jerusalem to the Sacred Mosque in Makkah, a moment that carried deep personal meaning for the Prophet, who had longed for a qibla tied to the heritage of Abraham. God honors that inner yearning by granting him a direction that answers his heart, while making clear that the turning is a divine command binding on all believers wherever they stand, so that unity of direction becomes a sign of unity of submission. The mention of the People of the Book knowing the truth of this change points to the fact that the new qibla is confirmed by their own scriptures, which foretold a prophet and a sacred house linked to Abraham, and the closing reminder that God is not heedless of what people do calls the community to sincere obedience even when the command tests their attachments and assumptions.

translation: And even if you brought to those who were given the Scripture every sign, they would not follow your qibla, nor are you one who will follow their qibla, nor are some of them followers of the qibla of others. And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, indeed you would then be among the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the direction of prayer is a matter of divine command rather than negotiation, and that no amount of evidence would win the People of the Book over to the Prophet's qibla, because their rejection stems from entrenched attachment and desire rather than lack of proof. It then warns the Prophet himself that yielding to their wishes after receiving revealed knowledge would be a grave wrong, showing that even the most upright person must hold firmly to truth and that such firmness is a safeguard against compromising the revealed guidance.

translation: Those to whom We gave the Scripture recognize it as they recognize their own sons. But indeed, a group of them conceal the truth while they know it.
interpretation: The verse points to a recognition that is deeper than mere knowledge: the People of the Book know the Prophet's message with the certainty a father has in recognizing his own children, so their concealment of the truth is not born of ignorance but of deliberate choice made against what they inwardly know. It exposes the gap between inner conviction and outward stance, showing that rejection of truth often stems from pride, worldly interest, or fear of losing standing rather than from a lack of evidence. For the believer, it is both a reminder of the clarity of the revealed message and a warning against allowing self-interest to silence what one knows to be right.

translation: The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the truth comes entirely from God, the Lord who nurtures and guides the Prophet, and therefore leaves no room for hesitation. The command not to be among the doubters is addressed to the Prophet, yet it carries a universal lesson: certainty is grounded in the source of revelation rather than in the shifting opinions of people. Doubt is presented not merely as an intellectual error but as a spiritual posture that turns away from a clear truth. The instruction calls the believer to firm conviction, to settle the heart upon what God has revealed, and to resist the wavering that comes from disputes and uncertainty.

translation: And for each there is a direction toward which it turns, so race to [all] good deeds. Wherever you may be, Allah will bring you all together. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse shifts the believers' attention from the dispute over the direction of prayer to what truly matters: the race toward righteousness. Every community has its own qibla and its own way of worship, so diversity of outward forms should not become a cause of division or rivalry over externals. The real contest is in good works, which the believers are commanded to hasten toward eagerly and competitively. The closing reminder that wherever one is, God will gather all people for judgment, and His power is absolute, gives urgency to this race: every person will ultimately be brought before God, so the question is not which direction one faces but how one's deeds stand before Him.

translation: And from wherever you emerge, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and indeed, it is the truth from your Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse reaffirms the change of the qibla from Jerusalem to the Sacred Mosque in Makkah, and it does so by repeating the command so that no believer could claim an exception based on location or circumstance. Turning toward the Ka'bah becomes a visible sign of submission and unity, binding the community together under a single direction of worship wherever they may be. By calling this direction 'the truth from your Lord,' the verse places the act of prayer within divine guidance rather than personal preference, and its closing reminder that Allah is not unaware of what they do points to sincerity: the outward turning must be matched by an inward turning of the heart toward God.

translation: And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque. And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it, so that people will have no argument against you, except those of them who do wrong. So do not fear them, but fear Me, that I may complete My favor upon you and that you may be guided.
interpretation: The verse makes the qibla, the direction of prayer toward the Sacred Mosque in Makkah, a universal obligation that applies wherever a believer is, so that the community's unity of direction is not bound to any one place. Its stated purpose is to remove the grounds of dispute that opponents might raise against the believers, leaving only the unjust, who will argue regardless of the evidence. God therefore directs the believers to stop fearing such people and to fear Him alone, and the reorientation of prayer becomes a test of obedience and a means by which divine favor is completed and guidance is attained.

translation: Just as We sent among you a messenger from yourselves, reciting to you Our verses, purifying you, and teaching you the Book and wisdom, and teaching you what you did not know.
interpretation: The verse presents the prophetic mission as a divine favor that completes a pattern of guidance: the Messenger is 'from among you' so that he is familiar to his people and their own, which makes the message relatable and accountable. The four functions named are sequenced deliberately: first recitation of the signs, which brings the revelation to the ear and heart; then tazkiyah, purification of the soul from inner corruption, which must precede genuine understanding; then teaching the Book and wisdom, uniting the letter of revelation with its inner purpose and practical judgment; and finally the broadening of knowledge to what humanity could never have reached on its own. The verse thus teaches that true knowledge is not merely informational but transformative, beginning with the self and extending outward to a whole civilization's enlightenment.

translation: So remember Me, and I will remember you. And be grateful to Me, and do not deny Me.
interpretation: The verse binds the believer to a reciprocal relationship with God: remembrance of Him (dhikr) is met with His own remembrance of the one who remembers, so the servant's turning toward God is answered by God's care and mention of him. Dhikr here is not limited to the tongue but encompasses an awareness of God in the heart and in conduct, so that a person recalls His presence in every state. Gratitude (shukr) is presented as the outward and inward counterpart of this remembrance, expressed through acknowledging His favors and using them in obedience. The warning against kufr, which in its root sense means concealing or covering over, calls the heedless to refuse the cover of forgetfulness and to recognize the blessings that point back to their Giver.

translation: O you who have believed, seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, Allah is with the patient.
interpretation: The verse presents patience (sabr) and prayer (salah) as the twin pillars for facing hardship and the trials of faith. Patience is not mere passive endurance but steadfast restraint of the self upon obedience, away from sin, and through trouble, while prayer connects the believer to God and renews his strength and reliance upon Him. By joining the two, the verse teaches that the believer's true aid comes from the Divine, and that the presence of Allah ('with the patient') is a special divine companionship of support, guidance, and success granted to those who persevere.

translation: And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah that they are dead. Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive it.
interpretation: The verse directs the believers to recognize that death in the cause of God is not an annihilation but a transition to a different mode of life that is beyond ordinary human perception. By forbidding them to call the martyrs dead, it corrects the instinctive judgment of the senses and invites faith to see what the senses cannot. The phrase 'but you do not perceive it' places the limit on human awareness rather than on the reality itself, teaching that the unseen dimensions of existence are real and that the believer's trust in God's word should outweigh the apparent evidence of loss. The verse thus consoles the grieving community, elevates the sacrifice of those who fell striving for God's cause, and reminds the living that their own perception is partial.

translation: And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth, lives, and crops. But give good tidings to the patient.
interpretation: The verse teaches that trials are a divine test woven into the fabric of human life, not a sign of abandonment. God names four domains where hardship strikes: fear, which unsettles the heart; hunger, which tests the body; loss of property and of lives, which tests attachment; and the loss of fruits, which tests one's reliance on the means of livelihood. By placing the announcement of good tidings directly after the warning of trials, the verse reframes suffering as an opportunity: the believer who meets loss with sabr, steadfast patience rooted in trust in God, is promised a reward that outweighs what was taken. Patience here is not passive resignation but an active holding fast to faith, and the tidings it receives are the nearness and mercy of God described in the verses that follow.

translation: Those who, when a calamity strikes them, say: "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we shall return."
interpretation: The verse describes the believer's response to affliction as a conscious act of submission and remembrance. By declaring that they belong to God and will return to Him, the afflicted acknowledge that their possessions, health, and loved ones were never truly their own but entrusted to them by their Creator, and that every loss is part of a divine wisdom and a temporary stage on the path back to God. This declaration transforms grief into patience and turns the moment of hardship into an opportunity to reaffirm one's relationship with the Divine, which is why the verses that follow promise blessings and mercy from the Lord to those who respond in this way.

translation: Those are the ones upon whom are blessings from their Lord, and mercy. And those are the ones who are guided.
interpretation: The verse identifies two marks of those who have been granted true guidance. First, divine favor is upon them: 'salawat' from their Lord, which in this context denotes a special blessing and honor that sets them apart, joined with 'rahmah,' the all-encompassing mercy that sustains them in this life and the next. Second, the verse closes by affirming that they are truly 'the guided' (al-muhtadun), meaning that their guidance is complete and acknowledged by God, not merely claimed by them. The repetition of 'ulaika' emphasizes that these people are singled out and distinguished. The passage thus teaches that genuine guidance is inseparable from receiving God's blessing and mercy, and that the signs of being rightly guided are both an inward orientation toward the truth and an outward assurance from the Lord.

translation: Indeed, as-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God. So whoever makes the pilgrimage to the House or performs the minor pilgrimage (umrah), there is no blame upon him for going around between them. And whoever volunteers good, then indeed God is Appreciative and All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse removes a scruple that some early Muslims felt about walking between the hills of as-Safa and al-Marwah, which had been associated with pre-Islamic idolatry. By declaring them among the signs of God, it sanctifies this rite and reframes it as an act of devotion tied to the worship of the One God, showing that God's law may correct a mistaken sense of impropriety. The closing sentence widens the lesson: whoever freely adds a good deed beyond what is required will find that God recognizes and rewards it, and He knows the sincerity behind it.

translation: Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance, after We have made it clear for the people in the Book, those are cursed by Allah, and cursed by those who curse.
interpretation: The verse condemns the deliberate concealment of divine truth by those who possess it. Clear signs and guidance revealed by God are not private matters; once they have been explained to people in the Scripture, withholding them becomes a grave moral failure that places the concealer under divine rejection and the condemnation of all who are capable of cursing. It establishes that the duty of religious scholars and the people of revelation is to make known what God has made clear, and that silence in the face of established truth, motivated by worldly interest or fear, is itself a serious sin. The phrase 'the cursers' is often understood to include angels, prophets, believers, and even creatures generally, indicating the scale of the condemnation.

translation: Except for those who repent, make amends, and clarify (the truth); those—I will accept their repentance, and I am the Accepting of repentance, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse opens an exception to the preceding condemnation of concealing what God has revealed, showing that the door of return remains open as long as the sinner's repentance is complete. Repentance alone is not enough: it must be followed by reform of one's conduct and by openly making clear what was hidden, so that the wrong is undone and the truth is restored to people. The closing divine names, al-Tawwab and al-Rahim, reveal that God's acceptance of repentance flows from His mercy, and that He is constantly turning toward His servants who turn back to Him.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, upon them is the curse of Allah, and of the angels, and of mankind, all together.
interpretation: The verse closes the door on the notion that the curse is limited to a single group: disbelief that persists until death brings a comprehensive, universal rejection, from the Creator, the angels, and all of humanity alike. The emphasis on dying in a state of disbelief points to the decisive role of one's final condition, since the verse ties the curse to a settled, unrepented rejection of faith rather than to a passing lapse. Its wording thus conveys both the gravity of persisting in unbelief and the solemn finality of a state that is not reversed before death.

translation: Abiding therein forever. Their punishment will not be lightened for them, and they will not be given respite.
interpretation: The phrase 'abiding therein' stresses that the state of the disbelievers in the Fire is permanent, not a temporary chastisement that might end. The denial of lightening (takhfif) shows that the torment is not softened at any moment, while 'nor will they be reprieved' (la hum yunzarun) removes even the hope of a brief postponement or a chance to make amends. Together these two negations close every avenue of relief, so that the verse conveys both the endlessness of the punishment and the total absence of any mitigation or delay, which is meant to awaken the listener to the gravity of persisting in disbelief and wrongdoing.

translation: And your God is One God. There is no deity except Him, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.
interpretation: The verse opens by addressing the whole of humanity as 'your God,' tying the oneness of God directly to the listener's own relationship with Him, so that tawhid is not an abstract doctrine but the foundation of every human being's worship. The phrase 'One God' is then sealed by the negation and affirmation 'there is no deity except Him,' which removes every rival claim to divinity and leaves no room for partners, intermediaries, or idols to share in what belongs to God alone. Immediately the verse pairs this stern exclusivity with two names of mercy, al-Rahman and al-Rahim, teaching that the same God who admits no associate is the One whose mercy encompasses all creation. Oneness and mercy are thus presented together: the unity of God is the ground of a sure and reliable compassion, and to recognize Him alone is to turn toward the source of all mercy.

translation: Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day, and the ships that sail through the sea with that which benefits people, and the water that Allah sends down from the sky, giving life thereby to the earth after its death, and dispersing therein every kind of moving creature, and the directing of the winds and the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth, are signs for a people who use their reason.
interpretation: This verse invites the thoughtful reader to see the whole cosmos as a chain of signs pointing to the One who orchestrates it. The heavens and earth, the cycle of night and day, the ships carrying goods across the seas, the rain that revives dead land, the living creatures spread across it, and the winds and clouds that move at God's command are not random occurrences but a unified system of mercy and provision. The phrase 'for a people who use their reason' shows that these signs are not seen merely with the eyes; they are recognized by minds that reflect, connecting the visible order of nature to the wisdom and power of its Creator. The sequence moves from the vast to the intimate, from the heavens to the revival of a single patch of earth, teaching that resurrection and renewal follow the same pattern as the reviving of dead soil, so that the believer who contemplates nature finds both evidence of God's existence and a reminder of life after death.

translation: And among the people are those who take other than Allah as equals, loving them as they should love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah. If only those who have wronged could see, when they see the punishment, that all power belongs to Allah, and that Allah is severe in punishment.
interpretation: The verse exposes the corruption of the heart that takes rivals to God: people give to created beings the love, reverence and devotion that belong only to the Creator, mistaking a borrowed affection for the true object of worship. Its contrast is with the believers, whose love for God is firmer and more sincere than any attachment to idols or intermediaries, because their love rests on knowledge of Him and not on fear or habit. The closing scene shows the wrongdoers at the moment of punishment, when the illusion of other powers collapses and they see that all strength belongs to God alone. The verse thus binds together the purity of tawhid in the heart, the sincerity of love for God, and the warning that the consequences of misplaced loyalty will be made plain on the Day when the false supports fail.

translation: When those who were followed will disown those who followed them, and they will see the punishment, and their means of connection will be severed from them.
interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Judgment as a scene in which the bonds of false leadership and blind following collapse. Those who were obeyed in worldly life, whether leaders, idols, or influential figures, will renounce their followers at the moment the punishment becomes visible, because the alliance was built on worldly interest and delusion rather than truth. The followers, who had surrendered their judgment to others, are left without any support, and every tie they once relied upon, whether kinship, alliance, or the claimed intercession of others, is cut off. The passage warns that no one can bear the responsibility of another's choices, and that true salvation depends on one's own faith and righteous deeds rather than on dependence upon those who themselves are powerless before God.

translation: And those who followed will say, "If only we had another chance, we would disavow them just as they have disavowed us." Thus does Allah show them their deeds as regrets upon them, and they will never emerge from the Fire.
interpretation: The verse portrays the reversal at the Day of Judgment, when the followers, who once obeyed their leaders, wish for a return to the world so they could sever ties with them, just as those leaders now disown them. Allah makes their own deeds appear before them as sources of anguish, so that the very actions they relied upon become the cause of their sorrow and remorse. The closing statement underscores that this torment is not temporary, for they will remain in the Fire without any exit. The passage thus reveals that blind allegiance and false dependence on others will bring no benefit when the reckoning comes, and it calls the listener to take responsibility for their own conduct before that day.

translation: O mankind, eat of what is lawful and good on the earth, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.
interpretation: The verse opens with a universal address to all of humankind, establishing that the bounties of the earth are generally permitted and wholesome, and that the permission is tied to two conditions: that what is eaten be lawful (halal) in its source and manner, and good (tayyib) in its nature, meaning pure, beneficial, and suited to human wellbeing. God then warns against following the steps of Satan, a phrase that points beyond food alone to the gradual path of temptation, where small deviations, such as appetites indulged without restraint or lawfulness disregarded, lead a person step by step away from guidance. By calling Satan a clear enemy, the verse frames the struggle against him as an ongoing and evident reality, urging believers to let their consumption and conduct be guided by revealed limits rather than by whim or the lure of what is forbidden.

translation: He only commands you to evil and immorality, and that you say about Allah what you do not know.
interpretation: The verse identifies the source of wrongdoing: the whispering of the self and of Satan, which urges a person toward evil deeds (al-su') and shameful acts (al-fahsha'). It also warns against the gravest form of this misguidance, which is attributing things to God without knowledge, such as false claims about His religion, His will, and His law. The verse thus teaches that whenever a person acts or speaks about God in ignorance, without sound knowledge or evidence, they are following the incitement of the enemy rather than guidance, and they must therefore examine their words and deeds against revealed knowledge before ascribing anything to Allah.

translation: And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we will follow what we found our fathers upon." Even though their fathers understood nothing and were not guided?
interpretation: The verse exposes the blind imitation of ancestral custom over revealed guidance. When the call is made to follow the revelation, the unbelievers answer by appealing to inherited tradition, as if the mere age and habit of the forefathers were a proof of truth. The Qur'an confronts this with a pointed question: what if those forefathers had no understanding and no right guidance? Then tradition alone cannot be a criterion, and the only sound standard is what God has revealed. The verse thus establishes a timeless principle that faith must rest on reasoned conviction and revelation rather than on unexamined loyalty to what one's community has always done.

translation: And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts to that which hears nothing except a call and a cry. Deaf, dumb, and blind, so they do not reason.
interpretation: The verse portrays the disbelievers as a listener who cannot truly hear: the shepherd calls out to his flock, yet the animals catch only the noise of his voice and not its meaning. The image shows that the disbelievers are not deprived of hearing, sight, or speech in a physical sense, but their faculties are spiritually disabled because they refuse to receive guidance. Their hearts are closed, so the Prophet's call reaches them only as sound without understanding, and their failure to reason is the consequence of their own willful turning away rather than a defect of creation.

translation: O you who have believe, eat of the good things We have provided for you, and be grateful to Allah, if it is Him that you worship.
interpretation: The verse joins two duties that belong together: enjoying lawful sustenance and returning thanks for it. Allah first permits the wholesome provisions He has given, meaning that faith does not require renouncing the good things of life, but that these good things must be taken in their proper, pure form. The call to gratitude then ties the enjoyment of provision to worship, so that eating becomes an act of recognizing the Giver. The conditional clause, 'if it is Him that you worship,' makes gratitude the evidence of sincere devotion: a believer who truly serves Allah will naturally acknowledge His bounty, and thanks is thus both a sign and a completion of that worship.

translation: He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than God has been invoked. But whoever is compelled by necessity, neither desiring it nor exceeding the limit, then there is no sin upon him. Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the prohibition of these foods is not an arbitrary restriction but a protection of human health and of the sacredness of worship, since carrion and blood carry harm and the dedication of an animal to other than God is a form of idolatry that corrupts the meaning of the act. Yet the law is built on mercy: when a person faces real compulsion, such as starvation, the ban is lifted to preserve life, provided he does not seek the forbidden thing out of desire or go beyond what is strictly needed. The closing divine names, Forgiving and Merciful, reveal that God's law balances firm boundaries with compassion for human weakness, so that religion never becomes a burden that destroys the one it is meant to guide.

translation: Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Scripture and exchange it for a small price — they consume nothing into their bellies but the Fire. Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse exposes the sin of deliberately hiding divine truth for worldly gain.
