interpretation: This verse, known as Ayat al-Kursi, establishes the absolute sovereignty and self-sufficiency of God, who needs neither rest nor assistance, and whose knowledge and power encompass all creation while remaining beyond the grasp of created beings except as He grants. Its emphasis on the unbroken living and sustaining nature of God points the believer away from any dependence on creatures and toward complete trust in the One who alone holds the heavens and earth without effort.

translation: There is no compulsion in religion. The right course has become clearly distinct from error. So whoever rejects false deities and believes in Allah has grasped the most reliable handhold, which will never break. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.
interpretation: The verse establishes that faith cannot be forced, because true belief rests on conviction that arises from clear understanding, and coercion can produce only outward submission. Its wording, 'the right course has become clearly distinct from error,' shows that God has already made guidance evident through reason and revelation, so the believer is called to choose freely. Rejecting the tyrannical powers that claim worship and affirming God alone is described as holding fast to an unbreakable bond, suggesting that a faith built on such a foundation is stable, while the closing names of God, the All-Hearing and All-Knowing, remind the reader that every human choice is known to Him and is ultimately accountable before Him.

translation: Allah is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out from the darknesses into the light. And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the false deities (taghut), who bring them out from the light into the darknesses. Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: The verse presents faith and disbelief as two opposed guardianships that determine a person's whole direction in life. Allah's wilayah over the believers is a continuous, active drawing of them out of the layers of ignorance, misguidance, and moral confusion into the clarity of guidance, so that faith is not merely a static belief but an ongoing journey of illumination. By contrast, those who reject faith have chosen as their protectors the taghut, whatever is worshipped or obeyed beyond God, such as desires, tyrannical authority, and false ideologies, and these forces gradually pull them from the light they once had back into deeper darkness. The verse thus shows that a person is always under some guardianship, and the choice of whom to take as protector is decisive, since it leads either toward the light of God or toward the darkness that ends in the Fire, where its people remain forever.

translation: Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, because God had given him kingdom? When Abraham said, "My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death," he said, "I give life and cause death." Abraham said, "Indeed, God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west." So the one who disbelieved was confounded. And God does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: The verse presents a confrontation between Abraham and a powerful ruler who, rather than acknowledging the Lord who grants life and death, claimed the same power for himself through a crude act of granting pardon or execution. Abraham then shifted the argument to a manifest sign of God's power over creation, the daily rising of the sun from the east, which exposed the emptiness of the claim. The ruler's confusion shows that arrogance founded on worldly authority collapses before clear reason, and the closing statement teaches that persistent injustice and denial of evident truth place a person beyond guidance.

translation: Or like the one who passed by a town while it lay fallen on its roofs. He said, "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?" So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then revived him. He said, "How long have you remained?" He said, "I have remained a day or part of a day." He said, "Rather, you have remained a hundred years. Look at your food and your drink, which has not spoiled, and look at your donkey, and We will make you a sign for the people. And look at the bones, how We raise them and then clothe them with flesh." And when it became clear to him, he said, "I know that Allah is over all things competent."
interpretation: The verse presents resurrection not as an abstract doctrine but as a lived sequence of signs: the man's question arises from witnessing a ruined town, and God answers him through his own body and surroundings. The unspoiled food and drink show that time has no power over what God sustains, the donkey's decay alongside his own preservation reveals the gap between human reckoning and divine reality, and the reassembling of bones into living flesh becomes a pattern of how the dead will be raised. Thus the story teaches that the revival of the dead is the same act of power that revives a ruined land, and that true knowledge is reached when the seeker moves from doubt to the conviction that God's power extends over all things.

translation: And [mention] when Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." [Allah] said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but [I ask] so that my heart may be assured." [Allah] said, "Take four birds and commit them to yourself [train them to come to you]. Then place on every hill a portion of them, then call them; they will come to you in haste. And know that Allah is Exalted in Might, Wise."
interpretation: The episode reveals that the prophet Abraham's request was not born of doubt in God's power but of a desire for the tranquility of certainty that comes through direct witnessing, and God answers this longing with a tangible lesson in resurrection: the scattered parts of the birds, called back by the Lord's summons, become a living image of how He will reassemble what has been dispersed by death. The verse thus teaches that faith and the heart's seeking of assurance can coexist, and that divine wisdom often conveys the unseen through the familiar. The closing reminder of God's might and wisdom reinforces that the one who calls the dead to life is both all-powerful and purposeful in every act of creation and restoration.

translation: The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of God is like a grain of corn that grows seven spikes, in each spike a hundred grains. And God multiplies for whom He wills. And God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse uses a vivid agricultural image to teach that charity given sincerely for God's cause is never lost but multiplies far beyond its outward size, as a single seed yields abundant harvest. The multiplication is not fixed but depends on God's will and generosity, which reflects His boundless bounty (wasi') and perfect knowledge ('alim) of the intention and sincerity behind every gift. The lesson is that the worth of spending lies not in the quantity given but in the purity of the heart that gives, and that God, who knows exactly what each person deserves, rewards accordingly.

translation: Those who spend their wealth in the cause of God and then do not follow up what they have spent with reminders of their generosity or with injury, theirs is their reward with their Lord, and no fear will befall them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the true value of charity lies not in the amount given but in the purity of intention and conduct that follows it. By forbidding both the reproach (al-mann), which wounds the recipient's dignity by reminding them of one's favor, and the harm (al-adha), which injures them in word or deed, the Qur'an teaches that giving must be a sincere act directed solely toward God, so that the giver's soul is protected from pride and the recipient's honor is preserved. The promise of a reward secured with the Lord and freedom from fear and grief shows that such sincere giving brings inner peace in this life and assurance in the next, and that generosity is completed only when it is free from self-regard and the wounding of others.

translation: Kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. And Allah is Free of need, Forbearing.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the inner moral quality of a giving is what matters most. A charitable act is undermined when the giver follows it with reproach, mockery, or hurt, because the recipient's dignity is then wounded and the gift loses its purpose of relieving need with compassion. A gentle word and a gracious pardon, even when no material gift is possible, are therefore presented as superior. The closing reminder that Allah is self-sufficient and forbearing points to the fact that God does not need our charity, and that His patience with human failings invites believers to emulate that same forbearance in how they treat others.

translation: O you who have believed, do not nullify your charities with reminders of your generosity or injury, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in Allah or the Last Day. His example is that of a smooth stone with a thin layer of soil on it; a heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare. They have no power over anything they have earned, and Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.
interpretation: The verse teaches that a charity's worth lies in its sincerity and in the spirit in which it is given, not merely in its outward act. Reminding the recipient of one's favor or hurting him with words wipes out the reward just as a hypocritical display of giving, done to be praised by people rather than for God's sake, does. Such deeds appear to stand as acts of kindness, but like the soil over the rock, they have no lasting root; when tested by the rain of the Hereafter, nothing remains. The image warns that a person may possess outward religiosity and generosity while lacking the inner faith that gives deeds their value, so the believer must guard his giving from pride, display, and harm to others.

translation: And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking the approval of Allah and for the strengthening of their souls is like a garden on a elevated ground: a heavy rain strikes it, and it yields its produce twofold; and if no heavy rain strikes it, then a light drizzle suffices. And Allah is Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse portrays sincere charity as a living, fruitful garden whose yield is multiplied by the favor of its location and the abundance of rain, and even a light drizzle does not leave it barren. The image teaches that the believer's giving is measured not by its size alone but by the sincerity behind it and the inner firmness it builds; a small gift given with a steadfast, pure heart still grows and bears fruit before the One who sees all that they do.

translation: Would any one of you like to have a garden of date palms and grapevines beneath which rivers flow, with every kind of fruit in it for him, and then old age overtakes him while he has weak offspring, and then a whirlwind containing fire strikes it and it is burned? Thus does God make the signs clear to you, so that you may reflect.
interpretation: The verse uses the image of a flourishing garden, destroyed just when its owner is most in need of it, to portray the fate of deeds whose reward is lost at the moment of greatest need. Old age and weak offspring stand for the helplessness of a person at the end of life, when he can no longer restore what he has lost. The fiery whirlwind shows how sudden and total such loss can be. God presents this parable so that people will reflect and recognize that pride in one's works, or spending them for show, can be annihilated, and so that they strive instead for what endures.

translation: O you who have believed, spend from the good things you have earned and from what We have brought forth for you from the earth, and do not aim at the bad of it to spend from it, while you would not take it yourselves unless you overlook in it. And know that Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse calls believers to give charity from the best of their wealth and produce, not from what is worthless or defective that they would be unwilling to accept for themselves. It reveals a principle of sincerity and generosity: one should not offer to God what one would reject, since God needs nothing from His creation, and therefore the giver's own spiritual benefit and the purity of his intention are what matter most.

translation: Satan threatens you with poverty and commands you to indecency, while Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty, and Allah is All-Encompassing and All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse exposes the two opposing voices that pull at the human heart when one is tempted to spend in the cause of good. Satan's whisper works on fear: it makes the prospect of loss feel immediate and certain, so that generosity appears to be a path toward destitution. Yet the same whisper also draws the soul toward fahsha, the shameful and corrupt deeds that disfigure both character and society, so that the very act of withholding becomes a gateway to moral decline. Against this, God's promise is set in contrast: maghfira, forgiveness that cleanses what has gone wrong, and fadl, a bounty that exceeds what was given. The closing names, Wasi' (the One whose reach and provision are vast) and 'Alim (the One who knows the hidden motives and needs of every person), assure the believer that the Giver is neither limited in resources nor unaware of the sincerity behind the giving. The lesson is that fear of scarcity is the tool of the devil, while trust in God's knowledge and generosity frees a person to do good.

translation: He gives wisdom to whomever He wills, and whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good. And none will be reminded except the people of understanding.
interpretation: The verse teaches that wisdom (al-hikmah) is a divine gift granted by God's sovereign will, not merely a product of learning or lineage, and that it is the greatest of goods because it enables a person to discern truth and act rightly. Its closing phrase links this gift to the faculty of 'ulu al-albab, the people of pure intellect, who are those capable of receiving admonition: the ability to be reminded and to benefit from guidance is itself a sign of the intellect that wisdom perfects. Thus the verse binds divine bestowal and human responsibility, calling the believer to humbly seek and cultivate the reasoning that makes one open to God's reminder.

translation: And whatever expenditure you spend or vow you vow, indeed Allah knows it. And the wrongdoers will have no helpers.
interpretation: The verse binds every act of giving and every vow made to God within the knowledge of God, so that nothing offered sincerely or pledged in devotion is lost or overlooked, while it simultaneously warns that those who persist in wrongdoing, and who thereby turn away from the sincerity that gives charity its worth, will find no one to shield them on the Day when all reliance on others falls away. The divine knowledge mentioned here is both a comfort to the faithful giver, whose hidden charity is recorded, and a reminder to the wrongdoer that no hidden injustice escapes the One who sees it.

translation: If you disclose your charities, then how excellent they are; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, that is better for you. And He will remove from you some of your misdeeds. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that charity is praiseworthy whether given openly or in secret, but it ranks the secret giving higher because it guards the giver's sincerity against showiness and protects the dignity of the recipient from public exposure. Open giving can inspire others and is not condemned in itself, so the believer should weigh intention above display. Because the giver's motive is hidden from people yet fully known to God, concealed charity becomes a means of expiation, through which Allah erases some of one's sins. The closing reminder that Allah is aware of all deeds calls the believer to sincerity, reminding that the true reward depends on what is in the heart.

translation: It is not upon you to guide them, but Allah guides whom He wills. And whatever good you spend, it is for yourselves, and you do not spend except seeking the Face of Allah. And whatever good you spend will be repaid to you in full, and you will not be wronged.
interpretation: The verse separates the Prophet's duty from the outcome of guidance: he is responsible for conveying the message, while the guidance of hearts belongs to God alone. It then turns the believers' attention from the recipients of charity to the spender, teaching that the benefit of giving returns to the giver himself, and that sincere charity is measured by the intention of seeking God's pleasure. Its reward is assured and complete, with no injustice in its recompense, so that generosity becomes an act of trust in God rather than a favor done for human regard.

translation: (Charity is) for the poor who have been restricted in the way of Allah, who cannot move about in the land. The ignorant person thinks them wealthy because of their restraint; you would recognize them by their mark. They do not beg people persistently. And whatever good you spend, indeed Allah is Knowing of it.
interpretation: The verse directs attention to a category of needy believers who have been confined by their commitment to the cause of God, perhaps through jihad or dedicated service, so that they cannot earn a livelihood by traveling and trading. Their dignified modesty makes them appear self-sufficient to the unaware observer, so the community must look beyond outward appearances and recognize them by their distinguishing marks of need, rather than by persistent begging. The closing line ties this social ethic to sincerity: whatever good is given, especially to such people, is known to God, who will reward it fully, so generosity should be directed with discernment and without expectation of human recognition.

translation: Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly, will have their reward with their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: The verse presents charity as a practice that is not confined to a single time or manner: it is offered at every hour and both in private and in public, which signals that generosity should be constant and sincere rather than performative. Its sincerity is shown by the balance between secret giving, which guards the giver from display and self-regard, and open giving, which can inspire others to follow. The promise that their reward rests with the Lord, and that fear and grief are lifted from them, ties the value of spending not to worldly recognition but to a reward that is sure and beyond the reach of loss, so that the believer's peace of heart is itself a fruit of giving freely.

translation: Those who consume interest will not stand [on the Day of Resurrection] except as one stands who is being driven to madness by Satan's touch. That is because they say, "Trade is only like interest," but Allah has permitted trade and forbidden interest. So whoever has received an admonition from his Lord and desists will have what is past, and his affair is up to Allah; but whoever returns [to it] - those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: The verse portrays the one who devours riba as rising in a state of frantic disorder, like a person struck and deranged by Satan, to expose the inner corruption that makes usury appear to be a form of sale. Its core claim is a rejection of the false equation between trade and interest: the difference is not one of appearance but of divine law, since Allah has made trade lawful and forbidden riba. The mercy in the verse lies in the door of repentance, where a person who heeds the reminder and stops is pardoned for what preceded, while persistence after clear warning places one among the people of the Fire. Thus the passage teaches that economic morality is ultimately a matter of obedience to the Lord's command, not of rationalization.

translation: Allah eliminates interest (riba) and gives increase for charities. And Allah does not love every ungrateful sinner.
interpretation: The verse sets two economic realities side by side to reveal a moral and spiritual law: what is gained through riba, the exploitative increase on wealth, is stripped of blessing and destined to dwindle, whether in this world or in the account of the Hereafter, while what is given freely in charity is made to grow, both in its worth before God and in its fruits in the heart and in society. The closing phrase ties this to the disposition of the one who persists in it: a person who keeps taking advantage of others while being ungrateful to God's bounty and persisting in wrongdoing is not beloved to God. The verse thus teaches that true increase lies not in the accumulation of gain at others' expense, but in generosity that binds a community together and is rooted in gratitude.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, and establish prayer and give zakat, will have their reward with their Lord, and no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: The verse ties salvation to a unified faith: true belief must be expressed in righteous action, and in the two pillars of worship and social responsibility, prayer connecting the believer to God and zakat connecting the believer to the community. Its promise that there is no fear or grief for them speaks to the inner peace that results when a person's life is aligned with faith, since their reward is secured with their Lord and not dependent on worldly outcomes.

translation: O you who have believed, fear Allah and give up what remains of interest (riba), if you are [truly] believers.
interpretation: The verse addresses the believers with a call to taww a (God-consciousness) and commands them to abandon whatever outstanding interest is still owed to them, making the abandonment of riba a direct test of the sincerity of their faith. By conditioning the command with "if you are believers," it presents financial dealings as an arena where belief is demonstrated: faith is not merely professed but proven by renouncing gain obtained through exploitation of others' need. The command to leave "what remains" points to the context of the period of revelation, when earlier interest contracts were still in effect, and it establishes that a principle of justice in wealth must govern the community's economic life once the prohibition is revealed.

translation: And if you do not do it, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger. But if you repent, you shall have your capital; you will not wrong, nor be wronged.
interpretation: The verse addresses those who persist in taking usury (riba) after the prohibition has reached them (Al-Baqarah 2:278-279). Its sense is that continued dealing in interest is tantamount to declaring war against Allah and His Messenger, a grave declaration that exposes the one who persists to the gravest consequence. Yet the door of repentance remains open: whoever turns back is entitled to the principal of his wealth, without adding interest, so that neither party is unjustly treated. Justice is thus established on both sides: the lender does not take what is not his, and the borrower is not burdened with what he cannot bear, since the debtor is not oppressed by compounded interest nor the creditor robbed of his due capital.

translation: And if the debtor is in hardship, then [grant him] postponement until a time of ease. But if you give charity as a gift, it is better for you, if you only knew.
interpretation: The verse establishes a principle of mercy in financial dealings: when a debtor is genuinely unable to pay due to hardship, the creditor is commanded to grant him respite until he is in a position of ease, rather than pressing him or seizing what he cannot afford. The closing words elevate the matter further, showing that remitting the debt altogether as charity is better for the creditor himself, since it brings reward and purifies the heart. The lesson is that wealth is entrusted to be used justly and compassionately, and that the believer's economic relations should be guided by mercy, patience, and generosity rather than by harshness and the pursuit of gain alone.

translation: And fear a Day on which you will be returned to Allah. Then every soul will be paid in full for what it earned, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: The verse calls the believer to constant awareness of God (taqwa) by reminding them that all human life ends in a return to Allah, where no one escapes accountability. The phrase "then every soul will be fully repaid" points to the perfect justice of the Day of Judgment: each person receives exactly what their deeds merit, neither reduced nor increased. The closing assurance that "they will not be wronged" highlights that this justice is free from any injustice, so the awareness of the Day should lead a person to act with responsibility, sincerity, and fear of God in this world.

translation: O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down. And let a scribe write it between you in justice. Let no scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him, so let him write. And let the one who has the obligation dictate, and let him fear Allah, his Lord, and not leave anything out of it. But if the one who has the obligation is of limited understanding or weak or unable to dictate himself, then let his guardian dictate in justice. And bring to witness two witnesses from among your men; but if there are not two men, then a man and two women from those whom you accept as witnesses, so that if one of the two errs, the other can remind her. And let the witnesses not refuse when they are called. And do not be weary of writing it, whether it is small or large, for its specified term. That is more just in the sight of Allah, more suitable as evidence, and closer to preventing doubt between you, except when it is an immediate trade that you conduct among yourselves; then there is no blame upon you for not writing it. And take witnesses when you conclude a sale, and let no harm befall a scribe or a witness. And if you do so, it is indeed deviance in you. And fear Allah; Allah teaches you, and Allah is all-knowing of everything.
interpretation: The verse establishes a comprehensive framework for documenting debts, placing the transaction under the awareness of God and treating the written record as an act of justice that protects both creditor and debtor from later dispute. By assigning the dictation to the debtor, who bears the obligation and is answerable to God, it makes honesty internal as well as procedural. The provisions for the incapacitated or weak party through a guardian show that the rights of the vulnerable are safeguarded within the contract, while the flexibility of witnesses reflects a practical concern for memory and reliability. The exception for immediate cash trades shows that the law calibrates its demands to the realities of commerce, and the closing prohibition on harming scribes and witnesses reveals that the entire system rests on the moral integrity of those who serve it.

translation: And if you are on a journey and cannot find a scribe, then a security taken in hand (shall suffice). But if one of you trusts another, let the one who is trusted fulfill his trust and let him fear Allah, his Lord. And do not conceal testimony, for whoever conceals it - his heart is indeed sinful. And Allah is Knowing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that when written documentation is impractical, as in travel, trust and tangible security may replace it, yet trust itself becomes a moral obligation: the trusted party must return what was entrusted, guarding it out of reverence for God. Concealing testimony is portrayed as a grave matter touching the heart, since honest witness is the foundation of justice in dealings between people, and the verse reminds believers that God is fully aware of their conduct, both public and hidden.

translation: To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Whether you reveal what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it. Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills, and Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse establishes that absolute dominion over everything in the heavens and earth belongs to Allah alone, and it extends this sovereignty into the inner world of the human heart, which is not hidden from Him. Its reference to being called to account for what one inwardly reveals or conceals points to the seriousness of intention and inner conviction, so that a person's moral responsibility is not limited to outward deeds but reaches to the thoughts and resolves they harbor. Yet the verse immediately pairs this accountability with the freedom of divine mercy and justice, forgiving whom He wills and punishing whom He wills, so that the believer is moved both to vigilant self-examination and to hope in Allah's forgiveness rather than despair. The closing affirmation of His power over all things grounds this awareness in the certainty that nothing escapes His knowledge or might.

translation: The Messenger believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord, and so do the believers. Each one believes in God, His angels, His books, and His messengers, (saying), "We make no distinction between any of His messengers." And they say, "We hear and we obey. Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return."
interpretation: The verse presents faith as a shared covenant between the Prophet and the believing community, where the Messenger's acceptance of revelation becomes the model for the believers' own acceptance. By placing belief in God, angels, scriptures, and messengers together as one indivisible creed, it establishes that faith is holistic: rejecting any single element undermines the whole. The refusal to distinguish among messengers signals the unity of the prophetic mission across generations. The closing formula of "hearing and obeying" joined with a plea for forgiveness reveals the proper posture of a believer, one that combines submissive readiness to comply with humble awareness of human shortcoming, and that orients the entire life toward the final return to God.

translation: Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. It shall have what it earned, and it shall bear what it has earned. Our Lord, do not impose blame on us if we forget or make mistakes. Our Lord, do not place upon us a burden like that which You placed upon those before us. Our Lord, do not burden us with that which we have no ability to bear. Pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy on us. You are our Protector, so give us victory over the disbelieving people.
interpretation: The verse opens with a foundational principle of divine justice: God's demands on each person are calibrated to that person's capacity, so no one is held responsible for what lies beyond their power, and each soul bears the moral weight of its own deeds, neither inheriting nor transferring guilt. The believers' supplication that follows reveals how this principle shapes the relationship between the servant and the Lord. Their plea to be spared blame for forgetfulness and error acknowledges that human frailty is itself part of the created condition, and God, knowing this, lightens what is laid upon them. The request not to be burdened as earlier communities were burdened reflects the mercy shown to this ummah through a more accommodating law, while the prayer not to be given what exceeds their strength teaches that true reliance is a humble admission of one's limits before the All-Powerful. Pardon, forgiveness, and mercy are sought as the complete remedy for human shortcoming, and the closing appeal to God as Protector, asking for help against those who reject truth, shows that the entire path of mercy and guidance is ultimately sustained by God alone.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Alif, Lam, Meem.
interpretation: The verse opens with the basmala, anchoring the reading of the text in the name of Allah and His two attributes of mercy, reminding the reciter that what follows is sought and received through divine mercy. The disjointed letters Alif, Lam, Meem stand among the muqatta'at, the enigmatic letters that open several chapters. Their meaning is known to God alone according to the majority of scholars, yet they carry a deliberate message: the Qur'an is composed of the same Arabic letters that the listeners use every day, and its challenge lies in their arrangement. The opening thus invites the reader to contemplate both the familiar letters and the mystery that surrounds the revelation they form.

translation: Allah - there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of [all] existence.
interpretation: This verse, the opening of Ayat al-Kursi (2:255), establishes the foundation of tawhid by affirming that divine worship belongs to Allah alone, since He alone possesses the attributes of true divinity. The two names al-Hayy (the Ever-Living) and al-Qayyum (the Self-Subsisting Sustainer) reveal that His life is intrinsic and eternal, not dependent on anything, while all else exists only because He sustains it. Thus the believer's reliance, fear, hope, and devotion are rightly directed to the One whose existence is necessary and whose care upholds every creature, making the verse a complete declaration that only the living, self-sustaining God is worthy of worship.

translation: He has sent down upon you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel.
interpretation: The verse establishes the continuity of revelation: the Qur'an comes from the same divine source as the earlier scriptures and is sent 'in truth,' meaning it is not an innovation but a confirmation of the message already entrusted to the prophets. By naming the Torah and the Gospel together with the Book sent to the Prophet, it presents all of them as stages of one divine guidance, which implies that the core truths they carry are shared and that the recipients of the earlier revelations are addressed within the same framework of faith. The phrase 'confirming what was before it' asks the reader to see the Qur'an not as a rupture with the past but as a renewal and a witness to what God had already revealed.

translation: Before this, as guidance for mankind, and He sent down the Criterion. Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah will have a severe punishment, and Allah is Exalted in Might, Owner of Retribution.
interpretation: The verse situates the revelation within a continuous chain of divine guidance: the Torah and the Gospel were sent as light for people before, and now the Qur'an, which is named the Criterion (al-Furqan) because it distinguishes truth from falsehood, right from wrong, and lawful from unlawful. The mention of this succession underscores that the message is not a novelty but the completion of one consistent divine purpose, so that rejecting its signs is not merely a rejection of a book but of the same God who sent all prior scriptures. The warning that such disbelief brings severe punishment is then anchored in God's attributes of might and retribution, reminding the listener that the authority behind revelation is absolute, and that its rejection carries real and inescapable consequences, while the divine name 'Owner of Retribution' conveys that justice will ultimately be enacted for those who knowingly reject clear signs.

translation: Indeed, Allah — nothing on the earth or in the heaven is hidden from Him.
interpretation: This verse affirms the comprehensive knowledge of Allah, which encompasses every created thing in all realms, both the visible and the unseen, in the earth and in the heavens. Nothing escapes His awareness, not even what is most concealed, so the believer is directed to a constant sense of accountability and sincerity, knowing that outward appearances and inward intentions alike are fully known to Him. The phrasing also reassures the believer that divine justice and mercy are rooted in perfect knowledge, and that no deed, however small or secret, is lost before the One who knows all things.

translation: It is He who forms you in the wombs however He wills. There is no deity except Him, the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: The verse points to the absolute power and wisdom of God over the process of human creation. The image of being shaped in the darkness of the wombs, in stages and in forms determined by God's will alone, reminds the human being of how utterly dependent his existence is on his Creator, from the first moment of his life. The closing affirmation of God's oneness and the attributes of might and wisdom ties this bodily origin to the theme of tawhid: the One who fashions every person with precision and purpose is the only one worthy of worship, and His creative acts are never arbitrary but grounded in perfect wisdom.

translation: It is He who has sent down to you the Book. In it are verses that are clear and precise (muhkamat), and they are the foundation of the Book, while others are allegorical (mutashabihat). As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is allegorical in it, seeking discord and seeking its hidden interpretation. But none knows its ultimate interpretation except God. And those firmly grounded in knowledge say, 'We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord.' And none takes heed except people of understanding.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the Qur'an's clear verses form its foundation, and that its ambiguous verses must be read in their light rather than in isolation. The decisive factor is the heart's intention: those with deviation in their hearts seize upon the ambiguous passages to create confusion and to impose their own meanings, whereas the sound approach is to accept the text with humility, recognizing that the final reality behind the ambiguous expressions belongs to God alone. The firmly grounded in knowledge do not claim to unveil what lies beyond human grasp; they affirm the whole revelation as coming from their Lord, and it is this humble faith, joined with reflection, that marks true understanding.

translation: Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us, and grant us mercy from Yourself. Indeed, You are the Bestower.
interpretation: This verse, from the supplication of those firmly rooted in knowledge (Surah Ali 'Imran 3:8), reveals that guidance is not a fixed possession once attained but a continuous divine bounty that must be sought anew. The believers acknowledge that the heart is by nature subject to turning, so their stability rests entirely on God's protection rather than on their own strength or past achievements. The request for mercy 'from You' (min ladunka) points to a gift that comes directly from God's own presence, beyond ordinary means. Ending with the name 'al-Wahhab' (the One who gives abundantly and without expectation of return) teaches that the believer should approach God with humility, recognizing that even the continuation of faith is a generous gift from Him.

translation: Our Lord, indeed You will gather the people for a Day about which there is no doubt. Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise.
interpretation: The verse is a supplication (or affirmation) made in awareness that the Resurrection is a certain event: the believers acknowledge that God will certainly assemble all of humankind on the Day of Judgment, a day whose arrival admits no uncertainty. By closing with the assurance that God never breaks His promise, the verse turns the certainty of that gathering into a source of reassurance and a call to prepare for it, since the same God who promised reward and accountability will surely fulfill both. It thus unites a confession of faith in the afterlife with trust in divine faithfulness.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve - their wealth and their children will never avail them anything against Allah, and they are the fuel of the Fire.
interpretation: The verse dismantles the illusion that worldly possessions and offspring can serve as a shield before God. Wealth and progeny, which people often trust as sources of security, honor, and support, become worthless when standing alone before Allah, since no worldly bond or resource can ransom a soul or alter its account. The phrase 'against Allah' points to the Divine judgment where human reliance on what is transient is exposed as empty. The closing image, that the disbelievers themselves become the fuel of the Fire, conveys the completeness of their ruin: the very things they accumulated and cherished yield nothing, while they are consumed by the consequences of their own rejection. It is a call to redirect trust from what can be possessed to what alone can benefit the soul, namely faith and righteous deeds.

translation: Like the manner of the people of Pharaoh and those before them. They denied Our signs, so Allah seized them for their sins. And Allah is severe in punishment.
interpretation: The verse draws a repeated pattern of divine justice: the people of Pharaoh and the generations before them are set as a precedent for those who now reject God's signs. The phrase "kada'b" (like the manner/custom) signals that the fate of earlier nations is not an isolated event but a consistent law of consequence, in which denial of clear revelation leads inevitably to seizure for one's sins. The sequence moves from denial ("kadhdhabu bi-ayatina") to the consequence ("fa-akhadhahum Allahu bi-dhunubihim"), showing that sin is not merely an abstract wrong but a path that ends in concrete accountability. The closing divine attribute, "shadid al-iqab" (severe in retribution), is paired with the earlier mention of seizure, so that the verse both warns and reminds the listener that divine mercy and severity operate together, and that the lesson of history is meant to prompt reflection before the same outcome befalls the present audience.

translation: Say to those who disbelieve: "You will be overcome and gathered to Hell, and wretched is the resting place."
interpretation: The verse addresses the disbelievers of Makkah with a clear warning delivered through the Prophet. Its first promise, that they will be overcome, was fulfilled in this world as the message of Islam prevailed over the opposition of the Quraysh, whose power in Badr and afterward was broken, so that the defeat they faced was both a worldly sign and an earnest of the greater reckoning to come. The second part turns the warning toward the Hereafter: they will be gathered, not as honored guests, but as those driven toward Hell, and the word mihad, meaning a bed or resting place, is used with bitter irony, since the place they chose for themselves in their rejection of truth becomes the most wretched couch imaginable. The verse thus teaches that worldly power and numbers are no guarantee of success, and that persistence in disbelief leads to a final gathering whose outcome is already decided.

translation: There has already been a sign for you in the two armies that met: one fighting in the cause of God, and another disbelieving. They saw them, with their own eyes, as twice their number. And God supports with His victory whom He wills. Indeed, in that is a lesson for those who have vision.
interpretation: The verse recalls the encounter at Badr, where a small band of believers faced a larger force of disbelievers, and it presents that event as a sign that victory is not determined by numbers or apparent strength but by God's support, which He grants according to His will. The apparent doubling of the enemy in the eyes of the observers points to how perception can be distorted by fear and circumstance, so the believers are called to look beyond surface appearances and to draw the moral from events, reading history as guidance about where true strength and reliance lie. The lesson is addressed specifically to those who possess insight, meaning the discerning ability to see the deeper reality behind what the senses report.

translation: Beautified for people is the love of desires: women, children, heaped-up piles of gold and silver, branded horses, livestock, and tilled land. That is the enjoyment of the worldly life, but with Allah is the best return.
interpretation: The verse explains that the natural human attraction to desirable things is presented as something made attractive to people, so that the heart may become absorbed in them. It lists the most cherished worldly goods, then reminds that these are only temporary provision of this life, and directs the believer's gaze toward the lasting reward with God, teaching that true contentment lies in measuring worldly attachments against what is with Allah.

translation: Say, "Shall I inform you of something better than that? For those who are mindful of God is with their Lord gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, and pure spouses, and approval from God. And God is Seeing of His servants."
interpretation: The verse is addressed to the Prophet to redirect human desire from the fleeting pleasures just mentioned in the preceding verse, namely worldly attractions such as wealth, women, and possessions. It presents the reward of taqwa as superior in kind, not merely in degree: lasting gardens, purity freed from the defects that mar worldly attachments, and above all God's pleasure, which the verse places as the crown of all blessings. By ending with God's perfect observation of His servants, it reminds the believer that their conduct is known and that the reward is measured by a just and all-seeing Lord, so that the pursuit of God's approval becomes the true measure of success.

translation: Those who say, "Our Lord, indeed we have believed, so forgive us our sins and protect us from the punishment of the Fire."
interpretation: The verse describes the humble supplication of true believers, who affirm their faith directly before their Lord and then ask for two things: forgiveness of their shortcomings and protection from the Fire. It teaches that genuine faith is accompanied by an awareness of one's own sins and a constant dependence on God's mercy, so that even those who believe never regard their deeds as sufficient to save them. Their prayer begins with acknowledgment of God's lordship and their own belief, which shows that sincere faith and humble seeking of pardon belong together, and that fear of divine punishment should drive the believer to continual repentance and reliance on God.

translation: The patient, and the truthful, and the devoutly obedient, and those who spend (in charity), and those who seek forgiveness in the hours before dawn.
interpretation: The verse describes a set of qualities that together form the character of the God-fearing believer, and it places the pre-dawn seeking of forgiveness at the summit of them. Patience (sabr) is listed first because it underlies every other virtue: truthfulness in speech and conduct, steadfast obedience to God (qunut), and generosity with one's wealth all require the self to be restrained and disciplined. The closing image of seeking forgiveness at the hours before dawn, when the night's stillness is deepest and the heart is most unguarded from worldly distraction, shows that true piety is sealed by humble, private turning to God. The sequence thus moves from inner self-discipline, to honesty, to devotion, to social responsibility, and finally to intimate repentance, suggesting that the believer's outward acts are sustained by an inner, ongoing dependence on divine mercy.

translation: God bears witness that there is no deity except Him, and so do the angels and those of knowledge, upholding justice. There is no deity except Him, the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse presents divine unity as the most solemn truth, attested by God Himself, by the angels, and by those endowed with knowledge, which makes it a standard that rational reflection and the heavenly order both confirm. Pairing 'upholding justice' with the declaration of oneness shows that belief in the one God is inseparable from justice: the one who alone deserves worship is also the one whose governance of the cosmos is perfectly equitable. The closing names, al-'Aziz and al-Hakim, tie the witness to God's power and wisdom, suggesting that the coherence of creation and the rightness of the divine law are evidence of the same truth that God testifies to about Himself.

translation: Indeed, the religion in the sight of Allah is Islam. And those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after knowledge had come to them, out of jealous animosity among themselves. And whoever disbelieves in the verses of Allah - indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning.
interpretation: The verse establishes that true religion before Allah is submission to Him, and it locates the source of division among the People of the Book not in any ambiguity of revelation but in envy and rivalry after clear knowledge had reached them. Such disputes are thus a moral failing rather than a genuine intellectual difficulty, and the warning at the end makes plain that rejecting Allah's signs carries a serious accountability, for His reckoning is swift.

translation: So if they argue with you, say, "I have submitted myself entirely to God, and so have those who follow me." And say to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered, "Have you submitted?" If they submit, then they have been guided; but if they turn away, then your duty is only to convey the message. And God is Seeing of His servants.
interpretation: The verse sets out the stance of the Prophet toward those who dispute with him, especially the People of the Book and the unlettered Arabs who were not given a prior scripture. Islam here is the wholehearted surrender of one's face and will to God, the same submission carried by all the prophets, so the Prophet's answer to argument is not a contest of rhetoric but a plain declaration of total submission shared by his followers. The question put to the People of the Book, whether they too have submitted, points to the common root of the revealed message and invites them to recognize it. The verse also fixes the limits of the Prophet's responsibility: guidance belongs to God and is granted to those who accept it, while his task is only to deliver the message clearly, leaving the outcome of refusal to God, who sees all of His servants.

translation: Indeed, those who deny the signs of God and kill the prophets without right, and kill those among the people who enjoin justice, give them the good news of a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse identifies a grave moral crime: rejecting God's signs is compounded by violence against the messengers and against those who stand for justice. Killing prophets without right shows that hostility to truth reaches its extreme when it turns against those who carry God's guidance, and killing the advocates of justice shows that tyranny seeks to silence whoever commands fairness. The ironic command to give them "good news" of painful punishment signals that their apparent success is in fact a path to ruin. The verse thus binds faith in God to the defense of justice in human society: to oppose justice is to oppose God, and the one who persecutes the upholders of equity has placed himself under the threat of a severe reckoning.

translation: Those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers.
interpretation: The verse describes the fate of those whose works are rendered null and void (habitat), meaning their deeds lose all value and produce no reward, because the foundation of their acts, such as sincere faith and conformity to God's guidance, was absent or corrupted. Their loss is total, spanning both worldly life, where their efforts bring no lasting benefit or true success, and the Hereafter, where they face the consequence of having nothing to show for their labor. The closing phrase, 'and they have no helpers,' emphasizes the utter abandonment they face: neither their idols, their associates, nor any worldly power can defend them or intercede on their behalf before God, so they stand alone in their disappointment and need for mercy.

translation: Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture? They are invited to the Book of Allah so that it may judge between them, and then a faction of them turn away, while they are refusing.
interpretation: The verse exposes a contradiction in those who possess a share of revealed knowledge: when they are called to submit their disputes to the Book of God, a party among them abandons that call out of stubbornness and habitual aversion to the truth. The verse is a rebuke that shows that claiming to follow scripture means little if one refuses its judgment when it is directly applied to oneself. It warns believers against selective adherence, in which a person accepts scripture only when it agrees with desire, and it teaches that true faith requires a sincere willingness to accept God's judgment even when it is unwelcome.

translation: That is because they said, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few counted days." And their falsehoods in their religion have deceived them.
interpretation: This verse exposes the root of the Children of Israel's false sense of security: a claim, unsupported by any divine warrant, that they were exempt from punishment because of their lineage or their status as a chosen people. Such self-assurance is a delusion that the verse traces to their own fabrications about religion, which they repeated until they believed them. The lesson is that a people's invented reassurances about God's judgment can blind them to accountability, and that deception of the self is more dangerous than deception by others, since no one else is there to correct it.

translation: So how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt, and every soul is paid in full for what it earned, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: The verse presents the Day of Judgment as a certainty that cannot be denied, and asks the listener to imagine the terror and regret of that moment. Its rhetorical question "how will it be" awakens the heart to the gathering of all creatures before God, where no excuse or intermediary will avail. The phrase "every soul is paid in full for what it earned" establishes that accountability is individual and exact, so that each person meets the true record of their own deeds. The closing assurance that "they will not be wronged" affirms God's perfect justice: no good is diminished and no sin is unjustly added. Thus the verse calls the believer to reflect now on what they are earning, since the reckoning is inevitable and perfectly just.

translation: Say: O Allah, Owner of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will; You endue with honor whom You will and You bring low whom You will. In Your hand is all good. Indeed, You are over all things Competent.
interpretation: The verse establishes that all true sovereignty belongs to Allah alone, and that worldly power, rank, and honor are His gift and His withdrawal, not the product of human merit or lineage. Because He alone raises and humbles, the believer is taught to seek power and dignity from Him rather than from creatures, and to accept changes of fortune with trust in His wisdom. Its closing emphasis on good in His hand and His power over all things points to the reality that every ascent and decline is governed by a Creator whose will is absolute, which should produce humility in the powerful and steadfast hope in the afflicted.

translation: You cause the night to enter into the day and You cause the day to enter into the night, and You bring the living out of the dead and You bring the dead out of the living, and You provide for whom You will without account.
interpretation: The verse presents the sovereign power of God over the natural order and over life and death as a single pattern of signs: the gradual merging of night and day shows that the cosmos is governed by a precise, continuous will, and the bringing forth of life from what is dead and death from what is living points to the same power of origination and return. The closing phrase, 'without account,' reveals that God's provision is boundless and not measured out by human calculation, so the believer is invited to recognize that all sustenance and all life flow from Him alone, and to trust in His generosity rather than in the limits of worldly reckoning.

translation: Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. And whoever does that has nothing with Allah, except when you fear a danger from them. And Allah warns you of Himself, and to Allah is the final return.
interpretation: The verse forbids believers from making disbelievers their closest allies, confidants, and protectors in preference to fellow believers, since loyalty and trust belong to the community of faith. It then makes a narrow exception: where real fear of harm compels caution, outward accommodation is permitted, while the heart's allegiance remains with God. The closing warning, that God cautions them about Himself, reminds the believer that God alone is to be feared and that all affairs return to Him, so no worldly alliance should override obedience to Him.

translation: Say: Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it, Allah knows it. And He knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and Allah is over all things Competent.
interpretation: The verse establishes that human inner life, with its intentions, thoughts, and hidden feelings, lies fully open before God, so that concealment before people offers no shelter before Him. Its wording moves from the hidden to the manifest and then to the whole cosmos, showing that divine knowledge is not limited to what is visible or spoken but embraces the inmost recesses of the heart as readily as the vastness of creation. The closing affirmation of His power reminds the believer that the One who knows every secret is also the One who holds every affair in His hand, so that awareness of being seen should lead to sincerity, self-accountability, and purity of intention rather than to mere outward appearance.

translation: On the Day every soul will find present whatever good it has done, and whatever evil it has done, it will wish that between itself and that evil there were a vast distance. And Allah warns you of Himself, and Allah is Kind to the servants.
interpretation: The verse places the reckoning of deeds at the center of human consciousness on the Day of Judgment, when every person will see their deeds laid bare and fully present before them, with no concealment. The good is recognized as a source of comfort, but the evil produces an anguished desire for distance from it, revealing how the soul's own record becomes its greatest burden. The closing phrase, 'Allah warns you of Himself,' calls the believer to heedfulness of God's majesty and justice, yet it is immediately softened by the declaration that Allah is Compassionate toward His servants. Thus warning and mercy are united: the fear of accountability is meant to draw the heart toward repentance and righteous action, not toward despair, since God's warning flows from His care for those He addresses.

translation: Say, "If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."
interpretation: The verse makes genuine love for Allah the root of obedience to the Prophet Muhammad, ﷺ, and shows that loving Allah is proven not by claims or feelings alone but by following the Messenger's guidance in belief and conduct. In return, divine love and forgiveness are promised, so the path to Allah's love runs through sincere imitation of the Prophet. The closing names, Forgiving and Merciful, reassure the believer that sins are not an obstacle when one turns back in sincerity, because Allah's mercy is vast and His pardon is ready for those who return to Him.

translation: Say: Obey Allah and the Messenger. But if they turn away, then indeed Allah does not love the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse makes obedience to Allah and His Messenger the single, inseparable path of faith: obeying the Messenger is not a separate matter but an expression of obeying Allah, since he conveys Allah's command. It places the burden of response on the listener, who is commanded to speak this message plainly to others. The final clause warns that turning away after clear guidance is not a neutral act but a form of rejection of the truth, and that Allah's love is withheld from those who persist in disbelief. The verse thus ties sincere faith to practical submission, showing that belief which does not translate into obedience to the revealed command is incomplete.

translation: Indeed, Allah chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of Imran over all the worlds.
interpretation: The verse presents divine selection (istifa') as the foundation of prophetic lineage and guidance: Allah chooses individuals and families not by accident of birth alone but as a sign of His sovereign will to convey His message through chosen vessels. By naming Adam, the first human and first prophet, alongside Noah, the restorer after the flood, and then the households of Abraham and Imran (the family of Mary and Jesus), the verse traces a continuous chain of revelation from the origin of humanity through the monotheistic prophets. The phrase 'over all the worlds' signals that this election is a distinction of honor and responsibility within the wider creation, which implies that such favor carries an accountability: those chosen are entrusted with bearing the divine trust, and their descendants and heirs are reminded that spiritual standing is ultimately measured by faith and obedience rather than by ancestry alone.

translation: Offspring, one descended from another. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.
interpretation: The phrase describes a chain of generations in which each people springs from those before it, so that human lineage forms a continuous bond linking the living to their ancestors and their descendants. By closing with the attributes of All-Hearing and All-Knowing, the verse reminds the believer that God perceives every word, intention, and circumstance within this succession, and therefore that the faith and conduct passed from one generation to the next are known to Him in full. The verse thus joins the reality of kinship with the assurance of divine awareness, inviting reflection on one's responsibility toward those who follow.

translation: When the wife of Imran said: "My Lord, I have dedicated to You what is in my womb, devoted entirely (to Your service), so accept it from me. Indeed, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing."
interpretation: The verse opens a window onto a mother's sincere vow made before the birth of her child, revealing a faith that offers the most precious thing she possesses without knowing its outcome. Her words show that true devotion begins with surrender: she places her unborn child wholly under God's care and service, trusting that her intention alone is worthy of acceptance. Her prayer that God hear and accept her offering reflects an awareness that God knows the hidden depths of the heart, including what the mother herself cannot yet see. The passage thus teaches that dedicating one's dearest blessings to God, with humility and reliance on His knowledge and mercy, is itself a form of worship that God accepts.

translation: So when she had delivered her, she said, "My Lord, I have delivered a female," and Allah knew best what she had delivered. "And the male is not like the female. And I have named her Mary, and I seek refuge for her and her offspring in You from the accursed Satan."
interpretation: The verse presents the mother of Mary, the wife of 'Imran, receiving her newborn with a mixture of humility and surprise, for she had vowed the child to the service of God and had hoped for a son who would serve in the sanctuary. Her words acknowledge that the outcome lies with God, who knows best what has been brought forth, and her statement that the male is not like the female reflects the expectations of her time regarding dedicated service, even as God would later honor the daughter above many. Her turning to God with the name Mary and her plea for protection of the child and her descendants from Satan reveal a heart that entrusts the newborn wholly to the Lord and seeks for her a life shielded from the whisperings of evil.

translation: So her Lord accepted her with a good acceptance and caused her to grow in a good growth, and placed her in the care of Zechariah. Every time Zechariah entered upon her in the prayer chamber, he found provision with her. He said, 'O Mary, from where is this for you?' She said, 'It is from Allah. Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without account.'
interpretation: The verse shows that Mary's purity and devotion were met with divine favor, so that her spiritual station was honored in both her upbringing and her sustenance. Zechariah's wonder at the provision he found beside her points to a sacred miracle that he could not explain by ordinary means, and Mary's reply directs the mind away from the visible causes toward the boundless generosity of God, who grants without measure to whomever He wills, teaching that true trust rests in Allah alone.

translation: There Zechariah prayed to his Lord. He said, "My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring. Indeed, You are the Hearer of supplication."
interpretation: The verse shows that Zechariah, in a moment of quiet devotion, turned to God in prayer at the place where he had witnessed the signs of divine care, seeking a righteous descendant. His request is framed not merely as a wish for a child but as a plea for a "good" offspring, one who would carry faith and goodness forward. By ending with the acknowledgment that God is the Hearer of supplication, the verse teaches that sincere prayer, even when it concerns something that seems beyond human means, is heard and answered by the One who controls all causes.

translation: Then the angels called to him while he stood in prayer in the sanctuary: "Indeed, God gives you good tidings of Yahya, confirming a word from God, and [he will be] a leader, chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous."
interpretation: The verse shows that the birth of Yahya (John) was announced to Zechariah at the very moment he was standing in devoted prayer, indicating that sincere worship opens the way to divine favor even when human circumstances seem closed. The three qualities given to Yahya reveal a balanced ideal of prophethood: he is a leader who confirms the truth of God's word (often understood as Jesus, who is called a 'word from God'), he is a man of self-restraint who keeps himself from worldly desires, and he is a prophet raised among the righteous. Thus the verse teaches that true leadership in religion combines faithful affirmation of revelation, purity of conduct, and closeness to God.

translation: He said, "My Lord, how can I have a son when old age has already overtaken me and my wife is barren?" He said, "Thus is Allah; He does what He wills."
interpretation: The verse captures Zakariya's (Zechariah's) moment of wonder and humble questioning when he receives the glad tidings of a son, not from doubt in God's power but from a human's natural astonishment at how the ordinary laws of nature could be overturned in his own life. The divine answer, "Thus is Allah," redirects his gaze from the apparent impossibility of his circumstances to the boundless will of the Creator, who is not bound by the causes and conditions He Himself established. The lesson is that when human means are exhausted, hope must rest entirely on the unlimited power of God, and that the miraculous birth of a child in old age is a sign that God's decree operates beyond what people can measure or predict.

translation: He said, "My Lord, appoint for me a sign." He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gestures. And remember your Lord much and glorify Him in the evening and the morning."
interpretation: The verse shows that Zechariah's request for a sign was answered with a trial that turned his tongue into a means of devotion rather than ordinary speech: his silence for three days, broken only by gesture, became a time set apart for remembrance of God. Being barred from speaking to people, he was directed to fill that very silence with abundant dhikr and tasbih at the beginning and end of the day, teaching that the sign of God's favor is often found in redirecting the believer's faculties toward the Lord, so that the moment of waiting for a promised blessing becomes an occasion of nearness to Him.

translation: And [mention] when the angels said, "O Mary, indeed God has chosen you, purified you, and chosen you above the women of the worlds."
interpretation: The angels' address to Mary elevates her station through a double election: first a selection for a particular grace, then purification that prepares her body and soul for a unique role, and finally a preference above all the women of her time. The repetition of the verb 'chosen' signals that her distinction is not merely personal but a divine decision that marks her as an exemplar, and the purification suggests that the honor she receives is grounded in moral and spiritual cleanliness, which in turn prepares her for the miraculous birth that the surrounding verses describe.

translation: "O Mary, be devoutly obedient to your Lord, prostrate yourself, and bow down with those who bow."
interpretation: The verse is God's address to Mary (Maryam), directing her to a complete devotion that unites inner obedience (qunut, steadfast devout submission) with outward worship expressed through prostration and bowing. By joining the bowing of those who bow, she is commanded to worship in congregation with the faithful, showing that her exceptional status as a chosen woman does not exempt her from the ritual acts of devotion; rather, it calls her to embody them fully, as a model of piety for the believers who follow.

translation: That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you; and you were not with them when they cast their pens (to see) which of them would take charge of Mary, nor were you with them when they disputed.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the account of Mary's upbringing and the dispute among the priests over her guardianship comes to the Prophet Muhammad solely through divine revelation, since he was not present at those events. It serves as a proof of his prophethood: an unlettered man relating precise, hidden details of past events could only know them by revelation. It also shows that the story of Zechariah and Mary is a reminder that God's providence chooses and protects those who are devoted to Him, and that the disputes of people over sacred matters are known fully to God.

translation: When the angels said, "O Mary, indeed God gives you good tidings of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, honored in this world and the Hereafter and among those brought near (to God)."
interpretation: The verse presents the annunciation as a divine honor bestowed upon Mary: the glad tidings concern not merely a birth but a 'word' from God, which the verse identifies with a figure named the Messiah, whose identity is defined by his maternal lineage, underscoring his full humanity while also marking him as a unique sign. Being 'honored in this world and the Hereafter' points to a dignity that is both prophetic and spiritual, and being 'among those brought near' places him in the company of the closest servants of God. The verse thus invites reflection on how God's command, expressed as His word, can bring about an extraordinary creation, and on the elevated station granted to Jesus through his relationship with God and with his mother, whom the verse also honors through the attention of the angels.

translation: And he will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity, and he will be among the righteous.
interpretation: The verse, spoken in the context of the annunciation to Maryam (Mary) about the child Jesus, presents the miraculous speech of the infant from the cradle as a sign of his special status and divine favor, affirming that he was granted wisdom and a mature voice of prophethood rather than being a mere ordinary child. Speaking to people in the cradle signals that his mission would begin from the earliest moments of his life, and that his words would carry authority and clarity in adulthood as well. The closing phrase, 'and among the righteous,' places him within the lineage of the prophets and the righteous servants of God, emphasizing that his prophetic role is grounded in piety, moral uprightness, and nearness to God, and thereby refuting claims that would elevate him beyond the human servant-prophet station.

translation: She said, "My Lord, how can I have a child when no man has touched me?" He said, "Thus is Allah; He creates what He wills. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is."
interpretation: The verse presents Mary's astonishment at the prospect of a child without marital contact, and God's reply that creation is not bound by ordinary causes. Divine power operates through a single command, so the miraculous birth of Jesus is an instance of the same absolute will that brings every thing into being. The verse teaches that what God decrees requires no intermediate means, and that human reckoning of what is possible is limited before His will.

translation: And He will teach him the Book, the wisdom, the Torah, and the Gospel.
interpretation: The verse, spoken in the context of Jesus being addressed by God in the Qur'an (Surah Al-Imran 3:48), presents divine instruction as a comprehensive education that joins the scripture given to him with wisdom and the earlier revelations. By naming the Torah and the Gospel alongside the Book, it affirms a continuity of revelation across prophets, showing that the message delivered through Jesus rests on the same divine source as the scriptures before him, and that true knowledge combines written revelation with the discernment that puts it into practice.

translation: And [he will be] a messenger to the Children of Israel: "Indeed, I have come to you with a sign from your Lord. Indeed, I will create for you from clay like the form of a bird, then I will breathe into it and it will be a bird by permission of Allah. And I will heal the blind and the leper, and I will give life to the dead, by permission of Allah. And I will inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses. Indeed, in that is a sign for you, if you are believers."
interpretation: This verse presents the miracles of Jesus, son of Mary, as the sign by which he confirms his prophethood to the Children of Israel, and it establishes a principle that runs through the Qur'an: every miracle is ultimately by the permission of Allah, never by the independent power of the messenger. Jesus's creation of a living bird from clay, his healing of the congenitally blind and the leper, and his raising of the dead are all acts that the Qur'an attributes to God's will, so that the prophet is shown to be a servant who channels divine power rather than a source of it. The final miracle, knowledge of what people eat and hoard in their homes, points to a knowledge granted by God that reaches into the hidden details of daily life. The closing phrase, "if you are believers," makes clear that these signs are meant to be recognized and accepted through faith, and that their evidentiary force is addressed to the open heart rather than compelled by spectacle alone.

translation: And confirming that which was before me of the Torah, and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you. And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, so fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: The verse presents Jesus, peace be upon him, affirming his mission as a continuation and confirmation of the earlier revelation given to Moses, rather than a rejection of it. Yet his message also carries a measure of divine relief: some prohibitions that had been placed upon the Children of Israel, often understood as a consequence of their transgressions, are lifted as a mercy from God. This shows that God's law can be adjusted in its details across prophetic stages while its essential truth remains constant. The phrase 'a sign from your Lord' points to the miracles that accompanied his message as evidence of his truthfulness and his commission. The verse closes by joining taqwa, the conscious awareness of God that guards the heart, with obedience to the messenger, teaching that true devotion to God is inseparable from faithful adherence to the one He has sent.

translation: Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path.
interpretation: The verse grounds true worship in the unity of lordship: because the One who creates, sustains, and governs all beings is the same for the prophet and his people alike, devotion must be directed to Him alone. The shared acknowledgment of one Lord removes any basis for division or for associating partners with Him, and it presents exclusive worship of God as the clear, upright way that leads to salvation, a path that is simple to recognize because it rests on the plain fact of God's sovereignty over all.

translation: So when Jesus perceived disbelief from them, he said, "Who will be my helpers toward Allah?" The disciples said, "We are the helpers of Allah. We have believed in Allah, so bear witness that we are Muslims (submitters)."
interpretation: The verse portrays the moment of decisive testing in the mission of Jesus, when he sensed the rejection of his people and turned from them to a call for sincere support in the cause of God. The response of the disciples shows that true faith expresses itself in active commitment, where believers take up the work of God's cause by becoming its helpers, and their declaration of submission stands as a witness that their loyalty belongs wholly to God alone.

translation: Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down, and we have followed the Messenger, so record us among the witnesses.
interpretation: The verse is a supplication of believers who unite two commitments: inner faith in the revelation sent down by God, and outward obedience by following the Messenger. Their faith is not merely verbal but is confirmed by action, since following the Prophet is the practical expression of belief in what was revealed.
