Its central lesson is that true steadfastness is measured by inner resolve rather than outcome: the faithful do not let wounds, losses, or setbacks sap their conviction, nor do they lower their heads in humiliation before the enemy. By recalling that the community of prophets endured similar trials, the verse reframes adversity as part of the path of God rather than a sign of divine abandonment, and it ties this firmness of spirit directly to the love of God for the patient.

translation: And their words were only that they said, "Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affair, and make our feet firm, and give us victory over the disbelieving people."
interpretation: The verse presents the true model of the believer's response to trial: rather than complaint or boasting, their speech is pure supplication that moves through a clear order. They first turn to God with humility, asking forgiveness for their wrongs and for their transgressions against themselves in matters of their own conduct, acknowledging that the fault lies with them. Then they ask for steadfastness, that their feet be made firm so that their resolve does not slip under pressure. Only after inward correction and firmness do they ask for victory over the opposing force. The lesson is that outward success is best sought by first purifying the heart and fortifying one's steadfastness, since divine help follows from sincere repentance and patient perseverance.

translation: So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the Hereafter. And Allah loves the doers of good.
interpretation: The verse closes a passage about the believers who stood firm after the trial of battle, showing that Allah's favor is not limited to worldly success but extends to the everlasting reward of the Hereafter. By tying the reward to their excellence in conduct and steadfastness, it teaches that ihsan, doing beautifully and sincerely, is the quality that earns Allah's love, and that such love is the true measure of a person's standing before Him, surpassing any gain the world can offer.

translation: O you who have believed, if you obey those who disbelieve, they will turn you back on your heels, and you will become losers.
interpretation: The verse warns believers against submitting to the counsel of those who reject faith, because such obedience gradually pulls a person backward from the path they have already entered, away from guidance and toward a state of loss. It presents a principle that the community's loyalty and decision-making must remain anchored in its own faith and its commitments to God, rather than being shaped by the desires or pressures of its opponents. The phrase 'turn you back on your heels' evokes a retreat from forward progress, suggesting that spiritual regression often begins with small concessions made under external influence. The consequence of 'losing' is therefore not only worldly but ultimately a loss of the eternal reward that faithfulness secures.

translation: Nay, but Allah is your Protector, and He is the best of helpers.
interpretation: The verse reassures the believers that their true ally and guardian is Allah alone, so their trust should rest in Him rather than in worldly alliances or their own strength. Since He is the best of those who give aid, whoever stands with Allah is never left without support, and the believer's security lies in turning to Him in every circumstance of hardship or conflict.

translation: We will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, because they associated with Allah that for which He had sent down no authority. Their refuge is the Fire, and wretched is the residence of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse presents the psychological reality of shirk as a burden that begins in the heart before it reaches the afterlife. The terror placed in the hearts of the disbelievers is a divine consequence: idolatry rests on no revealed proof, so it cannot give the soul security, and its adherents are left in fear and instability. The verse thus links the inner condition of the believer and the disbeliever with the outcome awaiting them, showing that the Fire is the destination of those who set up partners without any sanction from Allah, and that their state is one of injustice toward themselves.

translation: And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them by His permission, until when you lost courage and disputed about the matter and disobeyed after He showed you that which you love. Among you are those who desire this world, and among you are those who desire the Hereafter. Then He turned you away from them to test you. But He has pardoned you, and Allah is ever Bountiful to the believers.
interpretation: The verse recalls the Battle of Uhud, where the Muslims initially routed their enemy under divine support, but their loss of resolve, their quarrel over the spoils, and their disobedience to the Prophet's order to hold their positions reversed the outcome. It shows that divine help is tied to steadfast obedience, and that the believers are divided in their aims between worldly gain and the Hereafter. Allah's turning them away was a trial that exposed what was in their hearts, and His pardon that follows reveals that His mercy outweighs the lapse of the faithful.

translation: When you were ascending [the slope in flight] without turning aside for anyone, while the Messenger was calling you from behind you, so He rewarded you with grief upon grief, so that you would not grieve over what had escaped you nor over what had befallen you. And Allah is Aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse recalls the disorder at Uhud, when the believers fled up the mountain and the Prophet's voice called to them from the rear, and it teaches that the grief they suffered, a sorrow added to a sorrow through their own lapse and the rumor of the Prophet's death, was meant to train their hearts so that neither the loss of spoils and victory nor the wounds and deaths they had suffered would make them despair, since God knows precisely what they do and what lies in their intentions.

translation: Then after distress, He sent down upon you security in the form of drowsiness overcoming a faction of you, while another faction was concerned only with themselves, thinking about Allah other than the truth, the thought of the Jahiliyyah. They say, "Is there anything for us in the matter?" Say, "Indeed, the matter is entirely with Allah." They conceal within themselves what they do not reveal to you. They say, "If there were anything for us in the matter, we would not have been killed here." Say, "Even if you had been in your houses, those decreed to be killed would have gone out to their places of death." And [it was] so that Allah might test what is in your breasts and purify what is in your hearts. And Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts.
interpretation: The verse recounts the aftermath of the battle of Uhud, where God's gift of calm and sleep after the believers' grief was a mercy that settled some hearts, while others, driven by anxious self-concern, harbored doubts that treated the outcome as a matter of human fortune rather than divine decree. Their hidden resentment, expressed as questioning whether they had any share in the affair, is answered by the reminder that all command belongs to God, so that the defeat itself becomes a trial that exposes the concealed intentions of the heart and separates sincerity from hypocrisy, showing that nothing hidden from God can escape His knowledge.

translation: Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two armies met, it was only Satan who caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned. But Allah has already pardoned them. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.
interpretation: The verse shows that the flight of some believers at the battle of Uhud (or the encounter of the two hosts) was not left unexplained as mere cowardice, but traced to Satan exploiting an inner weakness produced by past deeds, such as worldly attachment or prior lapses. Yet the verse does not abandon them to that failure: it places the decisive emphasis on Allah's pardon, teaching that repentance and divine mercy follow a moment of weakness, and that a believer should neither deny his fault nor despair of forgiveness.

translation: O you who have believed, do not be like those who disbelieved and said about their brothers when they traveled through the land or went out to fight, "Had they remained with us, they would not have died or been killed." [They said this] so that Allah may make that aregret within their hearts. And it is Allah who gives life and causes death, and Allah is Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse warns believers against adopting the mindset of the hypocrites who attribute death and loss to staying away from the group, as if remaining home could avert fate. Its central point is that life and death belong solely to God, so a person's lifespan is not determined by travel, battle, or safety. The grief the disbelievers feel over their kin's fate is itself a result of their faulty belief, which leaves them with regret rather than trust. The believer is thus called to tawakkul, entrusting outcomes to God while acting sincerely, knowing that God observes every action and intention.

translation: And if you are killed or die in the cause of Allah, then forgiveness from Allah and mercy are better than whatever they accumulate.
interpretation: The verse reorients the believer's values away from worldly gain and fear of death toward the eternal reward of Allah. Dying or being killed in the path of God is not a loss but leads to a forgiveness and mercy that surpass everything the unbelievers amass in this life, which is fleeting and perishable. It thus frees the believer from attachment to the world and encourages steadfastness in striving for what is right, since the true outcome rests with God's pardon and compassion rather than with accumulated wealth or survival.

translation: And if you die or are killed, it is to Allah that you will be gathered.
interpretation: The verse reminds believers that death, whether natural or through being killed in the path of Allah, does not lead to a true loss or an escape from accountability, for every soul's final destination is the presence of its Lord. Since the return to God is certain regardless of how or where one dies, it urges a steadfastness that does not fear death and a readiness to strive sincerely, knowing that the gathering before God is the real and ultimate reality toward which all human effort must be directed.

translation: So by mercy from Allah, you were gentle with them. And had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you. So pardon them, and ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in the matter. And when you have decided, then rely upon Allah. Indeed, Allah loves those who rely upon Him.
interpretation: The verse shows that the Prophet's effectiveness as a leader rested on mercy and gentleness rather than harshness, for it was Allah's mercy that softened his heart toward the believers, and a hard-hearted leader would have driven them away. The divine instruction then sets out a pattern of leadership: forgiving the faults of those under one's care, seeking forgiveness for them, and involving them in deliberation on public affairs. Yet the final decision belongs to the leader once resolve is formed, and that resolve must be placed in complete trust in Allah, since consultation serves as a means while reliance on God is the true foundation of action.

translation: If Allah helps you, none can overcome you; but if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him? And upon Allah let the believers put their trust.
interpretation: The verse establishes that victory rests entirely with God's support, not with numbers, arms, or strategy alone. Divine help is the true source of strength, and its withdrawal leaves a person defenseless no matter how powerful they appear. Since no one can rescue the forsaken after God, the believers are called to place their reliance solely upon Him. This is a lesson in tawakkul: doing one's part in the struggle while recognizing that the outcome, and the real protection, belong to God alone.

translation: It is not for a prophet to defraud. And whoever defrauds will bring what he defrauded on the Day of Resurrection. Then every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: The verse establishes that betrayal of trust in public wealth is incompatible with prophethood, and by extension with integrity in any role of trust. Its wording, 'he will bring what he defrauded on the Day of Resurrection', makes the stolen property itself a burden the thief carries before all creation, so that concealed dishonesty is exposed and recompensed. The closing assurance that every soul receives exactly what it earned and is not wronged shows that divine justice is complete: no one is punished beyond their deeds, and no good or evil is overlooked. The verse thus joins the prohibition of embezzlement to the principle of accountability, teaching that a leader's or servant's trust is sacred and that every person answers fully for what he has taken or gained.

translation: Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah like one who has returned with anger from Allah, and whose refuge is Hell? And wretched is the destination.
interpretation: The verse draws a sharp contrast between two ways of life, framing the choice a person makes as a choice of ultimate destiny. Pursuing Allah's good pleasure means aligning one's intentions, actions, and loyalties with what He loves, and such a person is never equal to one who has earned divine displeasure through persistent disobedience and turning away. The rhetorical question leaves the listener to recognize, by their own reason and conscience, that these two paths cannot be treated as equal. The phrase 'returned with anger' conveys the image of someone who has drawn upon himself the wrath of his Lord, whose end is Hell, described as an evil abode. The verse thus calls the reader to reflect on where their own conduct is leading and to choose the path of divine pleasure.

translation: They are of [various] degrees in the sight of Allah, and Allah is Seeing of what they do.
interpretation: The verse establishes that people who differ in belief and conduct are not all equal before God: each is placed at a rank determined by his faith, sincerity, and deeds, not by worldly status or lineage. Since the divine ranking is based on what is hidden in the heart as well as what is outwardly done, the verse calls the believer to strive for sincerity, knowing that nothing of his actions escapes God's perfect observation, and it warns against self-deception or pride in one's standing among people.

translation: Indeed, Allah conferred a favor upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from themselves, reciting to them His verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom, although before that they had been in clear error.
interpretation: This verse presents the sending of the Prophet as the greatest of divine favors upon the believers, and it shows that the gift lies not merely in receiving revelation but in the complete transformation it brings. The messenger's origin "from themselves" makes the mission intimate: he shares their language, lineage, and human condition, so his guidance is understood and felt as coming from within their own community rather than from a distant or alien source. The four functions named in sequence (reciting, purifying, teaching the Book, and teaching wisdom) reveal a method of prophetic education that moves from the word of God heard aloud, to inner cleansing of the soul from moral corruption, to knowledge of the scripture, and finally to the deeper understanding of its purposes that wisdom provides. The closing phrase reminds the believers of the depth of their former state of clear error, so that gratitude arises from a recognition of how far guidance has raised them.

translation: Why is it that when a calamity struck you, although you had inflicted twice its like, you said, "From where is this?" Say, "It is from yourselves. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent."
interpretation: The verse, revealed after the Battle of Uhud, addresses the believers' bewilderment at their defeat after having inflicted double the losses at Badr. It redirects them from external causes to an inward reckoning: the setback was rooted in their own choices, such as disobeying the Prophet's instruction to hold their position on the archers' hill and their pursuit of worldly spoils. Yet the closing affirmation of God's power reminds them that every event lies within divine decree, so the lesson is to examine one's own conduct, take responsibility for it, and turn back to God rather than to despair or to blame others.

translation: And whatever afflicted you on the day the two armies met, it was by the permission of Allah, and that He might know the believers.
interpretation: The verse addresses the believers after the Battle of Uhud, when they suffered losses after the initial victory at Badr's sequel. It teaches that every calamity that befalls the community is not outside the knowledge and permission of God, so it should be received with trust rather than despair or confusion. It also reveals a purpose behind such trials: they serve to make visible the sincere believers, distinguishing genuine faith from weak or hypocritical profession, so that faith is tested and refined within the community.

translation: And that He may make evident those who practiced hypocrisy. It was said to them, "Come, fight in the cause of Allah or [at least] defend." They said, "If we had known there would be fighting, we would have followed you." They were nearer to disbelief that day than to faith, saying with their mouths what is not in their hearts, and Allah is most knowing of what they conceal.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites at the moment of testing: when called to the struggle, or at least to defend the community, they feign ignorance of any real fighting, revealing that their outward claims of faith were hollow and that their hearts leaned toward unbelief. Their excuse was a pretext, since their absence was a choice rather than a result of unawareness. The passage teaches that true faith is disclosed under pressure, and that the words of the tongue are not a reliable measure of belief; only God knows the concealed intentions of the heart, so the believer should examine his own sincerity rather than judge himself by mere profession.

translation: Those who said of their brethren while they themselves sat back, "If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed." Say: "Then avert death from yourselves, if you are truthful."
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrisy of those who stay behind from struggle and then, as safe spectators, pass judgment on the fallen, attributing their deaths to disobedience to them. Their own sitting idle is shown to be no shield from death, since death comes by God's decree whether one fights or stays home. The challenge "then avert death from yourselves" turns their claim back on them: if their counsel truly preserved life, they should be able to ward off death from themselves. The verse thus teaches that fate is in God's hand, and that rationalizing inaction by blaming others for the outcome of sacrifice is an empty and self-deceiving stance.

translation: And do not think of those who were killed in the cause of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive, with their Lord, being provided for.
interpretation: The verse lifts the believers' grief over their martyrs by revealing that death in the path of God is not annihilation but a transition into a higher form of life. Though their bodies are gone from the world of the living, their souls enjoy a real and honored existence in the presence of their Lord, receiving sustenance that is spiritual and unseen rather than material. The phrase 'with their Lord' points to a nearness and dignity beyond the reach of ordinary perception, so that the faithful should not regard such sacrifice as loss but as entry into a blessed state, which in turn encourages steadfastness and readiness to give one's life for the truth.

translation: Rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty, and receiving good tidings concerning those who have not yet joined them from behind them: that there is no fear upon them, nor shall they grieve.
interpretation: The verse portrays the martyrs in the state of the afterlife, who are not only content in their own station but also joyful for their brethren still in the world. Their gladness is not self-contained: they rejoice in the bounty Allah has granted them and take comfort in the knowledge that those who follow them will likewise be free of fear and sorrow, since the path of faith and striving leads to the same security. It thus reveals a true believer's ideal of felicity, in which personal peace is completed by hope and goodwill toward the community of the faithful who have yet to arrive.

translation: They rejoice in a blessing from Allah and bounty, and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers.
interpretation: The verse presents the joy of the martyrs and the faithful who have been received into the presence of their Lord, who rejoice not only in the grace and bounty they now behold but in the assurance that Allah never lets the wages of those who believe go to waste. Their happiness is thus rooted in a twofold certainty: the immediate favor of Allah bestowed upon them, and the enduring guarantee that every act of faith and sacrifice will be fully recompensed. It teaches that true joy for the believer lies in God's nearness and in trust that no good deed is ever lost before Him.

translation: Those who responded to God and the Messenger after wounds had befallen them—for those among them who did good and were mindful of God there is a great reward.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Imran (3:172), praises the believers who rose again to obey God and His Messenger immediately after the setback at Uhud, when they had been wounded in body and spirit. Their readiness to answer the call to pursue the enemy at Hamra al-Asad shows that true faith is measured not by the absence of hardship but by the willingness to return to obedience after it. The verse then singles out, among them, those who combined excellence in action with taqwa, teaching that the great reward is tied to both sincere good deeds and a constant awareness of God, so that wounds and trials become a path to elevation rather than a reason for despair.

translation: Those to whom people said, "Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them," and it only increased them in faith, and they said, "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs."
interpretation: The verse portrays the true believers at a moment of intense pressure, when rumors spread that a large enemy force had mustered to destroy them. Rather than being shaken into fear and retreat, their encounter with this threat deepened their trust in God, revealing that genuine faith grows stronger under trial. Their declaration "Allah is sufficient for us" expresses a complete reliance upon God alone, while calling Him "the best Disposer of affairs" acknowledges that all outcomes rest in His hands. The lesson is that worldly intimidation has no real power over one who has placed his affairs entrusted fully to the Creator, and that the fear of people should never displace the fear and trust due to God.

translation: So they returned with a blessing from Allah and a bounty, no harm having touched them, and they followed the pleasure of Allah. And Allah is the possessor of great bounty.
interpretation: The verse describes the believers who responded to the call to pursue the enemy after the battle of Uhud, despite their wounds and fatigue, and it shows that their obedience and sincere pursuit of Allah's pleasure transformed what could have been a hardship into a source of divine favor. The phrase 'no harm having touched them' indicates that Allah shielded them from the injury they might have expected, so that their reward was counted as blessing and bounty rather than loss. Their following of 'the pleasure of Allah' reveals that the true aim of faith is not worldly gain or the approval of people but Allah's contentment, and the closing words remind the reader that such pleasure is itself the greatest bounty, bestowed by the One whose grace is immense.

translation: It is only Satan who frightens you of his allies, so do not fear them, but fear Me, if you are believers.
interpretation: The verse exposes the true source of fear that seizes people when they are told of the power of others. Whatever threat is voiced, the one who speaks it is in truth the Shaytan, who magnifies his supporters in the eyes of the faithful so as to make them hesitate in the path of truth. The believer is therefore called to free his heart from the dread of creatures and to direct his awe solely toward God, for fear of God is the measure of faith: where it is genuine, the fear of men loses its hold. The conditional ending, 'if you are believers,' makes clear that such fearlessness before the allies of falsehood is itself a sign of sincere faith, and that wavering before them betrays a deficiency in it.

translation: And let not those who hasten into disbelief grieve you. Indeed, they will never harm Allah at all. Allah intends that they will have no share in the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) over the rapid rush of some people into disbelief, which might pain him as he longed for their guidance. It teaches that their rejection cannot diminish God's sovereignty or power, since no one can harm Allah in the slightest; the harm falls only upon themselves. By declaring that Allah wills them to have no portion in the Hereafter, it reveals that their eagerness for disbelief is a sign of divine abandonment to their own choices, and it assures the believer that God's justice will ultimately be fulfilled, while the great punishment awaits them. The lesson is patience and trust in God rather than sorrow over those who turn away.

translation: Indeed, those who have exchanged disbelief for faith will never harm Allah in the least, and theirs will be a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse frames disbelief as a deliberate bargain in which people trade away the guidance they were given for something of lesser worth, as though they were purchasing error with what should have been their treasure. Yet the consequence of this exchange falls entirely upon the one who makes it: Allah is in no need of anyone's obedience and is unaffected by their rejection, so the loss is wholly their own. The mention of a painful punishment underscores that the harm of this choice returns to the soul that chose it, and it invites the reader to reflect on how easily a person can sell a lasting good for a fleeting gain.

translation: And let not those who disbelieve think that the respite We grant them is better for themselves. Indeed, We grant them respite only that they may increase in sin, and for them is a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse warns that a delay in punishment is not a sign of divine approval or favor. What appears to the disbelievers as ease and prosperity is in reality a test that allows their wrongdoing to accumulate, so that their eventual humiliation becomes more complete. True benefit lies in turning back to God while there is still time, and the one who is given room to err should take that respite as a call to repentance rather than as proof of being right.

translation: Allah would not leave the believers in the state you are in until He distinguishes the wicked from the good. Nor would Allah give you knowledge of the unseen, but Allah chooses from among His messengers whom He wills. So believe in Allah and His messengers. And if you believe and are mindful of God, you will have a great reward.
interpretation: The verse was revealed after the Battle of Uhud, where hypocrites who had mixed with the believers were exposed by their conduct under hardship. It presents divine trials as a sifting process in which God lets the sincere and the insincere become visibly distinct, so that faith is shown through action and not merely through claim. The second part sets a limit on human knowledge: the unseen belongs to God, and whatever knowledge of it people receive comes through the messengers He selects. Thus the believer's certainty should rest on trust in God and in His messengers, not on demands for personal disclosures of hidden matters. The closing promise ties genuine faith and God-consciousness to a great reward, linking inner conviction to righteous conduct.

translation: And let not those who withhold what Allah has bestowed upon them of His bounty think that it is better for them. Rather, it is worse for them. They will have their necks encircled with that which they withheld on the Day of Resurrection. And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is All-Aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse warns that wealth withheld from its rightful due is not a gain but a loss, for what a person hoards out of stinginess becomes, on the Day of Resurrection, a burden fastened around the neck, a visible punishment of their own making. Since all that is possessed ultimately returns to Allah, who is the true heir of the heavens and the earth, human ownership is only a temporary trust, and the miser is reminded that his sole claim to what he holds is what he spends in obedience to the One who gave it to him.

translation: Allah has indeed heard the words of those who said, "Surely Allah is poor and we are rich." We will record what they have said, and their killing of the prophets without right, and We will say, "Taste the punishment of the burning."
interpretation: The verse exposes the gravity of blasphemous speech and of hostility toward God's messengers, showing that no utterance or act of injustice escapes divine knowledge and recording. The claim that God is poor, made in mockery of the call to charity and spending in His cause, is treated as a grave insult to Him, while the killing of prophets reveals a persistent pattern of rejecting divine guidance. The verse thus conveys that accountability is certain: the same God who hears every word will hold the speakers to account, and the punishment they face is the fitting consequence of their words and deeds.

translation: That is for what your hands have put forward, and that Allah is not ever unjust to the servants.
interpretation: The verse presents a principle of divine justice: the suffering that people face is the direct consequence of their own deeds, since the hands that performed wrongdoing sent it ahead of them. By affirming that Allah is never unjust to His servants, it places responsibility squarely on the human being rather than on God, so that a person reflecting on hardship is invited to examine his own conduct and to take accountability before God, knowing that the scale of reward and punishment is perfectly fair.

translation: Those who said, "Indeed, God has taken a covenant from us that we should not believe in any messenger until he brings us an offering that the fire consumes." Say, "There have certainly come to you messengers before me with clear proofs and with what you speak of. So why did you kill them, if you are truthful?"
interpretation: The verse exposes a pretext used by some who rejected prophethood: they claimed a divine covenant required a sign of a sacrificial offering consumed by fire as proof of a messenger's truth, a sign they invented to avoid accepting clear evidence. The reply turns their demand back on them by pointing out that earlier messengers already came with manifest signs and the very miracle they named, yet they still killed them, showing that the real obstacle was not a lack of proof but their stubborn refusal. The verse thus teaches that the demand for more signs can be a cover for unwillingness to submit to the truth, and that the consistent response of those who reject guidance is hostility toward those who bring it.

translation: And if they deny you, then messengers before you were certainly denied, who came with clear proofs, and the scriptures, and the illuminating Book.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad by placing his rejection within a long line of prophetic experience: denial is not a unique failure of his mission but a recurring pattern in which every messenger was met with disbelief despite bringing manifest evidence. The threefold description of what they brought, clear proofs, scriptures of wisdom, and the luminous Book, emphasizes that the truth they carried was complete and self-evident, so the fault lies with the deniers rather than with the clarity of the message. The verse thus teaches steadfastness, reminding the believer that the rejection of truth is an old human tendency and that the messenger's duty is only to deliver the clear message.

translation: Every soul will taste death. And you will only be paid your full rewards on the Day of Resurrection. So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise has indeed succeeded. And the worldly life is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion.
interpretation: The verse reminds the human being that death is a universal certainty that no soul can escape, and that the true accounting of a person's deeds is deferred to the Day of Resurrection, when recompense is complete. It sets the measure of success not in worldly gain or status but in being saved from the Fire and granted Paradise, and it frames the present life as a fleeting pleasure that deceives those who become absorbed in it, calling the believer to keep the eternal outcome in view.

translation: You will certainly be tested in your possessions and in your persons, and you will certainly hear much hurtful speech from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate partners with God. But if you are patient and mindful of God, then indeed that is among the matters requiring firm resolve.
interpretation: The verse presents trial as an inseparable part of the believer's path, meaning that faith is not tested only in moments of hardship but continuously, through loss of wealth and life and through the harm of words spoken by opponents. It shows that the community should expect such afflictions rather than be surprised by them, and it places patience (sabr) and God-consciousness (taqwa) as the twin inner resources that enable a believer to endure. By calling this steadfastness 'of firm resolve,' the verse elevates patient endurance and piety from passive suffering into a deliberate, courageous commitment that the Qur'an regards as among the highest of moral qualities.

translation: And [mention] when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture: "You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it." But they discarded it behind their backs and exchanged it for a small price. And wretched is what they were buying.
interpretation: This verse exposes a breach of trust at the heart of the People of the Book's relationship with their revelation. God's covenant bound them to two duties, to explain the Scripture openly and never to hide its truths, yet they treated it as something to be cast aside, 'behind their backs,' as though it were of no concern to them. Their motive was worldly gain, trading the eternal message of God for a fleeting, paltry return, whether that gain was status, leadership, income, or the preservation of their own authority over people. The verse teaches that knowledge carries an obligation to be shared honestly, and that concealing or distorting religious truth for material advantage is among the gravest forms of betrayal, one whose true cost is measured not in what is gained but in what is sold away.

translation: Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have brought, and love to be praised for what they did not do, are safe from punishment. For them is a painful torment.
interpretation: The verse exposes a hidden spiritual disease: the desire to be credited with virtue one does not possess. Those who take joy in their outward deeds and crave the praise of people for acts they never performed deceive themselves into thinking they are beyond accountability. God warns the believer not to assume such people escape reckoning; their self-deception and hypocrisy, which seeks reputation rather than sincere devotion, will itself bring a painful punishment. The lesson is to act sincerely for God alone and to guard the heart against vanity and the love of false recognition.

translation: And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. And Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse affirms that absolute sovereignty over everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah alone, so no created being holds ownership or authority that is independent of Him. Because this dominion is complete, His power is equally complete, reaching every thing without limit or difficulty. The believer is thereby invited to place trust in the One who both owns all that exists and is able to do whatever He wills, and to recognize that all worldly authority is borrowed and temporary, while divine sovereignty is unconditional and everlasting.

translation: Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and in the alternation of the night and the day, there are signs for those of understanding.
interpretation: The verse directs the mind beyond mere observation to reflection: the heavens and the earth, and the regular succession of night and day, are presented as signs (ayat) pointing to a wise and purposeful Creator. The phrase 'ulu al-albab' (people of pure intellect) signals that these signs are not perceived by the senses alone but are recognized by those whose reason is clear and free of heedlessness. The alternation of night and day, with its precise order and balance, becomes a model of constancy and measure, inviting the believer to recognize in the cosmos the evidence of divine wisdom and to let that recognition lead to awe, gratitude, and remembrance of God.

translation: Those who remember God while standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth: "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain. Glory be to You; so protect us from the punishment of the Fire."
interpretation: The verse portrays the believer whose remembrance of God is not confined to set times or postures but is continuous, accompanying every bodily state, so that dhikr becomes the inner orientation of the whole self. This constant remembrance leads naturally to contemplation (tafakkur) of the created order, where the cosmos is read as a sign pointing to its Creator's wisdom and purpose. The insight that creation is not purposeless then issues in a conviction of divine accountability, expressed in the prayer that exalts God's transcendence and seeks refuge from the Fire, showing that true knowledge of God joins intellectual reflection, devotion, and moral responsibility.

translation: Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit into the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him, and for the wrongdoers there will be no helpers.
interpretation: The verse reveals that true disgrace (khizy) is not merely worldly humiliation but being cast into the Fire, which exposes the complete failure of the wrongdoer's reliance on worldly status, alliances, and false supports. By stating that the zalimun have no nasir, it teaches that on the Day of Judgment every false refuge collapses, and that the believer's sole recourse is to beseech the Lord for protection from that fate, acknowledging that salvation rests entirely in God's mercy rather than in one's own deeds or the aid of others.

translation: Our Lord, indeed we have heard a caller calling to faith, saying, 'Believe in your Lord,' so we believed. Our Lord, forgive us our sins, remove from us our misdeeds, and cause us to die among the righteous.
interpretation: The verse presents a believer's prayer that rests on hearing the call to faith and answering it at once, with no hesitation. Having accepted that call, the believers ask for two things that follow from it: forgiveness that covers their past wrongs, and the removal of their evil deeds, so that their faith is matched by a cleansed record. Their final request, to die among the righteous, shows that they desire to be counted with the good people in this life and the next, so that their faith is sealed by a sincere and steadfast end.

translation: Our Lord, grant us what You promised us through Your messengers, and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, You do not fail in Your promise.
interpretation: The verse is a prayer of sincere believers who, having affirmed their faith, turn to God with humble dependence, asking Him to fulfil the promises of reward and victory He made through His messengers. Their request rests on a firm trust in God's perfect faithfulness, since He never breaks His word. Their plea against being humiliated on the Day of Resurrection reflects a deep awareness that honour and disgrace before God are decided by one's faith and deeds, and that only God's mercy can secure them from shame. Thus the verse teaches that true faith combines hope in God's promises with fear of His reckoning, and that the believer's ultimate refuge is the certainty that God's word is true.

translation: So their Lord responded to them: "Indeed, I will not allow the work of any worker among you to be lost, whether male or female; you are of one another. So those who emigrated, were driven out of their homes, were harmed in My cause, fought, and were killed—I will surely remove their misdeeds from them and admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, as a reward from Allah. And with Allah is the best of rewards."
interpretation: The verse establishes that God's reckoning is based on deeds rather than gender or lineage, affirming the equal standing of men and women before Him in the sight of their Lord's justice, since both are bound together in one human family and are equally accountable for what they do. It then singles out those who sacrificed their homeland, property, and even their lives for the sake of faith, showing that the greatest acts of devotion often arise from uprooting oneself for the truth. Their reward is presented as God's own gift, a forgiveness of wrongs together with everlasting paradise, implying that suffering endured for conscience is transformed by divine mercy into a gain that far exceeds the loss.

translation: Let not the movement of those who disbelieve throughout the land deceive you.
interpretation: The verse warns the believer against being misled by the apparent ease, prosperity, and freedom of movement enjoyed by those who reject faith. Their worldly comfort and commercial success across the lands is a temporary provision, not a sign of divine approval or of the truth of their path. The believer should measure things by their final outcome rather than their immediate appearance, trusting that the apparent security of the disbelievers is fleeting, as the following verses make clear that it is only a brief enjoyment that will lead to their destination in the Fire, while the righteous will have gardens beneath which rivers flow.

translation: A brief enjoyment, then their refuge will be Hell, and wretched is the resting place.
interpretation: The verse portrays the worldly prosperity of those who disbelieve and act arrogantly as fleeting, a passing comfort that offers no lasting security. By placing this brief enjoyment against the eternal abode that awaits them, it calls the listener to weigh the transient against the everlasting and to recognize that a life of ease in this world is no measure of success if it leads to Hell. The phrase 'wretched is the resting place' turns the image of a bed or cradle, a place of rest, into a bitter irony, showing that what they sought as comfort will become their torment.

translation: But those who have taqwa of their Lord will have gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, as a provision (hospitality) from Allah. And what is with Allah is better for the righteous.
interpretation: The verse draws a sharp contrast between the fleeting comfort of the disbelievers' worldly life and the lasting reward of the God-conscious believers. Their reward is not merely a gift but a noble welcome (nuzul) from Allah, the Generous Host, prepared before their arrival, which signals that the garden is the natural home of those whose hearts were bound to their Lord in fear and hope. By stating that what is with Allah is better for the righteous, the verse teaches that true value lies in the eternal and the divinely given, so the believer should measure success by what endures beyond this world rather than by its transient luxuries.

translation: And indeed, among the People of the Scripture are those who believe in Allah, and in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed to them, humbly submitting to Allah. They do not exchange the signs of Allah for a small price. Those will have their reward with their Lord. Indeed, Allah is swift in account.
interpretation: The verse corrects the sweeping assumption that the People of the Scripture are uniformly disbelievers by affirming that a sincere group among them believes in God, accepts the revelation given to the Prophet Muhammad, and continues to honor what was sent to their own prophets. Their defining marks are khushu', a humble inner submission before God, and integrity in refusing to trade God's signs for worldly gain, such as concealing or distorting the truth for wealth or status. The promise of reward with their Lord rests on this sincerity and not on group affiliation, so the verse teaches that divine recompense follows the reality of faith and conduct. The closing reminder that God is swift in reckoning warns that every act of concealment or sale of truth will be accounted for, urging vigilance and accountability in all communities.

translation: O you who have believed, be patient, endure together in patience, stand firm at the frontier, and fear Allah that you may be successful.
interpretation: The verse closes the Surah Al-Imran with a comprehensive program for the believing community: patience (sabr) in the face of hardship, a further stage of mutual perseverance (musabarah) that binds believers together so that no one endures alone, and steadfastness at one's post (murabatah), which both guards the community's frontiers and, more deeply, means holding fast to one's spiritual station against the forces that would breach it. These three duties are anchored in taqwa, the conscious awareness of God that governs every action, and the verse ties success (falah) to this integrated discipline, teaching that true prosperity in this world and the next is achieved not by isolated virtue but by a patient, united, vigilant, and God-conscious community.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O mankind, be mindful of your Lord, who created you from a single soul and created from it its mate, and from the two of them dispersed many men and women. And be mindful of God, through whom you ask one another, and of the wombs. Indeed, God is ever Watchful over you.
interpretation: The verse opens by addressing all of humanity together, grounding their shared dignity and kinship in a single origin, so that the diversity of men and women spread across the earth is seen as one family tree rooted in one soul. Taqwa is therefore called for not only toward the Creator but also in the bonds that join people to one another, since the mutual claims of kinship and the rights of the womb are sacred trusts that God holds people accountable for, and the closing reminder that God is ever watchful makes clear that no social obligation, however hidden, escapes His knowledge.

translation: And give the orphans their properties, and do not substitute the defective (bad) for the good, and do not consume their properties into your own properties. Indeed, that is a great sin.
interpretation: The verse establishes that guardianship of orphans is a trust that must be discharged with integrity: the wealth belonging to orphans must be handed over to them once they reach maturity, and the guardian must not exchange their good assets for his own worthless ones, nor merge their wealth with his own so as to devour it. By naming the act a great sin (hawban kabiran), God makes clear that the vulnerability of the orphan does not license exploitation but rather demands the strictest honesty, since the orphan has no protector other than the conscience of the one entrusted with his affairs.

translation: And if you fear that you will not deal justly with orphan girls, then marry from [other] women what seems good to you, two or three or four. But if you fear that you will not be just, then [marry only] one, or what your right hands possess. That is more suitable that you not incline toward injustice.
interpretation: The verse ties the permission of plural marriage to the fear of injustice toward orphans, placing the protection of vulnerable people's rights at the center of the ruling. It sets a ceiling of four wives and makes that permission conditional on the ability to be just among them, so that when justice cannot be assured the command narrows to one wife or to what the right hand possesses. The closing phrase, that this is nearer to avoiding oppression or excess burden, shows the underlying purpose: the law is oriented toward preventing wrong to the weak and securing fairness within the household rather than toward mere permission of multiplicity.

translation: And give the women their dowries as a gift graciously. But if they willingly give you something of it, then consume it with satisfaction and ease.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the mahr (bridal gift) belongs entirely to the wife as a sincere gift from the husband, given out of goodwill rather than as a price or obligation to be grudgingly paid. It protects the woman's ownership of her property: the husband may not take it back or appropriate it by pressure. Only when she freely and wholeheartedly chooses to give up part of it may he take it, and then he may enjoy it without guilt or unease. The phrase 'nafsan' (from her own self) emphasizes that the consent must come from genuine inner willingness, not coercion or social pressure. Thus the verse combines the honoring of women with the ethics of consent in marital finances.

translation: And do not give the foolish your wealth, which Allah has made a means of support for you; but provide for them from it and clothe them, and speak to them with kind and good words.
interpretation: The verse establishes that wealth is entrusted to a person by God as a means of sustenance and stability for the community, so it must not be handed over carelessly to those who lack the judgment to manage it wisely and would squander it or harm themselves and others with it. The guardian of such property is not thereby freed from responsibility toward these people: he is commanded to continue meeting their needs in food and clothing from that wealth, and to address them with gentle, reasonable speech that preserves their dignity while guiding them. Thus the verse joins prudent stewardship of property with compassion, showing that protecting wealth from waste and providing for the vulnerable are not opposed but belong together in the ethic of responsible care.

translation: And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age. Then if you perceive in them sound judgment, release their property to them. And do not consume it extravagantly and hastily, fearing that they will grow up. And whoever is wealthy should abstain, and whoever is poor may eat according to what is reasonable. Then when you release their property to them, have witnesses over them. And sufficient is Allah as Accountant.
interpretation: The verse establishes that guardianship of orphans carries a duty of gradual trust-building and accountability: the guardian must test the orphan's maturity and sound judgment before handing over his wealth, and must never treat the orphan's property as a resource to be consumed wastefully or in haste before the orphan comes of age. It sets an ethical standard of self-restraint, where the wealthy guardian abstains entirely from the orphan's money, while the poor guardian may take only what is customary and reasonable as compensation for his labor. The requirement of witnesses protects both parties from later suspicion, and the closing reminder that God is sufficient as Accountant places the entire trust under a moral oversight that transcends human supervision.

translation: For men there is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, and for women there is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, whether it is little or much, a share ordained.
interpretation: The verse establishes that inheritance rights belong to both men and women alike, breaking with the pre-Islamic custom that denied women and the young a share of the estate and granted it only to those who could fight. By affirming that each sex has a genuine, fixed portion regardless of the amount left behind, it makes the division of property a divinely ordained obligation rather than a matter of discretion, thereby securing the economic dignity and independent standing of women within the family and the wider community.

translation: And when the division (of inheritance) is attended by relatives, orphans, and the needy, provide for them from it and speak to them kind words.
interpretation: This verse teaches that wealth distributed through inheritance is not only a matter of legal shares for the direct heirs; it also opens a moral door for those who stand at the edge of the estate, the near relatives who were not named heirs, the orphans who have lost their protector, and the poor who have no claim at all. The believer is asked to give them a portion from what has been divided, out of compassion rather than obligation, so that the moment of dividing a family's property does not become a moment of exclusion and hurt. The command is completed by speech: when one cannot give much, one must still speak to them with gentleness, honor, and goodly words, so that no one leaves the gathering feeling belittled or ignored. In this way the verse makes generosity and courteous language part of justice, showing that the sharing of wealth is measured not only by what is given but by how the giver treats the hearts of those present.

translation: And let those fear [Allah] who, if they were to leave behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them. So let them fear Allah and speak words that are right and just.
interpretation: The verse addresses those standing at the bedside of the dying or entrusted with the affairs of an estate, urging them to act toward the orphaned and dependent heirs as they would wish others to act toward their own children after them. The principle is a mirror: one should feel for the helpless of others the same concern one feels for one's own weak descendants. Such empathy is to be expressed through piety (taqwa) in conduct and through sound, measured, truthful speech, meaning that when advising the dying or dealing with the property of orphans, one must avoid harshness, deception, or wasteful words, and instead speak what is correct and fair, guarding the rights of the vulnerable.

translation: Indeed, those who consume the properties of orphans unjustly are only consuming fire into their bellies, and they will soon enter a blazing Fire.
interpretation: The verse presents the wrongful seizure of orphans' wealth as one of the gravest injustices, because the orphan is the most vulnerable member of society and has no protector to defend his rights. By describing the act as eating fire into the belly, the Qur'an makes the consequence visible and bodily: the wealth taken unjustly becomes, in the hereafter, a burning punishment that the consumer literally carries within himself. The phrase 'unjustly' (ظلما) signals that the prohibition targets exploitation and theft, not the lawful management of an orphan's property by a guardian who acts with fairness, as other verses permit. The verse therefore calls believers to guard the trust placed in them over the weak, reminding them that the apparent gain of wealth seized from the helpless is in truth a fire that will be experienced in full on the Day of Reckoning.

translation: Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, the equal of the portion of two females. And if there are only daughters, more than two, they shall have two thirds of the inheritance; and if there is only one, she shall have half. And for each of his parents, a sixth of the inheritance if he left children. But if he left no children and the parents are his heirs, then for his mother is one third. And if he has brothers, for his mother is a sixth, after any bequest heorders or debt. Your fathers and your sons—you do not know which of them are nearer to you in benefit. This is an obligation from Allah; indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: The verse establishes the principle that inheritance is governed by a divinely fixed order rather than by human judgment of who benefits most, because people cannot know with certainty which relatives will be most useful to them. By fixing the shares, Allah removes the uncertainty and dispute that would otherwise arise, and the closing attributes of knowledge and wisdom affirm that these apportionments are perfectly suited to justice within the family, with the male receiving twice the female's share reflecting the financial responsibilities placed upon him. The condition that bequests and debts be settled first shows that the rights of the deceased and of creditors precede the distribution among heirs.

translation: And for you is half of what your wives leave, if they have no child. But if they have a child, then for you is a quarter of what they leave, after any bequest they make or debt. And for the wives is a quarter of what you leave, if you have no child. But if you have a child, then for them is an eighth of what you leave, after any bequest you make or debt. And if a man or a woman leaves neither ascendants nor descendants (a kalalah) and has a brother or a sister, then for each one of them is a sixth. But if they are more than that, they share in a third, after any bequest made or debt, without harm. This is a decree from Allah, and Allah is All-Knowing, Forbearing.
interpretation: The verse establishes the fixed shares of spouses and of siblings in inheritance as a binding divine ordinance, showing that the legal claims of heirs are fixed by God and that bequests and debts must be settled first, yet no bequest may be made to harm the heirs. The phrase 'without harm' (ghayra mudarr) marks the prohibition against a testator who deliberately diminishes the rights of his heirs through a will or a false debt, so that justice within the family is preserved. The closing names of Allah, All-Knowing and Forbearing, indicate that these precise distributions come from perfect knowledge of what benefits people, and that God delays punishment for human error while still holding people to His limits.

translation: These are the limits set by Allah. Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great triumph.
interpretation: The verse frames the divine commandments as boundaries (hudud) that protect the human being and define the space within which justice, order, and spiritual health are preserved; stepping beyond them is a self-inflicted harm. It links obedience to Allah and His Messenger as a single path, indicating that the Prophet's guidance is the practical expression of God's will, so that submission to one is submission to the other. The promised reward is presented not merely as material comfort but as an enduring, flourishing life in closeness to God, and the phrase "the great triumph" recasts success from worldly gain to eternal salvation, inviting the believer to measure achievement by its lasting spiritual consequence.

translation: And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits - He will admit him to a Fire, wherein he will abide eternally, and for him is a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse links two kinds of wrongdoing: disobedience to Allah and His Messenger, and the transgression of the divinely set boundaries. Disobedience is the rejection of what has been commanded, while transgressing the limits goes further, overstepping what is permitted and forbidden. The punishment is matched to the offence: the Fire, with its eternal abiding, is the consequence of persistent rebellion, and the 'humiliating punishment' reflects that the one who exalted his own desires over the command of God is brought low. The verse thus teaches that obedience to God is inseparable from obedience to His Messenger, and that the boundaries of the law are not to be treated lightly, since they mark the line between what God has protected and what He has forbidden.

translation: And those of your women who commit immorality, bring against them four witnesses from among you. And if they testify, then confine them to houses until death takes them or Allah ordains for them a way out.
interpretation: This verse, read together with its context in Surah An-Nisa, lays down an early legal stage for dealing with proven sexual immorality committed by women. It requires that such an accusation be established by the testimony of four witnesses from within the community, a deliberately high standard of proof that guards against casual accusation and protects reputations. Once established, the women are to be confined to their homes, a temporary and corrective measure rather than a final punishment. The phrase 'or Allah ordains for them a way out' points to the subsequent revelation that prescribed a specific penalty, and classical scholars differed on whether this verse was superseded by the later legislation of the hadd punishment or whether it remained a stage in a gradual process of reform. The verse thus reflects a broader Qur'anic pattern of progressive legislation, moving gradually toward clearer and more definitive rulings while emphasizing the seriousness of the offence and the importance of evidence and due process.

translation: And the two of you [men] who commit it, harm them both. But if they repent and reform, then leave them alone. Indeed, Allah is ever Accepting of repentance, Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, in its context within Surah An-Nisa, addresses the punishment for the grave sin of lewdness (fahisha) committed by two men, prescribing a form of reproach and harm to deter them. It then makes clear that sincere repentance and reform open the door to pardon, so the community should turn away from them and not persist in condemnation. The closing affirmation that God is oft-returning in acceptance and merciful emphasizes that the purpose of legal sanction is correction rather than unending punishment, and that divine mercy remains available to those who turn back to Him.

translation: Repentance accepted by Allah is only for those who do evil out of ignorance and then repent soon after; those are the ones to whom Allah turns in forgiveness, and Allah is ever All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the door of repentance is open, but its acceptance is tied to sincerity and promptness: the sinner who wrongs himself out of heedlessness or lack of full awareness of the gravity of his act, and who turns back to God before the sin becomes a settled habit or the moment of death arrives, is the one God mercifully receives. The phrase 'out of ignorance' does not mean the sin is excused in every sense, but that it arises from a momentary failure of judgment rather than deliberate defiance. The words 'soon after' point to the believer's obligation to hasten back to God immediately upon realizing his error, rather than postponing repentance. The closing divine names, All-Knowing and All-Wise, assure the believer that God knows the true state of the heart and orders His mercy with wisdom, so that hope in forgiveness is joined with reverence for His knowledge and justice.

translation: And repentance is not [accepted] from those who keep doing evil deeds until, when death comes to one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now," nor from those who die while they are disbelievers. Those - We have prepared for them a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse teaches that repentance is genuine only when it is made while there is still room for a real change of conduct and belief; a repentance uttered at the moment of death, when the reality of the unseen has already become evident and the choice is no longer free, carries no weight, just as dying in disbelief closes the door of forgiveness. It warns believers not to postpone turning back to God, since the time of acceptance is the lifetime in which a person can still act, and it underscores that God's mercy is wide but its acceptance is tied to sincere and timely return.

translation: O you who have believed, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion, nor to restrain them [from remarriage or keep them in marriage] to take away part of what you have given them, unless they commit a clear immorality. And live with them in kindness. For if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike something in which Allah has placed much good.
interpretation: The verse establishes that a woman is not property to be inherited against her will, and that the marital bond must not be used as a means of coercion to reclaim the dowry. Even when a husband feels aversion toward his wife, the command to live with her in kindness remains binding, and he should look beyond his momentary dislike, since what he finds disagreeable may hide a great good that God has placed within it.

translation: And if you wish to replace one wife with another, and you have given one of them a heap of gold, do not take back from it anything. Would you take it by slander and manifest sin?
interpretation: The verse forbids a husband from reclaiming any part of the mahr, the marriage gift, once it has been given, even when he wishes to divorce one wife in order to take another. The image of a qintar, a great treasure, underlines how generous the gift may have been, and the rhetorical question shows that to take it back would be an unjust seizure, a false accusation against the wife and a plain wrong. The ruling protects the woman's financial dignity and rights within marriage, and it reflects the Qur'anic principle that marital obligations must be honored with fairness and not reversed through oppression.

translation: And how could you take it back, when you have gone in unto one another and they have taken from you a solemn covenant?
interpretation: The verse is addressed to men who divorced their wives after intimacy and then wished to reclaim the mahr (dowry) they had given. God forbids this by highlighting the depth of what has already passed between the spouses, the intimate union they have shared, together with the firm, weighty covenant (mithaq ghalidh) made at the marriage contract. Such a bond is not to be treated lightly or reversed for material gain; the verse thus elevates marriage from a mere financial exchange to a sacred commitment grounded in mutual trust, intimacy, and reverence for God's covenant.

translation: And do not marry those whom your fathers married, except what has already passed. Indeed, it was an obscenity and hateful and an evil way.
interpretation: The verse forbids a son from marrying the women his father had married, a prohibition of the most severe kind that grows out of the sanctity of the family bond and the respect owed to the father's position. Its wording is deliberately graded: the act is called fahisha (a shameful indecency), maqt (an object of deep abhorrence), and an evil path, so that the ruling is not merely a legal limit but a moral condemnation that protects lineage, household honor, and the emotional order within the family. The exception, 'except what has already passed,' is a mercy that does not punish those who acted in the time of ignorance before the revelation, while it establishes a firm boundary for the future.

translation: Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brothers' daughters, your sisters' daughters, your mothers who nursed you, your milk-sisters, the mothers of your wives, your stepdaughters under your guardianship who are born of your wives with whom you have consummated marriage (but if you have not consummated the marriage, there is no blame on you), the wives of your sons who are from your loins, and that you combine two sisters in marriage, except for what has already passed. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse establishes the categories of women who are prohibited to a believer in marriage, grounding them in kinship, nursing, and in-law relations, and thereby protecting the integrity of the family and the bonds of blood and milk. By listing the mother and daughter first, it shows that the prohibitions rest on the sanctity of close lineage, which the wider community is to preserve. The conditional clause about stepdaughters, which excuses those whose marriages were never consummated, reveals the law's careful balance between firmness on the sacred boundaries and mercy toward those who acted without transgression. The closing mention of Allah's forgiveness and mercy, following the exception for what has already passed, indicates that the law looks forward to reform and does not condemn past practices that predated this revelation.

translation: And [prohibited to you are] married women, except those whom your right hands possess. This is the decree of Allah upon you. And lawful to you are all others beyond these, that you seek them with your wealth, chaste and not unlawful. So for whatever you enjoy [of marriage] from them, give them their compensation as an obligation. And there is no blame upon you in what you mutually agree to after the obligation. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: The verse closes the enumeration of forbidden women in Surah An-Nisa' by establishing that all women beyond the prohibited categories are lawful, provided the man seeks them through marriage, using his wealth as a dowry, with the aim of chastity rather than illicit fornication. It makes the mahr an obligatory right owed to the wife, fixed as a binding duty rather than a favor, while leaving room for mutual consent between spouses regarding adjustments after it is settled. The concluding names of Allah, All-Knowing and All-Wise, affirm that these rulings flow from divine knowledge and wisdom, protecting lineage, dignity, and the rights of women.

translation: And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free believing women, then let them marry from those whom your right hands possess of your believing young women. And Allah is most knowing of your faith; you are of one another. So marry them with the permission of their people and give them their due compensation according to what is reasonable, [they being] chaste, not unlawful fornicators nor those who take secret lovers. And when they are protected [in marriage], if they commit immorality, then for them is half the punishment for free women. That is for whoever among you fears hardship; but to be patient is better for you. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse addresses believers who lack the financial means to marry free chaste believing women, permitting them to marry believing bondwomen under their guardianship, with the emphasis that faith is the common bond among people and that the true measure of worth is faith, which Allah alone knows fully. It establishes that such marriages require the consent of the women's guardians, the giving of a fair dowry, and that the women be chaste and committed rather than prostitutes or those with secret lovers. It further sets the penalty for a married bondwoman's immorality at half that of a free married woman, reflecting the principle of graded responsibility. Finally, it presents patience and restraint as better than hastily entering such a union, while affirming Allah's forgiveness and mercy toward those who struggle with their desires.

translation: Allah wants to make clear to you, and to guide you to the ways of those before you, and to turn to you in forgiveness. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse presents God's will as an act of mercy toward believers, revealing that the purpose of the divine legislation that precedes it is threefold: clarity, guidance, and forgiveness. By 'making clear' (yubayyina) is meant the explanation of what is lawful and unlawful, so that human beings are not left in confusion about their duties. The 'ways of those before you' (sunan alladhina min qablikum) directs the reader to the lasting patterns of divine law and the consequences that followed earlier communities, so that the believers may learn from them and avoid their errors. Most striking is the final purpose, God's turning toward His servants in forgiveness, which shows that the commandments are not a burden meant to trap people but a path by which a merciful Lord brings His creatures back to Himself. The closing names, All-Knowing and All-Wise, confirm that these rulings flow from perfect knowledge of human nature and perfect wisdom in what is best for it.

translation: And Allah wants to accept your repentance, but those who follow their desires want you to deviate with a great deviation.
interpretation: The verse reveals two opposing wills acting upon the believers: the divine will that seeks to turn them back toward Himself in mercy and forgiveness, and the will of those driven by base appetites who wish to pull them away from the straight path into grave deviation. Repentance is thus presented as the way of Allah's favor, while the pursuit of desires is the means by which the heedless seek to draw people from righteousness. The believer is called to recognize where his inclinations lead and to choose the path that Allah has made open to him through turning back to Him.

translation: Allah wants to lighten [the burden] for you, and mankind was created weak.
interpretation: The verse places the divine wish to ease the believers' burdens alongside a fundamental truth about human nature: man was created weak, in body, resolve, and self-control. Because human frailty is part of how we were made, God's laws are not designed to crush us with impossible demands but to lighten what would otherwise be unbearable. Thus the verse grounds the permission of concessions, such as in matters of marriage, inheritance, and the prohibitions that follow it in its context, in mercy toward a creature who knows its own limitations and needs guidance. Recognizing one's weakness becomes a reason to turn to God for strength rather than to despair or to be proud.

translation: O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you. And do not kill yourselves. Indeed, Allah is ever Merciful to you.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the protection of property is grounded in justice: wealth may be exchanged only through lawful means, chiefly trade undertaken by the free and willing consent of both parties, so that no one is wronged or deprived of what is rightfully theirs. Placing the prohibition on killing oneself immediately after this principle links the sanctity of wealth with the sanctity of life, suggesting that both the body and one's possessions are trusts that must not be squandered through injustice or self-destruction. The closing reminder that Allah is Merciful frames these prohibitions as an expression of divine compassion, guarding believers from harm to themselves and to one another, and inviting them to conduct their economic and personal lives with mutual fairness and care.

translation: And whoever does that transgressively and wrongfully, We will certainly drive him into the Fire; and that is ever easy for Allah.
interpretation: The verse closes a passage on the rules of inheritance and the limits set by Allah (An-Nisa 4:14 context, here 4:30), warning that whoever deliberately transgresses those bounds out of hostility and injustice, consuming what is forbidden or violating what is commanded, will face the Fire. The phrase 'and that is ever easy for Allah' emphasizes that the punishment is no difficulty for Him, underscoring that no one can escape His justice and that deliberate defiance of divine limits, especially when it wrongs others, carries grave consequences. It is a call to fear the transgression that is born of arrogance and oppression rather than of ignorance or repentance.

translation: If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden from committing, We will remove from you your minor misdeeds and admit you to a noble entrance.
interpretation: The verse presents a conditional promise: steadfast avoidance of the grave transgressions God has prohibited becomes the means by which lesser faults are expiated, so that believers are not left burdened by every small failing. The reward is framed as a 'noble entrance' (mudkhalan kariman), an honorable admission into the Garden, suggesting that God's mercy honors those who keep away from what is gravest in the sight of the Lord. It encourages a balanced moral outlook: the believer should strive above all to shun the great sins, while trusting that God's forgiveness covers the ordinary shortcomings of a sincere servant who turns back to Him.

translation: And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others. For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned. And ask Allah for His bounty. Indeed, Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse forbids envious longing for what Allah has specifically granted to others, because distribution of bounties is His wisdom, not an arbitrary matter to be contested. It establishes that men and women each receive a just share matched to their own striving and earnings, so neither sex is to covet the other's portion, and it redirects the heart from comparison to asking Allah directly for His favor, since He knows all things and assigns each according to what is fitting.

translation: And for every one We have appointed heirs to what is left by parents and close relatives. And as for those with whom your oaths have bound you, give them their share. Indeed, Allah is ever Witness over all things.
