interpretation: The verse establishes that every person has rightful heirs (mawali) designated to inherit from what parents and near kin leave behind, so that inheritance is a divinely ordained entitlement rather than a matter of arbitrary custom. It then extends a gesture of provision to those bound by solemn pledges of alliance or support, who in the early community were given a portion as a recognition of their covenant, teaching that obligations sworn in good faith must be honored with concrete justice. The closing reminder that Allah is a witness over all things underscores that these distributions, both those fixed by law and those entrusted to human conscience, are observed by God, who holds people accountable for their fairness and faithfulness.

translation: Men are the protectors and maintainers of women, because Allah has given some of them more than others, and because they spend from their wealth. So righteous women are devoutly obedient, guarding in (the husband's) absence what Allah has guarded. As for those women from whom you fear disobedience, admonish them, forsake them in bed, and strike them. But if they obey you, then do not seek a way against them. Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted and Great.
interpretation: The verse establishes a principle of responsibility within the household: men bear the duty of provision and protection, grounded in both natural distinctions Allah has placed between them and the financial burden they carry, and this qualification (qiwamah) is understood as a role of care and leadership rather than domination. It describes the ideal wife as one who is devoutly obedient to Allah and faithful to her husband, guarding his honor and home in his absence through the trust Allah has entrusted to her. The graduated remedy for marital discord, beginning with advice and then temporary separation, is framed as a corrective process aimed at restoring harmony, and the verse closes by reminding husbands that if their wives return to obedience, they have no justification for further oppression, since Allah is above all and supremely great, holding them accountable for their own conduct.

translation: And if you fear a breach between the two of them, then send an arbitrator from his people and an arbitrator from her people. If they both desire reconciliation, Allah will bring about harmony between them. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Acquainted with all things.
interpretation: The verse establishes a structured, dignified mechanism for resolving marital discord before it results in separation. By requiring arbitrators drawn from both the husband's and the wife's families, it ensures that each side is represented by someone who knows the couple intimately and has a stake in their welfare, while guarding against the injustice of one party being judged by strangers or by a biased relative. The condition that the arbiters sincerely intend reconciliation shows that the process is meant to heal rather than to adjudicate blame or hasten divorce, and the promise that Allah will grant success in harmony places the human effort within a divine framework of sincerity and trust. The closing reference to Allah's knowledge and awareness reminds the parties and the arbiters that intentions are fully known to God, so that honesty in both motive and conduct is the true foundation of any reconciliation.

translation: And worship Allah and associate nothing with Him. And be good to parents, and to relatives, orphans, the needy, the neighbor who is near of kin, the neighbor who is far, the companion at your side, the wayfarer, and those whom your right hands possess. Indeed, Allah does not love one who is self-deluding and boastful.
interpretation: The verse opens with the foundation of all duties, the worship of Allah alone without any partner, and then ties faith directly to social conduct, showing that true devotion to God is made visible in kindness toward every rung of society, from the closest family to the stranger and the dependent. The graded list of recipients of goodness moves outward from kin to the orphan and the poor, then to the neighbor near and far, the companion beside you, the traveler, and those under your care, teaching that the measure of faith is how one treats those who are nearest and most vulnerable. The verse closes by naming arrogance and self-admiration as the opposite of this ethic: a person who sees himself as superior and glories over others stands outside the divine love, because pride is the inner root that severs a person from both God and fellow human beings.

translation: Those who are stingy and enjoin upon people stinginess, and conceal what Allah has given them of His bounty. And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse exposes a double failing: miserliness of the self, and the active urging of others toward it, which is compounded by concealing the blessings God has bestowed. Concealment of bounty is a form of ingratitude, since wealth and gifts are entrusted to be used rightly, and hoarding them both denies God's favor and cuts off the needy. The closing warning links this to disbelief: the one who hides God's grace and rejects its gratitude stands in denial of the Giver, and the humbling punishment reflects that the arrogance behind stinginess is itself a kind of self-abasement before wealth rather than before God.

translation: And those who spend their wealth to be seen by people and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day. And whoever has Satan as a companion, then evil is that companion.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hollowness of charity performed for display rather than for God's pleasure. Such spending is empty of sincere intention, and it flows from a heart that has turned away from faith in God and the Last Day, which is why its outward generosity cannot save its doer. The verse then makes the root of this condition plain: whoever takes Satan as an intimate friend and companion has chosen the worst of associates, for Satan's counsel leads to ostentation, stinginess, and heedlessness of the accountability that awaits. The reader is thus invited to examine the purity of their own giving and to choose righteous companions over the whispering of Satan.

translation: And what would it have cost them had they believed in God and the Last Day and spent from what God has provided for them? And God was ever Knowing of them.
interpretation: The verse turns a rhetorical question back on those who hesitate or hold back from faith and charity: their reluctance is not justified by any real loss, since belief in God and the Last Day, joined with generous spending from what God has granted, would only have benefited them. The phrase 'what would it have cost them' exposes the irrationality of refusing what is both easy and beneficial, while the closing reminder that God is fully Knowing of them signals that their inner intentions and outward conduct are not hidden from Him, so that their choices will be weighed with perfect knowledge.

translation: Indeed, Allah does not wrong even the weight of an atom; and if it is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward.
interpretation: The verse affirms the perfect justice of God, who withholds no due even in the smallest measure, and it reveals His generosity: He does not merely repay a good deed equally but multiplies it, and bestows from His own presence a vast reward. Thus the believer is invited to strive in good works, however small they may seem, trusting that none will be lost before the One who weighs every atom and amplifies every sincere act.

translation: So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and We bring you as a witness against these people?
interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Judgment as a scene of divine accountability in which every community is called to account through its own prophet, who testifies to whether he delivered the message. The rhetorical question "how then" conveys a sense of awe and dread at the reckoning that awaits, emphasizing that no one will be able to deny or evade it. By placing Muhammad as the witness over his own community, the verse elevates the Prophet's role: his testimony will be the decisive evidence against those who rejected his message, showing that the guidance he brought was clear and that the responsibility rests upon those who heard it. It also reflects the broader Qur'anic principle of a just, universal judgment in which each nation is measured against the message entrusted to it.

translation: On that Day, those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth could be leveled over them, and they will not be able to conceal from Allah any statement.
interpretation: The verse portrays the regret of the disbelievers and disobedient on the Day of Judgment, when the full reality of their situation is laid bare. Having rejected the Messenger, they will long to be swallowed up or flattened into the earth rather than face the reckoning and the exposure of their deeds. The final phrase makes clear that concealment is no longer possible: their tongues may try to deny or hide, but Allah knows every word and secret, so their attempt to hide anything before Him will be futile. The verse thus combines a warning against disobedience to the Messenger with a reminder of the absolute knowledge of God before whom nothing can be hidden.

translation: O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying, nor while in a state of major impurity, except when passing through, until you have washed yourselves. And if you are ill or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving himself, or you have had contact with women and find no water, then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it. Indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse begins by calling the believers to presence of heart before God: prayer demands a mind clear enough to understand its words, and a body and soul prepared to stand before the Lord. The outward purity it commands is a mirror of inner readiness, so that the one who prays is cleansed both in body and in awareness. Yet the verse does not leave the believer in hardship. By permitting tayammum with clean earth when water cannot be found, it shows that the purpose of the law is to keep the worshipper connected to God, not to burden him beyond his capacity. The closing names of God, 'Pardoning and Forgiving,' teach that when the servant falls short of the ideal because of illness, travel, or necessity, God's mercy meets him with ease and forgiveness.

translation: Have you not considered those who were given a portion of the Scripture? They purchase error, and they wish that you would go astray from the way.
interpretation: The verse exposes a grave moral failing among those who had received a share of divine revelation: rather than using their knowledge to guide, they trade away the guidance they possess for error, as though knowledge were a commodity to be bartered for worldly gain or status. Their desire that the believers stray reveals that their corruption is not merely personal but seeks to draw others down with them, out of envy and a wish to see the community of faith share their own condition. The verse thus warns that possessing scripture is no protection in itself; what matters is sincerity in acting upon it, and that the one who has been given knowledge bears a heavier responsibility to hold fast to the right path and not sell it cheaply.

translation: And Allah is most knowing of your enemies, and sufficient is Allah as a Protector, and sufficient is Allah as a Helper.
interpretation: The verse assures the believers that Allah, who knows their enemies completely, including their hidden plots and true intentions, does not leave them unprotected. Being sufficient as Protector (wali) and Helper (nasir) means the believers need not fear their enemies' strength or cunning, but should place their trust in Allah, who alone guards them and grants them victory. The repetition of "sufficient is Allah" emphasizes that reliance on Him alone is all the believers require, so their confidence rests not in their own power or alliances but in God's perfect knowledge and power.

translation: Among those who are Jews are those who distort words from their places and say, "We hear and we disobey," and "Hear, though you are not heard," and "Ra'ina," twisting with their tongues and attacking the religion. And if they had said, "We hear and we obey, and hear and look at us," it would have been better for them and more upright. But Allah has cursed them for their disbelief, so they do not believe except a few.
interpretation: The verse exposes a deceptive manner of speech practiced by a group among the Jews: outwardly they seem to show respect toward the Prophet, using words that sound courteous, while inwardly they intend mockery and insult, as with the ambiguous word "Ra'ina," which could be heard as a derogatory form. Their distortion of speech reflects a deeper distortion of the heart, since they hear the message but refuse to submit to it. The verse teaches that the true good lies in sincere obedience expressed plainly, and that hypocrisy in speech is a sign of spiritual corruption, which in turn brings about divine rejection and leaves faith rare among them.

translation: O you who were given the Scripture, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what is with you, before We obliterate faces and turn them back on their backs, or curse them as We cursed the companions of the Sabbath. And the command of Allah is always carried out.
interpretation: The verse addresses the People of the Book, principally the Jews, calling them to believe in the Qur'an as a confirmation of the message already in their hands, and warns them with a severe threat should they refuse. The threat of obliterating faces and turning them backward, or cursing them as the people of the Sabbath were cursed, points to the seriousness of persisting in disbelief after the truth has become clear, and to the certainty of Allah's decree, which will be executed when He wills.

translation: Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills. And whoever associates partners with Allah has certainly fabricated a tremendous sin.
interpretation: The verse singles out shirk (associating partners with Allah) as the one sin that God does not forgive if a person dies holding to it, because it breaks the very relationship of worship and acknowledgment on which all other forgiveness rests. Yet the verse also shows the vastness of divine mercy: all lesser transgressions fall under God's will to forgive, so that no sin below shirk is beyond hope for the one who turns back. The phrase 'fabricated a sin' reveals that shirk is not merely an error but an invented falsehood against the truth of creation, which is why its gravity is described as immense. The verse thus calls the believer both to fear the seriousness of associating anything with God and to hope in His forgiveness for everything else.

translation: Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves? Rather, it is God who purifies whom He wills, and they will not be wronged even by the thread of a date-palm seed.
interpretation: The verse exposes the spiritual vanity of those who publicly certify their own righteousness, piety, and moral worth, presuming to be the arbiters of their own purity. It redirects the believer's gaze from self-praise to the absolute sovereignty of God, the only true judge of who is truly purified, since inner sincerity and God's acceptance cannot be claimed by self-declaration. The closing phrase, 'not wronged even by the thread,' assures that whatever deeds and intentions are genuinely offered will not be diminished by even the smallest measure, so the believer's concern should be with sincere action before God rather than with reputation or self-justification.

translation: Look how they invent lies against Allah, and sufficient is that as a manifest sin.
interpretation: The verse exposes the gravity of attributing falsehood to Allah: it is not merely an error of opinion but a deliberate fabrication against the One who is the source of all truth, and the Qur'an declares that such a sin is itself enough to be a clear and manifest transgression. The call to 'look' directs the reader to observe the reality of this conduct, inviting reflection on how those who invent claims about God distort the religion and mislead people, while the phrase 'sufficient as a manifest sin' underscores that the very act of fabricating against Allah carries its own weight of wrongdoing, needing no further proof of its evil. It serves as a warning to believers to guard their speech about God, avoiding any ascription to Him of what He has not revealed.

translation: Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture? They believe in Jibt and Taghut, and they say to those who disbelieve, "These are better guided in the way than those who have believed."
interpretation: The verse exposes a grave inconsistency among those who possessed a share of revealed knowledge: instead of holding fast to the guidance they were entrusted with, they lend their faith to idols and false authorities, the Jibt and Taghut, and then, in a betrayal of their own trust, they flatter the disbelievers by declaring the pagans more rightly guided than the believers. The passage thus warns that knowledge of scripture without sincere adherence to its truth leads to a corrupted judgment that inverts right and wrong, valorizes falsehood, and undermines the faithful, and it addresses the believers by teaching them to recognize that worldly approval and the praise of those who reject God are no measure of the right path.

translation: Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed. And whoever Allah curses, you will not find for him any helper.
interpretation: The verse establishes that being cursed by Allah is a matter of divine judgment that no one can reverse: the cursed person, having forfeited Allah's mercy through their own persistent rejection and wrongdoing, is left without any protector or supporter. The phrase 'you will not find for him any helper' underscores that worldly alliances, tribal ties, or influence are worthless against a decree from the One who alone grants victory and support. It is a warning that true nasr (help) comes only from Allah, and that turning away from Him leaves a person utterly exposed, since the only shelter from divine curse is repentance and obedience.

translation: Or do they have a share of the kingdom? Then, they would not give the people even a speck (of a date-stone).
interpretation: The verse exposes the stinginess and selfishness of those who imagine they possess a share of divine authority or dominion. Were they to hold any such power, they would withhold even the smallest good from others, since their hearts are governed by greed and fear of losing what they have. By posing the question rhetorically and then describing the consequence, God shows the absurdity of their claim: a people so miserly in the tiniest matter could never be trusted with the kingdom, which belongs to God alone, who gives generously to whom He wills. It is a warning that true sovereignty and generosity both come from God, and that the one who clings to every speck of good in his hand reveals the poverty of his own soul.

translation: Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty? Indeed, We gave the family of Abraham the Scripture and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who begrudge others the favor Allah has granted them, reminding that such envy is misplaced because divine bounty is not withheld by human consent; the verse points to the precedent of the family of Abraham, to whom Allah gave the Book, wisdom and a mighty dominion, showing that Allah's favor is distributed by His own wisdom and that the envious should instead accept His decree and recognize that the blessings given to others do not diminish what He has given them.

translation: So among them is one who believed in it, and among them is one who turned away from it. And sufficient for those who turn away is Hell as a blazing fire.
interpretation: The verse presents the divide that the coming of a message creates among people: the same call that draws one soul to faith repels another into aversion, so that the truth itself becomes a test that sorts hearts. The phrase 'and sufficient is Hell as a blaze' is not merely a threat of punishment but a declaration that the consequence of turning away is already fixed and self-evident, as though the fire is the natural end of a heart that has chosen to shut itself off from guidance. It invites the listener to examine which of these two paths they are walking, since every person stands at the same crossroads the verse describes.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve in Our signs - We will surely burn them in the Fire. Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so they may taste the punishment. Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted in Might, Wise.
interpretation: The verse presents the punishment of those who reject God's signs as a deliberate, renewing process rather than a single event: the skin, which is the very organ that feels pain, is continually replaced so that the torment never ends and the suffering is never dulled by its own destruction. The closing names, 'Almighty' and 'All-Wise,' signal that this retribution is not arbitrary cruelty but the exercise of perfect power guided by perfect wisdom, matching each act of disbelief with a fitting consequence. The verse thus invites the listener to take seriously the gravity of denying the signs of God, and to see in the mercy of the warning an opportunity to turn back before the consequences are fixed.

translation: And those who believe and do righteous deeds - We will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. For them therein are purified spouses, and We will admit them to a shade, deep and ever-extending.
interpretation: The verse joins faith and righteous action as the two conditions for entering the gardens of Paradise, and it presents the reward as both physical and spiritual: eternal dwelling in beauty and abundance, purity in companionship, and enveloping comfort. The word "purified" suggests that the spouses are freed from every defect of this world, pointing to a relationship perfected in holiness and free from the flaws of earthly life. The closing image of a deep, lasting shade conveys protection, coolness and rest after the heat and struggles of worldly existence, so that the believer's reward is shown as complete ease, security and peace.

translation: Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts back to their rightful owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice. How excellent is what Allah instructs you. Indeed, Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing.
interpretation: The verse binds two great pillars of social order, the faithful return of what is entrusted and the justice of judgment, and grounds them in the divine gaze that hears and sees all. Trust (amanah) is understood broadly, covering not only deposits of wealth but also positions of authority, knowledge, and responsibility, all of which must be returned to those who rightfully deserve them. The command to judge with justice is addressed to anyone who arbitrates between people, so that rulings are free from favoritism, enmity, or bribery. By calling this instruction an excellent admonition, the verse presents justice and trustworthiness not as burdens imposed from outside but as the best guidance for human life, and it reminds believers that Allah's hearing and sight encompass every hidden intention behind their dealings.

translation: O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. And if you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you should be believers in Allah and the Last Day. That is better and more suitable in outcome.
interpretation: The verse establishes a framework for the believing community in which obedience is ordered and grounded: obedience to Allah is absolute and primary, obedience to the Messenger flows from it as the authoritative conveyor of divine guidance, and obedience to those in authority is bound to, and therefore limited by, the same foundation. The true locus of disputes is thus not personal preference or the will of rulers but the revealed text and the Prophetic example, so that the community's unity rests on a shared reference point rather than on power alone. The condition attached, 'if you should be believers in Allah and the Last Day,' indicates that such submission to ultimate judgment is an expression of faith itself, and that a believer's readiness to return to revelation in disagreement is a measure of genuine belief. The closing words, that this is better and fairer in its outcome, suggest that resolving conflicts by returning to God and His Messenger yields a more sound and beneficial result than resolving them through rivalry or arbitrary decision.

translation: Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, yet they desire to seek judgment from the transgressor (false judge), while they had been commanded to reject it? And Satan wants to lead them far astray.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrisy of those whose faith is only in their claims, not in their conduct: they profess belief in the revelation yet turn to a rival authority, such as a false judge or any power that stands against God's law, when disputes arise. Their behavior reveals that their profession is hollow, since true belief entails submitting to the judgment of what was revealed. The verse also shows that such a turning away is not a mere lapse of judgment but the work of Satan, who seeks to drive them into a deep and distant error, warning believers to recognize how the desire for convenient authorities can gradually lead the heart away from the truth.

translation: And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger," you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion.
interpretation: The verse exposes the inner state of the hypocrites (al-munafiqun): when they are called to submit their disputes and judgment to the revelation of God and to the Prophet, they do not respond sincerely but recoil, averting themselves from the Prophet with visible reluctance. Their outward profession of faith is thus contradicted by their conduct, since true belief is shown by willing acceptance of God's guidance and the Messenger's judgment. The verse also implies that the Prophet's authority is inseparable from the authority of revelation, so that turning away from him is in effect turning away from God's law, and it offers a timeless diagnostic: one can recognize hypocrisy by the reluctance to accept what is revealed when it runs counter to one's own interests or desires.

translation: So how will it be when a calamity strikes them because of what their own hands have sent forth, and then they come to you swearing by Allah, "We intended nothing but good and reconciliation"?
interpretation: The verse exposes a recurring human habit: when the consequences of one's own wrongdoing finally arrive, the wrongdoer rushes to cover guilt with pious language and sworn assurances of good intent. The rhetorical question "how then?" signals that their situation will be dire, because the calamity itself is traced back to their own deeds, and their oaths cannot change what their hands have done. The verse thus teaches that claims of good intention are no shield against accountability, and that a person's actions, not their professed motives, ultimately reveal the truth of their hearts.

translation: Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts, so turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them about themselves a far-reaching (eloquent and effective) word.
interpretation: The verse directs the Prophet to a mature, principled way of dealing with those whose hypocrisy or inner corruption is known to God, even though their outward conduct may conceal it. Allah, who knows the hidden intentions of hearts, does not require the Prophet to expose or punish them publicly; instead he is to turn away from their deceit without abandoning his duty, to keep admonishing them sincerely, and to address them directly in a way that penetrates their consciences. The 'eloquent word' suggests that true reform comes through speech that reaches the heart and touches the self, not through force or humiliation. The lesson extends to every preacher and reformer: deal with people according to what is apparent while leaving their inner state to God, and persist in gentle yet impactful counsel.

translation: And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by the permission of Allah. And if, when they had wronged themselves, they had come to you, [O Muhammad], and asked forgiveness of Allah and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse establishes that obedience to a messenger is not merely a human matter of following a leader, but is an obedience granted by Allah's permission, which makes the Messenger's authority a trust rooted in divine will. It then shows that when people sin against themselves, the door of return remains open: coming humbly to the Prophet, seeking forgiveness from Allah, and having the Messenger intercede for them is a path to finding Allah turning toward them in acceptance and mercy. The verse thus joins submission to the Prophet with repentance, presenting the Messenger as a means through which believers recognize their wrong and return to their Lord, while his life and presence remained a mercy to those who had transgressed.

translation: But no, by your Lord, they will not truly believe until they make you judge in what they dispute among themselves, and then find within themselves no discomfort at what you decide, and submit with full submission.
interpretation: The verse establishes that genuine faith is not merely verbal profession but requires a sincere inner acceptance of the Prophet's judgment in all disputes. Its oath by the Lord emphasizes the certainty of this principle. The phrase 'find no resistance within themselves' points to the heart being free of reluctance or resentment toward the ruling, and 'submit with full submission' shows that outward compliance must be joined by inward surrender. The occasion of revelation, traditionally linked to a dispute between a man from the Ansar and al-Zubayr over water rights, illustrates that a believer must accept the Prophet's verdict even when it goes against his own interest, so that the community is bound by justice and by willing acceptance of divine guidance as conveyed through the Messenger.

translation: And if We had decreed upon them, "Kill yourselves" or "Leave your homes," they would not have done it, except a few of them. But if they had done what they were being advised to do, it would have been better for them and stronger in firming them up (in faith).
interpretation: The verse shows that the hearts of many people are reluctant to sacrifice their lives or their homes when commanded, and that only a few would comply, which reveals how weak human resolve is when left to its own inclinations. Yet it also teaches that true good lies in obeying the admonitions that God sends through revelation, because such obedience brings a firmer, more steadfast faith and a better outcome in both this life and the next. The verse thus holds up a mirror to the weakness of the self and invites the believer to strengthen their resolve through sincere adherence to what they are advised.

translation: And if We were to give them from Us a great reward.
interpretation: The verse comes in the context of those who would have been firm in their faith and obedience had they been tested with what was asked of them, and it signals that Allah's generosity toward the sincere believer is unbounded. The phrase "from Us" (min ladunna) emphasizes that this reward is bestowed directly from the Divine presence, not merely earned through ordinary means, which elevates its dignity and magnitude. Thus the verse teaches that steadfastness in faith, even when the path is difficult, brings a recompense that surpasses human measure, and that God's gifts to the faithful are both immense and personally bestowed.

translation: And We would have guided them to a straight path.
interpretation: The verse speaks of a counterfactual: had certain people been sincere in their adherence to what they were commanded, or had they truly followed the guidance they were given, God would have granted them firm guidance along the straight path. Divine guidance is thus presented as following upon human readiness and sincere acceptance; the path is already laid out, and it is the turning of the heart toward it that brings one to walk upon it steadily.

translation: And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger - those will be with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favor of the prophets, the steadfast lovers of truth, the martyrs, and the righteous. And excellent are those as companions.
interpretation: The verse opens a path of companionship in the hereafter that is open to anyone who sincerely obeys Allah and His Messenger, showing that the highest rank is not reserved for a particular lineage or status but is reached through obedience. The four groups named form a graded ladder of excellence: prophets who receive revelation, the sincere in truthfulness who confirm it by their lives, the martyrs who give their lives for the cause, and the righteous who uphold good conduct in ordinary life. By placing the believer among them, the verse teaches that ordinary faithful people may aspire to the company of the greatest of God's servants, and that the closeness of such company, described as the best of companions, is itself the ultimate reward, so that love of the righteous and obedience to the Messenger become the means of joining them.

translation: That is the bounty of Allah, and sufficient is Allah as Knower.
interpretation: The verse closes a passage about the reward granted to those who strove in obedience and sincerity, declaring that such reward is not earned by the servant's deeds alone but is a grace (fadl) from Allah, Who extends it beyond what their works could merit. The phrase "wa kafa billahi 'alima" reassures the believer that Allah's knowledge encompasses every intention, effort, and sacrifice, so that nothing done for His sake is lost or overlooked, and that He alone suffices as the One who knows and rewards. The lesson is that a believer should neither rely on his own works in self-congratulation nor despair of the mercy of Allah, but should rest in the certainty that divine generosity surpasses human accounting.

translation: O you who have believed, take your precaution, then advance in companies or advance all together.
interpretation: The verse calls the believers to vigilance and preparedness in the face of the enemy: they must take their precautions and be fully ready, and then, as the situation demands, mobilize either in separate detachments or all together as one body. The command is not to recklessness but to a measured, strategic readiness, where the believers judge the appropriate form of going forth according to the circumstances. It teaches that faith is joined with prudence, organization, and collective responsibility, so that the community defends itself with both resolve and wise planning.

translation: And indeed, among you is one who lingers behind; so if a misfortune strikes you, he says, "Certainly Allah has blessed me that I was not present with them as a witness."
interpretation: The verse exposes the inner disposition of the hypocrites and the half-hearted who hang back from the struggle in the path of God. Their reluctance to go forth is revealed by their delight when calamity befalls the believers, for they rejoice at having escaped the hardship and danger, and their gladness is not born of faith but of self-preservation. The verse thus draws attention to the gap between outward association with the community and genuine commitment to it: a person may be physically among the believers while his heart is absent from their cause, measuring every trial by his personal safety rather than by the higher purpose that binds the community together. It is a warning that true allegiance is judged not by presence alone but by willingness to share both the hardship and the trust in God that accompanies it.

translation: And if a bounty from Allah should come to you, he would surely say, as if there had been no affection between you and him, "Oh, I wish I had been with them, so I would have attained a great attainment."
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrite who, when the believers are away fighting and are then granted victory and spoils, is not moved by fellowship with them but by envy and self-interest. Though there once was a bond of companionship between him and the believers, he severs it in his heart and speaks as if he were a stranger to them, lamenting that he was not among them to share their gain. His words reveal that his loyalty was conditional on worldly advantage, and his regret is not for the faith he lacks but for the profit he missed, showing that his attachment was to material success rather than to Allah and His cause.

translation: So let those fight in the way of Allah who sell the worldly life for the Hereafter. And whoever fights in the way of Allah and is killed or achieves victory - We will give him a great reward.
interpretation: The verse addresses those who have chosen the Hereafter over the fleeting pleasures of this world, calling them to fight in the cause of Allah. It frames the struggle as a transaction in which the believer exchanges worldly attachments for eternal reward: whether he is slain or triumphs, his recompense is a great reward from Allah. The emphasis falls on sincerity of purpose and detachment from worldly gain, so that the fighter's motive is the pleasing of God rather than worldly advantage. The verse thus ties courage in striving to a deep conviction that the outcome, whether martyrdom or victory, is ultimately secured with God.

translation: And what is [wrong] with you that you do not fight in the cause of Allah and of the oppressed among men, women, and children, who say: "Our Lord, bring us out from this city whose people are wrongdoers, and appoint for us from Yourself a protector, and appoint for us from Yourself a helper."
interpretation: The verse rebukes the believers for abandoning the defense of those who are persecuted and powerless, namely the weak men, women, and children who cry out to God for deliverance from a city ruled by oppressors. It establishes that fighting in God's cause is not merely a matter of personal conflict but a moral duty to rescue the vulnerable from injustice, and that the believers' sense of responsibility toward the oppressed is a central part of faith. The supplication of the oppressed, asking God for a protector and a helper from His own presence, shows that God's support comes to those who stand for justice, and it reminds the community that their own commitment to the helpless is tested by whether they answer such a cry.

translation: Those who believe fight in the cause of God, and those who disbelieve fight in the cause of the Taghut. So fight against the allies of Satan; indeed, the plotting of Satan is ever weak.
interpretation: The verse draws a clear line between two camps defined by their ultimate loyalty: believers struggle for the sake of God, while disbelievers fight for a false power that the Qur'an calls Taghut, meaning any object of worship or obedience beyond God. Because the cause, not the outward act of fighting, distinguishes them, the verse directs the believers to confront the agents of Satan with confidence, since the scheming of Satan, however cunning it appears, is inherently frail when set against the truth and the support of God. It thus offers reassurance to the faithful that evil's apparent strength is hollow, and it locates the moral meaning of conflict in its purpose rather than in its violence alone.

translation: Have you not seen those who were told, "Restrain your hands, establish prayer, and give zakah"? But when fighting was prescribed for them, a faction of them feared people as they should fear Allah, or even more intensely. They said, "Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You had delayed us to a near term." Say, "The enjoyment of this world is little, and the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful of Allah, and you will not be wronged even by a thread."
interpretation: The verse exposes a gap between professed faith and the inner readiness it demands. Those early believers had been ordered to restrain their hands while they were weak, and their patience was a discipline of trust in God. When the command to fight came, some were overwhelmed by fear of human enemies, a fear that equaled or surpassed their awe of God, which shows that their reverence had not yet settled in the right place. Their plea for a delayed deadline reveals a heart still attached to the comforts of this life, while the response reorients them: worldly gain is brief and fragile, whereas the reward of God-consciousness is lasting, and divine justice ensures that not even the smallest act is left unrewarded or unjustly diminished. The lesson is that fear of God must govern every other fear, and that obedience in hardship is measured by sincerity rather than by the ease of the moment.

translation: Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you should be in towers built up high. And if good comes to them, they say, "This is from Allah," but if evil befalls them, they say, "This is from you [O Prophet]." Say, "All is from Allah." So what is wrong with these people that they can hardly understand any statement?
interpretation: The verse exposes a flawed mindset that attributes blessings to God while blaming misfortune on the Prophet, revealing that their hearts are closed to the truth. By affirming that death is inescapable wherever one hides, it reminds them that no fortress can shield them from divine decree, and that both ease and hardship originate from Allah's will, whose wisdom they fail to grasp. Their inability to comprehend a plain message is thus presented as a consequence of their spiritual heedlessness rather than a lack of clarity in what is said.

translation: Whatever good reaches you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself. And We have sent you as a messenger to mankind, and Allah suffices as a witness.
interpretation: The verse teaches that every blessing a person receives is a gift from Allah alone, so gratitude and turning to Him are owed for it, while the misfortunes that come from a person's own misdeeds and errors should lead to self-examination and repentance rather than blaming fate or others. The verse then turns to the Prophet's mission, affirming that he was sent to all of humanity, and closes by assuring him that God's testimony to his truthfulness and to the message is sufficient, a reassurance against those who denied him.

translation: Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah; but whoever turns away, We have not sent you as a watcher over them.
interpretation: The verse establishes obedience to the Prophet as inseparable from obedience to God, so that submitting to the Messenger is itself submitting to Allah, since he conveys divine guidance rather than his own will. It then consoles the Prophet: his duty is delivery of the message, not compelling belief or being accountable for the choices of those who turn away, for responsibility for their faith rests with them and with God alone.

translation: And they say, "Obedience!" But when they go out from your presence, a group of them plots by night other than what you say. Allah records what they plot by night, so turn away from them and rely upon Allah. And sufficient is Allah as a Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: This verse exposes the hypocrisy of those who outwardly profess obedience to the Prophet while, in private, they conspire against his command, revealing a gap between speech and inner intention. It teaches that Allah records and knows every secret plan, so the believer need not be consumed by the schemes of such people. The Prophet is instructed to set them aside without anger or pursuit and to place his trust wholly in Allah, whose protection is sufficient against those who plot.

translation: Will they not then reflect upon the Qur'an? And had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy.
interpretation: The verse presents the consistency of the Qur'an across its length and its many themes, revelation spanning many years and circumstances, as an argument for its divine origin. Human speech, however eloquent, inevitably shows variation, contradiction, and change when produced over time and under shifting conditions, whereas the Qur'an's harmony of meaning, its sound legislation, its accurate reports, and its unified message are evidence that it comes from the One who knows all things. The verse thus calls the listener to sincere contemplation rather than heedless dismissal, since careful reflection is itself the path to recognizing its truth.

translation: When news of security or fear reaches them, they spread it around. But if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, those who can draw conclusions from it would have known it. And were it not for Allah's bounty upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan, except for a few.
interpretation: The verse addresses a habit of heedless publicity in the community: rumors about matters of safety or danger were broadcast before being verified, which can spread panic or false hope. It establishes a disciplined channel for handling public news, namely returning such matters to the Prophet and to those responsible for affairs, who possess the knowledge and judgment to discern what is true and what should be announced. The verse thus teaches that information of collective concern requires careful verification and responsible handling, and that the believers' unity and guidance depend on God's grace, without which many would have been led astray.

translation: So fight in the cause of God; you are not held responsible except for yourself. And urge the believers (to fight). Perhaps God will restrain the might of those who disbelieve; and God is stronger in might and stronger in punishment.
interpretation: The verse addresses the Prophet directly, commanding him to fight in God's way even if he must go alone, since each soul bears only its own responsibility and his duty is to deliver the message and stir the faithful to action rather than to compel the outcome. Its wording, 'perhaps God will restrain the might of those who disbelieve', reflects that victory and the restraint of enemies lie in God's hands, so the believers should act with resolve and trust, while holding in awe that God's power and retribution surpass that of any enemy.

translation: Whoever intercedes with a good intercession will have a share of it, and whoever intercedes with an evil intercession will bear a portion of it. And ever is Allah over all things Competent.
interpretation: The verse establishes that every act of mediation or advocacy among people is a moral deed for which one is accountable. Intercession is not neutral: one who supports and advances what is good, such as helping a person obtain a right, reconciling others, or encouraging righteousness, receives a share of its reward, and the good that results flows back to him. Conversely, one who lends his influence to wrongdoing, injustice, or the harming of others, whether by backing an unjust cause or shielding an oppressor, bears a corresponding share of the burden and consequence. The phrase 'kifl' suggests a weight or responsibility carried proportionately, so the verse calls believers to consider the moral direction of the causes they champion. It closes by reminding that Allah has complete power and watch over all things, so no act of advocacy, whether open or hidden, escapes His knowledge and recompense.

translation: And when you are greeted with a greeting, then greet with better than it, or return it [in kind]. Indeed, Allah is ever Accountable over all things.
interpretation: The verse establishes a principle of social courtesy grounded in accountability before God. When someone offers a greeting of peace, the believer is not merely to match it but is encouraged to respond with something finer, more generous, and more warmly expressed, and at minimum must return it equivalently. Because the greeting is an act of goodwill and a bond between people, neglecting to answer it or answering it grudgingly is a moral failing. The closing phrase reminds the believer that every word and gesture of social conduct is recorded and weighed by God, who keeps account of all things, so that even ordinary courtesies become acts of worship carrying moral consequence. The principle thus extends beyond the literal greeting to a general ethic of returning kindness with greater kindness and of treating others with dignity.

translation: Allah — there is no deity except Him. He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt. And who is more truthful in statement than Allah?
interpretation: The verse grounds the reality of the Resurrection in the absolute oneness of God: since none other than Allah possesses divinity, the One who alone is worthy of worship is also the One who holds full sovereignty over life and death, and therefore His promise to gather all people for judgment is certain. The closing question turns the certainty of this promise into a matter of trust in God's word, for no speech can surpass His in truth. The believer is thus invited to recognize that the reckoning of the Hereafter is not a matter for doubt, and that a life oriented toward the One God is the rational response to the coming gathering.

translation: So what is the matter with you that you have become two groups concerning the hypocrites, when Allah has returned them to their state of disbelief because of what they earned? Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has sent astray? And whoever Allah sends astray, you will never find for him a way.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the believers for their divided and hesitant stance toward the hypocrites, who had openly shown their disbelief by leaving the battlefield and siding with the enemy. Allah reminds them that these people's reversion into disbelief is the direct result of their own deliberate choices and inner corruption, not an accident of circumstance, so the believers should not waver in judging them. The closing lines teach that guidance belongs to Allah's will: those who persistently choose misguidance and are left by Allah to it cannot be led back by human effort, and the believers should therefore not exhaust themselves trying to guide those whose hearts have settled into hypocrisy.

translation: They wish that you would disbelieve just as they disbelieved, so that you would be equal. So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the cause of Allah. But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take from among them an ally or a helper.
interpretation: The verse reveals the hostile intent of those who had opposed the believing community: their aim was not mere coexistence but the believers' own abandonment of faith, so that all would stand on equal footing in disbelief. Friendship and alliance are therefore to be withheld from them until they demonstrate a genuine break with that hostility by migrating in the cause of God, which signifies a sincere commitment to the community of faith. The severe command applies to those who turn away and actively reject this covenant of loyalty, and it should be understood in its historical setting of armed enmity and treachery against the early Muslims, where the bond of trust could not be extended to those who were plotting their destruction.

translation: Except those who reach a people between whom and you there is a treaty, or who come to you with their hearts constricted from fighting you or fighting their own people. And if Allah had willed, He would have given them power over you, and they would have fought you. So if they remove themselves from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, then Allah has not made for you a way against them.
interpretation: This verse qualifies the harsh command of the preceding verse, which ordered that hostile enemies who turn away be seized and killed wherever found. It establishes that the permission to fight is bound to actual hostility, so those who are bound to the Muslims by a treaty, or who come to them with hearts too reluctant to fight either side, are not to be treated as enemies. The clause 'if Allah had willed, He would have given them power over you' shows that their restraint is itself a mercy from God, not a sign of the believers' strength, and so the believers should not presume on it. The closing phrase, 'Allah has not made for you a way against them,' sets down the principle that peace offered in good faith removes the justification for hostility, so that war is a defensive and conditional measure rather than a permanent state toward all non-believers.

translation: You will find others who wish to be secure from you and to be secure from their own people; whenever they are returned to temptation (to disbelief and fighting), they fall back into it. So if they do not withdraw from you, nor offer you peace, nor restrain their hands, then seize them and kill them wherever you encounter them. Those—We have given you clear authority over them.
interpretation: The verse describes a group who seek a double safety: they want assurance from the believers while also keeping security with their own tribe, by professing peace whenever it suits them, yet they are quick to revert to hostility whenever they are tempted or pressured toward it. The divine command draws a clear line: the measure of sincerity is concrete conduct, namely withdrawing from conflict, offering peace, and holding back their hands. Where those signs are absent, the believers are given explicit warrant to act decisively against such people, and the phrase "clear authority" signifies that this license rests on evident hostility rather than mere suspicion, so that the community's security is not left exposed to those who shift allegiance at will.

translation: It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake. And whoever kills a believer by mistake - then the freeing of a believing slave and a compensation (diyah) paid to his family, unless they forgo it as charity. But if the believer was from a people hostile to you, then [only] the freeing of a believing slave. And if he was from a people with whom you have a treaty, then compensation paid to his family and the freeing of a believing slave. But whoever does not find [the means], then fasting for two consecutive months - as a repentance from Allah. And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the taking of a believer's life is so grave that it is inconceivable for a believer to do it deliberately, and it limits the only excusable case to manslaughter by error, while showing that even an unintended death creates a binding obligation of atonement. The graded penalties reveal the moral logic of the law: the family of the slain and the wider community of covenant are to be compensated, and the freeing of a believing slave restores what was lost, with fasting as a substitute for those unable to afford it, so that repentance is made concrete through restitution and self-discipline. The distinction drawn between a victim from a hostile people and one bound by a treaty shows that the Qur'an does not let the sanctity of a believer's life depend on tribal enmity, yet it also recognizes the social realities of the time in calibrating the compensation. Closing with the names Knowing and Wise frames the whole ruling as an expression of divine knowledge of human frailty and of the wisdom that balances mercy with accountability.

translation: Whoever kills a believer intentionally - his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever, and Allah has become angry with him, and has cursed him, and has prepared for him a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse places the deliberate taking of a believer's life among the gravest of sins, and it does so by stressing the full weight of its consequences: the sinner is not merely punished but is subject to divine wrath and curse, and his punishment is named as eternal abode in Hell. The qualifier 'intentionally' (muta'ammidan) signals that the gravity lies in the premeditated and deliberate choice to extinguish a life that belongs to the community of faith, so that the verse directs the reader to see the sanctity of the believer's life as something whose violation the Divine Law treats with utmost seriousness. Scholars have debated whether this severity implies that such a killer is beyond forgiveness, and the wider Qur'anic message of God's mercy, together with the demands of sincere repentance and the rights of the victim's family, is generally understood to shape how this stern warning is to be read, while the verse itself leaves no doubt about the magnitude of the crime.

translation: O you who have believed, when you go forth in the cause of Allah, investigate carefully, and do not say to one who gives you [a greeting of] peace, "You are not a believer," seeking the goods of worldly life; for with Allah are abundant gains. Thus were you before, and Allah conferred His favor upon you, so investigate carefully. Indeed, Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.
interpretation: The verse commands believers to exercise deliberate care and certainty before passing judgment on others, especially in the midst of struggle and travel where the temptation to seize spoils or hasten to conclusions is strong. The one who offers the greeting of peace has already declared his submission, so to deny his faith out of worldly greed is a grave wrong; the believers are reminded that they themselves were once in a similar state and were guided by God's grace, so they should show the same patience and fairness toward others. The repeated call to investigate teaches that sincerity of heart is known only to God, and that human judgment must be tempered by mercy, justice, and awareness that God sees all actions and intentions.

translation: Those believers who sit at home, other than those with a disability, are not equal to those who strive in the cause of God with their wealth and their lives. God has preferred those who strive with their wealth and lives over those who sit at home by a degree. Yet to each God has promised the best reward, and God has preferred those who strive over those who sit at home with a great reward.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the believers are not all equal in their response to the call of striving in God's way: those who give of their wealth and their very selves for the cause of faith hold a higher rank than those who remain behind without a valid excuse. Yet the verse softens this distinction by affirming that God promises the good reward to all believers, so the difference in rank does not cancel the mercy extended to those who stayed back, and it is an exception for those truly prevented by harm, such as the disabled, who are excused entirely.

translation: (They are granted) higher ranks from Him, and forgiveness and mercy. And Allah has always been Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse closes the comparison in the preceding verses between those who strive in Allah's cause with their wealth and lives and those who remain behind without a valid excuse. It shows that the reward of the strivers is graded: first, elevated ranks that reflect the greater merit of their sacrifice; second, forgiveness that wipes away their shortcomings; and third, mercy, the enduring grace that completes their felicity. By ending with the divine names Al-Ghafur and Al-Rahim, the verse reminds believers that such rewards ultimately flow from Allah's own attributes of forgiveness and mercy rather than from the worth of their deeds alone, which should inspire both hope and humility.

translation: Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves, the angels will say, "In what condition were you?" They will say, "We were oppressed in the land." The angels will say, "Was not the earth of Allah spacious enough for you to emigrate therein?" For those, their refuge is Hell, and evil it is as a destination.
interpretation: The verse establishes that remaining in a place where one cannot practice faith or fulfill one's religious duties, while claiming helplessness, is a form of self-wronging, because God's earth is wide and emigration in pursuit of faith is always an available option. The angels' questioning at death reveals that excuses of weakness are not accepted when a person had the means to escape oppression and chose to stay in a state of negligence toward their own soul. The passage thus teaches that a believer bears responsibility to seek a setting where faith can be lived, and that those who neglect this obligation face the consequence of Hell.

translation: Except the oppressed weak among men, women, and children, who have no means and cannot find a way.
interpretation: The verse exempts from the condemnation of those who abandon emigration in the cause of faith (in the preceding verse about the angels questioning those who stayed among the polytheists while wronging themselves) those who are truly helpless: the genuinely oppressed and weak who lack the capacity to leave and have no route to guidance. Their exemption reveals that the moral judgment in Islam rests on one's real ability and opportunity; God does not hold responsible one who truly cannot act, and the phrase 'cannot find a way' shows that the duty to migrate is bound by what a person is able to do. It also highlights the mercy of God toward the vulnerable, especially women and children, who are placed alongside men as those whose circumstances must be accounted for.

translation: For those, perhaps Allah will pardon them. And Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse closes a passage about those who are excused for their failure to act because of genuine helplessness, and it expresses hope rather than certainty: 'asa' (perhaps) signals that forgiveness rests entirely with God's mercy, so the believer should neither presume upon it nor despair of it. Its ending, 'afuwwan ghafura', pairs two intensive divine names, the One who erases sins and the One who covers and forgives them, reassuring the sincere that God's pardon is abundant and that the true measure of a person is their sincere striving and intention before Him.

translation: And whoever emigrates in the cause of Allah will find on the earth many a refuge and abundance. And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to Allah and His Messenger and then death overtakes him, his reward has already become due from Allah. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse opens a door of hope for the one who abandons his homeland for the sake of his faith: far from being left without shelter, he will find in the earth wide places of refuge and an expansion of livelihood and spirit, so that migration becomes a path of liberation rather than loss. It then makes clear that the intention itself carries weight, for a believer who sets out toward Allah and His Messenger but dies before arriving still has his reward secured with Allah, since what is counted is the sincerity of the aim and not merely the completion of the journey. The closing divine names of Forgiveness and Mercy reassure the believer that Allah's generosity extends beyond what human effort can accomplish, and that the striving of a sincere heart is never wasted in His sight.

translation: And when you travel through the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer, if you fear that those who disbelieve may harm you. Indeed, the disbelievers are ever to you a clear enemy.
interpretation: The verse establishes a concession of ease for the traveling believer: the obligation of prayer remains, but its form may be shortened during journey, and the condition attached to this relief is fear of attack from those who reject faith. By tying the permission to a real danger, the verse shows that the dispensation is rooted in mercy and the removal of hardship, not in neglect of worship. Its closing reminder that the disbelievers are a manifest enemy situates the concession within the reality of hostility the early community faced, teaching that prudence and care for one's safety are compatible with devotion, and that God lightens the religious burden according to the circumstances in which people actually live.

translation: And when you are among them and lead them in prayer, let a group of them stand with you and let them take their weapons. When they have prostrated, let them go behind you, and let another group who have not yet prayed come forward and pray with you, taking their precaution and their weapons. Those who disbelieve wish that you would be heedless of your weapons and your belongings, so they could attack you in one assault. And there is no blame upon you if you put down your weapons because of rain or if you are ill, but take your precaution. Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse establishes the mode of congregational prayer in a situation of danger, where the community must remain vigilant even while worshipping. By dividing the believers into two groups, it ensures that the community's worship is never abandoned and that its defense is never neglected, teaching that faith and readiness are not opposed but joined: the believer turns to God in devotion while keeping guard against the enemy's treachery. The permission to lay down arms when rain or illness makes them burdensome shows that the law of precaution is adjusted to human capacity, while the repeated command to take one's caution reveals that vigilance itself is a form of trust in God rather than a lapse of it. The closing reference to the humiliating punishment prepared for the disbelievers underlines that the enemy's hostile designs will ultimately be frustrated by God's providence, and that the believers' safeguard lies in obeying His guidance.

translation: So when you have completed the prayer, remember God while standing, sitting, and lying on your sides. But when you are secure and at peace, establish the prayer. Indeed, the prayer has been prescribed for the believers at specified times.
interpretation: The verse teaches that remembrance of God is not confined to the formal prayer but accompanies the believer in every bodily posture and circumstance, so that the whole of life becomes an continuous act of mindfulness. By tying the ritual to fixed times and to moments of security, it shows that the discipline of prayer is meant to be carried out with composure, not in fear or haste, and that the outward structure of worship and the inward state of remembrance are meant to nourish one another.

translation: And do not weaken in pursuit of the enemy people. If you are suffering pain, then indeed they suffer pain as you suffer pain, but you hope from Allah for what they do not hope for. And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: The verse comes in the context of the aftermath of the battle of Uhud, where the believers had been wounded and were despondent. It addresses the weakness and despair that can creep in after setbacks and calls for steadfastness in pursuing the enemy. Its central lesson is that the pain both sides endure is a shared human reality, so the believers should not be distinguished by suffering alone; what sets them apart is their hope in God. Whereas the disbelievers have no assured hope of reward or victory from God for their struggle, the believers have a firm expectation of God's support, reward, and the fulfilment of His promise. The closing names of God, the All-Knowing and All-Wise, reassure the believers that their trials are governed by divine knowledge and wisdom, so that patience and resolve are rooted in trust in Him.

translation: Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth, so that you may judge between the people by what Allah has shown you. And do not be a advocate for the treacherous.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the Qur'an came with truth so that the Prophet would render judgment among people according to the guidance Allah granted him, not according to personal inclination or the wishes of others. The command 'do not be a disputant for the treacherous' warns against defending those who betray trust, even when they appear to be in the right, because a judge who is swayed to shield the dishonest corrupts justice. The verse thus binds rulers and judges to impartiality, anchoring judgment in divine revelation and protecting it from partisanship, and it teaches that the one who is known for betrayal must not be championed simply because of ties of kinship, tribe, or friendship.

translation: And seek forgiveness from Allah. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse directs the believer, even one who is already sinless in the case of the Prophet to whom it was addressed, to turn constantly to Allah in repentant seeking of forgiveness. The pairing of the command with the divine attributes of ghafur and rahim shows that the door of forgiveness is always open: the one who asks is met with Allah's abundant pardon and His compassionate mercy. It teaches that istighfar is both an act of humility, acknowledging one's shortcomings before God, and a means of drawing near to Him, since the Lord who commands it is known for forgiving and showing mercy to His servants.

translation: And do not dispute on behalf of those who betray themselves. Indeed, Allah does not love one who is constantly treacherous and sinful.
interpretation: The verse forbids a believer from pleading or arguing in defense of those who habitually act deceitfully, for in wronging others they are in truth wronging their own souls, since their treachery returns upon them. It teaches that the sincere faithful must not lend their voice to protecting persistent wrongdoers merely out of partisanship or loyalty, and that justice must take precedence over tribal or personal attachment. The closing phrase reminds that Allah's love is withheld from one who is repeatedly treacherous and persistently sinful, so that the believer's standing before God depends on uprightness rather than on advocacy for the dishonest.

translation: They hide themselves from people, yet they cannot hide themselves from Allah, for He is with them when they plot by night in speech that He does not approve. And Allah is ever encompassing of what they do.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hollowness of concealment practiced by those who scheme in secret. People may be deceived by outward appearances and hidden whispers, but the one who truly sees is Allah, who is never absent from them and knows their inner intentions as they devise words that displease Him. The verse thus calls the believer to inner sincerity, teaching that a person's conduct should be guided by awareness of God's constant presence rather than by fear of human judgment, since nothing done in darkness escapes the all-encompassing knowledge of the Creator.

translation: Here you are, those who argued on their behalf in the life of this world; but who will argue for them with God on the Day of Resurrection, or who will be their guardian?
interpretation: The verse confronts those who defended wrongdoers in worldly disputes, exposing the futility of such advocacy when the matter is weighed before God. In this world, human allies and advocates can sway judgments and appearances, but on the Day of Resurrection no one can plead on another's behalf against God's justice, and no protector remains to shield the guilty. The rhetorical question directs the listener to recognize that true reliance belongs to God alone, and that loyalty should be given to truth and justice rather than to partisan defense of falsehood.

translation: And whoever does wrong or wrongs himself and then seeks forgiveness of Allah will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse opens a door of hope that no sin can close. Wrongdoing, whether it harms others (sū') or harms the soul itself (ẓulm al-nafs), is not presented as a permanent condition or a final verdict. What decides the matter is the turning back: the sincere istighfār that follows the fault. Allah's forgiveness and mercy are described as something the believer will find, as if it were already waiting for the one who returns. The verse thus shifts the focus from the weight of past failure to the act of repentance, teaching that the gate of return remains open as long as a person lives, and that the human being's first response to sin should be humble return rather than despair.

translation: And whoever earns a sin, he earns it only against himself. And Allah is ever All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse establishes that moral responsibility is strictly personal: the consequence of wrongdoing falls upon the one who commits it, not upon another. Sin is presented as a self-inflicted burden, since each act of disobedience returns its harm to the doer's own soul, which undermines the notion of vicarious guilt or inherited blame. The closing attributes of Allah, 'All-Knowing' and 'All-Wise,' reinforce that this judgment is grounded in perfect knowledge of each person's intention and deed and in a wisdom that assigns every soul exactly what it has earned, so that no one is wronged and no injustice is done in the reckoning.

translation: And whoever earns a sin or an offense and then attributes it to an innocent person has certainly born the burden of slander and a manifest sin.
interpretation: The verse establishes that guilt cannot be shifted onto the innocent. Whoever commits a wrong and then falsely pins it on someone blameless doubles his wrongdoing: he first commits the transgression himself, then compounds it with a deliberate lie that damages another person's honor and standing. The phrase "has borne slander" conveys that he carries this weight as a heavy load, both the sin and the false accusation. The passage, revealed in connection with a case of theft where the guilty party tried to frame a Jewish man, teaches that justice requires careful truthfulness, and that false accusation is itself a grave, clearly visible sin before God.

translation: And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, a faction of them would have resolved to mislead you, but they mislead none except themselves, and they cannot harm you at all. And Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom, and taught you what you did not know. And the grace of Allah upon you has been ever great.
interpretation: The verse reassures the Prophet Muhammad that his steadfastness and the guidance he received are entirely owed to divine favour rather than his own strength, for a group among his opponents had plotted to lead him astray. Their scheme recoils upon themselves, since their deviation only destroys their own souls, and no plot can truly reach or harm the one protected by God. The verse then grounds this protection in the bestowal of the Book, wisdom, and knowledge, showing that the Prophet's sure guidance is a gift that surpasses anything he could have attained by himself, so that his trust should rest wholly on Allah's grace.

translation: There is no good in much of their secret consultation, except for those who enjoin charity, or what is right, or reconciliation between people. And whoever does that seeking the pleasure of Allah, We will give him a great reward.
interpretation: The verse reproaches the secret whispering and private conferring of people, most of which is idle, harmful, or conducive to discord and sedition, and so it strips such talk of any good. It makes a narrow exception for three kinds of speech that carry genuine benefit: urging almsgiving, enjoining what is known to be right, and mending breaches between people. The decisive condition is intention, for these acts earn their great reward only when they are done purely seeking God's good pleasure rather than for display, faction, or worldly gain. The lesson is that the value of private counsel lies not in its secrecy but in its purpose and its sincerity before God, so believers should measure their conversations by whether they build up justice, charity, and harmony.

translation: And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him and follows other than the way of the believers - We will leave him in that which he has turned to, and burn him in Hell, and evil it is as a destination.
interpretation: The verse establishes that opposition to the Prophet after the truth has become manifest is not merely a matter of error but a deliberate severance from the community of faith. Its sin lies in two linked acts: defying the Messenger, whose authority is the channel of divine guidance, and choosing a path other than that of the believers, which signals a settled preference for one's own direction over the path God has made clear. The phrase 'We will leave him in that which he has turned to' expresses a principle of divine justice: the one who turns away is granted what he has chosen, and his own orientation becomes his punishment, culminating in Hell. The verse thus ties the gravity of the consequence to the clarity of the guidance rejected, and it also serves to affirm the consensus of the believing community as a reliable guide to the meaning of revelation.

translation: Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills. And whoever associates partners with Allah has certainly strayed far astray.
interpretation: The verse establishes that shirk, associating partners with Allah, is the one sin that is not forgiven without repentance, because it breaks the very foundation of tawhid on which the relationship between the servant and the Creator rests. Its gravity lies in the fact that it misplaces worship and dignity, directing to creation what belongs only to the Creator. By placing forgiveness of all lesser sins under Allah's will, the verse keeps the believer between fear and hope: no one may presume upon divine mercy for a sin of shirk, yet no one should despair of mercy for other transgressions.
