The closing phrase describes the one who persists in shirk as having wandered into a remote and deep misguidance, far from the straight path that leads to truth and salvation.

translation: They do not invoke besides Him except female deities; and they invoke none but a rebellious devil.
interpretation: The verse exposes the emptiness of idolatry by showing that those who worship beside God are, in reality, calling upon nothing but names and images, which the pagans themselves gave feminine titles such as al-Lat, al-Uzza, and Manat, and which have no power of their own. Behind these lifeless idols, the verse reveals the true force being obeyed: a defiant Satan who continually seduces humanity away from the worship of the One God. Thus the idolater, in turning from the Creator to what is named and imagined, is in fact submitting to the influence of the devil, and the verse calls the reader to recognize that such devotion yields no benefit and only leads away from truth.

translation: Allah cursed him, and he said: "I will surely take from among Your servants a specified portion."
interpretation: The verse presents Satan's open declaration of enmity toward humanity after his expulsion from God's mercy. Having been cursed and distanced from divine grace, he vows to seize a determined share of the children of Adam, namely those who yield to his whispering and follow his desires. The phrase "a specified portion" conveys that his influence is limited and assigned, reflecting that he holds no authority over the sincere servants of God, and that his success lies only in the heedlessness and misguidance that people choose for themselves. The verse thus serves as a warning to be vigilant against the temptations that lead the heart away from its Lord.

translation: "And I will surely lead them astray, and I will arouse in them false desires, and I will command them so that they will slit the ears of cattle, and I will command them so that they will alter the creation of Allah." And whoever takes Satan as a guardian instead of Allah has certainly suffered a clear loss.
interpretation: This verse records Satan's vow, spoken after his expulsion, to misguide the children of Adam through three means: leading them astray from the truth, planting vain desires and hopes in their hearts, and commanding them to corrupt what God has established, whether by mutilating sacred animals as a pagan practice or by distorting the natural order God created. The closing sentence makes the conclusion explicit: to take Satan as a protector and ally in place of God is the gravest of losses, for it trades the eternal benefit of divine guardianship for a deception that ends in ruin. The passage thus reveals that the greatest harm lies not in Satan's power itself but in human willingness to follow him.

translation: He promises them and arouses their desires, but Satan does not promise them except as delusion.
interpretation: The verse exposes the nature of Satan's enticement: his promises are hollow and aim only to lure people into false hopes and heedlessness. Promising and raising expectations are the tools by which he draws the human soul away from the truth, so a believer must test every promise against what God has revealed, recognizing that what is sweet in appearance may be a deception that leads to loss.

translation: Those - their abode is Hell, and they will find no escape from it.
interpretation: The verse closes the account of those who, having wronged themselves by abandoning their flight from the Prophet's cause or by refusing to migrate when able, are left without excuse. Its wording is deliberate: 'maawahum' (their refuge or home) is turned into a grim irony, since the one who sought shelter in worldly ties and fear finds that his final dwelling is Hell itself. The phrase 'wa la yajiduna 'anha mahisa' stresses the total closure of every path of escape, for 'mahis' denotes a place of turning aside or a way out. The lesson drawn is that the true refuge is in obedience to God, and that worldly pretexts offer no protection on the Day of Reckoning.

translation: And those who believe and do righteous deeds - We will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. The promise of Allah is true, and who is more truthful in statement than Allah?
interpretation: The verse joins faith and righteous action as inseparable: belief alone, when it is not expressed in deeds, does not complete the promise, and deeds without faith lose their foundation. It presents Paradise not as a reward earned by the believer's effort alone but as a divine promise whose certainty is affirmed by God's own truthfulness, so that the believer's hope rests on the reliability of the One who makes the promise. The repeated emphasis on eternity (khalidina fiha abadan) conveys that the blessings of the Hereafter are free from the decline, loss, and anxiety that mark worldly attainments. The closing rhetorical question directs the heart away from doubting any other word and toward trusting God's speech above all speech.

translation: It is not by your wishful thinking, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Scripture. Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it, and he will not find for himself, besides Allah, any protector or any helper.
interpretation: The verse dismantles the illusion that salvation rests on mere desire, lineage, or group affiliation, whether claimed by the Muslims or by the Jews and Christians who boasted of being God's chosen. True standing before God is determined by one's actions: every wrongdoing carries its consequence, and no one can escape it by relying on a protector, intercessor, or community other than God. It calls the believer to sincere deeds rather than empty expectations, and to a humble accountability that leaves no room for complacency about one's own status.

translation: And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise and will not be wronged even by the amount of a naqir (a speck or the tiny mark on a date-pit).
interpretation: The verse establishes that salvation and entry into Paradise depend on faith combined with righteous action, not on gender; men and women are judged by the same standard and receive the same reward. The phrase 'they will not be wronged even a naqir' affirms the absolute justice of God, who will not diminish the smallest good deed. It thus conveys both the equality of the sexes before God in matters of reward and the assurance that no good work, however small, is lost.

translation: And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah while being a doer of good, and follows the creed of Abraham, inclining away from falsehood to truth; and Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend.
interpretation: The verse raises the standard of religion above lineage, ritual display, or mere claims by joining three inseparable qualities: sincere surrender of the whole self to God (aslama wajhahu), practical excellence in conduct (ihsan), and faithful adherence to the pure monotheism of Abraham, who turned away from every false deity. Its climax, that God 'took Abraham as a khalil,' shows that the highest religious rank is not earned by the prestige of community but by a heart wholly directed to God and a life that embodies goodness. The mention of the 'intimate friendship' of Abraham thus becomes a model: whoever imitates his sincerity and righteousness is brought near to the same divine favor, which is why the verse answers the People of the Book's claims of superiority by pointing to the essence of faith rather than to the external identity of a group.

translation: And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and ever is Allah, of all things, Encompassing.
interpretation: The verse affirms the absolute ownership and dominion of Allah over everything in the cosmos, the heavens and the earth alike, so that nothing escapes His possession. It then points to the reach of His knowledge and power: He is muhit, encompassing all things, meaning that nothing is hidden from His knowledge, nothing lies beyond His control, and no created thing can exist outside the sphere of His will. The believer is thereby led to recognize that all creation stands wholly under the sovereignty of its Creator, and that this comprehensive mastery is a ground for reliance upon Him, for fearing Him in private and public alike, and for turning to Him in all circumstances.

translation: They ask you for a ruling concerning women. Say: 'Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, and [also] what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women to whom you do not give what has been prescribed for them, while you desire to marry them, and concerning the helpless among the children, and that you stand firm for orphans with justice. And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is ever Knowing of it.'
interpretation: The verse exposes a corrupt motive that the guardian must abandon: a man who holds an orphan girl under his care may withhold her rightful inheritance and dowry while keeping her to himself, either out of greed for her wealth or desire for her beauty, rather than marrying her justly or releasing her to a better match. Allah makes clear that this exploitation is wrongdoing, and He restates the duty to uphold justice for orphans, including the weakest children, so that protection of the vulnerable is tied to fairness in property and in marriage. The closing reminder that Allah knows every good deed encourages sincere, unseen righteousness toward the orphan, since no act of kindness or justice toward the powerless is lost before Him.

translation: And if a woman fears ill-treatment or aversion from her husband, there is no blame upon them both if they make a settlement between themselves; and settlement is best. And souls have been made present to stinginess. But if you do good and fear God, then indeed God is ever Aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse opens a door to reconciliation within the marriage at the very moment strain appears, treating the wife's apprehension of her husband's nushuz (hostility or neglect) or i'rad (turning away) not as a cause for immediate rupture but as a situation that can be healed by mutual concession. The phrase 'there is no blame upon them both' removes the fear of sin from seeking peace, and the declaration that settlement is best establishes peace as the preferred course over separation. The sentence 'souls have been made present to stinginess' explains why compromise is hard: human nature inclines toward holding back one's rights and comforts, so reconciliation requires each party to overcome that self-interest. The closing call to doing good and piety ties the domestic matter to the wider ethic of God-consciousness, reminding believers that God observes their intentions and conduct in these private relationships.

translation: And you will never be able to be equitable between wives, even if you should strive to do so. So do not incline completely [toward one] and leave her [as if] suspended. And if you amend your conduct and fear Allah, then indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse recognizes a human limit: complete emotional equality between co-wives lies beyond a person's power, since the heart is not fully within one's control, so the Qur'an does not demand the impossible. What it does demand is that a man not abandon himself entirely to his preference for one wife, leaving the other neglected and suspended as if neither married nor free. The duty thus lies in outward justice in what is within one's capacity, such as provision, shelter, companionship and time, while avoiding deliberate, total partiality. The closing call to set things right and to be conscious of God, with the assurance of divine forgiveness and mercy, shows that God accepts sincere effort and repentance for lapses in what lies beyond human control.

translation: And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance. And Allah is ever All-Encompassing, Wise.
interpretation: The verse speaks of the reality that when a marriage cannot be sustained and the spouses part ways, this should not be feared as a catastrophe that leaves one destitute. Allah's provision is vast and does not depend on the marital bond; He can grant each party sufficiency and a better condition from His boundless bounty. The divine attributes of being Vast (wasi') and Wise (hakim) assure the believer that the separation is within God's knowing and wise ordering, so that trust in Him replaces anxiety over what remains after the union has ended.

translation: To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And We have certainly instructed those who were given the Scripture before you, and [it is] you [as well]: fear Allah. But if you disbelieve, then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And ever is Allah Free of need and Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse grounds the command to piety in the absolute sovereignty of God: since all that exists belongs to Him, He has no need of the obedience of His creatures, and the charge to fear Him is a mercy directed at humanity rather than a benefit to Him. The mention that earlier communities received the same charge shows that the call to taqwa is a continuous thread across revelations, and that the Muslim community inherits this covenant. The warning that disbelief does not diminish God in any way places the responsibility for rejection squarely on the one who rejects, turning the reader's attention inward toward moral accountability before a Lord who is self-sufficient and worthy of all praise.

translation: And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: The verse closes a passage by reminding the believer that absolute ownership and dominion over everything in the heavens and the earth belong to Allah alone. Since all things are His, nothing escapes His knowledge or power, and no creature can truly stand as a protector or ultimate authority over another. The word 'wakīl' conveys one who is entrusted with affairs and who manages them perfectly, so the verse teaches that a person should place full reliance upon Allah, for the One who owns all things is also the One fully capable of guarding, directing, and sustaining the affairs of those who trust in Him. Thus, the reference to universal possession becomes the foundation for tawakkul: the heart is freed from fear of creatures and anxiety over worldly outcomes, because the Owner of the heavens and the earth is sufficient as a trustee and guardian.

translation: If He wills, He can remove you, O people, and bring others (in your place). And Allah is ever capable of doing that.
interpretation: The verse reminds humanity that their continued existence and position are entirely at the discretion of God, who is able to replace them with another people at any time. It is a warning against arrogance and complacency: the favours granted to a community are not a permanent possession but a trust that can be withdrawn, and God's power to substitute one people for another is effortless and absolute. Faithfulness and obedience are therefore the only secure basis for a people's standing before Him.

translation: Whoever desires the reward of this world, then with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter. And Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the true reward is in Allah's hands, and a person's aim determines what they seek from Him. One who sets his sights only on worldly gain should recognize that Allah holds both worlds, so the Hereafter is available to whoever desires it, and worldly provision is not beyond His power to give. Since Allah hears every word and sees every intention, a person's striving, whether for this life alone or for the Hereafter, is known and weighed by Him. The verse thus calls the believer to examine his intention and to direct his effort toward the reward that endures.

translation: O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives. Whether one is rich or poor, Allah is more entitled to both of them. So do not follow [your own] desire, lest you deviate. And if you distort [your testimony] or refuse to give it, then indeed Allah is ever, with what you do, Acquainted.
interpretation: The verse establishes justice as an unconditional duty of believers, binding even when it runs against one's own interests, family bonds, or social standing. It shows that the judge or witness must not let wealth or poverty sway the verdict, since God's care for both the rich and the poor exceeds that of any human advocate. The root of injustice is identified as following whim and desire, which quietly steers a person away from fairness, so true justice requires the inner discipline to resist one's own inclinations. Finally, the warning against twisting testimony or withholding it makes clear that God, who is fully aware of every act, will hold a person accountable for the integrity of their witness.

translation: O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger and the Book He has sent down upon His Messenger and the Scripture He revealed before. And whoever disbelieves in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day has certainly strayed far astray.
interpretation: The verse addresses those who already profess faith and calls them to a deepened, continuous and comprehensive belief rather than a partial or merely nominal one. Faith here is presented as a unified whole: belief in God must be accompanied by belief in His Messenger, in the revelation given to him, and in the earlier scriptures that came before, since all of them proceed from one divine source and form one continuous guidance. The verse then shows that belief is not divisible at will, for rejecting any single pillar, whether God, His angels, His books, His messengers, or the Last Day, undermines the entire structure of faith, and the resulting error is described as a deep and distant straying from the path of truth.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and then disbelieve, then believe and then disbelieve, and then increase in disbelief - Allah will not forgive them, nor will He guide them to a path.
interpretation: The verse describes a state of persistent wavering in which a person repeatedly professes faith and then retracts it, moving back and forth until disbelief becomes entrenched and grows stronger. Because the cycle of belief and apostasy is not a sincere turning toward God but a pattern of hypocrisy and rejection, the door of forgiveness and divine guidance is closed to them. The lesson is that faith must be genuine and steadfast; repeated abandonment of it hardens the heart, and the one who keeps increasing in unbelief distances himself from the very guidance he has been offered.

translation: Give the hypocrites the good news that there is a painful punishment awaiting them.
interpretation: The verse (An-Nisa 4:138) addresses those who outwardly profess faith while concealing disbelief in their hearts, and it employs the rhetorical device of irony by calling their punishment "good news" (bishshir), the very term normally reserved for glad tidings to believers. This reversal exposes the hypocrites' condition: their deceit leaves them without the protection of true faith, and the painful torment that awaits them is the consequence of their duplicity. The verse thus warns that outward conformity without sincere belief in God offers no shelter on the Day of Judgment, and it implicitly calls the believer to inner sincerity, since God knows what is concealed in the breasts.

translation: Those who take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Do they seek honor with them? Indeed, all honor belongs to Allah.
interpretation: The verse exposes the inner motive behind taking disbelievers as protectors and friends in preference to the believers: a search for power, status, and security in the eyes of those who hold worldly dominance. It corrects this by declaring that true honor ('izzah) is not found in the favor of the powerful or in alliances of convenience, but belongs wholly to God, so that the believer who seeks esteem must seek it from Him alone. Such a reorientation of loyalty, the verse implies, frees the believer from dependence on the strength of others and anchors his dignity in his relationship with the One who holds all power.

translation: And it has already been revealed to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah being rejected and mocked, do not sit with them until they engage in a different conversation. Indeed, in that case you would be like them. Indeed, Allah will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers together in Hellfire, all of them.
interpretation: The verse establishes a clear ethical boundary for the believer: presence in gatherings where divine revelation is denied and ridiculed is itself a form of complicity, because sitting silently and enduring such mockery normalizes it and places the listener on the same footing as its perpetrators. The phrase "you would be like them" indicates that moral responsibility is shared by those who witness blasphemy and remain passive, not only by those who utter it. The believer is thus called to withdraw from such discourse and to honor the sanctity of God's signs, while the closing warning reminds that hypocrisy and disbelief, which often appear together in such settings, will be gathered and judged together.

translation: Those who wait and watch you: if a victory comes to you from God, they say, "Were we not with you?" and if the disbelievers have a share, they say, "Did we not gain mastery over you and protect you from the believers?" So God will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection, and God will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites (al-munafiqun) who hover between the believers and the disbelievers, positioning themselves to benefit from whichever side prevails. When the Muslims win, they claim loyalty to show they deserve a share of the gains; when the disbelievers gain ground, they claim they had protected the disbelievers from the believers, seeking favor from both camps. Their double-dealing reveals that their allegiance is driven by worldly calculation rather than sincere faith. The verse then consoles the believers: the ultimate judgment belongs to God on the Day of Resurrection, and His decree ensures that the disbelievers will never be granted a decisive dominion over the believers, so the believers should not be dismayed by temporary setbacks.

translation: Indeed, the hypocrites try to deceive Allah, but it is He who deceives them. And when they stand up to prayer, they stand lazily, showing off to the people, and they do not remember Allah except a little.
interpretation: The verse exposes the inner emptiness of hypocrisy: those who outwardly profess faith while concealing disbelief imagine they can outwit God, yet their scheme returns upon themselves, since God lets them persist in their self-deception and withholds from them the light of guidance. Their prayer, the clearest test of sincere devotion, reveals their true state, for they rise to it reluctantly, not out of longing for God but to be seen by others. Their remembrance of God is so scant that it hardly deserves the name, and the verse thus teaches that outward religious performance divorced from sincere intention and heartfelt remembrance is worthless before God, and that the believer must examine whether worship is for God alone.

translation: Wavering between that, belonging neither to these nor to those. And whomever Allah leaves astray, you will never find for him a way.
interpretation: The verse portrays the hypocrites as people suspended in an unstable middle state, unable to commit wholeheartedly either to the believers or to the disbelievers, so that their inner doubt keeps them drifting between two camps. Their wavering is not a neutral position but a spiritual condition that leaves them without a firm path. The closing statement shows that when Allah leaves a person to the direction he has chosen for himself, no guidance can reach him, because guidance follows sincere seeking and a genuine turning toward the truth. The verse thus warns that indecision in faith is itself a form of straying, and that a person who refuses to commit to clarity ultimately closes the way to guidance upon himself.

translation: O you who have believed, do not take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Do you wish to give Allah a clear proof against yourselves?
interpretation: The verse warns the believers against adopting the disbelievers as their closest friends, protectors, and confidants in place of fellow believers, since such alliance weakens the loyalty owed to the community of faith and draws the heart away from it. It then turns the question into a rebuke: by befriending those who oppose God, the believers would be handing Him a manifest justification against themselves, that is, giving grounds for accountability, because their conduct would evidence a clear departure from what they professed. The interpretation thus ties sincere faith to a clear, visible loyalty that the outward conduct of a believer must reflect.

translation: Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire, and you will not find for them any helper.
interpretation: The verse places hypocrisy among the gravest of spiritual conditions, for the hypocrite outwardly professes faith while concealing disbelief within, and so deceives both others and himself. By declaring that such people occupy the lowest level of the Fire, the verse indicates that their punishment is severe precisely because their duplicity corrupts the trust on which a community of faith depends. The closing phrase, that no helper will be found for them, teaches that the alliances, reputation, and worldly protection they relied upon will fail them on the Day of Judgment. It is a warning to every believer to examine the sincerity of his inner intention, since outward conformity without true faith offers no refuge before God.

translation: Except for those who repent, make amends, hold fast to Allah, and make their religion sincerely for Allah. Those are with the believers, and Allah will soon give the believers a great reward.
interpretation: The verse opens an exception for those who turn back from wrongdoing, a turning that is shown in action through reform and is anchored in holding fast to Allah and making the religion purely His. Their sincerity of intention is what distinguishes them, so that their being counted among the believers is not merely a claim of belonging but a status earned by genuine repentance and reform. The closing promise of a great reward for the believers, stated in the future tense, reassures the one who has erred that the door back to Allah remains open, and that the path of return leads not to disgrace but to honor and a place among the faithful.

translation: What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe? And Allah is ever Appreciative and All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse reveals that Allah's punishment is not an end in itself nor something He seeks out of spite or need; it is a consequence of persistent ingratitude and disbelief, which people bring upon themselves. When a servant turns to gratitude for the blessings received and faith in their Giver, the reason for chastisement disappears, and Allah's response is one of appreciation, since He rewards the sincere even for small good deeds. The closing names, Shakir and 'Alim, assure the believer that his gratitude is recognized and that Allah knows the true state of every heart, so that faith and thankfulness are the path by which a person is spared punishment and drawn near to his Lord's mercy.

translation: Allah does not like the public mention of evil in speech, except by one who has been wronged. And Allah is ever Hearing and Knowing.
interpretation: The verse sets a clear ethical boundary on speech: harsh, evil words spoken openly are disliked by God, and the only exception is the wronged person who is permitted to voice a grievance, since the injustice he suffered justifies complaint. The closing divine attributes of hearing and knowledge serve as a reminder that God perceives every word, whether spoken aloud or hidden, so believers should guard their tongues and let the pursuit of justice, rather than vindictive slander, govern how they speak of others' wrongs.

translation: If you disclose a good deed or conceal it, or pardon an evil, indeed Allah is ever Pardoning and All-Powerful.
interpretation: The verse teaches that God measures human conduct not only by outward acts but by the spirit behind them, and it invites believers to imitate His own attributes in their dealings. Whether a good deed is made public or kept hidden, its worth lies in sincerity, and the Qur'an places the act of pardoning a wrong on the same elevated plane as doing good, since forgiveness is a power that flows from strength rather than weakness. By closing with the names 'Pardoning' and 'All-Powerful,' the verse links the believer's capacity to forgive with the divine capacity to forgive while being able to punish, showing that clemency is most admirable when it comes from one who has the ability to retaliate. The passage thus reshapes the ethics of the community toward openness in good, discretion in charity, and generosity in overlooking injury.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers, and wish to make distinction between Allah and His messengers, and say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others," and desire to adopt a way in between—
interpretation: The verse exposes a subtle form of disbelief that does not openly reject faith but selectively accepts it according to personal preference. Faith in Allah cannot be separated from faith in His messengers, since accepting the message of Allah requires accepting all that He sent through those He chose to convey it. By dividing the prophets into those to be accepted and those to be rejected, such people treat revelation as a matter of desire rather than submission, and thereby reveal that their belief is in fact a rejection of the divine guidance as a whole. The verse thus warns that true faith is comprehensive and unconditional, and that a middle path between belief and disbelief is no path at all.

translation: Those are the disbelievers in truth, and We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse closes the passage on those who reject God and His messengers by affirming with emphasis ("haqqan," truly) that such people are the real disbelievers, meaning their disbelief is not a superficial or doubtful matter but a settled and genuine rejection. The phrase "We have prepared" (a'tadna) expresses that the punishment is already readied and certain, not merely a future possibility. The qualifier "humiliating" (muhin) indicates that the chastisement is not only painful but also degrading, matching the arrogance they showed toward divine guidance: those who refused to bow before the truth are repaid with a punishment that strips them of honor. The sequence thus pairs the reality of their condition with the certainty and fitting nature of its consequence.

translation: And those who believe in Allah and His messengers and do not make distinction between any of them - those, He will give them their rewards. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse identifies true faith as a unified commitment: belief in Allah must be accompanied by belief in all His messengers without selecting some and rejecting others, since all of them carry the same message from the same God. Its promise of reward is tied to this inclusive faithfulness, and the closing divine names of Forgiveness and Mercy show that Allah treats sincere believers with pardon for their shortcomings and with generous compassion, so the believer is invited to hold a faith that is comprehensive, humble, and free from partisan division in religion.

translation: The People of the Scripture ask you to bring down to them a book from the heaven. But they had asked Moses for greater than that, when they said, "Show us Allah openly," so the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing. Then they took the calf [for worship] after clear proofs had come to them, and We pardoned that. And We gave Moses clear authority.
interpretation: The verse exposes the recurring pattern of the People of the Scripture: their demands for miraculous signs are not born of sincere seeking but of stubborn defiance, as their ancestors' requests to Moses show, since they asked for the impossible sight of God and were struck for their presumption. Their history of rejecting clear proofs, culminating in the calf worship despite manifest evidence, is set forth as a warning to the Prophet's community that persistence in disbelief after clarity is the true sickness, while God's pardon of that sin and the clear authority given to Moses affirm that divine guidance was never lacking, only the will to accept it.

translation: And We raised above them the mountain by their covenant, and We said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating," and We said to them, "Do not transgress in the Sabbath," and We took from them a solemn covenant.
interpretation: The verse recalls the Children of Israel's binding covenant with God, sealed by the lifting of Mount Sinai (al-Tur) over them, a dramatic sign that compelled them to accept the commandments. Their entry through the gate in humble prostration was meant to express gratitude and submission, and the prohibition regarding the Sabbath tested their obedience in matters of observance. The phrase "a solemn covenant" underscores that this was no casual agreement but a weighty, binding trust between them and God, whose breach would bring accountability. The passage thus highlights a recurring theme in the Qur'an: divine favor and guidance are accompanied by responsibility, and the people's failures to honor their pledges are a warning to later generations to remain faithful to what they have promised God.

translation: So, because of their breaking their covenant, and their disbelief in the signs of God, and their killing of the prophets without right, and their saying, "Our hearts are uncovered" (i.e., sealed away from understanding). Nay, God has sealed them for their disbelief, so they do not believe, except a few.
interpretation: The verse traces the spiritual decline of the Children of Israel to a chain of causes: breaking their solemn covenant with God led to rejecting His signs, and that rejection culminated in killing His messengers unjustly. Their boast that their hearts are closed to admonition is answered by the verse's declaration that God has set a seal upon their hearts as a consequence of their persistent disbelief, not as an excuse for it. Thus the hardening of the heart is presented as the outcome of repeated choice, and only a small remnant among them retains the capacity for faith.

translation: And for their disbelief and their uttering against Mary a tremendous slander.
interpretation: The verse places the charge against Mary within a list of the Children of Israel's transgressions, showing that their rejection of divine signs culminated in a grave false accusation against the chaste mother of Jesus. Their 'great slander' (buhtan 'azim) is the accusation of unchastity, which the Qur'an elsewhere answers by affirming Mary's purity and her miraculous conception. The phrasing underscores that slander against the pure, especially one chosen and honored by God, is itself a severe sin, and that the people's disbelief led them into this serious wrong.

translation: And [for] their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the messenger of Allah" - but they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them. Indeed, those who differ concerning it are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption. And they did not kill him for certain.
interpretation: The verse denies the claim of the Jews that they killed Jesus, showing that the crucifixion was not a real event for him but a matter of apparent resemblance, a figure made to seem like him to his enemies. The disagreement among people over his fate is rooted in uncertainty rather than knowledge, since their claims rest only on conjecture. By stressing that they killed him not with certainty, the verse directs the believer away from disputed narratives toward what God has revealed, and it affirms that God protected His messenger from the humiliation his opponents sought to inflict upon him.

translation: Nay, Allah raised him up to Himself. And Allah is ever Exalted in Might, Wise.
interpretation: The verse affirms, in response to the claim that Jesus was crucified and killed, that Allah took him up to Himself in a manner beyond human perception, honoring and preserving him from his enemies' plot. The closing divine names, Al-'Aziz (the Almighty, who cannot be overcome) and Al-Hakim (the All-Wise, whose acts are perfectly ordered), indicate that the rejection of the crucifixion lies within Allah's power and wisdom: no one can thwart His will, and His decrees are never without purpose. The passage thus stands as a reminder that worldly appearances can mislead, while divine judgment and protection remain certain.

translation: And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in him before his death. And on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them.
interpretation: The verse speaks of the People of the Scripture, Jews and Christians, and the reference to 'him' is most commonly understood as Jesus, peace be upon him. Its meaning is that at the moment of death, when the veil of this world is lifted and the truth becomes plain, every person of the Book will recognize Jesus as the servant and messenger of God and will believe in him; yet that belief will come too late to benefit them, as belief at the time of death is not accepted. Some exegetes read the pronoun as referring to the Prophet Muhammad or to the coming of Jesus before the Last Hour, in which case the verse points to a universal acknowledgment at the end of time. The verse closes by affirming that on the Day of Resurrection Jesus will bear witness against those who denied him and distorted his message, so that their own admission of the truth will stand as a testimony against them.

translation: So, because of the wrongdoing of those who became Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them, and because of their frequent turning away from the way of Allah.
interpretation: The verse shows that the prohibition of certain good things upon the Children of Israel was not arbitrary but a consequence of their own injustice and persistent obstruction of others from the path of God. Their wrongdoing closed to them what had been permitted, teaching that disobedience and turning people away from guidance bring about the loss of blessings that were once within reach. It is a warning that divine restrictions often mirror the moral choices of a people, and that the harm of one's transgression extends beyond oneself to those who are led astray.

translation: And [due to] their taking of usury although they had been forbidden from it, and their consuming of people's wealth unjustly. And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse links two sins, usury and the unjust consumption of others' property, and shows that the Jews' transgressions were not merely ritual lapses but serious violations of justice in economic dealings. By stressing that they had been explicitly forbidden, it establishes that their wrongdoing was deliberate, and it implies that the punishment following from it is a consequence of persistent disobedience rather than ignorance. The phrase 'among them' limits the threatened painful punishment to those who persisted in disbelief, suggesting that the divine judgment is tied to a combination of economic injustice and rejection of the message. The verse thus teaches that wealth gained through exploitation, particularly through interest, is a grave moral offense that carries spiritual consequences.

translation: But those firm in knowledge among them, and the believers, believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you. And the establishers of prayer, and the givers of zakah, and those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, those We will give a great reward.
interpretation: The verse distinguishes the people of deep, rooted knowledge among the People of the Book from those who merely hold to inherited religion. Their firmness lies in accepting the continuity of revelation without reducing it to tribal loyalty or selective belief, so they affirm the Qur'an and the earlier scriptures together as one divine guidance. The sudden turn to prayer and zakah shows that true faith is not proven by claims of knowledge or lineage but by its fruits: devotion to God in worship and generosity toward others. Belief in God and the Last Day completes this picture, tying inward conviction to outward conduct, and the promise of a great reward is extended to whoever embodies this integrated faith, regardless of origin.

translation: Indeed, We have revealed to you, as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him. And We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Descendants (tribes), and Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon, and to David We gave the Psalms.
interpretation: The verse places the revelation given to Muhammad within one continuous chain of divine guidance running from Noah through the prophets to Jesus, establishing that the message is not a novelty but the same essential revelation entrusted to earlier messengers. By naming the prophets together, it affirms their unity of purpose and their common source, so that believers in Muhammad's message are reassured of its authenticity and are invited to recognize the shared origin of all scripture. The mention of David's Psalms as a gift shows that divine scripture took many forms, and that the diversity of books and communities does not divide the one message of worship and submission to God.

translation: And messengers We have already related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you. And Allah spoke to Moses directly, speaking [to him].
interpretation: The verse affirms that Allah sent many messengers, some whose accounts He has revealed to the Prophet Muhammad and others whose accounts He has not, so that the Prophet should not feel that his mission is unprecedented or that he alone bears the burden of prophethood. By singling out Moses, to whom Allah spoke directly without intermediary, the verse highlights a unique and intimate form of divine communication, showing that the divine word has been conveyed to prophets in varied ways, and reminding the listeners that revelation and prophecy are a continuous chain, with Moses's special closeness to God exemplifying the honor granted to some messengers over others.

translation: Messengers bearing good news and warning, so that people would have no argument against God after the messengers. And God is ever Mighty and Wise.
interpretation: The verse presents the sending of messengers as an act of divine mercy that removes any excuse people might offer on the Day of Judgment. Their dual mission, to bring glad tidings to those who believe and to warn those who deny, establishes a clear moral and spiritual framework, so that guidance is conveyed before accountability begins. The closing attributes of might and wisdom point out that this order is not arbitrary: God's power is joined with perfect wisdom, so that every sent message is part of a deliberate plan that holds humanity responsible only after the truth has truly reached them.

translation: But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you. He sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness too. And sufficient is Allah as a witness.
interpretation: The verse comes in response to the disbelievers who denied that the Prophet Muhammad was truly sent, or who refused to accept what was revealed to him. Allah answers their denial by affirming that the Qur'an is His own revelation, descended with His perfect knowledge, so it is not the invention of a man. Testimony of this kind carries the highest weight, since the Creator Himself and the angels, the messengers of revelation, bear witness to its truth. The phrase 'sufficient is Allah as a witness' assures the Prophet that his mission does not depend on the approval of his opponents, because the testimony of God outweighs all denial. The verse thus establishes that the authenticity of the message rests on divine attestation rather than on human acceptance, and it offers comfort to the believer who sees the truth rejected.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve and turn others away from the way of Allah have certainly strayed into a far-reaching error.
interpretation: The verse identifies a double offense: disbelief in one's own heart and the active obstruction of others from the path of God. The phrase 'وصدوا عن سبيل الله' shows that the harm is not confined to the individual's own unbelief but extends to barring others from guidance, which deepens the gravity of their error. The description 'ضلالا بعيدا' conveys a deviation so remote that it is difficult to return from, suggesting that the distance between such people and the truth grows with each act of obstruction. The verse thus warns that disbelief becomes more perilous when it is coupled with hostility toward the guidance that might save others.

translation: Indeed, those who have disbelieved and wronged [themselves or others] — Allah would never forgive them, nor would He guide them to a path.
interpretation: The verse establishes that persistent disbelief combined with injustice closes the two doors of divine mercy: forgiveness and guidance. Its emphasis lies on the word 'ليغفر' and 'ليهديهم' with the negation 'لم يكن', which signals that this is not merely a temporary state but a settled condition, the outcome of a soul that has persisted in rejecting the truth and in wronging itself and others. The verse thus reads as a warning that guidance is granted to those who seek it, and that the obstinate refusal of truth combined with oppression removes a person from the path that leads to God's forgiveness.

translation: Except the road of Hell, abiding therein forever. And that is ever easy for Allah.
interpretation: The verse, spoken of those who have wronged themselves by disbelief and by refusing the truth, closes the door of every escape except the road to Hell, where they will remain eternally. The phrase 'and that is ever easy for Allah' emphasizes that this fate is no burden or difficulty for God: His power is absolute, and the punishment and the sustained abiding in it follow effortlessly from His justice, so that the wrongdoers are left with no hope of relief, and the reader is reminded that nothing is beyond His ability to fulfill His decree.

translation: O mankind, the Messenger has certainly come to you with the truth from your Lord, so believe; it is better for you. But if you disbelieve, then indeed to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and Allah is ever All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse addresses all of humanity directly, establishing that the Prophet Muhammad brought the truth from their Lord, so faith is presented as the path of their own good. Disbelief does not diminish Allah's sovereignty, since everything in the heavens and earth belongs to Him alone; rather, the consequence of rejecting faith falls upon the disbelievers themselves. The verse closes by affirming Allah's perfect knowledge and wisdom, meaning that His judgment and dealings with people are grounded in full awareness and sound purpose.

translation: O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion, and do not say about Allah except the truth. The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was only a messenger of Allah and His word which He directed to Mary and a spirit from Him. So believe in Allah and His messengers, and do not say, "Three"; desist—it is better for you. Indeed, Allah is but one God. Glory be to Him that He should have a son. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: The verse calls the People of the Scripture, particularly Christians, back from exaggeration (ghuluww) regarding Jesus, which had lifted him from the station of a human messenger to divinity. It affirms his true status: a messenger, created by Allah's word 'Be' conveyed to Mary, and a spirit from Him, without any share in divinity. Faith is thereby to be grounded in Allah and all His messengers together, and the doctrine of the Trinity is explicitly rejected as a distortion. The closing declarations of Allah's oneness and transcendence above having offspring, along with His total ownership and sufficiency as guardian, establish that true devotion must be purified of any association or divine attribution to creatures.

translation: The Messiah will never disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor will the angels brought near (to Him). And whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant - He will gather them all to Himself.
interpretation: The verse affirms that servitude to God is no diminishment but the highest dignity, something even the Messiah and the closest angels do not refuse. It was revealed against those who exalted Jesus into divinity, showing that true honor lies in humble devotion, while arrogance that rejects worship leads inevitably to a final gathering before God, where every soul will be held to account.

translation: As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, He will give them their full rewards and increase them from His bounty. But as for those who disdained and were arrogant, He will punish them with a painful punishment, and they will find no protector or helper besides Allah.
interpretation: The verse closes the passage about Christ, who did not disdain to be a servant of Allah, by setting two conditions side by side. Faith joined with righteous action earns a full recompense, and Allah adds to it out of His grace, showing that divine reward exceeds what deeds alone could merit. The opposite path is rooted in istinkaf and istikbar, the refusal to submit to God's servanthood born of pride. Since the arrogant turn away from the only true source of help, they are left with no guardian or supporter other than Allah, who is the one they rejected.

translation: O mankind, there has certainly come to you a conclusive proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a clear light.
interpretation: The verse addresses all of humanity directly, announcing that the proof (burhan) has already arrived from their Lord, not as a distant promise but as a present reality. The 'proof' is understood by many commentators as the Prophet Muhammad himself, whose life, character, and message constitute an undeniable evidence of truth, and the 'clear light' (nur mubin) as the Qur'an, which illuminates the path so that people may distinguish guidance from error. The movement from 'proof' to 'light' suggests that the divine call first establishes its authenticity through evidence and then opens the way to understanding through illumination, so that the listener is left without excuse yet also gifted with clarity to walk the path.

translation: As for those who believed in Allah and held fast to Him, He will admit them into His mercy and bounty, and guide them to Himself on a straight path.
interpretation: The verse draws a clear line between two outcomes that follow from one inner stance: faith in Allah joined with actively holding fast to Him. Believing is the starting point, but the verse adds the word 'iʿtisam', which implies clinging to God as one clings to a firm rope or a secure refuge, so that faith becomes a living dependence rather than a mere assent. The reward is twofold. First, God 'admits them into mercy from Himself and bounty', meaning that what they receive is not earned in full by their own effort but is an overflow of divine generosity, with 'mercy' pointing to protection and forgiveness and 'bounty' to abundant favor. Second, God guides them to Himself along a straight path. The sequence is significant: the one who holds fast to God is brought closer to God, so that guidance is not only directed toward correct conduct but toward the very nearness of the Lord. The straight path thus becomes the path that leads to Him, and the believer's grasp on God is answered by God's guidance toward Him.

translation: They ask you for a ruling. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning the kalala (one who dies leaving neither parent nor child). If a man dies leaving no child but has a sister, she receives half of what he left, and he inherits from her if she has no child. If there are two sisters, they receive two-thirds of what he left. If there are brothers and sisters, the male receives the equivalent of two females' shares. Allah makes clear to you so that you do not go astray, and Allah has knowledge of all things.
interpretation: The verse closes the Qur'anic legislation on inheritance by addressing the rare case of kalala, where the deceased has no children and no surviving parents. Its wording, 'Allah gives you a ruling' and 'Allah makes clear to you lest you go astray,' presents clarity in the distribution of estates as a mercy that protects people from confusion, injustice, and disputes among heirs. The ruling also reveals a principle of balance: the sister's share is half, the two sisters' share is two-thirds, and where brothers and sisters combine, the male's double share reflects the Islamic financial responsibilities placed upon men, while the closing reminder that Allah knows all things affirms that these divinely set shares are perfectly just even when human reasoning cannot fully perceive their wisdom.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O you who have believed, fulfill your contracts. Lawful to you is the meat of grazing animals, except what is recited to you, but not hunting while you are in the state of ihram. Indeed, God decrees what He wills.
interpretation: The verse opens with a general command to honor one's covenants, placing the duty of faithfulness to commitments at the heart of the believer's relationship with God and with others. It then shows that divine law is an ordered whole in which permissions and restrictions are set by God's wisdom: cattle-type animals are made lawful, with the exception of what is explicitly named as forbidden, and hunting is suspended for those in the sacred state of pilgrimage. The closing phrase reminds the reader that God's judgment is absolute and that He legislates according to His own will and knowledge, so that obedience to these rulings is an expression of trust in His sovereign wisdom.

translation: O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah or the sacred month or the sacrificial animals or the garlands [of sacrifice] or those coming to the Sacred House seeking bounty from their Lord and His approval. But when you have come out of ihram, then hunt. And do not let the hatred of a people for having barred you from al-Masjid al-Haram incite you to transgress. And cooperate in righteousness and piety, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the sanctity of the rites of Allah, the sacred months, the offerings, and those who travel to the House must be respected, even when they belong to enemies, because the believers' loyalty is to God's commands rather than to their feelings of enmity. Their resentment toward a people who had blocked them from the Sacred Mosque must not drive them into injustice; instead, their social and moral action is to be built on cooperation in what is good and God-fearing, and the rejection of cooperation in wrongdoing and transgression. The closing reminder of God's severe punishment ties this ethical principle to accountability before Him, so that justice toward adversaries is itself a form of devotion.

translation: Forbidden to you are dead animals, blood, the flesh of swine, that which has been dedicated to other than Allah, the strangled, the beaten to death, the fallen from a height, the gored, that which a wild beast has partly eaten unless you slaughter it in time, that which is sacrificed on stone altars, and that you seek to know your fortune through divining arrows. That is grave disobedience. Today those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion, so do not fear them but fear Me. Today I have perfected your religion for you, completed My favor upon you, and approved Islam as your religion. But whoever is compelled by severe hunger, without inclining toward sin, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse joins two moments of closure: the fixing of the dietary and ritual prohibitions and the declaration that the religion is complete. By placing the prohibitions within a message of perfected religion, it presents the law not as an arbitrary burden but as a boundary that protects the community's purity, its devotion to God alone, and its distinct identity, especially at a time when the believers faced pressure from those who had hoped to see them fail. The call to fear God rather than the disbelievers points to the inner source of this order: obedience grows from awe of God, not from fear of human opposition. The exception for necessity then clarifies the spirit of the whole law. Prohibition is tied to the purpose of preserving life and the soul, so when survival itself is at stake and one does not willfully seek sin, the rule yields to mercy. Completion of the religion thus means a law that is both firm in its principles and attentive to human weakness.

translation: They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say: "Lawful for you are the good things, and [the game caught by] what you have trained among the trained hunting animals, teaching them from what Allah has taught you. So eat of what they catch for you, and mention the name of Allah over it, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is swift in account."
interpretation: The verse shows that the default in matters of food is permissibility: what is good and wholesome is lawful, and the question of what is permitted is answered by a broad principle rather than an exhaustive list. It then teaches that hunting trained animals, such as dogs and birds of prey, is a legitimate means of obtaining food, provided the trainer is skilled and has taught the animal by the knowledge Allah gave humanity, and that the game is eaten only after the hunter pronounces Allah's name. The closing reminder to fear Allah and that He is swift in reckoning ties this ordinary act of eating to moral accountability, teaching that even the everyday pursuit of sustenance must be carried out with awareness of God and responsibility before Him.

translation: Today, all good things have been made lawful for you. The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them. And [lawful for you in marriage are] chaste women from among the believers and chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you, when you have given them their due compensation, desiring chastity, not unlawful sexual intercourse or taking secret lovers. And whoever rejects faith, his deeds have become worthless, and he will be, in the Hereafter, among the losers.
interpretation: The verse opens a broad generosity of the Islamic law: what is good and wholesome is permitted, and the food of the People of the Book is allowed to the believers, showing that religious boundaries do not make ordinary human sharing unlawful. The permission to marry chaste women of the Scripture-people is tied to the seriousness of marriage itself: the dowry is a sincere right of the wife, and the union must be one of chastity and commitment rather than illicit affairs or secret liaisons. The closing warning ties the whole passage to faith, teaching that legal concessions never dilute the centrality of belief, since whoever abandons faith loses the value of his good works and stands among the losers in the Hereafter.

translation: O you who have believed, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe over your heads, and wash your feet up to the ankles. And if you are in a state of major impurity, then purify yourselves. But if you are ill, or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving himself, or you have had contact with women and you find no water, then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it. Allah does not intend to make difficulty for you, but He intends to purify you and to complete His favor upon you that you may be grateful.
interpretation: The verse opens with a call to believers that ties the outward act of ritual purity to the inward state of readiness for worship: before standing before God in prayer, the believer must cleanse the body, and this cleansing is itself a form of devotion. The command to wash the face, hands, head and feet, together with the rule of full bathing for major impurity, shows that Islam treats physical cleanliness as a path to spiritual purity, so that the worshipper approaches God clean in body and heart. The concession of tayammum, the dry ablution with clean earth when water is unavailable due to illness, travel, or other conditions, reveals the principle that hardship is lifted from the believer. The verse closes by declaring that God's purpose is not to burden people but to purify them and complete His blessing upon them, so that gratitude becomes the fitting response of the believer to this mercy.

translation: And remember the favor of Allah upon you and His covenant with which He bound you when you said, "We hear and we obey." And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts.
interpretation: The verse calls the believers to continuous awareness of divine blessing and of the covenant they accepted, which is the commitment to listen and obey. Their words of acceptance create a binding trust between them and their Lord, so remembrance of that bond should shape their conduct. God's favor is not merely a past gift but a standing reason for gratitude and faithfulness. Taqwa is presented as the guard over that covenant, since it grounds obedience in consciousness of God rather than in outward profession alone. The closing reminder that Allah knows what the breasts conceal means that sincerity of heart is the true measure of fulfilling the pledge, and that no inner intention escapes Him.

translation: O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses in justice, and do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness. And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do.
interpretation: The verse establishes justice as an unconditional duty of faith, and it makes the believer's own emotions the most demanding test of that duty: the believer must stand for justice even toward those whom he dislikes or who have wronged him, because enmity must never be allowed to tilt the scale. The repetition of the command to be just, placed right after the warning against letting hatred drive one away from it, shows that the real struggle lies in the heart rather than in the courtroom alone. Justice is thus tied to taqwa, since the closest path to God-consciousness runs through fairness toward one's adversaries, and the closing reminder that Allah knows all deeds means that a believer's partiality, even when hidden, is never beyond divine knowledge.

translation: Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: The verse establishes that divine promise is tied to a unified condition: genuine faith in the heart must be expressed in righteous action. Forgiveness (maghfirah) addresses what has passed, covering human shortcomings, while the great reward (ajr 'azim) points to what is awaited, a recompense whose greatness exceeds human measure. By placing forgiveness first, the verse suggests that the believer's hope rests less on the perfection of his deeds than on the mercy of the One who promised, so that faith and action are sustained by trust in divine generosity rather than by self-righteousness.

translation: But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs—those are the companions of Hellfire.
interpretation: The verse draws a sharp line between two groups by pairing two acts: disbelief in the heart (kufr) and the outward denial of God's signs (takdhib bi-ayatina). Ayat here carries both senses: the revealed verses of scripture and the signs woven into creation, so to deny them is to reject the evidence that points to God. The phrase 'companions of Hellfire' (ashab al-jahim) expresses not merely a destination but a lasting bond: such people have chosen the fire as their fitting company. The verse invites the listener to examine which path they walk, since the consequence follows from a chosen refusal to acknowledge what is plainly shown.

translation: O you who have believed, remember the favor of Allah upon you when a people determined to extend their hands against you, but He restrained their hands from you. So fear Allah, and upon Allah let the believers rely.
interpretation: The verse turns the believers' memory toward a concrete moment of divine protection, so that gratitude becomes the basis for taking God's side in every hard hour. Recalling how the hands of the hostile were held back is meant to train the heart to see that danger is never ultimately in the hands of enemies, but under the control of the One who restrains them. Taqwa, the watchful awareness of God, is then joined to tawakkul, the reliance that follows from having witnessed His help; the believer's fear of God and trust in Him are thus shown to be two faces of the same faith, with remembrance of past mercy feeding present steadfastness.

translation: And Allah had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised among them twelve leaders. And Allah said, "I am with you. If you establish prayer, give zakah, believe in My messengers, support them, and loan Allah a goodly loan, I will surely remove from you your misdeeds and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow. But whoever disbelieves after that among you has certainly strayed from the sound way."
interpretation: The verse presents the covenant with the Children of Israel as a pact built on a fourfold practical commitment: the ritual bond with God through prayer, the social duty of zakah, faith in all of God's messengers without distinction, and active support for them, crowned by the generous spending on God's cause described as a goodly loan. The promise of expiation of sins and entry into paradise is conditional on these acts, showing that divine favor is tied to a living fidelity that unites worship, charity, and allegiance to the prophets. The twelve leaders chosen from among them signify the organized responsibility borne by the community for upholding this covenant. The closing warning makes clear that rejecting this covenant after its terms have been made known is a deliberate departure from the straight path, indicating that the gravity of disbelief lies in turning away from a clear divine commitment already accepted.

translation: So because of their breaking of their covenant, We cursed them and made their hearts hard. They distort words from their places and have forgotten a portion of what they were reminded of. And you will not cease to discover treachery from them, except a few of them. So pardon them and overlook. Indeed, Allah loves the doers of good.
interpretation: The verse shows that hardness of heart is the consequence of repeatedly breaking a covenant with God, and that once the heart is hardened, it begins to corrupt meaning and neglect the guidance it was given. Distorting the words of revelation from their proper places is a form of betrayal that severs a people from the truth they were entrusted with. Yet the verse does not end in despair: the Prophet is commanded to pardon and forgive despite continual treachery, and this forbearance is tied to ihsan, the highest standard of good conduct, which God loves. The lesson is that righteous leadership can respond to betrayal with patience and magnanimity while remaining firm in principle.

translation: And from those who say, "We are Christians," We took their covenant, but they forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of. So We caused among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection. And Allah will inform them of what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse refers to the Christians who, like those before them, made a covenant with God to follow the guidance revealed to them, yet neglected a significant part of their message. Their abandonment of that part of the revelation led to internal division, sectarian enmity and hatred that would persist among them, and the verse closes by reminding that God will hold them accountable for their deeds on the Day of Judgment. The interpretation emphasizes that division arises when revelation is forgotten or partially abandoned, and that the enmity described is a consequence of their own choices rather than an arbitrary decree.

translation: O People of the Scripture, there has come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture and pardoning much. There has certainly come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book.
interpretation: The verse addresses the People of the Book directly, presenting the Prophet Muhammad as a messenger who exposes what they had hidden or altered of their own scriptures, while overlooking much of their concealment out of mercy and forbearance. The phrase 'light and a clear Book' signifies that the Qur'an itself is the divine illumination that dispels the darkness of distortion and makes the truth evident, so that the revelation both corrects the earlier scriptures and serves as a standing, lucid guide, inviting the People of the Book to recognize in it a continuation of the same message from God.

translation: Through it, God guides those who seek His good pleasure to paths of peace, and brings them out of darknesses into the light by His permission, and guides them to a straight path.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an as a divine guidance whose effect is progressive and conditional on sincerity: the one who genuinely pursues God's pleasure is led first to the paths of peace, which suggests that inner tranquility and reconciliation with God are the first fruits of such pursuit. The movement "out of darknesses into the light" describes a transformation from ignorance, confusion, and moral blindness to clarity of understanding and conduct, and the phrase "by His permission" reminds the believer that this transformation, though it requires human seeking, ultimately depends on God's grace. The closing reference to a straight path completes the picture by affirming that the guidance is not merely a momentary illumination but a stable direction of life.

translation: They have certainly disbelieved who said, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary." Say, "Then who could prevent Allah at all if He wished to destroy the Messiah, the son of Mary, and his mother and everyone on earth entirely? And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them. He creates what He wills, and Allah is over all things competent."
interpretation: The verse confronts the claim that God Himself became incarnate in the Messiah, son of Mary, by showing the absurdity of such a divinity: a being that can be destroyed, along with his mother and all mankind, cannot be God, since no one has power to resist God's will. Ownership of the heavens, the earth, and all between them belongs to God alone, and His creative act is free and unconstrained, so the creature's existence and death demonstrate his dependence rather than divinity. The verse thereby affirms God's absolute sovereignty and transcendence over all created things, including the prophet Jesus, whose humanity is established by his mother's humanity.

translation: The Jews and the Christians said, "We are the children of God and His beloved." Say, "Then why does He punish you for your sins? Rather, you are but human beings from among those He has created. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. And to God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, and to Him is the final return."
interpretation: The verse exposes the baseless claim of spiritual privilege by which the People of the Book considered themselves exempt from accountability before God, as if their lineage or closeness to Him placed them above moral judgment. The rhetorical question "then why does He punish you for your sins?" shows the contradiction in their own position: a loving father does not treat his children by punishing them for wrongdoing as if they were strangers to justice, and their very experience of consequences refutes the notion of a special status. By declaring them ordinary creatures like the rest of humanity, the verse restores the principle that divine favor and forgiveness are not inherited by descent or group identity but are granted by God's sovereign will, which is bound to no one, and that all people will ultimately return to Him for judgment, so that claimed kinship to God cannot replace righteous conduct.

translation: O People of the Scripture, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you [the truth] after a interval of [no] messengers, lest you say, "There came to us no bringer of good tidings and no warner." But there has certainly come to you a bringer of good tidings and a warner. And Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse addresses the People of the Book at a time when the chain of prophethood had lapsed, establishing that the Prophet Muhammad's mission removes any excuse they might offer on the grounds that no one came to guide them. Its emphasis on both good tidings and warning shows that divine guidance combines promise for those who respond with admonition for those who turn away, and the closing reminder of God's power underscores that the sending of this messenger is within His complete ability and wisdom.

translation: And [recall] when Moses said to his people, "O my people, remember the favor of Allah upon you when He appointed among you prophets and made you kings and gave you what He had not given anyone else among the worlds."
interpretation: The verse calls the Children of Israel to remember Allah's blessings as a basis for gratitude and obedience. Moses reminds them that the greatest of these favors is prophethood, which Allah placed among them, a distinction that carried a responsibility to live by the guidance they had received. Their being made kings points to a worldly authority and independence that expressed their dignity under divine favor. The phrase "what He had not given anyone else among the worlds" is understood by many commentators as referring to the particular privileges of their time, such as the sending of many prophets among them, the deliverance from Pharaoh, and the gifts granted in that era, rather than an absolute claim of superiority over all later peoples. The lesson is that remembrance of divine blessings should lead to gratitude, humility, and faithfulness, lest privilege become a cause of arrogance and deviation.

translation: O my people, enter the holy land which God has prescribed for you, and do not turn back on your heels, for you will then return as losers.
interpretation: The verse recalls Moses' call to his people to enter the land God had assigned to them, and it frames obedience to that command as a test of steadfastness. Retreating from a divine command out of fear or hesitation is portrayed as a backward step that forfeits what God has promised, so the loss it brings is not merely worldly but a loss of one's own good fortune and standing before God. The lesson is that trust in God's promise demands courage to advance when called, rather than yielding to doubt and reverting to former ways.

translation: They said, "O Moses, indeed there are in it a people of tyrants, and indeed we will never enter it until they leave it. So if they leave it, then we will enter."
interpretation: The verse reveals the spiritual and moral paralysis of a people who, having been given a promise, shrink from its fulfillment when faced with apparent strength. Their words expose a reliance on worldly calculation and fear rather than trust in the command of God delivered through Moses, and they make their obedience conditional on the removal of the obstacle rather than on faith that God would grant them victory. The verse thus teaches that hesitation born of fear of the powerful, when it replaces reliance upon God, becomes a barrier that keeps a people from the blessings promised to them.

translation: Two men from among those who feared (God), upon whom God had bestowed His favor, said: "Enter upon them through the gate; for when you have entered it, you will surely be victorious. And upon God put your trust, if you are (true) believers."
interpretation: The verse points to the decisive role of courage joined with trust in God: the two men, who were themselves God-fearing and blessed, do not merely counsel passivity or reliance on miracle, but urge the believers to take the bold, concrete step of confronting the enemy at the gate, and then anchor that action in tawakkul. The interpretation drawn here is that genuine trust in God does not cancel human effort but completes it; faith is shown by advancing with resolve while leaving the outcome to God, and the condition "if you are believers" makes clear that such reliance is the mark of true faith rather than an excuse for hesitation or cowardice.

translation: They said, "O Moses, indeed we will never enter it as long as they remain within it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed, we are sitting right here."
interpretation: This verse reveals the Children of Israel's collapse of resolve at the threshold of the Holy Land: having been commanded to enter it, they respond with a refusal rooted in fear of the inhabitants and a dependence on Moses' sole effort, rather than trust in God's promise. Their words expose a people who wished to be delivered without bearing the burden of struggle, and whose reluctance to act on divine command led them to forfeit the opportunity granted to them, a lesson on how hesitation before a clear command can translate into prolonged wandering and loss.
