translation: He said, "My Lord, I have no control except over myself and my brother, so separate us from the defiantly disobedient people."
interpretation: This verse is the prayer of Moses after his people refused to enter the holy land and rebelled against his command to fight the tyrannical nation within it. Having exhausted his capacity to lead a community that had repeatedly turned from obedience, he acknowledges the limits of his own authority, confining his responsibility to himself and his brother Aaron, and he appeals to God for a decisive separation between the faithful and those who persistently defy divine command. The supplication reveals a leader's trust in God as the ultimate judge, and a willingness to leave the outcome of a corrupted community to God's justice rather than to his own power.

translation: He said, "Indeed, it is forbidden for them for forty years; they will wander in the land. So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people."
interpretation: The verse shows that the Israelites' punishment for their refusal to enter the Holy Land was a forty-year period of aimless wandering, a divine consequence that tied the restoration of their promised inheritance to the passing of a generation shaped by their disobedience. The closing command to Moses not to grieve over them teaches the prophet that guiding people is ultimately God's affair, and that a messenger's duty is to deliver the message rather than to bear the anguish of those who persistently reject it. Thus the verse combines a lesson in accountability for collective defiance with consolation for the one who carries the burden of preaching.

translation: And recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam in truth, when each offered a sacrifice, and it was accepted from one of them but not accepted from the other. The latter said, "I will surely kill you." The former said, "Indeed, Allah accepts only from the righteous."
interpretation: The verse presents the story of Adam's two sons as a warning drawn from truth rather than legend, showing that acceptance before God depends not on the outward act of offering but on the inner piety of the one who gives. The envy of the rejected brother toward the accepted one reveals how resentment, when left unchecked, drives a person from covenant to crime. The reply of the righteous brother teaches that God's acceptance is tied to taqwa, so a believer who is wronged should hold fast to God-consciousness and not answer hatred with violence, since the true measure of a person's worth lies in his devotion to God rather than in the rivalries of this world.

translation: If you extend your hand toward me to kill me, I shall not extend my hand toward you to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allah, the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the righteous son of Adam in the account of the two sons of Adam, reveals a principle of restraint grounded in God-consciousness: the believer's fear of Allah outweighs the impulse of retaliation, even when facing a murderous aggressor. Rather than mirroring violence, he chooses to bear the wrong and entrust his cause to God, showing that true piety is anchored in the awareness of the Lord of all worlds, who sees both the act and the intention, and that the refusal to shed blood is itself a manifestation of faith.

translation: Indeed, I intend that you bear my sin and your sin, and so you will be among the companions of the Fire. And that is the recompense of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse is the words of one who, in the face of an opponent's hostility, declares that he would rather the other party carry the burden of his wrongdoing alongside their own, so that they end up among the people of the Fire. It conveys that the aggressor is ultimately made to bear the full weight of their own sin, and that the Fire is the fitting reward for those who wrong others. The phrasing reflects a moral principle that every soul is accountable for its deeds, and that intent to harm another does not escape the consequences of one's own injustice before God.

translation: So his soul induced him to the murder of his brother, and he killed him, and thereby became among the losers.
interpretation: The verse shows how the lower self can gradually make a grave sin appear acceptable: the soul first 'made easy' (taw'ala) the killing of his brother, so that the desire to act overcame restraint and conscience. The consequence is not only the loss of a brother but the loss of himself, since he forfeited his share in mercy, his moral integrity, and his standing before God. The passage warns that the first step toward a great wrong is the rationalization that lets the soul accept it, and that envy and resentment, left unchecked, can turn a family bond into a crime that ruins the one who commits it.

translation: Then Allah sent a crow scratching in the earth to show him how to conceal the body of his brother. He said, "Woe is me! Am I unable to be like this crow and conceal the body of my brother?" And he became among the regretful.
interpretation: This verse, from the story of the two sons of Adam, shows the first human response to death and the first murder: the killer, having no idea what to do with his slain brother, is taught by a crow that buries another to hide it. The lesson is that human beings, faced with a moral failure, often learn from the most unexpected sources, and that the sight of a creature performing a simple act of burial exposes the killer's own helplessness and lack of foresight. His cry of "Woe is me" reveals that the true punishment began with regret, which arose not from remorse for the crime itself but from shame at being outdone by an animal in a basic act of dignity. The verse thus highlights that the consequence of wrongdoing is often a painful awareness of one's own diminished humanity, and it points to the dignity owed even to the dead, whose body must be covered and respected.

translation: Because of that, We decreed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, unless it be for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as if he had killed all of mankind; and whoever saves a life, it is as if he had saved all of mankind. Our messengers had certainly come to them with clear proofs, yet many of them afterward were indeed transgressors in the land.
interpretation: The verse uses the Children of Israel's decree as a foundation for a universal principle: the sanctity of human life is so absolute that taking one innocent life is equated with destroying the whole human race, while preserving one life is equated with preserving all of humanity, since each soul carries the full weight of humanity within it. The sentence is framed by the reminder that this law was not given to them in ignorance but after clear signs from their messengers, so their later excesses in bloodshed and corruption reflect a deliberate transgression against known truth. The exception of retribution for murder or for corruption in the land limits the prohibition to lawful justice and public order, showing that the protection of life is tied to justice rather than to mere emotion, and that the sin of disregarding this principle is not confined to one nation but threatens the moral fabric shared by all people.

translation: The only recompense for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive to spread corruption in the land is that they be killed, or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or be exiled from the land. That is a disgrace for them in this world, and in the Hereafter they will have a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse addresses those who take up armed hostility against the divine order and the community that upholds it, and who spread disorder, terror, and bloodshed in society. It establishes that such conduct is not a private sin but a grave offense against public peace, and it sets out a graduated range of penalties, left to the authority responsible for justice, matched to the gravity of the crime, from execution to banishment. The phrase 'a disgrace in this world' shows that the punishment has a social and deterrent purpose, while the 'great punishment' in the Hereafter shows that the crime also carries accountability before God. Classical jurists differed on whether the options are alternatives chosen by the ruler according to the offense or fixed sequential stages, and on the precise scope of 'waging war' and 'corruption in the land', but the verse's central principle is that protecting security and life in the community is a serious religious obligation.

translation: Except for those who repent before you have power over them. So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, which closes the passage on the punishment of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and spread corruption in the land (Al-Ma'idah 5:33-34), establishes that the severe penalties mentioned earlier are lifted for the one who turns back in repentance before he is captured. The condition is precise: repentance made before the authorities gain power over the offender is accepted and its effect is to remove the legal punishment, since the state's coercion is no longer the decisive factor once the offender voluntarily returns. Repentance after capture, by contrast, does not cancel the public right that has already been enforced. The verse thus reveals the balance of divine justice, which demands accountability for harm to society while opening a door of mercy to the sincere penitent. The closing divine names, Forgiving and Merciful, signal that Allah's pardon extends to those who abandon rebellion, and that the rights of Allah are His to forgive, whereas the rights of people remain subject to their own claims and the justice owed to them.

translation: O you who have believed, fear Allah and seek the means of nearness to Him, and strive in His cause that you may succeed.
interpretation: The verse structures the believer's path in three ascending stages: first, taqwa, the inner vigilance that keeps the heart conscious of God in every act; second, wasīla, the active seeking of closeness to Him through what draws the servant nearer, such as worship, knowledge, and good deeds, since nearness is not reached by passive belief alone; and third, jihad in His path, the exertion of one's full capacity against whatever hinders the soul and the community from the truth. The closing promise of falāh, success, is tied to this whole sequence rather than to any single part, indicating that success in this life and the next comes from a disciplined heart that strives outward in service of God.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve—even if they had everything on earth, and the like of it along with it, to ransom themselves thereby from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them. And theirs will be a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse shows that on the Day of Resurrection no amount of worldly wealth, however vast, can buy release from the consequences of disbelief, because the true currency of that Day is faith and righteous deeds rather than possessions. It reminds the listener that what people hoard and value in this life becomes worthless before God, and that the only real ransom is sincere turning to Him before the reckoning comes, while the disbelievers' sufferings are compounded by the bitter realization that their attachment to the world has left them with nothing to offer.

translation: They wish to come out of the Fire, but they will not be able to leave it, and theirs is a lasting punishment.
interpretation: The verse portrays the desperate longing of the people of the Fire to escape, set against the certainty that this escape is denied them. Their wish is real but futile, which underscores that the torment is not a temporary trial but a fixed state. The closing phrase, a lasting punishment, signals the permanence of their condition, and the juxtaposition of their yearning with their inability to act on it intensifies the sense of irreversible loss, inviting the listener to reflect on the consequences of their choices in this world before that final reckoning.

translation: As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they have earned, and as an exemplary punishment from Allah. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse establishes the hadd punishment for theft as a deterrent rooted in divine justice, yet it is framed within the wider Qur'anic concern for the protection of property and social trust. The phrase "recompense for what they have earned" signals that the punishment is a direct consequence of the thief's own act, meaning the offender bears responsibility for choosing to take what is not theirs. The word "nakal" points to the purpose of the punishment: it is meant to be a visible lesson that restrains others, so that the wider community is protected from the breakdown of trust that theft produces. The closing names, "Aziz" (Mighty) and "Hakim" (Wise), remind the reader that the law comes from a source that is both able to enforce it and perfectly knowledgeable of what serves human welfare, so the ruling should be understood as part of a coherent divine wisdom rather than arbitrary severity. Classical jurists have debated the conditions, thresholds, and evidentiary requirements for applying this ruling, which reflects the principle that such a severe punishment demands strict standards of proof and due process.

translation: So whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms himself, indeed Allah will turn to him in forgiveness. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse opens a door of hope for the one who has transgressed: repentance is not closed to him merely because of what he has done. Its condition is twofold, sincere turning back after the wrong and genuine reform of conduct, since regret alone without amendment does not complete the return. When these are present, God's turning toward the servant is not a reluctant acceptance but an expression of His own attribute of mercy, and the closing names, Forgiving and Merciful, tie the promise of acceptance to the boundless compassion that makes the return possible in the first place.

translation: Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth? He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills, and Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse turns the believer's attention from the question posed to them toward a settled truth: sovereignty over all creation belongs to God alone, so no one stands outside His authority or can compel Him. Because the dominion is complete, His choices to punish or to forgive are exercised in full wisdom and justice rather than by any external constraint, and the mention of His power over everything reassures the faithful that no matter how the world appears to tilt, judgment and mercy both remain in His hands. The verse thus invites a response of humility, trust in His mercy, and awareness of accountability.

translation: O Messenger, let not those hasten to disbelief grieve you, from among those who say "We believe" with their mouths while their hearts have not believed, and from among the Jews—listeners for falsehood, listeners for another people who have not come to you. They distort words from their places, saying: "If you are given this, take it; but if you are not given it, beware." And whoever Allah wills to test, you cannot avail him anything against Allah. Those are the ones whose hearts Allah did not will to purify. For them in this world is disgrace, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet not to be saddened by those who rush headlong into disbelief, showing that the hypocrites' outward profession of faith masks a heart untouched by belief, and that the Jews who eagerly listen to falsehood and twist the meaning of revealed speech are bound by their own choices. Their distortion of the text and their conditional acceptance of rulings reveal a deliberate preference for what suits their desires over the truth. The statement that Allah has not willed to purify their hearts is not a denial of their capacity to change, but a sober declaration that their persistence in turning away has led to their spiritual state, so the Prophet's task is only to convey the message, not to guide everyone against their will.

translation: They are listeners for falsehood, consumers of what is unlawfully gained. So if they come to you, either judge between them or turn away from them; and if you turn away from them, they cannot harm you at all. And if you judge, judge between them with justice. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.
interpretation: The verse portrays a community whose leaders and listeners are drawn to lies and eat through ill-gotten gain, which shows that the corruption is both in their speech and in their livelihood, and that their willingness to bring disputes before the Prophet is not a sign of sincere submission to truth. It gives the Prophet a choice of judging or declining to judge, reflecting that he was not obligated to adjudicate for those who did not accept his authority in good faith, and that his independence protects him from their scheming. Yet once he undertakes judgment, the standard is absolute and not negotiable: justice ('qist') must be applied even-handedly, regardless of the parties' status or hostility. The closing statement that God loves the just ties the ethics of public judgment directly to divine favor, so that a judge's fairness is itself an act of worship and a reflection of God's own attributes of equity.

translation: And how would they make you judge while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah? Then they turn away after that. And those are not believers.
interpretation: The verse exposes a contradiction in the conduct of the People of the Book: they seek the Prophet's ruling while possessing their own scripture that contains God's judgment, showing that their appeal to him is not driven by sincere commitment to divine guidance but by convenience, since they reject that ruling when it does not suit them. By describing their turning away as following the rejection of a judgment they already claim to revere, the verse reveals that true faith is measured not by claiming allegiance to revelation but by submitting to its authority when it is applied to oneself. The final denial of belief underscores that nominal adherence to scripture without accepting its binding verdict is incompatible with genuine faith, and it reminds the believers that their own judgment should rest on the revealed law rather than on personal or communal preference.

translation: Indeed, We revealed the Torah, in which there is guidance and light. By it the prophets who submitted (to God) judged for those who were Jews, as did the rabbis and the scholars, by what they were entrusted to preserve of the Book of God, and they were witnesses over it. So do not fear the people, but fear Me, and do not exchange My signs for a small price. And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the earlier scripture was a divine source of guidance and light entrusted to its prophets and scholars as custodians and witnesses, and it binds the judges of every age to the revealed law. It warns that the true obstacle to upholding God's law is fear of people and the worldly gain of trading God's signs for a trivial price; sincere devotion requires fearing God alone. Its final statement, that rejecting judgment by God's revelation constitutes disbelief, is read by many classical scholars as applying to one who denies or willfully rejects the divine law, while those who judge unjustly from weakness or lapse are judged differently, so the verse calls for integrity, courage, and consistency in justice grounded in revelation.

translation: And We prescribed for them therein: a life for a life, an eye for an eye, a nose for a nose, an ear for an ear, a tooth for a tooth, and for wounds is legal retribution. But whoever forgoes it as a charity, it is an expiation for him. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - it is those who are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse establishes qisas, the principle of proportionate retribution, as a binding law in the Torah given to the Children of Israel, and by extension a principle affirmed in the Qur'an's own legal framework. Its deeper point lies in the moral weight placed on the victim: pardoning the offender is presented as a charitable act that brings expiation to the one who forgives, so justice is paired with the possibility of mercy. The closing condemnation ties the entire legal order to faithfulness to divine revelation, showing that abandoning God's law in favor of one's own judgment is a form of injustice, since true justice is measured by what God has revealed.

translation: And We sent, following in their footsteps, Jesus, son of Mary, confirming what was before him of the Torah. And We gave him the Gospel, in which was guidance and light, confirming what was before it of the Torah, and a guidance and an admonition for the righteous.
interpretation: The verse places Jesus within the continuous chain of prophetic revelation, presenting him not as a break from the earlier scripture but as a confirmer of the Torah that preceded him. The repeated emphasis on confirming the Torah signals that the Gospel completes and restores the same divine guidance rather than replacing it with something foreign. Its description as containing guidance and light, and its being addressed specifically as an admonition to the God-conscious, shows that the message is meant to awaken moral awareness in those who are already disposed to fear and obey God, drawing them toward the unity of the prophetic message.

translation: Let the People of the Gospel judge by what God has revealed therein. And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed - it is those who are the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse addresses the People of the Gospel, commanding them to adhere to the revelation given to them in their scripture as the standard for judgment, and it frames the abandonment of God's revealed law as a mark of moral transgression. Read in its context, which speaks of the Qur'an as a guardian over earlier scriptures, the verse establishes a principle that the duty to rule by divine guidance is binding on every community that has received revelation, and that deliberately setting it aside is a departure from obedience to God, described here as fisq, a going beyond the bounds of what is right.

translation: And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what came before it of the Book and guarding over it. So judge between them by what God has revealed, and do not follow their desires away from the truth that has come to you. For each of you We have made a law and a way. And had God willed, He would have made you one community, but He tests you in what He has given you, so race to good deeds. To God is your return, all of you, and He will inform you about that over which you used to differ.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an as both a confirmation of earlier revelation and a guardian standard over it, so that the believers' authority to judge rests on the divine revelation rather than on the wishes of people. The plurality of laws and methods given to each community is not a defect but a deliberate part of a divine test, in which the purpose of diversity is to turn people toward competing in goodness. Human disagreement is thus placed within a framework of accountability, where the final resolution of differences belongs to God alone at the return to Him.

translation: And judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires, and beware of them lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you. But if they turn away, then know that Allah intends to afflict them for some of their sins. And indeed, many of the people are defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the Prophet must rule among his community strictly by God's revelation, refusing to bend justice to the whims and preferences of those who seek to divert him from it, even through deception and enticement. It reveals that the reluctance of such people to accept divine judgment is itself a sign of a deeper rebellion, and that the worldly calamities they suffer are a consequence of their own past transgressions, which God uses as a warning. The closing remark, that most people are transgressors, draws a general lesson: obedience to revelation is rare, and a believer should not measure truth by the majority but by what God has sent down.

translation: Do they then seek the judgment of the time of ignorance? But who is better in judgment than Allah for a people who are certain?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who turn away from the revealed law of God to seek rulings rooted in the ignorance and whims of pre-Islamic custom, and it establishes that divine judgment is the most just and perfect standard. Its closing phrase ties the recognition of this truth to certainty of faith: only those whose hearts are firmly convinced of God's wisdom and justice will reject human desires in favor of His command. The verse thus presents submission to God's law as a direct expression of belief, and turning away from it as a sign of a deficient understanding of who truly deserves to govern human affairs.

translation: O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies. They are allies of one another. And whoever among you allies with them is indeed one of them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: The verse forbids believers from taking Jews and Christians as trusted allies and protectors in matters that bind their loyalty, because such alliance, when it becomes a true bond of loyalty, draws a person into the identity and cause of those they ally with, and it reflects a weakness of faith. The phrase 'they are allies of one another' points to a shared solidarity among these communities against outsiders, so aligning with one side places the believer among them. The final clause warns that persistent wrongdoing, here understood as betraying one's own community and its trust, closes the heart to guidance, so the believer is called to keep firm loyalty to God, His messenger, and the believing community.

translation: So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them, saying, "We fear that a misfortune may befall us." But perhaps Allah will bring a conquest or a decision from Himself, and they will become regretful for what they had concealed within themselves.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites who, wavering in their loyalty, rushed to ally themselves with the disbelievers out of worldly fear, dressing their calculation in the language of prudence. It reveals that the disease in their hearts is a spiritual one: doubt and lack of sincere faith, which the Qur'an elsewhere links to hypocrisy. Their excuse of fearing a reversal of fortune betrays that their allegiance was to the outcome rather than to God. The promise that God may bring victory or a decisive command shows that worldly power is in His hands, and that the schemes of those who trust in appearances will ultimately turn into remorse when their hidden intentions are laid bare.

translation: And those who believed will say, "Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that they were surely with you?" Their deeds have become worthless, and they have become losers.
interpretation: The verse portrays a moment of unmasking on the Day of Judgment or at the time of reckoning, when the hypocrites who had sworn solemn oaths of loyalty to the believers are exposed. The believers' astonished question reveals how the hidden reality of these people's hearts becomes visible, and their empty claims of allegiance collapse. The verse teaches that outward profession and emphatic swearing carry no weight without sincere faith and righteous action, since deeds are judged by their inner truth. Their works being nullified means that the appearance of closeness to the community brings no reward, and the consequence is genuine loss. It is a warning to believers against being deceived by eloquent oaths and to examine whether their own faith is sincere and backed by deeds.

translation: O you who have believed, whoever among you reverts from his religion - Allah will bring forth a people He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty over the disbelievers, striving in the cause of Allah and not fearing the blame of a critic. That is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills, and Allah is all-Encompassing and Knowing.
interpretation: The verse presents apostasy as a loss that Allah does not leave unanswered: He replaces those who abandon faith with a people marked by mutual love with Him, humility toward fellow believers, firmness against opponents of the truth, and fearless devotion to the cause of God regardless of social disapproval. The attributes described form a portrait of a community whose strength lies not in worldly power or popularity but in sincerity and steadfastness, and the closing reminder that this bounty is granted by Allah's will teaches that true honor comes from God's choice rather than from human approval.

translation: Your only guardian (walī) is Allah, and His Messenger, and those who have believed—those who establish the prayer and give zakah while they are bowing in prayer (rāki'ūn).
interpretation: The verse establishes that true authority of protection, loyalty, and leadership belongs to Allah, then to His Messenger, then to the believers who are defined by their sincere worship and generosity. Its occasion, traditionally linked to the incident of a believer who gave his ring to a poor man while in the state of bowing, shows that the believers' allegiance is anchored in devotion and charity. The verse thus teaches that the community's bonds of guardianship must rest on faith and righteous conduct, not on tribal or worldly alliances, and that the faithful community's leadership is inseparable from its spiritual discipline and its care for those in need.

translation: And whoever takes Allah and His Messenger and those who believe as allies - then indeed, the party of Allah - they are the victorious.
interpretation: The verse defines the true basis of belonging to the community of faith: loyalty and allegiance are owed to Allah, His Messenger, and the believers together. Those who bind themselves in genuine friendship and solidarity to this covenant of faith become part of 'the party of Allah' (hizb Allah), and the promise that they are the victorious is not merely worldly triumph but a assurance that a community united upon God's guidance will prevail, its strength rooted in its unity with its Lord and its righteousness. The verse thus calls believers to choose their allegiances carefully, placing their ultimate trust in God and in those who share their faith and its commitments.

translation: O you who have believed, do not take those who have taken your religion as a mockery and amusement from among those who were given the Scripture before you, or the disbelievers, as allies. And fear Allah, if you are [truly] believers.
interpretation: The verse addresses the believers with a call to guard their religious identity and loyalty. Mockery of faith is treated as a serious matter: those who make the community's religion a subject of ridicule and play have effectively placed themselves outside the circle of trusted companionship, so befriending them in matters of closeness, counsel, and alliance would erode the believers' own commitment. The closing command to be mindful of God ties the prohibition to the reality of faith itself, implying that true belief is shown by guarding one's loyalties and honoring what is sacred, rather than by mere profession.

translation: And when you call to prayer, they take it as a mockery and a game. That is because they are a people who do not use reason.
interpretation: The verse exposes a mindset that treats what is sacred as a source of amusement, and it traces this derision to a failure of intellect: those who do not reflect on the greatness of the call to worship and the purpose behind it end up ridiculing it. The call to prayer is thus a test of sincerity, revealing whether a person's heart responds to God's summons with reverence or with frivolity. The verse implies that true understanding ('aql) naturally leads to honoring the remembrance of God, so mockery of worship is itself a sign of a heedless and unreasoning state, and a warning to believers not to take up such company or be swayed by it.

translation: Say, "O People of the Scripture, do you resent us for no reason except that we believed in Allah and in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed before, and that most of you are defiantly disobedient?"
interpretation: The verse exposes the irrationality of the opposition faced by the believers from the People of the Book: their only 'fault' in the eyes of their critics is faith in God, a faith that embraces the revelation sent to Muhammad and the earlier scriptures sent to the prophets before him, which in essence are one message from the same source. The resentment thus reveals not a flaw in the believers but the moral corruption of those who, having been entrusted with revelation, turned away from its spirit and departed from obedience. By describing most of them as fasiqun, the verse shifts the accusation back onto them, teaching that when a community rejects the truth it once possessed, the blame lies with its own deviation rather than with those who uphold the common message of all the prophets.

translation: Say, "Shall I inform you of something worse than that as recompense from Allah? Those whom Allah has cursed and upon whom He has become angry, and of whom He made apes and swine, and who worshipped the false deity. Those are worse in position and further astray from the right way."
interpretation: The verse, addressing the People of the Book who mocked the believers for their faith, turns the accusation back on them: the true measure of standing before Allah is not lineage or claimed piety but whether one has been cursed and estranged from Allah for rejecting His guidance. Their hearts and conduct, having turned away from the truth and submitted to idols and false authority in place of Allah, have reduced them to a spiritual condition the Qur'an presents as a stark inversion of human dignity, symbolized by the transformation into apes and swine. The verse thus teaches that worth is measured by obedience and devotion to the One God, and that the one who abandons this devotion for the worship of tyrannical powers has indeed strayed furthest from the straight path.

translation: And when they come to you, they say, "We believe," but they had entered with disbelief and they had left with it. And Allah is most knowing of what they used to conceal.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites' duplicity: their outward profession of faith when meeting the believers is a mask, while their hearts entered and left the gathering with unbelief unchanged. The phrase "entered with disbelief and left with it" shows that the gatherings of faith did not alter their inner state, so their words were no evidence of true belief. The closing reminder that Allah knows what they conceal warns that no pretense can hide the heart from God, and it calls the believers to look beyond display to the inner reality of a person's faith.

translation: And you see many of them hastening toward sin and transgression and their consuming of what is unlawful. Evil indeed is what they have been doing.
interpretation: The verse portrays a people whose hearts are drawn eagerly toward wrongdoing, not merely committing it occasionally but racing to it with zeal. The pairing of sin (al-ithm) with aggression against others (al-'udwan) shows that their corruption runs both inward, against their own duty to God, and outward, against people's rights. Their appetite for al-suht, unlawful gain such as bribery and ill-gotten wealth, reveals a spiritual sickness in which greed has displaced conscience. The verse closes by condemning their conduct as truly evil, teaching that the gravity of an action lies in its wickedness, not in its outward profit, and that persistent eagerness for sin is the clearest sign of a hardened heart.

translation: Why do the rabbis and the scholars not forbid them from their sinful speech and their consuming of unlawful gain? Surely evil is what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the religious leaders of the community for their silence. Their failure to forbid the people from falsehood, sin, and taking forbidden wealth is itself a grave fault, since those entrusted with knowledge and guidance bear a greater responsibility. Their passivity, born of fear, worldly interest, or complicity, makes them equal partners in the wrongdoing. The verse teaches that enjoining good and forbidding evil is a duty that rests most heavily on those who hold religious authority, and that silence in the face of corruption is condemned as harshly as the corruption itself.

translation: The Jews say, "Allah's hand is tied up." Their own hands are tied up, and they are cursed for what they have said. Rather, His hands are both outstretched; He spends as He wills. And what has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief. We have cast among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection. Every time they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it. They strive throughout the land to cause corruption, and Allah does not love the corrupters.
interpretation: The verse exposes a theological distortion, the claim that God's hand is shackled, which is answered by affirming God's boundless generosity: His hands are outstretched and He gives as He wills, so the charge that He is restricted reflects on the speakers' own closed and grasping hearts. The verse then shows that the Qur'an's revelation, rather than healing their error, deepens their rebellion, as divine guidance tests and exposes what is already in people. Their enmity and mutual hatred are presented as a lasting consequence of their disunity, and their repeated attempts to ignite war are repeatedly frustrated by God, while their corruption on earth is condemned as a violation of the divine order that God does not love.

translation: And if the People of the Scripture had believed and feared Allah, We would have removed from them their misdeeds and admitted them to Gardens of Bliss.
interpretation: The verse presents faith and God-consciousness (taqwa) as the open door to divine mercy even for those who already possess revelation. Possessing a scripture is not in itself sufficient; what alone brings forgiveness of sins and entry into paradise is genuine belief joined with mindfulness of God in conduct. The conditional form, 'if they had believed,' places responsibility on the people themselves, showing that God's forgiveness is ready to meet sincere faith, and that the failure to attain it lies in their own refusal rather than in any lack of divine generosity.

translation: And if they had truly established the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet. Among them is a moderate community, but many of them do evil in what they do.
interpretation: The verse presents faithful adherence to revelation as the true source of abundance, for material provision flows from spiritual uprightness. The phrase 'from above them and from beneath their feet' conveys blessings coming from every direction, showing that when a people lives by its scripture, sustenance surrounds them fully rather than being scarce or grudgingly earned. The verse then turns from this ideal to the reality of the community, dividing it into a moderate, balanced group who uphold the revelation with equilibrium and a majority whose conduct is corrupt. The lesson is that blessings are tied to collective moral responsibility, and that the righteous few are a reminder that sincere faith, rather than mere affiliation with a scripture, is what determines a people's fate.

translation: O Messenger, proclaim what has been revealed to you from your Lord. And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message. And Allah will protect you from the people. Indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the full delivery of revelation is a duty that cannot be partially fulfilled: withholding any part of what was sent down is equivalent to not conveying the message at all, so the Prophet's mission is judged by completeness and courage rather than by selective or fearful omission. It is significant that this command is paired with divine assurance of protection from hostile people, teaching that the one who carries the truth is shielded by God even when opposition is strongest, while the closing statement makes clear that the obstinate rejection of the disbelievers is itself a barrier to receiving divine guidance, placing responsibility for that rejection on their own choice.

translation: Say, "O People of the Scripture, you are not upon anything until you establish the Torah, the Gospel, and what has been revealed to you from your Lord." But what has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in rebellion and disbelief. So do not grieve over the disbelieving people.
interpretation: The verse tells the Prophet that the People of the Book hold no genuine standing before God merely by possessing their scriptures; true standing requires living by what those scriptures contain and by the revelation now sent down through Muhammad, since the Torah and the Gospel both pointed toward the same message of God's guidance. Yet the verse also shows that the same divine revelation which guides the sincere will, for many who reject it, deepen their arrogance and denial, so that the Qur'an becomes a test that exposes hidden hearts. The closing command, not to grieve over them, consoles the Prophet and teaches that his duty is only to convey the message, and that the outcome of a people's stubbornness is not his burden.

translation: Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabeans, and the Christians — whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds — no fear will there be upon them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: The verse establishes that salvation is tied to genuine faith in God and the Last Day together with righteous action, not to belonging to a particular community or label. By naming the Jews, Sabeans, and Christians alongside the believers, it places the criterion of acceptance in the inward reality of belief and the outward reality of good conduct rather than in external affiliation. The phrase 'no fear and no grief' describes the state of security and inner peace that results from a sincere relationship with God and a life lived in accordance with righteousness. Read in its wider context, the verse also reflects a principle of divine justice that does not confine mercy to one religious group, while it still presupposes that faith in God and the Last Day remains the foundation of such a life.

translation: We certainly took the covenant of the Children of Israel and sent to them messengers. Whenever a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire, a group of them they denied, and a group they killed.
interpretation: The verse exposes a recurring pattern in the history of Banu Israel: a people bound by solemn covenant who nonetheless treated God's messengers according to their own inclinations rather than submitting to divine guidance. Their hearts measured the message by whether it pleased them, so any prophet who called them to what they disliked, whether to renounce desires, sins, or worldly interests, was rejected. The verse shows that the root of rejection is not a lack of evidence but the self's resistance to truth that demands its surrender. The gradation, with some denied and others killed, signals the escalation of stubbornness, and it warns the believers of later generations against the same disease: accepting only the teachings that flatter the ego while breaking faith with God's revelation.

translation: And they thought there would be no trial (consequence), so they became blind and deaf; then Allah turned to them in forgiveness, then they became blind and deaf again, many of them. And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do.
interpretation: The verse exposes the self-deception of a people who assumed their transgressions would go unpunished, so their hearts and senses grew dull: they stopped seeing the truth and stopped hearing the call. Allah's repeated mercy, in turning to them after their first lapse, was meant to awaken them, yet their relapse into blindness and deafness shows that divine patience offered as an opportunity is squandered when it only breeds complacency. The closing reminder that Allah sees all their deeds warns that the apparent respite is not neglect, and that a heart which repeatedly ignores guidance grows ever more insensible to it.

translation: Those who said, "Indeed, God is the Messiah, the son of Mary," have certainly disbelieved. But the Messiah said, "O Children of Israel, worship God, my Lord and your Lord." Indeed, whoever associates partners with God - God has forbidden him Paradise, and his refuge is the Fire. And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers.
interpretation: The verse confronts the claim that Jesus was God incarnate by placing the decisive proof in his own mouth: he calls the people to worship God as his Lord and theirs, thereby affirming his creaturely servanthood and rejecting any divinity attributed to him. The verse then generalizes the point into a principle that association of partners with God is the gravest error, cutting a person off from Paradise, and it closes by stating that those who wrong themselves in this way will find no one to rescue them, since salvation rests on pure monotheism and not on the status ascribed to any prophet.

translation: They have certainly disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three." And there is no god except one God. And if they do not desist from what they say, there will surely afflict the disbelievers among them a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse confronts the doctrine of the Trinity as understood by those who associate partners with God, declaring that such a claim amounts to disbelief because it breaks the absolute oneness of God (tawhid). Its logic rests on the single, indivisible divinity of Allah, which excludes any numerical division or partnership in the divine essence. The warning that follows is conditional: those who persist in this saying after the truth has been made clear will face a painful punishment, while the call to desist opens the door to repentance and return to pure monotheism.

translation: Will they not turn in repentance to Allah and seek His forgiveness? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse is a gentle rebuke and an open invitation at once. It questions those who persist in wrongdoing, asking why they do not simply return to God and ask for His forgiveness, as though the path back were obvious and within reach. The closing divine names, Ghafur and Rahim, reveal that the door of repentance is never closed: God's forgiveness is abundant and His mercy encompasses those who turn back. The verse thus joins accountability with hope, reminding the believer that sin calls for prompt turning to God, and that the very act of seeking forgiveness is met by a Lord who pardons and shows compassion.

translation: The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger; messengers had passed away before him, and his mother was a woman of truth. They both used to eat food. Observe how We make the signs clear to them, then observe how they are turned away.
interpretation: The verse strips away any claim to divinity from Jesus by pointing to the most ordinary human facts about him: he was a messenger like those before him, his mother was a truthful woman (siddiqa), and both needed food like every living being, which is incompatible with godhood. The closing call to observe reflects a pattern found throughout the Qur'an, where the clarity of the signs is set against the stubbornness that turns people away from them, so the reader is invited to see how plainly the truth is laid out and how strangely people still refuse it.

translation: Say, "Do you worship, besides Allah, that which possesses neither harm nor benefit for you? And Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing."
interpretation: The verse confronts the human tendency to direct worship toward created beings or objects that have no power to harm or benefit. Its logic is simple and decisive: true worship belongs only to the One who truly controls harm and benefit, and who hears every plea and knows every state. By closing with Allah's attributes of hearing and knowledge, the verse contrasts the living, attentive Lord with lifeless idols that can neither hear nor know, thereby calling the heart to sincere devotion grounded in reason and awareness of who truly holds power.

translation: Say, "O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion beyond the truth, and do not follow the desires of a people who had gone astray before and led many astray, and had strayed from the right way."
interpretation: The verse addresses the People of the Scripture and warns them against ghuluww, the excessive exaggeration in religion that moves beyond what truth allows, whether in venerating prophets or in distorting revealed guidance. It identifies the root of such deviation as following the whims and desires of earlier people who had themselves gone astray and misled others, so that error is perpetuated across generations. The call is thus to return to the pure truth of revelation, free from inherited passions and innovations, and to reject the blind imitation of those whose own path was already lost.

translation: Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed upon the tongue of David and Jesus, son of Mary. That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress.
interpretation: The verse shows that disobedience and persistent transgression against divine limits are what bring a people into a state of rejection, and that this condemnation was not new but had been voiced consistently through the prophets. The curse upon David and Jesus signals that the message of God's mercy and warning was delivered through a continuous chain of revelation, so that those who rejected it had no excuse. The stated cause, 'they disobeyed and used to transgress,' places the responsibility on the people's own conduct: the curse follows from a habit of defiance, not from an arbitrary decree. The verse therefore warns every community that the sustained pattern of disobedience, and not merely a single lapse, is what estranges a people from God's grace.

translation: They did not forbid one another from any wrong they committed. Wretched indeed was what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse condemns a community whose sin lay not only in their own wrongdoing but in their collective silence toward it. Their failure to restrain one another from evil revealed a corrupted social conscience, where the bond of mutual responsibility had dissolved. Enjoining good and forbidding evil is thus presented as a shared duty whose neglect makes the whole community accountable, and the verse warns that tolerating wrong in silence is itself a grave transgression that invites the same condemnation as the act.

translation: You see many of them allying themselves with those who disbelieve. Wretched is what their souls have sent forth for them: that Allah has become angry with them, and in the punishment they will abide eternally.
interpretation: The verse exposes the inner logic of alliance with the disbelievers: when people turn their loyalty away from God and His believers toward those who reject Him, they are not merely making a social or political choice but are sending ahead for their own souls a deed whose consequence is divine wrath. The phrase 'what their souls have sent forth' points to the principle that a person's own acts are the store of his account before God, so the ruin they face is the fruit of their chosen allegiance rather than an arbitrary sentence. The eternal abiding in punishment underscores that loyalty is a matter of the heart's direction, and that tying one's fate to those who oppose the truth carries a weight that endures beyond this world.

translation: And if they had believed in Allah, and in the Prophet, and in what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies; but many of them are defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse exposes the incoherence of a claimed faith that coexists with alliance to those who oppose God and His messenger. True belief in Allah and the Prophet, and in the revelation sent down to him, necessarily produces loyalty to the community of faith and distance from those who oppose it, so taking such people as allies is itself evidence that the professed belief is hollow. The closing phrase shifts the blame from belief as such to disobedience: the majority of them have chosen transgression over submission, which is why their words of faith do not translate into conduct. The lesson is that faith is tested by its practical commitments, especially in matters of loyalty, where the believer must prefer God's cause over worldly protection and kinship.

translation: You will surely find the most intense of people in enmity toward those who believe to be the Jews and those who associate partners with God; and you will surely find the nearest of them in affection toward those who believe to be those who say, "We are Christians." That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant.
interpretation: The verse draws a distinction within the religious landscape of early Medina rather than issuing a blanket judgment. Hostility toward the believers is attributed most strongly to the Jews and to the polytheists, reflecting the open opposition the early Muslim community faced from those groups. By contrast, those who call themselves Christians are described as nearer in affection, and the reason given is moral and spiritual: they include learned men devoted to worship and ascetic life, and they are free of the haughty refusal to accept truth that the verse attributes to others. The passage therefore links closeness to the believers with humility and devotion, teaching that disposition of heart, not mere label or lineage, determines how people stand before the truth.

translation: And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they have recognized. They say, "Our Lord, we have believed, so register us among the witnesses."
interpretation: The verse portrays the moment of recognition in the hearts of those who had received earlier scripture, particularly among the Christians who respond to the Qur'an. Their tears are not merely emotional but a sign that the truth they already knew has been confirmed in what is revealed to the Prophet, so the recognition pierces them to the eyes. Their prayer, asking to be written among the witnesses, expresses a desire to join those who bear witness to the truth of God's message, and it shows that true faith is a humble acknowledgment that moves the believer to stand with the community of witnesses to God's guidance.

translation: And why would we not believe in God and in what has come to us of the truth, while we hope that our Lord will admit us along with the righteous people?
interpretation: This verse is spoken by the believers of the people of Moses, who had been among those who recognized the truth of the message brought to them. Their words express a sincere and reasoned resolve: having received the truth, there is no justification for refusing belief, and their hope of admission among the righteous is not a presumption but a natural consequence of turning sincerely to God. It reflects the principle that faith is grounded in recognizing the truth when it arrives, and that the desire for God's mercy and companionship with the righteous should lead a person to firm and steadfast belief rather than to denial or arrogance.

translation: So Allah rewarded them, for what they said, with gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the recompense of the good-doers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that Allah's reward is tied to sincere words that are backed by sincere deeds: the believers' declaration of faith and their humble plea for forgiveness and steadfastness (in the preceding verses, 'Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excess in our affairs, and make firm our feet, and help us against the disbelieving people') is answered with an everlasting paradise. The phrase 'the recompense of the good-doers' shows that ihsan, doing beautifully and excellently, is the true measure of acceptance, and that the words of the heart become meaningful when they are lived out in action.

translation: But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs - those are the companions of Hellfire.
interpretation: This verse draws a direct contrast with the preceding description of the righteous, establishing that rejection of God's signs is not merely intellectual doubt but a active refusal that is coupled with denial. The Qur'an repeatedly presents the signs (ayat) as both the natural order and the revealed message, so to reject them is to reject the very evidence that points toward the Creator. The phrase 'companions of Hellfire' (ashab al-jahim) conveys a state of inseparable belonging: those who choose denial are described as bound to the consequence they have chosen, emphasizing that the Hellfire is the natural destination of a soul that persistently turns away from truth, rather than an arbitrary punishment.

translation: O you who have believed, do not prohibit the good things that Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not like transgressors.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the authority to declare things lawful or unlawful belongs to Allah alone, so a believer who voluntarily forbids for himself what God has permitted, in the name of asceticism or piety, is in effect encroaching upon the divine prerogative and thereby committing a form of transgression. Religious devotion is thus measured not by self-imposed deprivation but by gratefully accepting and enjoying the good provisions God has made lawful, within the bounds He has set. The closing warning against transgression ties this restraint to moderation: excess in renunciation is as much a departure from the balanced path as excess in indulgence, and God's disapproval attaches to both.

translation: And eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good, and fear Allah, in whom you are believers.
interpretation: The verse joins the command to eat with a condition of lawfulness and goodness: sustenance is a trust from God, so a believer's enjoyment of provision must be bounded by what God has made permissible and wholesome, both in its source and its nature. It then ties this discipline to taqwa, showing that consciousness of God is not confined to ritual but extends into the most ordinary acts such as eating, and that faith itself is sustained by vigilance over one's daily choices. The closing reminder of belief implies that mindfulness of God is the natural expression of having true faith.

translation: Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintentional in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have deliberately resolved upon in oaths. Its expiation is feeding ten needy people with the average of what you feed your own families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave. But whoever cannot find [the means], then fasting three days. That is the expiation of your oaths when you have sworn. And guard your oaths. Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses, that you may be grateful.
interpretation: The verse distinguishes between the empty, slips-of-the-tongue oath, which carries no blame, and the oath that is deliberately bound by the heart's intention, which creates real moral responsibility. By tying accountability to conscious commitment, it teaches that God judges the inner resolve behind speech. The prescribed expiation is graduated and merciful: it offers a generous, practical gift to the poor measured by what one ordinarily gives one's own household, with alternatives of clothing or freeing a slave, and only falls back to fasting for those lacking means. The closing call to guard one's oaths reflects a broader ethic of treating one's word as sacred, so that swearing by God's name is not treated lightly, and the purpose of such guidance is gratitude for God's clarity.

translation: O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificial] stones set up for worship, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.
interpretation: The verse presents the prohibition of intoxicants, gambling, idolatrous stones, and divining arrows as a single category of moral impurity, grouping them together as things that corrupt the soul and distance the believer from God. By calling them the work of Satan, it reveals that these practices are not merely harmful habits but instruments through which the devil sows enmity and distraction among people and turns them away from remembrance of God. The command to avoid them, rather than merely to refrain from their use in a narrow sense, points to a comprehensive turning away from whatever clouds reason, squanders wealth through chance, or seeks guidance from illusion instead of trust in the Creator. The closing promise of success ties the believer's flourishing to this purification, suggesting that true prosperity lies in a life cleansed of what Satan adorns, and that the path to felicity passes through deliberate abstention from such defilements.

translation: Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred among you through intoxicants and gambling, and to prevent you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?
interpretation: The verse exposes the hidden design behind intoxicants and gambling: they are not merely individual sins but instruments by which Satan sows discord within the community, dissolving the bonds of affection that hold believers together. Because these vices capture the heart and occupy the mind, they gradually displace the remembrance of God and the discipline of prayer, the two pillars that keep a person anchored to the Divine. The closing question is not a mere inquiry but a call to self-examination, urging the believer to recognize the trap and to halt before the damage to both social harmony and spiritual life becomes irreversible.

translation: And obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, then know that the duty of Our Messenger is only to convey (the message) clearly.
interpretation: The verse ties obedience to Allah directly to obedience to His Messenger, presenting the two as one inseparable command, since the Messenger's guidance is the means by which the divine will is known and followed. The call to beware (ihdharu) points to the danger of neglecting or evading this obedience, which is a warning that the consequences of turning away rest on the one who turns away. The final clause frees the Messenger from responsibility for those who refuse: his task is only the clear delivery of the message, not compelling belief or obedience. This places the burden of accountability on the individual's own choice while affirming that the message itself has been made plainly available.

translation: There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten, if they fear God and believe and do righteous deeds, and then fear God and believe, and then fear God and do good; and God loves the good-doers.
interpretation: The verse, revealed in connection with the prohibition of wine, teaches that past consumption made before a prohibition was legislated is not held against believers once they have turned to God's commands. The repeated cycle of piety, faith, and righteous action, climaxing in ihsan (excellence in conduct, worship, and dealing with people), shows that God's pleasure rests on those who progress from outward compliance to beautiful, sincere devotion, and that the sincerity of the heart and the quality of one's deeds matter more than mere avoidance of a single act.

translation: O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something of game that your hands and your spears can reach, so that Allah may make evident who fears Him unseen. And whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse presents the prohibition on hunting during the state of ihram as a trial of faith, in which the believer's hands and spears can reach the game but restraint is required. Allah's 'knowing' here refers to making the reality of faith manifest in action: the true measure of piety is fear of Allah when no one sees and no worldly consequence compels obedience. Those who violate the prohibition after this clear warning are threatened with a painful punishment, teaching that a believer's devotion is proven by self-restraint at the moment of temptation rather than by mere profession.

translation: O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram. And whoever kills it intentionally among you - then compensation is an equivalent of what he killed from the livestock, as judged by two just men among you, as an offering reaching the Kaaba, or an expiation of feeding needy people, or the equivalent of that in fasting, that he may taste the consequence of his deed. Allah has pardoned what was past. But whoever returns to it, Allah will take retribution from him. And Allah is All-Mighty, the Possessor of retribution.
interpretation: The verse addresses believers during the sacred state of ihram, forbidding the hunting of game, and establishes that deliberate violation carries a graduated expiation, with the equivalence of the slain animal judged by upright witnesses, so that the sin is felt in its real weight and the offender tastes the consequence of his act. The mention of pardon for what has passed together with the warning against repetition shows that divine mercy opens the door to repentance, while persistence in transgression brings a sure accountability, for God is Mighty and Lord of retribution. The passage thus joins reverence for the sanctity of the sacred place and time with a balance of justice and mercy in the moral life of the believer.

translation: Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you and for the travelers; but forbidden for you is the game of the land as long as you are in the state of ihram. And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered.
interpretation: The verse opens a door of ease alongside a boundary of sacred discipline: the sea's bounty is made freely available to the believers and to those passing through as travelers, showing that Allah's provision is generous and not confined to the settled. Yet the pilgrim in the sacred state is asked to restrain his hunting on land, so that the sanctity of the pilgrimage and the inner state of ihram train the heart to master its appetites even when something is permitted. The verse closes by tying all of this to taqwa, reminding that every restriction and every permission is ultimately measured before the One to whom all will return for judgment, so that the outward law of the pilgrimage becomes a mirror of accountability before God.

translation: God has made the Sacred House, the Kaaba, a means of standing (support) for people, and the sacred month, and the offerings and the garlands. That is so that you may know that God knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and that God is All-Knowing of everything.
interpretation: The verse presents the Kaaba, the sacred month, the sacrificial offerings and the garlanded animals as divinely appointed institutions that uphold human life, both spiritual and social: they sustain communal order, peace and the balance of society. By linking these institutions to God's comprehensive knowledge of the heavens and the earth, the verse teaches that the order of the sacred is not arbitrary but rooted in a Creator who knows all things, so that the believer, reflecting on these signs, comes to recognize the universality of divine knowledge and the wisdom behind the rites that sustain people.

translation: Know that Allah is severe in punishment, and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse places two divine attributes side by side so that the believer holds fear and hope in balance. Mentioning Allah's severity in punishment first awakens awareness of accountability and the seriousness of disobedience, so that a person does not become complacent about sin. Immediately following it with His forgiveness and mercy prevents that awareness from turning into despair, reminding the servant that repentance opens the door back to Allah's grace. The 'knowing' commanded at the start is therefore not mere information but a inner orientation: a heart that trembles before justice yet relies on mercy, walking steadily between the two.

translation: The duty of the Messenger is only to convey (the message). And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal.
interpretation: The verse establishes the limits of the Prophet's role: his responsibility ends with clear delivery of the revelation, while guidance and results rest with God. It then reminds the listener that nothing is hidden from God, so both outward declarations and inner intentions are known to Him, which calls the believer to sincerity and honesty before Him rather than reliance on appearances or on the messenger's power to compel belief.

translation: Say, "The corrupt and the good are not equal, even if the abundance of the corrupt impresses you. So be mindful of God, O people of understanding, that you may prosper."
interpretation: The verse establishes a principle that worth is measured by inner quality rather than by number or outward appeal: what is corrupt (khabith) and what is good (tayyib) can never be equal, however widespread the corrupt may be or however dazzling it may seem to the eye. Its address to "people of understanding" (ulu al-albab) signals that discernment is the faculty needed to see through quantity and popularity to real value, and that the remedy for being swayed by the crowd is taqwa, consciousness of God, which in turn leads to success. Read broadly, it warns against judging truth, goodness, or the lawful by how many follow them, and calls the believer to prefer the pure even when it is scarce.

translation: O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were made apparent to you, would distress you. But if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be made apparent to you. Allah has pardoned you concerning them, and Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.
interpretation: The verse warns believers against excessive and burdensome questioning about matters the revelation has not addressed, since answers to such questions could bring hardship or obligations they would find distressing. Its underlying lesson is that the believer should accept what is clearly commanded and refrain from probing into what has been left unspecified, which is a mercy from God, as the pardon at the end indicates that Allah has overlooked past inquiries of this kind and that His forgiveness and forbearance extend to those who turn back from such questioning.

translation: Indeed, a people before you asked such questions, and then they became disbelievers because of them.
interpretation: The verse warns believers against asking excessive or probing questions about matters that were not made necessary to reveal, since earlier communities who pressed such inquiries were given answers that burdened them, and their persistence in questioning eventually led them into disbelief. It teaches restraint and humility before revealed guidance: one should accept what is revealed, seek what is useful and clearly commanded, and avoid turning religion into a field of contentious speculation that breeds doubt rather than faith.

translation: Allah did not ordain any bahira, nor sa'iba, nor wasila, nor ham; but those who disbelieve invent lies against Allah, and most of them do not reason.
interpretation: The verse exposes the origin of the customs of the pagan Arabs, who attributed to God the prohibition of certain animals (the bahira, sa'iba, wasila and ham) that had no basis in divine law. By stating that God did not ordain these practices, the verse makes clear that religious legislation belongs to God alone, and that attributing prohibitions to Him without revelation is a fabrication against Him. The closing remark that most of them do not use their intellect points to the failure of reason when it abandons revelation and follows inherited tradition blindly, so that people accept falsehood about God without examination.

translation: And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," they say, "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers following." Even though their fathers knew nothing, nor were they guided?
interpretation: The verse exposes the blind imitation of ancestral custom as a barrier to accepting divine guidance. When the believers' rejecters are invited to return to what God has sent down and to the Messenger who conveys it, they reject the call not by argument but by appeal to inherited tradition, treating the practices of their forefathers as a sufficient standard. The rhetorical question then dismantles this stance: if the fathers themselves lacked knowledge and were not guided, then clinging to their way cannot be a path to truth. The lesson is that religious authority must rest on revelation and its messenger, and that inheritance alone, without knowledge or guidance, cannot justify error.

translation: O you who have believed, you are responsible for yourselves; those who have gone astray cannot harm you once you are guided. To Allah is your return, all of you, and He will inform you of what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse directs the believers' attention inward, reminding each person that their first duty is the reform and accountability of their own soul, since no one will be questioned for another's deviation once they have themselves followed guidance. Its meaning is not an abandonment of enjoining good and forbidding evil, which the Qur'an elsewhere makes binding, but a correction of the anxiety that can grip a community over the errors of others. The ultimate reckoning belongs to Allah alone, to whom all return, so the believer should measure success by sincerity and right conduct rather than by the conduct of those who stray.

translation: O you who have believed, when death approaches one of you and he makes a bequest, let there be testimony between you: two just men from among you, or two others from outside your own people if you are traveling through the land and the calamity of death strikes you. You shall detain them after the prayer, and they shall swear by Allah, saying: "We will not sell our testimony for any price, even if it concerns a near relative, and we will not conceal the testimony of Allah; indeed, we would then be among the sinners."
interpretation: The verse shows that faith is tested in the most serious matters of trust, such as a dying person's last will, where no worldly gain or family loyalty may corrupt honest testimony. By requiring the witnesses to swear after the prayer, when the hearts are turned toward God, it places the witness's word under the weight of divine accountability, so that a believer understands that to conceal or sell testimony is to betray God Himself. It also teaches that justice must be upheld even against one's own kin, and that the rights of the dead and of heirs are safeguarded through the honesty of those who bear witness.

translation: And if it is discovered that the two (witnesses) had committed a sin (by deceit), then let two others stand in their place from among those who were wronged by them, the two nearest (in right), and let them swear by Allah: "Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and we have not transgressed; indeed, we would then be among the wrongdoers."
interpretation: The verse establishes a safeguard for the integrity of testimony in a situation of suspicion, particularly during a bequest made on a journey. When the original witnesses are found to have betrayed the trust by concealing or distorting what they knew, the law does not leave the injured party without recourse. Two replacements from among those with a rightful claim take their place and swear an oath before God, which shifts the burden to a truthful counter-testimony. The lesson is that justice depends on exposing deception and that a sworn testimony made in God's presence carries grave moral weight, so that people are held accountable for what they witness and for the rights of others entrusted to them.

translation: That is more likely that they will give testimony in its proper form, or fear that oaths will be repeated after their oaths. And fear Allah and listen. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: This verse closes the rule on testimony given under oath during a bequest (Surah al-Ma'idah 5:106-108). Allah prescribes this procedure because it is the surest way to secure truthful testimony in its correct form: witnesses who know that their oath may be turned back against them, or that other witnesses may come forward to contradict them, are far more likely to speak honestly and precisely. The verse then calls the believers to taqwa and to attentive listening, the two qualities that make legal and moral guidance effective, and it warns that Allah does not guide those who persist in deliberate defiance (fisq). The lesson is that the integrity of testimony is a matter of both justice toward others and fear of God, and that rules of evidence exist to protect truth within a community of faith.

translation: On the Day when Allah will gather the messengers and say, "What was your response?" They will say, "We have no knowledge. Indeed, it is You who is the Knower of the unseen."
interpretation: The verse opens a scene of the Day of Judgment in which the messengers, who were sent to their peoples, are gathered and questioned about the reception of their message.
