Their reply, "We have no knowledge," is not a denial of their mission but an expression of profound humility before the infinite knowledge of God, since the true state of every community's response, including what happened after the messengers departed, is hidden from them and known only to Allah. By affirming that God alone is the Knower of the unseen, the messengers testify to His absolute knowledge and point to the limits of all human knowledge in the face of the divine reckoning, reminding the listener that accountability rests on the One who encompasses all that is hidden and manifest.

translation: When God said: 'O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My favor upon you and upon your mother, when I supported you with the Holy Spirit, you spoke to people in the cradle and in maturity; and when I taught you the Book, wisdom, the Torah, and the Gospel; and when you shaped from clay as the form of a bird by My permission, then you breathed into it and it became a bird by My permission, and you healed the blind and the leper by My permission, and when you brought forth the dead by My permission; and when I restrained the Children of Israel from you when you came to them with clear proofs, and those among them who disbelieved said, 'This is not but evident magic.'
interpretation: The verse recounts God's blessings upon Jesus as a reminder of divine favor and of the miracles that were, in every case, carried out only by God's permission, so that Jesus's power is shown to be a sign from God rather than an independent divine attribute. Its placement shows that the disbelievers' rejection of clear signs as mere sorcery is a recurring human response to truth, while the repeated phrase 'by My permission' guards against exalting Jesus beyond his role as a servant and messenger.

translation: And when I inspired the disciples, saying: Believe in Me and in My Messenger, they said: We have believed, and bear witness that we are Muslims (submitting ourselves).
interpretation: The verse shows that faith is a call that is answered by sincere submission. The disciples of Jesus, when inspired to believe in God and His messenger, responded immediately and without hesitation, taking on the testimony of their own submission to God. Their words, "we have believed" and "bear witness that we are Muslims," reveal that true belief is not merely spoken but is affirmed before God as a complete surrender of the self. The verse also implies that the messengers of God across time have called to one and the same message of faith and submission, so that the followers who answer that call share in a single path.

translation: When the disciples said, "O Jesus, son of Mary, can your Lord send down to us a table spread with food from the heaven?" He said, "Fear God, if you are believers."
interpretation: The verse reveals a moment in which the disciples' request, phrased as a question about whether God is able to send down a table from heaven, is met with a rebuke that turns their demand back on the heart of faith. Jesus does not dismiss the request outright but calls them to taqwa, a conscious awareness and fear of God, implying that a true believer should not place God's power under scrutiny or demand signs as a test of Him. The phrase "if you are believers" suggests that the question itself reflects a shortfall in certainty, and that genuine faith is measured by reverence and trust rather than by the demand for miraculous proof. The passage thus teaches that the seeking of signs must be grounded in humility before God, and that piety, not spectacle, is the proper foundation of belief.

translation: They said, "We wish to eat from it, and that our hearts may be assured, and that we may know that you have told us the truth, and that we may be among its witnesses."
interpretation: The disciples' request moves from bodily need to a quest for certainty: they want the table not merely to eat but so that their hearts may be at rest, so that their knowledge of Jesus's truthfulness may be confirmed by direct witness rather than report alone. Their wish to be among its witnesses shows a desire to bear testimony to the sign before others, making them active carriers of the truth they have seen. The verse thus portrays faith seeking to ascend from hearing to seeing, while also implicitly teaching that a sign granted in answer to such a request carries a weightier responsibility, since those who witness a clear miracle are accountable for how they respond to it.

translation: Jesus, son of Mary, said: "O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table spread with food from the heaven, which will be a festival for us, for the first of us and the last of us, and a sign from You. And provide for us, for You are the best of providers."
interpretation: The verse shows the disciples' request for a miraculous table from heaven to strengthen their faith, and Jesus' response turning to Allah in supplication. The true purpose of the sign is that it becomes a lasting reminder of gratitude and a visible proof of God's power and generosity, honored by every generation that follows. Jesus closes by acknowledging that provision ultimately comes from God alone, the best of all providers, teaching that even miraculous gifts are to be sought humbly through prayer and trust in Him.

translation: God said, "Indeed, I will send it down to you; but whoever among you disbelieves after that, I will surely punish him with a punishment that I will not inflict upon anyone else in all the worlds."
interpretation: The verse shows that God's gift of a miraculous sign, here the table spread down from heaven requested by the disciples of Jesus, carries a binding responsibility: having witnessed a clear sign, disbelief becomes far graver, since the one who denies after seeing is held to a uniquely severe accountability. It teaches that the greater the evidence and blessing received, the greater the moral weight of ingratitude and rejection, and that divine justice is measured against the light a person has been given.

translation: And [mention] when Allah said: "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah'?" He will say: "Glory be to You! It was not for me to say what I have no right to say. If I had said it, You would have known it. You know what is within myself, and I do not know what is within Yourself. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen."
interpretation: This verse presents a scene of the Day of Judgment in which Allah questions Jesus directly, and the answer reveals the complete absence of any claim to divinity on his part, which is a decisive refutation of the deification of Jesus and his mother Mary. Jesus's response begins by exalting Allah above any partner or deficiency, then affirms that speaking falsely about God is not something befitting him, since he has no right to utter what is untrue. His appeal to divine knowledge, that Allah knows even what is hidden within him, shows that the sincerity of his submission is known to God alone. The closing acknowledgment that only Allah knows the unseen emphasizes the boundary between the Creator's infinite knowledge and the creature's limited knowledge, and thereby uproots the notion that any created being shares in divinity.

translation: I said to them nothing except what You commanded me: 'Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.' And I was a witness over them while I remained among them; but when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them, and You are Witness over all things.
interpretation: This verse is spoken by Jesus, peace be upon him, on the Day of Resurrection in response to Allah's question to him about whether he told people to take him and his mother as gods besides Allah (Al-Ma'idah 5:116). He declares his complete fidelity to the message he was entrusted with: his only call was the pure monotheistic command to worship Allah alone, the Lord of both him and his people, rejecting any claim of divinity for himself. He affirms that while he lived among his people he bore witness over their conduct, but after his 'taking up' (tawaffi), the divine oversight passed entirely to Allah, who alone observes all things. The verse thus places the responsibility for the later distortions of his message upon those who deviated after him, while affirming that Allah is the ultimate Witness over everything, and it reflects the profound humility and sincerity of the prophets before their Lord.

translation: If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: In this verse, Jesus, peace be upon him, places the entire matter of his people's fate in the hands of God alone, speaking with a humility that refuses any claim over the outcome. He does not demand their punishment nor plead for their pardon as though he could decide it; he simply acknowledges that they are God's servants and therefore wholly subject to His judgment. The phrase 'You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise' affirms that God's justice in punishing and His mercy in forgiving both flow from perfect power and perfect wisdom, so the believer's posture before such a Lord is complete surrender and trust that whatever He decrees is just. The verse thus teaches that true prophetic intercession rests on submission to divine will rather than on the assertion of any independent authority.

translation: Allah said, "This is a day on which the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness. For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is the great triumph."
interpretation: The verse presents the Day of Judgment as a day of distinction, where the value of sincerity becomes fully manifest. Truthfulness, which in worldly life may be doubted, misunderstood, or left unrewarded, is revealed in its true worth, because the true benefit of one's word and conviction is only realized when it is measured by sincerity before God. The reward is described in two dimensions: the outward delight of eternal gardens and rivers, and the inward and more profound joy of mutual pleasure between the servant and his Lord. This mutual contentment suggests that the highest happiness is not merely in possessing blessings but in the perfect harmony of the heart with God, where the servant's acceptance of divine decree is met with divine approval. The phrase "the great triumph" thus points to a success that is not measured by worldly gain but by nearness to God and everlasting satisfaction.

translation: To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is within them, and He is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse grounds the believer's sense of reality in the absolute and exclusive sovereignty of God. Ownership and rule are not temporary loans to the powerful but belong entirely to the One who brought all things into being, so the ultimate authority over every creature and every created order lies with Him alone. The phrase 'and whatever is within them' extends this dominion to the full range of existence, reminding the reader that nothing escapes divine possession and direction, from the vast celestial bodies to the smallest beings on earth. The closing declaration that He is capable of all things joins sovereignty to power: the One who owns everything is also able to do anything He wills. For the believer, this combination brings both humility, since human claims to mastery are seen as borrowed and fleeting, and reassurance, since whatever hardship or circumstance one faces lies within a dominion that is neither careless nor limited.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light. Yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord.
interpretation: The verse opens by fixing praise exclusively upon Allah as the sole Creator of the heavens, the earth, the darkness and the light, which together encompass the whole of existence, both visible and hidden, material and spiritual. The making of darkness and light is mentioned alongside the cosmos to show that the Creator governs every mode of existence and every state of the soul, from ignorance to guidance. The sharp turn to 'then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord' exposes the absurdity of disbelief: the very creation that testifies to a single, unrivalled Creator is nonetheless taken by those who reject faith to set up equals with Him. The word 'ya'dilun' also carries the sense of deviating or swerving away from the truth, so the verse presents idolatry as a deliberate turning aside from the clear evidence of creation.

translation: It is He who created you from clay, then decreed a term (for you). And there is a specified term with Him. Yet you still doubt.
interpretation: The verse begins by pointing to the origin of humankind: God shaped the human being from clay, the humble and ordinary material of the earth, so that the one who might be proud is reminded of his lowly beginning. It then speaks of two terms. The first is the appointed lifespan decreed for each person, which begins at birth and ends at death. The second is the specified term that is held with God alone, which is the Last Hour or the final reckoning, known only to Him and not to any creature. By placing the two terms side by side, the verse shows that human life is bounded by the power of the Creator who both originated and ends it. The closing phrase, 'yet you still doubt' (thumma antum tamtarun), rebukes those who dispute the resurrection and the reckoning despite the clear evidence of their own creation from clay. The one who has witnessed the first creation has no sound reason to deny the second.

translation: And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth. He knows what you conceal and what you reveal, and He knows what you earn.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the one true God is worshipped and acknowledged throughout the heavens and the earth, and that His knowledge is total and encompasses every hidden and apparent act of a person. By stating that He knows both what is kept secret and what is openly displayed, it removes any illusion that human beings can escape His awareness through concealment. The mention of what 'you earn' points to deeds and their consequences, reminding the listener that every action, intention, and livelihood is recorded before a Knower who holds them accountable. The verse thus calls the heart toward vigilance, sincerity, and a consciousness of God that governs private as well as public conduct.

translation: And never does a sign come to them from among the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it.
interpretation: The verse describes a persistent habit of heedlessness among those who reject the message: every sign that reaches them from their Lord, whether in the revelation or in the created world, is met not with reflection but with aversion. The turning away is not caused by a lack of evidence but by a settled disposition that refuses to engage with what is clearly set before them. It warns that the problem lies in the heart's willingness to attend, so that the signs, however clear, remain ineffective for one who has chosen to look away.

translation: So they have denied the truth when it came to them, but there will soon come to them the news of what they used to mock.
interpretation: The verse describes a pattern of rejection: those who receive the truth at the moment it reaches them, yet deny it, are shown that their mockery is not without consequence. The phrase "anbaa'" (news) points to a certainty that the reality they scoffed at will be made manifest to them, whether in this world through its signs and outcomes or in the Hereafter. The delay implied by "fa-sawfa" (so they will surely come to know) underscores that the reckoning, though it may seem distant to the scoffers, is inevitable, and that the truth's own weight will eventually disclose the emptiness of their derision.

translation: Did they not see how many generations We destroyed before them, whom We had established on the earth in ways We have not established you, and We sent down abundant rain upon them from the sky and made rivers flow beneath them? Then We destroyed them for their sins and brought into being after them other generations.
interpretation: The verse directs the listeners to reflect on the fate of earlier peoples who enjoyed power, prosperity, and abundant provision, yet were seized by God when they persisted in sin, showing that worldly blessings are no guarantee of safety and that divine accountability is not bound to any nation's strength. By pointing to the generations that succeeded them, it also conveys that God's dominion is continuous and that the rise and fall of peoples is a warning addressed to every later community to heed the message before its own time comes.

translation: And even if We had sent down to you a written scripture on paper, and they had touched it with their own hands, those who disbelieved would have said, "This is nothing but clear magic."
interpretation: The verse shows that the rejection of the truth is not caused by a lack of evidence but by a settled disposition of denial. Even the most tangible form of proof, a written book they could see and physically handle, would not move those who have already decided to disbelieve; they would dismiss it as sorcery rather than acknowledge it as a divine revelation. Thus the verse consoles the Prophet by teaching that the obstinacy of the disbelievers stems from their hearts, not from any deficiency in the signs presented to them, and that guidance depends on sincere openness rather than on the demand for ever more visible miracles.

translation: And they say, "Why was an angel not sent down to him?" Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and then they would not be reprieved.
interpretation: The verse reveals the disbelievers' demand that the Prophet be accompanied by an angel as visible proof of his truth, a demand rooted in their expectation that a messenger must be supported by something beyond the human. God answers that such a request is self-defeating: if the sign they ask for were granted and they still denied it, the decisive judgment would have been executed immediately, leaving them no further respite. The divine wisdom therefore withholds spectacular signs that would only seal the fate of those who refuse to believe, and it implies that the message is to be accepted on its own clarity rather than on demanded miracles.

translation: And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man, and We would have covered them with [the same confusion] which they now cover themselves with.
interpretation: The verse addresses the disbelievers who demanded that the Messenger be accompanied by an angel or that an angel be sent down to them as a sign. God's reply shows that sending an angel would not have served their purpose: an angel sent as a messenger would have to appear in a human form so that people could see and deal with him, and this would only recreate the same doubt they already felt about the Prophet. Had they been shown an angel, they would have raised the same objection, so the confusion they wrap around themselves would be placed upon them in turn. The verse thus points to the fact that the problem lies not in the lack of evidence but in the disposition of hearts that refuse to accept the truth, and that God's wisdom in choosing the form of His messengers is aimed at guidance, not at satisfying demands made in bad faith.

translation: And messengers before you were certainly mocked, but those who ridiculed them were engulfed by that which they used to mock.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet and affirms a constant pattern in God's dealings with humanity: every messenger sent before him was met with derision, and this is a trial that accompanies the truth in every age. The verse reassures the believer that mockery of the message does not go unanswered. The phrase "ḥāqa bihim" conveys that the punishment encircled and befell them, so that the very thing they scorned came back upon them. Thus the ridicule that the disbelievers directed at the messengers returned to them in the form of the consequence they had denied, teaching that the mocker's own derision becomes the instrument of his undoing, and that patience in the face of ridicule is the path of the prophets.

translation: Say: "Travel through the earth and then observe how was the end of those who denied."
interpretation: The verse directs the reader to reflect on history through direct observation. Travel and witnessing the ruins of earlier peoples who rejected their messengers turns the past into a lesson: the same patterns of denial lead to the same consequences. It invites the believer to draw conclusions from visible evidence rather than heedless assumption, and warns that the fate of past deniers is a sign for those who come after them.

translation: Say, "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?" Say, "To Allah. He has prescribed for Himself mercy. He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt. Those who have destroyed their souls will not believe."
interpretation: The verse opens with a question put to the one who denies or neglects the Creator, then answers it immediately with "Allah," so that the questioner is left to acknowledge that all ownership and dominion in the heavens and earth belong to Him alone. Having established His absolute sovereignty, the verse discloses the manner of that sovereignty: He has bound Himself by a decree of mercy, a mercy that is not a mere sentiment but a commitment written upon His own essence. That mercy is the reason for the certainty of the gathering on the Day of Resurrection, which is announced as beyond doubt, so that human beings are reminded that their accountability is part of the same merciful order that created them. The closing sentence draws a sharp contrast: those who have ruined their own selves through their choices are precisely the ones who remain closed to faith, showing that disbelief is ultimately a form of self-inflicted loss rather than a failure that befalls the Creator.

translation: And to Him belongs whatever dwells in the night and the day. And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse points to the comprehensiveness of God's dominion: what is 'at rest' (sakana) in the night and what moves in the day both belong to Him, so that the cycle of darkness and light, rest and activity, is brought under a single ownership and governance. The closing names, As-Samee' and Al-'Aleem, then tie this sovereignty to awareness: the One who owns everything that stirs or settles in time is also the One who hears every utterance and knows every hidden state, so nothing in the ordered alternation of night and day escapes His hearing or knowledge.

translation: Say, "Shall I take as a protector other than Allah, the Creator of the heavens and the earth, while He feeds and is not fed?" Say, "Indeed, I have been commanded to be the first to submit (to Allah)." And do not be among the polytheists.
interpretation: The verse presents a rhetorical challenge to the idea of seeking any guardian or ally besides the One who originated the heavens and the earth and who sustains all creatures without needing sustenance Himself. Since true dependence and trust belong only to the Creator who provides for all and is self-sufficient, turning to any other as protector is both illogical and a form of associating partners with Him. The Prophet's declaration that he is commanded to be the foremost of those who submit places him at the head of the community of believers, showing that submission to God alone is the core of prophetic mission. The closing prohibition against being among the polytheists serves as a firm warning that association with God is incompatible with the sincere surrender that the verse calls for.

translation: Say, "Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous day."
interpretation: The verse presents the fear of God as the foundation of obedience: even a prophet who is sure of his mission expresses dread of disobedience, which shows that awareness of accountability should lead a believer to restrain himself from sin. The phrase "a tremendous day" points to the Day of Judgment, whose magnitude is meant to awaken the heart and turn it toward repentance and steadfastness in obedience.

translation: Whoever is spared from it on that Day, Allah has indeed shown him mercy. And that is the clear triumph.
interpretation: The verse points to the decisive truth that salvation on the Day of Judgment is not earned by one's own strength alone but is granted by Allah's mercy. The phrase "whoever is turned away from it" conveys that the punishment is something a person is either spared from or falls into, and being spared is itself a sign of divine grace. The closing words, "that is the clear triumph," call the believer to measure success not by worldly gain, which is fleeting, but by deliverance from the Fire and admission into Allah's mercy, which is the only victory that truly endures.

translation: And if Allah should touch you with harm, there is none who can remove it except Him; and if He touches you with good, then He is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse teaches that all power over harm and benefit belongs to Allah alone. Hardship cannot be lifted by any creature, and no good can be withheld from a person when Allah wills to grant it, because His power encompasses everything. Thus the believer's trust should be placed in Him alone, neither fearing created beings who cannot remove affliction nor depending on them for provision, since every outcome, whether trial or blessing, flows from His absolute ability and wisdom.

translation: And He is the Subduer over His servants, and He is the All-Wise, the All-Aware.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God's dominion over creation is absolute: His qahr (irresistible power) means that every creature, however strong or proud, is subject to His will and cannot escape it, and this sovereignty is not the tyranny of a capricious ruler but is joined with perfect wisdom (hikma) and complete knowledge (khubra), so that His dominance is always exercised with purpose and in full awareness of the inner states and deeds of His servants. The pairing invites the believer to find both awe and reassurance: awe before a power that no force can resist, and trust in a power that acts only in accordance with wisdom and knowledge of what is hidden.

translation: Say, "What thing is greatest as a testimony?" Say, "Allah is witness between me and you. And this Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you by it and whoever it reaches. Do you actually testify that there are other gods besides Allah?" Say, "I do not testify to that." Say, "He is only one God, and I am free from what you associate with Him."
interpretation: The verse establishes that the greatest witness is Allah, whose testimony in favor of the Prophet's message is decisive, and it shows that the Qur'an is a revelation whose purpose is warning all who hear it, with its reach extending to every generation that receives it. The challenge posed to the idolaters, asking whether they truly bear witness to other deities, exposes the baselessness of polytheism, and the Prophet's firm refusal to join that testimony reaffirms pure monotheism (tawhid) as the core of the message and the basis of his disassociation from shirk.

translation: Those to whom We have given the Scripture recognize it as they recognize their own sons. Those who have lost their souls, they are the ones who do not believe.
interpretation: The verse presents the People of the Book as possessing such clear knowledge of the Prophet's truth, as confirmed in their own scriptures, that their recognition of it is as certain as a father's recognition of his own children. Their rejection is therefore not born of ignorance but of self-inflicted loss: by refusing what they know, they forfeit their own souls, and it is this deliberate turning away, rather than any lack of evidence, that keeps them from faith.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or denies His verses? Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed.
interpretation: The verse establishes the gravest form of injustice as attributing falsehood to Allah or rejecting His signs, since such a person distorts the relationship between the Creator and creation at its foundation. By linking this wrongdoing to the certainty that the wrongdoers will not prosper, it shows that success is inseparable from truthfulness toward God and sincere acceptance of His revelation. The wrongdoer may appear to gain in worldly terms, yet the verse teaches that real failure lies in losing the guidance that leads to lasting salvation.

translation: And [mention] the Day We will gather them all, then We will say to those who associated others with Allah, "Where are your partners whom you used to claim?"
interpretation: The verse portrays the scene of the Day of Judgment in which all of humanity is brought together for reckoning, and it directs attention to the moment when the idolaters are confronted with their false beliefs. The question "Where are your partners?" is not merely a request for information but a rebuke that exposes the emptiness of what they once asserted: the deities and intermediaries they claimed would benefit or intercede for them are shown to be absent and powerless. The verse thus teaches that worship and devotion directed to anything besides God will be revealed as baseless when every pretense is stripped away, and it calls the listener to examine now the claims they hold about who truly deserves their trust and devotion before that day arrives.

translation: Then their trial would be only that they would say, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists."
interpretation: The verse depicts the moment of reckoning when the idolaters, having their false associations exposed, are left with no argument but a solemn oath of innocence. Their "fitnah" (test, or the outcome of their testing) is revealed to be empty of any real defense: the very denial they swear to is the last refuge of those whose hearts once turned away from God. It teaches that on the Day of Judgment, concealment and denial will not avail, and that the truth of one's inner allegiance becomes unmistakable before the Lord who knows what is hidden.

translation: Look how they lied against themselves! And what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them.
interpretation: The verse turns the reader's gaze to the self-deception of those who invented falsehoods about God and attributed partners or claims to Him. Their lie ultimately falls back upon their own souls, as they sank into a false belief that now blinds them to the truth of their own condition. The phrase 'and what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them' shows that the gods, intercessors, and fabricated claims they relied upon vanish at the moment of need, leaving them alone with the consequences of their fabrications. The verse thus warns that falsehood promises support but ultimately abandons its devotees, while the one who lies only deceives himself.

translation: And among them are those who listen to you, but We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness. And if they should see every sign, they would not believe in it. Until, when they come to you disputing with you, the disbelievers say, "This is nothing but the fables of the former peoples."
interpretation: The verse portrays a spiritual condition in which the listeners hear the Prophet's recitation only outwardly, their outward attendance producing no inner reception, because their hearts have become veiled and their ears closed as a consequence of their persistent refusal. The divine 'placing' of coverings is best understood as the confirmation of a chosen state of obstinacy: when a person repeatedly turns away from truth, the capacity to grasp it is progressively taken from him. Even the clearest sign would fail to move such hearts, showing that the obstacle lies within them rather than in the lack of evidence. Their dispute with the Prophet is therefore not a search for guidance but a defense of inherited habit, and dismissing the Qur'an as ancient legends is the final expression of this closed disposition.

translation: And they forbid others from it, and keep away from it themselves. And they destroy none but themselves, though they are not aware.
interpretation: The verse describes a people who not only refuse the truth themselves but also actively obstruct others from accepting it, while keeping their own distance from it. Their opposition is ultimately self-destructive: by turning away from guidance and hindering others, they bring ruin upon their own souls, yet their heedlessness prevents them from perceiving this harm. The verse thus exposes the blindness of those who, through arrogance and obstruction, unknowingly sacrifice their own salvation.

translation: If only you could see when they are made to stand before the Fire, and they say, "Oh, would that we were returned! Then we would not deny the signs of our Lord, and we would be among the believers."
interpretation: The verse portrays the moment of final exposure, when the deniers stand at the edge of the Fire and see the reality they once rejected. Their wish to be returned to the world is born of fear and regret rather than sincere conviction, and their vow to believe is the kind of promise that the verse, by its very framing, leaves in doubt, since the Qur'an elsewhere shows such people returning to their former ways even when given another chance. The passage thus warns the listener to accept the signs of God now, while choice is still possible, rather than waiting until the truth becomes undeniable and too late to act upon.

translation: Nay, there has become apparent to them what they used to conceal before; but even if they were returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden, and indeed they are liars.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites' concealed disbelief, which is revealed to them, or to others, when the truth of their condition becomes manifest, so that the hidden motive they once kept secret stands exposed. It then shows that their repentance would be false: even if granted a second chance and returned to the world, their nature would drive them back to the very prohibited conduct they had been warned against. Their claim of regret or belief is therefore a lie, and the verse warns that outward profession does not reflect what is truly within the heart.

translation: And they say, "There is nothing but our worldly life; we shall never be resurrected."
interpretation: The verse captures the denial of resurrection held by those who confine their entire reality to this present life. Their claim that life is only the worldly life reflects a materialist outlook that measures existence by what is immediately seen and felt, and so rejects the idea of being raised again after death. The verse thus exposes the root of disbelief in the afterlife: a heart that sees nothing beyond the near and the transient, and therefore dismisses accountability and the promised return to God.

translation: And if you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord. He will say, "Is this not the truth?" They will say, "Yes, by our Lord!" He will say, "Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."
interpretation: The verse presents the scene of the disbelievers' reckoning, where they are brought to stand before God and are compelled to confront the reality they once denied. Their answer, "Yes, by our Lord," is an admission made under the weight of undeniable truth, and it comes too late to benefit them. The verse teaches that the truth of the Resurrection and divine accountability will be plainly acknowledged on the Day of Judgment, even by those who rejected it in the world, and that the punishment they receive is the direct consequence of their persistent disbelief. It is a warning to the heedless to recognize the truth while there is still opportunity to act upon it.

translation: Those who denied the meeting with God have indeed lost, until when the Hour comes upon them suddenly, they will say, "Oh, our regret over what we neglected concerning it!" while they carry their burdens on their backs. Unquestionably, evil is what they bear.
interpretation: The verse portrays the ruin of those who reject the encounter with God as a self-inflicted loss that becomes fully visible only at the moment of the Hour's sudden arrival, when denial gives way to anguish over neglected duties. The image of bearing burdens upon their backs suggests that their sins are not left behind in the world but accompany them as a heavy, tangible weight, so that the consequences of their heedlessness are carried personally into the Hereafter.

translation: And the worldly life is nothing but play and amusement. But the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful of God. Will you not then use your reason?
interpretation: The verse sets the fleeting pleasures of this world, which are like play and diversion that quickly pass and distract the heart, against the enduring abode of the Hereafter, which is far better for those who guard themselves with consciousness of God. By posing a question, it calls the listener to reflect and to recognize that a rational person would not sacrifice what lasts for what is temporary. It invites a re-ordering of priorities, so that worldly life is enjoyed as a means toward the eternal rather than pursued as an end in itself.

translation: We certainly know that what they say grieves you, but it is not you they deny; rather, it is the wrongdoers who reject the signs of Allah.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in the face of his people's hostility. Its wording, 'they do not deny you' (fa-innahum la yukadhdhibunaka), indicates that the disbelievers' rejection was not a personal rejection of the Prophet, whom they knew to be truthful (al-amin, the trustworthy) before his mission, but a rejection of the truth he carried. Their denial was therefore driven by injustice and arrogance toward God's signs rather than by any flaw in him. The verse teaches the messenger, and every believer who calls to God, that grief over the rejection of guidance should be met with the understanding that the responsibility lies with those who wrong themselves by refusing the signs, and that the truth remains firm regardless of the response it receives.

translation: And messengers were certainly denied before you, but they were patient over being denied and harmed until Our victory reached them. And none can alter the words of Allah. And there has already come to you some of the news of the messengers.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad by showing that rejection is the common lot of all messengers before him, so the prophetic mission is not unique in facing denial. The key lesson is that steadfast patience in the face of denial and harm is the path that leads to divine victory, which is fixed by Allah's unalterable decree. The reference to the 'words of Allah' signals that His promise of support for His messengers cannot be changed or annulled, giving the Prophet assurance and steadiness. Finally, the reminder that news of earlier messengers has reached him directs him to reflect on those precedents as a source of strength and guidance.

translation: And if their turning away has been grievous to you, then if you are able to seek a tunnel into the earth or a ladder into the sky and bring them a sign, [do so]. But if God had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance, so do not be among the ignorant.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad at the stubbornness of his people in rejecting his message. It shows that the prophet's duty is to convey the message, not to compel belief, and that the miracles sought by the unbelievers would not change hearts that have chosen to turn away. Guidance rests in God's will alone, so the prophet's distress over their refusal must not lead him into the folly of impatience or of demanding what is beyond his power to give.

translation: Only those who listen will respond, while the dead—God will raise them up; then to Him they will be returned.
interpretation: The verse draws a contrast between two kinds of hearing. Those whose hearts are open to truth and who genuinely listen are the ones who answer the call, whereas those who are spiritually dead are unresponsive however often the message is delivered. The mention of the dead being raised by God points to the ultimate reality that only God can bring life, guidance, and awakening to hearts, and the closing reminder of return to Him frames human responsiveness within accountability before the Creator, so that the call of faith is ultimately answered through divine power and leads back to Him.

translation: And they say, "Why was a sign not sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "Indeed, Allah is able to send down a sign, but most of them do not know."
interpretation: The verse reveals the persistent pattern of those who rejected the Prophet ﷺ: they demanded a miraculous sign of a specific kind as if faith depended on their choosing the form of proof, while the Qur'an itself was already a sign. The reply shifts the question from the demand to the Divine power and wisdom: God is fully capable of sending any sign, yet He withholds or grants signs according to His wisdom, and sending one after the demand would not necessarily produce belief. The closing remark, "but most of them do not know," points to the root of the problem, which is not a lack of evidence but ignorance and heedlessness that prevent them from recognizing the signs already present in revelation and creation.

translation: There is no creature on the earth, nor any bird that flies with its two wings, but they are communities like you. We have not neglected anything in the Book. Then to their Lord they will be gathered.
interpretation: The verse places all living creatures within a single moral and existential order: animals and birds, though different from humans, are created communities subject to the same divine knowledge and destiny, so that human beings are reminded that they are not alone in being accountable to God. The phrase "we have not neglected anything in the Book" affirms that the revealed record encompasses all that is necessary for guidance and the understanding of creation, while the closing mention of gathering before the Lord recalls that every community, human and animal alike, will return to God for judgment, linking the natural world to the theme of resurrection and accountability.

translation: And those who denied Our signs are deaf and mute, in darknesses. Whomever Allah wills, He leaves astray; and whomever He wills, He places upon a straight path.
interpretation: The verse portrays denial of Allah's signs as a condition of sensory and spiritual deafness and muteness, combined with being immersed in layered darknesses, so that the faculties by which guidance is received are cut off. It then frames guidance and misguidance within the will of Allah, yet this is not a call to fatalism: the preceding clause shows that the people themselves chose denial, so the divine will responds to a person's own orientation, and the verse urges the listener to examine where their own heart stands.

translation: Say, "Tell me, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, would you call upon other than Allah, if you should be truthful?"
interpretation: The verse confronts the idolaters with a simple test of their own convictions. When calamity from God or the Final Hour overtakes them, they would be left with nothing but their Lord, since their false deities cannot save them in such moments. The question exposes the inconsistency of their worship: they turn to other gods only in ease, yet in the hour of real need their hearts naturally return to the One God. It calls them to honest reflection, implying that the instinct they feel in dire distress is the truth they ought to hold to at all times.

translation: Nay, it is Him you call upon, and He removes that for which you call upon Him, if He wills, and you forget what you associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse portrays the moment of distress in which the idolaters, who ordinarily turn to their false gods, instinctively call upon God alone, for only He can remove the hardship. Yet this sincere turning is not unconditional: it rests on His will, reminding the human being of his utter dependence and of how quickly the partners he has set up vanish from his memory when he is in need. The verse thus exposes the inconsistency of polytheism, since the very devotion that is directed to God in hardship should characterize the believer's relationship with Him at all times, in ease as in difficulty.

translation: And We had already sent messengers to nations before you, and We seized them with adversity and hardship so that they might humble themselves in supplication.
interpretation: This verse presents a consistent pattern in God's dealings with humanity: trials of hardship and affliction are sent not as mere punishment but as a means of awakening the heart. Hardship strips away human pride and self-reliance, exposing the fragility of worldly security, so that people turn back to their Lord with humility and sincere supplication. The verse thus addresses the Prophet and believers by showing that the rejection of earlier communities was often met with a mercy disguised as trial, and that the true test lies in whether a person responds to adversity by turning toward God or by hardening in arrogance and heedlessness.

translation: Why, when Our punishment came upon them, did they not humble themselves? But their hearts had hardened, and Satan made their deeds appear fair to them.
interpretation: The verse exposes a spiritual sequence: when hardship is sent as a warning, the natural response of a sound heart is humility and turning back to God, yet the hardening of the heart closes that door. Once the heart grows insensitive, Satan's work is to beautify wrongdoing so that it appears righteous to the person, and thus the very hardship that should have awakened them only deepens their heedlessness. The verse teaches that the real danger is not merely the calamity but the inner condition that prevents its lesson from being received.

translation: So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything, until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and at once they were in despair, utterly hopeless.
interpretation: This verse describes a pattern of divine testing and respite. When people neglect the reminders sent to them, Allah may open to them the outward doors of worldly abundance, not as a sign of favor but as a gradual trap that lulls them into complacency. Their joy in material gain makes them heedless of the Giver, and so the sudden punishment arrives when they least expect it, leaving them stunned and hopeless. The lesson is that worldly prosperity granted without gratitude and remembrance of God can be a form of deception, and that one should read abundance as a call to humility and accountability rather than as proof of being secure from consequence.

translation: So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off. And all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse closes the account of the destruction of the wrongdoing nations with a declaration of divine justice: when a people persists in injustice and rejects the messengers, Allah brings their existence to an utter end, leaving no trace of their arrogance. The immediate turn to praise, "Al-hamdu lillahi rabbil-'alamin," teaches that such a judgment is itself an act of mercy and wisdom that the believer should acknowledge with gratitude. The believers are thus reminded that the Lord who sustains all worlds is also the one who rightly deals with the oppressors, so that the faithful find both consolation in the fall of the unjust and a lesson in humility before the absolute justice of God.

translation: Say, "Have you considered: if Allah were to take away your hearing and your sight and seal over your hearts, what god other than Allah could bring them back to you?" Observe how We vary the signs in various ways, yet they still turn away.
interpretation: The verse turns the listener's attention from the gift of the senses to their fragility, showing that hearing, sight, and understanding are entrusted to a human being and can be withdrawn at any moment by the One who granted them. The question "what god other than Allah could return them?" establishes by implication that tawhid is the logical conclusion of a sound mind, since no false deity has any power over these faculties. The closing phrase, "yet they still turn away," exposes the deeper malady: the problem is not a lack of evidence but a heart that has been sealed against guidance. Thus the verse links the outward senses to the inward heart, teaching that real perception of the signs of God depends on an open heart, and that persistent aversion after clear signs is itself a form of spiritual blindness.

translation: Say: Have you considered, if the punishment of Allah should come upon you suddenly or openly, would anyone be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?
interpretation: The verse confronts the disbelievers with a question that leaves them no escape: whether Allah's punishment comes unexpectedly while they are heedless, or openly and visibly, its arrival cannot be avoided, and the only ones who face destruction in this way are those who have persisted in wrongdoing, that is, in injustice toward themselves through disbelief and toward others. It is a call to self-examination, reminding the listener that the decisive factor in ruin is not the mere passage of time but the injustice one chooses to hold to, so the wise person should turn to Allah before the sudden reckoning arrives.

translation: And We do not send the messengers except as bringers of good news and warners. So whoever believes and reforms, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: The verse establishes the mission of the messengers as twofold: to give glad tidings to those who respond and to warn those who turn away, so that divine guidance is conveyed with both hope and accountability. It then defines the path of salvation in two inseparable components, faith in the heart and righteous action in deeds, showing that belief is not complete without its outward fruit of reform in society and self. The promise that such people will be free of fear and sorrow points to a state of inner security that comes from a sound relationship with God, one that is not dependent on worldly circumstances. The verse thus balances the warning of divine justice with the assurance of divine mercy, inviting the believer to live with both awe and tranquility.

translation: And those who denied Our signs, the punishment will touch them because they used to defiantly disobey.
interpretation: The verse ties denial of God's signs to the consequence of punishment and places the root of that denial in a persistent pattern of fisq, a deliberate departure from obedience. Denial is not presented merely as an intellectual error but as the outcome of a habit of moral transgression: when a person repeatedly turns away from what is right, the heart grows resistant to the signs that would call it back. The punishment is thus described as the natural result of this chosen course, so that the verse warns that rejection of revelation is bound up with the disposition of one who has chosen disobedience over guidance.

translation: Say, "I do not tell you that I have the treasures of Allah, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I tell you that I am an angel. I only follow what is revealed to me." Say, "Is the blind equal to the seeing? Then will you not reflect?"
interpretation: The verse sets the Prophet's humility against the exaggerated claims people might project onto a messenger: he possesses no divine treasures, no knowledge of the hidden, and is not an angel, so his authority rests entirely on revelation he follows. The closing rhetorical question draws a sharp analogy between the blind and the seeing to show that those who receive guidance through revelation and those who refuse it are not equal, and it calls the listener to use reason to recognize this difference.

translation: And warn with it those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord, having no protector or intercessor besides Him, so that perhaps they will become righteous.
interpretation: The verse singles out those who are conscious of their accountability before God, for whom fear of being gathered to their Lord is a living reality. The Qur'an is presented as a warning meant first for such hearts, because awareness of the Day of Gathering, where no ally or intercessor can be relied upon apart from God, is what awakens them to taking piety seriously. The phrase "perhaps they will become righteous" indicates that the purpose of warning is moral transformation: fear of the encounter with God is meant to turn the believer toward taqwa, a conscious guarding of oneself against what displeases Him. It also teaches that true salvation rests on God alone, since no worldly patron or mediator can shield a person on that Day, which should drive a person to sincere reliance on Him rather than on any created being.

translation: And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face. Nothing of their account falls upon you, and nothing of your account falls upon them, that you should drive them away and thereby be among the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the worth of believers is measured by their sincere devotion to God, not by worldly standing or social status, and that the Prophet bears no responsibility for judging their inner reckonings. Because each soul answers for its own deeds, the Prophet's duty is only to convey the message, and to reject the humble sincere believers in favor of the powerful elite would itself be an act of injustice. It is a lasting warning against elitism in religious gatherings and a call to honor those who seek God's pleasure over those who seek worldly prestige.

translation: And thus We tested some of them through others, so that they would say: "Are these the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favor from among us?" Is not Allah most knowing of those who are grateful?
interpretation: The verse reveals that worldly provision and status are a trial rather than a sign of divine preference. The wealthy and privileged among the disbelievers looked at the poor believers with scorn, asking why God favored them over the elite. Allah answers with a question that dismantles this reasoning: He alone knows who is truly thankful, and He distributes His favor according to inner gratitude and sincerity, not according to social rank. The passage thus warns that measuring people by wealth or worldly standing exposes one's own spiritual blindness, and that the believer should look to gratitude and righteousness rather than envy or contempt toward others' circumstances.

translation: And when those who believe in Our verses come to you, say, "Peace be upon you. Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy: that whoever of you does evil in ignorance and then repents after that and makes amends, indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful."
interpretation: The verse opens a door of hope for the believers who come to the Prophet in a state of humility, and it instructs him to greet them with peace, a gesture that reassures them of their standing and of God's acceptance. The declaration that the Lord has written mercy upon Himself reveals that divine mercy is not a reluctant concession but a settled principle that governs God's dealings with His creatures. The conditions attached to forgiveness are significant: the sin is committed out of ignorance, meaning through lack of full awareness or through the heedlessness of passion, and it is followed by sincere repentance and a turning toward righteous action. Thus the verse teaches that no transgression is so final that it closes the way back to God, provided the one who erred returns with genuine remorse and reform, and that the community of faith should embrace such penitents rather than drive them away.

translation: And thus We detail the verses, that the way of the criminals may become clear.
interpretation: The verse points to a divine method of clarification: God explains His signs in distinct, graded detail so that the truth stands apart from falsehood. The purpose of this clarity is not only to illuminate the right path but also to make visible the path of those who persist in wrongdoing, so that a person can recognize where their own conduct is heading and turn away from it. Detailed revelation thus serves as both guidance and warning, leaving the listener without excuse, since the consequences of each way are laid out plainly.

translation: Say, "Indeed, I have been forbidden to worship those you invoke besides Allah." Say, "I will not follow your desires; for I would then have gone astray, and I would not be among the rightly guided."
interpretation: The verse establishes a clear boundary between the Prophet's mission and the desires of those who associate partners with God. Worship is a right reserved for Allah alone, and the Prophet's prohibition from serving the deities others call upon is presented as a divine command rather than a personal preference. The second part shows that adherence to revelation, not to the wishes of the people, is what safeguards one from misguidance: to follow human desires in matters of faith would be to abandon guidance itself. The verse thus teaches that truth is defined by God, and that even a messenger's own rectitude depends wholly on remaining faithful to what has been revealed to him.

translation: Say, "Indeed, I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, yet you have denied it. What you are asking to be hastened is not with me. Judgment belongs only to Allah; He relates the truth, and He is the best of deciders."
interpretation: The verse establishes the prophetic role as one of clear proof and conviction, grounded in a revelation from the Lord, while the denial of the messenger is portrayed as a denial of that very evidence. The Prophet disclaims any power over the timing of the threatened punishment that the disbelievers demanded be hastened, placing the decision entirely with God. Authority to judge is reserved to Allah alone, who narrates the truth without distortion and whose judgment is the most just. The verse thus directs the believer to rest in divine justice and patience rather than in impatient demands, trusting that the final verdict between truth and falsehood belongs to the One who knows all things.

translation: Say, "If I had what you are impatient for, the matter would have been decided between me and you. And Allah is most knowing of the wrongdoers."
interpretation: The verse shows the Prophet being commanded to disclaim any power over the timing of the punishment that the disbelievers mocked and demanded hastily. He tells them that if the decisive torment they seek were in his hands, the dispute would already have been settled between him and them, since he would have carried out what they asked for at once. The verse thus affirms that the timing of judgment rests solely with Allah, who knows best who among the wrongdoers deserves it and when, and that His delay is governed by His wisdom and knowledge rather than by the people's impatience.

translation: And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him. He knows what is on the land and in the sea. Not a leaf falls but that He knows it, nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth, nor anything moist or dry, but it is in a clear register.
interpretation: The verse presents God's absolute and comprehensive knowledge as the foundation of His unique authority over the unseen. The 'keys' of the unseen image full control over hidden realms, which no created being shares. By moving from the vast (land and sea) to the minute (a falling leaf, a seed in darkness), it shows that nothing escapes divine knowledge, and the 'clear register' signifies that all events are recorded and determined within a complete, preserved decree. The verse thus invites the reader to recognize human limitation and to place trust in a Lord whose knowledge encompasses every detail of existence.

translation: And it is He who takes you in death by night and knows what you have committed by day. Then He revives you therein so that a specified term may be fulfilled. Then to Him is your return; then He will inform you of what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse presents sleep as a lesser counterpart of death: at night the soul is taken back by God, and by day He raises the person again, so that each daily cycle mirrors the larger passage of life toward a fixed term. The repeated rhythm of sleep and waking thus serves as a sign prompting awareness that human life is wholly in God's hands, that He is fully aware of all deeds, including those done openly by day, and that the ultimate return to Him will end in a reckoning of what people actually did.

translation: And He is the Subduer over His servants, and He sends over you guardians until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him in death, and they do not fail in their duty.
interpretation: The verse presents divine absolute dominion (qahr) over all creation, which is not a tyranny but the assurance that no servant escapes God's control. That mastery is expressed concretely through the angelic guardians who record and protect human deeds, and through the messengers who carry out the appointed moment of death exactly as decreed. The phrase 'they do not fail' conveys that the angels neglect nothing entrusted to them, so human life, from its watching to its ending, is held within a precise and unfailing divine order that should prompt awareness, accountability, and reliance on God rather than heedlessness.

translation: Then they will be returned to God, their true Master. Unquestionably, judgment belongs to Him, and He is the swiftest of all reckoners.
interpretation: The verse points to the final return of all souls to God, whom it calls their true Lord (mawlahum al-haqq), stripping away every false master or idol that people served in this life. The phrase 'alā lahu al-ḥukm' affirms that ultimate authority to judge belongs to God alone, so no earthly tribunal, power, or claim has the last word. The closing description of God as 'the swiftest of reckoners' conveys that His accounting requires no delay, no investigation, and no effort, since He knows every deed completely. The verse thus calls the believer to live with constant awareness that the reckoning is certain and near, and that justice will be perfect.

translation: Say: "Who delivers you from the darknesses of land and sea, when you call upon Him in humility and in secret, [saying], 'If You deliver us from this, we will surely be among the thankful.'"
interpretation: The verse turns the human being back to the moment of crisis, when all the props of worldly security fall away and the soul, stripped of pretension, turns instinctively to its Creator. The 'darknesses of land and sea' point to the terrifying helplessness of being lost in deserts or storms, where no human power can rescue. The paired modes of prayer, 'humility' (tadarru') openly and 'secret' (khufyah) inwardly, reveal that true supplication is sincere both outwardly and in the heart. Yet the verse exposes a recurring human weakness: the promise made in distress to be grateful is so easily forgotten once relief arrives. Thus the question 'Who delivers you?' is not merely rhetorical; it calls the listener to recognize that the One who saves in extremity is the One who alone deserves gratitude and worship at all times, not only when fear compels them.

translation: Say: "It is Allah who saves you from them and from every distress, and yet you associate partners with Him."
interpretation: The verse confronts the human tendency to forget the source of relief once hardship has passed. Allah alone is the One who delivers people from danger and affliction, so when they are rescued, it is He who deserves their gratitude and devotion. Yet, having been saved, people return to associating others with Him, revealing how fleeting their sincerity becomes once ease returns. The verse calls the believer to recognize that every deliverance comes from Allah alone and to remain steadfast in pure monotheism, both in times of distress and in times of comfort.

translation: Say, "He is the One capable of sending upon you punishment from above you or from beneath your feet, or of confusing you into factions and making you taste the violence of one another. Observe how We vary the signs so that they may understand."
interpretation: The verse presents divine power over human society as a warning and a lesson: the same Almighty who can send calamity from above (such as storms or stones) or from below (such as earthquakes or floods) can also fragment a community from within, turning its members into rival factions that inflict harm on each other. Thus the true source of collective ruin is often not only external catastrophe but internal discord, which makes strife among people itself a form of punishment. The closing call to observe how the signs are varied points to the purpose behind this variety of warnings, which is to awaken understanding, so that people reflect, unite, and avoid the ruin that comes from division and injustice.

translation: Yet your people have denied it, though it is the truth. Say: I am not a guardian over you.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet after his people rejected the revelation, even though it is undeniably true. His duty is only to convey the message; he is not made responsible for compelling their acceptance or for their fate. Accountability for belief rests with each person, and the Prophet's role is limited to clear delivery, leaving guidance and judgment to God.

translation: Every prophecy has its appointed time of fulfillment, and you will come to know it.
interpretation: The verse (Al-An'am 6:67) assures that every news or promise announced by the Prophet has a fixed time and place where it will be realized, and that its truth will become evident. It is a warning to those who deny the message: they are not to be hasty in mocking it, for its reality will be revealed in due course, whether in this world or in the Hereafter. The phrase 'you will come to know' carries both a promise to the believers and a threat to the deniers, placing the final judgment of truth in God's hands and in the unfolding of His decree.

translation: And when you see those who engage in vain discourse concerning Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in a different topic. And if Satan should make you forget, then do not sit after the reminder with the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: The verse establishes a principle of disengagement from mockery and distortion of God's revelation: the believer is not to lend presence or validation to those who treat the signs of God with derision or sophistry, but to withdraw until they turn to other matters. The clause about Satan's making one forget shows that lapses can happen even to the conscious believer, and the remedy is immediate correction upon remembrance, leaving the company of the wrongdoers. The lesson extends beyond the Prophet's time to any gathering where the sacred is trivialized: a sincere person should not sit comfortably in such settings, since presence can imply consent and normalize blasphemy.

translation: And upon those who are mindful of God is nothing of their reckoning, but it is a reminder, that perhaps they may be mindful of God.
interpretation: This verse, revealed in the context of the Prophet's eagerness to guide the powerful leaders of Quraysh, teaches that the moral responsibility of the believer does not extend to bearing the account of those who reject guidance. The one who is conscious of God has fulfilled his duty when he delivers the message as a reminder; he is not held accountable for the choices of others, whose reckoning rests with God alone. The verse thus shifts the focus from anxious pursuit of others' conversion to sincere, patient admonition, while affirming that the purpose of the reminder is to awaken hearts to piety, and that the true measure of the believer is his own God-consciousness rather than the response of those he addresses.

translation: And leave those who have taken their religion as amusement and diversion, and whom the worldly life has deceived. But remind (them) with it, lest a soul be delivered to destruction for what it has earned; it will have, besides Allah, no protector and no intercessor, and if it offers every ransom, it will not be accepted from it. Those are the ones who will be delivered to destruction for what they earned; for them will be a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve.
interpretation: The verse portrays a people who reduced the religion of God to a game and a pastime, letting the lure of worldly life blind them to its reality, and it commands the believer to turn away from such mockers while still delivering the reminder, so that no soul is left to be seized by its own deeds with no one to shield it. The repeated denial of any protector, intercessor, or ransom shows that on the Day of Reckoning responsibility is purely personal and cannot be transferred or bought off, so the scalding drink and painful punishment are the natural consequence of their persistent rejection rather than an arbitrary sentence.

translation: Say, "Shall we call upon, instead of Allah, that which can neither benefit us nor harm us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us, like one whom the devils have lured away in the earth, bewildered, having companions who call him to guidance, saying, 'Come to us.'" Say, "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [true] guidance, and we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: The verse portrays the folly of abandoning true guidance after having received it, by likening the one who turns back from monotheism to a person led astray into a desert wasteland by devils, lost and confused while his companions call him back to the right path. It presents the reversal to idolatry as a return to disorientation, and affirms that Allah's guidance alone is the true path, so that submission to the Lord of the worlds is the only sound response to it.

translation: And that you should establish prayer and be mindful of Him. And it is He to whom you will be gathered.
interpretation: The verse binds together two pillars of a believer's life: the outward discipline of ritual prayer, which regularly turns the heart back to God, and taqwa, a watchful awareness of God that guards conduct in every matter. It then grounds both commands in the certainty of the Resurrection, when all people will be gathered before their Lord. Awareness of that final return is what gives prayer its sincerity and piety its steadiness, so that a person acts now as one who will stand accountable before God.

translation: And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth. And the day He says "Be," and it is, His word is the truth. And His is the dominion on the Day the Trumpet is blown. He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He is the Wise, the All-Aware.
interpretation: The verse binds creation to truth and purpose: the heavens and earth were brought into being not in vain but with a wise design, and the same divine word that called them into existence, "Be, and it is," shows that creation requires no effort or intermediary. Since His word is truth, what He promises, including the Resurrection, is certain. The mention of the Trumpet's blast ties the beginning and the end together, reminding the listener that sovereignty belongs to God alone at both moments, and that His complete knowledge of the hidden and the observed, together with His wisdom and awareness, makes accountability inescapable.

translation: And [mention] when Abraham said to his father Azar, "Do you take idols as gods? Indeed, I see you and your people in clear error."
interpretation: The verse presents Abraham's first direct confrontation with idolatry, and it begins with the most intimate relationship he had, that of a son to his father, showing that the duty of truth outweighs even family bonds and inherited custom. His question is framed as a gentle but piercing challenge rather than a harsh accusation: he asks whether the father truly takes lifeless images as deities, which invites reflection on the absurdity of worshipping what cannot hear, see, or benefit. By saying "I see you and your people" he places the error not on one man but on the whole community, yet his tone remains that of a sincere advisor who speaks plainly out of concern for them. The verse thus teaches that the rejection of false worship must be grounded in clear reasoning and sincere compassion, and that a believer should speak the truth candidly even when it confronts those closest to him and the prevailing norms of his society.

translation: And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among the certain (firm in faith).
interpretation: The verse presents Abraham's witnessing of the unseen dominion (malakut) of creation as a deliberate divine act of insight, granted so that his faith would move from inherited conviction or reasoned inference to certainty born of direct vision. Certainty of belief (yaqin) is thus shown to be a stage that comes through seeing the signs of God's sovereignty in the cosmos, not merely through assent. The prophet's inner conviction becomes a model for believers: the more deeply one contemplates the order and governance of the heavens and the earth, the more firmly one's faith is rooted, and the ground is laid for Abraham's subsequent steadfastness in confronting falsehood.

translation: So when the night covered him, he saw a star. He said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "I do not love those that set."
interpretation: The verse portrays Abraham's rational search for the true Lord. Through a progressive test of celestial bodies, first the star, then the moon and the sun, he demonstrates that whatever sets and vanishes cannot be a deity worthy of worship. His words "I do not love those that set" reveal that the disappearance of what was taken as divine exposes its limitation and dependence, turning the seeker toward the One who originates and sustains all things, the Creator of the heavens and the earth, and away from the created signs that merely point beyond themselves.

translation: So when he saw the moon rising, he said, "This is my Lord." But when it set, he said, "If my Lord does not guide me, I will surely be among the people who are astray."
interpretation: The verse presents Abraham's reasoned journey toward the recognition of the One true God. Through a sequence of observations of the stars, the moon, and the sun, each apparent deity is shown to be transient and to vanish, so that the seeker is led to renounce all that sets and to turn wholeheartedly toward the Creator who alone is unchanging. His words are less a confession of error than a method of inquiry, in which the human intellect, honestly searching, acknowledges its dependence on divine guidance as the ultimate condition for reaching truth.

translation: So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my Lord; this is greater." But when it set, he said, "O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate with Allah."
interpretation: This verse presents Abraham's reasoned journey toward monotheism through a progressive test of celestial bodies, which he uses to expose the inadequacy of what his people worshipped. Each heavenly object he considers as a possible lord, the sun included, is shown to be transient: it rises and then sets, and therefore cannot be a deity worthy of worship. His declaration of disavowal marks the point at which he refuses the authority of anything that vanishes and turns wholly toward the One who originates and sustains all things. The passage thus teaches that reflection on the created order should lead the mind beyond creation to its Creator, and that true faith requires a clear break from every form of associating partners with God.

translation: Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who originated the heavens and the earth, inclining (in pure monotheism), and I am not of those who associate partners with God.
interpretation: The verse expresses a complete and sincere reorientation of the whole self toward the Creator alone. 'Turning the face' signifies directing one's entire being, intention, and worship, and the description of God as the Originator of the heavens and the earth grounds that devotion in the evidence of creation itself. The word 'hanif' points to an upright, unswerving disposition that turns away from all false attachments and returns to the primordial natural faith (fitrah). The closing declaration that the speaker is not among the polytheists makes monotheism not merely a belief but an explicit disavowal of every form of associating others with God, so that sincere worship and pure tawhid are shown to be inseparable.

translation: And his people argued with him. He said, "Do you argue with me concerning Allah while He has guided me? And I do not fear those you associate with Him, unless my Lord wills something. My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. Will you not then be reminded?"
interpretation: The verse presents Abraham standing firm against his people's dispute over God, and his confidence rests not on his own strength but on divine guidance already granted to him. His fearlessness toward the idols they worshipped shows that true fear belongs only to Allah, since no created thing can harm anyone except by His will. By affirming that his Lord's knowledge encompasses all things, he directs the listeners from futile argument toward reflection and the recognition of God's comprehensive knowledge, ending with a call to remembrance that invites them to use their reason.

translation: And how should I fear what you associate with God, when you do not fear that you have associated with God that for which He has sent down no authority? So which of the two parties is more deserving of security, if you should know?
interpretation: The verse is Abraham's rebuttal to his people, who threatened him with harm from their idols. He turns the argument around: fear belongs to the one who has abandoned reason and revelation, not to the one who worships the One God.
