Idols have no power to harm or benefit, and they are given no authority by any clear proof or scripture, so the worshipper of idols is the one who should fear, having no sound basis for his trust. The rhetorical question directs the listener to reflect that security is owed to those who rest their faith on knowledge and evidence, namely monotheism, rather than to those who rest it on baseless claims. It thus establishes that true safety comes from sincere tawhid, which is grounded in certainty, and that tranquility of heart is found in exclusive devotion to God alone.

translation: Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing (injustice) — those shall have security, and they are the ones who are guided.
interpretation: The verse ties true security and guidance to a pure faith, one not clouded by zulm. Zulm here is not merely minor wrongdoing but the deepest form of injustice, which in the wider Qur'anic usage is shirk, the assigning of partners to God. The believer's inner peace and right direction are thus shown to depend on the integrity of belief itself: when faith is kept free of associating others with God, it becomes the source of both safety in this life and the hereafter, and of being rightly guided. The verse also suggests that security is not merely external, but flows from a heart that is unified in its devotion to God.

translation: And that was Our argument which We gave to Abraham against his people. We raise by degrees whom We will. Indeed, your Lord is Wise and All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse presents Abraham's rational argument against his people's idolatry (in the preceding verses, his reasoning about the stars, moon, and sun) as a divinely granted proof, meaning that true guidance is a gift from God rather than merely the product of human cleverness. The phrase 'We raise by degrees whom We will' shows that God elevates people in rank and insight according to His wisdom and knowledge, and Abraham's elevation is an example of this. The closing names of God, Wise and All-Knowing, assure the reader that this distribution of honor and understanding is never arbitrary but rests on perfect knowledge of who is worthy of it and on the wisdom of His decree.

translation: And We gave him Isaac and Jacob, each of whom We guided; and Noah We guided before, and among his descendants David, Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses, and Aaron. Thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: The verse, within the list of prophets mentioned in Surah al-An'am, shows that divine guidance and the gift of prophethood are bestowed by God's grace upon those whom He chooses, not earned by lineage alone; the family of Abraham is singled out as a line in which guidance and prophecy were passed on, and the closing phrase establishes that this honor is the reward God grants to those who do good, meaning that sincere righteousness in action is what brings a person under God's special favor and recompense.

translation: And Zechariah, John, Jesus, and Elijah. Each of them was among the righteous.
interpretation: The verse places these prophets within a single lineage of righteousness, grouping them together so that their shared standing among the righteous becomes the defining mark of their mission. By naming them in sequence and affirming that each was 'of the righteous' (min al-salihin), it presents righteousness not as the privilege of one era or one person, but as the common character of those whom God chose to guide and to carry His message. The verse invites the reader to see prophethood as the culmination of sincere devotion, and to recognize that the path of these men, despite their different circumstances, converged on the same essential goodness.

translation: And Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah, and Lot, and each We preferred over the worlds.
interpretation: The verse places these prophets within a chain of divine favor, showing that prophethood is a gift of God's choosing rather than a product of lineage or circumstance. By naming Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah, and Lot together, it presents them as examples of individuals whom God elevated above their peers in their own time. The phrase "preferred over the worlds" points to a distinction conferred by God's will, which calls the believer to recognize that such honor comes from divine election, and to respond with gratitude and faithful adherence to the guidance these messengers brought.

translation: And [We guided] some of their forefathers, their descendants, and their brothers; and We chose them and guided them to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse, placed within the passage listing the prophets (Zakariya, Yahya, Isa, Musa, Harun, Isma'il, Idris, and others), shows that divine election and guidance are bestowed upon a lineage that spans generations and kinship. The mention of 'their forefathers, their descendants, and their brothers' indicates that guidance is not confined to one individual but flows through families and communities who share a common commitment to God's message. The phrase 'We chose them' (ijtaba-nahum) highlights that prophethood is a divine selection, a gift rather than something earned by lineage alone, while 'We guided them to a straight path' affirms that those chosen were also continuously directed toward sound belief and righteous conduct. The verse thus teaches that the chosen ones are both recipients of God's grace and models whose lives display the path of straightness for those who follow them.

translation: That is the guidance of Allah; He guides thereby whom He wills of His servants. But if they had associated partners with Allah, that which they used to do would have been rendered worthless for them.
interpretation: The verse establishes that true guidance is a divine gift, not a human achievement: Allah grants it to whomever He wills among His servants, which is why it should prompt humility rather than self-reliance. It then issues a stern warning that shirk (associating partners with Allah) is the single act that nullifies all good deeds, because deeds are accepted only when they rest on sincere tawhid. Good works performed alongside idolatry lose their value, so the believer's worship must be purified of any rival to God, both in belief and in intention.

translation: Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book, the judgment, and prophethood. So if these (people of Makkah) disbelieve in them, then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad by placing him in the line of earlier prophets who were granted the Scripture, wisdom, and prophethood, and it warns that God's favor is not bound to any particular group. If the Quraysh reject this revelation and its message, God is not left without a witness: He has entrusted this trust to a people who will faithfully uphold and affirm it, such as the believers from among the Companions and those who follow them. The phrase "who are not disbelievers in them" points to a community that acknowledges these gifts rather than denying them, so the rejection of a few does not nullify the continuation of divine guidance.

translation: Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance. Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it; it is nothing but a reminder to all the worlds.
interpretation: The verse directs the Prophet to take the earlier messengers, whom God had guided, as the model to follow, so that his mission is anchored in the path already shown by divine guidance rather than in novelty or personal ambition. By stating that he seeks no wage for this message, the verse establishes its sincerity and disinterestedness, and by calling it a reminder for all the worlds it presents the Qur'an as a universal admonition that recalls humanity to the primordial truth God has always revealed.

translation: They did not measure God with His true measure when they said, "God has not revealed anything to a human being." Say, "Who revealed the Book that Moses brought, as a light and guidance for the people, which you make into scattered pages, showing some and concealing much? And you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew." Say, "God [revealed it]"; then leave them to their idle talk, playing.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who denied that God sent any revelation to humans, arguing that such a denial diminishes God's true greatness, since it contradicts the revelation granted to Moses, a book of light and guidance that they themselves handled selectively, displaying what suited them and hiding much of its content. By reminding them that they were taught knowledge unknown to them and to their forefathers, the verse exposes the inconsistency of their position, and the Prophet is commanded to answer decisively that God is the sender, then to disengage from them as they persist in their vain and frivolous disputation.

translation: And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed, confirming what came before it, that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it. And those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it, and they are steadfast over their prayer.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an as a blessed revelation that confirms the continuity of the divine message carried by earlier scriptures, and whose purpose is to warn Makkah, the 'Mother of Cities,' and the peoples around it. It then distinguishes true faith by its fruit: those who genuinely believe in the Hereafter embrace this Book, and their belief is evident in their constancy in prayer, showing that accountability before God is what animates both faith and worship.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God, or says, 'It has been revealed to me,' when nothing has been revealed to him, or who says, 'I will send down the like of what God has sent down.' If you could see when the wrongdoers are in the overwhelming agonies of death, and the angels extend their hands, saying, 'Release your souls! Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation for what you used to say about God other than the truth, and for being arrogant toward His verses.'
interpretation: The verse exposes the gravest form of injustice, which is fabricating claims about God and falsely attributing revelation to Himself, and it confronts such people with the scene of their death, where the angels demand their souls and announce a humiliating punishment. The verse teaches that arrogance toward God's signs and the false speech spoken against Him will be met with disgrace at the moment of death and beyond, so that the reality of the consequences of falsehood and pride becomes unavoidably clear.

translation: And you have certainly come to Us alone, just as We created you the first time, and you have left behind what We bestowed upon you, behind your backs. And We do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed were partners in your affairs. Your bond has indeed been severed, and what you used to claim has gone astray from you.
interpretation: The verse portrays the scene of the Day of Resurrection, where humanity returns to God stripped of all worldly possessions, status, and supports, just as they came into existence at first, in solitude and without wealth. It confronts the human tendency to attach oneself to the gifts of this world and to the false idols and intercessors invented in God's place, showing that these will utterly abandon the one who trusted in them. The severing of every tie and the vanishing of the associated partners expose the emptiness of polytheism and worldly reliance, and call the reader to turn toward the one Lord before that final reckoning comes.

translation: Indeed, Allah is the splitter of the grain and the seed. He brings the living out of the dead, and brings the dead out of the living. That is Allah; so how are you deluded away from the truth?
interpretation: The verse points to the signs of God's power in the natural world: the seed and the date-stone split open, and from what appears lifeless a living plant emerges, just as living things die and return to dust. This ongoing cycle of emergence and decay, repeated before the eyes of every generation, is a sign that the One who originates life is the One who alone deserves worship. The closing question is a rebuke: once this evidence is plain, turning away from God and attributing divinity to others is a kind of self-deception, as though the mind had been turned aside from what is manifestly true.

translation: He is the Splitter of the dawn, and He has made the night for rest and the sun and the moon for reckoning. That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse points to the precise order of creation as evidence of the Creator's power and wisdom. The One who cleaves the darkness of night to bring forth morning is the same One who appointed night as a time of stillness and repose for the living, and who set the sun and moon on a fixed measure so that days, months, and years can be counted and human affairs ordered. The regularity of these celestial movements is not accidental but the deliberate determination of the Mighty and All-Knowing, and so the believer is invited to reflect on this exact design, to recognize the Lord behind it, and to find in the dependable rhythm of day and night a sign that calls for gratitude and trust in Him.

translation: And it is He who placed for you the stars that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of the land and the sea. We have detailed the signs for a people who know.
interpretation: The verse points to the stars as a divine gift of guidance, joining the material world to the realm of signs. Its darknesses of land and sea represent the disorientation a person faces, both outwardly in travel and inwardly in life's uncertainties, and the stars are a reminder that Allah provides fixed points by which one may find the right direction. The closing phrase, that the signs are detailed for those who know, invites reflection: the ordered heavens are meant to be read by reason and knowledge, so that the observer moves from seeing the lights to recognizing the One who set them in their courses.

translation: And it is He who produced you from a single soul, and [for you is] a place of settlement and a place of storage. We have detailed the signs for a people who understand.
interpretation: The verse points to the common origin of all humanity from one soul, which underlies the unity of the human race despite its diversity. The phrase "a place of settlement and a place of storage" is read by many commentators as referring to the two stages of human existence: the lifetime in this world, where one is settled, and the stage in the womb or the grave, where one is kept in trust until the appointed time. Others understand it as the believer's dwelling and the soul's temporary stay. The closing statement ties this reflection to understanding: the signs of God are made clear for those who reflect, so that recognizing one's origin and destiny should lead to humility, mutual kinship among people, and awareness of accountability before the Creator.

translation: And it is He who sends down water from the sky, and with it We bring forth the growth of every thing; then We bring forth from it green (plants), from which We bring forth grain piled up in layers; and from the date palm, from its spathe, clusters hanging low within reach; and gardens of grapevines, and the olive and the pomegranate, similar and dissimilar. Look at their fruit when they bear fruit and at its ripening. Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe.
interpretation: The verse directs the believer's attention from the single act of rain to the graded diversity of plant life, moving from the general growth of all things, to grain stacked in ears, to palm clusters hanging near the hand, to vines, olives and pomegranates that resemble one another yet differ in form and taste. By commanding them to look at the fruit as it forms and ripens, it invites reflection on a process that unfolds by a precise order, showing that the same water yields varied results by a single Creator's design. Its signs are addressed specifically to those who believe, because it is faith that turns observation of nature into recognition of the One who sustains it.

translation: And they attribute to God partners among the jinn, though He created them; and they fabricate for Him sons and daughters without knowledge. Exalted is He above what they describe.
interpretation: The verse exposes a double error in the idolatry of its time: first, the assignment of partners to God from among the jinn, beings Himself created, which reverses the proper order of creator and creation; second, the invention of sons and daughters for Him, a claim made without any basis in knowledge, revelation, or reason. The phrase "without knowledge" shows that such beliefs are not rooted in certainty but in conjecture and inherited assumption. By ending with the declaration of God's transcendence above what they describe, the verse establishes that divinity cannot be shared, divided, or given offspring, since whatever is created is dependent and whatever is dependent cannot be a partner to its Creator. The passage thus calls the reader to tawhid, the affirmation of God's unity and absolute distinction from all creation, and to humility in speaking about Him only on the basis of what is known.

translation: The Originator of the heavens and the earth. How could He have a son when He has no companion? And He created everything, and He is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: The verse opens by naming God as Badi' (the Originator who brings things into being without precedent), and this creative power is the basis for denying that He could have offspring. A child implies a consort and a need for continuation, both of which are inconceivable for the One who alone originates all that exists, since everything other than Him is His creation and therefore cannot share in His divine nature. The closing affirmation that He created everything and knows all things underscores His absolute sovereignty and self-sufficiency: His knowledge encompasses every reality, so the attribution of a son to Him is shown to be a claim without any basis in truth.

translation: That is Allah, your Lord; there is no deity except Him, the Creator of all things, so worship Him. And He is Disposer of all things.
interpretation: The verse establishes the foundation of tawhid through a sequence of logical steps: first the identity of the Lord (Allah, your Lord), then the exclusivity of divinity (no god but Him), then the proof from creation (the Creator of all things), which in turn makes worship due to Him alone (so worship Him). The closing phrase, 'He is Disposer of all things' (wakil), shows that the one who creates is also the one who sustains, guards, and manages everything, so the believer should place complete trust in Him as well as devote worship to Him. Creation, worship, and trust (tawakkul) are thus shown to be inseparable: the One who alone brought everything into being is the only one deserving of both devotion and reliance.

translation: No vision can grasp Him, but He grasps all vision. And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware.
interpretation: The verse establishes the absolute transcendence of God over human perception: the faculties of sight cannot encompass or confine the Divine essence, since whatever the eye can reach is bounded and created, while God is not bounded by anything. Yet the verse turns from this limit of human knowing to God's comprehensive knowing: He perceives and encompasses all sight and all that is seen, so that the seer is himself within the gaze of the Seen. The closing names, al-Latif (the Subtle, who penetrates to the finest reality and whose workings are imperceptible) and al-Khabir (the All-Aware, who knows inner truths), reinforce that divine knowledge reaches where human perception cannot. The verse thus invites a humility that turns from the pursuit of seeing God with the eyes toward the awareness that one is always seen and known by Him.

translation: Clear evidences have certainly come to you from your Lord. So whoever sees, it is for his own benefit, and whoever is blind, it is to his own detriment. And I am not a guardian over you.
interpretation: The verse establishes that divine guidance is presented as clear insight, and that the choice to accept or reject it rests entirely with the individual, whose gain or loss returns to the self. The Prophet's role is therefore that of a conveyer of the message rather than a keeper who compels belief, which underscores personal moral responsibility and the sufficiency of the evidence already given.

translation: And thus We explain the verses in detail, so that they may say, "You have studied (these lessons)," and that We may make it clear to a people who have knowledge.
interpretation: The verse shows that God's revelation is deliberately varied and clearly articulated, so that its message reaches every mind in a form it can grasp. The disbelievers' response, "you have studied," reveals their habit of dismissing the Prophet's recitation as human learning rather than engaging with its truth, and it reflects the way people often deflect clear signs when their hearts are not inclined to accept them. Yet the clarity is not wasted: it is made manifest for those who truly seek knowledge, who recognize in these explained signs the guidance meant for them. The verse thus joins divine pedagogy with a call to honest reflection, where the same verses that provoke denial become a light for the knowing.

translation: Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord. There is no deity except Him, and turn away from the polytheists.
interpretation: The verse frames the Prophet's mission as a call to submit wholeheartedly to divine revelation rather than to human preferences or the pressures of his community. Its opening command to follow what is revealed establishes that prophetic authority is derived entirely from the Lord, not invented by the messenger. The declaration that there is no deity but Him is placed at the center as the core of that revelation, so that tawhid is presented as the foundational content every believer must hold to. The instruction to turn away from the polytheists is best understood not as a call to hostility but as a withdrawal from futile argument and from seeking their approval, allowing the message to stand on its own clarity. Thus the verse links steadfast adherence to revealed truth with a principled disengagement from those who reject it.

translation: Had God willed, they would not have associated others with Him. And We have not appointed you as a guardian over them, nor are you a trustee responsible for them.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet and reminds him that guidance and misguidance rest in God's will and not in his own effort. Shirk is not something the Prophet could prevent by force of insistence, because God permits human beings to choose. His role is to convey the message, not to be a guardian who compels faith or a custodian answerable for their deeds. By stating that the Prophet was not sent to watch over them, the verse lifts from him the burden of grief over their disbelief and places accountability for their choices where it belongs, with each person before God.

translation: And do not revile those whom they invoke besides Allah, lest they revile Allah in enmity without knowledge. Thus We have made attractive to every community their deeds; then to their Lord is their return, and He will inform them of what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that believers should refrain from insulting the objects of worship of others, because such insults, though perhaps intended to defend the truth, provoke those people to retaliate against Allah out of ignorance and hostility, and thus the believers would become the cause of blasphemy against God. It shows that the manner of calling to the truth must be wise and considerate, not leading to a greater evil. The verse also reveals a principle of divine wisdom: every community finds its own conduct appealing to itself, which is a test, and ultimately all will return to their Lord, who will make known to them the reality of their deeds on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And they swore by Allah their most solemn oaths that if a sign came to them, they would surely believe in it. Say, "Signs are only with Allah." And what would make you aware that even if they came, they would not believe?
interpretation: The verse exposes the hollowness of the oaths of those who demanded miraculous signs: their vows were made with maximum earnestness, yet their hearts were already closed, so the mere arrival of a sign would not move them. The Prophet is told that the power to bring signs belongs to God alone, who sends them according to His wisdom, and that he is not responsible for their obstinacy. The phrase "what would make you aware" signals that the Prophet cannot know the hidden state of their hearts, and it teaches that stubborn disbelief, once entrenched, is not cured by miracles alone but by a sincere turning toward the truth. It also serves as a warning to believers not to be swayed into hoping that these people would believe if only their demands were met.

translation: And We turn their hearts and their eyes away, just as they did not believe in it the first time, and We leave them wandering blindly in their transgression.
interpretation: The verse describes a divine consequence for persistent rejection: when people repeatedly refuse the truth despite its clear arrival, God lets their hearts and perception be turned away from guidance, mirroring their initial refusal. Their hearts and sight, which should have been the means of recognizing truth, become instruments of further deviation. The phrase "as they did not believe the first time" establishes a principle of measure: disbelief hardens into a condition where the faculties no longer respond to signs. Being left in their transgression is thus not an arbitrary abandonment but the natural outcome of their own chosen aversion, in which they wander aimlessly, unable to find their way, because they have repeatedly turned away from the light that was offered to them.

translation: Even if We had sent down to them the angels, and the dead had spoken to them, and We had gathered against them every thing face to face, they would not have believed, unless God willed. But most of them are ignorant.
interpretation: The verse shows that the refusal of the disbelievers is not a lack of evidence but a matter of their own obstinate hearts. Even if every sign they demanded were granted in its most visible and direct form, faith would not arise in them, because belief is ultimately under God's will and guidance, not merely under the force of proof. Their real affliction is ignorance, meaning a willful blindness to truth that no miracle can cure unless God opens their hearts. The verse thus consoles the Prophet: his duty is to convey the message, not to compel acceptance, and the stubbornness of his people should not grieve him beyond measure.

translation: And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy—devils among mankind and jinn, inspiring to one another decorative speech as deception. And had your Lord willed, they would not have done it, so leave them and what they fabricate.
interpretation: This verse consoles the Prophet by showing that opposition to prophets is an established pattern in the history of revelation, not a sign of his failure. The enemies are described as shaytans from both humans and jinn, indicating that evil is produced by both hidden and visible agents who whisper to one another in polished, attractive rhetoric whose purpose is only to delude. The verse also affirms that such deception operates within God's permitted will: had He willed, they would not have acted thus, which points to the trial and testing inherent in human freedom. The command to leave them to their fabrications teaches the believer to entrust the matter to God, to refrain from anxious engagement with falsehood that is destined to collapse, and to remain steadfast in the truth one carries.

translation: And so that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline toward it, and that they may be pleased with it, and that they may commit what they are committing.
interpretation: The verse reveals a causal chain in the deceptive whisperings described before it: the embellished, false speech of the devils is made to reach hearts that already lack faith in the Hereafter, so that such hearts lean toward it. Since the inclination of the heart follows its disposition, those who have severed their hope in the next life are the ones most receptive to falsehood, and their attraction to it becomes the means by which they accept it and persist in the sins they habitually commit. The verse thus shows that disbelief in the Hereafter is both a cause and a consequence of spiritual deafness, and that the heart's openness to deception is determined by what it has chosen to love and desire.

translation: Shall I seek a judge other than God, when it is He who has sent down to you the Book, fully detailed? And those to whom We gave the Book know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth, so do not be among the doubters.
interpretation: The verse establishes that true judgment belongs to God alone, since the Qur'an is itself a complete and clearly explained revelation that needs no outside arbiter. Its appeal extends to the People of the Book, whose own scriptures attest to its divine origin, so the Prophet is commanded to remain firm and free of doubt. The verse thus joins the authority of revelation to the testimony of prior revelation, teaching that the believer's reference point in disputes and in matters of truth must be God's Book rather than human preference or rival authorities.

translation: And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice. None can alter His words, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God's decrees and promises are complete and unfailing: what He has declared is true in its content and just in its outcome, so the believer can rest in certainty that no force, opposition, or human scheming can change what God has determined. Divine speech is not subject to revision or abrogation by any created being, and this immutability is grounded in God's perfect hearing and knowledge, which encompass every word spoken, every intention, and every circumstance. The passage thus draws the reader toward trust in God's word over the shifting claims of worldly power.

translation: And if you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you away from the way of Allah. They follow nothing but assumption, and they do nothing but guess.
interpretation: The verse is a warning against measuring truth by numbers. Majority opinion or popular consensus is not a reliable guide, since most people on earth may be led by conjecture rather than knowledge, and so following them blindly risks drifting from the path of God. The verse directs the believer to anchor belief and conduct in revealed guidance and sound knowledge rather than in what the crowd assumes or speculates, and it is a timeless principle that the many are not automatically right.

translation: Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.
interpretation: The verse assures the Prophet that the outcome of guidance and misguidance is not in his hands but in the knowledge of God, who perfectly knows the hearts and inclinations of every person. Divine knowledge encompasses both those who wander from the path and those who are rightly guided, so the Prophet should not be burdened by the refusal of his opponents, nor should he claim any authority over who is guided. This reflects the principle that God alone judges the true state of each soul, and that human beings are responsible for seeking the truth while the granting of guidance rests with Him.

translation: So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, if you are believers in His signs.
interpretation: The verse directs believers to eat only from what has been slaughtered or prepared with the mention of Allah's name, linking lawful sustenance to a conscious act of remembrance and gratitude toward God. It presents faith in God's revelations as something proven through discernment in what one consumes: a believer who acknowledges divine signs honors the sanctity of the act of eating by invoking God and distinguishing what is permitted from what is neglected of His name. The condition 'if you are believers' reframes the ruling not merely as a dietary law but as a test of sincere submission, where mindfulness of God transforms ordinary sustenance into an act of worship.

translation: And what is [the matter] with you that you do not eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned, when He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you, except what you are compelled to? Indeed, many [people] mislead [others] by their desires without knowledge. Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of the transgressors.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the permissibility of food is tied to the mention of God's name at its slaughter, and that God has already clearly specified what is forbidden, so believers have no reason to refuse lawful food on the basis of their own inclinations or the misguided whims of others. By pairing this clarity with the exception of necessity, it teaches that the prohibitions are not an arbitrary burden but a clear boundary, and that departing from revealed knowledge in favor of desires is a form of misguidance that God fully knows and will hold to account against those who transgress.

translation: And leave the outward and the inward of sin. Indeed, those who earn sin will be recompensed for what they used to commit.
interpretation: The verse calls for a total renunciation of sin in all its forms, whether it is openly displayed in action and conduct or hidden in the heart, intention, and private life. Sin is not divided into a visible part that matters and a hidden part that can be overlooked; a believer must purify both the outer self and the inner self. By tying this command to the warning that those who acquire sin will be requited for what they committed, the verse makes clear that every deed and inclination is accountable before God, so the pursuit of righteousness must be complete and sincere rather than superficial or selective.

translation: And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned, for indeed it is grave disobedience. And indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you. And if you obey them, indeed you would be associators of others with Allah.
interpretation: The verse ties a specific dietary rule to the wider question of whose authority is obeyed. Withholding the name of God at slaughter is presented as defiance (fisq), because it breaks the covenant of acknowledging God as the giver of what is lawful. The verse then shows the mechanism behind such disobedience: the whisperings of the devils, which work through human intermediaries who argue against the divine command. The decisive test is not the debate itself but submission. To follow those who reject God's guidance in matters of lawful and unlawful is to give them the place that belongs to God alone in legislation, and the verse therefore equates such obedience with associating partners with Allah. The passage thus teaches that tawhid is practical as well as doctrinal, and that it is expressed in ordinary choices such as what one eats, as much as in creed.

translation: Is one who was dead and We brought him to life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one who is in darkness, never to emerge from it? Thus has been made attractive to the disbelievers what they have been doing.
interpretation: The verse draws a sharp contrast between two states of the human soul: the dead heart that has no life of faith, and the one revived by guidance from God, which is given a light that illuminates its path in the world. Those who remain in disbelief are compared to a person trapped in darkness with no way out, and the verse reveals that their attachment to their own deeds has been made to appear appealing to them, so they cling to what harms them. The image teaches that faith is both a revival of life and a source of clear vision, and that the obstacle to guidance is often the self's contentment with its own errors.

translation: And thus We placed in every town its greatest criminals so that they would plot within it. But they plot only against themselves, and they do not perceive.
interpretation: The verse shows that the leaders of wrongdoing in every community are often the ones who hold power and influence, and that God permits them to be tested by the very authority they exercise. Their scheming against the truth and against God's messengers is, in the end, a self-inflicted harm: the schemes they weave to protect their privileges turn back upon their own souls, yet their blindness to this consequence is itself the clearest sign of their spiritual ruin. The verse thus turns the reader's attention from the apparent success of the powerful to the hidden reality that every deception directed at others is ultimately a deception of the self.

translation: And when a sign comes to them, they say, "We will never believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of God." God knows best where to place His message. Those who committed crime will be struck with humiliation before God and a severe punishment for what they used to plot.
interpretation: The verse exposes the arrogance of those who reject guidance: they do not seek truth for its own sake but demand a status equal to the prophets, as if prophethood were a prize to be claimed by rank or social standing. God's reply is that He alone knows who is fit to bear His message, placing it where He wills, which dismantles the claim of entitlement. The verse thus teaches that faith depends on humility before divine wisdom rather than on conditions set by human pride, and that the scheming and hidden malice of the guilty will ultimately bring them disgrace and punishment.

translation: So whoever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam; and whoever He wills to leave astray, He makes his breast tight and constricted, as if he were ascending into the sky. Thus does Allah place defilement upon those who do not believe.
interpretation: The verse presents guidance and misguidance as flowing from Allah's will, yet it describes the inner states that accompany each: the one who is guided finds his heart opened and at ease with submission to God, while the one who turns away finds his heart constricted, so that faith becomes as burdensome and unnatural to him as climbing toward the heavens for breath. The imagery suggests that spiritual resistance is felt as a physical suffocation, and that the defilement (rijs) placed upon unbelievers is the natural consequence of their persistent refusal, which hardens the heart further. The passage thus joins divine sovereignty with human responsibility, showing that a heart which persistently refuses light grows closed to it.

translation: And this is the path of your Lord, straight. We have detailed the verses for a people who take heed.
interpretation: The verse presents the divine guidance as a single, unswerving path that leads back to the Lord, in contrast to the many crooked ways that divert from it. By stating that the signs have been explained in detail, it shows that God has not left humanity without clarity; the responsibility lies with the heart's readiness to remember. Only those who reflect and recall, who keep their awareness of God alive, are able to benefit from these clear signs and to walk the straight path with understanding.

translation: For them is the Abode of Peace with their Lord, and He is their Protector because of what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse presents the reward of the righteous as a secure and peaceful dwelling in the presence of God, where the believers are free from fear, harm, and discord. Its mention of God as their 'walī', their close protector and ally, indicates that this divine nearness and care is the fruit of their deeds. The verse thus ties the blessing of lasting peace to God's own guardianship, which rests upon those whose actions were sincere and good, reminding the reader that true security lies in the Lord rather than in worldly achievements.

translation: And [mention] the Day He will gather them all, [saying], "O company of jinn, you have taken much of mankind." And their allies from among mankind will say, "Our Lord, we benefited from one another, and we have reached our term which You appointed for us." He will say, "The Fire is your residence, wherein you will abide eternally, except what Allah wills. Indeed, your Lord is Wise and Knowing."
interpretation: The verse portrays the collective reckoning of jinn and humankind as a single assembly, where the close bond formed in worldly life through mutual exploitation of desires, flattery, and misguidance is exposed. The humans who followed the jinn confess that each side gained something from the other, and that they have now reached the term appointed for them, a confession that lays bare how both parties had sought worldly advantage at the expense of truth. The divine reply, that the Fire is their abode, shows that this partnership in disobedience ends in shared punishment, while the exception "except what Allah wills" reminds the reader that the final judgment rests entirely with God's wisdom and knowledge, and that His mercy and will remain above all human calculation.

translation: And thus We make some of the wrongdoers allies of one another, because of what they used to earn.
interpretation: The verse presents a principle of divine justice in which the wrongdoers are left to be drawn toward one another, so that their corrupt alliances and shared injustice become the very consequence of their own deeds. Their mutual companionship is not a source of strength but a reflection of what they have chosen to acquire through their conduct, indicating that people are often given over to the company they have made for themselves. It serves as a warning that the bonds formed on the basis of wrongdoing are ultimately bound to their own earnings and their outcome.

translation: O assembly of jinn and mankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you, relating to you My verses and warning you of the meeting of this your Day? They will say, "We testify against ourselves." And the worldly life deceived them, and they will testify against themselves that they had been disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Judgment as a scene of accountability in which both jinn and humankind are gathered and confronted with the fact that God's messengers had already delivered His revelation and warnings to them. Their own confession is the decisive proof: the same faculties and deeds that were deceived by the allure of worldly life become the witnesses against them, showing that the sin lay not in ignorance of the message but in being seduced by the present life and turning away from it. The verse thus teaches that human and jinn responsibility is equal before God, that no one can claim lack of warning, and that the self itself will bear testimony on the Day when every person's conscience is laid bare.

translation: That is because your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people were unaware.
interpretation: The verse affirms the justice of God in His dealings with nations: He does not punish a community out of caprice or without first making the truth known to them. Destruction comes only after clear warning and the sending of messengers, so that no people can claim they were condemned while being ignorant of what was required of them. Their heedlessness does not excuse them when the message has reached them, yet God's justice ensures that punishment is never arbitrary. The verse thus places divine judgment within a framework of mercy and fairness, reminding believers that accountability follows knowledge and that God's law of consequence is grounded in His perfect justice.

translation: And for all there are ranks according to what they have done, and your Lord is not unaware of what they do.
interpretation: The verse establishes that people are placed in varied degrees before God, and that these degrees are determined by their deeds rather than by lineage, wealth, or outward status. The word 'darajat' (ranks) suggests a graded hierarchy in which each person's standing rises or falls in accordance with the sincerity and quality of their actions. The closing clause, 'your Lord is not unaware of what they do,' assures the believer that no act is overlooked: the reckoning is exact, so every degree is justly assigned. It thus combines a call to strive in good works with a reminder of divine justice and perfect knowledge, and it consoles those who labor unseen while warning those who imagine their conduct escapes notice.

translation: And your Lord is the Free of need, the Possessor of mercy. If He wills, He can take you away and replace you with whomever He wills, just as He produced you from the descendants of another people.
interpretation: The verse closes the address to the people with a reminder that God's self-sufficiency and boundless mercy are not diminished by their need of Him, and that their continued existence on earth is entirely by His will. The phrase "Free of need" (al-Ghani) establishes that God gains nothing from obedience nor loses anything from disbelief, while "Possessor of mercy" tempers this sovereignty with compassion, so that His power to remove them is held together with His patience toward them. The image of being raised up from "the descendants of another people" is a call to humility: the people addressed are themselves successors of earlier nations, and the Qur'an thereby presents human dominance as a trust that can be transferred at God's pleasure, urging them to recognize that their position depends on obedience rather than on lineage or power.

translation: Indeed, what you are promised is surely coming, and you cannot escape it.
interpretation: The verse affirms with emphatic certainty that the promised reckoning, the Resurrection and the requital for deeds, is inevitable and will certainly arrive. Its emphasis on the futility of resistance ("and you cannot escape") conveys that no human being can frustrate or outrun the divine decree; the fleeting power of people to avoid accountability is contrasted with the absolute power of God. The address thus calls the listener to moral awareness now, since the matter is settled and no one can flee from it.

translation: Say, "O my people, work according to your position; indeed, I am working. So you will soon know who will have the good outcome of the [final] abode. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed."
interpretation: The verse sets a clear contrast between two paths and two outcomes, and it closes with a principle of certainty. The Prophet is commanded to address his people with a firm and dignified challenge: each party should continue acting on its own course, since his own commitment to his mission is unwavering. The phrase "so you will soon know" conveys that worldly appearances can mislead, and that the true test of a way of life is revealed in its ultimate end in the Hereafter, where success belongs to the righteous. The final statement that wrongdoers do not prosper generalizes the lesson: oppression, whether against oneself, others, or God, may seem to flourish for a time, but it cannot achieve lasting success. The verse thus combines reassurance for the believer with a warning to the obstinate, urging patience and steadfastness rather than compromise.

translation: And they assign to God a share of what He has created of crops and livestock, and they say, "This is for God," by their claim, and "This is for our associates." But what is for their associates does not reach God, while what is for God reaches their associates. Evil is what they judge.
interpretation: The verse exposes a practice of arbitrary division in which people dedicate a portion of God's own bounty to Him while reserving another for the beings they associate with Him, and then manipulate the outcome in favor of those idols. The unfairness is laid bare: whatever was set aside for God may be diverted to the associates, yet what was set aside for the associates is never returned to God. Such a scheme reveals that their devotion is governed by self-interest and invented claims rather than by gratitude to the One who provided the harvest and the herds. The closing judgment, that their decision is wretched, condemns not only the injustice toward God but the corruption of their own reasoning, which places the created ahead of the Creator and treats divine right as something to be bartered.

translation: And likewise, their associates have made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children, to destroy them and to confuse them regarding their religion. And had Allah willed, they would not have done so. So leave them and what they invent.
interpretation: The verse exposes how polytheistic customs spread through social pressure and the influence of those who served as their 'partners' (whether idols, priests, or leaders who had them elevated to a sacred status). Those who were supposed to guide people toward truth instead beautified an atrocity, namely infanticide, presenting it as religious devotion or honor, thereby destroying both the lives of the children and the integrity of the faith of their parents. The phrase 'and had Allah willed, they would not have done so' does not excuse the crime; rather, it affirms that divine will permits human choice, so the responsibility for the deed rests with those who chose it. The closing command, 'leave them and what they invent,' signals the Prophet's disengagement from those who persist in fabricated beliefs, after the clear message has been delivered, and it teaches that every false religious innovation that justifies cruelty will ultimately be accounted for.

translation: And they say, "These are livestock and tilled crops, forbidden; none may eat of them except whom we wish, by their claim; and there are livestock whose backs are forbidden, and livestock over which they do not mention the name of God, fabricating against Him. He will recompense them for what they used to fabricate."
interpretation: The verse exposes a pagan practice of arbitrarily dividing their property into sacred categories without any divine authority: some animals and crops were placed under prohibitions whose sole basis was human claim and whim, with the right to eat them restricted to those they designated. Some animals were forbidden to be ridden, loaded, or otherwise used, and others were slaughtered without the name of God being invoked. The Qur'an identifies this as a fabrication attributed to God, and it shows that legislating in God's name without revelation is a grave offense, for which a reckoning is promised.

translation: And they said, "What is in the wombs of these cattle is exclusively for our males, and forbidden to our wives; but if it is stillborn, then they are all partners in it." He will surely recompense them for their attribution; indeed, He is All-Wise, All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse exposes a pagan practice of arbitrarily assigning the offspring of livestock between men and women, granting the male sex exclusive rights to what was born alive while sharing a stillborn animal among all, as if such distinctions carried divine sanction. It reveals how human custom, unmoored from revelation, presumes to legislate over God's creation and attributes its own rules to Him. The closing divine names, the All-Wise and All-Knowing, affirm that God perceives every such invented distinction and will hold those who fabricate them accountable for what they attribute to Him.

translation: Those who have killed their children foolishly, without knowledge, and have forbidden what Allah provided for them, fabricating lies against Allah, have certainly lost. They have indeed gone astray, and they were not guided.
interpretation: The verse exposes a double corruption that stems from one root: ignorance of Allah's wisdom and mercy. Killing children out of folly, whether by literal infanticide or by the modern equivalents of sacrificing the next generation to shame, poverty fears, or false notions of honor, reflects a loss of the sense that life is a trust from God. Forbidding what God has provided, by declaring lawful sustenance unlawful without any revelation, is the second face of the same error: a human presuming to legislate the boundaries of divine bounty. The phrase 'fabricating lies against Allah' identifies this as attributing to God what He never commanded, which makes it not merely a moral failing but a theological one. The verdict that they 'have lost' and 'were not guided' teaches that material gain obtained through such choices is no gain at all, since the true loss is the forfeiture of guidance itself. The verse calls the reader to trust in God as the provider and to honor life as His gift.

translation: And it is He who produced gardens, trellised and untrellised, and date palms and crops of varying taste, and olives and pomegranates, similar and dissimilar. Eat from their fruit when they bear fruit, and give its due on the day of its harvest, and do not be excessive. Indeed, He does not like those who are excessive.
interpretation: The verse shows that the bounties of the earth are the work of God's creative power, and it invites the believer to gratitude expressed through enjoying what is lawful while fulfilling the right of the poor on the day of harvest, so that blessing is neither hoarded nor squandered. Excess, whether in consumption or in giving, is a deviation from the balance God loves, and the diversity of the gardens, fruits and crops reflects a wise order in which moderation is the proper response to abundance.

translation: And of the cattle [He produced] those for burden and those for slaughter. Eat of what Allah has provided for you and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.
interpretation: The verse links the bounty of livestock, which serves both as a means of transport and as a source of food and provision, with a call to gratitude and lawful consumption. By placing the command to eat from God's provision directly beside the warning against Satan's footsteps, it shows that the boundaries of what is permitted are part of the same moral order as the blessings themselves. Satan's enmity is described as manifest, so the believer's gratitude for divine provision must be accompanied by vigilance against every path that leads away from what God has made lawful and good.

translation: Eight pairs: of the sheep two, and of the goats two. Say, "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females, or that which the wombs of the two females contain? Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful."
interpretation: The verse confronts the idolaters with a rational challenge against their arbitrary prohibitions on livestock. God has created eight pairs of cattle, male and female, and the Prophet is commanded to ask whether the prohibition they invent applies to the males, the females, or to what their wombs carry, since every such case leads to the same absurdity of forbidding what God has not forbidden. The demand for knowledge exposes that their rulings rest on no revelation or sound evidence, but on mere assumption and inherited custom. The lesson is that lawmaking in matters of what is lawful belongs to God alone, and any claim to forbid what He has permitted must be supported by clear proof.

translation: And of camels two, and of cattle two. Say, "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females, or that which the wombs of the two females contain? Or were you witnesses when Allah instructed you with this?" So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah to mislead people without knowledge? Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: The verse dismantles the pagan Arabs' arbitrary prohibitions on certain livestock by turning their own categories against them: if the prohibition concerns the males, the females, or what their wombs carry, then they must either show a divine decree that they could not possibly have witnessed, or admit they are attributing their own invented rulings to God. Its deeper point is that lawmaking belongs to God alone, and that declaring what He has not permitted or forbidden is a grave injustice, since it misleads people through falsehood rather than knowledge; the question of divine revelation is thus tied to the moral responsibility of not falsely attributing religious rulings to God.

translation: Say, "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who would eat it, except that it be carrion, or flowing blood, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is impure, or a deviant sacrifice over which the name of other than Allah has been invoked. But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, then indeed your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful."
interpretation: The verse establishes that the forbidden foods are limited to a specific, clearly enumerated set in the revealed message, in response to the pagan Arab practice of declaring arbitrary things unlawful. Its emphasis falls on the principle that prohibition belongs to God alone, so dietary law is defined by revelation rather than by human custom. The four categories are each marked by impurity or by a violation of the dedication owed to God: carrion and flowing blood are impure, swine is declared rijs, and an animal offered in the name of other than God is an act of shirk. The closing clause introduces the principle of necessity: one who is forced to eat them without willful disobedience or exceeding the bounds of need incurs no sin, because God's mercy removes hardship where it is unavoidable.

translation: And to those who were Jews We prohibited every animal with undivided hooves; and from the cattle and the sheep We prohibited to them their fat, except what their backs carried or the entrails or what is mixed with bone. That was a recompense We gave them for their rebellion, and indeed We are truthful.
interpretation: The verse presents this prohibition as a specific consequence imposed on the Children of Israel for their transgression (baghy), indicating that some of the dietary restrictions they faced were not an原 inherent part of the divine law for all, but a corrective measure tied to their own disobedience and wrongdoing. The exceptions granted, such as fat carried on the back, in the entrails, or mixed with bone, show that the restriction was precise and bounded, reflecting divine justice tempered with mercy. The closing affirmation of truthfulness underscores that this judgment was real and just, not arbitrary.

translation: And if they deny you, say: "Your Lord is the Possessor of vast mercy, and His punishment will not be turned away from the criminal people."
interpretation: The verse sets out a two-sided picture of God that the Prophet is to hold up in the face of denial: mercy that is boundless and extends to all, yet a justice that cannot be averted from those who persist in sin. The phrase "vast mercy" places God's compassion first, inviting the deniers back to Him, while the closing warning shows that this mercy does not cancel accountability. Mercy is not indifference to wrongdoing, and the one who clings to crime against the clear signs of truth removes himself from the reach of that mercy. The verse thus calls the messenger to patience and hope in his message, and calls the listener to recognize that the door of divine forgiveness remains open, but that rejection and persistent wrongdoing bring their own consequence.

translation: Those who associated partners with God will say: "Had God willed, we would not have associated anything with Him, nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything." Likewise did those before them deny until they tasted Our punishment. Say: "Do you have any knowledge that you can bring forth to us? You follow nothing but conjecture, and you do nothing but guess."
interpretation: The verse exposes the flawed reasoning of the polytheists, who used God's will as a justification for their idolatry and their self-declared prohibitions, as though whatever occurs must therefore be approved by Him. The argument confuses God's permitting of an act with His approval of it, and it is a pattern repeated by those who denied the prophets before them, who likewise rejected guidance until punishment befell them. The Qur'an then turns the burden of proof back on them: if they possess genuine knowledge, they should produce it; otherwise their creed rests on mere supposition and fabrication, which cannot stand as a basis for truth or for lawful rulings in religion.

translation: Say, "To Allah belongs the conclusive argument. So if He had willed, He would have guided you all."
interpretation: The verse establishes that the decisive proof belongs to God alone, and that guidance is ultimately in His hands. Its point is that divine will is absolute: had God willed universal guidance, no one would have remained in error, so the persistence of disbelief is not a failure of God's power but reflects the reality that guidance is bestowed by His will while humans are held accountable for their choices. The verse therefore humbles the believer's claim to certainty and reminds the one who disputes that the final word in argument belongs to God, prompting reflection on the difference between being persuaded by evidence and being guided by God's grace.

translation: Say, "Bring forward your witnesses who testify that Allah has forbidden this." And if they testify, do not testify with them; and do not follow the desires of those who denied Our signs and of those who do not believe in the Hereafter, and who ascribe equals to their Lord.
interpretation: The verse confronts the idolaters with a demand for proof: if they claim that Allah forbade what they had invented (the superstitious prohibitions concerning livestock and produce in the preceding verses), let them bring forth their witnesses. Since no genuine witness can testify to a divine prohibition that has not been revealed, the call exposes the emptiness of their claims. The believer is commanded not to join in such false testimony even if others sign it, because bearing witness to falsehood is a betrayal of truth. The closing warning turns from the act of testimony to the source of error itself: following the whims of those who reject God's revelation, who deny the Hereafter, and who set up rivals beside their Lord. Desires, not knowledge, drive such people, so the faithful must hold to revealed truth rather than the fashions of the crowd.

translation: Say, "Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you: that you associate nothing with Him; be good to your parents; do not kill your children because of poverty, We provide for you and for them; do not approach the shameful deeds, whether apparent or hidden; and do not kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right. This He has instructed you, that you may understand."
interpretation: The verse opens a set of divine prohibitions framed as a direct recitation from God, and it places the foundation of ethics in tawhid, the oneness of God, before moving to the social obligations of kindness toward parents, the protection of children, and the preservation of human life. The repeated command 'do not' moves from the sacred relationship with the Creator to the most intimate human bonds and then to the wider community, showing that faith is inseparable from justice in family and society. The rejection of killing children out of fear of poverty corrects a pre-Islamic practice and reminds believers that sustenance belongs to God, who provides for both the parent and the child, so anxiety about scarcity must not override mercy. The prohibition of approaching indecencies, both open and concealed, teaches that morality must govern outward conduct and inward intention alike. Ending with the sanctity of life and the phrase 'that you may understand' emphasizes that these commandments are not arbitrary but are meant to awaken reason and moral responsibility.

translation: And do not approach the property of the orphan, except in the way that is best, until he reaches his maturity. And give full measure and weight with justice. We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity. And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near relative. And fulfill the covenant of Allah. That is what He has enjoined upon you, that you may be reminded.
interpretation: This verse gathers a set of ethical obligations that rest on a single principle: justice that protects the vulnerable and binds the believer to his word. The guardianship of an orphan's wealth is entrusted to the one who is strongest and most capable, and it is restricted to what is best for the orphan until he reaches full maturity, so that the trust is guarded rather than exploited. The command to give full measure and weight, followed immediately by the statement that no soul is burdened beyond its capacity, shows that divine justice in commerce is not an impossible ideal; the believer is asked only to do what lies within his power, and the standard is exactness in dealings with others. The call to be just in speech, even against one's own kin, extends justice from property to testimony and words, showing that a person's ties of blood must never override the truth. Finally, the fulfilment of Allah's covenant is placed at the close as the root of all these duties, so that every act of justice toward orphans, traders, and relatives is understood as a response to the covenant made with God, and the verse ends by pointing to remembrance as the purpose of these commandments.

translation: And that this is My path, straight, so follow it. And do not follow [other] paths, for they will scatter you away from His way. That is what He has instructed you, that you may become righteous.
interpretation: The verse presents the straight path as a single, unified way that God has laid out, set in contrast to the many divergent paths that pull people apart from one another and from the truth. Its scattering effect is not only a matter of individual error but of social fragmentation: when people follow their own desires and separate roads, they lose the cohesion that comes from a common guidance. The closing phrase ties this command to taqwa, indicating that unity of direction and God-consciousness are inseparable, and that adherence to the one path is itself the means by which the believer guards against deviation.

translation: Then We gave Moses the Scripture, completed in perfection for the one who did good, and as a detailed explanation of all things, and as guidance and mercy, that perhaps they would believe in the meeting with their Lord.
interpretation: The verse presents the Torah as a complete and perfected revelation, granted to Moses, whose fullness is shown in its being a clear exposition of all matters needed for guidance. Its completeness is directed toward those who act righteously, indicating that the benefit of divine guidance is realized through sincere good conduct. The phrase 'that perhaps they would believe in the meeting with their Lord' ties the purpose of revelation to awareness of accountability before God, teaching that the ultimate aim of scripture is to awaken faith in the Hereafter and in the encounter with the Creator, which in turn transforms the believer's life into one of mercy and guidance.

translation: And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed, so follow it and be mindful of God, that you may be shown mercy.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an as a blessed revelation whose blessing lies in its abundant good, guidance, and lasting benefit for those who receive it. Its call is twofold: to follow its teachings in practice, and to be conscious of God (taqwa) in every matter. The verse links the two, implying that sincere adherence to revelation is itself a form of mindfulness of the Divine, and that the reward of this path is mercy, which is the believer's hope of divine grace in this life and the next.

translation: Lest you should say: "The Book was only sent down upon two groups before us, and we were indeed heedless of their study."
interpretation: The verse points to a justification the Arabs might offer on the Day of Judgment for not receiving revelation: that they were not addressed by it and were merely unaware of what previous communities had studied. By sending the Book to them in their own tongue, God closes this excuse, showing that the Qur'an was revealed to remove any plea of heedlessness and to establish a clear proof against them.

translation: Or [lest] you should say, "If the Book had been revealed to us, we would have been better guided than they." So there has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord, and guidance and mercy. Then who is more unjust than one who denies the signs of Allah and turns away from them? We will recompense those who turn away from Our signs with a terrible punishment for their turning away.
interpretation: The verse closes the argument that began with the Quraysh's and the People of the Book's claim that they would have been better guided had a scripture come to them, by showing that the Qur'an has in fact arrived as a clear proof, guidance and mercy, so that no excuse remains. The real injustice lies not in lacking a scripture but in rejecting the signs of God after they have been presented and deliberately turning away from them, and the punishment named is the natural consequence of that aversion rather than an arbitrary penalty.

translation: Are they waiting for anything but that the angels should come to them, or that your Lord should come, or that some of the signs of your Lord should come? On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come, no soul will benefit from its faith if it had not believed before, or had not earned good through its faith. Say: "Wait, indeed we are waiting."
interpretation: The verse warns those who refuse faith that they are only awaiting the decisive moment of accountability, whether through the angels' coming, the Lord's coming to judgment, or the manifestation of some of His signs, which the Prophet's commentators have variously related to the rising of the sun from the west and the great portents of the Hour. Once these signs appear, the door of repentance closes, and faith offered only under the pressure of certainty brings no benefit to one who had neglected it, so the true time for belief is now, while choice remains open. The closing command, "Wait, indeed we are waiting," is a stern rebuke that leaves the disbelievers to their expectation, while the believers are left to their own sincere readiness for the reckoning.

translation: Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects, you have nothing to do with them in anything. Their affair is only with Allah; then He will inform them of what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse addresses the danger of fragmenting the religion of God into rival factions, each claiming a partial truth and turning against the others. Its message is twofold: the Prophet is disassociated from those who split the community and make themselves into schismatic groups, since such division contradicts the unity of the message he brings; and the final judgment over their condition is left entirely to God, who will reveal the reality of their deeds on the Day of Reckoning. The verse thus calls believers to unity in faith and warns against sectarianism, while reminding them that they are not the judges of others' hearts and fates.

translation: Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times the like of it, and whoever comes with an evil deed will not be recompensed except with the like of it, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: The verse establishes the principle of divine justice in recompense: good deeds are multiplied generously, ten times over, reflecting God's abundant mercy and the value He places on even small acts of righteousness, while evil deeds are requited only with their equal, so no one is punished beyond what they committed. The closing phrase, "and they will not be wronged," affirms that the scale of reward and retribution is perfectly just, with generosity toward the good and exactness toward the wrongdoer, so that a person's accountability is measured with complete fairness. It invites the believer to hope in God's multiplying grace while recognizing that every action is weighed precisely.

translation: Say: Indeed, my Lord has guided me to a straight path, a firm religion, the creed of Abraham, a upright monotheist, and he was not of those who associate partners with God.
interpretation: The verse presents the Prophet being commanded to declare that divine guidance has led him to the straight path, and it identifies that path with the pure monotheism of Abraham. By describing Abraham as hanif, one who turns away from all false worship toward the one God, and by explicitly denying that he was among the mushrikun, the verse frames true religion as unwavering devotion to God alone, standing in contrast to the polytheism of the surrounding society. Its placement emphasizes that the Prophet's message is not a novelty but a restoration of the original, primordial faith of the prophets, grounded in the lineage and example of Abraham.

translation: Say, "Indeed, my prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: The verse condenses the whole orientation of a believer's life into a single declaration of sincere devotion. Prayer (salah) and sacrifice (nusuk) represent the most formal acts of worship, while living and dying represent the entirety of one's existence outside ritual. By placing the ordinary moments of life, and even death, under the same claim of belonging to God, the verse dissolves the boundary between the sacred and the everyday. Every act, from the most ritual to the most mundane, becomes an expression of a single loyalty to the Lord of all creation, so that the believer lives and dies as one who belongs wholly to God alone.

translation: He has no partner. And with this I have been commanded, and I am the first of the Muslims (those who submit).
interpretation: The verse is a declaration of pure monotheism (tawhid) made by the Prophet Muhammad in the name of his own submission to God. By stating that God has no partner, he rejects every form of associating others with God in worship, lordship, and authority, and this rejection is not a personal opinion but a command he has received. His words "I am the first of the Muslims" should be understood as a claim to be the first to surrender his whole self to God in this way, so that he becomes the model for all who follow him. The verse thus joins the content of faith with the act of submission: belief in the oneness of God must be accompanied by an active, willing surrender that the Prophet himself embodies first.

translation: Say, "Shall I seek other than Allah as a lord, while He is the Lord of all things? And no soul earns [blame] except against itself, and no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you about that over which you used to differ."
interpretation: The verse establishes that true lordship belongs to Allah alone, so seeking any other as a lord or authority is unreasonable when He is the Lord and Sustainer of everything. It then affirms the principle of personal accountability: each person bears the consequences of his own deeds and cannot be made to carry another's burden, which removes any hope of substitution or intercession for wrongdoing. Finally, it points to the certainty of the return to God, where the disputes that people held about religion and truth will be decided with full knowledge, so that each soul faces the reality of its own choices.

translation: And it is He who made you successors upon the earth and raised some of you above others in degrees that He may test you through what He has given you. Indeed, your Lord is swift in penalty, and indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse presents human diversity in worldly station, wealth, ability, and rank not as a sign of inherent superiority but as a trust and a test. Being made successors on the earth means that humanity holds what it possesses on loan from God, so each person's differing degrees become an arena in which gratitude, justice, and generosity are revealed or neglected. The verse then balances this serious warning with the reminder that God's punishment is swift when deserved, yet His forgiveness and mercy remain open to those who turn back to Him, so that the trial is ultimately meant to draw the believer toward accountability and hope rather than despair or arrogance.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Alif, Lam, Meem, Sad.
interpretation: The verse opens with the disjointed letters (muqatta'at) Alif, Lam, Meem, Sad, which appear at the beginning of certain surahs and are not given a literal word-by-word meaning in the text itself. The most convincing reading is that they draw the attention of the listener to the Qur'an as a revelation composed of the same letters from which human speech is formed, yet which they are unable to match. The opening invocation then establishes that what follows is to be received in the name of Allah, the source of all mercy. Taken together, the opening signals a challenge to hear and reflect deliberately, and it prepares the reader for the call to recognize the Book as a divine guidance free of doubt.

translation: A Book revealed to you, so let there be no discomfort in your breast about it, that you may warn thereby, and as a reminder for the believers.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet and steers him away from anxiety over the reception of the revelation. The phrase "let there be no constriction in your breast" depicts the burden of a heart that fears it will fall short of delivering a message that many will reject. God assures him that the Book was sent to him for a clear purpose: to warn, which is the duty of delivery, and to remind those who are already open to faith. The Prophet's task is therefore to convey the message faithfully, not to force its acceptance. Its benefit is determined by the hearts that receive it, and the believers are singled out as those who will truly profit from it, while the warning remains a proof for all.

translation: Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not follow other than Him as protectors. Little do you remember.
interpretation: The verse calls the believers to a single, clear source of guidance: the revelation sent from their Lord.
