The apparent blessing is thus revealed as a test and a trial, and true honor is measured by faith and the state in which one meets death, not by possessions or progeny.

translation: And when a surah is revealed [saying], "Believe in Allah and strive alongside His Messenger," those of wealth and ability among them ask your permission, saying, "Leave us to be with those who sit [at home]."
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites' reluctance to commit themselves to the cause of faith in its moment of trial. Those endowed with means and capacity, rather than rising to the call to jihad, seek exemption and prefer the company of those who stay behind. Their request reveals that their profession of faith was never accompanied by a willingness to sacrifice, and that comfort and worldly security had become their true measure. The verse thus teaches that genuine belief is tested by readiness to act and to bear cost for God's cause, and that ease used as a pretext for withdrawal is a sign of a divided and insincere heart.

translation: They were content to be with those who remain behind (the women and the infirm), and a seal was set upon their hearts, so they do not understand.
interpretation: The verse describes hypocrites who, rather than striving in the cause of God, chose the comfort of staying behind with those who were excused from fighting. Their contentment with this low station is itself a symptom of a heart that has been sealed: having repeatedly turned away from truth, their hearts became closed to guidance, so that they lost the capacity to grasp what is genuinely good for them. The verse thus links a person's choices to the state of their understanding, showing that persistent neglect of duty dulls the inner faculty by which one recognizes truth, and that the loss of comprehension is the consequence of such choices rather than an arbitrary decree.

translation: But the Messenger and those who believed with him strove with their wealth and their lives. For them are the good things, and it is they who are the successful.
interpretation: The verse distinguishes the true believers by their willingness to sacrifice what they most value, wealth and self alike, in the cause of God. Their striving is not merely outward action but the proof of the sincerity of their faith, and it is this sincerity that makes them deserving of the good things promised to them. The verse thus binds faith to sacrifice: a belief that costs nothing remains untested, while the one who gives of his property and his very self shows that his faith has taken root in his heart. Success here is not measured by worldly gain but by having been among those who chose God and His Messenger over every attachment of the self.

translation: Allah has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein they will abide forever. That is the great triumph.
interpretation: The verse presents the ultimate success as an eternal reward, where the believers' final victory is not merely worldly gain but a permanent state of blessing in gardens flowing with rivers. The word 'al-fawz' (triumph) points to having achieved what one truly sought, so that the greatness of this achievement lies in its everlastingness, in contrast with the fleeting nature of worldly goods. It calls the reader to measure success by the standard of eternity rather than of temporary advantage.

translation: And those with excuses among the Bedouins came seeking permission to stay behind, while those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat back. Those who disbelieved among them will be struck by a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse exposes a split among the desert Arabs who attached themselves to the community around the Prophet: some came forward with genuine or feigned excuses to seek exemption from the call to jihad, while others simply stayed behind without even offering an excuse, their absence revealing a lack of sincere faith. By distinguishing the excused from the deceitful, and then stating that the disbelievers among them will face a painful punishment, the verse teaches that outward claims of excuse do not shield one from accountability before God. Sincerity in faith is measured by one's readiness to answer the call of the Messenger when it matters most, and hypocrisy, which hides behind pretexts, is what brings the threatened chastisement.

translation: There is no blame upon the weak, nor upon the sick, nor upon those who find nothing to spend, if they are sincere toward Allah and His Messenger. There is no path (of blame) against the good-doers. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse lifts the burden of obligation from those who are genuinely unable to take part in struggle and giving, such as the weak, the sick, and the poor who have nothing to spend, so long as their hearts are sincere toward Allah and His Messenger. Religious duty is measured by capacity and intention, not merely by outward action, and sincerity (nush) is the condition that makes an excused person fully counted among the righteous. Those who do good are not subject to any charge against them, and the closing names of Allah, Forgiving and Merciful, affirm that divine mercy covers human limitation.

translation: Nor is there blame upon those who came to you asking to be given mounts, and you said, "I cannot find anything to mount you on"; they turned away while their eyes overflowed with tears of grief that they could not find anything to spend.
interpretation: The verse describes the sincere believers of the time of the Prophet who wished to join the campaign but lacked the means of transport, and it lifts any sin from them, showing that God judges by intention and capacity rather than by outward ability alone. Their grief at being unable to contribute is itself an act accepted before God, and it teaches that a sincere longing to do good, when one is genuinely prevented, is counted as good. It also reveals the Prophet's compassion, since he had no mounts to give, and the verse sets the principle that no one is burdened beyond what he can bear.

translation: The blame is only upon those who ask your permission while they are wealthy. They are content to be with those who remain behind (the women and the infirm), and Allah has sealed over their hearts, so they do not know.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrisy of those who had the means to join the struggle yet sought exemption from the Prophet on flimsy pretexts. Their excuse is not genuine hardship but a preference for ease and comfort over sacrifice. Their willingness to be counted among those who stay behind reveals a settled disposition of the heart, and the sealing of their hearts is presented as the consequence of their persistent choosing of worldly ease over duty. Their lack of understanding is thus self-inflicted: having repeatedly turned away from what is right, they lose the capacity to recognize it, so the verse warns that responsibility for exemption rests with those who are able, not with the sincere needy.

translation: They will make excuses to you when you return to them. Say, "Do not make excuses; we will never believe you. Allah has already informed us of your news. And Allah will see your deeds, and so will His Messenger. Then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do."
interpretation: This verse, revealed concerning the hypocrites who stayed behind from the Tabuk expedition, exposes the insincerity of their apologies after the Muslims return from battle. Allah instructs the Prophet to reject their excuses outright, because Allah has already disclosed their true inner state and actions to him, so their pretended remorse cannot deceive the believers. The verse thereby teaches that outward excuses are worthless when the heart is corrupt, that true accountability lies before Allah who sees all deeds, and that every person will ultimately be informed of and judged by what they actually did, not by what they claimed.

translation: They will swear to you by Allah when you return to them, that you may leave them alone. So leave them alone; indeed they are impure, and their refuge is Hell as recompense for what they used to earn.
interpretation: This verse, revealed concerning the hypocrites who stayed behind from the Tabuk expedition, exposes the nature of their oaths: they swear false oaths of sincerity upon returning to the Muslims, seeking to be left alone and spared reproach. The command to turn away from them is not a call to hostility but a directive to withdraw from honoring their excuses or entrusting them with confidence, since their inner corruption (rijs) makes them unfit for close fellowship. The verse ties their spiritual impurity to their destination in Hell, showing that outward oaths cannot cleanse what is hidden in the heart, and that accountability rests on what they have actually earned through their conduct.

translation: They swear to you in order that you may be pleased with them. But if you should be pleased with them, indeed Allah is not pleased with a defiant, wayward people.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites who swear oaths before the believers, not out of sincere repentance or loyalty, but to win their approval and secure their worldly acceptance. It teaches that true standing before God cannot be purchased by pleasing people through oaths or appearances, since divine pleasure follows righteousness and obedience, not the satisfaction of those who persist in defiance. The believer is warned not to be deceived by outward assurances, and that even if human hearts are won over by such deceit, Allah's favor is withheld from those who have deliberately departed from His command.

translation: The desert Arabs are more intense in disbelief and hypocrisy, and more likely not to know the limits of what Allah has revealed to His Messenger. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse distinguishes between the dwellers of the desert and the settled community not by lineage but by their relationship to revelation. Their greater hardness in kufr and nifaq is tied to their remoteness from the places where the Prophet taught and from the gatherings in which the revealed law was recited, explained and lived out. Ignorance of the bounds of what God has sent down is thus presented as a consequence of distance from knowledge and companionship, not as an inherent defect of a people. The closing names, the All-Knowing and the All-Wise, point to the fact that God understands the causes of such differences and that the verse is a summons to seek nearness to the source of guidance rather than a permanent judgment on a group.

translation: And among the Bedouin are those who consider what they spend [in charity] as a loss, and they wait for misfortunes to befall you. Upon them will be the misfortune of evil; and Allah is Hearing and Knowing.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocritical character of some desert Arabs who view almsgiving not as an act of devotion that brings them closer to God but as a burdensome tax imposed on them, a loss to be grudgingly paid. Their resentment is matched by their hostile expectation that the Muslims will suffer reversals, so that their hearts are turned against the community whose strength they begrudge. The Qur'an turns this calculation back upon them: the evil of the reversal they wish for will return to their own heads. The closing divine attributes of hearing and knowledge affirm that God is aware of the hidden intentions behind every outward expenditure, so that charity is judged by the sincerity of the heart rather than by the amount given.

translation: And among the Bedouin are those who believe in Allah and the Last Day and take what they spend as means of nearness to Allah and as [invocations of] blessings from the Messenger. Unquestionably, it is a means of nearness for them. Allah will admit them into His mercy. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse (At-Tawbah 9:99) distinguishes within the Bedouin community between those whose spending is sincere and those whose spending is merely a burden or a show. The true believers among them treat their charity as a way of drawing near to God and as a means of securing the Prophet's prayers for them, so that what they give becomes a genuine act of worship rather than a loss. The verse teaches that what determines the worth of an outlay is the intention behind it and the faith that animates it, not the amount or the social setting. God's promise to admit such people into His mercy, and the closing affirmation of His forgiveness and compassion, offer hope that even those from a harsher, less settled background can attain nearness to Him through sincere faith and generosity.

translation: And the foremost of the early emigrants and the helpers, and those who followed them in excellence, Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him, and He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great achievement.
interpretation: The verse honors the earliest Muslims, both the Muhajirun who left their homes for the sake of faith and the Ansar who sheltered and supported them, and extends the same divine favor to all who follow their path with sincere goodness. It teaches that acceptance before Allah rests on sincere faith and righteous conduct sustained across generations, and that mutual pleasure between the servant and his Lord is the highest reward, surpassing even the gardens promised to them.

translation: And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites, and among the people of Medina are those who have become accustomed to hypocrisy. You do not know them; We know them. We will punish them twice, and then they will be returned to a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse exposes a hidden hypocrisy within the early Muslim community, both among the nomadic Arabs of the surrounding desert and among the settled residents of Medina, where some had become so practiced in feigning faith that even the Prophet could not recognize them. The statement that God knows them while the Prophet does not affirms that true knowledge of the inner state of a person belongs to God alone, and that the Prophet's authority rested on revelation rather than on his own insight into hearts. The 'twofold punishment' is understood by many commentators as a worldly chastisement, such as disgrace, exposure, or hardship in this life, followed by the greater punishment in the Hereafter, which conveys that hypocrisy brings consequences both now and in the next world. The verse thus serves as a warning that outward membership in the community does not secure one's standing before God, and that sincerity of the heart is what He ultimately judges.

translation: And others have acknowledged their sins; they mixed a righteous deed with another that was bad. Perhaps Allah will accept their repentance. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse speaks of a group who, having fallen into wrongdoing, did not persist in denial but openly confessed their faults, and who combined good works with their earlier misdeeds. Its message is that sincere acknowledgment of sin, joined with a return to good conduct, keeps the door of repentance open: the phrase 'perhaps Allah will accept' places the believer between hope and humility, neither presuming upon divine mercy nor despairing of it. The closing names of Allah, the Forgiving and the Merciful, affirm that divine mercy is wide enough to embrace those who turn back to Him with honest contrition.

translation: Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow, and pray for them. Indeed, your prayer is a comfort for them. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse establishes that charity is not merely a financial transfer but a means of spiritual purification for the giver, lifting the soul from the attachment to wealth and cleansing it of greed. The Prophet's act of collecting it and his supplication over those who give are shown to be a bond that brings tranquility to the believers, reassuring them that their sacrifice is accepted. The verse thus joins the outward duty of almsgiving with the inward healing of the heart and the communal bond between leader and community.

translation: Did they not know that it is Allah who accepts repentance from His servants and takes charity, and that Allah is the Most Accepting of repentance, the Most Merciful?
interpretation: The verse directs the believers to a truth that should be settled in the heart: the door of return to Allah is never closed while a person lives. By asking 'Did they not know?', it reproaches those who have strayed or hesitated to repent, reminding them that the One who receives repentance is the same One who accepts sincere charity offered from what He has given. The pairing of repentance and charity shows that turning back to God is not merely a matter of words, but of a sincere inner turning joined with outward generosity toward others. The closing names, al-Tawwab and al-Rahim, reveal that Allah's acceptance of repentance flows from His mercy, so a servant should never despair of His forgiveness, but should hasten to repent and to give in His cause.

translation: And say, "Work, for Allah will see your deeds, and so will His Messenger and the believers. And you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do."
interpretation: The verse places human action under a threefold witness: God, who sees all things; the Messenger; and the believing community, whose scrutiny of conduct is a real and social form of accountability. Its address to the individual conscience is that no deed is hidden, whether done openly or in secret, and that the reality of one's work will ultimately be disclosed before the All-Knowing, who alone encompasses both the unseen and the witnessed. Thus the verse calls the believer to sincerity and integrity in action, since the true measure of work is not appearance but the knowledge of the One to whom every person returns.

translation: And [there are] others deferred until the command of Allah: either He will punish them, or He will accept their repentance. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse refers to the three companions who stayed behind from the Tabuk expedition, whose case was held in suspension (murjawn) until Allah's decision was revealed, rather than being judged hastily by the Prophet or the believers. Their matter teaches that human judgment on another's inner state and final standing belongs to God alone, and that a person under such uncertainty should neither despair nor presume. The verse holds out the open possibility of divine mercy through repentance, while affirming that Allah's outcome is governed by perfect knowledge and wisdom, so that every decision He makes, whether punishment or forgiveness, is placed in its rightful measure.

translation: And those who took a mosque for harm, disbelief, and division among the believers, and as a station for whoever had warred against Allah and His Messenger before. They will surely swear, "We intended nothing but good." And Allah bears witness that they are indeed liars.
interpretation: This verse refers to the hypocrites who built the mosque of Dirar (the mosque of harm) near Medina, which in reality was a base for undermining the Prophet's community: it was meant to cause harm, to strengthen disbelief, to split the believers into rival groups, and to serve as a refuge for those who had already opposed Allah and His Messenger, such as Abu 'Amir the monk. Their future oaths of good intention are exposed by Allah's testimony that they are liars, teaching that true faith is measured not by claims or pious appearances but by the actual purpose and effect of one's deeds upon the community of believers.

translation: Never stand in prayer therein. Surely a mosque founded upon righteousness from the first day is more worthy that you stand in it. In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah At-Tawbah (9:108), contrasts two mosques: the mosque of Quba, founded upon piety from its first day, and the mosque built by the hypocrites as a place of discord and disbelief. The Prophet was told never to stand in prayer in the latter. The verse teaches that the worth of a place of worship lies not in its structure but in the sincerity of its founding intention and in the purity of those who frequent it. Believers who love physical and spiritual cleanliness are beloved to God, so outward purity and inward sincerity together make a house of worship truly blessed.

translation: Is one who founded his building upon piety from God and His approval better, or one who founded his building on the edge of a crumbling bank that collapsed with him into the fire of Hell? And God does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: The verse uses the image of two buildings to contrast two foundations of a person's life. The first is a structure built on taqwa (God-consciousness) and the pursuit of God's good pleasure, which is firm and enduring because its base is sound. The second is built on the brink of a hollow, eroding cliff, so that the very ground beneath it gives way and it falls into the fire. The point is that actions and beliefs are only as stable as the intention and conviction underlying them: a life grounded in sincere devotion to God endures, while one grounded in falsehood, hypocrisy, or rebellion is inherently unstable and ends in ruin. The closing statement reminds that those who persist in wrongdoing deprive themselves of divine guidance, so their chosen foundation leads them astray rather than to security.

translation: Their building which they built will never cease to be a source of doubt in their hearts, unless their hearts are cut to pieces. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse speaks of the mosque built by the hypocrites (Masjid al-Dirar) to cause harm, divide the believers, and serve as a base for disbelief. Its construction remains a lasting cause of suspicion and inner turmoil for them, a sign that hypocrisy and deception produce perpetual unease in the hearts of those who practice them. The phrase 'unless their hearts are cut to pieces' points to the end of this inner conflict only through death or total destruction of their hearts, meaning that their doubt will persist until their lives end. The closing names, All-Knowing and All-Wise, affirm that Allah fully knows the intentions behind such deeds and that His judgment in them is perfectly wise.

translation: Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth in exchange for Paradise. They fight in the cause of Allah, so they kill and are killed. That is a true promise binding upon Him in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an. And who is truer to his covenant than Allah? So rejoice in the bargain you have concluded with Him, and that is the great triumph.
interpretation: The verse presents faith as a commercial contract in which God is the buyer and the believer sells his self and possessions, receiving Paradise as the price, which reveals that true belonging to God means surrendering what a person most values in exchange for an eternal reward that surpasses any worldly loss. By affirming that this covenant was sealed in the earlier scriptures as well, it places the Muslim community within a continuous line of prophetic commitment, and by calling the transaction a triumph it teaches that the sincere believer's sense of joy should come not from worldly gain but from having sold himself to the One whose promise is never broken.

translation: The repentant, the worshipful, the praisers, the wanderers (or fasting ones), the bowers, the prostrators, those who enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and those who observe the limits set by God. So give good news to the believers.
interpretation: The verse, from Surah At-Tawbah (9:112), describes the qualities of the believers who have sold their lives and wealth to God in exchange for Paradise. It sets out a sequence that begins with inner turning back to God (repentance) and sincere worship, moves through gratitude and praise, and then to outward devotion in bowing and prostration, and finally to social responsibility in commanding good and forbidding evil. Its closing phrase, 'those who observe the limits of God,' shows that faithful conduct must be bounded by divine law, so that piety is both a relationship with God and an ethical commitment to the community. The verse thus presents true belief as a complete way of life in which private devotion and public righteousness are inseparable, and it ends by directing the Prophet to announce good tidings to such believers.

translation: It was not for the Prophet or for those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were [close] relatives, after it had become clear to them that they are companions of Hellfire.
interpretation: The verse establishes a clear principle that the bond of faith takes precedence over ties of blood and kinship. Once the reality of the polytheists' condition has been made evident, continuing to seek forgiveness for them is no longer appropriate, because it would conflict with the truth that has been made manifest. The verse also reflects the moral seriousness of the Prophet and the believers: their loyalty and supplication must follow what is known to be right, and they must not be swayed by affection for relatives into praying for those who have persisted in rejecting God. It is a lesson that devotion to God requires clarity of conviction, and that sympathy must be disciplined by the knowledge of what is true.

translation: And the request of forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him. Indeed, Abraham was compassionate and forbearing.
interpretation: The verse clarifies that Abraham's plea for forgiveness on behalf of his father was not an expression of allegiance to disbelief but a fulfillment of a promise he had given out of gentleness and hope for his father's guidance. Once the reality of his father's persistent enmity toward God became undeniable, Abraham cleanly severed his bond with him, teaching that compassion for people must never become a compromise of loyalty to God. The closing description of Abraham as tender-hearted and forbearing shows that his firm disavowal of falsehood was joined with deep mercy and patience, so that even his rejection of his father flowed from sincere concern and a principled commitment to the truth.

translation: And Allah would never cause a people to go astray after He has guided them until He makes clear to them what they should avoid. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: The verse establishes that divine guidance is not a trap: Allah does not hold a people accountable for going astray after they have been guided until the path of righteousness has been made explicitly clear to them, so that they know what to beware of. Misguidance thus follows from a people's own rejection of clear guidance, not from arbitrary decree. The closing statement that Allah has full knowledge of all things affirms that His judgments are based on complete knowledge of each people's state, intentions, and circumstances, and that He is never unjust in what He lets them go astray in.

translation: Indeed, to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death. And you have not, besides Allah, any protector or any helper.
interpretation: The verse establishes that absolute sovereignty over all creation belongs to Allah alone, and that the power over life and death, the two greatest matters of human existence, rests exclusively with Him. Since everything in the heavens and earth is subject to His dominion, it follows that no creature can offer genuine protection or effective support against His will. The verse thus calls the believer to turn in trust and reliance only toward the One who owns and governs all things, rather than to any intermediary, idol, or worldly power that has no real authority over them.

translation: Indeed Allah turned in forgiveness toward the Prophet, and the emigrants and the helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship, after the hearts of a group of them had nearly swerved; then He turned to them in forgiveness. Indeed, He is Kind and Merciful to them.
interpretation: The verse shows that Allah's acceptance of repentance extends even to the noblest of believers, the Prophet and his companions, during the difficult campaign of Tabuk. It teaches that momentary wavering of hearts under extreme hardship is a human weakness, and that sincere return to Allah is met with His forgiveness and compassion, which in turn reflects the depth of divine mercy toward those who persevere in faith alongside the Messenger.

translation: And [He also turned in forgiveness toward] the three who were left behind, until when the earth became confining for them despite its vastness, and their souls confined them, and they thought that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him. Then He turned to them [in forgiveness] that they might repent. Indeed, Allah is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.
interpretation: The verse shows that divine forgiveness reaches those who were held back and isolated for their failings, and that Allah's turning to His servants comes first as a mercy that enables them to return to Him in repentance. The tightening of the earth and of their own souls describes the anguish of sincere remorse, which drives a person to realize that the only true refuge is Allah alone. Their acceptance was not merely the lifting of a punishment but a restoration that made their repentance itself possible, teaching that genuine turning back to God is ultimately sustained by His prior mercy.

translation: O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with those who are true (in word and deed).
interpretation: The verse calls the believers to two linked duties: taqwa, a conscious God-consciousness that guards one against disobedience, and companionship with the truthful. Taqwa is the inner source from which sincerity flows, and the command to be 'with' the truthful points to the need for believers to bind themselves to people of integrity, so that their faith is reinforced through example and fellowship. Truthfulness here is not only speech but the alignment of intention, word, and action, so that one who is true to God becomes a living witness whose sincerity others can rely upon and emulate.

translation: It was not fitting for the people of Medina and the Bedouins around them to stay behind from the Messenger of God, nor to prefer their own selves over his self. That is because no thirst, fatigue, or hunger afflicts them in the way of God, and they do not tread any path that enrages the disbelievers, nor gain anything from an enemy except that a righteous deed is recorded for them thereby. Indeed, God does not waste the reward of the good-doers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that every hardship borne in the cause of God, even the involuntary bodily suffering of thirst, weariness, and hunger, becomes a recorded act of worship, so that the believer's exertion is never lost. The reason given for this is not merely the suffering itself but the sincerity and the loyalty to the Messenger that moves a person to share his hardships, which is why the verse ends by tying the reward to being a muhsin, one who performs deeds with excellence. Thus the value of striving is measured by the intention and the excellence behind it, not by the outward result.

translation: And they do not spend an expenditure, small or large, nor do they cross a valley, except that it is recorded for them, so that Allah may reward them with the best of what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse shows that Allah's accounting of a believer's striving is exact and generous: even the smallest charity and the most modest physical effort on the path of good, such as a short journey or crossing a valley for a righteous cause, is recorded. The reward is measured not by the size of the deed but by its sincerity, and Allah repays the believer with the best of their actions. This should free the believer from thinking small deeds are worthless and encourage steady, sincere effort in the cause of faith, knowing that nothing done for Allah is lost.

translation: It was not for the believers to go forth all together. So why should there not go forth from every division of them a group, that they may gain understanding in the religion and warn their people when they return to them, that they may be cautious.
interpretation: The verse establishes a principle of division of labor within the Muslim community: not every believer must leave home for jihad or the frontier at once, lest society be left unattended. Instead, a portion from each group goes forth to acquire deep knowledge of the religion (tafaqquh), and then returns to instruct their people. Thus learning and the transmission of religious knowledge are presented as a communal obligation carried out by a qualified segment, and the purpose of that learning is not merely personal but the moral awakening of the community, so that they may be mindful of God and guard themselves against what displeases Him.

translation: O you who have believed, fight those adjacent to you of the disbelievers, and let them find in you harshness. And know that Allah is with the righteous.
interpretation: The verse directs believers to confront first the disbelievers nearest to them, not as an invitation to indiscriminate hostility but as a call to firmness and steadfastness in defending the community against those who threaten it. The phrase "let them find in you harshness" points to resolve and strength of character that the enemy should perceive, rather than weakness that invites aggression. The closing reminder that Allah is with the righteous anchors this resolve in piety: the strength demanded is to be exercised within the bounds of taqwa, so that courage never becomes injustice, and the believer's confidence rests not in numbers or force but in God's support for those who fear and obey Him.

translation: And whenever a surah is revealed, among them are those who say, "Which of you has had his faith increased by this?" As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice.
interpretation: The verse discloses two responses to revelation that reveal the state of the heart. The hypocrites, whose hearts are sick, mock or question the benefit of the revelation, unable to perceive any gain in it, because revelation only adds to those who already have a receptive heart. For the believers, each new revelation is an increase in faith: every command, promise and warning deepens their certainty and conviction, and this growth brings them joy. Thus the same message that increases the faith of the sincere is, for the diseased heart, only a further cause of doubt and aversion, so that the reception of guidance depends on the inner disposition of the one who hears it.

translation: As for those in whose hearts is a disease, it adds to their filth upon their filth, and they die while they are disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse describes a spiritual law: a heart already afflicted with doubt, hypocrisy, or moral sickness does not receive revelation as a cure but as an increase in its impurity. Each new verse that calls for truth exposes and deepens what the person has already chosen to harbor, so that their rejection becomes a layer added upon an earlier layer of corruption, until they die in unbelief. The text thus teaches that guidance and misguidance are both results of a person's own inner orientation, and that persistent refusal of truth hardens the heart rather than leaving it neutral.

translation: Do they not see that they are tested every year once or twice, and yet they do not repent, nor do they take heed?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who persist in heedlessness despite recurring trials. Their repeated afflictions, which come year after year, are meant as a reminder and a call to return to God in repentance, yet they neither turn back to Him nor reflect on the lesson these trials convey. The verse thus points to the danger of becoming desensitized to divine warnings, where hardship that should awaken the heart instead passes without change, and it urges the reader to learn from recurring tests rather than remain stubbornly unmoved.

translation: And whenever a surah is sent down, some of them look at others (asking), "Does anyone see you?" Then they slip away. Allah has turned their hearts away, because they are a people who do not comprehend.
interpretation: The verse portrays the hypocrites' evasive conduct in the presence of revelation: rather than attending to the message with sincerity, they furtively glance at one another, seeking an excuse to withdraw unnoticed, as though their concern were self-protection rather than receiving guidance. Their reluctance reveals a heart already inclined away from truth, and the verse suggests that persistent turning away from guidance leads to a deeper spiritual blindness, so that God turns their hearts further from understanding. Their failure is therefore not merely one of lacking knowledge but of an inner disposition that refuses to grasp what is set before them.

translation: There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves; grievous to him is what you suffer; he is anxious over you and, toward the believers, kind and merciful.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes the profound closeness and compassion of the Prophet Muhammad toward the community. Being one of them, of their own lineage and kind, he feels their hardships deeply, is distressed by whatever harms them, and is eager for their guidance and welfare. This reveals that the Messenger's mission flows from genuine mercy, so the believers should recognize his sincere care for them, accept his guidance with trust, and not regard his admonitions as harshness. The gentleness shown to believers also shows that his mercy is especially directed to those who have embraced faith, while his concern for all people is reflected in his eagerness that they be guided.

translation: So if they turn away, say, "Sufficient for me is Allah; there is no deity except Him. In Him I have placed my trust, and He is the Lord of the Great Throne."
interpretation: The verse teaches that when a message is rejected and its bearer is met with turning away, the believer's refuge is not in the approval of people but in God alone. The phrase "Sufficient for me is Allah" expresses a complete reliance that frees the heart from fear of opposition and from dependence on worldly support. Reaffirming the oneness of God ("there is no deity except Him") grounds this reliance in the recognition that all power belongs to Him. Ending with His lordship over the Great Throne, the greatest of creation, places the believer's concerns within the vastness of God's sovereignty, so that the rejection of the unbelievers becomes small in comparison and the messenger is consoled that his duty is only to deliver the message while the outcome rests with God.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the wise Book.
interpretation: The opening letters Alif, Lam, Ra stand as a sign that this revelation is composed of the same letters from which human speech is made, yet its eloquence and wisdom are beyond human capacity, so the verse directs the reader to recognize the Book as a distinct and authoritative divine communication. The description "al-Kitab al-Hakim" (the wise Book) indicates that its verses are firmly arranged, free from confusion, and full of wisdom, calling the listener to reflect upon its message with certainty and to accept its guidance as coming from the All-Wise.

translation: Is it a wonder for the people that We revealed to a man from among them: "Warn the people, and give good news to those who have believed that they will have a sure standing with their Lord"? The disbelievers said, "Indeed, this is clearly a magician."
interpretation: The verse answers the disbelievers' astonishment at the sending of a human messenger by showing that revelation through a man of their own kind is no strange matter, since guidance has always come through human messengers who speak their people's language. Its twofold mission, warning the unbelievers and giving glad tidings to the believers of a secure station of truth and nearness with their Lord, shows that the messenger's role is both to confront falsehood and to console the faithful. The accusation of sorcery leveled at the message reveals that the rejection lies less in any doubt about the message's clarity than in an unwillingness to accept its demands, so the believers are reassured that the charge of magic is a familiar refuge of those who refuse the truth.

translation: Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days; then He established Himself above the Throne, arranging every affair. No intercessor [can intercede] except after His permission. That is Allah, your Lord, so worship Him. Will you not then be mindful?
interpretation: The verse roots the believer's worship in the absolute lordship of God: the One who created the cosmos in six days and rose above the Throne is the sole manager of all affairs, so intercession is possible only by His leave, and therefore devotion must be directed to Him alone. The call to remembrance (tadhakkur) points to the rational consequence of this recognition: a mind that reflects on creation and divine governance cannot consistently give worship to any other power, since every intermediary's standing derives entirely from the Creator's permission.

translation: To Him you will all return. The promise of Allah is true. Indeed, He originates creation and then repeats it, so that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice. But those who disbelieved will have a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because of their disbelief.
interpretation: The verse grounds the certainty of resurrection in the argument from creation: the One who began the creation from nothing is fully capable of bringing it back again, so the return to Him is not a distant or doubtful matter but a divine promise that must be fulfilled. The emphasis on justice (bil-qist) shows that the final reckoning is not arbitrary; believers are rewarded in measure with their faith and good works, while disbelievers receive the consequence of their denial. The verse thus ties together God's power over origination and return, the truth of His promise, and the moral accountability that gives human action its ultimate meaning.

translation: It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light, and determined for it phases, that you may know the number of years and the reckoning. Allah did not create that except in truth. He details the signs for a people who know.
interpretation: The verse directs the reader from the observed order of the heavens to the purposeful design behind it. The distinction between the sun's brilliant radiance (diya') and the moon's reflected light (nur) reflects the different nature of the two luminaries, and the moon's fixed phases (manazil) become a practical measure of time, enabling people to count years and organize their affairs. Its closing words insist that this cosmic order is not random or idle but created with truth and wisdom, and that its signs are clearly set out for those who reflect and possess knowledge, thereby linking natural observation to faith and understanding.

translation: Indeed, in the alternation of the night and the day, and in what God has created in the heavens and the earth, there are signs for a people who are mindful of God.
interpretation: The verse directs the reader from the observable regularity of night giving way to day, and the vast order of the heavens and the earth, toward the recognition that these phenomena are signs (ayat) pointing beyond themselves to the wisdom and power of their Creator. Yet the verse specifies that these signs are fully legible only to those who are God-conscious (muttaqun): the capacity to perceive the sign depends on an inner disposition of taqwa, a watchful awareness of God that makes the cosmos speak as revelation rather than as mere mechanism. Thus natural phenomena and scripture are placed side by side as two books of guidance, and the moral condition of the observer is shown to be as necessary to understanding as the evidence itself.

translation: Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us and are content with the worldly life and feel secure in it, and those who are heedless of Our signs.
interpretation: The verse describes a condition of the heart in which a person's entire horizon is confined to this world: because they have ceased to hope for the encounter with God, they take comfort in the present life and find rest in its pleasures, so their attention is closed to the signs that point beyond it. The root of the fault is not merely disbelief in the afterlife but a settled contentment with the transient, which in turn produces heedlessness toward the divine signs in creation and revelation. The passage thus diagnoses how love of the fleeting world and forgetfulness of God reinforce one another, and it warns that such complacency is itself a form of spiritual loss.

translation: Those, their abode is the Fire, because of what they used to earn.
interpretation: The verse closes a passage about those who persist in wrongdoing and deceit by stating the consequence plainly: their final residence is the Fire, and the cause is attributed to their own acquisitions, that is, the deeds, wealth, and moral choices they habitually pursued. The phrase 'what they used to earn' (ma kanu yaksibun) frames sin as a kind of earning, a gain that returns to the earner as a reckoning. It teaches that punishment is not arbitrary but the outcome of one's chosen conduct, and it invites the listener to examine what they are accumulating in their own life.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, their Lord will guide them because of their faith; rivers will flow beneath them in the Gardens of Bliss.
interpretation: The verse links guidance to faith itself: God does not merely reward good deeds but guides the believer's heart and path through the faith that animates those deeds. Faith is thus the inner source from which guidance flows outward, and the rivers and Gardens of Bliss are the visible image of that inner light's fulfillment in the hereafter, showing that the reward is a continuation of the guidance received in this life.

translation: Their call therein will be, "Glory be to You, O Allah," and their greeting therein will be, "Peace." And the last of their call will be, "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: This verse, which closes the description of the people of Paradise in Surah Yunus (10:10), shows that the inhabitants of Paradise will be occupied with glorifying and praising God and in mutual peace. Their worship, which began in this world as the praise of God, becomes their constant and joyful occupation in the Hereafter. Their greeting is peace, reflecting the security and tranquility of that abode, where no harm, enmity or fear exists. The verse thus presents Paradise as the fulfillment of the believer's relationship with God: a state of perpetual remembrance, gratitude, and harmony, in which the praise of the Lord of all worlds is both the beginning and the end of their speech.

translation: And if God were to hasten evil upon people as they hasten for good, their term would surely have been decreed for them. So We leave those who do not expect to meet Us wandering blindly in their rebellion.
interpretation: The verse exposes the reversal in human nature: people ask for good quickly, yet if God answered their demands for harm with the same haste, they would be destroyed before they could repent. God's delay in punishing is therefore a mercy, giving room for reflection. Those who deny the meeting with God are left to their own insolence, and their wandering is a consequence of their chosen heedlessness rather than mere abandonment, a warning that persistent defiance turns into self-made blindness.

translation: And when harm touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side or sitting or standing; but when We remove his harm from him, he passes on as though he had never called upon Us to remove a harm that touched him. Thus has been made attractive to the transgressors what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse exposes a recurring human pattern: in distress, a person turns sincerely and urgently to God in every posture, yet once relief arrives he forgets that prayer and returns to heedlessness, as if his supplication had never been made. The image of calling 'on his side, sitting, or standing' conveys that no state of body or circumstance excuses neglect of God, since need is constant. The closing phrase, that their own deeds were made attractive to the transgressors, shows that the true root of this ingratitude is self-deception: wrongdoing is adorned in their eyes, so they mistake their forgetfulness for normalcy. The verse thus invites the believer to examine whether his devotion is tied only to hardship, and to cultivate gratitude and remembrance during ease as well.

translation: And We had already destroyed generations before you when they wronged; their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they were not going to believe. Thus do We recompense the criminal people.
interpretation: The verse establishes a pattern of divine justice that recurs throughout history: nations are destroyed not arbitrarily but because of their persistent wrongdoing, after clear signs have been conveyed to them. The phrase 'they were not going to believe' points to a settled stubbornness, where the rejection of truth is not merely a failure of evidence but a deliberate closing of the heart against it, so that the proofs themselves become the occasion of their ruin. The words 'thus do We recompense' present the fate of past peoples as a standing law that applies equally to the audience being addressed, warning them that the same consequences follow from the same conduct, and that the criminal, those who transgress against themselves and others, will be met with a requital that is fitting to their own choices.

translation: Then We made you successors in the land after them, so that We might see how you would act.
interpretation: The verse presents human beings as a deliberate divine appointment: having given earlier generations their turn on earth, God establishes the present generation as successors (khalā'if) in their place. This succession is not a privilege held without consequence but a trust that places responsibility on each generation to build, govern, and do justice in the land. The phrase 'so that We might see how you would act' expresses God's testing of humankind, meaning that the purpose of worldly authority is to reveal, and to hold accountable, the moral choices made by those who inherit it. Each generation thus learns from the fate of those who came before it, recognizing that power and prosperity are temporary and that what endures is the record of its conduct. The verse therefore calls believers to reflect that their place on earth is a test of righteousness rather than a possession to be used for corruption or heedlessness.

translation: When Our clear verses are recited to them, those who do not expect to meet Us say, "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it." Say, "It is not for me to change it on my own accord. I follow only what is revealed to me. Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great day."
interpretation: The verse exposes the root of rejection in the heart of those who do not hope for the meeting with God: their denial of the Hereafter makes them unwilling to accept a revelation that holds them accountable, so they seek a more agreeable scripture or a modified one. The Prophet is commanded to disclaim any authority over the revelation, affirming that he is only a faithful transmitter who follows what is revealed, not its author who can alter its content to suit people's desires. The closing statement shows that even the Messenger himself stands in awe before his Lord, fearing the consequences of disobedience, which makes clear that fidelity to divine revelation is the foundation of true prophethood and that the standard of truth is God's word rather than human preference.

translation: Say, "If God had willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made it known to you. I had already lived among you a lifetime before it. Will you not then reason?"
interpretation: The verse presents the Prophet's own life as proof of the authenticity of the revelation. Muhammad had spent forty years among his people known for his truthfulness and had never recited poetry, composed scripture, or displayed any sign of such knowledge before the revelation came. The sudden appearance of this Book after a lifetime of silence on such matters is thus an argument that it was not his own invention but a gift granted by God's will. The closing rebuke, 'Will you not then reason?', calls the hearers to use their intellect to recognize this plain evidence, showing that faith in revelation is meant to be grounded in reasoned reflection on the verifiable character and history of the messenger.

translation: So who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or denies His signs? Indeed, the criminals will not succeed.
interpretation: The verse establishes the gravest form of wrongdoing as fabricating falsehood against God, attributing to Him what He has not said or commanded, and rejecting His revealed signs. Such a person has placed themselves in direct opposition to the truth, and the verse closes by declaring that those who persist in this criminality will not prosper, meaning they will fail in attaining true success in this life and the next. The lesson is that the integrity of one's relationship with God rests on truthfulness about Him and humble acceptance of His guidance.

translation: They worship, besides Allah, that which can neither harm them nor benefit them, and they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah." Say, "Do you inform Allah of something He does not know in the heavens or on the earth?" Exalted is He above what they associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse exposes the emptiness of idolatry at its root: those who take intercessors besides Allah attribute to them a standing with God that no revelation or knowledge supports. By asking whether they would inform Allah of a partner He does not know of, the verse turns the claim against itself, since a real partner or intercessor would have to be known to the All-Knowing, and its absence from all of creation proves the claim false. The closing glorification of Allah above what they associate with Him shows that shirk is not merely mistaken worship but a misrepresentation of the divine nature, which is why the verse reasons from God's perfect knowledge rather than from mere assertion.

translation: And mankind was not but one community, so they differed. And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been decided between them concerning that in which they differ.
interpretation: The verse portrays humanity as originally united in one community of guidance or belief, with division arising afterward through human choice and disagreement. It points to a divine decree, a prior word of postponement, which allows human differences to persist until a final judgment settles them. Read this way, the verse explains why diversity of belief is tolerated in this life: the matter of dispute is deferred to God rather than being resolved immediately, which places responsibility on people to seek truth and calls believers to patience rather than to imposing uniformity on others.

translation: They say, "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?" So say, "The unseen belongs only to Allah, so wait; indeed, I am with you among those who wait."
interpretation: The verse reveals the disbelievers' habit of demanding a miraculous sign on their own terms, as though the truth of the message depended on their choosing the proof. The Prophet is commanded to answer that knowledge of the unseen, including when and how a sign will come, belongs to God alone, and that the decision about what to send rests with Him rather than with the one who asks. The closing words turn the matter into a shared waiting: the Prophet declares that he too awaits God's judgment and its outcome, so that the unbelievers' challenge becomes a call to patience and reflection on the clear signs already present, rather than an occasion for further demands.

translation: And when We let people taste mercy after adversity has touched them, behold, they scheme against Our signs. Say: "Allah is swifter in planning." Indeed, Our messengers record what you plot.
interpretation: The verse exposes a recurring human pattern: when hardship lifts and mercy is granted, people who ought to be grateful instead turn to deception, mocking or subverting the signs that point to God. The phrase "behold, they scheme" shows that the ingratitude is not a neutral forgetting but an active contriving against the truth. The reply, "Allah is swifter in planning," reframes their cunning: whatever stratagem they devise is already known to God, who acts with a speed and subtlety beyond their reach, so their schemes cannot ultimately succeed. The closing statement that Our messengers record what they plot serves as a warning and a comfort at once. It reminds the believer that nothing done in secret escapes divine accounting, and it encourages steadfastness in the face of opposition, since the record of every deceit is kept and will be disclosed on the Day of Reckoning.

translation: It is He who enables you to travel on land and sea. Until, when you are in ships and they sail with them by a good wind and they rejoice in it, there comes upon them a violent wind and the waves come at them from every place, and they think they are encompassed by it, they call upon God, sincere to Him in religion, saying: "If You deliver us from this, we will surely be among the grateful."
interpretation: The verse portrays the human being's instinctive turn to God in extremity: when the comforts of worldly means, such as a favorable wind and the safety of a ship, make a person feel self-sufficient and secure, a sudden reversal exposes how fragile those means are and how total one's dependence on the Creator is. In that moment of helplessness, people abandon their associates and false reliances and direct their devotion purely to God, yet the verse also reveals the fickleness of the heart, since its sincerity is tied to the escape from danger and its vow of gratitude is conditional on rescue, inviting the reader to cultivate a steady gratitude and sincerity that do not depend on hardship.

translation: But when He had delivered them, behold, they committed outrage on earth without right. O mankind, your outrage is only against yourselves—the enjoyment of the worldly life. Then to Us is your return, and We will inform you of what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse exposes the pattern of human moral failure: people who are rescued from distress often return at once to transgression, as if the deliverance had been forgotten. The verse observes that such wrongdoing ultimately rebounds on the wrongdoers themselves, since the injustice they inflict on others and on the earth corrodes their own souls, and the pleasures they pursue in this fleeting life are a brief enjoyment that cannot shield them. It thus turns the believer's attention from the temporary gains of oppression toward the certainty of the return to God, where every deed will be disclosed and weighed.

translation: Indeed, the example of the worldly life is like water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it, from which people and livestock eat, until when the earth takes on its adornment and becomes beautified, and its people think they have power over it, Our command comes to it by night or by day, and We make it into harvested stubble, as if it had not flourished the day before. Thus do We detail the signs for a people who give thought.
interpretation: The verse presents the fleeting nature of worldly life through a vivid image of rain bringing the earth to lush growth, only for it to be suddenly reduced to dry, cut stalks by a divine decree that can strike at any moment. Its lesson is that the splendor and apparent mastery people hold over their possessions and lands is borrowed and temporary, so one should not be deceived by it into forgetting the Hereafter, which is the enduring abode, and should instead reflect on how sudden the change of fortune can be.

translation: And Allah invites to the Abode of Peace, and guides whom He wills to a straight path.
interpretation: The verse presents divine guidance as an open invitation, the call of Allah to the Abode of Peace (Dar al-Salam), which is the realm of security, tranquility, and harmony with the Creator. Yet the verse pairs this universal call with the reality of divine will: the invitation is extended broadly, but the actual guidance into the straight path is granted to those whom Allah wills. This reflects a balance between human responsibility to respond to the call, through sincerity, openness, and seeking the truth, and the sovereignty of God in granting success. The reader is thus reminded that while the path is made clear and the summons is sincerely given, a heart's receptivity and its arrival at the straight path ultimately depend on Allah's mercy and guidance.

translation: For those who did good is the best reward and more. Neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces. Those are the companions of Paradise; therein they will abide forever.
interpretation: The verse sets the reward of the righteous above any mere measure of recompense: 'the best' (al-husna) is the reward promised for good deeds, and the addition 'and more' (ziyadah), which the tradition commonly understands as the beholding of God's face, points to a gift that exceeds what deeds could earn by justice alone. The contrast is drawn sharply: where the faces of the wrongdoers are darkened by dust and clouded by shame, the faces of the doers of good remain radiant and unburdened, so that the outward appearance on the Day of Reckoning becomes a sign of the inner state achieved in this life. Honor and the absence of humiliation are thus presented as the true completion of the good deed, and Paradise is named not merely as a place but as the enduring home of those whose righteousness has been recognized.

translation: And those who earned evil deeds - the recompense of an evil deed is its equivalent, and humiliation will cover them. They will have no protector from Allah. It is as if their faces were covered with pieces of the darkest night. Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: The verse presents a precise principle of divine justice: the requital for an evil deed is measured exactly by that deed, with no excess, so the punishment matches the wrong. Yet the verse also shows that the true harm of sin is not only the external penalty but the inner disgrace of humiliation that settles upon the sinner, which no worldly power or intercessor can lift, because protection from Allah cannot be bought or borrowed. The image of faces shrouded in dark fragments of night conveys how sin darkens the soul and its visible radiance, so that the wrongdoer carries the marks of his choices on his very countenance. The closing description of eternal dwelling in the Fire reminds the reader that the consequences of persistent wrongdoing reach beyond this life, urging the believer toward repentance before the ledger is closed.

translation: And [mention] the Day We will gather them all, then We will say to those who associated others with Allah, "Stay in your places, you and your partners." Then We will separate them, and their partners will say, "You did not used to worship us."
interpretation: The verse depicts the scene of the Day of Resurrection in which all people are brought together for judgment, and the polytheists are commanded to remain in their place alongside the false deities they had taken as partners with God. The separation that follows reveals the collapse of their false alliances: the idols and those they venerated are split from their worshippers, and the partners themselves disclaim any worship directed at them. This exposes the emptiness of the worship that was offered to beings that could neither hear, benefit, nor respond, and it underscores that on that Day no intercession or companionship in falsehood will avail the one who associated others with God.

translation: Sufficient is Allah as a witness between us and you; indeed, we were unaware of your worship.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by the believers, or by the messengers, to those who worshipped other than Allah. Having been rejected and having had their call dismissed, they appeal to Allah alone as the sole witness who is fully aware of the truth of their message and of the deeds of both sides. Their statement that they were unaware of the worship directed at them by the idolaters is an assertion that they never approved of it or was part of it, and that they were not responsible for it. The verse thus teaches that a sincere servant of Allah takes Him as sufficient judge and witness, relying on Him alone when the people turn away, and it warns that every act of worship offered to other than Allah will be disowned on the Day of Reckoning.

translation: There, every soul will be tested by what it sent forth before, and they will be returned to God, their true Lord, and what they used to fabricate will have vanished from them.
interpretation: The verse places the reckoning in a moment of truth where the deeds a soul sent ahead are laid bare, so that the illusions of self-deception and invented claims about God collapse. Stripped of every false support, humanity is returned to its rightful Master, the Truth, and discovers that the idols, falsehoods and partners it had attributed to Him have abandoned it, revealing that only genuine faith and righteous action endure before Him.

translation: Say, "Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? Or who owns hearing and sight? And who brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living? And who governs all affairs?" They will say, "Allah." So say, "Will you not then fear Him?"
interpretation: The verse confronts the idolaters with their own acknowledgment of God's sole lordship: they admit that provision, the faculties of hearing and sight, the cycle of life and death, and the governance of all affairs belong to Allah alone. Having conceded these premises, their refusal to worship Him exposes an inconsistency, so the closing question calls their conscience to reverent awareness (taqwa) and to the fear of incurring His displeasure by associating others with Him. Reflection on the signs of creation in one's own senses and in the rhythm of birth and death is thus meant to awaken the heart to fear and devotion.

translation: So that is Allah, your true Lord. So what is there after the truth except error? Then how are you turned away?
interpretation: The verse establishes a stark binary: once the truth of Allah's lordship is known, every alternative is error, leaving no neutral middle ground. The rhetorical question 'how are you turned away?' rebukes those who, despite clear evidence, turn from monotheism toward idols and falsehood, portraying their aversion not as a lack of proof but as a perverse deflection of the human mind and heart from what is plainly right. It invites the listener to reflect that to reject the Creator and Sustainer is to step out of truth into misguidance, and to ask honestly what drives such turning away.

translation: Thus has the word of your Lord been justified against those who defied (Him): that they will not believe.
interpretation: The verse presents the decree of God as an inevitable reality that follows from persistent rebellion. Those who have deliberately transgressed the bounds of truth and persisted in corruption have, through their own choices, closed their hearts to guidance, so that the divine word concerning their unbelief is fulfilled. This is not arbitrary injustice but the outcome of a moral trajectory: continued defiance hardens the heart until faith is no longer within its reach. The verse thus conveys both a warning against persisting in fisq and a reminder that God's decree operates according to the consequences of human conduct.

translation: Say, "Is there any of your partners who originates creation and then repeats it?" Say, "Allah originates creation and then repeats it, so how are you deluded away from the truth?"
interpretation: The verse confronts the idolaters with a simple test of reason: if their associated deities cannot begin creation, nor restore it after its end, then they have no claim to divinity. Since the answer can only be that Allah alone originates and resurrects creation, the verse exposes the absurdity of turning away from Him toward partners who possess no such power. The question "how are you deluded?" points to the fact that their turning away is not the product of sound judgment but of a perverse diversion of the mind and heart from what is plainly evident in creation itself, and it invites them to recognize the evidence of the origin and return of all things as proof of the Creator's exclusive lordship.

translation: Say, "Is there any of your 'partners' who guides to the truth?" Say, "It is Allah who guides to the truth. So is one who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or one who does not find guidance unless he is guided? What is wrong with you? How do you judge?"
interpretation: The verse confronts the polytheists with a rational test: if their associated deities cannot guide anyone to truth, then worship must belong to the One who does, namely Allah, since guidance is the basis for being rightly followed. Its reasoning shows that a being which itself lacks guidance and needs to be guided has no claim to divinity, so the disorder lies not in the evidence but in the people's unjust and illogical judgment, which the verse exposes through the question "How do you judge?"

translation: And most of them follow nothing but assumption. Indeed, assumption avails nothing against the truth. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do.
interpretation: The verse exposes the root of misguidance among the majority of people: they do not follow certain knowledge or revealed guidance but rely on conjecture, inherited habit, and unverified opinion. Such reliance is worthless in matters of belief, because it cannot reach or stand in the place of the truth, which must be sought through evidence and revelation. The closing reminder that Allah knows what they do warns that human conduct built on baseless assumption is not hidden from the One who will hold everyone accountable, so the believer is called to test his beliefs against knowledge rather than follow the majority or his own guesses.

translation: And it was not [possible] for this Qur'an to be fabricated apart from Allah, but it is a confirmation of what was before it and a detailed explanation of the Book, about which there is no doubt, from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse affirms the divine origin of the Qur'an by denying that any human could have produced it, since its character as a confirmation of the earlier revealed scriptures and its detailed clarification of the Book show it to be a revelation from the Lord of all creation. Its fulfilment of what came before and its exposition of the divine message together establish that its certainty is beyond any doubt, and that its source is Allah alone.

translation: Or do they say, "He has invented it." Say, "Then bring a surah like it, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you should be truthful."
interpretation: The verse confronts those who accuse the Prophet of fabricating the Qur'an with a direct challenge rather than a mere denial. By asking them to produce even one chapter of comparable eloquence, and to enlist every helper they can summon apart from God, it turns the accusation back on the accusers and exposes the claim as baseless. The inimitability of the Qur'an is thus presented as evidence of its divine origin: if human beings, with all their poets, orators, and idols, cannot match it, the charge of invention collapses under its own weight. The phrase "if you should be truthful" places the burden of proof squarely on the doubters, implying that their failure to meet the challenge is itself the answer to their doubt.

translation: Nay, they denied that which they did not encompass in knowledge, and its interpretation had not yet come to them. Likewise did those before them deny; so observe how was the end of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse exposes the root of disbelief as hasty rejection of what lies beyond one's grasp: people denied the message before understanding it or waiting for its fulfillment, the way a mind judges by what it already knows rather than by the evidence and its outcome. The denial is not a considered conclusion but a habit repeated across generations, which is why the verse points to the earlier nations. The call to observe the fate of the wrongdoers turns the reader from the heedless denial of the past toward reflection on where such rejection leads, so that the promised reality, once it arrives, becomes the proof that the unbelievers lacked the knowledge to dismiss.

translation: And among them are those who believe in it, and among them are those who do not believe in it. And your Lord is most knowing of the corruptors.
interpretation: The verse shows that people's response to divine revelation is varied: some open their hearts to it and some turn away, and this divergence is part of the testing built into human freedom of choice. The closing phrase reminds the Prophet, and every reader, that the final judgment on who is truly corrupt belongs to God alone, who knows the inner intentions and the lasting effects of each person's actions. It therefore calls the believer to patience and to leaving the outcome with God rather than to despair over those who reject the message or to claim knowledge of their hidden state.

translation: And if they deny you, say: "To me is my deed, and to you is your deed. You are free of what I do, and I am free of what you do."
interpretation: The verse sets out a clear principle of separation after the futility of persuading those who persist in denial: the Prophet is commanded to disengage from their rejection without hostility, leaving each party accountable for its own actions. It teaches that once the message has been delivered and rejected, the believer need not bear responsibility for the choices of others, and that moral accountability is individual, so each person will answer for his or her own deeds before God. The phrasing, with its reciprocal disavowal, conveys a firm but dignified boundary, rejecting both compulsion and further contention while keeping the door open to God's judgment that will ultimately distinguish the truthful from the deniers.

translation: And among them are those who listen to you. Can you make the deaf hear, even though they do not use their reason?
interpretation: The verse portrays those who sit before the Prophet and appear to listen, yet their hearing does not reach the heart, because they have closed themselves off from understanding. Guidance is not a matter of the messenger's ability but of the listener's openness; just as no one can make the deaf hear, the Prophet cannot force insight upon those who refuse to reflect. The verse thus consoles the messenger, reminding him that his duty is to convey the message, while the response depends on whether a person is willing to use their intellect and receptive heart.

translation: And among them are those who look at you, but can you guide the blind, even though they do not see?
interpretation: The verse portrays those who outwardly face the Prophet and seem to attend to him, yet their hearts and minds are closed to the truth. Their seeing is only physical; they lack the inner insight that would let them perceive the guidance he brings. Guidance is not something the messenger can impose on one whose faculty of perception has been deliberately sealed by his own refusal. The verse thus consoles the Prophet that his duty is to deliver the message, and that the responsibility for blindness of heart rests with those who choose not to see.

translation: Indeed, Allah does not wrong people at all, but it is the people who wrong themselves.
interpretation: The verse establishes that Allah's justice is absolute: wrongdoing originates in human choice, not in any injustice from God. Whatever harm people suffer through their own sins and misguided acts ultimately rebounds upon their own souls, since the moral consequences of disobedience fall on the one who commits it. It thus places personal responsibility at the center of human conduct, calling the believer to examine his own deeds rather than blame fate or the Creator, and it reassures that divine decree is never tyrannical, for Allah's mercy and fairness remain perfect even when humans fail themselves.

translation: And [mention] the Day He will gather them, [at which time it will seem] as if they had not remained [in the world] except for an hour of the day, recognizing one another among themselves. Those who denied the meeting with Allah have certainly lost, and they were not [rightly] guided.
interpretation: The verse portrays the shock of the Day of Resurrection: the long span of worldly life, which people felt was vast, will appear in retrospect as a brief hour, so that the brevity of the worldly life is revealed against the endlessness of the Hereafter. The mention of mutual recognition ('yatarafun') indicates that the bonds of acquaintance survive, and that people will know one another even as they stand in accountability, so that the deniers' shame is witnessed by those they knew. The closing declaration that those who denied the meeting with God are the losers, and were never truly guided, ties the vision of the gathering to the central sin of denying the encounter with the Divine, showing that the loss is not merely worldly but is the failure to have ever walked the path of guidance.

translation: Whether We show you part of what We promise them, or We take you in death, to Us is their return; then Allah is Witness over what they do.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, regarding the opponents who rejected his message.
