interpretation: The verse shows the Prophet Noah disclaiming the worldly and supernatural markers that his opponents expected of a messenger, namely divine treasures, knowledge of the unseen, and angelic nature, so that his mission rests solely on the revelation he carries and not on any claim to superiority. He then rejects the judgment of the powerful elite who despised the poor believers, because judging a person's inner worth belongs to God alone. To pass such a verdict on others without knowledge would be an injustice, and Noah declares that he would be a wrongdoer if he did so. The lesson is that human worth is measured by faith and sincerity, which are hidden from observers, and that social status must not determine how believers are valued or treated.

translation: They said, "O Noah, you have already argued with us and multiplied your arguments with us, so bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful."
interpretation: The verse shows the typical response of a people who have run out of rational answers: rather than engaging with Noah's repeated reasoning, they retreat into demanding the fulfillment of his warnings as a test of his sincerity. Their words reveal a hardened heart that treats prophetic admonition as mere debate, reducing a matter of eternal consequence to a contest of wits. The verse thus illustrates how persistent disbelief tends to mock the messenger and dismiss warning until the reality it describes arrives, and it invites the reader to consider that the promise of God is not undone by the scorn of those who ask for it hastily.

translation: He said: "Only Allah will bring it to you if He wills, and you will not be able to escape (Him)."
interpretation: The verse places the ultimate power over all things in Allah's hands alone: whatever is promised or threatened comes to pass only by His will and timing, and no created being can frustrate or escape His decree. It reminds the listener that human arrogance, cleverness, or attempts to evade accountability are powerless before the divine will, so one should rely on Allah rather than on one's own capacities, and remain mindful that no one can place himself beyond God's reach.

translation: And my advice will not benefit you, even if I wish to advise you, if Allah intends to lead you astray. He is your Lord, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: This verse is spoken by Prophet Nuh (Noah) to his people, and it reveals a subtle point about the limits of human guidance. Noah's sincere counsel cannot profit those whom Allah has determined to leave in misguidance, because guidance and misguidance ultimately rest in the Divine will, not in the eloquence or zeal of the messenger. Yet the verse does not dissolve human responsibility: the prophet's care for them is shown as genuine ("if I wish to advise you"), and the people are still called to account. The closing words, "He is your Lord, and to Him you will be returned," turn the listeners' attention from their rejection of the message to the ultimate reality of their dependence on God and their certain return to Him, where every heart's choice will be disclosed and judged. The verse thus combines a sober reminder of divine sovereignty over guidance with a call to reflect on one's own accountability before the Lord to whom all return.

translation: Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say, "If I had invented it, then upon me is my crime, and I am innocent of what you commit."
interpretation: The verse confronts the disbelievers' accusation that the Prophet Muhammad fabricated the Qur'an, and it answers with a principle of personal moral accountability. If the Prophet had invented the revelation, the consequence would fall solely on him, as the sin of forgery is his own burden. The phrase "I am innocent of what you commit" then turns the matter back on the accusers: the Prophet disowns their crimes, which may include denying the truth, slandering him, and persisting in disbelief. The verse thus presents a dual argument. It warns against fabricating speech about God, since such a crime bears its own consequence, and it shows that the messenger is answerable only for his own conduct, while each party bears responsibility for its own deeds.

translation: And it was revealed to Noah: "No one of your people will believe except those who have already believed, so do not grieve over what they have been doing."
interpretation: This verse presents Noah's situation as a model of consolation for the Prophet Muhammad. Divine revelation informs Noah that faith will not spread beyond those already committed to it, so the persistent rejection of his people is not a failure in his mission but a settled outcome of their own choices. The command not to grieve (fa-la tabtais) teaches that a messenger's duty is to deliver the message faithfully, while guidance rests with God. Sorrow over the disbelief of others must not consume the preacher, because the responsibility for accepting or refusing the truth belongs to each person. The verse thus combines comfort for the one who calls to faith with a reminder of the limits of human responsibility.

translation: And construct the ark under Our eyes and by Our revelation, and do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed, they are to be drowned.
interpretation: The verse presents Noah being commanded to build the ark under divine supervision and guidance, emphasizing that his work is carried out with Allah's watchful care and direct inspiration. The prohibition against pleading on behalf of the wrongdoers shows that the decree against them is settled and final, and that prophetic intercession cannot override divine justice when persistent wrongdoing has sealed a people's fate. It teaches that the righteous must submit to God's judgment and that kinship or closeness to a prophet does not spare those who persist in injustice, a lesson underscored by the subsequent account of Noah's son.

translation: And he was constructing the ark, and whenever chiefs of his people passed by him, they mocked him. He said, "If you mock us, then we will mock you just as you mock."
interpretation: The verse portrays Noah's steadfast perseverance in obeying God's command amid ridicule. The mockery of the eminent men of his people reveals their arrogance and their complacency toward the coming divine judgment, since they regarded a prophet building a vessel on dry land as absurd. Noah's reply is not a childish retort but a calm warning: their derision will turn back upon them, for their scorn is a sign of their heedlessness, and the reversal of mockery foreshadows the consequences they will face. It teaches that the believer who acts upon divine guidance need not be shaken by the scorn of the powerful, and that those who deride the truth are, in the end, the ones exposed to ridicule by their own fate.

translation: So you will come to know who it is that will receive a punishment that disgraces him, and upon whom will descend a lasting torment.
interpretation: The verse is a warning delivered with the certainty of future knowledge: the disbelievers who mock the message will eventually see for themselves who bears the true consequence. Their punishment is twofold, first a disgrace (yukhzihi) that strips them of honor and exposes the falsity of their pride in this world, and then an enduring torment (adhab muqim) that does not pass away. The phrasing leaves the matter open to the listener's own reckoning, emphasizing that the outcome will be made plain to all, and it places the weight of the threat on the contrast between the fleeting status the wrongdoers now enjoy and the lasting humiliation awaiting them.

translation: Until when Our command came and the oven gushed forth, We said: "Load into it two of each pair, and your family, except those against whom the word has already preceded, and those who believe." And none believed with him except a few.
interpretation: The verse depicts the moment of divine decree in the story of Noah: the sign of the coming punishment is the bubbling of the oven, a vivid image of the earth's waters erupting, and it marks the point beyond which no further delay is possible. The command to embark carries a double lesson. Salvation is granted to the pairs of creatures, which preserves the continuity of life, and to the household of faith, yet the verse explicitly excludes those whose fate was already sealed by previous divine judgment, showing that kinship alone does not save and that the decisive bond is belief and obedience. The closing remark that only a few believed with Noah, despite his long call, highlights the rarity of faithful response, a theme that turns the narrative into a warning that truth is often followed by a minority and that God's justice is exact in separating the saved from the condemned.

translation: And he said, "Embark upon it; in the name of God is its course and its anchorage. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful."
interpretation: The verse captures the moment of faith and trust at the threshold of salvation: Noah's call to board the ark is framed not as a leap into the unknown but as an act sanctified by the remembrance of God. By invoking the divine name over the vessel's departure and its eventual landing, the believers place their fragile means of survival entirely within God's hands, transforming a wooden ship on a flood into a vessel of mercy. The closing attributes of forgiveness and mercy reveal that the same Lord who brings judgment also opens a path of deliverance for those who turn to Him, so that the ark becomes a symbol of divine compassion amid universal destruction.

translation: And it sailed with them through waves like mountains, and Noah called out to his son, who was apart from them: "O my son, board with us and do not be with the disbelievers."
interpretation: The verse portrays the moment of the flood's fury, when the ark carries Noah and the believers through towering waves, and a father's compassion breaks through the crisis as he calls to his estranged son standing aside. The son's isolation from the ark is a picture of how distance from the community of faith, chosen by the heart's refusal, leaves a person exposed to the very waters meant to be escaped. Noah's plea shows that the bond of kinship does not replace the bond of belief: salvation is sought through joining the believers and rejecting disbelief, not through lineage alone.

translation: He said, "I will take refuge in a mountain that will protect me from the water." Noah said, "There is no protector today from the command of Allah, except for the one on whom He has mercy." And the waves came between them, so he was among the drowned.
interpretation: The verse portrays the moment of the flood's climax, where a son's stubborn reliance on worldly means of safety collapses before the absolute decree of God. His belief that a mountain could shield him reflects a misplaced trust in material causes and self-reliance, while the father's reply points to the truth that deliverance from divine judgment belongs to God alone and comes through His mercy, which is granted through faith and obedience rather than kinship or assumed status. The sudden separation by the waves signifies how decisively worldly ties and illusions are severed when the command of God takes effect, teaching that the only true refuge in the face of divine reckoning is God's mercy, sought through sincere submission to Him.

translation: And it was said: "O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold your rain." And the water subsided, and the matter was decided, and the ark came to rest on al-Judi. And it was said: "Away with the wrongdoing people!"
interpretation: The verse portrays the end of the Flood as a sovereign command addressed to the elements themselves, showing that all of creation is subject to God's will and responds immediately to it. The earth's swallowing of the water and the sky's ceasing of rain mark a return to order after cosmic disorder, and the resting of the ark on al-Judi signals the completion of the divine decree and the start of a new phase for Noah and the believers. The closing curse, "Away with the wrongdoing people," reveals that the catastrophe was not arbitrary but the just consequence of persistent injustice, so that the deliverance of the righteous and the destruction of the wrongdoers are presented together as the fulfillment of divine justice.

translation: And Noah called out to his Lord and said, "My Lord, indeed my son is of my family, and indeed Your promise is true, and You are the most just of judges."
interpretation: The verse captures Noah's appeal to God at the moment of his son's drowning, when he invokes the bond of family and God's previous promise of salvation for his household. Noah's plea rests on the truth of God's promise and on God's perfect justice, yet it reveals a human impulse of paternal affection that is then corrected by God's reply that his son was not of his family in the sense that matters, because his conduct was not righteous. The passage thus teaches that kinship alone does not secure salvation, that faith and action define one's true belonging, and that even prophets must submit their pleas to God's wisdom.

translation: He said, "O Noah, indeed he is not of your family; indeed, he is one whose conduct is other than righteous. So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge. I advise you lest you be among the ignorant."
interpretation: The verse teaches that kinship alone does not secure salvation; what decides a person's standing with God is righteous action, not blood ties to a prophet. When Noah pleaded for his son, God corrected him gently, showing that even a prophet must not press God for what lies beyond his knowledge or what is not his to decide. It is a lesson in humility before divine wisdom, and in the principle that faith must be accompanied by sound conduct, since the bond of prophethood cannot override the moral choices of an individual.

translation: He said, "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge. And unless You forgive me and have mercy upon me, I will be among the losers."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Prophet Noah (peace be upon him) after his son was drowned, shows that a believer must guard the tongue and heart against requests that rest on no sound knowledge, especially in matters of divine decree. It teaches humility before God's wisdom: even a prophet, upon realizing he had asked for something beyond his understanding, immediately sought refuge in God and turned to His forgiveness and mercy. The verse also reveals that true loss lies not in worldly misfortune but in being deprived of God's forgiveness and mercy, so that every person's ultimate hope rests in God's grace rather than in their own claims or merits.

translation: It was said: O Noah, descend in peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon nations from those with you. But there will be nations whom We will grant enjoyment, then a painful punishment from Us will touch them.
interpretation: The verse describes the conclusion of the Flood: after the waters subside, Noah is commanded to descend with divine peace and blessings, a promise of security and continuity for him and the righteous community that believed with him. The phrase 'nations from those with you' indicates that the lineages descending from the believers will multiply, while the mention of nations who are granted temporary enjoyment and then struck by painful punishment points to a universal divine principle: worldly provision given to those who persist in disbelief is a test and a delay, not a sign of acceptance, and it ends in accountability. The verse thus unites mercy toward the faithful with a sober warning that the Creator's justice ultimately reaches every people.

translation: These are among the tidings of the unseen which We reveal to you; you did not know them, neither you nor your people, before this. So be patient; indeed, the final outcome is for the righteous.
interpretation: The verse affirms the prophethood of Muhammad by pointing to the stories of Noah's people (in the surrounding passage, Surah Hud 11:49) as knowledge he could not have possessed through ordinary means, since neither he nor his community had known them before. Such revealed knowledge of the unseen is itself a sign of divine origin, and it becomes a source of consolation: the Prophet is commanded to bear the opposition of his people with steadfastness, because the ultimate triumph belongs to those who are conscious of God and act righteously, just as it did for the righteous in the earlier accounts. The verse thus links patience in the face of rejection with the certainty of God's promise to the God-fearing.

translation: And to ʿĀd (We sent) their brother Hūd. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. You are nothing but fabricators."
interpretation: The verse shows that every prophet is sent from among the people he addresses, which is why Hūd is called their "brother": he shares their lineage, language and social world, so his call carries the force of kinship and sincere concern. The core of his message is the same as that of all the messengers, tawḥīd, the exclusive worship of God, and it is framed as a rejection of the idols and false divinities the people had made. His closing charge, "you are nothing but fabricators," identifies their error not merely as a mistake of conduct but as a fabrication, a claim about the divine with no basis, so that the heart of the call is to replace invented authorities with the one true God and to recognize that worship must be directed to Him alone."}, 2)?>())}}}]}}?>()}?>?>}]]}]?>(

translation: O my people, I do not ask you for any wage for it. My reward is only from the One who originated me. Will you not then use your reason?
interpretation: This verse, spoken by a messenger calling his people to God, reveals the sincerity and disinterestedness of the prophetic mission: the messenger seeks nothing material from those he guides, so that his message cannot be suspected of being a means of worldly gain. His reward rests entirely with the Creator who brought him into being, which turns the listener's attention from the person of the messenger to the truth he carries. The closing question, 'Will you not then use your reason?', invites the people to examine the matter with their intellect, since a call that asks no payment and is free of personal interest is one that sound reason should accept and weigh carefully.

translation: And, O my people, seek forgiveness from your Lord and then turn to Him in repentance; He will send down the sky upon you in abundant rain and will increase you in strength upon your strength. So do not turn away as criminals.
interpretation: The verse presents a direct link between inner moral reform and outward material blessing: seeking forgiveness and turning back to God is not merely a private act of remorse but the condition under which divine bounty flows into a people's life. Rain, the foundation of agriculture and settled prosperity, stands here as a sign of God's generosity, and the increase of strength points to the renewal of a community's capacities, both physical and social. The warning at the end identifies the opposite path, turning away while persisting in wrongdoing, as a refusal that cuts a people off from these blessings. The message thus treats repentance as the true source of a society's renewal, where spiritual correction and worldly flourishing are shown to be inseparable.

translation: They said: "O Hud, you have brought us no clear proof, and we will not abandon our gods on your word, nor are we going to believe you."
interpretation: This verse shows the stubborn response of the people of 'Ad to their prophet Hud. Having no regard for the clear signs he presented, they demanded evidence yet rejected it, and their attachment to their inherited idols was so strong that it overrode reason and the truth of his call. Their refusal reveals a deeper pattern: when the heart is bound to familiar customs and false objects of worship, even manifest proof is dismissed, so faith is withheld not for lack of evidence but out of pride and attachment to what has always been worshipped.

translation: We only say that some of our gods have struck you with evil. He said: Indeed, I call Allah to witness, and you bear witness that I am free from what you associate with Him.
interpretation: This verse records the defiant reply of Hud (peace be upon him) to his people of 'Ad, who accused him of having been seized by madness through the displeasure of their idols. Rather than being shaken by their mockery and threats, he responds with a calm declaration of his innocence of their polytheism, invoking God as the sole witness to his sincerity and calling on his people themselves to bear witness. The statement reveals the prophetic confidence that rests entirely on God rather than on worldly power, and it teaches that a true messenger's firmness in tawhid is not diminished by accusations of insanity or threats from false gods. It also exposes the emptiness of idols that their worshippers believed capable of harm, for the prophet stands unafraid of what they claim to be able to do.

translation: Besides Him. So plot against me, all of you together, and give me no respite.
interpretation: This is Hud's defiant challenge to his people, who worshipped other gods besides God. Having declared that he is free of their idols and has placed his trust in God, his Lord and theirs, he tells them that they may scheme against him with all their power and delay no time in doing so. The statement reveals the unshakable confidence of a prophet who relies wholly on God rather than on any created power, and it shows that no plot of the disbelievers can harm one whom God protects. It also teaches that true tawakkul frees the believer from fear of people's threats.

translation: Indeed, I have relied upon Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path.
interpretation: The verse expresses the complete trust of the prophet Hud in God in the face of his people's threats. His reliance (tawakkul) rests on the recognition that God is the Lord of all, including his opponents, and that no living thing can escape His dominion, since He holds each creature by its forelock, a sign of absolute control and power over it. The phrase "on a straight path" affirms that God's governance is just and upright, so the believer who places his trust in Him is walking the same sound way. Thus the verse turns the threat of others into a reminder that every creature, the enemies included, is under God's sovereign command, and that steadfast reliance on Him is the surest refuge.

translation: But if you turn away, then I have certainly conveyed to you what I was sent with to you. And my Lord will bring after you a people other than you, and you will not harm Him at all. Indeed, my Lord is Guardian over all things.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Hud to his people 'Ad, shows that the prophet's duty is only to deliver the message clearly, while acceptance or rejection rests with the listeners. Hud's words carry a sober warning: when a people persist in refusing guidance, God is not diminished by their disbelief, and He can replace them with another nation, as He did with those before them. The closing affirmation that God is a watchful Guardian over everything points to His complete knowledge and control, meaning that no deed, whether of obedience or rebellion, escapes His account, and that human arrogance cannot threaten the divine order.

translation: And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and We saved them from a severe punishment.
interpretation: The verse presents the principle that divine judgment is executed only when its appointed time arrives, and that salvation is granted by Allah's mercy to those who believe alongside the messenger. Faith joined to obedience to a prophet is the means of deliverance, while those who reject the message are left to the consequences of their denial. The 'severe punishment' from which the believers were spared signals that mercy and divine justice operate together, and that Allah's rescue of the faithful is itself an act of grace rather than a reward earned by their own strength alone.

translation: And those were 'Ad: they denied the signs of their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.
interpretation: The verse holds up the people of 'Ad as a warning drawn from history, and it names the root of their ruin as a double rejection: they denied the clear signs of God in creation and revelation, and they refused the messengers God sent to guide them. Their deeper failure was surrender of judgment to arrogant leaders who set themselves against the truth; by following 'every obstinate tyrant' they traded obedience to their Lord for servility to human pride. The verse teaches that when a people stops heeding divine guidance and submits instead to domineering authority, it moves toward destruction, and that the stubbornness of tyrants is a recurring cause of communal downfall.

translation: And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection as well. Unquestionably, the 'Ad disbelieved in their Lord. Unquestionably, away with 'Ad, the people of Hud.
interpretation: The verse shows that the punishment of 'Ad did not end with their destruction in this world but extended into the Hereafter, as the curse pursued them from both realms. Their root sin was disbelief in their Lord, the denial of the One to whom they owed gratitude and obedience, and the repeated 'alert' (ala) signals the gravity of this rejection. The phrase 'away with 'Ad' conveys a complete distancing from them, a sentence of exile from God's mercy, and naming them 'the people of Hud' underscores that they had been sent a prophet of their own kin who called them to faith and was rejected, making their guilt the heavier.

translation: And to Thamud We sent their brother Salih. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. He has produced you from the earth and settled you in it, so seek His forgiveness and then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed, my Lord is near and responsive."
interpretation: The verse shows that the message of every prophet begins with the same call to pure monotheism, and Salih's appeal to his people rests on two foundations drawn from their own existence: Allah is their Creator, who brought them into being from the earth, and their Settler, who gave them dwelling and prosperity upon it, so gratitude and worship are owed to Him alone. The remedy for past sins is sincere seeking of forgiveness followed by a turning back to Allah in repentance, and the closing words, that the Lord is near and answers, convey that the door of return is always open and that Allah is close to those who call upon Him.

translation: They said, "O Salih, you were among us a man of hope before this. Do you forbid us from worshipping what our fathers worshipped? Indeed, we are in disquieting doubt about that to which you invite us."
interpretation: The people of Thamud's response reveals the depth of their attachment to inherited tradition: Salih had been held in high regard and was expected to lead them, so his call to abandon their ancestral idols is experienced as a betrayal of that expectation. Their words show that the obstacle to faith is often not a lack of evidence but the weight of custom and the fear of breaking with the community's accepted identity, which is why they describe the prophetic message as a source of troubling suspicion rather than engaging it on its merits.

translation: He said, "O my people, have you considered: if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, and He has given me mercy from Himself, then who will support me against Allah if I disobey Him? You would only be increasing me in loss."
interpretation: The verse presents the prophet Salih's (or Hud's, as in the wider context of this speech) plea to his people, grounded in the certainty of revelation and divine mercy. He argues that his prophethood rests on clear proof from his Lord, so disobeying Allah would be unthinkable, and no one could shield him from divine punishment if he betrayed his mission. His people's opposition therefore accomplishes nothing but their own ruin, since they only add to his loss by rejecting him and reinforcing their own perdition. The verse teaches that a messenger's firmness derives from sincere conviction and divine favor, and that rejection of truth ultimately harms those who reject it rather than the one who delivers it.

translation: And O my people, this is the she-camel of God, a sign for you, so leave her to graze on God's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest a near punishment seize you.
interpretation: The verse shows that the she-camel sent to Thamud was itself a clear sign of God's power and of the prophet's truthfulness, so it was entrusted to the people as something sacred that must not be harmed. Its freedom to graze on God's earth reflects that the earth and its provisions belong to God, and that people hold them only as trust. Harming it was not merely an injury to an animal but a violation of God's covenant, and the warning of a swift punishment teaches that a people who reject clear signs and wrong those who bring them become exposed to a consequence that comes quickly once the limits are crossed.

translation: But they hamstrung her, so he said: "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That is a promise not to be denied."
interpretation: The verse recounts the people of Thamud's defiance toward the she-camel sent to them as a sign from God. Having slaughtered her by hamstringing, they were granted a brief reprieve of three days, a respite that served as a final opportunity to reflect and repent before the punishment. The phrase "a promise not to be denied" signals that the warning is certain and will be fulfilled, so the temporary enjoyment of their dwellings is not a sign of safety but a countdown to inevitable retribution. The passage thus emphasizes that persistent rejection of divine guidance, especially after clear signs, brings a warning that God's threat is binding and unavoidable.

translation: So when Our command came, We saved Salih and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and from the disgrace of that day. Indeed, your Lord is the Strong, the Mighty.
interpretation: The verse presents divine deliverance as the fruit of mercy rather than of the believers' own strength: Salih and his companions were rescued at the moment of the divine decree, and the protection they received is linked to the shame and humiliation that fell upon the rejecters on that day. The closing names of God, al-Qawiy (the Strong) and al-Aziz (the Mighty), direct the reader to see that the victory and the punishment both flow from a power that cannot be resisted, so that faith is sustained by trust in the Lord's strength and His mercy toward those who stood with the prophet.

translation: And the wrongdoers were seized by the Blast, so they awoke in their homes lying prostrate, motionless.
interpretation: The verse points to the swift and inescapable nature of divine punishment upon those who persist in wrongdoing. The 'Blast' (al-sayhah) is a sudden overwhelming calamity that seizes them at the very moment they believe themselves secure, and the image of them found lifeless within their own dwellings, having been heedless of warnings, conveys that the places they relied upon for safety became the scene of their ruin. The verse thus warns that wealth, comfort and settled life provide no protection against the consequences of injustice, and that the reckoning may arrive when people least expect it.

translation: As if they had never dwelt therein. Unquestionably, Thamud disbelieved in their Lord. Unquestionably, away with Thamud!
interpretation: The verse portrays the people of Thamud as having vanished so completely that it is as though they never prospered in their homeland. Their downfall is traced to their ingratitude and denial of their Lord, who had sent them a prophet and a sign, and the repeated call "away with Thamud" conveys the finality of their divine rejection, leaving their name as a warning to later generations that prosperity without faith brings only annihilation.

translation: And certainly Our messengers came to Abraham with good tidings. They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace," and he did not delay before bringing a roasted calf.
interpretation: The verse portrays Abraham's exemplary hospitality and gentle manners toward unexpected guests, whom he first greets with a greeting of peace that is returned in kind. His immediate and unhesitating preparation of a fattened, roasted calf shows that generosity should be prompt and wholehearted, and that the honored guest is to be received with the best of what one has. Read alongside the good tidings mentioned at the beginning, the scene also prepares the reader for the announcement of a son, showing that divine blessing often arrives within ordinary acts of courtesy and welcome.

translation: So when he saw that their hands did not reach toward it, he became suspicious of them and felt a sense of fear within himself. They said, "Do not fear; we have been sent to the people of Lot."
interpretation: The verse shows Abraham's hospitality turning into unease when his guests refused to eat, a natural human response that reveals the gap between ordinary expectations of a guest and the nature of these messengers. Their reassurance that they were sent against the people of Lot reframes his fear: it is not a threat to him but a divine commission of judgment, and it prepares the ground for the good news that follows, teaching that fear of the unseen is met with God's messengers' calm and clarity.

translation: And his wife was standing, and she laughed, so We gave her the good news of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob.
interpretation: The verse portrays Abraham's wife receiving an unexpected announcement of divine favor in her old age, when hope of offspring seemed remote. Her laughter is best read as astonishment and disbelief at the promise rather than mockery, and it highlights the contrast between human expectation and God's power to bring life where natural means have ended. The mention of Isaac and then Jacob marks the continuity of the promise across generations, showing that God's blessing extends beyond the immediate recipient to the lineage that will carry the covenant forward.

translation: She said, "Woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman and this is my husband, an old man? Indeed, this is an astonishing thing!"
interpretation: The verse captures Sarah's astonishment when the angels bring her the good news of a son, despite her advanced age and that of Abraham. Her words express human amazement at a matter that seems beyond the ordinary course of nature, and yet they also reveal the moment where wonder gives way to recognition that divine power is not bound by the usual limits of cause and effect. Her exclamation invites the reader to reflect on how God's command operates beyond human expectation, and how faith is tested when the promised outcome appears impossible to the senses.

translation: They said: "Do you wonder at the decree of Allah? The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the household. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy and Glorious."
interpretation: The verse records the angels' reply to Sarah, who had laughed in astonishment at the news that she would bear a child in her old age while her husband Abraham was also aged. The angels rebuke her gently: wonder at Allah's command is misplaced, since His power is absolute and His decree is not bounded by ordinary custom. By addressing the household of Abraham, they confer upon it the mercy and blessings of Allah, showing that divine favor rests upon those whom Allah chooses. The closing names, Praiseworthy and Glorious, remind the believer that Allah's acts are worthy of praise and that His majesty surpasses every human expectation, so that one should submit with trust rather than doubt when faced with what seems impossible.

translation: So when the fear had left Abraham and the good tidings had come to him, he began to plead with Us concerning the people of Lot.
interpretation: The verse shows Abraham's compassion and moral sensitivity. After the angels brought him the glad news of a son and reassured him, his fear dissolved, and his tender heart turned toward the impending punishment of Lot's people. His 'pleading' (mujadalah) is not a dispute against God but an earnest intercession, a plea for mercy and delay for a community whose corruption had been made known. It teaches that true faith combines joy in divine promise with a deep concern for others, even those who have gone astray, and that a believer may appeal to God's mercy on behalf of people facing judgment.

translation: Indeed, Ibrahim was forbearing, grieving much (over others), and turning back in repentance to God.
interpretation: The verse portrays Ibrahim through three interrelated qualities that together form the character of a true believer. His "halim" (forbearance) describes a gentle, patient restraint that bears the harshness of his people and his opponents without retaliating, reflecting a self-command rooted in trust in God. His being "awwah" points to the tender heart that sorrows deeply over the state of others and over the distance of people from their Lord, a compassion that makes him pray and plead for them, as he does in other passages. Finally, "munib" shows that this tenderness is not passive: it is directed back to God in constant turning, so that his compassion for creatures is anchored in his devotion to the Creator. The verse thus presents prophetic character as the union of patience with others, empathy for their condition, and continual return to God.

translation: O Abraham, turn away from this; indeed, the command of your Lord has come, and indeed, a punishment that cannot be averted is coming upon them.
interpretation: The verse, addressed to Abraham, is a divine instruction to disengage from the matter at hand, which is understood as the futile dispute or obstinacy of those who refuse the truth. It conveys that God's decree has already been issued, so the matter is settled and no longer open to debate. The added assurance that a punishment which cannot be repelled awaits them points to the certainty of divine justice, reminding the believer that the outcome rests with God rather than with human persuasion, and that the prophet's duty is to deliver the message and then withdraw from fruitless argument.

translation: And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed on their account and felt helpless for them, and he said, "This is a difficult day."
interpretation: The verse portrays Lot's anguish at the arrival of the angelic messengers, whom he feared his people would molest because they came as handsome young men. His distress reflects the moral corruption of his community and his sense of powerlessness to protect his guests, which highlights the gravity of the trial he faced. His words "This is a difficult day" express the foreboding that a calamity was about to unfold, and they set the stage for the destruction of the people of Lot, showing that divine help comes to the righteous when human resources fail.

translation: And his people came rushing toward him, and before this they had been committing evil deeds. He said, "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear Allah and do not disgrace me concerning my guests. Is there not among you a single rightly-guided man?"
interpretation: The verse portrays Lot's confrontation with a people who had hardened themselves in vice, so that they rushed toward his guests with shameless desire, having long made a habit of sin. Lot's offer of his daughters is best understood as a plea that they turn to lawful union rather than the unnatural act they sought, and his appeal to God-consciousness and to their sense of honor reveals that he was calling them back to their own conscience. His final question, asking whether a single sound-minded man remained among them, expresses the deep grief of a prophet who finds no one willing to heed reason or restrain the corruption that had spread through his community.

translation: They said, "You already know that we have no claim or right to your daughters, and you certainly know what we want."
interpretation: The people of Lot's reply shows how far their corruption had gone: they openly confess their desire and treat the Prophet's warning as something he already knows, so they neither hide their sin nor feel any shame before him. Their words expose a hardened heart that has turned a lawful, pure alternative into a pretext for defiance, which is why the verses that follow describe the divine punishment that fell on them.

translation: He said: "If only I had against you some power, or could take refuge in a strong pillar (of support)."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Lut (Lot) to his people who were insisting on their wicked deeds and refusing his guidance and the guests who had come to him, expresses the helplessness of a righteous man faced with a corrupt community that rejects him. Having no tribe or army to protect him, he voices the longing for strength or a secure stronghold from which to resist them. It reveals the human sense of weakness before wrongdoing, while also pointing to the true refuge that the prophets turned to: God Himself, who was about to deliver Lut and his household and bring judgment upon the transgressors. The verse thus teaches that when worldly means fail, a believer's ultimate recourse is to the Almighty, the strongest of all supports.

translation: They said, "O Lot, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So travel with your family in a portion of the night, and let none of you look back, except your wife; indeed, she will be struck by what strikes them. Indeed, their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?"
interpretation: The verse shows the angels reassuring Lot that the wicked people of his town cannot harm him, and commanding him to leave secretly by night with his family before the punishment descends at dawn. The exception made for his wife, who will share the fate of the people because of her own inclination toward them, teaches that kinship with the righteous does not save one whose heart and conduct remain with the wrongdoers. The closing question, whether the morning is not near, urges immediate action and reminds the listener that the appointed time of divine judgment is closer than it seems.

translation: So when Our command came, We turned its highest part to its lowest and rained upon it stones of hardened clay, layered one upon another.
interpretation: The verse presents the destruction of the people of Lut as the final consequence of persistent moral corruption and refusal to heed warning. The overturning of the city and the rain of stones show that divine judgment is decisive and inescapable once it arrives, and that the sudden, total reversal of their dwelling mirrors the complete reversal of their values. The phrase 'layered stones of sijjil' suggests a judgment that was ordered and precisely marked, not random, reminding the reader that no place of settled comfort is beyond the reach of God's justice when its people persist in wrongdoing.

translation: Marked by your Lord. And they are never far from the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The stones were branded with distinct marks by God, so each one was aimed at a specific person, showing that the punishment was precise and deliberate rather than random. The closing phrase, 'and it is not far from the wrongdoers,' teaches that divine retribution is always within reach of those who persist in injustice. Its nearness is a warning that wrongdoing invites a consequence that may arrive sooner than the wrongdoer expects.

translation: And to Midian [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. And do not diminish the measure and the scale. Indeed, I see you in prosperity, and indeed I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing day."
interpretation: The verse shows that the prophet Shu'ayb's call began with the foundational command of tawhid, the exclusive worship of Allah, before addressing the social wrong of his people, which was cheating in weights and measures. Its wording suggests that their material prosperity had made them complacent and tempted them toward dishonest gain, so his warning of the encompassing day of punishment links economic injustice directly to the consequences of rejecting God. It teaches that trade and justice in the marketplace are inseparable from faith, and that the blessings of wealth are a trial that calls for honesty rather than exploitation.

translation: And O my people, give full measure and weight with justice, and do not deprive people of their due, and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief.
interpretation: The verse establishes that honest dealing in trade is an act of worship and a pillar of social order, for the measure and the scale are the instruments by which people's rights are secured. To cheat in weights is not merely a financial wrong but a form of corruption in the earth, because it erodes trust, distorts the just distribution of what God has provided, and spreads injustice through society. Its wider meaning reaches beyond the marketplace to every domain in which a person holds another's right in his hands: a judge, a ruler, an employer, or a witness must render to each their due exactly, since the balance of society rests on the balance of justice.

translation: What remains with Allah is better for you, if you are believers. And I am not a guardian over you.
interpretation: The verse, spoken by Shu'ayb to his people who cheated in measure and weight, contrasts the fleeting gain of dishonest trade with what Allah preserves: the lawful provision that comes through justice, and the reward of faith. Shu'ayb's words also show the limits of a prophet's role. He delivers the message and warns, but he is not a keeper who compels obedience. The responsibility for accepting or rejecting the truth rests with each person, and the believer is called to see that lasting good lies in what is with God rather than in wealth gained by wrongdoing.

translation: They said, "O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we should abandon what our fathers worshipped, or that we should not do with our wealth as we please? Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided."
interpretation: The verse shows the people of Shu'ayb mocking his call by treating his prayer and piety as a pretext for restricting their freedom in worship and property. Their sarcastic words expose a deeper refusal: they regard religious obligation as an intrusion upon inherited custom and personal autonomy, and they turn his moral reproach into an object of ridicule by calling him forbearing and rightly guided, as if to say that his very virtue is absurd in their eyes. It reflects a recurring pattern in the Qur'an, in which the reformers' ethical demands over economic justice and sincere devotion are rejected by those who equate tradition and wealth with ultimate authority.

translation: He said: "O my people, have you considered: if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, and He has given me good provision from Himself, [then how could I deviate?]. I do not intend to differ from you in that which I forbid you. I intend only reform as far as I am able. My success is only through Allah. In Him I have placed my trust, and to Him I turn back in repentance."
interpretation: Shu'ayb's words reveal that his prophetic mission rests on a clear proof from his Lord and on the sustenance and grace God has given him, so his conduct must match his preaching. He rejects any hidden motive of profiting from the people by doing what he forbids them, insisting that his sole aim is genuine reform within the limits of his ability. The verse teaches that the reformer's success depends entirely on God, which leads to reliance upon Him and constant return to Him in repentance.

translation: And O my people, let not my opposition to you bring upon you the like of what befell the people of Noah, or the people of Hud, or the people of Salih; and the people of Lot are not far from you.
interpretation: The verse shows Shu'ayb urging his people to reflect on the consequences of persisting in rejection and defiance. His call to them is not to be provoked into stubbornness by his opposition, since opposition is not the cause of their danger; rather, their own persistence in disbelief and wrongdoing would draw down the same divine punishment that overtook earlier nations. By invoking the destruction of Noah's, Hud's, Salih's and Lot's peoples, whose ruin is still fresh in memory and geographically near, he turns history into a warning, teaching that the nearness of past punishments should prompt repentance, and that God's justice reaches communities according to their conduct regardless of their worldly strength.

translation: And seek forgiveness from your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed, my Lord is Most Merciful and Most Loving.
interpretation: The verse presents a two-step path to restoring one's relationship with God: first, asking Him for forgiveness (istighfar), which acknowledges one's shortcomings and seeks erasure of their consequences; second, turning back to Him (tawbah), which is a sincere reorientation of the heart and conduct away from sin. The sequence shows that forgiveness is not merely spoken words but must be accompanied by a real return to God. The closing description of the Lord as Merciful (rahim) and Loving (wadud) assures the penitent that God's mercy is abundant and that He embraces those who return to Him with warmth and affection, not merely with grudging pardon. The phrase 'my Lord' in the verse, spoken by the prophet Shu'ayb in the surrounding context, also reflects a personal, intimate relationship with the Creator that encourages hope rather than despair.

translation: They said, "O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say, and we see you among us as weak. Were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you, and you are not mighty against us."
interpretation: The disbelievers of Madyan answer Shu'ayb with contempt, using his lack of worldly power as a pretext to dismiss his message: they claim not to grasp his words, regard him as feeble among them, and justify tolerating him only out of respect for his tribe rather than for him or his message. Their reasoning reveals a common error of the arrogant, who measure truth by social strength and tribal protection instead of by its own merit. The verse thus shows that the prophet's weakness in their eyes was a worldly appearance, while his true standing rested with God, and that rejection of the message often disguises itself as indifference or practical calculation.

translation: He said, "O my people, is my tribe more honored by you than Allah, and you have taken Him behind your backs as something cast away? Indeed, my Lord is encompassing of what you do."
interpretation: The verse shows the prophet Shu'ayb reproaching his people for valuing the protection of his worldly kin above the protection of God, whom they had neglected and thrust behind them as though He were of no account. Their error lay in measuring divine authority by tribal standing, when the one who truly guards and sees all is God. The closing phrase, that his Lord encompasses their deeds, turns the rebuke into a warning: nothing they do escapes divine knowledge and accountability, so their reliance on human loyalties will not shield them from the consequences of their conduct.

translation: And O my people, work according to your position; indeed, I am working. You will soon know who will receive a punishment that disgraces him and who is a liar. And wait; indeed, I am with you among those who wait.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the prophet Shu'ayb to his people, establishes a final challenge of certainty against those who reject him. Having exhausted persuasion, he tells them to continue in their chosen course while he continues in his, leaving the outcome to God. The statement shifts the matter from debate to consequence: the decisive difference between the truthful and the liar will be revealed through a punishment that brings humiliation upon the wrongdoer. The closing command to wait signals that his patience and trust in God's judgment are as firm as the warning itself, and that the truth of his mission will become evident in the events that follow.

translation: And when Our command came, We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and the blast seized those who had wronged, so they became prostrate lifeless in their homes.
interpretation: The verse shows that divine punishment comes only at the appointed time, after the messenger has delivered his call and the people have persisted in injustice. Salvation is not earned by lineage or social standing but granted by God's mercy to those who believed and stood with the prophet. The destruction of the wrongdoers in the very homes they relied upon teaches that worldly security offers no protection against the consequences of oppression and rejection of truth.

translation: As if they had never dwelt in it. Unquestionably, away with Midian, just as Thamud was taken away.
interpretation: The verse closes the account of the people of Midian by likening their destruction to that of Thamud: a people who prospered in their land are reduced to having never lived there at all. The phrase "as if they had never dwelt in it" presents total erasure as the ultimate form of divine retribution, where the material comfort and settled life they enjoyed vanish without a trace. The repeated call "away with" (alā bu'dan) expresses a divine curse and distance from mercy, placing Midian in the same category of rejected nations, so that the listener is warned that ingratitude, injustice, and rejection of the messenger lead to the same fate.

translation: And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs and a clear authority.
interpretation: The verse presents the mission of Moses as grounded in two complementary forms of proof: the 'ayat' (signs), which are the miraculous evidences given to him, and the 'sultan mubin' (clear authority), which is the manifest argument that leaves no room for doubt. The signs address the senses and wonder, while the clear authority speaks to reason and conviction, showing that divine guidance is supported both by visible wonders and by lucid, rational proof. The phrasing also reminds the listener that prophetic missions are never without evidence, so the rejection of Moses by Pharaoh and his chiefs was a matter of arrogance rather than a lack of clarity in the message.

translation: To Pharaoh and his chieftains. Yet they followed the command of Pharaoh, and the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided.
interpretation: The verse exposes the blind obedience that tyranny secures from its courtiers: the elite follow the ruler's directive not because it is sound but because it is his, so they surrender their own judgment and bind themselves to a path they know leads to ruin. By declaring that Pharaoh's command was not guiding toward right conduct, the Qur'an draws a firm line between legitimate authority and mere power, teaching that obedience is owed only to what accords with truth and justice, and that a community which abandons its discernment in favor of a leader's whims will be led astray.

translation: He will go before his people on the Day of Resurrection and lead them into the Fire. And wretched is the watering-place to which they are led.
interpretation: The verse portrays the leader who misguided his people in worldly life as one who will again walk at their head on the Day of Resurrection, only now toward the Fire. The image draws on the familiar scene of a caravan going to water: the people follow their leader to the water source, but here the destination is Hellfire, which is revealed as the worst possible place to be brought to. The imagery implies that those who follow falsehood and tyranny are not merely led astray but are brought to a final reckoning, and that the one who led them bears responsibility for guiding them to that end.

translation: And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection too. What evil gift is the gift they are given!
interpretation: The verse shows that rejection of God's guidance brings a double consequence: a curse that clings to a people in this life, and a further disgrace on the Day of Judgment. The word 'rifd' (gift, aid) is used ironically, since what these people receive as support and reward is in truth a burden. Their worldly reputation and the curse that trails them become the very 'gift' that accompanies them, and it is a dreadful one. The passage warns that the outcome of arrogance and defiance is not relief or honor but lasting shame that follows a person from this world into the next.

translation: That is from the news of the towns which We relate to you; some of them are still standing, and some have been reaped away.
interpretation: The verse points to the Prophet's own message as a divine report of the past, not a human invention: the histories of earlier communities are told to him so that he may see in them the outcome of rejecting prophets. The image is precise and striking. Some ruined towns still stand as visible witnesses, like walls or structures that remain, while others have been completely cut down and wiped out, as a field is harvested. Both conditions come from the same cause, so the believer is invited to reflect that divine justice spares no community and that continuance or destruction depends on conduct and response to truth, not on the strength of the people alone.

translation: We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves. So their gods that they invoked besides Allah did not avail them anything when the command of your Lord came, and they added nothing to them but ruin.
interpretation: The verse shows that the destruction of the past nations was not an act of injustice by God but the outcome of their own choices, since they persisted in denial and rebellion despite the warnings they received. It also exposes the futility of idolatry: the deities they trusted, and whom they had called upon for help and protection, vanished at the decisive moment when God's judgment arrived, leaving their worshippers with nothing but loss. The 'ruin' they gained from these false gods underscores that whatever is set up as a partner to God can only deepen a person's destruction, while true protection lies only with the One who commands the outcome of every event.

translation: And thus is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the cities while they are committing wrongdoing. Indeed, His seizure is painful and severe.
interpretation: The verse establishes that divine retribution is not arbitrary but follows a consistent pattern of justice: when a people persist in injustice, their destruction comes as a reckoning from a Lord who is fully aware of their conduct. The phrase 'and thus' links this to the preceding narratives of earlier nations, teaching that the same law of accountability governs every community. The description of the seizure as 'painful and severe' conveys both the gravity of the punishment and the fact that it is a genuine consequence rather than a mere warning. Its deeper message is a call to reflection: a society's wrongdoing is always carried out in the sight of God, and the respite granted to the unjust is a window for repentance rather than a sign of divine neglect.

translation: Indeed in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter. That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed.
interpretation: The verse directs the attention of the listener to the reality of the Day of Judgment by presenting it as a sign that is readily available to the one whose heart is moved by fear of the punishment of the Hereafter. Only such a person truly benefits from the sign, because fear opens the mind to what is coming. The verse then describes that Day in two ways: it is a Day when all of mankind will be brought together, the first and the last, the righteous and the wrongdoers, to be gathered before their Lord with no one left out; and it is a Day that is witnessed, a Day of visible and universal assembly in which all creation, angels and humans alike, will be present and observing. The emphasis on the gathering and the witnessing conveys that no deed will remain hidden and no one will be absent from the account, so that the reminder should move the believer to prepare for that encounter through righteous action.

translation: And We do not delay it except for a specified, limited term.
interpretation: The verse speaks of the divinely appointed timing of a matter, most naturally the punishment or the reckoning promised to the deniers, which God holds back only until a fixed, predetermined moment. The delay is not neglect or weakness but an expression of wisdom and precise measure: every affair has its appointed term, and nothing is postponed beyond what God has decreed. The phrase 'a counted term' calls the believer to patience and to awareness that all things, including the fulfillment of divine promises, unfold according to an exact and known limit that no one can advance or defer.

translation: On the Day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission; then among them will be the wretched and the happy.
interpretation: The verse points to the Day of Judgment, when the full authority of God over speech and intercession will be manifest: no soul may speak unless God grants it leave, so the eloquence of defense, pleading, or excuse is entirely subject to divine permission. The concluding division into the wretched and the happy shows that the outcome of that Day is not a matter of chance or of one's words in the moment, but the result of a prior distinction grounded in each person's deeds and faith. The verse thus calls the listener to reflect that the decisive account is settled by God's justice, and that preparation for that encounter must be made in this life, before the opportunity to speak on one's own behalf is no longer granted.

translation: As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, where they will have groaning and wailing.
interpretation: The verse divides humanity on the Day of Judgment into two destinies, and here it describes the fate of those who were 'shaqiyy', wretched, meaning those who chose misery for their souls through disbelief and disobedience. Their abode is the Fire, and the sounds of their distress, the deep, heaving sighs of zafir and the choked, sobbing shahiq, show that their suffering is total, both in the chest and in the voice, with no relief or escape. The scene is meant to awaken the listener to the reality that every person's end is the direct result of the path they chose in this world, and that the consequences of one's deeds are inescapable and sure.

translation: Abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills. Indeed, your Lord is the accomplisher of whatever He intends.
interpretation: The verse describes the abode of those who are destined for the Fire and the Garden, but it expresses the duration of their stay in terms of the heavens and the earth, which is a way of indicating a long span that has an end point known only to God. The exception clause, "except as your Lord wills," shows that even this duration is subject to the absolute will of God, leaving room for His mercy and His decision, while affirming that His power is unrestricted and that whatever He wills He carries out without any hindrance.

translation: As for those who were made happy, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills; a gift never cut off.
interpretation: The verse presents the final destiny of the blessed as an endless gift, and its phrasing about the duration of the heavens and the earth is best read as an idiom for eternity rather than a literal limit. The exception "except as your Lord wills" does not introduce an end to their bliss but affirms that God's will remains supreme and free, granting them more than their deeds could ever earn. The closing phrase "a gift never cut off" (ʿaṭāʾ ghayr majdhūdh) distinguishes this reward from the conditional and temporary goods of the world, pointing the believer toward a reward that is uninterrupted, unconditional in its continuance, and an expression of divine generosity.

translation: So do not be in doubt about what these people worship. They worship only as their fathers worshipped before. And indeed, We will give them their full share without any diminution.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet and reassures him against doubt about the idolatry of his people: their worship is no fresh truth but a blind imitation of ancestral custom, a pattern long established among those who came before them. Their error rests on inherited tradition rather than evidence. The closing promise that their portion will be rendered in full, without reduction, points to the certainty of recompense: whatever they earn, good or ill, will be paid back to them completely and justly, so the Prophet need not grieve over their rejection, since God's accounting leaves nothing unrecorded or unfulfilled.

translation: And We had certainly given Moses the Scripture, but it was disputed over. And were it not for a word that preceded from your Lord, the matter would have been judged between them. And indeed, they are in disquieting doubt concerning it.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet by showing that disagreement over revelation is an old pattern: the same Scripture given to Moses became a source of dispute among his people, not because the revelation lacked clarity but because human beings bent it to their desires and rivalries. The divine decree that postponed the final reckoning, a term already fixed by God's word, is what keeps the matter open rather than settled in this world. Their doubt is described as troubling and unsettling, which suggests that those who reject the message are not at ease in their rejection, and that the unrest in their hearts is itself a sign of the truth they resist.

translation: And indeed, [to] all [of them], your Lord will surely repay them in full for their deeds. Indeed, He is Acquainted with what they do.
interpretation: The verse assures the believer that no one's deeds will be lost or left unrewarded or unpunished. The word "kullan" (all) and the emphatic particles "inna" and the lam of oath, together with "layuwaffiyannahum" (He will surely pay them in full), stress that divine recompense is certain and complete, leaving nothing short. By closing with "Khabeer" (All-Aware), God ties this promise to perfect knowledge: the justice of the reckoning rests not on witnesses or records alone but on a Lord who knows the inner intentions and the hidden details of every action. The verse thus consoles those who are wronged by the powerful, who see the wicked prosper, and it warns the wrongdoer that every deed, however secret, is known and will be weighed.

translation: So remain steadfast as you have been commanded, and [so too should] those who have turned back with you [to God]. And do not transgress. Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse establishes uprightness (istiqamah) as the central duty of the Prophet and of the believers who share his path, grounding it in a direct divine command rather than personal preference. Steadfastness is not a single act but a continuous posture of balance that refuses both excess and deficiency, which is why the prohibition against transgression (tughyan) is joined to it. The closing reminder that God sees all actions gives the command its moral weight: the believer remains upright not merely before people but under the constant awareness of a Witness who observes the inner and outer conduct alike.

translation: And do not incline toward those who have wronged, lest the Fire touch you, and you would have no protectors other than Allah, and then you would not be helped.
interpretation: The verse forbids believers from leaning toward, relying upon, or being drawn into friendship and alliance with those who persist in wrongdoing and injustice. Such inclination, even if it appears to be a small compromise, gradually erodes one's commitment to truth and draws a person into the same path that leads to punishment. The warning makes clear that no worldly ally can shield anyone from Allah's consequences: once one has aligned oneself with the oppressors, there is no protector besides God, and no help will come. The verse thus calls the believer to firm moral independence, to loyalty to God and to the righteous, and to vigilance about the company one keeps and the sources of support one depends upon.

translation: And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in some hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds. That is a reminder for those who remember.
interpretation: The verse ties the steadiness of worship to the rhythm of daily life: prayer at dawn and dusk, and in the approaching hours of the night, keeps the believer continually turned toward God, so that the day's bodily and spiritual lapses are gradually erased by sincere good deeds. Its concluding words suggest that this is not a mere command but a remembrance, a waking of the heart in those who are truly mindful, so that worship becomes both a purifying discipline and an ongoing act of recollection that guards the soul against sin.

translation: And be patient, for indeed Allah does not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost.
interpretation: The verse ties patience directly to ihsan, the excellence of doing good, and grounds that patience in the certainty that God never wastes the reward of those who persevere in goodness. Patience here is not passive endurance but an active, steadfast commitment to righteousness in the face of hardship, injustice, or opposition. By assuring the believer that no effort made sincerely for God's sake is lost, the verse transforms the experience of trial into a meaningful stage on the path toward divine recompense, reinforcing the inner dignity and hope that sustain the one who does good when it is difficult.

translation: So why were there not, among the generations before you, people of virtue who would forbid corruption in the land, except a few of those whom We saved from among them? And those who did wrong pursued the luxuries they had been given, and they were guilty people.
interpretation: The verse laments the absence of a remnant of righteous people in earlier nations who stood against corruption, and shows that the destruction of those societies came because the wrongdoers, absorbed in the comfort and indulgence they were granted, abandoned moral responsibility. Only the small number who forbade evil were spared, which teaches that a community's survival depends on the presence of those who actively resist corruption, and that prosperity without moral vigilance leads to ruin.

translation: And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people were reformers.
interpretation: The verse reveals a principle of divine justice: God does not punish communities arbitrarily or in a manner contrary to justice, least of all when their inhabitants are upright and work for good. Destruction falls upon a people on account of wrongdoing, so that where righteousness and reform prevail, the mercy and fairness of God shield the community from annihilation. It also implies that the measure of a society is its conduct: when its members act to set things right, they become the grounds on which God's forbearance rests, and the assurance is given to believers that divine judgment is never a capricious act but always follows from a just cause.

translation: And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community, but they continue to differ.
interpretation: The verse shows that diversity of belief, outlook and way of life among people is not an accident but part of the divine decree, since God could have compelled all humanity into a single community of faith had He willed it. Because His wisdom chose to leave human beings free, their disagreements persist, and this persistence becomes a test that distinguishes those who seek truth with sincerity from those who hold to their own partisanship. The lesson for the believer is to accept that difference will endure, to refrain from presuming to force uniformity on others, and to focus on his own conduct and on sincere, patient calling to the truth.

translation: Except for those upon whom your Lord has mercy. And for that He created them. And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind all together."
interpretation: The verse points to a divine decree that separates the destiny of humanity and jinn by the operation of mercy versus the consequence of persistent rejection. Its phrase "and for that He created them" is read by many commentators as referring to the purpose of creation being the test of worship and the choice between obedience and disobedience, so that the final outcome is not arbitrary but the fruit of what each soul chose. The clause "except for those upon whom your Lord has mercy" shows that Allah's mercy is the decisive path of salvation, which the verse holds out as a reality even amid the warning of Hell. The fixed word of God that Hell will be filled signals the certainty of the consequence for those who deliberately turn away, and it addresses the Prophet with consolation, assuring him that the stubbornness of the majority is part of a known and decreed course, while mercy remains open to whoever turns to God.

translation: And each [of these] we relate to you from the news of the messengers, by which We strengthen your heart. And there has come to you in this [account] the truth, and an admonition and a reminder for the believers.
interpretation: The verse presents the stories of the earlier messengers as a deliberate divine provision for the Prophet ﷺ, meant to steady his heart amid the rejection and hardship he faced from his people. Such narratives show him that the call of every messenger met opposition and that God's support and final victory were certain for those who stood firm. Their significance lies not only in consolation but in the truth they carry, which warns the disbelievers by example and gives the believers counsel and a renewed awareness of God's ways. The heart's firmness is thus strengthened through remembering how God's justice and mercy unfolded in the lives of His messengers.

translation: And say to those who do not believe: "Work according to your position; indeed, we are working (according to ours)."
interpretation: The verse sets out a clear separation between the believer and the disbeliever at the level of conduct and final accountability. Rather than engaging in endless argument with those who refuse faith, the Prophet is instructed to state the matter plainly and step back: each party is left to act upon its own convictions and way of life. The phrase "on your position" (ʿalā makānatikum) points to the standing, condition, and path a person has chosen for himself, and the words "we too are working" affirm that the believer's own labor is equally real and purposeful. The verse thus conveys both a firm dignity in asserting one's path and a reminder that every deed will ultimately bear its consequence, leaving judgment to the outcome of what each has done.

translation: And wait; indeed, we too are waiting.
interpretation: This verse, spoken in the context of the Prophet's opponents who rejected his message and demanded signs, is a closing warning that sets the two sides on a clear footing. The Prophet is told to leave the matter in God's hands: the disbelievers may await whatever outcome they wish, and the believer likewise awaits God's decree, which will vindicate truth and expose falsehood. The verse conveys both divine patience with those who persist in denial and the assurance that the final judgment belongs to God alone, so that the deniers' waiting carries the weight of their own consequences.

translation: And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and to Him the whole matter is returned. So worship Him and rely upon Him. And your Lord is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse directs the believer's heart toward absolute tawhid by affirming that Allah alone possesses the hidden knowledge of all that is in the heavens and the earth, which places all affairs under His sole authority and return. Because every matter ultimately comes back to Him, the proper response is twofold: sincere worship that is directed to Him alone, and complete reliance upon Him rather than upon one's own plans, strength, or other beings. The closing assurance that the Lord is not heedless of human deeds joins this trust with accountability, teaching that the one who entrusts his affairs to Allah should also remain conscious that every action is known to Him and will be weighed on the Day of Return.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Clear Book.
interpretation: The opening letters Alif, Lam, Ra are among the muqatta'at, the disjointed letters that begin several surahs, and they point to a deliberate challenge: the Qur'an is composed of the very letters of the Arabic language that its audience already uses, yet they cannot produce its like. By calling the revelation 'the Clear Book,' the verse affirms that its guidance is lucid and self-evident, not hidden in riddles, so that the mystery of the letters draws the listener's attention to the sheer clarity and inimitability of the text that follows. The invocation of the Merciful names before it frames the revelation as an act of divine compassion, indicating that the Book's clarity is itself a mercy meant to lead people out of darkness into light.

translation: Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an, so that you may reason.
interpretation: The verse presents the revelation's Arabic language as a deliberate means of making its meaning accessible, so that the listener can understand it and be moved to think. Its clarity in a familiar tongue is an invitation to engage the mind, not merely to recite words. Reason (ta'qilun) is thus named as the purpose of revelation: the Qur'an calls people to reflect on its message, weigh its signs, and draw conclusions about God, themselves, and the world, so that understanding leads to faith and right conduct.

translation: We relate to you the best of stories by Our revelation to you of this Qur'an, although you were before it certainly among the unaware.
