interpretation: The verse presents the revelation of the story of Joseph as the finest of narratives, given to the Prophet Muhammad so that he might learn what he had not known before. Its emphasis on the Prophet having been among the unaware before revelation highlights that knowledge of the unseen and of earlier prophetic history came solely through divine inspiration, not through his own learning. The 'best of stories' is understood as best because it combines a complete account of patience, betrayal, chastity, forgiveness and divine providence, offering a model of trust in God's plan and a consolation to the believers facing their own trials.

translation: When Joseph said to his father, "O my father, indeed I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me."
interpretation: The dream Joseph relates is a early sign of the prophetic destiny God has prepared for him, and it is delivered as a private confidence to his father, Jacob, who alone is positioned to understand its significance. The cosmic imagery of eleven stars, the sun, and the moon bowing to him gathers the whole household into a single symbolic scene: the sun and moon traditionally read as his parents and the stars as his brothers, so the vision foreshadows the eventual humbling of the family before him. The verse also teaches the importance of guarding such revelations from those who might envy or plot against the one who receives them, a lesson Jacob immediately draws in the verses that follow.

translation: He said, "O my son, do not relate your vision to your brothers, lest they plot against you a scheme. Indeed, Satan is to mankind a clear enemy."
interpretation: Jacob's counsel to Joseph reveals a wise principle of guarding blessings from envy. A vision of divine favor is a trust, and sharing it indiscriminately with those whose hearts may harbor jealousy can invite their scheming. The verse teaches discretion in speech and awareness that the whisper of Satan works to sow enmity among people, especially among kin. The believer is thus reminded to protect what is precious through prudence, seeking refuge in God from the envy of others and from the open enmity of the devil.

translation: And thus your Lord will choose you and teach you the interpretation of events, and complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Jacob, just as He completed it upon your two forefathers before, Abraham and Isaac. Indeed, your Lord is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse, spoken to Joseph after his dream, shows that divine election is bestowed by God's knowledge and wisdom rather than by human merit, and that the gift of understanding the meaning of things behind appearances is itself a sign of being chosen. Joseph's favor is presented as a continuation of the covenant blessings already granted to Abraham and Isaac, so that his trials and rise are read as part of a single, unfolding divine plan in which God's completion of His grace is both certain and wise.

translation: Indeed, there were in Joseph and his brothers signs for those who ask.
interpretation: The verse points to the story of Joseph and his brothers as a source of lessons for those who seek knowledge with a sincere and open heart. Its 'signs' are not merely historical events but reflections of God's wisdom in the trials, jealousy, repentance, and eventual reconciliation that unfold within one family, showing how divine providence works through what appears to be harm. The phrase 'for those who ask' suggests that such signs are unveiled to the inquiring soul who reflects and questions, rather than to the heedless or the merely curious.

translation: When they said: Joseph and his brother are dearer to our father than we are, though we are a strong band. Indeed our father is in clear error.
interpretation: This verse opens the account of the brothers' jealousy toward Joseph and his full brother Benjamin. Their envy was rooted in the father's visible preference for the two younger sons, which they experienced as a slight against their own number and strength as a group. Their words reveal how resentment can turn into a self-justifying judgment: they label their father's affection as misguidance, thereby excusing the wrong they are already contemplating. The verse thus shows how unchecked envy corrupts one's view of others, even of a righteous parent, and leads to moral blindness that hides one's own fault behind a claim of collective strength and rightness.

translation: Kill Joseph, or cast him out to some land, so that your father's face will be turned toward you alone, and after that you will be a righteous people.
interpretation: This verse records the scheming of Joseph's brothers, who, jealous of their father Jacob's special love for Joseph, plotted to remove him. Their proposal reveals how envy can lead people to rationalize grave wrongs, presenting murder or abandonment as a path to restored favor and even to future righteousness. The verse thus exposes the self-deception inherent in jealousy: they imagine that eliminating the object of envy will bring them honor and goodness, when in fact it is the first step in a chain of sins. It serves as a warning that corrupt intentions often disguise themselves as reasonable solutions, and that a people's claim to righteousness is hollow if it is built upon injustice against their own kin.

translation: A speaker among them said: "Do not kill Joseph, but cast him into the depths of the well; some of the travelers will pick him up, if you are going to act."
interpretation: The verse shows the brothers' jealousy reaching the point of plotting murder, and how one of them, seeking a middle course, proposes abandonment instead of bloodshed. His suggestion reflects a conscience that still recoils from killing, yet it is a compromise that still embraces the sin of betrayal and cruelty toward a brother. The phrase "if you are going to act" underscores that their resolve is conditional on their own choice, placing the moral responsibility squarely on them. Read more broadly, the passage reveals how envy can gradually corrode a person's restraint, leading from harboring resentment to contemplating harm, and how Divine providence nevertheless carries forward the destined course of Joseph's life through the very schemes meant to end it.

translation: They said: "O our father, what is wrong with you that you do not entrust us with Joseph, while we are truly sincere well-wishers toward him?"
interpretation: The brothers' words expose a tension between outward affection and inward intent: they feign concern and sincere goodwill toward Joseph while concealing the plot they are shaping against him. Their insistence on being trusted with him reveals how easily sincerity can be performed in speech, and the verse invites reflection on how the sincerity of one's claims must be tested by deeds rather than accepted at face value. Jacob's hesitation, which follows, is read as the wisdom of a parent who senses that the protestations of goodwill conceal something amiss.

translation: Send him with us tomorrow so that he may enjoy himself and play, and indeed we will be his protectors.
interpretation: The words of the brothers of Joseph reveal the tension between a father's deep anxiety and the sons' eagerness to win his consent. Their request to take Jacob's son out to graze and play is framed as harmless, and their pledge to guard him is a bid for trust. The verse invites reflection on how assurances of safety can be sincere yet still fail when the one giving them is not truly in control, and on how Jacob's later reply, that he would trust only God's protection, points the believer toward reliance on God rather than on human promises.

translation: He said: "Indeed, it grieves me that you take him away, and I fear that a wolf may devour him while you are heedless of him."
interpretation: The verse reveals Jacob's deep paternal anguish and his reluctance to entrust Joseph to his sons. His words express that his sorrow is not merely emotional but rooted in a fear born of their careless attitude, suggesting that he sensed their lack of genuine care and vigilance toward their brother. It also reflects the tension between a father's trust in God and his human caution: he voices his worry openly, yet his grief is shown as a test of patience, teaching that concern for loved ones must be balanced with reliance upon the One who protects them.

translation: They said: "If the wolf were to devour him while we are a group, then indeed we would be losers."
interpretation: The brothers' words reveal how envy and collective pride can disguise a plot as mere caution: they invoke the strength of their numbers and the apparent safety of a wolf-attack as a pretext, while their true intent is hidden beneath a show of concern. The verse exposes the self-deception of those who measure their worth by their group and their ability to act together, and warns that the hearts that conceal malice often speak in the language of protectiveness and calculated fear.

translation: So when they took him away and agreed to put him at the bottom of the well, We revealed to him: "You will surely inform them of this matter of theirs, while they do not perceive."
interpretation: The verse marks the turning point in Joseph's trial, where his brothers' jealousy hardens into a collective decision to cast him away, yet God's providence is already at work behind their scheme. The revelation sent to Joseph in the depths of the well is a sign of divine assurance: his abandonment is not the end of his story but the first step toward his future elevation, and the phrase "while they do not perceive" reveals the gap between human plotting and the hidden wisdom that brings it to fulfillment. The verse teaches that those who are wronged in the darkest places are never beyond God's knowledge, and that the hearts of the oppressors are unaware of the consequences their acts will bring back upon them.

translation: And they came to their father in the evening, weeping.
interpretation: This verse, from the story of Yusuf (Joseph), shows the brothers' deceit being carried out under the cover of grief. Having thrown Yusuf into the well and planned to present a false account, they return at nightfall performing sorrow, a tears-filled display meant to convince their father Ya'qub (Jacob) of a tragedy that never happened. The verse thus exposes how falsehood can be dressed in the outward signs of mourning, and it foreshadows the patient, trusting endurance of Ya'qub, who recognizes the lie and responds with beautiful patience.

translation: They said, "O our father, indeed we went racing with one another and left Joseph by our belongings, and the wolf devoured him. But you will not believe us, even if we are truthful."
interpretation: The brothers of Joseph come to their father with a fabricated account, having already concealed their crime, and the verse exposes the psychology of guilt that seeks to pre-empt doubt: by framing the event as an innocent game and blaming a wolf, they attempt to secure acceptance of a story they know to be false. Their closing remark, that the father will not believe them even if they speak the truth, is itself a telling irony, since it reveals their awareness that their words lack credibility and that their own conduct has given them reason to be distrusted. The verse thus stands as a lesson on how deception, once begun, requires further deception, and how the one who has wronged others often finds that trust, once broken, is not easily restored even when he speaks honestly.

translation: And they came with his shirt stained with false blood. He said, "Rather, your souls have beguiled you into something. So patience is most fitting, and Allah is the one sought for help against what you describe."
interpretation: The verse shows how deceit can be dressed in the appearance of grief: the brothers presented a bloodied garment as proof of a loss they had themselves engineered, and their false evidence was meant to close the matter. Jacob's response refuses to accept the surface story and places the real cause within their own inner dispositions, which had been made to appear acceptable to them, teaching that self-deception often precedes and enables wrongdoing. His answer of beautiful patience (sabr jamil) is not passive resignation but a steadfast refusal to be pushed into despair or false accusation, with his trust directed entirely toward God as the only true support against the lies being told. It stands as a model for the believer who must bear a painful trial with dignity, neither denying the reality of hardship nor surrendering to the narrative of deceivers.

translation: And there came a caravan, so they sent their water-drawer, and he lowered his bucket. He said, "Good news! This is a boy!" And they concealed him as merchandise, but Allah was Knower of what they did.
interpretation: The verse portrays the moment of Joseph's discovery at the well: a passing caravan sends its water-drawer, who lets down his bucket and, finding a boy, cries out in joy. The mercantile sphere reduces a human being to a commodity to be hidden and sold, mirroring the brothers' own treachery. Yet the closing phrase reminds the reader that the divine knowledge encompasses every hidden scheme, so the apparent triumph of the plotters is already within the all-knowing gaze of God, who will bring about the outcome He has decreed.

translation: And they sold him for a paltry price, a few dirhams counted out, and they were among those who had no desire for him.
interpretation: The verse describes the brothers of Joseph selling him for a trifling sum, a handful of silver coins, revealing how readily envy and resentment can cause people to trade away a person of great worth for almost nothing. The phrase 'they were among those who had no desire for him' shows that they valued him so little that they cared nothing for him once he was gone, so their betrayal was rooted not in necessity but in indifference and spite. The verse thus teaches that the worth of a righteous person is not diminished by the low esteem of those who fail to recognize it, and that God's plan proceeds regardless of the cruelty and shortsightedness of human beings.

translation: And the one who bought him from Egypt said to his wife, "Make his residence honorable; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son." And thus We established Joseph in the land, and that We might teach him the interpretation of events. And Allah is predominant over His affair, but most of the people do not know.
interpretation: The verse shows that Joseph's rise to a position of authority in Egypt was not the result of chance but of divine design: the Egyptian who purchased him unknowingly became the first step in God's plan, as his wife's care for Joseph's dwelling placed him in a setting where his gifts could develop. The phrase "and that We might teach him the interpretation of events" points to the knowledge God bestows upon him, which is later manifested in his interpreting dreams and guiding a nation through famine. The closing statement affirms that God's command is always fulfilled, even when it moves through the apparently ordinary decisions of people, while the majority remain unaware of this hidden wisdom and continue to interpret events only by their surface appearances.

translation: And when he reached his maturity and was fully grown, We gave him judgment and knowledge. And thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: The verse, belonging to the story of Joseph, marks the stage at which his inner and outer faculties reached full maturity, and God responded to that maturity by granting him wisdom (hukm), the capacity to judge rightly and place things in their proper order, along with knowledge of the realities of things and of the meaning of events. The connection drawn by 'thus' shows that this gift is not arbitrary but follows a principle: those who act with sincerity and excellence (ihsan) in their conduct, especially when tested by temptation and hardship, will be recompensed by God with clarity of judgment and deeper understanding. Ihsan here is not merely outward good deeds but a state of worship and sincerity toward God, which Joseph displayed in resisting what was unlawful, so that the reward of knowledge and wisdom is presented as the natural fruit of such devotion.

translation: And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him from himself; she bolted the doors and said, "Come, you". He said, "I seek refuge in Allah! Indeed, he (my master) has treated me well in my residence. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed."
interpretation: The verse presents Joseph's steadfastness in the face of temptation as an act of moral integrity grounded in gratitude and God-consciousness. By refusing the woman's advances, he recognizes that his master's kindness to him creates an obligation of loyalty, and he places his trust in God as his refuge. His declaration that the wrongdoers do not prosper reveals that he sees the path of sin as ultimately self-defeating, so that his resistance is both a protection of his own soul and a witness to the principle that betrayal of trust and transgression lead only to loss.

translation: And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus [it was], that We might avert from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was among Our sincere, chosen servants.
interpretation: The verse presents Yusuf's steadfastness as the fruit of divine protection: his desire was restrained not by his own unaided strength but by a clear sign (burhan) from his Lord that turned his heart from temptation. The phrase 'had he not seen the proof of his Lord' is best read as showing that the sincere servant of God is protected by the vision of his Lord's presence and accountability, so that what could have become sin is averted. The verse thus teaches that true chastity is rooted in sincerity (ikhlas) and in God-consciousness, and that God shields those who are devoted to Him from evil and indecency, with the emphasis falling on the inner cause of his purity rather than on the outward circumstances of the temptation.

translation: And they raced each other to the door, and she tore his shirt from behind, and they found her master at the door. She said, "What is the punishment for one who intended evil against your wife, other than imprisonment or a painful torment?"
interpretation: The verse portrays the decisive moment at the door, where the race toward it reveals the contest between Yusuf's innocence and the woman's desire, and the shirt torn from behind becomes a silent witness to the truth that Yusuf was fleeing rather than pursuing. Her immediate turn to accuse him before her husband shows how deception rushes to shift blame, and her words cloak her own guilt in the language of justice, framing a sincere man's chastity as a crime. The verse thus exposes how desire, once thwarted, seeks to protect itself by condemning the innocent, while God's justice works through the very evidence she creates.

translation: He said, "It was she who sought to seduce me from myself." And a witness from her own family testified: "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth and he is among the liars."
interpretation: The verse shows the reasoning of justice applied through circumstantial evidence. The witness does not rely on accusation or oath but on the physical sign of the garment: a shirt torn at the front indicates resistance and self-defense against an aggressor, while a shirt torn at the back indicates flight and pursuit. The method teaches that careful examination of visible traces can reveal truth where testimony is contested, and that justice must follow evidence rather than status or the pressures of a household. It also shows that truth can be brought forth even from within the accused party's own circle, so that the one who is wronged is vindicated and the false accusation is exposed.

translation: And if his shirt is torn from behind, then she has lied, and he is of the truthful.
interpretation: The verse presents a piece of circumstantial evidence used to discern the truth in a case of accusation. Joseph's shirt being torn from the back indicates that he was the one fleeing while being pursued, which means the woman who accused him of attempting to seduce her was the aggressor and is the liar. The verse shows that God allows reason and careful examination of physical signs to reveal the truth, and that justice may be established through such evidence even when there are no direct witnesses, placing the innocent man's truthfulness beyond doubt.

translation: So when he saw that his shirt was torn from the back, he said, "Indeed, it is from your scheming, surely your scheming is great."
interpretation: The verse shows the decisive role of evidence in exposing the truth where accusation and passion had obscured it. The torn shirt, pulled from behind, testified that Joseph had been fleeing rather than pursuing, so the sign itself refuted the false charge. Yet the husband does not simply accept the innocence of the one he had trusted; he attributes the whole affair to the women's cunning, reflecting how the human tendency to shift blame and to weave deception can exceed the bounds of reason. By calling their scheming great, the verse highlights how seductive falsehood, when it gathers the powerful and the envious together, can strike with a force that only divine protection can withstand.

translation: Joseph, turn away from this. And ask forgiveness for your sin, for indeed you have been among the sinners.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by the nobleman of Egypt's household, addressed to his wife and to Joseph in the context of the affair that had come to light. Its instruction to Joseph to let the matter pass and not dwell on it reflects a counsel of discretion and of protecting a dignified silence in the face of scandal. The command to the wife to seek forgiveness is not merely a rebuke but a call to acknowledge wrongdoing before God and before men, showing that true repentance begins with recognizing one's own fault rather than deflecting blame. The passage thus models how the wronged may choose dignity and forgiveness, while the wrongdoer is reminded that sin must be confessed and its consequences faced with humility.

translation: And women in the city said, "The wife of the minister is seeking to seduce her young man away from himself. He has certainly captivated her with love. Indeed, we see her in clear error."
interpretation: The verse shows how private matters become public talk: the women of the city, who themselves are not named, turn Zulaikha's passion into gossip and mockery, reducing her to a scandal. Their words reveal that they judge by appearances and social reputation rather than by justice or compassion, and the phrase "clear error" exposes their own hypocrisy, since they condemn in another the very desire that the verse presents as a love so overpowering it seizes the heart. The passage thus invites reflection on how easily society condemns the weakness of others, and on how love and desire, when they overtake a person, can lead to both suffering and moral testing, a theme that runs through the whole story of Yusuf.

translation: So when she heard of their scheming, she sent to them and prepared for them a reclining banquet, and gave each one of them a knife, and said, "Come out before them." So when they saw him, they were struck with awe at him and cut their hands, and said, "Far be God from imperfection! This is not a human being; this is none other than a noble angel."
interpretation: The verse shows Zulaykha turning the women's gossip against them: by inviting them to a feast and handing each a knife, she set a trap in which their own astonishment at Joseph's beauty exposed their hypocrisy. Their overwhelming awe made them cut their own hands unknowingly, revealing that the same women who had mocked her were themselves undone by his presence. Their exclamation that he is no mere human but a noble angel underscores the extraordinary dignity and purity that Joseph displayed, which vindicated his steadfastness and exposed the emptiness of the criticism directed at both him and Zulaykha.

translation: She said, "That is the one you blamed me for. I did seek to seduce him, but he refused. And if he does not do what I order him, he will surely be imprisoned and will be among the humiliated."
interpretation: The verse shows the wife of the ruler, after the women of the city have condemned her, turning their blame into a defiant display: she presents Joseph before them as the reason for her shame, openly admitting her pursuit of him while confirming his chastity. Her threat of imprisonment and humiliation reveals how power, when joined with desire, seeks to coerce what it cannot win by persuasion, and it exposes the moral corruption that a worldly court can produce, in contrast with the steadfast purity of the one who refuses it.

translation: He said, "My Lord, prison is more beloved to me than what they invite me to; and unless You turn away from me their plotting, I would incline toward them and be among the ignorant."
interpretation: Yusuf's words reveal a profound awareness that worldly temptation, when dressed in the appeal of pleasure and social pressure, can weaken the heart more than hardship does. He does not trust his own strength alone; he recognizes that the will is fragile without divine support, and so he turns to God for protection. His choice of prison over sin is a deliberate preference for the trial that preserves his integrity over the comfort that would corrupt it. The phrase "among the ignorant" shows that he understands yielding to wrongdoing as a form of folly, a departure from true knowledge of what is good, and that sincere humility before God is the safeguard against it.

translation: So his Lord responded to him and turned away from him their plotting. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse shows that when a sincere servant turns to God in distress, the response of the Lord comes in the form of protection: the schemes that were woven against him are averted, not by the servant's own power but by the One who hears every plea and knows every hidden intention. The divine attributes of hearing and knowledge are mentioned to assure the believer that no cry goes unheard and no plot escapes the knowledge of God, so that trust in Him, rather than fear of human cunning, becomes the stance of the one who has been wronged.

translation: Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs, to imprison him for a while.
interpretation: The verse, from Surah Yusuf, shows how authority can override evidence when its own reputation is at stake. Though the signs of Yusuf's innocence had become plain to those in power, they chose to silence him rather than face the truth, sacrificing justice to protect their image. The phrase "after they had seen the signs" exposes the moral gap between knowing what is right and acting on it, a recurring human failing. The temporary imprisonment ironically becomes a further trial for Yusuf, and the passage warns that when people suppress truths they have recognized, the injustice they commit ultimately falls on the innocent while revealing their own inner corruption.

translation: And there entered the prison with him two young men. One of them said, "Indeed, I see myself pressing wine." And the other said, "Indeed, I see myself carrying bread on my head, of which the birds are eating. Inform us of its interpretation; indeed, we see you to be of the good-doers."
interpretation: The verse shows Joseph in prison being approached by two fellow inmates, each recounting a dream that weighed on them, and turning to him precisely because his conduct had earned their trust. Their request to be told the dream's meaning reveals that they recognized in him a person of integrity and insight, which is why they called him one of the good-doers. Within the surah, this scene prepares the ground for Joseph's role as a interpreter of dreams and, through it, a witness to God's guidance reaching people even in the confines of a prison, where his patience and righteousness were visible to those around him.

translation: He said: "No food will come to you as provision except that I will inform you of its interpretation before it reaches you. That is of what my Lord has taught me. Indeed, I have abandoned the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah and who are disbelievers in the Hereafter."
interpretation: The verse shows that Prophet Yusuf, imprisoned with two companions, uses his prophetic gift as a sign of his trust in God: before he interprets their dreams, he demonstrates a knowledge that comes from his Lord rather than from himself. He then grounds this knowledge in his rejection of the polytheistic creed of his surroundings, presenting faith in God and the Hereafter as the basis of a true religious path, and tying the gift of knowledge to the rejection of disbelief.

translation: And I follow the religion of my forefathers: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It was not for us to associate anything with Allah. That is from the bounty of Allah upon us and upon mankind, but most of mankind are not grateful.
interpretation: The verse presents the speaker's faith as a inheritance of prophetic monotheism, rooted in the line of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and grounded in the absolute refusal to associate partners with God. It shows that true tawhid is not merely a private conviction but a received mercy from God, extended to all people through the guidance He sent. The closing remark turns this into a moral reproach: humanity at large fails to recognize and give thanks for this favor, so that the grace of guidance is left unacknowledged by most.

translation: O my two fellow prisoners, are many lords scattered better, or Allah, the One, the Irresistible?
interpretation: Joseph opens his call to the two cellmates by asking them to weigh two kinds of lordship against each other. On one side stand many divided masters, each claiming a share of obedience, whose authority is fragmented and whose power is partial and contradictory. On the other stands the One God, whose oneness brings unity of purpose and whose irresistible dominion (al-Qahhar) leaves no rival able to override Him. The question is not merely theological but practical: a person who serves many lords is pulled in conflicting directions, while one who turns to the single true Lord finds a coherent and secure direction for life, even in the midst of imprisonment.

translation: You do not worship besides Him except names you and your forefathers have named, for which God has sent down no authority. Judgment belongs only to God; He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.
interpretation: The verse exposes the emptiness of idolatry: the gods worshipped besides God have no reality beyond the names people invented and inherited from their ancestors, names unsupported by any revealed proof. Since all authority to judge and legislate belongs to God alone, true worship must be directed to Him exclusively, and this pure monotheism is the straight, enduring religion. Yet the verse laments that most people remain ignorant of this truth, not because it is hidden, but because they follow custom and inherited assumptions rather than reason and revelation.

translation: O my two fellow prisoners! As for one of you, he will give his lord drink of wine; but as for the other, he will be crucified, and birds will eat from his head. The matter has been decided about which you both inquire.
interpretation: Yusuf, peace be upon him, responds to the two men's dream-inquiry by delivering a decisive interpretation that is also a test of faith. Through the phrase 'O my two fellow prisoners' he gently establishes a bond of companionship before revealing an outcome that separates their fates: one will be restored to his former service and position, while the other faces execution. The closing words, 'The matter has been decided about which you both inquire,' show that the outcome is not merely a guess but a fixed decree, and they point the listener toward the truth that knowledge of what will come belongs to God alone, who has conveyed it through His prophet. The verse thus joins prophetic knowledge of the unseen with a call to reflect on the certainty of divine decree in a setting of hardship.

translation: And he said to the one he knew would be saved among them, "Mention me in the presence of your lord." But Satan caused him to forget the mention of his lord, so he remained in prison for several years.
interpretation: The verse shows that even a prophet of God, in a moment of human reliance on worldly means, may turn to a created person for deliverance, and that this turning away from total trust in God is met with a consequence: the forgetting that Satan induced and a prolonged confinement. Joseph's request reveals how the heart can become entangled in hope placed in people rather than in the Lord alone, and how the dhikr of the Lord can be obscured by heedlessness, which the verse attributes to the whisperings of Satan. The years in prison are thus presented as a lesson on sincerity of reliance, patience, and the need to return the heart wholly to God, who in His wisdom arranges the timing of relief.

translation: And the king said, "Indeed, I see seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green spikes of grain and others withered. O chiefs, explain to me my vision, if you are able to interpret visions."
interpretation: The king's dream, relayed in this verse, sets up the central test of the Joseph narrative: the court's inability to read a symbolic vision. The contrast between the plenty of the fat cows and green ears and the leanness and dryness of their counterparts foreshadows a cycle of abundance followed by famine. The king's appeal to his chiefs, framed as a challenge to their expertise in dream interpretation, exposes the limits of worldly wisdom and prepares the way for Joseph, who alone is granted the knowledge to decode the vision and, through it, to guide Egypt through its coming hardship.

translation: They said, "These are confused jumbles of dreams, and we are not versed in the interpretation of dreams."
interpretation: The verse records the response of the courtiers of the king of Egypt when Yusuf's dream-interpretation was sought after the king's disturbing vision. Dismissing the dream as meaningless 'aḍghāth aḥlām' (tangled, incoherent dream-jumbles), they reveal a common human tendency to reject what they cannot understand and to exempt themselves from responsibility for knowledge beyond their grasp. Their words expose the gap between worldly expertise, which had failed to explain the vision, and the divinely granted insight that Yusuf possessed, a theme that prepares the reader for his release from prison and his rise to authority.

translation: And the one of the two who was saved and remembered after a period of time said, "I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me forth."
interpretation: This verse comes from the story of Prophet Yusuf in the prison, where he was asked to interpret the dreams of two fellow prisoners, one of whom was to be released and return to serving the king's drink. When that man was spared and, after a long interval, recalled Yusuf, he came back with a request to be sent to the one who could explain the dream. The verse shows that knowledge given by God can open doors even for one who has been forgotten in confinement, and that the truthful servant of God is ultimately remembered and sought out. It also reflects the patience of Yusuf, whose release was delayed for years, teaching that God's timing for relief, though it may seem long, is always in accordance with His wisdom.

translation: Joseph, O man of truth, give us your opinion concerning seven fat cows which seven lean ones devour, and seven green ears of grain and others dry; perhaps I may return to the people so that they may know.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the royal cupbearer after years in prison, marks the moment he recalls Joseph's gift of dream interpretation and seeks his counsel on the king's troubling vision. The title "al-Siddiq" (the truthful one) reflects the reputation for integrity Joseph had earned, which makes him the trusted source of a true explanation. The dream's imagery of plenty followed by famine foreshadows the coming years of abundance and scarcity in Egypt. The cupbearer's desire to "return to the people" shows a hope of restoration to his former position and of relieving the uncertainty of those who await an answer, while the closing phrase "so that they may know" points to knowledge as the purpose of his mission, and by extension to the wider lesson that divine guidance is conveyed through a sincere servant of God who is patient through hardship.

translation: He said: "You will sow for seven years in succession; so whatever you harvest, leave it in its ears of grain, except for a little which you may eat."
interpretation: The verse presents Joseph's interpretation of the king's dream as a practical plan grounded in foresight and discipline. Seven years of abundance are to be met not with indulgence but with restraint: the harvest is stored in its stalks, which protects the grain from spoiling and decay, and only a small portion is consumed. The message is that prosperity demands planning and self-control, and that wise stewardship during good times is what allows a community to endure the hardship that follows.

translation: Then after that there will come seven hard years, which will consume what you had stored up for them, except a little of what you guard.
interpretation: The verse uses the image of a seven-year famine to teach that prosperity is not permanent and that hardship follows ease as surely as night follows day. The grain stored during the years of plenty is consumed by the lean years, and only a small portion survives, which is the part that was carefully guarded. Read spiritually, worldly wealth and provision, however carefully gathered, are eventually spent, and what endures is what has been protected through wise foresight, discipline, and trust in God. The verse thus calls the believer to plan responsibly in times of abundance while not placing final reliance on the stores themselves.

translation: Then after that there will come a year in which the people will be given rain (relief), and in which they will press (juice and oil).
interpretation: The verse, spoken in the context of Joseph's interpretation of the king's dream, foretells that after seven years of abundant harvest there will follow a year of relief, in which the people will receive abundant rain and their crops and produce will flourish again so that they can press fruits and oils. It teaches that hardship is not permanent: God's providence brings ease after difficulty, and the prudent planning that Joseph advised during prosperity is what allows a community to endure scarcity and then recover. The verse also points to the reality that sustenance and relief come ultimately from God, who sends rain and restores abundance to those who trust in Him and act wisely.

translation: The king said, "Bring him to me." But when the messenger came to him, he said, "Return to your lord and ask him what was the matter with the women who cut their hands. Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plotting."
interpretation: This verse shows Yusuf's (peace be upon him) dignity, patience, and integrity. Though he had been unjustly imprisoned for years, he refuses to leave prison hastily and instead insists that his innocence be established publicly before he is released. He does not seek personal vindication through haste or mere release, but demands that the truth of the women's conduct be brought to light, so that his reputation and the justice of his case are clearly affirmed. His words also reveal his trust in God's complete knowledge: the cunning and deceit of those who wronged him are known to his Lord, who will judge them justly. The passage teaches that a believer should bear hardship with composure, seek justice through legitimate means, and rely on God as the ultimate witness over all deceit.

translation: [The king] said, "What was your situation when you sought to seduce Joseph?" They said, "Far be God from imperfection! We know of him no evil." The wife of the nobleman said, "Now the truth has become evident. It was I who sought to seduce him, and indeed he is among the truthful."
interpretation: This verse marks the moment when the truth about Joseph's innocence is finally brought to light before the court. The women who had earlier gathered and slandered him are compelled to admit they found no wrong in him, and the wife of the nobleman, no longer able to conceal the matter, openly confesses her own attempt to seduce him. Her words "now the truth has become evident" show that sincere acknowledgment of wrongdoing is the path by which hidden falsehood is exposed and integrity is restored. Joseph's patience through imprisonment and false accusation is thereby vindicated, illustrating that God ultimately reveals the truth of those who remain steadfast and upright.

translation: That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that Allah does not guide the plotting of the treacherous.
interpretation: The verse is the words of the woman of the Aziz's household, who, after the truth of the matter had emerged, acknowledges that her accusation against Joseph was false and that he remained innocent even when unseen by the king. Her declaration that she never betrayed him in secret teaches that true integrity is preserved even when one is not observed, since God knows what is hidden. Her closing remark, that Allah does not guide the schemes of the treacherous, sets forth a general principle: deceit and intrigue, however carefully planned, cannot achieve lasting success, because divine guidance and favor do not accompany those who betray trust. The verse thus binds a personal confession to a broader moral lesson about the futility of treachery and the vindication that comes to the truthful.

translation: And I do not declare myself innocent; indeed, the soul is certainly inclined to evil, except those upon which my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse expresses a profound humility and self-scrutiny: even one who has been honored and entrusted cannot claim moral purity on his own strength. It reveals that the nafs (the self) by its nature tends toward wrongdoing, pulling a person toward desire and evil, so that safety from this tendency comes not from one's own merit but from divine mercy. The closing divine names, Forgiving and Merciful, direct the believer to hope in Allah's grace rather than in self-assurance, teaching that true integrity lies in recognizing one's weakness and continually seeking God's protection and forgiveness.

translation: And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself." So when he spoke with him, he said, "Indeed, you are today with us established and trusted."
interpretation: This verse, from the story of Yusuf (Joseph), marks the turning point where his integrity and wisdom, proven through patience in adversity, are finally recognized by the ruler. The king's desire to keep him close reflects how sincerity and competence eventually open doors that injustice had closed. It also shows that Yusuf's trustworthiness was not merely claimed but witnessed directly in conversation, as the king came to see in his character what the prison had concealed. The verse teaches that divine providence can elevate a person who remains faithful to truth, and that true standing comes from established character rather than from circumstance.

translation: He said, "Appoint me over the storehouses of the land; indeed, I am a knowledgeable guardian."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Joseph (peace be upon him) to the king of Egypt, reveals a principled request for responsibility rather than a mere desire for power. Having shown his integrity and wisdom in interpreting the king's dream, Joseph does not seek office for personal gain but offers his qualifications, namely his trustworthiness (hafiz) and his knowledge ('alim), as the grounds for entrusting him with the nation's resources. It teaches that a person may legitimately present their competence when the public good depends on it, especially in a time of coming hardship, while the stewardship of wealth must rest on careful preservation and sound knowledge.

translation: And thus We established Joseph in the land, to settle therein wherever he willed. We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will, and We do not waste the reward of the good-doers.
interpretation: The verse shows that Joseph's deliverance from the well, prison, and servitude was not merely a personal rescue but a divine establishment of him in authority over the land, reached through patient steadfastness in goodness. Its central teaching is that God's mercy is a sovereign gift, granted to whomever He chooses, yet it is never arbitrary toward the one who does good: their reward is preserved and will not be lost. Joseph's trials and his ascent thus express the pattern by which hardship endured with righteousness is ultimately turned into a station of honor and influence, placing responsibility on the believer to remain virtuous while trusting in God's wisdom over the timing and form of his reward.

translation: And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and were mindful of God.
interpretation: This verse draws a clear contrast between the fleeting rewards of this world and the enduring recompense of the Hereafter. Its promise is not merely that the next life is better, but that it is better specifically for those who combine faith with taqwa, a consciousness of God that guards them in their conduct. Faith is thus shown to be inseparable from righteous behavior: belief that does not express itself in mindful, disciplined living falls short of the standard the verse sets. The verse also invites the believer to reorder priorities, measuring worldly gains and losses against what lasts, so that patience, honesty, and restraint in this life are understood as investments in a far greater reward.

translation: And the brothers of Joseph came and entered upon him, so he recognized them, while they did not recognize him.
interpretation: The verse marks a turning point in the narrative: the brothers who once cast Joseph away now stand before him in Egypt as supplicants, unaware that the one whom they had abandoned holds authority over them. Joseph recognizes them immediately, while they remain blind to who he is, which reveals the reversal of positions that divine providence has arranged. Their non-recognition reflects how their own past deeds have veiled them from the truth, while Joseph's recognition shows the steadfast memory and inner clarity of one who has endured hardship with patience. The scene thus carries a lesson that what is hidden from people's eyes is fully known to God, and that the consequences of one's actions can return in unexpected ways.

translation: And when he had equipped them with their supplies, he said: "Bring me a brother of yours from your father. Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of hosts?"
interpretation: Joseph, having provided his brothers with their provisions, sets a condition for their return: they must bring the brother who shares their father, Benjamin. His words combine a claim of integrity, that he gives full measure and does not cheat, with a claim of generous hospitality toward guests. The verse shows him testing his brothers' honesty and their attachment to their family, while planting the means by which the scattered family will eventually be reunited, all under a plan that serves a larger wisdom the reader is only beginning to glimpse.

translation: But if you do not bring him to me, then there will be no measure (of grain) for you from me, and do not come near me.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Yaqub (Jacob) to his sons in Surah Yusuf (12:60), reflects a condition set by a just but firm father who, having already entrusted Benjamin's safety to them once before, now refuses to be deceived again. The withdrawal of the grain allotment is a practical consequence that exposes the brothers' material need and dependence, and the prohibition against approaching him signals a severing of access until they fulfil the test of faithfulness. It teaches that trust, once broken, must be rebuilt through deeds, and that providence often operates through the very hardships that compel people to reconsider their conduct and return to what is right.

translation: They said: "We will seek to win him over from his father, and indeed we will do it."
interpretation: The brothers of Yusuf, having agreed among themselves on their scheme, reveal their resolve with a firm commitment: they will employ persistent effort and cunning to draw their father's favor and attention away from Yusuf, and they affirm that they will certainly carry it out. The verse exposes how envy can harden into deliberate plotting, and how the wrongdoer often speaks with confident determination about a harm he has already decided to commit, a warning that resolve in evil is no less dangerous for being spoken calmly.

translation: And he said to his servants, "Put their merchandise back into their saddlebags, so that they may recognize it when they return to their family, that perhaps they will come back."
interpretation: The verse shows Yusuf's careful strategy in dealing with his brothers: by secretly returning their goods into their baggage, he creates a pretext that obliges them to come back, while his hidden purpose is to reunite with his family. It reveals a wisdom that works through subtle means, leaving the brothers to discover the gift themselves, and it also foreshadows the moral reckoning that their return will eventually bring about.

translation: So when they returned to their father, they said: "O our father, measure is withheld from us, so send with us our brother that we may get our measure, and indeed we will be its guardians."
interpretation: The verse shows the brothers approaching their father with a practical need turned into a plea: the denial of grain is a trial that compels them to seek trust again. Their request to take Benjamin along is wrapped in a promise of protection, which reveals that their earlier failure with Joseph has made them aware that words of assurance must be backed by deeds. The passage thus points to the moral weight of trust, the tension between necessity and reliance on God, and the way hardship can open the path toward reconciliation with the past.

translation: He said: Shall I trust you with him except as I trusted you with his brother before? But God is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful.
interpretation: The verse shows Jacob's hesitation to entrust Benjamin to his sons after their earlier failure with Joseph, so his refusal rests on painful experience rather than mere suspicion. His reply turns from human promises to reliance on God, the best guardian, whose mercy surpasses all others. The lesson is that when human assurances have failed, the believer's true security lies in placing trust in God, while still acting with prudence.

translation: And when they opened their belongings, they found their merchandise had been returned to them. They said, "O our father, what more could we want? This is our merchandise, returned to us. And we will provide for our family, and guard our brother, and gain an extra camel's load. That is an easy measure."
interpretation: The brothers' words reveal a shift from anxious doubt to renewed hope. Discovering that their payment had been returned, they see it not as a hardship but as a sign of good fortune and fair dealing, and they take it as a reason to go back to Egypt. Their speech lays out their reasoning in measured steps: securing food for their households, returning with Benjamin to keep him safe, and gaining an additional measure of grain. Their closing remark that this measure is easy points to the ease that God grants when a person turns to Him with trust, even after past failures. The passage quietly contrasts their ready eagerness with the trust they had yet to show in their father's promise to protect their brother, inviting reflection on how a sense of provision can lead people toward commitment before their hearts are fully ready.

translation: He said, "I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn covenant in Allah's name that you will surely bring him back to me, unless you are completely overpowered." And when they gave him their solemn covenant, he said, "Allah is Witness over what we say."
interpretation: The verse shows Ya'qub's caution after the sons' earlier failure with Yusuf: he refuses to entrust Benjamin to them without a binding oath sworn by Allah, making divine witness the guarantee of their trust. His stipulation of an exception, being overpowered, reflects a realistic acknowledgment that human will has limits and that only God's ultimate decree is beyond human control. His closing words place the matter entirely under God's oversight, teaching that reliance (tawakkul) should rest on Allah, who witnesses every pledge and every word spoken.

translation: And he said, "O my sons, do not enter from one gate but enter from different gates. And I cannot avail you anything against Allah. Indeed, the decision is only for Allah. In Him I have placed my trust, and upon Him let those who trust rely."
interpretation: Ya'qub's counsel to his sons reveals that taking lawful means and precautions is itself part of trusting God, yet no measure of human planning can override divine decree. By entering through separate gates, he avoids giving the appearance of a single threatening group that might provoke suspicion or harm, showing that prudent action is compatible with reliance on God. His immediate disclaimer that he can benefit them not at all against God establishes that the ultimate authority rests with Allah alone, so that caution never becomes a source of false security. Thus the verse teaches a balanced tawakkul: exert effort wisely, but place the final outcome entirely in the hands of the One whose judgment alone prevails.

translation: And when they entered from where their father had instructed them, it did not avail them anything against Allah; it was only a need within the soul of Jacob, which he fulfilled. And indeed, he was a possessor of knowledge because of what We had taught him, but most of the people do not know.
interpretation: The verse shows that Jacob's precaution, though sound and commanded by a father's care, could not shield his sons from what Allah had decreed; it was a means he employed out of paternal concern, a need he discharged within himself, while true reliance and knowledge come from Allah's teaching. Jacob's prior knowledge was a divinely granted insight, yet most people fail to grasp that such knowledge, like all means, operates only by Allah's permission, and that a believer must both take the means and place his trust wholly in the One who decrees outcomes.

translation: And when they entered upon Joseph, he drew his brother close to himself and said, "Indeed, I am your brother, so do not grieve over what they used to do."
interpretation: The verse shows Joseph reaching out to Benjamin in a private, tender moment after the brothers' long ordeal in Egypt. Having withheld his identity, Joseph first offers the one brother who was not party to the old wrong the comfort of recognition, assuring him that the sorrow inflicted by the others need not weigh on his heart. The phrase "do not grieve" points to a deeper lesson: that God's plan transforms past injustice into a means of reunion and mercy, so that a believer may release old pain and rest in the wisdom of what has unfolded.

translation: So when he had furnished them with their provisions, he put the drinking cup into his brother's baggage. Then a crier called out: "O caravan, you are indeed thieves!"
interpretation: The verse shows Joseph devising a stratagem, with divine guidance, to keep his full brother Benjamin with him under a lawful pretext, since the king's law did not allow him to seize him otherwise. The accusation of theft is thus a planned test that brings the brothers to confront their past treatment of Joseph and their earlier betrayal. It also teaches that worldly provisions and outward arrangements are ultimately under God's command, which is why the narrative places Joseph's plan within a larger providential design that reconciles the family in the end.

translation: They said, turning toward them: "What is it that you are missing?"
interpretation: The verse depicts the moment when the king's servants (the officials of the king of Egypt) are searching for the missing drinking cup, which was in fact placed in Benjamin's baggage as part of a plan devised by Joseph. Their turning toward the brothers and their question carry the tone of an official inquiry: the scene shows the brothers being confronted and forced to face an accusation they did not expect. Beneath the surface, the verse is a turning point in the narrative, in which Joseph arranges circumstances that test his brothers' character and open the way to the eventual reconciliation between them. It also reminds the reader that worldly accusations can be a means through which divine wisdom unfolds, even when the innocent appear to be under suspicion.

translation: They said: "We have lost the king's goblet, and for whoever brings it is a camel's load, and I guarantee it."
interpretation: The verse, from the story of Joseph, shows the brothers' officials announcing a reward of a camel's load for the return of the king's goblet, with the speaker personally guaranteeing payment. It reflects the setting of a formal public proclamation, in which a pledge of compensation is made with binding assurance. Within the narrative, the scene prepares the way for the stratagem by which Joseph keeps his brother Benjamin, and it highlights how the brothers are drawn into a situation they cannot easily escape, since the reward is openly sworn by a responsible guarantor.

translation: They said, "By God, you know well that we did not come to cause corruption in the land, and we were not thieves."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the brothers of Joseph when they were accused of theft in Egypt, reveals a defensive appeal to shared knowledge and oath. They invoke God as witness and appeal to what the officials already know of their conduct, asserting that their purpose in coming to Egypt was honest, namely to obtain food during the famine, not to spread corruption or steal. The verse shows how a person facing unjust suspicion may turn to their track record and to an oath to establish innocence, while also reflecting the anxious tension of brothers whose past deeds still weighed on them.

translation: They said, "Then what will be its recompense, if you are liars?"
interpretation: The verse records the words of the brothers of Yusuf (or the interrogators in the narrative, as the context of the speech indicates), who, having been accused of theft, are asked to bear the consequences of their own claim. By asking for the penalty to be fixed in advance on the one found guilty, they accept a principle of self-binding justice: the one who is shown to have taken what was not his shall bear the due consequence. The conditional phrase "if you are liars" reveals a moral seriousness in which a person who stakes his word must also stake his liability, so that truth and accountability are bound together. The verse thus teaches that a claim of innocence is best demonstrated when the claimant willingly submits to a just standard of recompense that he himself would accept.

translation: They said, "The penalty for it: whoever is found to have it in his bag, he himself is its penalty. Thus do we requite the wrongdoers."
interpretation: The verse reflects an ancient legal custom in which the thief himself bears the consequence of his act, becoming the one who pays for what he took, which underscores personal accountability and the principle that a wrongdoer must answer for his own wrong. The closing phrase, "Thus do we requite the wrongdoers," shows that this was not an arbitrary punishment but a divinely sanctioned measure of justice applied to those who violate others' rights, and it reminds the reader that wrongdoing inevitably returns upon the one who commits it. Read within the story of Joseph, the ruling also reveals a providential plan: by the custom of the land Joseph could not seize his brother under the king's law, yet under the custom of the household the law of restitution allowed him to keep Benjamin, so that the wrong of the brothers' earlier conduct was brought to light in a way that led toward reconciliation.

translation: So he began with their bags before the bag of his brother, then he brought it out from his brother's bag. Thus did We plan for Joseph. He could not have taken his brother under the king's law, except that Allah willed it. We raise in degrees whom We will, and over every possessor of knowledge is one more knowing.
interpretation: The verse shows that Joseph's stratagem, though it appeared as a harsh deception toward his brothers, was a divinely guided plan (kidna) that Allah arranged so that Joseph could keep his brother Benjamin under the king's own legal system, which otherwise offered him no lawful means of detaining him. The phrase 'except that Allah wills' teaches that every human device succeeds only by God's permission, and the closing statement that God raises whom He wills in rank, and that above every knowing person there is one more knowledgeable, reminds the reader that human knowledge and cleverness are always bounded and surpassed by the infinite knowledge of God.

translation: They said, "If he steals, then a brother of his has indeed stolen before." So Joseph concealed it within himself and did not reveal it to them. He said, "You are worse in position, and Allah is most knowing of what you describe."
interpretation: The brothers, seeking to free their youngest brother, falsely accuse Benjamin by pointing to an earlier theft attributed to Joseph, whose true nature they had concealed. Joseph, stung by the slander yet controlling his feelings, hides his anguish and does not disclose his identity or the matter to them. His reply turns their accusation back on them: their own conduct toward Joseph and their father was far worse, and God alone knows the truth of what they fabricate and claim.

translation: They said, "O you who hold authority, indeed he has an elderly father, so take one of us in his place. Indeed, we see you are among the doers of good."
interpretation: The brothers of Joseph, faced with the loss of Benjamin, approach the Egyptian ruler with humility and appeal to his compassion by invoking the grief of their aged father, while flattering him as a benefactor. Their plea reveals both the weight of their guilt toward Joseph and a shift in their character: they now offer themselves as substitutes out of concern for their father, a sign of the moral growth that the unfolding story is meant to bring about in them.

translation: He said: "God forbid that we should take anyone except him with whom we found our property; indeed, then we would be wrongdoers."
interpretation: The verse shows Joseph's brothers' insistence on the principle of justice and integrity: they are unwilling to take an innocent person in place of the one who was found holding the king's cup, because doing so would be a clear injustice. Joseph, having arranged for the cup to be placed in Benjamin's bag, now stands at a moment of testing where the brothers' conduct, which earlier betrayed him, is shown to have changed. Their refusal to commit wrong, even when it benefits them, reflects a moral transformation and reveals the depth of their sense of accountability before God. The statement also underlines the Qur'anic teaching that one is not held responsible for another's wrongdoing, and that taking the innocent in place of the guilty is itself a form of zulm.

translation: So when they despaired of him, they withdrew to confer privately. The eldest of them said: Did you not know that your father had taken from you a solemn pledge in the name of God, and that before this you had failed in regard to Joseph? So I will never leave this land until my father permits me, or God decides for me. And He is the best of judges.
interpretation: The verse shows the brothers of Joseph, having lost hope of securing the release of their younger brother Benjamin, turning inward to deliberate in secret, and it is their eldest, who had been the most resolute in his restraint, who reminds them of the covenant their father exacted from them and of their earlier betrayal of Joseph. His resolve to remain in Egypt rather than return empty-handed reflects a moral reckoning: the guilt of the past compels him to accept responsibility and to entrust the outcome to God's judgment, the wisest of judges, rather than to his own strength or to despair.

translation: Return to your father and say, 'O our father, indeed your son has stolen, and we did not testify except to what we knew, and we were not witnesses of the unseen.'
interpretation: The brothers of Joseph, returning from Egypt without Benjamin, are sent back with a carefully worded report that protects them from blame. Their statement that they testify only to what they knew reveals a guarded honesty: they speak about what they witnessed, while admitting they could not guard against what happened in secret. The verse exposes the limits of human knowledge and responsibility. It also shows how the brothers, still burdened by their past treatment of Joseph, are cautious in what they claim, and it prepares the reader for the father's grief and his trust in God.

translation: And ask the town in which we were and the caravan in which we came, and indeed, we are truthful.
interpretation: The brothers, accused of theft in Egypt, do not rely on oaths alone but invite their accusers to verify their account through witnesses, the people of the town they left and the travelling company they journeyed with. Their appeal shows that sincerity is best established through open, checkable evidence, and that a person who is truthful has nothing to fear from investigation. Their closing declaration of truthfulness is thus backed by a challenge to test it, reflecting the confidence of those who are innocent of what they are charged with.

translation: He said: "Rather, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you. So patience is most fitting. Perhaps Allah will bring them all back to me. Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."
interpretation: The verse shows Jacob's response to the news of his sons' return without Benjamin and of the story they told him. He recognizes that the outward account was not the whole truth and that their inner selves had adorned a grim deed as if it were acceptable, so he does not deny what he senses but turns his grief toward beautiful patience. Rather than despairing, he places his hope in Allah, trusting that the One who knows all hidden matters and governs with wisdom can reunite him with his children. The verse teaches that when a trial exposes the deceptions of the self, the believer responds with sincere patience and steadfast reliance on God's knowledge and wisdom.

translation: And he turned away from them and said, "Oh, my grief over Joseph!" and his eyes turned white from the sorrow, and he was suppressing (his anguish).
interpretation: The verse portrays Jacob (Ya'qub) as a father whose grief is so deep that it bodily consumes him: his eyes whiten from weeping, yet he does not voice complaint against his sons, but restrains his sorrow in silent patience. His 'kazm' (suppression of anger and grief) is a form of inner dignity and trust in God, the same patience (sabr) that he will later express when he says that his only recourse is to God. The verse thus teaches that true patience does not mean the absence of pain, but the containment of pain within faith, so that grief becomes a sign of love rather than despair.

translation: They said, "By God, you will not stop remembering Joseph until you become consumed with grief or become among the perishing."
interpretation: The verse captures the alarm of Joseph's sons as they watch their father Jacob's relentless sorrow over Joseph, whom he has not stopped mourning. Their words reveal how grief that has no end can wear down the body and spirit until a person is reduced to a shadow of himself. Yet the sons speak from outside the depth of Jacob's faith and patience, which the surah presents elsewhere as steadfast trust in God. Their concern is human and understandable, and it highlights the contrast between worldly despair at the loss of a loved one and the hope in God's mercy that Jacob ultimately affirms.

translation: He said, "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah what you do not know."
interpretation: Jacob's words reveal a heart that, even while mourning the loss of his sons, refuses to surrender to despair. By turning his complaint toward Allah alone, he models a faith that places sorrow before the One who can relieve it, rather than before people who cannot. His added statement that he knows from Allah what they do not know points to a hope grounded in divine knowledge: he trusts that Allah has information and purposes hidden from his sons, and that the trials he endures may conceal mercy and a future reunion that they cannot yet perceive. The verse thus teaches that grief is not incompatible with trust in God, and that true patience is a complaint lodged with Allah rather than a complaint against Him.

translation: O my sons, go and seek news of Joseph and his brother, and do not despair of relief from God. Indeed, no one despairs of relief from God except the disbelieving people.
interpretation: The verse shows that despair of God's mercy is itself a form of disbelief, since it presumes that God's power and compassion have limits. Jacob's command to his sons teaches that a believer must keep striving and hoping even amid long trials and loss, acting on the means available while trusting that relief (rawh) from God can come at any moment. Hope in God's mercy is thus presented as an integral part of faith, and giving up on it as a mark of those who reject Him.

translation: So when they entered upon him, they said, "O Chief, adversity has touched us and our family, and we have come with meager merchandise, so give us full measure and be charitable to us. Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable."
interpretation: The verse shows the brothers of Yusuf approaching him in a state of humble need, having been reduced to poverty and hardship in a famine. Their appeal is marked by candor rather than pride: they admit their goods are inferior and rely entirely on the nobility of the one they address, asking for justice in measure and for generosity beyond what they deserve. Their closing remark, that Allah rewards those who give in charity, is a subtle plea that quietly invokes the principle of divine recompense to move his heart, and it prepares the scene for the moment of recognition that follows, where mercy and forgiveness are shown to them.

translation: He said: "Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother, when you were ignorant?"
interpretation: The verse captures the moment of reckoning in which Joseph, now established in power in Egypt, confronts his brothers with their past wrongdoing without immediately revealing his identity. His question is not merely an accusation but a gentle invitation to self-examination: it draws their attention to the gravity of what they had done, framed by the phrase "when you were ignorant," which suggests that their act was born of blindness and jealousy rather than settled malice. The mention of Joseph together with his full brother (Benjamin) also points to the wound of their favoritism and their casting-off of the innocent. By recalling the past in this way, the verse opens the path to repentance, forgiveness, and the reconciliation that the surah ultimately brings about, showing that acknowledging a wrong is the first step toward its healing.

translation: They said, "Are you indeed Joseph?" He said, "I am Joseph, and this is my brother. Allah has certainly been gracious to us. Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient - then indeed, Allah does not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost."
interpretation: The verse captures the moment of recognition between Joseph and his brothers, after years of separation, trial, and hidden identity. Joseph's answer does not dwell on the wrongs done to him but acknowledges that his elevation and reunion are a favor (mann) from Allah, shifting the focus from personal grievance to gratitude. He then grounds this grace in a general principle: taqwa joined with patience is the path by which Allah's favor is secured, and no good deed is ever wasted. The verse thus teaches that patience through hardship and God-consciousness, when sustained, lead ultimately to honor and reward, and that a believer should attribute success to God rather than to his own merit.

translation: They said: "By Allah, indeed Allah has preferred you over us, and we were certainly sinners."
interpretation: The brothers of Yusuf, confronted with the evident greatness that Allah had bestowed upon him, are compelled to acknowledge both his elevated station and their own wrongdoing. Their words reveal a belated humility born of guilt: they recognize that Allah chose Yusuf for honor and favor while they had erred against him. The verse shows that true repentance begins with an honest admission of fault, and that divine preference, though it may be resented in the moment, is ultimately revealed as justice and grace.

translation: He said, "No reproach upon you today. May Allah forgive you, and He is the most merciful of the merciful."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Yusuf to his brothers who had wronged him, shows that true forgiveness lifts the burden of blame at the very moment of reconciliation, closing the past rather than keeping it open as a weapon. By directing them to Allah's forgiveness and mercy, he also teaches that a person who forgives should not claim for himself the role of judge over others' sins, but should point the repentant toward the infinite mercy of their Lord. The verse thus joins magnanimity toward people with humility before God, presenting pardon as both a social healing and a reflection of the divine attribute of mercy.

translation: Go with this shirt of mine and cast it over my father's face; he will regain his sight. And bring to me all your family.
interpretation: The verse, spoken by Joseph to his brothers in Surah Yusuf (12:93), shows that his request is not merely a practical arrangement but a sign of the trust that bond with his father sustained through long separation. The shirt becomes a vehicle of divine mercy: the same garment that had carried the false evidence of his loss now carries the means of restoring sight, so that grief is reversed by the very object that once symbolized it. Joseph's call to gather the whole family reflects a movement from estrangement toward reconciliation, where the brothers who wronged him are invited into a restored household, and the scattered family is made whole again under the sign of patience and God's providence.

translation: And when the caravan departed, their father said, "Indeed, I perceive the scent of Joseph, if you would not think me senile."
interpretation: The verse marks the moment of separation from the caravan, when Jacob, though far away and without any physical means of knowing, senses the presence of Joseph through a scent. This points to the intimate bond between the prophet and his son, and to the way divine favor can grant a believer knowledge beyond ordinary perception. Jacob's words also reveal his fear of being mocked by those around him for speaking of what they cannot see, yet he chooses to speak the truth he feels, teaching that sincere conviction in God's mercy should not yield to the doubts of others.

translation: They said, "By God, you are surely in your old error."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the sons of Jacob to their father Ya'qub (Jacob) concerning his persistent grief over Yusuf (Joseph), reveals how those who measure matters only by outward appearances can mistake the steadfast hope of a believer for foolishness. Their words reflect a worldly reckoning that cannot grasp the bond between a heart and the mercy of God, and the verse thereby teaches that the one who trusts in God's relief may appear to others to be lost in an old delusion, while in truth he is anchored in a certainty that they do not yet perceive.

translation: So when the bearer of good news arrived, he cast it (the shirt) over his face, and he regained his sight. He said, "Did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?"
interpretation: The verse shows that Ya'qub's (Jacob's) certainty rested on a knowledge granted to him directly by Allah, which his sons lacked. Despite years of grief and apparent despair, his trust in God's mercy never wavered, and when the good news came, it was confirmed exactly as he had hoped. The restoration of his sight is presented as a sign that patient, steadfast hope in Allah is rewarded, and that what appears impossible to people is never beyond God's power. The reminder to his sons is a call to recognize that human judgment is limited, while divine knowledge encompasses what people cannot see.

translation: They said, "O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins. Indeed, we have been sinners."
interpretation: The brothers of Joseph, having been confronted with the enormity of what they had done to him and to their father, turn to Jacob in a moment of humbled confession. Their request reveals a shift from envy and deceit toward repentance: they do not merely seek their father's favor but acknowledge that their wrongdoing stands before God and needs His pardon. By placing the plea for forgiveness through their father, they show that they recognize the weight of his fatherly standing and the bond they had broken. The verse teaches that genuine repentance begins with the plain admission of fault, spoken without evasion, and that seeking forgiveness, whether from God or from those we have wronged, is the path by which broken relationships and a troubled heart may be restored.

translation: He said: "I will ask my Lord to forgive you. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) to his father or to his people, reveals the tender patience of a prophet who, even after being rejected, responds with a promise of prayer rather than harshness. It teaches that the believer's sincere concern for others persists beyond disagreement, and that turning to God for forgiveness is the proper refuge.
