Their tireless and precise orbits are not merely cosmic phenomena but signs of a wise Creator who has ordered the universe so that human life may be sustained, ordered and made meaningful. Man is thus invited to recognize that the reliability of the heavens is a gift and a call to gratitude, reflection and orderly living, since the same law that keeps the celestial bodies in motion also governs the rhythm of time by which people work, rest and worship.

translation: And He gave you of all that you asked of Him. And if you should count the favors of Allah, you could not enumerate them. Indeed, mankind is [generally] a wrongdoer and ungrateful.
interpretation: The verse points to the vast, uncountable bounty of God, which He bestows on people beyond what they even request, so that the very inability to number His favors should humble the heart. The verse then turns to the human condition: the wrongdoing (zulm) of mankind lies in failing to recognize these gifts, placing things where they do not belong, and the ingratitude (kufr) it names is the concealing of blessings. Gratitude, in this light, is the recognition that every good thing is a gift and the response of worship and right conduct toward the Giver.

translation: And [mention] when Abraham said: "My Lord, make this city secure, and keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols."
interpretation: The supplication reveals that the foundation of a righteous society and a secure home is tawhid: Abraham asks for safety for the land before anything else, yet he immediately links that worldly security to protection from idolatry, showing that spiritual peace is inseparable from physical peace. His plea also reflects a prophet's awareness of his own vulnerability to temptation, for he asks God to keep even himself and his descendants from idol-worship, teaching that true faith is a constant request for divine protection rather than a settled achievement.

translation: My Lord, indeed they have led astray many of the people. So whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me, then indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse is the supplication of Abraham (Ibrahim), peace be upon him, as recorded in Surah Ibrahim (14:36), in which he speaks of the idols he had prayed to be kept away from. He attributes the misguidance of many people to the idols, which were the means by which they strayed from the worship of God. His words "whoever follows me is of me" express a bond of spiritual kinship rooted in the adherence to the path of monotheism, while his turning to God's forgiveness and mercy for those who disobey reveals a compassionate heart that does not curse them but leaves their matter to the boundless mercy of the Lord. The verse teaches that a prophet's concern extends even to those who oppose him, and that the true refuge of the believer, when facing the widespread deviation of people, is to entrust them to God's forgiveness and mercy.

translation: Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a barren valley near Your sacred House, our Lord, that they may establish prayer. So make hearts among people incline toward them, and provide for them with fruits, that perhaps they may be grateful.
interpretation: This verse is the supplication of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) after he left his wife Hajar and son Isma'il in the arid valley of Makkah beside the Sacred House. Its central theme is the purpose of settling the family there: not merely to dwell in a desolate place, but to establish the prayer, so that the sanctuary becomes a center of worship and devotion to God. Ibrahim then asks for two provisions: that hearts be drawn toward them, so that people would come to them and the place would be inhabited and sustained, and that they be given sustenance from the fruits, which reflects God's answer in making Makkah a destination for all kinds of produce. The verse closes with the hope that they would be thankful, showing that the ultimate aim of divine provision is gratitude, and that worship and thankfulness are the purpose behind sustenance and the blessing of a sacred place.

translation: Our Lord, You indeed know what we conceal and what we disclose. And nothing is hidden from Allah, on the earth or in the heaven.
interpretation: The verse, spoken by the believers in their supplication (it is from Surah Ibrahim, 14:38, where Ibrahim addresses his Lord after settling his offspring in the barren valley near the Sacred House), turns the act of prayer into an admission of total dependence on a Lord whose knowledge encompasses the inner world of the heart. The one praying does not need to explain his need in words, because what he hides in his chest and what he openly expresses are equally known to God. This knowledge is meant to produce two effects in the servant: sincerity, since there is no point in performing for an audience that cannot see the heart, and hope, since the One who knows the hidden anguish of the heart is also the One who can relieve it. The closing affirmation that nothing on earth or in heaven escapes Him frames the believer's entire life, so that every secret intention, private sin, and hidden longing is held before a Lord who is never absent from it.

translation: All praise is due to Allah, who has granted me, in my old age, Ismail and Isaac. Indeed, my Lord is the Hearer of supplication.
interpretation: This verse is the grateful exclamation of Abraham after receiving glad tidings of children in his advanced age. It teaches that true gratitude follows the fulfillment of a prayer, and that a believer should recognize divine generosity even when it arrives after long patience and when natural means seem exhausted. Abraham's words also reveal a deep trust in God's responsiveness: the one who has answered past prayers is the one who hears every plea, so hope should never be abandoned, however late the answer may come.

translation: My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and [among] my descendants. Our Lord, and accept my supplication.
interpretation: This verse is the supplication of Abraham (Ibrahim), peace be upon him, made after he settled part of his family in the barren valley of Mecca near the Sacred House. Having just completed the building of the Ka'bah, he turns to God not only asking for his own steadfastness in prayer but extending the request to his offspring, showing that true faith includes concern for the spiritual continuity of one's family and future generations. The phrase "establisher of prayer" (muqim al-salat) points to more than performing the prayer occasionally; it means maintaining it with its outward forms, inner presence, and consistency. The closing plea, "accept my supplication," reflects the humility of a believer who, even after great acts of obedience, recognizes that acceptance rests entirely with God and asks for it with sincerity.

translation: Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the day the reckoning is established.
interpretation: This supplication, placed in the Qur'an as the prayer of the believers, reveals the proper posture of a servant before the Day of Judgment: rather than relying on his own deeds alone, he turns to God's mercy and seeks forgiveness first for himself, then extends his prayer to the parents who raised him and to the wider community of believers. The verse thus binds personal repentance to a sense of collective responsibility and filial gratitude, reminding the reader that on the day when accounts are settled, the hope of salvation rests on divine pardon, and that love for one's family and fellow believers is part of a sincere faith that seeks good for others even in the moment of standing before God.

translation: And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do. He only delays them until a Day when eyes will stare fixedly in horror.
interpretation: The verse addresses the heart that might be deceived by the apparent respite granted to oppressors, reading their continued ease as a sign that God has forgotten or overlooked their injustice. It corrects this assumption by making clear that the delay is not neglect but a measured postponement, a suspension of their reckoning until a day when the full consequence of their deeds will be exposed. The image of fixed, staring eyes conveys the overwhelming dread of that moment, when the illusions of power and impunity vanish and every person confronts what they have done. The lesson is one of patience for the oppressed and a warning to the oppressor: divine justice is certain even when it appears slow.

translation: Hastening forward, with their heads raised high, their gaze not returning to them, and their hearts empty as air.
interpretation: The verse portrays the people on the Day of Judgment in a state of overwhelming terror and bewilderment. Rushing headlong toward the summons, with heads lifted and eyes fixed in a frozen stare, they are stripped of all composure and self-awareness, and their hearts have become hollow and void of understanding, as though emptied of courage, reason, and hope. It is a vivid image of the utter helplessness of those who once stood in heedless arrogance before their Lord, now confronted with the reality they had denied.

translation: And warn mankind of the Day when the punishment will come to them, and those who wronged will say, "Our Lord, delay us for a short term; we will answer Your call and follow the messengers." [They will be told], "Did you not swear before that there would be for you no cessation?"
interpretation: The verse portrays the moment of reckoning as one in which the wrongdoers, faced with the punishment they once denied, seek a brief reprieve they would never have granted to themselves in life. Their plea reveals that the truth of the messengers has become evident to them only when it is too late to act on it, and their promise to obey is exposed as hollow by the rebuke that they had earlier sworn they would never face decline or end. The verse thus warns that arrogance in worldly life, which treats the prospect of accountability as impossible, is itself the means by which a person is ensnared when the appointed time arrives.

translation: And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who had wronged themselves, and it became clear to you how We dealt with them, and We set forth for you the examples.
interpretation: The verse directs the listeners' attention to the ruins of past peoples who denied their messengers and oppressed their own souls, places the believers could still see and walk through. Their dwelling in those abandoned homes should prompt reflection that the same divine justice applies to every community that persists in wrongdoing, so that the stories of destruction become a lesson rather than mere history. By stating that the examples have been struck for them, God makes the lessons of earlier generations a clear, accessible guide, asking the hearers to draw the moral conclusion and turn away from the path that led those peoples to ruin.

translation: And they have planned their scheme, but with Allah is their scheme [recorded], though their scheme was such that the mountains would be moved by it.
interpretation: The verse portrays the disbelievers' conspiracies against the message as immense and fearsome, so much so that they could shake the mountains, yet it assures the believers that every such plot is fully known to God and encompassed by His knowledge and power. Their scheming, however great it appears, is ultimately within God's control and cannot overturn His decree or harm His truth. The imagery conveys both the gravity of the opposition faced by the Prophet and his community and the steadfast reassurance that divine planning surpasses all human designs.

translation: So do not think that Allah will fail to fulfill His promise to His messengers. Indeed, Allah is Exalted in Might, Owner of retribution.
interpretation: The verse reassures the Prophet and the believers that Allah's promise of victory and support for His messengers is certain and will not be broken, even when the messengers seem overwhelmed by opposition and delay. The apparent delay is not a failure of divine promise but part of a wisdom that tests and refines the believers. Allah's might ensures He is never thwarted, and His being the Owner of retribution means that those who oppose His messengers and persist in wrongdoing will ultimately face the consequences of their actions. Thus the verse joins hope for the righteous with a sober warning to the wrongdoers, grounding trust in God's justice and power rather than in the immediate appearance of events.

translation: On the Day when the earth will be changed into a different earth, and the heavens as well, and they will come forth before God, the One, the Subduer.
interpretation: The verse points to the final reckoning as a cosmic transformation, not merely the end of the present world but its replacement by a new order. The earth and heavens, which humans take for granted as fixed, are shown to be contingent creations that will be remade at God's command. The phrase 'they came forth' (wa-barazu) conveys that all of creation, the righteous and the wicked alike, will stand openly exposed, with nothing hidden and no shelter from judgment. The closing divine names, the One (al-Wahid) and the Subduer (al-Qahhar), frame the scene: all plurality dissolves before the absolute oneness of God, whose power is irresistible. The verse thus invites reflection that worldly distinctions, pride, and power are temporary, while the ultimate reality is God's sovereign unity before whom every creature must appear.

translation: And you will see the criminals that Day bound together in shackles.
interpretation: The verse presents the scene of the Day of Judgment as a vivid image of the guilty being gathered and chained together in pairs or groups, bound to one another as their companions in wrongdoing and their shared fate. The imagery of shackles conveys humiliation, helplessness and the loss of all freedom and dignity, showing that those who were arrogant and defiant in worldly life are reduced to utter powerlessness. The 'pairing' of the criminals also suggests that each person's deeds and associations are brought before them, so that they are bound to the company they chose, and it warns the listener to reflect on the consequences of persisting in crime before that reckoning arrives.

translation: Their garments will be of pitch, and the Fire will cover their faces.
interpretation: The verse portrays the torment of the wrongdoers in the Hereafter through a vivid image of total encompassment. Their outer garments (sarabil, the garments worn over the body) are made of qatran, a tar or pitch that burns quickly, catches fire easily, and clings to the skin. This reflects that the punishment surrounds them entirely, leaving no part of them untouched, and the mention of the face, the seat of honor and expression, shows the humiliation and anguish that accompany the torment. The imagery conveys that the fire they chose in this life, through disbelief and wrongdoing, will become the very covering that envelops them, so that their own deeds return to them in a form that is inescapable and visible.

translation: So that Allah may recompense every soul for what it has earned. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning.
interpretation: The verse points to the principle of complete divine justice: every person will be held accountable for exactly what they themselves have done, neither more nor less. Because each soul bears its own deeds, the believer is driven to vigilance over his conduct, knowing that no action, whether good or wrong, is lost before God. The closing phrase, that Allah is swift in reckoning, is a warning that the account is not delayed indefinitely; it comes quickly, so one should not presume on time and should prepare for the settlement of accounts.

translation: This is a message for mankind, that they may be warned by it, and that they may know that He is but one God, and that those of understanding may take heed.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an as a clear proclamation (balagh) addressed to all people, and it names three purposes that together form a complete path of guidance. First, it is a warning (indhar), so that people may be roused from heedlessness before the consequences of their conduct overtake them. Second, it directs them to tawhid, the knowledge that the true object of worship is one God alone, which is the foundation of the whole message. Third, it calls the people of intellect (ulu al-albab) to remembrance (tadhakkur), indicating that reason is not an end in itself but must lead to reflection, recollection of God, and moral awakening. The sequence moves from delivery of the message, to warning, to knowledge of God's oneness, and finally to the reflective heart that understands and acts upon it.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book and a clear Qur'an.
interpretation: The opening letters Alif, Lam, Ra are among the muqatta'at, disjointed letters whose precise meaning is known to God alone; their presence before the revelation draws the listener's attention to the miraculous nature of the Book, which is composed of the very letters of the Arabic language yet cannot be matched. The verse then identifies this revelation in two complementary ways: as 'the Book', the established and preserved scripture that confirms the messages of earlier prophets, and as 'a clear Qur'an', a recitation whose guidance is manifest and whose meaning is evident to anyone who reflects upon it with an open heart. Thus the verse presents the Qur'an as both a fixed, authoritative revelation and a luminous, understandable message, inviting the reader to recognize its clarity as a sign of its divine origin.

translation: Those who disbelieved will perhaps wish that they had been Muslims.
interpretation: The verse points to the regret that the disbelievers will feel at the moment of reckoning, when the truth becomes clear and the worldly distractions that kept them from submission fall away. Their wish to have been among those who submitted to God is a sign that they recognize, too late, the consequences of their rejection. It also serves as a warning to the listener in this world to turn toward faith before that regret becomes unavoidable, since the wish of the disbelievers at that point brings them no benefit.

translation: Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them; but they will soon come to know.
interpretation: The verse presents a divine permission granted to the heedless: they are left to indulge in worldly pleasures and to be occupied with distant hopes, which become a veil that keeps them from remembering their ultimate accountability. Their delay is not a sign of divine approval but a respite that will end in a reckoning they will come to know, at the moment when their false sense of security and endless expectations collapse. The verse thus warns that the pursuit of present enjoyment and the deception of long hopes are among the most dangerous forms of negligence, since they lull the soul into forgetting what is truly coming.

translation: And We did not destroy any town except that it had a known decree (a appointed term written in a Book).
interpretation: The verse teaches that every community has a predetermined, fixed term set by God, known to Him and recorded in the Book of decree, so that no nation perishes before or after its appointed time. This divine measure of destiny underscores that the rise and fall of peoples is not random but governed by God's precise knowledge and wisdom, and it calls people to recognize that their own deeds within that limited span determine how they stand before Him.

translation: No nation can precede its appointed term, nor can it delay it.
interpretation: The verse affirms that every community has a fixed, divinely determined term (ajal) for its existence and for the consequences it faces. Neither its destruction nor its respite can be advanced or postponed by a single moment beyond what God has decreed. This reminds believers that human planning, wealth, and power operate within a predetermined order, so one should neither despair at a delayed reckoning nor presume upon divine patience, but rather live with awareness that the appointed time is known only to God.

translation: And they said, "O you to whom the Reminder has been revealed, indeed you are a madman."
interpretation: This verse records the disbelievers' mockery of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. By addressing him sarcastically as the one to whom the Reminder (al-Dhikr, the Qur'an) was sent, they turn his claim to revelation into an accusation of madness. Their words reveal a pattern that recurs across the prophetic story: when messengers brought a message that exposed the heedlessness of their people, the powerful and comfortable often answered with ridicule and labels of insanity rather than engaging the substance of the call. The verse thus offers consolation to the believers and the Prophet, showing that the charge of madness is a familiar tool of those who prefer their habits to the reminder, and that the true measure of the message lies in its content and its effect on the heart, not in the mockery of its opponents.

translation: Why do you not bring us the angels, if you are among the truthful?
interpretation: The disbelievers' demand reflects a recurring pattern in which people reject the message and ask for a sign of their own choosing, here the descent of angels as visible proof of the Prophet's truthfulness. The verse shows that they judged the revelation by their own standards of evidence rather than by its substance. The divine response in the following verses makes clear that angels do not descend merely to satisfy such demands, since their descent carries a decisive consequence, and that the refusal to believe lies in the hearts of those who ask, not in any lack of proof.

translation: We do not send down the angels except with truth, and they would not then be given respite.
interpretation: The verse affirms that angels descend only with a true purpose, namely to carry out a decree of divine justice, such as the punishment of a people or the confirmation of a truth. Their appearance is therefore never idle or arbitrary; it marks the moment when God's judgment is final. The statement that they would not then be granted respite conveys that once the angels come with this decisive command, the delay that people had been given to repent or to persist in denial comes to an end. It is a warning that the period of reprieve is limited and that God's measure, once it reaches its appointed time, is not postponed.

translation: Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will be its guardian.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an, referred to as the Dhikr (Reminder), is a revelation whose origin is directly from God, and it singles out its preservation as a divine commitment. The emphatic phrasing, with its repeated 'inna' and the use of the first-person plural, underscores both the certainty of the revelation and God's personal oversight of it. Its guarding means that the text has been protected from corruption, alteration, or loss across generations, so that it remains a continuous source of guidance and remembrance for humanity, in contrast to earlier scriptures whose preservation was entrusted to their own communities.

translation: And We had already sent messengers before you to the sects of the former peoples.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad by showing that he is not the first to be sent with a message that is rejected. God had sent earlier messengers to earlier communities, and those communities divided into factions and sects, some believing and others denying. This places the Prophet's mission within a continuous divine pattern: the same resistance and dispute he faces is the lot of every prophet, so he should remain steadfast, knowing that the outcome of truth prevailing over denial has been established in God's way with the nations before him.

translation: And no messenger came to them except that they used to mock him.
interpretation: The verse points to a recurring pattern in the history of revelation: the people who were sent a messenger did not simply fail to notice him, but met him with ridicule. Their mockery was not an isolated reaction but a habitual one, reflecting an attitude in which the message was dismissed before it was examined, and the messenger was reduced to an object of laughter rather than being heard. The verse thus shows that scorn toward the bearers of truth is a spiritual disease that tends to repeat itself across generations, and it implicitly warns that such arrogance blinds people to guidance that could have saved them. It also offers consolation to the Prophet, indicating that the rejection he faced was part of a long-established human response rather than a personal failing on his part.

translation: Thus do We cause it to enter into the hearts of the guilty.
interpretation: The verse refers to the Qur'an's reception by those who persist in sin: just as We have sent it down clearly and made it a reminder, We let it penetrate the hearts of the criminals (mujrimin), yet they do not believe in it, because their hearts have been hardened by denial and arrogance. Divine guidance and warning reach them, but their own obstinate disposition keeps it from taking root, so the same message that brings life to the believers becomes for them a source of further resistance and proof against them.

translation: They will not believe in it, though the way of the earlier peoples has already passed.
interpretation: The verse shows that the obstinate rejection of the Qur'an by the disbelievers is not a new or unforeseen phenomenon but follows a divine pattern (sunnah) seen in earlier nations: when the messengers came with clear signs, their hardened hearts refused them, just as the verse before describes the Qur'an being placed in the hearts of the guilty so that they still reject it. Thus the Qur'an comforts the Prophet by reminding him that his people's disbelief repeats a familiar course, and warns that the consequences meted out to former peoples remain the outcome of persistent denial.

translation: And even if We opened for them a gate from the heaven, and they continued to ascend through it.
interpretation: The verse portrays the obstinacy of those who reject the truth: even if God granted them a visible, miraculous sign, opening a gate into the heavens so that they could ascend and witness it with their own eyes, their hearts would remain closed. Their denial stems not from a lack of evidence but from a settled disposition of stubbornness, so that even the most direct proof would only be dismissed as illusion or sorcery. The verse thus teaches that faith depends on receptiveness of the heart rather than on the quantity of signs presented.

translation: They would say: "Our eyes have only been dazzled; rather, we are a people bewitched."
interpretation: The verse portrays the reaction of those who witness a clear sign and refuse to accept it: rather than admitting the truth of what they see, they attribute their perception to a mere trick upon their senses, as if their eyes had been clouded. By claiming to be "bewitched," they dismiss the miracle as sorcery, thereby shielding themselves from the demands of faith. The passage reveals a recurring human tendency to explain away evidence rather than yield to its implications, and it warns that a heart closed by pride can turn even undeniable signs into illusions.

translation: And We have certainly placed in the sky great constellations (zodiacal mansions), and We have beautified it for the observers.
interpretation: The verse points the reader's gaze upward to the sky as a deliberate act of divine craftsmanship: the 'buruj' are not random scatterings of light but ordered stations, and the beauty they display is offered specifically to those who look and reflect. Creation is thus presented as an invitation to contemplation, where the observer's wonder at order and splendor becomes itself a form of recognition of the One who arranged the heavens.

translation: And We guarded it from every accursed devil.
interpretation: The verse speaks of the protection granted by God to the heavens, which are guarded from every rebellious, accursed devil so that they cannot reach the higher realm to eavesdrop on the angels' counsel. It affirms that divine wisdom shields the cosmic order from corruption and from the deceptive whisperings of those who seek to pry into what is hidden, pointing the believer to trust in the Almighty's safeguarding of truth against every form of satanic interference.

translation: Except one who steals a hearing, so he is pursued by a clear flaming meteor.
interpretation: The verse describes the protection God placed around the heavens against the devils. Those jinn who attempted to eavesdrop on the angelic discourse of the higher realm, catching fragments of what was decreed, were struck down by a piercing, luminous shooting star. This shows that the heavens were guarded so that the unseen could not be known through illicit means, and that the transmission of revelation remained under divine control, the knowledge of the unseen belonging to God alone and granted only to whom He chooses.

translation: And the earth — We spread it out, and cast into it firm mountains, and caused to grow therein of every thing in measured balance.
interpretation: The verse presents the earth as deliberately shaped for life: its expanse (madd) is not accidental but designed, and the firmly set mountains (rawasi) serve to stabilize it so that it can bear its inhabitants. The phrase 'of every thing in measured balance' (min kulli shay'in mawzun) points to a cosmos governed by precise proportion, where plant life and the vegetation of the earth grow according to a calculated measure. The verse thus invites the reader to recognize in the earth's geography and fertility an ordered wisdom, in which stability, nourishment and balance are interwoven as signs of the Creator's exact design.

translation: And We have made for you therein means of livelihood, and [also] for those whom you do not provide for.
interpretation: The verse points to the breadth of divine provision: the earth is not merely a place where humans struggle for their own sustenance, but a setting prepared by God with sources of living for mankind. By pairing 'for you' with 'those whom you do not provide for,' it reminds the believer that the one who gives sustenance is God alone, who extends His provision to creatures beyond the reach of human effort or responsibility. This should cultivate gratitude in the one who benefits, and humility in recognizing that one's own earnings are not the sole source of others' or one's own life. It also implicitly warns against the illusion that wealth and provision depend on one's own power, since the sustainer of those one cannot feed is God Himself.

translation: And there is not a thing but that Our are its depositories, and We send it down only in a known measure.
interpretation: The verse affirms that everything that exists has its source and reserve with God alone, so nothing is unlimited in the sense of belonging to itself; its origin is in His treasury. What reaches creation comes down in a precise, determined measure, fixed by divine wisdom and knowledge according to what benefits each thing and each time. This points the believer to trust in God's provision: material and spiritual blessings are not scattered by chance but are apportioned with exactness, so that no one should despair of what is withheld nor become heedless of what is given, and so that the whole order of the world is seen as a sign of a Lord who measures all things.

translation: And We sent the winds fertilizing, then We sent down water from the sky and gave you drink from it, and you are not its keepers.
interpretation: The verse presents rain as a deliberate act of divine provision: the winds are sent as fertilizers that set the clouds and vegetation in motion, water is brought down from above, and humans are given drink from it. By stating that people are not its storers or keepers, it reminds them that they hold no control over the water's supply and must therefore recognize that sustenance depends entirely on God, prompting gratitude and humility rather than a false sense of self-sufficiency.

translation: Indeed, it is We who give life and cause death, and We are the Inheritors.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God alone holds absolute sovereignty over life and death, the two fundamental realities that bind every creature. Giving life and causing death are acts of the Creator alone, and the human being, who is subject to both, is reminded of his dependence and mortality. The closing declaration that God is the Inheritor points to the ultimate truth that all worldly possessions, power, and created things pass away, and that everything returns to Him once the created order has run its course. The verse thus invites the believer to detachment from the transient and to reflection on the certainty of returning to the One who remains after all things have perished.

translation: And We have certainly known those who go before you among you, and We have certainly known those who come after.
interpretation: The verse is spoken in the context of the Qur'an's account of the angels and the ranks of worshippers standing in lines before God (Surah al-Hijr 15:24 and the surrounding verses, and related passages on the sincere ranks). It affirms God's complete knowledge of every generation of humankind, whether those who came earlier or those who come later, so that none of them is hidden from Him. Classical exegetes such as al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi read it as a statement of divine knowledge that encompasses all people across time, and some related to it the idea that God knows who among the earlier and later generations responds to truth and who holds back. The verse thus reminds the believer that deeds, intentions, and the timing of each person's life are fully known to God, and that accountability rests on that perfect knowledge.

translation: And indeed, your Lord—He will gather them. Indeed, He is Wise, All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse assures the Prophet that the final gathering of all creatures rests entirely with God, who alone has the power and the wisdom to assemble them on the Day of Judgment. The divine attributes of wisdom and all-knowledge are invoked to show that this gathering is not arbitrary but perfectly ordered, and that nothing in the scattered and disputing affairs of humankind escapes God's knowledge. The reader is thereby reminded that disputes left unresolved in this world will be brought to their rightful conclusion before the One who knows every hidden matter and acts with perfect judgment.

translation: And We had certainly created man from clay, from black mud altered and molded.
interpretation: The verse points to the humble material origin of the human being: a clay that was dried and shaped like pottery (ṣalṣāl), drawn from black, decayed mud (ḥamaʾ masnūn). By naming this lowly beginning, it reminds humanity of its dependence on and createdness by God, and invites reflection on how a being formed from such earth was given a unique station, the breath of God and the capacity for knowledge and moral responsibility, so that pride is set aside and gratitude and humility before the Creator take its place.

translation: And the jinn We had created before from the fire of scorching wind.
interpretation: The verse places the jinn's origin in a fire of intense, scorching heat, specifically the 'samum' (a burning, searing wind), which stands in contrast to the clay from which humans were fashioned. This distinction of substance points to the jinn being a created order with its own nature, distinct from humanity, endowed with free will and accountability like humans, and whose pre-human creation before Adam signals a prior stage in God's creative activity. The fiery nature implied by the verse highlights the difference in their constitution rather than any inherent moral quality, since the Qur'an elsewhere makes clear that both jinn and humans are judged by their conduct.

translation: And [mention] when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to create a human being from clay, from black mud altered and molded."
interpretation: The verse opens the account of the creation of Adam by presenting it as a deliberate divine decree announced in advance to the angels, which signals that humankind holds a distinguished place in God's plan from its very origin. The material described, clay from altered black mud, points to the humble and earthly substance from which the human being is made, reminding the reader of human dependence and limitation, while the divine act of shaping it implies the dignity that God later confers upon this creature. The announcement "I am going to create" frames human existence as a purposeful creation rather than an accident, setting the stage for the subsequent exchange with the angels that reveals the human capacity for knowledge and the responsibility entrusted to Adam as God's vicegerent on earth.

translation: So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, then fall down before him in prostration.
interpretation: The verse marks the completion of the creation of Adam: after God shapes and perfects his form, He breathes into him something of His own spirit, which sets the human being apart as a creature honored with a divine dignity. The command to the angels to fall prostrate is thus not worship of the clay or of Adam himself, but a recognition of the spiritual trust God has placed within humanity, and it establishes the honor due to the human being as the bearer of that breath, while the refusal of Iblis to bow reveals the danger of arrogance that places one's own origin above the command of God.

translation: So the angels prostrated themselves, all of them together.
interpretation: The verse describes the immediate and unanimous obedience of the angels to God's command to prostrate before Adam. Their word 'kullahum ajma'un' (all of them, every one without exception) emphasizes that no angel held back, showing that true submission to the divine order is complete and collective. It stands in contrast to Iblis, who refused, and thus highlights the honor God bestowed upon humanity and the seriousness of obeying God's clear command.

translation: Except Iblis, who refused to be among those who prostrate.
interpretation: The verse singles out Iblis as the one exception to the universal prostration before Adam commanded by God to the angels. His refusal (ibā') was not mere inability but a deliberate act of arrogance, for he chose his own judgment over the explicit command of his Lord. The verse thus teaches that the root of disobedience lies in pride and the refusal to submit, and it presents Iblis as the archetype of the proud soul that rejects humility before God's will.

translation: He said, "O Iblis, what is wrong with you that you are not among those who prostrate?"
interpretation: The verse captures the moment of direct confrontation between God and Iblis after his refusal to bow before Adam. The question "what is wrong with you" is not a request for information, since God knows the answer, but a rebuke that exposes the absurdity of his refusal and invites him to justify his disobedience. It shows that Iblis was not merely failing to follow an order but had stepped outside the ranks of the obedient who prostrate in submission. The verse thus frames arrogance and refusal to submit to God's command as the root of rebellion, and it places the reader before the same choice between humble obedience and self-exaltation.

translation: He said: "I would not prostrate myself to a human whom You created from clay, from black mud molded into shape."
interpretation: This verse records Iblis's refusal when God commanded the angels to prostrate before Adam. His refusal rests on a claim of superiority based on his own origin: he regards himself as created from fire, and therefore nobler than a being formed from clay that has been shaped from dark, fermented mud. The core sin it exposes is arrogance (kibr) that places personal judgment about one's own worth above the explicit command of the Creator. The verse also reveals that the human being's material origin, though humble, was the very thing God chose to honor with the angelic prostration, so that disdain for the human form becomes a rejection of God's wisdom in creation.

translation: He said, "Then get out of it, for indeed you are expelled (accursed, stoned)."
interpretation: The word "rajim" carries the sense of one who is pelted and driven away, and the command to leave the heavenly abode marks the immediate consequence of Iblis's refusal to prostrate before Adam. The expulsion is not only a removal from a place but a stripping of his former station and nearness to God, so that his arrogance becomes the very cause of his exile. The verse thus teaches that pride severs a creature from the mercy that once sheltered it, and that disobedience transforms a former servant into one cast out.

translation: And indeed, upon you is the curse until the Day of Recompense.
interpretation: This verse is spoken to Iblis (Satan) after his refusal to prostrate to Adam, when Allah expels him from His presence. The curse (al-la'nah) signifies his complete removal from divine mercy and nearness, and it is linked to the Day of Judgment, the Day of Recompense, when every soul will receive what it has earned. The verse thus establishes that Satan's rejection is sustained and final, and that the ultimate accountability he faces lies beyond this world. It also serves as a reminder to human beings that arrogance and refusal to submit to the command of Allah lead to the same loss of mercy, and that the believer should guard against pride by humbly obeying the divine will.

translation: He said: "My Lord, then give me respite until the Day they are resurrected."
interpretation: Iblis, having been cast out for refusing to prostrate to Adam, does not ask for forgiveness but petitions God for a postponement of his punishment until the Day of Resurrection. The request reveals a defiant persistence in his enmity: he seeks not repentance but a reprieve in which he may pursue his purpose of misleading humankind. God's granting of this respite, as the subsequent verses show, is granted only up to a known appointed time, so the verse teaches that delay of judgment is never a sign of approval, and that those who ask for time in order to rebel are seeking an extension of their own test rather than an escape from accountability.

translation: He said: "Indeed, you are among those given respite."
interpretation: This is Iblis's request, after his refusal to prostrate to Adam, to be granted respite until the Day of Resurrection. God grants it, showing that His permission to test humankind extends even to its arch-enemy, and that the respite is a trial rather than a reward. The verse reminds the believer that Satan's time to mislead is limited by divine decree, and that the path of resisting his whispers rests on sincere reliance on God.

translation: Until the day of the appointed time.
interpretation: The phrase shows that divine respite is bounded by a fixed term known only to God. The delay granted to Iblis (and, by extension, to all human beings) is not an oversight or a sign of abandonment but a measured trial that runs its course until the predetermined moment arrives, when the matter will be decided and every reprieve comes to an end. It reminds the believer that time itself is under God's appointment, so one should not mistake postponement of punishment for escape from it, and should use the allotted period in obedience before the set time concludes.

translation: He said: "My Lord, because You have sent me astray, I will surely make evil seem appealing to them on earth, and I will mislead them all."
interpretation: The verse records Iblis's response to his punishment and expulsion. By attributing his misguidance to God ("because You have sent me astray"), he attempts to shift responsibility from his own arrogance and refusal to prostrate before Adam onto the Divine decree, a recurring pattern in which the rebellious self seeks justification for wrongdoing. His vow to beautify falsehood for humanity reveals the nature of his enmity: he works not through open force but through making sin attractive and worldly enticements alluring, so that people are drawn away from their Lord while believing they act reasonably. The phrase "all of them" shows the scope of his ambition, and the verse thereby highlights for the believer the importance of sincere devotion and reliance upon God, since only those whom God protects are safe from this seduction, as the subsequent verses make clear.

translation: Except Your sincere servants among them.
interpretation: This phrase, spoken in the context of Iblis (Satan) vowing to mislead humankind (Surah Sad 38:82-83 and Surah al-Hijr 15:40), marks a decisive exception. Iblis's power of misguidance is absolute over those who follow him, but it has no authority over the 'mukhlasin', those whose devotion has been purified and made sincere for God alone. Sincerity (ikhlas) is thus shown to be the protective shield against Satan's whisperings: a heart cleansed of hypocrisy, worldly motives, and divided loyalties cannot be captured by his deception. The verse thereby affirms both God's sovereignty over Satan's reach and the human responsibility to cultivate sincere devotion.

translation: He said, 'This is a straight path leading to Me.'
interpretation: The verse presents the path of sincere servitude to God as a direct, unerring route that leads straight to Him, and it is God who vouches for its straightness. Within this framing, Satan's authority does not extend over those who rely upon their Lord, because the one who walks this path is protected from his misguidance. The verse therefore assures the believer that the way to God is clear and secured by divine promise, while the path of deviation remains open only to those who choose to follow Satan.

translation: "Indeed, My servants - you have no authority over them, except those who follow you among the misguided."
interpretation: The verse marks a decisive boundary in the relationship between Satan and humanity. Satan's power is not a force that compels people; it operates only through the person's own choice to follow him. The sincere servants of God, who rely on Him and keep their hearts turned toward Him, are beyond his reach, while those who willingly adopt his suggestions and deviate from the path have, by that very act, placed themselves under his influence. Thus the verse places moral responsibility squarely on human will: the seduction is real, but its success depends on the believer's own inclination and surrender to it.

translation: And indeed, Hell is the promised meeting place for all of them.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the final destination of all those who turn away from God, without exception, is Hell. The word 'ajma'een' (all together) emphasizes that no one escapes this appointed place: those who followed misguidance and those who led others astray are gathered there alike. The term 'maw'id' (appointed meeting) conveys that this is a certain, fixed reckoning that awaits them, and that it is a meeting they cannot evade. The verse thus underscores the certainty of divine justice and calls the listener to reflect on their own path before that appointed gathering.

translation: It has seven gates; for each gate there is an allotted portion of them (who are assigned to it).
interpretation: The seven gates point to the graded and distinct paths by which people arrive at the Fire, not a single undifferentiated entrance. Each gate is assigned a 'divided portion' of the deniers and transgressors, which conveys that the reckoning is precise and individualized: each person is placed according to the nature and degree of his own disbelief, sins, and misdeeds. The verse thus affirms divine justice, in which no one is punished beyond what he earned and everyone is sorted by the specific deeds that led him there.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and springs.
interpretation: The verse presents the reward of those who are conscious of God (al-muttaqun) as a state of lasting security and abundance: gardens of lush life and flowing springs. Its placement and brevity invite the listener to see taqwa as the decisive condition for entering this promised felicity. The imagery of water and greenery, which were precious in the arid Arabian setting, conveys both physical delight and spiritual serenity, suggesting that the believer's ultimate fulfillment lies in a harmony with the Creator that outlasts worldly scarcity.

translation: Enter it in peace, secure.
interpretation: The verse is spoken as an address to the righteous at the threshold of Paradise, welcoming them to enter it with safety and peace. The phrase "bi-salam" conveys that they are free from every fear, harm, and sorrow, while "aminin" stresses the lasting security of those who enter, so that the believers' reward is presented not merely as a place to dwell but as a state of complete tranquility that they will never lose.

translation: And We will remove whatever rancor is in their breasts; they will be as brothers, facing each other on thrones.
interpretation: The verse depicts the people of Paradise being purified of inner resentment, envy, and ill will that may have lingered from worldly life. Their hearts are cleansed so that the bonds among them become sincere brotherhood, free of jealousy or grudges. The image of them seated face to face on couches expresses mutual ease, intimacy, and the absence of any estrangement or turning away from one another, so that their joy is complete and shared.

translation: No fatigue will touch them therein, and they will not be removed from it.
interpretation: The verse describes the state of the dwellers of Paradise, who are spared all weariness, toil, and exhaustion, and who abide there forever with no fear of expulsion. Its emphasis is on the completeness of their rest and security: the bodily and spiritual burdens that mark worldly life are lifted, and the permanence of their abode removes the anxiety that even pleasure can carry when it might be lost. The verse thus presents Paradise as a place of perfect ease joined with lasting stability, the reward that God grants for faith and righteous action.

translation: Inform My servants that I am the Most Forgiving, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse opens a window onto the very heart of the divine relationship with humanity: before any command or warning, God first declares His own nature as endlessly forgiving and merciful. The phrase "Inform My servants" carries a tender insistence, as if God is urging the Prophet to make this good news known to all who have strayed or despaired. It teaches that the gate of return is never closed; a servant burdened by sin should not conclude that their failings have placed them beyond reach, because the Lord's forgiveness is wider than any transgression. The juxtaposition of the verse with the surrounding narrative of Abraham's guests and Lot's people, where divine punishment is also described, shows that mercy and justice are not opposites but are held together in God's wisdom, with mercy always being the more prominent attribute. The believer is thus invited to approach God with hope, repentance, and trust, while the sense of the verse also calls the one who proclaims faith to convey this hope to others rather than to preach only fear.

translation: And that My punishment is indeed the painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse follows directly after the assurance of God's mercy toward His servants, and it establishes the counterbalance: the same Lord who is forgiving and merciful is also the One whose punishment is severe and painful. The juxtaposition is meant to hold the believer between hope and fear, so that the awareness of divine mercy does not slide into complacency, and the awareness of divine justice does not slide into despair. The emphasis on 'My punishment' (عذابي) situates the chastisement entirely within God's own agency, while the definite article in 'the painful punishment' (العذاب الأليم) signals a punishment that is singular in its severity and recognized as such, pointing the listener toward repentance as the path that keeps one from its reach.

translation: And inform them about the guests of Abraham.
interpretation: The verse opens a narrative that Allah commands the Prophet to recite to those who deny or dispute him, namely the account of the honored guests who came to Abraham. By telling it, the message reminds listeners of Abraham's exemplary hospitality and of the angelic messengers sent on a mission of mercy and of punishment, showing that Allah's signs and His dealings with nations are real and that the past holds lessons for those who reflect.

translation: When they entered upon him and said, "Peace." He said, "Indeed, we are fearful of you."
interpretation: The verse depicts Abraham's guarded reaction to his unexpected guests, who greet him with peace, and his initial unease at their arrival. Ibrahim's wariness reflects the customary hospitality of his time, in which a stranger's visit was typically met with food and welcome; his apprehension, expressed as fear of them, is the opening of a scene that will soon reveal the guests to be angels bearing glad tidings. The verse thus teaches that a believer's first response to the unknown may be caution, yet this caution gives way to recognition and reassurance when the true purpose of the visitors is made known.

translation: They said: "Do not fear. We give you good news of a boy who will be knowing (endowed with knowledge)."
interpretation: The verse records the angels' reassurance to Abraham after they came to him bearing news that could seem improbable given his age and Sarah's barrenness. Their words "Do not fear" respond to his unease at unexpected visitors, and the announcement of a son described as 'alim' points to the coming of a child who would be endowed with knowledge and wisdom, a sign that divine promise can bring life and hope where human expectation sees none.

translation: He said: "Do you give me good tidings even though old age has touched me? Then with what do you give good tidings?"
interpretation: The verse captures Prophet Ibrahim's astonishment when the angels brought him the news of a son despite his advanced age and that of his wife. His question is not a rejection of divine power but an expression of human wonder at how such a thing could occur naturally, which leads him to ask on what basis the glad tidings are being given, seeking clarity about the means by which this blessing would come about. It reflects a sincere heart that marvels at Allah's favor while still seeking understanding.

translation: They said: "We give you good news of the truth, so do not be among the despairing."
interpretation: This verse comes from the account of Abraham and the angels who came to him with the news of a son despite his old age. When they announced the glad tidings, they reaffirmed that the promise was true and firm, and they urged him not to despair. The lesson drawn is that even when natural means seem exhausted, one must not lose hope in God's mercy and power, for the truth of His promise stands regardless of human expectation.

translation: He said: "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except those who are astray?"
interpretation: The verse establishes that losing hope in Allah's mercy is itself a mark of straying from the path. Despair (qunut) implies a false assumption that one's sins or circumstances have placed them beyond forgiveness and divine care, which contradicts the attributes of a Lord whose mercy encompasses all things. Thus true faith requires holding fast to hope even in hardship, as hope in God's mercy is inseparable from sound belief, while despair opens the door to further error and distance from Him.

translation: He said, "What is your business, O messengers?"
interpretation: This verse (Adh-Dhariyat 51:31 context, spoken in the story of Abraham's guests, here framed as a direct question) shows Abraham, after receiving the visitors and their greeting, turning to inquire about the purpose of their coming. His question is a courteous and measured one: having recognized that they are not ordinary guests but envoys sent with a specific mission, he seeks to learn what they have been commissioned to do. It reflects the prudence of a host who welcomes strangers with hospitality first and then, with dignity, asks the reason for their visit, and it points to the reader that divine messengers carry a definite task whose nature becomes known in its own time.

translation: They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a people who are criminals."
interpretation: This verse comes from the account of Lot's people in Surah Al-Hijr (15:58), where the angelic messengers, having come to Abraham with glad tidings, reveal their mission to destroy the town. The phrase "qawm mujrimeen" (a people of criminals) points to the nature of the community: its persistent, deliberate transgression, especially the sin of its people in rejecting the moral order and indulging in outright depravity. The word "mujrimeen" also conveys that their wrongdoing is not accidental but a settled, open defiance of God's guidance, which is why the punishment is announced as justified. The verse thus frames the destruction as the just consequence of a people who had hardened themselves in sin, and it reminds the listener that divine judgment follows when warnings are persistently ignored.

translation: Except the family of Lot; indeed, We will save them all together.
interpretation: The verse speaks of the divine decree concerning the people of Lot, who were to be destroyed for their grave transgressions. The exception made for Lot's household shows that God's justice is accompanied by His mercy: those who remain faithful to the truth and stand apart from wrongdoing are rescued, even amid a general punishment. The phrase 'all together' emphasizes the completeness of their deliverance, assuring that none of the believing family is left behind, and it reminds the reader that salvation rests on God's care for those who uphold righteousness rather than on their social ties alone.

translation: Except his wife; We had decreed that she would be among those who remain behind.
interpretation: The verse refers to the family of Lot (Lut), whom the angels were sent to rescue from the people of Sodom. Lot's wife is exempted from the rescue, not because of any unfairness, but because of her own inner allegiance: she remained aligned with the disbelieving town and its ways, even though she was physically part of Lot's household. The word 'qaddarna' (We decreed) underlines that her fate was determined by divine knowledge of her choices, teaching that kinship with the righteous does not by itself secure salvation; each person's faith and conduct are what ultimately count. The phrase 'among those who remain behind' (al-ghabirin) points to those who are left to perish with the wicked, and it serves as a warning that being near the believers is no substitute for believing and aligning oneself with them.

translation: So when the messengers came to the family of Lot,
interpretation: The verse marks the moment of arrival: the angelic messengers, sent by God, reached the household of Lot (Lut). Their coming was the turning point that set in motion the divine judgment upon his people. It underscores that God's messengers, whether prophets or angels, are never sent without purpose, and that Lot's family stood at the threshold between the mission of mercy to the righteous and the reckoning awaiting those who persisted in wrongdoing.

translation: He said, "Indeed, you are a people unknown (to me)."
interpretation: The verse comes from the story of Abraham and the angels who visited him in the form of guests (Surah Al-Hijr 15:62, and Surah Adh-Dhariyat 51:25). Abraham does not recognize them, so he says they are strangers to him, and this marks the beginning of his cautious reception of unfamiliar visitors. His words reflect the caution and hospitality of a host who is uncertain about the identity and purpose of the people who have come to him. The verse thus opens a moment of tension that is resolved when the angels reveal their mission: the announcement of a son and the coming punishment upon the people of Lot.

translation: They said: Rather, we have come to you with that about which they used to doubt.
interpretation: The verse records the response of the messengers' interlocutors (the angels sent to Abraham's guests or, in the wider context of Surah al-Hijr, the messengers sent to the people of Lot) who, when asked by the people of the town what brought them, reply that they have come bringing the punishment that these people had long disputed and doubted. The phrase 'yamtarun' carries the sense of persistent, argumentative doubt and hesitation, showing that the threat which the prophets had warned of was not an empty claim but a certain reality now arriving. The verse thus underscores that the denial of prophetic warning does not cancel its fulfilment: what was mocked as a fiction becomes the very thing that overtakes the disbelievers, and the mercy of God is revealed in the sending of warning before the reckoning.

translation: And We have brought you the truth, and indeed we are truthful.
interpretation: This verse, spoken in the context of the messengers' address to their people (in the surrah of Yasin, where it follows the account of the messengers sent to a town), affirms that the messengers come with a clear and certain message from God, not with falsehood or personal ambition. The emphatic phrasing, with its oath-like assertion of sincerity, is a deliberate reply to the disbelievers who doubted them, and it establishes that the authenticity of the prophetic mission rests on the truth of its content and the truthfulness of its bearers. The verse thus invites the listener to weigh the message on its own merits and to recognize that prophethood is grounded in divine truth rather than in mere claims.

translation: So set out with your family in the depth of the night, and follow behind them, and let none of you look back; and proceed to where you are commanded.
interpretation: The verse depicts Lot being commanded by the angels to leave Sodom under cover of night, with his household, so that the departure is secret and swift before the divine punishment descends. Following behind the group serves both to protect the family and to keep them together as they flee, while the prohibition against looking back signals that attachment to the doomed city must be abandoned entirely. Lot's wife, who looks back, is the one who does not escape. The final command, to go where they are directed, places the believers' fate fully in God's guidance, teaching that salvation requires obedience to the divine command and a decisive break with the past, even when the destination is not yet known.

translation: And We decreed to him that matter: that the last remnant of these would be cut off by morning.
interpretation: The verse reveals the divine decree conveyed to Lot concerning the people of his town, whose wrongdoing had reached its limit. The phrase "dabir" (the last remnant, literally the tail or the one who comes last) signals a complete and total eradication, not merely a punishment, and "musbihin" (at morning) points to the suddenness of the destruction, arriving when the people least expected it. The verse thus teaches that divine justice, though it may be delayed, is precise in its timing, and that once a people persist in corruption and reject guidance, their end is determined with certainty and no trace of their arrogance is allowed to remain.

translation: And the people of the city came, rejoicing.
interpretation: The verse depicts the arrival of the townspeople in Sodom (the city of Lot) in the Surah Hud/Al-Hijr narrative, when they heard of the handsome young visitors who had come to Lot's house. Their coming is marked by eager, joyful anticipation (yastabshiruna), a sign of their eagerness to commit wrongdoing. The word conveys how their desires had overtaken their sense of decency, so that they approached Lot's home with delight in their transgression, which sets the stage for Lot's distress and his plea to them to fear God and not disgrace his guests.

translation: He said, "Indeed, these are my guests, so do not disgrace me."
interpretation: Lot's words here reveal the sanctity of the rights of hospitality (ḍiyāfah) in the Arabian moral world and the depth of his sense of honor and responsibility. Though his people were pressing toward the arrival of the two angels in the form of young men, he placed the duty of protecting his guests above his own standing and comfort. By saying "do not disgrace me," he appeals to their remaining sense of shame and manhood, reminding them that to violate guests is to bring dishonor upon him and upon themselves. The verse thus presents the ethical principle that protecting the vulnerable and the one who seeks refuge is a trust, and that a community that abandons this trust has lost the very basis of its dignity.

translation: And fear Allah and do not disgrace me.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the Prophet Hud (or Salih, depending on the reading in context) to his people, is a call to taqwa, the conscious awareness of God that guards one against wrongdoing. The words 'do not disgrace me' (wa la tukhzun) carry a double meaning: they ask the people not to dishonor the messenger who has been sent to them, and, by extension, to avoid the shame that comes from rejecting divine guidance. The verse teaches that righteous conduct toward God is inseparable from honorable treatment of those He sends to guide, and that opposing the truth ultimately brings disgrace upon the one who opposes it.

translation: They said, "Did we not forbid you from (hosting or dealing with) the people of the world?"
interpretation: Their question turns Lot's hospitality to strangers into a charge against him, so the community's own boundary-keeping becomes a pretext for hostility. The verse shows how a society that has grown accustomed to policing outsiders and resisting moral correction treats the reformer's ethical integrity as a violation of its authority, using its prior prohibitions to silence the one who calls it back to righteousness.

translation: He said, "These are my daughters, if you must act (lawfully)."
interpretation: Lot, peace be upon him, faced a people who had given themselves over to the abomination of desire for men, and when they came to his guests he offered them his daughters as a lawful alternative, saying "these are my daughters" (Q 11:78; 15:71). The phrase "if you must act" is a conditional rebuke: if their intent is to fulfil their desire, let them turn to what is lawful, and it exposes the futility of their pursuit. Many commentators read in it a call to conscience and a reminder that the natural and permitted path is open to them, while others understand Lot's words as a deliberate offer of marriage, with his daughters standing for the community's women in a spiritual sense as well as a literal one. The verse thus joins moral urgency with a father's protective concern for his guests and his people.

translation: By your life, indeed they were wandering blindly in their intoxication.
interpretation: The verse is an oath by the Prophet's own life, a mark of his exalted honor in God's sight, and it turns to describe those who reject him as lost in a drunken-like heedlessness. Their 'intoxication' is not wine but the grip of desire, pride and attachment to the familiar, which numbs the heart so that it cannot perceive the truth set before it. Their wandering (ya'mahun) is the aimless stumbling of one who has lost the path while believing himself guided. The imagery warns that such spiritual stupor is itself a form of self-deception, and that the remedy lies in awakening the heart to the signs of God rather than in mere outward religious show.

translation: So the blast seized them at sunrise.
interpretation: The verse describes the sudden destruction of a people at the moment of dawn, when they were already up and about, as the Cry overtook them in the bright morning light. The timing underscores the completeness of their downfall: the very hour that should have brought them ease and the start of their daily affairs became the moment of their annihilation. It serves as a reminder that divine punishment can arrive without warning, at a time when people feel most secure and occupied with their own pursuits, and that no appearance of prosperity or daylight security can shield those who persist in denial and wrongdoing.

translation: So We turned its highest part to its lowest, and rained upon them stones of hardened clay.
interpretation: The verse describes the punishment that befell the people of Lut (Lot), whose cities were overturned and then struck by a rain of baked stones, as the culmination of their persistence in transgression after warnings. The sequence of upheaval from above and destruction from the sky shows that no human power or settled prosperity can shield a people from divine accountability when they persist in corruption. Its deeper lesson is that the consequences of moral defiance are real and comprehensive, reaching every part of a community, so that what appears most secure and elevated can be brought to ruin, and that the signs of such destruction are meant to be contemplated by the reflective believer as a warning.

translation: Indeed, in that are signs for those who observe closely (or discern through insight).
interpretation: The verse points to a faculty of perceptive insight given to those who look beyond the surface of things and read the traces of God's creation and events with a discerning, attentive heart. The word 'mutawassimin' comes from the root wasama, meaning to mark or to bear a sign, so these are people who recognize the marks that reveal the truth of a matter, such as character, consequence, or the hidden meaning behind outward appearances. The verse teaches that the signs of God are not reserved for the careless; they are made manifest to the one who reflects, contemplates, and reads the world with a mind attuned to the wisdom behind it. In this sense, the verse calls believers to cultivate a discerning gaze that sees God's guidance in the natural order and in the lives of earlier peoples mentioned in the surrounding passage.

translation: And indeed, it (the ruined towns) lies on a road that remains (in plain view).
interpretation: The verse refers to the ruins of the destroyed peoples of earlier generations, such as the towns of Lot's people, which lie along a well-traveled route that passing travelers see by day and night. Their continuing presence is a standing sign for those who pass by, calling them to reflect on the consequences of denying the messengers and of persisting in wrongdoing. The word "muqim" (lasting, standing) emphasizes that the sign is permanent and visible, so that it remains available as a lesson for every generation that comes after.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign for those who believe.
interpretation: The verse directs the believer to reflect on a particular event or natural phenomenon mentioned in the surrounding context, presenting it as a clear sign (ayah) of God's power, wisdom, and mercy. The phrase "for those who believe" indicates that while the sign is objectively present to all, it is truly perceived and benefited from only by those whose hearts are open to faith and reflection. Thus the verse links faith with the capacity to read the signs of creation and to recognize in them the presence of the Creator.

translation: And indeed, the companions of the thicket (Al-Ayka) were surely wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse refers to the people of Al-Ayka, the community to whom the prophet Shu'ayb was sent, and it is placed as a warning that injustice in dealing with others, particularly cheating in measure and weight and corruption in the land, brings a people to ruin. The repeated emphasis with 'indeed' and the particle of confirmation shows that their wrongdoing was clear and not in doubt, so that the listener understands that persistence in oppression and rejection of guidance is what destroyed them. The verse thus directs the reader to reflect on the consequences of injustice as a lesson that moral conduct in trade and social life is inseparable from faith.

translation: So We took retribution from them, and indeed, both of those cities lie on a clear highway.
interpretation: The verse follows the account of the destroyed peoples and points to the consequence of their denial: divine retribution overtook them. By saying that their ruined settlements lie on a manifest road (imam mubin), the Qur'an invites those who pass by them, such as the Meccan travelers journeying to Syria, to observe with their own eyes the traces of past wrongdoing as a clear warning. The 'clear imam' signifies a visible path or record that leaves no excuse for heedlessness, so that the listener reflects on the fate of the disbelievers and draws the lesson that persistence in rejecting the messengers brings inevitable accountability.

translation: And the companions of al-Hijr certainly denied the messengers.
interpretation: The verse points to the people of al-Hijr, the Thamud, as a warning that rejecting the messengers is not a matter of rejecting one man alone but of rejecting the whole chain of guidance sent by God. Their denial is presented as a collective act of stubbornness, in which they refused the signs brought to them and turned away from the one who called them to their Lord. The phrase 'the messengers' in the plural carries a further lesson: whoever denies a single prophet is, in effect, denying all of them, since they all bring the same truth from the same source. The story thus stands as a reminder to the listeners of the Qur'an that persistent denial of clear guidance invites the same consequences that befell those who came before them.

translation: And We gave them Our signs, but they turned away from them.
interpretation: The verse points to a state of spiritual heedlessness that is more blameworthy than ignorance: the clear signs were not withheld from them, yet they chose to turn their backs on them. Divine guidance had reached them in full, so their aversion reflects a deliberate refusal of the truth rather than a lack of evidence. It warns that receiving revelation carries a responsibility to attend to it, and that the heart can become so absorbed in its own concerns that it deliberately looks away from the very signs meant to awaken it.

translation: And they used to carve out houses from the mountains, feeling secure.
interpretation: This phrase, drawn from the story of the people of Thamud (in Surah al-Hijr, 15:82), points to the remarkable engineering and material confidence of a civilization that hewed dwellings directly out of rock. Their sense of safety in these stone houses became a source of arrogance, leading them to believe that their achievements and fortified security could protect them from divine judgment. The verse thus teaches that worldly mastery and a feeling of invulnerability offer no shelter against God's command, and that human security rests ultimately on faith and righteousness rather than on the strength of what one builds.

translation: So the blast seized them at sunrise.
interpretation: The verse describes the sudden destruction that overtook a disbelieving people: the 'sayha' (a mighty cry or blast) struck them while they were still in the morning, at the very time they assumed they were secure and going about their day. The timing underscores how swiftly divine punishment can arrive without warning, catching people in the midst of their ordinary affairs and heedless complacency. It serves as a reminder that worldly comfort and apparent safety offer no protection against the consequences of rejecting the messengers of God, and that the moment of reckoning may come when least expected.

translation: So what did their earnings avail them?
interpretation: The verse poses a rhetorical question to show the futility of worldly wealth and achievements when they are relied upon in place of faith and righteous action. Whatever a person has amassed or gained through his efforts cannot shield him from the consequences of his disbelief and wrongdoing on the Day of Reckoning, for true benefit lies only in what one has sent forward in obedience to God. The verse thus directs the reader to reassess where he places his trust, reminding him that material gain, however substantial, is no substitute for sincere devotion.

translation: We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth. And indeed, the Hour is coming, so overlook (their faults) with gracious forgiveness.
interpretation: The verse binds two truths together: creation is not idle or random but rests on the truth, and therefore it has a purpose and an end, namely the Hour, which is certain to come. Because accountability is certain and the cosmos is ordered by truth, the believer is not called to take vengeance or to be consumed by the provocations of opponents. Instead, the command is to turn away from their harm with a beautiful pardon, entrusting justice to the One who will judge all deeds on the Day when every soul is repaid. Forbearance here is grounded in trust that truth will ultimately prevail, so patience and graceful forgiveness become a reflection of faith in the cosmic order and the reality of the coming reckoning.

translation: Indeed, your Lord is the All-Creator, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse closes a passage by joining two attributes of God that together ground the trust a believer places in Him. Al-Khallaq, the Creator, refers to the One who brings things into being and shapes them with precise measure, so that all of creation is the product of His deliberate will rather than chance. Al-'Alim, the All-Knowing, signifies that this creative act is accompanied by complete knowledge of every created thing, its nature, its condition, and its end. The juxtaposition teaches that the one who designed existence is also the one who fully comprehends it, and therefore the Prophet and every reader can rely on the Lord's wisdom in matters that appear hidden or unjust to human eyes. Creation and knowledge are thus presented as inseparable: a Lord who fashioned all things cannot be ignorant of what He has fashioned, and this assurance is meant to steady the heart in the face of opposition and uncertainty.

translation: And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated (verses) and the Grand Qur'an.
interpretation: The 'seven oft-repeated' are understood by many commentators to be the opening chapter, al-Fatihah, whose seven verses are recited in every prayer and thus repeated constantly by the believer.
