By naming it alongside 'the Grand Qur'an,' the verse presents the Fatihah as a compact summary of the whole revelation, a gift given to the Prophet that is both a sustained act of worship and a comprehensive key to the message he carries. The verse thus points to the centrality of the believer's continual remembrance and praise of God, which the Prophet is reminded to hold as a precious treasure.

translation: Do not extend your eyes toward what We have given enjoyment to pairs of them, nor grieve over them, and lower your wing to the believers.
interpretation: The verse addresses the Prophet with a lesson in spiritual detachment and humility. Its first command, not to fix one's gaze longingly on the worldly comforts granted to others, guards the heart against envy and covetousness, since such goods are a fleeting adornment of this life and not a measure of worth. The prohibition on grief over those who turn away from faith frees the messenger from carrying a burden that belongs to God's judgment alone. The closing image of lowering the wing is a gesture of tenderness and gentleness, calling the Prophet to treat the believers with compassion, kindness, and a humble heart, so that his concern for the wealthy and powerful does not cause him to neglect those who are sincerely faithful.

translation: And say, "Indeed, I am only a clear warner."
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet to declare the limits of his own role: he is a plain and unambiguous warner, charged with delivering the message clearly rather than with forcing belief or controlling outcomes. The word "mubin" points to clarity in both the content and the manner of the warning, so that no one can claim they were left in confusion. By defining himself as a warner, the Prophet is freed from any claim to divine powers, and the responsibility for acceptance or rejection rests with each listener, while the warning itself stands as a sincere act of mercy that gives people the chance to turn back before the consequences arrive.

translation: As We sent down upon the dividers (who divided the Qur'an into parts).
interpretation: The verse likens the disbelievers who split the revelation into fragments, accepting some parts and rejecting others, to the earlier groups who did the same with their scriptures, and it warns that such selective faith invites the same consequences that befell those who came before.

translation: Those who have broken the Qur'an into fragments (who have made it into parts, believing in some of it and rejecting the rest).
interpretation: The word 'adin, from 'idah, means pieces or parts. The verse condemns those who split the Qur'an into divided portions, accepting what suits their desires and rejecting what does not, or dismissing it as a collection of disconnected sayings such as poetry, sorcery, or soothsaying. The Qur'an is a single, coherent revelation whose parts confirm one another, so to take only selected verses and discard the rest is to deny its unity and to treat God's guidance as something to be reshaped by human inclination.

translation: So by your Lord, We will surely question them all, every one of them.
interpretation: The verse opens with a solemn divine oath, 'By your Lord,' which underscores the absolute certainty of the reckoning that awaits all people. The accountability is universal, reaching every individual without exception, and it points to a day when each soul will be called to answer for its beliefs and deeds. The emphasis on 'all of them' conveys that no one can escape or be overlooked, and that the questioning is both personal and comprehensive, meant to awaken the heedless to their responsibility before their Lord.

translation: about what they used to do
interpretation: The phrase points to God's complete knowledge and accountability: no deed of those who went astray is hidden from Him, and their conduct, repeated over time, will be weighed and answered for. It calls the listener to examine their own habitual actions, since the record of what people habitually do is what their reckoning will be based on.

translation: So proclaim openly what you are commanded, and turn away from those who associate others with Allah.
interpretation: The verse marks a turning point in the Prophet's mission: after a period of private and gentle outreach, he is commanded to make his message public and unambiguous, declaring the truth without fear or concealment. The word fa-sda' evokes splitting something open, suggesting that the truth must break through the walls of resistance and denial. Yet this boldness is bounded by the command to turn away from the obstinate polytheists, teaching that the messenger's duty is to deliver the message clearly, not to compel acceptance or to be drawn into endless argument with those who refuse it. Clarity of proclamation and dignified withdrawal from hostility together form a model for every believer who carries a truth that others reject.

translation: Indeed, We suffice you against the mockers.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Hijr 15:95) is a consolation to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who was being ridiculed and scorned by the leaders of Quraysh. God assures him that He Himself will protect him from those who mock his message and person, so he need not be distressed by their derision or fear their harm. The verse teaches that the believer's reliance rests on God's sufficiency, and that the mockery of the arrogant will ultimately be turned back upon them, while the one who trusts in God is shielded and sustained.

translation: Those who set up with God another god; but they will come to know.
interpretation: The verse confronts the sin of associating partners with God (shirk) by pairing it with a solemn warning of future knowledge. The phrase "fa-sawfa ya'lamun" ('but they will surely come to know') points to a reckoning in which the illusions of those who invoked other deities will be exposed. Their knowledge will arrive at the moment of truth, when the futility of what they worshipped becomes evident and the sole sovereignty of God is unveiled, so that the error they clung to in this life is revealed as a loss they can no longer deny.

translation: And We certainly know that your breast is constricted by what they say.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Hijr 15:97) consoles the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in the face of the mockery, denial, and slander directed at him by his opponents. God, who knows every hidden thing, acknowledges the emotional burden and distress this causes him, showing that divine knowledge encompasses the Prophet's inner state. The remedy prescribed immediately after it is not retaliation or despair but glorifying God with praise, prostrating before Him, and worshipping until certainty comes, which teaches that patience in the face of hostility is sustained through remembrance and devotion.

translation: So glorify your Lord with His praise, and be among those who prostrate.
interpretation: The verse directs the Prophet, and by extension every believer, to answer the burdens of the message with two acts of devotion joined together: tasbih, the glorification of God that affirms His perfection and freedom from every deficiency, and prostration, the bodily posture of humility before Him. The phrase 'with His praise' (bihamdihi) shows that glorifying God is not a silent or abstract exercise but one that is woven together with gratitude and acknowledgment of His blessings. The command to 'be among those who prostrate' points beyond a single ritual act to a whole way of life in which the believer lowers the self before the Creator, so that worship becomes the natural response to hardship, opposition, and the weight of responsibility.

translation: And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty (death).
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet, and by extension every believer, to persist in worship of God continuously for the whole of life, without interruption or slackening, until death, which is the 'certainty' that arrives without doubt. Worship is thus not a seasonal or conditional duty tied to circumstances, but a lifelong bond of devotion that ends only at the moment of death.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it. Exalted is He and high above what they associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse, which opens the Surah An-Nahl, speaks to the believers and the disbelievers alike about the certainty of the divine decree. The phrase 'the command of Allah has come' may be read as the imminent arrival of the Hour, of divine judgment, or of the revelation itself that was sent down as a clear guidance; either way it signals that what Allah has determined is already set in motion and need not be pressed forward by human impatience. The mockery of the disbelievers, who challenged the Prophet to bring the punishment swiftly, is answered by a reminder that Allah's timing is perfect and beyond human reckoning. The closing declaration of Allah's exaltation above the partners they ascribe to Him ties the certainty of the promise to the absolute sovereignty of the One God, so that trust in His wisdom replaces restlessness and the rejection of associating partners with Him is affirmed as the foundation of the whole message.

translation: He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command upon whomever He wills of His servants, [saying]: Warn that there is no deity except Me, so fear Me.
interpretation: The verse establishes that revelation is a divine act: God alone chooses whom He will, and He sends the angels bearing the Spirit, which is the revealed guidance, by His command. The core message delivered through this revelation is a call to pure monothean tawhid, that no one deserves worship but God, and this is the duty of every prophet to warn people of. The verse ends by turning this doctrine into a practical demand: awareness of God and heedfulness toward Him (taqwa) is the proper response to the recognition of His oneness, since true reverence arises from knowing that He alone is the one to be worshipped and obeyed.

translation: He created the heavens and the earth with truth. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse begins by affirming that the creation of the heavens and the earth was not idle or meaningless but was done bi-l-haqq, with truth, purpose, and wisdom, so that the cosmos itself bears witness to a deliberate Creator whose will is just and whose order is sound. The sublime order of the heavens and earth is thus a sign pointing beyond itself to the One who fashioned it. From this recognition the verse moves to the declaration of divine transcendence, ta'ala 'amma yushrikun: God is exalted far above the partners that those who disbelieve ascribe to Him. Since the one who created everything with truth alone holds absolute sovereignty over it, the attribution of partners to Him is revealed as a grave incongruity, a claim that contradicts the very evidence of creation that surrounds the human being.

translation: He created man from a drop of fluid, and yet he is an open adversary, disputing against his Creator.
interpretation: The verse begins with the humble origin of the human being, a mere drop of seminal fluid, to remind him of the source of his existence and the power of his Creator who shaped him from such a meager beginning. Against this lowly origin, the verse exposes a striking paradox: the very creature who owes his existence entirely to God becomes a clear and open disputant, arguing against the truth and contending with his Lord. The word khasim suggests one who contends fiercely and persistently in argument, and mubin emphasizes that this opposition is manifest rather than hidden. The verse thus invites reflection on human pride and forgetfulness, urging the person to recall his modest origin and to abandon vain disputation in favor of humility before the One who created him.

translation: And the cattle—He created them for you; in them is warmth and (other) benefits, and from them you eat.
interpretation: The verse directs the believer's attention to the cattle as a concrete sign of divine providence: they are not merely animals but a gift created for the sake of humankind. Their wool and hide provide warmth against the cold, their milk, labor and other uses supply ongoing benefit, and their meat sustains life. By naming these everyday blessings, the verse invites reflection on gratitude, teaching that the ordinary provisions of life, when pondered, reveal the mercy and wisdom of the Creator who arranged the natural world for human welfare.

translation: And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home in the evening and when you send them out to pasture in the morning.
interpretation: The verse directs attention to the beauty that God places in the ordinary, daily rhythms of life. The evening return and the morning departure of the herd, which may seem like routine labor, are presented as sources of dignity and delight. By naming this beauty as a gift, the verse teaches that gratitude belongs not only to extraordinary blessings but also to the familiar cycles of provision that sustain human life, so that the believer learns to perceive God's generosity in what is commonly overlooked.

translation: And it carries your loads to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves. Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse recalls the blessing of transport given to people so that they can reach distant lands that they could never have reached by their own strength alone. The hardship that would have attended such journeys is lifted by Allah's provision, and this is itself a sign of His compassion. The closing words, "Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful," direct the listener to see in ordinary comforts a reflection of God's tenderness toward His creation, so that gratitude and trust in Him follow naturally from reflecting on these favors.

translation: And horses, mules, and donkeys [He created] for you to ride and as adornment. And He creates what you do not know.
interpretation: The verse points to the bounty of God's provision in animals made useful to humanity, first for transport and then for beauty and display, and it closes by reminding the believer that God's creation extends beyond what human beings currently know. The phrase "and He creates what you do not know" invites humility before the vastness of divine creative power, suggesting that the means of travel and comfort will continue to be disclosed to people in ages to come, as indeed the later invention of vehicles and machines testifies. Thus the verse links gratitude for present blessings with an open horizon of future knowledge that remains within God's unlimited creation.

translation: And upon Allah is the direction of the way, and among the ways is one that deviates. And had He willed, He would have guided you all.
interpretation: The verse presents guidance as something that belongs to Allah: the straight path is 'qasd al-sabil', literally the way that reaches its destination directly, and the Qur'an places its clarity upon God. Yet 'wa minha ja'ir' reminds the listener that many roads branch off into crookedness, so the seeker must discern rather than assume that every path leads home. The closing clause, 'had He willed, He would have guided you all', shows that universal guidance by compulsion was within divine power but was not the chosen design. God granted human beings the capacity to choose, so the responsibility to follow the straight way lies with each person, who must turn toward the guidance that God has made clear and seek it sincerely.

translation: It is He who sent down water from the sky; from it you have drink, and from it [grows] vegetation in which you pasture your livestock.
interpretation: The verse directs the reader's attention from the simple, everyday fact of rain to the Creator who makes it a provision on which life depends. Water is first given as drink for humans, and then, through the plants it brings forth, as pasture for the animals that sustain them. The sequence moves from the basic need of the body to the wider web of nourishment that links the earth, its animals, and its people. The reflection it invites is gratitude: a person who drinks and grazes his herds is being reminded that every sip and every harvest traces back to a single gift from the One who sends the water down.

translation: He causes to grow for you thereby the crops, the olives, the date palms, the grapes, and of all the fruits. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who give thought.
interpretation: The verse directs the mind from the ordinary act of rain bringing forth vegetation to a deeper reflection on the orderly design behind it. Each plant named, from grain to olive, date and grape, draws on the same water yet yields differing fruits, pointing to a single Creator who arranges diverse forms of life from one source. The closing phrase makes clear that this sign is not evident to everyone, but is perceived by those who reflect, so the verse invites the believer to turn daily provision into an occasion for contemplation and gratitude toward its Giver.

translation: And He has subjected to you the night and the day, the sun and the moon; and the stars are subjected by His command. Indeed, in that are signs for a people who use their reason.
interpretation: The verse directs the reflective mind from the orderly movements of the heavenly bodies to their Creator: the regularity by which night alternates with day and the sun, moon, and stars follow fixed courses shows that they are made subservient to human benefit and bound by a command that is not their own. Such constancy is not self-generated, so it points to a single, wise Originator whose will governs the cosmos. The verse makes this recognition the special province of those who truly reason, implying that understanding the order of creation is itself a form of faith and a path to gratitude and devotion.

translation: And what He has created for you on the earth of varied colors. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who are mindful.
interpretation: The verse directs the reflective mind toward the vast diversity of created things spread across the earth, whose differing colors, forms, and kinds are not accidents but deliberate marks of a single Creator's art. Such variety in creation is offered as a sign that rewards those who remember, meaning those who recall God and their own accountability, and who draw from the visible world a lesson about the wisdom and power behind it.

translation: And it is He who subjected the sea, that you may eat from it tender flesh and extract from it ornaments which you wear; and you see the ships ploughing through it, that you may seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful.
interpretation: The verse presents the sea as a sign of divine grace: it is made subservient to human benefit, providing fresh food and adornment, and serving as a route for commerce and travel. Yet the verse frames these gifts not as ends in themselves but as means toward gratitude, inviting the believer to recognize that the ability to draw sustenance, beauty, and livelihood from a vast and otherwise dangerous element is a manifestation of the Creator's mercy. Seeking God's bounty through trade is thus wedded to thankfulness, so that worldly provision becomes a path to acknowledging the One who subjected the sea to human use.

translation: And He placed in the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you, and rivers and roads, that you may be guided.
interpretation: The verse presents the earth as a carefully prepared dwelling: its stability is secured by mountains set firmly upon it so that it does not sway beneath its inhabitants, while rivers and pathways are provided for their sustenance and movement. The mention of guidance at the end turns this physical arrangement into a lesson: the same wisdom that fixed the earth and ordered its features calls the human being to reflect on the signs of his Creator and to find the right direction in life, both on the land and in the heart.

translation: And landmarks; and by the stars they are guided.
interpretation: The verse points to the natural signs God has placed for human beings, such as landmarks on the earth and the stars in the sky, which guide travelers across deserts and seas. Through these visible, ordered signs, people are led to find their way, and this everyday guidance invites reflection on the Creator who made the heavens and the earth as a means of direction and mercy.

translation: Is then He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not then be reminded?
interpretation: The verse poses a rhetorical question that exposes the absurdity of equating the Creator with what cannot create. Creation is the clearest sign of divine power and sole lordship, so the one who brings things into being alone merits worship, while idols that create nothing are unworthy of any share of it. The closing question, 'Will you not then be reminded?', calls the listener back from heedlessness: a mind that considers the wonders of its own origin and the world around it cannot fail to recognize that the Creator is the only one deserving to be served.

translation: And if you were to count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate them. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse points to the boundlessness of Allah's blessings: a person who tries to reckon them all will fail, because they encompass every breath, sense, provision, and guidance given to human beings, most of which go unnoticed. Such a realization should humble the believer and lead to gratitude rather than self-satisfied reckoning. The closing names, Forgiving and Merciful, indicate that human beings inevitably fall short in thanking Allah, and that His mercy covers this shortfall, so that the awareness of one's inability to count His favors becomes a reason for hope and turning back to Him rather than despair.

translation: And Allah knows what you conceal and what you reveal.
interpretation: The verse reminds believers that Allah's knowledge is complete and encompasses every hidden intention, secret thought, and outward action alike. Nothing escapes Him, so the one who is mindful of Allah should align their inner intentions with their outward conduct, knowing that sincerity of heart is as accountable before Him as what is openly displayed to people.

translation: And those whom they invoke besides Allah create nothing, while they themselves are created.
interpretation: The verse confronts the idols and false deities worshipped beside Allah with a stark logical contrast: they are themselves fashioned by human hands or otherwise brought into being, yet they are presented as creators. Their total inability to create anything exposes the absurdity of directing worship toward beings that possess no power of creation, provision, or benefit. Since creation is the first and clearest mark of divinity, the one who is created cannot be the one who deserves to be worshipped, and the verse calls the reader to turn sincerely toward the true Creator alone.

translation: They are dead, not alive; and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected.
interpretation: The verse describes those who are worshipped besides God as lifeless things that possess no life of their own, and it points to the helplessness of those who call upon them. Their lack of awareness even of the time of their own raising emphasizes that such deities cannot benefit or respond to anyone, in contrast with the living and all-knowing God who alone holds power over resurrection. It thus invites the listener to recognize the emptiness of associating partners with God and to turn toward the One who alone gives life and will raise all people on the appointed Day.

translation: Your God is one God. As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are denying, and they are arrogant.
interpretation: The verse establishes the core of tawhid in its opening words, that the one who deserves worship is the single God, and then ties disbelief in the Hereafter directly to a disease of the heart and a posture of pride. The denial of the afterlife is not presented merely as an intellectual error but as a state of the heart that has closed itself off, a heart that refuses what it cannot see and therefore refuses the humility that faith demands. Arrogance (istikbar) is the natural companion of this denial: a person who does not expect to answer before God feels no need to bow before Him or before the truth brought by His messengers. The verse thus reveals a causal chain, where the unwillingness to accept accountability leads to the refusal of guidance, and the refusal of guidance hardens into self-exaltation. Oneness of God and belief in the Hereafter are shown to be inseparable, since acknowledging the One Lord means recognizing that He will gather creation and judge it, and this recognition softens the heart and makes it receptive to submission.

translation: Without doubt, Allah knows what they conceal and what they disclose. Indeed, He does not love the arrogant.
interpretation: The verse closes a warning about inner and outer conduct by establishing that nothing hidden escapes God's knowledge: the arrogant may keep their pride private or display it openly, yet both are equally exposed before Him. The phrase "la jarama" is an emphatic affirmation that this truth is beyond question. The concluding statement that God does not love the arrogant shows that istikbar, the inflated self-regard that refuses truth and looks down on others, is not merely a social flaw but a condition that cuts a person off from divine love. The verse thus joins the themes of sincerity and humility: what matters is the heart's posture as much as its visible actions, because God sees both.

translation: And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they say, "Legends of the former peoples."
interpretation: This verse exposes a habitual evasion: when the message of revelation is put to the disbelievers directly, they neither engage with its content nor deny it openly, but dismiss it in advance as the old tales of earlier generations, already known and empty of truth. Their reply is a refusal to think, since calling revelation "myths" spares them from weighing its claims, and it shows how the familiar narratives of the past can be turned into a shield against guidance. The verse thus warns that the question "what has God sent down?" is answered not by a fair examination but by a reflexive labeling that closes the heart to what it is asked to consider.

translation: That they may bear their own burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. Unquestionably, evil is what they bear.
interpretation: The verse shows that those who call others astray bear a double load: the full weight of their own sins, and a share of the sins of those they misguided, since their misguidance was carried out without knowledge and so their responsibility is not diminished by the errors of those who followed them. Leading people astray does not transfer guilt away from the one who did it; rather, it adds to his own burden, and the verse highlights the gravity of misleading others by describing the bearing of such burdens as the worst of loads.

translation: Those before them had already plotted, but Allah came at their structure from its foundations, so the roof fell down on them from above, and punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive.
interpretation: The verse uses the image of a building collapsing from its foundations to show that the schemes of the wicked turn back against them. Those who plot against the truth believe they are building something secure, yet Allah undermines the very base of their plans, so what they raised as a shelter becomes their own ruin. The punishment comes from a direction they never anticipated, teaching that human calculation cannot secure itself against the decree of God, and that deceit ultimately destroys its own author.

translation: Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them and say, "Where are My partners, for whose sake you used to oppose [the believers]?" Those who were given knowledge will say, "Indeed, disgrace today and evil are upon the disbelievers."
interpretation: The verse portrays the exposure of idolatry on the Day of Resurrection, where the humiliation of the polytheists is made complete by God's direct rebuke concerning the partners they associated with Him and defended in opposition to the truth. The phrase "those who were given knowledge" points to the righteous among the people of revelation and the believers who understood the reality of tawhid, and their words affirm that the true disgrace belongs to those who rejected faith. The verse thus teaches that worldly pride and attachment to false associates bring shame that becomes fully manifest at the Resurrection, while knowledge of God is the means by which the believer is spared that shame.

translation: Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves; then they will offer submission, (saying): "We were not doing any evil." Yes, indeed; surely Allah is Knowing of what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse portrays a scene at the moment of death for those who wronged themselves through disbelief and sin. Confronted by the angels, they attempt to deny their misdeeds and throw down their submission in a futile show of innocence, a reflex that betrays their guilt. The angelic reply, "Yes indeed," overturns their denial, affirming that nothing escapes Allah's perfect knowledge. The lesson is that concealment before people is pointless, since the reckoning rests with the One who knows the hidden and the apparent, and that self-deception through denial only deepens the soul's loss.

translation: So enter the gates of Hell, abiding therein forever. How wretched is the abode of the arrogant.
interpretation: The verse portrays the final consequence of arrogance (takabbur): those who refused to submit to God and disdained His truth are told to enter Hell through its gates, to remain there eternally. The phrase "how wretched is the abode" is an ironic reversal of their worldly pride, since the one who considered himself above the truth and above others is given a place of humiliation as his lasting dwelling. Arrogance here is not merely a personality trait but a spiritual condition that closes the heart to guidance, and the verse warns that its outcome is the loss of every honor the proud sought in this life.

translation: And it will be said to those who were mindful of God, "What has your Lord sent down?" They will say, "Goodness." For those who did good in this world there is good, and the Hereafter is better still. And excellent indeed is the abode of the God-conscious.
interpretation: The verse sets two responses to revelation side by side, and draws a contrast between them. The God-conscious answer the question about what was sent down with a single word, "goodness," because they have received it as a true gift and recognize its benefit. That answer is then matched by a reward that mirrors it: those who do good receive good in this life, and the Hereafter is greater still, so the reward of the righteous is not confined to this world but reaches its fullest form in the abode to come. The verse thus teaches that the believer's grateful acceptance of guidance and the believer's good deeds are repaid in kind, with the greater reward reserved for the next life.

translation: Gardens of perpetual residence which they will enter, beneath them rivers flow; they will have therein whatever they wish. Thus does Allah reward the righteous.
interpretation: The verse presents paradise as a place of enduring settlement (adn), where the believers' joy is complete: the flowing rivers signify abundance, purity and ever-renewing life, and the promise that they will have whatever they desire shows that every longing of the soul is fulfilled without lack or fear of loss. The closing phrase links this reward directly to taqwa, indicating that the state of God-consciousness that guided a person's conduct in this world is precisely what qualifies them for this eternal honor, so that the reward is a natural fruit of righteousness rather than an arbitrary gift.

translation: Those whom the angels take in death while they are good, saying, "Peace be upon you; enter Paradise for what you used to do."
interpretation: The verse portrays the moment of death for the righteous as a gentle and honorable departure rather than a painful one. Their souls are received by angels in a state of purity and goodness, and the angels greet them with peace, announcing that they are destined for Paradise. The verse thus links the serene ending of a life with the deeds that were done in it: the reward of Paradise is presented as the fruit of the believer's own good conduct, and it offers reassurance that a life of sincere faith and righteous action is met with tranquility at its close and with honor in the hereafter.

translation: Are they waiting for anything but that the angels should come to them, or that the command of your Lord should come? Thus did those before them act. And Allah did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who persist in denial by showing that they are, in effect, waiting only for the inescapable reckoning: either the angels come to take their souls and carry out the decree of death, or the decisive command of God arrives in the form of the promised punishment or the Final Hour. This is the same pattern that befell the earlier nations who rejected their messengers. The closing statement makes clear that the destruction was not an act of injustice by God; rather, people brought their own ruin through their persistent wrongdoing, since every refusal of guidance is ultimately a harm done to one's own soul.

translation: So the evils of what they had done struck them, and what they used to mock surrounded them.
interpretation: The verse shows that the consequences of wrongdoing are not random but are the direct result of one's own deeds, returning upon the doers themselves. Those who mocked the message of the prophets and treated its warnings as a jest found that the very thing they ridiculed encompassed them in the form of punishment. It is a reminder that disbelief and arrogance toward divine guidance carry their own inevitable reckoning, and that what a person dismisses as mere amusement may become the reality that overtakes him.

translation: And those who associated others with Allah said, "If Allah had willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have prohibited anything without His permission." Likewise did those before them act. So is there upon the messengers except clear conveyance?
interpretation: This verse exposes a common argument of the polytheists: they attribute their idolatry and their self-invented prohibitions to the divine will, reasoning that whatever they do must be what Allah wants since He could have prevented it. The Qur'an does not refute them by denying divine will, but by showing that such reasoning would excuse every falsehood, and that this is the same pattern of denial followed by earlier nations. The verse then reminds that the duty of the messengers is only to convey the message plainly, while accountability rests with the people who choose to accept or reject it.

translation: And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying], "Worship Allah and avoid false deities." So among them were those whom Allah guided, and among them were those upon whom error was deserved. So travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the deniers.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the central mission of every prophet across all nations was one and the same: calling people to exclusive worship of Allah and to rejecting everything worshipped besides Him, which is what the term taghut denotes. Yet the verse makes clear that the prophetic message, though universal in its sending, did not produce uniform results: guidance is granted by Allah to those who respond, while those who persist in denial have, by their own choices, come to deserve the error they chose. The closing command to travel and observe turns the reader's attention to history, inviting reflection on the fate of past communities that rejected their messengers, so that the consequences of denial become a lesson in the sincerity and seriousness of the call to faith.

translation: If you are eager for their guidance, indeed Allah does not guide those whom He sends astray, and for them there will be no helpers.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) when his strong desire for the guidance of his people grows heavy on him. It teaches that guidance ultimately rests with Allah alone, and that the Prophet's duty is to convey the message, not to force faith upon hearts. Those who persistently turn away from the truth and choose misguidance, Allah leaves to the consequences of their own choice, and they will find no one who can rescue them from that state. The verse thus combines comfort for the messenger with a sober warning to those who insist on error.

translation: And they swear by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that Allah will not resurrect those who die. Yes! It is a promise binding upon Him, true, but most people do not know.
interpretation: The verse exposes the deniers of resurrection who, despite their most solemn oaths, insist that the dead will never be raised, thereby revealing that their certainty rests on ignorance rather than knowledge. The word "bala" overturns their denial with emphatic affirmation, and "wa'dan 'alayhi haqqan" frames resurrection not merely as a possibility but as a divine promise that Allah has bound Himself to fulfil, so the reality of the Hereafter is anchored in God's own truthfulness. The closing phrase locates the root of the error in the majority's lack of knowledge, suggesting that denial of the afterlife is less a matter of evidence than of failing to reflect on the creation and origin that make return entirely within God's power.

translation: So that He may make clear to them that about which they differ, and that those who disbelieved may know that they were liars.
interpretation: The verse points to a purpose behind the revelation of the Book: it is sent down to resolve the disputes that people have fallen into about matters of faith and truth, so that the confusion is removed and the truth is distinguished from falsehood. It also indicates that the outcome will expose the disbelievers' claims, making plain to them, and to the observer, that the denial and the accusations they made were untrue. Thus clarity of guidance and the unmasking of falsehood go together, and the truth is ultimately shown to stand while the claims of those who rejected it are revealed as false.

translation: Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is.
interpretation: The verse expresses the absolute ease of divine creation: God's will needs no effort, process, or time, since the mere command "Be" brings the thing into existence at once. This shows that all created things depend entirely on the divine decree, and that God's power is not limited by the means or resistances that govern human action. It also invites the believer to reflect on the reality of resurrection and the origin of all things, for the One who creates by a word is certainly able to bring back what has ceased to be.

translation: And those who emigrated for the sake of Allah after they had been wronged - We will surely settle them in this world in a good place, and the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew.
interpretation: The verse presents migration undertaken for Allah's sake as a supreme act of faith that follows upon suffering injustice, and it links the believer's patience and sacrifice to a double recompense: a worldly settlement of goodness and an even greater reward in the Hereafter. The phrase "if only they knew" implies that the true measure of worth lies beyond the immediate, and that those who grasp the value of the unseen will see that loss of home and status for God's sake is repaid far more abundantly than any earthly comfort. It reassures the oppressed that displacement endured with sincerity is not a defeat but a path toward divine honor, both here and in the eternal life to come.

translation: Those who are patient and upon their Lord they rely.
interpretation: The verse describes the two inner qualities of the believers who are steadfast in faith: sabr (patient endurance in obedience, in avoiding sin, and in bearing hardship) and tawakkul (placing complete trust in God). Patience is the active discipline that holds a person firm under trials, while reliance on the Lord is the heart's settled confidence that God alone manages affairs. The verse indicates that true success in the face of difficulty comes from combining perseverance in one's own striving with trust that the outcome rests with God.

translation: We sent not before you except men to whom We revealed; so ask the people of remembrance if you do not know.
interpretation: The verse affirms that every messenger sent before Muhammad was a human man chosen and inspired by God, which refutes the objection that a messenger must be an angel or someone outside human nature. It then directs those who lack knowledge to consult those who possess the scriptural record, namely the People of the Book who had received earlier revelation, so that prophethood is confirmed through transmitted knowledge rather than through doubt. The verse thus establishes both the humanity of the prophets and the principle that unlearned people should rely on informed authorities in matters of revealed truth.

translation: With the clear proofs and the scriptures. And We have sent down to you the Reminder, that you may make clear to mankind what has been sent down to them, and that they may reflect.
interpretation: The verse presents the Prophet's mission as a twofold trust: he was sent with manifest proofs and with the earlier scriptures as a confirmation of the same message, and he was given the Reminder so that its clarity would not remain confined to him. The phrase 'what has been sent down to them' signals that the Prophet's explanation is not an addition to revelation but a faithful unfolding of it, so that people may grasp the guidance meant for them. The final aim is not mere recitation or memorization but reflection, since the purpose of making the message clear is to awaken thought and understanding in the hearts of its hearers.

translation: Do those who devise evil schemes feel secure that God will not cause the earth to swallow them up, or that the punishment will not come upon them from where they do not perceive?
interpretation: The verse confronts those who plot wickedness with a pointed question about their sense of security. Their confidence that they are beyond reach is shown to be unfounded, since divine justice can strike suddenly and from directions they never anticipated, whether through a catastrophe that engulfs them in the earth or a punishment that arrives unnoticed. The verse thus calls the reader to vigilance and humility, reminding that worldly power and cunning offer no real protection against God, and that heedlessness toward one's own wrongdoing is itself a dangerous state.

translation: Or He seizes them in their going to and fro, so they cannot escape Him.
interpretation: The verse presents Allah's complete power over those who plot against the truth or defy Him: whether He seizes them suddenly while they are busy with their daily affairs, travelling, trading, and moving about in their own cycles of life, or gradually through a slow decline, they can never frustrate His will or flee from His grasp. Their constant movement and apparent freedom give them a false sense of security, yet it is entirely within His command, which should prompt the listener to heed warning, reflect on past nations destroyed in similar ways, and turn back to Him before the decree comes.

translation: Or He seizes them gradually, [wearing them down] by fear. Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse presents God's patience and mercy as the reason behind a gradual form of punishment. Rather than striking the wrongdoers at once, God may diminish them step by step, so that their fear and loss become a warning that invites repentance. The closing words, 'Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful,' show that even this measured chastisement flows from divine compassion, giving people time and reason to turn back before the consequences become final.

translation: Have they not considered what things Allah has created, how their shadows turn from the right and the left, prostrating to Allah while they are humbled?
interpretation: The verse invites the heedless to reflect on the created order, where even inanimate things such as shadows, which swing from side to side as the sun moves, are shown to be in a state of submission to their Creator. Every shadow falls in obedience to the laws Allah set, so the believer is reminded that all of creation, in its own manner, bows before God, and that human pride is out of place before a universe that is already humbled in His worship. The image thus turns the observer's gaze from the shadow itself to the Lord who governs it, calling the one who has eyes to recognize that submission is the natural state of all that exists.

translation: And to Allah prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures, and the angels, and they are not arrogant.
interpretation: The verse presents all of creation, from the creatures of the earth to the angels in the heavens, as united in a single act of submission before God, so that prostration becomes the natural state of the cosmos. The angels are singled out and described as free of arrogance, which highlights that pride is the very trait that led Iblis to refuse prostration, so the verse contrasts the humility of the angelic host with the defiance of those who refuse to bow to God. The message calls the human being to recognize that true dignity lies in lowering oneself before the Creator, and that the refusal to submit is a form of spiritual disorder that the whole created order stands against.

translation: They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded.
interpretation: The verse portrays the angels who dwell in the presence of God as beings whose reverence is rooted in awe of His supreme majesty, which is described as 'above them', signifying His absolute dominion and transcendence over all creation. Their fear is not dread born of guilt but a conscious, humble awareness of the One who is exalted above them, and this awareness expresses itself in complete and immediate obedience. The verse thus joins inner reverence with outward submission, teaching that true fear of God is the foundation of unwavering compliance with His commands. The prostration marker at its end invites the reader to enact this same humility before the Lord.

translation: And Allah said, "Do not take two gods. He is but one God, so fear only Me." (An-Nahl 16:51)
interpretation: The verse establishes the absolute oneness of God (tawhid) as the foundation of true faith: since divinity belongs to a single, unique Lord, multiplicity of objects of worship is rejected at its root. The command to take no two gods is followed by a direct address in the first person, "fa-iyya-ya fa-rhabun" (so fear Me alone), which shifts from declaring the truth about God to demanding a reverent awe that is directed exclusively toward Him. The verse thus connects belief in God's unity with the inner disposition of awe, teaching that reverence, which is the heart of worship, must not be divided among rivals, whether these are idols, desires, or worldly powers that a person might fear more than God.

translation: And to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and to Him is obedience due always. Will you then fear other than Allah?
interpretation: The verse establishes that all dominion over the heavens and the earth belongs exclusively to God, and therefore the religion, meaning the obedience, submission and due worship, is His alone and is owed to Him perpetually. Having affirmed His absolute ownership and right to be obeyed, the verse turns into a rhetorical rebuke: it is unreasonable to direct the awe, dread and piety that belong to God toward anyone else. Fear of harm, hope of benefit, and reverence are properly placed only in the One who possesses everything, so turning that fear toward idols or created powers reflects a misplaced and illogical devotion.

translation: And whatever blessing you have is from Allah; then when adversity touches you, to Him you cry for help.
interpretation: This verse exposes a recurring human weakness: the tendency to forget the Source of one's blessings during ease and to remember it only when hardship strikes. Every favor, whether health, provision, or safety, is traced back to Allah alone, so gratitude should be constant rather than reserved for moments of need. The image of crying out (tajarru') to Him in distress reveals that deep within human nature lies an instinctive recognition of a single Lord, even among those who deny Him in comfort. The verse thus calls the believer to a consistent awareness, turning to Allah in prosperity with thanks and not only in calamity with supplication.

translation: Then, when He removes the harm from you, behold, a group of you associate others with their Lord in worship.
interpretation: The verse exposes a recurring human pattern: in hardship, people turn sincerely to God, but once relief comes, a segment of them quickly returns to associating partners with Him. The word "إذا" (behold/suddenly) conveys how abrupt this reversal is, as though gratitude is forgotten the moment fear lifts. It is a warning that true faith should be consistent in prosperity as in adversity, and that the shirk criticized here is rooted in ingratitude and forgetfulness of the One who actually granted relief, rather than in any reasoned belief. The phrase "فريق منكم" also signals that this tendency belongs to a part of the community, not all of it, leaving room for those who remain steadfast.

translation: So that they may deny what We have given them. So enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know.
interpretation: The verse describes a people who, having been granted blessings, respond by ingratitude and denial, using those very favors as a reason for disbelief. The command "enjoy yourselves" is not an honor but a warning: their worldly pleasures are temporary and deceptive, given as a respite that only deepens their heedlessness. The closing threat, "you will soon know," points to the certain reckoning that will expose the emptiness of their enjoyment and the consequence of their ingratitude. The lesson is that abundance without gratitude becomes a trial, and that God's patience with the ungrateful should not be mistaken for neglect.

translation: And they assign to what they do not know a share of what We have provided them. By Allah, you will surely be questioned about what you used to fabricate.
interpretation: The verse exposes a practice of idolatrous people who set apart a portion of the sustenance Allah granted them for deities and objects of worship they have no knowledge or basis for, as though these had any claim to it. This reflects a deeper fault: attributing to false gods a right that belongs only to the One who provided the livelihood, and doing so on the authority of mere conjecture and invention. The oath that follows, with its emphatic future tense, warns that these acts of fabrication will not go unexamined, and that they will be called to account for the falsehoods they attributed to God and to what they chose to honor. The lesson is that sharing one's gifts in God's name must rest on knowledge revealed by Him, and that any ruling or devotion built on ignorance and invention carries accountability before Him.

translation: And they attribute daughters to God, glory be to Him, while for themselves they have what they desire.
interpretation: The verse exposes a double standard in the pagan Arabs' beliefs: they assigned daughters to God, even though they themselves considered daughters a source of shame (as stated elsewhere in the surah, where a father receiving news of a daughter's birth turns dark with grief), while reserving for themselves the sons they preferred. The phrase 'glory be to Him' rejects such attributions and affirms God's transcendence above having offspring of any kind. The closing clause, 'and for themselves they have what they desire,' is ironic: they claim for themselves what they most value and deny God what they consider inferior, showing that their theology was shaped by their own desires rather than by reason or revelation.

translation: When one of them is given tidings of a female child, his face darkens and he is filled with suppressed grief.
interpretation: The verse exposes the inner contradiction of those who attributed daughters to God while holding them in contempt for themselves. Their reaction to the birth of a daughter reveals a deep-seated shame and a valuation of human beings based on status and lineage rather than on the worth God has placed in them. The darkening of the face is an image of humiliation and inner anguish, showing that their disdain was not grounded in any reasoned principle but in a distorted pride. By depicting this reaction so vividly, the verse invites reflection on the injustice of judging a creature by social prejudice, and it implicitly calls the reader to recognize that the value of a child lies in the mercy and wisdom of the One who grants it.

translation: He hides himself from the people because of the evil of that which he has been given good news of. Shall he keep it in humiliation or bury it in the dust? Unquestionably, evil is what they decide.
interpretation: The verse portrays the mindset of those who, upon being given news of a daughter, feel shame and disgrace, and so weigh whether to keep her in humiliation or bury her alive. By exposing the absurdity and cruelty of this judgment, it shows that the pre-Islamic practice of female infanticide stemmed from false values, and that the people's standard of judgment is corrupt. The verse thus calls the reader to reject such inherited prejudice and to recognize that true honor and worth do not lie in the sex of a child but in the divine decree and in righteous conduct.

translation: For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the worst description, and to Allah belongs the highest description. And He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: The verse sets two contrasting 'likenesses' side by side: those who deny the Hereafter are given a base and ugly portrayal, a state of spiritual poverty in which their own disbelief reflects back on them as the worst of examples, while God alone possesses the sublime attributes of perfection, untouched by any deficiency. The disbelief in the Hereafter is shown to distort a person's whole measure of value, since one who sees no accountability beyond this life tends to reduce himself to lowly aims and a lowly self-image. By contrast, the 'highest likeness' belongs to God, whose might and wisdom are complete, so the verse invites the reader to measure reality by the Divine standard rather than by the narrow standards of a life that forgets its Creator and its return to Him.

translation: And if Allah were to seize the people for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it (the earth) a single creature; but He defers them until a specified term. So when their term comes, they will not remain behind an hour, nor will they precede it.
interpretation: The verse reveals the mercy and forbearance of Allah toward humanity: were He to hasten punishment in response to every act of injustice, no living creature would survive on the earth, since human wrongdoing is constant. Instead, He grants respite until a fixed appointed time decreed in His knowledge, and this delay is itself a form of grace that gives room for repentance and reform. When that appointed term arrives, no one can delay it even for a moment or bring it forward, reminding the reader that the timing of accountability belongs entirely to God and that the opportunity given in this life should not be squandered.

translation: And they assign to Allah what they dislike for themselves, and their tongues utter the lie that for them is the best (reward). Without doubt, for them is the Fire, and they will be left neglected therein.
interpretation: The verse exposes a twofold contradiction in the thinking of those who associate partners with God: they attribute to Him daughters, which they themselves detest, while they claim for themselves the best reward in the Hereafter, a claim that has no basis in revelation. The verse rebukes this self-serving presumption by affirming that their true destiny is the Fire, and that they will be hastened to it or abandoned to it, having been rendered heedless and left behind. It reveals a principle that human beings often project onto God what they would reject for themselves, and that a false sense of entitlement to divine favor, detached from righteous conduct, is itself a form of deception that the Qur'an firmly unmasks.

translation: By Allah, We certainly sent messengers to nations before you, but Satan made their deeds appear attractive to them, so he is their ally today, and theirs will be a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse shows that Satan's most dangerous method is not open command but making wrongdoing look appealing, so that people mistake their own corrupt deeds for goodness. Those who follow him in this way become his companions, and the phrase "today" points to the reality that the one who chose him as a guide will find that his alliance offers no protection, leaving only the painful consequence of their choices. The verse is therefore a warning to every generation to examine what has been adorned for them and to test their desires against the guidance sent by God.

translation: And We did not send down to you the Book except that you may make clear to them that about which they differ, and as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.
interpretation: The verse establishes the purpose of the revelation given to the Prophet Muhammad: it is not merely a text sent down but a clarifying instrument, meant to resolve the disputes that had arisen among the people, particularly among earlier communities who divided over their scriptures. The Prophet's role as an explainer is thus tied to the Qur'an's own function of distinguishing truth from falsehood in matters of belief and practice. The verse then names two fruits of this clarity, guidance and mercy, but specifies that they are realized only for those who believe, showing that the Book's illumination is received in proportion to the openness of the heart that accepts it. Clarity, in this reading, is not only a property of the text but a relationship between the message and a receptive human response.

translation: And Allah sends down water from the sky and by it gives life to the earth after its death. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who listen.
interpretation: The verse draws the listener's attention from the familiar act of rain to a deeper lesson about resurrection and divine power. The dead, barren earth that suddenly revives when water reaches it is a visible pattern of what God can do with the dead on the Day of Judgment, so the cycle of nature becomes a daily reminder of the Hereafter. The phrase "a people who listen" indicates that such signs are perceived not by eyes alone but by those who open their hearts and attentively hear the message, whereas the heedless pass over the same evidence without reflection.

translation: And indeed, in grazing livestock there is a lesson for you: We give you to drink from what is in their bellies, from between digestive waste and blood, pure milk, palatable to those who drink it.
interpretation: The verse directs the reader's attention from the familiar act of drinking milk to a deeper reflection on divine wisdom and care. The milk is produced inside the animal from materials that are themselves unclean, yet it emerges pure, wholesome, and pleasant, showing that Allah brings good out of what appears base and that His creation operates with precise, purposeful design. The 'lesson' (ibrah) is thus a call to recognize the Creator's power, mercy, and provision in everyday natural phenomena, and to be grateful for sustenance that comes through means one might never have imagined.

translation: And from the fruits of the date palms and grapevines you derive intoxicants and good provision. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who use reason.
interpretation: The verse draws attention to a contrast within the same produce: the date and the grape yield both sakar (an intoxicant, or what is made from them that may intoxicate) and rizq hasan (good sustenance). Placed in a Meccan context, where it reflects the gradual process of the prohibition of wine, it invites the reader to reflect that the same divine gift can be turned to harm or to nourishment depending on human choice. The phrase 'a sign for a people who reason' makes the lesson an appeal to the intellect: discernment between what corrupts the mind and what sustains life is itself a sign of God's wisdom, perceptible to those who reflect.

translation: And your Lord inspired to the bee: "Take for yourselves houses in the mountains, and in the trees, and in what they construct."
interpretation: The verse presents the bee as a creature guided by a direct divine inspiration (wahy) that is instinctive rather than rational, so that it builds its dwellings in mountains, trees, and structures raised by people. This points to the wonder of natural guidance: the same Lord who orders the cosmos also places within a tiny insect the knowledge needed to construct its precise and orderly home, inviting the reader to reflect on divine wisdom manifest in the creatures.

translation: Then eat from all the fruits and follow the ways of your Lord, made easy. From their bellies comes a drink of varying colors, in which there is healing for people. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who give thought.
interpretation: The verse, addressed to the bee, shows that divine guidance works through instinct and obedience: the bee is commanded to feed on the fruits of many plants and to move through the paths its Lord has made smooth for it, and from its own body issues honey of varied hues, a substance that heals. The reflection the verse calls for is that the wondrous products of creation are not accidental; they point to a single, wise Creator who channels even the humblest creature toward beneficial ends, and that the Qur'an invites people to ponder such signs in nature, which bring human beings to recognize and be grateful to their Lord.

translation: And Allah created you, then He causes you to die. And among you is one who is returned to the most decrepit age, so that he knows nothing after having known. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Powerful.
interpretation: The verse points to the stages of human life as a sign of God's absolute power over creation and its end: the one who created humanity from nothing is the same who decides its death, and the return to feebleness in old age shows that the strength, knowledge, and capacities people possess are lent to them and can be taken away. Its closing names, All-Knowing and All-Powerful, invite the reader to recognize that nothing escapes divine knowledge or outside divine control, and so to humility before God, reflection on one's own fragility, and gratitude for the faculties one still enjoys.

translation: And Allah has favored some of you over others in provision. But those who have been favored will not hand over their provision to those whom their right hands possess, so that they would be equal therein. Is it then the blessing of Allah that they deny?
interpretation: The verse uses the unequal distribution of provision among people as a sign pointing to God's wisdom and the reality of His blessing. If people themselves do not accept sharing their wealth equally with those they own or are responsible for, how can they then claim equality with God's own dispensation, to Whom they owe all they have? The rhetorical question rebukes those who deny or are ungrateful for Allah's favor, since everything they possess, including their ability to earn and their share of sustenance, is a gift from Him and not a product of their own merit alone.

translation: And Allah has made for you spouses from among yourselves, and made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren, and provided for you from the good things. Then in falsehood do they believe, and in the favor of Allah do they disbelieve?
interpretation: The verse points to a sequence of divine favors that flows from the human being's own nature: Allah created spouses from within the self so that companionship and tranquility arise from the same kind, then extended this bond into lineage and continuity through children and grandchildren, and finally supplied sustenance from good and wholesome things. Having enumerated these blessings, which are plain and undeniable in everyday life, the verse turns to a rhetorical rebuke: it is incongruous that people would give their trust to falsehood, such as idols and baseless beliefs, while ungratefully rejecting the very bounties that testify to the Creator's grace. Belief and gratitude are thus shown to be intertwined, and disbelief is portrayed as a denial of what is evident in one's own life.

translation: And they worship, besides God, that which possesses for them no provision from the heavens and the earth, not the least, and they are not able (to do anything).
interpretation: The verse exposes the emptiness of idolatry by showing that the objects of worship have no power whatsoever over sustenance, which belongs to God alone; they can neither provide anything from the heavens or the earth nor act on anyone's behalf. Since true worship must be directed to the one who controls provision and has the power to grant or withhold it, the verse calls the human being to recognize that devotion given to powerless beings is both unreasonable and a misplacement of trust that cannot bring any benefit.

translation: So do not set forth comparisons for Allah. Indeed, Allah knows, and you do not know.
interpretation: The verse forbids believers from coining likenesses or analogies for God, since human reasoning, shaped by limited experience and knowledge, cannot fathom His nature or properly liken Him to His creation. Allah alone possesses complete knowledge of what is fitting for Him, while people are ignorant of the reality they try to describe. The call is therefore to humility before divine knowledge: to affirm God as unique and incomparable, and to refrain from speculation that attributes to Him human forms, qualities, or equals.

translation: Allah presents an example: a slave owned by others, who has no power over anything, and a man on whom We have bestowed good provision from Us, so he spends from it secretly and openly. Are they equal? All praise is for Allah. But most of them do not know.
interpretation: The verse sets before the reader a concrete parable drawn from the institution of slavery to expose the absurdity of associating others with God. A slave under another's ownership cannot act independently, and so cannot truly dispose of anything, whereas the free man who has been granted sustenance by God can give freely in public and in private. The comparison is designed to show that just as no sensible person would equate these two, it is equally unreasonable to equate the Lord, the sole true Provider who owns and gives all things, with the idols and false objects of worship that possess no power over anything. The rhetorical question 'Are they equal?' answers itself, and the closing praise of God affirms that the proof is clear. The statement that most people lack knowledge points to the fact that the clarity of this reasoning is apparent to the mind, yet most remain heedless of it, failing to draw the obvious conclusion about the unique sovereignty of God.

translation: And Allah presents an example: two men, one of them mute, unable to do anything, a burden upon his master, wherever he directs him he brings no good. Are they equal, he and one who commands justice while he is on a straight path?
interpretation: The verse sets two figures side by side to expose the difference between dependence and guidance. The mute man, incapable of speech or initiative and a liability to his master, stands for one who has no true benefit to offer and whose every undertaking yields nothing good, while the one who enjoins justice stands for a person whose words and conduct are anchored in clear, upright principle. The rhetorical question, which expects the answer no, shows that usefulness, clarity and righteousness cannot be equated with their opposites. Read more broadly, the parable warns against the idol-worshippers who, like the mute servant, depend on lifeless things that can neither speak nor act, and it invites the believer to recognise that the one who calls to justice and walks the straight path is of an entirely different worth.

translation: And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. And the matter of the Hour is not but like the blink of an eye, or it is even nearer. Indeed, Allah is over all things Competent.
interpretation: The verse directs the heart from the visible world to the realm of the unseen that belongs exclusively to God, and then turns the believer's attention to the Hour, which is a matter of that unseen knowledge. Its arrival, though it may seem distant to human reckoning, is as sudden and certain as a blink of the eye, or even nearer, because for God time is not measured as humans measure it. The closing affirmation that God has power over all things reminds the listener that the One who controls the hidden realms and who will bring the Hour is fully capable of doing so, so the proper response is constant readiness, humility, and trust rather than either denial or presumptuous speculation about its timing.

translation: And Allah brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers knowing nothing, and He made for you hearing, sight, and hearts, that perhaps you would be grateful.
interpretation: The verse reminds humanity of its origin in helplessness: a person emerges from the mother's womb with no knowledge at all, entirely dependent on others. Within this state of total ignorance, God endows the human being with the faculties of hearing, sight, and the heart (af'ida), which are the very means by which knowledge is acquired and understanding is formed. The verse thus links the gift of these faculties to the purpose of gratitude: the recognition that one's capacity to learn, perceive, and comprehend is a divine bounty, and that the proper response to it is to use these faculties in acknowledging and thanking the Giver.

translation: Have they not considered the birds, made subservient in the atmosphere of the sky? Nothing holds them up except Allah. Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe.
interpretation: The verse directs the believer's attention from the ordinary sight of birds in flight to a sign of divine power. A bird suspended in the air, sustained against the pull of gravity and moving through the open sky by a body and an instinct it did not create for itself, displays a constant dependence on a Sustainer who alone holds it aloft. The question "have they not seen?" reproaches heedlessness: the phenomenon is before every eye, yet it is passed over without reflection. The phrase "made subservient" (musakhkharat) indicates that the birds are bound to a law set by God, just as the rest of creation is subjected to His will, so their flight is not an independent power but an act of obedience to the order He established. The verse then narrows its focus to those who believe, implying that faith is what allows one to read these signs, since only the one who is inwardly attentive to God perceives in the familiar what points to Him. The lesson is that tawhid is affirmed through the observable world: nothing in the heavens or the earth sustains itself, and reliance should be placed on Allah alone.

translation: And Allah has made for you from your homes a place of rest, and He has made for you from the hides of cattle tents which you find light to carry on the day of your traveling and the day of your settling, and from their wool, their fur, and their hair [He has made] furnishings and provisions for a time.
interpretation: The verse points to the way God's favor is woven into the ordinary material conditions of human life: the home is a source of tranquility (sakan), and even the portable dwellings of the nomadic Arabs are made from the animals God created, lightened so they can be carried on the journey and used at rest. The wool, fur and hair of livestock become household goods and comforts, all for a limited span of time. The lesson is that human security, mobility and provision all come from God's bounty, and that the worldly enjoyments they provide are temporary, inviting gratitude and remembrance that they are for 'a time' only.

translation: And Allah has made for you shade from [among] what He has created, and has made for you places of refuge in the mountains, and has made for you garments that protect you from the heat, and garments that protect you from your [mutual] violence. Thus does He complete His favor upon you that you might submit [to Him].
interpretation: The verse presents shade, mountain shelters, and garments as signs of divine provision that answer the basic human needs for protection from harm, whether from the elements or from enemies, so that the believer sees in ordinary comforts a continuous favor that calls for gratitude and submission. By naming both the heat and the 'violence' that men inflict on one another, it suggests that God's care covers both physical and social dangers, and that completing His blessing upon people is meant to lead them to surrender to Him in Islam.

translation: But if they turn away, then your duty is only to convey the clear message.
interpretation: The verse places the full weight of the Prophet's responsibility where it truly belongs: delivering the message clearly and completely. Guidance is not something the messenger can force into hearts. Once the truth has been presented plainly, the outcome of a person's acceptance or rejection rests with God, and the messenger is free of blame for those who refuse. This reminds every later bearer of the message that sincere, lucid communication is their duty, while the results lie beyond their control.

translation: They recognize the favor of Allah, then they deny it, and most of them are disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse exposes a painful inconsistency of the heart: knowledge alone does not produce gratitude. These people do not lack awareness of Allah's blessings; they know them clearly, yet their knowledge does not lead to acknowledgment, and so they turn their recognition into denial. The lesson is that true faith requires more than intellectual acknowledgment of divine favor; it demands that one live that recognition through sincere thankfulness, humility, and obedience. The verse's closing judgment that most of them are disbelievers points to how widespread this condition of knowing yet rejecting becomes among a people, warning the believer to guard against letting familiarity with blessings dull them into ingratitude.

translation: And [mention] the Day when We will raise up from every nation a witness, then none will be permitted to the ones who disbelieved [to make excuses], nor will they be asked to make amends (or be allowed to return to good standing with their Lord).
interpretation: The verse points to a day of accountability in which every community is judged through its own prophet or witness, who testifies to what was conveyed to them and how they responded. Once the testimony is established, the disbelievers are denied the opportunity to offer excuses or plead for a reprieve, and they cannot earn back divine pleasure by repentance at that point. The verse thus underlines that the window for repentance and reconciliation belongs to this worldly life, and that on the Day of Judgment the case is closed, with justice leaving no room for appeal.

translation: And when those who did wrong see the punishment, it will not be lightened for them, nor will they be given respite.
interpretation: The verse portrays the moment of confrontation with punishment as final and irreversible for the wrongdoers. Their sudden sight of the torment strips away any hope of relief, since the chance to amend has already passed, and the delay that might have been granted in worldly life is withdrawn. It conveys that justice is not softened by pleading once the reality is laid bare, and it calls the listener to act while respite is still available, before the moment when no reprieve can be given.

translation: And when those who associated others with God see their associates, they will say, "Our Lord, these are our associates whom we used to invoke besides You." But they will throw back at them the word: "Indeed, you are liars."
interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Judgment, when idolaters, confronted with the beings they had made partners with God, will blame those partners for their misguidance. Their false gods, once the objects of their hope and worship, are now presented as witnesses to their own error. The reply of the 'partners' that they are liars (in Q 16:86 and related passages, they deny that the idolaters ever worshipped them) exposes the emptiness of the claims made for them. The scene rebukes the futility of associating anything with God, since on that day no intercessor or ally can be relied upon, and the false bonds built in this life collapse and turn into mutual denial.

translation: And they will offer submission to God on that Day, and what they used to fabricate will be lost to them.
interpretation: The verse depicts the moment of final reckoning, when those who had persisted in arrogance and denial are compelled to surrender in humble submission before God, the one true Lord, having no more defiance left in them. The 'submission' (al-salam) they cast forth is a yielding that comes too late to benefit them, since it is forced by undeniable reality rather than freely given in faith. Their false claims, the partners and fabrications they had invented and relied upon in the world, vanish and abandon them, revealing the emptiness of everything they had trusted apart from God. The verse thus invites the listener to embrace sincere submission now, while it still profits, rather than awaiting a day when every illusion collapses.
