Since true power over harm and relief belongs to God alone, devotion must be directed to Him exclusively, and the verse thereby establishes tawhid through the logic of demonstrated helplessness.

translation: Those whom they call upon themselves seek the means of access to their Lord, competing as to which of them is nearest, and they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is something to be feared.
interpretation: The verse exposes the futility of worshipping others besides God: those who are invoked, such as prophets, angels, and righteous servants, are themselves seeking nearness to their Lord through good deeds and supplication. Their own condition of hope and fear mirrors that of the worshippers, showing that all creation is dependent and humble before God. The true path is therefore to direct one's devotion to the One who alone deserves it, seeking the means of drawing near to Him through obedience, balancing hope in His mercy with awareness of His justice.

translation: And there is no city but that We will destroy it before the Day of Resurrection or punish it with a severe punishment. That was written in the Book as inscribed.
interpretation: The verse establishes that every community's fate is bound to a divine decree already recorded in the Preserved Book: no town escapes, whether through destruction before the Final Day or through severe chastisement, so that worldly ruin is presented not as random misfortune but as a predetermined consequence of a people's conduct. Its emphasis on the fixity of the written decree calls the listener to reflect on accountability in this life, reminding that the arrogance of prosperous communities is the very thing that brings about their reckoning, and that God's knowledge and justice encompass all histories in advance.

translation: And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them. And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign, but they wronged themselves through it. And We send not the signs except as a warning.
interpretation: The verse explains God's wisdom in sending miracles: the signs were not withheld out of inability, but the earlier nations' rejection made further signs pointless for them, so a miracle that was denied brought down a warning rather than mercy. The she-camel given to Thamud was a clear, perceptible sign, yet they responded with injustice, turning the very proof meant to guide them into their own wrongdoing. The sign is thus a trial that either leads to guidance or, when rejected, becomes a warning of consequences.

translation: And [remember] when We told you, "Indeed, your Lord has encompassed the people." And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people, and [like] the accursed tree mentioned in the Qur'an. And We warn them, but it increases them only in great transgression.
interpretation: The verse links three things: the all-encompassing knowledge and power of God over humanity, the night-journey vision that was shown to the Prophet, and the cursed tree in the Qur'an, all of which served as a test that separated those whose hearts were receptive from those who rejected the message. The warnings sent to people did not produce belief in those who were already fixed in defiance, so their rebellion only grew. The passage teaches that a sign or a warning reveals the inner disposition of a person rather than creating faith by itself, and that God's encompassing reach means no one escapes accountability even when they resist.

translation: And [mention] when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," so they prostrated, except Iblis. He said, "Shall I prostrate to one whom You created from clay?"
interpretation: The verse recalls the pivotal moment of creation when God honored Adam by commanding the angels to prostrate before him, an act of reverence rather than worship. The angels obeyed immediately, while Iblis refused out of arrogance, measuring Adam by his material origin of clay and considering himself superior because he was made of fire, as mentioned elsewhere in the Qur'an. His refusal reveals the root of disobedience: pride that judges another by lineage or substance rather than by the favor and command of the One who created both. The passage thus establishes the nature of Iblis's sin as haughty self-regard, and it presents the humility of obedience as the proper response to divine command, while also foreshadowing the human struggle against the same pride that led to his downfall.

translation: He said: "Have you considered this one whom You have honored over me? If You delay me until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely seize control of his descendants, except for a few."
interpretation: The verse reveals Satan's arrogance and envy toward Adam, whom God honored above him, and his defiant challenge to God. His boast to dominate Adam's offspring reflects the nature of temptation: the enemy of humanity openly declares his intent to lead people astray, while the exception of "a few" points to the sincere servants of God who resist his influence. It is a reminder that human honor in God's sight is a trial, and that the true safeguard against misguidance is sincere faith and devotion to God.

translation: He said, "Go, and whoever follows you among them, indeed Hell is your recompense, a full and ample recompense."
interpretation: The verse records Iblis's expulsion-and-challenge scene in its context: after refusing to prostrate, he is told to depart, and the warning is directed at him and at those among his followers who go astray. The phrase "jaza'ukum jaza'an mawfuran" presents Hell not as a random punishment but as a complete, deserved repayment, measured to match the choice each party made. The wording emphasizes that following the deceiver carries its own inevitable consequence, so the verse shifts the reader's attention from Satan's boast to the moral responsibility of whoever chooses to follow him.

translation: And incite to rebellion whomever you can among them with your voice, and urge against them your cavalry and your infantry, and share with them in wealth and children, and make promises to them. But Satan promises them nothing except delusion.
interpretation: The verse depicts Satan's declared plan to lead humanity astray by every means at his disposal: seductive speech, mobilizing his forces, and entangling people in wealth and offspring, which are often the very things that absorb hearts and distract them from their Lord. The phrase 'share with them in wealth and children' points to how worldly attachments become channels of misguidance when they are pursued without regard to God. The closing words emphasize that Satan's promises are hollow and deceptive, offering false hope that leads people away from truth. The verse therefore serves as a warning to believers to recognize these subtle tactics and to ground their lives in sincere faith rather than in worldly illusions.

translation: Indeed, My servants - you have no authority over them. And sufficient is your Lord as a Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: The verse reveals that Satan's power extends only over those who choose to follow and align themselves with him, not over the sincere servants of God who place their trust in Him. Authority over the believer is not granted by force but is surrendered by the person's own inclinations and choices. The closing phrase points to the assurance that God is the sufficient guardian and guarantor of those who rely upon Him, so that the one who entrusts his affairs to the Lord need not fear the whisperings of the enemy. Thus the verse links protection from misguidance to sincere reliance (tawakkul) and to the servant's own devotion.

translation: Your Lord is He who drives the ships for you through the sea, that you may seek of His bounty. Indeed, He is ever Merciful to you.
interpretation: The verse presents the sea-faring ship as a sign of divine mercy: the very act of human commerce and travel across the waters, which might seem a product of human skill alone, is traced back to the Lord who makes the vessel move and sustains the conditions that allow it. Seeking His bounty through trade is thus not severed from worship but framed as a grace that He opens for His servants. The closing affirmation that He is Merciful toward you invites the reader to recognize that provision, safety, and livelihood are all expressions of a compassion that accompanies humanity even in the most precarious and unpredictable places, such as the open sea.

translation: And when harm touches you at sea, those you call upon vanish except Him. But when He brings you safely to land, you turn away. Indeed, man is ever ungrateful.
interpretation: The verse exposes a recurring pattern in human nature: in moments of extreme helplessness, when the storm leaves no refuge and every human support falls away, the heart turns instinctively and sincerely toward God alone, and all the false powers one usually relies on are revealed as empty. Yet the same heart is quick to forget this sincerity once danger passes and ease returns. The turning away after deliverance is therefore not merely a historical act of the idolaters of Mecca but a warning about a standing tendency in the self, which treats the mercy of God as a temporary debt to be forgotten rather than a continual bounty to be remembered. The final word, kafur, signals that this forgetfulness is a form of ingratitude that conceals the favor received. The lesson is that true faith is tested not only in distress but in ease, and that one's gratitude should be as constant as one's dependence proved to be in the hour of need.

translation: Do you feel secure that He will not cause the earth to swallow you on the side of the land, or send against you a violent storm of pebbles, and then you will find for yourselves no protector?
interpretation: The verse confronts human complacency toward divine power. Those who feel safe on dry land, even after escaping the perils of the sea, are reminded that safety is never self-generated: the same Creator who can cause the earth beneath them to give way, or send a destructive wind laden with stones from the sky, can strip away every human defense. When every means of protection fails, no ally or guardian remains except God. The verse thus calls for humility, gratitude, and constant awareness that security is a gift that rests entirely in God's hands.

translation: Or do you feel secure that He will not return you to it another time and send against you a violent wind-storm and drown you for your disbelief, then you will not find for yourselves any pursuer against Us therefor?
interpretation: The verse addresses those who feel safe from divine retribution on land after being delivered from the sea. Having shown them mercy by bringing them safely ashore, God warns that the same Power that controls the elements can at any time return them to the sea and unleash a destructive wind that drowns them as a consequence of their ingratitude and disbelief. The verse thus calls for reflection on the fragility of human security, the obligation of gratitude for deliverance, and the recognition that no one can avenge or pursue them against God's decree once it is executed.

translation: And We have certainly honored the children of Adam, carried them on land and sea, provided for them from the good things, and preferred them over many of those We have created with a definite preference.
interpretation: The verse establishes that human dignity (karāmah) is an inherent divine gift that belongs to humankind as a whole, prior to any distinction of faith, race, or achievement. The honor is expressed through concrete blessings: the capacity to travel and transport across land and sea, the provision of good and wholesome sustenance, and a preferred station above much of creation. Its significance lies in reminding the human being that the dignity he possesses is a trust rather than a possession, so that it obliges him to honor that same dignity in others and to respond to such favor with gratitude and righteous conduct.

translation: On the Day We will call every people with their leader; so whoever is given his record in his right hand, those will read their record, and they will not be wronged even a thread.
interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Judgment as a gathering in which each community is summoned according to the guide or model it followed in life, whether a prophet, a righteous leader, or a misguiding figure, so that the reckoning is tied to the path a people chose. Receiving the record in the right hand signifies success and honor, as the believer joyfully reads an account that is exact and complete. The closing assurance that no one will be wronged even by the thinness of a date-fiber's thread affirms the perfect justice of God, where every deed, however small, is recorded and weighed, urging the listener to take responsibility for the leader they follow and the deeds they inscribe.

translation: And whoever is blind in this (world) will be blind in the Hereafter, and even further astray from the way.
interpretation: The verse ties spiritual perception in this life to one's condition in the Hereafter. Blindness here is not merely physical but refers to the inability to perceive the signs of God in creation, in the revelation, and in one's own self; whoever closes their heart to these signs in this world will find that same blindness continuing and deepening in the next, where the veil is lifted for everyone yet the one who was blind will see nothing of the truth they neglected. The phrase 'even further astray from the way' indicates a progressive loss: the blind person not only fails to see the path but wanders further from it, so that the consequence of present heedlessness is an intensified misguidance rather than a mere continuation. The verse thus calls the listener to use the sight that God has given in this world, since the faculties neglected here become the very deficiencies that define one's state in the afterlife.

translation: And indeed, they came close to tempting you away from that which We revealed to you, so that you would invent [something] other than it against Us; and then they would have taken you as a close friend.
interpretation: The verse portrays the intense pressure exerted by the opponents of the Prophet, who nearly succeeded in drawing him away from the revelation by offering him an alternative, which would have amounted to fabricating falsehood against God. Its message is that the Prophet's steadfastness was sustained by divine protection, and that had he deviated even slightly, his relationship with his opponents would have shifted into a false intimacy, underscoring that faithfulness to revelation is the foundation of true closeness to God and that compromise with falsehood, however subtle, leads to a false alliance.

translation: And had We not made you firm, you would have almost inclined toward them a little.
interpretation: The verse, addressed to the Prophet Muhammad, is a reminder that his steadfastness was a sustained gift of divine grace rather than a product of his own strength alone. It comes in the context of the Meccan pressure to make concessions and compromise on the message, and it shows how close even the most upright soul can come to yielding to worldly pressure without God's support. It teaches that firmness in truth depends on Divine help, and that believers should continually seek that support, while the Prophet's near-inclination, though slight, is presented as a warning against any tilt toward compromise with falsehood.

translation: Otherwise, We would have made you taste a double portion of life and a double portion of death; then you would not have found for yourself any helper against Us.
interpretation: The verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad and, through him, every person, in the context of the Prophet's steadfastness against pressure from his opponents who sought to make him incline toward them. It shows that a messenger's firmness is sustained by divine support alone: had God not strengthened him, he would have been exposed to a severe punishment in both this life and the next, and no one could have protected him from it. The phrase 'double the life and double the death' conveys an intensified chastisement, here and in the hereafter, and the rhetorical emphasis lies in the absence of any helper against God, teaching believers that true protection and victory come only from Him.

translation: And indeed, they almost tried to drive you out of the land to expel you from it, but then they would not have remained after you except for a little while.
interpretation: This verse belongs to the narrative of the Prophet's departure from Mecca and the hostility of his opponents, who sought to remove him from his homeland. It conveys a divine warning that persecutors who force a prophet out of his land are not granted lasting security in it: the same land that they wished to clear of him would soon be emptied of them. The phrase 'after you' points to the principle that God's way with His messengers is established, so that the aggressors who expel a messenger are themselves swept away shortly after. The verse thus offers consolation to the believers and a sober reminder to the oppressors that their power is brief and their plotting will recoil upon them.

translation: [This is Our] way with those We sent before you of Our messengers, and you will not find any change in Our way.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God's established pattern (sunnah) applies uniformly to the prophets sent before Muhammad: when a people rejected their messenger and persisted in denial and hostility, the consequences followed by divine decree. Since this law is constant and cannot be altered or diverted, the Prophet is consoled and reassured that the opposition he faces is part of an unchanging divine order, and that the outcome will be governed by the same fixed principles that governed previous generations.

translation: Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night, and [establish] the recitation of dawn. Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed.
interpretation: The verse directs the believer to uphold the prayer across a span of the day, from the sun's decline after its zenith until the night grows dark, which encompasses the noon, afternoon, sunset and night prayers, and it singles out the dawn recitation (the Fajr prayer) as a special act of worship. Its statement that the dawn recitation is 'witnessed' points to the belief that the angels of night and day gather at that hour to witness it, so that standing in prayer at dawn is a moment of heightened spiritual presence in which the believer is made conscious that the whole creation bears witness to his devotion.

translation: And during part of the night, pray with it as an additional devotion for you; it may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station.
interpretation: The verse directs the Prophet to devote a portion of the night to prayer, beyond the obligatory prayers, as a voluntary act of worship that is special to him, reflecting the depth of his closeness to God. The word "nafilah" (additional) signals that this night vigil is a surplus of devotion that elevates his rank rather than a mere duty. The promise that his Lord may raise him to a "maqam mahmud" (praiseworthy station) is understood by many commentators as the station of intercession (al-shafa'ah) on the Day of Judgment, though it also points to a spiritual elevation in this life. The verse thus links sincere, sustained nighttime worship with the attainment of honor and high standing before God.

translation: And say, "My Lord, cause me to enter a sincere entrance and cause me to exit a sincere exit, and grant me from Yourself a supporting authority."
interpretation: The verse teaches the believer to turn to God with a prayer that asks for a righteous beginning and a righteous ending to every undertaking, so that one's entry into affairs and one's departure from them are both marked by truthfulness, sincerity, and rightness of purpose. The request for a "sincere entrance" and "sincere exit" points to the whole course of a person's life and works, from the moment of commencing a task to its completion and to one's final passage from this world. The petition for "authority" from God's presence, which is a helping power, reflects the recognition that true strength and victory come only from Him. In its context, which is often read as directed to the Prophet and his mission of migration and establishment of truth, the verse expresses the hope that God will make his movements, whether departure from a place or arrival at a new one, an occasion of truth and that He will grant him the support needed to establish the truth against opposition.

translation: And say, "The truth has come, and falsehood has vanished. Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish."
interpretation: The verse is a divine command to the Prophet to proclaim a decisive reality: with the arrival of revelation, the truth has manifested and falsehood has been exposed and dislodged from its place. Its closing emphasis, that falsehood was by its very nature destined to perish, roots this vanishing not in the strength of believers but in the inherent fragility of what is baseless. Falsehood may appear firm for a time, yet it has no foundation to sustain it, so its collapse is a settled law. The verse thus offers reassurance to those who carry the truth amid opposition, teaching that their confidence should rest on the certainty that what is false cannot endure before what is real.

translation: And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, but it increases the wrongdoers in nothing except loss.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an as a single revelation whose effect depends on the disposition of the one who receives it. For the believer who opens his heart to it, its guidance works as a cure for spiritual and moral ailments such as doubt, confusion, and corrupt desires, and it becomes a source of divine compassion that draws him nearer to God. For the wrongdoer who persists in injustice and arrogance and turns away from its message, the same words add only to his ruin, because every rejection hardens his heart and deepens his loss. The Qur'an itself is not the cause of harm; the difference lies in how human beings respond to it, so that its healing and its harm both arise from one source according to the state of the receiver.

translation: And when We bestow favor upon man, he turns away and distances himself (with his side); but when harm touches him, he is despairing in utter hopelessness.
interpretation: The verse exposes a recurring human weakness: in times of ease and blessing, a person grows heedless, turning away from gratitude and from remembrance of the One who granted it, as though he needed nothing. Yet the same person collapses into despair the moment hardship strikes, forgetting that relief is also from God. The verse calls the believer to a balanced state, thankful in prosperity and hopeful in adversity, since both blessing and trial are tests and neither ease nor hardship is permanent.

translation: Say: 'Each acts according to his own manner, but your Lord knows best who is best guided on the path.'
interpretation: The verse places before the human being a truth about moral responsibility and divine knowledge. Every person acts in accordance with his own shakla, that inner disposition, character, and orientation which has been shaped by his beliefs, habits, and choices, so that conduct reveals what is within the heart. Yet the verse does not leave judgment to appearances or to the claims of people; it reminds the believer, and especially the one who is confronted by opponents, that only God fully knows who has truly taken the most rightly guided way. This calls for humility in judging others, patience in the face of disagreement, and a firm trust that the final assessment of guidance belongs to the One who sees hearts and intentions, while each person remains accountable for the direction he chooses to walk.

translation: And they ask you about the soul. Say, "The soul is of the affair of my Lord, and you have not been given of knowledge except a little."
interpretation: The verse sets a boundary on human knowledge: when the questioners ask about the rūḥ, the Prophet is told to answer that its reality belongs to the command of God (amr Rabbī), a realm whose true nature lies beyond what humans can fully grasp through the senses and reason. The phrase "and you have not been given of knowledge except a little" does not condemn inquiry, but reminds the seeker of the limits of created understanding and directs the heart toward humility before the Creator, who alone encompasses the knowledge of the soul's essence, while humans are left with the portion of knowledge God chooses to grant.

translation: And if We willed, We could surely take away that which We have revealed to you; then you would find for yourself no advocate against Us in that matter.
interpretation: The verse reminds the Prophet, and through him every believer, that the Qur'an is a sheer gift from God and not a possession that belongs to the Messenger. God's power to withdraw the revelation is absolute, so the Prophet has no guardian or defender who could restore it or shield him from that loss. This humbles the human recipient before divine grace, and it teaches that gratitude for guidance must be joined with awareness that it rests entirely on God's will and mercy.

translation: Except as a mercy from your Lord. Indeed, His bounty upon you has ever been great.
interpretation: The verse is spoken in the context of the Prophet Muhammad's Night Journey and the earlier verses about the Israelites' Scripture and the Prophet's own guidance. It teaches that whatever the Prophet received, whether revelation, guidance, or the honor of his mission, came not from his own merit or the power of his enemies' plots but purely from God's mercy. The phrase 'except as a mercy from your Lord' reminds the believer that nothing in the spiritual life is owed to human effort alone; every grace is a gift. The closing words, 'indeed His bounty upon you has been great,' turn this into an expression of gratitude and reassurance: the Prophet is singled out for an abundance of divine favor, and by extension the believer is encouraged to recognize that God's generosity far exceeds what he could claim or earn, so that gratitude and humility should mark his response.

translation: Say, "If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like, even if they were to be aides to one another."
interpretation: The verse presents a challenge issued to all of humanity and the unseen jinn together: the Qur'an is so singular in its eloquence, wisdom, and content that no collective human and jinn effort could match it, even with mutual support. Its inimitability is thus placed as a sign of its divine origin, and the Prophet is commanded to declare the challenge openly. The phrasing 'even if some of them were aides to others' stresses that cooperation and pooling of strength do not overcome what is beyond created capacity, inviting reflection on the Qur'an as a miraculous proof that transcends the limits of human and jinn ability.

translation: And We have certainly diversified for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, but most of the people refused except to be ungrateful.
interpretation: The verse reveals that God repeatedly varies and explains His guidance through diverse parables and illustrations so that the truth may be grasped from many angles, yet the obstinacy of most people lies not in a lack of clarity but in a deliberate choice to reject. Their refusal is presented as a moral failing rooted in ingratitude: they are offered abundant signs and reminders, and rather than receiving them with thankfulness, they persist in denial. The verse thus shifts the problem from the message to the disposition of the hearer, teaching that the sufficiency of evidence does not guarantee acceptance where the heart is closed by pride or habitual disbelief.

translation: And they said, "We will never believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth,"
interpretation: The verse exposes a recurring pattern of the disbelievers who, having already been shown clear signs, demanded yet another miracle as a condition for faith. Their demand reveals that the obstacle was not a lack of evidence but a stubborn refusal to accept the messenger's truth. By making faith contingent on a spectacular, self-chosen sign, they placed themselves as judges over God's signs, while the true sign of revelation was already in front of them. The verse thus teaches that faith is answered by sincerity and openness of heart, not by the demand for miracles tailored to one's own expectations.

translation: Or you should have a garden of palm trees and grapevines, and you cause rivers to gush forth within it in abundance.
interpretation: The verse is part of the Meccan challenge in Surah Al-Isra (17:90–93), in which the disbelievers, refusing to accept the Prophet's message, demand miraculous signs from him. Here they mock him with the image of a lush, self-sustaining paradise of date palms and vines watered by abundant rivers, as if wealth and material abundance were the proof of prophethood. The verse exposes the shallowness of such demands: the Prophet is a human messenger, not one who controls the bounty of the earth, and the true measure of a message lies in its truth rather than in worldly splendor. It also implicitly contrasts the fleeting gardens of this world with the true abundance that God alone grants.

translation: Or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed, or you bring God and the angels before us as a group of witnesses.
interpretation: The verse is part of the disbelievers' demands made to the Prophet, in which they set conditions for their faith as a challenge rather than a sincere search for guidance. They ask that the heavens be made to collapse upon them in fragments, as the Prophet had warned, or that God and the angels be brought before them face to face, as a visible guarantee of the message. The verse thereby exposes the arrogance of those who demand sensory proof while refusing the clear signs already present, and it implies that the proper response to such demands is the reminder that the true proof lies in the revelation itself and in the Prophet's sincere call, not in the spectacular display they seek.

translation: Or you have a house of gold, or you ascend into the sky, and we will not believe in your ascent until you bring down to us a book we can read. Say: Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?
interpretation: This verse belongs to a passage in which the disbelievers of Makkah set out a series of demands to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, as conditions for their faith: a house adorned with gold, an ascent into heaven, and a written book they could read. The Qur'an presents these demands as a pretext rather than a sincere search for guidance, since the proof offered already sufficed. The Prophet's reply, delivered in the form of a command to glorify God, points to the true nature of his mission: he is a human being chosen as a messenger, not a being with powers that exceed human limits. Divine signs are not granted according to the desires of those who ask for them, and the measure of a messenger is his fidelity in conveying the message, not the spectacular miracles he is asked to produce. The verse thus reminds the believer of the balance between the reality of prophethood and the humility of the human being who carries it.

translation: And what prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them except that they said, "Has God sent a human as a messenger?"
interpretation: The verse exposes the root of disbelief as an objection rooted in expectation rather than evidence: people rejected the message not because it lacked clarity, but because they found it hard to accept that a mortal man like themselves could carry a divine message. Their stumbling block was a preconceived notion of what a prophet should be, which blinded them to the guidance actually placed before them. The lesson is that God's wisdom in choosing His messengers from among humankind is itself a mercy, since a messenger who shares human nature can be understood, imitated, and trusted, and that resistance to the truth often hides behind an insistence on how it must appear.

translation: Say: If there had been angels walking calmly upon the earth, We would have sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a messenger.
interpretation: The verse argues that guidance is sent in a form suited to its recipients. Humans, who live on the earth and are bound to it, receive a messenger who is one of their own kind, so that they can hear, understand, and follow him. Had the inhabitants of the earth been angels, who are at home in the heavens and move about at ease there, the messenger would likewise have been an angel. The point is that God's message is fitted to the nature and capacity of those it addresses, and that the prophethood of a human being is a mercy suited to human beings rather than a deficiency in the message.

translation: Say, "Sufficient is Allah as Witness between me and you. Indeed, He is ever Acquainted and Seeing of His servants."
interpretation: The verse places the Prophet in a position of total reliance on God when his message is rejected and his truthfulness is disputed. Since God alone is the witness whose testimony settles the matter, the believer need not seek validation from the skeptics or fear their denial; the divine witness is both knowing (khabir), aware of inner intentions and hidden realities, and seeing (basir), observing every act. The closing description of God's knowledge of His servants thus works as both consolation for the messenger and a warning to the opponents that their conduct, however concealed, is fully before the One who will judge between them.

translation: Whoever Allah guides is the one truly guided, but whoever He leaves astray - you will not find for them any protectors besides Him. And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, mute, and deaf. Their refuge is Hell; whenever its fire subsides, We increase it for them in blaze.
interpretation: The verse establishes that true guidance belongs entirely to Allah's will, so the one who is guided is guided by Him alone, and the one who strays has no ally who can rescue him from the consequences of his own persistent turning away. Their blindness, muteness, and deafness on the Day of Resurrection mirror their spiritual condition in this life, where they had eyes, tongues, and ears but failed to perceive, speak the truth, or listen. The image of the fire being renewed whenever it dies down conveys that their punishment is unceasing and that the very means by which they rejected truth becomes the measure of their torment.

translation: That is their recompense, because they disbelieved in Our signs and said, "When we have become bones and crumbled dust, will we really be resurrected as a new creation?"
interpretation: The verse shows that disbelief in God's signs and denial of resurrection are linked: the people who deny the afterlife treat the question of bodily resurrection as absurd, reasoning from the decay of their bodies into dust to conclude that return is impossible. The verse answers this by framing their punishment as the fitting consequence of their rejection, implying that the one who created humans from nothing is fully able to bring them back. Their incredulity reveals a narrow view of God's power, measuring the Creator's capacity by the limits of their own perception, and so the verse calls the reader to reflect on creation and renewal as evidence for the certainty of the Hereafter.

translation: Do they not see that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth, is capable of creating the likes of them? And He has appointed for them a term about which there is no doubt. Yet the wrongdoers refuse anything but disbelief.
interpretation: The verse directs the mind from the immense creation of the heavens and the earth to the plain logic of resurrection: the One whose power brought forth the greater creation is certainly able to recreate humankind, who are lesser in comparison. The appointed term, which is beyond all doubt, signals that the Hereafter is a certainty set by divine wisdom, not a matter of conjecture. The closing phrase exposes the root of denial, which is not a lack of evidence but a deliberate stubbornness of those who wrong themselves by rejecting clear signs, persisting in ingratitude and disbelief.

translation: Say: "Even if you possessed the treasuries of the mercy of my Lord, you would surely withhold them for fear of spending; and man is ever tight-fisted."
interpretation: The verse points to the limitless nature of Divine mercy and the innate human tendency toward stinginess. Even if people were given control over the storehouses of God's mercy, their natural anxiety about loss and their fear of depletion would make them hold back, so the verse exposes the miserliness rooted in the human soul. Its deeper lesson is that the believer should overcome this trait through trust in God's boundless provision and generosity in giving, since what is with God does not diminish when shared.

translation: And We had certainly given Moses nine clear signs. So ask the Children of Israel: when he came to them, Pharaoh said to him, "Indeed, I think you, O Moses, are bewitched."
interpretation: The verse affirms that God granted Moses nine manifest signs as undeniable proof of his prophethood, and it directs the reader to the testimony of the Children of Israel, who witnessed his mission firsthand. Pharaoh's response reveals the typical stance of arrogant rulers who, faced with clear evidence, dismiss the messenger as a sorcerer or one deluded rather than confront the truth. The accusation of being bewitched is a means of discrediting what cannot be refuted, showing that rejection of guidance is often driven by pride and worldly authority rather than by a lack of evidence.

translation: He said: "You know well that none has sent down these (signs) except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as clear evidences, and indeed I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed to destruction."
interpretation: Moses affirms to Pharaoh that he knows with certainty that the miraculous signs (the staff, the white hand, and the rest) are not the work of sorcery or human contrivance but were sent down by the Lord of the heavens and the earth as clear insights that open the eyes of the heart to the truth. Pharaoh's arrogant denial was not born of ignorance of the signs' divine origin, since his own soul recognized them, so Moses, speaking in response to Pharaoh's accusation of being bewitched, turns the charge back: he judges that Pharaoh, having rejected what was plainly evident, is headed for ruin and loss. The verse thus shows that persistent refusal of manifest truth, when it is pursued out of pride, brings a person toward destruction.

translation: So he intended to drive them out of the land, but We drowned him and those with him, all together.
interpretation: The verse presents Pharaoh's scheme to expel the Children of Israel from their land as a reflection of arrogant tyranny that seeks to remove a people from their place by force. Yet the plan is turned against its author: the one who sought to uproot others is himself uprooted by drowning, along with his followers, so that no one is spared from the consequences of their collective wrongdoing. The verse thus teaches that oppression tends to return upon the oppressor, and that divine justice can overturn the schemes of the powerful at the very moment they believe they have secured their dominance.

translation: And We said after him to the Children of Israel: "Dwell in the land, and when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you forth as a mixed multitude."
interpretation: The verse points to a recurring pattern in the history of the Children of Israel: after the removal of a tyrant or the passing of a leader, they are granted settlement in the land, yet their security remains conditional on their conduct. The "promise of the Hereafter" is best understood as the appointed time of their second corruption and the consequences that follow it, when they are gathered together from every direction, indicating that worldly dominion is a trial and a test rather than a permanent privilege. The phrase "lafifa" (a mixed multitude) conveys the image of people gathered from scattered places, drawn together for judgment and accountability, so that the verse ultimately warns that all communities, not only one, will be summoned to account for how they used the blessings given to them.

translation: And with truth We sent it down, and with truth it descended. And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good news and a warner.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an is entirely grounded in truth: it was sent down by God with truth as its source and content, and it arrived intact with that same truth, untouched by falsehood or distortion. The Prophet's mission is then defined in its simplest and most essential terms. He is a bringer of good tidings to those who believe and act righteously, and a warner to those who turn away. The verse thus links the authenticity of the revelation to the sincerity and limited role of the messenger, reminding the listener that the prophet's function is to convey and clarify, not to compel, and that guidance and accountability rest on the truth he carries.

translation: And a Qur'an We have divided into parts, that you might recite it to the people at intervals, and We have sent it down in gradual stages.
interpretation: The verse points to the manner of the Qur'an's revelation: it was sent down piece by piece over about twenty-three years rather than all at once. This gradual descent served the Prophet's ability to retain and recite it calmly and steadily before people, and allowed it to address events, questions and circumstances as they arose, so that its guidance would be absorbed patiently and firmly into the lives of the believers.

translation: Say: Believe in it or do not believe. Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it, when it is recited to them, fall down upon their faces in prostration.
interpretation: The verse shows that faith in the Qur'an does not depend on the approval of the unbelievers, who are free to accept or reject it, while the true measure of sound knowledge is its reaction to revelation. Those who had genuine knowledge of the earlier scriptures recognize the truth of what is recited and respond with humble prostration, falling on their faces in reverence. Their prostration is an outward sign of an inward submission that the recitation of God's words naturally produces in a person of true understanding, so the verse teaches that real learning leads to humility before the Creator rather than to pride or denial.

translation: And they say, "Glory be to our Lord! Indeed, the promise of our Lord has certainly been fulfilled."
interpretation: This verse, from Surah al-Isra (17:108), describes the response of those who were given knowledge before the Qur'an when it is recited to them: they fall prostrate in humility and glorify God, affirming that His promise is necessarily realized. The phrase "the promise of our Lord" points to the divine promise of resurrection, reckoning, and reward, which is not a distant hope but a reality that will certainly come to pass. Their exclamation of glory (subhan) expresses a recognition that God is far above any failure or breaking of His word. The verse thus portrays true knowledge as producing reverent submission, as the heart that truly understands God's revelation is moved to affirm His exaltation and the certainty of His promises.

translation: And they fall down upon their faces weeping, and it increases them in humility.
interpretation: The verse describes the response of those who have been given knowledge of the earlier revelations when the words of God are recited to them: their reaction is not mere intellectual assent but a bodily and emotional submission. They fall prostrate on their chins in reverence, and their tears flow, a sign of a heart softened before the truth. The closing phrase shows that this act is not a one-time emotional outburst but a continual growth: each recitation deepens their humility and awe, so that devotion becomes an ever-increasing state of the soul rather than a fixed achievement. It teaches that true knowledge of God leads to lowliness, and that the Qur'an is meant to move both the mind and the heart toward reverent submission.

translation: Say, "Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names." And do not be loud in your prayer or silent therein, but seek between that a way.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the believer's worship should avoid both extremes: excessive loudness that becomes ostentation or disturbance, and excessive silence that becomes neglect or lack of presence. The 'middle way' between them is a balanced sincerity in which the heart and tongue are both engaged. Linking this to the preceding statement that all of God's names are beautiful, the verse suggests that God may be invoked by any of His excellent names, and that the manner of remembrance should reflect reverence, moderation, and attentiveness to the One being addressed.

translation: And say: "All praise is due to Allah, who has not taken a son, and who has no partner in the dominion, and who has no protector out of weakness; and magnify Him with full magnification."
interpretation: The verse places the praise of God at the center of the believer's speech and ties it to a threefold negation that defines His absolute sovereignty. By denying Him a son, a partner in dominion, and any protector arising from weakness, it removes every trace of dependency, need, and deficiency from the divine nature, so that the one who praises Him can stand before Him as a servant who owes everything to a Lord who needs nothing. The command to magnify Him 'with full magnification' turns this theological clarity into an act of devotion: the believer is to exalt God not merely in words but in the whole orientation of the heart, recognizing that true greatness belongs to Him alone and that every claim to power, lineage, or allies in the world is dwarfed by His reality.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. All praise is due to Allah, who has sent down to His servant the Book, and has not made in it any crookedness.
interpretation: The opening praise directs the heart to the source of revelation: the Book is praised not merely for its descent but for its perfect straightness. Its rectitude is both a quality of its wording and meaning, free of contradiction, distortion, or deviation, and therefore a reliable guide. Its perfection is linked to the Prophet's servanthood, showing that the highest honor is to be a servant of God who bears this Book. The verse thus teaches that gratitude for guidance begins with recognizing that the path it offers is upright, and that a believer should seek to walk in that straightness.

translation: Upright, to warn of a severe punishment from Him and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a goodly reward.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an as an upright, straight guidance (qayyim), free of crookedness, whose twofold function is to warn and to reassure. The warning concerns a severe divine reckoning that comes 'from Him,' emphasizing that its source is God's own authority and not merely human disapproval. The good tidings are reserved for those who combine inner faith with outward action, since iman and 'righteous deeds' (amal salih) are joined throughout the Qur'an as inseparable. The reward is described as 'good' (hasan), suggesting one that is complete, beautiful, and fitting to the believer's effort. The structure thus teaches that revelation balances fear and hope, calling people to accountability while opening the path of mercy to those who translate belief into righteous conduct.

translation: Abiding therein forever.
interpretation: The phrase describes the endless duration of the good reward promised to the righteous in Surah Al-Kahf (18:2-3). Their stay in that reward is not temporary or subject to ending, and the word 'abadan' stresses that this bliss has no limit of time, which gives the believers lasting security and hope in place of the fleeting pleasures of this world.

translation: And to warn those who say, "God has taken a son."
interpretation: The verse identifies the specific theological error it addresses: the claim that God has begotten or adopted a son. Its warning is directed at this assertion about God's nature, which the Qur'an consistently rejects as an attribution to God of something unbefitting His absolute oneness and self-sufficiency. By singling out this statement, the verse establishes that ascribing offspring to God is not a minor doctrinal matter but a grave falsehood that calls for a clear warning, reinforcing the Qur'anic insistence on pure monotheism (tawhid) and on God's transcendence above any need for progeny.

translation: They have no knowledge of it, nor did their fathers have any. Terrible is the word that comes out of their mouths; they say nothing but a lie.
interpretation: The verse condemns the claim that God has begotten a son (as in the preceding verses about those who say "God has taken a son"). Its point is that such a claim is not grounded in any real knowledge, neither in revealed guidance nor in inherited sound tradition, since the claimants merely follow the assumptions of their forebears. The gravity of the statement is conveyed by calling it "kabura kalimatun", a word enormous in its wrongness, because it attributes to the Creator something unworthy of His majesty and oneness. The verse thus teaches that speech about God must rest on knowledge, and that imitation of ancestors cannot replace evidence, so that what is said without knowledge is only falsehood.

translation: Then perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over them, if they do not believe in this message.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, for the intensity of his concern over the disbelief of his people. His care for their guidance was so great that it consumed him with sorrow, and God addresses him gently, as if to say that he should not wear himself out grieving over those who turn away. The burden of guidance rests with God and the delivery of the message, not with compelling belief. The verse thus teaches that a messenger's duty is to convey faithfully, while the outcome lies in God's hands, and it reflects the mercy and compassion the Prophet bore toward humanity.

translation: Indeed, We have made whatever is on the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed.
interpretation: The verse presents the world's beauties and possessions as a trial rather than an end in themselves. Everything on earth is adorned to attract the human heart, and this very attraction is the means of testing people, revealing whether they will let these allurements distract them from God or will use them rightly and do good works. The measure of worth is not the quantity of worldly adornment one gathers but the excellence of one's conduct, so the believer is called to view the earth's splendor with discernment, enjoying it lawfully while keeping their eyes fixed on the reckoning that follows.

translation: And indeed, We will make what is upon it a barren, dry wasteland.
interpretation: The verse points to the transience of worldly splendor: the lush gardens, fields, and adornments that cover the earth are destined to be reduced to barren dust. Just as the living earth is stripped bare by God's command, so the beauty that people cherish in this life is temporary and will vanish, directing the reader's heart toward what endures beyond it.

translation: Or do you think that the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription were among Our signs as a wonder?
interpretation: The verse turns the Prophet's attention away from the question of the sleepers toward a broader lesson: the story of the youths who fled with their faith to the cave is not an isolated marvel but one of God's signs, and the believer should recognize that God's power over life, death, and time is equally evident in the created order around him. By framing the tale as a question, it invites reflection rather than mere astonishment, urging the listener to see that the true wonder lies in God's protection of those who take refuge in Him, and that such stories are meant to strengthen faith and steadfastness in the face of persecution.

translation: When the young men retreated to the cave and said, "Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself and prepare for us right guidance in our affair."
interpretation: The verse presents the moment of the youths' withdrawal into the cave as an act of faith made in utter reliance on God. Having left behind the society that threatened their belief, they turn not to their own strength or plans but to God's direct mercy, which they ask to come "from Yourself," signifying a grace that is entirely divine and beyond human means. Their request for "right guidance" in their affair shows that their concern is not merely for safety or comfort but for a sound path in their religious situation. The passage thus teaches that when a believer must separate from a corrupt environment for the sake of faith, the proper refuge is prayer, trust in God's mercy, and a sincere petition for guidance, since God alone can prepare the way out of hardship.

translation: So We sealed their ears in the cave for a number of years.
interpretation: The verse describes the Companions of the Cave (Ashab al-Kahf) being put into a deep sleep for many years, during which their hearing was, as it were, shut so that no outside noise could rouse them. The phrase 'darabna 'ala adhanihim' (We struck over their ears) conveys a divine act that cut them off from the world, showing that God's power over time and consciousness is absolute: the years passed unfelt by them, and the sleep became a sign of God's care for those who held fast to their faith, and a lesson that the reckoning of time belongs to Him alone, not to human measurement.

translation: Then We woke them up, that We might know which of the two parties was more precise in computing the time they had remained.
interpretation: The verse comes after the account of the Companions of the Cave, who slept for a long period. The phrase "that We might know" is understood by many commentators in terms of manifestation rather than新 discovery: God's knowledge is eternal, so the purpose is to make visible to people which of the two disputing groups, regarding how long the sleepers stayed, reckoned the duration more accurately. The verse thus turns a seemingly trivial dispute about time into a lesson on humility before divine knowledge, showing that the true measure of the matter belongs to God alone, who knows the unseen and the exact count of every moment.

translation: We relate to you their story in truth. Indeed, they were young men who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance.
interpretation: The verse presents the account of the People of the Cave as a true narrative revealed to the Prophet, emphasizing that faith is a matter of sincere youthful commitment to God, and that divine guidance is not static but grows for those who turn to Him with conviction. Their steadfastness in a hostile environment becomes a model that the believer is invited to reflect upon, showing that God's increase of guidance follows upon the individual's own resolve to stand firm in belief.

translation: And We strengthened their hearts when they stood up and said, "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth; we will never invoke any deity other than Him. Certainly we would have uttered, then, an excessive transgression."
interpretation: The verse portrays the Companions of the Cave as young men whose resolve was divinely fortified at the decisive moment when they rose up against their people's idolatry. Divine steadiness (rabṭ 'alā al-qulūb) is shown to be the source of their courage: they did not merely hold a private belief but publicly declared tawhid, the oneness of the Lord of all creation, and renounced any worship besides Him. Their reasoning is embedded in their words: to call upon other gods would be to utter something far from reason and justice (shaṭaṭ), a deviation from the truth. The verse thus teaches that faith which withstands social pressure is a gift sustained by God, and that sincere monotheism is grounded in the recognition of the Creator as the sole rightful object of worship.

translation: These, our people, have taken gods besides Him. Why do they not bring for them a clear authority? Who then is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God?
interpretation: The verse is the words of the people of the cave's companions (Surah al-Kahf 18:15), who reject their people's worship of other gods as baseless. Their argument rests on a simple demand for evidence: a belief in divinity must be supported by a clear proof, or else it is mere invention. By declaring that attributing partners to God without authority is the gravest injustice, the verse shows that faith must be grounded in reason and revelation, and that to speak about God without knowledge is to commit the worst form of falsehood against Him.

translation: And when you have withdrawn from them and what they worship other than Allah, then take refuge in the cave; your Lord will spread out for you of His mercy and will prepare for you from your affair an easy outcome.
interpretation: The verse, spoken by the youths of the Cave (Ashab al-Kahf) to one another, models the principle that when faith is endangered by a corrupt society, the believer must physically and spiritually separate from its idolatry and seek a sanctuary in which worship of God alone can be preserved. The withdrawal is not mere flight but a deliberate choice to protect one's conviction, and it is precisely in that act of trust that God opens mercy and makes the path ahead smooth. It teaches that hardship embraced for the sake of faithfulness is met with divine provision, and that the seeker who places his affairs in God's hands will find ease where human options appear to be closed.

translation: And you would see the sun, when it rises, inclining away from their cave to the right, and when it sets, passing away from them to the left, while they were in a spacious chamber of it. That is among the signs of Allah. Whomever Allah guides is the one rightly guided, but whomever He leaves astray, you will never find for him a guardian who could lead him to the right course.
interpretation: The verse presents the sleepers of the cave as sheltered by a divine arrangement of nature: the sun's path is turned aside so that its direct rays never fall upon them, preserving their bodies while they remain in a wide, airy hollow that keeps them in a protected and comfortable state. Described as a sign of Allah, this scene shows that the Creator governs even the cosmic movements to serve His chosen servants, and it turns the reader's attention from the marvel of the event to the greater truth that guidance belongs to Allah alone. The closing statement links the miraculous care given to the youths with the principle that true guidance is a divine gift; those whom God guides possess the right path, while those He leaves to their own deviation have no protector able to set them aright, so the story of faith in the cave becomes a lesson on reliance upon God's guidance.

translation: And you would think them awake, while they were asleep. And We turned them to the right and to the left, while their dog stretched out its forelegs at the threshold. Had you looked upon them, you would have turned away from them in flight, and been filled with dread of them.
interpretation: The verse portrays the People of the Cave in a state that seems to be wakefulness while they are in fact asleep, so that whoever sees them is deceived about their condition. God's turning of their bodies from side to side protects them from the earth consuming them, and the dog at the entrance adds a sense of guarding and of being a living witness to their miraculous rest. The awe-inspiring appearance is meant to keep onlookers at a distance, shielding the sleepers from curiosity and showing that their preservation is wholly by divine design, a sign that calls the reader to reflect on God's power over time, life, and death.

translation: And thus We roused them so that they might question one another. A speaker among them said, "How long have you remained?" They said, "We have remained a day or part of a day." They said, "Your Lord knows best how long you have remained. So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city, and let him look for which of its food is purest, and bring you provision from it, and let him be discreet, and let no one become aware of you."
interpretation: The verse shows that the awakening of the sleepers was itself a divine act whose purpose was to open a space for mutual inquiry and reflection, so that their waking became a moment of recollection about the passage of time. Their uncertainty about how long they had slept teaches humility before the knowledge of God, who alone measures time exactly, and the believers' instinct to defer the final answer to Him. Their concern for pure food and for remaining hidden reveals a community that, even while sheltered by God, carries the weight of vulnerability and the need for prudence in a hostile world, reminding the reader that trust in God is joined with wise and careful action.

translation: Indeed, if they gain the upper hand over you, they will stone you or force you back into their religion, and you will never prosper then, ever.
interpretation: The verse describes the enemies' hostility toward the believers, who are warned that if their opponents gain dominance, the consequence would be violent persecution or coerced return to disbelief. It implies that such a reversal would mean the believers' ultimate failure, since prosperity in this world and the next is tied to steadfastness in faith. The verse thus reinforces the importance of holding firm to one's religion under pressure, and it reminds believers that their enemies' aim is not merely conflict but the uprooting of their faith.

translation: And thus We caused them to be found, that they might know that the promise of God is true and that the Hour is not to be doubted. When they disputed among themselves about their affair, they said, "Build over them a structure; their Lord knows best about them." But those who prevailed over their affair said, "We will surely take over them a place of worship."
interpretation: The verse points to the Companions of the Cave, whose sleep and awakening after centuries became a sign for their contemporaries of the resurrection that the people of the time disputed. Their discovery settled the question of the Hour by showing God's power to restore life after death, and the dispute over how to honor their tomb reveals how a community can turn a sign of God into a matter of rivalry, with some wanting a mere structure and others a mosque built in reverence over the sleepers, a contest of interpretation over sacred remains that reflects the human tendency to claim authority over what belongs to God alone.

translation: They will say, "They were three, the fourth of them being their dog"; and they will say, "Five, the sixth of them being their dog," guessing blindly; and they will say, "Seven, and the eighth of them being their dog." Say, "My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few. So do not argue concerning them except with an outward argument, and do not seek a ruling about them from any of them."
interpretation: The verse shows that the number of the Companions of the Cave was a matter of conjecture rather than certain knowledge, so the Prophet is commanded to leave the exact count to God alone, who knows it perfectly, and to avoid disputing with those who argue about it. By calling the guesses "blind" and affirming that only a few know the number, the verse teaches that in matters beyond revealed certainty one should not claim knowledge, and that the true reference for such unseen matters is God's knowledge, while the story's real purpose lies in its lessons of faith and steadfastness rather than in its numerical details.

translation: And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow,"
interpretation: The verse forbids a person from making unconditional promises about the future as though their own plans were fully within their control. Human beings do not know what tomorrow holds, and every intention is subject to the will of God; therefore one should attach the qualification "if God wills" to one's statements about future actions. This is a lesson in humility and reliance on God, recognizing that all planning and ability ultimately depend on Him. The verse is connected to the account in which the Prophet was asked about matters and promised an answer the next day without adding that God willed it, which led to a delay in revelation until the qualification was taught.

translation: Unless God wills. And remember your Lord when you forget, and say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is nearer than this in right direction."
interpretation: The verse comes in the context of the story of the people of the cave and the prophet's promise to do something tomorrow. It teaches that a person should never make an absolute pledge about the future without attaching it to the will of God, and that whenever one forgets, one should return to remembering God and seek His guidance. Hope in God's guidance toward what is closer to right conduct and sound judgment is itself a form of trust. The verse thus joins submission to God's will with the discipline of remembrance, and shows that true guidance is sought from the Lord rather than relied upon from one's own certainty.

translation: And they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine [more years].
interpretation: The verse records the duration of the Companions of the Cave's sleep as three hundred solar years, then adds nine. The Qur'an's own clarification follows immediately: the difference between the lunar and solar calendars accounts for the extra nine years, since three hundred solar years equal roughly three hundred and nine lunar years. This subtle reckoning reminds the reader that God's knowledge encompasses all time, and that the length of a sleep or an era is ultimately known only to Him, as the following verse affirms: 'Say, God knows best how long they remained.' The verse thus turns a miraculous tale into a lesson in humility before divine knowledge and in reflection on the signs embedded in time itself.

translation: Say, "Allah knows best how long they remained." To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. How clearly He sees and hears! They have no protector besides Him, and He does not share His command with anyone.
interpretation: The verse closes the account of the People of the Cave by returning the question of their duration to its proper source: divine knowledge, which alone encompasses what is hidden. Their dispute over the number of years is rendered trivial once one recognizes that the One who holds the unseen of all creation needs no witnesses or calculations. The phrase "How clearly He sees and hears" is an emphatic affirmation that nothing escapes His perception, so the believer should rest in His knowledge rather than in human conjecture. The final statements, that no protector exists beside Him and that He shares His rule with no one, establish tawhid as the conclusion of the entire narrative: the sleepers were preserved by the One who alone governs, and all security and guidance belong to Him alone.

translation: And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord; none can alter His words, and you will never find any refuge besides Him.
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet to hold fast to and recite the revelation entrusted to him, assuring him that divine words are immutable, so no one can distort or change them despite opposition. By stressing that no one can alter God's words and that there is no shelter outside Him, it strengthens the believer's trust that the message will endure and that true protection and refuge belong to God alone, not to any created power or false patron.

translation: And keep yourself patient, [O Muhammad], with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face. And let not your eyes pass beyond them, desiring the adornment of the worldly life. And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his own desire and whose affair has become excess and loss.
interpretation: The verse teaches that the Prophet must bind himself in steadfast companionship with the sincere poor believers who devote themselves to worship at the beginning and end of each day, seeking only God's pleasure, rather than being drawn toward the wealthy elite of Quraysh for the sake of worldly status. The heedless man, whose heart has been turned from the remembrance of God and who is ruled by his whims, is shown to be a model of disorder and ruin, so that obeying such a person is the real danger. The lesson is that spiritual worth is measured by sincerity and remembrance of God, not by worldly display, and that a leader must keep company with those who truly seek the Divine.

translation: And say, "The truth is from your Lord, so whoever wills, let him believe; and whoever wills, let him disbelieve." Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire whose walls will enclose them. And if they ask for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten brass that scalds the faces. Wretched is the drink, and evil is the resting place.
interpretation: The verse places the choice of faith and disbelief squarely before the human being, not as coercion but as a moral responsibility: the truth has been made clear by God, and each person bears the consequences of the path he chooses. The stark imagery of the Fire enclosing the wrongdoers and the scalding, molten-like water that they are given to drink when they plead for relief shows that the outcome of disbelief and injustice is not merely unpleasant but inescapable. The contrast between the freedom given to choose and the certainty of the reckoning that follows underscores that the wrongdoers have themselves determined their fate by rejecting what was plainly revealed.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—indeed, We do not allow the reward of anyone who does good deeds to be lost.
interpretation: The verse establishes that faith and righteous action are inseparable in the divine reckoning: belief gives direction to deeds, and deeds give belief its practical witness. By affirming that God never wastes the reward of those who act well, it removes any fear that sincere effort will vanish unnoticed or unrewarded. Every good intention carried into action is recorded and preserved before God, so the believer is called to steadiness and perseverance, knowing that no measure of goodness is insignificant in His sight. The phrase 'those who do good in action' (aḥsana ʿamalan) also points to excellence, not mere completion, suggesting that God honors the quality and sincerity of deeds, not only their outward form.

translation: Those, for them are Gardens of Eden beneath which rivers flow; they will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold, and they will wear green garments of fine silk and brocade, reclining therein upon couches. How excellent is the reward, and how good is the resting place.
interpretation: The verse portrays the honor of the righteous in the Hereafter through a contrast with the worldly life: the gardens of Eden, flowing rivers, and gold bracelets and fine garments signal a complete and dignified rest in which their bodily comfort and sense of honor are fulfilled. The reclining on couches expresses tranquility and security, while the closing phrases, 'how excellent is the reward and how good the resting place,' affirm that this recompense is the highest good, surpassing anything the earthly life can offer, and that the believers' final abode is a place of rest and nobility.

translation: And present to them an example: two men, for one of whom We had made two gardens of grapevines, and We had surrounded them with date palms, and between them We had placed fields of crops.
interpretation: The verse opens a parable of two men, one blessed with abundance and the other without, to show that worldly wealth and prosperity are a trust that can breed arrogance and heedlessness in the one who possesses it. Its lesson is that a person's fortune is a test from God, not a measure of his worth, and that gratitude and humility before the Giver are what distinguish the faithful. The image of lush gardens nourished by water and fertile land invites reflection on how quickly such bounty can be transient, pointing the listener toward the enduring value of faith over the fleeting display of possessions.

translation: Both gardens yielded their produce and did not fall short in anything from it, and We caused a river to gush forth within them.
interpretation: The verse belongs to the parable of the two men in Surah al-Kahf, where the believer's two gardens are described as a sign of abundance that is never withheld, since the fruit is delivered in full and no shortfall occurs. The gushing river between them completes the image of a self-sustaining, flourishing place, which stands in pointed contrast to the arrogant owner's pride in his wealth. The verse thus implies that true provision comes from God, who gives generously and completely, and that a person should recognize this favor rather than attribute prosperity to his own efforts.

translation: And he had fruit, so he said to his companion while conversing with him, "I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in men."
interpretation: This verse, from the parable of the two men in Surah al-Kahf, shows the arrogance that arises from worldly abundance: the wealthy man measures his worth by his property and his supporters rather than by gratitude to God, and he uses his advantage to belittle the believing companion. The verse warns that material possessions and social power can breed pride and a false sense of self-sufficiency, causing a person to forget that all blessings are a trust from God and are not a sign of personal merit.

translation: And he entered his garden while he was wronging himself. He said, 'I do not think that this will ever perish.'
interpretation: The man in this verse, the owner of one of the two gardens in the parable, is deluded by his wealth into believing that his prosperity is permanent and self-sustaining, forgetting that it is a trust granted by God and can be taken away at His will. His wronging of himself is primarily spiritual: his ingratitude, arrogance, and denial of accountability harm his own soul more than anyone else. His confident claim that the garden will never perish exposes the heedlessness that comes from measuring worth by possessions rather than by faith and righteous deeds, which the surrounding parable goes on to show as the true and lasting wealth.

translation: And I do not think the Hour will ever come to pass; and even if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a destination.
interpretation: The verse portrays a man who, filled with arrogance over his worldly garden and wealth, denies the Resurrection and assumes that even if there is a return to God, he will be granted something better than what he has in this world. It exposes a heedless self-deception in which material prosperity is mistaken for divine favor and a sign of worth, so that a person comes to imagine that the blessings enjoyed here are a guarantee of future reward. The verse thus warns against confusing worldly abundance with proof of one's standing before God, and against the delusion that accountability can be dismissed while one remains absorbed in possessions.

translation: His companion said to him while conversing with him, "Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then fashioned you into a man?"
interpretation: The verse comes from the parable of the two men in Surah Al-Kahf, where a believer rebukes his arrogant, disbelieving companion who boasted of his wealth and denied the Hour. The believer's question exposes the absurdity of denial: the one who originated a human being from lifeless dust, then from a small drop, and then gave him a complete, balanced form, is surely capable of resurrection and of granting a better end in the Hereafter. The verse thus turns the disbeliever's own origin into proof of divine power, teaching that gratitude and recognition of the Creator should follow from reflecting on one's own creation, and that pride in worldly possessions is baseless when one's very existence testifies to a Creator who can bring him back to account.

translation: But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I associate none with my Lord.
interpretation: The verse, spoken by a believer confronting a disbelieving companion, reflects the purity of tawhid: the speaker affirms unequivocally that Allah alone is his Lord and refuses any form of shirk. The opening 'But as for me' (lakinna) sets his steadfast faith in deliberate contrast to the arrogance and denial of the other man, showing that true gratitude and humility before the Creator are founded on exclusive devotion. The phrase 'my Lord' repeated twice emphasizes a personal, sincere relationship with the One who created him from dust and then from a drop, so that his conviction rests not on worldly status or wealth but on recognition of God's sole lordship.

translation: And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, "What Allah wills [will be]; there is no power except through Allah"? Though you see me as less than you in wealth and children.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the owner of the garden for his arrogance and self-reliance in the face of his blessings. Upon entering his orchard, he should have recognized that all he possessed came from Allah's will and grace, and acknowledged his own powerlessness, saying "What Allah wills" and "there is no power except through Allah." Instead, his pride in his wealth and progeny led him to measure his worth by material abundance and to look down on his poorer companion. The speaker, the humble believer, reminds him that worldly possessions are a trust that can be lost in an instant, so gratitude and humility before the Creator are the proper response to prosperity.
