translation: Perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden, and will send upon it a calamity from the sky, so that it becomes a barren, slippery ground.
interpretation: The verse belongs to the account of the two men, one of whom was blessed with gardens yet grew arrogant and denied the Hereafter. His companion, who admonished him, responds with a hope rooted in trust in God rather than in wealth: he expresses the expectation that his Lord may grant him something better in this world or the next, and warns that God may strike the proud man's garden with a divine decree from heaven, leaving it stripped bare and treacherous. The lesson is that worldly abundance is entrusted and can be taken away at any moment, so one's confidence should rest in God's power and not in possessions or self-importance.

translation: Or its water will become sunken deep down, so you will never be able to find it.
interpretation: The verse, spoken in the context of the signs of God's power and His provision, pictures the possibility that the water that sustains life could be made to sink into the depths of the earth, beyond human reach. It reminds the listener that water, which humans take for granted, is a bounty entirely in God's hand: He can withdraw it at will, and no human effort, digging or searching, could restore what He has taken away. The image thus invites reflection on gratitude for provision and on humility before the One who grants and withholds it.

translation: And his fruits were encompassed (by ruin), so he began to wring his hands over what he had spent on it, while it lay fallen upon its trellises, and he said, "Oh, would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord!"
interpretation: The verse depicts the man who, in his arrogance and pride in his wealth and gardens, denied the Resurrection and forgot his Creator; when his worldly possessions were suddenly destroyed, his regret was not merely over the loss of his property but over his prior shirk, the attributing of partners to God, which he now recognized as the root of his ruin. It teaches that material abundance is a trust that can vanish in an instant, and that true loss lies in turning away from the One Lord, whose favor alone sustains all things.

translation: And he had no company to help him against God, nor was he able to defend himself.
interpretation: The verse teaches that worldly power, numbers, and alliances are worthless when God's decree arrives, because the only real protection belongs to God. The man who trusted in his wealth and followers and denied the Resurrection is shown that no group can shield him once his arrogance has brought divine judgment. The lesson is that a person should place their trust in God rather than in what is transient, and should recognize that every strength is borrowed from Him and can be withdrawn in an instant.

translation: There, the authority (or protection) belongs to Allah, the Truth. He is the best in reward and the best in outcome.
interpretation: The verse points to a moment of ultimate reckoning and reversal, where all false claims to power, protection, and allegiance collapse, and only Allah's sovereignty remains manifest. Its emphasis is that true guardianship belongs to the Real, so a believer should anchor their hope and loyalty in Him rather than in transient worldly supporters. The phrase "best in reward and best in outcome" directs the heart to measure success not by immediate gains but by what is ultimately good and lasting, thereby reorienting one's choices toward the eternal.

translation: And present to them the example of the life of this world: it is like water which We sent down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingled with it, and then it became dry stubble scattered by the winds. And Allah is ever Able over all things.
interpretation: The verse uses the image of rain-fed vegetation to portray the transience of worldly life: what flourishes green and luxuriant is soon reduced to brittle debris carried off by the wind, so that a person should not place their trust in wealth, status, or beauty that passes away. The closing affirmation that Allah is capable of all things points to the absolute power behind this cycle of growth and decay, reminding the believer that the One who brings life from the earth and withers it is the only lasting reality, and that human hopes must be anchored in Him rather than in what is fleeting.

translation: Wealth and children are adornment of the worldly life; but the enduring good deeds are better in the sight of your Lord for reward and better for hope.
interpretation: The verse teaches that wealth and children, though beloved and pleasing to the soul, are only an adornment that belongs to the fleeting life of this world, and so they should not be mistaken for the true measure of worth. What remains lasting is the set of righteous deeds, the good works whose effect endures beyond the passing of this life. Such deeds bring a reward from God that is far better than any worldly gain, and they give the believer a firmer hope than the expectations that people place in possessions and offspring. The verse thus redirects the heart from attachment to what decorates the present life toward what carries value before the Lord.

translation: And [mention] the Day when We will set the mountains in motion, and you will see the earth laid bare, and We will gather them all, leaving none of them behind.
interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Resurrection as a moment of total upheaval in the natural order: the mountains, which stand as the most enduring symbols of permanence, are set moving and dissolve, while the earth is stripped of its hills, valleys, and structures and lies open and exposed. The image of a bare, levelled earth becomes a stage on which the whole of humankind is assembled, with not a single soul excluded. The sequence conveys that no created thing, however solid it seems, escapes the dissolution of this world, and that the reckoning is universal, leaving the listener to reflect on how thoroughly the present order is bound to end and on the certainty of being gathered before the Lord.

translation: And they will be presented before your Lord in rows: "You have certainly come to Us just as We created you the first time. But you claimed that We would never appoint for you a appointed time."
interpretation: The verse depicts the Day of Resurrection, when humanity is brought forth in ranks before God, stripped of worldly pretensions and returned to the same bare state in which they were first created. The rhetorical address reproaches those who denied resurrection and assumed no reckoning would ever be set for them. It conveys that the denial of the Hereafter was rooted in a false assumption that human life would end without accountability, and that the reality of God's promise will be confronted directly, leaving no room for excuse or delay.

translation: And the record will be placed, and you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it, and they will say, "Woe to us! What is this record that leaves out nothing small or great except that it has enumerated it?" And they will find what they did present, and your Lord does not wrong anyone.
interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Judgment as a moment of exposure in which every person's deeds are laid bare in a complete and exact record, so that the guilty, confronted with the full scope of their actions, are overwhelmed by dread and remorse. The statement that the record omits nothing, small or great, conveys the absolute precision of divine accountability, where no act is forgotten or overlooked. The closing assurance that they find their deeds present before them and that the Lord wrongs no one establishes that the reckoning is perfectly just: each soul meets the true consequences of what it did, and nothing is added to or taken from its account.

translation: And [mention] when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," so they prostrated, except Iblis. He was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord. Will you then take him and his descendants as allies instead of Me while they are an enemy to you? Wretched is the exchange for the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse uses the story of the prostration to Adam to expose the root of disobedience: Iblis refused out of arrogance and rebelled against his Lord's clear command, and the verse presents this as a moral warning that whoever takes the enemy of mankind as a guardian has accepted a corrupt substitute for loyalty to God. The phrase "he was of the jinn" explains that his disobedience was not the result of being one of the angels, so his rebellion was a deliberate choice rather than a lack of capacity, which makes his allies' betrayal all the more blameworthy. The rhetorical question addresses people directly, implying that turning to Satan and his offspring for guidance, protection, or companionship is an act of folly that exchanges the Creator's guardianship for the guardianship of an open enemy. The closing words, "wretched is the exchange," make the consequence plain: those who choose this path are wronging themselves, since the bargain they strike gives up eternal benefit for a deceptive and destructive alliance.

translation: I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves, nor would I take as helpers those who lead others astray.
interpretation: This verse, spoken in the context of the polytheists' claims about the divine and their reliance on intermediaries, establishes that God alone is the sole Creator who needed no assistants or witnesses in bringing the cosmos and humanity into being. Since no created being was present at the origin of creation, no one can claim knowledge of it independently or share in God's authority over it. The final clause affirms that God does not take misguiding figures as supporters; the Qur'an thereby implicitly warns against following those who lead people astray, since true help and guidance come only from God.

translation: And on the Day He will say, "Call upon My partners whom you claimed," so they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them, and We will place between them a barrier of destruction.
interpretation: The verse depicts the Day of Judgment as a scene of exposure and abandonment: those who associated partners with God are summoned to call upon the very beings they had claimed as intercessors or equals, only to find those beings deaf to their pleas. The phrase "mawbiqan" suggests a dividing chasm or a place of mutual ruin, indicating that the false bonds of worship that once united the worshippers and their idols are severed, leaving each side in a shared but separate destruction. It teaches that falsehood collapses under the weight of the truth, and that every claimed partnership with God will be revealed as empty when no help can be obtained from it.

translation: And the criminals will see the Fire and will think that they are about to fall into it, and they will not find any escape from it.
interpretation: The verse presents the moment of confrontation with the Fire as one in which the guilty, who had dismissed the warnings of the Prophets, finally perceive its reality with overwhelming certainty; their expectation of being cast into it reflects the dread of a fate they cannot avert. The phrase 'lam yajidu anha masrifan' (they find no place of turning away from it) underscores the closing of every avenue of escape: the worldly means of evasion, denial, and excuse that they relied upon are gone. The verse thus conveys that the consequences of persistent wrongdoing become inescapable once the reckoning arrives, and it invites the listener to recognize the Fire now, while turning away from it through faith and righteous conduct is still possible.

translation: And We have certainly presented to the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, but man is ever the most contentious of things.
interpretation: The verse reveals a tension between the abundance of divine guidance and human disposition. God has varied and repeated the parables and proofs in the Qur'an so that they reach the human mind from every angle, leaving no pretext for those who seek the truth. Yet the verse points to the human tendency toward dispute, where man, driven by pride, attachment to inherited opinions, or the desire to defend his own views, argues against clear evidence rather than submitting to it. The Qur'an thus shows that the failure to accept guidance lies not in a lack of clarity in the message but in the human inclination to contention, and this is a call to self-examination, humility, and openness to the truth.

translation: And what prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them, and from seeking forgiveness of their Lord, except that the way of the former peoples should befall them, or that punishment should come upon them face to face?
interpretation: The verse exposes the real obstacle standing between people and faith: it is not any lack of evidence, since guidance has already arrived in clear form, but a stubborn refusal that keeps them from turning back to God and asking His forgiveness. Their hesitation is therefore self-chosen, and the verse warns that they are waiting only for one of two outcomes, either the same fate that overtook earlier nations who rejected their messengers, or a direct and visible punishment. The implicit lesson is that delay in responding to guidance is itself dangerous, because the opportunity to repent is not indefinite, and a person who postpones returning to God risks being overtaken by the consequences that were already set for those who persisted in denial.

translation: We send not the messengers except as bringers of good news and warners. But those who disbelieve argue with falsehood to refute thereby the truth, and they have taken My signs and what they were warned of as a mockery.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the role of the messengers is limited to delivering glad tidings to the obedient and warning those who persist in error, so their mission is one of clear guidance rather than coercion. It then turns to the response of the disbelievers, who do not engage the message honestly but deploy false arguments in an attempt to overturn the truth, a pattern in which dispute is used as a tool of evasion rather than inquiry. Their mockery of God's revelations and of the warnings given to them reveals that the problem lies not in insufficient proof but in a settled refusal to take the signs seriously, showing that ridicule can become a means of shielding oneself from accountability.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord but turns away from them and forgets what his hands have put forward? Indeed, We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness. And if you invite them to guidance, they will never be guided, ever.
interpretation: The verse describes a closed disposition that turns the reminder itself into a barrier: having repeatedly chosen to turn away from God's signs, a person gradually loses the capacity to receive them, so that the hearing and the heart are sealed as a consequence of the person's own aversion rather than as an arbitrary imposition. The phrase 'what his hands have put forward' points to the deeds he has committed, which he neglects to reckon with, and this forgetting is itself the root of his injustice. The attribution of the coverings to God is best understood as the divine principle that persistent refusal is answered by the withdrawal of guidance, so that the verse warns the listener to respond to the call while the heart remains open.

translation: And your Lord is the Forgiving, the Possessor of mercy. If He were to seize them for what they have earned, He would have hastened for them the punishment. But for them there is an appointed time, and they will never find from other than Him a refuge.
interpretation: The verse presents God's forgiveness and mercy as the primary attributes governing His dealings with humanity, explaining that His restraint from immediately punishing the wrongdoers is an expression of that mercy rather than indifference. Their sins would justify immediate retribution, yet God delays it until a fixed appointed time, which gives space for repentance and reflection. The closing warning makes clear that this delay is not an escape: when the appointed time comes, no one can find any shelter or refuge apart from God, so the mercy described should lead people to turn toward Him while there is still opportunity.

translation: And those towns—We destroyed them when they wronged, and We appointed for their destruction a fixed appointed time.
interpretation: The verse presents the destruction of earlier communities as a lesson in divine justice and patience. Those towns were not annihilated arbitrarily; their ruin came only after they persisted in wrongdoing, which shows that Allah grants respite and warnings before punishment. The phrase 'We appointed for their destruction a fixed time' indicates that every nation has a term set by God, beyond which no people can delay or hasten their reckoning. For the listener, this is a call to heed the signs of past destruction, to recognize that injustice carries consequences, and to take the opportunity of respite as a chance to repent before one's own appointed time arrives.

translation: And [mention] when Moses said to his young servant, "I will not cease [traveling] until I reach the junction of the two seas, or I will continue for a long period."
interpretation: The verse opens the story of Moses's journey in search of the one of profound knowledge, showing that the seeker of truth must be willing to persevere without limit, even if it demands years of travel. Moses's resolve to reach the meeting point of the two seas, or to go on for ages, reflects the sincerity of a student who values knowledge above comfort and fatigue. The place where the two seas meet is a symbolic threshold where two realms of understanding converge, and the destination is less a geographical point than a spiritual horizon that only the patient and humble can attain.

translation: So when they reached the junction of the two seas, they forgot their fish, and it took its way into the sea, making a passage.
interpretation: The verse marks the point where Musa and his young companion reach the meeting place they were seeking, and the forgetting of the fish signals that the appointed sign has been reached without their noticing. The fish's escape into the sea as a tunnel-like path shows that the sought-after knowledge and guidance lie beyond the ordinary markers of human planning; the miraculous sign is made known through forgetfulness, teaching that true insight often arrives where one is not consciously looking. The wondrous passage through the water foreshadows the encounter with the servant of God who possesses knowledge granted directly from Him.

translation: So when they had passed beyond it, he said to his young servant, "Bring us our morning meal; indeed we have suffered fatigue from this journey of ours."
interpretation: The verse marks the point where Moses and his companion pass the place they had been seeking, and the weariness that follows the journey becomes a quiet signal that they have moved beyond the appointed meeting point. Moses's request for food reveals both the human need of the traveler and his humility in acknowledging exhaustion, which prepares the narrative for the forgetting of the fish and the subsequent discovery of the servant at the rock. The verse thus shows that the pursuit of divine knowledge is not exempt from physical hardship, and that the seeker is still bound by ordinary needs even as he seeks the extraordinary.

translation: He said: "Did you see? When we took refuge at the rock, I indeed forgot the fish, and none but Satan made me forget it, so that I did not mention it. And it took its way into the sea in a wondrous manner."
interpretation: The verse shows the moment of forgetfulness on the journey of Moses and his servant, where the servant's lapse over the fish is attributed to Satan's whispering, which reflects how even the most diligent seekers of knowledge may be distracted by the whisperings of the devil. Yet the fish's miraculous escape into the sea becomes the sign that marks the place of the meeting with the servant of God, so that a human lapse is turned into the path toward a greater knowledge, teaching that Allah's wisdom can bring about the fulfillment of His purpose through what appears to be a mistake.

translation: He said, "That is what we were seeking." So they went back, retracing their footsteps.
interpretation: Moses's words reveal that the vanishing of the fish was the sign marking the very place he had been seeking, so the disappearance of the provision became the guide to the meeting with the servant of God. Their retracing of their own footsteps shows that the seeker of knowledge must return along the path of his earlier steps, reading the signs he once passed over, until he arrives at the destination that his trust in God had promised.

translation: So they found one of Our servants, to whom We had given mercy from Us and had taught him knowledge from Our own presence.
interpretation: The verse points to a servant of God who possessed a direct, divinely granted knowledge ('ilm min ladunna) that is not acquired through ordinary means of learning, combined with mercy from God that shapes how he acts. This knowledge is not the outward law that Moses had been taught, but an inner understanding of the hidden wisdom behind events that appear unjust on the surface. The lesson is that human judgment is limited, and that true insight comes from God, who may teach what He wills to whom He wills, so one should submit to what one cannot yet comprehend.

translation: Musa said to him, "May I follow you so that you may teach me of what you have been taught, [as] right guidance?"
interpretation: The verse captures Musa's humility and eagerness for knowledge: even as a prophet of great stature, he approaches another servant of God seeking to be taught, asking permission to accompany him on condition of learning. It teaches that true seeking of knowledge requires modesty, respect for those who possess a knowledge one lacks, and a willingness to be guided, and that the purpose of knowledge is rushd, a sound, rightly directed understanding that leads to righteous action.

translation: He said: "Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me."
interpretation: This verse comes from the story of Musa (Moses) and Al-Khidr in Surah Al-Kahf. When Khidr warns Musa in advance that he will not be able to bear patience with him, the statement reveals the gap between human judgment, which relies on outward appearances and immediate understanding, and divine wisdom, which sees the hidden purpose behind events. It teaches that true patience requires trust in what one does not yet comprehend, and that humility before knowledge beyond our reach is a necessary part of faith.

translation: And how can you be patient about that which you have not encompassed in knowledge?
interpretation: This verse is spoken by Moses's companion (al-Khidr, in the story of Surah al-Kahf) to Moses, who had accompanied him on a journey and was about to witness actions whose wisdom he could not yet grasp. The point is that patience requires a foundation of knowledge: one cannot be steadfast regarding matters whose inner reasons and outcomes lie beyond one's understanding. The verse thus invites humility before the limits of human knowledge, and reminds the seeker that true patience is tied to trust in the wisdom of the One who sees what we do not. Yet it also implies that the one who undertakes to learn must be prepared to bear with what appears strange until its meaning is revealed.

translation: He said, "You will find me, if Allah wills, patient, and I will not disobey you in any command."
interpretation: Musa's pledge reflects the humility of a seeker of knowledge before a teacher. By attaching "if Allah wills" to his promise of patience, he acknowledges that his own steadfastness depends on God's will and not on his self-confidence, so his commitment rests on reliance on God. His promise not to disobey any command shows that he accepts the discipline of learning from Khidr without questioning its wisdom in advance, which the rest of the story then tests.

translation: He said, "So if you follow me, then do not question me about anything until I myself mention it to you."
interpretation: The condition Khidr sets reveals that true knowledge granted from God cannot be fully grasped through immediate demand for explanation; it unfolds in its own time and wisdom. Musa, a prophet who had been given the Torah, is asked to surrender his impulse to judge events by their outward appearance and to accept a patience that opens the heart to hidden purposes. The verse therefore teaches that the seeker must place trust in a guide's knowledge, and that questioning born of haste can obstruct understanding, while patient companionship allows meaning to emerge at its appointed moment.

translation: So they set out, until when they boarded the ship, he tore it open. Said he, "Have you torn it open to drown its people? You have certainly committed a grave thing."
interpretation: The verse portrays Moses' shock at an act that appears to be pure destruction, and it carries a lesson about the limits of human judgment when it meets events whose inner wisdom is hidden. Moses sees only the visible harm, the breaking of a vessel that carries people to their deaths, and so he responds with the natural indignation of one who holds to justice and the sanctity of life. The phrase "shay'an imra" conveys something monstrous and grievous in the eyes of the observer. Read within the larger narrative, the scene shows that a seeker of knowledge must be patient with what he does not yet understand, because the apparent evil may conceal a mercy, and the true meaning of an act may only be revealed later.

translation: He said: Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Moses's companion (al-Khidr) in Surah al-Kahf, is a gentle rebuke recalling an earlier warning. Moses had agreed to accompany him on condition of patience, and the reminder exposes the limits of human patience when one is confronted with events whose wisdom lies beyond immediate understanding. It teaches that true knowledge of God's decree requires humility and trust, since what appears troubling may conceal a deeper mercy and purpose known only to Allah.

translation: He said: Do not take me to task for what I forgot, and do not burden me with difficulty in my affair.
interpretation: The verse is the plea of Moses, spoken to Khidr during their journey, and it reveals the posture of a servant who has accepted the authority of a teacher yet still feels the human pull of forgetfulness and the fear of being overwhelmed. By calling his lapse 'what I forgot,' he places his failure within the mercy that excuses the unintentional, and by asking not to be burdened with hardship he shows that he seeks ease from his Lord in the trials of obedience. The lesson is that sincere commitment to the path of knowledge and patience is joined with humble dependence on God, who lifts the weight of error from those who turn to Him.

translation: So they set out until, when they met a boy, he killed him. Moses said, "Have you killed a innocent soul without (its having killed) another? Indeed you have committed a grave wrong."
interpretation: The verse shows Moses, bound by his covenant to remain patient and not to question, reacting with alarm at an act that appeared to be an outright, unprovoked killing of an innocent person. His words express the sacred weight the Qur'an places on human life, since taking a soul is justified only by retribution for another soul. The scene also reveals the limits of human judgment: Moses judges by outward appearance, while the hidden wisdom behind the act, which only the companion knows, lies beyond what he can perceive, thus setting up the lesson about trust in God's knowledge over one's own immediate understanding.

translation: He said: Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?
interpretation: The verse records Musa's companion (al-Khidr) reminding Musa of the condition he had already been given: that patience is beyond what Musa could sustain when witnessing actions whose wisdom is not yet visible to him. The rebuke is gentle yet pointed, exposing the gap between a student's zeal for knowledge and the endurance that true learning requires. It teaches that trust in God's hidden wisdom, and restraint from judging by appearances, are essential to walking the path of guidance alongside one who has been granted knowledge from God.

translation: He said: "If I ever ask you about anything after this, then do not keep me in your company. You have indeed received an excuse from me."
interpretation: This is Moses speaking to Khidr after the third incident, when he had broken his word twice before out of eagerness to understand. Having seen the wisdom behind the actions, he accepts that his patience has been tested to its limit and binds himself to a condition: any further questioning will end their companionship. The phrase "you have received an excuse from me" shows a humble acknowledgment that he has given Khidr every reason to part ways, leaving no grounds for blame. It teaches that the seeker of knowledge must submit to the conditions of learning, that patience with a teacher whose methods are not yet understood is essential, and that a person of sincerity admits his own lapses and accepts the consequences of breaking his commitments.

translation: So they set off, until when they came to the people of a town and asked its people for food, they refused to host them. Then they found in it a wall about to collapse, so he set it upright. [Moses] said, 'If you had wished, you could have taken a payment for it.'
interpretation: The verse shows that true generosity is not conditional on the worthiness or hospitality of its recipients. Khidr repairs a wall for a people who turned away two travelers in need, which reflects the mercy and patience of God's servants, who answer hardness with kindness. It also reveals the limits of human judgment: Moses sees only the apparent unfairness of working without pay for an inhospitable town, while the hidden wisdom behind the act, later disclosed in the story, is beyond his immediate understanding. The lesson is that one should act for the sake of what is right and merciful, trusting that God's purposes often lie beyond what the observer can see.

translation: He said, "This is the parting between me and you. I will inform you of the interpretation of that which you could not bear with patience."
interpretation: The verse marks the moment when the companion of Moses, having fulfilled the conditions of the test, declares the end of their companionship. The events he was asked to witness were judged by outward appearances, which Moses could not accept in patience, yet each act carried a hidden wisdom. By explaining the inner meaning of what had troubled Moses, the verse teaches that divine knowledge reaches beyond human perception, and that trust in God's wisdom is required even when His ways are not immediately understood. It also reminds the believer that the apparent harm may conceal a greater good, and that true knowledge comes through patience and submission rather than hasty judgment.

translation: As for the boat, it belonged to poor people who worked on the sea, so I wished to damage it, for behind them was a king who seized every boat by force.
interpretation: The verse reveals that apparent harm can conceal a greater mercy: the damaging of the boat, which seemed wrongful to Moses, was in fact a protection of the poor owners from a tyrant's confiscation. It teaches that divine wisdom often operates beyond human perception, so that a believer should trust Allah's knowledge over the limits of his own sight, and that caring for the vulnerable may sometimes require an action that looks harmful on the surface.

translation: As for the boy, his parents were believers, and we feared that he would burden them with rebellion and disbelief.
interpretation: The verse, spoken by al-Khidr in the Surah of the Cave, reveals that the boy's killing was rooted in divine foresight rather than arbitrary harm. Since he was destined to grow into a rebellious disbeliever who would pressure his devout parents toward transgression and unbelief, God's mercy chose to remove him, and in exchange to grant the believing parents a purer and more compassionate child. It teaches that apparent evil in events may conceal a wisdom beyond human sight, and that faith itself is a trust whose protection rests with God's knowledge of what lies ahead.

translation: So We wished that their Lord would replace for them one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion.
interpretation: The verse shows that what appears to be harm may hide divine mercy. The boy's parents were believers, and the child was destined to bring them hardship through rebellion and disbelief, so God removed him and granted them a child who was purer in character and closer to them in affection and kindness. The lesson is that human knowledge is limited, and believers should trust God's wisdom even when His decrees seem painful, because He sees the consequences that people cannot.

translation: As for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them. Their father had been righteous, so your Lord wished that they would reach their maturity and extract their treasure, as a mercy from your Lord. And I did not do it of my own accord. That is the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience.
interpretation: The verse reveals that the seemingly unjust act of repairing the wall for free was rooted in divine mercy and wisdom: the protection of an orphan's inheritance, preserved because of their righteous father, shows that God's care extends to the children of the righteous, and that apparent harm or wasted effort may hide a greater good that only becomes clear through trust in the Lord's plan, not through human judgment alone.

translation: They ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn. Say, "I will recite to you about him a reminder."
interpretation: The verse opens a narrative in which the Prophet is asked about Dhul-Qarnayn, a figure whose story is withheld until the question is answered. The reply, "I will recite to you from him a reminder," makes the account itself the answer: the tale is not offered as idle history but as a remembrance meant to admonish the listener. The phrase "منه ذكرا" suggests that what is recounted is a portion of his story chosen for its moral and spiritual weight, so that the reader is directed toward reflection on power, justice, and accountability rather than toward mere curiosity about the man. Dhul-Qarnayn thus becomes an exemplar of a ruler whose strength was placed in the service of God and the protection of the weak, and the verse establishes that the Qur'anic narrative answers questions by turning them toward guidance.

translation: Indeed, We established him firmly in the land, and We gave him a means to everything.
interpretation: The verse refers to Dhu al-Qarnayn, whom God empowered on earth and provided with the resources and means needed to accomplish his undertakings. The phrase "a means to everything" signals that his strength lay not only in power but in the wisdom and tools God granted him, so that his success was a trust that obligated him to act justly and to use his capabilities for the benefit of others, rather than for arrogance or conquest.

translation: So he followed a course (of means).
interpretation: The word sabab means a cause, a means, or a path by which something is reached. Here it shows that Dhul-Qarnayn's power and conquests were carried out through the means God had placed at his disposal, and that he pursued them as an instrument of justice rather than of mere ambition. The verse teaches that human striving is real and must be exerted through lawful, available means, while the authority and the success of those means ultimately belong to God, who enables them.

translation: Until, when he reached the setting place of the sun, he found it setting in a murky spring, and found near it a people. We said, "O Dhul-Qarnayn, either you punish them or you adopt kindness toward them."
interpretation: The verse presents the sun's setting as seen from the observer's position, not as a literal account of the sun entering a body of water, so that the 'murky spring' describes how the horizon appeared to Dhul-Qarnayn. Its real significance lies in the moral choice that follows: a ruler who holds power over a people is given the right to either punish or be gracious, which establishes justice and mercy as the two poles of governance. The divine address directly to him, rather than through an intermediary, marks him as one entrusted with responsibility, and the open-ended choice shows that his conduct toward the defeated will be judged by how he uses his authority.

translation: He said: As for whoever does wrong, we will punish him; then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a terrible punishment.
interpretation: The verse presents a stark principle of divine justice: the one who persists in wrongdoing (zulm) is not left unchecked, first facing consequence in this world and then, after being returned to his Lord, facing a far more severe and unfamiliar torment. The phrase 'adhaban nukra' (a dreadful, unprecedented punishment) conveys that the final reckoning exceeds anything the person has known, so the verse serves as a warning against persisting in injustice toward oneself and others, while implying that accountability is certain and comes in stages.

translation: But as for whoever believes and does righteous work, he will have the best reward, and we will speak to him of our command with ease.
interpretation: The verse sets the reward of faith and good deeds against the ease that accompanies it: the believer who acts rightly is promised the finest recompense, and God will make the matters of His command easy for him to understand and to carry out. Faith joined with action is thus shown to lighten the path, so that what might seem burdensome becomes accessible to the one who sincerely turns toward God.

translation: Then he followed a means (or path).
interpretation: The phrase comes from Surah Al-Kahf (18:85), where Dhul-Qarnayn, after receiving power on the earth, follows a route toward the west. The word "sabab" means a means, cause, or way by which something is reached; here it signifies the material resources, knowledge, and tools God granted him to accomplish his journey and his mission of justice. The verse teaches that true power is exercised through legitimate means, and that a righteous ruler uses what God has given him to pursue his goals, while always recognizing that the ultimate success belongs to God.

translation: Until, when he reached the rising-place of the sun, he found it rising over a people for whom We had made no shelter against it.
interpretation: The verse describes a journey to the far eastern limit of the inhabited world, where the sun rises over a people who lived without any natural or built protection from its heat. It conveys the sovereign power of God over the whole earth and the extent of Dhu al-Qarnayn's travels, showing that the people he reached were exposed to the sun with no cover, a state of simple, unsheltered existence that reflects God's knowledge of His creation's conditions, and it directs the reader to reflect on the vastness of God's dominion and the diversity of human circumstances across the earth.

translation: Thus it is; and We have encompassed with knowledge all that is with him (Dhu al-Qarnayn's account of his journey and his knowledge). Or, in the sense of the verse in Surah al-Kahf (18:91): Thus it was, and We had full knowledge of what was with him.
interpretation: The phrase signals that God's knowledge fully surrounds everything that the figure described possessed, whether his power, his resources, or his understanding; nothing of his affairs escapes the divine awareness. It affirms that the story is recounted from a source of complete knowledge, so its details are trustworthy, and it reminds the listener that human achievements and capacities, however great, are encompassed by and dependent upon God's all-encompassing knowledge.

translation: Then he followed a way (a means).
interpretation: The verse, from Surah Al-Kahf (18:85) in the story of Dhul-Qarnayn, shows that after his conquests he did not stop at achieving power but continued to pursue specific means and causes, each suited to its purpose. The phrase reflects a principle that a righteous ruler uses the available means, planned and systematic, to accomplish a just goal, while remembering that the ultimate success belongs to God, who grants the means.

translation: Until, when he reached between the two barriers, he found beneath them a people who could barely understand any speech.
interpretation: The verse describes Dhul-Qarnayn's journey to the furthest inhabited region in the east or west, where he meets a people isolated from the world by the two barriers. Their inability to grasp speech points to a people so remote and culturally distant that communication itself was nearly impossible, which in turn highlights the reach of divine guidance and power that carried the righteous ruler to them. Read more deeply, the phrase suggests a human condition of limited understanding, where people are cut off from the wisdom that would otherwise be available to them, and the story invites reflection on the responsibility of the powerful to bridge such divides with justice and mercy.

translation: They said, "O Dhul-Qarnayn, indeed Gog and Magog are spreading corruption in the land, so may we pay you a tribute on condition that you build a barrier between us and them?"
interpretation: The verse presents a moment of human vulnerability before a righteous ruler: a people beset by destructive enemies turn to Dhul-Qarnayn, recognizing that power given by God can be used for protection. Their offer of payment reflects the natural human impulse to seek security through material means, while the request for a barrier points to a boundary between order and chaos. The verse invites reflection on how authority entrusted with strength should answer the cries of the weak, and on the limits of worldly resources in the face of corruption that threatens communal life.

translation: He said: "That in which my Lord has established me is better; so help me with strength, and I will place between you and them a barrier."
interpretation: Dhul-Qarnayn refuses any payment for his service, recognizing that the power and provision Allah has given him are far better than what the people offer. Instead of accepting wealth, he asks them for physical labor and effort, so that together they might build a strong barrier against the destructive peoples of Gog and Magog. The verse teaches that true sufficiency comes from God, that a person of means should act with integrity and not seek material reward for a public good, and that collective cooperation in a righteous cause, backed by sincere effort, accomplishes what no single party could achieve alone.

translation: "Bring me sheets of iron" — until, when he had leveled [the gap] between the two mountain-sides, he said, "Blow [with bellows]"; until, when he had made it fire, he said, "Bring me molten copper to pour over it."
interpretation: The verse portrays a deliberate, step-by-step act of construction carried out under divine guidance: the barrier is built only after the materials are gathered, the gap is made level and sealed, and the metal is heated and then cast. It conveys that protection against a destructive people is achieved through patient human labor and skill, sustained by faith and wisdom, and that the completion of such a barrier is itself a sign of God's power working through human effort.

translation: So they were not able to scale it (the barrier), nor were they able to dig through it.
interpretation: The verse, spoken by Dhu al-Qarnayn after building the iron barrier between two mountains against Gog and Magog, expresses the completeness of the protection he built. The people who came to him could neither climb over the wall, which was smooth and high, nor tunnel beneath it, which was made solid and deep. Their failure shows that human strength and ingenuity, when set against a barrier built by a righteous ruler with divine permission, are limited. It also reminds the reader that every means of protection is ultimately a mercy granted by God, and that Dhu al-Qarnayn himself attributes the strength of the barrier to his Lord rather than to his own power.

translation: He said, "This is a mercy from my Lord. But when the promise of my Lord comes, He will reduce it to dust, and the promise of my Lord is ever true."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Dhul-Qarnayn after he built the barrier against Gog and Magog, attributes the strength of the barrier to divine mercy rather than to his own power, acknowledging that every human achievement is a favor from God. Yet the mercy is temporary: the barrier is bound to crumble when God's appointed time arrives, a reminder that all worldly structures are subject to decline. The verse thus joins gratitude with an awareness of mortality and the inevitability of God's promise, which is certain to be fulfilled.

translation: And We will leave them, that Day, surging against one another, and the Horn will be blown, and We will gather them together in a single gathering.
interpretation: The verse portrays the disorder of the Day of Judgment, when humanity is left to surge in confusion, each crowd pressing against the next as the Trumpet is sounded. The scene is one of overwhelming upheaval, after which God gathers all of creation into one assembly for reckoning, showing that the scattered and tumultuous state of the world before that day ends in a complete and unified gathering before the Lord.

translation: And We will present Hell on that Day to the disbelievers, exposed to view.
interpretation: The verse portrays the final reckoning as a scene in which Hell is not hidden but openly displayed before those who denied the truth, so that the reality they once dismissed becomes undeniable. The word 'ard' (presentation) conveys both exposure and confrontation: the disbelievers are brought face to face with the consequence of their rejection, and the vivid imagery teaches that the denial of faith ultimately collapses under the weight of an unavoidable, visible truth. It is a warning that what was obscured in the world will be laid bare on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Those whose eyes were under a covering from My remembrance, and who were unable to hear.
interpretation: The verse describes those whose spiritual perception was veiled from the remembrance of God, so that their eyes, which should see the signs of God in creation and revelation, were closed to guidance. Their inability to hear points to a deafness of the heart that refuses to receive the message, even when it is spoken plainly. The imagery suggests that the obstacle is not in the faculties themselves but in a inner covering that arises from heedlessness and aversion, so that the outward senses fail to convey the truth to the soul.

translation: Do those who disbelieve think that they can take My servants as protectors instead of Me? Indeed, We have prepared Hell as a lodging for the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who disbelieve for presuming that they may take as allies and protectors, in place of God, those He has created as His servants, whether these be angels, prophets, saints, or idols and false deities they worship in His stead. Such a presumption is a grave error, for all true protection belongs to God alone, and those who set up others beside Him will find no refuge in them. The phrase 'prepared Hell as a lodging' conveys that the consequence of this disbelief is already readied, so that the one who chooses to rely on what is other than God is warned of the abode awaiting him, an abode that is a guest-house of punishment rather than a place of rest.

translation: Say: Shall we inform you of the greatest losers in respect of their deeds?
interpretation: The verse turns the believer's attention from outward appearances to the question of where true loss lies. Those most deeply ruined are not necessarily the poor or the openly unbelieving who are easily recognized, but those whose efforts were directed toward a goal they thought was good while their striving was in fact wasted. Their labor was spent in the wrong direction, so when they stand before their Lord they find that everything they hoped to gain has vanished. The verse therefore calls for sincere self-examination: a person should ask whether his deeds are rightly intended and rightly grounded, since sincere effort that is misdirected can still leave a soul in the greatest loss.

translation: Those whose efforts have gone astray in the life of this world, while they think that they are doing good work.
interpretation: The verse describes a tragic self-deception: a person may labor diligently and sincerely believe his deeds are righteous, yet his striving is wasted because it was not directed toward the truth or guided by faith and obedience to God. The gravity lies not only in the failure of the effort but in the false confidence that hides the failure from its doer, so that he is neither warned nor corrected in this life. It is a call to self-examination, to measure one's actions by the standard revealed by God rather than by one's own sense of having done well.

translation: Those are the ones who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord and in meeting Him, so their deeds have become worthless, and We will not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection.
interpretation: The verse shows that disbelief in God's signs (both the revealed verses and the signs in creation) and denial of the meeting with Him go together, and that such denial empties a person's deeds of value. Because those deeds were not built on faith in the Lord who would judge them, they carry no weight in the balance on the Day of Resurrection. The image of the scale without weight conveys that outward works divorced from true belief count for nothing before God, so a person's standing is measured by the reality of faith and sincerity rather than by the appearance of good deeds.

translation: That is their recompense: Hell, because they disbelieved and took My signs and My messengers in mockery.
interpretation: The verse presents a direct causal link between disbelief and its punishment: the reward of those who mock God's revelations and His messengers is not arbitrary but the natural consequence of their own choice. Their treatment of the signs as objects of ridicule reveals a heart that has turned away from reverence, and the mockery of the messengers is an assault on the very channels through which guidance reaches humanity. Hell is thus framed not merely as a penalty imposed from outside but as the fitting outcome of a stance that trivializes truth, teaching that frivolity toward the sacred carries grave moral weight.

translation: Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds, for them will be the Gardens of Paradise as a lodging.
interpretation: The verse ties salvation to a two-fold condition: inward faith and outward righteous action, which are presented as inseparable, since faith that produces no good works remains incomplete in the Qur'anic view. The phrase "Gardens of Firdaws" uses the word for the highest and most enclosed of paradises, suggesting that the reward is matched to the sincerity and excellence of the believer's deeds. The word "nuzul" (lodging or welcoming provision) evokes the image of a host preparing a generous reception for a guest, so the reward is portrayed not as a wage earned by mere exchange but as an honored hospitality granted by God's generosity. The verse thus invites the reader to see worship and ethical conduct as the path by which a person prepares a home in the next life.

translation: Abiding therein forever; they will not desire any change from it.
interpretation: The phrase describes the eternal and unchanging nature of the abode of the righteous in Paradise. Its inhabitants will be content with their station, having no wish to be moved from it or to exchange it for anything else, since they will possess complete and lasting satisfaction. The word 'hawlan' (change or removal) emphasizes that their state is free from any desire for alteration, conveying a sense of perfect, undisturbed bliss that is never subject to decline, boredom, or longing for something other than what they have been granted.

translation: Say: Even if the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord are exhausted, even if we brought the like of it as a supplement.
interpretation: The verse points to the boundlessness of divine knowledge, wisdom and creative speech, which no created measure can contain or exhaust. Human beings, and all of creation, are limited in their capacity to comprehend or record the realities of God, so even the most vast resources imaginable, such as an ocean turned into ink and multiplied, would fall short. It calls the believer to humility before the infinite majesty of God and to recognize that whatever knowledge humanity gains is only a small portion of what belongs to Him alone.

translation: Say, "I am only a human being like you. It has been revealed to me that your God is one God. So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord."
interpretation: The verse establishes the Prophet's humanity as a corrective to any exaggeration about his station, placing him on the same level as the people he addresses while distinguishing himself by revelation alone. From that revealed basis comes the core of the message, pure monotheism, which the verse then links to the practical life of the believer. Hope in meeting the Lord is shown to be inseparable from two things: righteous action and sincere worship free of any partner. Faith in the hereafter thus becomes a daily discipline in which deeds and undivided devotion to God are the sign of genuine expectation of Him.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ain, Sad.
interpretation: The verse opens with the mysterious disjointed letters (muqatta'at), which the Qur'an leaves without explicit lexical gloss, as a sign that the revelation is composed of the same letters human beings use, yet inimitable in its eloquence. Their placement before the mention of Allah's mercy invites the listener to pause before a text that is at once familiar in its alphabet and beyond human capacity to produce. The opening invocation then anchors this opaque signal in mercy, suggesting that the coming account of Zakariyya and his prayer for a child is framed by the divine attribute of compassion that answers quiet supplication.

translation: An account of the mercy of your Lord toward His servant Zakariyya.
interpretation: The opening words of this passage (Surah Maryam 19:2) establish its central theme before the narrative begins: divine mercy (rahmah) is not an abstract idea but something God actually bestows on a particular servant. By calling Zakariyya 'His servant' ('abdahu), the verse frames his story as one of devoted worship and humble submission, showing that mercy is extended to those who turn to God. The word 'remembrance' (dhikr) signals that the account is meant to be recalled and reflected upon, so that the listener sees in Zakariyya's experience of answered prayer, despite advanced age and a barren wife, a pattern of how God responds to sincere supplication in circumstances that seem humanly hopeless.

translation: When he called out to his Lord in a secret, low voice.
interpretation: The verse presents Zakariyya's supplication as an intimate, hidden prayer rather than a loud public appeal. This quiet invocation reflects sincerity and humility before God, and a closeness in which the servant need not raise his voice for the Lord to hear him. It also suggests that the most authentic supplication often arises from a heart that turns to God in private, far from display, and the subsequent verses show that this hidden plea was answered with the gift of a son in his old age.

translation: He said, "My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened and my head has glistened with grey hair, and I have never been unsuccessful in my supplication to You, my Lord."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Zakariya (Zechariah), is a prayer of humble intimacy born of age and long hope. He describes his physical decline, the weakening of his bones and the whitening of his hair, not as a complaint but as a plea grounded in his lifelong habit of calling upon God. His statement that he has never been left wretched in his supplication expresses a deep trust that God has always answered him, and it sets the stage for his request for an heir, showing that faith is strongest when a person recalls God's past graciousness while facing an apparently impossible situation.

translation: And indeed, I fear my relatives after me, and my wife is barren, so grant me from Yourself an heir.
interpretation: This verse is the supplication of Zakariyya (Zechariah), peace be upon him, who, advanced in age and with a barren wife, turns to God in humble and sincere prayer. His fear concerns the conduct of his kinsmen after his death, who might fail to carry on the faithful mission of guiding the Children of Israel and preserving the religious trust. The phrase 'from Yourself' (min ladunka) points to a gift that comes solely from divine grace, beyond the ordinary means of nature, which is why he asks for an heir who will inherit his knowledge, prophethood, and responsibility. The verse teaches that a believer, when faced with personal limitations and anxiety about the future of the faith, should direct his concern to God and ask with trust that He can bring about what appears impossible by ordinary measures.

translation: "He will inherit me and inherit from the family of Jacob; and make him, my Lord, pleasing [to You]."
interpretation: Zechariah's prayer reveals a father's deep concern for the continuity of his prophetic mission after him. Fearing that his kinsmen would not carry on the faithful service of God, he asks for a son who will inherit both his worldly role and the spiritual legacy of the family of Jacob, a legacy of prophethood and guidance. The phrase "inherit" here is best understood as inheriting prophetic knowledge, wisdom, and the mantle of guiding the community, rather than merely material property. His closing request, that the son be "pleasing" to the Lord, shows that his true desire is not merely an heir but one whose character and devotion are acceptable to God, placing righteousness above lineage.

translation: O Zechariah, indeed We give you good news of a boy whose name is Yahya; We have not assigned to anyone before him that name.
interpretation: The verse marks the singular honor of Yahya, the son given to Zechariah in his old age and after his wife had been barren. The good news comes from God directly, and the naming of the child before his birth, a name no one had borne before, signals that Yahya is set apart by a distinction unique in creation. This is a sign of divine favor and mercy that answers a prayer offered in quiet devotion, showing that God can bring life where human means seem exhausted, and that the one who was 'nameless in precedent' is chosen for a special mission of purity and prophethood.

translation: He said, "My Lord, how can I have a son when my wife is barren and I have reached extreme old age?"
interpretation: Zechariah's question is not a denial of God's power but an expression of wonder and humble seeking of clarity. Having long prayed for an heir, he now sees both himself and his wife as beyond the natural age and condition for childbearing, and so asks how the promise will come to be. The verse thus shows the believer's honest amazement before divine favor, a question that stems from awareness of human limitation rather than doubt about the Lord who is able to do all things, and which is answered in the following verses by the assurance that what seems impossible is easy for God.

translation: He said: "So it will be. Your Lord says: 'It is easy for Me, and I created you before, when you were nothing.'"
interpretation: The verse conveys that what seems impossible to human reasoning is effortless for God, who created the human being from nothing. Zechariah, who asked how he could have a child in his old age and with a barren wife, is reminded that the One who brought him into existence from non-existence can easily grant him a son. The argument moves from the greater act of creating a person out of nothing to the lesser act of granting a child, so that divine power, not natural causes, is the decisive factor. It is a lesson in trust that God's promise is not limited by the ordinary order of things, and that the origin of human life itself is proof of His capacity to do what He wills.

translation: He said, "My Lord, appoint for me a sign." He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three nights, while sound and well."
interpretation: Zechariah asked for a sign so that he could know with certainty when the good news of a son, promised to him, had taken hold. God made his sign a voluntary silence: his tongue was restrained from ordinary speech with people for three nights, though he was physically sound and able. The affliction was not of the body but of communication, so that his devotion would be turned wholly toward remembrance and glorification of God, and the miracle of the promised birth would be witnessed in the very stillness that preceded it.

translation: So he came out to his people from the prayer niche and conveyed to them by inspiration: Glorify (God) morning and evening.
interpretation: The verse shows that Zechariah, after receiving the sign that he would be unable to speak to people for three days except by gesture, came out from the sanctuary and communicated the command of God to his people through signs rather than speech. The inspired message he conveyed is a call to continuous remembrance and glorification of God at the beginning and end of each day, teaching that even when ordinary human communication is restricted, the believer's tongue and heart may remain devoted to praising the Creator. It also highlights that dhikr and tasbih are to be sustained at the fixed times of morning and evening, which frames daily life around the remembrance of God.

translation: O Yahya, take the Scripture with determination. And We gave him judgment while he was still a boy.
interpretation: The verse presents Yahya as a child who was given wisdom and prophetic judgment at an early age, and it commands him to hold fast to the Scripture with resolve. This suggests that the true measure of a person's readiness for religious responsibility is not age but sincerity, seriousness, and firm commitment to God's revelation. Yahya's early maturity becomes a model: devotion to the divine message should be pursued earnestly and without wavering, and the capacity to understand and bear that trust can be granted even in youth when the heart is prepared to receive it.

translation: And compassion from Us and purity, and he was devout and God-fearing.
interpretation: The verse describes three gifts bestowed upon Yahya (John), the son of Zechariah, and then his character. The phrase "hanānan min ladunnā" (compassion from Our presence) points to a tenderness of heart that is not merely a natural disposition but a divine gift, enabling him to be merciful toward others and to feel deeply for the suffering of people and creatures. "Zakāh" here conveys purity of soul and inner cleanliness, a state of being free from sin, corruption and moral defilement, which he attained in his youth. The final words, "wa-kāna taqiyyan," present the fruit of these gifts: he was a man of taqwā, constantly mindful of God, guarding himself from what displeases Him. The sequence suggests that divine mercy and purity of heart are what make a person truly God-conscious, and that piety is not only outward ritual but a tender, pure inner life that reaches out to others with compassion.

translation: And dutiful toward his parents, and he was not arrogant or disobedient.
interpretation: The verse describes the character of Yahya (John), son of Zakariyya, in the surah of Maryam, presenting filial piety as the foundation of his moral excellence. His kindness toward his parents is named first, showing that goodness toward those who gave us life is a primary sign of righteousness. The two negations that follow, 'not arrogant' (jabbar) and 'not disobedient' (asi), reveal that true devotion to God is inseparable from humility before creation and obedience to what is right. A person who is gentle with parents is thereby shielded from the pride of the tyrant and the rebelliousness of the one who refuses guidance, so the verse ties the social duty of honoring parents to the spiritual discipline of humility and submission to God.

translation: And peace be upon him the day he was born, and the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by John the Baptist (Yahya) in Surah Maryam, is a declaration of divine peace and security that spans the three critical junctures of human existence: birth, death, and resurrection. Its significance lies in the fact that the three moments are the points where a person is most vulnerable and most dependent on God's protection. Birth marks the entry into a world of trials, death marks the departure from it and the unknown, and resurrection marks the final accounting before God. By placing these together, the verse presents a complete arc of a believer's life under divine care, affirming that the prophet is shielded from the fear and harm that accompany each of these stages. It also reflects the tender, reassuring language of the surah as a whole, which emphasizes God's mercy toward His chosen servants, and it stands in contrast to the pattern of the wider narrative, where the same peace is elsewhere granted to the prophets and righteous as a sign of their nearness to God.

translation: And mention in the Book Mary, when she withdrew from her family to a place toward the east.
interpretation: The verse opens a narrative in which Mary is singled out as a model of devotion, her withdrawal to an eastern place signaling a deliberate separation from her people in order to devote herself to worship and solitude before God. Her retreat prepares the ground for the miraculous annunciation that follows, showing that God's chosen servants are often placed in circumstances of withdrawal and trial before receiving His favor. The command to "mention" her underscores that her story is a lesson to be remembered, affirming her purity and the sanctity of her position among the righteous.

translation: So she took a screen apart from them, and We sent to her Our Spirit, and he appeared to her as a man in all respects.
interpretation: The verse shows Mary withdrawing from her people into a secluded place to devote herself to worship, and it presents solitude with God as a sacred space for devotion. The sending of the Spirit, understood as Gabriel, in the form of a perfectly formed man shows that divine revelation and command reach people in a form they can perceive and bear, which prepares the reader for the miraculous conception that follows.

translation: She said: "Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are one who fears Allah."
interpretation: This verse, from the story of Maryam (Mary), captures the moment she is confronted by the angel who appears before her in human form. Her immediate response is not panic but a turn to God: she seeks refuge in al-Rahman, the Most Merciful, placing her protection entirely in the divine mercy rather than in her own strength or in any human help. Her words also contain a measured challenge, reminding the visitor that if he is truly God-fearing, he should refrain from what he is approaching her with. The verse thus shows that true piety recognizes the presence of God as a restraint on wrongdoing, and that a person of faith, when threatened, instinctively takes refuge in God's mercy.

translation: He said: I am only a messenger from your Lord, to give you a pure boy.
interpretation: The verse, spoken by the angel to Maryam (Mary), shows that the birth of the boy Jesus comes not from human means but from a direct divine gift, announced through a messenger who clarifies that his role is only to convey the Lord's command. The description "zakiyyan" (pure) points to the holiness and blamelessness of the child from his very beginning, and it prepares the reader to see the miraculous nature of his birth as a sign of God's power to create as He wills, free of any sin or impurity.

translation: She said: "How can I have a son when no man has touched me, and I have not been unchaste?"
interpretation: Maryam's question is not a denial of God's power but an expression of wonder and of her chastity, which she had preserved under deep social pressure. Her words show that she understood the announcement as a miracle requiring a means beyond the ordinary course of nature, and they prepare the reader for the divine answer that God creates what He wills: when He decrees a matter, He says to it 'Be,' and it is. The verse thus places the miraculous birth of Jesus within the framework of God's absolute sovereignty over the laws of causation, while affirming the purity and honor of Maryam as a model of faithful devotion.

translation: He said, "So it will be. Your Lord says, 'It is easy for Me; and We will make him a sign for mankind and a mercy from Us. And it is a matter already decreed.'"
interpretation: The verse presents the divine decree concerning the birth of Yahya (John) to the aged Zachariah and his barren wife, even though it seemed impossible by ordinary human measures. God declares that this matter is easy for Him, for His power is not bound by natural causes, and it is He who creates the means and the outcome alike. The child is made a sign, a clear proof of God's power and of His ability to bring life where none seems possible, and he is a mercy from God to his parents and to those who witness his story. The phrase 'a matter already decreed' affirms that what God has determined will certainly come to pass, so the believer should find in this a reason for hope and trust in God even when circumstances appear closed.

translation: So she conceived him, and withdrew with him to a remote place.
interpretation: The verse describes Maryam (Mary) withdrawing to a secluded, distant place after conceiving the child, which reflects her modesty, her need for privacy and protection from the judgment of her people, and her turning away from the world to face a momentous and trying event alone. The seclusion also prepares the setting for the miraculous birth of 'Isa (Jesus) that follows, showing that God's sign arises in circumstances of solitude and hardship, and that the faithful servant bears such trials with patience and reliance upon God.

translation: So the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree. She said, "Oh, I wish I had died before this and had been a thing forgotten, completely forgotten."
interpretation: The verse shows Maryam at the most vulnerable moment of her life: alone, in labor, far from her people, and facing the shame she expected them to attach to a child born outside marriage. Her wish for death and oblivion reveals the depth of her distress, yet it also prepares the reader for the divine relief that follows immediately after, when she is comforted and provided for. Her human anguish is presented honestly, as a reminder that trust in God does not remove the pain of trials but opens the way to relief beyond what the sufferer can see.

translation: Then he (the one below her) called out to her: "Do not grieve; your Lord has placed beneath you a stream."
interpretation: The verse recounts the moment of comfort granted to Maryam (peace be upon her) in her solitude and distress after giving birth in a remote place. The call from beneath her, whether understood as the infant Jesus or as a voice from the angel, reveals that divine care reaches the believer precisely when human strength is exhausted. The stream (sariyyan) that God provides is both a literal provision of water and a symbol that Allah does not leave His servant without sustenance and consolation. The command "Do not grieve" teaches that sorrow, though natural, should give way to trust in the Lord who has already arranged relief beneath the very feet of the one who suffers, so that patience is rewarded by unseen mercy.

translation: And shake toward yourself the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you fresh, ripe dates.
interpretation: The verse, spoken to Maryam (Mary) during her labor, teaches that divine provision comes through human effort: she is commanded to act, shaking the palm trunk, though the fruit that falls is wholly God's gift. It shows that trust in God (tawakkul) does not cancel the duty to take action, and that God can cause nourishment to reach a person in her weakest and most isolated moment. The fresh dates also signal that God's care for her and her child is complete, meeting her need for food, strength and comfort before she faces her people.

translation: So eat and drink and be comforted. And if you see any human being, say, "Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, so I will not speak today to any human."
interpretation: The verse comes in the story of Maryam (Mary) after the birth of Jesus, when she was physically and emotionally exhausted and facing the anxiety of her people's reaction. God instructs her to nourish her body with food and drink and to find consolation in the infant at her side, and to answer any questioner through a sign rather than words. The vow of silence (sawm, literally abstention) is a form of trust in God: she entrusts her defense to the miracle that will follow, as the infant Jesus will speak on her behalf. The passage teaches that when a person faces hostility or misunderstanding, patience, self-care, and reliance on God's support can be more effective than argument, and that the Creator provides comfort and vindication at the right time.

translation: Then she brought him to her people, carrying him. They said, "O Mary, you have certainly come with a strange and monstrous thing."
interpretation: The verse presents the moment of public shock that follows Mary's return with the infant Jesus. Her people, who knew her as a chaste and devoted woman dedicated to the sanctuary, read the sight of a newborn in her arms as proof of a scandal, and their words reveal how readily appearances were judged against her. The word fariyyan, rendered as strange or monstrous, conveys something so unprecedented that it provokes outrage rather than curiosity. The episode anticipates the miraculous answer that follows, in which the child himself speaks in his mother's defense, so that the vindication of Mary comes not through her own argument but through a sign from God that silences the accusation.

translation: O sister of Aaron, your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother an unchaste woman.
interpretation: The verse is spoken to Mary (Maryam) by her people after she returns to them carrying the infant Jesus, when they accuse her of immorality. Their words, "O sister of Aaron," are an address that recalls her noble lineage, placing her among a family of righteous standing, and they stress the purity of her parents as a rebuke against the charge brought upon her. The phrasing exposes the contradiction in their accusation: a family known for uprightness cannot readily produce such a shameful act, and the reproach is thus directed at the unjust suspicion rather than at her ancestry. The miraculous circumstances that follow, in which the newborn speaks from the cradle to vindicate his mother, form the answer to this accusation and affirm her chastity and the divine sign surrounding the birth of Jesus.

translation: So she pointed to him. They said, "How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a young child?"
interpretation: The verse shows Maryam (Mary) responding to the miracle of the newborn by gesturing toward her infant rather than speaking, following the instruction to abstain from speech. The people's reaction reveals their astonishment and their rejection of the idea that a baby in the cradle could converse, which sets the stage for the miraculous speech of 'Isa (Jesus) that follows. The scene underscores that God's sign was meant to be a clear proof, confronting the onlookers with something beyond ordinary expectation while Maryam is shown to be relying wholly on God's guidance rather than on her own defense.

translation: He said: Indeed, I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by the infant Jesus from the cradle, answering the accusations made against his mother Mary. Before anything else, he affirms his humble servanthood to Allah, rejecting any notion of divinity that Christians would later attribute to him. The sequence is significant: servitude comes first, then the gift of the Scripture, then prophethood. This shows that revelation and prophetic mission are bestowed by Allah's grace alone, and that the true vocation of a messenger is to direct people to the worship of the One God rather than to himself.

translation: "And He has made me blessed wherever I may be, and has enjoined upon me prayer and zakah as long as I remain alive."
interpretation: The verse, spoken by Prophet Jesus from the cradle, shows that true blessing (barakah) is not tied to place, circumstance, or status but is a divine gift that accompanies a servant wherever he goes, and its outward sign is the faithful performance of worship. By linking prayer, which joins the servant to God, with zakah, which joins him to his fellow human beings, the verse presents a complete devotion that is vertical and horizontal together. The phrase "as long as I remain alive" teaches that these obligations are lifelong and not restricted to a particular period or condition, so that the believer's blessing is measured by his steadfastness in them until the end of his life.

translation: And dutiful toward my mother, and He has not made me domineering or wretched.
interpretation: Jesus's words here, spoken from the cradle, place filial devotion at the center of his mission. Honoring his mother is presented as the first duty he is given, showing that reverence for parents is the foundation of a righteous life.
