His statement that God did not make him 'jabbaran' (tyrannical or arrogant) and 'shaqiyyan' (wretched) shows that true honor and sanctity are tied to humility in the face of God and gentleness toward those closest to us. The verse thus suggests that a person who is kind to parents is protected from both arrogance and misery, since obedience and humility bring a blessed life.

translation: And peace be upon me the day I was born, and the day I die, and the day I am raised alive.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Yahya (John, son of Zakariya) in Surah Maryam (19:15), is a declaration of divine protection and blessing that spans the whole course of a person's existence. The three moments it names, birth, death, and resurrection, mark the beginning, end, and final reckoning of human life, and the peace (salam) asked for in each is a security granted by God rather than one that depends on worldly circumstances. Its placement immediately after the account of Yahya's birth and his dutifulness to his parents suggests that the peace given to him is the reward of his piety and gentleness. The verse thus presents a life that is sanctified from its first moment, shielded in its final hour, and secure on the Day of Judgment, and it offers the believer a model of a life lived in God's peace from start to finish.

translation: That is Jesus, son of Mary — the word of truth about which they doubt.
interpretation: The verse affirms, in response to the disputes over Jesus, that he is the son of Mary and that his account is the true word (qawl al-haqq) revealed from God, not the fabrications of those who deny or distort it. The phrase 'about which they doubt' (yamtarun) points to the people's persistent hesitation and disputing over his nature and status, despite the clarity of the truth. The verse thus calls the listener to put aside doubt and accept the plain reality of Jesus as a human messenger born of Mary, the true statement concerning him that stands in contrast to the conflicting claims of the disputants.

translation: It is not for God to take a son; exalted is He above that. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it "Be," and it is.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's absolute transcendence and self-sufficiency by denying that He could ever take a child, since having a son presupposes need, division, or likeness to creatures, none of which befit the One whose nature is perfect. It then displays the nature of His power: creation requires no effort, no process, and no intermediary. His command alone brings a thing into existence at the moment it is willed. The reasoning moves from the rejection of the claim that God has offspring to the demonstration that the one who creates by a mere word has no need of any helper or heir, so the notion of a divine son is incompatible with the majesty of a sovereign whose will is immediately realized.

translation: Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is the straight path.
interpretation: The verse grounds the call to worship in a shared lordship: the Prophet 'Isa (Jesus) affirms that God is both his Lord and theirs, so the worship of God alone is not a sectarian demand but the common foundation that the messengers brought to all people. By placing the command to worship within the affirmation of God's sole lordship, it defines the straight path as nothing other than sincere devotion to the One Creator and Sustainer, free from any partner or intermediary that would displace Him in the heart and the practice.

translation: So the factions differed among themselves, so woe to those who disbelieved from the scene of a tremendous day.
interpretation: The verse points to the division that arose among the various groups who received or opposed the message, each adopting its own position and turning away from the truth. Their disagreement is presented as the prelude to a reckoning, and the words "woe" and "the scene of a tremendous day" warn that those who persisted in disbelief will face a terrible fate on the Day of Judgment, when the consequences of their choices will become manifest before all witnesses.

translation: How clear of hearing and sight they will be on the Day they come to Us! But the wrongdoers today are in clear error.
interpretation: The verse sets a stark contrast between the worldly life and the Day of Judgment. Those who were deaf and blind to truth in this world will become acutely perceptive when the reality of their situation is laid bare, but that clarity will come too late to benefit them. The 'clear error' they are in today is veiled from them by their own choices, yet on the Day it will be plain to all. The verse implies that the real blindness lies in misusing the faculties of hearing and sight that God granted, and that the reckoning will expose what worldly denial concealed.

translation: And warn them of the Day of Regret, when the matter will be decided, while they are in heedlessness and do not believe.
interpretation: The verse directs the Prophet to warn people about a day of profound regret, when the affair is finalized and the consequences of a life of heedlessness become irreversible. Their unbelief and inattention in this world are presented as the very cause of their later anguish, so the warning aims to awaken the heedless now, before the opportunity to act is gone. The phrase 'when the matter is decided' suggests that the final judgment leaves no room for amendment, which makes present reflection and faith all the more urgent.

translation: Indeed, it is We who will inherit the earth and whatever is upon it, and to Us they will be returned.
interpretation: The verse reminds human beings of their transience and of God's ultimate dominion. Possessions, lands, and power pass from one generation and one owner to another, and all of it finally reverts to its true Owner, who alone remains. The statement that all will be returned to God points to the Day of Judgment, where every person will stand before Him and be held accountable for how they used what was entrusted to them. The verse thus calls the believer to hold worldly attachments lightly, to act with humility, and to keep in mind that every action will be returned to its doer.

translation: And mention in the Book Abraham. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a prophet.
interpretation: The verse directs the Prophet to recall Abraham from the Book, presenting him as the model of sincerity and truthfulness (ṣiddīq) combined with the high station of prophethood (nubuwwah). By joining these two qualities, the verse shows that true prophetic mission rests on an unwavering inner honesty, so that the one who carries revelation to others must first embody truthfulness in word and deed. The command to 'mention' him is also an invitation to reflect on his steadfast faith and submission, offering believers a exemplar whose life confirmed the message he conveyed.

translation: When he said to his father, "O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees and cannot benefit you at all?"
interpretation: The verse presents Abraham's gentle but firm call to his father to abandon idolatry. By pointing out that the objects of worship lack hearing, sight, and any power to benefit, he uses reason rather than harshness, showing that true worship must be directed only to the One who hears, sees, and provides. The respectful address "O my father" combined with the pointed question reveals that sincere reform of belief can coexist with compassion and filial courtesy, and that the basis of faith is the rational recognition of what is truly worthy of worship.

translation: O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you, so follow me; I will guide you to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Abraham to his father (traditionally identified as Azar), shows the dignity of gentle, reasoned persuasion in calling someone to the truth. Abraham addresses him respectfully as 'O my father' while presenting the knowledge he has received from God, which the idolatrous father lacks. The phrase 'knowledge that has not come to you' is not arrogance but a humble claim to divinely given insight, offered as a basis for following. The call to 'follow me' places the speaker as a guide, and the promise of a 'straight path' frames faith not as a burden but as the clear and sound way that leads to salvation, in contrast with the misguidance of idol worship.

translation: "O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed, Satan has always been disobedient to the Most Merciful."
interpretation: The verse, spoken by Abraham to his father (Q. 19:44), reveals that worship (ʿibada) is ultimately a matter of obedience: to serve Satan is to follow him, and to follow him is to rebel against the Merciful. Its force lies in the connection it draws between Satan's defining trait, persistent defiance of God, and the danger of taking him as a guide. The phrase "the Most Merciful" (al-Raḥmān) is pointedly chosen: the one who has shown boundless mercy to humanity is the one whose authority Satan refused, so disobedience toward Him is presented as the greatest ingratitude. Abraham's tender address, "O my father" (yā abati), contrasts with the gravity of his plea, teaching that sincere concern for those we love must be expressed with gentleness yet without compromise on truth.

translation: O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so you would become a companion of Satan.
interpretation: The verse reveals the tender yet firm plea of a believing son to his idolatrous father, rooted in sincere concern rather than arrogance. The son grounds his warning in the mercy of God, showing that the fear he expresses is not merely of wrath but of losing the protection of that mercy through persistence in worship of other than God. By describing the outcome as becoming a "wali" (ally or companion) of Satan, the verse teaches that taking Satan as a guide and friend is itself the path to punishment, since loyalty is given to the one who leads away from truth. It thus portrays the proper manner of calling to faith: gentle address ("O my father"), sincere compassion, and clear reasoning, while leaving the final choice to the listener.

translation: He said: "Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham? If you do not desist, I will surely stone you, so leave me alone for a long time."
interpretation: The verse captures the confrontation between Abraham and his father, who rejects his son's call to abandon idol worship. The father's anger escalates from disbelief to open threat, warning of stoning if Abraham persists, and then curtly dismisses him for an extended period. The passage highlights the cost of monotheistic conviction within a family and society rooted in idolatry: faith in God may bring estrangement, hostility, and even danger, yet Abraham's call to truth stands firm, reminding believers that loyalty to the One God takes precedence over familial and social bonds.

translation: He said: "Peace be upon you. I will ask my Lord to forgive you. Indeed, He has always been gracious to me."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Abraham to his idolatrous father (Surah Maryam 19:47), shows a gentle and patient manner in the face of rejection and harshness. Though his father had threatened him, Abraham responds with a farewell of peace rather than anger, and he promises to pray for his father's forgiveness. His words reveal a heart that remains loyal to his duty of calling to God, while reflecting a tender concern for his father's fate. The phrase "He has always been gracious to me" expresses deep gratitude and trust, recognizing that God's kindness has been constant in his life, and it teaches that a believer should combine firmness in faith with courtesy, mercy, and reliance on God's grace.

translation: And I will withdraw from you and from what you invoke besides Allah, and I will call upon my Lord; perhaps I will not be unblessed in my supplication to my Lord.
interpretation: Abraham, having confronted his people's idolatry, declares a clean separation from them and their false deities, choosing instead to devote himself to worshipping the one true Lord. His words express both firm conviction and humble trust: he does not claim certainty of acceptance, but hopes that sincere devotion to his Lord will bring him success rather than wretchedness. The verse thus teaches that true faith requires disassociation from falsehood, coupled with sincere reliance on God and hope in His mercy.

translation: So when he had withdrawn from them and from what they worshipped besides Allah, We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and each of them We made a prophet.
interpretation: The verse presents Abraham's withdrawal from his people and their idols as the turning point that opened the way to divine favor: having given up false worship for the sake of Allah alone, he was rewarded with a lineage of prophets. Separation from what is worshipped besides God is thus shown to be the precondition for receiving guidance and blessing, and the gift of Isaac and Jacob signals that faithful renunciation of idolatry is answered by continuity of prophethood within his family.

translation: And We bestowed upon them of Our mercy, and We granted them a tongue of truth, elevated (and exalted).
interpretation: The verse refers to the prophets mentioned just before it in Surah Maryam (Ibrahim, Ishaq, Ya'qub, and others), whom God honored with His mercy and guidance. The phrase "lisan sidq 'aliyy" describes a lofty and enduring good repute: their memory is kept alive on the tongues of every generation with praise and honor. It shows that true, lasting distinction comes from God's mercy and from sincere truthfulness, and that a righteous legacy is itself a gift from God, granted in answer to the faithful service of those who were chosen.

translation: And mention in the Book Moses. Indeed, he was sincere (chosen and purified), and he was a messenger and a prophet.
interpretation: The verse calls the believer to remember Moses through the Book, not as a mere historical tale but as a model to be recalled and emulated. Two qualities are singled out: his sincerity (ikhlas), meaning he was wholly devoted to God, purified of divided aims, and so was chosen for the mission; and his dual station as rasul, one sent with a specific message to a people, and nabi, one who receives and conveys divine news. The sequence teaches that true prophethood rests on sincere devotion, and that remembrance of the prophets is itself a means of renewing faith and sincerity in the one who recites.

translation: And We called to him from the right side of the mountain, and We drew him near in confidence and intimate conversation.
interpretation: The verse portrays Moses receiving the divine call at the blessed western side of Mount Sinai, the side nearest to him as he approached the fire. The phrase 'najiyyan' conveys more than physical nearness: it describes a private, confidential communion, as one speaks secretly with a trusted companion. Thus the verse emphasizes that revelation is a gift of divine closeness and honor bestowed upon a chosen prophet, and that the one who is drawn near by God is granted intimacy with Him that surpasses ordinary speech and distance.

translation: And We gave him, out of Our mercy, his brother Aaron as a prophet.
interpretation: The verse shows that divine mercy often comes through the support of companions. Moses, burdened with the mission to confront Pharaoh, was granted his brother Aaron, who was elevated to prophethood as a helper for the message. It teaches that God does not leave His servants alone in their struggles but provides them with partners who strengthen their resolve and share the weight of their duty.

translation: And mention in the Book Ishmael. Indeed, he was true to his promise, and he was a messenger and a prophet.
interpretation: The verse singles out Ishmael for remembrance, and its emphasis on his faithfulness to promises shows that keeping one's word is a defining mark of a prophet. Joining 'messenger' with 'prophet' suggests that he received a commission to convey God's message to his people while also being granted prophetic insight. Placing him within the broader command to recall the Book invites the reader to see that the scripture's stories of the prophets are meant as moral examples, especially in integrity and steadfastness toward God.

translation: He used to enjoin on his family prayer and almsgiving, and he was pleasing to his Lord.
interpretation: The verse presents a model of responsibility that begins at home: the one praised here does not keep his devotion to himself but carries it to those closest to him, commanding them to establish prayer and give zakat. Prayer anchors the relationship with God, while almsgiving expresses care for others, so the two together show that true faithfulness joins worship of the Creator with compassion for creation. The closing phrase, that he was 'pleasing to his Lord,' indicates that such an integrated life, which seeks to guide one's family as well as oneself, is what earns divine approval (riḍwān).

translation: And mention in the Book Idris. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a prophet.
interpretation: The verse calls the Prophet to recall Idris, a figure whose remembrance is presented as part of the scripture's own testimony to earlier messengers. By describing him as ṣiddīq (one who is steadfastly truthful, whose words and deeds accord) and as a prophet, the verse establishes that truthfulness in conduct and faithfulness to revelation are the marks of God's chosen servants. The mention of Idris within the Book also reinforces the continuity of prophetic guidance across generations, inviting the reader to see in his example a model of sincerity and devotion to God.

translation: And We raised him to a lofty station.
interpretation: The verse, from Surah Maryam (19:57) concerning Idris (Enoch), describes God elevating him to a high rank. Classical commentators such as al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi understood this 'lofty place' as a spiritual and honorific exaltation, marking him as a prophet distinguished by piety and high standing with God. Some exegetes, relying on reports in the tradition, also took it to mean his physical elevation to heaven, though the wording itself emphasizes elevation in rank and nearness to God, pointing to the reward of a steadfast, truthful servant who was exalted for his devotion.

translation: Those are the ones upon whom Allah bestowed His favor from among the prophets of the descendants of Adam, and of those whom We carried with Noah, and of the descendants of Abraham and Israel, and of those whom We guided and chose. When the verses of the Most Merciful were recited to them, they fell down prostrating and weeping.
interpretation: The verse portrays the lineage of the chosen prophets as a single chain of divine favor, spanning from Adam through Noah, Abraham and Israel, and it ties their elevated status to two things: Allah's guidance and their own choosing by Him. Their response to the recitation of the divine verses, falling in prostration and tears, shows that true knowledge of God produces humility and emotional submission rather than mere intellectual assent, and it sets the believer's reaction to revelation as the model of reverence the verse calls for.

translation: Then there succeeded them a generation who neglected the prayer and followed their desires, so they will meet with destruction (Ghayy).
interpretation: The verse marks a decline across generations: when people abandon the prayer, which is the core link between the servant and his Lord, they soon abandon the discipline that restrains the soul, and surrender to appetites. Neglecting the prayer is shown as the first step of moral collapse, since prayer keeps the heart attentive to God and guards against heedlessness. Following desires without restraint leads to the outcome named as ghayy, a word suggesting going astray into ruin or a deep pit of loss. The verse warns that religious neglect is not a private matter but a process that corrupts a community over time, and that the consequence is real and awaits those who choose it.

translation: Except for one who repents, believes, and does righteous work; those will enter Paradise and will not be wronged in the least.
interpretation: The verse opens with an exception that opens the door of mercy: whoever turns back to God in sincere repentance, returns to faith, and backs that faith with righteous deeds is granted entry into Paradise. The triad of repentance, belief, and action shows that turning back to God is not merely an inner regret but a complete reorientation of the heart and conduct. The closing phrase, 'and they will not be wronged in the least,' assures that their reward will be given in full, with no diminishment of any good they have done, so that God's justice and mercy are both affirmed.

translation: Gardens of perpetual residence, which the Most Merciful has promised His servants in the unseen. Indeed, His promise is ever fulfilled.
interpretation: The verse presents the reward of the believers as a certainty grounded in trust rather than sight: the 'Gardens of Eden' are promised to those who believe in the unseen, so faith itself is the bridge between the present world and a future that cannot yet be perceived. By describing the promise as coming from 'the Most Merciful' and as something that will certainly arrive ('ma'tiyyan', that which is bound to come), the verse links divine mercy with divine reliability, teaching that the servant should live with patient hope, knowing that God's word is not broken and that the hidden reality of paradise is more secure than anything visible.

translation: They will not hear therein any vain speech or sin, but only the word "Peace." And they will have their provision therein morning and evening.
interpretation: The verse describes the peace of Paradise as a realm free from the idle, hurtful, and sinful speech that marks worldly gatherings; the only words the righteous hear there are greetings of peace, so that their inner and social life is wholly tranquil. The phrase "morning and evening" conveys that their provision is continuous and effortless, not a matter of toil or scarcity, pointing to a state of complete security, ease, and dignity in which material and spiritual needs are满足 without anxiety.

translation: That is the Paradise which We will cause to inherit from among Our servants those who were God-conscious (righteous).
interpretation: The verse presents Paradise not as something earned merely by lineage, association, or outward claims, but as an inheritance bestowed upon those whose hearts are marked by taqwa, a vigilant awareness of God that governs conduct. The word "nuwrith" suggests that Paradise is like a legacy that comes to the righteous as the rightful heirs of their faithful lives, and the phrase "from among Our servants" emphasizes that the bond of servanthood to God, expressed through piety, is the true basis of this honor. Thus the verse directs the believer to see salvation as the fruit of sustained God-consciousness rather than of mere profession.

translation: And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs what is before us, what is behind us, and what is between those two. And your Lord is never forgetful.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by the angel Gabriel in response to the Prophet Muhammad's delay in receiving revelation, which had caused him distress and prompted the question of whether he had been forsaken. The angels' descent is shown to be entirely subject to God's will and timing, not to their own choice. By affirming that God possesses all of space and time, the past, present, and future, and all that lies between, the verse reassures the believer that divine wisdom governs even apparent delays. The closing words, that God is never forgetful, teach that what seems to be neglect is in truth a perfectly ordered plan, and that the Prophet's trust should rest in God's constant awareness of him.

translation: The Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, so worship Him and be patient in His worship. Do you know of anyone who is equal to Him in name?
interpretation: The verse calls the believer to a single, exclusive devotion: since the One who created and sustains the heavens, the earth, and all that lies between them is the true Lord, worship must be directed to Him alone. The command to be steadfast (istibar) in worship signals that devotion is not a passing mood but a sustained discipline that requires perseverance through its demands and distractions. The closing question, 'Do you know of anyone equal to Him in name?', is rhetorical and pointed: the sense of 'sami' here is one who shares His name or equal standing, and since no one truly shares His attributes of lordship and creation, there is no rightful object of worship besides Him. Thus the verse links tawhid (the oneness of God) with patient, continuous worship as the proper response of a creature to its Creator.

translation: And man says, "When I have died, shall I really be brought forth alive?"
interpretation: The verse captures a recurring human denial of resurrection, voiced as incredulous doubt about being raised alive after death. Its phrasing, with the emphatic particle "لسوف" and the question form, reveals a mind that measures the unseen by the limits of its own experience and dismisses what it cannot witness. Yet the verse also points to a deeper forgetfulness: the same power that brought the human being into existence from nothing is fully able to return him to life. The denial is thus less a matter of logic than of heedlessness toward one's origin and one's accountability, and the Qur'an answers such doubt elsewhere by reminding the listener of the first creation as proof of the second.

translation: Does not man remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?
interpretation: The verse directs man's attention to his own origin as a reminder of his dependence on God and of the reality of resurrection. The one who brought him from non-existence into being is able to bring him back after death. Man, who was once nothing, has no ground for arrogance or for denying his Creator, and his forgetting of his beginning is itself a cause of heedlessness toward the account that awaits him.

translation: So by your Lord, We will surely gather them, and the devils too, then We will surely bring them forth around Hell, on their knees.
interpretation: The oath by the Lord of the Prophet underscores the certainty of the Resurrection and the reckoning, showing that no one escapes the gathering. The verse pairs humankind with the devils, who were their companions in misguidance, so that they stand together in the same place of accountability. Their being brought around Hell 'on their knees' (jithiyyan) depicts their humiliation and helplessness before the sight of the punishment they had denied, a fitting contrast to the arrogance they displayed in the world.

translation: Then We will surely drag out from every sect those among them who were most insolent against the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse points to the principle that those who rebel most fiercely against God's mercy and authority are singled out for the greatest punishment. The word 'shi'a' refers to groups united by a common allegiance, and the divine selection of 'the most defiant' from each group shows that the Judgment will separate individuals by the intensity of their arrogance and opposition rather than simply by their collective affiliation. It warns that belonging to a party or following a tradition does not shield a person; each is judged by the degree of their own defiance toward the Merciful, and the gravest rebels will be brought forward first for their due reckoning.

translation: Then We are most knowing of those most deserving of being burned therein.
interpretation: The verse ties the final sorting of humanity to God's perfect knowledge rather than to crowds, sects, or outward claims. Those assigned to the Fire are not chosen by chance or by collective label but are identified through full knowledge of each person's inner disposition and deeds, so the judgment is precise and free of injustice. Its placement right after the gathering and selection described in the preceding verses reinforces that no soul is wronged, because every outcome rests on exact divine awareness of what each person has chosen.

translation: And there is none of you but will pass through it. That is upon your Lord an absolute decree that must be carried out.
interpretation: The verse refers to the passage over Hell (al-Nar), which every person must encounter, as the Qur'an states in this same chapter of Maryam. Scholars have understood 'wurud' in different ways: some take it as passing over or near the Hellfire, with the righteous being delivered from it, while others read it as arrival at it before salvation. Either way, the verse conveys that this crossing is a divinely decreed matter that cannot be avoided, which should prompt reflection on accountability, the seriousness of one's deeds, and reliance on God's mercy for deliverance.

translation: Then We will save those who were mindful of God, and We will leave the wrongdoers therein, kneeling down.
interpretation: The verse of Surah Maryam (19:72) speaks of the final gathering around Hell. After all have been brought near it, the righteous are delivered from it by God's mercy, while the wrongdoers are left within it, humbled and kneeling in helplessness. The image conveys a sharp reversal: those who lived in awareness of God (taqwa) are rescued from the very place their opponents are left to suffer, showing that piety, not worldly power or status, determines one's fate on the Day of Judgment. The word "jithiyyan" (kneeling) depicts the wrongdoers' humiliation and their inability to rise or resist, a fitting end for those who were arrogant in this life.

translation: When Our clear verses are recited to them, those who disbelieve say to those who believe: Which of the two groups is better in position and finer in assembly?
interpretation: The verse exposes a recurring pattern in the response of the disbelievers to the message: they measure truth by worldly standing rather than by the evidence of revelation. Confronted with clear signs, they turn to the outward marks of prosperity, rank, and social prestige, as though the favor of this world were a proof of who is upon the right path. The believers, often poor and marginalized in Makkah, are thus dismissed by their material comparison. The verse implicitly warns that such a standard is misguided, since honor before God rests on faith and righteousness, and that worldly splendor is fleeting, as the surrounding verses make clear regarding the fate of those who were once outwardly more favored.

translation: And how many generations before them did We destroy, who were better in furnishings and in appearance?
interpretation: The verse points to a recurring pattern in history: worldly prosperity, luxurious possessions, and an impressive outward display are no guarantee of safety from divine judgment. The Qur'an asks the listeners to reflect on the earlier peoples who were materially superior to the Quraysh yet were destroyed for their denial and arrogance, so that the believers may not be deceived by wealth and status. The rhetorical question, 'how many,' emphasizes the vast number of such nations, and the true measure of a person or community is found in faith and righteous conduct rather than in outward appearance and possessions.

translation: Say, "Whoever is in error, the Most Merciful will extend for him an extension, until, when they see that which they are promised, either the punishment or the Hour, they will know who is worse in position and weaker in forces."
interpretation: The verse describes God's patient respite granted to those who persist in misguidance: the prolonging of their days is not a sign of approval but a test and a delay that allows their arrogance to grow until the reality they denied is unveiled. When the promised punishment in this world or the Hour of judgment arrives, the true measure of their state becomes clear, as the supposed strength of their numbers and the prestige of their position vanish, and they recognize that they were the ones lacking in standing and support. The verse thus turns the believers' gaze away from the apparent prosperity of opponents and toward the ultimate reckoning, where worth is measured by faith and righteousness rather than by worldly power.

translation: And Allah increases those who are guided in guidance. And the lasting good deeds are better in the sight of your Lord for reward and better for return.
interpretation: The verse teaches that guidance is not static but grows: when a person responds sincerely to the guidance already received, Allah adds to it, opening the heart further to truth and strengthening steadfastness. It then directs the believer's attention from fleeting worldly ornaments to the 'lasting good deeds' (al-baqiyat al-salihat), such as sincere prayers, remembrance of God, honest conduct, and acts of charity whose effects endure. Such deeds are the true investment, surpassing worldly wealth and status both in the reward they bring in this life and the Hereafter and in the eventual outcome to which a person returns before their Lord.

translation: Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our verses and said, "I will surely be given wealth and children"?
interpretation: The verse points to a man who rejects the signs of God while boasting that worldly abundance (wealth and offspring) is proof of his standing and a sign of favor he has earned. It exposes a common error: equating material blessing with divine approval, and presuming that one's worldly success guarantees a good outcome in the hereafter. The arrogance of denying the revelation while feeling secure in possessions is presented as the root of his downfall, and the following verses show that his claims about the unseen will be exposed on the Day of Judgment, when his wealth and children will be of no benefit to him.

translation: Has he attained knowledge of the unseen, or has he taken a covenant from the Most Merciful?
interpretation: The verse confronts a boastful disbeliever who claimed that he would be given wealth and children in the Hereafter. Its two rhetorical questions expose the baselessness of that claim: either he has looked into the unseen (al-ghayb), which is reserved for God alone, or he has secured a binding pledge from the Most Merciful guaranteeing him such reward. Since neither is possible, his assertion is revealed as presumption. The verse thus teaches that entitlement to divine reward rests on sincere faith and righteous deeds, not on worldly arrogance or on an unfounded assurance of God's favor, and that knowledge of the unseen belongs to God alone.

translation: No! We will record what he says, and We will extend for him of the punishment, extending it greatly.
interpretation: The verse rebukes a man who arrogantly rejected the revelation and boasted of wealth and Qur'anic claims he dismissed as mere magic. The opening "Kalla" (No!) sharply refuses his vain claim to divine favor. "We will record what he says" points to the certainty that every word of defiance and mockery is preserved in the divine account, so nothing he utters escapes accountability. The phrase "We will extend for him of the punishment" turns his own expectation of increase against him: the worldly abundance he expected as a sign of favor becomes a growing torment, and the doubling of "extending, extending" conveys a punishment that is continuous and ever-intensifying, a fitting measure for one whose arrogance grew with every warning.

translation: And We will inherit from him what he says, and he will come to Us alone.
interpretation: The verse speaks of a boastful disbeliever who claims wealth and children in the afterlife. God declares that He will take away from him the very things he boasts of, stripping him of his claimed worldly possessions and status. Left with nothing but his own deeds, he will return to God as a solitary individual, with no wealth, family, or helpers to accompany him. This reflects the Qur'anic theme that on the Day of Judgment every person stands alone before God, and that false pride in worldly claims and promises will be exposed as worthless.

translation: And they have taken, besides Allah, gods so that they might be for them a source of might (honor and strength).
interpretation: This verse exposes the illogical reasoning of those who worship other than Allah: they seek power, honor, and protection from idols they have fashioned, when those objects are powerless and cannot benefit or defend anyone. The verse reveals that true might belongs to Allah alone, and that placing one's trust in created things for dignity or security leads only to disappointment and loss. It calls the believer to seek honor through faithfulness to the One who holds all power.

translation: No! They will soon deny their worship of them, and they will become opponents against them.
interpretation: The verse describes the futility of the false deities that people took for worship. On the Day of Judgment, those who were worshipped will disown their worshippers, and the very objects of devotion will reject the worship directed at them, becoming adversaries to those who had relied on them. The word "kalla" (No!) rejects the hope or claim that these idols would intercede or benefit them, exposing the emptiness of shirk, which ends in disappointment and reversal, as the supposed helpers turn into accusers and enemies.

translation: Have you not seen that We sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with relentless incitement?
interpretation: The verse portrays the devils as active forces that stir up disbelievers toward wrongdoing, pushing them persistently and forcefully rather than merely tempting them lightly. The rhetorical question 'Have you not seen' directs the listener to a reality that is evident in human conduct: when a person turns away from guidance, he becomes susceptible to every whisper that drives him toward denial and transgression. The word 'azz' conveys a violent, driving pressure, indicating that those who reject faith are left to be carried along by their own inclinations and by the suggestions of evil. The verse thus serves as a warning that persistent rejection of truth opens the heart to ever stronger incitement, and it reminds believers of the necessity of seeking refuge with God against the whisperings of Satan.

translation: So do not be hasty against them. We are only counting out for them a countdown (of days and breaths).
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet and the believers by forbidding them to seek a hastened punishment for the disbelievers. Divine retribution is not rushed or neglected; it is precisely measured and reckoned for each person, with every moment and breath counted toward its appointed time. The believer is thus taught patience and trust in God's perfect timing, knowing that the delay of the wrongdoers is not forgetfulness but a reckoning that is already numbered.

translation: On the Day We will gather the righteous to the Most Merciful as a delegation honored.
interpretation: The verse portrays the believers who feared God in this world being gathered on the Day of Judgment not as captives or a driven crowd, but as honored guests received with dignity. The word "wafdan" denotes a delegation sent to a king or a notable person, so the image is one of welcome, respect and reward: those who were conscious of their Lord are brought near to the All-Merciful, whose mercy they had hoped for and whose pleasure they had sought. It thus sets the destiny of the pious in contrast to the later verses describing the wrongdoers driven to hell like thirsty cattle, and it urges the listener to see present piety as the path to that honorable reception.

translation: And We will drive the criminals to Hell in a thirsty herd.
interpretation: The verse portrays the guilty being herded toward Hell like thirsty cattle driven to water, but with the crucial reversal that the water is the fire itself. The image of the wretched, parched animals hurried along in a sorry procession conveys their humiliation, helplessness, and total lack of dignity on the Day of Judgment, in stark contrast to the honored believers who are gathered to the Merciful as a delegation (Surah Maryam 19:85). Their own deeds, rather than any external force alone, have led them to this state, so the scene underscores the justice of the Divine recompense and the inversion of the worldly pride of those who once refused the truth.

translation: They shall not possess intercession, except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse denies that anyone, whether idols, false deities, or people, has the power to intercede on the Day of Judgment in their own right. Intercession belongs entirely to God's permission, and it is granted only to those who have secured a covenant with the Most Merciful, meaning those who have held fast to faith and righteous conduct, and who have been bound to God through a pledge of sincere obedience. Thus the verse directs the believer away from reliance on created intermediaries and toward cultivating a genuine bond with God through faith and good deeds, since that bond alone is the means by which one may hope for acceptance of intercession.

translation: And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."
interpretation: The verse records the claim of those who attributed offspring to God, a claim the Qur'an firmly rejects elsewhere. By calling God "al-Rahman," it highlights the contradiction: divine mercy encompasses all creation as servants, and the idea of God begetting a son implies a need, likeness, or division incompatible with absolute divine oneness and self-sufficiency. The verse thus serves as an introduction to the stark refutation that follows in the surrounding passage, which describes the enormity of this utterance and the near-cataclysmic reaction it would provoke in the heavens.

translation: Indeed, you have brought forth a monstrous thing.
interpretation: The word "idd" describes an assertion so grave and offensive that it nearly tears apart the heavens, the earth, and the mountains, as the following verses state. The verse rebukes the claim that the All-Merciful has begotten a son by presenting that claim as an enormity, not a mere error of opinion. Its force lies in showing that attributing offspring to God is a deviation from the pure tawhid that the surrounding verses affirm, since all that is in the heavens and earth comes to the All-Merciful as a servant.

translation: The heavens are almost splitting apart from above them, and the earth is cleaving open, and the mountains are collapsing in ruin
interpretation: The verse depicts the cosmic magnitude of the utterance attributed to those who claim that God has a son (Maryam 19:88-91): so monstrous is this assertion that the very fabric of creation seems on the verge of rupture. The heavens, earth, and mountains, which are obedient to their Creator and bear witness to His oneness, are portrayed as trembling at such an affront. The imagery conveys that attributing offspring to the All-Merciful is not a minor error but a grave transgression against the cosmic order, whose stability rests on God's perfect unity and independence from any need of progeny.

translation: That they attribute to the Most Merciful a son.
interpretation: The phrase 'an da'aw lil-Rahmani waladan' refers to those who claimed that the Most Merciful has begotten a child, a claim the Qur'an firmly rejects as incompatible with God's absolute oneness and transcendence. The verse thus frames the attribution of offspring to God as a grave assertion, one whose enormity is emphasized in the surrounding verses, since it implies that God would share in created nature or require a successor, which contradicts His self-sufficiency and the nature of His mercy, which is expressed through His creation rather than through a filial bond.

translation: And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.
interpretation: The verse denies that the Most Merciful could ever take a son, because taking a son is incompatible with His absolute perfection and transcendence. The word 'ought not' (ma yanbaghi) signals that such a claim is not merely false but unfitting to His majesty, since begetting or adopting a child implies need, deficiency, or a division of divine authority, none of which can apply to the One whose mercy encompasses all things. It is a rebuttal of the claims of those who attributed offspring to God, and it affirms that His mercy is expressed through His creation and His kindness toward His servants, not through familial kinship with any being.

translation: There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant.
interpretation: The verse declares that every being in creation, whether in the heavens or on earth, stands in the same relation to God: all must come before Him in utter submission and dependence, as servants. This universal servanthood levels every distinction of rank, power, or wealth, since no one can claim independence from the Creator, and it reveals that true honor lies not in self-sufficiency but in recognizing and fulfilling one's created station before the Merciful, who is the source of all mercy even as He is the Lord to whom all shall return for accounting.

translation: لقد أحصاهم وعدّهم عدّاً. (Indeed, He has enumerated them and counted them with an exact counting.)
interpretation: The verse speaks of Allah's perfect knowledge and comprehensive accounting: nothing escapes His awareness, not even the smallest detail of a person's existence, deeds, or number. Every individual is known to Him by name and count, which conveys both the certainty that no one is overlooked before Him and the seriousness of the reckoning that awaits each soul, since every act is recorded and will be weighed exactly.

translation: And every one of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection, alone.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that on the Day of Resurrection each person stands before God individually, stripped of worldly ties, companions, status, and false supports. No one can rely on another's merit or be shielded by family, wealth, or intercession that God has not permitted. This solitary return calls the believer to personal accountability: one's faith, deeds, and sincerity will be judged directly, and the reality of this aloneness should motivate a person to prepare for that meeting while still in this world.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, the Most Merciful will bestow upon them affection.
interpretation: The verse links two things: faith in the heart and righteous action in the world. Together they open the way to a divine love that God places in the hearts of His servants, so that the believers are loved by Him and drawn to one another. It teaches that true faith is not a private claim but is proven by deeds, and that the affection God grants is the fruit of this harmony between belief and conduct. The divine name al-Rahman, the Most Merciful, signals that this love flows from the boundless mercy of God rather than from any merit that could compel it.

translation: So indeed, We have made it easy by your tongue, that you may give glad tidings thereby to the righteous and warn thereby a stubbornly quarrelsome people.
interpretation: The verse points to the purpose behind the revelation's being made easy in the Prophet's own language: it is not meant to be a burden of incomprehensible speech but a clear message whose reach is shaped by its audience. Its two functions are paired deliberately: good news for those who guard themselves with God-consciousness, who receive it and are moved toward it, and warning for the 'quarrelsome' (lodd), those hardened in contention and dispute who turn the truth into a matter of argument for its own sake. The ease of the Qur'an is therefore not only linguistic but moral, since its guidance becomes accessible to the heart that is open and remains a source of admonition to the heart that is closed.

translation: And how many generations did We destroy before them? Do you perceive any of them, or hear from them even a faint sound?
interpretation: The verse, spoken in the context of the warnings to the Makkan disbelievers, points to the fate of past nations as a lesson in the transience of worldly power and wealth. Its rhetorical question draws the listener's attention to the complete disappearance of earlier peoples, so that not a trace of them is perceived and not a whisper of their existence remains. The implication is that those who now live in pride and heedlessness will face the same end, and that the only lasting reality lies beyond the visible world, where accountability awaits.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ta-Ha.
interpretation: The verse opens the surah with the basmala, placing the entire revelation under the name of Allah and His two attributes of mercy, al-Rahman and al-Rahim, so that what follows is framed as a gift of mercy. The isolated letters Ta-Ha stand as a disjointed letter (muqatta'at) that draws the listener's attention to the Qur'an as a清 divine speech composed of the same letters of the Arabic language, yet inimitable, and they signal that the revelation is given to be a source of guidance and a call to pay attention. Their precise meaning is known only to Allah, and the wise course is to accept them as a sign of the Qur'an's miraculous and mysterious character, while understanding them as an opening that prepares the heart to receive the message of mercy that the surah will unfold.

translation: We did not send down the Qur'an upon you to be distressed.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who was deeply grieved by the refusal of his people to accept the message. God clarifies that the revelation was not sent to burden him with anguish or to make him suffer over those who turn away. His duty is only to convey the message, and the outcome rests with God. The verse thus teaches that a messenger is responsible for delivering the truth, not for compelling its acceptance, and that excessive sorrow over others' disbelief is not what God requires of him. It also reflects God's mercy toward the Prophet, reminding him that the Qur'an is a source of guidance and mercy rather than a cause of hardship.

translation: Except as a reminder for those who fear (Allah).
interpretation: The verse says that the Qur'an was revealed not to burden the Prophet but as a reminder, and that only those whose hearts are inclined to fear God truly benefit from it. Its guidance is like rain on fertile ground, reaching those who are receptive, while those who are heedless and indifferent turn away from it. Thus, the capacity for fear of God, a sincere consciousness of accountability, is the key that opens the heart to the message of revelation.

translation: A revelation from He who created the earth and the high heavens.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an as a descent (tanzīl) from the One who brought into being both the earth and the lofty heavens, thereby linking the authority of the revelation to the Creator's absolute sovereignty over the whole cosmos. The phrase "al-samāwāt al-ʿulā" (the high heavens) emphasizes the exalted and vast dimension of creation, suggesting that the one who fashioned such a grand order is the only one worthy to send down guidance to humankind. Thus the recipients are invited to recognize that the message they hold comes from the same power that governs the visible and invisible universe, and that its origin is as elevated as the heavens themselves.

translation: The Most Merciful settled Himself firmly upon the Throne.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God, described by His attribute of boundless mercy (al-Rahman), is exalted above His creation and has established Himself upon the Throne in a manner befitting His majesty. Classical scholars, following the early generation's principle, accepted this without asking 'how' (bi-la kayf), affirming the meaning of 'istawa' as an act of sovereign elevation while denying any resemblance to created beings. The verse thus joins God's mercy with His sovereign rule: the One who governs all things from above does so with compassion toward His creatures.

translation: To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens, whatever is on the earth, whatever is between them, and whatever is beneath the soil.
interpretation: The verse extends divine ownership across every realm of existence: the heavens above, the earth beneath our feet, the space between them, and even what lies hidden beneath the surface of the earth, the depths of the soil that no human eye can see. By naming the hidden as well as the visible, it teaches that God's dominion is total and that nothing escapes His knowledge or possession. For the believer this is a source of both humility and reassurance: whatever one holds is held in trust from the One to whom all things ultimately belong, and nothing in creation stands outside His sovereign care.

translation: And if you speak aloud, indeed He knows the secret and that which is yet more hidden.
interpretation: The verse establishes that God's knowledge is absolute and not dependent on the volume or manner of human speech. Whether a person openly proclaims a word or keeps it concealed, it is equally known to Him. Beyond the outward secret that a person harbors in the heart, He knows what is even more hidden, such as intentions not yet formed into thought and what lies within the unseen. The lesson is to cultivate sincerity and mindfulness in one's words and inner states, since nothing escapes the One who knows what is hidden and what is more hidden still.

translation: Allah — there is no deity except Him. To Him belong the most beautiful names.
interpretation: The verse opens by affirming the absolute oneness of God: no being has any right to worship except Him, and this declaration of tawhid is the foundation of the whole faith. The phrase "the most beautiful names" (al-asma' al-husna) points to the perfection of God's attributes, which are free of any deficiency; each name reveals a dimension of His mercy, power, knowledge, and majesty. Thus the believer is invited not merely to acknowledge God's uniqueness in worship, but to know Him through His names, calling upon Him by them and letting that knowledge shape a life of devotion and reverence.

translation: And has there reached you the story of Moses?
interpretation: The verse opens with a question that serves to draw the Prophet's attention and heighten anticipation for what follows. By asking whether the account of Moses has reached him, it signals that this story is significant and worthy of careful attention. It establishes that the narrative about Moses is not merely a historical recollection but a divinely conveyed reminder, meant to console the Prophet and to instruct the listener in the reality of prophetic struggle, divine support, and the consequences of rejecting God's messengers.

translation: When he saw a fire and said to his family, "Stay here; indeed I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I will bring you from it a burning brand, or find at the fire some guidance."
interpretation: The verse portrays Moses at the moment of his first encounter with the sacred, wandering in the desert with his family and seeking only a practical comfort: a brand to warm them or a path to guidance. Yet the ordinary search for fire becomes the threshold of prophethood, teaching that divine revelation often arrives unannounced within the routines of life. The word "hudan" carries the deeper turn: what he sought as physical light and direction would soon become the guidance of God Himself, so that the seeker of a flame is led instead to the light that illuminates the soul.

translation: So when he came to it, he was called: "O Moses,"
interpretation: The phrase reveals that Moses' call to prophethood came at the exact moment he reached the fire, marking the divine initiative that opens his mission. The passive form "was called" emphasizes that the summons came from God alone, without Moses seeking it, and the direct address by name signals intimacy and attentiveness, preparing him to receive a weighty charge.

translation: Indeed, I am your Lord, so take off your sandals. Indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa.
interpretation: The command to remove the sandals marks the place as holy ground and calls Moses to inner humility before the presence of God. Stripping away the outward marks of ordinary life, he is to approach the divine address with full attention and reverence, recognizing that the encounter at the burning bush is a moment set apart from everything profane, and that true readiness to receive revelation begins with the stripping away of self-reliance and worldly attachment.

translation: And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Ta-Ha (20:13), is God's address to Moses at the burning bush, in which He declares that He has selected him for a unique role as a prophet and messenger. The command to listen to what is revealed (yuha) establishes the foundation of prophetic mission: Moses is not to act on his own understanding but to receive and attend closely to divine revelation. The verse thus frames the relationship between the chosen messenger and the divine speaker as one rooted in attentive reception, humility, and obedience, a pattern that the subsequent verses develop through the commands to worship God alone and to establish prayer.

translation: Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance.
interpretation: The verse opens with a direct divine self-declaration that establishes tawhid, the absolute oneness of God, as the foundation of all worship: there is no god besides Him, so devotion must be directed to Him alone. The command to worship is immediately tied to the establishment of prayer (salah), showing that prayer is the central and most concrete form of that devotion. The phrase 'for My remembrance' (li-dhikri) reveals that the purpose of prayer is to remember God, so that the heart and the act of worship are oriented toward Him, making the ritual a living expression of constant awareness of the Divine rather than a mere outward obligation.

translation: Indeed, the Hour is coming—I almost conceal it—so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for.
interpretation: The verse presents the certainty of the Final Hour as a settled reality, and it emphasizes that its timing is withheld from creation, which keeps people in a state of constant readiness rather than complacency. The phrase "I almost conceal it" conveys the intensity of divine concealment: the Hour is so firmly decreed that it is as if God has nearly kept it entirely hidden. The stated purpose—that every soul be recompensed according to its striving—establishes accountability as the moral foundation of the Hereafter. Human effort, in its full range of intention and action, is not lost but will be weighed and answered, so the believer is called to direct their striving toward what will bear fruit on that Day.

translation: So let not one who does not believe in it and follows his own desire turn you away from it, lest you perish.
interpretation: The verse addresses Moses, warning him not to be diverted from the Hour and the resurrection by those who disbelieve in it and are ruled by their desires. Such people, driven by appetite rather than by reason and revelation, seek to pull the believer away from faith, and the verse teaches that yielding to their influence leads to ruin. It implies that the true safeguard of the believer is steadfastness in truth, since a person who is lured from the path by the passions of others has already fallen into destruction.

translation: And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?
interpretation: This question, posed by God to Moses at the burning bush, is not asked for information, since God knows exactly what is in Moses' hand. It serves to draw Moses' attention to the ordinary object he holds, a simple staff, so that he will recognize it as something he can reflect on and then be prepared for the miracle that is about to transform it. It teaches that Allah often begins His great acts with what is humble and already within a person's reach, and that the believer should acknowledge what he possesses before being commissioned with a greater task.

translation: He said, "It is my staff; I lean upon it, and I beat down leaves with it for my sheep, and I have in it other uses."
interpretation: Moses' answer to the Lord's question about what is in his right hand is simple and humble, and it opens a door to a deeper lesson. He names the staff plainly, but then lingers on its everyday functions: support for the weary traveler, a tool for gathering foliage for his flock, and many other benefits. The verse thus turns an ordinary object into a sign of the intimate relationship between the prophet and the ordinary means of his life. The question seems to prepare him for the miracle that follows, when this familiar, mundane thing will be transformed into a serpent, showing that God can turn the commonplace into a sign of His power, and that the one called to prophethood must learn to trust in what he already holds.

translation: He said, "Throw it down, O Moses!"
interpretation: This phrase comes from the account of Moses' encounter with God at the valley of Tuwa, where Moses is commanded to cast down his staff. The command is the first step in a sign meant to establish his authority and prepare him for his mission before Pharaoh. The staff turning into a serpent shows that the divine command, when obeyed in trust, transforms what is ordinary into a clear proof, and that Moses need not fear what he is sent to do, since God is with him.

translation: So he threw it down, and suddenly it was a serpent, moving swiftly.
interpretation: This verse depicts the moment Moses, at Allah's command, cast down his staff, and it transformed before his eyes into a living serpent gliding rapidly. The miracle is presented as a direct sign of divine power, given to Moses so that he would be confident in his mission before Pharaoh. The swift movement of the serpent underscores the reality and force of the transformation, showing that the staff, an ordinary object in the hand of a shepherd, could become an instrument of God's will. It teaches that what appears humble and familiar can be made into a sign of overwhelming truth when Allah wills it, and that the prophet's reliance rests not on his own strength but on the command and support of his Lord.

translation: He said, "Take it and do not fear. We will return it to its original state."
interpretation: This verse comes from the account of Musa (Moses) after his staff was transformed into a serpent, as described in Surah Ta-Ha. When he was frightened by it, God commanded him to seize it without fear, and promised that it would be restored to its former form as a staff. The verse teaches that the one who trusts in God's protection need not fear the very sign God has given him. It also shows that the miracle was under divine control: the serpent that caused alarm would be returned to its original nature, emphasizing that the power behind the sign belongs to God alone, who can bring about the change and reverse it at will.

translation: And draw your hand close to your side; it will come out white, without harm, as another sign.
interpretation: The verse presents Moses with a second miraculous sign, given alongside the staff that turns into a serpent. By drawing his hand back against his side and bringing it out, it emerges luminous and white yet unharmed, a sign of God's power over nature. Its purpose is to show Pharaoh and his people that the messenger carries clear, undeniable proof from the Lord, so that the sign itself becomes evidence of the truth of Moses' mission rather than a mere wonder.

translation: So that We may show you of Our greatest signs.
interpretation: This phrase comes from Surah Ta-Ha's counterpart in Surah Al-Isra (17:1), where it follows the mention of the Prophet's night journey from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque. It indicates that the purpose of the journey was to make the Prophet witness the greatest of God's signs, showing that the miraculous ascent was itself a divine revelation meant to affirm his mission and strengthen his certainty, granting him a direct vision of realities beyond ordinary perception.

translation: Go to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed beyond all bounds.
interpretation: The command given to Moses is a direct mission against a tyrant who has exceeded every limit of justice and humility. Its force lies in the word 'taghā' (transgressed, rebelled beyond measure), which marks Pharaoh's arrogance as a condition that has become total: he claims divinity over his people and oppresses them. The verse thus establishes that the prophetic summons must be delivered even to the most powerful oppressor, and that the one who sends Moses is the one who knows the true extent of this rebellion. It also reveals that the believer's courage rests not on his own strength but on the commission from God.

translation: He said, "My Lord, expand for me my breast (open up my chest for me)."
interpretation: This is Moses' prayer at the moment of his commission, as he is about to confront Pharaoh. Before asking for any external help or success, he asks God for inner expansion of the breast, meaning relief, tranquility, steadiness of heart, and capacity to bear the heavy burden of prophethood and the harshness of his mission. The verse teaches that the strength needed for any great responsibility begins with an opened heart, and that a servant should seek God's help first for the inner readiness that makes outward tasks bearable.

translation: And ease for me my task.
interpretation: This plea, spoken by Moses after he asked God to expand his breast and loosen his tongue, shows that the believer's effort is incomplete without God's facilitation. Moses has been commanded to confront Pharaoh, a task far beyond his own strength, so he recognizes that the outcome depends on God making the difficult path passable. The verse teaches that inner readiness, clarity of speech, and the removal of obstacles all come from God, and that a servant should undertake the work he is given while seeking God's help to accomplish it.

translation: And loosen a knot from my tongue.
interpretation: This is the plea of Moses (peace be upon him) when God commissioned him to confront Pharaoh, as recounted in Surah Taha (20:27). Having been sent with a mission of great weight, he asks God to remove the impediment in his speech, which likely refers to a hesitancy or difficulty in articulation that could hinder his delivery of the message. The request reflects a recognition that eloquent and clear communication is essential for the prophetic task, and that success depends on God's assistance rather than human ability alone. It is an expression of humility and reliance on the Divine, seeking that the message be understood by its hearers.

translation: "So that they may understand my speech" (Qur'an 20:28, spoken by Moses, following his request: "And loosen a knot from my tongue").
interpretation: Moses' request shows that the purpose of speech in the prophetic mission is comprehension, not eloquence for its own sake. He does not ask for a grand or impressive tongue but only that the knot be loosened so his message reaches its hearers intact. Divine guidance depends on being understood, so the messenger must make the truth clear and accessible, and the burden of communicating it clearly falls on the one who carries it.

translation: And appoint for me a minister from my family.
interpretation: This is the supplication of Prophet Musa (Moses) when he was commissioned by God to confront Pharaoh. Aware of the immense burden of the mission and his own difficulty in speech, he asked God to make his brother Harun (Aaron) a helper and supporter from his own household. The verse reveals the prophetic awareness that a great task cannot be carried out alone, and that trusted, capable companionship, especially among those bound by close trust and kinship, is a means of strength for those who bear the message of truth.

translation: Aaron, my brother (Ta-Ha 20:30: 'Aaron, my brother'). Moses asks God to appoint his brother Aaron as a helper from his own family.
interpretation: The phrase reveals that Moses, sensing the enormity of confronting Pharaoh, looks to his family for support, and the naming of Aaron as 'my brother' expresses a bond of trust and shared purpose rather than mere kinship. It implies that a prophet's mission is strengthened not only by divine commission but also by a companion who shares the burden, and that the request is an expression of humility, since Moses acknowledges his own need for a trusted partner to speak and act alongside him.

translation: Strengthen my back through him (Aaron).
interpretation: Moses' request reveals that a prophetic mission, however great, is not carried by one person alone. By asking God to make his brother Aaron a support to his strength, Moses acknowledges his own human need for a trusted partner in the confrontation with Pharaoh, and he shows that God's cause is best advanced through shared responsibility, mutual reliance, and the reinforcement of one faithful companion by another.

translation: And let him share in my task
interpretation: This is the prayer of Moses (peace be upon him) when God commissioned him to confront Pharaoh. Having been sent to a mission far beyond his own strength, he asked God to appoint his brother Aaron as a partner in the prophetic charge, so that the burden could be shared. The request reveals that a prophet's mission is a collective responsibility that benefits from the support of a capable companion, and that eloquence and steadfastness in a great task are sought from God, Who alone grants the means to fulfill what He commands.

translation: So that we may glorify You abundantly.
interpretation: Musa's request for his brother Harun to share his burden is framed not as a worldly ambition but as a means to an end: that the two of them might glorify God abundantly. This shows that the purpose of any prophetic mission, and of every act of cooperation within it, is to fill life with remembrance and praise of God, so that the work itself becomes an act of worship.

translation: And that We may remember You much.
interpretation: This phrase, from Surah Taha (20:34), is spoken by Aaron and Moses as they are sent to Pharaoh, asking that they be able to glorify God abundantly. The verse, in this reading, presents remembrance of God (dhikr) as the foundation of the prophetic mission: the messengers' strength for confronting tyranny lies not in their own power but in constant, frequent turning of the heart to God. Their request for much remembrance reveals that the ability to bear a heavy trust, and to keep the goal of worship at the center of their work, is sustained through continual mindfulness of the One who sent them.

translation: Indeed, You have always been Seeing of us.
interpretation: The phrase comes in Musa's supplication (Ta-Ha 20:35), where he asks God to grant him the strength to glorify and remember Him abundantly, and then affirms that God has always been fully aware of him and his circumstances. This is a statement of trust: Musa is confident that his request is made to One whose knowledge and care encompass him, so his mission and his need for support rest on God's constant watchfulness rather than on his own capacity.

translation: He said, "You have been granted your request, O Moses."
interpretation: The verse comes at the moment Moses asks God for what he has requested, and the answer is given with immediate reassurance: the petition is accepted and fulfilled. It shows that God responds to the sincere supplications of His prophets, and that a servant who turns to Him with a clear, humble request is not left unanswered. Moses's request in this context is a stage in a larger dialogue in which divine favor is extended to him, reminding the reader that the one who asks must do so with trust, and that God's granting of a need is an expression of His mercy toward those He has chosen.

translation: And We had already bestowed Our favor upon you another time.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Taha (20:37), recalls to the Prophet Musa (Moses) the many past blessings God had granted him since infancy, when he was placed in the chest on the river and returned safely to his mother, to reassure him before he is sent to Pharaoh. The repeated favor is a reminder that the One who has sustained him so far will not abandon him now, so the mission ahead rests on trust in God's continuous grace rather than on Musa's own strength.

translation: When We inspired into your mother that which is inspired:
interpretation: The verse recalls a moment of divine favor toward Moses, placed in the Nile as an infant in obedience to a revealed command. It emphasizes that God's guidance reaches even a mother's heart in a time of fear, prompting a response of trust that set in motion Moses' rescue and his later role as a prophet. The inspiration to his mother is presented as a sign that divine providence works through ordinary human acts, and that God's care for the chosen can be realized through the faithful obedience of those closest to them.

translation: That you cast him into the chest, then cast the chest into the river, and the river will throw it onto the bank, and there an enemy of Mine and his enemy will take him. And I bestowed upon you love from Me, so that you might be raised under My watchful eye.
interpretation: The verse shows God's providence working through a sequence of ordinary, obedient acts. The mother's instructions are given step by step, and the river and its current become instruments of a plan she cannot see. The very enemy who sought to destroy the infants becomes the household in which Moses is nurtured, so Pharaoh's hostility ends up serving the rearing of the one who will confront him. The love placed upon Moses is both the affection that draws hearts to him and a divine favor, and the phrase 'so that you might be raised under My eye' points to a childhood guarded by God's direct care, preparing him for the mission that lies ahead.

translation: When your sister walked and said, "Shall I direct you to one who will nurse him?" So We returned you to your mother that her eye might be comforted and she would not grieve. And you killed a soul, but We saved you from distress and tested you with a [severe] testing. Then you remained for years among the people of Madyan; then you came [here] at the appointed time, O Moses.
interpretation: This verse recounts the stages of Moses' early life as a sequence of divine favors and trials, framing his whole history as the work of God's providence. God's hand is seen first in his rescue as an infant, when his sister's offer returned him to his own mother, fulfilling the promise that she would be consoled and not grieve. The killing of a man is then recalled not as an isolated lapse but as part of a testing that God turned into deliverance from distress, showing that even a person's mistakes can be woven into a larger path of guidance. The years spent among the people of Madyan are presented as a period of preparation, and his arrival at the appointed time signals that his prophetic mission was decreed in advance. The address "O Moses" at the end personalizes the recollection, inviting the listener to recognize that every stage of hardship and rescue was measured out with precision by God.

translation: And I have chosen you for Myself.
interpretation: This phrase, spoken by God to Moses (Ta-Ha 20:41), expresses a special divine selection and intimate bond. The word 'istana'tuka' (I have made you for Myself, or fashioned you for My own purpose) signifies that Moses was raised up and prepared under God's direct care, as the Qur'an describes his upbringing in Pharaoh's household, the way he was nurtured under God's eye, and then sent with a mission. The phrase 'for Myself' indicates that his life and calling belong exclusively to God, reserved for a unique role in delivering His message, and it reflects the honor and closeness granted to the prophets chosen for a sacred task.

translation: Go, you and your brother, with My signs, and do not slacken in remembering Me.
interpretation: The command given to Moses and Aaron carries a double charge: outward, to deliver the message of God's signs to Pharaoh with courage and clarity; inward, to keep the heart constantly mindful of God. The verse teaches that the one who calls others to God must first sustain his own remembrance of Him, for dhikr is the fuel that keeps the mission from weakening. Mentioning the brother alongside him also shows that sincere cooperation in the service of truth is a source of strength, and that the burden of prophetic work is not meant to be borne alone.

translation: Go, both of you, to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed beyond all bounds.
interpretation: The command to Moses and Aaron to go to Pharaoh carries the weight of a mission entrusted to prophets who must confront tyranny without fear, relying on God's support. The phrase "he has transgressed" (innahu taghā) identifies the root of Pharaoh's corruption as arrogant overreach: he claimed a divinity that belongs to God alone and exceeded every limit of justice and humility. The verse thus teaches that the prophetic duty is to speak truth to power directly, and that the gravest sin of rulers is to exceed their bounds, making themselves unaccountable.

translation: So speak to him with gentle words, perhaps he will be reminded or fear (God).
interpretation: The verse, addressed to Moses and Aaron as they are sent to Pharaoh, teaches that the method of calling people to truth matters as much as the truth itself. Even against a tyrant who claimed divinity, the prophets are commanded to speak softly, because gentleness opens the heart and removes the defensiveness that harshness provokes. The aim is not victory in argument but the awakening of remembrance and conscience. The word "perhaps" (la'alla) is significant: the outcome rests with God and the listener's free response, so the messenger's duty is sincere, kind delivery, not guaranteed success. It offers a lasting principle for every caller to faith: be patient, compassionate, and gentle, leaving the results to God.

translation: They said: Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will hasten against us, or that he will transgress (in his insolence) against us.
interpretation: The words are spoken by Moses and Aaron when God commanded them to go to Pharaoh. Their plea reveals a human, prudent fear that a tyrant might act hastily against them before they could deliver their message, or that he might exceed all bounds in insolence and cruelty. Yet the very act of turning to the Lord as 'our Lord' shows that their fear is placed in the hands of the One who sends them.
