interpretation: The verse exposes a path of blind contention in matters of faith: a person who disputes about God not on the basis of sound knowledge or revelation, but on whim, inherited prejudice, or the suggestions of misleading voices. Its phrase 'every rebellious devil' shows that such disputation is not an independent exercise of reason but a surrender to whatever inner or outer voice leads away from truth, so that the arguer becomes a follower rather than a seeker. The verse therefore calls for intellectual honesty in religious discourse: that claims about the Divine be grounded in knowledge, and that one's allegiance be given to guidance rather than to rebellion against it.

translation: Whoever takes him as an ally, it is decreed against him that he will mislead him and guide him to the punishment of the blazing Fire.
interpretation: The verse speaks of the consequence of turning to Satan as a protector and follower. Such a person has, by his own choice, placed himself under the influence of one whose entire aim is to lead humanity astray. Divine decree here signifies the natural outcome of a path freely chosen: whoever surrenders his heart to misguidance is left to it, and that misguidance inevitably leads to the torment of the Blaze. It is a warning that loyalty given to the enemy of God shapes the destiny of the one who gives it, so the believer must guard his allegiances carefully.

translation: O mankind, if you are in doubt about the resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed, that We may make clear to you. And We settle in the wombs whatever We will for a specified term, then We bring you out as infants, then [We develop you] that you may reach your maturity. And among you is one who is taken in death, and among you is one who is returned to the most decrepit age, so that he knows, after knowledge, nothing. And you see the earth barren, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs, swells, and grows every beautiful kind of plant.
interpretation: The verse argues for the resurrection from the observable stages of human creation and from the revival of dead land: the same power that shapes a human being gradually from dust through successive stages, and that brings life out of a lifeless, parched earth, is able to bring the dead back to life. The stages of human development, along with the varied fates of life and death and the decline into feeble old age, display God's dominion over life and death and show that the one who began creation can surely restore it, so that doubt about the Hereafter is shown to be unreasonable.

translation: That is because God is the Truth, and it is He who gives life to the dead, and He is over all things capable.
interpretation: The verse grounds the preceding claims in three divine attributes that together explain why God's works, including the resurrection and the granting of reward, are certain. Because God alone is the Real (al-Haqq), whatever proceeds from Him and whatever He promises is true and stable, in contrast with the falsehood of what is worshipped besides Him. His power to bring the dead to life is the clearest proof that He can restore creation after its dissolution, so the Hour is no more difficult for Him than the first creation. His capability over all things means nothing resists His will, so the promise He makes is fully within His power to fulfil. The verse thus moves the believer from knowledge of God's essence to trust in His promises, asking that one ground hope and fear in the reality of the One who is the Truth and the Giver of life.

translation: And that the Hour is surely coming, there is no doubt about it, and that Allah will resurrect those who are in the graves.
interpretation: The verse affirms two linked truths of faith: the certainty of the Final Hour, which is beyond all doubt, and the resurrection of the dead, when Allah will raise those in their graves for judgment. By placing these together, it shows that the promise of Resurrection is not a distant or uncertain myth but a divine reality grounded in Allah's power over creation. Its emphasis on the absence of doubt calls the heedless to prepare for the meeting with their Lord and to recognize that the same power which first brought creation into being can restore life to the dead, so that every soul receives its recompense.

translation: And among the people is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge or guidance or an illuminating Book.
interpretation: The verse exposes the baselessness of argument about God that is not anchored in any of the three sources of certainty: reasoned knowledge ('ilm), divine guidance (huda), or revealed scripture (kitab munir). Such disputation is not a search for truth but an assertion driven by desire, inherited prejudice, or arrogance, and it stands in contrast to the believer who approaches questions of the divine with humility, evidence, and reliance on revelation. The phrase 'among the people' indicates that this condition is a recurring human tendency rather than the trait of a single individual, and the verse thus serves as a warning to examine one's own claims about God against honest knowledge and the clear light of revelation.

translation: Turning aside with his neck arrogantly, to lead others astray from the way of Allah. For him in this world is disgrace, and We will make him taste on the Day of Resurrection the punishment of the burning Fire.
interpretation: The verse portrays a man who turns away from the truth with pride, bending his neck as a gesture of haughty disdain toward the guidance being recited. His aim is not merely his own disbelief but to mislead others from the path of Allah, so his sin is doubled: he deviates himself and draws others after him. The verse links his worldly humiliation with the severe torment awaiting him in the Hereafter, showing that arrogance against revelation brings disgrace in this life and the fire in the next, and that those who misguide others bear the weight of their own misguidance as well.

translation: That is for what your hands have sent forth, and that Allah is never unjust to His servants.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the suffering or recompense a person meets is the direct consequence of their own deeds, since the hands are the instruments by which a person acts and so stand for the deeds themselves. By affirming that Allah is not a wrongdoer toward His servants, it removes any suspicion that punishment could be arbitrary: the one who is held to account is the one who chose and performed the wrong. The sentence thus joins personal responsibility with the perfect justice of God, urging the listener to examine their actions and to recognize that no one is wronged by God, and that a person's own conduct is what returns to them.

translation: And among the people is he who worships Allah on the edge. If good befalls him, he is reassured by it; but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face. He has lost this world and the Hereafter. That is the clear loss.
interpretation: The verse exposes a faith that is conditional and self-serving, held only as long as worldly comfort confirms it. Such a person does not stand firm in worship of God as a matter of conviction and gratitude, but measures devotion by his own gain. The image of worshipping 'on the edge' portrays a believer standing at the rim of a valley, ready to step away at the first tremor. When fortune smiles, he feels secure in his religion; when hardship strikes, he abandons it and turns back to his former ways, thereby forfeiting both the goods of this life and the reward of the next. The verse calls the believer to a steadfast faith that endures through prosperity and adversity alike, recognizing that trials are a test that reveals and refines the sincerity of one's devotion.

translation: He calls upon, besides Allah, that which can neither harm him nor benefit him. That is the far-reaching error.
interpretation: The verse exposes the irrationality of idolatry: the one who worships other than God directs his supplication to something that possesses no power to harm or to benefit, so his devotion is misplaced at its root. Its wrongness is not merely a matter of inherited custom but a departure from reason and from the nature of true reliance, which can only rest upon the One whose power alone determines harm and good. The phrase 'the far-reaching error' conveys that such misguidance has wandered very far from the truth, so that a person who has strayed into it may find the way back only with great difficulty.

translation: He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit. Surely wretched is the protector, and wretched is the companion.
interpretation: The verse exposes the absurdity of idolatry: the false deities that people invoke cannot benefit them, and their harm is closer to them than any good they might hope for, since worshipping them leads only to loss in this life and the next. Calling upon such a patron is a grave misjudgment, and the verse sharpens this by condemning both the protector who is chosen and the companion who is kept, showing that a bond with what cannot truly help is a bond of ruin rather than support. The lesson turns the reader toward seeking refuge and guidance only in the One whose nearness brings real benefit.

translation: Indeed, Allah will admit those who have believed and done righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed, Allah does whatever He wills.
interpretation: The verse joins a promise of reward with a reminder of divine sovereignty. Entry into the gardens is granted to those whose faith is matched by righteous action, showing that in the Qur'an belief and deeds are inseparable, and that the believer's hope rests on God's generosity rather than on a claim of merit. The closing phrase, that Allah does what He wills, places the promise within the absolute freedom of God: the reward is certain because it comes from One who is not bound by any constraint, and the believer is thereby directed to trust in His power and mercy rather than to measure Him by human expectations.

translation: Whoever thinks that Allah will not grant victory to him (the Prophet) in this world or in the Hereafter, let him stretch a rope up to the sky and then cut it off, and let him see whether his scheme removes that which enrages him.
interpretation: The verse uses a sharp, ironic challenge aimed at those who were consumed by rage at the believers' rising strength and hoped that God's support would never reach them. It pictures the enraged man reaching for the most extreme measure available, climbing to the sky to sever the source of help he resents, and then asks him to examine whether such a desperate act could change anything about the cause of his fury. The implied answer is that no human scheme, however drastic, can cut off what God has decreed, so his anger is powerless and his plotting is futile. The verse thus turns the opponents' hostility back on them, showing that their attempts to stop divine victory only expose the limits of their own power.

translation: And thus We have sent it down as clear verses, and indeed Allah guides whom He wills.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an as a revelation whose clarity is itself a sign: its verses are manifest in their meaning and argument, so that anyone who reflects on them can recognize their truth. Yet the closing clause makes clear that clarity alone does not produce guidance. Guidance belongs to Allah's will, which He grants to those who sincerely seek it and open their hearts to what is clear. The verse thus joins the divine gift of a lucid revelation with the sovereign act of divine guidance, reminding the believer to be grateful for the light of the Qur'an and to humbly seek Allah's help in following it, while recognizing that the failure of some to be guided is not due to any lack in the message but to the reality of divine will and human disposition.

translation: Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabeans, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associated others with God — indeed, God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, God is, over all things, a witness.
interpretation: The verse places the believers alongside the adherents of earlier revealed and other traditions and declares that the ultimate distinction among them belongs to God alone, who will separate them on the Day of Resurrection, so that human claims of superiority or exclusive salvation are left to His judgment. By stating that God is a witness over all things, it affirms that His knowledge encompasses every deed, intention and belief, so that no one's sincerity or error escapes Him, and it calls the reader to humility regarding others' fates while keeping firm in their own faith and conduct.

translation: Have you not considered that to Allah prostrate all who are in the heavens and all who are on the earth, and the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the trees, the creatures that move, and many of mankind? But many among mankind have deserved the punishment. And whoever Allah disgraces, for him there is no one to honor him. Indeed, Allah does whatever He wills.
interpretation: The verse reveals a cosmic order of submission in which all creation, through its own nature and way of being, bows to its Creator, so that prostration becomes the natural state of the universe. Against this backdrop, the verse singles out humans, who alone can choose between recognizing their Lord and turning away from Him. Their refusal to prostrate in willing obedience is what makes them deserving of punishment, and honor is found only in submission to Allah. Thus the verse presents honor and disgrace as determined by one's relationship with God, and it closes by affirming that His will is absolute and unrestrained.

translation: These are two adversaries who dispute concerning their Lord. But those who disbelieved will have garments of fire cut out for them; boiling water will be poured over their heads.
interpretation: The verse presents the Day of Judgment as a courtroom dispute between two opposing parties over their Lord, where the believers and the disbelievers stand as rival claimants before God. The image of the disbelievers being clothed in cut garments of fire and scalded by boiling water portrays their punishment as fitting and inescapable, mirroring the way they are surrounded on every side by the consequences of their denial. It conveys that the contest between truth and falsehood, faith and rejection, ends with a decisive and visible outcome, underscoring the seriousness of choosing disbelief in the face of divine guidance.

translation: Whereby there will be melted what is in their bellies, and [their] skins.
interpretation: The verse depicts the torment of the Fire as something that reaches the very core of the body: what is in their bellies, including their inner organs, and their skins, which are the outer covering that feels pain. The melting is a graphic image of the total and inescapable nature of the punishment, affecting both the hidden interior and the exposed surface of the disbelievers, so that no part of the body is spared. It also conveys that the physical suffering is a direct consequence of their defiance, mirroring how they dismissed the reality of the Hereafter in the world.

translation: And for them are maces of iron.
interpretation: The phrase describes the punishment awaiting the disbelievers in the Hereafter, depicting the instruments of their torment as iron maces (maqamie), which are heavy striking rods used to beat and subdue. The image conveys the severity and inescapability of the chastisement, emphasizing that the people who arrogantly rejected God's guidance will face a humiliating and painful retribution fitting the harshness of their defiance.

translation: Every time they wish to get out of it, out of distress, they will be returned into it, and it will be said to them: Taste the punishment of the burning fire.
interpretation: The verse portrays the fire of Hell as a place from which the inhabitants have no escape: their repeated attempts to flee its anguish are met with being driven back into it, so that their suffering is both continual and inescapable. The words 'Taste the punishment' point to the reality of the torment as something experienced directly and fully, and the phrase 'from distress' suggests that the sorrow of the Fire is not merely physical but also a deep grief of the soul that seeks relief and is denied it. The verse thus invites reflection on the consequences of one's choices, warning that the same reality that is ignored in this life becomes an unavoidable and lasting experience in the next.

translation: Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk.
interpretation: The verse presents the reward of faith joined with righteous action as entry into gardens of lasting bliss, where rivers flow beneath them, emphasizing that true belief is inseparable from deeds that give it substance. The adornment with gold bracelets and pearls and the garments of silk depict the honor and comfort granted to the believers in the Hereafter, a dignity that stands in contrast to the worldly life where such luxuries were often denied or reserved for the powerful. It invites the reader to see that the highest ornament of a person is their faith and righteousness, which the Hereafter will reveal and reward in full measure.

translation: And they were guided to the good speech, and they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse describes those who, in the Hereafter or in their worldly lives when they were rightly disposed, are led by God to what is pure and good in speech, namely the sound words of faith, testimony, and praise, which are the fruit of a heart that has accepted the truth. Their guidance is not merely to speak well but to be directed to the path of the One worthy of all praise, so that their words and their way of life harmonize with their Lord, the Praiseworthy, and the ultimate result of their guidance is their arrival at His pleasing way. The verse thus links inner purity of speech with the straight path that leads to God, showing that true guidance manifests first in what a person says and then in the course he follows.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar others from the way of God and from the Sacred Mosque, which We have made equal for all people, the resident and the visitor alike, and whoever intends therein a violation through wrongdoing - We will make him taste a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse links disbelief with obstructing access to God's worship and to the Sacred Mosque, showing that the sanctity of the place is a shared trust rather than a private possession of any group. Because the Haram is open equally to its local inhabitants and to outsiders, anyone who would deny others their rightful access or violate its sanctity through injustice is committing a grave offense against God's order. The verse teaches that the gravest sin lies not only in the act itself but in the intention to transgress sacred boundaries wrongfully, and it warns that such wrongdoing carries a severe accountability before God.

translation: And [recall] when We settled Abraham at the site of the House, [saying]: Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circumambulate it, those who stand [in prayer], and those who bow and prostrate.
interpretation: The verse recalls the divine appointment of Abraham to the sacred site of the Ka'bah, and frames the purpose of the House around pure monotheism: its foundation rests on the absolute prohibition of associating partners with God. The command to purify the House links outward sanctity with inward and communal worship, so that the sacred space is cleansed of idolatry and reserved for those who orbit it, stand in devotion, and bow and prostrate before the One God. Thus the sanctity of the place is inseparable from the sincerity of the worship performed there, and Abraham's mission becomes the model for keeping sacred places dedicated to God alone.

translation: And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every distant mountain pass.
interpretation: The verse is a divine command to Abraham, after the house was built, to call humanity to the Hajj, and it shows that the call is answered by willing hearts rather than by compulsion. Coming 'on foot' and 'on lean camels' that have traveled through deep, far-off passes signifies that the sacrifice of effort, fatigue, and distance is itself part of the act of worship, so that the pilgrim's journey becomes a sign of sincerity and devotion. The verse also points to the universal reach of the message, since the summons is addressed to all people and the answer comes from every corner of the earth, uniting diverse peoples around a single center of worship.

translation: That they may witness benefits for themselves and mention the name of God over known days, over what He has provided for them of the livestock animals. So eat from them and feed the distressed poor person.
interpretation: The verse ties the pilgrimage sacrifice to a dual purpose: it opens the rite to spiritual and communal benefit, as the worshipper gathers with others in a sacred setting and remembers God through the act of slaughter. By commanding that the meat be shared both with the one who sacrifices and with the destitute, it establishes that devotion to God is inseparable from generosity toward those in need, so that worship is completed through social responsibility rather than ritual alone.

translation: Then let them end their state of ihram and complete their rituals, fulfill their vows, and circumambulate the Ancient House.
interpretation: The verse lays out the closing stages of the pilgrimage after the sacrifice at the place of offering. Having shed the restrictions of the sacred state, the pilgrim is to cleanse himself of the dust and disarray of the journey (al-tafath), keep the vows he made, and perform the circumambulation of the Ancient House, the Ka'bah, which marks the completion of the rite. The sequence moves from the outward discipline of ihram to the inward fulfillment of promises and the return to the sanctuary, showing that the sacred journey ends not in mere release from prohibitions but in renewed devotion centered on the House of God.

translation: That is so. And whoever honors the sacred rites of Allah, it is better for him with his Lord. And the grazing livestock has been made lawful for you, except what is recited to you (as prohibited). So avoid the abomination of idols, and avoid the saying of falsehood.
interpretation: The verse binds reverence for what God has sanctified to the purity of worship and speech: honoring Allah's sacred matters is presented as a good that returns to the believer from his Lord, and the lawfulness of livestock is a mercy whose boundaries are set by revelation rather than by human whim. The call to shun the filth of idolatry and the falsehood of words joins the outward and inward realms, teaching that a heart cleansed of false worship must also guard the tongue from deceit, so that the whole person stands in truthfulness before God.

translation: Turning in pure devotion to God, associating no partners with Him. Whoever associates partners with God is as though he had fallen from the sky and the birds snatched him away, or the wind hurled him into a faraway place.
interpretation: The verse portrays shirk (associating partners with God) as a total collapse from a lofty state of uprightness. The one who rises above the world toward the pure monotheism of hanif faith is compared to a soul that has been lifted to the heavens, while the one who turns to idols is like someone who falls from that height and is seized by predatory birds or swept off by a violent wind into a remote abyss. The image conveys that shirk is not merely an error but a self-inflicted annihilation: the person is torn apart, left with no stable ground, and carried far from any refuge, showing that a heart divided among false objects of worship is exposed to every destructive force and ultimately lost.

translation: That [is so]; and whoever honors the symbols of Allah, indeed it is from the piety of hearts.
interpretation: The verse ties the veneration of Allah's sacred symbols to the inner state of the heart. Exalting what Allah has made sacred is not merely an outward ritual but a sign of taqwa residing within the heart, so that outward reverence and inward God-consciousness are shown to be inseparable. The sincerity of devotion is thus measured by the heart's reverence, which gives rise to honoring the rites and places dedicated to God.

translation: For you therein are benefits until a specified term; then their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House (the Ka'bah).
interpretation: The verse refers to the sacrificial animals (the hady) dedicated to God at the sanctuary. Before they are slaughtered, they bring the pilgrims various benefits, such as their milk, wool, and use for riding or carrying loads, for as long as they remain in the believer's care. Their final destination and place of sacrifice is the Ancient House, the Ka'bah in Mecca, where they are offered in devotion. The verse thus joins the lawful use of God's gifts with the ultimate purpose of dedicating them to Him at His sacred house, teaching that worldly benefit and worship are not in conflict but meet in gratitude and obedience.

translation: And for every community We have appointed a rite of sacrifice, that they may mention the name of Allah over the livestock He has provided for them. So your God is one God, so submit to Him. And give good tidings to the humble (who are submissive).
interpretation: The verse establishes that the ritual of sacrifice (manasik) is an ancient, universal institution given to every community, not a practice unique to one nation. Its essence lies not in the blood or flesh, which do not reach God, but in remembrance of His name over what He has provided, acknowledging that all sustenance comes from Him. The verse then moves from the particular rite to the core of faith: the unity of the one God, which all prophetic communities share, and which calls for full submission (islam) to Him. The closing promise of good tidings is directed to the mukhbitun, those whose hearts are lowered in humility before God, as the true fruit of this worship is a soul that yields to Him with gentleness and reverence.

translation: Those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble; and those who are patient over what befalls them; and those who establish prayer; and from what We have provided them, they spend (in charity).
interpretation: The verse portrays the inner and outer marks of true believers as a unified character: awe that makes the heart tremble at the remembrance of God is the root from which patience in trials grows, and that patience is anchored in steadfast prayer, which in turn overflows into generous giving from what God has granted. Faith here is not merely a claim of the tongue but a living disposition where reverence shapes endurance in hardship, worship in the heart and body, and generosity toward others, so that each dimension sustains and completes the others.

translation: And the camels [as offerings] We have made for you among the symbols of Allah; in them is good for you. So mention the name of Allah over them while they are lined up [standing]. Then when their sides fall [after slaughter], eat from them and feed the contented one and the beggar. Thus We have subjected them to you that you may be grateful.
interpretation: The verse reframes the sacrificial camel as one of the visible markers (sha'a'ir) of Allah's religion, so that its value lies not in the animal itself but in the devotion it expresses. Its benefit to the worshipper is real, yet the decisive act is the remembrance of Allah's name at the moment of slaughter, which turns a physical act of sustenance into an act of worship. The command to eat and to feed both the one who asks with dignity and the one who asks openly teaches that the fruits of devotion must flow outward to the needy, so that gratitude for subjugated beasts becomes social generosity. The closing phrase ties the whole arrangement to gratitude: the ease with which humans control such great animals is itself a blessing that calls for thankfulness.

translation: It is not their meat that reaches God, nor their blood, but what reaches Him is your piety. Thus He has subjected them to you so that you may glorify God for guiding you. And give good tidings to the doers of good.
interpretation: The verse (22:37) shifts the meaning of sacrifice from the physical act of offering animals to the inner state that animates it. God is not in need of the flesh or blood of the sacrificed animals, which were the material of pre-Islamic offerings; what ascends to Him is taqwa, the conscious awareness and fear of God that guides the worshipper's intention and conduct. The subjection of the animals to humans is presented as a divine favor, and the proper response to it is takbir, magnifying God for the guidance He has granted. The closing promise of good tidings to the muhsinun ties the ritual to ihsan, excellence in worship and in dealing with others, so that the outward rite becomes meaningful only when it expresses a sincere and virtuous heart.

translation: Indeed, Allah defends those who have believed. Indeed, Allah does not love every treacherous ingrate.
interpretation: The verse presents divine protection as a dual relationship of divine defense and moral accountability: God actively stands in defense of the believers, who are called to trust in Him amid hostility, while at the same time He withholds love from those who betray trust and persistently reject gratitude and truth. Read in its context of the early Muslim community facing persecution, it assures the believers that their cause is under God's protection, and it implies that true standing before God rests on faithfulness and sincere gratitude rather than on mere claims of belief or on the treachery and ingratitude of those who oppose them.

translation: Permission has been given to those who are being fought because they were wronged, and indeed, Allah is capable of giving them victory.
interpretation: The verse marks the first divine permission granted to the early Muslim community to take up arms in self-defense after years of persecution in Makkah. Its wording ties the permission to a clear moral cause: the believers were not aggressors but people who had been wronged, driven from their homes and harassed for their faith. The closing assurance that Allah is able to grant them victory reinforces their trust in God at a moment of vulnerability, connecting the right to resist oppression with reliance on divine support. The verse thus establishes that armed response is legitimate only as a defense against injustice, not as an end in itself.

translation: Those who have been expelled from their homes without right, only because they said, "Our Lord is Allah." And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others, there would have been demolished monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques in which the name of Allah is much mentioned. And Allah will surely support those who support Him. Indeed, Allah is Strong and Mighty.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the expulsion of believers from their homes was an unjust act whose only cause was their faith in the one God, and it reveals a divine law of mutual restraint: Allah holds back the aggression of some people through others, so that places of worship of every community, which bear His name, are protected from destruction. This protection is itself a form of divine support, and the verse ties it to a promise that whoever supports God's cause will be supported by Him, since His strength and might are absolute and no one who stands for Him is left alone.

translation: Those who, if We establish them in the land, establish prayer, give zakat, enjoin what is good, and forbid what is wrong. And with Allah is the outcome of all matters.
interpretation: The verse defines the true marks of a believing community when it is granted power and authority: its strength is not an end in itself but a trust to be used for worship and for reform. Establishing prayer ties the community to its Lord, zakat secures justice and mutual care among its members, and enjoining good and forbidding evil make it a force for moral order in society. The closing phrase reminds the believers that power is granted and withdrawn by God, so success is ultimately measured by faithfulness to these duties rather than by worldly dominance, and that the final consequence of every affair belongs to Allah alone.

translation: And if they deny you, then the people of Noah, 'Ad, and Thamud had already denied (their messengers) before them.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad by showing that rejection of prophets is an established pattern in human history, not a personal failure on his part. Denial of messengers by their own peoples is shown to be a recurring response to divine guidance, from Noah's people to 'Ad and Thamud. By placing his own situation within this long lineage, the verse offers reassurance that the Prophet's mission is part of a continuous prophetic chain, and that the obstinacy of his opponents follows a familiar course that has already played out before. It thus encourages steadfastness, reminding the believer that the outcome of denial rests with God, who has always upheld His messengers and held the deniers accountable.

translation: And the people of Abraham and the people of Lot.
interpretation: This brief verse links two prophetic communities, those of Abraham and Lot, as examples of nations that were given the message and then faced the consequences of rejecting it. Placed within the surrounding passage, it serves as a warning that the pattern of denial and divine judgment recurs across history, so that the listeners of the Prophet Muhammad would reflect on the fate of earlier peoples who turned away from their messengers.

translation: And the companions of Madyan, and Musa was denied. So I granted respite to the disbelievers, then I seized them; so how was My rejection (of them)?
interpretation: The verse places the people of Madyan and the denial of Musa within the chain of earlier nations that rejected their messengers, showing that a single pattern runs through history: messengers are sent, they are rejected, and divine respite is given for a time. The phrase "I granted respite" reveals that delay is a form of testing and a stretch of opportunity for return, not a sign of approval, and the sudden seizing that follows warns that such respite can end. The closing rhetorical question, "how was My rejection?", is meant to make the listener reflect on the consequences that befell those nations, so that the hearers of the message take warning from their fate rather than assume that their own security is permanent.

translation: So how many a town did We destroy while it was wrongdoing, so it lies in ruins upon its foundations, and [how many] an abandoned well and a lofty palace [lie in desolation].
interpretation: The verse presents the ruined cities as a lesson drawn from history: a community that persists in injustice and wrongdoing carries within itself the seeds of its own collapse, and its once-thriving houses, wells, and palaces become silent witnesses to the consequences of its corruption. The image of the fallen roofs and the idle well and the high palace stripped of its inhabitants addresses the reader with the reminder that worldly power, wealth, and grandeur are fragile, and that divine justice operates through history, so that those who observe these ruins should reflect, turn away from oppression, and recognize that the true and lasting dominion belongs to God alone.

translation: Have they not traveled through the land, so that they would have hearts with which to understand, or ears with which to hear? For indeed, it is not the eyes that go blind, but it is the hearts within the chests that go blind.
interpretation: The verse directs attention to the faculty of true perception: sight, hearing, and understanding are not merely physical organs but are fulfilled only when the heart is open to reflection. Travelling through the earth and observing the remnants of earlier peoples is meant to awaken contemplation, yet the verse reveals that blindness is not located in the eyes of the head but in a heart that has grown closed and unresponsive to the signs before it. The passage thus warns that outward exposure to evidence is worthless without an inward readiness to reason and to hear the truth, and it locates the true seat of spiritual insight and of its failure in the heart.

translation: They ask you to hasten the punishment, but God will never fail to fulfill His promise. Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count.
interpretation: The verse addresses the disbelievers who mocked the Prophet and demanded that the threatened punishment be brought at once. God reassures the believers that His promise is certain and will not be broken, even though its timing is in His hands alone. The apparent delay is not neglect: God's measure of time differs from human reckoning, so that a span which seems immensely long to people is a single day in the sight of their Lord. Human haste is therefore set against divine patience, teaching that the believer should trust God's timing rather than demand a hastened outcome, since what is promised will certainly come at the moment God has appointed.

translation: And how many a town did I give respite while it was wrongdoing, then I seized it, and to Me is the final return.
interpretation: The verse teaches that Allah's delay of punishment for a wrongdoing community is not neglect but a trial and a grace of time to repent, and that when the appointed time comes the seizure is certain, leaving every soul accountable before Allah alone at the final return. It calls the listener to heed the warnings of past nations, to avoid being deceived by prolonged ease, and to recognize that all worldly authority and success are ultimately subject to the Creator's judgment.

translation: Say, O mankind, indeed I am to you a clear warner.
interpretation: The verse establishes the core role of the Prophet Muhammad as a messenger whose function is limited to clear warning: he is not commanded to compel belief, control outcomes, or claim divine powers, but to deliver the message with unmistakable clarity. The address to all of mankind (ya ayyuha al-nas) shows that his mission is universal rather than confined to one people, and the word mubin, 'clear' or 'manifest,' places responsibility on the warning itself to be understandable, so that whoever rejects it does so with the truth made plain to them. The verse thus joins humility about the prophet's authority with the seriousness of a message that leaves humanity without excuse.

translation: So those who believe and do righteous deeds will have forgiveness and a noble provision.
interpretation: The verse joins faith and good action as inseparable: belief alone is not complete without deeds that express it, and righteous deeds rest on a sincere inner commitment. The reward is twofold. Forgiveness (maghfirah) addresses what has gone wrong in the past, cleansing the believer of sins and restoring the relationship with God, while the 'noble provision' (rizq karim) points to a generous, honorable sustenance that is not merely material but includes the peace, honor, and nearness to God that the faithful enjoy. The phrasing suggests that God's gifts to the righteous are abundant and dignified, so that the one who turns to faith and good works is met first with pardon and then with a lavish, dignified bounty.

translation: And those who strive against Our verses, seeking to frustrate them, those are the companions of Hellfire.
interpretation: The verse identifies the true cause of a person's damnation as active opposition to God's signs: the word "sa'aw" (strove) describes a deliberate, purposeful effort, and "mu'ajizin" (seeking to thwart or render powerless) shows that this striving aims to nullify the revelation and escape its authority. The signs are not merely doubted but actively combated, and the verse thus ties the fate of the Hellfire to a stance of hostility toward divine guidance, which in turn implies that the revelation's reach is meant to be met with sincere reception rather than contrived resistance.

translation: And We did not send before you any messenger or prophet except that when he recited [the revelation], Satan cast [something] into his recitation. But Allah abolishes what Satan casts, then Allah makes His verses firm. And Allah is Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: This verse (Surah al-Hajj 22:52) consoles the Prophet by showing that every messenger and prophet before him faced the same obstacle: when they conveyed the divine message, the devil sought to insert false suggestions, distortions, or misunderstandings into what they recited, so that people would be confused or tempted to doubt. The verse affirms that such interference is never allowed to stand: Allah nullifies whatever the devil inserts, and then firmly establishes His own revelation so that its meaning is preserved and clear. The closing names of Allah, All-Knowing and All-Wise, indicate that this divine process of abrogating falsehood and securing the revealed verses is grounded in perfect knowledge and wisdom, and that the trials of the messengers serve a purpose in testing the hearts of people.

translation: So that He may make what Satan throws in as a trial for those in whose hearts is a disease and those whose hearts are hardened. Indeed, the wrongdoers are in extreme dissension.
interpretation: The verse shows that God permits what Satan casts into the minds of people, through the suggestions and distortions that accompany the message of prophets, as a test that separates those whose hearts are sick and hardened from the sincere believers. For the one who has a disease of doubt or a heart that refuses to soften before the truth, the insinuation becomes a source of confusion and deeper rejection, while for those with sound hearts it clarifies the difference between truth and falsehood. The closing phrase reveals that the wrongdoers, by persisting in opposition, have fallen into a remote and irreconcilable split from the truth, so that the trial itself exposes where each person truly stands.

translation: And that those who have been given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord, so that they believe in it and their hearts humbly submit to it. And indeed, Allah is the guide of those who believe to a straight path.
interpretation: The verse links true knowledge with recognition of the Qur'an as truth from God, and shows that genuine knowledge is meant to culminate in faith and humility of heart rather than mere intellectual possession. The phrase 'their hearts humbly submit' (fatakhbata) points to the inner softening and reverent surrender that knowledge of the divine should produce, so that understanding becomes transformative. The closing assurance that Allah guides the believers to the straight path reveals that the journey from knowledge to faith is itself divinely facilitated, placing both the human effort to understand and the grace of guidance within a single movement toward God.

translation: And those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt about it until the Hour comes upon them suddenly, or there comes to them the punishment of a barren day.
interpretation: The verse portrays the persistent state of those who reject faith: their doubt about the revelation and the Hour does not lift on its own, but continues until the reality they denied breaks upon them without warning. The phrase 'a barren day' (yawm 'aqim), a day that brings no good or relief, points to a day of destruction that offers no respite or mercy, so that the consequences of their disbelief arrive at a moment they neither expect nor can prepare for. The verse thus warns that prolonged doubt is not a neutral condition but a path that ends in sudden accountability.

translation: The dominion on that Day belongs to Allah; He will judge between them. So those who believed and did righteous deeds will be in Gardens of Bliss.
interpretation: The verse points to the absolute and unshared sovereignty of God on the Day of Judgment, when every pretense of worldly authority collapses and no one holds any power except by His leave. The division that follows is not a matter of lineage, status, or wealth but of faith joined with righteous action, which together form the true criterion by which a person is judged. The phrase 'Gardens of Bliss' also suggests that the reward is the natural fulfillment of a life lived in faithful response to God, so that those who recognized His sovereignty in this world are granted a dwelling of lasting joy in the next.

translation: But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs—those will have a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse draws a sharp contrast between the fate of the believers and that of the deniers: rejection of God's signs is not merely intellectual error but a wilful refusal to acknowledge them, and its consequence is a punishment that strips away dignity. The word 'muhin' conveys humiliation, suggesting that the arrogance which led people to reject the revelation is answered with a disgrace fitting to that arrogance. The pairing of disbelief (kufr) with denial (takdhib) indicates that the problem lies both in the heart's refusal and in the active repudiation of what has been made clear.

translation: And those who emigrated in the cause of Allah and then were killed or died - Allah will surely provide for them with a good provision. And indeed, Allah is the best of providers.
interpretation: The verse establishes that migration for the sake of God is an act whose reward is not cut off by death or martyrdom, since God Himself guarantees a provision that is both good and abundant, a provision that surpasses worldly sustenance and points to the honorable and lasting reward in the hereafter. By ending with the declaration that God is the best of providers, it directs the believer's trust away from worldly means and toward the Creator, teaching that sacrifice made for God's sake is never lost, and that the one who leaves home, property, and comfort in His path is placed under His direct and generous care whether he lives to see the outcome or not.

translation: He will surely admit them to an entrance that they will be pleased with. And indeed, Allah is Knowing and Forbearing.
interpretation: The verse promises the righteous believers a final abode that will fully satisfy them, an entrance they will find pleasing in every respect, so that their hearts will be content with their destination. It closes by reminding the listener that this promise rests on Allah's perfect knowledge of who truly deserves it, and on His forbearance, which gives people room to repent and return before the reckoning. The divine names 'Knowing' and 'Forbearing' together assure the believer that reward follows sincere faith and that Allah's patience with human failings does not diminish His justice.

translation: That is so. And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was made to suffer, and then is wronged again, Allah will surely help him. Indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse establishes that retaliation is permitted only in proportion to the injury suffered, never beyond it, so that the one who is wronged keeps within the bounds of justice. Its closing words, that God is Pardoning and Forgiving, remind the believer that although rightful response is allowed, pardon is the higher and more God-like course, and that God Himself will support the one who is oppressed after he has been wronged a second time, so the believer need not transgress his limits to secure his right.

translation: That is because Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and because Allah is All-Hearing and All-Seeing.
interpretation: The verse points to the precision of the cosmic order as evidence of God's power and mastery over creation: the gradual lengthening and shortening of night and day, each merging into the other, shows that time itself is under divine governance rather than random chance. The closing names, All-Hearing and All-Seeing, tie this observable order to God's perfect knowledge, indicating that the One who orders the heavens also perceives every word and deed, so the believer is invited to reflect on the signs in nature and to live with awareness of being constantly known by God.

translation: That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood, and because Allah is the Most High, the Most Great.
interpretation: The verse grounds the preceding signs of God's power in a fundamental truth about reality: divinity belongs to Allah alone, because He alone is the ultimate, self-subsisting Reality, while everything worshipped apart from Him is empty and baseless, lacking any real power or claim to worship. The closing affirmation of His loftiness and greatness reinforces this, directing the heart away from idols and created intermediaries toward the One whose sovereignty is absolute. Thus the verse calls the reader to discern between what is true and what is illusory, and to recognize that awe, reliance, and worship are rightly due only to the Most High and Most Great.

translation: Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky, and the earth becomes green? Indeed, Allah is Subtle and Acquainted with all things.
interpretation: The verse directs the reader's gaze to the ordinary, repeated miracle of rain turning dry, lifeless land into greenery, so that the one who reflects on it recognizes that the same Lord who revives the earth after its death is the One whose subtle knowledge reaches into every hidden detail of creation and of the human heart. Its closing names, al-Latif and al-Khabir, link the visible act of providence to an intimate, penetrating knowledge: God's care for creation is gentle and precise, reaching what human perception cannot, and therefore the believer should trust Him, both in the revival of the earth and in the unseen matters of his own life.

translation: To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse establishes absolute divine ownership: everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah alone, so nothing in creation is independent of Him. Yet this ownership is not a need on His part. Because He is Al-Ghani, utterly self-sufficient, He gains nothing from His creation's obedience or loss from its disbelief, and because He is Al-Hamid, He is praiseworthy in His essence and deeds whether or not anyone praises Him. The believer is thus invited to see that all dependence is owed to Allah, while turning to Him is a mercy to the servant rather than a benefit to God.

translation: Do you not see that God has subjected to you whatever is in the earth, and the ships that sail through the sea by His command? And He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth, except by His permission. Indeed, God is Kind and Merciful toward mankind.
interpretation: The verse directs the mind from the familiar to the awe-inspiring: the human being is reminded that the resources of the earth, the vessels that cross the seas, and the vast canopy of the sky are not self-sustaining marvels but gifts placed at his disposal by a Lord who both empowers and restrains. The subjection (taskhir) of the earth to humankind is a sign that human agency is real yet entirely dependent on divine permission, since the ship moves only because the sea and wind obey a command, and the heavens stand only because God holds them. The closing affirmation of God's raʾfa and raḥma reveals that this cosmic order is not indifferent to humanity but is the very expression of mercy, so that the act of seeing these signs should lead to gratitude, humility, and recognition of the One who sustains all.

translation: And it is He who gave you life, then will cause you to die, then will bring you back to life. Indeed, the human being is ungrateful.
interpretation: The verse moves from the signs of God's power over human life, giving life, causing death, and restoring it, to a sharp observation about human nature: despite having received existence and every stage of it from God, the human being tends to deny or be ungrateful for these blessings. The sequence of life, death, and resurrection is presented as a reminder that the one who controls every stage of a person's existence deserves recognition and gratitude, and that human ingratitude is a failure to acknowledge this reality.

translation: For every community We have appointed a rite which they observe, so let them not dispute with you about the matter, and invite (them) to your Lord; indeed, you are upon a straight guidance.
interpretation: The verse establishes that divine law has given each community its own specific form of worship and ritual practice, which they keep as their way of devotion. Because this diversity of rites is part of the divine plan, the Prophet is told not to be drawn into fruitless quarrels over religious observances, which are a matter of the community's own practice. Instead, he is commanded to keep calling people to his Lord, with the assurance that he stands on a clear and sound path. The passage thus teaches that a messenger's firmness should rest on conviction and steady invitation rather than on argument for its own sake, and that disagreement over outward forms should not divert the call to God.

translation: And if they dispute with you, say: "Allah is most knowing of what you do."
interpretation: The verse instructs the Prophet, when faced with argument and contention from those who reject him, not to be drawn into an endless or heated debate, but to leave the matter to Allah, who has full knowledge of their deeds and intentions. It teaches that the ultimate judgment over disputed truths belongs to God, who will hold each person accountable for what they actually did and believed, so the believer can respond with calm dignity, stating his position and entrusting the outcome to the One who knows the hearts and actions of all people.

translation: Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein you used to differ.
interpretation: This verse points to the certainty that all disputes among people, especially those arising from differences in religious belief and conduct, will ultimately be settled by God alone. In this world, truth and falsehood often remain tangled and contested, and people hold firmly to their own views; but the Day of Resurrection will strip away illusion and self-justification, leaving no room for doubt about who was right. The verse thus calls believers to humility in disagreement, patience with those who differ, and a sober awareness that final judgment belongs to God, whose knowledge encompasses every hidden intention and every choice made in the course of one's life.

translation: Do you not know that Allah knows whatever is in the heaven and the earth? Indeed, that is in a Book. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.
interpretation: The verse turns the believer's attention from the question of knowledge to the certainty of divine records: Allah's knowledge encompasses all that is hidden in the heavens and the earth, and this complete knowledge is preserved in a written decree, the Preserved Tablet, which makes the recording and accounting of all deeds effortless for Him. The rhetorical question 'Do you not know?' reproaches the heedless for failing to reflect on a truth their own reason and faith should already grasp, so that awareness of being fully known should produce vigilance in conduct and humility before the One whose knowledge and power require no exertion.

translation: And they worship other than Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and about which they have no knowledge. And the wrongdoers will have no helper.
interpretation: The verse exposes the baselessness of idolatry: its adherents devote worship to beings for which no divine revelation or clear proof has been granted, and their devotion rests on no knowledge, only on assumption and inherited custom. Worship must rest on authority from God and on genuine understanding, so whoever abandons this foundation for false objects of devotion has abandoned the only firm ground of faith. The closing declaration that the wrongdoers have no helper points to the reality that those who associate partners with God, and thereby wrong their own souls, will find on the Day of Reckoning that the false powers they relied upon cannot save them, and that true protection belongs to God alone.

translation: When Our clear verses are recited to them, you can recognize denial on the faces of those who disbelieve; they nearly assault those who recite Our verses to them. Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that? The Fire, which Allah has promised to those who disbelieve, and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: The verse portrays the inner hostility of those who reject revelation as becoming visible in their faces and conduct: when the clear signs are recited, their discomfort turns into anger and near-violence against the messengers and believers who carry the recitation. The believer is thus shown that the clarity of the message provokes resistance precisely from those who have closed their hearts, and that such hostility should not shake one's steadfastness. By directing the question toward a greater reality, the verse redirects the believer's attention away from the immediate threat of the opponents toward the ultimate reckoning, the Fire that God has promised, which is the true measure of loss and the only destination that outweighs every worldly harm.

translation: O mankind, a parable is presented, so listen to it. Indeed, those you invoke besides God will never create a fly, even if they gather together for that purpose. And if the fly should snatch away something from them, they could not retrieve it from it. Weak are the seeker and the sought.
interpretation: The verse exposes the utter powerlessness of the objects of worship besides God by choosing the smallest of creatures, the fly, as the measure. If all of creation's false gods combined could not produce even a fly, nor recover a trifle the fly seizes from them, then their claim to divinity collapses on its own terms. The closing phrase, 'weak are the seeker and the sought,' turns the lens back on the worshipper who petitions something as helpless as himself, and on the idol that is petitioned, so that the parable calls the human heart to recognize where true power and true sufficiency lie, and to turn in sincere reliance to the One who alone creates and restores.

translation: They did not measure God with the true measure of His worth. Indeed, God is All-Powerful, All-Mighty.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who fail to grasp God's greatness in their beliefs and conduct, reducing Him to something their limited understanding can contain. To know God 'with His due measure' is to recognize that His power is absolute and that He is unbound by any human reckoning. The closing words, 'Indeed, God is All-Powerful, All-Mighty,' serve as the reason for this reverence: a Being whose strength and dominion are beyond all comparison deserves to be honored in heart, speech, and action, and no created thing can rival or diminish Him.

translation: Allah chooses messengers from among the angels and from among mankind. Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the selection of messengers is an exclusive prerogative of Allah, who alone knows where prophetic mission should be placed, whether among the angelic host or among human beings. This divine choosing is not based on lineage, worldly status, or human request, but on Allah's perfect knowledge of the hearts and capacities of those He selects. The closing names, All-Hearing and All-Seeing, point to the fact that this choice is made with full awareness of every word, deed, and intention, so that the bearers of revelation are chosen by the One who hears all speech and sees all that is concealed, and this should lead believers to trust His wisdom in the guidance He sends.

translation: He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and to Allah all matters are returned.
interpretation: The verse affirms the comprehensive knowledge of Allah, which encompasses everything that lies before and behind His creatures, that is, their past and future, their visible and hidden circumstances, and what they can see and what remains beyond their reach. Human beings act within a limited field of knowledge, so they should not presume to grasp the full reality of their affairs. The verse then points to the final return of all matters to Allah, meaning that ultimate authority, judgment, and the outcome of every affair belong to Him alone. Awareness of this should lead the believer to humility, trust in God's perfect knowledge, and readiness for the accountability that awaits.

translation: O you who have believed, bow down, prostrate, worship your Lord, and do good that you may succeed.
interpretation: The verse addresses the believers directly and gathers the core of their practice into a single sequence: outward acts of submission (rukū' and sujūd), inward and continuous devotion (worship of the Lord), and broader righteous conduct (doing good). The order moves from the physical posture of humility in prayer, to the worship that gives that posture its meaning, and finally to goodness toward others and the world beyond the ritual act. The closing promise, 'that you may succeed,' ties salvation to the integration of these three dimensions, showing that prostration without ethical action or worship without sincerity falls short of true success. The prostration mark at the end signals that this is a verse of sajdah, prompting the reader to prostrate in recognition of the command.

translation: And strive for Allah with the striving that is due to Him. He has chosen you and has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion. It is the religion of your father Abraham. He named you 'Muslims' before this and in this (Revelation), so that the Messenger may be a witness over you and you may be witnesses over mankind. So establish the prayer, give the zakah, and hold fast to Allah. He is your Protector, and what an excellent Protector and what an excellent Helper.
interpretation: The verse grounds the believers' whole mission in divine election and in the ease of the religion: because God chose this community and removed hardship from its faith, its striving must be sincere and total, directed wholly toward God. The Abrahamic identity links the community to a shared prophetic lineage, and its title of 'Muslims' marks a continuity of submission running through earlier revelation and the Qur'an alike. Its purpose is to make the Prophet a witness over his followers and the followers witnesses over humanity, so that the community becomes a moral standard for the nations. Prayer, zakah, and holding fast to God are the practical means of sustaining that role, and the closing affirmation that God is the Protector and Helper places the entire burden of this mission in reliance on Him.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Successful indeed are the believers.
interpretation: The opening declaration of Surah Al-Mu'minun establishes success (falah) as the defining reward of faith, and it is framed as a settled certainty rather than a hope. By placing the name of Allah and His mercy at the head of the verse, the text signals that this success flows entirely from divine grace, not from human merit alone. The word 'believers' (al-mu'minun) is given with the definite article, pointing to a recognized category of people whose character the following verses go on to describe in detail: humility in prayer, turning away from idle talk, purity, guarding chastity, faithfulness to trusts and covenants, and attentiveness to prayer. The sura thus teaches that true belief is not a mere verbal claim but a lived inner and outer discipline, and that its fruit is a success that is both immediate in the heart's tranquility and final in the hereafter.

translation: Those who are humbly attentive in their prayer.
interpretation: The verse describes the believers whose defining mark in prayer is khushu', a state of inward humility, stillness of heart, and focused submission before God. Khushu' is not merely a bodily posture but a condition of the heart in which the worshipper is conscious of standing before the Almighty, so that the prayer becomes a genuine encounter rather than an empty ritual. By placing this quality at the center of the believers' portrait, the verse teaches that the outward acts of worship are only fulfilled when they are animated by reverence, sincerity, and attentiveness.

translation: And those who turn away from idle talk.
interpretation: The verse describes the believers who deliberately withdraw from vain, frivolous, and pointless speech and conduct. Their turning away from what is useless reflects a refined character that guards the tongue and time, avoiding gossip, mockery, and every empty pursuit that serves no benefit. It shows that true faith is measured not only by acts of worship but also by discipline over one's words and attention, so that a person's life is occupied with what is meaningful and beneficial.

translation: And those who are active in giving zakat (purifying alms).
interpretation: The phrase describes believers who do not merely pay zakat as an occasional obligation but actively engage in it as a continuous practice of purification. Zakat here is understood both as the purification of wealth through giving a due share to those in need and as the purification of the soul from greed and attachment to possessions. The verse places this active, deliberate giving among the defining marks of the righteous, showing that faith is measured not only by ritual worship but by a practical commitment to social responsibility and generosity.

translation: And those who guard their private parts (from unlawful sexual intercourse),
interpretation: The verse describes a defining quality of the believers: the guarding of their chastity. This restraint is not merely a negative prohibition but a comprehensive discipline of the self, confining sexual desire within the lawful bond of marriage or the lawful possession permitted by the Shariah, and thereby protecting the individual, the family, and the wider social order from the corruption that unbridled desire brings. Its placement within the description of the successful believers, alongside humility in prayer and care for trusts and promises, shows that inner purity and outward conduct are inseparable in the Qur'anic vision of faith.

translation: except with their spouses or what their right hands possess, for indeed they are not blameworthy.
interpretation: The verse, in its context (Surah al-Mu'minun 23:6 and al-Ma'arij 70:30), defines the lawful boundary of sexual relations for the believers who guard their chastity: relations are permitted only within marriage or with those whom one's right hand possesses, meaning captives or slaves under the legal framework of the time. By placing this exception directly after the command to guard the private parts, the verse establishes that the moral exemption from blame applies only within these two lawful bonds, and it thereby affirms the sanctity of marriage as the primary institution regulating intimacy, while the reference to what the right hand possesses reflects the historical reality of slavery addressed through the Qur'an's gradual approach toward its eventual limitation and the encouragement of manumission.

translation: So whoever seeks beyond that, it is those who are the transgressors.
interpretation: The verse, which comes in the context of the believers' guarded chastity (al-Mu'minun 23:5-7, and its parallel in al-Ma'arij 70:29-31), defines the only lawful outlets for sexual desire as marriage and what the right hand possesses. Anyone who seeks gratification beyond these limits has crossed the boundary God set, and the verse names such people 'al-'Adun', those who exceed their bounds. The word 'wara'a' (beyond) conveys that the forbidden lies on the far side of the permitted, so the transgression is not merely a lapse but a deliberate overstepping of divine limits. The verse thus teaches that restraint is a mark of the faithful, and that the boundaries of permissibility are part of God's guidance for preserving the individual's dignity and the integrity of family and society.

translation: And those who are faithful to their trusts and their covenants, keeping them.
interpretation: The verse describes the believers as people who guard what has been entrusted to them and honor the commitments they have made, whether these are agreements with others or their pledges to God. Here faithfulness is presented as a defining mark of the righteous: trustworthiness in worldly dealings and fidelity in covenants are not separate from piety but are a direct expression of it. The Arabic word ra'un, meaning those who watch over and tend carefully, suggests not a passive avoidance of betrayal but an active, vigilant guardianship of what is owed to others, so that a believer is one who protects the rights and expectations that others have placed in his keeping.

translation: And those who are constant in guarding their prayers.
interpretation: The verse describes the believers who do not merely perform their prayers but persistently watch over them, preserving their timing, their completeness, their humility, and their inner presence before God. Guarding the prayer means protecting it from neglect, distraction, and carelessness, so that it remains a living bond between the servant and his Lord rather than an empty ritual. Its placement among the qualities of the successful believers shows that steadfastness in prayer is a foundation from which all other righteous conduct grows.

translation: Those are the inheritors.
interpretation: The verse comes from Surah Al-Mu'minun (23:10–11), where it concludes the description of the believers who attain Paradise. After listing their qualities, such as humility in prayer, turning away from vain talk, giving zakat, guarding their chastity, keeping their trusts and covenants, and maintaining their prayers, God declares that these are the inheritors, who will inherit Paradise and dwell therein eternally. The imagery of inheritance suggests that Paradise is received as a rightful legacy earned through faithful conduct, much as an heir receives what was left behind, rather than merely being a reward bought by isolated acts. It also conveys that the believers are the true heirs of the earth's blessings in the hereafter, while those who are deprived of it lose what they could have inherited.

translation: Those who will inherit Paradise; they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: The verse presents paradise (al-Firdaws) as an inheritance, a reward that comes to those who have earned it through their faith and righteous deeds, much as an heir receives what was prepared for them rather than something earned by mere effort alone. The word "inherit" conveys both the certainty and the dignity of the reward, while the closing phrase "they will abide therein forever" emphasizes its eternal permanence, in contrast to the transient pleasures of this world. It reassures the believer that the final outcome of faithful conduct is not temporary success but everlasting felicity, with no fear of loss or expulsion.

translation: And We did certainly create man from an extract of clay.
interpretation: The verse points to the humble material origin of humankind. Man, who may appear to be the pinnacle of creation and inclined toward pride, is traced back to something as ordinary as clay, which reminds him of his dependence on his Creator and of the need for humility. The word 'sulalah' (extract, essence) suggests that the human being is drawn out of the finest part of the earth's substance, so the same verse that recalls his lowly origin also honors the dignity of his creation, as the subsequent verses describe the stages of his development from a drop of fluid. Read this way, the verse invites reflection on the Creator's power to fashion a conscious, responsible being from the simplest of materials.

translation: Then We made him a drop of semen in a firm resting place.
interpretation: The verse traces the stages of human creation with precision: after the earlier stage of clay and the making of the human being, the process continues with the seed being placed in a secure, stable vessel, the womb, where it is protected from harm and given the time and conditions to develop. The phrase 'firm resting place' points to the womb's protective enclosure, which safeguards the nascent life from the external world. The verse invites reflection on the wonder of how a minute drop becomes a human being, and it reminds the reader that this unfolding is the work of a deliberate divine design that shelters and sustains life at its most fragile beginning.

translation: Then We made the sperm-drop into a clinging clot, then We made the clot into a lump of flesh, then We made the lump into bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced it as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators.
interpretation: The verse traces the stages of human embryonic development in a sequence of successive transformations, each created by God's deliberate act, and it moves from the humble drop of fluid to a fully formed human being endowed with a distinct nature. The phrase 'another creation' points to the qualitative leap when the fetus receives its soul and emerges as a living, conscious person, which is why the verse ends by exalting God as the best of creators. The passage thus invites reflection on human origins as evidence of divine power and artistry, and it calls the believer toward gratitude and humility before the Creator who shapes each human being with precision and care.

translation: Then indeed you, after that, will surely die.
interpretation: The verse, appearing in Surah Al-Mu'minun (23:15) within the sequence describing the stages of human creation, marks a turning point: after the formation of the human being from clay, the drop of sperm, the clinging clot, the lump of flesh, and the bones clothed with flesh, the human being is brought forth as a new creation, yet this very beginning of life is immediately followed by the reminder of its certain end. The emphatic particles (inna and the lam of emphasis) stress that death is an absolute reality that no one can escape, which places human life in a fleeting frame and calls the listener to reflect on their dependence on the Creator who brought them from nothing, and to prepare for the Hereafter in which they will be resurrected and held accountable.

translation: Then, indeed, you will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection.
interpretation: The verse follows the preceding announcement of death with the certainty of resurrection, marking the transition from the temporal life to the final accounting. The word 'thumma' (then) signals a sequence of stages: after the death that all creatures must undergo, comes a second, decisive event in which humanity is raised from the graves to stand before its Lord. The emphatic 'innakum' (indeed you) and the passive 'tub"athun' (you will be raised) affirm both the inevitability of this rising and that it is ordained from above rather than left to human will. The phrase 'yawm al-qiyamah' (the Day of Standing up) points to the moment when all beings rise to give account, so the verse calls the listener to recognize that this worldly life is not final, and that their deeds will be weighed on a day when no aspect of their existence remains hidden.

translation: And indeed, We created above you seven heavens (paths), and We were never unaware of creation.
interpretation: The verse points to the vastness and order of the cosmos: the phrase 'seven paths' (tara'iq) is read by many commentators as the seven heavens, layered above the believer's head, and the closing clause affirms that God's creative act is never heedless or careless. Taken together, the verse invites reflection on the precision of the created order as evidence of a knowing Creator who attends to all that He has made, so that human beings, living beneath this structured sky, should recognize that nothing in creation escapes divine knowledge and care.

translation: And We sent down from the sky water in measure, and We caused it to settle in the earth; and indeed, We are able to take it away.
interpretation: The verse presents rain as a deliberate, measured provision: God sends water down in a precise quantity suited to what the earth can hold and what life needs, not in excess that would destroy, nor in scarcity. The water that is made to dwell in the ground becomes a stored reserve, feeding springs, wells, and the roots of plants, so that life continues between rains. The closing statement turns the reader's attention from blessing to vulnerability: the same God who gives this water can withdraw it entirely, through drought or by sinking it deeper into the earth, so that human security in sustenance rests on divine power rather than on human control. Gratitude for what is given and awareness of its fragility are thus the two responses the verse calls for.

translation: So We produced for you thereby gardens of date-palms and grapevines; in them you have abundant fruits, and from them you eat.
interpretation: The verse presents the water sent down from the sky as the living source of abundance: from it God brings forth gardens of palms and vines, not as mere scenery but as provision for human life. The phrase 'for you' repeated twice shows that these gifts are made for the benefit of people, so that the bounty of the earth becomes a sign that the Creator cares for and sustains His creatures. Ordinarily one reflects on the chain from rain to fruit and on the gratitude owed for it, since the same power that brings a garden out of dry ground is the power that gives the believer daily sustenance and calls for thankfulness.

translation: And a tree that springs forth from Mount Sinai, growing with oil and a relish for those who eat.
