interpretation: The tree of Mount Sinai (the olive tree, as the Qur'an itself names it in Surah al-Mu'minun 23:20) is presented as a source of nourishment that gives both oil for light and fuel and a condiment for food, so that the verse ties the sacred landscape of revelation to the everyday sustenance that sustains people. Its growing out of the mountain where Moses received the revelation suggests that divine blessing reaches the physical world through ordinary, humble means, and that the same God who guides the soul also provides for the body. Read in its context in Surah al-Mu'minun, the olive is one of the signs of God's bounty, inviting the reader to reflect on the gifts of creation as evidence of the Creator's care.

translation: And indeed, in livestock there is a lesson for you: We give you to drink from what is in their bellies, and for you in them are many benefits, and from them you eat.
interpretation: The verse invites the believer to reflect on the cattle not merely as property but as a sign (ʿibrah) pointing to the Creator's care and design. The image of pure milk produced from within the animal's body, between digested matter and blood, reveals a precise and merciful providence that sustains human life. Their many benefits, from wool, mounts, and burdens to food, teach gratitude, since the blessings of the created world are a continual reminder that human sustenance flows from a generous Lord rather than from human effort alone.

translation: And upon them (the cattle) and upon the ship you are carried.
interpretation: The verse points to the two means of transport by which people were carried in the time of revelation: the land animals, which bear loads and riders across the earth, and the ship, which carries them across the sea. Placing them together reminds the listener that human movement and livelihood depend on God's subjection of these creatures and of the waters to human use, so that gratitude is owed for the ease of travel over both land and sea.

translation: And We certainly sent Noah to his people, and he said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. Will you not then be mindful of Him?"
interpretation: The verse presents the foundational message shared by all the prophets: pure monotheism, the worship of Allah alone, and the rejection of any partner or rival deity. Noah's call begins with the people's own community bond ("O my people"), signaling that his concern is compassionate and sincere rather than adversarial. The closing question, "Will you not then be mindful?", does not merely ask for intellectual agreement but calls the heart to taqwa, a conscious awareness of God that guards against heedlessness and shapes conduct. The verse thus teaches that true reform begins with restoring the correct relationship between the human being and the Creator, and that belief must be translated into God-consciousness in daily life.

translation: So the chiefs of those who disbelieved among his people said: "This is not but a human being like you who wants to make himself superior over you. And if Allah had willed, He would have sent down angels. We have not heard of this among our forefathers, the earliest ones."
interpretation: The verse exposes the reasoning of the disbelieving elite, who reject the prophetic message not on its content but on the grounds that its bearer is merely human, and who seek to preserve their social standing by denying that a man from among them could be singled out with a revelation. Their objection that God would have sent angels if He wished to send guidance reflects a common pattern of resistance in which the form of the messenger becomes the pretext for refusing the message, while their appeal to ancestral custom shows that inherited tradition was valued over the claims of new revelation. The verse thus teaches that truth is often rejected by those who measure it against worldly hierarchy and familiar habit rather than by its own merit.

translation: He is nothing but a man possessed by madness, so wait with him for a time.
interpretation: The verse reports the hostile words of the disbelievers about the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: they accuse him of being mad, attributing his message to a derangement of the mind rather than to genuine revelation. The phrase "fatarabbasu bihi hatta hin" carries a note of contempt and of deliberate waiting, as though they told one another to hold off and see whether the matter would pass or collapse on its own. Read in its setting, the verse exposes a pattern that recurs throughout the Qur'an, in which the messengers are dismissed as sorcerers, poets, or madmen so that the truth they bring can be set aside without being weighed. The verse thus teaches that the charge of madness is often a way of avoiding argument, and it offers the believer consolation that such accusations are an old and expected response to prophetic guidance.

translation: He said, "My Lord, support me, because they have denied me."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the prophet Noah according to the context of Surah Al-Mu'minun (23:26), reveals the prophetic posture in the face of persistent rejection: after long years of calling his people with no response, he turns entirely away from his own efforts and places his cause in the hands of God alone. His words express the reliance of the believer on divine help when human support is absent and when falsehood has been used to dismiss the truth he carries. The phrase "bima kadhdhabun" points to the pain of being denounced as a liar, and his plea teaches that the true refuge of one who is mistreated for the sake of the message is the Lord who sees and who is able to grant victory.

translation: So We revealed to him, "Build the ship under Our eyes and Our inspiration. Then when Our command comes and the oven overflows, load into it a pair of every kind, and your family, except those against whom the word has already preceded; and do not address Me concerning those who have wronged. Indeed, they are to be drowned."
interpretation: The verse presents Noah's obedience as a process carried out under divine watch and guidance, where the construction of the ark is itself an act of trust in God's command before any sign of the flood appears. The overflowing oven signals the onset of the catastrophe, and the instruction to save a pair of every kind and the believing family, while excluding those already condemned by the prior decree, shows that divine justice separates those bound to perish by their own choices from those spared through faith. The prohibition against pleading for the wrongdoers marks a firm boundary: intercession cannot override the outcome of persistent injustice, and the prophet is taught that the consequences of wrongdoing, once settled by God, are not to be contested.

translation: So when you and those with you are settled upon the ship, then say: "All praise is due to God, who has saved us from the wrongdoing people."
interpretation: The verse teaches that deliverance from danger is to be met first with gratitude rather than self-congratulation. Having been commanded to board the ark and be borne safely over the flood, Noah is taught the proper response to every completed rescue: to recognize that the ability to reach safety comes from God alone, and to acknowledge that the wrongdoers who rejected the message were the ones who perished. The moment of settling into the vessel becomes a lesson that the believer's security is a divine gift, and that the praise of God must accompany the end of every hardship, linking the ordinary act of gaining stability with a deeper awareness of divine mercy and of the distinction between the righteous and the unjust.

translation: And say, "My Lord, cause me to land at a blessed landing place, and You are the best of those who bring to land."
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Mu'minun (23:29), is a prayer taught to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in the context of the storm and the sinking of the wrongdoers. It teaches the believer to turn to Allah at moments of danger, uncertainty, and displacement, asking for a blessed settling place, whether a literal shore after a voyage or a secure station in life. The phrase "best of those who bring to land" affirms that true provision of shelter and safety belongs to Allah alone, and it models a humble dependence in which one asks for blessing rather than merely for comfort. It also reminds the reader that every journey, whether of the sea or of life, ends in a settling that only God can make blessed.

translation: Indeed, in that are signs; and indeed, We were ever testing [mankind].
interpretation: The verse points to the story that precedes it in the surah (the tale of the people of the garden in Surah Al-Qalam, or the trial of the owners of the orchard in Surah Al-An'am context) and draws a lesson from it: the events recounted are clear signs for those who reflect, because they reveal that wealth, harvest, and blessings are themselves a trial from God. The word 'mubtalin' signals that the test is deliberate and purposeful, meant to expose whether a person will respond with gratitude and humility or with arrogance and heedlessness. Thus the verse calls the believer to see the outcomes of worldly favor and loss as examinations of character, and to recognize divine wisdom in both abundance and deprivation.

translation: Then We brought into being after them another generation.
interpretation: The verse points to the divine pattern of succession in history: after one community is destroyed or passes away, Allah raises up a new generation in its place. This reminds the listener that worldly power and prominence are lent for a time, and that the cycle of rise and fall is governed by God's will, so each generation is accountable for how it uses the opportunity it has been given.

translation: So We sent among them a messenger from among themselves, [saying]: Worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. Will you not then be mindful of Allah?
interpretation: The verse shows the mercy of Allah in not leaving a people without guidance: He raised up a messenger from among their own kin, one who knew their language, their circumstances and their character, so that his call would be clear and understandable to them and no excuse would remain. The core of his message is tawhid, the singling out of Allah in worship, since every other object of devotion is false and powerless. The closing question, 'Will you not then be mindful?', is a gentle rebuke that turns the listener from heedlessness to taqwa, reminding that awareness of Allah and fear of displeasing Him are the natural response to a clear message that has been delivered.

translation: And the chieftains of his people who disbelieved and denied the meeting of the Hereafter, and whom We had given luxury in the worldly life, said: "This is none but a human being like you. He eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink."
interpretation: This verse (23:33-34) reveals a recurring pattern in the rejection of prophets: the leaders of a people, who were made complacent by material comfort and luxury, reject the messenger not on the basis of his message but on the basis of his ordinary humanity. Their objection rests on a worldview in which status and wealth are signs of worth, so they cannot accept that a man with the same mundane needs as themselves could be chosen to convey a divine message. The verse links this arrogance to denial of the Hereafter: those who are absorbed in the pleasures of this life and refuse to reckon with the accountability to come are most prone to dismiss guidance that calls them beyond it. The reasoning reflects a deeper truth that God's wisdom often works through what appears ordinary, and that prosperity without faith in the meeting with God hardens hearts against the truth.

translation: And if you obey a human being like yourselves, then indeed you would be among the losers.
interpretation: The verse is spoken in the context of the people of Shu'ayb, who warned their own community that submitting to a mortal man like themselves would lead to ruin. It exposes a recurring rejection of prophethood on the grounds that the messenger is merely human, as though a message from God could only come through a superior being. The verse teaches that obedience to a messenger is not a diminishment of one's dignity but the path to success, and that the real loss lies in turning away from guidance because of the messenger's ordinary human form. It also reminds believers that the measure of truth is the message itself and the one who sent it, not the outward status of the person who delivers it.

translation: Does he promise you that when you die and become dust and bones, you will indeed be brought forth (alive again)?
interpretation: The verse confronts the disbelievers' denial of resurrection by repeating their own objection in its starkest form: the body, reduced to dust and scattered bones, seems beyond any possibility of return. Its rhetorical question sets the human assumption of irreversibility against the promise of the Messenger, inviting the listener to reflect that the one who originated creation from nothing is not bound by the decay that appears to us as final. Thus the verse turns a mocking doubt into a call to recognize that death is a passage, not an end, and that the scale of what seems impossible to human eyes is no measure of what is possible for God.

translation: Far, far is that which you are promised.
interpretation: This verse, spoken in the Qur'an (al-Mu'minun 23:36) by the disbelievers as they dismiss the warning of the Messenger of their own resurrection, expresses the mocking denial of the Hereafter. The repeated word "hayhat" conveys an intense sense of remoteness and impossibility, as if the promised rising from the dead were something utterly unreachable and absurd. Its emphatic doubling reveals a heart that has grown so distant from belief that it regards the certainty of accountability as a fantasy, thereby exposing how worldly heedlessness hardens into outright rejection of the divine promise.

translation: There is nothing but our life of this world: we die and we live, and we will not be resurrected.
interpretation: The verse records the words of those who deny the Hereafter, who reduce human existence to the cycle of this worldly life alone, a cycle of death and birth with no return to account. Its interpretation lies in the sharp contrast it draws between a life bounded by the material world and the reality of resurrection and accountability that the Qur'an affirms throughout. By quoting the denial in their own voice, the verse exposes the poverty of a worldview that sees no purpose beyond the present, and invites the listener to reflect on the origin and end of human life, so that the brevity of worldly existence becomes a reason for moral responsibility rather than heedlessness.

translation: He is nothing but a man who has invented a lie against God, and we are not going to believe him.
interpretation: The verse records the stance of the disbelieving leaders of a people toward a messenger sent to them. Unable to answer his message on its merits, they dismiss him by reducing him to an ordinary man and accusing him of fabricating speech and attributing it to God. Their conclusion, "we are not believers in him," shows that their rejection was settled in advance and rests on prejudice rather than evidence. The passage reflects a recurring pattern in the Qur'an: prophets are charged with falsehood precisely when their message challenges the comfortable beliefs and social standing of their audience. It also reminds the believer that rejection of a truth does not make the truth false, and that the accusation of lying against God is among the gravest charges, one that the accusers themselves bear responsibility for.

translation: He said, "My Lord, support me, because they have denied me."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the prophet Noah according to the context of Surah al-Mu'minun (23:26), reveals the posture of a messenger who, having exhausted every means of guidance and been met only with rejection, turns entirely to God. The word "انصرني" asks for divine help against the opposition, and the phrase "بما كذبون" ("because they have denied me") grounds the plea in the people's denial, not in personal grievance. The prophet does not seek vengeance for himself but places his cause before the One who alone can decide between him and his people. It teaches that when human efforts in calling to truth meet persistent denial, the believer's refuge is prayer and reliance on God's support, and that patience combined with this turning to God is the way of the prophets.

translation: He said, "Within a little while they will surely become regretful."
interpretation: This verse, spoken in the context of the story of the people of the garden (Surah al-Qalam, 68:17-33) or in a parallel narrative setting, conveys that the wrongdoers who chose greed and deception over obedience to God will soon face the consequences of their actions. The phrase "ʿamma qalīl" (within a little while) emphasizes that the punishment is near and certain, while the word "nādimīn" (regretful) points to the inner anguish that follows when worldly gain turns into loss. It is a reminder that regret, though it arrives too late to undo the deed, is the natural outcome of forsaking what is right, and that every person should act with foresight before the moment of accounting arrives.

translation: So the blast seized them in truth, and We made them as debris carried away by a flood. So away with the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: The verse portrays the sudden and total destruction of a people who persisted in wrongdoing. Their end is depicted as a justified outcome rather than an arbitrary catastrophe: the scream or cry that overtook them came in accordance with truth, which means their ruin matched their own conduct and the consequences of rejecting the messengers. The image of them becoming like driven foam or wreckage swept along by a torrent conveys how their apparent strength, pride and social standing vanished into worthlessness, leaving nothing of lasting value. The closing phrase, calling for distance and removal from mercy, expresses the finality of their exclusion, and it stands as a warning that persistent injustice invites divine judgment and ultimately severs a people from God's favor.

translation: Then We produced after them other generations.
interpretation: The verse points to the continuity of divine providence in history: after each people is destroyed for its wrongdoing, God brings forth a new generation to inherit the earth and be tested in turn. Each successive community is thus given its own opportunity to believe and act rightly, and the sequence of nations reminds the reader that worldly power is lent, not owned, and that those who follow are placed under the same scrutiny as those who came before.

translation: No nation can precede its appointed term, nor can it delay it.
interpretation: The verse affirms that every community has a fixed, divinely decreed time (ajal) set for its existence and its destruction or reckoning. Neither can any people hasten that appointed term by a single moment, nor postpone it once it has arrived. This establishes that the rise and fall of nations, as well as the individual's lifespan, are governed by a precise divine measure, which should humble human beings who may think they can control their own fate, and should encourage reflection on the certainty of the Divine decree. It also implies that the delay of punishment for a people is not neglect; rather, it is a mercy granting them time until their appointed moment comes.

translation: Then We sent Our messengers in succession. Every time a messenger came to a nation, they denied him, so We made some follow others [to destruction], and We made them into tales. So away with a people who do not believe.
interpretation: The verse portrays a recurring pattern in sacred history: God sends His messengers one after another, not as a single isolated call but as a continuous chain of guidance, so that every community is given the opportunity to hear the truth. The repeated refusal of each nation to accept its messenger shows that the obstacle has never been a lack of evidence but a stubborn disposition of heart. The phrase "We made them into tales" points to the fate of such peoples: their destruction left them as stories for later generations, a warning to be remembered rather than a legacy to be imitated. The closing curse, "away with a people who do not believe," is not merely condemnation but a statement that persistent rejection, after clear signs, removes one from God's mercy. The verse thus addresses the listeners of the Prophet, urging them to learn from the past and to respond to the final message before they too become a cautionary tale.

translation: Then We sent Moses and his brother Aaron with Our signs and a clear authority.
interpretation: The verse presents the mission of Moses and Aaron as a divinely authorized commission: they are equipped with two distinct sources of proof, the signs (ayat), which are miraculous evidences that call the mind and heart to recognition of God, and a manifest authority (sultan mubin), a clear and undeniable argument that establishes their legitimacy before Pharaoh and his chiefs. Mentioning Aaron alongside Moses highlights the value of brotherly support in bearing a prophetic burden, and the pairing of signs with clear authority shows that prophetic guidance rests on both wondrous evidence and rational clarity, leaving the audience without excuse once the truth has been made plain.

translation: To Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they acted arrogantly, for they were a haughty people.
interpretation: The verse shows that Pharaoh and his court were not merely unbelievers but people who, having been shown the truth through Moses' mission, deliberately chose pride over submission. Their arrogance (istikbar) was the root of their rejection, and it was reinforced by their sense of social and political superiority, which made them regard the call of a messenger from among the Children of Israel as beneath them. The phrase 'a people who were high and exalted' (qawman 'alin) points to a self-image of lofty dominance over others, which the Qur'an elsewhere ties to oppression and corruption on earth. The lesson is that worldly rank and power become a barrier to accepting truth when they breed the conceit that one is too great to be guided, and that such pride ultimately leads to ruin.

translation: So they said: "Shall we believe two mortals like ourselves, while their people are servants to us?"
interpretation: This verse, from Surah al-Mu'minun (23:47), records the arrogance of the elite among the people of Noah's and Moses' era... wait, precisely: it is the reply of the disbelieving chieftains of the nations of the earlier messengers, who rejected the prophets Musa and Harun (in the context of Surah al-Mu'minun, the nations after Noah) by pointing to their humanity and their own worldly dominance. Their reasoning reveals a recurring pattern in which social status and the assumption that a messenger must be of a superior, non-human nature become grounds for denying revelation. The Qur'an answers this throughout by affirming that messengers were human beings chosen by God, and that truth is not measured by rank, wealth, or the submission of others to one's own authority, but by the guidance that the messenger brings.

translation: So they denied the two of them, and so they were among those destroyed.
interpretation: The verse closes a narrative of rejection: when a people persisted in denying the two messengers sent to them, their denial became the cause of their own ruin. The phrase "among those destroyed" signals that such destruction is not an isolated accident but a recurring consequence in the Qur'an's account of earlier nations, where persistent disbelief after clear warning brings divine punishment. It serves as a warning to the listener that rejecting the messages of God's prophets carries real and grave consequences, and that the fate of past communities is meant to be a lesson for the present.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture, that they might be guided.
interpretation: The verse presents the giving of the Scripture to Moses as a divine favor whose purpose is guidance. The phrase "that they might be guided" (la'allahum yahtadun) shows that revelation is not an end in itself but a means by which people are led to the right path, so the verse implicitly calls the community that receives the Book to read it as a living source of direction and to act upon it. By linking Moses' Scripture to the hope of guidance, it also underlines the continuity of prophetic revelation: each Book sent to a people carries the same purpose, which is to bring humanity from confusion to clarity and from error to truth.

translation: And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign, and We gave them refuge upon a high ground, a place of settling and flowing water.
interpretation: The verse presents Jesus and his mother Mary as a sign of God's power and favor: their miraculous circumstances, and the protection granted to them, point to God's ability to act beyond ordinary causes. The 'high ground with stable settlement and flowing spring' evokes a place of security, peace and provision, suggesting that those who remain faithful and trust in God are sheltered and sustained even amid hardship and opposition, much as Mary was given rest and sustenance after the difficult birth and the accusations against her.

translation: O messengers, eat from the good things and act righteously. Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse addresses the messengers collectively and joins two duties that cannot be separated: consuming what is lawful and wholesome (tayyibat), and performing righteous deeds. Lawful sustenance is the foundation that makes good action sound, since what nourishes the body shapes the disposition of the soul, and the prophets are thereby taught that their own conduct must be exemplary before they call others to it. The closing reminder that God is fully aware of their actions carries a call to sincerity and vigilance, assuring the righteous that their efforts are not overlooked and warning them that every deed is recorded before the One who knows it completely.

translation: And indeed, this, your community, is one community, and I am your Lord, so fear Me.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the believers form a single community bound by one faith and one source of guidance, rather than being divided into rival sects, since all messengers and their followers ultimately trace back to the same Lord. The address moves from the collective unity of the community to a personal command of taqwa, indicating that genuine unity rests on each individual's conscious awareness of God and mindfulness of His commands. Unity of the ummah is thus not merely social or political but is rooted in shared worship of the one Lord, and the call to be wary of Him is the means by which that unity is preserved against fragmentation.

translation: But they divided their affair among themselves into sects, each party rejoicing in what it has.
interpretation: The verse portrays how a community that received a single trust from God fragments its unity into rival factions, each becoming enamored of its own doctrine and self-justification. The rejoicing is the telling detail: the sect's satisfaction with what it possesses blinds it to the truth it has abandoned, so division is not merely a historical accident but a spiritual condition born of complacency and self-admiration. It warns believers that the surest sign of drifting from the message is the pride that takes its partial portion for the whole.

translation: So leave them in their confusion until a time (appointed).
interpretation: The verse is a divine command to the Prophet to withdraw from arguing further with those who persist in denial and heedlessness. Their being plunged in 'ghamra'—a deep, engulfing heedlessness that blinds them as floodwaters cover everything—is presented as their own chosen state, and God grants them respite until their appointed reckoning. It teaches that once truth has been clearly conveyed and rejected, the believer's responsibility is discharged, and the matter of their guidance and punishment rests with God's timing.

translation: Do they think that what We provide them with of wealth and children
interpretation: The verse confronts those who take their worldly abundance as a sign of divine favor and a guarantee of their standing. Wealth and offspring are a trial and a respite, not proof of God's approval; by asking whether they imagine these gifts to be a form of advancement, it exposes the error of measuring one's worth before God by material blessings, and turns the reader toward the reality that such provision may be a means of testing and of drawing people further into heedlessness.

translation: "Do they think that We extend to them wealth and children as a means of hastening good things for them? Nay, they do not perceive." (Surah al-Mu'minun 23:56) — More literally: "Shall We hasten for them in good things? Nay, they do not perceive."
interpretation: The verse exposes a deceptive reading of worldly favor: when a person sees abundance flowing to him, he may take it as proof that God approves of him, when in fact such ease can be a trial that draws him further from the truth. The phrase "nusari'u lahum fi al-khayrat" can be read as a divine respite that lets people think they are being rewarded, while the closing "bal la yash'urun" (nay, they do not perceive) shows that the real danger lies in their lack of awareness. The lesson is that worldly blessings are not in themselves a sign of acceptance, and that true insight requires examining one's state before God rather than being lulled by prosperity.

translation: Indeed, those who are, out of fear of their Lord, apprehensive (fearful with reverent awe).
interpretation: The verse describes the true believers as those whose awe of God is rooted in an intimate consciousness of His majesty and their own accountability. Their fear (ishfaq) is not mere dread but a tender, watchful anxiety that they may fall short of what their Lord requires, and this inner trembling is what drives them to sincere devotion and careful conduct. The verse thus places reverent fear at the heart of faith: it is the emotional root from which righteous action grows, distinguishing those who truly know their Lord from those who are heedless of Him.

translation: And those who believe in the signs of their Lord.
interpretation: The verse describes the true believers as those whose faith is not merely a matter of words but is directed toward the signs of God. These signs (ayat) include both the revealed verses of scripture and the evident signs manifest in creation. To believe in them is to accept them with conviction, to reflect upon them, and to let them shape one's conduct, so that faith becomes a living, attentive relationship with the Lord who makes His signs known.

translation: And those who do not associate anything with their Lord.
interpretation: The verse describes the believers' pure monotheism, a sincere devotion in which they direct their worship, trust, and reliance solely to their Lord, free from any form of shirk, whether open idolatry or subtle forms of hidden association such as seeking the praise of others or placing hope in creatures rather than the Creator. Their faith is thus not merely a verbal claim but a consistent orientation of the heart and conduct toward the One God, which is the foundation upon which the other qualities of the righteous in this passage rest.

translation: And those who give what they give while their hearts tremble, because they will be returning to their Lord.
interpretation: The verse describes a believer whose charity and good deeds are accompanied by fear rather than complacency. Their giving is not a display of merit but an act performed with a heart that is aware of its accountability before God. The trembling of the heart springs from the certainty of the return to the Lord, which keeps the believer humble, sincere, and watchful over the purity of intention. Thus the ideal of faith in this verse is not merely outward performance of duty, but the union of action with inward awe, so that the very act of giving becomes a means of drawing nearer to God while remaining mindful that all is ultimately owed to Him and that every deed will be weighed before Him.

translation: Those hasten toward good deeds, and they are foremost in them.
interpretation: The verse describes a believer whose inner drive is not merely to perform good when it is convenient, but to race toward it eagerly, as one who sees virtue as the highest prize. The phrase 'they are foremost in them' indicates that such people do not stop at the minimum obligation; they lead the way, anticipating opportunities for charity, worship, and service before others do. Their hastening reflects a heart that is awake to the value of the hereafter and that treats time and opportunity as precious and fleeting. The verse thus invites the reader to cultivate a spirit of initiative and urgency in doing what is right, measuring success not by how little one can get away with, but by how far one can outpace others in seeking God's pleasure.

translation: And We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity. And with Us is a record that speaks with truth, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: The verse establishes two foundations of divine justice: God never imposes upon a person a burden beyond what they are able to bear, so accountability is measured by one's capacity, intention, and means. It then assures that every deed is recorded in a book that speaks the truth without distortion or omission, so no one will be unjustly treated on the Day of Judgment. Together these affirm that the ultimate reckoning is perfectly fair, leaving the believer both mindful of responsibility and reassured against injustice.

translation: Nay, their hearts are in confusion about this, and they have deeds other than that which they are doing, [deeds] they will persist in.
interpretation: The verse describes the disbelievers' hearts being immersed in heedlessness and bewilderment regarding the revealed message, so that they remain absorbed in the affairs of this world and in their own chosen conduct. Their preoccupation with other deeds is presented as the root of their rejection: the heart, when sunk in ghafla, becomes unable to perceive the truth, and so they persist in their ways with determination. The verse thus warns that the cause of disbelief is not a lack of evidence but a heart that has been drawn away and buried beneath its own pursuits.

translation: Until, when We seize their affluent ones with punishment, behold, they cry out in supplication.
interpretation: The verse depicts the moment of reckoning for the wealthy and comfortable elite who were immersed in luxury and heedless of their Lord. Only when the punishment actually overtakes them do they turn to loud, desperate wailing, a cry that comes too late to be answered. It conveys that the pride and ease that made them deaf to the truth in life leave them helpless in the face of divine justice, and that the true measure of their state is revealed not in their prosperity but in their distress when it is taken from them.

translation: Do not cry out for help today; indeed, you will not be given any victory from Us.
interpretation: The verse depicts the moment of reckoning in the Hereafter, when the disbelievers who had arrogantly rejected revelation are told to stop their loud wailing and pleas. Their screaming has no benefit, because the help they once relied on, whether their idols, their allies, or their own strength, is gone, and no one can rescue them from God's judgment. It serves as a warning that worldly pride and false reliance collapse completely before the Divine court, and that true deliverance comes only from sincere faith and submission before the Day arrives.

translation: "My verses were indeed recited to you, but you used to turn back on your heels."
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who, having heard the clear revelations recited to them, abandoned the truth and retreated from it. Turning back on one's heels (nukus) pictures a deliberate, shameful withdrawal from guidance after it has been made plain, showing that the fault lies not in a lack of evidence but in a refusal to follow what was already known. It warns that clarity of revelation brings accountability, and that turning away from it after recognition is a grave form of spiritual regression.

translation: Being arrogant about it, you would gather by night telling tales and speaking nonsense, dismissing the revelation.
interpretation: The verse traces rejection of the revelation to pride rather than to a lack of evidence. The night gatherings, where they talked idly about the Qur'an, show that their dismissal was deliberate and social: they chose to mock and distract instead of listening with humility. Arrogance is the root, and the nightly chatter is its visible form, a way of keeping the message at arm's length while appearing to discuss it.

translation: Do they not then reflect upon the Word? Or has there come to them what did not come to their forefathers of old?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who refuse to contemplate the Qur'an, challenging them to reflect deeply on its message rather than dismissing it. It then suggests their resistance may stem from a claim that the message is unprecedented, that something has come to them which was never sent to their ancestors, so they reject it as novel. The verse implies that genuine reflection would reveal the continuity of the divine message with earlier revelations and the prophets sent before, and that a sincere heart, by pondering the Word, would recognize its truth instead of hiding behind inherited assumptions.

translation: Or did they not recognize their Messenger, so that they deny him?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who reject the Prophet by posing a pointed question: their denial is not born of genuine ignorance, since they knew him well, being his own people who had known his truthfulness, integrity, and character from his youth. Their rejection, then, is not the result of an unfamiliarity that would excuse them, but of stubbornness and a refusal to acknowledge what their own knowledge of him should have compelled them to accept. The verse thus shows that disbelief often lies not in a lack of evidence but in a willful turning away from a truth that is already recognized within the heart.

translation: Or do they say, "There is madness in him"? Rather, he has brought them the truth, but most of them are averse to the truth.
interpretation: The verse exposes the logic of those who rejected the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: unable to deny the clarity and sincerity of his message, they fall back on the accusation of madness, which is an evasion rather than a reasoned judgment. The verse then turns the charge around, affirming that what he brought is the truth itself, so the real problem lies not in the messenger's reason but in the hearts of the majority who dislike the truth because it confronts their desires, habits, and worldly interests. It thus teaches that rejection of guidance is often rooted in aversion of the soul rather than in genuine lack of evidence, and it consoles the believers by showing that the Prophet's mission is grounded in truth even when it is met with hostility.

translation: And if the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted. Rather, We have brought them their reminder, but they, from their reminder, are turning away.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the order of the cosmos rests on truth, which is by nature aligned with the real good and cannot bend to the caprices of human desire; were the divine truth to be reshaped according to what people wish for, the balance of creation would collapse. The phrase 'Rather, We have brought them their reminder' turns from hypothetical to fact: God has not left humanity without its message, and the Qur'an itself is that reminder addressed to them in their own tongue and concern. Yet the tragedy lies in their turning away, which exposes the real conflict not between truth and falsehood in the abstract but between the self's inclinations and the call to remembrance. The verse thus teaches that the failure is not in the reminder's clarity but in the heart that prefers its appetites to the message that would guide it.

translation: Or do you ask them for a payment? But the payment of your Lord is better, and He is the best of providers.
interpretation: The verse contrasts the Prophet's mission with the worldly motives of those who would demand compensation for guidance. Since the message is a mercy from God, its reward cannot be measured by human wages or material gain. The Prophet is thus shown to be disinterested, seeking nothing from his people, because the provision and recompense that truly matter come from God alone, whose sustenance is the most generous and enduring. The verse thereby affirms the sincerity of the call and directs the heart away from dependence on people toward trust in the Provider.

translation: And indeed, you invite them to a straight path.
interpretation: The verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad, affirming that his call is directed toward a path that is upright and unswerving. The phrase "you invite them" conveys both the sincerity and the persistence of his summons, while the "straight path" (sirat mustaqim) signifies the clear, balanced guidance of monotheism and righteous conduct that leaves no crookedness or ambiguity. The verse thus offers consolation and reassurance: the Prophet's mission is rightly guided, even when those who hear him turn away, and the responsibility of his call rests on delivering the message clearly.

translation: And indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are surely deviating from the path.
interpretation: The verse identifies disbelief in the Hereafter as the root of deviation from the straight path. Accountability in the afterlife gives human conduct its ultimate direction and moral weight; when a person no longer expects to answer before God for his deeds, his choices lose their anchor and he drifts away from guidance. Thus the verse presents belief in the Hereafter not as a peripheral doctrine but as the foundation that keeps the soul upon the path of righteousness, so that the denial of the Last Day becomes the cause from which turning away from divine guidance follows.

translation: And even if We were to have mercy upon them and remove the harm that is upon them, they would persist in their rebellion, wandering blindly.
interpretation: The verse exposes the depth of human obstinacy in the face of divine mercy. Hardship often serves as a moment of awakening, yet when relief comes, the heart that has not truly turned to God returns to its old arrogance and transgression, as if the warnings of suffering were forgotten the moment it passed. Their wandering is not the result of lacking guidance, but of a chosen attachment to their own excess, so that even grace becomes a further occasion for going astray. The verse thus warns the believer to recognize God's kindness as a call to gratitude and steadfastness, rather than merely a respite to return to heedlessness.

translation: And We had already seized them with punishment, yet they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor did they supplicate.
interpretation: This verse points to a recurring human failing: hardship is meant to awaken humility and turn the heart back toward its Creator, yet many people respond to affliction with obstinacy rather than submission. The punishment was not only a trial in itself but a summons to repentance, and the verse's emphasis lies on the missed opportunity, as the two verbs, istikanah (to abase oneself, to yield in meekness) and tadarru' (to plead humbly and with lowliness), describe the inner and outward posture that a sincere response would have taken. Its warning is that adversity which fails to soften the heart becomes a sign of spiritual hardness, and that the door of return remains open only so long as one chooses to walk through it.

translation: Until, when We open upon them a door of severe punishment, at that moment they will be plunged into despair.
interpretation: The verse shows that divine respite can be a test that ends abruptly. Those who persist in heedlessness are given room to continue, until the door they had long dismissed opens onto a punishment they can no longer avoid. The word mublisun, from iblas, signals a despair that strips away all their former confidence, showing that the hopes and arrogance that sustained them collapse the moment the reality they denied becomes visible.

translation: And it is He who produced for you hearing, sight, and hearts; little are you grateful.
interpretation: The verse directs attention to three faculties that are given to humans before any effort of their own: hearing, sight, and the heart (intellect and conscience). These are the very instruments through which a person receives signs, perceives the order of creation, and comes to knowledge and belief. Their ordering as a gift from the Creator makes the reproach sharper: the one who has been equipped to hear, see, and understand is expected to use these faculties to recognize the Giver, yet the Qur'an notes that gratitude is rare. Gratitude here is not merely verbal thanks but the directing of one's senses and reason toward obedience and acknowledgment of God's blessings.

translation: And it is He who multiplied you upon the earth, and to Him you will be gathered.
interpretation: The verse joins two great signs of divine power: the first is the creation and dispersal of humankind across the earth, which reveals that life on earth is a trust granted by God rather than a self-made achievement, so people should recognize their dependence and their accountability to the One who brought them into being. The second is the certainty of resurrection, for the same Lord who scattered humanity over the land will gather them again before Him on the Day of Judgment. Thus the verse links the beginning of existence with its end, urging the reader to live mindful that every person's journey on earth ends in a return to God, where deeds will be reckoned.

translation: And it is He who gives life and causes death, and His is the alternation of the night and the day. Will you not then use your reason?
interpretation: The verse directs the listener's attention from the self to the cosmos: the same Power that grants life and brings death also governs the regular succession of night and day, so the orderly alternation of time is itself a sign of a single, purposeful Creator who is not bound by the cycles He set in motion. By closing with a rhetorical question about reason, it calls for reflection rather than mere acceptance, implying that rational contemplation of birth, death, and the ordered passing of day and night should lead a person to recognize divine sovereignty and to act accordingly. The alternation of night and day may also remind the believer that human life itself is measured in such cycles, urging attentiveness to the time granted before one's own inevitable death.

translation: Nay, but they said the like of what the earlier ones had said.
interpretation: The verse describes the stubbornness of those who denied the messengers: when faced with the truth, they did not offer new reasoning but simply repeated the same objections their predecessors had raised against earlier prophets. Their denial is thus shown to be inherited and imitative rather than the result of honest reflection, a pattern that reveals that rejection of revelation often rests on tradition and habit instead of examination of evidence. The verse warns that repeating the excuses of past generations does not make them valid, and that the same heedlessness can recur in every age.

translation: They say: "When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we really be resurrected?"
interpretation: The verse captures the disbelievers' incredulity toward bodily resurrection. Their question is not a sincere inquiry but a denial rooted in the assumption that what has decayed into dust and scattered bones cannot be reassembled and given life again. By repeating the question with emphatic particles, they express certainty that resurrection is impossible. The Qur'an frequently answers such objections by pointing to the same God who first created humanity from nothing, implying that restoring what was once made is no greater a feat than originating it, and thus turning the verse's skepticism into a call to reflect on creation and accountability.

translation: "We have been promised this, we and our fathers before us. This is nothing but the fables of the ancients."
interpretation: The verse reflects the stance of those who deny the Resurrection and the promise of reckoning. Their claim that the warnings are merely old tales inherited from earlier generations shows how they dismiss the message of the Prophet by treating it as a repetition of unfounded legends rather than examining its truth. Their reliance on what their forefathers said, rather than on reason and revelation, exposes a heedlessness that the Qur'an repeatedly confronts, reminding them that the promise of God is true and that past generations who rejected the prophets were not spared the consequences of their denial.

translation: Say: "To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it, if you should know?"
interpretation: The verse poses a challenge that turns the questioner back on himself: ownership of the earth and all within it cannot be claimed by anyone but God, the Creator and Sustainer of all things, and the rhetorical 'if you know' exposes the obviousness of the answer to anyone who reflects honestly. Its force lies in leading the listener to acknowledge, through their own reasoning, that dominion is God's alone, so that submission to Him becomes the only rational response to the evidence of creation.

translation: They will say, "To Allah." Say, "Will you not then remember?"
interpretation: The verse is a rhetorical challenge posed to those who are asked whom the earth and whoever is in it belong to, and who insist that the answer is God, yet fail to draw the logical conclusion. Their own acknowledgment that ownership and dominion belong to Allah ought to awaken them to the reality of His sovereignty, and the question "will you not remember?" calls them back from heedlessness to reflection. The verse thus shows that the recognition of God as Lord is often present in the human heart, but it becomes meaningful only when it is remembered and allowed to shape one's conduct and belief.

translation: Say, "Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?"
interpretation: The verse poses a direct challenge to the reasoning of the listeners, asking them to name the One who holds dominion over the seven heavens and the vast Throne, the greatest of created things. By framing the question as a plain matter to be answered, it draws the mind toward a truth its audience already acknowledged: that the ultimate Lord of the cosmos is God alone. The exalted image of the Throne and the layered heavens conveys boundless sovereignty, so that the question itself becomes a call to reflect on who truly deserves worship, obedience, and trust, and to recognize that a Lord of such majesty cannot be shared with any other.

translation: They will say, "(It belongs) to Allah." Say, "Then will you not fear Allah?"
interpretation: The verse exposes the inconsistency of those who, when asked about the ownership and dominion of the earth and its contents (as in the preceding verses, 23:84-89), readily acknowledge that it all belongs to God, yet fail to draw the logical conclusion. Their own admission should lead them to reverence and God-consciousness, since the One who holds absolute sovereignty is the One who is owed obedience and awe. The rhetorical question, 'Will you not then be mindful of God?', calls the heart back from heedlessness to taqwa, reminding that acknowledging God's lordship in word must be matched by fearing Him in conduct.

translation: Say: "In whose hand is the dominion of all things, who protects and against whom no protection can be given, if you should know?"
interpretation: The verse presents a challenge to reason and conscience: if the idolaters and doubters truly possess knowledge, they must acknowledge that absolute sovereignty over everything belongs to God alone. Since He is the one who grants protection (yujir) while none can shelter anyone against Him, it follows that no one else is worthy of worship or of being placed beside Him. The phrase "if you should know" turns the question into a rebuke, inviting the listener to recognize through their own answer the unity of divine lordship and the futility of seeking refuge in any power other than God.

translation: They will say, "[It belongs] to Allah." Say, "Then how are you deluded?"
interpretation: The verse confronts those who, when asked about the owner and ruler of the earth and its inhabitants, readily concede that it all belongs to God, yet still turn away from Him. The question "Then how are you deluded?" exposes the inconsistency of their position: having acknowledged God as the source of all things, they nonetheless are led astray from the truth they already affirm. It calls the listener to reflect on how the mind can be bewildered after recognizing its own admission, and to draw the logical conclusion that worship and obedience belong to the One they confess as Lord.

translation: Nay, We have brought them the truth, and indeed they are liars.
interpretation: The verse rejects the claim of those who opposed the Prophet that he was a fabricator or a madman, asserting instead that God has conveyed to them the clear truth of revelation, the message of monotheism and resurrection that they had the means to recognize. Their denial is not due to any lack of clarity in what was presented but to their own obstinacy and attachment to falsehood; the accusation of lying is thus turned back upon them, showing that the fault lies not with the message but with those who reject it despite its evident truth.

translation: God has not taken any offspring, and there is no god alongside Him; otherwise each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overpowered others. Glory be to God above what they describe.
interpretation: The verse uses a rational argument from the unity of creation to refute the claim that God has a son or partners. If there were multiple deities, each would be independent in his own creation and would seek to keep it for himself, which would lead to conflict, separation of domains, and the domination of some over others. The observable order, harmony, and unity of the universe testify that one absolute Creator governs it. Therefore the verse concludes by declaring God exalted above all the false attributes that the polytheists ascribe to Him, affirming that absolute perfection belongs to Him alone.

translation: (He is) the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed; so exalted is He above what they associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's complete knowledge, encompassing both what is hidden from human perception (al-ghayb) and what is observed and present (al-shahada), so nothing escapes His awareness. Having established this perfect knowledge and sovereignty, the verse declares Him far above the partners that the idolaters attribute to Him. The logic is that a being who knows all things, both concealed and apparent, is uniquely worthy of worship, and any association of others with Him is therefore both baseless and a diminishment of His absolute transcendence.

translation: He said: "My Lord, if You should show me that which they are promised..." (Surah al-Mu'minun 23:93, with the verse's wording rendered as: "Say: My Lord, if You show me that which they are promised.")
interpretation: The verse teaches the believer to turn to Allah with humble supplication when faced with the prospect of the punishment and the promised threat that the disbelievers mock. It expresses a desire not to be left among the wrongdoers when that torment descends, so the Prophet is instructed to ask his Lord to keep him clear of what befalls the transgressing people. It reflects the principle that a servant should seek refuge in God from the consequences of injustice and place his trust entirely in God's mercy and justice.

translation: My Lord, do not place me among the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: This is a supplication of Prophet Musa (Moses) with his Lord, which comes after a plea for mercy and forgiveness for the wrong he had committed. Its meaning reflects a profound awareness that one's standing among people is ultimately determined by God's guidance and protection. The believer asks to be kept away from the company, path, and fate of those who persist in injustice, recognizing that the greatest safeguard against being counted among the wrongdoers is divine protection, sincere repentance, and a steadfast refusal to follow the ways of oppression. It teaches humility before God and the importance of seeking refuge in Him from becoming like those who transgress against truth and against themselves.

translation: And indeed, We are able to show you what We have promised them.
interpretation: The verse assures the Prophet that Allah's promised punishment for the disbelievers will certainly come to pass, and that Allah has full power to let him witness its fulfillment in his lifetime. It also conveys that the timing of divine retribution rests entirely with Allah, not with human desire or challenge, so the Prophet is to remain steadfast and trust in God's perfect power and wisdom rather than be disturbed by the disbelievers' delay or mockery.

translation: Repel evil with that which is better. We are most knowing of what they describe.
interpretation: The verse instructs the believer to meet wrongdoing not with the same harshness but with the finest response available, such as patience, forgiveness, gentleness, and good conduct. Such a response has the power to transform a hostile opponent into a close friend, as the verse goes on to describe in the following lines. The closing phrase reminds the believer that God knows fully the slander and false descriptions that the wrongdoers voice, so the believer need not retaliate in kind, but can entrust the matter to God's knowledge and justice.

translation: And say, "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the incitements of the devils."
interpretation: The verse teaches the believer to turn directly to God as Lord (Rabb), the One who nurtures and protects, and to seek refuge in Him alone against the subtle whisperings and promptings of the devils. The word 'hamazat' (sudden stirrings or pricks) points to the faint, quick impulses that stir the heart toward evil before a person is fully aware of them, so the remedy is not only to resist sin but to take shelter in God at the very first movement of such suggestion. It shows that spiritual safety comes from constant reliance on God's protection rather than from one's own strength alone.

translation: And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, from their presence (from their coming near) to me.
interpretation: The verse expresses the believer's humble dependence on God as the sole refuge against the whisperings and harmful influences of evil forces, the devils (shayatin), whose presence is to be feared. By asking God's protection not only against their deeds but against their very approach, the speaker acknowledges human vulnerability and places complete trust in the Lord, who alone can shield the heart from corruption. It teaches that a sincere servant seeks protection through prayer and turning to God, especially at moments when evil seems near, rather than relying on his own strength.

translation: Until, when death comes to one of them, he says: "My Lord, send me back,
interpretation: This verse depicts the moment of a person's final reckoning, when the reality of death lifts the veil from the heedless and they suddenly long for a second chance. The plea "send me back" reveals that what was once dismissed as trivial, the worldly life and its distractions, now appears in its true light as a lost opportunity for good deeds. Its placement within the surrounding context, which speaks of those who squandered their lives in denial, underscores that regret arrives only at the threshold of death, when repentance and return are no longer possible. It is a warning to the living to act while action remains within their power.

translation: "So that I may do righteous work in what I have left behind." No! It is merely a word he is saying, and behind them is a barrier until the Day they are resurrected.
interpretation: The verse depicts a soul at the moment of death, seeing the reality of the Hereafter, and pleading to return to the world to make amends for what it neglected. Its request is rejected with the emphatic "No!", for the return it seeks is only a empty utterance that cannot be fulfilled. Between the dead and the world they left stands a barrier (barzakh), a state of separation that lasts until the Day of Resurrection, when all will be raised. The verse thus warns the living that the opportunity for righteous deeds is bounded by this life, and that regret after death will not grant a second chance.

translation: And when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship ties among them that day, nor will they ask about one another.
interpretation: The verse points to the moment of the Resurrection, when the blast of the Trumpet ends the world and every human bond that once defined a person's identity and status collapses. Lineage, tribe, and family, which in worldly life gave honor and protection, lose all their force before the Day of Judgment, so each soul stands alone and is judged by its own deeds. The phrase that they will not ask one another signals the overwhelming preoccupation of that Day, in which the fear of one's own fate absorbs every person and mutual concern is suspended. The verse thus teaches that true and lasting worth rests not on ancestry or social connection but on faith and righteous conduct, the only things that can be carried into the presence of God.

translation: So as for those whose scales are heavy, it is they who will be the successful.
interpretation: The verse ties success in the Hereafter directly to the weight of one's good deeds on the Day of Reckoning. The 'scales' (mawazin) are the instrument by which each person's actions are measured, and their heaviness signifies that good conduct, faith, and righteousness have outweighed evil. Those who attain this are the 'muflihun,' the ones who achieve true and lasting salvation, having escaped the loss that the Qur'an describes for those whose scales are light. The imagery teaches that a person's eternal fate is determined by the substance of what they have actually done in this life, so that salvation is earned through sincere and sustained righteous action.

translation: And as for those whose scales are light, those are the ones who have lost their souls, abiding eternally in Hell.
interpretation: The verse presents the Day of Judgment as a moment of weighing deeds, where the scale stands for the true measure of a person's faith and conduct. Lightness of the scale signals that good works and sincere belief did not outweigh what was wrong, so the real loss is not of wealth or worldly status but of the self itself, the soul's own potential for nearness to God. The mention of eternal abiding in Hell underscores that this loss is final when it is not repaired in life. The verse thus calls the listener to examine the weight of their actions now, while there is still time to turn back and make the balance heavy with righteousness.

translation: The Fire scorches their faces, and they therein are grim-faced, with their lips drawn back from their teeth.
interpretation: The verse portrays the hellfire as striking the most sensitive and honored part of the human being, the face, so that the sinners are shown in a state of utter disfigurement and anguish. The word kalihun describes the grimace of severe pain and distress, in which the lips recede from the teeth as the burning takes hold. The image conveys that the punishment is not merely external but total, reaching the very countenance that once expressed pride and heedlessness, and so it reverses the dignity they displayed in the world. It also serves as a warning that the ugliness of sin, which the soul hides in this life, will be made visible on the face in the Hereafter.

translation: Were not My verses recited to you, and yet you used to deny them?
interpretation: The verse is a rebuke addressed to the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, reminding them that Allah's signs were conveyed to them clearly through the messengers and the revelation, leaving them without excuse. Their question-form reproach highlights that the denial was not born of ignorance of the message but of wilful rejection after it had been plainly presented. It thus underscores human responsibility: the guidance reached them, and their own choice to call it false is what brings them to account.

translation: They will say: "Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us, and we were a people who had gone astray."
interpretation: The verse depicts the people of the Fire acknowledging, too late, that their own misfortune and deviation were the cause of their ruin. The word shiqwa, rendered as wretchedness, points to the wretched state their own choices produced, which overpowered them, so that they did not follow the guidance when it came. By confessing that they had been a people who strayed, they admit that the fault lay with them and not with God. The verse thus teaches that persistent disobedience hardens a person until it becomes a force that controls him, and that the admission of error comes only when it can no longer benefit the one who makes it.

translation: Our Lord, bring us out of it; then if we return (to disbelief and wrongdoing), indeed we will be wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by the people of the Fire (as in Surah al-Mu'minun, 23:107), who beg to be released from it, and it reveals a profound moment of recognition: having been shown the truth of their condition, they confess their own culpability in advance. Their words express a sincere resolve that they would never again return to the deeds that brought them there, yet the verse also exposes the deep human tendency to revert to what is familiar and harmful once the immediate fear passes. It thus teaches that true repentance is not merely the request for deliverance but a lasting commitment, and that every person who relapses into wrongdoing after knowing better takes on the very injustice from which they prayed to be spared.

translation: He said, "Remain in it with contempt, and do not speak to Me."
interpretation: This verse comes at the end of the scene in Surah al-Mu'minun (23:108) in which the dwellers of the Fire plead to be taken out, only to be rebuffed. The command "ikhsa'u" is a harsh word of rejection, used for a dog driven away in disgrace, and it expresses the complete severance of the disbelievers from any mercy or hope of relief. The added words "and do not speak to Me" shut the door on their pleading and their attempts at negotiation, so that the punishment is not only physical but also a final humiliation and a silence imposed upon them. The verse teaches that in the Hereafter the means of appeal that were available in this world are gone, and that the consequence of persistent denial is a sealed and definitive exclusion, which should move the listener to reflect and turn to God while there is still time.

translation: Indeed, there was a group of My servants who used to say, 'Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy on us, and You are the best of the merciful.'
interpretation: The verse reveals the character of the believers who are described as a distinct group among God's servants, marked by humble supplication rather than pride or self-reliance. Their prayer begins with faith ('we have believed'), which they present as the foundation for seeking forgiveness and mercy, showing that true belief is joined with an awareness of one's own shortcomings. By concluding with an acknowledgment that God is the best of the merciful, they place their hope entirely in His boundless compassion. The verse thus teaches that the surest path to divine mercy is sincere faith coupled with humble, hopeful reliance on God's mercy and forgiveness.

translation: But you took them in mockery, until they caused you to forget My remembrance, and you used to laugh at them.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who made the faithful a target of ridicule. Their mockery became so absorbing that it drew them away from the remembrance of God, so that the very act of scorning others turned into a neglect of their own accountability to Him. It warns that treating sincere believers with contempt is not a harmless pastime but a path that can weaken one's own heedfulness of God, and that the laughter of the heedless will be answered by the consequences of their forgetfulness.

translation: Indeed, I have rewarded them today for their patience; indeed, they are the ones who are the triumphant.
interpretation: The verse presents patience (sabr) as the decisive quality that earns divine recompense, and it ties that recompense to ultimate success (fawz), which in the Qur'anic sense is not worldly gain but deliverance and acceptance before God on the Day of Judgment. The word 'today' points to the moment of reckoning, when the true value of endurance under trial becomes visible. The repetition of 'indeed' (inna) emphasizes the certainty of the promise, so that the faithful who endured hardship, temptation, and opposition are assured that their steadfastness is not lost but fully repaid.

translation: He said, "How long did you remain on the earth, counted in number of years?"
interpretation: This verse belongs to the story of the People of the Cave (Ahl al-Kahf) in Surah al-Kahf, and more precisely to the story of the sleepers' awakening after a long sleep. Allah, through the speaker (who is one of them, or a questioner who has come to know their state), poses a question that turns their attention from the immediate to the measure of time: how long they stayed on earth, counted in years. The question is not asked for information Allah lacks, but to awaken them to the reality of time as a created thing that is subject to the Creator's will. The verse thus teaches that a human being's sense of time is limited and relative, and that the one who sleeps for years may feel he has slept only a day or part of a day. This highlights the sign of God's power over life and death, and invites reflection on the brevity of worldly life compared with the reckoning that lies ahead.

translation: They said, "We remained a day or part of a day, so ask those who keep count."
interpretation: The verse comes from the story of the People of the Cave (Surah Al-Kahf), who slept for centuries and, upon waking, were uncertain of how long they had stayed. Their answer reflects the limits of human perception of time: when the mind is cut off from the normal flow of events, it cannot reliably measure duration, and so they defer the question to others who can count. The phrase "those who keep count" points to the broader lesson that true knowledge of time and of events belongs to God alone, who knows exactly how long they remained, and that humility before that knowledge is the proper response to what we cannot verify ourselves.

translation: He said: "You remained but a little, if only you knew."
interpretation: The verse places the speaker's words in a moment of stark reckoning, where the sense of time that people carried in the world is revealed as brief and hollow once the truth is laid bare. The phrase "if only you knew" turns the statement into a rebuke: the duration that once seemed long to them was short, and their failure lay not in the length of their stay but in their lack of true knowledge while they lived. It invites the listener to measure worldly time against the eternal, so that the brevity of the life they spent becomes a lesson in what should have been known and acted upon before it was too late.

translation: Did you then suppose that We created you without purpose, and that you would not be returned to Us?
interpretation: The verse confronts the human assumption that existence is purposeless and free of accountability. By posing a rhetorical question, it exposes the incoherence of such a belief: creation carrying no aim would be inconsistent with the wisdom of the Creator. Creation is thus framed as purposeful, and the certainty of return to God follows from that purpose, since a meaningful creation implies a reckoning in which deeds are weighed. The verse calls the listener to reflect on the reason for their own existence and to live with awareness of the eventual return to their Lord.

translation: So exalted is Allah, the True King. There is no deity except Him, the Lord of the Honorable Throne.
interpretation: The verse opens with a declaration of God's transcendence (ta'ala), placing Him above every imperfection and every partner ascribed to Him, and it immediately follows with the ultimate sovereignty of Allah as al-Malik al-Haqq, the King whose kingship is real and whose authority is not borrowed or temporary, in contrast to the apparent and fleeting kingships of the world. The affirmation that there is no deity but Him returns the heart to pure monotheism, and the reference to Him as Lord of the Mighty Throne (al-'Arsh al-Karim) directs the believer to contemplate the vastest of created things as under His absolute dominion, so that the exaltation of God is tied to the recognition that all power, governance, and majesty belong to Him alone.

translation: And whoever invokes along with God another deity, for which he has no proof, then his reckoning is only with his Lord. Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed.
interpretation: The verse identifies the sin of associating partners with God as rooted in the absence of any evidence: a claim to divinity made without proof is empty, and so the one who makes it bears full responsibility before his Lord, who alone will judge him. By stating that the disbelievers will not prosper, the verse ties worship to reason and accountability, inviting the listener to examine on what basis he directs his devotion. The emphasis on the lack of proof suggests that sound belief must rest on clear evidence, and that true success lies only in sincere devotion to the one God.

translation: And say, "My Lord, forgive and have mercy, and You are the best of the merciful."
interpretation: This verse, which closes Surah al-Mu'minun (23:118), teaches the believer to end all supplication and conduct by turning humbly to God with a plea for both forgiveness and mercy. The pairing is significant: forgiveness (maghfirah) removes the burden of past sins, while mercy (rahmah) grants what is needed for the future, so the servant asks to be cleared of wrongdoing and sustained by divine compassion. By calling God "the best of the merciful," the supplicant acknowledges that no human or created source of mercy can equal God's, and places complete reliance on Him. The verse thus models a posture of humility, dependence, and hope, reminding the believer that the most fitting response to the trials and disbelief described throughout the surah is to seek refuge in the boundless mercy of the Lord rather than in one's own merit.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. A surah We have sent down and made obligatory, and in it We have sent down clear verses, that you may remember.
interpretation: The opening declares the surah a divine gift and a binding command at once: it is sent down by God's own will and its contents are made obligatory upon the believers, so that revelation is not merely received as information but accepted as a law to be lived by. The phrase "and in it We have sent down clear verses" points to the surah as a vessel of unambiguous signs, where the clarity of the verses is the means by which hearts are guided. The closing purpose, "that you may remember," frames the whole revelation as a call to recollection: the purpose of clear guidance is not intellectual display but awakening the human being to his forgotten covenant with his Creator, so that obligation and remembrance become one movement of the soul.

translation: The adulterous woman and the adulterous man - flog each one of them with a hundred lashes. And let not pity for them take hold of you in the religion of Allah, if you should believe in Allah and the Last Day. And let a group of the believers witness their punishment.
interpretation: This verse establishes the prescribed punishment for illicit sexual intercourse (zina) between unmarried persons: a hundred lashes applied equally to both man and woman, without distinction of status or gender. It forbids allowing compassion to override the execution of God's law, tying the strictness of enforcement to the sincerity of one's faith in God and the Last Day, since mercy misplaced in the application of divine ordinance would undermine justice itself. The requirement that a group of believers witness the punishment serves a public function: it makes the penalty a visible deterrent, and it ensures that the sentence is carried out openly and not in private, so that the community as a whole shares in upholding moral boundaries and learns from the consequences of transgression.

translation: The adulterer does not marry except an adulteress or a polytheist, and the adulteress is not married except by an adulterer or a polytheist. And that has been made unlawful to the believers.
interpretation: The verse establishes a moral boundary on marriage by linking it to the character and faith of the spouses. A person known for illicit sexual conduct is, in this ruling, paired with one of similar character or with one outside the community of faith, and the believers are commanded to avoid such unions. Read in its context, the ruling addresses the honor of the believing household and the sanctity of marriage as a covenant built on chastity and shared faith, rather than merely describing a social reality of the time. The phrasing 'and that has been made unlawful' signals that the prohibition is binding upon the community, pointing to marriage as an institution that should protect lineage, dignity, and the spiritual unity of the believers.

translation: And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses - lash them eighty lashes and do not accept from them testimony ever. And those are the defiantly disobedient.
