interpretation: This verse establishes the legal penalty for slander against chaste women (qadhf) in the context of the Qur'anic principle of protecting honor and reputation. Because the accusation of unchastity is grave and carries severe social consequences, Islam requires the accuser to substantiate it with four eyewitnesses, a standard so demanding that it effectively discourages baseless accusation and shields the innocent from public defamation. Those who fail to meet this burden are punished with eighty lashes and are permanently disqualified as witnesses, since a person who casts unfounded charges has forfeited the trust essential to testimony. The verse thus joins legal deterrence with moral judgment, labeling such slanderers as fasiqun, those who have departed from obedience, and teaches that the tongue must be restrained where proof is absent, reflecting the broader Qur'anic concern that justice, honor, and the integrity of the community be protected.

translation: Except for those who repent after that and make amends, for indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse opens an exception to the preceding severe judgment, showing that the door of repentance remains open so long as a person turns back sincerely. Repentance alone is not enough in the sense of mere words; it must be accompanied by reform (islah), meaning the repentant person repairs what was corrupted, makes amends for the harm done, and returns to righteous conduct. The closing names of Allah, Ghafur (the One who veils and forgives sins) and Rahim (the One whose mercy is continuous and encompassing), reassure the believer that divine forgiveness is greater than any transgression once it is genuinely sought, and that God's mercy is the ground on which human reform becomes possible.

translation: And those who accuse their wives [of adultery] and have no witnesses except themselves - then the testimony of one of them is four testimonies by Allah that he is certainly among the truthful.
interpretation: This verse establishes the procedure of li'an, the oath of mutual condemnation, for a husband who accuses his wife of adultery without having witnesses other than himself. Since the husband cannot produce four eyewitnesses as required for a charge of zina, the law grants him a substitute: he swears four times by Allah that his accusation is true, which in effect places his own word in the position of the required testimony. The emphasis on the oath being sworn by Allah reflects the gravity of the matter, since the one swearing calls down God as witness to his sincerity, and the surrounding verses show that the wife can likewise refute the charge with her own oath, with the fifth oath invoking divine curse or wrath upon the liar. The ruling thus protects against the baseless besmirching of a spouse's honor while keeping the burden of proof within a framework of solemn accountability before God.

translation: And the fifth [testimony will be] that the curse of Allah be upon him if he is among the liars.
interpretation: This verse completes the procedure of li'an, the oath of mutual cursing between spouses who accuse one another of adultery without witnesses. After the husband has sworn four times by Allah to the truth of his charge, the fifth oath calls down Allah's curse upon himself should he be lying. The solemn structure reflects the gravity of accusing a spouse of unchastity, and it places the matter under divine judgment rather than human proof. By binding the accuser to a self-imprecation, the law protects both the honor of the marriage and the principle that a false accusation carries a consequence the accuser must bear before God.

translation: And it shall avert the punishment from her if she swears four oaths by Allah that he is surely among the liars.
interpretation: This verse completes the legal procedure of li'an between spouses, where a wife accused by her husband of adultery, and unable to produce witnesses, is shielded from punishment by her own solemn testimony. Four times she swears by God that her husband is lying, and the repeated oath, sworn in the name of the Divine, makes her claim weighty and binding before God, lifting the threat of the prescribed punishment from her. The mechanism reflects the Qur'an's concern for justice where one's word alone cannot be verified, placing the matter before God as the ultimate witness, and it protects the dignity of a woman against an accusation without proof while ensuring that a false accusation is itself weighed in the sight of God.

translation: And the fifth (oath) is that the Wrath of Allah be upon her if he is among the truthful.
interpretation: This verse belongs to the rite of li'an, the mutual oath-taking between spouses when a husband accuses his wife of adultery without witnesses. After the husband's four oaths testifying to his truthfulness, the fifth oath invokes God's wrath upon himself if he lies; the verse's phrasing as applied to the wife in this context is the counterpart of the wife's own oath that follows. The lesson emphasized is the gravity of invoking God as witness in matters of honor and lineage, so that the matter is placed entirely under divine judgment when human proof is lacking, and it protects both the accused from unjust punishment and the family from unfounded slander by requiring that a false accusation be answered before God, whose knowledge of the hidden surpasses any human court.

translation: And were it not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, and that Allah is Accepting of repentance and Wise...
interpretation: The verse reminds the believers that the very fact that they were spared from the consequences of their error was itself a manifestation of Allah's grace and mercy, not a result of their own merit. Its closing names, the One who accepts repentance and the All-Wise, teach that divine forgiveness is open to those who turn back, and that Allah's judgments and dealings are governed by perfect wisdom, so that the believer should respond to His favor with gratitude, humility, and a sincere return to Him.

translation: Indeed, those who came with the slander are a faction among you. Do not think it bad for you; rather, it is good for you. For every person among them is what he earned of sin, and he who took upon himself the greater part of it will have a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse refers to the incident of the slander against 'Aisha, the Prophet's wife, may God be pleased with her, in which a group among the believers spread the false accusation. God consoles the wronged household and the community by revealing that what seemed a trial is in truth a good, since it exposed hypocrisy, purified the believers, and revealed their innocence through revelation. It establishes personal moral responsibility: each participant bears the sin proportionate to his own share in spreading the falsehood, while the one who led and magnified the slander, bearing the greatest share of it, faces a severe punishment. The lesson is that a community must guard its honor and reputation from baseless accusation, and that trials can carry hidden benefits for those who remain steadfast.

translation: Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think well of one another and say, "This is an obvious lie"?
interpretation: The verse rebukes the believers for not immediately rejecting the slander against 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, when it first reached them. It teaches that a community of faith should give its members the benefit of the doubt, and that when a serious accusation is spread without evidence, one's own conscience and the bond of brotherhood and sisterhood demand that it be dismissed at once as a fabrication rather than repeated or believed. The phrase 'think well of themselves' points to the ideal of the believers being one body, where what harms one member is felt as harm to all, so that suspicion of a fellow believer is treated as suspicion of oneself.

translation: Why did they not bring four witnesses for it? Since they did not bring the witnesses, it is they who are the liars in the sight of God.
interpretation: The verse addresses the slander against the chaste believers, where the accusers are required to produce four eyewitnesses to a charge of adultery; the requirement of four witnesses sets an exceedingly high standard of proof, protecting honor and preventing reckless accusation. The failure to produce such witnesses renders the accusers liable to be judged as liars before God, shifting the moral weight of the accusation back onto those who spread it. The divine judgment here reflects a principle that the reputation of a person must not be damaged on the basis of rumor, and that anyone who makes a grave charge without proof bears the responsibility for that falsehood.

translation: And had it not been for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, in this world and the Hereafter, a great punishment would have touched you for what you plunged into.
interpretation: The verse addresses the believers after the slander against A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, which spread among them through careless repetition. It shows that the only thing that spared them a severe consequence was Allah's grace and mercy, not their own merit. The phrase "what you plunged into" points to the way they eagerly took up and spread baseless accusation without knowledge, treating it lightly while it was grave in the sight of Allah. The verse thus teaches that idle speech about the honor of others is a serious matter, and that a believer's safety from its consequences depends on Allah's mercy, which should prompt humility, vigilance over one's tongue, and care not to repeat what one cannot verify.

translation: When you received it on your tongues and said with your mouths what you had no knowledge of, and you considered it trivial while it was, in the sight of Allah, grave.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who spread a grave accusation (the slander against 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, in the Hadith of the Slander) without verifying it. Their error lay in three stages: their tongues passed the lie along readily, their mouths uttered what they had no knowledge of, and they regarded it as a minor matter when in God's estimation it was a serious sin. The lesson is that speech about others, especially damaging speech, carries weight before God regardless of how casually it is treated, and that believers should respond to rumor with verification and restraint rather than repetition.

translation: And why, when you heard it, did you not say, "It is not for us to speak of this. Glory be to You! This is a tremendous slander."
interpretation: The verse rebukes the believers for failing to react immediately and instinctively when they first heard the vicious rumor (the slander against the Prophet's wife A'isha). A sound faith should recognize at once that such an accusation is baseless and unthinkable, so the true believer must reject it outright, glorify God by declaring Him free from any such imperfection, and label the allegation for what it is: a monstrous lie. The passage teaches that a community must guard its honor and that repeating or entertaining slander, rather than refuting it, is a grave failure of moral judgment.

translation: Allah admonishes you never to return to the like of this, ever again, if you are [truly] believers.
interpretation: The verse, addressed to believers, warns against repeating a grave wrong that has just been condemned, here the matter of slandering the chaste wives of the Prophet in the incident of the false accusation (al-ifk), and by extension any similar transgression. It presents the admonition as an act of divine guidance and care rather than mere prohibition: God advises the community never to revisit such conduct. It then ties the command to faith itself, implying that true belief is proven by heeding this counsel, so that persistence in such harm would contradict the sincerity of one's iman.

translation: And Allah makes clear to you the verses (signs), and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse presents divine clarification as an ongoing act of mercy: Allah does not leave His guidance vague, but explains His signs so that human beings can distinguish truth from falsehood and act accordingly. The closing names, the All-Knowing and the All-Wise, tie this clarity to divine knowledge and wisdom, indicating that the laws and guidance He makes plain are precisely fitted to human needs, and that the believer's task is to reflect on these signs with humility and trust in the One who explains them.

translation: Indeed, those who love that indecency should spread among those who believe will have a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter. And Allah knows, while you do not know.
interpretation: The verse warns against a subtle corruption of the heart: taking pleasure in seeing immorality and scandal circulate among the believers. Such a desire is itself sinful, because it turns a community's moral fabric into a field for gossip, slander, and the publicizing of others' faults. The threat of painful punishment in both worlds shows that Allah judges intentions as well as deeds, and the closing reminder that Allah knows what people do not know calls for humility, restraint in judging others, and guarding the honor of fellow believers, especially by concealing their private failings rather than exposing them.

translation: And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, and that Allah is Kind and Merciful, [you would have been ruined].
interpretation: The verse turns the believers' attention from the sin they committed to the source of their salvation: the only reason they were not destroyed for their fault is Allah's bounty and mercy, not their own merit. Its repetition of Allah's gentleness and compassion (ra'uf rahim) teaches that divine mercy is the ground on which human weakness is covered, so the proper response is gratitude, humility, and a renewed turning back to Him rather than despair or self-justification.

translation: O you who have believed, do not follow the footsteps of Satan. And whoever follows the footsteps of Satan - indeed, he enjoins immorality and wrongdoing. And if not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, not one of you would ever have been pure, but Allah purifies whom He wills. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.
interpretation: The verse warns believers that Satan's path always leads toward what is shameful and evil, so the safeguard against it is not self-reliance but the grace and mercy of God, which alone makes any person pure. Recognizing one's own dependence on divine favor should therefore produce humility, vigilance against temptation, and a sincere turning back to God, who hears all and knows every heart and what each person truly deserves.

translation: And let not those of virtue and wealth among you swear not to give to close relatives, the needy, and those who emigrated in the cause of Allah. Let them pardon and overlook. Do you not like that Allah should forgive you? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, revealed concerning Abu Bakr after he swore to stop supporting Mistah ibn Uthathah who had joined the slander against 'A'ishah, teaches that generosity must not be withdrawn out of anger or wounded pride. Those blessed with status and means are commanded to continue giving to kin, the poor, and the emigrants, and to replace resentment with pardon and forgiveness. The verse links human forgiveness to divine forgiveness: one who wishes to be forgiven by God must be forgiving toward others, so that the reward of mercy returns to the one who shows it.

translation: Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unwary, believing women [of adultery] are cursed in this world and the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment.
interpretation: This verse, part of the passage on the slander of 'A'isha, establishes the gravity of false accusation of chastity against honorable believing women. By describing them as cursed in both worlds and as facing a great punishment, it treats the injury to a woman's honor and reputation as a grave sin whose harm reaches beyond the individual to the integrity of the community. The qualities named, being chaste, unwary of such charges, and believing, highlight the innocence of the victims and the cruelty of the accuser, and the verse thereby urges believers to guard their tongues and to protect the dignity of others before spreading unverified accusations.

translation: On the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will testify against them concerning what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse presents a vivid image of the Day of Judgment in which the body itself becomes a witness against the one who misused it. The tongue, hand, and foot, the very instruments through which a person speaks, acts, and moves, are shown turning against their owner, so that no deed remains hidden and no excuse can be made. This conveys a moral lesson: every faculty entrusted to a person is a trust that will be accounted for, and the self that is now the author of its actions will then be exposed by those same limbs. It invites the believer to align speech, conduct, and movement with righteousness now, since the body's testimony is inescapable.

translation: On that Day, Allah will pay them their full due, their true recompense, and they will know that Allah is the Manifest Truth.
interpretation: The verse points to the Day of Judgment as the moment when the hidden reality of every human deed is laid bare. Allah's justice ("al-Haqq") will be fully manifest: each soul receives its exact due, neither more nor less, so the recompense itself becomes a proof of the truth of what was promised. The disbelievers who denied the Hereafter or mocked the idea of divine accountability will then see with certainty that Allah is the Real, the one whose existence, promise and judgment are unshakeable and self-evident. The verse thus connects the reality of justice with the reality of God: the final reckoning is the place where the truth that was obscured in the world becomes visible to all.

translation: Wicked women are for wicked men, and wicked men are for wicked women; and good women are for good men, and good men are for good women. Those are cleared of what they say; for them is forgiveness and an honorable provision.
interpretation: The verse establishes a principle of moral correspondence in human relationships: people of corrupt character tend to be drawn to and matched with their like, while those of purity and goodness find their fitting companions among the upright. Its context, traditionally linked to the slander against 'A'isha, shows that the righteous are vindicated against false accusations, since those who are truly pure are placed beyond the reach of the lies spread about them. The verse thus assures the innocent of God's protection of their honor, and promises them forgiveness and abundant, noble reward, while calling the community to measure people by their character and to refrain from casting baseless accusations.

translation: O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you have asked permission and greeted their occupants with peace. That is better for you, that you may be mindful.
interpretation: The verse establishes the sanctity of the private home as a space of personal dignity and privacy, even among believers. Seeking permission (istі'nas) before entering is an act of courtesy that protects the inhabitants from intrusion and preserves trust between people. Greeting them with salam before entering turns the act of access into an act of peace and mutual goodwill, so that the household is approached as a place of safety rather than a place to be surprised. The closing phrase, 'that you may be mindful,' shows that these manners are not mere social etiquette but a discipline of the heart: by respecting the boundaries of others, a person trains his or her consciousness of God, who sees what is hidden and who loves that people guard one another's honor.

translation: And if you find no one therein, then do not enter them until permission is given to you. And if it is said to you, "Go back," then go back; it is purer for you. And Allah is Knowing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse establishes a principle of respect for the rights of others and of inner discipline: one must not intrude upon a private dwelling even when it appears empty, because the owner's privacy and permission remain binding regardless of whether anyone is visible. Returning when told to return is presented as the course that brings greater spiritual purity, since it trains the believer to restrain the ego's impulse to insist on access and to submit willingly to the limits set by others. The closing reminder that Allah knows what is done reinforces that outward compliance with these etiquettes is tied to sincerity, as the one who observes them is accountable before the One who sees even what remains hidden from people.

translation: There is no blame upon you for entering uninhabited houses in which there is benefit for you. And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal.
interpretation: The verse lifts a burden of scruple that people may have felt about entering houses that belong to no one residing in them, such as empty dwellings, storehouses, or lodgings meant for travelers and public use, where a person has a legitimate benefit like shelter, goods, or rest. It teaches that the sanctity of property does not forbid every entry, provided the purpose is lawful and sincere, and it reminds the believer that while people may judge only outward actions, Allah knows the hidden intentions behind them, so one's conduct must be guided by honest intent as well as permissible practice.

translation: Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do.
interpretation: The verse opens the moral code of modesty by addressing believing men first, placing the responsibility for restraint on the one who is first to be tempted by the eye. Lowering the gaze is the gateway to guarding the chastity of the body, for the heart is often corrupted through what the eye lingers upon before any deed is committed. The phrase 'that is purer for them' shows that this discipline is not a burden imposed for its own sake but a means of cleansing the soul and protecting it from desire that leads to ruin. The closing reminder that Allah is Acquainted with what they do turns the command inward, teaching that the believer's restraint must be sincere and observed by God even when no human eye sees, so that modesty becomes a matter of conscience rather than mere outward conformity.

translation: And tell the believing women to lower their gaze, guard their chastity, and not reveal their adornment except what appears of it; let them draw their headcoverings over their chests, and not reveal their adornment except to their husbands, their fathers, their husbands' fathers, their sons, their husbands' sons, their brothers, their brothers' sons, their sisters' sons, their women, what their right hands possess, male attendants lacking desire, or children who have not yet attained awareness of women's private matters. And let them not stamp their feet so as to reveal what they conceal of their adornment. And turn to God in repentance all together, O believers, that you may succeed.
interpretation: The verse establishes a moral discipline that begins with the inner orientation of modesty: lowering the gaze and guarding chastity precede any rule about dress, showing that the Qur'an locates the root of decency in the heart and in self-restraint rather than in outward covering alone. The instruction to draw the headcovering over the chest reframes visible adornment as something to be concealed from strangers, while the broad list of permitted persons reveals a balance between social reality and protection: family and those in close domestic life may see the woman in her ordinary presentation, and the prohibition on stamping the feet extends the principle to subtle signals, teaching that even small gestures should not draw attention to what is hidden. The verse closes by linking this whole ethical structure to repentance, suggesting that modesty is not merely a set of external rules but a continual turning back to God, through which the believing community attains success.

translation: And marry off the unmarried among you, and the righteous among your male and female servants. If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty, and Allah is All-Encompassing and All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse directs the community to facilitate marriage for those who are single, including the pious among its slaves, and removes the fear of poverty as a barrier to it. By promising that Allah will enrich those who marry from His bounty, it teaches reliance on God's provision rather than delaying marriage out of anxiety over wealth. Its reference to Allah's vastness and knowledge reassures the believer that divine provision is boundless and that God knows the sincere intentions behind marriage, so that chastity and family life are supported rather than hindered by material concerns.

translation: And let those who cannot find the means to marry keep themselves chaste until Allah enriches them from His bounty. And those among your slaves who seek a deed of emancipation, write it for them if you know good in them, and give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you. And do not force your slave girls into prostitution when they desire chastity, seeking the fleeting goods of worldly life. And whoever forces them, then indeed Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse sets out a graduated moral framework for a society in transition. It first commands restraint for those unable to marry, tying their chastity to a trust that Allah will provide. It then turns to the enslaved, requiring that their right to purchase freedom through a written agreement be honored, with the community helping them to obtain it, so that a route out of bondage is opened rather than closed. Finally it forbids the exploitation of slave women for illicit gain, especially when they themselves seek purity, and it shows that the wrongdoing lies with the one who compels them, for Allah pardons what was done under coercion. The passage thus unites personal self-discipline, social justice toward the vulnerable, and the principle that dignity and the sanctity of the person must be protected against the pursuit of worldly profit.

translation: And We have certainly sent down to you clear verses, and an example from those who passed away before you, and an admonition for the God-fearing.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an as a self-evidently clear revelation whose clarity is meant to dispel doubt and guide the reader toward understanding. By pairing the 'clear verses' with 'an example from those who passed away before you,' God directs the listener to history: the fates of earlier communities serve as living lessons, showing how truth was received and rejected and what consequences followed. Yet the verse adds that this admonition truly reaches only the God-fearing, because the heart that is conscious of God is the one that opens to reminder and reflection, while the heedless remain unmoved by even the clearest signs. Thus the revelation is both a light and a test, illuminating the path for all while benefiting most those who approach it with reverence and a readiness to change.

translation: Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. His light is like a niche within which is a lamp, the lamp inside a glass, the glass as if it were a pearly star, lit from a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it. Light upon light. Allah guides whomever He wills to His light. And Allah presents examples for the people, and Allah is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: The verse uses the image of a layered light to show that the divine light is the source of all guidance and existence, and that the believer's heart, when it receives this light, is like a niche housing a lamp, illuminated from a pure source that is neither bound to one direction nor to one worldly limit. Its brightness is light stacked upon light, because divine guidance meets the receptive heart and multiplies its clarity, so that the heart nearly radiates before the revelation even fully reaches it. Guidance is thus not merely taught from outside but kindled within a prepared soul, and the examples in the verse are given so that people may reflect and recognize where true illumination comes from.

translation: In houses which God has permitted to be raised up and in which His name is mentioned; therein glorify Him morning and evening.
interpretation: The verse points to the sanctity of places dedicated to the remembrance of God. Such houses are honored by God's permission, and they are meant to be elevated in status and purpose through the mention of His name and the worship performed in them. The verse presents them as places where people devote themselves to glorifying God at the beginning and end of each day, so that the mosque becomes a center of constant devotion that shapes the believer's daily rhythm and draws the community toward remembrance, prayer, and sincere submission to God.

translation: Men whom neither trade nor commerce distracts from the remembrance of God, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakat. They fear a Day when hearts and eyes will be turned about.
interpretation: The verse portrays a people whose hearts are anchored by something higher than worldly gain: even when commerce is their livelihood, it does not pull them away from remembering God, from prayer, or from purifying their wealth through charity. Their fear of the Day of Judgment is what keeps their priorities in order, since on that Day the hearts that were once fixed on profit and the eyes that once gazed at worldly gain will be overturned in dismay. The lesson is that true success lies not in being free of work or trade, but in never letting the market become the master of the soul.

translation: So that Allah may reward them with the best of what they did, and increase them from His bounty. And Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning.
interpretation: The verse presents God's justice and generosity together: He repays the righteous not merely in proportion to their deeds but with the finest of them, and then adds from His own grace beyond what deeds could earn. The phrase 'without reckoning' signals that divine giving exceeds any measure of human accounting, so believers should hope in God's abundant mercy rather than calculating their merits as though they were owed a fixed wage. The verse thus balances accountability with trust in boundless divine favor.

translation: As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level desert: the thirsty one thinks it is water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it is nothing, and he finds God with him, and He pays him his account in full. And God is swift in reckoning.
interpretation: The verse portrays the deeds of the disbelievers as a mirage that deceives the parched traveler, appearing to offer life-giving water only to vanish upon approach. Their works, though they seem substantial to them and may appear valuable in worldly eyes, will be found empty of the reality they were supposed to have, because they were not built upon faith in God. Yet the verse emphasizes that nothing escapes God: when the person arrives at the reckoning, he finds God present, Who settles his account fully and justly, and God's reckoning is swift, leaving no deed unaccounted for.

translation: Or like darknesses in a vast deep sea, covered by waves, above which are waves, above which are clouds—darkness upon darkness. When one extends his hand, he can barely see it. And whoever Allah does not give light, for him there is no light.
interpretation: This verse completes the parable begun earlier in the same surah, where the disbelievers' deeds are likened to a mirage and now their state of heart and mind is likened to a person lost in the depths of a turbulent ocean, enveloped by layered waves and dense clouds, so that even his own hand is invisible to him. The imagery conveys the multiplied and suffocating darkness of ignorance, misguidance, desires, and worldly passions that stack upon one another until the soul cannot perceive the truth even when it is right before it. The closing statement makes the lesson explicit: true guidance is a light that comes from God, and one who is denied that light by his own persistent turning away has no other source from which to find his way.

translation: Have you not seen that to God glorify whoever is in the heavens and the earth, and the birds spreading their wings? Each one has indeed known its prayer and its glorification, and God is All-Knowing of what they do.
interpretation: The verse opens by drawing the listener's attention to a universal reality that is visible to anyone who looks: all creation, from the celestial bodies and the inhabitants of the heavens and earth down to the birds in flight, is engaged in glorifying its Creator. The mention of the birds held aloft in their ranks is especially striking, since their suspended flight is itself a sign of the power that sustains them, reminding the human being that what he takes for granted in nature is an act of devotion. The phrase 'each one has indeed known its prayer and its glorification' points to a conscious, though non-human, form of worship suited to each creature's nature, which the human being may not perceive but which God fully knows. The verse thus invites humility: if every creature has its own way of glorifying God, then human beings, who are given understanding and free choice, are called to recognize this harmony and to worship with sincerity, knowing that God is fully aware of all their deeds.

translation: And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and to Allah is the final return.
interpretation: The verse establishes two foundational truths about God: His absolute sovereignty and the certainty of return. Possession of the heavens and the earth means that every creature, every event, and every law of the cosmos is under His sole authority, so no power outside Him can ultimately command or protect anyone. The mention of the final destination (al-maṣīr) immediately follows, reminding the believer that this dominion is not merely a fact of creation but a reality before which all human affairs will be judged. Together these ideas invite a posture of humility in prosperity and steadfastness in hardship: since the one who owns all things is also the one to whom all things return, the believer is called to place trust in Him alone and to orient one's actions toward the accountability that awaits.

translation: Have you not seen that Allah drives the clouds gently, then joins them together, then makes them into a heaped mass, and you see the rain coming out from their midst? And He sends down from the sky mountains of hail in it, so He strikes with it whom He wills and averts it from whom He wills. The flash of its lightning nearly takes away the sight.
interpretation: The verse uses the phenomenon of the storm cloud as a sign of God's absolute power and sovereignty over nature, showing that rain, hail, and lightning are not random but are directed by His will, granting or withholding benefit and harm as He chooses. By reminding the listener of something observable, it calls the heart to recognize that human beings, who depend entirely on these forces, must acknowledge the One who governs them, and it implicitly warns that the dazzling power of the lightning is a reminder of how easily sight and certainty can be overwhelmed by divine majesty.

translation: Allah alternates the night and the day. Indeed, in that is a lesson for those who have insight.
interpretation: The verse directs the believer's gaze to the constant alternation of night and day, a phenomenon so regular and familiar that it is easily overlooked. Its recurrence, with its precise order and balance, points to a Creator who governs time with wisdom and power. The phrase "those who possess sight" (ulu al-absar) suggests that true seeing goes beyond the eyes: it is the perceptive insight that reads the signs of creation and draws from them recognition of God, reflection on the transience of life, and moral awareness. Thus the verse calls for a contemplative vision that turns the ordinary rhythms of the world into lessons for the heart and mind.

translation: And Allah has created every moving creature from water. Among them are those that move on their bellies, and among them are those that walk on two legs, and among them are those that walk on four. Allah creates what He wills; indeed, Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse points to the common origin of all living creatures in water, a fact that invites reflection on the unity of creation amid its extraordinary diversity. The variety of locomotion, from crawling to walking on two or four limbs, is presented as a sign of God's power to shape creation as He wills, reminding the reader that the same Creator who brought forth such varied forms from one substance is able to do all things.

translation: Indeed, We have sent down clear signs, and Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an's revelation as a source of clarity: its signs are evident in their meaning and self-evident to a sincere seeker, leaving no excuse for doubt. Yet the verse also affirms that clarity alone does not compel guidance; the reception of guidance rests with Allah's will, which He grants to those who turn toward Him with an open heart. The believer is thus called both to reflect upon the clear signs and to seek Allah's guidance, recognizing that the straight path is reached through the combination of divine illumination and sincere human response.

translation: And they say, "We believe in Allah and in the Messenger, and we obey," then a faction of them turn away after that. And those are not [truly] believers.
interpretation: The verse exposes a hypocritical attitude in which a person verbally professes faith and obedience while his conduct contradicts the claim. The turning away of a group "after that" shows that the profession was not rooted in the heart, so that when obedience demanded real commitment they withdrew. The verse teaches that true belief is proven by sincere and steadfast obedience to God and His Messenger, not by words alone, and it warns that the mere utterance of faith does not make one a believer when it is not matched by action and inward submission.

translation: And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger that he may judge between them, behold, a party of them turn away, refusing.
interpretation: The verse exposes a hypocritical disposition that claims faith yet recoils the moment divine and prophetic authority is invoked to settle a dispute. The turning away is not merely a practical reluctance but reveals that their professed submission was conditional, accepted only so long as its outcome suited their own interests. The sudden shift from calling them to judgment to their open aversion shows that the test lies in the heart's readiness to accept a ruling that may go against its desires. True faith is therefore measured not by words of belief but by willing acceptance of God's and His Messenger's judgment, especially when it is inconvenient to the self.

translation: But if the right was theirs, they would come to him willingly, in submission.
interpretation: The verse exposes the opportunism of those who turn away from the Prophet's judgment when they suspect it will go against them. Their readiness to come eagerly to him when they believe they will win reveals that their allegiance is not to truth or justice but to their own interests. Their conduct shows that they seek a judge only when the judgment serves them, so that they treat the divine guidance as a convenience rather than as a binding authority. The verse thus teaches that true faith is measured by submission to what is right even when it is unwelcome, and that a heart which accepts justice only when justice favors it is revealing its underlying disease.

translation: Is there in their hearts a disease, or have they doubted, or do they fear that Allah and His Messenger will wrong them? Rather, it is they who are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hidden motives behind the reluctance of the hypocrites to accept the judgment of Allah and His Messenger. It poses three possibilities: a sickness of the heart (hypocrisy and spiritual disease), doubt about the truth of the message, or fear that the Prophet would rule unjustly against them. The answer comes decisively: the fault lies not with the Messenger's justice but with them, for by turning away from a just judgment they themselves commit injustice. The verse thus teaches that true faith requires full submission to divine and prophetic judgment, and that suspicion of the one who judges justly is itself a form of wrongdoing.

translation: The only saying of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger that he may judge between them, is that they say, "We hear and we obey." And it is those who are the successful.
interpretation: The verse defines true faith by its response to the divine and prophetic call: a believer's authentic reaction to being summoned to the judgment of Allah and His Messenger is not reluctance or argument but immediate acceptance expressed in both word and deed, "we hear and we obey." The phrase "the only saying" (innama kana qawl) restricts the proper stance to this submission, contrasting it implicitly with the hypocrites described in the preceding verses who turn away when judgment is sought from the Prophet. Hearing here implies understanding and acceptance, not mere perception, so obedience follows naturally from it. The closing declaration that these are "the successful" (al-muflihun) ties salvation and prosperity in this world and the next to a heart that submits to God's law, showing that genuine success lies in surrendering personal preference to the authority of revelation rather than in worldly gain or self-vindication.

translation: And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, and fears Allah and remains conscious of Him, those are the victorious.
interpretation: The verse ties success to a single inner orientation expressed in outward conduct: obedience to Allah and His Messenger is the visible form of a heart that fears Allah and keeps Him in awareness (taqwa). Obedience without God-consciousness risks becoming mere formalism, while taqwa that does not issue in obedience remains abstract. By joining the two, the verse defines true triumph not as worldly gain but as the state of a person whose whole life is aligned with the divine will, so that victory (fawz) is understood primarily as nearness to God and salvation from the consequences of turning away from Him.

translation: And they swore by Allah their most emphatic oaths that if you commanded them, they would surely go forth. Say, "Do not swear; known obedience is better. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do."
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites' habit of exaggerated oath-taking to display a devotion that their hearts do not hold. Their solemn vows to go out for jihad at the Prophet's command are contradicted by the reality of their conduct, so the Prophet is told to reject the oaths outright and to point instead to a sincere, recognized obedience, which alone has genuine worth. The closing reminder that Allah is fully aware of their actions warns that no display of oaths can conceal inner disposition from Him, turning the believer's attention from outward protestation to the honesty and consistency of actual deeds.

translation: Say: "Obey Allah and obey the Messenger." But if you turn away, then upon him is only what he has been assigned, and upon you is what you have been assigned. And if you obey him, you will be guided. And the duty of the Messenger is only to convey clearly.
interpretation: The verse establishes a clear division of responsibility between the Messenger and the believers: obedience to Allah and His Messenger is inseparable and is the path to guidance, while the Messenger's duty is limited to delivering the message plainly, and he bears no compulsion over whether people accept it. Each person is accountable for their own response, so turning away does not transfer the burden of guidance onto the Prophet, whose task is fulfilled through clear conveyance. The verse thus underscores that guidance is reached through sincere obedience, and that the call's success rests on the listener's own choice to follow it.

translation: Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors upon the earth, just as He made successors those before them, and that He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them, and He will surely replace their fear with security. They worship Me, not associating anything with Me. But whoever disbelieves after that, those are the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse establishes a divine covenant linking faith and righteous action to the promise of political and spiritual empowerment, showing that true security after fear is grounded in exclusive devotion to God, so that the community's stability is inseparable from its sincere monotheism; the one who turns away after such clear favor has rejected the very condition on which the promise rests, and thereby places himself outside the obedience that God's favor requires.

translation: And establish prayer, give zakat, and obey the Messenger, that you may receive mercy.
interpretation: The verse joins three pillars of communal and personal worship, namely the ritual prayer, the giving of zakat, and obedience to the Prophet, and presents them as the path to divine mercy. Prayer ties the believer's heart directly to God, zakat turns that devotion outward into care for the needy and the purification of wealth, and obedience to the Messenger secures the believer's conduct within the guidance that God sent through him. The phrase "that you may receive mercy" indicates that mercy is not merely a reward owed to deeds but a grace that follows when these obligations are kept with sincerity, so that the believer's relationship with God and with society is brought into harmony under the Prophetic model.

translation: Do not think that those who disbelieve can escape [Allah] in the earth. Their refuge is the Fire, and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: The verse addresses the Prophet and believers, forbidding them from supposing that the disbelievers can outpace or escape the power of God on earth. Their apparent freedom and success is no sign of escape from accountability; their true end is the Fire, a destination the verse describes with stark finality. The statement reassures the faithful that worldly defiance does not place the unbelievers beyond the reach of divine justice, and it warns that the consequence of rejecting faith is a grim and inescapable outcome.

translation: O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess and those among you who have not reached puberty ask your permission three times: before the dawn prayer, and when you put off your clothing at midday, and after the night prayer. These are three times of privacy for you. Beyond these, there is no blame on you or on them to go about without permission, as you move about attending to one another. Thus does Allah make clear to you the verses, and Allah is Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: The verse establishes a rule of domestic privacy and the protection of personal boundaries within the household, teaching that even those who are dependent or under one's care must observe the sanctity of the three moments of intimate undress and rest, because these are times when the body is exposed and the family is most vulnerable to intrusion. By singling out the hours before dawn, midday, and after the night prayer, the text reflects a pedagogy of modesty that begins at home and extends the adab of seeking permission from the Prophet's household to every dwelling. The clause that follows the three times relaxes the rule, acknowledging the constant mutual service within the house, so that the law balances dignity with the practical ease of daily life. Ultimately the verse ties ethics to divine clarity: Allah explains these details so that believers may internalize respect for privacy, and the closing names of Knowing and Wise remind the reader that such detailed regulation flows from wisdom that understands human nature.

translation: And when the children among you reach puberty, let them ask permission (to enter) just as those before them asked permission. Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses, and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the onset of puberty marks a moral and social threshold, after which a young person must observe the same discipline of seeking permission before entering private spaces that adults are bound to observe. It shows that the rules of privacy and modesty within the household are not arbitrary but grounded in the dignity of each individual, so that the family is taught to respect the boundaries of its members. The reference to those before them indicates that this courtesy is an established and universal practice rooted in revealed guidance. Closing with Allah's knowledge and wisdom reminds the believer that these precise regulations are given by the All-Knowing for the good ordering of human life.

translation: And as for women past child-bearing who no longer hope for marriage, there is no blame upon them if they put aside their outer garments, without displaying adornment. But to be modest is better for them. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse grants a concession to elderly women beyond the age of desire and marriage: they are relieved of the obligation to keep the outer garments on, so long as they do not intend to display their adornment. The ruling is framed by the principle that restraint and modesty remain better for them, so the relaxation is not an invitation to exposure but a mercy that lightens a burden no longer suited to their condition. The closing reminder that God hears and knows all underlines that intentions and conduct are fully known to Him, and that true virtue lies in what a person sincerely intends and does.

translation: There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick, nor upon yourselves, that you eat from your own houses, or the houses of your fathers, or the houses of your mothers, or the houses of your brothers, or the houses of your sisters, or the houses of your paternal uncles, or the houses of your paternal aunts, or the houses of your maternal uncles, or the houses of your maternal aunts, or from that whose keys you possess, or from the house of your friend. There is no blame upon you whether you eat together or separately. So when you enter houses, greet one another with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good. Thus Allah makes clear to you the verses, that you may understand.
interpretation: The verse lifts a burden that people of the time felt about sharing meals, especially with those who were physically impaired, who feared that eating from others' homes or with them would be improper or dishonorable. It reveals that family ties and close friendship create a natural trust that permits ease in eating from one another's houses, whether together or apart, so long as the spirit of kindness and good faith is kept. The closing instruction to greet the household when entering, with a blessed and pleasant greeting from God, teaches that a home is to be entered with peace and goodwill, so that each visit becomes a source of divine blessing and mutual affection, and the whole passage calls the believers to reason and to understand the clear signs of God's guidance in social life.

translation: The believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger, and when they are with him on a matter of common concern, they do not leave until they have asked his permission. Indeed, those who ask your permission are the ones who believe in Allah and His Messenger. So when they ask your permission for some affair of theirs, give permission to whom you will among them, and ask Allah's forgiveness for them. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse defines true faith through disciplined loyalty to the Prophet's leadership in communal affairs: believers who gather with him on a matter of collective importance do not depart without his leave, showing that faith is expressed in respect for legitimate authority and in the seriousness of shared responsibility. The permission granted to those with genuine personal needs is left to the Prophet's judgment, which teaches that leaders may weigh necessities case by case with discernment rather than rigidly. The closing request for forgiveness, and the reminder of Allah's forgiveness and mercy, shows that even when a leader's discretion is exercised, compassion and pardon remain the framework, and that asking permission honorably is itself a mark of those who truly believe.

translation: Do not make the summoning of the Messenger among you like your summoning of one another. Allah already knows those among you who slip away, hiding behind others. So let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial afflict them or a painful punishment strike them.
interpretation: The verse establishes a standard of reverence toward the Prophet: his call to gather is not to be treated as the casual summoning people make of one another, since it carries the weight of divine guidance and must be answered with seriousness and respect. The image of those who slip away furtively, covering each other, shows that hypocrites and the careless attempt to evade a gathering unnoticed, yet God sees them fully. The warning that follows ties obedience to the Prophet's command to obedience to God himself, so that opposing his order exposes a person to worldly trial or to a painful punishment in the Hereafter.

translation: Surely, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. He already knows the condition you are in, and on the Day they are returned to Him, He will inform them of what they did. And Allah is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: The verse establishes that absolute ownership of everything in the heavens and earth belongs to God alone, and it links this sovereignty to complete knowledge. Because nothing lies outside His dominion, nothing about a person's inner state or outward conduct is hidden from Him, so the believer is reminded that his hidden intentions and public actions alike stand in full view of God. The mention of the Day of Return turns this divine knowledge into accountability: the same God who knows every condition will, on the Last Day, make people aware of their deeds, so that the awareness of being watched should lead to sincerity and carefulness in conduct rather than heedlessness.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion (al-Furqan) upon His servant, that he may be a warner to the worlds.
interpretation: The verse opens by declaring the blessedness of God, whose greatness is shown by the very act of revelation. The term al-Furqan, the Criterion, names the Qur'an as that which divides truth from falsehood, guidance from error, and so gives believers a clear standard by which to judge their lives and the world. By calling Muhammad His 'servant' ('abd), the verse roots prophethood in humble devotion rather than in worldly rank, which is the highest honor a human being can hold. The purpose of this descent is universal: the message is not confined to one people but addressed to all the worlds, and the prophet's role is that of a warner, one who alerts humanity to the consequences of turning away, so that they may choose the path of accountability before it is too late.

translation: He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, who has not taken a son, and who has no partner in the dominion, and who created everything and determined it with precise measure.
interpretation: The verse establishes the absolute sovereignty and oneness of God through a sequence of negations and affirmations: the dominion over all of creation belongs to Him alone, so He needs no offspring to continue His rule nor any associate to share in governing, since both would imply deficiency or need that cannot apply to the Creator. The declaration that He created every thing and measured it with precise determination points to the orderliness of creation, where each being is given its specific nature, proportion, and purpose, so that the universe is understood as the product of a wise and deliberate will rather than chance. Thus the verse links God's transcendence above human notions of begetting and partnership with His active providence over every detail of existence.

translation: And they have taken, besides Him, gods that create nothing while they themselves are created, and they possess no power to harm or benefit themselves, and possess no control over death or life or resurrection.
interpretation: The verse exposes the absurdity of idolatry by contrasting the true Creator with the false gods people chose besides Him. Those worshipped beings cannot create anything; rather, they are themselves created, so they are lesser than the one who brought them into being. Lacking even the power to avert harm or secure benefit for their own worshippers, let alone for anyone else, they hold no authority over the decisive matters of human existence: death, life, and the raising of the dead on the Day of Resurrection. Its lesson is that worship belongs only to the One who alone holds dominion over creation, sustenance, and the final return, and that trusting in anything that cannot protect or benefit even itself is a grave error of reason as well as faith.

translation: And those who disbelieve say, "This is nothing but a lie he has fabricated, and other people have helped him with it." But they have certainly committed an injustice and a falsehood.
interpretation: The verse exposes the rhetorical strategy of those who rejected the Prophet's message: when they could not refute the Qur'an on its own merits, they attributed it to human fabrication and to outside assistance from others. Their claim is itself presented as a form of wrongdoing, a zulm (injustice) that distorts the truth and a zur (falsehood) that they knowingly speak. The verse thus teaches that denial often rests on slander and unfounded accusation rather than on sound evidence, and it implicitly reaffirms the divine origin of the revelation by showing how weak and unjust the charge against it is.

translation: And they say, "Tales of the ancients, which he has had written down; they are dictated to him morning and evening."
interpretation: The verse records the disbelievers' dismissal of the Prophet's recitation as mere legends of earlier peoples, copied and read back to him at all hours. Their charge is an attempt to strip the revelation of its divine origin by reducing it to borrowed human stories, a pattern of denial the Qur'an repeatedly confronts. The phrase "morning and evening" exaggerates the supposed constancy of his sources, implying a deliberate, continuous process of composition that they imagine rather than observe. In answering this, the verse exposes the weakness of their accusation: they cannot explain the Qur'an's content, its unlettered source, or its moral force, and so they fall back on the claim that it is inherited tradition.

translation: Say, "He has sent it down, who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth. Indeed, He is ever Forgiving, Merciful."
interpretation: The verse places the revelation under the direct knowledge of God, who knows what is hidden in the heavens and the earth, so the Qur'an is not a human invention but a message sent down from the One who encompasses all unseen things. The closing pair of divine names, Forgiving and Merciful, then turns this knowledge toward the believers: the same all-knowing God who sees every hidden thought and deed also pardons and shows mercy to those who turn back to Him, which invites the listener to trust the revelation and to seek its guidance with hope rather than despair.

translation: And they said, "What is this messenger who eats food and walks through the markets? Why was an angel not sent down to him so that he would be with him as a warner?"
interpretation: The verse reveals a recurring objection of the disbelievers against the prophethood of Muhammad: they judged a messenger by worldly standards and found it incompatible that a true envoy of God should share the basic human conditions of eating and moving among people in the marketplaces. Their reasoning assumes that a messenger from the Divine must be elevated above human needs and visible commerce, and therefore they demand an angel as a companion who would confirm the warning. The Qur'an elsewhere answers this by pointing out that God sent human messengers to human communities, since a human can be a model and a teacher to other humans, and that the rejection stems less from a genuine lack of evidence than from a refusal to accept a message delivered through one of their own. The verse thus exposes how the standard of human dignity and status can become a pretext for denying guidance.

translation: Or a treasure be thrown down to him, or he be given a garden from which he eats. And the wrongdoers said, "You are only following a man affected by magic."
interpretation: The verse records the disbelievers' mockery of the Prophet Muhammad, peer-pressure-driven objections that reveal their refusal to judge his message on its merits. They demand material signs of status, such as a hoard of wealth or a private garden, as though prophethood must come with worldly grandeur, thereby measuring divine guidance by worldly standards. Their final accusation, that the Prophet is bewitched, is a way of dismissing his clear message as the product of an unsound mind rather than confronting its truth. The verse thus teaches that the rejection of truth often rests not on evidence but on attachment to worldly values and on slander against those who bring it.

translation: Look how they strike for you the examples, so they have gone astray and cannot find a way.
interpretation: The verse turns the Prophet's attention to the disbelievers' habit of coining comparisons against him, calling him a madman, a sorcerer, or a poet, and of setting forth images of his message to dismiss it. Their very method of striking such examples is itself the sign of their misguidance: having abandoned sound reasoning, they wander from the truth and are left with no true path to reach guidance. The wording implies that those who persist in such mockery and distortion close off for themselves every route to the right way, so that they cannot find it, not because the path is hidden, but because their hearts and judgment have turned away from it.

translation: Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that: gardens beneath which rivers flow, and He will assign for you palaces.
interpretation: The verse points to the boundless generosity of God, who is able to give far more than what people imagine or desire in this world. The mention of 'if He wills' reminds the believer that all bounty rests in divine choice, not in human deserving or calculation, which should cultivate humility and trust. The promise of gardens with flowing rivers and palaces is offered in the context of the Qur'an's broader message that the true, enduring reward lies in the Hereafter, and that the blessings of the next life surpass whatever worldly goods a person might be tempted to cling to. It invites the reader to measure their hopes by eternal rather than fleeting standards.

translation: Nay, but they have denied the Hour, and We have prepared for those who deny the Hour a blazing Fire.
interpretation: The verse points to the root of the disbelievers' rejection: it is not a lack of evidence but a refusal to accept accountability before a Day of reckoning. The word "bal" (nay, rather) turns the reader from their stated objections toward the true motive, which is the denial of the Hour. Denying the Hour is not a neutral intellectual position; it dissolves the moral meaning of action, since if there is no return to God there is no ultimate justice, and so the denial itself becomes the gateway to heedlessness. The verse ties this denial to a concrete consequence, the prepared blaze, so that belief in the Last Day is shown to be inseparable from moral responsibility in this life.

translation: When it sees them from a distant place, they will hear its raging and its roaring.
interpretation: The verse depicts the Fire of Hell as a living, conscious presence that perceives the wrongdoers from far away, and the sound it makes, a furious seething and a deep roar, is itself a terrifying foretaste of the punishment. Its rage is directed at those who denied and defied God, so that the very approach of the Fire inspires dread before any contact with it. The imagery conveys that the torment begins with the fear and anguish of seeing and hearing it, emphasizing the severity of the account that awaits the disbelievers and the powerlessness of those who once considered themselves beyond reckoning.

translation: And when they are thrown into it, into a narrow place, bound together in chains, they will call out there for destruction.
interpretation: The verse depicts the final state of the disbelievers in Hell, where they are cast into a confined and suffocating place, shackled together in companionship of their misguidance. Having been bound to one another in the world by shared denial and sin, they are now bound in punishment, and the cry 'thubur' (utter ruin) expresses their despair at being overtaken by a destruction they can no longer escape. The narrowness of the place reflects the constriction of their hearts in the world, and the chaining together signifies that their earthly alliances now become a source of torment rather than support.

translation: Do not call out today for one destruction, but call out for many destructions.
interpretation: The verse is spoken to the people of the Fire on the Day of Judgment, mocking their despair. When they cry out for ruin and destruction, they are told that their single lament will not help; instead, they should cry out for countless destructions, because the torment they face is multiplied and endless. It underscores the futility of their wailing and the severity of the punishment that their deeds have brought upon them.

translation: Say: "Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity which has been promised to the righteous? It shall be for them a reward and a final destination."
interpretation: The verse presents a question meant to draw the listener toward a clear comparison. After describing the fate of those who deny the Hour, the Qur'an contrasts the torment of the disbelievers with the garden promised to the God-conscious. The phrase "a reward and a final destination" signals that the believers' paradise is not merely a temporary recompense but their ultimate abode, so the rhetorical question leaves the hearer to recognize, by their own reasoning, that the eternal garden is far superior to the worldly and hellish alternatives the verse has just set before them. It thus calls the heart to choose piety, since the stakes are the everlasting outcome of one's conduct.

translation: They will have therein whatever they wish, abiding eternally. That is a promise incumbent upon your Lord, one to be asked of Him.
interpretation: The verse presents the reward of the righteous as a divine promise that is absolute and binding upon God, whose fulfilment is assured. The phrase "whatever they wish" conveys the completeness of the believers' felicity, where no desire goes unmet, and "abiding eternally" stresses that this bliss is free from any fear of loss or end. The word "mas'ūlan" suggests a promise that the faithful may rightfully request and hold God to, underscoring both the certainty of the reward and the intimate relationship between the Lord and His servants in which hope is grounded in His own pledge.

translation: And [mention] the Day He will gather them, and those they worshipped besides Allah, and He will say, "Did you lead these servants of Mine astray, or did they themselves stray from the way?"
interpretation: The verse depicts the Day of Gathering, when all who were worshipped besides Allah are brought together with their worshippers, and it presents a scene of judgment in which responsibility for misguidance is put to the test. The question directed at the false deities is not asked for information, since Allah knows all things, but serves as a rebuke and an exposure of the falsehood of those who were worshipped. The phrase "My servants" shows that those who went astray remain Allah's creation and servants, and it sharpens the reproach against those who led them away from His worship. The closing alternative, whether they themselves chose to stray, points to the human moral agency that the Qur'an repeatedly affirms: people bear responsibility for their own choices, and no one can escape accountability by blaming those they followed.

translation: They will say: "Glory be to You! It was not fitting for us to take any protectors besides You, but You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the remembrance, and they became a people ruined and lost."
interpretation: The verse depicts the worshippers of others besides God, and the false deities they followed, speaking together on the Day of Judgment. Those who were worshipped declare God's absolute transcendence and deny that they ever called people to take them as allies or partners, affirming that such a claim was never proper for them. The verse then locates the true cause of this misguidance not in the deities but in the worshippers themselves: God granted them and their forefathers prolonged worldly comfort and ease, which led them to neglect the reminder of God and the guidance sent to them. Heedlessness born of material enjoyment is thus presented as the root of their ruin, and their condition is described as one of perdition, a people who had turned away from the path of truth and brought destruction upon themselves.

translation: Indeed, they have denied you in what you say, so you can neither avert [the punishment] nor gain help. And whoever among you does wrong, We will make him taste a great punishment.
interpretation: The verse is addressed to those who had taken false deities and claimed partners with God, who are told that their gods have already contradicted their claims: the things they worshipped have denied what they asserted about them, so they possess neither the power to turn away harm nor the ability to bring help. The closing warning widens the address to all the believers and hypocrites among the community: wrongdoing, meaning the persistent injustice of associating others with God or of turning away from His guidance, will bring a severe torment. The passage thus joins a rebuke of false worship with a general lesson that no intermediary can shield a person from the consequences of his own choices.

translation: We never sent before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets. And We have made some of you a trial for others: will you be patient? And your Lord is ever Seeing.
interpretation: The verse dismantles the expectation that a true messenger must stand apart from ordinary human life. Eating and walking in the marketplace are the marks of shared human need and public life, and God deliberately placed the messengers within that common condition so that their message would be measured by its truth rather than by any exemption from human frailty. The turn to 'some of you a trial for others' shows that the same condition becomes a test for the people themselves: the one who is mocked, the poor, and the one who is envied are each tested by what they are given and by how they respond to one another. The closing question, 'will you be patient?', places the burden on the listener's steadfastness, and the final reminder that your Lord is Seeing assures the believer that every act of patience, and every act of envy or scorn, is fully witnessed by God.

translation: And those who do not expect to meet Us say, "Why were the angels not sent down upon us, or why do we not see our Lord?" Indeed, they have become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great insolence.
interpretation: The verse exposes the root of disbelief as a combination of arrogance and denial of the Hereafter. Those who do not hope for the encounter with God demand either that angels be sent to them or that they see God directly, reflecting a wish to set the terms of revelation and faith on their own terms rather than humbly accepting the message. Their request is not born of sincere seeking but of pride, which the Qur'an identifies as the true cause of their rebellion: they have magnified themselves within their own souls and exceeded all bounds in defiance. The passage teaches that genuine faith requires humility before the signs that God sends, and that demands for spectacular proofs often conceal an unwillingness to submit.

translation: On the Day they see the angels, there will be no good tidings that Day for the guilty, and they will say, "A barrier forbidden [to you]!"
interpretation: The verse depicts the terror of the Day of Judgment for the disbelieving sinners: the sight of the angels, which for the righteous is a sign of mercy and glad tidings, becomes for the guilty a moment of dread, since the angels bring no good news to them but rather herald their doom. Their cry "ḥijran maḥjūran" is a plea, as they were accustomed in the world to saying such words to ward off what they feared, asking that a forbidding barrier be placed between them and what they dread, yet on that Day no such refuge is granted. The verse thus contrasts the fate of the wrongdoers with the believers, reminding the listener that the gate of hope closes for those who persist in crime until they face their reckoning.

translation: And We will turn to whatever deeds they did, and make them scattered dust motes.
interpretation: The verse speaks of deeds done without sincere faith or without seeking God's face: though they may appear weighty to their doers, they are stripped of any value on the Day of Reckoning. Just as the scattered dust in a sunbeam looks substantial yet has no substance, such works, lacking the spirit and sincerity that give them life and worth, come to nothing. It warns that outward accomplishment is not enough; only deeds rooted in genuine intention and faith will endure before God.

translation: The companions of the Garden, on that Day, will be better in their resting place and finer in their place of repose.
interpretation: The verse sets the believers' final destination against the scene of the Day of Judgment described just before it, where the wrongdoers are shown in dread and distress. Their 'resting place' (mustaqarr) is the settled abode of eternal security, and their 'place of repose' (maqil) recalls the midday rest taken in the shade, here elevated to a restful respite free of the terror of that Day. The verse thus teaches that the reckoning which frightens the guilty becomes a day of honor and tranquility for those who lived in faith and righteousness, and that the true measure of a place is not its worldly comfort but the peace and dignity granted by God in the Hereafter.

translation: And on the Day the sky is split open with clouds, and the angels will be sent down in a descent.
interpretation: The verse points to the great Day of Judgment, when the orderly structure of the heavens will be torn apart, the sky splitting open amid clouds as a sign that the cosmic order that humans take for granted has come to an end. The descent of the angels in a grand, solemn procession underscores the seriousness of that moment, when the unseen realm becomes visible and the authority of God is displayed without any veil. Its message is a warning to the heedless: the worldly pride and denial that seemed so secure will be exposed, and every soul will face the reality of its deeds before the majesty of the Creator.

translation: The sovereignty on that Day will be truly for the Most Merciful, and it will be a difficult Day for the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse points to a day when all pretended and borrowed authority collapses, and the true and unchallenged dominion belongs to God alone, the Most Merciful. Mercy, which in this world is shared with the believers and offered to all, becomes in that moment the very quality that governs the entire order of reckoning. The hardship of that Day is not a random cruelty but the natural result of the disbelievers' refusal to acknowledge the One whose mercy they neglected, so that their own choices make the Day heavy for them while it remains a day of ultimate truth for everyone else.

translation: And [mention] the Day when the wrongdoer will bite his hands, saying, "Oh, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger."
interpretation: The verse depicts the regret of the wrongdoer on the Day of Judgment, when the one who oppressed himself through disbelief and disobedience will gnaw on his own hands in anguish. His wish to have followed the path of the Messenger reveals that the true loss is the forsaking of guidance in this world, and that the reckoning will expose the futility of the choices he made while he still had the opportunity to turn back. It is a warning to every soul to take the way of the Prophet while there is still time, before remorse becomes of no benefit.

translation: "Woe to me! Would that I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend."
interpretation: The verse captures the anguish of a person on the Day of Judgment who regrets having made a companion of someone who led him away from the remembrance of God and the right path. The phrase "so-and-so" (فلانا) is left unnamed, which many commentators understand as a general reference to any misguiding friend, so that the verse warns believers to choose their intimate companions carefully, since a close friendship built on heedlessness or sin will turn into enmity and remorse on that Day, as the surrounding verses (Al-Furqan 25:27-29) make clear.

translation: He had certainly led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me. And Satan is ever a deserter, forsaking man.
interpretation: The verse captures the anguish of one who, having been given the Reminder and yet turned away from it, now sees that the real fault lay in following a misleading companion.
