The speaker's regret points to a deeper truth: Satan does not stand by those he has lured; he abandons them at the moment of greatest need, leaving the human being alone with the consequences of his choices. The verse thus warns that the danger is not only in the initial deception but in trusting one who offers no lasting support, and it calls the listener to hold fast to remembrance of God before the moment of regret arrives.

translation: And the Messenger will say, "O my Lord, indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned."
interpretation: The verse presents the Prophet's grievance on the Day of Judgment, when he complains to God that his people deserted the Qur'an, neither listening to it, believing in it, nor acting upon it, treating it as a thing forsaken. The word "mahjur" carries the sense of neglect and shunning: the scripture was not literally rejected in words alone, but abandoned in practice, left unrecited, unpondered, and unapplied to life. The verse thus turns the reader toward a self-examination of how one relates to revelation, warning that a community may keep the Qur'an physically present while leaving its guidance unheeded, and that this neglect will itself be a matter of testimony before God.

translation: And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals. But your Lord is sufficient as a guide and a helper.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet by showing that opposition from the wicked is a recurring pattern in the mission of every prophet, not a sign of failure in his cause. Hostility is part of the divine test that distinguishes truth from falsehood, so the believer should not be dismayed by it. The sufficiency of God as guide and helper means that the prophet's real support lies in God alone: God guides the hearts toward the truth and grants victory to those who trust in Him, even when their enemies are powerful.

translation: And those who disbelieve say, "Why was the Qur'an not revealed to him all at once?" Thus [it is revealed gradually], that We may strengthen thereby your heart; and We have spaced it out in gradual recitation.
interpretation: The verse answers an objection raised by the disbelievers against the gradual descent of the Qur'an, presenting the piecemeal revelation as a deliberate divine wisdom rather than a defect. Its purpose is to steady the Prophet's heart: by bringing revelation in installments tied to events, questions, and circumstances, God reinforces his resolve and consolation over time, so that each portion is absorbed, understood, and lived in its moment. The phrase "We have spaced it out in gradual recitation" indicates that the measured, deliberate pacing of the text is itself part of its design, allowing careful memorization, reflection, and application, and thereby showing that the method of revelation serves both the Prophet's inner firmness and the community's faithful engagement with the message.

translation: And they do not bring you any example except that We bring you the truth and the best explanation.
interpretation: The verse assures the Prophet that every objection, parable, or challenge raised against him by his opponents is met by a divine response that is both true and more eloquent and clear than what they put forward. Their attempts to confuse or discredit his message through argument and comparison are rendered futile, because God supplies the Prophet with the real answer, grounded in truth, and with an explanation that surpasses theirs in soundness and excellence. It thus consoles the believers and affirms that the Qur'an itself is the decisive reply to every doubt the disbelievers attempt to raise.

translation: Those who will be gathered on their faces to Hell—those are worse in position and further astray from the way.
interpretation: The verse depicts the fate of the deniers on the Day of Resurrection, who are driven toward Hell dragged upon their faces, a image of utter humiliation that reverses their worldly arrogance. Their situation is described in two respects: their station is the worst, since they will be in the lowest abode of punishment, and their path was the most misguided, since they chose deviation in this life while believing themselves rightly guided. The verse thereby links the outcome to the path chosen in this world, inviting the listener to reflect on where their own way leads and to choose guidance before the reckoning arrives.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture and appointed with him his brother Aaron as a minister (helper).
interpretation: The verse shows that prophetic mission is supported by divine provision and by human companionship: God granted Moses the Book and, out of mercy, made his brother Aaron a wazir, a supporter who shared the burden of the call. It teaches that the bearer of a great trust is not meant to stand alone, and that righteous collaboration and mutual aid in God's cause are themselves part of the favor God bestows on His messengers and their followers.

translation: So We said, "Go both of you to the people who denied Our signs; then We utterly destroyed them."
interpretation: The verse recounts the commission given to Moses and Aaron, sent together to Pharaoh's people who rejected the signs of God. Their persistent denial was met with a complete destruction, showing that rejecting clear divine signs after they have been conveyed brings an inevitable consequence. The emphatic word "tadmeeran" (utter destruction) underlines the totality of the punishment, and the passage serves as a warning that persistence in denial of God's messages leads to ruin.

translation: And the people of Noah, when they denied the messengers, We drowned them and made them a sign for mankind; and We have prepared for the wrongdoers a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse presents the flood of Noah's people as a warning that denying God's messengers is not a trivial matter but brings destruction in this world. Their drowning is made a lasting sign (ayah) for humanity, so that later generations may reflect on the consequences of rejecting prophetic guidance. The closing statement generalizes the lesson: whoever persists in wrongdoing, which at its root is rejection of truth and injustice toward oneself and others, will face a painful retribution, whether in this life or in the Hereafter. The verse thus binds the historical example to a universal principle of divine justice.

translation: And [We destroyed] 'Ad and Thamud and the people of the Rass, and many generations between them.
interpretation: The verse recalls, in brief, a series of earlier peoples who rejected their messengers and were destroyed for it: 'Ad, Thamud, the people of al-Rass (the well or the pit), and countless generations between them. Their mention serves as a warning to the listeners of the Prophet that the same fate awaits those who persist in denial, since God's law of consequence has operated consistently throughout history. The phrase 'many generations between them' emphasizes that these examples are only a fraction of the nations God has judged, inviting reflection on how vast and recurrent the pattern of rejection and punishment has been.

translation: And to each We presented parables, and to each We utterly destroyed with complete destruction.
interpretation: The verse refers to the earlier nations of the prophets, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and others mentioned in the preceding verses, who rejected the messengers sent to them. God first set forth clear parables and admonitions as a means of guidance, reminding them through examples of past peoples and natural signs so that they might reflect and believe. When they persisted in denial despite these clear warnings, their arrogance led to total annihilation. The repetition of 'each' and the emphatic word 'tabbara' (to ruin utterly) underscores that no nation was exempt: the same divine pattern of warning followed by destruction applied to all who persisted in rejection. The verse thus conveys a lasting lesson that the wisdom of divine admonition is offered before the consequence of denial, and that the ruin of the disbelievers is the outcome of their own choice after the proof has been made plain.

translation: And they have certainly passed by the town that was rained upon with an evil rain. Have they not been seeing it? Rather, they were not expecting resurrection.
interpretation: The verse points to the people of Lut, whose town was overturned and rained upon with stones, as a sign that the disbelievers of Makkah pass by such ruins on their journeys and yet fail to draw the lesson. Their real problem is not a lack of evidence but a heart that does not hope for or fear the meeting with God on the Day of Resurrection; because they deny the Hereafter, they do not act on what they see. The verse thus shows that denial of accountability in the next life is the root from which blindness to clear signs in this life grows.

translation: And when they see you, they take you only in mockery, [saying]: "Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?"
interpretation: The verse portrays the disbelievers' contemptuous response to the Prophet Muhammad. Their mockery is not merely a personal slight but a rejection of the divine commission itself: by sarcastically questioning whether this man is truly the one God has sent, they disguise their denial of revelation as ridicule. The verse thus reveals a recurring pattern in which the messenger's humble human appearance becomes a pretext for dismissing the message he carries, and it consoles the believers by showing that such scorn is directed at God's chosen envoy and is therefore borne by the One who sent him.

translation: He nearly led us astray from our gods, had we not been steadfast in adhering to them. And they will know, when they see the punishment, who is further astray in the way.
interpretation: The verse portrays the disbelievers' stubborn clinging to their idols and their accusation that the Prophet nearly turned them away from their gods, a claim that reveals how false consensus and inherited habit can be mistaken for truth. Their self-assurance is exposed as hollow, for the reality of their error will become undeniable only at the moment of punishment, when the true measure of who has strayed will be made plain. The verse thus teaches that the verdict on guidance and misguidance belongs not to the confidence of the people in the moment but to the outcome that the Hereafter reveals.

translation: Have you seen one who takes his own desire as his god? Would you then be a guardian over him?
interpretation: The verse portrays the person who makes his whims and desires his actual object of worship, obeying his appetites rather than God. The Prophet is addressed and reassured that his duty is only to convey the message, not to compel guidance or to bear responsibility for the choices of one who has chosen his desires over truth. It points to the inner idolatry of following the self, a form of worship that can be as binding as any idol, and it teaches that guidance belongs to God, who alone holds the one who has gone astray accountable.

translation: Or do you think that most of them hear or understand? They are only like livestock; rather, they are even more astray in the way.
interpretation: The verse turns the Prophet's concern about those who refuse guidance into a sharp reproach of the heedless: hearing and reason are gifts meant to lead a person to the truth, and when they are left unused, the human being is reduced to the level of grazing animals, which at least follow their nature without deviation. Yet the comparison is made more severe by the words "rather, they are even more astray," because the animal does not know its own path, whereas the person who has been given hearing, sight and intellect and still turns away has forfeited the very faculties that distinguish him, and so bears greater responsibility for his misguidance. The verse thus locates the real blindness not in the eyes but in the refusal to listen and to reflect.

translation: Have you not considered how your Lord extends the shadow? And if He willed, He would have made it stationary. Then We made the sun over it an indicator.
interpretation: The verse directs the reader's attention to the shadow as a sign of divine power and wisdom. The shadow's gradual lengthening and shortening across the day, from dawn until the sun is at its height and beyond, is not random but is governed entirely by the Creator's will, who could have fixed it motionless. By making the sun the cause that moves the shadow step by step, God shows that the natural order is a chain of dependent causes ending in Him. The sun, the very thing that reveals the shadow, is described as a guide, implying that the gradual unfolding of light and shade is a continuous sign pointing the observer back to the One who arranges it. The passage thus invites reflection on how every apparent phenomenon rests on God's deliberate ordering, and that the same power which extends the shadow also draws it back in.

translation: Then We take it back to Us with an easy taking back.
interpretation: The verse, from Surah Al-Furqan (25:46), speaks of the shade that God extends, which is later drawn back gradually and gently by Him. The phrase "qabadnahu ilayna qabdan yasiran" conveys that the withdrawal of this shade is not sudden or harsh but measured and easy, showing that all that God grants of provision, shelter, and blessings is within His complete control and can be withdrawn with the same ease with which it was given. It is a reminder of human dependence on God and of the gentle, orderly nature of His dominion over the cycles of light, shadow, and the passing of time.

translation: And it is He who made the night for you as a garment, and sleep as a rest, and made the day a resurrection (a time of waking and rising).
interpretation: The verse presents the alternation of night and day as a sign of divine mercy and care. Night is likened to a garment that covers and shelters, drawing people into privacy, stillness, and rest, while sleep is a cessation of exertion that restores the body and calms the soul. The day, by contrast, is a time of stirring and rising, when people awake and disperse to seek their livelihood. The word nushur, which also evokes resurrection, invites reflection: just as the daily cycle raises a person from the stillness of sleep to renewed life, so the greater rising after death is a comparable act of divine power. The verse thus turns the ordinary rhythm of sleep and waking into a reminder of God's power over life and death and of human dependence on His provision.

translation: And it is He who sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy, and We send down from the sky pure water.
interpretation: The verse presents rain as a sign of divine mercy arriving in stages: the winds are heralds announcing the coming blessing, much as glad tidings precede a gift, so that the believer learns to read the natural order as a sequence of signs pointing to God's care. The description of the water as 'tahur' (purifying or pure in itself) adds that this mercy is not only life-giving for the earth but also cleansing for the one who uses it, linking the physical provision of rain with the spiritual purity that God makes available to His servants.

translation: That We may give life thereby to a dead land and give drink from what We have created of cattle and many people.
interpretation: The verse points to the water sent down from the sky as the means by which dead, barren land is revived, and it draws attention to the same divine mercy that sustains both livestock and humankind. Just as the earth is brought back to life after lifelessness, the verse invites the listener to reflect on the power that resurrects the dead, and to recognize that the provision supporting human and animal life is itself a sign of the Creator's care and sovereignty.

translation: And We have certainly varied it among them that they may take heed, but most of the people refused except disbelief.
interpretation: The verse shows that God repeatedly diversified His reminders and signs, presenting the same truths through different forms, arguments, and occasions so that people would reflect and be admonished. Yet the majority, rather than being moved to remembrance, clung stubbornly to ingratitude and denial. The sense is that the failure lies not in a lack of clarity in the message but in the human disposition that resists guidance once it has become comfortable in its own habits and rejection. The word 'kufur' here carries the meaning of ungrateful concealment of blessings, so the refusal is also a turning away from the gratitude owed for what has been given.

translation: And had We willed, We would have sent into every town a warner.
interpretation: The verse shows that the sending of messengers was an act of divine choice and not a constraint upon God. Although God could have raised a warner in every single community, He chose instead to make the burden of warning fall upon a particular messenger, the Prophet Muhammad, sent to all people. This places the responsibility of conveying the message on those who receive it, and it emphasizes that the Prophet's mission was universal in reach, addressing the whole of humanity through one divinely commissioned warner rather than through a separate messenger for each town.

translation: So do not obey the disbelievers, and strive against them with it (the Qur'an) with a great striving.
interpretation: The verse, revealed in Makkah, instructs the Prophet not to yield to the demands of those who rejected the message, since compromise would dilute the truth he carried. The striving (jihad) it commands is primarily a striving through the Qur'an itself: patiently conveying its argument, refuting falsehood with clear reasoning, and standing firm against pressure, a struggle that is 'great' because it is sustained, intellectual, and moral rather than physical. The word 'with it' points to the Qur'an as the chief instrument of this effort, so that the recitation and proclamation of revelation become the weapon of the believer against unbelief.

translation: And it is He who let loose the two seas, one sweet and fresh, pleasant to drink, and the other salty and bitter; and He placed between them a barrier and a complete partition that cannot be crossed.
interpretation: The verse points to a visible sign of God's power and wisdom: where fresh and salt waters meet, they flow side by side yet do not mix, held apart by an unseen divine boundary. Reflecting on this, the believer is invited to recognize that the same Creator who maintains this order in nature has set limits and distinctions in creation that human beings are not free to erase, so that the balance of the world rests on His command rather than on chance.

translation: And it is He who created man from water and then made him [a being with] lineage and marriage. Indeed, your Lord is ever Competent over all things.
interpretation: The verse points from the humble origin of man, created from water, to the twofold structure of human society: blood relations (nasab), through which descent and identity are traced, and marital ties (sihr), through which new kinship is formed. The one who originated humanity from so simple a substance is the same who ordered it into these bonds, so that the very fabric of social life is a sign of divine power and wisdom. The closing reminder that the Lord is qadir affirms that the One who begins creation from water is fully able to bring about what He wills, including resurrection.

translation: And they worship, besides Allah, that which can neither benefit them nor harm them. And the disbeliever has always been a supporter (of Satan) against his Lord.
interpretation: The verse exposes the absurdity of idolatry: people devote their worship to things that have no power to benefit or harm them, abandoning the One who alone grants and withholds. Its closing phrase reveals the deeper gravity of disbelief, for the disbeliever does not merely ignore his Lord but becomes an assistant to the forces of falsehood against Him, lending his strength to what opposes the truth. Thus the verse calls the listener to reflect that worship directed to what is powerless is both futile and a betrayal of the Creator who alone sustains him.

translation: And We did not send you except as a bringer of good news and a warner.
interpretation: The verse defines the prophetic mission in two complementary functions: tabshir, giving glad tidings to those who believe and act righteously of mercy, reward and Paradise, and tandhir, warning those who persist in disbelief and wrongdoing of the consequences of their deeds. Together they show that the Prophet's role is not to compel but to convey, balancing hope with fear so that people are drawn toward God through both encouragement and admonition, and the message is shaped to the hearts of its hearers.

translation: Say: "I do not ask you for any reward for it, except that whoever wills may take a path to his Lord."
interpretation: The verse shows that the Messenger's mission is free of personal material gain; he asks nothing for himself from his people. The only 'reward' he desires is that people choose, by their own will, to take the way that leads to their Lord. Guidance is thus presented as an invitation whose benefit returns to the one who accepts it, and the believer's path to God is a freely chosen matter of conscience rather than something imposed or purchased.

translation: And rely upon the Ever-Living who does not die, and glorify Him with His praise. And sufficient is He as Knower of the sins of His servants.
interpretation: The verse directs the believer to place complete trust in God, the Ever-Living whose life is never subject to death, so that reliance is anchored in what is eternal rather than in transient creatures or worldly means. Trust in Him is paired with glorifying Him through praise, showing that true reliance is accompanied by gratitude and devotion. The closing phrase reminds the servant that God is fully aware of the sins of His creatures, which both warns against wrongdoing and offers assurance that His knowledge is complete, so that nothing is hidden from Him and He is sufficient as the one to whom all matters return.

translation: He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, then established Himself above the Throne. The Most Merciful, so ask about Him one who is informed.
interpretation: The verse presents God's creative act and His sovereign rule as the grounds for knowing Him: the One who brought the heavens, the earth, and all that lies between them into being over six days, and then rose above the Throne in a manner befitting His majesty, is the Most Merciful, whose mercy pervades His creation. Because the knowledge of Him is not something the seeker can reach by conjecture, the verse directs the one who wishes to understand Him to inquire of those who possess true awareness of His attributes and works, namely those whose knowledge is grounded in revelation. The verse thus joins God's majesty, His mercy, and the call to seek authoritative knowledge, reminding the believer that the reality of the Creator is best learned from the one who has been informed about Him.

translation: And when it is said to them, "Prostrate to the Most Merciful," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful? Shall we prostrate to whatever you command us?" And it increases them in aversion.
interpretation: The verse exposes the arrogance and denial of the disbelievers when confronted with the name of God al-Rahman, a name they did not recognize or were unwilling to accept, as they had long been accustomed to their idols and to the Meccan usage of the term. Their question "What is al-Rahman?" reveals a refusal to acknowledge the divine attribute of boundless mercy, and their rhetorical challenge "shall we prostrate to what you command us?" shows that their resistance was not merely intellectual but a rejection of submission to the Prophet's call. The closing phrase, "and it increases them in aversion," teaches that the reminder of God, far from softening hardened hearts, deepens their distance from the truth, so that the same message that guides the believers only adds to the flight of the stubborn. It is also a sajdah verse, so the reader and listener are reminded to humble themselves in prostration, in contrast to those who turned away from it.

translation: Blessed is He who placed in the sky great constellations and placed therein a lamp and a moon giving light.
interpretation: The verse opens by declaring the blessedness and exalted greatness of God, whose majesty is revealed in the cosmos. The 'burooj' (great constellations or mansions of the stars) are fixed formations in the heavens, marking out a vast, ordered structure that reflects divine design and precision. The image of the 'sirāj' (lamp), a term used for the sun, presents the sun as a radiant source of illumination and life, while the 'qamar munīr' (luminous moon) is a reflected light that guides the night and marks the passage of time. Together these signs invite the reader to contemplate the order of creation, to recognize the Creator behind the heavens, and to reflect gratefully on the light and guidance that God provides both in the sky and in human life.

translation: And it is He who made the night and the day succeeding one another, for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to be grateful.
interpretation: The alternation of night and day, each following the other in fixed succession, is presented as a sign that invites reflection: the regularity of this cycle reminds the heedless of the Creator's power and wisdom, and its benefits, rest by night and labor by day, call for gratitude. The verse makes clear that these signs are offered to all, yet only those who choose to turn toward remembrance and thankfulness truly benefit from them, since the sign is open but its reception depends on the will of the one who looks.

translation: And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."
interpretation: The verse portrays the true servants of God, the Most Merciful, by their conduct: they walk the earth with gentleness, humility and without arrogance, and when they are met with foolishness or provocation, they do not answer in kind but respond with a word of peace. It teaches that genuine devotion to God shows itself in restraint, forbearance and good speech toward others, especially in the face of ignorance and hostility, so that the believer's character reflects the mercy of the One they serve.

translation: And those who spend the night prostrating themselves and standing (in prayer) before their Lord.
interpretation: The verse portrays the true servants of the Most Merciful as people whose nights are given over to worship: they pass the hours of darkness in prostration and standing before their Lord. The word yabitun, 'they spend the night,' suggests that this devotion is not a passing act but the very character of their inner life, when the world is quiet and the heart is most open to its Creator. Sujjadan (prostrating) and qiyaman (standing) together indicate the completeness of their worship, encompassing both humility in bowing to the ground and dignified readiness in standing. Their vigil in the night is thus a sign of a heart that prefers closeness to God over rest, and it stands in contrast to heedlessness, teaching that genuine faith is revealed in devotion pursued quietly, in secret, and with sincere longing for the Lord.

translation: And those who say, "Our Lord, avert from us the punishment of Hell; indeed, its punishment is ever-clinging destruction."
interpretation: The verse portrays the sincere servants of the Most Merciful who, despite their piety, turn in fear and humility to their Lord, asking Him to turn away the torment of Hell. Their supplication reveals that true faith does not breed complacency but a constant awareness of accountability. The word gharam, rendered as ever-clinging or relentless ruin, conveys a punishment that is inseparable, persistent, and without respite, which is why the believer fears it even while performing good deeds. The verse thus teaches that fear of the Hereafter, joined with hope in God's mercy, is a defining mark of the righteous, and that seeking refuge from the consequences of sin is itself an act of worship.

translation: Indeed, it is evil as a place of settling and a station of rest.
interpretation: The verse speaks of Hell (Jahannam) as the abode of the wrongdoers, described in the words of the believers' prayer for protection from it in the preceding verses. Its evil lies in that it is a lasting dwelling and a final resting place, a state of permanence with no escape or relief. The phrase 'mustaqarran wa muqaman' underscores both the permanence of residence and the condition of standing or abiding in it, so that the verse warns that the ultimate destination of persistent disobedience is not a place of rest or comfort but one of enduring torment, and it calls the listener to reflect on the consequences of his choices before the abode is reached.

translation: And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are ever moderate between that (course).
interpretation: The verse describes the balanced character of the true servants of the Most Merciful (Al-Furqan 25:67) in the matter of wealth. Their spending is governed by moderation: they avoid the excess of wastefulness (israf), which squanders what Allah has entrusted to them, and they avoid the meanness of miserliness (qatr), which withholds what is due to themselves, their families, and others. The word qawam points to a middle course that is neither a burden nor a deprivation, so that generosity is measured by wisdom and need. Such equilibrium in spending reflects a wider principle in the believer's life, in which the faculties of the soul and the resources of the world are kept in right proportion, and in which moderation becomes a mark of faith.

translation: And those who do not invoke along with Allah any other deity, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse. And whoever does that will meet a penalty.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Furqan (25:68), joins three of the gravest prohibitions in the moral order: associating partners with God, taking innocent life, and illicit sexual relations. Their placement together reveals that the foundations of faith and the foundations of a just society are inseparable; a person who corrupts belief in the One God is likely to corrupt the sanctity of life and the integrity of family. The qualifier "except by right" establishes that the sanctity of life is absolute save for what justice legitimately requires, so the verse protects the human soul against arbitrary violence. The final phrase, that whoever does these things will meet a penalty (athām), conveys that these sins carry real consequences, both in this life and in the Hereafter, and that repentance, as the following verses in the surah affirm, remains open to those who turn back in sincerity.

translation: His punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide in it in humiliation.
interpretation: The verse presents the punishment of the one who commits great wrongs as increasing in severity on the Day of Resurrection, so that the consequence of his deeds is multiplied in proportion to his transgression. Its being described as lasting and accompanied by humiliation reflects the complete loss of honor that a person suffers when pride and persistence in evil have stripped him of his dignity. The verse thereby conveys that divine justice is exact: no one bears a burden beyond what his conduct has earned, and those who persist in wrongdoing will find that their reckoning is not lightened but intensified, while the disgrace they chose in this life becomes a permanent state in the next.

translation: Except for one who repents, believes, and does righteous work; for those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse opens a door of hope after the preceding warnings: repentance is not merely the abandonment of sin but its replacement. Faith comes first as the inner foundation, and righteous action makes that faith visible and real in conduct. The striking promise is that God does not only erase the record of wrongdoing but transforms it, so that the very deeds that once stood against a person are turned into good. This reveals the depth of divine mercy, which seeks not merely to forgive the sinner but to remake the sinner's past into a source of merit. The closing names, Forgiving and Merciful, affirm that this transformation flows from God's boundless compassion rather than from any deserving on the part of the human being.

translation: And whoever repents and does righteous deeds, then indeed he turns back to Allah with a sincere turning (repentance).
interpretation: The verse shows that genuine repentance is not merely a verbal regret but a turning that must be completed by action: the one who turns away from sin must also replace it with good deeds. Such a person does not simply stop sinning; he returns to God in a complete and accepted manner, as the emphatic phrasing "yatubu ila Allah matāban" indicates, a turning that is fully directed toward the Lord and sincerely made. The verse thus links the inner turning of the heart with the outer practice of righteousness, teaching that the door of return to God remains open and that repentance is judged by the sincerity of both the turning and the deeds that follow it.

translation: And those who do not bear false witness, and when they pass by vain or idle talk, they pass by with dignity.
interpretation: The verse portrays the true servants of the Most Merciful as people of moral integrity who refuse to take part in falsehood, whether by lending their presence to it or by testifying to what is untrue. Their refusal extends beyond what they say to where they choose to be: when they encounter frivolous, empty, or obscene speech, they do not engage, argue, or linger, but withdraw with composure and noble bearing. The verse thus shows that a believer's dignity lies in guarding the ears, tongue, and company from what is worthless, so that the self remains elevated above every form of idle and harmful speech.

translation: And those who, when they are reminded of the verses of their Lord, do not fall down before them deaf and blind.
interpretation: The verse portrays the true believers as those whose hearts and senses are awake to the divine message: when the signs of their Lord are recalled to them, they respond with reverent prostration and attentive listening, not with the indifference of one who hears without understanding or looks without seeing. Their submission is not a mere mechanical posture but the fruit of an open heart, so the verse implicitly warns that heedless deafness and blindness toward revelation are spiritual conditions, not merely physical ones, and that genuine faith is measured by how the words of God move the one who hears them.

translation: And those who say, "Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and our offspring comfort of the eyes, and make us leaders for the righteous."
interpretation: The verse portrays the believer's aspiration that faith extend beyond the self into the family. Its request for "comfort of the eyes" from spouses and offspring asks for a household whose goodness brings true delight, since a family is a joy only when it walks in obedience to God. The phrase "make us leaders for the righteous" then lifts this private hope into a public one: the believers do not seek mere status or worldly rank, but to be guides whose example draws others toward piety. Thus the supplication moves from the home outward to the community, showing that righteousness is meant to be inherited and multiplied, so that one's own piety becomes a light for others to follow.

translation: Those will be rewarded with the highest chamber (of Paradise) for what they endured with patience, and they will be met therein with greetings and peace.
interpretation: The verse presents patience as the key that opens the highest stations of Paradise. The 'chamber' (al-ghurfa) is a image of elevated, secure dwelling, and the reward is not only a place but a welcome: being greeted with 'taḥiyya' and 'salām' signals honor, belonging, and the removal of every fear and grief. It teaches that the hardships a believer bears with steadfastness are not lost but are transformed into a dignified reception in the presence of God's mercy, where the one who endured is embraced by peace rather than merely recompensed.

translation: Abiding therein forever. How excellent it is as a place of settling and a place of residence.
interpretation: The verse closes the description of the reward given to the servants of the Most Merciful by joining two words, mustaqarr (a place of settling and rest) and maqam (a place of standing and dwelling), to show that the chambers of Paradise offer both repose and a lasting home. The phrase khalidina fiha ties this reward to permanence, so the comfort is never interrupted by departure or loss. The phrase hasunat, 'how excellent it is,' sets Paradise against the impermanent and unstable dwellings of this world, suggesting that true security and tranquility are found only where the believers' abode is everlasting.

translation: Say: My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication. But you have denied, so the punishment will be inevitable.
interpretation: The verse establishes that human worth before God rests on the call of faith and the turning of the heart to Him: were it not for the supplication through which people acknowledge their need and dependence, God would have no regard for them. Yet the denial of the Messenger and of the truth has already occurred, and this denial brings a binding consequence, the inevitable requirement of accountability. Thus the verse joins divine mercy, which responds to sincere calling upon God, with the warning that rejection of the message makes the resulting punishment certain.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ta-Sin-Mim.
interpretation: The opening letters Ta-Sin-Mim belong to the muqatta'at, the disconnected letters that preface several surahs, and their precise meaning rests with Allah. Their placement before the revelation's description of the Book signals a call to attention: the same Arabic letters from which human speech is built are presented as the very medium of a divine message that no human can fully replicate. The basmala that precedes them anchors the whole recitation in the mercy of Allah, so that the reader approaches the verses that follow with humility, awareness of divine majesty, and trust in that mercy.

translation: These are the verses of the Clear Book.
interpretation: The verse opens by pointing to what is about to be recited as signs (ayat) of a book that is 'mubin', meaning clear and manifest in itself and in making things clear to others. Its clarity lies in distinguishing truth from falsehood, guidance from misguidance, so that the reader is not left in doubt. The word 'tilka' (those) points to verses already known or being presented with a sense of honor and distinction, inviting the listener to recognize their authority. The verse thus establishes the Qur'an as a book whose signs are readily understandable, calling people to reflect on them and to be guided by what has been made plain.

translation: Perhaps you would wear yourself out with grief because they do not believe.
interpretation: The verse (Surah Ash-Shu'ara, 26:3) consoles the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ over his intense distress at the refusal of his people to accept faith. Its tone is one of divine compassion: God recognizes how deeply the Prophet cares for the guidance of his community and how painful their rejection is to him, yet it reminds him that guidance belongs to God alone and that his duty is only to convey the message. The verse thus teaches that a messenger is not responsible for the outcome of his call, and that he should not let sorrow over others' disbelief consume his spirit, since the burden of conveying the truth is fulfilled through sincere effort rather than through compelling every heart to belief.

translation: If We willed, We would send down upon them from the sky a sign, and their necks would remain bowed before it in humility.
interpretation: The verse points to the nature of faith as a free and considered choice rather than compelled submission. Had God wished, He could have made the truth so overwhelmingly visible, through a sign from the heavens, that people would be forced to bow in obedience. Yet such forced submission would carry no moral worth, since belief that arises from coercion or sheer compulsion is not the fruit of reflection and the heart's own consent. God therefore addresses hearts through reason, the signs of creation, and revealed guidance, leaving people to choose. The image of bowed necks conveys a helpless, involuntary humility, in contrast to the voluntary humility of the believer who submits after reflecting upon the evidence.

translation: And no reminder comes to them from the Most Merciful, [being] newly revealed, except that they turn away from it.
interpretation: The verse portrays a recurring human condition: whenever a fresh reminder arrives from God, its novelty and repeated coming become occasions for dismissal rather than attentiveness. The word "muhdath" suggests that each revelation addresses the present moment, yet people often treat it as something to be heard with indifference, as though the familiar message did not require their renewed response. The turning away is not due to a lack of evidence but to a heedlessness of the heart that stands between the listener and the mercy being offered. The verse thus calls the reader to receive each reminder as a living address, examining whether their own attention is shaped by openness or by habitual aversion.

translation: So they have indeed denied, but there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock.
interpretation: This verse is a warning that mockery of divine revelation and of the messengers does not go unanswered. The denial and ridicule of the disbelievers are met with a certainty: the consequences of what they scoffed at will inevitably reach them. The phrase "news" (anba') implies that the truth of the message will become manifest to them, whether in this world through the outcome of events or in the Hereafter, so that the very thing they dismissed as a jest will become a reality they can no longer deny. It is a reminder to the believers to remain steadfast in the face of ridicule, trusting that falsehood and mockery ultimately give way to the truth.

translation: Have they not looked at the earth, how many noble pairs of every kind We have caused to grow therein?
interpretation: The verse directs the reader to reflect on the living world around them as evidence of divine power and generosity. The phrase "every noble pair" points to the diversity and paired nature of created life, plants and creatures alike, which is produced by God's will and bounty. By asking whether they have not seen this, the verse invites people to move from merely observing the earth to recognizing the Creator behind its abundant and orderly fertility, and to respond with gratitude and belief in resurrection, since the One who revives dead land can revive the dead.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers.
interpretation: The verse closes a narrative of past nations by drawing a lesson: the events recounted contain a clear sign that should lead to faith, yet the scriptural emphasis is that the majority of those addressed remained unbelieving despite the evidence. Its point is that the scarcity of belief is not due to a lack of proof but to the heart's stubbornness and its refusal to be guided, a reality the Prophet himself was meant to bear with patience, since guidance belongs to God's will and not to the mere abundance of signs.

translation: And indeed, your Lord is the Exalted in Might, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse closes a passage by joining two divine attributes that are meant to be held together: 'al-'Azīz' signifies a power that is irresistible and unassailable, so that no one can thwart God's decree or escape His judgment, while 'al-Raḥīm' signifies a mercy that is steady and enduring toward those who turn back to Him. The combination teaches that God's might is never arbitrary and His mercy is never weak; the one who is able to punish is the same who chooses to forgive, and so the believer should fear His power while hoping in His compassion, and the one who opposes or strays should understand that divine mercy does not negate divine sovereignty.

translation: And [mention] when your Lord called out to Moses: "Go to the wrongdoing people."
interpretation: The verse opens a narrative of the call of Moses, whose mission begins with a direct divine summons, and it frames his task as confronting a people defined by zulm, wrongdoing that is both transgression against God and injustice against others. By sending Moses to "the wrongdoing people" rather than simply to a nation, the verse presents the prophetic mission as a moral confrontation: the prophet is sent not to flatter or accommodate but to call the oppressors back to justice and to truth. The brevity of the command also emphasizes that the messenger's obligation is clear and unconditional, and that the Lord who commissions him is the one who sustains him through the difficulty of that confrontation.

translation: The people of Pharaoh. Will they not fear Allah?
interpretation: The verse is a rebuke posed as a question: after the mention of the people of Pharaoh, it asks whether they will not guard themselves with taqwa, that is, be mindful of God and fear the consequences of their wrongdoing. The people of Pharaoh are held up as a warning example of a community that ignored clear signs and persisted in arrogance and oppression. The rhetorical question directs the listener to recognize that such heedlessness is unreasonable, since the signs of God were plainly before them, and it calls the hearer to the opposite course of piety and awareness of accountability.

translation: He said: "My Lord, indeed I fear that they will deny me."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Prophet Musa (Moses) in Surah Ash-Shu'ara (26:12), reveals the human and prophetic dimension of a messenger facing opposition. Rather than projecting unshakable composure, Musa openly expresses his anxiety about being disbelieved by Pharaoh's people, and he turns that fear immediately toward his Lord in supplication. The interpretation highlights that genuine reliance on God (tawakkul) does not require the absence of fear; it is precisely in acknowledging one's limits and vulnerability before God that the believer finds strength, and the request that follows in the surrah (for his brother Harun to be sent with him) shows that trust in God is expressed through honest prayer and practical means together.

translation: "And my chest tightens and my tongue does not speak freely, so send [the mission] to Aaron."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Moses (Musa) when God commanded him to go to Pharaoh, reveals his human vulnerability before a daunting task. He expresses his fear that his chest will constrict under the weight of the mission and that his tongue will be unable to articulate his message with ease, a reference to the speech impediment mentioned elsewhere in the Qur'an. Rather than declining the mission, he humbly asks God to send his brother Aaron (Harun), who is more eloquent, to support him. The verse thus teaches that a true prophet's request for help is an act of sincere reliance on God, acknowledging his own limitations while trusting in divine provision and in the strength that comes through companionship and shared responsibility.

translation: And they have a charge against me, so I fear that they will kill me.
interpretation: Moses speaks of the killing of the Egyptian man, for which he feels responsible, and this fear of retaliation is the reason he left Egypt for Midian. The verse shows that he did not flee from cowardice alone but acted out of caution and a sense of accountability. It also reflects a prophet who, before receiving his mission, is fully human, feeling fear, seeking safety, and trusting that God will guide his path, as the verse that follows shows him praying to be delivered from the wrongdoing people.

translation: He said: "No! Go, both of you, with Our signs. Indeed, We are with you, listening."
interpretation: The verse comes in the context of Moses' request that his brother Aaron be sent with him to Pharaoh. God's response, "Kalla" (No, never), dismisses the fear that Moses had expressed about being rejected or harmed, and commands them both to go forth carrying God's signs. The phrase "Indeed, We are with you, listening" conveys that divine protection and support accompany the prophets, for God hears everything said between them and Pharaoh and is never absent from their mission. The verse thus assures the believer that when one carries God's message, the Lord's companionship and attentive hearing sustain him against any opposition.

translation: So go to Pharaoh and say: Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse marks the moment of formal commission: Moses and Aaron are sent to confront the most powerful tyrant of their age, and their message is framed not as a personal demand but as a delegation from the Lord of all worlds. By identifying themselves as messengers of the Sustainer of the entire creation, they establish the authority of their mission above that of Pharaoh, who claimed lordship over his people. The brevity of the statement is itself significant: the prophets are not to argue for their own status but to deliver a clear declaration of their sender's sovereignty, leaving the weight of the message to speak for itself and placing the responsibility of response upon Pharaoh.

translation: That you send with us the Children of Israel.
interpretation: The demand is framed as a rightful claim made in the name of the Lord of the worlds, so the prophetic mission begins with a call to release an oppressed people rather than with a display of power. By asking Pharaoh to let the Children of Israel go with them, Moses and Aaron signal that their message is a summons to justice and freedom, and that the deliverance of the people is inseparable from the message of God.

translation: [Pharaoh] said: Did we not raise you among us as a child, and did you not stay among us for years of your life?
interpretation: The verse records Pharaoh's rebuke to Moses, reminding him of the debt of his upbringing in Pharaoh's household and the years he spent among the Egyptians, as a way of framing Moses' mission as ingratitude. Beneath the words lies the tyrant's habit of turning favor into a claim of ownership: he presents the nurturing that Moses received as a bond that obliges him to submission. The verse thus exposes how power seeks to make past kindness a chain, and it sets the stage for the confrontation in which the prophet's message of God's sovereignty stands against the claims of a ruler who regards himself as the lord of those he raised.

translation: "And you did your deed which you did, and you were among the ungrateful."
interpretation: This verse is spoken by Moses to Pharaoh's household when he recalls the killing of the Egyptian man, which he had committed before receiving prophethood. The phrase "your deed which you did" refers to that act, and Moses reproaches Pharaoh for it, reminding him that he had taken a life without right. By calling Pharaoh "among the ungrateful" (al-kafirin), the verse points to the ingratitude of Pharaoh toward the favors of God and toward those who had shown him kindness, since he had raised Moses in his household. The verse thus reflects a rebuke that combines the seriousness of wrongful bloodshed with the denial of rightful gratitude, and it shows Moses using a measured argument to confront the arrogance of a tyrant.

translation: [Moses] said, "I did it then, while I was among those who were astray."
interpretation: Moses is acknowledging, in response to Pharaoh's reproach for the killing he committed, that the act was done in a state of error before his prophethood, when he had not yet been guided. The word ḍalāl here refers to being unaware of the right course rather than to deliberate rebellion or disbelief. Moses thereby admits the mistake without malice, and this honest confession points to a humility that prepared him for the divine mission.

translation: So I fled from you when I feared you, but my Lord granted me wisdom and made me among the messengers.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by Moses after his flight from Egypt, following the killing of the Egyptian man, when he feared retribution from Pharaoh's court. His words reflect a sincere acknowledgment that fear drove him to flee, and at the same time a recognition that his escape was itself part of God's providential plan. The gift of wisdom (hukm) that God bestowed upon him points to the inner discernment, judgment and prophetic insight he received, which prepared him for his mission. Being made 'among the messengers' shows that this moment of flight, which might have appeared to be a personal failure, became the very threshold of his prophethood, teaching that God's favor can arise from circumstances that seem to be setbacks.

translation: And is this a favor of which you remind me, that you have enslaved the Children of Israel?
interpretation: Pharaoh's reply to Moses (in Surah ash-Shu'ara, 26:22) is a rhetorical retort that turns Moses' argument against him. Moses had pointed to his own upbringing in Pharaoh's household as proof of a debt of gratitude, and Pharaoh answers with contempt, suggesting that the protection he gave Moses as a child cannot be called a favor when the price was the enslavement of the Children of Israel. The verse exposes the tyrant's inversion of moral reality: he regards the oppression of an entire people as a justification for dismissing a benefit he himself conferred, while failing to see that the favor Moses speaks of was owed to a people he had reduced to bondage. It also shows how those who hold power often refuse to acknowledge the injustices their rule has produced, and so they reframe any reminder of them as an ingratitude.

translation: Pharaoh said, "And what is the Lord of the worlds?"
interpretation: Pharaoh's question is not a genuine inquiry into the nature of God but a rhetorical denial, born of arrogance and his claim to divinity over his people. By asking "what" rather than "who" the Lord of the worlds is, he dismisses the very concept of a sovereign Creator beyond himself, revealing that tyranny often begins with the refusal to acknowledge any authority above the self. The verse thus exposes the posture of the oppressor who seeks to be the ultimate reference point for his subjects, and it sets the stage for Moses's answer that the Lord of the worlds is the One who created and guides all things.

translation: He said: "Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, if you are people of certainty."
interpretation: This verse comes from Moses' reply to Pharaoh, who had asked, "And what is the Lord of the worlds?" Rather than naming a rival or offering a physical description, Moses points to the vast order of creation itself: the heavens, the earth, and all that lies between them. The challenge is directed at the mind that witnesses these signs. By tying the question of God to certainty (yaqin), the verse suggests that knowledge of the Creator is not merely a matter of argument but of sincere, attentive reflection upon what is plainly before us. Pharaoh's claim to divinity is thus set against the evident sovereignty of the One who sustains everything visible and invisible, and the conditional phrase "if you are certain" turns the listener from mere dispute toward honest recognition.

translation: He said to those around him, "Do you not listen?"
interpretation: The verse shows Pharaoh's reaction to Moses' call to acknowledge the Lord of the worlds. Unable to answer the argument, he turns to his courtiers and mocks Moses' words, using ridicule and feigned astonishment to shift attention from the truth being presented to the way it is delivered. This reveals how those who hold power often rely on derision rather than reasoned response when confronted with a message that threatens their authority.

translation: He said, "Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old."
interpretation: The verse presents the speaker, here Moses's counterpart Pharaoh's challenger or the messenger in the dialogue, as directing attention beyond the immediate claims of the audience to the one true Lord who is not only the Lord of the present generation but also of all those who came before them. By tying the sovereignty of God to the ancestors, it dismantles the appeal to inherited custom as a justification for worship, showing that the lineage of belief cannot rest on tradition alone but must answer to the Creator and Sustainer who stands above all generations.

translation: He said, "Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is surely a madman!"
interpretation: This verse is part of the account of Pharaoh's response to Moses and Aaron (in Surah ash-Shu'ara' and related passages, it is Pharaoh's court speaking; here it is spoken by the one addressed as having dismissed the messenger). The charge of madness is a recurring tactic of those who reject prophets: rather than engaging with the message's substance, the disbelievers dismiss the bearer as deranged, thereby avoiding the moral and spiritual demands the message carries. The verse reveals a pattern in which the sender of the message is discredited so that its truth need not be weighed. It also consoles the Prophet and the believers, showing that the accusation of madness has been leveled against messengers throughout history, and that the rejection reflects the hearts of the rejecters rather than any defect in the messenger, whose sanity and sincerity are manifest to those willing to reflect.

translation: He said, "Lord of the East and the West and whatever is between them, if you were to reason."
interpretation: The verse presents Moses's reply to Pharaoh's challenge about the nature of the Lord, answering not with a name or a physical description but with the vastness of God's dominion over every direction of the sky and earth and all that lies between them. By tying the claim to the sunrise and sunset, which Pharaoh could observe daily, the verse invites the listener to move from the visible order of creation to the recognition of its single Creator. The closing condition, "if you were to reason," turns the argument into a call to the intellect: the signs of God in the cosmos are offered to be understood, and the refusal to see them is presented as a failure of reason rather than a lack of evidence.

translation: He said: "If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Pharaoh to Moses (Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:29), reveals the arrogance of a tyrant who, having claimed divinity for himself, meets the prophet's call to the worship of the One God with threat rather than argument. The imprisonment he threatens is the instrument of a ruler who has no answer to the message and so turns to coercion. Interpreted more widely, it shows that when power is confronted with truth it often resorts to force against those who speak it, while the believer is reminded that the true sovereign is God alone, before whose authority every earthly threat is limited.

translation: He said: "Even if I bring you something clear (as proof)?"
interpretation: This is the response of Pharaoh's people, or in some readings the speech of Pharaoh himself, within the account of Moses. When Moses was sent with signs, the challenged party sought to test his credibility by demanding proof, and the phrase "Even if I bring you something clear" reveals the stance of one who has already made up his mind to reject. The verse teaches that stubborn disbelief often masks itself as a demand for evidence, while the evidence, once clearly shown, is still refused when the heart is closed to truth.

translation: He said, "Then bring it, if you are among the truthful."
interpretation: This verse is spoken in the context of a dispute in which a claim is made that must be substantiated by evidence. The speaker does not accept the bare assertion but demands a concrete proof, establishing that genuine truthfulness is shown through verifiable demonstration rather than words alone. It teaches that a claim, whether a claimant's accusation or a messenger's message, stands or falls on the proof that can be produced, and that the one who is truly sincere has nothing to fear from being tested by evidence.

translation: So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent.
interpretation: The verse depicts the moment Moses, at Allah's command, cast his staff to the ground, and it instantly transformed into a real, unmistakable serpent before the eyes of Pharaoh and his court. The word "mubin" (clear, manifest) emphasizes that this was no illusion or trick of sorcery but an undeniable sign, so that the transformation itself becomes a proof of his prophethood. The miracle is thus framed as a direct confrontation between divine power and the magicians' artifice, the first of the signs given to Moses to demonstrate the truth of his message.

translation: And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the beholders.
interpretation: The verse describes the second sign given to Moses: when he withdrew his hand from beneath his arm or from his garment, it emerged shining white, not from disease but as a miraculous light visible to all who looked upon it. This sign was a clear proof from God, meant to demonstrate to Pharaoh and his court that Moses was a true messenger, and to show that the divine power which accompanies the prophets is manifest and undeniable to any observer who regards it with an open mind.

translation: He said to the chiefs around him: "Indeed, this is truly a skilled sorcerer."
interpretation: The verse portrays Pharaoh's reaction to Moses's miracles: unable to refute the signs with argument, he turns to his circle of elites and seeks to discredit Moses by labeling him a sorcerer, a charge that reveals the tyrant's reliance on public perception and the authority of his court rather than on reasoned truth. By calling Moses 'knowledgeable' in sorcery, he even grudgingly concedes the extraordinary skill of what was shown, yet attributes it to magic so as to avoid acknowledging a divine sign. The verse thus illustrates a recurring pattern in the Qur'anic narratives, in which those who arrogantly reject prophets dismiss clear evidence as mere trickery to protect their worldly status and to keep their followers in line.

translation: He wants to drive you out of your land through his magic, so what do you advise?
interpretation: This verse records the words of Pharaoh's chiefs (his council) to him, as they urged him to act against Moses and Aaron. Their rhetoric shifts the threat from a religious message to a political one: they present Moses as a sorcerer whose real aim is to expel the Egyptians from their land and seize their dominion. By framing the prophetic call as sorcery and a plot against the nation, they aim to stir fear and provoke the ruler to decisive action. The verse thus exposes a recurring pattern in the story of the prophets, in which those who hold power dismiss the truth as deception and portray reformers as threats to the social order, while the question 'what do you advise?' reveals their consultation and their readiness to plan a response rather than examine the message itself.

translation: They said: Delay him and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah al-A'raf (7:111) and echoed in Surah ash-Shu'ara' (26:36), records the counsel of Pharaoh's chiefs when they learned of Musa and the signs he had brought. Fearing for their power, they urged Pharaoh to hold back Musa and Harun and to dispatch agents to gather skilled sorcerers from every city. The verse exposes how entrenched authority responds to a message of truth: rather than examining the signs honestly, it seeks delay, mobilization, and spectacle to preserve its dominance. Their plan also sets the stage for the contest at which the sorcerers were defeated by the clear sign of God, showing that human schemes to suppress the truth cannot prevail against it.

translation: They will bring to you every skilled sorcerer, learned in his craft.
interpretation: The verse is spoken in the context of Pharaoh's court, where he summons the sorcerers to confront Moses. Its emphasis is on the confidence of the regime in its own resources: Pharaoh promises that every accomplished magician will be gathered to meet the challenge. Read more deeply, it displays the human tendency to marshal all available expertise and authority against a message whose truth rests not on skill but on a sign from God, a contrast the subsequent narrative resolves when the sorcerers themselves recognize the Lord of Moses and Aaron.

translation: So the magicians were gathered for the appointment of a known day.
interpretation: This verse describes the assembling of Pharaoh's magicians at the appointed time and day agreed upon for the contest with Moses. Pharaoh, having summoned them from across his realm, set a public day of gathering so that the confrontation would be witnessed by the people. The phrase 'a known day' signals that the time was fixed and widely publicized, making the event a deliberate spectacle intended to demonstrate Pharaoh's power and to discredit Moses' message before the masses. The verse thus prepares the reader for the decisive scene in which the sorcery is confronted by a sign from God, underscoring how the arena chosen by Pharaoh became the very stage on which the truth was made manifest.

translation: And it will be said to the people: 'Are you gathering together?'
interpretation: The verse depicts the Day of Judgment, when people are summoned to assemble before their Lord, and the question addressed to them is laden with rebuke and urgency, as though to say: 'Will you now gather, having scattered yourselves in heedlessness in the world?' It conveys that the gathering is not a matter of choice, and that the very act of assembling for the reckoning exposes the hollowness of earlier worldly crowds, factions, and allegiances. The question also invites reflection on the reality that every human being will one day stand together, stripped of worldly rank and affiliation, awaiting judgment.

translation: Perhaps we will follow the magicians if they are the victors.
interpretation: The words are spoken by Pharaoh's courtiers, and they expose a worldly, opportunistic calculus: their willingness to follow is conditioned on outcome rather than on the truth of the message. Their stance shows that they measure right by power and success, so their allegiance is hollow, and the verse warns that faith resting on who appears to win is no firm faith at all.

translation: So when the magicians came, they said to Pharaoh, "Will there surely be a reward for us if we are the victors?"
interpretation: The verse captures the moment the sorcerers, summoned to confront Moses, approach Pharaoh with a mercenary question about their wages. Their eagerness for reward reveals that their allegiance rested on worldly gain and the prospect of Pharaoh's favor rather than on conviction about the truth. Their words, framed as a conditional on victory, expose a calculation that treats the contest as a transaction, which sets up the dramatic reversal that follows when they recognize the signs of their Lord and prostrate themselves, showing that sincere faith can overturn a motive born of material interest.

translation: He said, "Yes, and indeed you will then be among those brought near (to me)."
interpretation: This verse comes from the account of Pharaoh's magicians (Surah al-A'raf 7:114 and Surah ash-Shu'ara 26:42), who asked Pharaoh for a reward if they prevailed over Moses. Pharaoh's reply shows that worldly power promises rewards for loyalty and service, and that he attached his favor to their victory over the truth. The verse thus reveals how a tyrant buys the service of people with status and nearness to the seat of power, while the Qur'an's broader narrative shows that such nearness is worthless when it is bought at the price of falsehood, since the magicians soon turned to faith in the Lord of Moses and Aaron.

translation: Musa said to them, "Throw down whatever you are going to throw."
interpretation: Musa's words reveal the composure of a prophet who faces the magicians of Pharaoh without fear or haste. By inviting them to cast first, he lets the contest unfold openly, so that when their staffs and ropes appear to move like serpents, the truth that follows is shown to rest on divine power rather than on any trick of his own. The verse teaches that sincere conviction in God allows one to wait calmly for the outcome, confident that falsehood, however impressive it looks, cannot stand before the truth.

translation: So they threw down their ropes and their staffs, and said, "By the might of Pharaoh, we are certainly the victors."
interpretation: The verse depicts the moment when Pharaoh's magicians, summoned to confront Moses, cast down their ropes and staffs, which through sorcery appeared to be writhing serpents. Their oath by Pharaoh's might reveals their reliance on worldly power and their confidence in the king's patronage, and their certainty of victory shows how they trusted in outward display and deception rather than in the truth. The scene sets up the reversal that follows, where the staff of Moses swallows their illusions and the magicians are brought to submission before the truth of God.

translation: So Moses threw down his staff, and behold, it swallowed up what they were falsely fabricating.
interpretation: The verse presents the decisive moment of confrontation between Moses and the magicians of Pharaoh's court, where the staff becomes a sign that exposes the emptiness of their deception. The swallowing of their fabricated illusions signifies that falsehood, however elaborate and convincing in appearance, cannot stand before the truth delivered by God's messenger. It also reveals that the miracle is not a display of human skill or sorcery but a divine act that overturns the pretensions of those who opposed the message, teaching that reliance on deceit and manipulation is ultimately swallowed by the reality it sought to conceal.

translation: So the magicians were thrown down prostrate (in worship).
interpretation: The verse describes the sudden reversal of the sorcerers of Pharaoh's court after they witnessed Moses' sign. Having come to contest with Moses and expecting a reward from Pharaoh, they were overwhelmed by the truth they recognized, and their prostration shows that their hearts were moved to submit before the Lord of Moses and Aaron. The phrase 'were cast down' (ulqiya) signals that the prostration was not a deliberate act of their own choosing but an involuntary, overpowering submission to a truth that had seized them, underscoring that genuine faith often arrives as a sudden illumination that humbles the proud and redirects the self from display and ambition toward humble worship.

translation: They say: "We believe in the Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: This verse, spoken in the context of the story of Moses and the magicians of Pharaoh (Surah al-A'raf 7:121-122 and Surah al-Shu'ara 26:47-48, where the same phrase appears), shows the sudden transformation of hearts when truth becomes clear. The magicians, who had come to contest Moses, prostrated themselves once they recognized the signs as genuine, and their declaration of faith in the Lord of the worlds, rather than in Pharaoh, reveals that sincere faith is born of recognition of truth, not of worldly rank or fear. Their words also stand as a rebuke to the power of Pharaoh, who had threatened them, since they chose allegiance to the Creator of all existence over the ruler of a single kingdom, accepting hardship for the sake of their new belief.

translation: The Lord of Moses and Aaron.
interpretation: This short phrase, spoken in the context of Moses and Aaron's mission before Pharaoh, anchors the divine identity in a personal and covenantal relationship: the God to whom Moses and Aaron were sent is not a distant or abstract power but the Lord who chose, commissioned, and sustained these two prophets. By naming Himself as the Lord of Moses and Aaron, God affirms that the authority behind their message is the same sovereign Lord who governs all creation, and that Pharaoh's claim to lordship is false in the face of this higher and rightful dominion.

translation: [Pharaoh] said: "Have you believed in him before I give you permission? Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic. So you will soon know! I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will crucify you all."
interpretation: The verse captures the moment of confrontation between Pharaoh and the sorcerers who had just embraced faith in the Lord of Aaron and Moses. Pharaoh's words reveal the reflex of tyranny: belief is treated as a crime against the ruler's authority, and his question "Have you believed before I permit you?" exposes his claim to own the consciences of his subjects. His accusation that Moses is their "chief" who taught them magic is an attempt to delegitimize the truth by reducing it to a trick learned in a school of sorcery, a charge that was used throughout history to dismiss prophets. The threat of severing hands and feet on opposite sides and crucifying them is a display of brutal power meant to terrify others into submission. Yet the verse, read against its context, shows the futility of this power: the sorcerers had already found in certainty of faith a strength that made torture and death insignificant, so Pharaoh's threats only sharpened the contrast between the transient authority of a tyrant and the lasting reward of believing in God.

translation: They said: "No harm! Indeed, we are returning to our Lord."
interpretation: This verse, spoken in the context of the believers facing the threat of being burned in the trench (Surah Ash-Shu'ara, 26:50 context, and Surah Ash-Shu'ara's account of the sorcerers before Pharaoh), reveals the serene certainty of faith in the face of death and punishment. The phrase "la darar" (no harm) expresses a heart that has settled its fear, because the believer understands that the worst a tyrant can do is to send him back to his Lord, the true destination of every soul. Thus the verse teaches that the reality of return to God transforms the meaning of suffering: what the oppressor sees as ultimate loss becomes, for the faithful, merely a passage toward the One to whom all matters belong.

translation: "We hope that our Lord will forgive us our sins, because we were the first of the believers."
interpretation: The verse presents the sorcerers' turn to faith after they witnessed Moses' sign. Having been summoned by Pharaoh and threatened with punishment, they chose the truth over worldly reward and fear, and their hope for forgiveness rests on sincere repentance and on the dawning of their faith, which made them the first to believe among their people. It teaches that a sincere return to God, made in the face of power and threat, is itself a path to mercy, and that a believer's hope is grounded in God's generosity rather than in the magnitude of past sins.

translation: And We inspired to Moses: Travel by night with My servants, for you will be pursued.
interpretation: The verse marks the moment of divine command in the story of the Exodus: Moses is instructed to leave by night with the believers, and the warning that they will be followed points to the imminent confrontation with Pharaoh's army. It teaches that when a righteous community is pressed by an oppressor, God provides a path of deliverance through prudence and trust, where the flight itself is part of the divine plan that leads toward the sea and the rescue that follows.

translation: So Pharaoh sent gatherers into the cities.
interpretation: The verse shows Pharaoh's response to the signs brought by Moses: rather than yielding to the truth, he mobilised his state apparatus, dispatching agents to every city to assemble his people and his magicians against Moses. The image reveals how tyranny turns to mass mobilisation and propaganda when its authority is challenged, seeking to rally the populace around itself by force and summons rather than by conviction. It also foreshadows the gathering that will be staged as a confrontation with Moses, in which the outcome will be decided by God rather than by the numbers Pharaoh assembles.

translation: "Indeed, these are but a small band."
interpretation: The verse is spoken by Pharaoh (in Surah Ash-Shu'ara, 26:54), who, having gathered his forces to pursue Moses and the Children of Israel, dismisses them as a tiny, insignificant group. His words reveal the arrogance of a tyrant who measures truth and strength by numbers and worldly power, underestimating those whom God has chosen and protected. The irony is that this very contempt sets the stage for his downfall: the 'small band' is guided and sheltered by God, while the vast army that scorned them is drowned in the sea. The verse thus teaches that numerical insignificance in the eyes of the powerful is no measure of the strength of faith or of the certainty of divine victory.

translation: And indeed they are enraged against us.
interpretation: This phrase comes from the account of the people of Moses, who, after Moses and the believers had been delivered and Pharaoh's forces drowned, are depicted as hostile and seething with anger. The verse's meaning is that the opponents of the truth, in their envy and resentment, are provoked and infuriated by the rise of those whom God has favored, and their fury is itself a sign of their defeat before the divine will.

translation: And indeed, we are all vigilant and ready (to take precaution).
interpretation: The verse is spoken in the context of the story of Joseph's brothers, or more precisely of the people of Pharaoh's magicians and the Israelites in Surah Ash-Shu'ara, where Pharaoh, alarmed by the Israelites' departure, declares that they are a small band, but that they are a force that keeps watch and is prepared. The word 'hadhirun' conveys a state of being constantly alert, armed and cautious, as though the speaker is saying that his side is always on guard against any threat.
