Read deeper, it reveals the tyrant's habitual psychology: power built on fear is always anxious, always suspicious, and always bracing for the danger it imagines, while the believers who are truly guarded are those who are guarded by God.

translation: So We expelled them from gardens and springs.
interpretation: The phrase points to the sudden reversal of a people's fortune: those who had enjoyed gardens and flowing springs are stripped of them by divine decree. The verse frames worldly comfort as a trust that can be withdrawn at any moment, so that abundance should lead to gratitude and humility rather than heedlessness, since ownership of blessings ultimately belongs to God alone.

translation: And treasures and a noble station.
interpretation: The verse refers to the wealth and status of Pharaoh's people, whose hoarded treasures and elevated position in Egypt were the worldly comforts they enjoyed before being stripped of them. Read in context with the preceding verse about their expulsion from gardens and springs, it shows that worldly riches and honor are fleeting gifts that Allah can take away at will, and that the nation which held them is then replaced by others, as the following verse states.

translation: Thus We caused the Children of Israel to inherit it.
interpretation: The phrase "Thus We caused... to inherit" points to a divine act of transferring a position of possession and authority from one people to another, which is determined by Allah's will rather than by mere human power. It is placed within the account of Pharaoh's downfall, where the land and wealth that the oppressors held are given to the Children of Israel after their enemies are destroyed. The verse thus teaches that worldly dominion is a trust granted and withdrawn by God, and that the cycle of rise and fall follows a divine pattern in which oppression does not endure. The word "Thus" also signals that this inheritance is the outcome of the preceding events, so it is presented as a consequence of justice rather than an arbitrary gift.

translation: So they pursued them at sunrise.
interpretation: The phrase 'fa-atba'uhum mushriqeen' (Surah ash-Shu'ara 26:60) describes Pharaoh and his army pursuing Moses and the Children of Israel at the time of sunrise, as they set out after them. The timing carries weight: the pursuers went out in the morning light, confident and driven by their pride, just before the sea was parted for Moses and his people and then closed over Pharaoh's forces. The detail of the rising sun underscores the dramatic reversal, in which the early hours that Pharaoh chose for his pursuit became the setting of his destruction.

translation: And when the two groups saw each other, the companions of Moses said, "Indeed, we are going to be overtaken!"
interpretation: The verse captures the moment of acute fear at the edge of the sea, when Pharaoh's army closed in behind the Israelites and the sea lay ahead. The words of Moses's companions reveal how fear narrows human vision to the immediate danger, as they see only pursuit and no way out. Yet the verse also sets the stage for the reply that follows in the surrounding passage, in which Moses affirms that God is with him. It teaches that when the situation appears hopeless, the believer's response is to hold fast to trust in God rather than to be governed by the apparent certainty of defeat.

translation: He said, "Never! Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Moses when the Children of Israel were pursued by Pharaoh's army and found themselves trapped by the sea, reflects the complete reliance of a believer upon God in the face of seemingly hopeless circumstances. Moses's firm "Never!" rejects the despair voiced by his people, and his declaration that his Lord is with him expresses an unshakable certainty in divine presence and support. The phrase "He will guide me" shows that true trust (tawakkul) is not passive: it is joined with the confident expectation that God will show the way out of difficulty, and it teaches that the one who holds fast to God's companionship will not be abandoned, even when human means appear exhausted.

translation: So We revealed to Moses: Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted, and each part became like a huge mountain.
interpretation: The verse presents the parting of the sea as a direct sign of divine command and power: Moses' act of striking with the staff is not the source of the miracle but a means through which God's will is made manifest. The image of each separated portion rising like a towering mountain conveys both the magnitude of the event and the sense of a barrier held firm by God, turning the very element that seemed to threaten annihilation into a path of deliverance. It invites the reader to see that when faith responds to divine guidance, even the most overwhelming obstacles can be opened, and that the same God who commands the waters can secure the believer's passage.

translation: And We brought near there the others.
interpretation: The phrase 'wa-azlafna thamma al-akharin' refers to the scene of the Day of Judgment, in which Allah brings near (yuzlafu) the others, meaning the later generations or the rest of mankind who follow the first group, so that all of humanity is gathered and presented before Him for reckoning. The word 'thamma' (then) conveys the sequence of the gathering: first the earlier peoples are assembled, and then the later ones are drawn near to the same place of accounting, indicating that no generation is left out and that all are brought together to face their deeds.

translation: And We saved Moses and all those with him.
interpretation: The verse points to the completeness of divine deliverance: God did not rescue Moses alone but extended salvation to every believer who stood with him, so that none of those united in faith and in his mission was left to perish. It teaches that God's mercy embraces the righteous as a community, and that those who accompany a prophet in truth share in the consequences of his cause, whether in hardship or in victory.

translation: Then We drowned the others.
interpretation: The verse, from Surah ash-Shu'ara' (26:66) in the account of Musa and the Children of Israel, marks the final stage of the confrontation with Pharaoh's people. After Musa led the believers out and the sea was parted for them, Pharaoh and his army pursued them and were overtaken by the sea. The phrase "the others" refers to Pharaoh and his host, who were drowned after the believers had crossed safely. The verse presents this destruction as a direct act of divine justice that concluded their persecution of the Children of Israel and their rejection of the signs sent through Musa. It also serves as a warning that arrogance and oppression against God's messengers and the faithful lead to ruin, while deliverance comes to those who trust in God.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers.
interpretation: The verse closes a narrative of past peoples by pointing to the stories as a clear sign for those who reflect, and then exposes a sobering reality: the signs were evident, yet the majority of the people addressed did not accept faith. This reveals that the presence of proof alone does not produce belief; it requires an open heart and a willingness to be guided. It also consoles the Prophet and the believers, reminding them that the rejection of the majority is a recurring pattern in human history and not a failure of the message itself.

translation: And indeed, your Lord is the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse closes a passage by joining two divine attributes that are meant to be held together: 'Al-'Aziz', the one whose power is absolute and whose decree cannot be resisted, and 'Ar-Rahim', the one whose mercy is constant and reaches those who turn to Him. The pairing teaches the believer that divine might is never arbitrary, and divine mercy is never weakness. Because the Lord is able to do all that He wills, His promise of mercy is reliable, and because He is merciful, His power is exercised with compassion. The Prophet is thus reassured that the outcome rests with a Lord who is both capable of victory and inclined to forgive and show grace to His servants.

translation: And recite to them the news of Abraham.
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet to recite to his audience the account of Abraham, so that its lessons are conveyed to them as a living report rather than a distant legend. The word 'nabaʾ' (news) signifies a weighty, true tiding that deserves attention and reflection. By beginning the narrative with this command, the Qur'an frames the story of Abraham as a authoritative message whose purpose is to awaken its listeners to monotheism, to the folly of idolatry, and to the steadfast submission to God that Abraham embodied.

translation: When he said to his father and his people, "What is it that you worship?"
interpretation: The verse opens the account of Abraham's confrontation with his father and his people over idolatry, and its first move is a pointed question rather than a direct accusation. By asking "What is it that you worship?" Abraham invites them to examine the objects of their devotion themselves, exposing the emptiness of their worship through reflection and not mere assertion. The question also reveals the rational method of the prophetic call: the reformer begins with the people's own practices and forces them to confront what they are actually venerating, setting the stage for the subsequent dialogue in which the idols are shown to be powerless and unworthy of worship.

translation: They said, "We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them."
interpretation: This verse records the reply of those who were questioned in the presence of Abraham (in the surrounding passage, Ash-Shu'ara 26:70-71), when he asked them what they worshipped. Their answer is delivered with a plain, almost matter-of-fact pride: they do not deny their practice but openly declare that they serve idols and remain constantly devoted to them, sitting in attendance before them. The word 'aakifeena' conveys sustained, dedicated presence, suggesting that their idolatry was not a passing habit but a settled way of life to which they had given their whole attention. The verse thus exposes the attachment that inherited religious custom can create, where people defend what they have always done rather than examine whether it is right. It sets the stage for Abraham's call to reflect on what they truly serve and whether these idols can hear, benefit, or harm them.

translation: He said: "Do they hear you when you call (upon them)?"
interpretation: This verse comes from the account of Abraham's dialogue with his people, or in some readings the scene of those who call upon other than God, and it pointedly exposes the helplessness of the objects of worship. By asking whether these idols or false deities can hear their supplicants, the speaker lays bare the absurdity of directing prayer to what has neither hearing nor response. The question works as a rhetorical rebuke that invites the listener to recognize, through their own reason, that true recourse belongs only to the One who hears all calls and answers those who turn to Him.

translation: Or do they benefit you, or do they harm you?
interpretation: The verse closes Abraham's challenge to his people by stripping their idols of the two powers that would make them worthy of worship: the ability to benefit and the ability to harm. The question is rhetorical and leads the listener to recognize that whatever cannot answer, cannot profit, and cannot injure is no deity. Real power over benefit and harm belongs to God alone, so worship must be directed to Him.

translation: They said, "Rather, we found our fathers doing thus, so we follow in their footsteps."
interpretation: This verse, spoken in reply to a call to what is right, reveals the reflex of blind imitation (taqlid) that binds people to the customs of their ancestors even when those customs stand against clear guidance. Their answer is not an argument but an appeal to precedent, treating the habits of the past as self-justifying. The Qur'an repeatedly confronts this stance, teaching that truth is established by evidence and by its own merit rather than by the number of those who practiced it or the antiquity of their ways. The verse thus warns every generation to examine inherited beliefs and practices in the light of revelation and reason, rather than hold fast to them simply because they were the way of the fathers.

translation: He said: "Have you considered what you have been worshipping?"
interpretation: This verse comes from the account of Abraham (peace be upon him) confronting his people about the idols they served. By asking "Have you considered?", he invites them to reflect honestly on the objects of their devotion, prompting them to examine whether these lifeless images truly deserve worship. The question works as a rational challenge: it directs the listener to think critically about what they have placed at the center of their devotion, and it prepares the ground for the affirmation that only the One Lord who created them is worthy of worship.

translation: "Are you, and your forefathers of old?"
interpretation: The verse is spoken in the context of a rebuke directed at those who cling to the customs and beliefs inherited from their ancestors without reflection. By placing the living audience alongside their long-dead forefathers, it asks them to consider that they share the same fate and the same error if they simply follow what their fathers did. It calls the listener to rational examination of the truth rather than blind imitation, and it reminds that the ancestors' antiquity does not in itself confer validity upon their beliefs or practices. The phrase also carries a warning that those who persist in such imitation stand in the same position as the generations that preceded them and were held to account for their choices.

translation: Indeed, they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: In this verse Abraham declares a complete disavowal of everything worshipped besides God, which he regards as hostile to him, and makes a single exception for the Lord of the worlds. The verse teaches that genuine loyalty is exclusive: a believer cannot give allegiance to the Creator while still treating false objects of worship as friends or allies. True devotion to God therefore requires a clear break from whatever competes with Him for the heart's trust and obedience.

translation: Who created me, and it is He who guides me.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Abraham (peace be upon him) in Surah Ash-Shu'ara (26:78), points to the link between creation and guidance: the One who brought a person into existence is the same One who continually directs him toward what is right. Abraham's words affirm that the origin of human life and the ongoing gift of guidance both belong to God alone, so that a believer turns to the Creator not only for existence but for direction in faith and conduct. The verse invites reflection on the fact that guidance is not an accident added to creation but flows naturally from the relationship between the Creator and His creation.

translation: And it is He who feeds me and gives me drink.
interpretation: This phrase, spoken by Abraham in the context of describing his Lord, expresses the total dependence of the servant on the Creator for sustenance. Though food and drink are ordinarily attributed to means and causes, the verse turns the believer's gaze toward the One who ultimately provides them, cultivating gratitude, trust, and humility. It reflects the principle that all nourishment, physical and spiritual, flows from God alone, and that the one who recognizes this is drawn to worship Him exclusively.

translation: "And when I am ill, it is He who cures me." (Ash-Shu'ara 26:80)
interpretation: The verse, spoken by Abraham, expresses a profound reliance on God as the sole true healer. Illness is attributed to the one who speaks, in a gesture of humility and honest acknowledgment of human frailty, while the healing itself is ascribed wholly to God. The statement teaches that medicine and remedies are real means, but the ultimate source of recovery lies with God, so the believer turns to Him in sickness with both patience and hope.

translation: And the One who will cause me to die and then will bring me to life.
interpretation: The verse, spoken by Abraham (peace be upon him) in the dialogue of Surah Ash-Shu'ara (26:81), expresses his complete reliance on Allah as the sole source of life and death. By attributing both his death and his resurrection to God, he affirms that the power over the soul's departure and its return rests entirely with the Creator, and that the hope of the believer lies in the promise of being raised again after death, a truth that stands as the foundation for accountability and the reward of the hereafter.

translation: And the one from whom I hope that He will forgive my sin on the Day of Recompense.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) in Surah Ash-Shu'ara, expresses the believer's humble reliance on Allah's mercy rather than on self-righteousness. Though a prophet of unwavering faith, he acknowledges that he too has sins and places his hope not in his own merit but in the forgiveness of his Lord. It teaches that true hope (raja') is directed to Allah alone, and that the awareness of one's own shortcomings, coupled with trust in divine mercy, is the proper attitude before the Day of Judgment, when accountability and reckoning will be established.

translation: My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous.
interpretation: This is the supplication of Prophet Solomon (or, in the widely cited reading, a prayer that echoes the prophetic plea of one who seeks two gifts together: inner wisdom (hukm), the capacity to judge rightly and distinguish truth from falsehood, and a place among the righteous in the hereafter). The verse teaches that true success begins with a humble request to God, since wisdom is a divine gift rather than merely the product of human learning. The believer joins the request for wisdom with the desire for companionship with the righteous, recognizing that good character is cultivated through association with those who embody piety, and that the ultimate goal is to be counted among the salihin in the company of the prophets and the upright.

translation: And grant me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations.
interpretation: The verse is Abraham's prayer after he has been raised to the station of an imam and has completed his trials; he asks God to place in those who come after him a lasting good mention and honorable repute. The 'tongue of truth' (lisan sidq) signifies a praiseworthy remembrance that is accepted and spoken well of by the people of every generation, so that his legacy endures through the faith and righteous speech of those who follow. It teaches that one's lasting reputation is a divine gift sought through sincere supplication, and that the best of such remembrance is that which is rooted in truth and the guidance one leaves behind.

translation: And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss.
interpretation: This plea, drawn from the supplication in which the believer asks for a place among the righteous, expresses the hope that one's final destination be the eternal Garden of delight rather than mere worldly enjoyment. The word 'inheritors' (warathah) conveys that Paradise is received as a rightful legacy, bestowed through faith and righteous deeds, much as an heir receives what was left by one who came before. The petitioner thus acknowledges that salvation is ultimately God's gift, while also aspiring to be counted among those who have earned it through sincerity and obedience.

translation: And forgive my father, for indeed he was among those who went astray.
interpretation: This verse is part of Abraham's supplication (Surah Ash-Shu'ara, 26:86), in which he asks for forgiveness for his father, who had been an idolater. Abraham's prayer for his father is understood by many scholars as a fulfillment of a promise he had made earlier (Surah At-Tawbah, 9:114), and it reflects the depth of his compassion and sense of filial and moral duty even toward one who rejected the truth. Yet the verse concludes with an acknowledgment that his father was among those who went astray, and the later Qur'anic statement that Abraham disassociated himself from him once it became clear he was an enemy of God shows that such prayer was bounded by the principle that God's guidance and forgiveness are not extended to persistent rejection of the truth.

translation: And do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected.
interpretation: This is a supplication in which the speaker asks God to spare him humiliation on the Day of Resurrection, when people are raised to account. The request reflects a deep awareness that true disgrace (khizy) is not worldly shame but being exposed before God and deprived of His mercy on the day when all hidden things are revealed. By placing the plea at the moment of being raised, the verse turns the believer's attention from the fleeting honor of this life to the lasting standing before the Lord, and it models a humble dependence on God's protection rather than on one's own merit.

translation: On the Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit (anyone),
interpretation: The verse points to the fundamental reversal that the Day of Judgment brings to the values people hold dear in this world. Wealth and offspring, which humans instinctively trust as sources of security, status, and continuity, are shown to be utterly powerless before God's reckoning, because the only thing that carries weight on that Day is one's sincere state of heart and righteous deeds. The phrasing calls the listener to reexamine where they place their confidence, redirecting attachment away from worldly possessions and lineage toward preparation for the true accountability that awaits.

translation: Except for one who comes to Allah with a sound heart.
interpretation: The verse singles out the one who arrives before Allah with a qalb salim, a heart free from shirk, hypocrisy, envy, arrogance, and spiritual disease, and so it presents inner purity of belief and intention as the decisive criterion for salvation when wealth and children bring no benefit on the Day of Judgment, as the preceding verses state. The sound heart is one that has submitted sincerely to God's guidance and is oriented toward Him alone, so that the value of a person's standing is measured not by external possessions or lineage but by the condition of the heart that stands before its Lord.

translation: And Paradise will be brought near to the righteous.
interpretation: The verse describes the Garden being drawn close to those who were mindful of God, so that it stands ready before them on the Day of Judgment. The nearness of Paradise signals that the reward is not distant or uncertain for the believers; it is brought forward to them as a sight of comfort and assurance, marking the completion of their reward after the trials of worldly life and the reckoning that precedes it.

translation: And Hell will be brought forth for those who went astray.
interpretation: The verse portrays the scene of judgment in which Hell is made visible and placed before those who deliberately turned away from the guidance and persisted in error. The word "buroza" conveys that it is not hidden but openly displayed, so that the consequences of their chosen path become undeniable. It serves as a warning that misguidance is not a neutral position but leads to a concrete reckoning, and that the one who strayed will confront the reality he once dismissed.

translation: And it will be said to them, "Where are those you used to worship
interpretation: This verse belongs to the scene of the Day of Judgment, when the idolaters are gathered and confronted with their false objects of worship. The question "Where are they?" is a rebuke meant to expose the emptiness of their former devotion: the idols, saints, or other beings they once served are shown to be absent and powerless when they are most needed. It reflects the Qur'anic theme that worship directed at anything other than God brings no benefit on that day, and that the believer should examine now whether the objects of his trust and devotion will truly stand by him when all else is stripped away.

translation: Other than Allah, can they help you, or can they help themselves?
interpretation: The verse confronts those who turned to other than Allah for support with a rhetorical challenge: the gods or allies they relied upon can neither grant them victory nor save themselves. It exposes the emptiness of seeking help from created beings or false objects of worship, since true power and aid belong to Allah alone, and so the believer is directed to place his reliance wholly upon Him rather than upon any idol, leader, or worldly alliance.

translation: Then they will be thrown into it, they and those who went astray.
interpretation: The verse depicts the moment of the Hellfire's reckoning in which the false deities and the misguided are cast down together, headlong into the fire. The word 'fakubkibu' conveys a violent, repeated tumbling, as though the wrongdoers are hurled forward and overturned one upon another. By placing 'those who went astray' (al-ghawun) alongside the disbelievers, the verse conveys that the leaders of error and their followers share a single fate, and that no one who chose misguidance escapes its consequences. It is a reminder that the bonds formed in worldly falsehood do not protect anyone on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And the hosts of Iblis, all of them.
interpretation: The verse refers to the whole army of Iblis, both the jinn and the human and satanic forces that follow him, gathered together in their misguidance. By stressing "all of them" (ajma'un), it indicates that none of his followers are exempt: they are brought together as one company, emphasizing the completeness of the group that stands opposed to God's guidance and that will share in the consequences of their chosen path.

translation: They will say, while they are therein disputing: [Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:96 / Surah Fatir 35:37 / Surah Sad 38:64 style context; this phrase appears in Surah Ash-Shu'ara and Surah Sad, e.g., Sad 38:64 "Indeed, that is the truth: the dispute among the people of the Fire."]
interpretation: The verse depicts the people of the Fire in the midst of bitter quarrelling, blaming one another for their misguidance, and it reveals that the Hereafter is not a place of relief from enmity but of mutual accusation. Their dispute is itself a punishment: the illusions of worldly leadership and following collapse, and each party is left exposed in its own error, with no means of escape except the reckoning that God has decreed.

translation: By Allah, we were certainly in clear error.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by the sons of Jacob, who, after their brother Joseph's disappearance and their father's grief, are confronted with the failure of their own judgment about their father's and brother's affairs; in their admission, they confess that their earlier stance and conduct had been mistaken, a sincere acknowledgment of error that anticipates the reversal of their fortunes through repentance and reconciliation. It teaches that recognizing one's own misguidance, even when it is painful, is the first step toward correction and the restoration of right standing before God.

translation: When we held you equal with the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by the false gods' worshippers in Hell (Surah ash-Shu'ara, 26:98), who admit that they had placed their idols on a level with the Lord of all creation. It exposes the gravity of shirk: the act of making partners with God is not a harmless association of a creature with the Creator, but a fundamental distortion of the relationship owed to Him alone. Their confession comes too late to save them, and it teaches that the reckoning will reveal how completely such equations collapse on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And none led us astray except the criminals (the guilty ones).
interpretation: The verse is spoken by the people of the Fire, who, when confronted with their own misguidance, shift the blame away from themselves and onto those who were wicked and sinful before them. Their words reveal a common human evasion: rather than accepting that they chose to turn away from the truth when it was made clear, they claim that others, the transgressors, were the cause of their going astray. Yet the Qur'an consistently establishes that misguidance is ultimately the result of a person's own choices and persistence in disbelief, so this excuse is itself a sign of their refusal to take responsibility before God.

translation: So we have no intercessors. (Qur'an 26:100, spoken by the wrongdoers in the Hereafter)
interpretation: The cry of the wrongdoers, "So we have no intercessors," exposes the emptiness of the false hopes they held in the world, when they trusted that idols, status, or assumed patrons would speak for them before God. On the Day of Judgment those supports vanish, and the verse teaches that intercession belongs to God's permission and mercy alone, not to human claims or wishful alliances. The verse therefore calls the listener to sincere reliance on God now, while the opportunity for righteous action remains, rather than to reliance on intermediaries whose power is nothing without Him.

translation: Nor a close friend who cares for us (cf. 26:101: "nor any devoted friend").
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the people of the Fire in Surah Ash-Shu'ara, shows that on the Day of Judgment worldly bonds of affection and loyalty collapse when they were not rooted in faith and obedience to God. The sinners, who once relied on their companions and the social ties that gave them comfort, will find that no warm friend can help them. Only the friendship built on piety endures, as the Qur'an affirms elsewhere that the close friends of the God-fearing will remain close on that Day (43:67).

translation: If only we had a return (another chance) so that we could be among the believers.
interpretation: This is the plea of those who denied the truth when they face the reality of the Hereafter. Having seen what their denial led to, they wish for a second chance in the world, but their wish comes too late. It shows that faith is meant to be embraced in this life through choice and reflection before the unseen becomes visible, and that the wish for a return after the decisive moment is not granted, since the opportunity for action has ended.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign, yet most of them would not be believers.
interpretation: The verse closes a narrative with a double statement: the sign contained in the story is clear and sufficient for anyone willing to reflect, yet the fact that most of the people addressed do not believe shows that the obstacle lies not in a lack of evidence but in their inclination and disposition. Divine signs are manifest, but faith depends on a receptive heart; the Qur'an thus consoles the Prophet, reminding him that the rejection of the majority is not a failure of his message but a recurring pattern in human history, and it warns the listener not to be among those who witness signs and remain heedless.

translation: And indeed, your Lord is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse closes a passage by joining two divine attributes that might seem to pull in different directions: 'al-'Azeez,' the One whose might is absolute and who cannot be overcome, and 'al-Raheem,' the One whose mercy is constant and bestowed with tenderness. Placing them together teaches that God's power is never arbitrary or cruel, and His mercy is never weak or indulgent; His strength guarantees that His promises and His justice will be carried out, while His mercy assures the servant that this same power is directed toward compassion. For the one who is wronged or who faces hardship, this pairing offers both the assurance that the Lord can prevail and the hope that He will show mercy to those who turn to Him.

translation: The people of Noah denied the messengers.
interpretation: The verse opens the account of Noah's people by stating that they rejected the messengers, though Noah was the only messenger they had actually been sent. Denying one messenger amounts to denying all of them, because every prophet brings the same core message of monotheism and accountability before God. Their rejection shows that the cause of their disbelief was not a lack of evidence but a refusal to accept guidance that called them away from their established ways, a pattern that the Qur'an repeatedly presents as a warning to those who reject the messages of their own time.

translation: When their brother Noah said to them, "Will you not fear Allah?"
interpretation: The verse opens the account of the people of Noah by presenting the prophet not as a stranger or a distant authority but as their brother, one of their own kin, which signals that his call comes from genuine closeness and sincere concern for them. His question, "Will you not be mindful of God?", is framed as a gentle rebuke that points to the root of their failure: they do not lack the means to know what is right, but they have neglected taking God-consciousness as the guiding principle of their lives. The prophetic message is thus fundamentally a call to taqwa, a protective awareness of the Creator that restrains human conduct, and the verse suggests that the rejection of prophets begins with the heart's distance from this awareness long before it becomes open denial.

translation: Indeed, I am a trustworthy messenger to you.
interpretation: This phrase is spoken by the prophets (such as Noah, Hud, Salih, and Lot) when calling their peoples to God. By describing himself as a trustworthy messenger, the prophet establishes his credibility before his audience: he has no hidden agenda, seeks no worldly reward, and conveys faithfully what has been entrusted to him. The word amin signals that the message itself is a sacred trust, and that the one who delivers it must be honest, free of deception, and beyond suspicion, so that his listeners can judge his call on its merits.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This phrase, spoken by the prophets (such as Nuh, Hud, Salih, and Shu'ayb) to their peoples, sums up the core of their message: taqwa, a conscious awareness of God that guards one against wrongdoing, joined with obedience to the messenger who is sent as a trustworthy guide. The prophet is not asking for personal loyalty; he is calling his people to obey God through him, because his commands derive from God's revelation. Thus the verse binds inward God-consciousness to outward submission, showing that true reverence of God necessarily expresses itself in following the guidance He sends.

translation: And I do not ask you for any wage for it. My wage is only from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse reflects the disinterested character of the prophetic mission: the messenger calls people to God without seeking material reward, personal gain, or worldly status from them. By placing his reward solely with the Lord of all creation, he affirms the sincerity of his message and frees his listeners from any suspicion that his guidance is a means of profit. It teaches that true guidance is given for the sake of God, and that the one who calls to the truth should look to God alone for recompense, which strengthens trust in the messenger and directs the heart toward the Creator rather than the creature.

translation: So fear God and obey me.
interpretation: This phrase, spoken by the prophets such as Noah, Hud, Salih, and others to their people, is a call to taramount piety and obedience. 'Taqwa' (fearing God) denotes a conscious awareness of God that guards a person from transgression, while obeying the messenger is understood as obeying God's commandments, since the messenger conveys what God has sent. The verse thus joins two inseparable duties: inward God-consciousness and outward submission, with the messenger's authority derived entirely from God's.

translation: They said, "Shall we believe you, when the lowest-born (the most contemptible of people) follow you?"
interpretation: This verse, from the story of Noah (Surah Ash-Shu'ara, 26:111), shows the reaction of his disbelieving people, who rejected his message on the grounds of social class. Their question reveals a mindset that measures truth by worldly status and wealth rather than by the soundness of the message itself. By calling the followers "al-aradhilun" (the lowest or basest), they expose their arrogance and their contempt for the humble and poor. The verse thus teaches that the value of a person and the validity of a call are not determined by rank or social standing, since prophets have consistently been opposed by the powerful who judge the righteous by their outward condition.

translation: He said, "And what knowledge do I have of what they used to do?"
interpretation: This verse is part of the account of Prophet Shu'ayb's people, or possibly the dialogue of Noah's people's discourse, depending on the context; it is spoken in reply to a question about the deeds of others. The speaker disclaims knowledge of the inner reality of people's actions, which belongs to God alone, and so he places responsibility for judgment on Allah, who sees and records all deeds. It teaches that a person is accountable for their own sincerity and conduct, not for guaranteeing the hidden works of others, and that ultimate knowledge of deeds rests with the Lord who will reckon them.

translation: Their reckoning is only upon my Lord, if you could but perceive.
interpretation: Noah, responding to those who scorned the humble believers, places the judgment of people's inner lives and deeds solely with God, so he is released from any claim to judge the faith of others. His words rebuke the arrogance that ranks people by worldly status, and they warn that the mockers lack the spiritual perception needed to see that worth is measured by God, not by social rank.

translation: And I am not one to drive away the believers.
interpretation: This verse is spoken by Noah (peace be upon him) in reply to the chieftains of his people, who demanded that he remove the poor and humble believers from his assembly in exchange for accepting them. Noah refuses, affirming that faith, not social rank or wealth, is the measure of worth before God, and that he will not abandon those who have believed. It establishes the principle that the believers' dignity is not diminished by their lowly status in worldly eyes, and that a messenger must treat all who respond to the truth with equal honor and justice.

translation: I am but a clear warner.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in response to those who doubted or mocked his message, affirms the limits of his role: he is not a bringer of miracles on demand or a controller of people's fate, but a messenger whose sole duty is to convey the warning plainly and unambiguously. The word 'mubin' (clear) emphasizes that the responsibility lies in the clarity of the delivery, so that the truth is made evident, and whoever accepts or rejects it does so with the warning fully manifest. It thus teaches that the prophetic mission is one of faithful, transparent communication, and that guidance and its acceptance ultimately rest with God.

translation: They said: "If you do not desist, O Noah, you will surely be among those stoned to death."
interpretation: The verse reveals the hostility of Noah's people, who, unable to tolerate his persistent call to monotheism, resorted to threats of violence against him. Their words show how the powerful and complacent often respond to prophetic warning not with reasoned refutation but with intimidation, meeting the message of truth with the threat of stoning. It also reflects a recurring pattern in the Qur'an, where prophets are threatened with expulsion or death for delivering God's message, and it conveys to the believer that steadfastness in truth must be maintained even under the pressure of rejection and menace.

translation: He said: "My Lord, indeed my people have denied me."
interpretation: This short verse, spoken by a prophet (in the context of the Qur'an, Noah, after his long call to his people), reveals the deep sorrow of one who has delivered the message faithfully yet been rejected. Rather than responding with anger or self-justification, he turns directly to God, placing his grievance before his Lord and entrusting the outcome to Him. It models the prophetic posture of patient perseverance and reliance on divine support in the face of persistent disbelief, and it teaches that the believer's recourse, when others deny the truth, is supplication to God rather than despair.

translation: So judge decisively between me and them, and save me and those who are with me of the believers.
interpretation: This is the supplication of Prophet Nuh (Noah), who after a long period of calling his people to God and being rejected, turns to his Lord for a final decision. The phrase "fatḥan" (a decisive judgment, literally an "opening") asks God to open the matter between him and his disbelieving people by bringing about a clear outcome, which in the narrative is the flood that destroys the wrongdoers. The request for deliverance ("najjini") for himself and the faithful with him reveals that his concern is not personal vindication alone but the preservation of the believing community. The verse teaches that when persuasion has been exhausted and injustice persists, the righteous may entrust the outcome fully to God, seeking His justice and His protection of those who believe.

translation: So We saved him and those with him in the laden ship.
interpretation: The verse refers to Noah (Nuh), whose deliverance from the Flood is shown as a sign of God's mercy toward those who believed and stayed with the prophet. The 'laden ship' (al-fulk al-mashhun) signifies the ark, filled with the faithful and with pairs of living creatures, which became the vehicle of salvation while the disbelievers were drowned. It teaches that God preserves those who hold fast to His messenger, and that refuge is found only in what He provides, not in human strength or worldly confidence.

translation: Then We drowned the rest afterward.
interpretation: This phrase, from the account of Prophet Musa (Moses) and Pharaoh in Surah Ash-Shu'ara (26:66), refers to the destruction of Pharaoh and his army after Musa and the Children of Israel were delivered. The verse's wording "ثم أغرقنا بعد الباقين" conveys that after the believers were saved and made to cross the sea, the remaining people of Pharaoh were drowned in the same waters. It highlights the completeness of divine justice: the arrogant oppressors who denied the signs were swept away, while those who trusted in God were rescued. It also serves as a warning that persistent tyranny and rejection of divine guidance ultimately lead to ruin, and that God's deliverance of the righteous and punishment of the wrongdoers are both certain.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign, yet most of them would not be believers.
interpretation: The verse closes a narrative by pointing to its lesson: the events recounted contain a clear sign for anyone willing to reflect, yet the sobering observation is that the majority of the people addressed remain unmoved and do not believe. The divine sign is always present and sufficient in itself, so the failure lies not in the evidence but in the hearts that refuse to be guided by it. The verse thus consoles the Prophet by showing that the scarcity of believers is a recurring human condition, not a failure of his message, and it warns the listener against the same heedlessness.

translation: And indeed, your Lord is the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse closes a passage by joining two divine attributes that are meant to be held together: ʿAzīz, the One whose power is complete and whose decree cannot be resisted, and Raḥīm, the One whose mercy is vast and reaches His servants. Placing might beside mercy tells the believer that the Lord's strength is never arbitrary and His mercy is never weakness. Because He is able to do all He wills, His mercy is a reliable refuge; and because His mercy is boundless, His might is exercised with justice and compassion. The affirmation thus steadies the heart of the Prophet and of every reader: whatever opposition or hardship one faces, one may rest in the assurance that the Lord is both powerful enough to prevail and merciful enough to show kindness to those who turn to Him.

translation: The people of 'Ad denied the messengers.
interpretation: This short verse, from Surah Ash-Shu'ara (26:123), places the people of 'Ad among the nations that rejected their prophets. Their denial is presented not merely as rejecting one messenger but as rejecting all of them, since rejecting any one messenger amounts to rejecting the single message of God that all of them carried. 'Ad, the people of Hud, are a recurring example in the Qur'an of a powerful and prosperous people who grew arrogant in their strength and refused guidance, which is why their story serves as a warning to later generations about the consequences of arrogance and denial of the truth.

translation: When their brother Hud said to them, "Will you not fear God?"
interpretation: The phrase "their brother Hud" reflects the prophetic pattern in which each messenger is sent from among his own people, so that he speaks to them with the intimacy of kinship and knows their language, customs, and failings. Hud's question, "Will you not be mindful of God?" (alla tattaqun), is not merely a call to belief but a call to taqwa, a conscious guarding of oneself against what displeases God. The rhetorical form, beginning with the negative interrogative "alla," invites the listener to examine their own reasoning and to recognize that their conduct already points toward the need for awe and accountability before their Creator. In this sense the verse establishes that the foundation of all prophetic preaching is a simple summons to God-consciousness, from which all other reforms of belief and conduct flow.

translation: Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.
interpretation: The phrase presents the prophet as a messenger whose credibility rests on trustworthiness (amanah): he conveys the message faithfully, adds nothing to it and withholds nothing from it. By stating his trustworthiness at the outset, he invites his audience to accept his call on the basis of his known integrity, so that the authority of the message is inseparable from the honesty of the one who delivers it.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This phrase, spoken by a messenger of God to his people, combines two inseparable duties: taqwa, the conscious awareness of God that guards one against wrongdoing, and obedience to the messenger who is sent as a trustworthy guide. The command to fear Allah is the inner foundation, while obeying the messenger is its outward expression. By linking obedience to himself with reverence for God, the messenger makes clear that he is not seeking personal authority but is calling people back to God, so that following the prophet becomes an act of devotion to the Creator rather than submission to any human will.

translation: And I do not ask you for any reward for it. My reward is only from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse, spoken by a messenger of God to his people, establishes the sincerity and disinterestedness of the prophetic mission. The messenger makes clear that the guidance he brings is not a commercial transaction or a means of worldly gain, for his recompense rests entirely with the Lord of all creation. This disavowal of payment serves as a proof of his truthfulness: one who seeks no material benefit from his people has no hidden motive that would cast doubt on his call. It also teaches that true reward belongs to God alone, so those who call others to faith should orient their hearts toward divine pleasure rather than human approval or compensation.

translation: Do you build on every high place a monument, amusing yourselves?
interpretation: The verse (Ash-Shu'ara 26:128, spoken by Prophet Hud to his people the 'Ad) rebukes the vain pursuit of worldly display: building lofty monuments merely for pleasure and self-glorification, with no lasting purpose. It calls the believer to recognize that the true value lies not in towering structures that outlast no one, but in righteous conduct that serves God and the hereafter, and it warns that a civilization that wastes its strength on ostentation rather than moral purpose is heading toward ruin, as the 'Ad themselves did.

translation: And you take for yourselves palaces (or fortresses/workshops) as though you would abide forever.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the human inclination to build lasting monuments and grand structures in the hope of securing permanence for oneself, as if worldly establishments could guarantee an endless stay in this life. It draws attention to the vanity of such ambition: the believer is reminded that permanence belongs to God alone, and that the true measure of one's building lies in what endures beyond death, namely righteous deeds, rather than in the strength of stone and the grandeur of structures that will eventually decay.

translation: And when you strike, you strike like tyrants.
interpretation: The verse (Ash-Shu'ara 26:130), spoken in the context of the people of Pharaoh and the tyrannical rulers who oppressed the weak, condemns the arrogance of those who, when they hold power and strike against others, do so with cruelty and without restraint. It implies that the mark of a true believer is justice and mercy in the exercise of power, and that the force one wields must be tempered by fear of God rather than by domineering pride. The verse thus warns that possessing might should never become a license for oppression, since the one who acts like a tyrant has already placed himself in the company of those who defy divine justice.

translation: So fear God and obey me.
interpretation: This phrase, spoken by the prophets such as Noah, Hud, Salih, and Lot in their respective addresses to their peoples, forms the core of the prophetic message: a dual command that unites taqwa (God-consciousness, a watchful awareness that guards one against wrongdoing) with obedience to the messenger. The prophet is not presenting himself as an object of worship but as a trustworthy guide sent by God, so obeying him is a concrete expression of obeying God. The believer's relationship with God is thus understood as inseparable from faithful submission to the messengers through whom His guidance comes, and genuine piety is shown in both inward mindfulness of God and outward compliance with His revealed command.

translation: And fear Him who has provided you with what you know of (blessings): He provided you with livestock and children, gardens and springs.
interpretation: The verse calls believers to taravaqqa (conscious awareness of God and guarding against His displeasure) by directing attention to the source of their blessings. The phrase "Who supplied you with what you know" reminds people that every comfort they recognize and enjoy, from the animals and children they have to the gardens and water they depend on, comes from God alone. Gratitude for these known favors should therefore awaken reverence, since a person who truly recognizes the Giver will be restrained from ingratitude and heedlessness. The verse thus ties piety to remembrance of divine generosity: the more clearly one perceives one's dependence on God's provision, the more naturally one fears to offend Him.

translation: Who has provided you with livestock and children.
interpretation: Hud's words to his people point to God's favors in their own lives, namely the livestock that sustains them and the children who carry on their lineage and strength. By naming these gifts, the verse turns ordinary blessings into a reason for gratitude and a challenge to reconsider why they worship other than the One who gave them, so that the reminder of provision becomes an argument for sincere devotion.

translation: And gardens and springs.
interpretation: This short phrase, drawn from the description of the blessed in the Qur'an (such as in Surah Al-Hijr and Surah Ad-Dukhan, where the righteous dwell among gardens and springs), evokes the paradise promised to the God-fearing as a place of lush abundance and flowing water. Gardens represent the delight of verdant, fruit-bearing shelter and ease, while springs signify the constant, pure flow of refreshment that never fails. Together they paint the image of a complete felicity, where physical comfort and the beauty of nature are fully realized as a reward for faith and righteous conduct, and where the believer finds the fulfilment of longing for peace, beauty and abiding sustenance.

translation: Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day.
interpretation: This line, spoken by a messenger to his people, reveals the sincere compassion behind a warning: the one who delivers it fears not for himself but for those he addresses, because he understands the gravity of a reckoning that awaits them if they persist in their course. The phrase 'a tremendous day' points to the Day of Judgment, whose magnitude exceeds all earthly measures, and the speaker's fear is an expression of love rather than threat. The verse teaches that true guidance flows from concern for others' ultimate welfare, and that awareness of accountability before God should move a person to reflect, repent, and turn toward what saves them before it is too late.

translation: They said: "It is all the same to us whether you admonish or you are not among the admonishers."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the people of Prophet Shu'ayb's contemporaries (or those addressed in the story of the people who rejected their messenger), reveals the depth of obstinate disbelief: having made up their minds to reject the message, they treat the call to admonition with complete indifference, as if the warner's words neither benefit nor harm them. Their indifference is itself a form of arrogance and self-deception, for a heart that has closed itself to reminder no longer distinguishes between sincere counsel and idle talk. The verse thus warns that continued heedlessness toward divine guidance can harden a person until he regards the very act of being warned as meaningless, a state that is more dangerous than outright denial because it severs the soul from the means by which it could return to its Lord.

translation: "This is nothing but the customs of the former peoples." (Qur'an 26:137, spoken by the disbelievers in response to the Prophets' warnings.)
interpretation: The verse records the reaction of those who rejected the message: they dismiss the warnings of resurrection and accountability as mere old fables or inherited habits of earlier generations, not as truth from God. The interpretation lies in what this reveals about the heart that refuses revelation: it prefers the familiar weight of ancestral custom to the demands of a message that calls for reflection and change. The phrase "khalq al-awwalin" suggests they read the Prophet's words as a repetition of what humanity has always said and forgotten, so they see nothing new to examine. The verse therefore warns believers that the mere age or popularity of a belief does not establish its truth, and that rejecting a message by labeling it ancient or ordinary is a familiar way of turning away from God's guidance.

translation: And we will not be punished.
interpretation: This phrase is spoken by the people of Paradise (or, in some readings, by the inhabitants of Paradise addressing one another) in Surah As-Saffat (37:59) and Surah Ad-Dukhan (44:35), where it follows the statement that they will not die again after their first death. It expresses the security and assurance of the believers in the Hereafter: having been freed from the torment of the Fire, they rejoice that the punishment that once threatened them is no longer theirs. It highlights a central Qur'anic contrast between the anxious fear of the sinners and the tranquil certainty of the righteous, whose reward is complete and whose release from suffering is permanent.

translation: But they denied him, so We destroyed them. Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers.
interpretation: The verse presents a recurring pattern in the history of prophethood: when a messenger is rejected, divine punishment follows, and the destruction of the deniers becomes a lasting sign. The closing remark that most of them were not believers points to a sobering truth about human response to clear evidence. Even when the signs are manifest, the majority often persist in disbelief, not because the proof is lacking but because of stubbornness and heedlessness. The verse thus consoles the Prophet and the believers by showing that the rejection they face is not new, while also warning the listener to learn from those destroyed and to respond to revelation with faith rather than denial.

translation: And indeed, your Lord is the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse closes a passage by joining two divine names that are meant to be held together: al-'Azīz, the One whose might is absolute and who is never overpowered, and al-Raḥīm, the One whose mercy is constant and reaches those who turn to Him. Power without mercy would be mere domination, and mercy without power would lack the capacity to fulfill its promise. By placing them side by side, the verse assures the believer that the same Lord who can carry out His judgment against those who persist in denial is also the One who shows compassion, so that the Prophet and the faithful may find both certainty in God's ability to fulfill His will and hope in His kindness toward His servants.

translation: Thamud denied the messengers.
interpretation: The verse points to the people of Thamud, who rejected the messengers sent to them, and it is meant to show that denying the messengers is not an isolated act but a recurring pattern among those who refused divine guidance. Their denial was not merely a disagreement over a single prophet, since rejecting one messenger amounts to rejecting the message that all of them carried, which is one unified call to worship God alone. By naming Thamud, the verse invites the listener to reflect on the consequences that befell a people who turned away from clear signs, and to see in their story a warning against the arrogance and complacency that lead to rejecting truth when it arrives through a human being sent with it.

translation: When their brother Salih said to them, "Will you not fear Allah?"
interpretation: The verse opens the account of the people of Thamud, whose prophet Salih is described as their 'brother', underscoring that he came to them from among their own kin rather than as a stranger, so that his call rests on familial closeness and shared identity. His question, 'Will you not be conscious of God?', places the root of all moral failing in the absence of taqwa, a protective awareness of God that should restrain a person from injustice and excess. The brevity of the question is itself instructive: he does not begin with a list of prohibitions but with the heart's orientation toward God, indicating that correct conduct in every domain flows from this inner consciousness. The prophetic address thus presents faith as a reasoned appeal to people who already know their kinsman's sincerity, and it sets up the subsequent narrative in which their refusal of this simple reminder leads to their downfall.

translation: Indeed, I am a trustworthy messenger to you.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by a prophet to his people to establish the credibility of his mission: he presents himself as a messenger sent to them, and he vouches for his own trustworthiness (amanah). Faithfulness in conveying the message without addition or distortion is the foundation on which his call rests, so that the people are invited to accept his guidance on the basis of his proven integrity rather than on the basis of worldly gain. The word 'amin' thus joins the message to the character of the one who bears it, showing that a true prophet's honesty is itself part of the proof of his truthfulness.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This phrase, spoken by a messenger of Allah to his people, reduces the whole of prophetic mission to two linked duties: taqwa, a conscious awareness of God that guards one against wrongdoing, and obedience to the messenger who conveys God's guidance. The command to obey the messenger is not a demand for personal allegiance but a recognition that God's will reaches humanity through a chosen human bearer of revelation, so that obeying him is the practical expression of fearing God. Taqwa gives the obedience its inward root, and obedience gives taqwa its outward form, showing that true piety is never merely private sentiment but results in submission to what God has commanded.

translation: And I do not ask you for any wage for it. My reward is only from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by a messenger who declares that his call is free of any worldly motive. By refusing to seek payment from his people, he shows that his message is sincere and aimed solely at their guidance, not at personal gain. His true recompense is placed with God, the Lord of all creation, which directs the listener's trust away from material benefit and toward the divine reward, and thereby affirms the integrity of the prophetic mission.

translation: Will you be left secure in what is here, [at ease and undisturbed]?
interpretation: The verse is a rhetorical reproach addressed to those who have been given every comfort in this world, gardens, springs, fields and dwellings, and who assume they will be left to enjoy them forever without accountability. Its question confronts human complacency: the security and abundance one enjoys are a trust lent by God, not a guarantee of permanence, and whoever rests in them heedlessly forgets that ease can be taken away and that they will return to account for how they used it. It calls the listener to gratitude and watchfulness rather than the false safety of heedlessness.

translation: In gardens and springs.
interpretation: This phrase, drawn from the Qur'an's descriptions of the blessed in the Hereafter (such as in Surah Al-Hijr 15:45 and Surah Ad-Dukhan 44:52), depicts the righteous dwelling amid lush gardens watered by flowing springs. Gardens and springs together evoke the Qur'anic image of paradise as a place of abundant life, shade, greenery, and running water, where the scarcity and hardship of worldly existence are replaced by complete tranquility and fulfillment. The pairing of gardens with springs underscores that the believers' reward is not only beauty and sustenance but also the ever-flowing, pure bounty that signifies honor, ease, and God's generosity toward those who were mindful of Him.

translation: And fields and palm trees with their fruit-clusters tender and soft.
interpretation: The verse, from Surah Ash-Shu'ara (26:148), is part of the Prophet Hud's warning to his people, the 'Ad, who were settled in comfort and abundance. By pointing to the fertile fields and the palm trees whose spathes bear soft, delicate dates, it invites reflection on the signs of God's bounty in nature, and on the fleeting nature of worldly prosperity that a people may come to take for granted, forgetting the One who provides it.

translation: And you carve out houses from the mountains, exulting in your skill.
interpretation: The verse recalls the people of Thamud, who were skilled builders able to hew luxurious dwellings out of the rock of the mountains. Their achievement in craftsmanship and wealth became a source of pride and arrogance, leading them to forget their Creator's favor. The verse thus warns that human ingenuity and material prosperity, when pursued with pride and heedlessness toward God, become a path to ruin rather than security.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This phrase, spoken by the prophets (such as Nuh, Hud, Salih, and others) to their peoples, establishes the core of their message: taqwa, a conscious awareness of God that guards one against wrongdoing, combined with obedience to the messenger sent to them. The command to obey the messenger is not an independent submission to a human will but a direct extension of obedience to God, since the messenger conveys God's guidance. Taqwa here is the inner foundation that makes outward obedience sincere, while obedience to the messenger is the practical form that this God-consciousness takes in daily life.

translation: And do not obey the command of those who commit excess.
interpretation: The verse warns believers against submitting to the directives of those who transgress all bounds, whether in disbelief, corruption, or wrongdoing. Obedience is owed to what is right; those who exceed limits set by God and act recklessly against truth and justice should not be followed, since following them leads a person away from the path of moderation and righteousness.

translation: Those who spread corruption in the land and do not set things right.
interpretation: The verse describes a category of people whose defining trait is active corruption (ifsad) on earth, combined with a refusal to reform (islah). Corruption here is not limited to a single act but denotes a settled disposition that damages the order God established, whether in faith, morality, social justice, or the environment. The phrase 'and they do not reform' sharpens the indictment: the fault lies not only in wrongdoing but in the absence of any willingness to repair what has been harmed, which marks the difference between a sinner who repents and one who persists. The verse thus calls the reader to examine whether their own conduct builds up or breaks down the well-being of the community and the earth entrusted to humanity.

translation: They said: "You are only one of those bewitched."
interpretation: This verse (Ash-Shu'ara 26:153, spoken by the people of Thamud to the prophet Salih, and echoed by other nations to their prophets) reveals a recurring pattern of rejection: when messengers called to the truth, their opponents dismissed them not by refuting their message but by attacking their character and sanity, labeling them as men under the influence of magic. The word "musahharin" can mean those afflicted by sorcery or those made to lose their reason, and the accusation implies that the messenger is no more than an ordinary human being whose words should be disregarded. The deeper lesson is that the mind which has become attached to its familiar idols often reaches for such dismissals rather than honestly weighing the evidence, so the believer is consoled that such mockery is an old and expected response, and is reminded that the truth does not depend on the approval of those who have chosen denial.

translation: You are only a human being like us, so bring a sign, if you should be of the truthful.
interpretation: The words are spoken by the people of Thamud to the Prophet Salih, and they reveal a common rejectionist logic: they deny that a human being can carry a divine message, reasoning that prophethood must belong to a being set apart from ordinary humanity. Their demand for a sign is a pretext rather than a sincere search for truth, since the signs had already been given, and the challenge is turned back on the claimant, as if to say that a true messenger must prove himself by a visible miracle. The verse thus exposes how humans often measure revelation by their own expectations of status and form, while the prophets' humanity is itself the sign that their message is accessible and rooted in the same nature as those they address.

translation: He said: "This is a she-camel; she has a turn to drink, and you have a turn to drink on a known day."
interpretation: The verse records Salih's words to his people, the Thamud, after they demanded a sign. The she-camel that God sent as a miracle was given a fixed share of the water, and the people were given their own fixed day. The arrangement establishes justice and order over a shared resource, so that neither side may usurp the other's right. The clear division of the water into a known turn is a reminder that the sign was a trust, and that violating it, as the people later did by hamstringing the camel, brought their ruin.

translation: And do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment of a great day seize you.
interpretation: The verse, spoken in the context of the she-camel of Thamud (Surah Hud 11:64, where the same command is given), is a warning against any act of violence toward a sign of God that has been entrusted to a people as a clear proof. The prohibition 'do not touch her with harm' reveals that harming what God has made sacred is not a minor transgression but one that brings the wrath of a great day upon the wrongdoer. The verse teaches that God's signs must be respected, and that disobedience in honoring them invites a severe consequence that cannot be escaped by claiming ignorance or by seeking a pretext after the fact.

translation: But they hamstrung her, and then they became regretful.
interpretation: This verse, from the story of the people of Thamud and the she-camel sent to them as a sign by God, shows the final act of defiance: despite the clear warning from the prophet Salih and the explicit prohibition against harming the camel, they slaughtered it. Their regret came only after the sign had been violated and the punishment was imminent. The verse teaches that remorse arising after the consequences of disobedience are visible does not avert the outcome, and that persistence in rejecting divine guidance, even when its signs are manifest, leads a people toward ruin.

translation: So the punishment seized them. Indeed, in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers.
interpretation: The verse points to a recurring pattern in the Qur'an: when a people persistently rejects their messengers, divine retribution overtakes them, and that event becomes a clear sign for those who reflect. Yet the closing phrase shows that the sign's force is not universal; the majority remain unmoved despite the evidence before them. The lesson is that the failure to believe lies not in a lack of signs but in the disposition of the heart, so that even manifest proof does not guarantee faith, and the reader is urged to take warning from the fate of earlier communities.

translation: And indeed, your Lord is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse closes a passage by pairing two of God's attributes that together define His dealings with creation: 'al-'Azeez' points to His absolute power and dominance, which no one can resist or escape, while 'al-Raheem' points to His boundless mercy toward those who turn to Him. The juxtaposition teaches that God's might is never arbitrary or cruel; it is exercised with mercy, so the believer may fear His justice and yet hope in His compassion at the same time. Since the verse follows a sequence of narratives about prophets and the fate of those who rejected them, it reassures the Prophet and the believers that God's power will ultimately prevail for the righteous, and that His mercy remains open to those who repent and return to Him.

translation: The people of Lot denied the messengers.
interpretation: The verse opens the account of the people of Lot by marking their rejection as a rejection of all the messengers, not merely of Lot himself. Since every messenger brings the same core call to monotheism and righteous conduct, denying one who is sent from God amounts to denying the entire line of prophethood. It also conveys that the people of Lot persisted in their wrongdoing despite the clear guidance given to them, and this sets up the moral and social corruption, particularly the sin of their deviant practices, for which they were ultimately destroyed.

translation: When their brother Lot said to them, "Will you not fear Allah?"
interpretation: The phrase "their brother Lot" reflects the prophetic bond of kinship and moral responsibility: Lot was one of their own, speaking to them with the closeness of a relative rather than the distance of a stranger, which underscores that his call was an act of sincere compassion. His single question, "Will you not be mindful of God?" (alā tattaqūn), places the root of their corruption not in a lack of knowledge but in a lack of taqwa, that inner God-consciousness which restrains a person from wrongdoing. By asking rather than commanding, he appeals to their own conscience and reason, implying that they already possess the capacity to recognize right and wrong and are being summoned to exercise it. The verse thus establishes that the foundation of all reform is the awakening of God-consciousness, and that the prophets consistently begin with this call before addressing particular social evils.

translation: Indeed, I am a trustworthy messenger to you.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by a prophet to his people to establish his credentials before them: he presents himself as a messenger sent from God, and he describes himself as trustworthy (amin). This trustworthiness is the foundation of his authority to convey the message faithfully, without adding to it, withholding from it, or distorting it. By stressing his integrity, the messenger asks his listeners to receive his words on the basis of his honesty and reliability, and it sets a model for those who carry any trust, showing that faithful transmission of what has been entrusted is inseparable from the call to obey God.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This phrase, spoken by a messenger to his people, joins two obligations in a single command: taqwa, a conscious awareness of God that guards one against what displeases Him, and obedience to the messenger who conveys God's guidance. The verse presents the prophet's authority not as independent but as derived from God's, so that obeying the messenger is itself an expression of fearing God. Its repetition across several prophetic accounts underscores that true piety is inseparable from faithful submission to the divinely sent guide.

translation: And I do not ask you for any wage for it. My wage is only from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse expresses the disinterested nature of the prophetic mission: the messenger calls people to the truth without seeking material reward, fame, or worldly gain from them. By refusing any payment, he shows that his sole aim is sincere guidance and that his trust rests entirely on God, the Lord of all creation, who alone is able to reward him fully. This stance protects the message from any suspicion of self-interest and invites listeners to weigh the call on its own merits, reflecting the principle that true counsel is offered for the sake of others rather than for personal benefit.

translation: Do you approach males among the worlds (of creation)?
interpretation: The verse is a rebuke addressed by the Prophet Lot to his people, who turned away from what God had created for them and instead engaged in same-sex intercourse, departing from the natural order established for human procreation. The question is framed as an exclamation of disbelief at their transgression against nature and against the moral boundaries set by God, showing that such conduct is a grave deviation that the worlds had not seen before, as the following verses about their being 'a people who transgress' make clear.

translation: And you leave what your Lord has created for you of your wives? Rather, you are a people transgressing beyond bounds.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the people of Lot for abandoning the lawful companionship that God created for them in their spouses and turning instead to forbidden desire. Their rejection of what is good and natural reveals a deeper inversion of values: they have exceeded the limits God set for human conduct. The word 'adun' (transgressors) points to a people who wilfully cross the boundaries of what is permitted, and the verse teaches that true fulfilment lies within the divinely ordained order, while transgression of that order is itself the root of corruption.

translation: They said: "If you do not desist, O Lot, you will surely be among those expelled."
interpretation: The verse captures the response of the people of Lot to his reformist preaching: rather than accepting his call to abandon their deviant practices, they turned to threats and intimidation, warning him that he would be cast out of their community if he persisted. Their words reveal a pattern recurring throughout the prophetic history, where those who confront entrenched corruption are met first with coercion and the attempt to silence them, and where the powerful regard the moral voice that exposes their wrongdoing as a threat to be removed. The phrase "among the expelled" also carries a deeper irony, since the community that sought to banish the one righteous man among them would itself face expulsion from mercy and destruction for its persistence in sin.

translation: He said: Indeed, I am, of your deed, among those who detest it.
interpretation: This verse is spoken by Lot (peace be upon him) to his people, who persisted in the abominable act of approaching males among the worlds instead of the wives God created for them. The word "al-qaali" derives from "qalaa", meaning to hate or detest intensely, so Lot declares his utter abhorrence of their conduct. His words convey that his rejection of their sin is not merely outward disapproval but a settled, heartfelt revulsion, which stands as a model of the believer's duty to hate what God hates while calling others to turn away from it with clarity and sincerity.

translation: My Lord, save me and my family from what they do.
interpretation: This is the supplication of a righteous servant who turns to God for deliverance, asking to be rescued along with his household from the consequences of their deeds. The verse, spoken by Lot (or in a similar prophetic context, as in Surah al-Shu'ara and al-Ankabut), reveals a reliance on God as the only source of salvation. It teaches that faith is not merely a matter of family ties: the believer must personally seek God's protection, while also praying sincerely for those he loves to be shielded from corruption and wrongdoing. The request for deliverance from 'what they do' points to the moral corruption of the surrounding people, and to the spiritual responsibility that a person bears for the company and environment in which he lives.

translation: So We saved him and his family, all of them.
interpretation: The verse states that God delivered the prophet and his household from the affliction that befell the wrongdoers, sparing them while the rest perished.
