The word "أجمعين" (all of them) emphasizes the completeness of the deliverance, indicating that not a single member of his family was left behind to suffer the destruction. It reflects the principle that divine salvation is extended to the righteous and their close kin, as an expression of God's mercy and justice toward those who believe and obey Him.

translation: Except an old woman who remained among those who lagged behind.
interpretation: The verse refers to Lot's wife, who was not among the household that was saved. Although she was bound to his family by kinship, her inclination toward his people's ways and her remaining with those left to be destroyed placed her among those who were 'left behind' in the punishment. The verse teaches that blood ties and association with the righteous do not protect a person whose own conduct and allegiance are opposed to faith.

translation: Then We destroyed the others.
interpretation: The verse, which appears in Surah Ash-Shu'ara and Surah Al-Muminun contexts, speaks of the swift and complete destruction of the earlier rejecting nations after the messengers were denied. It conveys that divine justice is not delayed indefinitely: those who persist in denying the signs and rejecting the prophets are eventually overtaken by consequences, while the believers who were saved stand as a testimony that Allah's promise to His messengers is true. The brevity of the phrase, with its emphasis on 'the others,' underscores how the memory of those nations is reduced to a warning for every generation that follows.

translation: And We rained upon them a rain, so evil was the rain of those who were warned.
interpretation: The verse refers to the destruction that befell a people who had been warned by their messengers and persisted in denial. The 'rain' is not a blessing but a shower of punishment, and its evil lies in the fact that it came upon those who had been given fair warning and chose to ignore it. The phrasing 'the rain of those who were warned' emphasizes that the warning itself was clear, so the consequence was the justice of their own refusal. It stands as a reminder that divine mercy, when rejected, can turn into a chastisement, and that the one who has been warned bears responsibility for heeding the warning.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers.
interpretation: The verse closes a narrative of past nations (in the surrounding passage, the story of Abraham and the people of his time, and the signs given to them) by drawing a lesson for the reader. The 'sign' (aya) is not merely a miracle witnessed by those people but a clear indication of God's truth available to anyone who reflects. Yet the divine observation that 'most of them were not believers' shows that the presence of evident signs does not by itself produce faith; the obstacle lies in the human heart's stubbornness, heedlessness, and attachment to inherited customs. The verse thus consoles the Prophet and the believers by affirming that the rejection of the majority is a recurring pattern in history, and it warns each listener that the decisive question is whether he will open his heart to the sign rather than whether the sign is present.

translation: And indeed, your Lord is the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse closes a passage with two of God's names paired together, al-'Aziz (the Almighty, whose power is absolute and who cannot be overcome) and al-Rahim (the Most Merciful, whose mercy is constant and enduring). Its meaning is that the same Lord who holds full power over all things is also the one who shows mercy, so the Prophet and believers can rest assured that divine power is never exercised without compassion. The pairing also directs the listener to hold fear and hope together: the might of God calls for reverence, while His mercy invites trust and return to Him.

translation: The companions of the Thicket denied the messengers.
interpretation: The verse points to the people of al-Ayka, the community to whom Shu'ayb was sent, who rejected him as a messenger. Their denial was not merely a rejection of one man but of the divine guidance he carried, which is why the verse speaks of 'the messengers' in the plural: whoever rejects a true prophet rejects all the messengers who call to the same truth. The verse thus warns that persistent refusal of clear guidance, rooted in arrogance and complacency about worldly prosperity, invites the same fate that befell the earlier nations that denied their prophets.

translation: When Shu'ayb said to them, "Will you not fear Allah?"
interpretation: The verse opens the prophet Shu'ayb's address to his people with a direct, gentle question that appeals to their own reason and conscience rather than issuing a bare command. By asking "Will you not be mindful of God?", he calls them to taqwa, the inner awareness that restrains a person from wrongdoing and keeps them conscious of being accountable before Allah. The rhetorical form suggests that the truth he brings is already known to their hearts, and that their failure to fear God is a choice rather than a lack of understanding. Shu'ayb's mission, as the surrounding narrative shows, centers on rejecting corruption in measure and trade, so this call to taqwa is the root from which their social and economic reform must grow.

translation: Indeed, I am a trustworthy messenger to you.
interpretation: This phrase is spoken by a prophet to his people to establish the credibility of his mission. By calling himself a trustworthy messenger (rasul amin), he affirms that he faithfully conveys what he has been commissioned to deliver, neither adding to nor subtracting from the divine message, and that he is free of any personal motive or deceit. The word amin signals integrity and reliability, qualities that make his call worthy of being heard and accepted, and it invites his listeners to trust in the message through trust in the one who brings it.

translation: So fear God and obey me.
interpretation: This phrase, spoken by the prophets (such as Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb in their respective accounts), is a direct call to two linked duties: taqwa, the conscious awareness of God that guards one against wrongdoing, and obedience to the messenger sent to convey God's guidance. The structure reveals that obedience to God cannot be separated from obedience to the one He commissions to deliver His message; the messenger is not to be followed for his own sake but as the trustworthy channel of divine command. Taqwa is thus presented as the inner foundation from which outward submission flows, so that faithfulness to the messenger becomes an expression of reverence for God rather than a rival loyalty.

translation: And I do not ask you for any wage for it. My wage is only from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse reveals the sincerity and disinterestedness of the prophetic mission. The messenger declares that he seeks no material recompense from his people for delivering the message, so that no suspicion of self-interest can cloud the call to truth. His reward rests entirely with God, the Lord of all creation, which teaches that true guidance is offered freely and that those who call others to faith should look to God alone for their due, not to worldly gain or the favor of people.

translation: Give full measure and weight, and do not be among those who cause loss (who give less than their due).
interpretation: The verse commands honesty in trade and dealings: when one measures or weighs for others, one must give what is fully and rightly due, without shortchanging. Measure and weight stand here for every form of exchange and every obligation toward others, so the principle reaches beyond the marketplace to all dealings in which one party could wrong another by taking more than its share. The warning against being among 'those who cause loss' shows that cheating harms not only the one defrauded but ultimately the cheater himself, who forfeits his own well-being, trust, and standing before God. Justice in measure is thus tied to faith: a believer who truly fears God cannot allow his gain to rest on another's loss.

translation: And weigh with a true, upright balance.
interpretation: The verse commands honesty and justice in commercial dealings, requiring that measures and weights be exact and that one never cheat others by giving less than their due. Weighing with the straight scale signifies that economic transactions must be governed by fairness and integrity, reflecting a broader moral principle that the believer's conduct in the marketplace should embody the same balance and equity that God has established in creation.

translation: And do not deprive people of their due, and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief.
interpretation: The verse links economic justice directly to the preservation of social order. To withhold from people what is rightfully theirs, whether by cheating in measure and weight, by fraud, or by usurping their property, is a form of corruption that disturbs the balance God established on earth. Honest dealing in trade and possessions is therefore not merely a commercial matter but an act of worship and a safeguard of the community's well-being, since injustice in exchange spreads harm far beyond the individuals involved.

translation: And fear Him who created you and the previous generations.
interpretation: The verse calls the listeners to taqwa, a conscious awareness of God that guards one from wrongdoing, by reminding them of the most basic truth of their existence: that the One who brought them into being is the same One who brought into being every generation before them. The word al-jibilla, rendered as 'the previous generations' or 'the earlier creation,' points to the continuity of the human race and to the shared origin of all people, which ought to humble the proud and draw the heart back to its Creator. Since every person owes his or her existence to God alone, fearing Him is not a burden imposed from outside but the natural response of a creature to its Maker, and the awareness that the same Power shaped those who came before implies that the same accountability awaits those who come after.

translation: They said, "You are only one of those who have been bewitched."
interpretation: The disbelievers, addressing the Prophet, dismissed his message by claiming he was not a true messenger but a man whose faculties had been clouded by sorcery, so that his speech was the product of some deception rather than revelation. The phrase al-musahharin, from the root sahara, carries the sense of one who has been subjected to magic or who has been deprived of sound judgment, and in this way they attempted to discredit his claim to prophethood by attributing his condition to an external affliction rather than to the truth of what he conveyed. The verse thus reveals a recurring pattern in the response of those who rejected the prophets, who, when confronted with clear signs and a message they could not refute, resorted to labeling the messenger as deranged or enchanted in order to avoid submitting to the call.

translation: You are only a human being like us, and we think you are certainly among the liars.
interpretation: The verse records the disbelieving elders of a people rejecting a messenger on the ground that he is merely human and therefore cannot be a source of divine guidance. Their argument rests on an assumption that prophethood must belong to someone superior in status or nature to ordinary people, a pattern the Qur'an repeatedly confronts by affirming that God sends messengers from among humankind so that they may be relatable teachers, and that their humanity is precisely what allows them to embody and convey the message. The accusation of lying shows how rejection can harden into a prior judgment that forecloses any honest examination of the messenger's words, so that the perceived ordinariness of the bearer becomes a pretext for dismissing the message itself.

translation: So cause a piece of the sky to fall upon us, if you are among the truthful.
interpretation: This verse is spoken by the disbelievers of the people of Shu'ayb (or, in some readings, the companions of the Forest, as in Surah ash-Shu'ara), who, after being warned, mock the Prophet's claim and challenge him to prove his truthfulness by bringing down a punishment from heaven. Their demand reveals a common pattern in the Qur'an: the rejecters do not seek guidance but demand a visible, coercive sign, treating the messenger's warnings as empty threats. The verse thus exposes the arrogance of those who set the terms of truth for the prophets, while implicitly reminding the listener that the timing and form of divine punishment belong to God alone, and that the destruction they mockingly invite is in fact the consequence of their own denial.

translation: He said, "My Lord is most knowing of what you do."
interpretation: The speaker places his final judgment and his trust in God's perfect knowledge rather than in the opposition of his audience. Since God alone sees the hidden intentions and deeds of people, the speaker leaves the outcome to Him, freeing himself from the burden of proving his case to those who refuse to hear it. The reply also reminds the listeners that their actions are not hidden from their Lord, who will hold them accountable for them.

translation: So they denied him, and the punishment of the Day of the Canopy seized them. Indeed, it was the punishment of a tremendous day.
interpretation: The verse refers to the people of Shu'ayb (or, in the wider reading of the surah, a people who rejected their messenger), whose denial led to a catastrophe that came upon them from above in the form of a cloud-canopy that shaded them before unleashing fire and destruction. The 'Day of the Canopy' signifies that the very sign they mocked as a shade of relief became the instrument of their annihilation, teaching that comfort which is turned to a means of punishment is a warning that divine justice can arrive in the form they least expect. The phrase 'a tremendous day' emphasizes the severity and magnitude of the reckoning, pointing to the lesson that rejection of prophetic guidance carries consequences that are both certain and grave.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers.
interpretation: The verse closes a narrative with a double message: the sign contained in the story is clear and sufficient for anyone who reflects on it, yet the lesson is wasted on the majority, whose hearts remain closed to faith despite the evidence before them. The phrase 'most of them' reveals a recurring pattern in the Qur'an, where the availability of signs is never the true obstacle; rather, it is stubbornness, heedlessness, and an unwillingness to submit that keep people from belief. The verse thus turns the story into a mirror for the listener, inviting them to examine whether they are among those who see the sign and truly believe, or among those who witness it and remain unmoved.

translation: And indeed, your Lord is the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse closes a passage by joining two divine attributes that are meant to be held together: 'al-'Aziz', the One whose power is absolute and whose decree cannot be resisted, and 'al-Rahim', the One whose mercy is constant and tender toward His creatures. Placing might beside mercy teaches that God's power is never arbitrary or cruel; it is exercised with wisdom and compassion. For the believer this is a source of both awe and hope, reminding that the Lord who can grant victory and enforce justice is the same Lord who shows mercy to those who turn back to Him, and that the strength of the one who addresses the Prophet and his community is ultimately rooted in care rather than domination.

translation: And indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse affirms the divine origin of the Qur'an by declaring it a descent sent down from Allah, the Lord (Rabb) of all creation. The word "tanzil" conveys that the message was sent down from above rather than composed by a human author, and naming Him "Lord of the worlds" signals that the revelation is not meant for one people or age but addresses all of creation, establishing its universal scope and the authority of its Sender over every realm of existence.

translation: The trustworthy Spirit came down with it (the Reminder).
interpretation: The verse (Ash-Shu'ara 26:193) affirms that the Qur'an was brought down by a trusted, faithful messenger, identified as the Spirit, i.e., Gabriel. The epithet 'al-Ruh al-Amin' highlights two qualities: he is a pure, angelic being of revelation, and he is entrusted and faithful, delivering the divine message without addition or loss. This establishes the authenticity and reliability of the transmission, since the Qur'an is not the product of human invention or of the jinn, but was conveyed through a faithful intermediary from God.

translation: Upon your heart, that you may be among the warners.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the revelation was received by the Prophet Muhammad through his heart, a faculty of understanding and receptivity, so that he would become one of those who warn humanity of the consequences of disbelief. It shows that prophetic mission is a divinely entrusted responsibility: the message descends into a sincere and prepared heart, and its purpose is to awaken people to accountability before God, making the Prophet a bearer of warning rather than merely a recipient of inspiration.

translation: In a clear Arabic tongue.
interpretation: The phrase identifies the Qur'an's language as plain, eloquent Arabic, so that its message is intelligible to the people it was first addressed to. Its clarity is the means by which the warning reaches the heart: the revelation is meant to be understood and reflected upon, not kept as an obscure or unreachable text. The verse thus ties the Qur'an's miraculous eloquence to its purpose of guidance and warning.

translation: And indeed, it is [mentioned] in the scriptures of the former peoples.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an's message is not an isolated novelty but is attested in the earlier revealed books sent to previous nations. Its presence in the 'Zubur of the ancients' serves as a witness to its continuity with the prophetic tradition, placing it within the same divine line of guidance and reinforcing its authenticity for those who had access to earlier scriptures, while also pointing to the unity of the message delivered through the prophets.

translation: Was it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel knew it?
interpretation: The verse points to the testimony of the learned among the Children of Israel, whose knowledge of the earlier scriptures confirmed the prophethood of Muhammad and the truth of the revelation. For the Meccan audience, this knowledge held by the People of the Book served as an evident sign, since the message agreed with what those scholars already recognized in their own tradition. The verse thus challenges those who denied the revelation to reflect on this independent witness, and it reminds believers that sincere knowledge of God's scripture leads to recognition of the truth rather than to rejection of it.

translation: And if We had sent it down upon some of the non-Arabs (a‘jamiyyin),
interpretation: The verse imagines a hypothetical: had the Qur'an been revealed in a non-Arabic tongue and recited to a foreign-speaking people who could not understand Arabic, they would have used this as a pretext to reject it, saying, 'Why are its verses not made clear to us?' This points to the principle that a message must be intelligible to its audience in order to fulfill its purpose of guidance, and it also underscores that God chose to reveal the Qur'an in clear Arabic so that its Arab recipients could comprehend and reflect upon it.

translation: So he recited it to them, but they were not going to believe in it.
interpretation: The verse points to the stubbornness of those who have already decided to reject the truth. Even when the message is recited clearly to them, their hearts are closed, so the recitation alone does not produce faith. Faith depends on sincere openness and willingness to accept guidance, and the verse warns that when that openness is absent, clear evidence and eloquent recitation do not, by themselves, lead people to belief.

translation: Thus We cause it to enter into the hearts of the guilty.
interpretation: The verse refers to the Qur'an's own reception among those who persist in sin: just as We have made the message enter the hearts of the guilty, so their hearts are closed to it and it finds no acceptance there. The image of 'causing it to enter' suggests that the revelation is delivered into their very hearts, yet because of their stubborn disbelief and denial it does not take root in them, showing that the fault lies not in the message's clarity but in the disposition of the hearts that reject it.

translation: They will not believe in it until they see the painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse describes the stubbornness of those who reject the message: their disbelief is so entrenched that they will hold out until the torment itself is before their eyes, at which point faith comes too late to benefit them. It points to a recurring pattern in the Qur'an, where people demand visible proof and only believe once the consequences are upon them, as with those whose faith at the moment of punishment was not accepted. The lesson is a warning to respond to guidance while there is still time, rather than waiting for compelling evidence that arrives only when repentance no longer avails.

translation: So it will come upon them suddenly while they do not perceive it.
interpretation: The verse warns that the punishment or the Hour will arrive unexpectedly, catching people in their heedlessness. Their unawareness is itself part of the trial: because they neither anticipate nor notice its approach, they have no opportunity to prepare, so the verse calls the listener to constant readiness and mindfulness of God rather than to complacency about the time that remains.

translation: Then they will say, "Are we to be given respite?"
interpretation: The verse depicts the moment when the disbelievers, having been confronted with the reality of their situation, seek a final delay or reprieve, asking whether they will be granted time. Their plea reveals the futility of their hope, since the opportunity for deliberation and repentance has passed, and it underscores that respite is a mercy granted in this life rather than something to be expected once the matter has been decided.

translation: Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?
interpretation: The verse is a rhetorical rebuke directed at those who mocked the Prophet and demanded that the threatened chastisement be brought upon them immediately. The question implies astonishment at their folly: they urge on the very thing that would bring them harm, failing to recognize that divine punishment, though delayed, is certain and will arrive at its appointed time. The delay is itself a mercy and a period of respite, not a sign of its absence, and the verse calls the hearer to reflect on the danger of heedlessness and to respond to warning before the consequence overtakes them.

translation: Have you considered: if We gave them enjoyment for years,
interpretation: The verse (Ash-Shu'ara 26:205-207, which begins with this phrase) turns the listener's attention to the deceptive nature of worldly comfort. The question "Have you considered?" invites reflection on a scenario in which the disbelievers are granted prolonged worldly enjoyment, and it sets up the warning that follows: that such years of ease will not avail them when the promised punishment finally arrives. The passage teaches that a long delay of reckoning or abundance of provision is not proof of divine approval, and that the true measure of benefit is what a person's enjoyment brings them when faced with the consequence of their conduct.

translation: Then there came to them what they had been promised.
interpretation: The verse speaks of the moment when the threat that the disbelievers had long been warned of and had mocked finally arrives. Its phrasing, 'then there came to them,' emphasizes the sudden and unavoidable nature of the divine decree: the promise they had dismissed as empty is fulfilled exactly as it was announced. It serves as a reminder that God's promises, both of reward for the righteous and of punishment for the heedless, are certain, and that delay in their fulfillment should not be mistaken for their negation.

translation: What their enjoyment of worldly things availed them nothing, nor did what they used to enjoy (accumulate and rely upon) avail them.
interpretation: The verse points to the hollowness of worldly comfort when it is trusted as a substitute for faith and righteousness. Wealth, status, and pleasures seem secure while a person lives, but at the moment of reckoning they provide no shield against the consequences of one's choices. The lesson is to measure success by what endures before God rather than by temporary enjoyments that vanish with the end of this life.

translation: And We did not destroy any town except that it had warners sent to it.
interpretation: The verse declares that divine justice is never arbitrary: no community was punished without first being given clear warning through messengers or admonishers. Destruction follows upon rejection of a warning, so the verse emphasizes that God's mercy precedes His judgment, and that every people is held accountable only after the truth has reached them. It also serves as a reminder to every generation that heeding the warnings sent to it is the way to avoid the ruin that befell earlier nations.

translation: As a reminder, and We were never unjust.
interpretation: The verse affirms that divine punishment comes only after warners have been sent to remind people, so that no community is destroyed without first receiving the message. God's justice is shown in this: the warnings serve as a mercy and a proof, and when a people is destroyed it is because they were reminded and chose to persist in wrongdoing, not because God treated them unjustly. The verse also implies that the reminder itself is an act of divine grace, giving every generation a clear opportunity to turn back before accountability falls upon them.

translation: And the devils did not bring it down (with them).
interpretation: This phrase comes from Surah Ash-Shu'ara (26:210), where God denies that the Qur'an was carried down by the devils (shayatin), in direct response to the accusation that the revelation was the work of soothsayers or jinn. The verse affirms the Qur'an's divine origin by stating that it is unfit for the devils and they are incapable of producing or conveying it: it is not in their nature to desire it, nor could they bear it. Read in its context, the verse is a rebuttal of those who claimed the Prophet was possessed or inspired by satanic forces, establishing a clear distinction between the pure, truthful revelation brought by the angel and the lying, corrupt suggestions of the devils, who typically descend upon every sinful liar.

translation: Neither is it proper for them, nor are they able to (do it).
interpretation: The verse denies that the Qur'an could be the work of devils, on two grounds. First, it is not fitting for them by their nature, since the Qur'an's purity, truth, and divine guidance are incompatible with their corrupt and deceptive character. Second, they lack the capacity to produce it, because they are kept far from the heavenly revelation and cannot reach or imitate it. The verse thus affirms that the revelation's source is God alone and protects it from the claim that the devils inspired it.

translation: Indeed, they have been removed far from hearing (the heavenly revelation), being cut off from it.
interpretation: The verse (Ash-Shu'ara' 26:212, or the parallel in Ash-Shu'ara' context regarding the devils) depicts the shayatin being barred from eavesdropping on the upper realm, where the angels discuss the heavenly decree. Their being 'mu'zaloon' (removed or isolated) from hearing points to a divine protection of the revelation: the unseen messages cannot be intercepted or corrupted by those who would mislead humanity, so the Qur'an reaches the Prophet pure, and those who claim to receive knowledge from the jinn are shown to be deceived about the source of what they hear.

translation: So do not invoke another god along with Allah, lest you be among those who are punished.
interpretation: The verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad, but its real audience is every believer, and it establishes tawhid, the absolute oneness of God, as the foundation of the whole message. Directing the warning to the most honored of creation shows that no one is exempt from this principle, and that even the slightest turning toward other objects of worship carries the gravest consequence. The phrase "lest you be among those who are punished" presents the punishment as the natural outcome of associating partners with God rather than as an arbitrary sentence. Worship is therefore to be directed to God alone, and any divided loyalty, whether in the form of idols or of inner attachments that displace God, undermines the very purpose of human existence.

translation: And warn your nearest kindred.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Ash-Shu'ara (26:214), is a divine command to the Prophet Muhammad to begin his public preaching by warning his closest relatives first. It establishes that the duty of conveying the message starts with those nearest to the messenger, who are the most directly accountable to hear it and who bear a special responsibility because of their closeness. It also shows that the message of monotheism and accountability before God is not limited by ties of blood: the warning is first directed at family, yet the mission as a whole is universal, and kinship alone offers no exemption from the truth. The verse thus teaches that personal sincerity and faithful delivery of the message must begin at home, with the people one is most responsible for and most able to influence.}

translation: And lower your wing (in humility) to those believers who follow you.
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet to show gentleness, humility, and tenderness toward the believers who follow him. The image of lowering the wing evokes a bird that spreads its wings over its young to protect and shelter them, so the Prophet's leadership is to be marked by compassion, mercy, and nearness rather than arrogance or harshness. It teaches that true authority in guiding a community rests on care for its members, making them feel protected and honored, and that humility toward the faithful is a central quality of righteous leadership.

translation: So if they disobey you, then say, "Indeed, I am free of what you do."
interpretation: The verse instructs the Prophet, when faced with disobedience and rejection, to step back from responsibility for those who refuse. His duty is only to convey the message; he is not accountable for their deeds, and he should clearly disassociate himself from their conduct. This sets a principle that a messenger's concern is faithful delivery, while each person bears the consequences of their own choices before God.

translation: And put your trust in the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse directs the believer to place complete reliance upon God alone, joining two of His names: al-'Aziz, the Mighty and Invincible whose power no one can resist, and al-Rahim, the Most Merciful whose compassion embraces His servants. Tawakkul, or trust, is thus shown to rest on both aspects of the divine: confidence that God's power can accomplish what He wills, and assurance that His mercy will not abandon those who turn to Him. The believer is taught that strength and tenderness are not opposed in God, and that surrender to Him is the fullest security, since the One who prevails is also the One who cares.

translation: Who sees you when you stand (up for prayer).
interpretation: This verse (Ash-Shu'ara 26:218) affirms God's constant, all-seeing watchfulness over the Prophet Muhammad, especially when he stood in prayer at night. It is a reassurance that his devotion, solitude, and movements in worship are never hidden from God, and it implicitly invites every believer to stand before God with the awareness that He sees both outward actions and inward intentions.

translation: And [He sees] your movements among those who prostrate.
interpretation: The verse, spoken in the context of the Prophet Muhammad's prayer, indicates that God watches over the Prophet's turning and movement among those who bow and prostrate in worship, whether standing, bowing, or prostrating alongside the believers. It conveys divine awareness and care over the Prophet's devotion, assuring him that his worship in the company of the faithful is seen and known by God, and that his station among the righteous is under God's constant observation.

translation: Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse closes a statement with two of God's most intimate attributes: as-Samee' (the All-Hearing) and al-'Aleem (the All-Knowing). Hearing here is not merely the perception of sound but a complete attentiveness that encompasses every utterance, whether spoken aloud or hidden in the heart, and knowledge encompasses every intention and outcome. Coupled together, these names assure the reader that nothing said or meant escapes the divine awareness, which calls for both sincerity in speech and reliance on Him as the one who truly hears and knows.

translation: Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?
interpretation: The verse poses a rhetorical question that draws the listener's attention to the nature of those who receive the descent of the shayatin. It implies that such inspiration is not given to just anyone: the devils descend upon every lying and sinful person (akhhaf kathdhdhab athim), the one who wrongly claims revelation or speaks falsehood and sin. The verse thus distinguishes the true revelation granted to the prophets from the baseless talk of soothsayers and poets, pointing to the moral corruption of those who are receptive to the whisperings of the devils.

translation: Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend? They descend upon every lying, sinful wrongdoer.
interpretation: The verse answers the accusation that the Prophet Muhammad received his revelation from devils by stating the defining mark of those who receive satanic inspiration: they are habitual liars and persistent sinners. Their speech is false and their conduct is corrupt, so the inspiration they attract matches their own nature. The Prophet, known for truthfulness and integrity, is the opposite of this description, and the Qur'an's own content, which calls to truth and righteousness, shows that its source is not the satanic realm. The verse thus turns the charge back on its makers and offers a moral test: one should judge the source of a message by the character of the person who conveys it.

translation: They lend their ears (to the unseen), but most of them are liars.
interpretation: The verse describes the soothsayers and deceivers of the pre-Islamic and early era who would eavesdrop on the angelic discourse or receive whispers from the devils, and then pass them on to their followers. By saying they "lend their ears" the Qur'an points to a deliberate, attentive listening aimed at acquiring hidden knowledge that is not truly theirs. The phrase "and most of them are liars" exposes the fraud: even what they claim to have heard is mixed with falsehood, so that those who trust them are misled. The verse thus warns against credulity toward claimed sources of hidden knowledge and affirms that genuine guidance comes only through revelation, not through the unreliable whisperings of those who profess to see the unseen.

translation: And the poets—those who go astray follow them.
interpretation: The verse presents the poets as leaders whom the deviant and misguided people follow, implying that those who are lost in error are drawn to and gather around such figures. The following of the poets is not a sign of guidance but of straying, since those who follow them are shown to be taking their direction from voices driven by desire and fancy rather than by truth. It points to a principle that one should examine whom one follows, because the company one keeps and the voices one heeds shape the path one walks.

translation: Have you not seen that they wander aimlessly in every valley, [like the poets who say what they do not do]?
interpretation: The verse, from Surah ash-Shu'ara' (26:225), describes poets who are led astray by their own desires and fancies: they roam through every valley of imagination, speaking of things they never do, pursuing vanity and flattery without any firm principle. The image of wandering in every valley conveys a restless, purposeless drifting, in contrast with the believing poets who are exempted in the verses that follow because they act righteously, remember God often, and defend themselves after being wronged.

translation: And that they say what they do not do.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Ash-Shu'ara (26:226) in the context of the poets, and echoed in the broader Qur'anic condemnation of hypocrisy, rebukes those who make claims or promises through speech while their conduct contradicts their words. Its meaning extends to a moral warning against the gap between saying and doing: the Qur'an repeatedly treats such inconsistency as a serious failing, since words unaccompanied by action expose the speaker to disapproval, both before people and before God. The verse thus calls the believer to align speech with deed, so that one's sincerity is shown through practice rather than mere declaration.

translation: Except for those who believe and do righteous deeds and remember Allah often, and defend themselves after they have been wronged. And those who have done wrong will soon know what [kind of] return they will be returned to.
interpretation: This closing verse of Surah Ash-Shu'ara' (227) makes an exception to the preceding condemnation of poets who wander in every valley and say what they do not do. The true believers among poets are distinguished by four qualities: faith, righteous action, abundant remembrance of God, and standing up in defense after being oppressed. Their retaliation is not a license for transgression but a legitimate, measured response to injustice, which is why it is framed as victory after wrong was done to them. The verse then turns to a stark warning: those who persist in wrongdoing will come to know the ultimate outcome awaiting them, where their destination will be revealed as a reversal of their worldly position. The passage thus teaches that the value of speech and art lies in its moral truthfulness and faithfulness to God, and that justice and dignity are compatible with faith.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ta, Sin. These are the verses of the Qur'an and a clear Book.
interpretation: The opening letters Ta and Sin are among the disjointed letters (muqatta'at) that introduce several chapters, and they draw the listener's attention before the speech begins. The verse then points to what is being revealed: its verses are the Qur'an itself, and it is described as a 'clear Book' (kitab mubin), meaning one that makes truth distinct from falsehood, explains guidance, and is manifest in its meaning. The verse thus establishes the Qur'an's identity and its self-evident clarity, inviting the reader to recognize its authority and to reflect on its verses with the certainty that it is a clarifying revelation.

translation: Guidance and good tidings for the believers.
interpretation: The verse describes the Qur'an itself, or the revelation it contains, as a source of guidance (هدى) that leads the heart and conduct onto the straight path, and as good news (بشرى) specifically for those who have believed. Guidance is presented as something received and then actualized: the Qur'an shows the way, but it is the believers who, by accepting and acting upon it, come to benefit fully from it. The tidings of reward and mercy are thus tied to faith, indicating that the Book's blessings are most completely realized in those who open their hearts to it.

translation: Those who establish prayer, give zakah, and they are certain of the Hereafter.
interpretation: The verse defines true believers by a unity of inner conviction and outward practice. Certainty of the Hereafter (yaqin) is the root that drives the two pillars named: establishing prayer (iqamat al-salah), which is the ongoing bond between the servant and God, and giving zakah, which is the practical service to others through wealth. The verse shows that faith is not merely a belief held privately, since the certainty about the Hereafter is what makes a person keep up worship and share their wealth. The grammar also stresses this: the phrase 'they are certain' is given as a separate clause, marking that this conviction is the defining quality, and the acts of worship and charity flow from it. Thus the Hereafter is not only a doctrine to affirm but a reality that reshapes how one lives in the present.

translation: Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter—We have made their deeds appear attractive to them, so they wander blindly in confusion.
interpretation: The verse identifies disbelief in the Hereafter as the root from which spiritual blindness grows. When a person severs the thought of accountability beyond this life, his own deeds stop being measured by any higher standard and begin to look good simply because they are his. The phrase "zayyanna lahum a'malahum" points to a divinely permitted consequence: the one who turns away is left to the adornment of his own choices, so that what he pursues feels right to him. This self-admiration is precisely what makes him "yaʿmahun," wandering aimlessly and unable to find the path, because a life without a final reckoning has no fixed direction. The verse thus teaches that faith in the Hereafter is not a peripheral belief but the compass that keeps human conduct oriented and protects the heart from mistaking its own desires for guidance.

translation: Those are the ones for whom is the worst of punishment, and in the Hereafter they are the greatest losers.
interpretation: The verse closes a description of those who chose the fleeting life of this world over guidance and clearly-known truth. Its message is that their loss is not merely worldly but total, since the consequence they bring upon themselves reaches into the Hereafter, where the very gains they pursued are revealed as ruin. The phrase "al-akhsarun" (the greatest losers) points to a loss that is comparative and absolute at once: they forfeit both the reward that a sound soul would have gained and the peace that sincere faith offers even in hardship. The verse thus warns the listener to weigh where true profit lies, since a life spent in heedlessness and denial is, in the final reckoning, the most costly bargain a person can make.

translation: And indeed, you are receiving the Qur'an from One who is All-Wise, All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse assures the Prophet Muhammad that the revelation he receives is not his own invention nor the product of human reasoning, but is delivered to him from the presence of Allah, whose wisdom encompasses every purpose and whose knowledge encompasses every detail. Because its source is perfect in wisdom and knowledge, the Qur'an carries that same perfection: its guidance is sound, its laws are purposeful, and its message is trustworthy. The verse thus grounds the Prophet's confidence and the believer's certainty in the divine origin of the scripture.

translation: When Moses said to his family, "Indeed, I have perceived a fire. I will bring you from it some news, or I will bring you a burning brand from it, that you may warm yourselves."
interpretation: The verse opens a scene of quiet human need and divine encounter: Moses, traveling with his household in the dark and cold of the desert, sees a light far off and tries to secure something for those he loves. His words reveal a man of humble responsibility, hoping either to gain guidance about the path or to bring back a brand for warmth, so that the ordinary comfort of his family is the immediate concern that leads him toward the greater revelation that awaits at the fire. The verse thus shows that the call of the sacred often comes through the most natural acts of care, and that a seeker who moves toward a distant light for the sake of others may find himself met by a word far greater than what he sought.

translation: So when he came to it, he was called: "Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it. And glory be to God, Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: The verse describes Moses at the blazing fire on the mountain, which is in fact the place of divine manifestation rather than a mere source of heat. The call that reaches him declares blessing upon the one within the fire and upon those around it, meaning that what appeared to be fire was the presence of the Divine, and the sanctity of the spot derives from the One who speaks from it. Its closing glorification of God as Lord of all worlds turns the scene from astonishment at a wondrous sight into recognition of God's transcendence above any form, place, or created thing, teaching that the true encounter with the Sacred humbles the seeker and directs him to proclaim God's purity beyond all that the senses can perceive.

translation: O Moses, indeed it is I, Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse opens with a direct divine address to Moses, and the emphatic particle "innahu" with the explicit "I" (anā) marks a personal self-disclosure by God at the moment of Moses' encounter with the Divine, as if to remove any doubt about the speaker. The pairing of the names "al-'Azīz" (the Almighty, who is invincible and cannot be overcome) and "al-Ḥakīm" (the All-Wise, whose acts are purposeful and well-ordered) prepares Moses for the mission ahead: the one who sends him is both powerful enough to accomplish what he commands and wise enough that every command serves a sound purpose. The interpretation thus frames the subsequent miracles and the confrontation with Pharaoh as expressions of these two attributes, grounding Moses' confidence not in his own strength but in the authority and wisdom of the One who speaks to him.

translation: And throw down your staff. But when he saw it moving as if it were a serpent, he turned back fleeing and did not look back. "O Moses, do not fear; indeed, those who are messengers do not fear in My presence."
interpretation: The verse presents the staff's transformation as the first sign given to Moses at the moment of his commission, and it shows that the fear that seized him is a natural human reaction to the sudden and awesome, which is why God immediately reassures him. The phrase "those who are messengers do not fear in My presence" links Moses's calm to his status as one chosen by God: the one who is sent and rests in divine protection has no cause for dread before the Lord, even when facing a power that terrifies others. The verse thus teaches that true security before God comes from trust in His nearness and the assurance that His messenger is under His care, so that the miracle that frightens becomes the very means by which Moses's authority is confirmed.

translation: Except for one who wrongs, then substitutes good after evil; indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse opens with an exception that rests on a condition of repentance: the door of forgiveness remains open to the one who has wronged, provided he changes his course, replacing the evil he committed with good. The phrase 'substitutes good after evil' points to sincere transformation rather than mere regret, meaning that the true measure of return is the actual exchange of a sinful deed for a righteous one. The closing divine names, Forgiving and Merciful, indicate that God's pardon is not reluctant but flows from His mercy toward those who turn back, so that no past wrong should lead a person to despair of God's grace.

translation: And insert your hand into your pocket; it will come out white without blemish. (It is one) of nine signs to Pharaoh and his people. Indeed, they have always been a defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: The verse presents Moses' hand turning white without disease as a clear sign of divine power, one of nine miracles sent to Pharaoh and his people. Its purpose was to establish the truth of his prophethood before a nation that had strayed into transgression. The closing statement reveals that their refusal was not due to a lack of evidence but to a settled habit of defiant wickedness, meaning that persistent rebellion hardens the heart against even undeniable proofs.

translation: But when Our clear signs came to them, they said, "This is obvious magic."
interpretation: The verse shows the habit of those who reject the truth: when the evidence arrives in plain, undeniable form, they do not engage with its clarity but dismiss it by labelling it sorcery. Calling the manifest signs "magic" is a way of avoiding the moral and spiritual demands they carry, since admitting their divine origin would require a change of conduct. The passage thus points to a recurring human response in which clarity is met not with reflection but with a convenient explanation that protects existing certainties and preserves the comfort of disbelief.

translation: And they denied them, though their souls had been convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance. So see how was the end of the corrupters.
interpretation: The verse exposes the paradox of obstinate disbelief: these people were not ignorant of the signs, for their own inner selves recognized their truth with certainty, yet pride and injustice drove them to reject them. Denial here is not a failure of knowledge but a choice rooted in arrogance, which turns the knowing heart against itself. The command to look at the fate of the corrupters directs the reader to history and to the consequences that follow when one persistently overturns clear truth and spreads disorder on earth, teaching that the outcome of such conduct is inevitably ruinous.

translation: And We certainly gave David and Solomon knowledge, and they said, "All praise is due to Allah, who has preferred us over many of His believing servants."
interpretation: The verse shows that divine knowledge is a blessing that calls for gratitude rather than pride. David and Solomon, though granted exceptional knowledge and status, immediately acknowledge that the favor comes from Allah alone, and they recognize that among His servants many are equally or more deserving. Their words model humility and thankfulness: the true response to being distinguished is to praise the Giver, not to boast in one's own merit.

translation: And Solomon inherited David. He said, "O people, we have been taught the speech of birds, and we have been given of everything. Indeed, this is evident favor."
interpretation: The verse presents prophetic succession not merely as inheritance of wealth but as inheritance of divine knowledge and authority: Solomon receives from David the gift of wisdom and sovereignty, and he frames his special knowledge, including the understanding of birds' speech, as a communal trust rather than personal pride. By addressing "O people" and attributing both his knowledge and his provision to God's bounty, he models gratitude, acknowledging that every capacity he holds is a favor from God, and that such favor is meant to be recognized, shared, and used responsibly.

translation: And there were gathered before Solomon his armies, of the jinn and the humans and the birds, and they were being marshaled in ranks.
interpretation: The verse portrays Solomon's dominion as a comprehensive kingship that unites three realms of creation (jinn, humankind, and birds) under one organized command. The word 'yuzaʿūn' (they are held back and arranged in order) suggests that his host was not a mere crowd but a disciplined, orderly assembly, reflecting that true sovereignty joins diverse beings in harmony under rightful authority. It also hints that the power granted to Solomon was a trust, exercised with order and purpose rather than chaos, and that the marshaling of creatures serves a wise and purposeful governance.

translation: Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants, an ant said, "O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his soldiers crush you while they do not perceive."
interpretation: The verse presents an ant as a figure of foresight and collective responsibility: she perceives a danger that the creatures around her cannot see, and she calls her own kind to shelter before harm comes. Her speech, addressed to the whole colony, reveals that even the smallest beings possess a language, an awareness of their community, and a concern for its safety. The phrase "while they do not perceive" points to the nature of unintended harm, where a mighty host passes by without awareness of what it tramples, and it invites the reader to reflect on the moral duty of the powerful to be mindful of the lives they may crush without intent. Through this scene, the Qur'an also highlights Solomon's exalted station, for his vast army moves in procession, yet his power is shown to be bounded by a justice and care that extend even to the ants, as the subsequent verse reports his smile at her words.

translation: So he smiled, laughing at her speech, and said: "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents, and that I may do righteous deeds which please You, and admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants."
interpretation: The verse shows Solomon's reaction to the ant's words: his smile and laughter are not mockery but joy and wonder at God's grace that has made him aware of the speech of creatures and granted him dominion. He immediately turns this blessing back toward its source, asking God for the inner capacity (awza'nī) to be thankful, which is itself a gift that must be sought from God. Gratitude is thus joined to righteous action, and his prayer for his parents indicates that divine favor extends through family and lineage. Finally, he seeks not merely worldly power but to be counted among the righteous, showing that the true measure of a ruler's success is his closeness to God through mercy rather than through his kingdom.

translation: And he inspected the birds and said, "Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent?"
interpretation: The verse shows Solomon, endowed with knowledge of the speech of birds and dominion over creation, carefully reviewing his assembly of birds as a responsible ruler who notices every member of his realm. His question about the hoopoe reflects attentive leadership that does not overlook even the smallest creature under his charge, and it prepares the ground for the hoopoe's report from Sheba, where the lesson lies in the importance of accountability, the duty to verify information before judgment, and the honest account that a subordinate may bring to correct a ruler's understanding.

translation: "I will surely punish him with a severe punishment, or I will slaughter him, or he must bring me a clear authority."
interpretation: This is the words of the hoopoe's report to Solomon (Sulayman) in Surah An-Naml, where the hoopoe is speaking of the threat Solomon makes against a absent bird that failed to appear before him. Solomon's stern threat reveals the seriousness with which he held to discipline and order among the creatures under his command, and his insistence on a manifest justification shows that he would accept no unfounded excuse. The verse teaches that authority, when exercised, should be tempered by a demand for clear evidence rather than acting on mere assumption, since Solomon's ultimate standard was not the severity of punishment but the presence of a clear and convincing proof.

translation: So he (the hoopoe) stayed not long, and said: "I have encompassed [knowledge of] what you have not encompassed, and I have come to you from Sheba with certain news."
interpretation: The verse presents the hoopoe as a messenger who returns to Solomon after a brief absence and boldly claims a knowledge Solomon himself lacked, namely the reality of a distant kingdom. The phrase "what you have not encompassed" shows that true knowledge is not the monopoly of the one in authority, and that a humble subordinate may possess information that the powerful do not. The bird's report is rooted in certainty ("nabaʾ yaqīn"), which teaches that a reliable message should be grounded in verified knowledge and delivered with confidence and honesty, and that the wise ruler must remain open to correction from those under his care.

translation: Indeed, I found a woman ruling over them, and she has been given of everything, and she has a mighty throne.
interpretation: The hoopoe's report to Solomon presents the Queen of Sheba as a sovereign who possesses worldly abundance and majestic authority, yet the bird's words also reveal a subtle contrast: her great material power and splendid throne stand in contrast to the true and complete kingship that Solomon holds through divine favor. The verse thus invites reflection on the nature of worldly dominion, which can be vast and impressive while still lacking the guidance of faith, and it prepares the narrative for the Queen's eventual recognition of the one God.

translation: "I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah. Satan has made their deeds appear attractive to them and has barred them from the path, so they are not guided."
interpretation: The verse, spoken by the hoopoe (al-hudhud) to Solomon, reveals the root of the Queen of Sheba's people's error: they had turned from worshipping the One God to venerating the sun, a natural and dazzling created thing. The phrase "Satan made their deeds appear attractive" shows that misguidance often comes dressed as ordinary custom and comfortable habit, so that people come to regard their own wrong as good and never question it. Satan's work is not always open defiance; it is often the gradual beautifying of what is false, which blocks the way to truth. The closing words, "so they are not guided," present the consequence: when a person lets what is attractive override the call of guidance, the heart loses its ability to see the right path, and the verse thus warns that the self's adornment of its own errors is the deepest obstacle to faith.

translation: Why do they not prostrate themselves to God, who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth, and knows what you conceal and what you reveal?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who turn away from worshipping God by pointing to the boundless reach of His knowledge: He brings out into the open what has been concealed across all of creation, from the hidden provisions of rain and growth to the secrets of the unseen, and nothing escapes His awareness, whether hidden in the heart or displayed in speech and deed. The question 'Why do they not prostrate' is therefore a call to reason: the one who alone knows the hidden and reveals it deserves exclusive prostration, and the act of prostration itself becomes a recognition that human beings stand transparent before the One who knows their inner and outer lives.

translation: Allah — there is no deity except Him, the Lord of the Mighty Throne.
interpretation: This phrase, drawn from the Verse of the Throne (Ayat al-Kursi, 2:255) and its surrounding declarations, establishes the core of tawhid: the absolute oneness of God as the only object of worship. By naming Him as Lord of the Mighty Throne, it links His exclusive divinity to His sovereignty over the greatest of all created things, the throne that encompasses the heavens and the earth. The believer is thus reminded that the One who alone deserves worship is also the One who alone governs and sustains all of creation, so that devotion, reliance, and submission must be directed to Him alone.

translation: He said, "We will see whether you have told the truth or whether you were among the liars."
interpretation: This verse, spoken in the context of the messenger's mission to Pharaoh's court, shows a measured response to a claim that seemed to require verification rather than immediate acceptance. The phrase "We will see" places the matter under the test of evidence and outcome, teaching that a claim to prophethood or truth is judged by what follows from it. It also reflects a principle of patience and restraint: the one who speaks is not dismissed outright, but the sincerity of his words is left to be shown through their fruits and the result of the encounter.

translation: Take this letter of mine and deliver it to them, then turn away from them and see what they will return with.
interpretation: The verse, spoken in the context of the letter of Solomon sent to the Queen of Sheba (Bilqis), shows the method of prophetic and diplomatic address: a clear message is conveyed directly, and then the messenger withdraws to observe the response, leaving the recipients to reflect freely upon the message. It teaches that the duty of the bearer of truth is to deliver the message faithfully, while the outcome and the reaction of the listeners rest with them, and that a calm, patient observation of how people respond is part of wise conduct.

translation: She said: O assembly, indeed there has been delivered to me a noble letter.
interpretation: The verse presents the Queen of Sheba (Bilqis) addressing her council of chiefs with a measured and dignified opening, announcing that a letter of honorable character has been cast to her. Her choice of words, calling the letter 'noble' (karim), signals both its importance and its respectful tone, which stands in contrast to the arrogance of the kings who wrote in such a manner. It shows a wise ruler who does not immediately act on impulse but first brings the matter to her counsel for deliberation, modeling consultation (shura) in governance and the proper weighing of serious communications before decision.

translation: Indeed, it is from Solomon, and indeed it reads: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.
interpretation: Solomon opens his letter with the basmala, placing the whole message under the name of God before any other words. This shows that his authority is not his own but derives from God, and that his purpose is to call the Queen of Sheba to submit to God rather than to assert his own power. The opening also sets the tone of mercy and rational persuasion that follows, since the letter invites her to come to him in submission, which is why the verse frames the message as a sincere call to faith.

translation: Do not exalt yourselves over me, and come to me in submission (as Muslims).
interpretation: The verse, spoken by Solomon in his letter to the Queen of Sheba (Bilqis), calls for humility before the truth: he forbids arrogance and self-exaltation and invites the recipients to come before him in submission to God. Its message is that true dignity lies not in pride or power but in surrendering to the one God and accepting the guidance that comes from Him, which is the essence of islam, meaning submission.

translation: She said: O chiefs, advise me in my matter; I would not decide any matter until you are present and witnessing.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the Queen of Sheba (Bilqis) to her counsellors, shows the principle of consultation (shura) in governance: a wise ruler does not act alone in weighty affairs but seeks the counsel of her notables before reaching a decision. Her words reveal humility and prudence, as she refuses to commit to a course of action without the shared judgment of those whose opinion carries weight. The verse thereby models responsible leadership that binds rulers to deliberation with their people, and it sets up the subsequent narrative in which her council's response, and her own discernment, lead to the recognition of the truth delivered through Solomon's message.

translation: They said: "We are people of strength and people of great might, but the decision is yours, so consider what you will command."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the warriors and men of power who were summoned by the Queen of Sheba (Bilqis) in response to Solomon's letter, shows a council that offers its readiness and military strength while deferring the final judgment to the ruler. It reflects the wisdom of a leader who consults her counsel and weighs her options carefully before acting, and the courtiers' respectful submission to her authority. The passage teaches that strength should be placed at the service of sound deliberation, with the decision resting on careful reflection rather than on force alone.

translation: She said: Indeed, when kings enter a town, they corrupt it and make the most honorable of its people humiliated. And thus do they behave.
interpretation: The verse, spoken by the Queen of Sheba (Bilqis) as she addresses her counsellors in Surah An-Naml (27:34), reflects her political wisdom and caution before deciding how to respond to Solomon's letter. Her statement is a general observation that powerful rulers, when they conquer or enter a land, tend to ruin its order and degrade its noblest inhabitants, so that the honored are reduced to lowliness. By framing the matter this way, she shows that she is wary of aggressive kingship and prefers to examine the nature of the sender before submitting or resisting. The verse thus conveys a lesson about the corrupting effect of worldly power when it is exercised by rulers who seek dominance, and it invites the reader to judge authority by its conduct rather than by its pomp.

translation: And indeed, I am going to send them a gift, and will wait to see what the messengers bring back.
interpretation: The Queen of Sheba, having heard of Solomon's power and of the letter delivered to her, chose a diplomatic route rather than immediate confrontation. By sending a gift, she tests whether Solomon is a mere king who can be appeased with wealth or a prophet whose concern is not worldly treasure. Her decision to wait and observe the response reflects prudence, a measured judgment that weighs the consequences before committing her people to war or submission. The verse thus shows the value of wise deliberation and careful assessment of those who claim authority over you, a stance that the subsequent events confirm, as Solomon rejects the gift and calls her to submit to God.

translation: So when the envoy came to Solomon, he said: "Would you provide me with wealth? What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you. Rather, it is you who exult in your gift."
interpretation: The verse presents Solomon's refusal of the Queen of Sheba's gift as a lesson in spiritual self-sufficiency and integrity. Solomon recognizes that the divine blessings bestowed upon him, including prophethood, wisdom, and dominion, far exceed any worldly riches the people could offer, so he has no need to be enticed by material bribery. His rebuke turns the matter back on the messengers: the true test is not the gift but whether the recipients will be moved by it, and his words expose the pride and worldly attachment that cause people to rejoice in presents rather than in the guidance that truly matters. The verse thus teaches believers to measure value by what Allah grants, and to remain free from being swayed by offers of worldly wealth when they conflict with truth.

translation: Return to them, for we will surely bring them armies they cannot withstand, and we will surely expel them from it in humiliation, and they will be debased.
interpretation: The verse is spoken in the context of Prophet Moses' account with Pharaoh's magicians and the Children of Israel, and it has been read as a threat of the consequences awaiting the arrogant who oppose God's truth. Pharaoh's people are told that they will face a force they have no power to resist, and that they will be driven out of their land in disgrace, stripped of the pride and dominion they relied upon. The phrase 'lā qibala lahum bihā' conveys the overwhelming and irresistible nature of the divine decree, showing that worldly power and political authority are ultimately subject to God's will. The word 'ṣāghirūn' points to a humiliation that is not merely external but a state of inner abasement that befalls those who persist in arrogance and rejection. The verse thus reflects a recurring Qur'anic lesson: that tyranny and pride lead to inevitable downfall, while humility before God brings honor.

translation: He said: "O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?"
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Solomon (peace be upon him) in the Surah An-Naml, shows his desire to demonstrate a miracle to the Queen of Sheba before her arrival, so that the proof of his prophethood and the truth of his message would be evident to her. By asking for the throne before she arrives in submission, he expresses the aim that she come to Islam willingly, moved by clear signs rather than by force or display of power. It also reflects the wisdom of a leader who seeks to win hearts through evidence and to show that the true sovereignty belongs to God, Who grants His servants knowledge and abilities beyond their own.

translation: A powerful one among the jinn said: "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place; indeed, I am strong and trustworthy for it."
interpretation: The verse, from the account of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, shows that Solomon's courtiers included a strong and trustworthy jinn who offered to bring the throne before the Queen could leave her seat. Its deeper meaning lies in the contrast between brute power and knowledge: the jinn's strength is matched by his reliability, yet the one who possessed knowledge of the Book (as the following verse reveals) accomplishes the task in the blink of an eye. The passage teaches that true capability is not measured merely by force, but by the knowledge and faith granted by God, which surpass even the might of creatures who seem formidable.

translation: The one who had knowledge from the Scripture said, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." And when he saw it settled in his presence, he said, "This is from the favor of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful. And whoever is grateful, his gratitude is only for himself; and whoever is ungrateful, indeed my Lord is Free of need and Generous."
interpretation: The verse shows that the true source of this marvel is divine favor, not personal power: the man with knowledge from the Scripture attributes the swift transfer of the throne to his Lord, recognizing that such blessings are a trial that reveals whether a person will give thanks or turn away. Gratitude benefits only the grateful person himself, since God needs nothing from His creatures, and ingratitude does not diminish His generosity, which remains boundless. The passage thus teaches that knowledge of revelation should lead to humility, acknowledgment of God's favor, and sincere thankfulness rather than pride in one's own accomplishments.

translation: He said: "Disguise her throne for her; we shall see whether she will be guided or whether she will be among those who are not guided."
interpretation: The verse comes from the story of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba (Bilqis). Solomon, wishing to test her intellect and to show her a sign of his prophetic authority, orders that her throne be altered in appearance so that she might fail to recognize it when she arrives. The test is not merely a trick of perception but a means of examining whether her reason and insight will lead her to recognition and faith. The phrasing "we shall see" reflects that the outcome is left open to her own discernment: guidance here is shown to depend on the willingness to reflect upon signs, and the verse highlights that the one who is truly guided is the one who responds to evidence rather than merely to appearances.

translation: So when she arrived, it was said, "Is your throne like this?" She said, "It is as if it were it. And we were given knowledge before this, and we had been Muslims (submitting to God)."
interpretation: The verse presents the Queen of Sheba's reply as a measured, intelligent response that neither affirms nor denies outright, reflecting her discernment and caution in recognizing the miraculous nature of what she sees. Her words that knowledge was given to them before this, and that they had already submitted, suggest that her wisdom and faith in God preceded the sign, so that Solomon's miracle confirmed rather than created her submission. The verse thus highlights the value of reasoned judgment and humble surrender to God when confronted with signs beyond ordinary experience.

translation: And it was prevented from what it used to worship besides Allah. Indeed, it was from a disbelieving people.
interpretation: The verse describes the queen of Sheba (Bilqis) after she came to Solomon and witnessed the wonders of his kingdom. Her former worship of the sun, which her people had adorned for her, had kept her from the true worship of God; the phrase "and it had prevented her" points to the way inherited custom and the influence of a disbelieving community barred her from recognizing the truth. The verse teaches that the obstacle to faith is often not a lack of evidence but the hold of ancestral habits and the pressure of one's social environment, and that a person born into such a community must consciously break free from it to find guidance.

translation: It was said to her, "Enter the palace." And when she saw it, she thought it was a body of water, and she uncovered her shins. [Solomon] said, "Indeed, it is a palace paved smooth with glass." She said, "My Lord, I have wronged myself, and I have submitted with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: The verse shows the Queen of Sheba being led by Solomon's wisdom from her own misjudgment to clear recognition of the truth. The glass-floored palace deceived her eyes so that she mistook it for water, and her uncovering of her shins reflects that confusion. Her reaction reveals an honest humility: rather than defending her error, she admits that she had wronged herself, and she turns in submission together with Solomon to God, the Lord of all worlds. The episode thus portrays the faith that follows when a person sees the truth plainly and abandons what was false.

translation: And We had certainly sent to Thamud their brother Salih, [saying], "Worship Allah," but they became two factions disputing with each other.
interpretation: The verse shows that the call of the prophets is one and unified in its essence, namely the worship of Allah alone, yet human beings, once given the message, often divide themselves into rival camps. Thamud's split into two quarreling factions after Salih's call reveals how the truth, when it arrives, exposes hearts and exposes the tendency of people to turn a shared revelation into a source of discord and partisanship rather than unity in obedience. The verse thus teaches that division in religion is frequently a consequence of ignoring the single command to worship God, and it warns believers against allowing worldly interests, pride, and factionalism to replace sincere submission to the one Lord.

translation: He said: O my people, why do you seek to hasten the evil before the good? Why do you not ask forgiveness of Allah, that perhaps you may be shown mercy?
interpretation: The verse reveals a reversal common to those who turn away from guidance: people eager for immediate worldly results or for punishment to come upon them, yet reluctant to seek what would truly bring them mercy. The prophet's rebuke exposes a heedlessness that prefers the hasty and visible over the lasting good. The remedy offered is simple and near at hand, namely turning back to Allah in repentance and seeking His forgiveness, since forgiveness is the gateway through which mercy is reached. The phrasing 'perhaps you may be shown mercy' also reminds the believer that mercy is a gift from God, not a debt owed, so humble repentance is the proper posture toward it.

translation: They said, "We see an omen of ill in you and those with you." He said, "Your omen is with Allah; rather, you are a people being tested."
interpretation: The verse records the reaction of a people who blamed their misfortunes on the messenger and his followers, treating them as a bad omen, a common reflex of those who reject guidance when hardship comes. The reply redirects the matter to its true source: whatever befalls people, good or ill, is decreed by Allah, so the cause of misfortune lies not in the believers but in the disbelievers' own deeds and state. The closing phrase, "a people being tested," reveals that their superstition is itself a trial exposing their heedlessness, and that hardship and ease alike are occasions by which people are tested to see how they respond.

translation: And there were in the city nine men who spread corruption in the land and did not reform.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah An-Naml (27:48), describes the leaders of the nine-man conspiracy in the city of Thamud, the people of Salih, who plotted against him and his family by night. Their corruption was twofold: it was moral and social, as they opposed the prophet and sought to kill him, and it was a corruption of the order of the land, since they rejected the signs of God and spread harm rather than good. The phrase 'and they did not reform' emphasizes that their nature was fixed in destruction; they were not merely wrongdoers who occasionally erred, but people who made corruption their practice and refused every opportunity to mend their ways. It warns that when a community is ruled by a small group of people who choose mischief over righteousness, the resulting harm reaches the entire land, and that the schemes of the corrupt are ultimately turned back upon themselves, as the story that follows shows in their destruction.

translation: They said: "Swear to one another by God that we will surely attack him and his family by night, and then we will say to his heir, 'We did not witness the destruction of his family, and indeed we are truthful.'"
interpretation: The verse depicts a conspiracy hatched by a group who, bound by an oath sworn in God's name, plotted to secretly kill Prophet Salih's people (the family of the man who was to be slain, as commonly understood from the surrounding narrative of the men of Thamud or the people of the story) under cover of night, and then to deny all knowledge of the crime to his heir. The passage exposes how religious oaths can be perverted into instruments of treachery, and how deceit is compounded by a false claim of innocence and truthfulness.
