The closing statement, "But most of them do not know," points to a gap between knowledge and understanding: they possess the premise of tawhid without grasping its implications for how one should live, worship, and surrender. The verse thus calls the listener to move from a merely verbal or inherited belief in God to a conscious recognition that the consequences of creation belong entirely to Him.

translation: To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Indeed, Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse establishes that absolute ownership and dominion over all that exists in the heavens and the earth belong to Allah alone, so nothing in creation is independent of Him. Because He possesses everything, He has no need of His creation's worship, obedience, or wealth; His self-sufficiency (al-Ghani) is complete and does not diminish by what He gives or withholds. Yet He is also al-Hamid, praiseworthy in His essence and deeds, deserving of gratitude even when people fail to render it. The verse thus calls the believer to recognize that any benefit humanity gains is from a Lord who needs nothing from them, which should inspire humility, sincere devotion, and gratitude rather than arrogance or reliance on anything other than Him.

translation: And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens, and the sea, replenished by seven more seas after it, (were ink), the words of Allah would not be exhausted. Indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse points to the boundlessness of Allah's knowledge, wisdom, and creative command, which no created thing can measure or exhaust. By placing the most abundant imaginable resources, every tree turned into a pen and the oceans multiplied sevenfold as ink, against the endlessness of His words, it shows the limitation of all creation before the infinity of the Creator. The closing names, Al-Aziz (the Mighty) and Al-Hakim (the Wise), indicate that this inexhaustibility is joined to power and perfect wisdom, so that the believer is reminded of the vastness of divine reality and of the humility proper to a finite human mind contemplating it.

translation: Your creation and your resurrection are not except like that of a single soul. Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.
interpretation: The verse tells the multitude of humanity that bringing all of them into being and raising them after death is no greater a matter for God than doing so for one soul, because His power is not strained by numbers. It is followed by the attributes of hearing and seeing to show that this ease rests on His complete knowledge: He perceives each individual soul in its details, so the mass of creatures poses no confusion to Him, and the same God who hears and sees every person is able to gather them all again on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Have you not seen that Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and has subjected the sun and the moon, each running to a specified term, and that Allah is Acquainted with what you do?
interpretation: The verse directs the reader's attention to the observable order of creation: the gradual lengthening and shortening of night and day, which is the continuous 'merging' of one into the other across the seasons, is not random but the work of a single Lord who governs it precisely. The sun and moon, made to serve humanity and to mark time, move along fixed orbits toward an appointed end, and this regularity is a sign that points the heart toward the Creator's power and wisdom. The verse closes by reminding the human being that the One who orders the heavens is fully aware of every deed, so that a person who contemplates the cosmos should also examine and correct his own conduct, knowing that nothing he does is hidden from God.

translation: That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood, and because Allah is the Most High, the Most Great.
interpretation: The verse closes the story of the divine signs and the marvels of creation by fixing a firm principle of belief: reality belongs wholly to Allah, the one who is established in being and cannot be otherwise, while every object of worship taken alongside Him is empty of any true power or reality, existing only by borrowed names and imagined claims. The repetition of Allah's exalted and great attributes after the stress on the falsehood of rival gods turns the believer's gaze from the transient and the imagined toward the one whose height and greatness no creature can rival. The lesson is that true worship is the recognition of what is real, and that every act of devotion directed elsewhere collapses before the truth of Allah's sovereignty.

translation: Have you not seen that the ships sail through the sea by the grace of Allah, that He may show you of His signs? Indeed, in that are signs for every patient, grateful person.
interpretation: The verse directs the reader's attention to the familiar sight of ships gliding over the sea, asking whether one has not truly seen it, so that ordinary experience becomes a window onto divine favor. The vessel stays afloat and moves across a vast, unstable element only because Allah sustains it, so every safe voyage is a form of His grace and a demonstration of His power. The purpose stated is that He shows people His signs, meaning that creation itself points to the One who governs it. The closing phrase limits the benefit of these signs to those who are sabbar, steadfast in patience during hardship and fear at sea, and shakur, thankful in ease and gratitude for blessings. Thus the verse teaches that recognizing divine signs requires a heart that endures trials with patience and acknowledges favors with gratitude.

translation: And when a wave covers them like canopies, they call upon God, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them to the shore, some of them remain moderate. And none rejects Our signs except every treacherous ingrate.
interpretation: The verse portrays human nature under extreme duress: when surrounded by overwhelming peril at sea, where every false support collapses, people turn sincerely to God alone, abandoning their associates and pretensions. Yet the relief of safe arrival often reveals the fragility of that sincerity, as forgetfulness returns. The verse divides humanity into those who hold to their gratitude and balance, and those whose denial of God's signs is persistent, treacherous, and ungrateful. It implies that real faith is tested not in crisis alone but in ease, and that the signs of God in creation and in revelation are rejected not for lack of evidence but from a heart that betrays its own covenant.

translation: O mankind, fear your Lord and dread a Day when no father will avail his son at all, nor will a son avail his father in anything. Indeed, the promise of Allah is true, so do not let the worldly life deceive you, and do not let the Deceiver deceive you about Allah.
interpretation: The verse calls all people to taking responsibility for their own souls before a Day on which every person stands alone, since the bonds of kinship that mattered in worldly life will no longer shield anyone from the consequences of their deeds. Its warning is directed at the seduction of this world, which tempts the heart to presume upon God's mercy and to assume that worldly status, lineage, or the intercession of others will suffice. By affirming that Allah's promise is true, it anchors the summons to piety in certainty of the Hereafter, and by naming the Deceiver (al-gharur, identified in classical exegesis as Satan) it reveals that the greatest danger is the false comfort that leads a person to neglect God while believing himself secure.

translation: Indeed, Allah has with Him the knowledge of the Hour, and He sends down the rain, and He knows what is in the wombs. And no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Acquainted.
interpretation: The verse identifies five matters that belong exclusively to God's knowledge, which the human mind cannot reach by its own means: the exact time of the Hour, the descent of rain, the hidden sex and nature of the unborn child, the outcome of one's deeds tomorrow, and the place of one's death. By placing these together, the verse teaches that real knowledge of the unseen rests with God alone, so that a person should not presume to know his destiny and should live in awareness of his dependence on Him, planning and acting responsibly while leaving the future in His hands.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Alif, Lam, Meem.
interpretation: The verse opens with the formula of the basmala, placing the recitation under the name of Allah, the Most Gracious and Most Merciful, so that the reader begins by acknowledging that all that follows is a mercy from the One whose names are mercy. The three disjointed letters Alif, Lam, Meem belong to the muqatta'at, the letters that open several chapters of the Qur'an. Their precise meaning is known only to God, and their function is to arrest the listener's attention and to draw the mind toward the miraculous character of a revelation composed of the same letters of Arabic that its first audience used, yet impossible for them to match. The interpreter's humility lies in leaving their hidden meaning with God while recognizing in them a sign that the Qur'an is a discourse from beyond human making.

translation: The revelation of the Book, about which there is no doubt, is from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse establishes the Qur'an's divine origin by stating that its descent is from the Lord of all creation, and it asserts with emphatic certainty that the Book is free from any doubt. The phrase 'la rayb fihi' is not merely a claim that no reasonable person should doubt it, but a declaration that its authenticity rests on its own clarity and the evident truth of its message, so that the believer's confidence is grounded in the Book itself. By tying the revelation to 'Rabb al-'Alamin,' the verse also highlights God's universal lordship: the same Sustainer who governs all worlds is the one who sends this guidance, which therefore addresses humanity as a whole rather than a single people.

translation: Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"? Rather, it is the truth from your Lord, that you may warn a people to whom no warner has come before you, that they may be guided.
interpretation: The verse answers the accusation that the Prophet Muhammad invented the Qur'an by affirming that it is the truth descended from God, not a human fabrication. Its purpose is mercy and guidance: the Prophet is sent to a people who had received no prior warner, so that the message might awaken them to the right path. The verse thus joins the defense of the revelation's authenticity with a statement of its mission, indicating that the Qur'an's divine origin is shown by its truth and its beneficial aim of guiding hearts rather than by mere assertion.

translation: It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them in six days; then He established Himself above the Throne. You have, besides Him, no protector and no intercessor. Will you not then be reminded?
interpretation: The verse grounds the call to monotheism in the evidence of creation: the One who alone created the cosmos and then ordered its affairs from the Throne is the only One deserving worship and reliance. Since no one other than Him can give protection or intercede without His permission, placing hope or trust in any other power is both futile and a departure from reason. The closing rhetorical question invites the listener to awaken the heart's faculty of remembrance, so that the signs of creation lead back to the recognition of the Creator's sole sovereignty over all things.

translation: He arranges every matter from the heaven to the earth; then it ascends to Him in a Day whose measure is a thousand years of what you count.
interpretation: The verse presents God as the sole director of the affairs of creation, with commands descending from the highest realm to the earthly one and then their outcome returning to Him. The 'day' of this ascent is not measured by human reckoning: the same word for day denotes vastly different spans depending on the order of reality in which it is measured, so that the human mind, bound to its own time, is invited to recognize that divine time transcends its counting. The verse thus combines a lesson in divine sovereignty over all levels of existence with a reminder of the limits of human perception of time.

translation: That is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse closes by presenting God through two pairs of divine attributes that together encompass the whole of creation and the whole of His relation to it. 'The unseen and the witnessed' (ghayb and shahada) means that nothing is hidden from Him, neither what lies beyond human perception and the realm of the hereafter nor what is open to the senses, so His knowledge is total and does not depend on what is observed. 'Al-Aziz' (the Almighty) affirms His overpowering might, which makes His judgment and decree irresistible, while 'al-Rahim' (the Most Merciful) shows that this power is joined to compassion, so that His knowledge and might are not cold or threatening but directed toward the mercy by which He guides and forgives. The placement of these names at the end of the verse thus reminds the listener that the One who sees all that is concealed and manifest is also the One who is both able to hold them to account and merciful toward those who turn to Him.

translation: Who perfected everything He created, and began the creation of man from clay.
interpretation: The verse presents divine craftsmanship as both complete and purposeful: God does not merely create, but makes each thing in the best form suited to its nature, so that creation itself testifies to His wisdom and mastery. By then tracing the origin of humankind to clay, it joins this perfection with humility, reminding the human being that the same Creator who shaped the most intricate details of the cosmos began the human story from the simplest and most lowly of materials. The reflection it invites is twofold: awe at the precision of divine creation, and recognition that human dignity rests not on self-made origins but on the grace of the One who fashioned us with care.

translation: Then He made his descendants from an extract of a liquid, despised (base) water.
interpretation: The verse points to the humble origin of the human being: the continuation of the human line comes through a fluid drawn from a weak and lowly source, which is meant to awaken reflection on how much a person owes to the Creator's power and how little ground there is for arrogance. The contrast between the fine, perfected form that follows and this despised beginning turns the reader's attention from pride in one's own self toward gratitude, humility, and recognition that the one who shaped humanity from so modest a start is able to bring it back and to hold it accountable.

translation: Then He proportioned him and breathed into him of His spirit, and made for you hearing, sight, and hearts; little is it that you give thanks.
interpretation: The verse traces the creation of the human being in stages: after shaping and perfecting his form, God breathed into him something of His own spirit, which marks his unique dignity and his capacity for knowing and responding to the divine. The faculties of hearing, sight, and understanding are the means by which he receives guidance, perceives the signs of God in creation, and reflects on them. The closing rebuke, that few are the ones who give thanks, points to how rarely people recognize these gifts as blessings and turn them into gratitude expressed through obedience and acknowledgment of their Giver.

translation: And they say: "When we have gone astray in the earth, will we indeed be in a new creation?" Nay, they are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord.
interpretation: The verse reports the denial of the resurrection by those who deny the Hereafter: their question, "When we have lost ourselves in the earth, will we really be re-created?", expresses their astonishment that scattered dust and decayed bodies could ever be gathered and brought back into life. The phrase "gone astray in the earth" depicts the body dissolving and vanishing into the soil, so that it seems beyond recovery. The Qur'an answers with "Nay" (bal), rejecting their doubt, and then locates the true cause of their denial not in any lack of evidence but in their disbelief in meeting their Lord. Their rejection of resurrection is thus rooted in a deeper spiritual estrangement: they do not truly acknowledge that they will stand before their Creator to be judged, and it is this refusal of accountability that makes the idea of a new creation seem unthinkable to them.

translation: Say: The angel of death who has been entrusted with you will take you back; then to your Lord you will be returned.
interpretation: The verse affirms that death is not random or beyond divine control but is carried out by an appointed angel who acts under God's command, so that each person's term ends exactly as decreed. It places human life between two points: the moment the soul is taken, and the return to the Lord, where every person will stand accountable. The reminder is that a person's mortality should prompt readiness for that return, since the appointed time is known only to God and the return to Him is certain.

translation: And if you could see when the criminals will hang their heads before their Lord, (saying): "Our Lord, we have seen and heard, so return us, and we will work righteousness; indeed we are now certain."
interpretation: The verse presents the scene of the Day of Judgment as a vivid image of the guilty's humiliation and regret. Their bowed heads express shame and the collapse of their former arrogance before the Lord, and their plea reveals that the truth which was hidden from them in the world has now become undeniable through sight and hearing. Yet their request to be returned comes too late, for the opportunity of action has passed, and their certainty arrives only when it can no longer benefit them. The verse thus teaches that faith and righteousness must be pursued in this life, before the reality of the Hereafter becomes plain to every eye and ear.

translation: And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance, but the word from Me has come into effect: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind all together."
interpretation: This verse, from Surah As-Sajdah (32:13), shows that guidance is ultimately a matter of divine will, yet it does not negate human responsibility. Had God willed, He could have compelled every soul to guidance, but He created humans with the capacity to choose, and guidance granted by compulsion would not be the true guidance that is meant to be freely embraced. The "word" that has gone forth is God's decree, grounded in His foreknowledge and in the choices people make after persistent rejection and arrogance. The verse thus warns that those who knowingly turn away from the truth, whether among jinn or humankind, bring upon themselves the consequence they have chosen, while also reminding believers that guidance is a mercy from God that must be sought sincerely.

translation: So taste [the punishment] for your forgetting the meeting of this your Day; indeed, We have forgotten you. And taste the everlasting punishment for what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse reveals that forgetting the Day of Meeting is not a mere lapse of memory but a deliberate neglect that shapes one's whole conduct, so the recompense mirrors the offense: as they forgot the encounter with their Lord, they are now left to be forgotten by Him, meaning they are abandoned to the consequences of their own choices. The phrase "We have forgotten you" is best understood as a measured retribution, not a literal lapse in divine knowledge, expressing withdrawal of mercy and attention. The closing reference to the everlasting punishment ties the punishment to their deeds, teaching that a heedless life, lived as though accountability were absent, is itself the seed of the torment that awaits.

translation: Only those believe in Our verses who, when they are reminded of them, fall down prostrating and glorify the praise of their Lord, and they are not arrogant.
interpretation: The verse identifies true faith with a particular inner disposition: the believer's heart is so receptive that a mere reminder of God's signs brings him to humble submission. His prostration is not an empty bodily act but the outward expression of an inner surrender that leaves no room for pride. Praising the Lord with His praise and being free of arrogance are two sides of the same reality, since the one who truly recognizes his Creator sees his own station as that of a servant. Thus faith is revealed not by claims made with the tongue but by the prompt, humble response of the heart to the remembrance of God's revelation.

translation: Their sides forsake their beds, as they call upon their Lord in fear and in hope, and they spend out of what We have provided for them.
interpretation: The verse portrays believers whose inner devotion draws them away from the comfort of sleep to stand in prayer at night, so that their nightly worship becomes a living expression of a heart suspended between dread of God's justice and longing for His mercy. This inward tension is not allowed to remain a private emotion: it is completed by generosity, as those whose bodies rise from rest are also those whose hands give from what God has granted them. The verse thus binds the intimacy of worship to the discipline of charity, suggesting that true closeness to the Lord shows itself both in the watches of the night and in the open sharing of one's provision.

translation: So no soul knows what is hidden for them of comfort for the eyes as a reward for what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse points to the limits of human knowledge regarding the reward prepared for the righteous: no one can fully conceive the joy and delight that God has concealed for them. The phrase 'qurrat a'yun' (coolness of the eyes) conveys the deepest contentment and consolation, the kind of gladness that brings the eyes comfort and tranquility. Its hiddenness signals that the bliss of the Hereafter surpasses all description and imagination, and that it is granted as a recompense ('jaza'an') proportioned to their deeds, showing that what they did in this world is the cause for which this reward is given. The verse thus invites the believer to hope, to strive in good works, and to remain humble before a reward whose full reality is known only to God.

translation: Is then one who was a believer like one who was defiantly disobedient? They are not equal.
interpretation: The verse poses a rhetorical question that settles the matter by its own form: faith and moral corruption are not alike, and whoever stands in belief cannot be placed on the same footing as whoever has departed from obedience. The denial 'they are not equal' carries the weight of the lesson, pointing the listener toward a moral clarity that the human conscience already recognizes. Its force lies in showing that inequality between the righteous and the wicked is not a matter of opinion but of the nature of their deeds and their ends, so that a person reflecting on it is urged to choose the path of faith and to avoid being counted among the defiant.

translation: As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will have the Gardens of Refuge as a lodging, because of what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse sets the believers' reward in direct contrast with the fate of the wicked mentioned just before it in the surah (As-Sajdah), showing that faith joined with righteous action is what earns a secure and honored abode. The word "nuzul" (lodging) evokes the image of a host preparing a welcome for a guest, so the Gardens are presented not as a wage earned by mere effort but as a generous hospitality, while the phrase "bima kanu ya'malun" ties the reward to their deeds, teaching that outward works are the visible measure of inward faith. The name "Gardens of Refuge" suggests that those who take shelter in God through belief and good conduct find in the Hereafter a lasting place of safety and rest.

translation: And as for those who defied (were defiantly disobedient), their refuge is the Fire. Whenever they wish to get out of it, they will be returned into it, and it will be said to them: "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."
interpretation: The verse draws a sharp contrast with the preceding description of the righteous, presenting fisq (defiant transgression that departs from obedience to God) as a condition that leads its bearer to the Fire as a settled dwelling place. The image of their repeatedly trying to escape only to be driven back conveys the inescapable nature of the punishment and the futility of their longing for release once they are in it. The final address, "Taste," frames the torment as the direct consequence of their own denial in the world, so that the punishment is shown to be the very reality they had rejected, linking the outward act of wrongdoing to the inward refusal to believe.

translation: And We will surely make them taste the lesser punishment before the greater punishment, so that perhaps they will return (to the right path).
interpretation: The verse points to a mercy woven into divine punishment: the 'lesser punishment' (al-'adhab al-adna) is not merely a sample of suffering but a corrective warning meant to awaken the heedless before the final reckoning. Worldly hardships, losses, illnesses, and calamities serve as a summons to self-examination, so that a person who has strayed may recognize the emptiness of their course and turn back in repentance. The greater punishment is reserved for the Hereafter, while the nearer one is given in this life as a gentle shaking of the heart. The verse thus reveals that God's chastisement is ultimately aimed at guidance and return, not at destruction alone, and it invites the believer to read every trial as an opportunity to return to God before it is too late.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the verses of his Lord and then turns away from them? Indeed, We will take vengeance upon the criminals.
interpretation: The verse establishes a link between injustice and the deliberate rejection of divine reminder. Being admonished through God's signs is not merely an occasion to be informed but a test of one's receptiveness; to hear the verses and then deliberately turn away is to wrong oneself most grievously, since the signs were given precisely to guide. The phrase 'the criminals' (al-mujrimun) denotes those who persist in such heedlessness and sin, and the closing declaration that God will exact retribution from them underscores that the opportunity to heed is not without accountability. The verse thus warns that indifference to revelation, once it has reached a person, carries a weight of responsibility before God, and that divine justice will ultimately settle the account of those who persist in it.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture, so do not be in doubt about meeting him, and We made it a guidance for the Children of Israel.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the revelation given to Moses was a genuine divine book, and it counsels the Prophet Muhammad not to be in doubt about receiving or encountering the revelation (or, in the widely cited reading, about meeting Moses in the Night Journey), since the Scripture of Moses came from God. By making it a guidance for the Children of Israel, the verse presents the continuity of revelation: the same divine source that guided earlier communities underlies the Qur'an, and the reader is invited to recognize the shared origin of the messages and to trust the reality of the divine communication.

translation: And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient, and they were certain of Our signs.
interpretation: The verse shows that spiritual leadership in religion is earned through two qualities, patience in the face of hardship and firm certainty in God's signs. Their guidance of others by God's command was not a matter of worldly rank but a consequence of their steadfastness and conviction. Leadership that guides people toward the truth thus rests on inner perseverance and sure faith, and the verse implies that when such qualities are lost, the authority to guide is lost with them.

translation: Indeed, your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that about which they used to differ.
interpretation: The verse assures the Prophet that the disputes among people over matters of faith and truth are not left unresolved; God Himself, the true Lord, will be the ultimate judge on the Day of Resurrection, separating the parties and making clear what they had disagreed about. This points to the finality of divine judgment, which stands above all human argument, and invites the believer to patience and trust in God's justice when truth is contested in this world.

translation: Did it not guide them how many generations We destroyed before them, among whose dwellings they walk? Indeed, in that are signs. Will they not then listen?
interpretation: The verse directs the heedless to reflect on the ruins of earlier peoples whom God destroyed for their denial, since those who now walk through the very dwellings of those nations can see the consequences of rejecting prophets with their own eyes. History itself becomes a guidance that the people of Makkah had failed to heed, and the rhetorical question 'will they not listen?' presses them to draw the lesson from what is visible to them, rather than remaining deaf to the warning that such signs carry.

translation: Do they not see that We drive the water to the barren land and bring forth thereby crops from which eat their livestock and themselves? Will they not then see?
interpretation: The verse directs the human gaze toward the ordinary, repeated miracle of rain revived dead earth, presenting it as a sign that the one who gives life to barren land is able to bring the dead back to life. Those who witness this cycle daily and still fail to perceive its meaning are rebuked for a blindness that is not of the eyes but of insight, since the sustenance that feeds their animals and themselves is itself a proof of divine power, mercy, and the reality of resurrection.

translation: And they say, "When will this victory be, if you are truthful?"
interpretation: The verse records the disbelievers' mocking challenge to the believers regarding the promised 'fath' (decisive victory or judgment), which they demanded be brought about if the Prophet and his companions were truthful in their claims. Their question reflects a dismissive denial of the promise of a coming reckoning and divine decision, treating it as a distant or impossible event. The implicit answer in the wider context is that the decisive matter is known only to God, and that their demand for its immediate arrival will not spare them from its reality when it comes. The verse thus combines the rejection of the believers' message with a reminder that the timing of divine judgment lies entirely with God and that the disbelievers' hasty mockery is no argument against its truth.

translation: Say: "On the Day of Victory, the faith of those who disbelieved will not benefit them, nor will they be given respite."
interpretation: The verse points to a decisive moment at which the opportunity for faith ends. Belief is only of value when it is embraced freely and in time; once the reality of the Hereafter or the decisive divine judgment becomes manifest, professing faith out of fear or compulsion carries no weight, as the Qur'an elsewhere shows with those who believed only when they saw the punishment. The phrase "nor will they be given respite" reinforces that there will be no delay or extension of time for repentance. The verse thus calls the listener to seize the present moment for sincere faith before the window closes, and it underscores that the timing of belief is itself part of its sincerity.

translation: So turn away from them and wait; indeed, they too are waiting.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet and reassures him in the face of his people's persistent rejection: he is commanded to withdraw from their stubborn disbelief and mockery rather than exhaust himself in argument, and to entrust the matter to God's timing. The phrase "they too are waiting" points to the fact that those who deny the message are themselves awaiting a reckoning, a fate of punishment or defeat that will in due course overtake them. The verse thus joins patience with a firm assurance that truth will prevail and that the outcome lies with God, not with the deniers.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O Prophet, fear Allah and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites. Indeed, Allah is ever All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse addresses the Prophet directly with the command to maintain taqwa, that is, constant consciousness of Allah in all his affairs, and it links this with a prohibition on yielding to the disbelievers and the hypocrites. The pairing is significant: the disbelievers oppose the message openly, while the hypocrites undermine it from within by feigning faith, so the Prophet is warned against accepting either their counsel or their pressure, especially when such counsel seeks to bend the community's policies toward their own interests. The closing names, Knowing and Wise, reassure the believers that Allah has full knowledge of the schemes of these groups and that His judgments and legislation are grounded in perfect wisdom, so the Prophet's steadfastness rests on trust in divine knowledge rather than on the approval of men.

translation: And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord. Indeed, Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.
interpretation: The verse directs the Prophet, and by extension every believer, to take revelation as the sole guide for conduct, placing unwavering obedience to the divine message above personal inclination or the pressures of opposition. It links this command to God's complete awareness of human deeds, so that the call to follow revelation is also a reminder of accountability: nothing done in sincerity or hypocrisy escapes the One who knows them fully, and the believer's conduct should be shaped with the constant consciousness of being observed by the All-Aware.

translation: And rely upon Allah. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: The verse directs the believer to place complete trust in Allah after the preceding guidance, teaching that true reliance (tawakkul) is not passive resignation but a settled confidence that arises from acting faithfully while surrendering the outcome to the One who manages all affairs. The phrase 'sufficient is Allah as Disposer' (wakil) reassures the believer that whoever entrusts his affairs to God will find in Him a protector who is adequate for every need, so that fear of people or worldly loss loses its hold on the heart.

translation: God has not made for any man two hearts within his body. Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar (declaring them as your mothers) your mothers, nor has He made your adopted sons your sons. That is merely your saying with your mouths. But God says the truth, and He guides to the way.
interpretation: The verse dismantles three social fictions that had been treated as binding realities, showing that law must rest on what is true rather than on words or assumed identities. Just as no person has two hearts, so a man cannot be bound to a single wife in two opposite ways at once, nor can a wife become a mother through a mere utterance, nor can an adopted child acquire the blood-ties and legal status of a natural child. The point is that a declaration spoken by the mouth does not alter reality; the heart's actual truth and God's word are the measure. By removing these false equivalences, the verse prepares the ground for the reform of family rules, establishing that kinship and obligation follow from genuine facts and divine guidance rather than from customary fictions.

translation: Call them by [the names of] their fathers; that is more just in the sight of Allah. But if you do not know their fathers, then [they are] your brothers in religion and your protégés. And there is no blame upon you for what you have done in error, but [blame lies in] what your hearts intended. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse establishes that lineage is a matter of truth and justice, so adopted children should be attributed to their real fathers rather than to those who raised them, which protects the integrity of family identity and rights. Where a true father is unknown, the believer is not left without a bond: the adopted child is a brother in faith and a protégé with a place in the community. The mercy in the closing lines shows that unintended mistakes are forgiven, while accountability rests on deliberate intention, so that the law of truthfulness is balanced with compassion for human error.

translation: The Prophet has more right over the believers than they have over themselves, and his wives are their mothers. And those of blood relationship are more entitled to one another in the Book of Allah than the (other) believers and the emigrants, except that you do to your allies a kindness. That is, in the Book, inscribed.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the Prophet's authority over believers exceeds their own claims over themselves, since his guidance is aimed at their true welfare, and it makes his wives honored as mothers of the believers, bound to them in reverence and forbidden to them in marriage after him. It then restores the principle that kinship by blood takes precedence in inheritance under God's decree, abrogating the earlier arrangement of brotherhood between emigrants and helpers as a basis for inheritance, while permitting believers to leave a bequest of kindness to their allies. The closing phrase affirms that this ordinance is fixed and recorded in the divine Book, so that the social order of the community rests on both spiritual loyalty to the Prophet and the natural bonds of family.

translation: And [mention] when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus the son of Mary; and We took from them a solemn covenant.
interpretation: The verse points to a covenant that God took from all the messengers, and it singles out five of the greatest among them, beginning with Muhammad, to show that the commitment to deliver God's message and stand by it was not a casual matter but a binding, weighty pledge that the prophets themselves were bound to keep. By naming the Prophet first among these, the verse honors his place within the single chain of revelation that runs from Noah through Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, and it implies that faithfulness to this trust is the measure by which the messengers, and those who follow them, are judged. The word 'solemn' (ghaliz) conveys that the pledge was heavy and serious, so that the sincerity of the prophets in conveying and supporting one another's mission is presented as the foundation of the religious order God established through them.

translation: That He may ask the truthful about their truthfulness; and He has prepared for the disbelievers a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse points to a divine purpose behind the accountability of the Day of Judgment: God will call the sincere to account for the sincerity of their words and deeds, so that truthfulness is shown to be a matter of real weight before Him, while those who reject faith face a severe, painful punishment prepared in advance. The contrast between the truthful and the disbelievers highlights that sincerity of heart is the dividing line between reward and retribution.

translation: O you who have believed, remember the favor of Allah upon you when hosts came to you and We sent upon them a wind and armies you did not see. And Allah is ever Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse calls the believers to dhikr of Allah's blessing at a moment of acute danger, the siege of Medina by the confederates (al-Ahzab). Remembrance here is not mere recollection but a recognition that the believers' survival was not the product of their own strength or numbers, but of a hidden divine intervention, the wind and unseen hosts, which turned the enemy back. The phrase 'armies you did not see' teaches that Allah's help often operates beyond human perception, so that faith requires trust in what is unseen. The closing reminder that Allah sees what they do links gratitude with accountability: having witnessed such deliverance, the believers are to remain steadfast and conduct themselves in a way worthy of that favor.

translation: When they came upon you from above you and from below you, and when the eyes shifted in fear and the hearts reached the throats, and you were thinking about Allah with various (doubtful) thoughts.
interpretation: This verse depicts the crisis of the Battle of the Trench (al-Ahzab), when the believers in Medina were encircled from every direction by the allied forces, and felt the full weight of fear and distress. The imagery of hearts rising to the throats conveys extreme terror and anxiety, which tested the sincerity of faith. The verse exposes the inner turmoil of the believers, some of whom entertained doubts and misgivings about God's promise of help, thereby showing that true faith is revealed in moments of severe trial rather than in times of ease.

translation: There the believers were tested, and they were shaken with a severe shaking.
interpretation: The verse refers to the Battle of the Trench (al-Ahzab), when the believers faced a combined siege from enemies within and without Medina. The word 'there' points to that critical moment, and the trial is described as a severe shaking that exposed the true state of hearts. Its meaning is that hardship is a crucible that separates the sincere from the wavering, and that the believers' firmness under such fear is itself a sign of faith tested and proven.

translation: And when the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease say, "Allah and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion."
interpretation: This verse, from Surah al-Ahzab, portrays the inner state of those whose faith was only outward during the Battle of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), when the believers were surrounded and severely tested. The hypocrites and those with sickness in their hearts, whose faith was weak and whose commitment was doubtful, took the hardship as proof that the divine promises of victory were empty. Their words reveal that their real problem was not the lack of evidence but the weakness of their trust in God and His Messenger. The verse teaches that trials expose what people truly believe: sincere believers see in hardship a confirmation of God's promise, while those with hypocrisy in their hearts interpret the same events as a sign of deception and failure.

translation: And when a faction of them said, "O people of Yathrib, there is no place for you, so return." And a group of them asked permission of the Prophet, saying, "Indeed, our houses are exposed," while they were not exposed. They only intended to flee.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites of Medina during the battle of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), who, seeking to abandon the front at a moment of great fear, invented a pretext that their homes were unprotected, when in truth their hearts sought escape from the struggle. It reveals how fear and worldly attachment can clothe desertion in the language of concern, teaching the believer to examine the true motive behind his excuses and to stand firm alongside the community in times of trial.

translation: And if an invasion had entered upon them from all its sides, and then they had been asked to commit disbelief, they would have given it at once, and they would have hesitated over it only briefly.
interpretation: This verse (33:14) exposes the hollowness of the hypocrites of Medina who had sworn to stand firm and had claimed their homes were exposed when they were in fact seeking to flee the battle of the Confederates. It shows that their apparent attachment to faith was fragile: under pressure, a call to abandon their principles or to join the enemies of the community would have been accepted almost instantly, with no real resistance. The Qur'an thereby teaches that outward profession without inner steadfastness collapses when tested, and that true faith is measured by perseverance under trial rather than by verbal commitments made in comfortable times.

translation: And they had certainly pledged to Allah before this that they would not turn their backs (in flight). And the pledge of Allah is ever to be questioned about.
interpretation: The verse exposes the gravity of breaking a sworn covenant with God: those who had already committed themselves to steadfastness in battle and then fled reveal that their word to God was hollow. By stating that the covenant "will be questioned," it teaches that every pledge made to God is a moral debt that will be held to account, so a believer's commitments—whether made in worship, in battle, or in ordinary dealings—must be honored, since fleeing from a promise is ultimately fleeing from accountability before God.

translation: Say: Flight will never benefit you if you flee from death or killing, and then you will not be allowed to enjoy (worldly life) except for a little.
interpretation: The verse addresses the hypocrites and those who shrank from jihad, reminding them that fleeing from fighting cannot save them from the decree of death, which comes at its appointed time wherever a person is. Whoever tries to escape the battlefield to preserve his life gains nothing lasting, since his share of this world is brief and fleeting. The message is that true security lies in obedience to God and not in running from what He has decreed, and that the enjoyment of worldly life is short compared to what lies ahead in the Hereafter.

translation: Say, "Who is it that can protect you from God if He intends harm for you, or intends mercy for you?" And they will not find for themselves, besides God, any protector or any helper.
interpretation: The verse establishes that no created being can shield a person from the decree of God once He wills either hardship or grace for them, so true reliance and refuge belong to God alone. By posing the question as a rhetorical challenge, it exposes the emptiness of seeking protection from idols, rulers, or any human power, since whoever turns to them finds neither a guardian nor a helper. The lesson is that a believer's trust should rest on the One whose will governs both harm and mercy, while recognizing that all other sources of support are powerless without His permission.

translation: Allah already knows those among you who hinder others and who say to their brothers, "Come to us," and they come not to battle except a little.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites who, under the cover of their own weakness and reluctance, discourage their fellow believers from joining the struggle and call them back to comfort and safety. Allah's knowledge of them is presented as a warning that their inner dispositions are fully exposed to Him, however they conceal them from the community. Their participation in the fighting is minimal and grudging, revealing that their loyalty lies with ease and self-preservation rather than with the cause of faith. The verse thus teaches that obstructing good work and undermining others' resolve is a serious spiritual fault, and that true commitment is measured by sincere action rather than by words of pretended solidarity.

translation: Stingy toward you. So when fear comes, you see them looking at you, their eyes rolling like one fainting before death. But when the fear departs, they assail you with sharp tongues, greedy for good things. Those have not believed, so Allah has nullified their deeds, and that is ever easy for Allah.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites' character through their conduct in moments of crisis. In the danger of the battle, their fear makes them wild-eyed and frantic, clinging to self-preservation rather than standing with the Prophet and the believers. Their stinginess is not only with wealth but with loyalty, sacrifice, and commitment to the community. Once the threat passes and the spoils or advantages appear, they become bold and aggressive in speech, claiming a share of the good they did nothing to earn. The verse teaches that faith is revealed by steadfastness under pressure and generosity in service, not by words or by seeking benefit. Their outward appearance of belonging is hollow, and their deeds, lacking sincere faith, come to nothing before God.

translation: They think the confederates have not withdrawn; and if the confederates should come, they would wish that they were out in the desert among the Bedouins, asking about your news. And even if they were among you, they would fight only a little.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites during the Battle of the Trench (al-Ahzab). Their fear was so great that they imagined the allied confederates had not yet retreated, and should those forces return, the hypocrites would prefer to be far away in the desert, merely inquiring anxiously from afar about the news of the Muslims rather than sharing their peril. Even when present among the believers, their participation in fighting would be minimal and grudging, reflecting a heart detached from the cause and a reluctance to bear hardship for the sake of God and His Messenger.

translation: There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example for whoever was hoping for Allah and the Last Day and remembering Allah often.
interpretation: The verse presents the Prophet Muhammad as a living model to be imitated, and it ties the sincerity of following him to two inner conditions: hope in Allah and the Last Day, which give a person a reason to seek the good, and frequent remembrance of Allah, which keeps the heart attentive so that its imitation is not merely outward. Its wording, 'an excellent example' (uswa hasana), indicates that the Prophet's conduct in worship, patience, courage, mercy and trust in God is meant to shape the believer's character, not only to be admired. The verse, revealed in the context of the Battle of the Trench, thus teaches that steadfastness in hardship is best nourished by taking the Prophet as a guide while keeping God constantly in mind.

translation: And when the believers saw the confederates, they said, "This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us, and Allah and His Messenger have spoken the truth." And it increased them only in faith and submission.
interpretation: The verse presents the believers' reaction to the massing of the confederate armies around Medina (the Battle of the Trench) as a test that confirmed rather than shook their faith. What they saw of overwhelming enemies was, for them, the fulfillment of a divine promise of trial that precedes victory, so their certainty in Allah and His Messenger grew. The increase is described in two dimensions: inner conviction (iman) and outward, active surrender to God's command (taslim). The lesson is that adversity, when met with trust, deepens belief and obedience rather than diminishing them, and that a believer reads hardship through the promises of God rather than through the apparent balance of power.

translation: Among the believers are men who have been true to what they covenanted with Allah. Among them is one who has fulfilled his vow (died), and among them is one who awaits, and they have not changed in the least.
interpretation: The verse honors those believers who kept their sincere pledge to God, showing that faithfulness is measured by steadfastness rather than by outward circumstance. Some have completed their commitment through martyrdom or death in the path of God, while others remain ready and waiting to fulfill theirs, and neither group has altered or weakened their resolve. The phrase 'they did not change in the least' stresses that true faith is marked by constancy: a believer's promise to God is not discarded under pressure, delay, or temptation, but is held firmly until its fulfillment, whether that comes in this life or is still awaited.

translation: So that Allah may reward the truthful for their truthfulness, and punish the hypocrites if He wills, or turn to them in forgiveness. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse reveals the purpose behind the trials and events described before it: divine justice is meant to separate the sincere from the hypocritical. Allah rewards those whose truthfulness was tested and proven in deed as well as word, so their sincerity becomes the very cause of their reward. As for the hypocrites, their fate remains in Allah's hand. He may punish them for their concealed disbelief, or He may open the door of repentance to them, which shows that His punishment is tied to His wisdom and that His mercy is never closed to a sincere return. The verse closes by affirming that Allah's attributes of forgiveness and mercy are constant, so the believer is reminded both to hold fast to truthfulness and to never despair of His pardon.

translation: God turned back those who disbelieved in their rage, they gained no good; and God sufficed the believers in fighting, and God is ever Strong, Mighty.
interpretation: The verse portrays God's sufficiency for the believers in a situation of conflict: the disbelievers who came with fury and hostility were sent back empty-handed, unable to achieve their aim, their rage turning into a defeat that gained them nothing. The phrase 'and God sufficed the believers in fighting' points to divine protection that spares the community from having to carry the full burden of battle on its own strength, so that their reliance on God is itself the decisive factor. The closing attributes of strength and might reaffirm that this outcome flows from God's power, which no hostile force can overcome, and that trust in Him is the source of the believers' security.

translation: And He brought down those among the People of the Scripture who had supported them (the confederates) from their fortresses, and cast terror into their hearts. A group of them you killed, and another group you took captive.
interpretation: The verse recounts the episode of the Banu Qurayza after the Battle of the Trench (al-Ahzab), whose betrayal of the Muslims in Medina while the confederate armies besieged the city left them exposed to danger. Their collapse came not through the strength of the believers alone but through God's casting of fear into their hearts, which made them abandon their fortresses and surrender. The verse thus presents the outcome as a divine act: the one who withdraws the protection of the treacherous and humbles them is God, and the believers are reminded that victory and reversal lie in His hands, so that trust in Him rather than in one's own strength remains the source of security.

translation: And He caused you to inherit their land, their homes, their wealth, and a land you had not yet trodden. And Allah has power over all things.
interpretation: The verse, revealed in the context of the early Muslim community's struggles and the battles against their adversaries, is a promise of divine succession: God grants the believers possession of lands, dwellings, and property that had belonged to their opponents, and even territories they had never set foot upon, so that the believers learn that worldly dominion is entirely in the hands of God, who transfers it according to His will. The closing phrase reminds the reader that nothing is beyond His capacity, so the believers should place their trust in Him rather than in their own numbers or strength, and should recognize that the inheritance of the earth follows from steadfastness and faithfulness to Him.

translation: O Prophet, say to your wives: If you desire the worldly life and its adornment, then come, I will provide for you and release you with a graceful release.
interpretation: The verse presents the Prophet with a choice to offer his wives, granting them freedom to choose between the fleeting pleasures of this world and its finery on one hand, and God and His Messenger and the abode of the Hereafter on the other. It reveals a principle that the household of the Prophet must be bound to sincerity and devotion, and that the wives of the Prophet, as the mothers of the believers, were held to a higher standard of conduct. By offering provision and a kindly release, the verse shows that God's justice and mercy accompany even moments of hard choice, and that worldly attachment is to be weighed against a higher purpose.

translation: And if you desire Allah and His Messenger and the Last Abode, then indeed Allah has prepared for the doers of good among you a great reward.
interpretation: The verse presents a clear choice placed before the wives of the Prophet ﷺ: their preference for God, His Messenger, and the hereafter over the worldly adornment they had sought. Its wording ties the great reward specifically to those among them who are muhsinat, that is, who combine sincere devotion with excellence in conduct, so that closeness to the Prophet's household is measured not by status alone but by faith and good deeds. The passage thus teaches that God's favor is earned through sincerity of intention and the pursuit of righteousness, and it sets an enduring standard that the honor of association with the Prophet must be matched by piety.

translation: O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clearly outrageous act of immorality, her punishment will be doubled twice over; and that is ever easy for Allah.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the wives of the Prophet are held to a higher standard of accountability precisely because of their elevated position and closeness to the Prophet, so that a transgression which might be lighter for others carries a doubled penalty for them. The doubling reflects the gravity of their example to the believing community, since they were the mothers of the believers and the visible models of conduct in the Prophet's household. The phrase 'and that is ever easy for Allah' reminds the listener that this doubling is no burden for the Divine, who is able to requite each person precisely and without difficulty, and that the rule rests on justice rather than arbitrariness. The verse thus teaches that nearness to sources of guidance increases responsibility, and that the stakes of conduct grow with the trust placed in a person.

translation: And whoever of you devoutly submits to God and His Messenger and does righteous deeds - We will give her her reward twice, and We have prepared for her a generous provision.
interpretation: The verse addresses the wives of the Prophet and establishes that their closeness to the Prophet's household does not grant them special immunity or privilege; rather, their standing before God depends on their own devotion (qunut), obedience to God and His Messenger, and good conduct. Their doubled reward reflects the greater responsibility and the exemplary role they bear as the wives of the Messenger, so that their obedience carries a weight beyond that of other believing women. The phrase 'generous provision' (rizq karim) points to the abundant honor and blessing God reserves for them in the hereafter, showing that God's reckoning is based on piety and righteous action rather than on lineage or association.

translation: O wives of the Prophet, you are not like any other women. If you are mindful of God, then do not be soft in speech lest one in whose heart is a disease should become covetous, but speak in a known, proper manner.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the wives of the Prophet hold a unique station that carries heightened responsibility, so their conduct is held to a standard above that of ordinary women. Their piety (taqwa) is the condition for this distinction to be meaningful. The prohibition on a yielding, seductive tone is not a general restriction on women's speech but a guard against provoking desire or false hope in those who are spiritually diseased, which teaches that the manner of speech, and not only its content, carries moral weight. The command to speak in a 'known and proper' way (qawlan ma'rufan) directs that their words be dignified, clear, and free of any suggestive softness, thereby protecting both the sanctity of the Prophet's household and the social integrity of the community.

translation: And stay in your houses and do not display yourselves as was the display of the former times of ignorance. And establish prayer, give zakah, and obey Allah and His Messenger. Allah only intends to remove from you the impurity, O people of the household, and to purify you with complete purification.
interpretation: The verse, addressed to the wives of the Prophet, sets out a principle of modesty and dignity for the believing women: they are commanded to remain composed within their homes and to avoid the flaunting of beauty and adornment that marked the pre-Islamic age of ignorance. This restraint is not meant as mere confinement but as a protective framework within which their devotion is anchored in prayer, charity, and obedience to God and His Messenger. The closing phrase, speaking of God's will to remove impurity and purify the 'people of the household,' expresses divine care for the moral cleanliness of the Prophet's family, understood by many commentators to include the Prophet's wives and, by extension, the wider household, and reveals that the outward commands of modesty are rooted in an inward purification of the heart.

translation: And remember what is recited in your houses of the verses of God and the wisdom. Indeed, God is ever Subtle, All-Aware.
interpretation: The verse, addressed to the wives of the Prophet in the context of the Prophet's household, directs them to keep in mind and to guard within their homes the revelations recited there and the wisdom that accompanies them, since this recitation is a trust that shapes the moral life of the household and, through it, the wider community. It links remembrance with gratitude and mindfulness: the sacred words are not merely heard but are to be internalized and lived. The closing names of God, Subtle (latif) and All-Aware (khabir), remind the believers that God perceives the finest details of what is done and intended within the private sphere of the home, and that His gentle guidance reaches even into the most hidden corners of human life.

translation: Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women, the devoutly obedient men and devoutly obedient women, the truthful men and truthful women, the patient men and patient women, the humble men and humble women, the charitable men and charitable women, the fasting men and fasting women, the men who guard their chastity and the women who guard theirs, and the men who remember Allah often and the women who remember Him. For them Allah has prepared forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: The verse answers the question of whether women are included in the religious standing that the Quran describes, and it does so by pairing each quality with its feminine counterpart, so that no one can read the earlier address to believers as addressed only to men. The ten pairs move from the basic commitment of submission and faith, through obedience, truthfulness, patience, humility, generosity, fasting, and chastity, to constant remembrance of God. This sequence presents a complete spiritual path in which each virtue is a stage that a person of either sex can reach. The verse therefore establishes that closeness to God is measured by inner qualities and sincere practice, not by gender, and that the reward of forgiveness and great recompense is promised to both equally.

translation: It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decided a matter, that they should have any choice in their affair. And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger has certainly strayed into clear error.
interpretation: The verse establishes that true faith entails surrendering one's own preference to the decree of Allah and His Messenger once a matter has been decided by them. Its wording addresses believers in general, and it was revealed in connection with the marriage of Zaynab bint Jahsh to Zayd ibn Harithah, when the families initially resisted the proposal. The 'choice' denied to the believer is not a rejection of legitimate consultation or personal reflection before a ruling, but the freedom to override or set aside a clear command once it has come. Obedience is thus presented as the measure of sincere belief, and deliberate disobedience as a drift into manifest misguidance, since the believer's will must align with the will of God as conveyed through His Messenger.

translation: And [remember, O Muhammad] when you said to the one on whom Allah bestowed favor and you bestowed favor, "Keep your wife to yourself and fear Allah," while you concealed within yourself that which Allah was to disclose, and you feared the people, while Allah has more right that you fear Him. So when Zayd had no longer any need for her, We married her to you so that there would be no discomfort for the believers concerning the wives of their adopted sons when they had no longer any need for them. And the command of Allah is ever accomplished.
interpretation: The verse shows the Prophet inwardly holding a divine decree that he had not yet been commanded to announce, and his reluctance stemmed from concern over public reproach in a society that treated adopted sons as true sons. Allah's correction teaches that the human fear of people, however understandable, must yield to the fear of God, and the marriage was a deliberate act that dismantled the pre-Islamic custom linking adoption to the prohibitions of marriage, so that the community's practice would rest on truth rather than on custom.

translation: There is no blame upon the Prophet concerning what Allah has ordained for him. That has been the way of Allah with those who passed away before; and the command of Allah is a decree determined in advance.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Prophet was not burdened by any restriction or guilt in carrying out what Allah had permitted or prescribed for him, particularly in matters of marriage that were lawful to him alone. It places this within a divine pattern (sunnah) established for earlier prophets, showing that Allah's commands are not arbitrary but follow a fixed and wise decree. The closing phrase emphasizes that every affair is measured and determined by Allah in advance, so the believers should accept what He ordains with certainty and without doubt.

translation: Those who convey the messages of Allah and fear Him, and do not fear anyone except Allah. And sufficient is Allah as Reckoner.
interpretation: The verse defines the true character of the messenger-bearers by two intertwined marks: they faithfully deliver what God has entrusted to them, and their inner fear is directed toward God alone. Their courage in proclaiming the message thus springs not from self-confidence but from a settled awareness that no human power can harm them beyond God's will, which frees them from the paralyzing dread of people's disapproval or threats. The closing phrase, that Allah suffices as a reckoner, assures them that their accountability rests with the One who sees their deeds and will judge them justly, so that they need not measure their success by the approval of others. It is a call to every believer who carries a truth, especially in times of opposition, to prioritize God's pleasure over human approval.

translation: Muhammad is not the father of any one of your men, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the seal of the prophets. And Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse clarifies that Muhammad's role was not defined by biological fatherhood over the men of the community, a point made in the context of his adopted son Zayd and the abolition of the pre-Islamic custom of treating adopted sons as true sons. His true and enduring station is that of Messenger of God and 'Seal of the Prophets,' meaning that prophethood is concluded with him, so that no prophet follows him and his message stands as the final and complete revelation for humanity. The closing words, that God has knowledge of all things, affirm that this ordinance and its finality rest upon divine wisdom and complete knowledge, not upon social convention or human lineage.

translation: O you who have believed, remember Allah with much remembrance.
interpretation: The verse addresses believers directly, calling them to a constant and abundant remembrance of Allah, which is not confined to set times or places but should permeate every state of their lives. Such dhikr, whether through the tongue, the heart, or action in obedience, keeps faith alive and vigilant, guarding the believer against heedlessness, which is the root of moral failure. By making God-consciousness habitual, the believer's conduct, worship, and dealings are brought under the awareness that Allah is always near and watching, so that remembrance becomes both the fruit of faith and the means of strengthening it.

translation: And glorify Him morning and evening.
interpretation: The verse commands the believers to glorify God (tasbih) at the beginning and end of the day, namely dawn and dusk. The word 'bukrah' refers to the early morning and 'asil' to the late afternoon or evening, so the phrase signifies constant, continuous remembrance and praise of God throughout the day. By dedicating the two ends of the day to His glorification, the believer's whole life is framed by devotion, so that remembrance of God becomes a steady rhythm rather than an occasional act, and the praise of God is set as the principal activity that opens and closes each day.

translation: It is He who sends blessings upon you, and so do His angels, that He may bring you out of darknesses into light. And He is ever Merciful toward the believers.
interpretation: The verse reveals that divine blessing (salawat) flows from Allah toward the believers, and the angels join in this mercy, so that the believers' bond with the Divine is itself the instrument of their rescue. The phrase "from darknesses into light" frames faith not as a single event but as a continual journey, in which each step of guidance pulls the soul out of ignorance, desire, and heedlessness into clarity and nearness to God. The closing attribute, Raheem, is placed beside the believers specifically, indicating that this mercy is a special, intimate care that accompanies those who turn toward Him, so that the verse calls the believer to trust that the very act of being blessed is the beginning of being led out of spiritual darkness.

translation: Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be "Peace," and He has prepared for them a generous reward.
interpretation: The verse portrays the believers' destiny as one of honor and tranquility: on the Day of meeting with God, the mutual greeting that surrounds them is peace, signifying that the fear, strife and anxiety of the world have been left behind. The word "salam" thus becomes both the speech of the blessed and a sign of their security in God's presence. The phrase "a generous reward" (ajran kareeman) then sets this peace within a larger frame of divine generosity, suggesting that what God gives far exceeds what human deeds could have merited, so that the very encounter with Him is itself the highest fulfillment of faith.

translation: O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good news, and a warner.
interpretation: The verse presents the Prophet's mission through three complementary roles. As a witness (shahid), he bears testimony over his community and over the truth of the message, and is a model whose conduct attests to what he conveys. As a bringer of good news (mubashshir), his primary call is an invitation of hope, promising mercy and reward to those who believe and act righteously. As a warner (nadhir), he alerts people to the consequences of rejecting the truth. Together these roles show that guidance in Islam balances hope and fear, and that the Prophet's role is both testimony and mercy, calling people to God with wisdom and sincerity.

translation: And [as] one who calls to Allah by His permission, and as a illuminating lamp.
interpretation: The verse describes the Prophet Muhammad as a caller to Allah whose call succeeds only by Allah's permission, which teaches that guidance belongs to God alone while the messenger's duty is to invite sincerely and patiently. The image of a lamp that gives light means that his message dispels the darkness of ignorance and misguidance, and that he himself serves as a clear example by which people can find their way. The phrase "by His permission" also guards the believer against pride, reminding him that the success of his efforts in da'wah rests with God.

translation: And give good news to the believers that for them is a great bounty from Allah.
interpretation: The verse directs the Prophet to convey glad tidings to those who have faith, assuring them that Allah has reserved for them a immense favor, a grace far exceeding what they could earn by their own deeds. It turns the believers' gaze from their own limited merits toward the boundless generosity of God, so that faith is met not merely with reward but with abundant bounty. The phrase 'fadlan kabiran' conveys that this favor is vast in scale and quality, inviting the believer to hope in Allah's mercy while remaining steadfast in belief.

translation: And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and disregard their harm, and rely upon Allah. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: The verse commands the believer to stand firm against the pressures of those who reject faith and those who conceal disbelief behind a face of belief. Obedience here means yielding to their wishes in matters of religion and conduct, which would compromise the community's principles. The instruction to "disregard their harm" does not mean passivity toward injustice, but rather refusing to let their hostility or slander divert the believer from the path of truth or cause fear that paralyzes action. The closing call to trust in Allah and the reminder that He is sufficient as Guardian (wakil) point to the source of security: when a person's reliance is placed fully on God, the schemes of opponents lose their power over his resolve. The hypocrites are singled out because their danger lies in their deception from within, which makes steadfastness and reliance on God even more necessary.

translation: O you who have believed, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them, then there is no waiting period for you to count concerning them. So provide for them and release them in a graceful release.
interpretation: The verse establishes that when a marriage is dissolved before consummation, the wife owes no waiting period ('iddah) to her former husband, which removes a burden from her and shows the law's concern for ease and clarity in divorce. It then obligates the husband to make a provision (mut'ah) for her, so that the separation is not left bare of kindness, and to release her 'graciously' (sarahan jamilan), meaning without harm, public disgrace, or withholding what is due. The passage teaches that even the ending of a marital bond must be carried out with justice and beautiful conduct, preserving the dignity of the woman and the moral responsibility of the believer.

translation: O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful for you your wives whose bridal gifts you have given, and those whom your right hand possesses from what Allah has granted you as spoils, and the daughters of your paternal uncles and the daughters of your paternal aunts, and the daughters of your maternal uncles and the daughters of your maternal aunts who emigrated with you, and a believing woman if she gives herself to the Prophet and the Prophet wishes to marry her, exclusively for you, apart from the believers. We have certainly known what We have enjoined upon them concerning their wives and those whom their right hands possess, so that there will be no difficulty upon you. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse identifies a special dispensation granted to the Prophet Muhammad in matters of marriage, which was not extended to the believers in general, and it does so to remove any sense of constraint upon him in his personal and public responsibilities. Allah first defines the lawful circle of marriage for him, emphasizing that the bridal gifts were honored and that his wives and captives of war came to him through legitimate means. The inclusion of his cousins who shared the hardship of migration signals that closeness of kinship and faith together formed the basis of this circle. The provision regarding a believing woman who offered herself to him shows that consent and sincerity were central, and that the arrangement was a unique privilege. The verse then reminds that the rules binding the believers were known to Allah, so the Prophet's exemption is not a license for disorder but a divinely specified allowance for his unique mission. Ending with forgiveness and mercy reassures that the divine ordinance is tempered with compassion.

translation: You may defer whom you will of them, and take to you whom you will; and whomever you seek of those you had set aside, there is no blame upon you. That is more suitable that their eyes be comforted, and that they not grieve, and that they all be pleased with what you give them. And Allah knows what is in your hearts, and Allah is ever Knowing and Forbearing.
interpretation: The verse grants the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ a special latitude in managing the affairs of his wives, letting him postpone or bring near whom he wished, so that the household's domestic arrangements were lifted from the rigid rotation expected of ordinary husbands. This was a mercy and a relief, both to him and to them: by knowing that the choice rests with God's messenger under divine permission, their hearts would be settled, their eyes comforted, and their contentment assured, since no one could feel slighted by a rule that treated them all equally in what truly mattered. The closing reminder that God knows what lies in hearts and is Forbearing points to the inner intention behind such decisions, calling the believers to sincerity and to patience with one another in matters of the heart that lie beyond human control.
