translation: It is not lawful for you [to take] women after this, nor to exchange them for other wives, even if their beauty pleases you, except what your right hand possesses. And Allah is ever, over all things, Watchful.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Ahzab 33:52) comes after the Prophet Muhammad was given permission regarding his wives and restricts him from taking additional wives or replacing those he already had with others, even if another's beauty attracted him, while exempting captives or bondwomen that his right hand possessed. Classical scholars such as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understood it as a special distinction for the Prophet, who had been granted a limited number of wives and was ordered to remain content with those he had, a restriction that did not extend to ordinary believers. The closing reminder that Allah is Watchful over all things signals that the Prophet's conduct and inner inclinations are under divine oversight, emphasizing that his obligations toward his household were to be guarded with integrity and God-consciousness.

translation: O you who have believed, do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless you are permitted for a meal, without waiting for its preparation. But when you are invited, then enter; and when you have eaten, disperse without seeking familiarity for conversation. Indeed, that would cause harm to the Prophet, and he is shy of you, but Allah is not shy of the truth. And when you ask them [his wives] for something, ask them from behind a screen. That is purer for your hearts and their hearts. And it is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah or to marry his wives after him, ever. Indeed, that would be an enormity in the sight of Allah.
interpretation: The verse establishes a code of conduct for the believers toward the household of the Prophet, grounded in respect for his privacy and dignity. Entering his home is conditioned on invitation, and guests are told not to linger after eating so as not to burden him, even though he himself is too modest to ask them to leave. The lesson extends beyond that setting: the Prophet's household is a sanctuary of trust, and the believers' manners there reflect the purity of their hearts. The prohibition on marrying his wives after him reflects their unique station as mothers of the believers, and the whole passage teaches that harming the Messenger, whether directly or through his family, is a grave matter before God.

translation: Whether you show forth something or conceal it, indeed Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse establishes that Allah's knowledge encompasses every outward act and every hidden intention alike, so no distinction between the open and the secret escapes Him. Its force lies in turning the believer's attention inward: since nothing is concealed from the One who knows, sincerity must govern not only what one displays to others but also what one keeps within the heart. Concealment therefore offers no shelter from accountability, and the verse invites constant awareness that one stands before a Lord whose knowledge is complete.

translation: There is no blame upon them (concerning) their fathers, their sons, their brothers, the sons of their brothers, the sons of their sisters, their women, or those whom their right hands possess. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is ever, over all things, Witness.
interpretation: The verse (Surah al-Ahzab 33:55) lifts the strictness of seclusion from the women of the Prophet's household and, by extension, the believing women, permitting them to appear without veil before those whose kinship or bond makes such contact natural and familiar, while the closing command to fear Allah reminds that the lawful latitude does not dissolve their accountability: since Allah witnesses everything, outward propriety must be joined with inward God-consciousness, so that the permission is exercised with modesty and integrity rather than as a loophole.

translation: Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. O you who have believed, send blessings upon him and greet him with the greeting of peace.
interpretation: The verse shows that honoring the Prophet Muhammad is a matter in which the believers are commanded to share with the heavens: while Allah and His angels bestow blessings (salawat) upon him, the faithful are called to do the same through prayers for him and sincere submission in greeting him with peace. Its meaning is that true faith is completed not merely by belief in the heart but by visible reverence, love, and devotion expressed toward the one through whom the message reached humanity. By joining their voices to the divine and angelic praise, believers acknowledge their debt to him and align themselves with the cosmic order of honoring the chosen messenger, so that salutation becomes both an act of worship and a pledge of loyalty to his way.

translation: Indeed, those who abuse Allah and His Messenger, Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter, and has prepared for them a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse identifies harming Allah and His Messenger as among the gravest transgressions, since it is an assault on the one who is the source of guidance and on the Messenger who conveys it. Its double curse, in this world and the next, shows that such hostility removes a person from Allah's mercy at every stage of existence, while the phrase 'humiliating punishment' points to the fact that the arrogance behind such harm is met with a corresponding disgrace. The verse thus calls the believer to guard their tongue and conduct against any form of injury to what is sacred, and to recognize that honoring the Messenger is inseparable from honoring Allah.

translation: And those who harm believing men and believing women without their having earned (it) have certainly borne a slander and a manifest sin.
interpretation: The verse establishes that injuring believers, whether men or women, through accusation, slander, or any other form of harm undeserved by them is a grave wrong that the wrongdoer carries as a burden upon himself. The phrase 'without their having earned it' makes clear that the sin lies entirely in attacking the innocent, since the believers have done nothing that justifies the injury. Calling the act 'bahtan' (a lie that dumbfounds the hearer with its falsehood) joins the sin of the tongue to the sin of deceit, and calling it 'ithman mubinan' (a manifest sin) shows that its wrongness is plain and not open to excuse. The verse thus extends protection to the honor and dignity of the community's members and warns against treating their reputations or bodies as fair targets.

translation: O Prophet, tell your wives and your daughters and the women of the believers to draw their outer garments close around them. That is more suitable so that they will be known and not be harmed. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse establishes a principle of distinguishing modest, honorable women from others through outer covering, so that they are recognized as respectable and thereby spared harassment. Its wisdom lies in protecting dignity and social order rather than in confining women, and the closing reminder of God's forgiveness and mercy signals that the command is given with compassion, leaving room for human weakness in observing it sincerely.

translation: If the hypocrites, and those in whose hearts is a disease, and the agitators among the people of Medina do not cease, We will surely incite you against them; then they will not remain your neighbors therein except for a little while.
interpretation: The verse warns that persistent hypocrisy, spiritual sickness in the hearts, and the spreading of rumors and sedition in the community will not go unanswered. Their continued malice is met with a divine decree that the Prophet will be empowered to confront them, after which they will be expelled or destroyed and will have only a brief stay among the believers. It teaches that a society's stability depends on confronting public corruption and that persistent deceit against the community brings its own consequence.

translation: Cursed are they; wherever they are found, they shall be seized and slain with relentless slaughter.
interpretation: The verse describes those who spread falsehood and sow unrest in the community (Q. 33:60-61, in the context of the hypocrites, those with disease in their hearts, and the agitators of Medina). Its force lies in the phrase "cursed" (mal'unin), which expresses their expulsion from God's mercy, and in the image of them being pursued wherever they are found, so that no refuge remains for those who persist in undermining the social order through rumor and sedition. The stern wording is not an endorsement of indiscriminate violence; classical commentators such as al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi tie it to a specific situation of open hostility and conspiracy, and the verse conveys that a community which tolerates organized subversion cannot be left defenseless. The moral lesson for later readers is the gravity of spreading lies that endanger public peace, and the warning that persistent, unrepentant malice invites divine and social consequences.

translation: This was the way of Allah with those who passed away before, and you will never find any change in the way of Allah.
interpretation: The verse establishes that Allah's sunnah, His established law and consistent pattern of dealing with nations, is fixed and unchanging. Just as He dealt with earlier communities who rejected their messengers, so the same principles of divine reward and consequence apply to every people. The believers are thereby reminded that God's promise of victory for the righteous and ruin for the wayward is not subject to alteration by circumstance, power, or human desire, and that its certainty should strengthen trust in the divine order rather than fostering despair or complacency.

translation: People ask you about the Hour. Say: its knowledge is only with God. And what would make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near.
interpretation: The verse teaches the Prophet, and through him every believer, to be honest about the limits of human knowledge: the precise timing of the Last Day is a matter reserved to God alone, and no one can claim to know it. The question "what would make you know?" is a rhetorical reminder of human limitation, yet the phrase "perhaps it is near" keeps the reality of the Hour alive in the heart, so that a person remains ready, mindful, and accountable at all times rather than either denying it or postponing preparation until a fixed date.

translation: Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blazing Fire.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Ahzab (33:64), declares two linked realities about those who persist in rejecting faith: first, that they are removed from Allah's mercy, which is the meaning of being cursed, since they have distanced themselves from the source of guidance; second, that the consequence awaiting them is a fire that is kindled and intensified, a 'sa'ir' that burns without cease. The verse is placed within a passage warning those who harm the Prophet and the believers, so its message extends beyond a general statement about disbelief to a warning against hostility toward the truth and its bearers. It also reminds the believer that divine justice is certain, and that the outcome of rejection is determined by the choices people make in this world.

translation: Abiding therein forever. They will find no protector or helper.
interpretation: The phrase "abiding therein forever" emphasizes the permanence of the punishment or reward described in the surrounding context, underscoring that it is not temporary. The closing words, "no protector or helper," reveal the complete abandonment of those who will face this state: having severed their bond with God, they will find no one, whether an intercessor, friend, or ally, who can shield them from what they face. The verse thus teaches that worldly alliances and supports vanish on the Day of Judgment, and that true refuge lies only in God, the ultimate Protector and Helper.

translation: On the Day when their faces are turned over in the Fire, they will say: "Oh, would that we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger!"
interpretation: The verse portrays the regret of those who, in the Hereafter, see the consequences of their disbelief and disobedience. The image of faces being turned about in the Fire conveys the total reversal of their state, from the honor they might have sought in this world to humiliation and torment. Their wish, "Would that we had obeyed Allah and the Messenger," reveals that they now recognize the truth they had rejected, and that true salvation lies in obedience to God and His Messenger. The verse thus warns the listener that the cry of regret comes too late, and urges that obedience be embraced in this life before the reckoning arrives.

translation: And they will say, "Our Lord, indeed we obeyed our leaders and our elders, so they led us astray from the way."
interpretation: The verse portrays the people of the Fire, at the moment of their regret, shifting blame onto the leaders and the powerful figures they once followed blindly. Their plea reveals a recurring human tendency: surrendering personal judgment to status, lineage, or authority rather than weighing truth for oneself, and then disowning the consequences of that surrender. Implicit in their words is the acknowledgment that they had the capacity to choose the path of guidance, yet relinquished it. The verse thus warns that no earthly hierarchy can absolve a person before God, since each soul is accountable for the direction it chose to follow.

translation: Our Lord, give them double the punishment and curse them with a great curse.
interpretation: The verse, spoken by the believers in the Hereafter or by those who suffer at the hands of misguiding leaders, reflects the principle that those who lead others astray bear a double burden: their own sin and the sin of those they misled. The plea for a 'double punishment' and a 'great curse' expresses a longing for justice against the chief architects of falsehood, the ones who, having deviated themselves, caused the downfall of their followers. It conveys that divine justice is exact, and that responsibility for misguidance weighs more heavily than the misguidance alone, a warning to every person of influence to consider the weight of the paths they open for others.

translation: O you who have believed, do not be like those who harmed Moses; then Allah cleared him of what they said, and he was distinguished and honored in the sight of Allah.
interpretation: The verse warns believers against emulating those who wronged Moses, by slandering or accusing him falsely, and it shows that the true measure of a person's worth is vindication by God rather than the accusations of others. Moses, who bore their harm patiently, was cleared by Allah and granted a high station in His presence, teaching that the righteous who endure false accusation with patience will ultimately be exonerated and honored, while the believers are commanded to guard their tongues and conduct against causing hurt to any righteous person.

translation: O you who have believed, fear Allah and speak words that are upright and on target.
interpretation: The verse joins taqwa, God-consciousness that guards a person in every act, with the discipline of speech. Sound faith is shown not only in ritual but in the honesty, precision, and rightness of what one says. Qawl sadid is speech that is straight, sincere, and free of deceit or distortion, and the believer who keeps his tongue to this standard is promised in the following verse that Allah will set his deeds right and forgive his sins. The verse thus treats truthful speech as a path to moral and spiritual wholeness, since the words we utter reveal and shape the state of the heart.

translation: He will set right your deeds for you and forgive you your sins. And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger has certainly achieved a great attainment.
interpretation: The verse links two things: Allah's reform of a person's actions and His forgiveness of their sins, both granted as the fruit of sincere obedience. Correcting one's deeds is presented as the inward and outward renewal that follows from turning to God, while forgiveness clears the record of past failings. The closing statement frames obedience to Allah and His Messenger not merely as a duty but as the true path to success, a 'great triumph' whose greatness lies in its being the lasting reward of a righteous life rather than the fleeting gains of this world. The verse thus binds the believer's present conduct to an eternal outcome, showing that obedience to the Prophet is inseparable from obedience to God himself.

translation: Indeed, We offered the trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they refused to bear it and were apprehensive of it; and man bore it. Indeed, he has always been unjust and ignorant.
interpretation: The verse presents the 'amanah (trust) as a moral and spiritual responsibility, the freely accepted burden of conscious obedience, choice, and accountability before God. The heavens, earth, and mountains, vast as they are, lacked the capacity for such free and discerning responsibility, so they declined it out of reverence rather than defiance. Man accepted it, yet the verse immediately names his defining flaws: zulm and jahl, injustice toward oneself and others and ignorance of the weight of what he has taken on. The interpretation thus reads human greatness and human failing together: the very capacity that elevates man to bear a divine trust is the same capacity that makes him prone to wrong when he neglects it.

translation: So that Allah may punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women and the polytheist men and polytheist women, and that Allah may accept the repentance of the believing men and believing women. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Ahzab 33:73, closing the passage on the trust offered to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, and on humanity's bearing of it) presents the outcome of that bearing as a divine sorting. Those who betrayed the trust through hypocrisy and polytheism are made to bear the consequence of their chosen inner duplicity and false worship, while those who kept faith with it, the believing men and women, are met with God's acceptance of their turning back to Him. The mention of hypocrisy alongside polytheism shows that outward profession without sincere inner allegiance is itself a form of betrayal. The closing divine names, Forgiving and Merciful, indicate that even this judgment is framed within God's mercy: the door of repentance remains open, and the final word is one of compassion toward those who return.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. All praise is due to Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Him belongs all praise in the Hereafter. And He is the Wise, the All-Aware.
interpretation: The verse opens by establishing praise as belonging to God alone, grounded in His absolute ownership of everything in the heavens and the earth, which makes Him the only rightful object of gratitude and glorification. By extending this praise into the Hereafter, it teaches that the praiseworthiness of God is not confined to the transient world, where His favors are often obscured or misattributed, but is revealed fully when all dominion is seen to be His. The closing attributes of wisdom and all-encompassing knowledge link this universal sovereignty to purposeful action and perfect awareness, inviting the believer to recognize that the trials and blessings of this life, as well as the final reckoning, are governed by a wisdom that surpasses human understanding, and thus to respond with sincere praise in both this world and the next.

translation: He knows what enters into the earth and what emerges from it, and what descends from the sky and what ascends into it. And He is the Most Merciful, the Oft-Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse points to the all-encompassing knowledge of God that reaches every hidden movement in creation, from what sinks into the soil and what springs forth from it, to the descent of revelation and provision from above and the ascent of deeds and angels back toward Him. Such comprehensive awareness is paired with mercy and forgiveness, suggesting that the One who sees every secret and every return is also the One who waits patiently for the sinner to turn back. The verse thus invites the believer to live with constant awareness that nothing escapes God, and to find in that awareness not fear alone but hope in His boundless compassion.

translation: And those who disbelieve say, "The Hour will not come to us." Say, "Yes, by my Lord, it will surely come to you. [He is] the Knower of the unseen; not an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth escapes Him, and no smaller than that or greater, but it is in a clear register."
interpretation: The verse presents the denial of the Resurrection by the disbelievers as a matter that the Prophet is commanded to answer with a solemn oath by his Lord, affirming with certainty that the Hour will arrive. The grounds for this certainty are God's complete knowledge of the unseen, which encompasses even the smallest particle, so that every deed and every created thing is recorded and known with perfect precision in a clear Book. The truth of the Hour is thus tied to the all-encompassing knowledge of the One who will bring it about and hold all accounts.

translation: So that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds. Those will have forgiveness and an honorable provision.
interpretation: The verse presents the purpose behind God's creation and judgment as justice and grace: those who combined inner faith with righteous action are not left unrewarded. Their reward is twofold, forgiveness that cleanses their past shortcomings and a generous provision that is noble in its quality and dignity. The pairing of belief with deeds shows that true faith is inseparable from action, and that divine recompense is measured by God's generosity rather than merely by human merit.

translation: And those who strive against Our verses, seeking to frustrate them, for them is a punishment of painful, humiliating torment.
interpretation: The verse identifies those who work with determined effort against God's signs, aiming to discredit, obstruct, or defeat them, as people who believe they can escape accountability. Their striving is described as 'mu'ajjizin,' meaning they seek to render the divine message powerless, yet they are the ones who will be overcome. The 'rijz' (a dreadful, abasing chastisement) that awaits them is fitting, since their arrogance in opposing revelation is met with a humbling punishment that matches the contempt they showed toward God's words. The passage thus conveys that resistance to the clear signs of God, whether through ridicule, suppression, or distortion, is itself a grave moral failing with consequences that cannot be evaded.

translation: And those who have been given knowledge see that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth, and it guides to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse points to a kind of knowledge that recognizes the Qur'an's truth by its own weight, not merely by inheritance or assumption. Those who have true knowledge, meaning people of sound understanding among earlier revealed communities and believers alike, are presented as witnesses to the revelation's authenticity, since it confirms what they know of God's guidance. The phrase "the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy" links the Qur'an's guidance directly to God's attributes: its path leads toward the One whose power is absolute and whose praiseworthiness is complete, so that following the revelation is itself a movement toward God rather than toward any lesser authority. The verse thus ties knowledge, recognition of truth, and right guidance into a single chain, showing that genuine learning should lead the heart to God.

translation: And those who disbelieved said, "Shall we direct you to a man who will tell you, when you have been completely torn apart, that you will indeed be in a new creation?"
interpretation: The verse captures the mockery of the disbelievers toward the Resurrection. Their statement is framed as a sarcastic offer to point out a man who claims that, after the body has been scattered and decomposed into utter dispersal, a person will be recreated and restored to life. By presenting the prophetic message as an absurd claim about a 'man' who 'tells' such things, they belittle its source and deny the possibility of being gathered again after death. The verse thus highlights a recurring theme in the Qur'an: the denial of bodily resurrection was rooted less in intellectual inquiry than in a dismissive rejection of the idea that scattered remains could ever be reassembled and brought into a new existence.

translation: Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there in him madness? Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in the punishment and far error.
interpretation: The verse records the disbelievers' accusation against the Messenger: either he fabricates lies about God, or he is afflicted with madness. The Qur'an then rejects both charges and redirects the matter to its true cause, which is not a defect of intellect or a deliberate falsehood but the refusal to believe in the Hereafter. Because they deny the accountability of the Final Day, their judgment of the truth is distorted, and so they fall into a torment now and into a distant straying from the right path. The verse thus shows that disbelief in the afterlife is the root of the errors that lead people to slander the truth and its bearer.

translation: Have they not looked at what is before them and behind them of the heaven and the earth? If We willed, We could cause the earth to swallow them, or drop upon them fragments from the sky. Indeed in that is a sign for every servant who turns back in repentance.
interpretation: The verse directs the heedless to reflect on the visible cosmos surrounding them on every side, the heavens above and the earth below, as evidence of God's dominion and power. Since the same Lord who holds up the sky and spreads the earth can at any moment make it a cause of their destruction, their security is revealed as dependent entirely on His will and not on their own strength. The sign, however, is clear only to the one who is 'munib', who turns back to God with sincere humility, for such a heart perceives in creation a call to submission and repentance.

translation: And We certainly gave David bounty from Us. O mountains, echo back the praise with him, and the birds as well. And We made iron soft for him.
interpretation: The verse presents David's prophethood as a divine favor, and shows that this favor extended to the natural world: the mountains and birds were made to join him in glorifying God, so that creation itself becomes a chorus of worship. The softening of iron for him points to the power God grants to those who serve Him faithfully, transforming a hard and stubborn material into something he could shape for the benefit of people. Together these signs suggest that true strength and skill come from God's grace, and that gratitude and devotion are the proper response to such gifts.

translation: That make full coats of mail and measure well in the links (of the armor), and work righteousness. Indeed I am Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse, addressed to David's family in the context of the revelation given to David, shows that skilled and productive labor is itself a form of devotion when joined with righteous conduct. God granted David the craft of forging perfect, well-fitted armor, and the command to measure the rings of the mail precisely signals that excellence in one's trade is part of obeying God. The phrase 'work righteousness' places ordinary livelihood under the same moral sight of God, and the closing reminder that God is All-Seeing of what they do ties every craft and deed to accountability before Him, so that work done with integrity becomes worship.

translation: And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind, its morning course being a month's journey and its evening course a month's journey, and We caused a fountain of molten copper to flow for him, and among the jinn were those who worked before him by the permission of his Lord. And whoever deviated among them from Our command, We would make him taste the punishment of the blaze.
interpretation: The verse presents Solomon's dominion as a sign of divine favor granted by God alone: the wind serving him across vast distances in a single day, the flowing source of copper, and the jinn laboring under his command all occur only by God's permission. The mention of the punishment of the blaze for those who turn away from God's command establishes that even this extraordinary subjection operates within the bounds of divine law, so that obedience to God's order is the governing principle over all creation, visible and unseen.

translation: They made for him whatever he willed: sanctuaries (of worship), statues, basins like reservoirs, and fixed great cooking-pots. "Work, O family of David, in gratitude." But few of My servants are truly grateful.
interpretation: The verse presents the jinn serving Solomon as an image of divine favor placed under a righteous ruler's command, yet it turns quickly to the call to gratitude addressed to David's family, the very act of thankful labor being the proper response to blessing. The closing remark that few of God's servants are grateful shifts the lesson from a king's wealth to the general human tendency to receive favors without acknowledging their Giver, so that the magnificence of the works becomes a measure not of power but of the thankfulness that should accompany it.

translation: So when We decreed death upon him, nothing indicated his death to them except a creature of the earth eating away at his staff. And when he fell down, the jinn realized that if they had known the unseen, they would not have remained in humiliating punishment.
interpretation: This verse, concerning Prophet Solomon, shows that the jinn who labored for him were deceived about the unseen: his death went unnoticed while he leaned on his staff, and only the termite gnawing at it revealed it. The fall of his body exposed the jinn's false claim to knowledge of the unseen, and it shows that their continued toil under compulsion was not the product of any real knowledge of what lay hidden. The verse thus teaches that knowledge of the unseen belongs to God alone, and that human and jinn power is bounded by what God chooses to reveal.

translation: There was certainly a sign for Sheba in their dwelling place: two gardens, one on the right and one on the left. "Eat from the provision of your Lord and be grateful to Him. A good land and a forgiving Lord."
interpretation: The verse presents the prosperity of the people of Sheba as a sign meant to be read, not merely admired: their abundance was a trust that obligated gratitude, and the phrase "a good land and a forgiving Lord" joins material blessing to divine mercy, teaching that sustenance is sustained by thankfulness and that forgiveness is the mercy that remains when gratitude is neglected. The sequence of the verse, which moves from sign to command to praise, implies that the people's later downfall, described in the verses that follow, arose from turning away from this gratitude.

translation: So they turned away, and We sent upon them the flood of the dam, and We replaced their two gardens with two gardens bearing bitter fruit, tamarisk, and a little lote-tree.
interpretation: The verse portrays the consequence of ingratitude and disregard for divine blessings: when the people of Sheba turned away from the signs and bounty granted to them, their prosperity was stripped away by a sudden catastrophe, and their lush, fruitful gardens were replaced by meager growth. The reversal teaches that abundance is a trust that can be withdrawn, and that material wealth without gratitude and obedience becomes a source of loss rather than security.

translation: That is how We repaid them for their disbelief. And do We repay anyone except the ungrateful?
interpretation: The verse presents recompense as a direct consequence of one's own choices: the punishment is tied to the disbelief (kufr) that the people chose, so that divine justice appears not as arbitrary but as the natural outcome of rejecting the signs of God. The rhetorical question affirms that such requital is reserved for those who are ungrateful, meaning those who conceal and reject the blessings and truth they were given. The word kufr carries the dual sense of disbelief and ingratitude, suggesting that the root of their wrongdoing was a refusal to acknowledge what God had bestowed upon them, and therefore the consequence they face is a fitting mirror of that refusal.

translation: And We placed between them and the towns which We had blessed other towns visible (in plain view), and We measured out between them the journey: "Travel through them by night and by day, secure."
interpretation: The verse points to the ease and security of travel that God granted to the people of Sheba (Saba') in their prosperity: the route between their settlements and the blessed lands of Syria and Palestine was dotted with visible, closely spaced towns so that a traveler's stages were measured out and never far apart, allowing journeys to be made at any hour without fear. Read in its context, this is a reminder of divine favor that was meant to prompt gratitude, and the people's later ingratitude and their request for longer, more difficult journeys shows how easily blessings of security and provision are taken for granted when they are not acknowledged.

translation: But they said, "Our Lord, make the distances of our journeys farther apart," and they wronged themselves; so We made them into tales, and scattered them completely. Indeed, in that are signs for every patient, grateful person.
interpretation: The verse portrays the people of Sheba (Saba') who, having been granted abundant blessings and a continuous chain of towns along a safe, close route, grew ungrateful and asked for longer, more difficult journeys, thereby wronging their own souls. Their request reflects a restless disdain for ease and a preference for the illusion of greater independence over the gifts they already possessed. God's response was to strip them of their prosperity and dispersal them, so that they became mere stories told among others, a warning that heedless ingratitude turns blessing into ruin. The closing phrase identifies the true lesson: only the one who endures trials with patience and recognizes God's favors with gratitude can read such events as signs, while the complacent and ungrateful remain blind to them.

translation: And certainly Iblis confirmed his assumption about them, so they followed him, except for a group of the believers.
interpretation: The verse shows that Iblis's expectation of human weakness proved accurate: most people, once they had the means to be led astray by desire and whim, surrendered to his suggestion rather than to their own reason and conscience. The exception, a faithful minority, signals that the path of resisting temptation remains open to everyone, and that true faith is measured by steadfastness against the whispers of misguidance. Iblis's boast in the Qur'an that he would mislead most of humankind thus becomes a warning that the decisive factor is not the enemy's power but the believer's choice to follow God rather than him.

translation: And he had no authority over them, except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from one who is in doubt about it. And your Lord is Guardian over all things.
interpretation: The verse clarifies that Satan's power over people is not coercive but limited to whispering and enticement. Its purpose is a divine test: God permits this influence so that what is hidden in human hearts becomes manifest, separating the one who truly believes in the Hereafter from the one whose heart wavers in doubt. The knowledge spoken of as 'that We may know' refers to making the reality visible and distinguishing the sincere from the hesitant, since God's knowledge encompasses all things beforehand. The closing reminder that the Lord is watchful over everything assures the believer that no action, intention, or hidden state escapes divine oversight, and that every soul is preserved and accounted for.

translation: Say, "Call upon those you claimed besides Allah. They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth, nor do they have in them any share, and He has among them no helper."
interpretation: The verse exposes the emptiness of the idols and intermediaries that people set up beside Allah. Having no ownership, even of the smallest weight, and no partnership in creation, nor any assistance to offer Him, they are shown to be powerless objects of supplication. Its lesson is that true dependence and prayer belong only to the One who alone owns and governs the heavens and the earth, so worship directed at anything else rests on a false claim that cannot be sustained by reason or by the reality of creation.

translation: And intercession with Him does not benefit except for one whom He has permitted. Until, when fear is removed from their hearts, they say, "What has your Lord said?" They say, "The truth." And He is the Most High, the Most Great.
interpretation: The verse teaches that no one can intercede before Allah on their own authority; intercession is wholly dependent on His prior permission and His will, so that even the most honored of intercessors cannot speak until He grants leave. It also portrays the awe that overtakes the celestial beings and the hearts of all creatures when the divine command is heard: their fright is only lifted after a pause, and when they ask one another what the Lord has decreed, the answer is simply "the truth," affirming that His word is justice and reality. The closing names, Al-'Aliyy and Al-Kabir, remind the listener that the one who decides such matters is exalted above all and greater than all, so that true dominion over the outcome of the Hereafter belongs to Him alone.

translation: Say, "Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?" Say, "Allah. And indeed, either we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error."
interpretation: The verse turns the debate with the disbelievers into a test of reason rather than a contest of assertions. Having first been asked who provides for them from heaven and earth, and having been forced to accept that the answer is God alone, the Prophet is then told to present the matter as an open question of right and wrong: the phrasing "either we or you" deliberately leaves the opponents to draw the conclusion themselves. The mention of "clear error" is not a casual insult but a call to self-examination, since those who acknowledge God as the true Provider have already conceded the premise on which their own worship of others collapses. The verse thus teaches that persuasion should proceed from shared premises, and that a believer may hold his position with confidence while still leaving room for the listener to reflect honestly.

translation: Say: You will not be asked about what we committed of sin, nor will we be asked about what you do.
interpretation: The verse establishes a principle of individual moral accountability, each party answerable only for its own deeds, and it is delivered as a pointed rebuttal to those who sought to hold the believers responsible for the sins of others or to dispute the path of the Prophet. By declaring that the guilt of one side will not be imputed to the other, it dissolves the claim of collective blame and leaves each soul to bear its own burden before God. It also carries a tone of dignified detachment: the Prophet is told to leave the matter in God's hands, since the final reckoning belongs to Him alone and each person will answer for what he himself has done.

translation: Say: Our Lord will bring us together, then He will judge between us with truth. And He is the Judge, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse places the believer's dispute with those who deny or oppose him within the certainty of a final gathering before God. The word "yajmaʿu" (will gather) points to the resurrection as the moment when scattered claims and divisions are brought together before one Lord, and "yaftaḥu" (will open/decide) suggests that the matter will be resolved and laid open, as a closed door is opened. The judgment is made "bil-haqq," with truth, so no injustice or distortion will remain. The closing names, al-Fattāḥ (the Opener, the Judge) and al-ʿAlīm (the All-Knowing), tie the verdict to perfect knowledge: nothing hidden in hearts or deeds escapes Him. The Prophet is thus instructed to leave the matter to God, finding in this promise both consolation for the wronged and a warning to the arrogant.

translation: Say, "Show me those whom you have attached to Him as partners. No! Rather, He is Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Wise."
interpretation: The verse confronts the idolaters with a direct challenge: point out the so-called partners you have joined with God, and let them be shown. The sharp negation "Kallā" (No!) dismisses the claim outright, and the verse then affirms that the true reality is Allah alone, whose absolute power ('Azīz) and perfect wisdom (Ḥakīm) make any association with Him baseless. The argument rests on the emptiness of the alleged partners, who possess no creative power, no benefit, and no share in the divine attributes, in contrast with the one God who alone holds might and governs all things with wisdom.

translation: And We have not sent you except as a comprehensive messenger to all of mankind, bearing good tidings and warning, but most of the people do not know.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the mission of the Prophet Muhammad is universal rather than confined to a single people, tribe, or region: the word kaffah conveys that his message encompasses all of humanity across every time and place. His role is defined by two complementary functions, giving glad tidings to those who believe and do good, and warning those who turn away from truth, so that his message offers both hope and accountability. The closing clause, 'but most of the people do not know,' points to the gap between the clarity of the message and the widespread heedlessness of humankind, implying that the obstacle to guidance is not a lack of evidence but a lack of knowledge and reflection that the believer is called to remedy by conveying the message.

translation: And they say, "When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?"
interpretation: The question is posed by those who deny the Resurrection and the Last Day, mocking the Prophet and the believers by demanding a date for the threatened punishment and reckoning. Its wording, "if you are truthful," reveals a challenge meant to show that the promise is doubtful in their eyes. The verse is best understood as a reminder that the timing of the promise belongs to God alone, so that the believer's trust rests not on knowing when it will come but on certainty that it will come, and the denier's haste is a sign of heedlessness rather than of a genuine search for truth.

translation: Say: For you is an appointed day, from which you cannot delay by an hour, nor advance.
interpretation: The verse addresses those who deny the Hereafter with a stark reminder that the Day of Judgment has a fixed, divinely appointed time that no one can postpone or hasten. Its force lies in the precision of the phrase 'not an hour': human beings, who imagine themselves in control of their affairs and their time, are shown to be utterly powerless before the decree of God. The command to 'say' places the warning on the Prophet's tongue as a clear, unavoidable announcement, inviting the listener to reflect on the limits of human agency and to prepare for an encounter that is certain and cannot be evaded.

translation: And those who disbelieve say, "We will never believe in this Qur'an, nor in that which came before it." If you could but see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord, [and] they refer the statement back and forth among themselves. Those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant, "Were it not for you, we would have been believers."
interpretation: The verse portrays the scene of mutual blame on the Day of Judgment, where the wrongdoers, once standing before their Lord, cannot escape the consequences of their choices. Their stubborn rejection of revelation, both the Qur'an and the earlier scriptures confirming it, is shown to be rooted in a social dynamic: the weak, who followed the powerful, now accuse the arrogant leaders of misleading them, while the leaders are themselves bound by the same accountability. The verse thus teaches that false pride and blind following both lead to ruin, and that no one can shift full responsibility onto another when faced with the truth before God.

translation: Those who were arrogant will say to those who were oppressed: "Did we turn you away from guidance after it had come to you? Rather, you yourselves were criminals."
interpretation: The verse depicts the Day of Judgment dialogue in which the arrogant leaders deny responsibility for misguiding their followers. Their question feigns innocence, asking whether they were the cause of the weakened ones rejecting guidance after it reached them, and then they turn the blame back on the followers themselves, calling them criminals. The passage exposes a recurring human evasion: those who held power and led others astray shift accountability onto the very people they deceived, while the truth is that each soul bears responsibility for its own choices in rejecting clear guidance.

translation: And those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant: "Rather, it was your scheming by night and day, when you were ordering us to disbelieve in Allah and to set up rivals to Him." And they will conceal their regret when they see the punishment, and We will put shackles around the necks of those who disbelieved. Will they be recompensed except for what they used to do?
interpretation: The verse exposes the moral accountability that remains even when followers blame their leaders. The weak, who were led astray, direct the blame at the arrogant who constantly devised deception and pressed them toward shirk, yet the Qur'an shows that this shifting of blame cannot erase the responsibility of each soul. Their hidden remorse at the sight of punishment reveals that they grasp the truth only when it is too late, and the shackles on the necks signify how their own choices have bound them. The closing question affirms the principle of divine justice: every person is repaid only according to his own deeds, so no one can escape accountability by pointing to others.

translation: And We did not send a warner into any town except that its affluent people said, "Indeed, we disbelieve in what you have been sent with."
interpretation: The verse shows a recurring pattern in the history of prophethood: the wealthy and comfortable elite of every community are typically the first to reject messengers. Their rejection is rooted less in the evidence itself than in attachment to their privileges, status, and worldly ease, which they fear will be threatened by a message calling for humility, justice, and accountability. Thus the verse consoles the Prophet by revealing that the opposition he faced was part of a long-established human tendency, and it warns that wealth and luxury often blind people to the truth.

translation: And they said, "We have more wealth and children, and we will not be punished."
interpretation: This verse (Surah Saba, 34:35) exposes a common error of the arrogant who judge their standing before God by worldly abundance. Those who reject the messengers measure divine favor by their possessions and progeny, concluding that what they enjoy in this life is a sign of acceptance and a shield against consequence. The verse teaches that material wealth and large families are trials rather than proofs of righteousness, and that the assumption of immunity from accountability is itself a form of heedlessness. Prosperity can deceive a person into complacency, making them forget that every blessing is a loan to be answered for, and that the Hereafter is not determined by the measures of this world.

translation: Say, "Indeed, my Lord extends provision abundantly to whom He wills and restricts it (to whom He wills), but most of the people do not know."
interpretation: The verse teaches that the distribution of sustenance is entirely in the hands of God, who grants expansion or constriction according to His wisdom and will, not according to merit alone or the apparent circumstances of people. By commanding the Prophet to declare this, it corrects the human tendency to read wealth as a sign of divine favor and poverty as a sign of rejection. The closing remark, that most people do not know, points to the widespread ignorance of this reality: people often mistake worldly abundance for honor and scarcity for disgrace, and so they fail to grasp that provision is a trust and a test. The believer is thereby directed toward trust in God, contentment with what is allotted, and a realization that the true measure of a person lies in faith and righteous conduct rather than in material holdings.

translation: And it is not your wealth nor your children that bring you near to Us in closeness, except those who believe and do righteous deeds; for those, there is a double reward for what they have done, and they will be secure in the upper chambers.
interpretation: The verse teaches that worldly possessions and offspring, though often regarded as markers of status and divine favor, do not by themselves draw a person closer to God. What brings nearness to God is genuine faith joined with righteous action, which is the true measure of worth. The phrase 'double reward' (jaza' al-di'f) indicates that God multiplies the recompense of the faithful far beyond what their deeds alone would seem to merit, reflecting His generosity. The 'upper chambers' (al-ghurfat) symbolize the elevated station of safety and peace granted to the believers, a reminder that spiritual rank is determined by inner conviction and conduct rather than by material abundance or family lineage.

translation: And those who strive against Our verses, seeking to frustrate them, those will be brought forth into the punishment.
interpretation: The verse portrays those who work energetically to undermine the signs of God, trying to outmaneuver and defeat them, as people who imagine they can escape the reckoning. Their striving is described as a contest they believe they win, yet the phrase 'brought forth into the punishment' reveals the reversal: their very efforts summon them before the consequence they sought to evade. It conveys that opposition to divine revelation is not a clever escape but a self-chosen path ending in a certain, inescapable accountability on the Day when all are presented before their Lord.

translation: Say, "Indeed, my Lord extends provision for whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him. And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it; and He is the best of providers."
interpretation: The verse establishes that the expansion and restriction of sustenance are both under God's sole will and wisdom, so that wealth is not a sign of a person's worth nor poverty a sign of divine rejection. It turns the believer's attention from the amount of what one holds to the reality that every act of giving is met by God's replacement, whether in this world or in the reward to come. Thus it calls the human being to generosity without fear of loss, and to trust in God as the one true and most generous source of provision, rather than in one's own calculations or in the uncertain accumulation of possessions.

translation: And [mention] the Day when He will gather them all, then say to the angels, "Did these people used to worship you?"
interpretation: The verse portrays a scene of the Day of Gathering in which Allah assembles all of creation, including those who took others as objects of worship, and then poses a direct question to the angels about whether they were the ones being worshipped. The question is less a request for information, since Allah knows the answer, than a means of exposing the falsehood of such worship before all witnesses. It implies that the angels, who are obedient servants devoid of any claim to divinity, will disown this worship, and that the worshippers will be confronted with the futility of venerating beings who never called them to it. The verse thus conveys that the rejection of false deities is a matter of accountability, and that on that Day the true nature of every object of worship will be laid bare.

translation: They will say, "Exalted are You; You are our Protector, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them were believers in them."
interpretation: The verse depicts a scene of the Day of Judgment in which those who were worshipped are asked about their worshippers, and they disclaim any part in that worship by affirming God's absolute transcendence and sole guardianship over them. Their statement turns the accusation back onto the worshippers, showing that the true object of their devotion was not God's angels or prophets but the jinn, whom they obeyed and trusted. The closing phrase, "most of them were believers in them," reveals the root of their error: a deep-seated faith in unseen beings that drew them away from the one God. The passage thus teaches that misplaced reliance on invisible powers, rather than sincere devotion to God alone, is a form of worship that will be exposed and rejected on that Day.

translation: So today none of you will have power to benefit or harm one another, and We will say to those who did wrong: "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."
interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Judgment as a moment when every human bond of protection, patronage, and mutual reliance collapses, so that the only real authority is God's, and the mutual dependence people relied on in worldly life (of kin, friends, leaders, and idols) is revealed as empty. The command to "taste" the Fire conveys the immediacy and the bitter, personal experience of a punishment that was once dismissed as falsehood, suggesting that denial in this life is answered with a reality no one can contest or avert in the next.

translation: And when Our verses are recited to them as clear proofs, they say, "This is not but a man who wants to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship." And they say, "This is not but a fabricated lie." And those who disbelieved said about the truth when it came to them, "This is not but obvious magic."
interpretation: The verse depicts the reaction of the disbelievers of Makkah to the clear revelation recited to them: rather than engaging with its evidence, they dismiss the Messenger as a man with an agenda to pull them away from the inherited worship of their forefathers, then call the message a fabrication, and finally label the truth itself as manifest sorcery. The progression shows how resistance to guidance often moves from personal suspicion to outright denial and then to slander against the truth, not because the proof is lacking, but because it threatens established custom and worldly attachments.

translation: We did not give them any books which they could study, nor did We send to them any warner before you.
interpretation: The verse addresses the Meccan disbelievers who denied the Prophet Muhammad and questioned his message. It establishes that their rejection did not rest on any prior divine scripture they were studying, nor on any earlier warner sent to their people, so their claim to be guided by revelation or precedent is baseless. Their position is thus one of unfounded assumption, and the Prophet is consoled that he is being sent to a people who lacked a previous scriptural basis for their stance, making the clarity of the new revelation the decisive proof against them.

translation: And those before them denied, and they had not attained one-tenth of what We had given them, yet they denied My messengers. So how was My rejection (of them)?
interpretation: The verse points to the earlier nations who rejected their prophets despite having been granted far greater worldly power, wealth, and capacity than the Makkan audience possesses. Their superior strength did not protect them, and the question 'how was My disapproval?' is a rhetorical warning that their denial brought a devastating and deserved punishment. The message to the listeners is that material advantage offers no immunity from divine accountability, and that persisting in rejecting the messengers leads to the same fate.

translation: Say: "I only advise you of one thing: that you stand up for Allah in pairs and individually, and then reflect. There is no madness in your companion; he is only a warner to you before a severe punishment."
interpretation: The verse calls the disbelievers to a sincere, disciplined form of inquiry, free from the pressures of crowds and prejudice: whether one meets in pairs or stands alone, the aim is to stand before God in earnest seriousness and then to think deeply. Such reflection is the path to recognizing that the Prophet, far from being possessed, is a clear warner whose message is rooted in concern for his people in the face of a grave reckoning. The command to reflect, rather than to follow habit or reject the messenger out of hand, places the responsibility for judgment on the listener's own reasoned consideration.

translation: Say, "Whatever reward I have asked of you is yours. My reward is only from Allah, and He is Witness over all things."
interpretation: The verse shows the sincerity of the Prophet's mission: he disclaims any worldly motive or payment for his call, so that his message cannot be suspected of self-interest. By declaring that any recompense he sought benefits the people themselves, he places his entire reward with Allah alone. The closing phrase, "He is Witness over all things," reminds the listeners that Allah sees the intentions of both the messenger and those who hear him, so that trust in the message rests on God's knowledge rather than on the messenger's wealth or status.

translation: Say: Indeed, my Lord casts the truth upon falsehood, and He is the Knower of the unseen.
interpretation: The verse presents the Prophet with a decisive reply to those who deny his message: the truth is not merely asserted but is actively sent forth by God, like a projectile hurled against falsehood so that it breaks and vanishes. The image of 'casting' (yaqdhifu) conveys force and certainty, assuring the believer that divine truth will ultimately prevail over error. The closing divine attribute, 'Knower of the unseen' ('allam al-ghuyub), anchors this assurance in God's perfect knowledge: He knows what is hidden in hearts and what lies beyond human perception, so His judgment between truth and falsehood is exact and final, and no pretense can escape it.

translation: Say: The truth has come, and falsehood can neither originate anything nor restore it.
interpretation: The verse is a decisive declaration that divine truth, the revelation brought by the Prophet, has now arrived and established itself, leaving falsehood powerless. Falsehood has no creative power: it cannot initiate a new reality (yubdi') nor bring back what has perished (yu'id). This points to the futility of idols and false beliefs, which can create nothing and resurrect nothing, in contrast to God, the true Originator who begins creation and brings it back. The verse thus calls the listener to recognize the emptiness of what is worshipped besides God and to embrace the truth that alone has lasting substance and effect.

translation: Say, "If I should go astray, I only go astray to my own detriment; but if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me. Indeed, He is All-Hearing, Ever-Near."
interpretation: The verse places the Prophet in a position of complete personal accountability and humble dependence. His going astray would fall on himself alone, while any guidance he possesses is not his own achievement but a gift from God through revelation, so his authority is derived entirely from what is revealed to him rather than from himself. The closing names, All-Hearing and Ever-Near, assure the believer that the One who hears every word and is close to every servant is the true source of guidance, and that prophethood and human responsibility both rest on that divine nearness and attentiveness.

translation: And if you could see when they are seized with terror, but there will be no escape, and they will be seized from a nearby place.
interpretation: The verse presents a scene of the disbelievers at the moment of their seizure, where the fear that overtakes them is so overwhelming that it is as if they were already caught. The phrase "no escape" (fawt) conveys that flight is impossible: whatever refuge they hoped for in this world, or whatever hiding place they imagined, will fail them. Their being seized "from a nearby place" suggests that the punishment is not distant or hidden from them; it reaches them from the very ground they stand on, meaning that they cannot claim ignorance of its approach or assume it is far off. The verse thus turns the reader's attention to the inescapability of divine reckoning and invites reflection on the reality of the moment before it arrives, when the heedless are left with nothing but dread.

translation: And they will say, "We have believed in it." But how can they reach [acceptance of faith] from a place far away?
interpretation: The verse depicts the futility of belief sought too late. When the disbelievers are removed from the world of choice and see the unseen reality, they claim faith, but that faith cannot be grasped from the distance they now stand at. Just as one cannot reach something that is far beyond his grasp, their sudden profession of faith, made after the opportunity for free choice has passed, is not accepted. The verse thus warns that true faith must be attained in this life, while it still can be reached and acted upon, before the moment of seeing the truth makes belief meaningless.

translation: And they had already disbelieved in it before, and they would hurl conjectures about the unseen from a distant place.
interpretation: The verse portrays the disbelievers as persistent in their rejection: they denied the message earlier, and now they throw out baseless accusations and guesses about what is hidden, as if shooting arrows at a target they cannot reach. Their claims about the unseen are reckless and unfounded, made from a remote position far from the truth they are trying to hit. The image conveys both the distance of their reasoning from certainty and the presumptuous, careless way they speak about matters beyond human knowledge, which is attributed only to God.

translation: And a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire, just as was done with their like before them. Indeed, they were in disquieting doubt.
interpretation: The verse portrays the fate of those who persisted in denial: when the moment of reckoning comes, they are cut off from the very things they longed for in the world, as were earlier generations who followed the same path. Their root cause is named as a troubling, unsettling doubt that never let their hearts find rest in faith, and so their desires, which had governed their choices, become the very barrier that separates them from the good they sought. The passage thus teaches that persistent doubt, when it hardens into a settled way of life, leads to a loss that mirrors the fate of those who came before.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. All praise is due to Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, who made the angels messengers having wings, two or three or four. He increases in creation what He wills. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse opens by establishing God as the sole source of praise because He is the originator (fatir) who brings the heavens and earth into being from nothing, and it presents the angels as messengers whose wings, in pairs, triples and quadruples, display a creation of varied forms and capacities beyond human imagining. The closing phrase, that He adds to creation what He wills, teaches that the scope of divine creativity is not fixed or exhausted by what is known to people, and that the power behind it is absolute, reaching every thing.

translation: Whatever mercy Allah opens up for people, none can withhold it; and whatever He withholds, none can release it after Him. And He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse affirms that all of God's mercy, whether bounty, provision, guidance, or relief, lies entirely in His hand. Human beings cannot block what He grants, nor can anyone release what He restrains, so people should turn to Him alone with hope and dependence rather than to created means. The verse closes with His names al-'Aziz and al-Hakim, which tie this absolute power to perfect wisdom: whatever He opens or withholds is exactly what is best, so trust in His decree is joined with trust in His wisdom.

translation: O mankind, remember the blessing of Allah upon you. Is there any creator other than Allah who provides for you from the sky and the earth? There is no deity except Him, so how are you turned away?
interpretation: The verse opens by calling all of humanity to remembrance, directing the mind first to the countless favors already received, since gratitude begins with recognizing them. It then poses a rhetorical question that exposes the absurdity of associating partners with God: provision from heaven (rain, light, air) and from earth (growth, sustenance) is undeniably the work of One Creator, so no other can share in the claim to worship. The closing question, 'how are you turned away?', is a reproach that marks the perverse turning of the heart from clear evidence, suggesting that the wrong in idolatry is not merely intellectual error but a wilful aversion from a truth that everyday experience already confirms.

translation: And if they deny you, then messengers before you were certainly denied. And to Allah all matters are returned.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad by placing his experience within a long line of prophetic history: rejection is not a sign of personal failure or of falsehood in his message, since earlier messengers faced the same denial. The Prophet is thereby reminded that his responsibility is to convey the message faithfully, while the outcome and the judgment of deniers rest with God, to whom every affair ultimately returns. The closing phrase shifts the reader's attention from the immediate hostility of opponents to the final accountability before God, offering both reassurance and a measure of patience to the believer who faces opposition.

translation: O mankind, indeed the promise of Allah is true, so let not the worldly life deceive you, and let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah.
interpretation: The verse calls humanity to awareness that the divine promise, whether of reward, accountability, or the Resurrection, is certain, and therefore the fleeting pleasures and allurements of this world must not lure a person away from preparing for the Hereafter. It warns that the greatest deception is the false hope that one may presume upon God's mercy while neglecting obedience, or that Satan, the arch-deceiver, may mislead a person into believing that Allah will overlook sin without repentance. Thus the verse joins a sober recognition of mortality with a call to sincere faith and righteous action.

translation: Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy. He only calls his party so that they may be among the companions of the blazing Fire.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the believer must treat Satan not as a mere distant temptation but as a declared, active enemy whose entire purpose is to draw people into his camp. Taking him as an enemy means refusing his whispers, guarding against his methods, and recognizing that every invitation to disobedience is a step toward the Fire. The phrase 'his party' reveals that evil operates through organized allegiance, so the believer's vigilance must be equally deliberate: to know who calls to what, and to choose instead the party of God.

translation: As for those who disbelieve, there is a severe punishment; and those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them is forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: The verse sets two destinies side by side to make the choice between them unmistakable. Disbelief is not presented as a neutral stance but as a path that ends in a severe reckoning, while faith joined with righteous action is linked to two gifts: forgiveness, which removes what has gone wrong, and a great reward, which crowns what has been done well. The pairing of belief with deeds shows that faith in the heart is meant to be made visible in conduct, so that a person is judged not only by what he professes but by how he lives it. The contrast also teaches that divine mercy is generous toward the one who turns back in sincerity, since forgiveness is placed before reward, indicating that the believer's first need is to be pardoned and only then to be rewarded.

translation: Is then one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him so that he sees it as good [equal to one who is guided]? For indeed, Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. So do not let your soul waste away in regret over them. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do.
interpretation: The verse poses a rhetorical question contrasting the one whose corrupt conduct has been adorned in his own eyes, so that he regards it as good, with the one who is rightly guided; the implied answer is that they are not equal. The phrase 'zuyyina lahu' points to the self-deceiving nature of sin: once a person persistently chooses wrongdoing, his inner vision is distorted and he no longer perceives his error as error. Attributing this to God's will (yudil and yahdi) is then qualified by the consistent Qur'anic principle that such divine decree follows a person's own persistent choices and turning away. The Prophet is consoled, told not to consume himself with grief over those who refuse guidance, because his duty is only conveyance; the matter of their hearts rests with God, who knows fully every action they perform and will hold them accountable for it.

translation: And it is Allah who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, and We drive them to a dead land and give life thereby to the earth after its death. Thus will be the resurrection.
interpretation: The verse draws a deliberate parallel between the natural cycle and the resurrection. Just as the lifeless, barren earth is revived by rain carried by the winds, so the dead will be brought back to life on the Day of Resurrection. The same power that quickens dry land after it has lain dead is the power that will raise the dead from their graves, so the observable renewal of nature serves as a sign pointing the human being toward the reality of resurrection and accountability.

translation: Whoever desires honor - then to Allah belongs all honor. To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deed raises it. But those who plot evil deeds will have a severe punishment, and the plotting of those will perish.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true honor (al-'izzah) is not found in worldly status, power, or the approval of people, but belongs entirely to Allah, so whoever seeks it must seek it from Him alone. The path to that honor is ascent toward Allah through sound speech, meaning faith, remembrance, and truthful words, joined with righteous action, which gives the words their weight and lifts them up to Him. By contrast, those who scheme with evil deeds, conspiring against truth and against others, are warned that their own plots are doomed to ruin and will bring them severe punishment. The verse thus binds inward belief, spoken word, and deeds into one whole, and shows that elevation comes through goodness while deceit defeats itself.

translation: And Allah created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then He made you into pairs. No female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge. And no one is granted long life or has his life shortened except that it is in a Record. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.
interpretation: The verse traces the human being's origin from lifeless dust through the stages of the seed to the formation of male and female pairs, then turns to show that the whole course of human life, from conception to birth and from its length to its end, is encompassed by Allah's knowledge and recorded in a decree that is fixed before it happens. Its purpose is to awaken the believer to the completeness of divine knowledge and power, so that a person relies on Allah rather than on his own control over his life, and understands that what seems like a matter of chance or human effort is in fact known and measured by Allah, which is easy for Him.

translation: And the two bodies of water are not alike: this one is fresh and sweet, pleasant for drinking, and that one is salty and bitter. From both you eat fresh, tender flesh, and you extract ornaments that you wear. And you see the ships plowing through them, that you may seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful.
interpretation: The verse sets the sweet and the salty seas side by side to show that two things sharing one world can differ profoundly in their nature and benefit, and that this difference is itself a sign pointing to the Creator's wisdom. The same waters that carry ships and yield food and adornment are sweet in one place and bitter in another, so divine favor is shown to be found in the variety of creation rather than in uniformity. The closing image of ships cutting through the sea to seek provision makes the lesson practical: the human being is invited to recognize these gifts, to strive for livelihood through God's bounty, and to answer that bounty with gratitude rather than heedless enjoyment.

translation: He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term. That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs dominion. And those you invoke other than Him do not possess even a speck (of a date-seed's membrane).
interpretation: The verse points to the precise, continuous alternation of night and day and the orderly motion of the sun and moon, all under divine subjugation toward a fixed end, as evidence that the true Lord who alone governs this cosmic order alone holds sovereignty; by contrast, the deities worshipped besides Him own not even the thinnest membrane of a date-seed, so their worship is shown to be utterly baseless and unworthy of any share in what belongs to Allah alone.

translation: If you call upon them, they will not hear your call; and even if they heard, they would not respond to you. And on the Day of Resurrection they will disavow your associating them with God. And none can inform you like the One who is All-Aware.
interpretation: The verse exposes the utter powerlessness of the deities that people invoke besides God. They are incapable of hearing a supplicant, and even if they could hear, they could never answer or grant what is asked. Their claimed partnership with God is shown to be empty: on the Day of Judgment, they will themselves deny the worship offered to them. The closing phrase points to the unparalleled knowledge of God, who is the only true Informer about reality, so that no one can give a truer account of these matters than He does. The verse thus calls the believer to turn sincerely to the One who hears and knows all, rather than to beings that are unable to respond.

translation: O mankind, you are the ones in need of Allah, while Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse establishes the fundamental relationship between the human being and the Creator: poverty and need are the essential condition of creatures, while sufficiency and praiseworthiness belong to Allah alone. Human need is not merely material but extends to every moment of existence, since one's being, sustenance, guidance, and capacity to act all subsist through God. Recognizing this need is the root of humility and worship, and it frees the believer from dependence on other creatures, for the only true wealth is closeness to the One who is independent of all. The address to 'mankind' emphasizes that this truth is universal, binding the rich and the poor, the powerful and the weak alike.

translation: If He wills, He can take you away and bring forth a new creation.
interpretation: The verse points to God's absolute power over His creation: the removal of the people addressed is not beyond His will, and He is able to replace them with an entirely new creation. Its force lies in reminding the listener that human existence and the order of the earthly world depend entirely on God's choice, so that arrogance or reliance on one's own strength is shown to be baseless. It also implies that disobedience does not hold God back; if people turn away from His command, He can remove them and bring others in their place who will carry out His purpose.

translation: And that is not difficult for Allah.
interpretation: The verse affirms that Allah's power is absolute and unlimited, so that what may seem extraordinary or hard to human reckoning, such as bringing back the dead or creating anew, is effortless for Him. Since He is the One who originated creation without precedent, restoring it presents Him with no difficulty at all. The phrase directs the believer to measure what is possible by the infinite might of the Creator rather than by the limited capacities of human beings, and so to trust in the promise of resurrection and divine recompense.

translation: And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. And if a heavily laden soul calls [another] to its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he were a close relative. You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen and establish prayer. And whoever purifies himself does so only for his own soul, and to Allah is the final return.
interpretation: The verse establishes the principle of individual moral accountability: each soul bears its own responsibility before God, and no one can shift the weight of its deeds onto another, not even a close kinsman in the hour of need. Because accountability is personal, the warning of the Prophet truly benefits only those whose hearts are open to their Lord, who fear Him in private as well as in public and who give form to that fear through prayer.
