By forgetting the origin of his own creation, he reasons about God's power only through the lens of decay, as if the act that first brought him from nothing were beyond the same Creator's capacity to restore him. The rhetorical question marks the heedlessness of one who sees the dust of the bones yet fails to see the Originator who shaped him, and the verses that follow answer him by pointing to the green tree turned to fire and to the One who created the heavens and earth, showing that the power which initiated creation is fully able to bring it back.

translation: Say: He who brought them into being the first time will give them life again, and He is All-Knowing of every creation.
interpretation: The verse answers the disbelievers' denial of resurrection with a argument from origins: the One who originated creation from nothing has the power to bring it back. Recreation is therefore no greater a matter than the first creation, and it is not beyond the capacity of the Creator. The closing phrase affirms that God's knowledge encompasses every created being in all its detail, including the scattered remains of the dead, so nothing is hidden from Him when He restores them. The verse thus joins divine power with divine knowledge to establish the certainty of the Hereafter.

translation: Who has made for you, from the green tree, fire, so that from it you kindle [your fires].
interpretation: The verse points to a sign of God's power and grace hidden in the ordinary: the green, moisture-laden tree seems the very opposite of fire, yet through the natural order God established, fire is drawn from it, so that people may kindle it for their needs. It invites the reader to reflect on how the Creator who brings fire out of what appears to be its contrary is able to bring about resurrection and the renewal of life, as the surrounding context of the chapter of Ya-Sin suggests. Thus the mundane act of lighting a fire becomes a reminder of divine authority over creation and of the bounty that sustains human life.

translation: Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them? Yes, indeed; and He is the All-Creating, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse turns the listener's own acknowledgment of God as Creator of the vast heavens and earth into a proof against doubt about resurrection. If the One who brought into being something as immense and intricate as the cosmos is plainly capable of it, then re-creating human beings after death, which is a far lesser undertaking in comparison, lies squarely within His power. The answer 'Yes, indeed' is offered as the self-evident conclusion that reason and fitra (innate disposition) already grant. The closing names, al-Khallaq (the All-Creating) and al-'Alim (the All-Knowing), reinforce that creation flows from both boundless power and perfect knowledge, so nothing about the individual, however scattered or forgotten, escapes His command to bring them back.

translation: His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.
interpretation: The verse presents divine creation as effortless and absolute: God's will needs no process, instrument, or time, and the mere word "Be" brings the thing into existence at once. This shows that the created order depends entirely on the Creator's decree, and it teaches the believer to rely on the One whose command alone governs all that exists, and whose power is never limited by resistance or delay.

translation: So glorified is He in whose hand is the dominion of all things, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: The verse opens with tasbih, the declaration that God is free of every deficiency and worthy of exalted glory, and it grounds this declaration in two facts about Him. First, malakut, the inner sovereignty and hidden dominion over all things, is in His hand, meaning that nothing escapes His governance, neither the visible nor the unseen. Second, the return of all created beings is to Him alone, so human life has a destination and a final accountability. The sequence moves the believer from awe at God's absolute power to the sobering awareness that every person will stand before Him. Glorifying God thus becomes both an act of worship and a reminder that one's conduct in this world is ultimately answerable to the One who owns it.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By those (angels) arranged in ranks, standing in rows,
interpretation: The oath by the ranked ones (al-Saffat) draws the listener's attention to the angels in their orderly, disciplined formation before their Lord, standing in devoted readiness to carry out His command. The swearing by this image of perfect order points to the sacred structure of the cosmos and to the believer's own duty to stand firm and united in worship and in the path of truth, as the rows of prayer and of the righteous mirror the ranks of the heavenly host.

translation: Then by those who drive forcefully, driving (them) with force.
interpretation: The oath is sworn by the angels, or possibly by the ranks of those who drive and restrain, who forcefully drive away and repel (the devils and evil suggestions, or the clouds and creatures they govern), as an emphatic affirmation that the matter of resurrection and the Hereafter is true, and that there is one God whose Oneness the following verses will establish.

translation: And by those who recite the reminder,
interpretation: The oath is sworn by the angels who ceaselessly recite and glorify God's revelation and remembrance, carrying the divine message to the heavens and to the prophets. Their devoted recitation of the reminder stands as a sign of the sincerity of their service, and the oath prepares the listener for the affirmation that follows, that God alone is the one true God.

translation: Indeed, your God is One.
interpretation: This verse, drawn from the Qur'an's affirmation of divine oneness, declares that the Lord to whom people turn is a single, unique God with no partner, equal, or associate. Its emphasis falls on tawhid, the core principle that all worship, trust, and devotion must be directed to the one Creator alone, and it stands as a corrective to any division of allegiance among multiple deities or created intermediaries.

translation: Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, and Lord of the easts.
interpretation: The verse establishes God's absolute lordship by first encompassing the whole created order, the heavens, the earth, and everything between them, and then specifying 'the easts' (al-mashriq), the points where the sun rises across its changing seasons and positions. This points the believer to a Lord who is not confined to one place or one moment, but who governs the cosmos in its full breadth and in its recurring rhythms of dawn and sunrise. Such a comprehensive sovereignty is the proper ground for trust, worship, and reliance, since the One who ordains the movements of the heavens and the sun is the One to whom all affairs ultimately belong.

translation: Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven with an adornment of the stars.
interpretation: The verse presents the lower heaven as beautified by the stars, so that the visible sky, which human beings behold every night, becomes a sign of God's power and artistry. This adornment is not merely aesthetic: it reflects an ordered cosmos, in which the stars are both a delight to the eye and a guide for travelers and a protection against the outermost reaches of the unseen realm, pointing the attentive reader from the beauty of creation to the Creator who fashioned it with purpose.

translation: And as a protection from every rebellious devil.
interpretation: The verse refers to the heavens being guarded and protected from every rebellious, defiant devil (shaytan marid), so that these jinn cannot ascend to eavesdrop on the higher assembly. The word marid denotes one who is insolent and has transgressed beyond bounds in evil, showing that the protection is against the most obstinate and wicked of the devils. It affirms that the cosmos is ordered under divine guard, and that no created being can escape the command of its Lord.

translation: They cannot listen to the Exalted Assembly (the angels above), and they are pelted from every side.
interpretation: The verse describes the devils, who once tried to eavesdrop on the heavenly council to snatch news of the unseen, but are now barred from it. Whenever they attempt to steal a hearing, they are driven off by burning flames from every direction, so that the heavens are guarded and the knowledge of the unseen is kept from those who would corrupt it with falsehood. It points to the sealing of the heavens against the rebellious jinn after the mission of the final Prophet, a sign that divine revelation is protected from distortion and that the sources of deception have been cut off.

translation: Repelled, and for them is a constant punishment.
interpretation: The verse describes the fate of the rebellious spirits who try to eavesdrop on the heavenly assembly: they are driven away and repelled by the shooting flame, and beyond this worldly rejection awaits them a punishment that is lasting and unceasing. The word 'wasib' conveys a punishment that does not relent or end, emphasizing that their expulsion from the heavens is only a prelude to an enduring torment, and that those who persist in arrogance and disobedience face a consequence that is continuous rather than momentary.

translation: Except one who snatches a fragment, and he is pursued by a piercing flame.
interpretation: The verse describes the eavesdropping of devils on the higher assembly, in which a stray listener who manages to snatch a stolen fragment of the heavenly secrets is immediately pursued and struck by a bright, piercing meteor. It conveys that the heavens are guarded against the jinn, so that no one can obtain divine knowledge except by the permission of God, and it affirms the protection of the revealed message from distortion and interference.

translation: So ask them: are they harder to create, or those (others) whom We have created? Indeed, We created them from sticky clay.
interpretation: The verse confronts those who deny resurrection with a simple rhetorical challenge: if creation itself is the measure, then the human being, formed from humble, clinging clay, is hardly beyond the power of the One who first brought them into existence. The question turns their own disbelief back on them, since the origin they already witness testifies that re-creation is no greater a feat. Its force lies in the argument from origin, placing the sheer capacity of the Creator before the eyes of the doubter so that denial of the Hereafter appears as a failure to reason from what is plainly seen.

translation: Nay, you marvel, and they mock.
interpretation: The verse (Surah As-Saffat 37:12) describes the disbelievers' response to the clear signs and the message of the Prophet: rather than reflecting, they mock what is presented to them. The Prophet's 'marvelling' (عجبت) at their state, whether read as his own astonishment or as God's expression of wonder at their denial, highlights the gap between the clarity of the truth and the heedlessness of those who ridicule it. The word 'بل' (nay) turns the reader from the preceding description of the reminders toward the stubbornness of those who dismiss them with scorn, showing that mockery of revelation is a common refusal to accept evident truth.

translation: And when they are reminded, they do not remember.
interpretation: The verse describes a spiritual condition in which people who are given admonition and reminders fail to heed them, their hearts having grown heedless and unresponsive. Reminder, when it reaches a heart that has closed itself off through habitual neglect or arrogance, produces no real recollection of God or of the truth, so the verse points to the danger of a hardened heart that hears the message yet does not let it take hold.

translation: And when they see a sign, they mock it.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah As-Saffat (37:14), describes the attitude of those who deny the truth when confronted with clear signs from Allah. Rather than reflecting on the evidence, they respond with ridicule, a habit that reveals a heart closed to guidance. Their mockery is not born of ignorance of the signs but of arrogance and an unwillingness to submit, showing that the problem lies not in the lack of proof but in the refusal to accept it.

translation: And they said, "This is nothing but clear magic."
interpretation: The verse records the reaction of those who rejected the message when they encountered it: rather than engaging with its substance, they dismissed it as sorcery, a label that attributes the impact of the revelation to trickery rather than truth. Their charge of 'clear' magic reveals a deliberate and confident denial, one that prefers to explain away undeniable effects instead of acknowledging their source. The verse thus shows a recurring pattern in the response of the unbelievers to the prophets, in which the evident power of the message is reduced to a manipulative illusion so that its claim upon the hearer can be avoided.

translation: "Would we, when we have died and become dust and bones, really be raised again?"
interpretation: The verse voices the disbelievers' astonishment at resurrection, measuring it against the ordinary human experience of death and decay: once the body has turned to dust and crumbled bones, return to life seems to them impossible. The question is less a request for information than a denial, and its rhetorical form invites the listener to reflect on how a Creator who first brought humanity from nothing is fully capable of reconstituting what has dissolved into earth. Its context in the surah answers this incredulity by pointing to the origin of creation and to the certainty of the Day of Judgment, so that the doubt itself becomes the occasion for reflection on God's power over life and death.

translation: "Or our forefathers, the earliest ones?"
interpretation: This phrase is taken from the Qur'anic report of the disbelievers' challenge to the resurrection, where they ask whether they and their earliest ancestors will be raised again after death (as in Surat As-Saffat 37:17 and Surat Al-Waqi'ah 56:48). The question expresses their reliance on inherited tradition and their incredulity that the dead, including the ancient generations, could be brought back to life. The Qur'an answers such doubts by affirming the certainty of resurrection and the accountability that follows, directing the listener to reflect on creation's beginning as evidence of God's power to restore life.

translation: Say, "Yes, and you will be humbled and abased."
interpretation: The command to answer "Yes" affirms the resurrection with emphatic certainty, and the word "داخرون" (humbled, abased, reduced to lowliness) points to the reversal of the pride these disbelievers displayed in this life. Those who scoffed at being raised from dust and bones will be brought low before the reality they denied, so the verse turns their mockery into a sign of their coming humiliation.

translation: Then it will be but a single shout, and at once they will be looking on.
interpretation: The verse describes the moment of the Resurrection as sudden and effortless: a single cry (zajra) is all that is needed to bring the whole of creation to life and to assembly before God. The Arabic word zajra suggests a forceful, startling call, and the phrase 'fa-idha hum yanzurun' ('and at once they are looking') emphasizes the immediacy of the event, where those who once denied the Hereafter find themselves suddenly awake, gazing at what they had been told about. It conveys that the reckoning is not a distant or laborious undertaking for God, but an instant act of His will, leaving the disbelievers no time for escape or delay.

translation: And they will say, "O woe to us! This is the Day of Recompense (Judgment)."
interpretation: The cry "O woe to us!" is the spontaneous confession of people who, now facing the reality they once denied, recognize that their own deeds have brought them to ruin. The verse presents the Day of Judgment not as a distant abstraction but as an immediate, undeniable fact that strips away every excuse. The phrase "Day of the Din" (yawm al-din) points to the day when every soul is repaid according to what it did, so the anguish expressed here is the awakening of conscience that comes too late for denial. It is a warning to the believer to live now in the awareness of that accounting, since the reckoning that the heedless dismissed will then be seen as true.

translation: This is the Day of Decision, which you used to deny.
interpretation: The verse speaks to the deniers at the moment of judgment, when the separation between truth and falsehood, and between the righteous and the wrongdoers, becomes manifest. The 'Day of Decision' (yawm al-fasl) is the day on which God renders the final judgment among creatures, so that what was previously disputed and dismissed as a lie is revealed as undeniable reality. The phrase 'which you used to deny' turns the rejection they once held back on them, exposing the futility of their former disbelief and making their denial itself part of the reckoning, so that the verse functions as both a rebuke and a warning to heed the reality of accountability before it arrives.

translation: Gather those who did wrong, along with their companions, and what they used to worship
interpretation: The verse depicts the Day of Judgment, when a command is issued to gather together all wrongdoers, together with their like-minded companions and the false objects they once worshipped instead of God. The gathering is not only of the persons but of the whole network of their sin: the oppressors are assembled with those who shared and enabled their injustice, so that each is brought to account in the company of the very partners in wrongdoing they chose in this life. The mention of what they 'used to worship' underscores that their idols and false deities, which offered them nothing, are brought forth to be exposed, leaving the worshippers without any refuge in the very things they had trusted.

translation: Besides Allah, so lead them onto the path of the Hellfire.
interpretation: The command to guide them to the path of Hellfire is a sign of their own choices, which led them away from the worship of Allah alone. Those who set up beings other than God as objects of devotion are shown walking the road they freely chose, and the verse presents their destination as the consequence of that chosen path.

translation: And stop them, for they are [to be] questioned.
interpretation: The verse belongs to the scene of the Day of Judgment, where those who went astray are gathered and then halted before being examined. The command to "stop them" is addressed to the angels, and the reason given, "they are to be questioned," points to the accountability that awaits every person for their beliefs and deeds. The brief statement conveys that no one escapes reckoning: each soul, and each group that followed false leaders, must stand and give account before God. It also reminds the listener that the pause before judgment is itself part of the justice, since the accused are made to face their own conduct before the questioning begins.

translation: What is wrong with you that you do not help one another?
interpretation: The question is a rebuke spoken on the Day of Judgment to those who denied the Hereafter and mocked the believers. The alliances they relied on in worldly life, their tribal loyalties, their idols, and their mutual support in opposing the message, have all vanished, and they are left helpless. Their inability to help one another exposes the hollowness of the solidarity they once boasted of, since no one can rescue another from the consequences of their deeds. The verse thus shows that true help belongs to God alone, and that bonds formed on falsehood dissolve when the reckoning comes.

translation: Nay, but on that Day they will be submitting (surrendering in submission).
interpretation: The verse portrays a moment of complete capitulation on the Day of Judgment, when those who had been stubbornly defiant, denying and arrogantly resisting, will be unable to keep up their pretense. Their former pride and resistance collapse, and they are left with no choice but to submit before the reality of their accountability. The word "مستسلمون" conveys an involuntary surrender, a recognition that the power and authority belong entirely to God, and that the veil of worldly self-assertion is lifted. It serves as a warning that the submission demanded of believers in life is ultimately inescapable, and that those who refuse it in this world will be compelled to it in the Hereafter.

translation: And they will turn toward one another, questioning each other.
interpretation: The verse depicts the people of the Garden or the Fire in the Hereafter, turning to one another in mutual inquiry after their reckoning has begun. It conveys the vivid social dimension of the Day of Judgment: the bonds of worldly companionship are reactivated as the righteous and the wayward recall their past lives, seek news of one another's fate, and reflect on what led them to their present state. It also hints at the reflective, conversational quality of the blessed and the condemned alike, where questioning becomes a means of recollection, accountability, and the unfolding of truth between former companions.

translation: They will say, "Indeed, you used to come to us from the right side."
interpretation: This verse (Surah As-Saffat 37:28) depicts the followers speaking to their leaders in the Fire, reproaching them for having misled them. The phrase "coming to us from the right" (ta'tunana 'an al-yamin) is a metaphor for deception disguised as sincere counsel: the leaders approached their followers as though they were truthful guides, presenting falsehood in the guise of goodness and piety, much as one approaches from the side of blessing and righteousness. The verse thus reveals that misguidance often wears the appearance of good, and that those who followed such misleaders will bear the blame of having surrendered their judgment to them, while the misleaders themselves are now exposed in the reckoning.

translation: They will say: Rather, you were not believers.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the followers who are misled, reflects the reproach they direct at their former leaders during the reckoning, who had led them astray. Their words turn back on themselves: the accusation that they were misled is answered by the claim that the misguided themselves never possessed genuine faith, so their own refusal of the truth was the true cause of their ruin. It reveals that the responsibility for disbelief rests ultimately on the disbelievers' own choice and inner disposition, rather than solely on outside influences, and that a heart not open to faith will find pretexts to blame others when facing the consequences.

translation: And we had no authority over you; rather, you were a transgressing people.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by the followers in the Hereafter, who are shown to be disclaiming responsibility for their own misguidance before their leaders. Their words reveal that the leaders' influence was never a compelling force: they had no real power to compel anyone into disbelief. The statement "we had no authority over you" (sultan) points to the fact that persuasion and misleading suggestions cannot override a person's free will and moral accountability. The verse therefore places the blame back on the people themselves, who chose to persist in transgression (tughyan), that is, in overstepping the bounds set by God and rebelling against the truth, having been warned and having freely accepted that path. It is a reminder that every soul bears responsibility for its own choices, and that the excuse of being led astray will not be accepted on the Day of Judgment.

translation: So the word of our Lord has come true against us: indeed, we are going to taste (the punishment).
interpretation: The speakers, having gathered in the Hereafter after their companion's account, affirm that the divine decree of punishment has been fulfilled upon them. Their words are a confession of collective accountability: they acknowledge that they, like all who rejected the messengers, are bound to taste the consequence that God had promised. The verse conveys a sober acceptance of divine justice, where the reality of the threatened punishment is no longer a matter of doubt but a settled truth that they now must endure.

translation: So We misled you, for indeed we were ourselves misguided.
interpretation: The verse records the words of those who were led astray, spoken on the Day of Judgment as they stand before their Lord and blame the ones who misled them, a reflection of the reality that those who call others to error bear their own deviation. It reveals that the followers and their misleaders share in the same fate, since neither the one who strayed nor the one who led him to straying can escape responsibility; the admission 'we were ourselves misguided' exposes the emptiness of the claims made in this world, where the misguided cling to one another in mutual justification, only to find that their shared error brings them together in the same punishment.

translation: So on that Day they will be sharing in the punishment.
interpretation: The verse points to the solidarity of wrongdoers in their fate: those who once joined together in disbelief, in following falsehood, and in mutual support will find themselves bound together in the same torment on the Day of Judgment. Their former alliances, which gave them a sense of shared strength in this world, will bring them no relief there, for the common suffering they share only deepens their reckoning, and each is left to bear his own share of the consequences of what he did.

translation: Indeed, that is how We deal with the criminals.
interpretation: The verse presents God's justice as a settled pattern rather than an arbitrary act: those who persist in guilt and wrongdoing, especially those who deliberately oppose the truth, will face consequences of the same kind that God has always applied to such people. The word 'kadhalika' (thus, in this same manner) points to a consistent divine practice, so that the fate of earlier wrongdoers stands as a warning and a reassurance that moral accountability is real, and that no one escapes it by denial or by numbers and power.

translation: Indeed, when it was said to them, "There is no deity except Allah," they would become arrogant.
interpretation: The verse exposes the root of rejection as pride rather than lack of evidence. The disbelievers understood the demand of La ilaha illa Allah: to renounce every claim to worship and authority apart from God and to submit to Him alone, and that demand threatened their status, their inherited customs, and their sense of self-importance. Their istikbar, or arrogance, was therefore a refusal to humble themselves before the truth once it was made known. The passage teaches that faith requires humility, and that the heart's pride can close the mind to a message whose clarity it already recognizes.

translation: And they say, "Are we to abandon our gods for a mad poet?"
interpretation: The verse captures the reaction of the disbelievers of Quraysh to the Prophet Muhammad's call to renounce idolatry. Unable to refute his message with reason, they dismissed him as a madman and a poet, labels meant to discredit his revelation and to make people see his summons as the ravings of a deranged man rather than a message from God. Their rhetorical question reveals the attachment of their society to inherited idols, and their refusal to abandon what their forefathers worshipped, even as the clarity of the Qur'an stood before them. The verse thus shows a recurring pattern in the history of prophethood: the messenger's truthfulness is met with ridicule and slander, and tradition is defended against the call to pure monotheism.

translation: Nay, he has brought the truth, and he has confirmed the messengers.
interpretation: The verse answers those who denied the Prophet Muhammad by affirming that he came with the truth itself, not with falsehood or invention. The phrase "and he confirmed the messengers" shows that his message is not a break from the prophets before him but a renewal and confirmation of their common call to monotheism and the truth they delivered. The verse thus teaches that authentic prophethood forms one continuous chain, and that rejecting the final messenger is, in effect, a rejection of the truth carried by all the messengers.

translation: Indeed, you will surely taste the painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse addresses those who persist in disbelief and rejection, warning them with absolute certainty that they will experience the agony of divine retribution. The emphatic particles 'inna' and the lam of emphasis underscore that this is not a mere possibility but a settled reality. The image of 'tasting' suggests that the punishment will be experienced directly and fully, though it is only a brief sip compared to the complete reckoning, and the adjective 'painful' conveys the severity of the suffering awaiting them. The verse thus serves as a call to reflection, urging the listener to reconsider their path before the consequences become unavoidable.

translation: And you are not recompensed except for what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse establishes the principle of strict and exact accountability: a person's reward or punishment is precisely the fruit of their own deeds, neither more nor less. Its wording places the emphasis on the reality of one's actions in this life, so that every human being is called to reflect on what they are actually doing, since the outcome in the Hereafter will be a direct mirror of that conduct. It thus combines a warning against complacency with a reassurance of divine justice, in which no good work is lost and no wrong goes unaccounted for.

translation: Except for the sincere servants of Allah.
interpretation: The verse makes an exception: the sincere servants of Allah, those whom Allah has purified and chosen, are not subject to the seduction or misguidance that Satan had vowed to bring upon humanity. Their sincerity (ikhlas) in devotion, freed from any admixture of hypocrisy, worldly motives, or idolatry, is what shields them from Satan's influence, so that their worship is pure and wholly directed to Allah alone.

translation: "For those there is a known provision." (Qur'an 37:41)
interpretation: The verse describes the sincere servants of God who are granted a provision that is specific, known, and fixed, in contrast to the uncertainty of worldly sustenance. Its 'knownness' signals that God's reward for them is not vague or arbitrary but precisely ordained, honored, and fitting to their faith and deeds. It is a reminder that the believer's ultimate sustenance rests with the One who assigns each good thing its measure, so one should seek the Hereafter's provision through righteousness rather than being anxious over worldly shortfall.

translation: Fruits, and they will be honored.
interpretation: The verse describes the delight of the righteous in Paradise, where abundant fruits are provided for them, and the honor (ikram) bestowed upon them signifies that their sustenance and station are given with dignity and esteem, reflecting the divine generosity that awaits those who did good in this world.

translation: In Gardens of Bliss.
interpretation: The phrase "fi jannati n-na'im" (in Gardens of Bliss) describes the place of the righteous in the Hereafter as a setting of complete delight and ease. The word jannah evokes a garden, a image of lush, shaded, flowing abundance that the desert-dwelling audience of the Qur'an would have found especially precious, while na'im (bliss) signifies a pleasure that is whole, untroubled and free of the hardship and want of worldly life. The verse thus teaches that the ultimate reward is not merely the absence of punishment but a positive, enduring state of joy, and that the believer's true home is one where every need of body and soul is fulfilled in peace.

translation: Reclining on thrones, facing one another.
interpretation: The verse describes the joy and companionship of the righteous in Paradise: they recline comfortably on elevated couches, seated face to face, so that no one turns away from another. This face-to-face posture signifies mutual affection, equality, and the absence of rancor or envy among them, as elsewhere the Qur'an promises that any lingering resentment will be removed from their hearts. Their closeness reflects a社会 of harmony and intimacy in which the bliss of Paradise is shared rather than competed for.

translation: They will be served around with a cup from a flowing spring.
interpretation: The verse describes the delights of the righteous in Paradise, where cups of pure, flowing drink are circulated among them. The image of a cup drawn from a running spring (ma'in) conveys abundance, purity, and continuous availability, and it stands in contrast to the worldly drink that the Qur'an elsewhere describes as intoxicating and defiling. It points to a joy that is clean, untainted, and given freely, so that the blessings of the afterlife are presented as both honorable and fully satisfying.

translation: White, a delight to those who drink.
interpretation: The verse presents the drink of Paradise as white and pleasant to the taste, which points to a purity free of the defects of worldly drink. Its whiteness signals clarity and untainted goodness, and calling it a delight ties the reward to complete sensory pleasure. Read alongside the following verse, which says it neither causes harm nor intoxication, the drink is a sign that Paradise's blessings are perfected versions of the good things people know in this world, granted without their corruption and offered to those who have earned them.

translation: There is no harm (intoxication) in it, nor are they affected by it or made to lose their reason.
interpretation: This phrase describes the wine of Paradise as set apart from the wine of this world. Its drink does not bring the headaches, corruption of mind, or loss of sense that intoxicants cause in worldly life, and the people of Paradise are not dulled or confused by it. The verse thus presents Paradise as a realm of pure delight in which the pleasure of drink is free of every harm, and it implicitly invites the believer to forsake what dulls the intellect in this life in hope of that purer reward.

translation: And with them will be women restraining their gaze, with beautiful, wide eyes.
interpretation: The verse describes the companions awaiting the righteous in Paradise as spouses who are modest and chaste, whose gaze is directed only toward their own mates and not toward others, and whose eyes are large, lustrous and beautiful. Beyond the literal image, it points to a pure and undisturbed joy in the hereafter, where the sources of delight are free from jealousy, betrayal, or any inner unrest, and where the beauty of the companions reflects the beauty and peace of the blessed abode itself.

translation: As if they were preserved eggs (or: as if they were hidden/guarded eggs), kept safe within their shells.
interpretation: The simile of 'hidden eggs' (bayd maknun) evokes the houris of Paradise as pure, untouched, and carefully protected, like an egg nestled in its shell away from dust and the hand of any toucher. Its whiteness and smoothness suggest radiant beauty, delicacy, and a purity of form that has never been marred, conveying the honor and preciousness of the companions promised to the righteous.

translation: Then they turned toward one another, questioning each other.
interpretation: The verse depicts the people of Paradise or the companions of the Fire in the Hereafter turning to one another to ask questions, as they recall their former life in the world and reflect on their destinies. It conveys the mutual reckoning and reflection that arises once the realities of the Hereafter have become manifest, where worldly bonds and conversations take on a new and solemn character, and where the seekers of truth and the heedless alike confront the consequences of their beliefs and deeds.

translation: Said a speaker among them: "Indeed, I had a companion (who used to say to me...)."
interpretation: This verse belongs to the scene of the people of Paradise conversing in the Hereafter, as recounted in Surah As-Saffat (37:51). One of them recalls, with a tone of wonder and reflection, a companion he once had in the world. The phrase "qarin" denotes a close associate who shared his life and outlook, and the speaker's recollection sets up the account of that companion's doubt in resurrection and his fate in the Fire. It conveys that the believer's gratitude and joy in Paradise are tied to remembering the worldly life he was spared from, and that close companionship in this life carries real weight for a person's final destiny.

translation: He says, "Are you truly among those who believe it?"
interpretation: The words are spoken by a believer who is in Paradise and is recalling a former companion on earth who mocked the idea of resurrection and reckoning. Asking "Are you truly among those who affirm this?" expresses his astonishment and his gratitude that God has spared him from that companion's doubt, so the scene shows that the blessed will remember worldly relationships and reflect on how close they came to ruin.

translation: "Is it that when we have died and become dust and bones, we will indeed be brought to account (or be recompensed)?"
interpretation: The verse voices the disbelievers' incredulous denial of resurrection and final reckoning, treating the dissolution of the body into dust and bones as proof that a person can never be gathered again or held responsible. Its rhetorical doubling of the question ('Is it that... is it that...') reveals a mind that considers bodily decay an insurmountable barrier to divine judgment. The verse thus frames denial of the Hereafter as rooted less in lack of evidence than in a limited view of God's power over creation, which the surrounding passages answer by pointing to the original creation of humankind from a humble origin.

translation: He said: "Would you like to look down (and see)?"
interpretation: This verse comes from the story of Moses in Surah As-Saffat (37:55), or rather from the account of the people of the Fire in the dialogue between the believers and the disbelievers. Here it is spoken by one of the believers in Paradise, who, having been granted a view, asks his companions whether they wish to look down into the Fire to see the condition of a former companion who denied the Resurrection. The question reveals the believer's gratitude for his salvation and the contrast between the bliss of the righteous and the torment of those who rejected the truth, prompting reflection on how close a person may come to ruin through disbelief and how great a favor Allah bestows through guidance.

translation: So he looked, and saw him in the midst of the Blazing Fire.
interpretation: The verse depicts the moment a man among the companions of the Garden looks down from his elevated place and sees his former companion in the depths of the Hellfire, located at its very center. This sight, presented in the context of the dialogue in Surah As-Saffat, serves as a vivid picture of the reality of divine justice: the believer is granted a view of the fate of the one who denied the Resurrection, which heightens his gratitude for the favor of his salvation and underscores how a single choice in worldly life determines an eternal destination.

translation: He said: By Allah, you have almost brought me to ruin.
interpretation: This is the words of Ya'qub (Jacob) to his sons, spoken when they came back with the news that the brother they had taken to Egypt was accused of theft and that they had been forced to leave him behind. His oath 'By Allah' expresses that he feels they nearly destroyed him through grief and their earlier wrongdoing toward Yusuf. The phrase 'to ruin' conveys a state of near-death from sorrow, and it reveals how deeply the old wound of losing Yusuf had worn him down, while his reply also reflects a patient reliance on God that follows immediately in the surrounding verses.

translation: And were it not for the grace of my Lord, I would certainly have been among those brought forward (to punishment).
interpretation: The verse is spoken by a man who, on the Day of Judgment, is shown what befell him and his companion in the worldly life; it expresses the recognition that his deliverance from the fate of those summoned to punishment was purely by the bounty of God, not by his own merit. It teaches that divine mercy alone sustains a servant from ruin, so that the believer's safety should be attributed to God's grace rather than to self-regard, and that gratitude and humility are the fitting response to having been spared. The 'muhdarun' are those brought forth and presented for chastisement, and the phrase conveys how narrowly one may escape destruction when God's favor intervenes.

translation: Is it not that we shall not die (again)? — Qur'an 37:58: "Are we not to die [again]?"
interpretation: The verse is spoken by the people of Paradise as they converse with one another, recalling their earthly life. Having been granted the bliss of Paradise, they marvel at their security and ask, in a tone of rhetorical wonder and gratitude, whether they will still die after their first death. Their question highlights the completeness of their everlasting felicity: death, which they once knew in the world, has been permanently left behind, and they are secure in an eternal state from which there is no return to mortality.

translation: Except for our first death, and we will not be punished.
interpretation: This verse is spoken by the people of Paradise, who, having entered the Garden and tasted its bliss, reassure one another that they will never die again after their first death in the world. Their statement expresses the certainty of eternal life and security in Paradise, where there is no return to death and no punishment. It highlights the contrast between the trials of worldly life, which ended with a single death, and the everlasting ease that awaits the righteous in the Hereafter.

translation: Indeed, this is the great triumph.
interpretation: The phrase, spoken in the context of the righteous and the reward prepared for them, declares that the true success is the attainment of the Garden and the pleasure of God. It teaches that the greatest victory is not worldly gain or status, which is fleeting, but the everlasting felicity that results from faith and good deeds. By calling it "the great triumph" with emphasis, the verse directs the believer's heart toward valuing what endures over what passes away, and measuring success by its outcome before God.

translation: For the likes of this let those who would strive, strive.
interpretation: The verse, taken from Surah As-Saffat (37:61), turns the believer's gaze from the transient pleasures of this world toward the eternal reward of Paradise described just before it, the fruit and the gardens of bliss. The repetition of the call to 'work' signals that such a prize is worth a sustained, wholehearted effort, and that the true measure of a person's ambition should be what endures beyond death. It implicitly contrasts the competitive pursuit of worldly status and wealth with the nobler competition for closeness to God, urging the believer to make righteous action the object of their striving.

translation: Is that better as a welcoming feast, or the tree of Zaqqum?
interpretation: The verse poses a rhetorical contrast between the hospitality prepared for the righteous in Paradise and the food of the damned. The question is framed so that the answer is obvious to any reasoning listener: the blessed reward of the garden is far superior to the bitter, torment-laden tree of Zaqqum that grows in the depths of Hell. It serves as a warning that the consequences of one's choices in this life are as different as these two hosts, and it invites the listener to weigh the eternal outcomes of faith and disbelief and to choose accordingly.

translation: Indeed, We made it a trial for the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse refers to the tree of Zaqqum described in Surah As-Saffat (37:63-64), which Allah made a source of trial for the wrongdoers. Its mention as a test reveals that the same reality can become a means of misguidance for those whose hearts are already inclined to denial and injustice, while for believers it strengthens faith. The wrongdoers, in their arrogance, mock what they do not understand: they reject the warning of a tree growing in the depths of Hellfire and use it as a pretext for disbelief, thereby exposing their own corrupted reasoning. Thus the verse teaches that divine signs are not themselves the cause of error; rather, the trial lies in how a person responds to them, and injustice toward the truth turns guidance into a snare.

translation: Indeed, it is a tree that springs forth from the root of Hellfire.
interpretation: The verse presents the zaqqum as a fitting consequence of the wrongdoers' own choices: its roots lie at the bottom of the Fire, so the very source of their nourishment is the place of their punishment. Its mention alongside those who mocked it when it was described shows that what worldly minds reject as absurd can be the true reality of the Hereafter, and that the rejection itself becomes part of their trial. The image suggests that the fruits of disbelief and transgression grow from roots that lie in the Fire they have chosen.

translation: Its shoots are as if they were the heads of devils (Shayatin).
interpretation: The verse, from Surah As-Saffat (37:65), describes the fruit-bearing spathes of the zaqqum tree, the tree that grows in the depths of Hellfire. Since no one has seen a devil's head, the image is deliberately drawn from what the listeners could imagine: a horrifying, grotesque form, twisted and ugly, so that the very look of the tree conveys its repulsiveness. The comparison leaves the hearers with a sense of dread and revulsion before the fruit is even mentioned, and it prepares them for the next verses, in which the people of the Fire are made to eat from it and drink boiling water. The image thus ties the sensory horror of the tree to the punishment of those who denied the truth.

translation: Then indeed they will eat from it, and fill their bellies with it.
interpretation: The verse portrays the food of the people of the Fire, the zaqqum tree, as something they are forced to consume in great quantity despite its repulsiveness. Their hunger drives them to eat, yet what they eat yields no nourishment or satisfaction, only torment. The image reverses the worldly experience of eating for pleasure and sustenance: the belly that was filled with comfort in this life becomes a vessel of suffering in the Hereafter, teaching that every indulgence pursued in heedlessness of God may return as its own punishment.

translation: Then indeed for them over it is a mixture of boiling water.
interpretation: The verse describes the continuation of the punishment of the disbelievers in the Fire: after their return to the blazing place, they are given a drink mixed with scalding water (hamim), so that the torment is not only in the burning itself but in what they are made to consume. The phrase "over it" (alayha) suggests that this mixture is placed upon or added to their dwelling or their food, reinforcing the sense of an inescapable and layered suffering. Read in its context, the verse serves as a warning that the consequences of rejecting the truth extend beyond the grave into a state where even what should sustain a person becomes a source of agony, pointing the listener toward reflection on the seriousness of their choices in this world.

translation: Then indeed their return is to the Blazing Fire (Jahim).
interpretation: The phrase "thumma inna marji'ahum la-ila al-jahim" (from Surah al-Saffat, 37:68, where it follows the mention of the ancestors of the disbelievers who were led astray) emphasizes that the ultimate destination of those who persist in misguidance is Hell, and that their return is certain and inescapable. The word "thumma" (then) introduces a sequence and a sense of progression: after the worldly life and the blind following of their forefathers comes the final reckoning. The emphatic particles "inna" and the lam of emphasis ("la-ila") affirm the certainty of this outcome, warning the listener that the path of inherited error leads not to safety but to the fire. The verse thus serves as a call to reflect on the consequences of following others blindly rather than seeking the truth through one's own reason and revelation.

translation: Indeed, they found their fathers astray.
interpretation: The verse describes the reason some people rejected the message of the prophets: they blindly adopted the beliefs and customs of their forefathers without examining whether those beliefs were true. Their attachment to inherited tradition became a barrier to guidance, since they treated the mere fact that their ancestors held a belief as sufficient proof of its correctness. The verse thus warns against unquestioning imitation (taqlid) in matters of faith and calls the believer to reflection and to following evidence rather than familiarity and lineage.

translation: So they were hurrying along in their footsteps.
interpretation: The verse portrays those who reject guidance as blindly rushing after their forefathers' ways, following the traces of their predecessors without examining whether those ways are true. Their eagerness is not the eagerness of seeking truth but the momentum of inherited custom, which replaces reflection and leaves them following the path of error.

translation: And certainly, most of the earlier generations went astray before them.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet and the believers by showing that the straying of the majority is not a new phenomenon. Every nation before them had its own multitude who turned away from the guidance sent through their messengers. Divine guidance has always been received by a minority, while the majority of people, following inherited custom and the crowd, have fallen into error. The lesson is that the numbers of those who follow a path are no proof of its truth, and the believer should measure the right way by revelation rather than by the majority.

translation: And We had certainly sent among them warners.
interpretation: The verse affirms that Allah does not leave any community without guidance: messengers were sent into the midst of the people themselves, not from afar, so that they could warn them of the consequences of their deeds. The word 'fihim' (among them) emphasizes that the warners were of their own society, familiar with their language, circumstances, and conduct, which makes the warning direct and establishes the proof against them. The plural 'munthirin' indicates that this divine mercy of warning was repeated across generations and places, and that the purpose is to awaken hearts to accountability before the consequences arrive.

translation: So observe how was the end of those who were warned.
interpretation: The verse directs the listener to reflect upon the fate of past communities that received divine warnings through their messengers and yet rejected them. Their destruction serves as a lesson that heeding or ignoring the warnings of God has real consequences in this world, and it urges the reader to take the admonition seriously rather than assume that delay in punishment means escape from it.

translation: Except for the sincere servants of Allah.
interpretation: The verse singles out 'the sincere servants of Allah' (ʿibād Allāh al-mukhlaṣīn) as an exception to the general fate of those who are led astray or condemned. These are people whose devotion has been purified of hypocrisy, worldly motives, and association with others in worship, so that their faith and actions are sincerely directed toward God alone. Their sincerity (ikhlāṣ) is what protects them, showing that the decisive factor before God is not mere lineage or outward claim, but the purity of intention and devotion of the heart.

translation: And Noah had certainly called Us, and how excellent were We as Responders.
interpretation: The verse presents Noah's supplication as a model of prayer answered: his call to his Lord was heard, and the phrase 'how excellent were the Responders' expresses God's own praise of Himself for answering, highlighting that true reliance and turning to God in distress is met with the most generous response. It invites the believer to see that Divine answering is the best of answers, and that Noah's persistence in calling upon God, even amid rejection by his people, was ultimately vindicated by deliverance.

translation: And We saved him and his family from the great distress.
interpretation: This verse refers to Noah (or possibly Nuh's deliverance from the flood), and it speaks to God's mercy toward a prophet who remained steadfast amid rejection and overwhelming calamity. The 'great distress' points to the catastrophe that befell those who denied the message, from which God rescued the believer and his household. It teaches that divine deliverance comes to those who remain faithful to their Lord, and that God's salvation extends to the righteous and their families, reflecting the principle that steadfastness in faith is met with God's protection in the hour of greatest trial.

translation: And We made his descendants the ones who remain (survive).
interpretation: The verse refers to Noah (nuh) and the Flood: after the deluge destroyed the disbelievers, God made Noah's offspring the sole surviving lineage, so that the human race afterward descends from the righteous family that was saved in the ark. It signals that God's continuation of humanity rests on those He preserves, and that the survival of the believers' line is a sign of divine favor following judgment upon the wicked.

translation: And We left for him (a good remembrance) among the later generations.
interpretation: The verse refers to Abraham (Ibrahim), peace be upon him, from the preceding verses of Surah As-Saffat. God made His praise and good mention endure for him among those who came after him, so that every community following the prophets honors him, and he remains a model of sincere monotheism and submission. The phrase points to the lasting legacy a righteous person leaves behind, which is granted by God as a reward for steadfast faith and devotion.

translation: Peace be upon Noah among the worlds.
interpretation: This short verse, found in Surah As-Saffat (37:79), is a divine greeting bestowed upon Noah, honoring him among all the peoples and generations of mankind. The phrase "fi al-'alamin" indicates that the peace and honor granted to him are not confined to his own time but are recognized across the ages and among all the worlds, marking him as one of the great messengers whose steadfastness in calling his people to God earned him a lasting and universal remembrance. It reflects God's reward for the righteous who endure opposition with patience, and it stands as a reassurance to believers that faithfulness to the divine message is rewarded with enduring honor.

translation: Indeed, that is how We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: The verse presents divine reward as a direct and just response to ihsan, the excellence of conduct that goes beyond mere obligation, combining sincere faith with beautiful action toward God and creation. It teaches that Allah's recompense is not arbitrary but follows the pattern of the believer's own striving, so that the one who perfects his worship and conduct will find that his good deeds are met with generous and fitting reward. The phrase 'kadhalika' (thus, in this manner) signals that this is a established principle of divine justice, encouraging the believer to aspire to ihsan in every station of life.

translation: Indeed, he was among Our servants, the believers.
interpretation: The verse, spoken of a servant chosen for his faith, identifies the person it describes by two marks: he is one of God's servants ('ibad), a status of humble devotion and closeness to God, and he is a believer (mu'min), whose faith is sincere and firm. By joining these two qualities, the verse presents true servanthood to God as inseparable from genuine belief, and it honors the believer with God's own attribution of him as 'Our servant,' signaling that such a person is under God's protection and is worthy of His favor.

translation: Then We drowned the others.
interpretation: The "others" are Pharaoh and his army, who pursued Moses and the Children of Israel into the sea. Their drowning completes the rescue of the believers and shows that God's justice overtakes those who oppose His messengers and rely on their own power, so that the tyrant who sought to crush the truth is himself erased, leaving the verse as a warning that no worldly force can withstand the decree of God.

translation: And indeed, from among his followers was Abraham.
interpretation: The pronoun in 'his' refers back to Noah (nūḥ), mentioned in the preceding verses, so the verse places Abraham within the lineage of those who followed the path of Noah's message. It highlights that the prophetic mission of monotheism is a continuous chain passing from one messenger to the next, with Abraham as a chief example of steadfast faithfulness to the one God, who came with a sound heart and turned away from idolatry. By naming him as belonging to the same community of faith, the verse affirms the unity of the message across the prophets and offers the believers a model of loyalty to that shared tradition.

translation: When he came to his Lord with a sound heart.
interpretation: The verse describes the state in which a person reaches God: not merely with outward deeds or possessions, but with a heart that is free from shirk (associating partners with God), hypocrisy, arrogance, rancor, and attachment to worldly desires. A 'sound' heart (qalb salim) is one that is whole, sincere, and turned entirely toward its Lord, so that its devotion is genuine and its inner state matches its worship. The phrase thus locates the criterion of acceptance before God in the purity and soundness of the inner self, which is the true condition for meeting Him on the Day of Judgment.

translation: When he said to his father and his people, "What is it that you worship?"
interpretation: Abraham's question is not a request for information but a pointed challenge that opens a path to reasoning with those closest to him. By asking about the objects of their worship, he invites them to examine what they have inherited and to confront the emptiness of practices they have never questioned. The verse reveals the prophetic method of beginning with a simple, direct question that unsettles blind imitation of ancestors and prompts the listener to reflect on whether what they revere truly deserves that reverence.

translation: Is it falsehood, gods other than Allah, that you desire?
interpretation: The verse is a rebuke addressed to those who turn away from the truth toward fabricated deities. By asking whether they truly desire 'ifk' (falsehood, lies) in the form of gods besides Allah, it exposes the absurdity of exchanging the One true Lord for beings that have no reality or power. The rhetorical question draws the listener to recognize, through their own reason, that such worship is a deliberate choice of illusion over certainty, and it calls them to return to sincere devotion to God alone.

translation: So what do you think of the Lord of the worlds?
interpretation: This phrase, appearing in Surah As-Saffat (37:87) in the context of the disbelievers who worshipped idols, is a rhetorical challenge that confronts them with the question of how they could imagine they will escape the consequences of their conduct before the One who is Lord of all creation. The verse invites the listener to reflect on the sheer magnitude of God's sovereignty and mastery over all worlds, so that one would never presume that He will leave falsehood unaccountable or that He is like the lifeless idols they served. The word 'ẓann' here carries the sense of firm conviction or assumption, and the question therefore urges a serious examination of one's own assumptions about the Creator, pressing the heart toward awareness, humility, and a correct estimation of the Lord before whom all must stand.

translation: And he looked a look at the stars.
interpretation: This verse (As-Saffat 37:88, in the account of Abraham) describes him glancing up at the stars as he was about to respond to his people, who had invited him to a festival. The glance was a deliberate, pointed act: he looked at the stars to convey that he was feigning illness, so that he could remain behind and carry out his plan against their idols. It reveals his cleverness and his resolve to reject their idolatry, using a sign of the heavens to set up the argument that follows.

translation: So he said, "Indeed, I am sick."
interpretation: This is spoken by Ibrahim (Abraham) when his people invited him to join their festival, and he sought an excuse to remain behind so he could carry out his plan against their idols. By declaring himself ill, a statement that was literally a feigned excuse, he avoided the gathering without outright lying in a way that harms anyone, and this allowed him to be alone to act against the idolatry of his people. The verse shows that a believer may use a discreet, indirect expression to achieve a righteous purpose, and that his words were a form of strategic wisdom meant to expose the emptiness of their worship.

translation: So they turned away from him, retreating.
interpretation: The phrase describes the reaction of those who were confronted with the truth through the Prophet's call: rather than engaging with the message, they turned their backs on it and withdrew in flight from it. The word 'mudbirin' (retreating, turning their backs) conveys not merely indifference but an active, deliberate aversion, as though they fled from the summons itself. The verse thus portrays the stubborn refusal of those who, having been shown the signs, chose to avoid reflection and to abandon the guidance that was placed before them.

translation: Then he turned aside to their gods and said, "Will you not eat?"
interpretation: The verse portrays Abraham's clever mockery of the idols. Having slipped away unnoticed from the people who had gone out to their festival, he approached the idols that were set up for worship and, addressing them as though they could hear and respond, asked why they do not eat the food placed before them. His question exposes the absurdity of worshipping objects that have no power to eat, speak, or act, and it is a pointed rebuke that prepares the way for his subsequent act of breaking them, thereby calling his people to recognize the emptiness of what they serve in place of God.

translation: What is the matter with you that you do not speak?
interpretation: The question is a sharp, ironic rebuke. Abraham addresses the idols as if they were capable of answering, so that their silence exposes the absurdity of worshipping things that cannot speak, hear, or act. The verse turns the idolaters' own reasoning against them: if the objects they honour cannot even respond to a question, they cannot deserve worship, and devotion belongs only to the One who speaks and commands.

translation: Then he turned upon them, striking them with his right hand.
interpretation: The verse depicts Abraham, after his people had left for their festival, turning decisively against their idols and smashing them with force. The 'right hand' signifies strength, skill, and resolute purpose, showing that his act of breaking the idols was a deliberate, powerful assault on false worship. It portrays the prophet's courage in confronting idolatry openly, placing monotheistic conviction above social pressure and the fear of his people.

translation: So they came hastening toward him, rushing along.
interpretation: The verse (Surah As-Saffat 37:94) depicts the people of Abraham's community, having been told by their idols' worshippers of his destruction of their idols, coming rushing toward him in agitated haste to confront him. The word yazifun conveys a sense of being driven forward with urgency, like a camel's gait or people hurrying together in a state of excited zeal, which highlights the intensity of their anger and the rashness of their reaction. It implicitly contrasts their frenzied, collective haste with Abraham's calm composure, suggesting that those who rely on blind tradition often act in disorder when confronted with truth.

translation: He said: "Do you worship what you carve?"
interpretation: This verse comes from the story of Abraham (Ibrahim) with his people, as recounted in Surah As-Saffat (37:95). Abraham challenges the idolaters by exposing the absurdity of venerating objects that they themselves shape with their own hands. The rhetorical question turns the logic back on them: the carved image is a product of human workmanship, so it cannot be the proper object of worship, and its maker is the one who has more claim to be acknowledged. The verse thus establishes the principle that true worship belongs only to the Creator who made both the worshipper and the thing made, a theme that runs throughout the Qur'an's critique of idolatry.

translation: And Allah created you and what you make.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah As-Saffat (37:96), affirms that Allah is the sole Creator of human beings and of their handiwork. It was revealed in the context of people who carved idols and then worshipped them, and it points out the absurdity of worshipping something one has shaped with one's own hands, since the very act of making is itself a creation granted by God. The verse thus establishes God's absolute power over both the maker and the made, calling the believer to direct worship to the One who is the origin of all existence and of all human skill and effort.

translation: They said, "Build for him a structure, then throw him into the blazing fire."
interpretation: This verse (Surah As-Saffat 37:97) recounts the climax of Prophet Ibrahim's confrontation with his people. Having been unable to refute his monotheistic message and having smashed their idols, they resolved to punish him in the most severe way, choosing to burn him alive. Their plan reveals how the powerful, when confronted with truth they cannot answer, turn to brute force and public spectacle to silence the one who calls them back to God. Yet the verse that follows shows that God rendered their scheme futile, which teaches that no human plot can prevail against the one whom God protects, and that persecution of the righteous often becomes the very means by which God manifests His power and vindicates His messenger.

translation: So they intended to scheme against him, but We made them the lowest.
interpretation: The verse presents a pattern of divine justice in which those who plot against the righteous are turned back upon themselves. Their deliberate scheme, meant to destroy Moses and his people, becomes the very means of their humiliation: the one who was to be cast down rises, while the plotters are brought to ruin. The word 'al-asfalin' (the lowest) carries both a literal sense of being placed beneath and a moral sense of abasement, showing that worldly power and cunning count for nothing against the will of God. The verse thus encourages trust in God's protection of the faithful, and warns that arrogance and the planning of injustice inevitably lead to one's own degradation.

translation: And he said, "Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Abraham (peace be upon him) as he withdrew from his people after they turned away from the worship of God, reveals the sincere reliance of a believer who, having separated himself from falsehood for the sake of truth, places his full trust in God alone. His words "I am going to my Lord" express a complete turning of the heart and the self toward the Creator, a migration of the spirit even when the body must leave familiar ground. The phrase "He will guide me" reflects a firm conviction that whoever forsakes all for God will not be abandoned, and that divine guidance follows the one who sincerely seeks it. It teaches that when a person is compelled to leave a corrupt or hostile environment for the sake of faith, the hope and assurance placed in God's guidance is the true source of steadfastness and direction.

translation: My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous.
interpretation: This is the supplication of Prophet Zakariya (Zechariah), who, having reached old age with a barren wife, turned to God with a sincere and humble plea for an heir of righteous character. The verse reflects that true longing for offspring is best directed toward their piety and goodness, not merely their existence. It teaches that a believer should seek from God not only worldly blessings but a lineage that will carry faith and righteousness forward, and that sincere supplication, even when circumstances seem impossible, is answered by the One who is able to bring life where there was none.

translation: So We gave him good tidings of a forbearing boy.
interpretation: The verse refers to the announcement to Abraham of a son who would be forbearing (halim), a quality that signals the child's future patience, gentleness, and self-restraint. Its placement in the narrative shows that this good news comes after a long trial and submission, so the promised son is presented as a reward and a mercy that answers a faithful servant's devotion. The word 'halim' also conveys that the boy's later readiness to accept his father's command, as the story continues, springs from a character of composure and inner strength rather than mere obedience.

translation: And when he reached with him the age of exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so see what you think." He said, "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast."
interpretation: The verse presents the complete surrender of both father and son to a divine command conveyed through a dream, which in the prophetic tradition is a form of revelation. Abraham does not impose his will but consults his son, showing the value of mutual counsel within the family, while the son's reply joins obedience to God with humble dependence on God's will ('if Allah wills') and patient endurance. The episode thus establishes submission (islam) to God as the foundation of faith, where trial is met with patience, and it foreshadows the ransoming of the son with a great sacrifice, teaching that God tests His servants to refine their devotion.

translation: So when they both submitted (to Allah), and he laid him down upon his forehead (for sacrifice).
interpretation: The verse captures the moment of complete submission shared by Ibrahim and his son Isma'il: the father, obeying the command he received in a dream, prepared to sacrifice his son, while the son yielded willingly to the divine will. The phrase "aslama" points to the essence of islam, the surrender of the whole self to God, which is enacted here not merely in words but in the readiness to give up what is most beloved. The laying down upon the forehead conveys the seriousness and totality of that surrender, and it is precisely this perfect submission that the subsequent ransom with a great sacrifice honours, showing that God desires the heart's submission rather than the act of bloodshed itself.

translation: And We called out to him, "O Ibrahim (Abraham)!"
interpretation: The verse marks the moment of direct divine address to Ibrahim, a call that signals his selection and nearness to God. Coming after the trials described just before it, the call highlights that Ibrahim's faithfulness was met with God's immediate attention, and that the prophetic mission begins with God's own voice reaching him, establishing the bond of close, personal communication between the Creator and His chosen servant.

translation: You have indeed fulfilled the vision. Thus do We reward the good-doers.
interpretation: The verse comes from the story of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph), spoken after the dream of the king's cupbearer or baker is realized. It affirms that the divine vision was true and fulfilled exactly as interpreted, showing that dreams can carry real knowledge from God when rightly understood. The closing principle, that God rewards those who do good, is stated as a general law: Yusuf's steadfast patience, chastity, sincerity, and trust in God during his imprisonment were met with honor, deliverance, and eventual authority. The verse thus links faithful conduct under hardship with the certainty of divine recompense.

translation: Indeed, this is surely the manifest trial.
interpretation: The verse refers to the test of Moses and the Children of Israel, as in the context of Surah As-Saffat (37:106), where God says that the deliverance of Abraham's son was itself a manifest trial. The word "balaa'" here denotes a test that reveals what is in a person's heart: whether they will submit with patience and gratitude when given a hardship, or whether they will falter. The clear trial is therefore not merely suffering but an examination that brings out true faith, showing that ease and hardship alike are means by which God distinguishes the sincere believer from the heedless.

translation: And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.
interpretation: This verse, from the story of Abraham and Ishmael (As-Saffat 37:107), describes God's redemption of the son offered in obedience. The 'great sacrifice' (dhibhin 'azim) signifies that the divine command was a test of submission, and that God accepted the willingness of the father and son in place of the act itself. It teaches that true devotion is measured by sincere surrender to God, and that God's mercy substitutes a ransom for what faith was prepared to give, establishing the sacrifice as a lasting remembrance of obedience and generosity.

translation: And We left for him (a good mention) among the later generations.
interpretation: The verse, found in Surah As-Saffat (37:78) in the context of Prophet Abraham, indicates that Allah preserved a lasting good remembrance of Abraham among those who come after him. Abraham's honor is so widely recognized that he is revered by the followers of the three Abrahamic faiths, and this enduring praise is itself a sign of the sincerity and devotion for which he was chosen. The verse thus teaches that true righteousness leaves a legacy that outlasts a person's lifetime, and that Allah grants lasting esteem to those who are steadfast in faith and submission to Him.

translation: Peace be upon Abraham.
interpretation: This brief verse (As-Saffat 37:109) is a divine greeting of peace bestowed upon Abraham after his steadfastness in submission to God, including his willingness to sacrifice his son and his faithfulness through trials. It honors him as a model of devotion, and the greeting marks God's acceptance of his righteousness, showing that those who sincerely submit to God are granted lasting honor and peace in the memory of later generations.

translation: Thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: The verse presents divine recompense as a general law: those who act with ihsan, perfecting their conduct and performing their deeds sincerely and excellently, will be rewarded by God. The word 'thus' (kadhalika) links this reward to the preceding context, indicating that God's justice and generosity toward the righteous follow a consistent pattern. It conveys that excellence in worship and in dealing with others is never lost before God, and that the reward is given according to the quality of the good done, reminding the believer that sincerity and beauty of action are themselves the path to divine favor.

translation: Indeed, he was among Our servants, the believers.
interpretation: The verse testifies to the high station of the one it describes by placing him among 'Our servants' (ʿibādinā), a title of honor that God bestows on the righteous, and by specifying that he is among the 'believers' (al-mu'minīn), indicating that his faith was sincere and firm. Being counted among God's believing servants is presented as the highest distinction, since it unites true faith with humble devotion and the intimate relationship of servanthood to the Creator.

translation: And We gave him good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous.
interpretation: The verse points to the tender mercy of God toward Abraham, who is given the glad tidings of Isaac as a prophet, after years of longing for a child. The phrase "from among the righteous" shows that prophethood here is joined with uprightness of character, indicating that the honor God bestows on His servants is rooted in their righteousness. Isaac's selection as a prophet also confirms that the blessing of guidance continued through Abraham's line, as God had promised, and it reminds the believer that God's gifts often arrive at the moment when human hope seems most distant.

translation: And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are the good-doer and the one who wrongs himself openly.
interpretation: The verse shows that divine blessing upon the forefathers does not automatically pass to all their offspring; lineage alone is not a guarantee of righteousness. Within the same family line there are those who do good and those who clearly wrong their own souls through disobedience, so each person is judged by their own conduct. Blessing is thus tied to a person's deeds, and the verse warns against relying on ancestral merit while neglecting one's own responsibility before God.

translation: And We had already bestowed Our favor upon Moses and Aaron.
interpretation: The verse opens with 'wa-laqad' (and indeed), a emphatic particle signaling that what follows is a settled, well-known divine kindness. The word 'mannā' (We bestowed favor) comes from the root m-n-n, and in the Qur'an divine favor ('minna') is often given without the recipient having earned it, which highlights that Moses and Aaron's prophethood and deliverance were acts of pure grace. By pairing the two brothers, the verse frames them as partners in a single mission, and the broader passage (37:114-122) goes on to recount their deliverance and the Israelites' rescue from great distress, which reminds the listener that God's favor often arrives as salvation after hardship.

translation: And We saved them and their people from the great distress.
interpretation: This verse refers to the deliverance of Musa (Moses) and Harun (Aaron) together with their people from the great calamity that afflicted them, most likely the oppression and torment inflicted by Pharaoh and his regime.
