interpretation: The verse speaks of a select group of prophets, most likely those named just before it (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and others in Surah Sad 38:45–47), praising them as chosen by God and virtuous. Their election (istifa') is not a mere privilege but a divine distinction grounded in their righteousness, and the word 'al-akhyar' (the excellent) signals that moral goodness is what marks out the truly chosen. The verse thus invites believers to see prophetic status as bound up with ethical excellence, and reminds them that God's favor rests on those who embody that excellence before Him.

translation: And mention Ishmael, Elisha, and Dhul-Kifl, for each of them was among the good ones.
interpretation: The verse places these three prophets among the 'akhyar' (the good and chosen), a title that signals how the Qur'an groups them within a single line of righteous servants who were purified and guided. By commanding the Prophet to 'remember' them, the verse turns the recounting of their stories into a form of moral instruction: their steadfastness in duty, patience under trial, and devotion to God are set forth as models for the believers to emulate. The brevity of the mention, with no detail given, also invites reflection on the shared character of these chosen servants rather than on their individual histories, emphasizing that goodness, not lineage or circumstance alone, is what elevates a person in God's sight.

translation: This is a reminder. And indeed, for the righteous there is a good place of return.
interpretation: The verse opens by calling what precedes it a 'dhikr', a reminder that recalls the human soul to its origin and purpose, so that the believer does not forget the covenant with God. It then turns to those who are mindful of God (al-muttaqun), who guard themselves against wrongdoing through awareness of their Lord, and promises them a 'husn ma'ab', a beautiful place of return. The word ma'ab signifies the final homecoming to God, so the verse ties present piety to the ultimate destiny: the goodness of the end is the fruit of conscious fear and devotion in this life, and the reminder itself is the means by which a person is guided toward that homecoming.

translation: Gardens of perpetual residence, whose doors will be opened for them.
interpretation: The verse portrays the reward of the righteous as a dwelling of lasting settlement ('adn, meaning to abide and remain), not a passing stay. The phrase 'its doors opened for them' conveys honor and immediate welcome: nothing bars the believers from entry, and they are received as honored guests rather than admitted grudgingly. It thus joins the promise of permanence with the assurance of unhindered access, inviting the reader to hold onto faith and good deeds with the hope of a home that will never be lost.

translation: Reclining therein, they will call for abundant fruit and drink.
interpretation: The verse portrays the people of Paradise in a state of complete ease and honor: reclining in comfort, they are free to ask for whatever they desire, and what is granted is abundant rather than scarce. The fruit and drink mentioned stand for the full satisfaction of bodily and spiritual delight that the believers will enjoy without any lack or anxiety. The imagery of reclining and calling freely reflects a station of security, dignity, and fulfillment, in which the pleasures of the hereafter are presented as generous, plentiful, and completely unrestricted.

translation: And with them will be women restraining their gaze, [and] equal in age.
interpretation: The verse describes the spouses awaiting the righteous in Paradise as chaste companions who are devoted only to their husbands and do not look with desire upon others, and who are of matching age, so that the bond of love is complete and free from the disparities that often trouble earthly marriages. This points to the perfection of the joys of Paradise, where the believer's companionship is pure, harmonious, and free of jealousy or discord, and where the highest reward is shown to be not only in sensory delight but in the serenity and dignity of intimate fellowship.

translation: This is what you were promised, for the Day of Reckoning.
interpretation: The verse addresses the righteous, announcing that the reward promised to them is now at hand, and that it is kept for the Day of Reckoning, when every soul will be called to account for its deeds. It reminds the believer that accountability is certain and that the promise of God is not forgotten, so one should live with awareness that every action will be weighed on that Day.

translation: Indeed, this is Our provision; it has no end or exhaustion.
interpretation: The verse, spoken in the context of the blessings of Paradise, points to the perfection of divine provision: what is granted to the people of Paradise is not a temporary supply that diminishes with use, as worldly provisions do, but an unending bounty that never runs out. Its mention of 'Our provision' attributes these gifts directly to God's generosity, indicating that the blessings of the hereafter are a direct expression of the Lord's boundless mercy and power, and that the believers' satisfaction there will never be interrupted by scarcity, loss, or the fear of depletion.

translation: This (is a reminder). And indeed, for the transgressors is an evil place of return.
interpretation: The verse closes the description of the righteous in the preceding passage by drawing a sharp contrast: after the reminder of the blessed gardens prepared for the God-fearing, it turns to those who are overstepping bounds, rebelling against God and His guidance. Their 'return' (ma'ab) is not a home of peace or rest but the Hellfire toward which their own choices lead them. The word 'taghin' suggests excess and arrogance, a persistent transgression of limits, and the verse teaches that the ultimate destination of every person is determined by the path they chose in this life, so that the believer is reminded to weigh their own conduct against the reality of the final return.

translation: Hell — they will burn therein, and wretched is the resting-place.
interpretation: The verse presents the final destination of those who turn away from truth as a place of burning from which there is no escape, and it underscores the moral consequence of their choices: the bed they prepared for themselves in this life becomes, in the Hereafter, a place of dreadful repose. The word 'mihad' (resting-place or cradle) is pointedly ironic, since what is normally a place of comfort and rest is described as the opposite, inviting the listener to reflect that a life of heedlessness and rejection of God's guidance leads to a bitter end rather than to ease.

translation: This, so let them taste it: boiling water and dark, pus-like discharge.
interpretation: The verse presents the punishment of the wrongdoers as an immediate, sensory reality they are commanded to experience. The phrase "فليذوقوه" (let them taste it) uses the imperative with the language of tasting, which conveys both the bitterness of the torment and the inescapability of its consequence. The two items named, scalding fluid (حميم) and a foul, cold, putrid liquid (غساق), are paired to suggest the extremes of the torment: an unbearable heat and an unbearable cold and repulsiveness. The contrast between these two opposites emphasizes that no comfort or relief awaits them, and the verse thus turns the deeds of the wrongdoers back upon them as the very substance of their recompense.

translation: And [there are] others of similar kind, in pairs.
interpretation: The phrase 'min shaklihi azwaj' points to the manifold and matched nature of the torment prepared for the rebellious. Following the description of the boiling water and the dark, putrid liquid, the verse indicates that the chastisement is not a single kind but comes in varied forms, each paired with another of its own sort, so that the punishment of the transgressors is complete and fitting, leaving no aspect of their wrongdoing unrequited.

translation: This is a host rushing in with you. No welcome for them; indeed they will burn in the Fire.
interpretation: The verse depicts the scene of the Fire in which a group of the misguided, having followed their predecessors into disbelief, is driven in together with those they once followed. Their entry is met with a curt rejection, "no welcome for them," signaling that the bond of company that united them in the world yields no honor or mercy in the Hereafter. The Qur'anic phrasing conveys that every soul bears the consequence of its own choices, and that the crowd rushing into the Fire will find no comfort in numbers, for the reckoning falls upon each of them and they are destined for the burning that their deeds had earned.

translation: They will say: Rather, it is you! There is no welcome for you. You have brought this upon us, so what a wretched abode it is.
interpretation: This verse depicts the mutual reproach of the followers and their leaders in the Fire. When the followers are met by the leaders, the leaders are rebuked and the followers answer them with the same kind of harsh greeting, placing on them the responsibility for leading them into disbelief. The phrase "you brought this upon us" shows that misguidance is shared: those who led others astray bear the burden of their own misdeeds and of those they misled, and no one can escape accountability by blaming another. The closing words "what a wretched abode" reveal that the Fire itself is the resting place that their own choices prepared, a sober reminder that every person is answerable for the path they chose to follow.

translation: They will say, "Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, increase for him a double punishment in the Fire."
interpretation: The verse depicts the people of the Fire, in their torment, turning to blame those who led them astray. Their cry reveals that they recognize the source of their misguidance, yet it does not spare them from their own responsibility. The request for a doubled punishment for their misleaders reflects the Qur'anic principle that those who call others to error bear a share of the burden of the sin they caused, as in the saying that whoever establishes an evil practice carries its weight and the weight of those who follow it. The verse thus conveys that the punishment of the Fire is shaped by justice, where every soul is answerable for what it did, while the misleaders are not excused from the harm they spread.

translation: And they will say: 'What is wrong with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the wicked?'
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Sad (38:62), depicts the people of the Fire questioning their own state in the Hereafter. Having been blinded in the world by their judgments, they assumed that the believers they once mocked and reckoned as evil were absent from the scene of reward. Their question reveals a reversal of values: the criteria they used on earth to label people as wicked are exposed as false, and the conspicuous absence of those they despised signals that the true measure of people is their faith and righteousness, not worldly standing. It is a warning that a person's habit of dismissing the sincere as malefactors can become a source of bewilderment and regret when reality is unveiled.

translation: Did we take them as objects of mockery, or have their eyes turned away from them?
interpretation: The verse is spoken in the context of the unbelievers in the Hereafter, who look around in the Fire and wonder why the people they once mocked in this world are not among them. Their question reveals a double bewilderment: they ask whether they had wrongly taken the believers as objects of ridicule, or whether the believers have simply vanished from their sight, as though their eyes had failed to find them. The rhetorical form lays bare the inner confusion of the arrogant, whose scorn for the faithful in worldly life is shown to have been built on false measures, and whose own gaze, once so quick to mock, now finds nothing but their own loss. It is a warning that worldly standards of honor and contempt collapse before the truth of the Hereafter, where the true position of each soul becomes manifest.

translation: Indeed, that is the truth: the dwellers of the Fire disputing with one another.
interpretation: The verse points to the reality of the bitter quarrel among those in the Hellfire, which is set within the wider context of the Surah (Sad, 38:64) where it follows the account of the people of the Fire being shown their fate. It affirms that this mutual argument is not mere imagination but a true and certain event. The dispute reveals the futility of their earlier loyalties and false leaders: the followers and their leaders blame each other, and each seeks to shift responsibility onto the other. By presenting this scene as truth, the verse warns the listener that worldly pride, blind following, and misguidance will turn into mutual recrimination and regret in the Hereafter, when no justification will avail.

translation: Say, "I am only a warner. And there is no deity except Allah, the One, the Subduer (Irresistible)."
interpretation: The verse places the Prophet in his true role: he is a warner, not a source of power over the unseen or a divine being, and his mission rests on one core truth, that there is no god but Allah. The two closing names, al-Wahid (the One, with no partner or equal) and al-Qahhar (the Subduer, whose dominion is absolute and irresistible), frame that tawhid as both a matter of pure oneness and of total sovereignty. The warning is thus inseparable from the proclamation of God's unity: to hear the message is to face the reality that all power belongs to the One who cannot be overcome, and to respond accordingly.

translation: The Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, the Mighty, the Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse opens by affirming God's absolute lordship over all of creation, the vast heavens, the earth, and everything that lies between them, which points the believer to a sovereignty that encompasses the whole cosmos and leaves nothing outside His dominion. The two divine names that close it balance each other: al-'AzIz, the Mighty, whose power is unassailable and whose rule cannot be resisted, and al-Ghaffar, the One who repeatedly covers over sins and forgives. Read together, they teach that the same Lord who holds absolute power over everything is also the One who readily pardons those who turn back to Him, so that awe at His might is joined with hope in His mercy.

translation: Say: It is a momentous news.
interpretation: The verse introduces the Qur'an (or the matter it conveys) as a great and weighty announcement, directing the Prophet to proclaim it with emphasis. The word "nabaʾ" denotes news of real consequence, and calling it "ʿaẓīm" (great) signals that its importance is not trivial: it concerns the truth of prophethood, resurrection, and the accountability that follows. The imperative "Say" places the burden of delivery on the messenger, while the subsequent verses in the surah show that the listeners' heedlessness toward this news is precisely what makes it so striking.

translation: "And you turn away from it" (or: "you are averse to it").
interpretation: The phrase is addressed to those who disregard or refuse the message being presented to them. It rebukes the listeners for their deliberate aversion: they are not ignorant of the truth so much as they consciously turn their backs on it. The verse highlights that the failure lies not in a lack of evidence but in a heedless, self-chosen indifference that leaves them unprepared to accept guidance when it reaches them.

translation: I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly when they were disputing.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by the Prophet Muhammad, instructed to tell his listeners that he had no prior knowledge of the heavenly council's debate about the creation of Adam, which was revealed to him only by divine inspiration. This affirms that his knowledge of the unseen comes solely from God, thereby establishing the authenticity of his prophethood against those who doubted that the account of the angels' dispute could come from a mere human. The verse thus turns the argument back on the disbelievers: a man who had never witnessed these events could only know them through revelation.

translation: "It is only revealed to me that I am but a clear warner." (Qur'an 38:70, Surah Sad)
interpretation: The verse establishes the limits of the Prophet's mission: his sole authority derives from divine revelation, and his role is confined to conveying a plain and unambiguous warning. By emphasizing that he is only a warner, it shows that he holds no power to compel belief or to control outcomes, and that the responsibility lies in delivering the message clearly. The word "mubin" (clear) signals that the warning must be free of obscurity, so that the listener has no excuse for failing to understand what is at stake, leaving the choice of acceptance or rejection to the one addressed.

translation: When your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to create a human being from clay."
interpretation: The verse sets the creation of Adam as a deliberate, announced decision of God, made known to the angels before it happened. By calling the first human simply "basharan" (a human being, emphasizing his physical, mortal nature) and tying his origin to clay, it highlights humanity's modest material substance joined to a lofty divine purpose. The announcement to the angels anticipates the later test of Adam's position as God's vicegerent on earth, and it shows that human beings are honored not by their origin in clay but by the breath of God and the knowledge God grants them.

translation: So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, then fall down to him in prostration.
interpretation: The verse describes the moment of the creation of Adam: after God gives him his complete form and breathes into him from His spirit, the angels are commanded to prostrate before him. The breath of God's spirit marks the honor and distinction of the human being, lifting him above the rest of creation and making him the bearer of a unique divine dignity. The prostration is not worship of Adam himself but an act of obedience to God and recognition of the special trust placed in humankind, a trust that the angels, who had questioned the creation of a being who would cause corruption, were now called upon to acknowledge.

translation: So the angels prostrated themselves, all of them together.
interpretation: The verse shows the immediate and complete obedience of the angels to God's command to honor Adam. Their prostration is total and unanimous, with none of them holding back or hesitating, in contrast with Iblis, who refused. It teaches that true submission to the divine command is whole-hearted and collective, and that honoring what God has chosen is itself an act of worship of Him.

translation: Except Iblis, who refused in arrogance; he was among the disbelievers.
interpretation: This phrase, drawn from the story of Adam's creation in Surah al-Baqarah (2:34) and elsewhere, shows that Iblis's downfall was rooted in pride (istikbar) rather than mere ignorance. When God commanded the angels to prostrate before Adam, Iblis considered himself superior, having been created from fire while Adam was created from clay, and so his refusal became an act of open rejection of God's command. The verse teaches that arrogance toward divine guidance is itself a gateway to disbelief, since it leads a person to place his own judgment above the clear word of God. Iblis is thus presented as the archetype of the proud soul that refuses to submit, and the verse warns the believer that humility before God's command is the true safeguard of faith.

translation: He said, "O Iblis, what prevented you from prostrating to that which I created with My two hands? Did you become arrogant, or were you among the exalted?"
interpretation: The verse presents God's direct challenge to Iblis after his refusal to prostrate to Adam, and it shows that the true root of his disobedience was not ignorance but pride. By asking whether he grew arrogant or considered himself among the exalted, God exposes the inner disease of self-elevation that led Iblis to measure himself against the command of his Creator. The phrase "created with My two hands" honors Adam with a special mark of divine care and distinction, so the refusal becomes an act of contempt toward what God had uniquely honored. The verse thus warns that arrogance, when it claims superiority over divine wisdom, is the gateway to rebellion and ruin.

translation: He said, "I am better than him; You created me from fire, and You created him from clay."
interpretation: This verse records Iblis's refusal to prostrate before Adam when God commanded the angels to do so. His refusal rests on a claim of superiority based on material origin: he regards fire as nobler than clay. The interpretation lies in the sin of arrogance (kibr) that stems from judging worth by one's substance rather than by obedience to the Creator's command. By setting his own reasoning against the explicit divine order, he exposes the root of disobedience, which is pride, and shows how a self-assessment of superiority can lead a being to reject truth and submission.

translation: He said, "Then get out of it, for indeed you are accursed."
interpretation: This verse is God's command to Iblis (Satan) after his refusal to prostrate before Adam. Being cast out of the heavenly abode signifies his expulsion from divine mercy and nearness due to his arrogance and disobedience. The word "rajim" carries the sense of one who is stoned or driven away, and it points to the state of being rejected and distanced from God's grace. The verse teaches that pride in the face of clear divine command leads to banishment from the sphere of God's favor, and it establishes the framework of the enmity between Satan and humankind that the following verses develop.

translation: And indeed, upon you is My curse until the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: This verse is part of Iblis's expulsion from the presence of God after his refusal to prostrate to Adam. God declares that the curse will rest upon him until the Day of Recompense, marking the complete severance of his standing before God. The phrase 'until the Day of Judgment' signifies that the curse is bounded in time, extending to the final reckoning, when every soul will be judged for its deeds. It underscores that arrogance and disobedience to a clear command lead to exile from divine mercy, and that the consequences of such rebellion persist until the ultimate accountability.

translation: He said: My Lord, then reprieve me until the day they are resurrected.
interpretation: This is the request of Iblis (Satan) after his refusal to prostrate to Adam, when he asks God for respite until the Day of Resurrection. The request is granted in a later verse, but its purpose is not mercy: it reveals his intention to mislead humankind for as long as he is given room to do so. The verse shows that the defiant tempter seeks to postpone his accountability and to extend his influence over the children of Adam, and it reminds the believer that the time granted to evil is a test, not a sign of approval, and that the final reckoning on the Day of Resurrection is certain.

translation: He said: "Indeed, you are among those given respite."
interpretation: This verse records Iblis's request, after his refusal to prostrate to Adam, to be granted respite until the Day of Resurrection, and God's answer that he is indeed among those reprieved. The granting of respite is not an honor or a sign of favor but a trial and a permitted delay that allows the consequences of disobedience to unfold. It teaches that God gives the wrongdoer room to act, so that his persistence in arrogance and rebellion becomes his own undoing, while the believer is reminded that every moment of life is a test in which the choice between obedience and the whisperings of the devil is real.

translation: ...until a known appointed day.
interpretation: The phrase 'ila yawm al-waqt al-ma'lum' (until the appointed known time/day) refers to a fixed, predetermined term set by God, after which a matter reaches its completion. It conveys that every affair, whether the lifespan of a person or the duration of a respite granted to a people, has a definite limit known only to God, so that nothing is hastened or delayed beyond the time He has decreed, and it points the believer toward patience and trust in the divine timing.

translation: He said: "By Your might, I will surely mislead them all,"
interpretation: Iblis, having been cursed and expelled for refusing to prostrate to Adam, swears by God's majesty and power that he will lead all of humanity astray. The oath reveals that his enmity is directed at the children of Adam as a consequence of his own arrogance, and it shows that he seeks to turn people away from God's path through deception and temptation. The verse also implicitly reminds the reader that God's power is absolute, and that the only protection against such misguidance lies in sincere devotion to God, as the following verses make clear through the exception of the sincere servants of God.

translation: Except Your sincere servants among them.
interpretation: The verse refers to the exception made by Iblis (Satan) in his oath to mislead humanity: he will not be able to lead astray those servants of God who have been purified and made sincere (mukhlasin) in their devotion. The word "mukhlasin" is read with a kasra on the lam by those who mean those whom God has chosen and purified, and this indicates that sincerity is not merely a human achievement but also a divine gift. The verse thus teaches that true protection from misguidance lies in sincerely devoting oneself to God, since a heart made wholly sincere for Him is beyond the reach of Satan's deceptions.

translation: He said: So the truth, and the truth I say.
interpretation: Here God's speech stands as its own guarantee: by repeating al-Haqq twice, He binds His absolute truthfulness to His word, so what He declares, including His oath to fill Hell with Iblis and those who follow him, is certain and cannot be altered. The verse thus answers the defiance of Iblis with a divine pledge that truth is both the basis of His command and the content of His promise.

translation: "I will surely fill Hell with you and with those among them who follow you, all together."
interpretation: The verse, spoken by Iblis in response to Allah's command to the angels to prostrate before Adam, expresses a solemn divine decree that disobedience and the following of misguidance bring a shared fate. It shows that the leader who misleads and those who choose to follow him are bound together in accountability, and that the consequence of rejecting divine guidance is certain and inescapable. The emphatic oath-like phrasing (la-) underscores that this judgment is firm and that no one who chooses to follow the path of arrogance and deception can escape its result.

translation: Say: "I do not ask you for any reward for it, and I am not one of the pretentious."
interpretation: The verse shows that the Prophet's call was sincere and free of worldly motive: he asks no payment or material gain from those he addresses, so his message stands on its own merit. By disclaiming any pretense or affectation (takalluf), he affirms that he speaks only what he has been commanded to convey, without adding to it or claiming a status beyond that of a messenger. This sets a standard for all who call others to truth, that their aim should be sincerity and their words free of vanity or contrived display.

translation: It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an, or the message it carries, is solely a reminder (dhikr) addressed to all of creation, not to one people alone. Its purpose is to recall humanity to what is already present in their nature and in the primordial covenant with God: awareness of the Creator, accountability, and the truth of guidance. By calling it a reminder rather than a novelty, the verse presents the revelation as a restoration of an ancient and universal message, whose benefit extends to every rational being who is willing to heed it.

translation: And you will surely come to know its news after a while.
interpretation: The verse is a solemn warning spoken as a promise of certainty: whatever truth has been announced, whether a prophetic message or the reality it foretells, will become manifest in time. The phrase "after a while" (bad hin) indicates that the fulfilment is delayed rather than denied, so that the listener is called to patience and not to disbelief. Its reference to the disbelievers' scoffing at the warning is understood by many commentators as a reminder that human beings are not the judges of when divine truth will be shown, and that the reckoning, whether in this world or in the Hereafter, will surely reveal what was previously dismissed.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The opening of this surah establishes the divine origin and authority of the Book before anything else is said: its descent is not human composition but a revelation from Allah, whose attributes of might (al-Aziz) and wisdom (al-Hakim) guarantee that what it contains is both binding and purposeful. By placing the Name of Allah with the Names of mercy at the head of the Basmala, the verse also signals that this revelation, though it comes with power and judgment, flows from a mercy that precedes and encompasses it. The reader is thus invited to approach the Book with reverence for its majesty and trust in its wisdom.

translation: Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth. So worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion.
interpretation: The verse grounds the command to worship in the revelation itself: the Book was sent down with truth, so its call is not arbitrary but rooted in reality. The phrase "mukhlisan lahu al-din" makes sincerity (ikhlas) the defining condition of worship, meaning that every act of devotion must be directed to Allah alone, free from hypocrisy, show-seeking, and any associating of others with Him. Thus the Prophet is addressed first, implying that the core mission of revelation is to purify the heart's intention and restore pure monotheism as the foundation of religion.

translation: Surely, to God belongs pure religion. And those who take protectors besides Him say, "We only worship them so that they may bring us nearer to God in closeness." Indeed, God will judge between them concerning that over which they differ. Indeed, God does not guide one who is a liar and ungrateful.
interpretation: The verse establishes that sincere devotion (al-din al-khalis) belongs exclusively to God, and it exposes the flawed logic of those who take intermediaries as objects of worship on the pretext that these beings draw them closer to God. Such a claim turns intercession into a substitute for the direct relationship with God that true faith requires. The verse closes by affirming that God is the final judge of their disputes, and that guidance is withheld from those who persist in falsehood and ingratitude, meaning that the root of misguidance lies in a willful choice to deny the truth rather than in any lack of clarity about it.

translation: Had God wished to take a son, He would have chosen whomever He willed from what He creates. Glory be to Him! He is God, the One, the Subduer.
interpretation: The verse refutes the claim that God has a son by showing that the very idea presupposes a need or a choice that is unbecoming of the absolutely self-sufficient Creator. If He were to choose any offspring, it would be by His sovereign will from among His creation, which would make the chosen one a created being subject to Him rather than a partner in His divine nature. The declaration of His glory (tasbih) places Him beyond all such attributions, and the closing names, the One and the Subduer, affirm His absolute unity and His dominion over all things, leaving no room for a rival, a partner, or a begotten son.

translation: He created the heavens and the earth in truth. He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night, and He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term. Unquestionably, He is the Mighty, the Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse presents the creation of the heavens and earth as an act grounded in truth rather than in vanity, and it points to the orderly alternation of night and day, the subjection of the sun and moon, and their courses toward an appointed end, as evidence that the Creator is the one who governs the cosmos with wisdom and purpose. The image of the night and day 'wrapping' over one another conveys a smooth, continuous enfolding of light into darkness and darkness into light, inviting reflection on the gradual and seamless nature of divine order. The closing divine names, al-'Aziz (the Mighty, whose power is absolute) and al-Ghaffar (the Constant Forgiver), juxtapose majestic sovereignty with mercy, suggesting that the same One who ordains the cosmos with immense power is abundantly forgiving toward His creatures, so that awareness of cosmic order should lead to humility and hope in divine pardon.

translation: He created you from a single soul, then made from it its mate, and He sent down for you eight kinds of livestock in pairs. He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation, in three layers of darkness. That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs the dominion. There is no deity except Him, so how are you turned away?
interpretation: The verse moves from the origin of humanity in a single soul to the detailed stages of human formation within the womb, presenting the unfolding of life in successive creations through three veils of darkness as a sign of divine power and wisdom. By grounding the reality of Divine Lordship in both the human origin and the provision of livestock, it invites reflection that the One who shapes life step by step in hidden darkness alone deserves sovereignty and worship, and it rebukes the heedless who turn away from this clear truth.

translation: If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is free of need from you. And He does not approve disbelief for His servants; but if you are grateful, He approves it for you. And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you of what you used to do. Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts.
interpretation: The verse establishes that God's self-sufficiency is absolute: human faith or unbelief adds nothing to or subtracts anything from Him, yet He does not will disbelief for His servants as a good for them, since it is a corruption of the innate disposition in which they were created. Gratitude, by contrast, is the path He approves, and it returns its benefit to the one who practices it. Moral responsibility is strictly individual, so each soul answers only for its own deeds, and the reckoning at the return to the Lord will disclose every action. Finally, the mention of His knowledge of what the breasts conceal reminds the believer that intentions, not merely outward conduct, are fully known to God, which makes sincere inner orientation the true measure of accountability.

translation: And when harm touches a person, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance; then when He grants him a favor from Himself, he forgets what he had been calling upon Him for before, and sets up rivals to God in order to lead others astray from His way. Say: "Enjoy your disbelief for a little while; indeed, you are among the companions of the Fire."
interpretation: The verse exposes the inconsistency of the human heart in times of need and ease: when adversity strikes, a person sincerely turns to God, yet once blessing returns he quickly forgets that sincerity and attributes his well-being to other causes or deities. Setting up rivals to God is shown as both a personal lapse and a means of misguiding others, which makes the sin heavier. The closing command to say "Enjoy your disbelief for a little while" carries a stern warning that worldly comfort gained through ingratitude and denial is brief, and its end is the Fire, so the verse calls the listener to remember God in prosperity as sincerely as in distress.

translation: Is one who worships devoutly during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord (equal to one who does not)? Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know? Only the people of understanding take heed.
interpretation: The verse sets devout night worship, combining prostration and standing, as the mark of one whose heart is balanced between fear of the Hereafter and hope in God's mercy, and it presents the contrast with the ignorant as a question that the intellect itself must answer. By ending with 'people of understanding' (ulu al-albab), it links true knowledge not merely to information but to inner awareness that moves a person to devotion, so that learning and worship are shown as inseparable, and the one who truly knows is the one whose knowledge leads him to stand before his Lord in the night.

translation: Say, "O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord. For those who do good in this world is good, and the earth of God is spacious. Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account."
interpretation: The verse opens with a direct address to the believers, calling them "My servants," which joins the command of taqwa (God-consciousness) to a warm intimacy with the Lord. It then links good conduct in this world to a good reward, and it presents the vastness of God's earth as an invitation to emigrate from places where faith is oppressed, so that no believer is trapped in a place that prevents worship. Finally, it singles out patience as the quality that brings reward beyond measure, "without account," showing that steadfastness through hardship is among the highest forms of devotion and that God's generosity to the patient exceeds any calculation.

translation: Say, "Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion."
interpretation: The verse establishes that the central command given to the Prophet is pure monotheistic worship directed solely to Allah, and it specifies that this worship must be free of any association or hypocrisy. The word "mukhlisan" (sincere) points to the inner purity of intention: every act of devotion must be performed purely for God's sake, not for display, worldly gain, or the approval of people. By placing "religion" (al-din) as that which is made sincerely for Him, the verse shows that faith is not merely outward ritual but a total orientation of the heart and life toward God alone. The verse thus frames sincerity (ikhlas) as the essence of the message brought by all the prophets, the axis around which the rest of religious practice turns.

translation: And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims (those who submit).
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the Prophet as part of a declaration of his devotion to God (in Surah al-An'am, 6:14, and parallel passages), expresses the principle that true submission to God is a personal obligation that the believer takes up first and foremost. The phrase 'first of the Muslims' does not merely denote chronological priority but signifies leading by example: the one who is charged with conveying God's message must himself be the foremost in embodying the surrender of the will to the Divine. Thus the verse binds the authority of the messenger to his own exemplary sincerity, teaching that calling others to submission is credible only when one's own life is marked by complete devotion to God alone.

translation: Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous day.
interpretation: The verse places the Prophet in the role of one whose fear of God is the foundation of his obedience. Even a messenger chosen by God is commanded to declare that he himself is not exempt from accountability; his awareness of the Day of Judgment is what keeps him devoted to his Lord. The phrase "a tremendous day" conveys the immensity of that reckoning, and the conditional "if I disobey" teaches that fear of punishment is a motive for righteousness that every believer shares, whatever his station. The verse thus calls the listener to examine his own conduct in the light of the certainty of accountability and to let reverent fear of God restrain him from disobedience.

translation: Say, "It is Allah I worship, sincerely devoted to Him in my religion."
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet to declare that his worship is directed to Allah alone, and that he dedicates his faith to Him with pure sincerity, free of any associating of partners with Him. The repeated emphasis on the word "Allah" at the head of the statement, placed before the verb, signals exclusivity: worship is not shared, and the religion is entirely His. Sincere devotion (ikhlas) here is shown to be the essence of the message, a call for the heart and the act to be purified so that every form of devotion, belief and practice is directed toward God without hypocrisy or rivalry.

translation: So worship whatever you wish besides Him. Say, "Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss."
interpretation: The verse closes the address with a stark warning delivered as a divine permission that is in fact a rebuke: those who insist on worshipping other than God are free to do so, but the real consequence falls on themselves. The true loss is not material but existential and relational. By forfeiting their own souls through misplaced devotion, they also cost their families and dependents, who might have been guided by them, and this becomes fully evident on the Day of Resurrection when every illusion of gain collapses. The phrase "the manifest loss" emphasizes that this ruin is unmistakable and clear, underscoring that worldly profit pursued against faith is the greatest bankruptcy.

translation: For them there will be layers of fire above them, and beneath them layers (of fire) as well. That is what Allah instills fear with, to His servants. O My servants, then fear Me.
interpretation: The verse presents hell not merely as a place of punishment but as an encompassing reality: the believer's fear of God is meant to be awakened by imagining the fire pressing in from every side, leaving the soul no escape from its consequences except through taking refuge in God. The shift from the third person to the direct address "O My servants" turns the warning into an intimate call, suggesting that the true response to the terror of the Last Day is not dread that paralyzes but taqwa, a conscious and loving guarding of oneself in obedience, which is the only shelter that the fire cannot penetrate.

translation: And those who avoided the false gods, not worshipping them, and turned back in repentance to Allah — for them is good news. So give good tidings to My servants.
interpretation: The verse defines the true servants of God by two inseparable acts: turning away from every power that claims a worship due only to God (tāghūt, whatever transgresses its limits and is taken as an object of devotion), and turning penitently and devotedly toward Allah. Avoidance alone is not enough; the negative rejection must be completed by the positive return to God. Because they have made this double turn, the good news is addressed to them directly, and the verse's final command, 'give good tidings to My servants,' places them within the intimate circle of God's servants, whose identity is established by the choice of allegiance rather than by lineage or outward claim. The passage thus shows that the heart's orientation, freed from idols of every kind and directed wholly to the Divine, is the true ground of hope.

translation: Those who listen to the word and follow the best of it. Those are the ones whom Allah has guided, and those are the people of understanding.
interpretation: The verse describes a mark of sound guidance: a person who is open to hearing many kinds of speech, whether truth or falsehood, and who, having heard, deliberately chooses the most excellent of what is said. Their guidance is shown not merely by receiving words but by discernment that recognizes and adopts what is best, such as the clearest command, the most beautiful counsel, or the path closest to truth. Because such selection requires reflection and a sound heart, Allah names them the people of intellect, showing that true understanding is proven by its fruit in right choice and conduct.

translation: Is then one against whom the word of punishment has been justified [equivalent to one who will be in the Fire]? Would you then save the one who is in the Fire?
interpretation: The verse addresses the Prophet with a rhetorical question that underscores a fundamental truth about divine decree and human responsibility: guidance belongs to God alone. Once the word of punishment has become binding upon a person because of his persistent rejection and obstinacy, no human effort, however sincere or earnest, can rescue him. The Prophet's role is to convey the message clearly, and his grief over the disbelief of his people is thereby gently lifted, reminding him that he is not accountable for their choice. The verse thus calls the believer to strive in delivering the call with wisdom and compassion, while entrusting the outcome of guidance to the Almighty.

translation: But those who have feared their Lord will have chambers above which are built chambers, beneath which rivers flow. It is the promise of Allah; Allah does not fail in His promise.
interpretation: The verse draws a contrast between the fleeting, deceptive comforts of worldly life and the lasting reward prepared for the God-conscious. Taqwa, the awareness of God that shapes conduct, is the criterion that determines one's place in the Hereafter, not wealth or worldly status. The imagery of layered, elevated chambers with rivers flowing beneath them conveys both honor and abundance, and tiers of dwellings suggest that rank in the afterlife corresponds to the degree of one's piety. By calling it a promise of Allah who never breaks His word, the verse grounds the believer's hope in divine certainty, encouraging perseverance in righteousness even when the present world seems to favor the wicked.

translation: Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky, and He makes it flow as springs in the earth; then He brings forth by it crops of varying colors; then it withers and you see it turning yellow; then He makes it into crumbled debris. Indeed, in that is a reminder for those of understanding.
interpretation: The verse directs the reader's attention to the familiar cycle of rain, groundwater, plant growth, decay, and dissolution as a sign of God's power over creation and as a lesson about the transience of worldly life. The sequence of water descending, being channeled into springs, producing varied vegetation, then fading and crumbling mirrors the passage of human life from vitality to decline and ending. The phrase 'those of understanding' addresses the reflective mind, calling it to recognize in this ordinary natural process the signs of the Creator who sustains and then ends all things, and to draw from it a reminder to orient oneself toward what endures beyond the world.

translation: Is one whose heart Allah has expanded to Islam, so that he is upon light from his Lord, [equal to one whose heart is hardened against the remembrance of Allah? Those are in manifest error. Woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah; those are in clear error.]
interpretation: The verse sets two states of the human heart side by side: a heart opened by Allah to submission, which walks in light from its Lord, and a heart hardened against the remembrance of God, which has turned away from the very source of guidance. The contrast is not merely between two opinions but between two conditions of the inner self, so that the one whose breast Allah has expanded is shown to be on illumination that clarifies his path, while the hardened heart is left in a darkness that it has chosen by refusing to be reminded. The warning 'woe' is directed at hardness itself, implying that a heart that stops receiving admonition has lost its capacity to see, and that the remedy lies in turning back to remembrance through which the heart softens and light is received.

translation: God has sent down the best of speech, a Book consistent with itself and repeating its teachings. At it shiver the skins of those who fear their Lord; then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of God. That is the guidance of God, by which He guides whom He wills. And whomever God leaves astray, for him there is no guide.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an as the finest of speech, whose internal harmony and repeated themes make its message reach the deepest layers of the human being. The physical trembling of the skin and the softening of heart and body signal a sincere, embodied awe that turns from fear into tender remembrance of God, showing that true reverence is not merely intellectual but transforms the whole person. The closing lines make clear that this receptivity is itself a divine gift: guidance is God's choice to bestow, and one who is left to his own inclination has no one to lead him back.

translation: Is one who shields with his face the terrible torment on the Day of Resurrection [equal to one who is safe]? And it will be said to the wrongdoers: "Taste what you used to earn."
interpretation: The verse presents a stark contrast between the believer who is secure and the wrongdoer who is destined for punishment. The image of the disbeliever having to use his face to ward off the torment is a vivid depiction of his utter helplessness and humiliation: the face, the most honored part of the human being, becomes the very thing that must bear the brunt of the fire, as in other verses where faces are described as blackened. The rhetorical question leaves the obvious answer unspoken, emphasizing that the two can never be equal. The closing command, "Taste what you used to earn," frames the punishment as the natural consequence of one's own deeds, so that the torment is not arbitrary but the direct fruit of the earnings of one's own wrongdoing, and a reminder that every person will be held to account for what they acquired in this world.

translation: Those before them denied (the truth), so the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive.
interpretation: The verse points to a recurring pattern in history: when earlier communities rejected their messengers, their own denial drew them toward a reckoning they never anticipated. The phrase "from where they do not perceive" suggests that the danger was not seen coming, since people who are heedless of warnings tend to assume they are safe, and their complacency is precisely what leaves them exposed. The lesson addressed to the listeners is that persistent denial is itself a path to ruin, and that the truth should be received while there is still time to respond.

translation: So Allah made them taste disgrace in the worldly life, but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew.
interpretation: The verse shows that worldly humiliation is only a foretaste of a far greater punishment awaiting in the Hereafter, where the consequences of disbelief and defiance are unmistakably heavier than anything endured in this life. The closing phrase, "if only they knew," points to the root of their error: they were not ignorant of the truth through lack of means, but chose to neglect knowledge and reflection, so their failure to grasp the gravity of their end is itself a condemnation. The verse thus calls the reader to weigh the temporary against the eternal and to pursue true knowledge before it is too late.

translation: And We have certainly presented to the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, so that they might take heed.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an as a deliberate act of divine pedagogy: God does not merely command but illustrates, using parables, comparisons, and concrete images drawn from ordinary life so that abstract truths become graspable to every mind. The phrase 'from every kind of example' signals the comprehensiveness of this method, which addresses people of differing capacities and temperaments. The purpose stated, 'that they might remember' (or 'be mindful'), reveals that the aim of such examples is not intellectual display but awakening: the recollection of what the human soul already knows of its Creator, its accountability, and its origin, which heedlessness has dulled. Thus the verse invites the reader to approach the Qur'an reflectively, letting its similitudes pierce the veil of forgetfulness and turn the heart back toward remembrance.

translation: A Qur'an in Arabic, without any crookedness, that they may be mindful of God.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that the revelation was sent in a clear, eloquent Arabic tongue that is free of any deviation, contradiction, or distortion, so that its meaning is directly accessible to its hearers. Its straightness is the very reason it can guide people to God-consciousness: a message without crookedness leaves no excuse for confusion, and the clarity of its language is meant to open the way to taqwa, a watchful awareness of God that shapes conduct.

translation: God presents an example: a man owned by several partners who quarrel with one another, and a man belonging wholly to one master. Are the two alike in comparison? Praise be to God. But most of them do not know.
interpretation: The verse uses the image of a slave held by quarreling partners, each pulling him in different directions, against a slave devoted entirely to a single master, to show that the one who serves many conflicting lords cannot be at peace like the one who serves only one. Applied to belief, it exposes the divided soul that bows to many idols and competing desires, versus the sincere monotheist whose heart and devotion rest in the one God. The rhetorical question makes the answer self-evident, and the closing remark indicates that most people fail to grasp this plain truth, which is why they keep serving many masters.

translation: Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Az-Zumar (39:30), addresses the Prophet Muhammad directly and affirms the universal mortality of all human beings, including the Messenger himself, thereby dispelling any notion of his divinity or immortality. By declaring that both he and his opponents will die, it places the disputants on equal footing before death, reminding the believers that the true reckoning lies ahead, when all will be brought before their Lord to judge between them concerning their disputes.

translation: Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord will be disputing with one another.
interpretation: The verse places the human dispute at the center of the final reckoning: those who argued, denied, and blamed one another in this world will be brought face to face before their Lord, where the pretenses and mutual accusations that dominated worldly life are laid bare. The word 'takhtasimun' implies a back-and-forth contention in which each party attempts to shift responsibility, reminding the listener that no false claim, alliance, or worldly authority will shield anyone from the truth on that Day. It is a call to humility and sincerity now, since the disputes of this life will be resolved only by the Judge whose knowledge encompasses all things.

translation: So who is more unjust than one who lies about Allah and denies the truth when it has come to him? Is there not in Hell a residence for the disbelievers?
interpretation: The verse establishes a standard of judgment by posing a rhetorical question that leaves no room for doubt: the greatest wrongdoer is the one who both fabricates falsehood against God, attributing to Him what He did not say, and rejects the truth at the very moment it reaches him. The fault lies not in ignorance of the message but in the deliberate refusal of a truth that has clearly arrived. The closing question, answered implicitly, points to Hell as the fitting abode of those who persist in this disbelief, so that the consequence is presented as the natural outcome of a choice rather than an arbitrary punishment. The passage thus joins two offenses, slander against God and rejection of His revelation, showing that they are inseparable, since whoever invents lies about God will inevitably turn away from the truth that exposes those lies.

translation: And the one who brings the truth and confirms it - those are the righteous (al-muttaqun).
interpretation: The verse identifies two marks of the God-fearing: the one who brings the truth (the Prophet and those who convey the message) and the one who affirms it in his own conduct and belief (the believer who accepts and lives by it). The verse thus joins the role of the messenger who delivers the truth with the role of the believer who sincerely confirms it, and it makes taqwa the fruit of both: genuine piety is not merely speaking the truth but accepting it and being sincere in its acceptance, so that the words and the heart stand in agreement.

translation: They will have whatever they wish with their Lord. That is the reward of the good-doers.
interpretation: The verse points to a reward that exceeds human limitation: the believers' desires are not restricted or deferred, but are fully answered in the presence of their Lord, which signals that what is promised is complete and secure. The phrase "with their Lord" elevates the recompense beyond worldly goods to a nearness and honor granted by God Himself. By calling it the reward of the muhsinun, the verse ties this abundance to the quality of ihsan, that is, worship performed as if one sees God and good conduct toward others, showing that God's generosity is measured by sincerity and excellence in action.

translation: So that Allah may remove from them the worst of what they did and reward them with their best deeds, according to the best of what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse presents a dual mercy of God toward those who believe and do righteous deeds: He erases the gravest of their misdeeds, so that their sins do not define their record, and He rewards them not merely in proportion to their deeds but with a recompense surpassing them, as if their finest works are given precedence in the reckoning. It reveals that divine accounting is generous, forgiving the worst while magnifying the best, which should instill both hope in God's mercy and a drive to strive toward the excellence of one's deeds.

translation: Is not Allah sufficient for His servant? Yet they threaten you with those other than Him. And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.
interpretation: The verse assures the Prophet that God alone is sufficient protection and support for His servant, so he need not fear the idols and false deities his people set up as threats against him. Those who worship other than God possess no real power to harm or benefit, and their intimidation is hollow. The closing phrase reflects that guidance belongs to God's will: those who persistently reject the truth and turn away from it, God leaves to their chosen misguidance, and no one can guide them afterward. The passage thus strengthens trust in God's sufficiency while placing the responsibility for acceptance or rejection on the human heart's own choices.

translation: Whoever Allah guides, there is no misleader for him. Is not Allah Mighty, Owner of Retribution?
interpretation: The verse establishes that guidance and misguidance rest ultimately in the hands of Allah: the one whom He guides cannot be led astray by any other, because true guidance is His gift and no created power can override it. The closing question, by way of rhetorical affirmation, reminds the listener that the One who holds this absolute authority is almighty and not to be defied, and that His justice will take its course against those who persist in rejecting the truth. The interpretation thus joins two dimensions: the comfort of trust in divine guidance for the believer, and the sobering warning that those who turn away bear responsibility for their own deviation before a Lord who is both powerful and just.

translation: And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Have you considered what you invoke besides Allah? If Allah should intend harm for me, could they remove His harm? Or if He intends mercy for me, could they withhold His mercy?" Say, "Sufficient for me is Allah; upon Him rely those who rely."
interpretation: The verse exposes an inconsistency in the position of the polytheists: they acknowledge that Allah alone is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, yet they direct worship to others besides Him. Having conceded that the creation belongs to Allah, the Prophet is commanded to ask them to reflect on the idols they call upon, since none of them can avert a harm that Allah wills nor withhold a mercy He wishes to grant. The argument thus shows that power over harm and benefit rests with Allah alone, so reliance and trust must be placed in Him exclusively, as the Prophet declares that Allah is sufficient for him.

translation: Say: O my people, work according to your position; indeed, I am working. So you will soon know
interpretation: The verse sets out a principled parting of ways between the Prophet and those who reject his message. Rather than engaging in further argument or compromise, he is commanded to announce a clear separation: each party acts upon its own course and stance, and the outcome will reveal who was right. The phrase "according to your position" (ʿalā makānatikum) conveys that the disbelievers are free to persist in their chosen state, while the believer continues steadfastly in his own path. The closing "so you will soon know" points to a certainty of accountability, whether in this worldly life through the triumph of truth or in the Hereafter, when the consequences of every action become manifest. The verse thus teaches steadfastness in the face of opposition and places final judgment in God's hands rather than in human disputation.

translation: Whoever will receive a punishment that disgraces him, and upon him will descend a lasting torment.
interpretation: The verse portrays the fate of the wrongdoer in two stages: first a worldly humiliation that strips him of dignity and exposes his falsehood before others, and then a punishment that does not end, settling upon him as a consequence he cannot escape. The pairing of disgrace with everlasting torment suggests that the outward shame of this life is a foretaste of an enduring reckoning, urging the listener to recognize that defiance of God brings degradation both here and in the hereafter.

translation: Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book for mankind in truth. So whoever is guided, it is for his own soul; and whoever strays, he only strays to its detriment. And you are not a guardian over them.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the revelation is given to all of humanity with the truth as its foundation, and that guidance and misguidance are each individual's own responsibility, since the benefit or harm of one's choice falls upon the self alone. It consoles the Prophet by clarifying that his role is to convey the message, not to compel belief or to hold people accountable for their acceptance; the final judgment of their choices belongs to God, who alone watches over all affairs.

translation: Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died during their sleep. He retains those upon whom He has decreed death and releases the others until a specified term. Indeed, in that are signs for a people who reflect.
interpretation: The verse presents sleep as a kind of partial, temporary taking of the soul, paralleling death as its complete form, so that the nightly withdrawal of consciousness and its return each morning becomes a continual reminder of the greater reality of death and resurrection. The distinction drawn between the souls retained and those released to a appointed term points to the sovereignty of God over the moment of every soul's departure, a truth that is apprehended not through mere observation but through reflective contemplation, which is why the verse closes by singling out those who think deeply as the ones who truly perceive its signs.

translation: Or have they taken intercessors besides Allah? Say, "Even if they own nothing and do not reason?"
interpretation: The verse confronts those who take objects of worship as intercessors besides Allah by exposing the absurdity of their choice: these intercessors possess no power over anything and lack any faculty of understanding, so how could they be fit to mediate with the One who alone owns all intercession? The rhetorical question ("even if they...") shows that lifelessness and absence of reason disqualify them outright, and it calls the listener to reflect on the emptiness of seeking help from what cannot benefit or perceive. True intercession belongs to Allah alone, as the Qur'an elsewhere states that no one may intercede except by His permission.

translation: Say: To Allah belongs all intercession. To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; then to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the power of intercession is entirely in Allah's hands, not in those who are worshipped besides Him. Since all sovereignty over the heavens and earth belongs to Him alone, no one can intercede except by His permission, and the true source of any benefit sought through intercession is Him. The closing reminder that you will ultimately be returned to Him directs the believer's attention to accountability, urging that one's hope and fear be directed solely toward the One to whom all matters ultimately return, rather than toward intermediaries who possess no independent authority.

translation: And when Allah alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter recoil with aversion; but when those other than Him are mentioned, behold, they rejoice.
interpretation: The verse exposes a telltale sign of hypocrisy and spiritual sickness: the heart's true inclination is revealed not by what a person claims but by how it reacts to remembrance. Where the Oneness of God is proclaimed, the unbeliever's heart contracts in revulsion, because pure monotheism demands the surrender of every rival loyalty, every idol of wealth, status, or self. Yet the same heart opens with delight when the names of partners or false objects of devotion are raised, since they flatter its desires and require nothing of it. The contrast also reflects the Hereafter-blindness the verse names: a person who looks only to worldly gain feels no pull toward the Lord of Judgment and finds in the lesser gods a comfortable companionship. The lesson for the believer is to examine the heart's joy and discomfort as a mirror, and to cultivate delight in the remembrance of God alone.

translation: Say, "O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You will judge between Your servants concerning that over which they have been differing."
interpretation: The verse teaches that the ultimate resolution of human disputes, especially those concerning religion, rests with Allah alone, who created the heavens and the earth and knows both what is hidden and what is apparent. The Prophet is commanded to turn to Him in this supplication, which expresses humble reliance on the One who knows the truth of matters that people have fragmented over. It reminds believers that differences among them should not lead to hostility or arrogance, since final judgment belongs to the all-knowing Creator, who will reveal the truth of what they disputed.

translation: And if those who did wrong possessed everything on earth, and the like of it along with it, they would surely offer it as ransom from the terrible punishment on the Day of Resurrection. And there will appear to them from Allah what they had never reckoned.
interpretation: The verse portrays the total futility of worldly wealth before God on the Day of Judgment. Those who committed injustice, who in this life measured success by possessions and reckoned themselves secure, will find that no amount of wealth, even multiplied to the full extent of the earth, can buy their release from the punishment they face. The 'appearing from Allah of what they had not reckoned' points to the sudden unveiling of realities they had dismissed or never anticipated: the consequences of their deeds, the certainty of accountability, and the true nature of their situation. The verse thus calls the reader to reorient their values now, since the only currency accepted in that Day is sincere faith and righteous action, not material abundance.

translation: And the evils of what they had earned will become apparent to them, and what they used to mock will surround them.
interpretation: The verse depicts the moment of reckoning when the disbelievers face the true nature of their deeds, which they had previously dismissed or hidden. The 'evils they earned' are revealed as they truly are, stripped of the justifications and illusions behind which they had concealed them. The verb 'haqa' (to encompass or befall) conveys that the punishment they once scoffed at closes in on them completely, so that their mockery of the divine warnings turns back upon them. The verse thus teaches that worldly arrogance and derision toward revelation are ultimately exposed, and that the consequences of one's conduct are inescapable.

translation: So when harm touches man, he calls upon Us; then when We bestow upon him a favor from Us, he says, "I was only given it on account of knowledge." Rather, it is a trial, but most of them do not know.
interpretation: The verse exposes a recurring human tendency: in hardship a person turns humbly to God, but once relieved and blessed, he attributes his good fortune to his own merit, cleverness, or acquired knowledge, forgetting its divine source. God corrects this claim by declaring that such blessings are a test rather than a reward for personal worth, so that gratitude or ingratitude is revealed. The closing remark that most people do not know points to the widespread ignorance of this truth, namely that prosperity is a trial that calls for thankfulness and humility rather than self-congratulation.

translation: Those before them said it too, but what they used to earn did not avail them at all.
interpretation: The verse points to a recurring pattern in human history: those who denied the truth and attributed their success to their own knowledge or resources, as Qarun did in the verses preceding this one, found that their worldly gains gave them no protection when the consequence of their conduct arrived. It teaches that wealth, status, and accumulated possessions are worthless as a shield before God unless they are accompanied by true faith and righteous action, and it warns the reader not to be deceived into thinking that material abundance is a sign of divine approval.

translation: So the evil consequences of what they earned afflicted them, and as for those who did wrong among these (people), the evil consequences of what they earned will afflict them too, and they will not be able to escape.
interpretation: The verse presents a general law of divine justice: wrongdoing carries its own consequences, and these are not random but are the natural outcome of what people themselves acquired through their deeds. The repetition of the phrase about the earlier generations and the present audience signals that the same principle that struck the past peoples applies equally to those who follow the same path of injustice, so no one is beyond the reach of this accountability. The closing statement that they cannot escape (or frustrate Allah) emphasizes that human power cannot override this decree, reminding the listener that refusing to heed warnings only brings upon oneself the same measure of harm.

translation: Have they not considered that Allah extends provision to whomever He wills and restricts it. Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe.
interpretation: The verse directs the reader to reflect on a fundamental truth of divine providence: sustenance is not earned by human effort alone nor distributed by chance, but is wholly in the hands of Allah, who expands it for whom He wills and measures it out according to His wisdom. Expansion and restriction are both acts of divine decree, and the believer who contemplates this sees in the daily flow of provision a sign pointing to God's sovereignty, which should cultivate trust in Him, freedom from anxiety over livelihood, and gratitude in abundance. The phrase 'signs for a people who believe' indicates that such signs are perceived fully only by those whose hearts are open to faith, for the same phenomenon that appears ordinary to the heedless becomes a clear indication of the Creator's power to the attentive believer.

translation: Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.
interpretation: This verse opens a door of hope for those who have burdened their own souls with sin and excess. Addressed directly and tenderly as 'My servants,' the sinners are reminded that their wrongdoing, however grave and prolonged, does not sever them from God's mercy. The prohibition against despair (qunoot) is itself a warning that despair is a greater danger than sin, since it closes the heart to repentance and return. The verse grounds this hope in the universality of divine forgiveness, 'all sins,' and in the names of God as the Most Forgiving and Most Merciful, teaching that the believer's response to wrongdoing should be prompt turning back to God rather than resignation to one's ruin.

translation: And turn in repentance to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you, after which you will not be helped.
interpretation: The verse calls people to a two-fold return: inward turning (inabah) in sincere repentance to God, and outward submission (islam) to His will, both to be undertaken now, while there is still opportunity. The warning is that once the torment arrives, there will be no escape and no one to come to one's aid, since the window for repentance closes with the onset of punishment. It thus joins heartfelt contrition with actual surrender of the self to God, and frames timely repentance as the only real protection against a loss that cannot later be reversed.

translation: And follow the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive.
interpretation: The verse calls people to embrace the finest of what God has sent down to them, which is the Qur'an with its clear guidance, its commands, and its good counsel, rather than clinging to heedlessness. It warns that the chastisement may arrive unexpectedly, catching the negligent off guard when they have no awareness of its approach. The implicit lesson is urgency: a person should hasten to act upon divine guidance now, while there is still time to repent and reform, because the hour of reckoning is hidden and cannot be anticipated. Following the best of revelation thus means taking its moral and spiritual instruction seriously as the path of safety from sudden loss.

translation: Lest a soul should say: "Oh, my regret over what I neglected concerning Allah, and indeed I was among those who mocked."
interpretation: The verse portrays the fear of a soul on the Day of Judgment that, faced with its own neglect, cries out in anguish over having squandered its duty toward God. Its regret is compounded by the admission that it was once among those who scoffed at the truth and at the messengers who called to it. The verse thus warns that mockery of divine guidance is not a harmless pastime, but a grave matter whose consequences will be felt in the hereafter, and it urges the listener to take heed before such remorse becomes inescapable.

translation: Or [that] it say: "Had Allah guided me, I would have been among the righteous."
interpretation: The verse captures the moment of a soul confronted with the reckoning, when it seeks an excuse and attributes its failure to divine withholding of guidance, wishing for a second chance in this world. The wish is a form of self-justification that the Qur'an answers elsewhere by affirming that guidance came through the messages sent, and that the person's own refusal and neglect were the cause. It thus exposes the futility of such regret, since the desire to be among the righteous arrives only when it can no longer change the outcome, and it warns the listener to respond to guidance while it is still within reach.

translation: Or that it would say when it sees the punishment: 'If only I had another chance, so that I could be among the doers of good.'
interpretation: The verse depicts the regret of a soul that, when it faces the reality of punishment, wishes for a return to the world so it could correct its conduct and become among the righteous. Its wish reveals that the true recognition of one's failure comes too late, when the opportunity for action has passed. The verse thus calls the listener to seize the time of life for doing good before the moment of accountability arrives, when every excuse becomes void and only deeds remain.

translation: Yes, indeed My verses had come to you, but you denied them, grew arrogant, and were among the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse, spoken in the context of the scene in which the people of the Fire are reproached on the Day of Judgment, shows that the rejection of divine guidance is not merely a failure of knowledge but a moral failing rooted in pride. The person was not left without a clear sign: the revelations reached them, and the sin lay in their response, first in denying the truth, and then in the arrogance that prevented them from submitting to it. Denial and arrogance are presented as linked, since the proud heart refuses to accept a message that asks it to humble itself before its Creator. The final phrase, 'among the disbelievers,' shows that this conduct places the person in the category of those who cover over the truth and persist in it, so the verse calls the listener to examine whether pride has closed their own heart to the signs of God.

translation: And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied against Allah with their faces blackened. Is there not in Hell an abode for the arrogant?
