interpretation: The verse presents a vivid contrast between the fate of those who fabricated lies against God and the destiny of the arrogant. Blackened faces are a visible sign of their inner state: the shame of falsehood and the disgrace of having claimed what God never said or willed. The rhetorical question at the end affirms that Hell is the rightful dwelling of the proud, who, out of self-exaltation, refused to humble themselves before the truth. Attributing false words to God and refusing to accept the truth are shown to be closely linked forms of arrogance, both of which place a person in a position of rebellion against the Creator, and the verse warns that such conduct will be exposed and recompensed on the Day of Resurrection.

translation: And Allah will save those who were mindful of Him by their achievement; no harm will touch them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: The verse presents salvation as a gift that comes through taqwa, the conscious awareness of God that shapes a person's conduct. The word mafaza, which literally refers to a place of safety or a winning, suggests that the righteous are carried across the dangers of the Hereafter into a state of secure triumph. The verse then describes that state negatively: evil does not touch them and sorrow does not overtake them. This implies that the believer's inner peace is not merely the absence of punishment but a settled security rooted in having lived with God-consciousness, so that fear and grief lose their hold on the soul.

translation: Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is, over all things, Disposer of affairs (Wakeel).
interpretation: The verse affirms that God alone brings all of creation into being, and that the same absolute power which created everything also sustains and governs it. Because He is both the Creator and the one entrusted with all affairs, the believer is invited to place complete reliance on Him, recognizing that no creature possesses independent power, and that true trust (tawakkul) rests only in the One who originated and directs all existence.

translation: To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth. And those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah – it is they who are the losers.
interpretation: The verse places the absolute sovereignty of God over all creation first: the 'maqālīd' (keys) of the heavens and the earth, the power to open and close, to grant and withhold, belong to Him alone, so nothing in the cosmos escapes His control. Against this backdrop of universal dominion, the verse turns to the human response. Rejecting the 'āyāt' of God, whether the signs manifest in the natural order or the revelations sent through the prophets, is depicted as the true loss: a person may gain wealth, status, or worldly comfort, yet by refusing to recognize the One who holds the keys of all things, he forfeits his own well-being and his place of nearness to his Lord.

translation: Say, "Is it other than God that you order me to worship, O ignorant ones?"
interpretation: The verse presents a rhetorical challenge directed at those who called the Prophet to worship their idols. Its force lies in the reversal of expectation: the one who is commanded to worship God alone is being urged to take up a worship that the ignorant ones themselves would be willing to direct toward something other than God. By addressing them as "ignorant" (al-jahilun), the verse indicts not merely their error but their lack of discernment, since the ignorance it names is a failure to recognize that worship belongs exclusively to the One who created and sustains all things. The question thus turns the idolaters' own demands back upon them, exposing the absurdity of directing devotion to what has no claim to it, and it establishes the prophetic stance of tawhid as the only reasonable response to the reality of God.

translation: And it has already been revealed to you, and to those before you: "If you associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely be rendered worthless, and you will surely be among the losers."
interpretation: The verse establishes that the message given to the Prophet Muhammad is continuous with the revelation granted to all earlier prophets, and its core is one unchanging warning: shirk (associating partners with God) is the one act that nullifies all good deeds, however righteous they appear. The conditional phrasing addressed even to the Prophet himself shows that no one's standing, however exalted, exempts them from this principle, and it teaches that sincerity of worship is the foundation on which the value of every action rests. Deeds without tawhid are like a structure built on nothing, so the true loss is not material but the forfeiture of one's entire spiritual account before God.

translation: Rather, worship Allah alone, and be among the grateful.
interpretation: The verse directs the listener to single out Allah alone for worship, turning away from any other object of devotion, and to make gratitude the defining character of that worship. Its phrasing, placed right after a call to reflect on the bounty of Allah, shows that true worship is not merely ritual but an active recognition of divine blessings, so that the one who worships Allah becomes one who constantly acknowledges and thanks Him in heart, speech, and action.

translation: They did not measure God with His true measure, while the whole earth will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand. Glory be to Him, exalted above what they associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who reduce God to human standards and then associates partners with Him, by portraying the entirety of creation as utterly subordinate to Him: on the Day of Resurrection the earth is held in His grip and the vast heavens are folded up in His right hand with no effort or strain. The imagery is meant to awaken awe and proportion, so that the believer's sense of God's greatness corresponds to His true majesty, which no created thing can rival or share, and so that the idea of partnership with Him is recognized as an absurd diminishment of His unmatched power.

translation: And the Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will fall unconscious, except whom Allah wills. Then it will be blown again, and suddenly they will be standing, looking on.
interpretation: The verse depicts the two blasts of the Trumpet as the decisive turning point of the Last Day, marking the dissolution of the present order and the gathering for judgment. The first blast brings terror and annihilating dread upon all creation, so that even the strongest beings are overwhelmed, with only those whom God exempts spared from that collapse, which underscores that absolute power belongs to God alone. The second blast reverses the state entirely: humanity rises in sudden standing and gazing, alert and awaiting their account. The imagery teaches that death and resurrection are both fully under divine command, and that the sudden shift from annihilation to standing before the Lord should awaken the listener to prepare for that moment while life remains.

translation: And the earth will shine with the light of its Lord, and the Record will be placed, and the prophets and the witnesses will be brought, and judgment will be passed between them with truth, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: The verse depicts the Day of Judgment as a scene of complete and perfect justice. The earth, once dark and ordinary, is illuminated not by the sun but by the radiance of its Lord, signalling that God's own presence and justice fill the scene. The books of deeds are set down, the prophets who delivered the message are summoned as witnesses against those who rejected them, and the martyrs testify to the truth. Everything is settled by the standard of truth, and no soul is wronged even by a particle, so the verse assures the believer that no injustice will prevail and that every human being will receive exactly what they deserve.

translation: And every soul will be paid in full for what it did, and He is most knowing of what they do.
interpretation: The verse establishes that accountability is complete and exact: no soul will be cheated of any of its deeds, whether good or evil, because the reckoning is carried out by the One whose knowledge encompasses every hidden intention and every outward act. The phrase "and He is most knowing of what they do" removes any possibility of error, omission, or deception in the judgment, so that the believer is reminded that no action goes unrecorded and no one can escape what they have earned. This should inspire sincerity in deeds and restraint from wrongdoing, since the scale of justice is in the hands of One who knows precisely what each person has done and why.

translation: And those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups, until, when they reach it, its gates will be opened, and its keepers will say to them, "Did there not come to you messengers from among you, reciting to you the verses of your Lord and warning you of the meeting of this Day of yours?" They will say, "Yes, but the word of punishment has come due upon the disbelievers."
interpretation: The verse portrays the disbelievers' final reckoning as a procession of humiliation, driven in herds rather than honored as guests, which reflects that they chose the crowd of error in life. The gates of Hell open only upon their arrival, showing that the punishment is the consequence of their own choices, made after the truth had been delivered to them through their own people. The keepers' question exposes that no excuse of unawareness remains, and the disbelievers' admission that the messengers did come shows they recognize their guilt; their final words, that the decree of punishment was justly fulfilled upon them, express a sealed judgment that comes from persistent rejection rather than from God's injustice.

translation: It will be said: Enter the gates of Hell, abiding therein forever. Evil, then, is the abode of the arrogant.
interpretation: The verse portrays the final reckoning of those who lived in pride, refusing to submit to God and disdaining His messengers and guidance. Their arrogance, which made them see themselves as above truth and above humility before their Creator, is shown to lead to its own consequence: they are commanded to enter the gates of Hell, a place without end. The phrase 'the abode of the arrogant' reveals a moral principle that pride is not merely a personal flaw but a condition that shapes one's destiny, since the very state of self-exaltation that kept a person from bowing to God becomes the enclosure in which they dwell eternally. Hell is thus presented not as an arbitrary punishment but as the fitting home for a self-chosen posture of rejection.

translation: And those who feared their Lord will be driven to Paradise in groups, until, when they arrive at it and its gates are opened, its keepers will say to them, "Peace be upon you; you have been good, so enter it to abide forever."
interpretation: The verse portrays the believers' final journey not as a lonely or uncertain walk but as an honored procession, gathered in groups and escorted toward Paradise, which suggests that God's reward is presented to the God-conscious with dignity and joy. The phrase "and its gates were opened" before they arrive reflects the readiness of their reward, as though Paradise had been prepared and was waiting for them. The keepers' greeting of peace and their declaration that they are good ties the reward to their taqwa: their inner state of guarding themselves before God in this life is what the goodness recognized at the gate reflects. The closing word, abiding forever, marks the end of all fear and loss, completing the contrast with the driven, humiliated procession of the disbelievers mentioned just before in the surah.

translation: And they will say, "Praise be to God, who has fulfilled His promise to us and has caused us to inherit the earth, that we may settle in Paradise wherever we wish. How excellent is the reward of those who do good."
interpretation: The verse portrays the moment of the righteous's arrival at their final reward, where gratitude replaces striving. Their praise is directed to God alone because they recognize that the fulfillment of His promise was an act of His grace rather than a debt owed to them by their deeds. The phrase "inherit the earth" evokes the Qur'anic theme that the righteous are the true heirs of what the wicked once held, and the "earth" here may be understood as the land of Paradise itself, which is granted to them as a settled and unrestricted dwelling. The freedom to settle "wherever we wish" signals a state of complete contentment in which no desire is left unfulfilled. The closing remark, that the reward is excellent for those who labored in faith and action, reminds the listener that God's recompense surpasses every effort, so that the righteous experience their deeds as seeds whose harvest exceeds all expectation.

translation: And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne, glorifying the praise of their Lord. And it will be judged between them with truth, and it will be said: "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: The verse closes the sûrah with a vision of the final judgment, in which the angels circle the Throne in devotion, not in a position of their own authority. Their glorification of God signals that the whole of creation acknowledges His sovereignty as the scene of judgment unfolds. The decisive point is that the judgment is rendered with truth (bil-haqq), so that every soul receives what its deeds deserve, and the verse ends with a declaration of praise to God, Lord of all worlds, showing that the completion of divine justice is itself the ground for universal gratitude and the fulfillment of the sûrah's theme of God's majesty and mercy.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ḥā Mīm.
interpretation: The verse opens the chapter with the disjointed letters Ḥā Mīm, which are among the muqatta'at (the isolated letters that begin certain surahs). Their precise meaning is known only to Allah, and the scholarly tradition generally treats them as a sign of the Qur'an's inimitability: the same Arabic letters from which human speech is formed are presented here as the basis of a divine revelation that no human can match. The formula of the Basmala that precedes them places the recitation under the mercy of Allah, so that the reader approaches the surah with humility and reverence, acknowledging that the revelation that follows comes from the Most Gracious and Most Merciful.

translation: The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse establishes the divine origin of the Qur'an at its very opening: its descent is not the product of human authorship but comes from Allah, whose attributes of 'Al-Aziz' (the Mighty, whose power cannot be resisted and whose authority is absolute) and 'Al-Alim' (the All-Knowing, whose knowledge encompasses everything hidden and manifest) guarantee both the authority and the perfect wisdom of what is revealed. The pairing of might and knowledge implies that the scripture is binding because it comes from a sovereign who cannot be overcome, and trustworthy because it comes from one whose knowledge is complete, so that its guidance is neither arbitrary nor mistaken. The listener is thereby invited to receive the Book with submission and confidence, recognizing that the one who sent it both has the power to enforce its command and the knowledge to make it wise.

translation: Forgiver of sin and Accepter of repentance, severe in punishment, Owner of bounty. There is no deity except Him; to Him is the final return.
interpretation: The verse presents God through a pairing of mercy and justice: He is the one who forgives sin and accepts the repentance of those who turn back to Him, yet He is also severe in retribution against those who persist in defiance. Naming Him as possessor of bounty (al-tawl) reminds the believer that His favor is abundant and that the forgiveness He grants flows from generosity rather than obligation. The declaration of His oneness that follows ties this divine attributes to the central truth of tawhid, so that the hope of pardon and the fear of punishment both direct the soul toward Him alone. The closing reference to the final return makes clear that all of these attributes will be displayed in full at the moment when every person is brought back to account before Him.

translation: None dispute concerning the signs of Allah except those who have disbelieved, so do not be deceived by their movement throughout the land.
interpretation: The verse establishes that outright rejection of God's signs, whether the revealed verses or the signs in creation, is the mark of those who have chosen disbelief, and that such opposition is not a matter of honest inquiry. It then directs the believer not to be misled by the apparent ease, prosperity, or freedom of movement these disbelievers enjoy in their worldly affairs. Their comfort is a temporary respite, not evidence of divine approval or of the soundness of their position. The lesson is one of steadfastness: worldly success is no measure of truth, and the believer should keep his gaze fixed on the reality of the Hereafter rather than on the fleeting status of those who reject the message.

translation: Before them the people of Noah denied (the truth), and the factions after them; and every nation plotted against their messenger to seize him, and they argued with falsehood to refute thereby the truth, so I seized them. So how was My punishment?
interpretation: The verse presents a recurring pattern in the history of prophecy: each community that rejected its messenger not only denied the message but sought to physically destroy the one who carried it, and tried to neutralize the truth through empty disputation rather than honest reasoning. The phrase 'li-ya'khudhuhu' (to seize him) shows the hostility reached the level of intended violence against the prophets. Their use of falsehood to 'refute' the truth reveals that rejection was often a matter of obstinate argument rather than genuine inquiry. God's rhetorical closing question, 'how was My punishment?', is meant to make the listener reflect on the terrible consequences that befell these nations, warning the Quraysh and every later audience that persisting in the same conduct invites the same fate.

translation: And thus the word of your Lord has been justified against those who disbelieved: that they are companions of the Fire.
interpretation: The verse reveals that the decree of Allah concerning the disbelievers is not arbitrary but is the fulfilment of a word already established by His justice and knowledge. Their persistence in rejecting the truth, having been given every clear sign, has sealed their destiny, so that their own chosen course becomes the very reason their end is the Fire. The phrasing 'the word of your Lord' points to the unchangeable divine judgment, which is addressed to the Prophet to console him: the obstinacy of those who refuse guidance is not his failure, and the outcome for them is already determined by their own disbelief, not by any lack of divine mercy in offering the message.

translation: Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with His praise, believe in Him, and seek forgiveness for those who believe: "Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge, so forgive those who repent and follow Your way, and protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire."
interpretation: The verse opens a window onto the angels who carry the Throne and those surrounding it, showing that the highest of created beings are occupied with glorifying God and believing in Him, and that their devotion turns outward in intercession for the believers. Their prayer reveals that God's mercy and knowledge embrace everything, so the believer's hope rests not on his own sufficiency but on that all-encompassing mercy. The request is precise: forgiveness for those who turn back in repentance and walk the path of God, and protection from the Fire. Thus the verse teaches that true faith joins belief, praise, and sincere repentance, and that believers are bound together by mutual supplication across the whole of creation.

translation: Our Lord, and admit them into the Gardens of Eden which You have promised them, along with whoever was righteous among their forefathers, their spouses, and their descendants. Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: The verse is a supplication of the angels who bear the Throne and those around it, found in Surah Ghafir (40:8), asking God to bring believers into the everlasting gardens He promised them. Its significance lies in the principle that salvation is not an isolated individual matter but extends through family bonds: the righteous are granted the company of their parents, spouses and offspring, so that the mercy of God reaches those whose faith and good deeds merit it, even if their own deeds fall short. The closing divine names, al-'Aziz (the Almighty) and al-Hakim (the All-Wise), remind the believer that this admission is an act of perfect power exercised with perfect wisdom, and that the believer's hope rests not on his own merit alone but on the justice and mercy of the One who decides.

translation: And protect them from evil consequences. And whoever is protected from evil consequences on that Day, Allah will have granted him His mercy. That is the great triumph.
interpretation: The verse presents the Day of Judgment as the true measure of success: the decisive question is not worldly gain but whether a person is shielded from the consequences of their misdeeds. Being preserved from sins' penalty on that Day is itself an expression of divine mercy, so mercy and salvation are shown to be inseparable. The verse teaches that the ultimate triumph is not worldly prosperity or status but being drawn near to Allah's grace and spared the reckoning that the wrongdoers will face, which is why it calls this the great success.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieved will be called out to: "God's aversion toward you is greater than your aversion toward yourselves, when you were called to faith and you disbelieved."
interpretation: The verse portrays the moment of reckoning in the Hereafter, when the disbelievers, gripped by regret in the Fire, realize that their own self-loathing over their plight is dwarfed by God's far greater displeasure with their rejection of faith. The call to faith had been clear and repeated through the messengers, yet they chose denial, and the verse exposes the true root of their torment: not merely the consequences of their disbelief, but the deliberate turning away from a summons they had already heard. It thus teaches that God's wrath against persistent rejection of truth is absolute, and that the self's remorse at that point is a pale reflection of the divine judgment already deserved.

translation: They will say: "Our Lord, You have made us die twice and You have given us life twice, so we have acknowledged our sins. Is there any way out (of the Fire)?"
interpretation: The verse depicts the people of Hell, after their confrontation with the reality of their condition, confessing their sins and seeking an exit. Their words "You made us die twice and gave us life twice" are commonly understood as referring to the first death before worldly life (being non-existent, then given life in creation), the first life in this world, the second death at the end of worldly life, and the second life of resurrection; this reading lets the verse affirm the sequence of creation, death, and resurrection. Their acknowledgment of sins comes too late to benefit them, and their final question about a way out underlines the irreversibility of the Hereafter, where the opportunity for action has passed and only the consequences remain, a call to the listener to act while there is still time.

translation: That is because, when God alone was invoked, you disbelieved; but when others were associated with Him, you believed. So judgment belongs to God, the Most High, the Most Great.
interpretation: The verse exposes the inner logic of disbelief: it is not a lack of evidence but a reluctance to accept exclusive devotion to God. When the oneness of God is proclaimed alone, the heart that has grown attached to its idols recoils, yet the same heart readily accepts partners once they are added to Him, revealing that the true issue is the surrender of ownership over one's worship and loyalties. The closing phrase shifts the matter from human preference to divine authority: since judgment rests with the Most High and Most Great, human acceptance or rejection of truth does not alter it, and the believer is called to make God's sovereignty, rather than popular custom or personal desire, the standard by which all claims are weighed.

translation: He is the One who shows you His signs and sends down for you provision from the sky. But none remembers except one who turns back in repentance.
interpretation: The verse directs the heart to see God's power in the world around it: His signs appear in the natural order, and the rain that descends from the sky is a tangible provision that sustains human life, so the very means of sustenance becomes a reminder of the One who grants it. Yet the verse makes clear that seeing signs is not enough; true remembrance belongs only to the one who turns back to God with humble return (inabah), for it is the sincerely returning heart that is opened to reflection and gains benefit from the signs.

translation: So call upon Allah, making your devotion sincerely His, even though the disbelievers detest it.
interpretation: The verse calls the believer to direct all worship and supplication exclusively to Allah, purifying the religion (ad-din) from any association with others, and it assures that this sincere devotion must be maintained regardless of the opposition or aversion of those who deny the truth. Sincerity in faith is thus shown to be independent of the approval of the disbelievers; it is the believer's steadfast commitment to Allah alone that matters, even when that commitment is met with hostility.

translation: Exalted in degrees, Lord of the Throne. He casts the Spirit by His command upon whomever He wills of His servants, that he may warn of the Day of Meeting.
interpretation: The verse presents God's absolute sovereignty and transcendence: He is exalted above all creation and rules from the Throne, and it is by His sole command that revelation (the 'Spirit') is sent down to whichever of His servants He chooses. The purpose of this chosen mission is warning, so that people are made aware of the Day of Meeting, when all will stand before God, and thus the prophetic message is bound up with accountability in the hereafter.

translation: On the Day when they will come forth, nothing of them will be hidden from God. [It will be asked:] "Whose is the dominion this Day?" [The answer is:] "God's, the One, the Subduer."
interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Judgment as a moment of complete exposure, when all human beings stand visible before their Creator with no concealment of deed, intention, or inner state. The ancient question of who holds sovereignty, answered by God alone, dismantles every claim to power, wealth, and authority that people clung to in the world. Its rhetorical force lies in stripping away illusions: the same divine oneness and irresistible dominion that the believer affirms in this life becomes undeniably manifest then, calling the soul to live now in a way that it would not be ashamed to see revealed.

translation: This Day every soul will be recompensed for what it earned. No injustice will there be today. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning.
interpretation: The verse places the reader before the Day of Judgment and establishes that accountability is exact and personal: each soul receives exactly what its deeds have merited, neither more nor less. The declaration that there is no injustice on that Day reassures the wronged and warns the wrongdoer, since no one's deeds can be lost, overlooked, or wrongly attributed. The closing phrase, that Allah is swift in reckoning, conveys both the certainty that the account will be settled without delay and the total command of the One who counts every action, so that the believer is moved to live with constant awareness that every deed is being recorded for a reckoning that will come.

translation: And warn them of the Day of the Approaching, when hearts will be at the throats, choking with grief. The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend, nor any intercessor who will be obeyed.
interpretation: The verse presents the Day of Resurrection as 'the Approaching' because its reality is imminent and certain, and it draws the image of hearts leaping up into the throats in terror and suppressed anguish, so that people can neither speak freely nor cry out. The phrase 'choking with grief' conveys the inner state of a soul overwhelmed, unable to express what it feels. The closing lines strip away every false source of hope: the wrongdoers will find no loyal friend who can help them, and no intercessor whose word is heeded. The warning thus teaches that worldly alliances, status, and borrowed hopes of rescue collapse on that Day, and that only one's own conduct in this life remains of consequence.

translation: He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the chests conceal.
interpretation: The verse points to the comprehensiveness of God's knowledge, which reaches beyond outward action to the most hidden things. The 'treachery of the eyes' refers to the furtive glances by which a person betrays a secret intention, such as a stolen look at what is forbidden or a glance that signals deceit, while 'what the chests conceal' refers to the thoughts, intentions, and inner feelings kept hidden within the heart. By naming both the subtlest outward signs and the innermost concealed states, the verse teaches that nothing escapes God's awareness, and it calls the believer to sincerity and watchfulness over both gaze and heart, knowing that accountability extends to what others never see.

translation: And Allah judges with truth, while those whom they invoke besides Him do not judge anything. Indeed, Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.
interpretation: The verse sets a clear contrast between the true Judge and the false objects of worship. Allah alone decides matters in accordance with the truth, and His judgment is perfect because it is grounded in knowledge and justice, whereas the idols and false deities that people call upon besides Him possess no power to decide or affect anything at all. Their helplessness exposes the emptiness of directing worship toward them. By closing with Allah's attributes of hearing and sight, the verse assures the believer that nothing said or done is hidden from Him, so He hears every plea and sees every deed, and His judgment will be made on the basis of complete awareness.

translation: Have they not traveled through the land and observed how was the end of those before them? They were greater than them in strength and in the traces they left upon the earth, yet Allah seized them for their sins, and they had no protector from Allah.
interpretation: The verse calls the heedless to direct observation of history: the ruins and remnants of earlier peoples, who surpassed the present audience in power and monumental achievement, are presented as a witness that material strength does not shield against divine accountability. Their destruction was not arbitrary but the consequence of their own sins, and the closing phrase underscores that no intercessor or guardian can stand between a people and Allah's decree. The lesson is an invitation to reflection, where the traces of the past become a mirror that turns the mind toward moral responsibility in the present.

translation: That is because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs, but they disbelieved, so Allah seized them. Indeed, He is Powerful, Severe in punishment.
interpretation: The verse establishes a clear principle of divine justice: the destruction of earlier peoples was not arbitrary but the direct consequence of their rejection of guidance after clear signs had been presented to them. Allah's seizing of them is shown to follow from their own choice to disbelieve, so the verse places responsibility squarely on human conduct. The closing attributes of might and severity in punishment serve as a warning that Allah's power is absolute and that His retribution is certain for those who persist in denial after the truth has been made plain, while also underscoring that the messengers' role was to deliver clear evidence, leaving the accountability with the people who received it.

translation: And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs and a clear authority.
interpretation: The verse presents the mission of Moses as grounded in two complementary supports: the miraculous signs (ayat) that testify to the truth of his message, and a manifest authority (sultan mubin) that compels recognition through clear proof and undeniable argument. Together they show that divine guidance is never left to mere assertion; it is accompanied by visible evidence addressed to both the senses and the reason. The term sultan, meaning authority or proof, also hints that the one who brings the message is granted a legitimate mandate, so that rejecting him becomes a rejection of clear evidence rather than an honest uncertainty. The verse thus frames the prophetic mission as a deliberate act of divine sending, equipped with clarity so that the people may be left without excuse.

translation: To Pharaoh and Haman and Qarun, and they said, "A sorcerer, a liar."
interpretation: The verse presents Moses being sent with his message to the three most powerful figures of the establishment: Pharaoh, the political ruler; Haman, his minister and the organizer of his affairs; and Qarun, the wealthy magnate. Their response is a reflexive dismissal that labels the messenger a sorcerer, to discredit the miracles he brought, and a liar, to discredit the message itself. The pattern shows that those whose worldly position depends on the existing order tend to answer clear signs with accusation and slander rather than examination, and that the charge of sorcery is a familiar tool for neutralizing a prophetic call without engaging its substance.

translation: So when he brought them the truth from Us, they said, "Kill the sons of those who believe with him, and spare their women." But the plotting of the disbelievers is nothing but in error.
interpretation: The verse portrays the reaction of Pharaoh's establishment to Moses's arrival with the truth from God: rather than yielding to clear evidence, they resorted to the same tactic of terror against the believers, targeting their sons to crush the emerging community while sparing the women to humiliate and subjugate them. The closing statement reveals the futility of such schemes, since the stratagems of those who reject faith are ultimately misguided and bound to fail, however powerful they appear. It suggests a recurring pattern in which tyrants, confronted with truth, turn to oppression, and God's reassurance is that their plotting leads only to their own confusion and ruin.

translation: And Pharaoh said, "Leave me to kill Moses, and let him call upon his Lord. Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land."
interpretation: This verse reveals the mindset of a tyrant who, unable to answer the message brought by Moses, resorts to the pretext of protecting the public order and the established faith. Pharaoh cloaks his intent to murder in the language of religious and social concern, presenting the prophet as a threat to the people's religion and the stability of the land, a classic strategy of those who hold power and fear losing it. His sarcastic dismissal of Moses calling upon his Lord suggests contempt for the prophet's appeal to God, as if prayer were a harmless matter he need not fear. The verse thus exposes how false accusations of corruption and fitna have repeatedly been used against reformers, and how the powerful equate their own dominance with the good of society.

translation: And Moses said, "Indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning."
interpretation: The verse reveals that true refuge is sought in the Lord who is the Lord of all people, not in any worldly power. Moses frames his seeking of protection in the language of shared lordship, inviting his people to recognize the same Creator and Sustainer as his own. His plea against the arrogant man is not merely a personal grievance but a stance against pride that severs a person from accountability before God. The arrogance he names is rooted in disbelief in the Day of Reckoning: a heart that feels no answerability to a final judgment inflates itself and becomes a source of oppression. Thus the verse teaches that the remedy for tyranny is taking refuge in God, and that faith in the Last Day is the safeguard that restrains human pride.

translation: And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh, who concealed his faith, said: Will you kill a man because he says, "My Lord is Allah," when he has brought you clear evidences from your Lord? And if he is a liar, upon him is his lie; but if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you. Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar.
interpretation: The verse shows that the believer's wisdom lies in reasoning with his people on their own terms rather than confronting them with open defiance. He does not claim the prophet's message as his own, but builds a rational case: if the man is a liar, his falsehood will harm only himself, so there is no need to kill him; if he is truthful, then even a part of his warning will strike them, so they risk punishment by opposing him. The closing statement that Allah does not guide the excessive and the habitual liar teaches that persistent transgression and lying close the heart to guidance, and it implicitly distinguishes the sincere seeker of truth from the arrogant oppressor who rejects clear signs.

translation: O my people, the kingdom is yours today, dominant upon the earth; so who will help us against the might of Allah should it come to us? Pharaoh said, "I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the path of right judgment."
interpretation: The verse captures Pharaoh's rhetoric toward his people at a moment of apparent dominance, where he presents his worldly power as a reason to dismiss the warning of Moses and the believer. The sudden appeal to 'who will help us against Allah's might' is ironic, since it reveals that Pharaoh's own reasoning recognizes a higher power yet he refuses to submit to it. His claim to show them only what he sees and guide them only to righteousness exposes the deceptive nature of tyranny, where personal opinion is elevated above divine guidance and the appearance of rule is mistaken for true direction.

translation: And the one who believed said, "O my people, indeed I fear for you a day like the day of the factions (al-Ahzab)."
interpretation: The believing man from Pharaoh's household, who had concealed his faith, now speaks openly to his people, warning them that their rejection of Moses risks bringing upon them a fate like that of the earlier nations destroyed for denying their messengers, such as the peoples of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and those after them. By invoking the 'day of the factions,' he reminds them of the calamities that overtook the disbelieving communities of the past, urging them to reflect on history, to avoid arrogance and injustice, and to heed the sincere counsel offered before the punishment arrives.

translation: Like the custom of the people of Noah, and 'Ad, and Thamud, and those after them. And Allah does not desire injustice for His servants.
interpretation: The verse places the present audience within a recurring pattern of history: the fate that befell the peoples of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud and their successors was the consequence of their own denial and wrongdoing, not a sign of divine caprice. By stating that God does not will injustice toward His servants, it establishes that punishment is never arbitrary; it is the just outcome of persistent rejection after the truth has been made clear, and it is a warning that people's choices carry real consequences.

translation: And O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Calling-out (the Day of mutual calling).
interpretation: The verse reveals the compassion of the believing man from Pharaoh's household, who addresses his people with tender concern, fearing for them not for himself. By naming the Day of Tanad, the day when people call out to one another in distress, bewilderment, and mutual appeal, he awakens their awareness of the reckoning to come, when the bonds of worldly alliance and kinship will be exposed as insufficient. His fear is a call to sincere admonition: he urges them to reflect on their accountability before the moment when no one can help another, and to turn from the arrogance and injustice that threaten their fate.

translation: On the Day you turn back in retreat, you will have no protector against Allah. And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.
interpretation: The verse presents a stark contrast between human weakness and divine sovereignty. When people turn their backs in flight from what they fear, they discover that their strength, numbers, and allies cannot shield them from the decree of Allah, and that no one can rescue them from it. The closing statement carries a deeper spiritual warning: guidance is ultimately in God's hands, and one who persistently turns away from the light, having been given every sign, may be left to the path of his own choosing. The verse therefore calls the listener to turn toward Allah now, while turning toward Him is still possible, rather than fleeing from Him in the moment of reckoning when no refuge remains.

translation: And Joseph had certainly come to you before with clear proofs, but you remained in doubt about what he brought you. Then when he died, you said, "Allah will never send after him a messenger." Thus does Allah leave astray whoever is a transgressor and a doubter.
interpretation: The verse exposes a recurring human pattern: people who receive clear guidance but withhold conviction through habitual doubt tend to conclude, once the messenger is gone, that no further guidance will come, thereby closing the door to revelation on their own terms. Their doubt is not born of lack of evidence but of a settled disposition of excess and suspicion, so their misguidance is portrayed as the natural consequence of their own choices, which Allah confirms by letting them persist in the error they have chosen.

translation: Those who dispute concerning the signs of God without any authority having come to them—it is greatly hateful in the sight of God and in the sight of those who have believed. Thus does God seal every arrogant, tyrannical heart.
interpretation: The verse identifies the root of rejecting divine signs not in lack of evidence but in arrogance: disputation that is not grounded in any true authority is a willful defiance that stems from a heart inflated with pride. Its gravity is measured by its being detestable both to God and to the believers, who recognize the emptiness of such argument. The sealing of the heart is presented as a consequence rather than an arbitrary decree: when a person persistently chooses self-exaltation and domination over submission to truth, the heart gradually loses its capacity to receive guidance. The passage therefore warns that the true danger lies in the disposition of pride that makes a person impervious to signs, more than in any single act of doubt.

translation: And Pharaoh said, "O Haman, build for me a tower so that I may reach the means of access."
interpretation: Pharaoh's demand for a lofty tower reveals the arrogance of a tyrant who, having claimed divinity over his people, seeks to make his pretension tangible by reaching the heavens through human engineering. The verse exposes the vanity of relying on worldly power, architecture, and technical means to attain what lies beyond human reach, and it sets up the subsequent account of Moses' God, who answers such presumption by bringing Pharaoh's schemes to nothing. It serves as a warning that material ambition, unmoored from submission to the Creator, leads only to ruin.

translation: "The means of the heavens, so that I may look upon the God of Moses, though I truly think he is a liar." Thus was the evil of his deeds made attractive to Pharaoh, and he was barred from the path. And the scheming of Pharaoh was nothing but ruin.
interpretation: The verses expose how arrogance turns into self-deception. Pharaoh's claim to ascend to the heavens is a mask for his refusal to accept the truth he had already been shown, and his conviction that Moses is a liar is a rationalization for his pride. The Qur'an then identifies the mechanism behind this: his own wrongdoing was made appealing to him, so he came to see his corruption as sound judgment and his obstruction of the way of God as a service to his power. The closing phrase, that his scheming led only to ruin, teaches that when a person's plans are built on denying the truth, those plans are defeated from within, because what they aim to protect is the very thing that destroys him.

translation: And the one who believed said, "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the path of right conduct."
interpretation: The believer from Pharaoh's household (Surah Ghafir 40:38) speaks with the courage of faith within a hostile court, turning from the role of a passive listener to that of a sincere counselor. His appeal rests on a simple logic: whoever has found the way of truth has a duty to show it to others, and his call is made in the language of affection ("O my people") rather than of confrontation. The verse also suggests that guidance is a trust that a believer carries into the public sphere, where even someone in a position of worldly proximity to power may bear witness to what is right at personal risk.

translation: O my people, this worldly life is nothing but a fleeting enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of permanence.
interpretation: The verse contrasts two states of existence: the present life, which is brief and passing like a provision enjoyed for a short time, and the Hereafter, which is the enduring home where one's final settlement lies. By calling the worldly life 'mata' (a temporary possession or enjoyment), it teaches the believer not to let attachment to fleeting pleasures displace concern for what lasts. The address 'O my people' also carries a tone of sincere counsel, as the speaker urges his community to reorient their priorities toward the eternal abode, where the consequences of their choices will truly be settled.

translation: Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its equivalent, and whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise, being provided for therein without account.
interpretation: The verse sets two different scales of divine justice side by side. For evil, it allows only an exact equivalent, so no one is punished beyond what they did, which guards against excess and injustice. For good, it opens an unmeasured generosity, since the provision in Paradise is given "without account," showing that God's reward exceeds what deeds could ever earn. By placing male and female together and making faith the condition for righteousness, it also ties the worth of a person to their belief and action rather than their gender, so that both are judged by the same standard of faith and deed.

translation: And O my people, what is [wrong with] me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire?
interpretation: The believer from the family of Pharaoh, who had concealed his faith, turns to his people with a tender and urgent appeal, framing his call as a rescue rather than a challenge. His question "what is with me" expresses his bewilderment at their stubbornness: he is offering them the path to deliverance, yet they are pulling him toward destruction by their disbelief and their opposition to the one who calls to God. The verse thus reveals the reversal at the heart of misguidance, where the sincere counselor is treated as the enemy and the true path of salvation is rejected in favor of the path that leads to the Fire.

translation: You invite me to disbelieve in God and to associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge, while I invite you to the Exalted in Might, the Perpetual Forgiver.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by a believing man of Pharaoh's people who confronts his community with a stark reversal of their claims. They call him toward disbelief and associating partners with God, partners for which they have no sound knowledge or evidence, while he calls them to the Almighty, who is able to enforce His will and who is abundantly forgiving toward those who turn back to Him. The contrast is between worship grounded in mere assumption and worship directed to the One whose power and mercy are real. His words show that true guidance is measured by knowledge and by the character of the One worshipped, not by the weight of social pressure or inherited custom.

translation: Certainly, what you call me to is not a call to anything in this world or the Hereafter, and indeed our return is to God, and indeed the transgressors are the companions of the Fire.
interpretation: The believer, addressing his people, sets a clear contrast between the idols they worship and the God he calls them to. The false deities have no claim to be invoked, neither in this worldly life nor in the Hereafter, because they neither answer nor benefit anyone. By contrast, the return of all people is to God alone, who will judge them. The verse thus ties the rejection of false worship to the certainty of accountability, and it identifies the excessive, transgressing people, who persist in their wrongdoing, as the ones destined for the Fire.

translation: So you will remember what I say to you. And I entrust my affair to Allah. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of [His] servants.
interpretation: The verse expresses the believer's stance of reliance upon God after delivering a warning or message despite opposition: the speaker accepts that his hearers will eventually recall his words, most likely when the consequences become visible, and he hands over the outcome of his mission entirely to God. Preaching is thus separated from the obligation of forcing results, and trust (tawakkul) becomes the proper response to threat. The closing reminder that God is All-Seeing of His servants assures the believer that his sincerity and his opponents' deeds are both fully known to God, who will judge justly.

translation: So Allah protected him from the evils of what they plotted, while the terrible punishment closed in upon the family of Pharaoh.
interpretation: The verse shows that God's protection of the believer from the schemes of his enemies is complete, while the same divine justice that shields the righteous turns the plotters' own devices back upon them. The phrase 'what they plotted' points to the cunning designs that the people of Pharaoh intended against Moses and the believing man among them, and God rendered those evils ineffective. The word 'haqa' (closed in, encircled) conveys that the punishment did not merely approach them but surrounded and seized them entirely, leaving no escape. The contrast between the protected believer and the encompassed household of Pharaoh teaches that reliance upon God safeguards against the malice of tyrants, and that injustice ultimately recoils upon its perpetrators.

translation: The Fire—they are exposed to it morning and evening. And on the Day the Hour is established, [it will be said]: "Admit the people of Pharaoh into the most severe punishment."
interpretation: The verse presents the punishment of Pharaoh's household in two stages: before the Final Day, they are brought before the Fire each morning and evening, so that their torment begins in the barzakh and is a continuous reality rather than a distant threat. On the Day of Resurrection the command shifts from exposure to full entry, and they are sent into the severest form of chastisement. The sequence teaches that the arrogance of tyranny and the leading of others astray do not escape divine accountability, and that the punishment of the grave is an earnest of what awaits the wrongdoer in the Hereafter.

translation: And [mention] when they will argue with one another in the Fire, and the weak will say to those who were arrogant, "Indeed, we were your followers, so will you bear from us any portion of the Fire?"
interpretation: The verse portrays the scene of mutual recrimination in Hell, where the followers, who once submitted to the authority of their leaders, now appeal to them for relief. Their plea exposes the futility of blind following and worldly pride: the arrogant who led others astray cannot shoulder the punishment of others, and each soul is ultimately bound by its own deeds. It is a warning that no one can be excused on account of the status or influence of those they obeyed, and that the responsibility for one's beliefs and actions remains personal before God.

translation: Those who were arrogant will say: Indeed, we are all within it. Indeed, Allah has already judged between the servants.
interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Judgment, when the arrogant, who once refused to submit to God and to His messengers, are gathered in the Fire together with those they misled and followed. Their words admit that they share the same fate, and that no one can escape it or be excused by their former status. The verse ends by affirming that God has already rendered His judgment among His servants, so the outcome is settled by His justice alone. It warns that pride, which exalts the self above truth, ends in shared humiliation, and that no worldly rank or position can shield anyone before the Lord.

translation: And those in the Fire will say to the keepers of Hell, "Call upon your Lord to lighten for us a day of the punishment."
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Ghafir (40:49), reveals the desperate reversal of the inhabitants of the Fire, who, having been arrogant in the world, now turn humbly to the guardians of Hell and ask them to intercede with their Lord. Their request is modest, seeking only a lightening of punishment even for a single day, which shows how the hope for relief becomes the most precious thing when all worldly pride has vanished. The verse implies that the guardians, who are angels, are beyond granting mercy themselves and can only convey the plea to God, underscoring the finality of the separation between the believers' path of supplication and the condemned's loss of agency. It serves as a warning that the opportunity for prayer and repentance belongs to this world, where a person can still call upon the Lord before the consequences become irreversible.

translation: They will say: "Did your messengers not come to you with clear proofs?" They will say: "Yes indeed." They will say: "Then call upon [your gods]. But the supplication of the disbelievers is nothing but in error."
interpretation: The verse portrays a scene of the Hereafter in which the disbelievers are confronted with their own admission: the messengers had already come to them with clear signs, and they had acknowledged this truth, so no excuse remains. Their final appeal to their false deities or to any refuge is shown to be futile, because the supplication of those who rejected the truth is lost in its own misguidance. The verse thus teaches that when clear guidance has been received and rejected, the recourse to falsehood at the moment of judgment brings no benefit, and the responsibility lies entirely with the one who denied the proofs.

translation: Indeed, We will surely help Our messengers and those who believe in the life of this world and on the Day when the witnesses will stand.
interpretation: The verse grants a firm divine promise that the cause of God's messengers and their faithful followers will ultimately prevail, a victory that may appear delayed in worldly life yet is certain both in this world and in the Hereafter. By linking this assurance to the Day when the witnesses rise, it places worldly struggle within the larger framework of final accountability, where the righteous are vindicated and the truth of their testimony is made manifest before all creation. Believers are thus encouraged to persevere in patience, knowing that God's support is not measured only by immediate outcomes but by the ultimate justice that will be revealed on that Day.

translation: On the Day when their excuses will not benefit the wrongdoers, and for them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode.
interpretation: The verse points to the finality of the Day of Judgment, when the usual means of escape from accountability, such as offering excuses, will be of no use to those who persisted in wrongdoing. Their rejection of the truth has already closed the door to mercy, so what remains for them is exclusion from God's grace and the miserable dwelling of the Hereafter. It implies that sincere repentance is valued in this life, since the Hereafter offers no opportunity to revise one's account through pleas or justifications.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses the guidance, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit the Scripture.
interpretation: The verse points to a divine pattern of election and responsibility: guidance was first bestowed upon Moses, and the Book was then passed down as an inheritance to the Children of Israel. The word "inheritance" suggests that scripture is not merely a possession acquired by lineage but a trust that must be actively received, understood, and lived by; the gift of revelation carries with it the obligation to act upon it. Its placement in the Qur'an also implicitly reminds the reader that earlier communities received revelation, and that the continuity of divine guidance across prophets is meant to be recognized and honored rather than neglected.

translation: A guidance and a reminder for those of understanding.
interpretation: The phrase describes the Qur'an (or the revealed guidance it belongs to) as having a twofold function: it guides people toward the truth, and it serves as a reminder that awakens what is already present in the human heart. The word "ulul-albab" refers to people of pure, discerning intellect, whose minds are not clouded by desire or heedlessness. The verse thus implies that the Qur'an's benefit is realized fully only by those who reflect deeply and use their reason, because guidance requires an open and thoughtful mind to be received and acted upon.

translation: So be patient, indeed the promise of Allah is true. And seek forgiveness for your sin, and glorify your Lord with praise in the evening and the morning.
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet to hold fast to patience in the face of opposition and denial, grounding that patience in the certainty that Allah's promise of victory and reward will be fulfilled. It pairs this steadfastness with inner turning back to God: seeking forgiveness, which reflects humility even for one who is guarded from grave sin, and continual remembrance through praise at the beginning and end of the day. Thus outward perseverance is sustained by inward devotion, and the believer's endurance of hardship is rooted in constant worship and reliance on the Lord.

translation: Indeed, those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah without any authority having come to them—there is nothing in their breasts but pride, which they will never attain. So seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.
interpretation: The verse exposes the true root of disputation against God's revelation: it is not born of knowledge or evidence but of an inner arrogance that seeks superiority and refuses submission to truth. Their pride is a barrier they can never overcome, since it prevents them from reaching the goal they covet, namely dominance and the rejection of what is right. The command to seek refuge in God is directed at the Prophet and by extension at every believer, teaching that the remedy against such hostile contention is turning to the One who hears every word and sees every intention, rather than being drawn into futile argument.

translation: The creation of the heavens and the earth is indeed greater than the creation of mankind, but most of mankind do not know.
interpretation: The verse directs the reader's attention from the human being's sense of self-importance toward the vastness of the cosmos, suggesting that if people truly grasped the immensity of creation in the heavens and the earth, they would recognize both the limits of human pride and the greatness of the Creator. The phrase "most of mankind do not know" points to a deficiency not in the available evidence but in the reflection and understanding that would lead people to faith and humility. The verse thus calls for contemplation of creation as a path to knowledge of God and to a proper sense of one's place in the universe.

translation: And the blind and the seeing are not equal, nor are those who believe and do righteous deeds equal to the wrongdoer. Little do you reflect.
interpretation: The verse draws a contrast through paired images: the blind and the seeing, the believers who do good and the evildoer. Just as no sensible person would deem the one who cannot see equal to the one who can, the moral and spiritual difference between faith joined with righteous action and wrongdoing is real and cannot be erased. By closing with the remark that people seldom reflect, the verse rebukes the heedlessness that makes people overlook this difference, and it calls the listener to use the faculty of reason and insight that God has given, so that the distinction between light and darkness, truth and falsehood, becomes clear to them.

translation: Indeed, the Hour is surely coming, there is no doubt about it, but most of the people do not believe.
interpretation: The verse affirms with emphasis the certainty of the Day of Resurrection, placing it beyond any doubt, since its arrival is part of the truth God has decreed. Yet the verse turns from the certainty of the promise to the condition of humanity: the obstacle is not a lack of evidence but the heedlessness and stubbornness of the hearts of most people, who turn away from what reason and revelation make plain. The verse thus joins a reminder of the reality of accountability with a sober observation that faith is often rejected not because the truth is unclear, but because people are reluctant to accept what it demands of them.

translation: And your Lord says: "Call upon Me, I will respond to you. Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell in humiliation."
interpretation: The verse joins a direct divine invitation to prayer with a warning about arrogance. God makes supplication accessible and promises an answer, presenting du'a as a direct bond between the servant and his Lord that requires no intermediary. The contrast with those who 'turn away in arrogance' from worship shows that the root of disbelief is pride, the refusal to acknowledge one's dependence on God. Such pride is punished with a humiliation that mirrors the inner state it arose from: those who would not bow before God in this life enter Hell abased. Worship is thus understood broadly, encompassing both the ritual act of calling upon God and the humble posture of the heart toward Him.

translation: It is Allah who made for you the night that you may rest therein, and the day giving sight. Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind, but most of mankind do not give thanks.
interpretation: The verse directs the believer's attention to the everyday mercies that are so familiar they are overlooked. Night is made a provision of stillness and rest, a withdrawal from the exertions of the day, while day is made luminous so that one may see, act, and seek sustenance. By joining these two signs in a single breath, the verse teaches that the alternation of light and darkness is itself a gift, not a mere mechanical fact of the cosmos. The statement that most people are ungrateful exposes a spiritual poverty: the abundance of blessing is constant, yet heedlessness dulls the heart to it. Thus gratitude is shown to be the proper response to the ordinary, and the sign of faith is an awakened awareness that every rhythm of one's life is sustained by the bounty of the Creator.

translation: That is Allah, your Lord, the Creator of all things; there is no deity except Him. So how are you turned away?
interpretation: The verse establishes the core of tawhid by linking the lordship of Allah (rububiyyah) with His exclusive creation of everything, and from this premise draws the conclusion that worship belongs to Him alone. The rhetorical question 'how are you turned away?' exposes the absurdity of those who, having acknowledged that the sole Creator is Allah, nonetheless turn their hearts and worship toward others. The verb 'tu'fakun' carries the sense of being deluded or diverted from the truth, implying that such aversion is not born of evidence but of a deviation that the intellect itself should reject.

translation: Thus are turned away those who used to deny the signs of God.
interpretation: The verse presents a divine principle that those who persistently reject the clear signs of God are, as a consequence of their own obstinacy, turned away from guidance and truth. The word 'yu'fak' implies being diverted or perverted from the right path, suggesting that repeated denial hardens the heart until it no longer perceives the truth even when it is plainly before it. It is a warning that denial is not merely an intellectual error but a moral choice whose outcome is a progressive loss of the capacity to recognize God's signs, and the verse thus links disbelief with self-inflicted spiritual blindness.

translation: God is the One who made the earth a stable resting place for you, and the sky a canopy; and He shaped you and perfected your forms, and provided you with good things. That is God, your Lord. So blessed be God, the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse directs the human being to recognize the divine favor woven into the very structure of existence: the earth is fashioned as a settled dwelling so that life can be stable and grounded, the heavens are raised as a protective architecture above, and the human form itself is shaped with deliberate beauty and balance. The provision of wholesome sustenance completes this gift, so that the believer's gratitude must extend from the cosmos to the body to the daily table. By concluding with the declaration of God as the true Lord and the blessing of His sovereignty over all worlds, the verse turns the reflection on creation into worship, calling the heart from admiring created things to glorifying their Creator alone.

translation: He is the Ever-Living; there is no deity except Him, so invoke Him, being sincere to Him in religion. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: The verse grounds the call to sincere worship in the unique life and sole divinity of Allah: because He alone is the Ever-Living, the One who neither dies nor depends on anything, He alone deserves to be called upon. Sincerity of religion (ikhlas) means directing every act of supplication and worship to Him exclusively, free from association and from seeking the approval of others. The closing declaration that all praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all creation, completes the thought by tying gratitude and worship to the One who sustains every being.

translation: Say, "Indeed, I have been forbidden to worship those you invoke besides Allah, since clear proofs have come to me from my Lord, and I have been commanded to submit myself to the Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: The verse establishes that the Prophet's exclusive devotion to Allah rests on clear evidence (al-bayyinat) he has received from his Lord, so his refusal to worship the deities of his people is not arbitrary but a conclusion drawn from revealed knowledge. The command to 'submit' (aslama) links the verse to the core meaning of Islam: complete surrender of the self to the Lord of all creation, the one whose lordship embraces every world. Worship is thus shown to be a matter of rational certainty grounded in revelation, and the rejection of idols is inseparable from the positive affirmation of total submission to the one true Lord.

translation: It is He who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then from a clinging clot, then He brings you forth as a child, then that you may reach your full maturity, then that you may become elders; and among you is one who dies before that, so that you may reach a specified term, and perhaps you will use your reason.
interpretation: The verse traces the human being's life as a sequence of stages, each a gift of divine power moving the person from the humblest origin toward a set end. The progression from dust to the clot, then to infancy, maturity, and old age, shows that human existence is not self-originating but continuously sustained by the Creator, who alone determines when each stage arrives and when life ends. The mention of those who die before old age and the appointed term reminds the listener that every life is bounded by a decree that cannot be delayed or extended. The closing phrase, 'perhaps you will use your reason,' directs the reader from observing this natural course to reflecting on it, so that recognizing one's humble beginning and one's dependence on God becomes the basis for true understanding.

translation: He is the One who gives life and causes death, and when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.
interpretation: The verse establishes God's absolute sovereignty over existence: the same power that brings the living into being and brings them to their end governs all things. Its emphasis is that creation and command require no effort, no intermediary, and no resistance; God's decree is immediate and complete, since the thing decreed exists the moment the word of God reaches it. Because nothing can be withheld from this will, the believer is directed to place full reliance on the One whose word alone brings reality into being, and to recognize that every created thing, including the human being's own life and death, is wholly contingent on that single divine word.

translation: Have you not considered those who dispute concerning the signs of God—how are they turned away?
interpretation: The verse turns the Prophet's attention to those who argue against God's signs, meaning the revealed verses and the evident proofs of His existence and oneness, with contentious disputation rather than sincere seeking of truth. The rhetorical question 'have you not considered' presents their condition as already known and observable, and the phrase 'how are they turned away' (anna yusrafun) asks in wonder by what means, and from what direction, they are diverted from the truth. The verse implies that their persistent rejection is not a neutral intellectual position but a deflection caused by their own stubbornness, so that the very signs they dismiss become a mirror showing them their own turning away.

translation: Those who deny the Book and that with which We sent Our messengers—they will come to know.
interpretation: The verse sets forth a warning of certain consequence: the denial of revelation, both the Book itself and the message carried by every prophet, is not a matter that goes unnoticed or unanswered. The phrase "they will come to know" points to a knowledge that is deferred rather than denied, a truth that will be laid bare when the reality of their choice is unveiled, whether at the moment of death, on the Day of Reckoning, or in the unfolding of their own consequences. The verse also binds the scripture of the Qur'an to the wider chain of prophetic messages, implying that rejecting one part of God's guidance amounts to rejecting the whole, since all revelation proceeds from the same source and calls to the same truth.

translation: When the shackles are around their necks and the chains; they will be dragged along.
interpretation: The image is of the disbelievers in the Hereafter bound in humiliation and helplessness: the iron collars and chains that once symbolized their arrogance and refusal to submit to God become the very instruments of their disgrace. Being dragged through boiling water and into the fire shows that the pride they clung to in this world is stripped away entirely, leaving them powerless before the consequences of the choices they made. The verse invites the listener to reflect on how the stubborn heart, which resists guidance, ultimately binds itself, and to turn toward humility before the chains of the Hereafter are placed upon the neck.

translation: Then in the boiling water they will be dragged, and then in the Fire they will be burned.
interpretation: The verse depicts the sequence of punishment awaiting the deniers: after being seized and dragged, they are first thrust into scalding water (al-hamim), and then cast into the Fire to be kindled. The ordering conveys an escalating torment, in which the chastisement of the wrongdoers progresses from one agony to a greater one, and it reminds the listener that the consequences of rejecting the truth are both real and inescapable.

translation: Then it will be said to them, "Where are those you used to associate with God?"
interpretation: This verse depicts the moment of reckoning on the Day of Judgment, when the idolaters are confronted with their false beliefs. The question "Where are they?" is a rhetorical rebuke that exposes the emptiness of their trust in partners made equal to God. Those they once invoked, whether idols, intermediaries, or their own desires, are shown to be absent and powerless, so that the futility of shirk is laid bare before them. The verse thus teaches that tawhid alone endures, and that every claimed partner will vanish when the truth is revealed.

translation: They will be asked, "Where is what you used to worship besides Allah?" They will say, "They have vanished from us. Rather, we had not been calling upon anything before." Thus does Allah leave the disbelievers astray.
interpretation: The verse shows the disbelievers' idols and false objects of worship abandoning them at the moment they most need help, and the worshippers themselves denying that they had ever truly called upon anything real. Their denial exposes the emptiness of their former devotion, since what they took as partners never existed as a true power. The closing phrase indicates that such misguidance is a consequence of their own persistent rejection: having chosen falsehood and turned away from guidance, they are left to the error they embraced, so that Allah's leaving them astray is the just outcome of their disbelief rather than an injustice.

translation: That is because you used to exult in the land without right, and because you used to behave insolently and boastfully.
interpretation: The verse ties the punishment to the root of arrogance: joy in worldly pleasures and display of pride, taken without any truth or justification. Exultation (farah) here is not merely happiness but a self-satisfied elation that forgets God and looks down on others, while mirth (maraḥ) points to the swaggering, insolent conduct that flows from it. The verse teaches that the true measure of a person is not in what they possess or how they strut upon the earth, but in their humility before the truth, and that such unjustified pride stands at the heart of the wrongdoing that leads to ruin in the Hereafter.

translation: Enter the gates of Hell, abiding therein forever. How wretched is the abode of the arrogant.
interpretation: The verse portrays the final destination of those who were proud and refused to submit to God. The words "enter the gates" evoke the image of a fixed, sealed dwelling with multiple entrances, each reserved for a category of the wrongdoers, and the phrase "abiding therein" stresses that this punishment is not temporary. The closing phrase "how wretched is the abode" reverses the expectation of a place of rest: the arrogant, who regarded themselves as too great to bow before the truth, are given a dwelling that reflects their own self-exaltation, now transformed into humiliation. The verse thus links the sin of takabbur, arrogance toward God and His signs, directly to its consequence, showing that spiritual pride closes the soul off from mercy and leads to a lasting and degrading abode.

translation: So be patient. Indeed, the promise of God is true. Whether We show you some of what We promise them, or We take you in death, to Us they will be returned.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad in the face of the opponents' denial and mockery by commanding steadfast patience, grounded in the certainty that God's promise of punishment and victory will be fulfilled. Whether the Prophet lives to witness the fulfilment of the threatened chastisement in this world or dies before it, the outcome rests with God, and in the end all people will return to Him for accounting. The Prophet's responsibility is therefore only to convey the message and to trust in the justice of the divine decree, not to hasten what God has appointed in its time.

translation: And We certainly sent messengers before you; among them are those We have related to you, and among them are those We have not related to you. And it was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by permission of Allah. So when the command of Allah comes, it will be concluded in truth, and the falsifiers will lose therein.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad by reminding him that a long line of messengers preceded him, some of whose stories were revealed to him and some of whose stories were not, so that he would not feel alone in facing rejection. It also establishes that no messenger has power over the miraculous signs himself; every sign comes only by Allah's leave, so the demands of the disbelievers for particular miracles are ultimately in Allah's hands and not the Prophet's. Finally, it points to the Day of Judgment or the decisive moment of divine command, when truth will be vindicated and those who sought to nullify the truth through falsehood will be shown to have lost everything.

translation: It is Allah who made for you the grazing livestock, that you may ride upon some of them and from some of them you eat.
interpretation: The verse points to Allah's mercy in subjecting animals to human benefit: the cattle are not merely sources of food but also means of transport, so that human life is sustained and eased through them.
