The word "maḥīṣ" denotes a refuge or a way of escape, and its negation conveys that no avenue of evasion, whether through denial, cunning, or appeal to false allies, will be open to them. The verse thus links intellectual obstinacy in the face of divine revelation with an inescapable accountability, inviting the listener to examine their own posture toward the signs and to approach them with humility rather than combative disputation.

translation: So whatever you have been given is but the enjoyment of the worldly life; but what is with Allah is better and more lasting for those who believe and rely upon their Lord.
interpretation: The verse places worldly possessions in their true rank: they are merely a passing provision, while what Allah has prepared is superior in value and enduring in permanence. The believers are described by two qualities, faith and complete reliance upon their Lord, which teach that a person should not let the fleeting goods of this life define their worth or their anxieties, but should anchor their hopes in God's lasting reward and entrust their affairs to Him. The verse thus redirects the heart from attachment to what is gained and lost toward a trust that makes the believer content with what is given and steady in the face of its loss.

translation: And those who avoid the major sins and the immoralities, and when they are angered, they are the ones who forgive.
interpretation: The verse describes a believer whose moral character rests on two pillars: restraint from grave wrongdoing and gracious self-control under provocation. Avoiding 'the major sins and indecencies' marks a disciplined conscience that keeps distance from what is gravely wrong, while the phrase 'when they are angered, they forgive' shows that anger, the most natural impulse of the wronged, is not allowed to dictate their conduct. Their strength lies not in never being provoked but in choosing pardon over retaliation at the very moment they have the power and the justification to retaliate. The juxtaposition suggests that true righteousness is measured by how one behaves when the passions are most roused, and that forgiveness is itself a sign of inner mastery and nearness to God.

translation: And those who respond to their Lord, establish prayer, and whose affairs are [conducted by] consultation among themselves, and who spend from what We have provided them.
interpretation: The verse portrays the ideal believing community through four intertwined qualities: obedient response to God's call, steadfast worship through prayer, collective decision-making by mutual consultation, and generous giving from God's bounty. Placing public consultation between worship and charity shows that governance of shared affairs is itself an act of faith, to be carried out with the same sincerity and sense of accountability as prayer, and that wealth is a trust to be shared rather than hoarded. The believers' social life is thus grounded in their relationship with God and expressed in justice, participation, and care for others.

translation: And those who, when tyranny (oppression) afflicts them, they defend themselves (they help themselves / stand up for themselves).
interpretation: The verse describes believers who, when wronged or subjected to transgression, do not submit passively to injustice but rise to defend their rights. This is not a call to aggression, since the surrounding verses make clear that retaliation must be proportionate and that forgiveness is virtuous, but it establishes that resisting oppression is a noble quality. Standing up against wrongdoing, rather than accepting humiliation, is part of the dignity the Qur'an assigns to the faithful community, and it reflects a balanced ethic in which justice is upheld without transgressing its limits.

translation: And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah. Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse establishes justice as the baseline for responding to wrong: retaliation is permitted in measure, equal to the injury suffered, and not exceeding it. Yet it immediately elevates the ideal above strict equity, for the one who forgives and restores what was broken through reconciliation earns a reward that rests directly with God rather than with any human party. The closing clause, that God does not love the wrongdoers, warns that the one who transgresses the measure of retribution, returning more harm than was received, places himself among those who wrong. The moral architecture thus moves from the right of redress, through the nobler path of pardon joined to repair, toward a society in which justice and mercy are complementary rather than opposed.

translation: And whoever defends himself after he has been wronged, those — there is no blame upon them.
interpretation: The verse (Ash-Shura 42:41) establishes that retaliating against an injustice after it has been inflicted is not sinful, and it sets a principle of proportionate self-defense: a believer who is wronged may seek redress, and no one should hold him accountable for doing so. Yet the verses that follow (42:42-43) make clear that this permission is a measured right rather than a duty to seek vengeance, for pardoning and reconciling are presented as more praiseworthy. The verse thus balances justice for the wronged with the moral ideal of forbearance, showing that the believer may stand up against oppression without transgressing, while remaining free to choose forgiveness when it leads to good.

translation: The blame is only upon those who wrong people and transgress upon the earth without right. For those there is a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Ash-Shura (42:42), clarifies that moral responsibility for oppression lies entirely with the oppressors, not with the victims who seek redress. The 'way' or 'path' of blame is directed at those who commit injustice against others and spread corruption on earth through transgression that has no legitimate basis. By distinguishing between lawful response and unjust aggression, the verse establishes a principle that wrongdoing is defined by its violation of others' rights, and that God reserves a painful reckoning for such people. It thus protects the dignity of the wronged while warning the aggressor that their injustice is the true source of culpability.

translation: And whoever is patient and forgives - indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination (resolve).
interpretation: The verse elevates patience and forgiveness to the level of firm resolve, the kind of steadfast commitment that God regards as among the most important matters. Patience here means restraining one's anger and enduring harm without retaliation, while forgiveness goes a step further by releasing the wrongdoer from the debt of injury. The phrase "lamin 'azm al-umur" presents these virtues not as passive weakness but as a deliberate, courageous choice that demands strength of character. Their weight lies in the fact that it is far easier to respond to offense with revenge than to master oneself, so the one who chooses this path shows a higher form of resolve and moral greatness.

translation: And whoever Allah leaves to stray, for him there is no protector after Him. And you will see the wrongdoers, when they see the punishment, saying, "Is there any way to return?"
interpretation: The verse sets two scenes side by side: the one whom God leaves astray has no one to guide or protect him once divine guidance is withdrawn, and the wrongdoers, when faced with the torment they once denied, seek a way back to the world to undo their choices. Their plea comes too late, since the moment of reckoning reveals that the real opportunity to turn back was in life, and it suggests that persistent rejection gradually closes the door to guidance until only regret remains.

translation: And you will see them being presented before the Fire, humbled by disgrace, glancing furtively. And those who believed will say, "Indeed, the losers are those who lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, the wrongdoers will be in lasting torment."
interpretation: The verse portrays the scene of the wrongdoers standing before the Fire, their pride broken and their gaze stolen in humiliation, as their own choices now appear before them in full clarity. It then shifts to the believers, who define true loss not in worldly wealth or status but in the ruin of the soul and of those entrusted to one's care, since a person who forfeits faith forfeits both self and kin. The closing declaration affirms that injustice, whether against oneself or others, leads to an enduring punishment, so the verse calls the listener to reflect on where their own life is heading before that reckoning arrives.

translation: And they will have no protectors to support them against Allah. And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no way (to guidance).
interpretation: The verse establishes a stark principle: those who turn away from the truth cannot rely on any allies, idols, or worldly powers to shield them from the consequences of their choices, since no one can rescue them from Allah's decree. Its second clause points to the sequence of human choice and divine permission: one who persistently chooses misguidance is, by his own repeated turning away, left to the path he has chosen, and no guide or means can open a road for him that he has himself refused to walk. The verse thus calls the listener to sincere seeking of guidance and to attachment to God alone as the only true refuge.

translation: Respond to your Lord before there comes a Day that cannot be averted from Allah. You will have no refuge that Day, nor will you have any denial (of your sins).
interpretation: The verse calls humanity to immediate obedience and submission to the Lord before the Day of Judgment arrives, a Day whose decree no one can reverse. Its warning is that on that Day every human being will find no shelter from the consequences of their deeds, and no one will be able to deny or reject what is recorded against them. The urgency of the call lies in the fact that the opportunity to respond is limited to this life, so the wise person hastens to answer the call of faith and righteousness now, while repentance and good works are still accepted.

translation: But if they turn away, [know that] We did not send you as a guardian over them. Your duty is only to convey [the message]. And indeed, when We let man taste mercy from Us, he rejoices in it; but if an evil befalls them because of what their hands have put forward, then indeed man is ungrateful.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet and reassures him that his responsibility ends with delivering the message; he is not a watcher who compels faith, and the outcome rests with God. It then exposes a recurring human weakness: when blessings come, a person exults in them forgetting their Giver, and when hardship strikes, he attributes it to his own deeds and is quick to forget gratitude. The word 'insan' here points to a human disposition that, without awareness of God, slides into ingratitude, so the believer is called to be grateful in ease and patient and self-examining in adversity.

translation: To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He creates what He wills. He bestows female children upon whom He wills, and He bestows males upon whom He wills.
interpretation: The verse establishes that absolute sovereignty over all creation belongs to Allah alone, and that the creation of human beings, including the determination of their sex, is entirely within His will and wisdom. By mentioning the bestowal of daughters and sons in succession, it reminds people that children are a gift from God rather than something human beings can command or claim as their own right. This undercuts the pre-Islamic tendency to favor sons over daughters and to treat daughters with disdain, since the one who grants offspring is the Creator who alone decides their form. The verse thus calls the believer to humility before divine decree, gratitude for whatever is given, and acceptance that the wisdom behind each gift belongs to God.

translation: Or He grants them both males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren. Indeed, He is All-Knowing, All-Powerful.
interpretation: The verse presents the absolute sovereignty of God over human procreation: children are a gift bestowed by His will alone, not a matter of human planning, desire, or entitlement. By granting some believers sons, others daughters, and leaving some without offspring, God shows that the distribution of lineage follows His perfect knowledge and wisdom rather than human preference, which often favored sons. The closing names, All-Knowing and All-Powerful, tie this divine allocation to His complete knowledge of what is best for each person and His unlimited capacity to act, thereby inviting humans to submit to His decree and to be content with what He grants.

translation: It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who reveals by His permission what He wills. Indeed, He is Most High, Most Wise.
interpretation: The verse establishes the categories through which divine communication reaches humanity: direct inspiration placed in the heart, speech from behind a veil as was granted to Moses, and the sending of an angelic messenger who conveys the revelation. Each mode is absolutely under God's will and permission, so that no human being can claim unmediated access to God's speech, and the emphasis on His elevation and wisdom reminds the listener that the manner and timing of revelation follow His perfect knowledge rather than human expectation.

translation: And thus We have revealed to you a spirit from Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was, but We made it a light by which We guide whomever We will of Our servants. And indeed, you guide to a straight path.
interpretation: The verse presents the revelation to the Prophet Muhammad as a divine favor that came entirely from God's command, not from his own prior knowledge or seeking, so that his role as a guide is derivative of the Book he received. Calling the revelation a 'spirit' and a 'light' shows that it gives life to hearts and illuminates the way, and the statement that God guides whom He wills affirms that the guidance it brings is ultimately under divine choice, while the Prophet's own guidance to the straight path is a real but dependent role.

translation: The path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Unquestionably, to Allah all matters return.
interpretation: The verse closes the surah of Ash-Shura by tying the call to the straight path to the absolute ownership of Allah over all creation, so that the one who follows that path is walking toward the One who owns every thing and to whom every affair ultimately returns. The 'path of Allah' is thus not a human invention but a way anchored in the reality of divine sovereignty, and its destination is the same Lord who will judge all affairs. The verse thereby reminds the believer that guidance and accountability both belong to God alone, and that the final outcome of every matter rests in His hands.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ha, Mim.
interpretation: The verse consists of the disjointed letters Ha and Mim, which open Surah Ghafir and several other surahs (40 through 46). Such letters are read as mysterious signs belonging to the divine knowledge of Allah, and their precise meaning is left to Him alone. Their placement at the head of a surah signals a revelation of great significance, drawing the listener's attention before the message that follows. Many scholars also see in them a reminder that the Qur'an is composed of ordinary Arabic letters, yet no human being can produce its like, which points to its miraculous and divine origin.

translation: And by the Clear Book.
interpretation: The verse swears by 'al-Kitab al-Mubin,' the Clear Book, which in this context refers to the divine record that makes matters plain and unambiguous. Its clarity lies in its being fully manifest: it distinguishes truth from falsehood and leaves nothing obscure concerning what it contains. By swearing an oath upon it, God affirms the seriousness and authenticity of the message that follows, directing the reader to regard this Book as a sure and trustworthy source of guidance, the very standard by which the matter at hand is to be judged.

translation: Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an, so that you may reason.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that the revelation was deliberately sent in the Arabic tongue, the language its first audience understood, so that its meaning would be accessible and its message could be grasped through reflection. Divine guidance is thus tied to human intellect: the purpose of making the Qur'an clear in a known language is to invite the listener to ponder, comprehend, and act upon its wisdom rather than merely recite it. Understanding is presented as the gateway through which revelation becomes transformative for the believer.

translation: And indeed, it is in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and full of wisdom.
interpretation: The verse affirms the exalted status of the Qur'an by placing its source in Umm al-Kitab, the preserved original record kept with Allah, beyond any alteration or corruption. Describing it as 'Ali' (sublime) and 'Hakim' (wise) points to its elevated rank above all other scriptures and to the perfection of its wisdom, which is both lofty in origin and precise in its laws, guidance, and purposes. The verse thus invites the reader to recognize that the message they hold is anchored in a divine, unchanging source, and that its wisdom reflects the wisdom of the One who authored it.

translation: Shall We then turn away from you the Reminder, out of neglect, because you are a people who transgress?
interpretation: The verse expresses a rhetorical rebuke, asking whether God would cease sending the Reminder, the revelation, simply because the people have been excessive and heedless in their conduct. The phrase "afanadribu" (shall We turn away) is a question of astonishment, suggesting that divine mercy is not withdrawn so easily; the people's transgression (israf) is the very reason the message is still being sent to them, as a call to return. It implies that God's patience and guidance continue even toward those who have gone to excess, and that the Qur'an itself is the Reminder that should awaken them from their heedlessness.

translation: And how many prophets did We send among the earlier peoples?
interpretation: The verse is a rhetorical question that consoles the Prophet Muhammad and reminds the listeners that God's practice has been consistent throughout history: He has sent a prophet to every nation of former times, so the people of every age have had messengers calling them to the truth. The phrasing 'how many' emphasizes the vast number of prophets sent, and by pointing to this long-established pattern it implies that the disbelief faced by the present messenger is nothing new. It is a reminder that rejection of the messengers has been a recurring human response, and that the same divine mercy of guidance has accompanied every generation.

translation: And no messenger came to them except that they used to mock him.
interpretation: The verse reveals a recurring pattern in the history of human response to divine guidance: the arrogant and heedless, confronted with a messenger sent to them, often met his call not with sincere reflection but with ridicule. Mockery serves as a shield for those who are unwilling to change their ways, allowing them to dismiss truth without examining it. The verse thus consoles the Prophet Muhammad by showing that rejection and derision are not unique to his mission, and it warns later generations that treating the bearers of revelation or its teachings with scorn is a grave error that places a person in the same condition as those who were destroyed for their denial.

translation: So We destroyed those who were stronger than them in might, and the example of the former peoples had already passed.
interpretation: The verse points to a recurring divine pattern: those who exceeded their predecessors in physical power and worldly strength were not spared when they rejected their messengers, for strength is no shield against the decree of God. The phrase "and the example of the former peoples has passed" directs the listener to history as a lesson, urging the present generation to recognize that the fate of earlier nations stands as a warning and a sign, so that they may reflect, heed the message, and avoid the same arrogance that brought ruin upon those who came before.

translation: And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing."
interpretation: The verse exposes a tension within the consciousness of the polytheists of Makkah: they acknowledged God as the Creator of the cosmos, yet they did not draw from this acknowledgment the necessary consequence of exclusive worship and submission to Him alone. Their confession of God's power (al-'Azīz) and knowledge (al-'Alīm) in creation shows that the basic knowledge of the Creator is inherent in human nature, so the dispute with them was not primarily about the existence of the Creator but about recognizing His rightful sovereignty in worship, law, and obedience. The pairing of the divine names of might and knowledge with the act of creation also reminds the reader that the majestic order of the heavens and earth is itself a sign pointing to a Lord who is both powerful and all-knowing, so that the one who admits this must logically admit that He alone deserves to be worshipped.

translation: Who has made the earth for you a bed (spread out and made smooth), and has made for you therein pathways, that you may be guided.
interpretation: The verse presents the earth as a deliberately prepared dwelling: it is made level and stable like a resting-place, so that humanity can settle and live upon it securely. The making of roads and routes within it shows that the same Creator who provided the ground also arranged the means of movement, so that people can travel, trade, and seek their needs. The closing phrase, 'that you may be guided,' turns these material blessings into a call to reflection: the orderly earth and its paths point to the One who designed them, so that human beings may find guidance both on their journeys across the land and on the straight path toward their Lord.

translation: And the One who sent down from the sky water in measure, and We revived thereby a dead land. Thus you will be brought forth.
interpretation: The verse draws an analogy between the revival of barren land and the resurrection of human beings. Just as rain falls from the sky in a measured amount, sufficient for life without excess or destruction, and brings a lifeless earth back to fruitfulness, so God will bring the dead out of their graves. The same power that gives life to the parched earth after its death is the power that will raise people on the Day of Resurrection, so the sight of renewed vegetation becomes a sign pointing the believer toward the certainty of being brought forth again.

translation: And He who created all the pairs, and made for you ships and cattle upon which you ride.
interpretation: The verse points to the principle of duality and complementarity that runs through all of creation: every created thing is made in pairs, male and female, night and day, heaven and earth, which reflects that only the One who is without pair (the Creator) stands beyond such multiplicity. Having established this cosmic order, the verse turns to human benefit: God has subjected to people the vessels of the sea and the animals of the land, so that what sustains and carries them is itself a sign of divine provision. The reminder is that the same Creator who ordered the universe in pairs also arranged the means by which human beings move and travel, so that gratitude and recognition of His power should accompany every journey.

translation: So that you may sit firmly upon their backs, and then remember the favor of your Lord when you are seated upon them, and say: Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, though we were not capable of subduing it ourselves.
interpretation: The verse presents the riding animals as a gift that reveals divine mercy: humans, physically weaker than these creatures, are enabled to mount and control them, so that gratitude is meant to arise at the very moment of benefiting from the favor. Remembering the Lord 'when you are seated upon them' turns an ordinary act of travel into an occasion of worship, teaching that God's blessings are to be acknowledged in every act of using them. The declaration of God's glory acknowledges that human power alone could never have tamed such creatures, so the sense of mastery is replaced by humility and dependence on the One who subjected them.

translation: And indeed, to our Lord we are surely returning.
interpretation: The verse expresses the believer's awareness that all of life's journey ends in a return to God, so the one who keeps this in view is steadied in hardship and in the face of loss, measuring every outcome against the final meeting with the Lord rather than against the fleeting circumstances of this world.

translation: And they have attributed to Him a portion from His servants. Indeed, mankind is clearly ungrateful.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who assign to God a share from among His own creation, as though He had offspring or partners born of His servants, which contradicts His absolute oneness and transcendence. It then turns to the root of this error in the human soul: man, when he forgets his total dependence on God for every blessing, becomes manifestly ungrateful, and this ingratitude is what drives him to distort the truth about his Creator by ascribing to Him what is unworthy of Him.

translation: Or has He taken for Himself daughters from among what He creates, and chosen sons for you?
interpretation: The verse confronts the polytheistic claim that angels are God's daughters while the pagans themselves preferred sons. It exposes the inconsistency and injustice of attributing to God what they would find distasteful for themselves, and it shows that such claims rest on no knowledge but on human preference and assumption. The rhetorical question is a sharp reproach meant to awaken reason: if sons are honored among you, how can you assign to the Creator the lesser share? It implicitly affirms God's absolute transcendence above begetting, need, and any resemblance to His creation.

translation: And when one of them is given the good news of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful as a likeness, his face becomes darkened, and he is filled with suppressed grief.
interpretation: The verse exposes the inconsistency of those who ascribe daughters to God while they themselves dislike daughters. When one of them is told of the birth of a daughter, the news that should be a cause for joy fills him with shame and anger, his face darkening as he suppresses his rage. By portraying his reaction, the verse shows how the attribution he makes to God contradicts his own values, and it implicitly rebukes the entire framework of assigning to God what people themselves find demeaning.

translation: Is one who is brought up among ornaments, and who is unclear and unable to make his case in disputation (while he is in contention), [equal to one who is not like that]?
interpretation: The verse describes a mindset that equates adornment and softness with worth, while its owner lacks the clarity to express a reasoned argument. The verse shows that a person raised in luxury and ornament, who is unable to present clear proof when disputing, is depicted as deficient in the qualities that truly matter, such as sound reasoning and eloquent, lucid speech. It is a rebuke to those who judge by outward display and who, in contending over matters of truth, cannot express themselves clearly. Rhetorically it also reminds the listener that genuine value lies in clarity of mind and soundness of expression rather than in the ornaments of appearance, and this is consistent with the Qur'an's broader critique of those who were proud of their wealth and status while lacking true understanding.

translation: And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females. Did they witness their creation? Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned.
interpretation: The verse exposes the baselessness of the polytheists' claim that the angels are daughters of God. Those who attribute to God offspring they would reject for themselves ascribe to the angels, honored servants of the Merciful, a sex and kinship they have no knowledge of. The rhetorical question, 'Did they witness their creation?', dismisses such claims as mere conjecture unsupported by any witness or evidence, and the statement that their testimony will be recorded and they will be held accountable warns that such unfounded assertions about the unseen will be called to account on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And they say, "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them." They have no knowledge of that; they are merely guessing.
interpretation: This verse exposes the flawed reasoning of those who justify idolatry by appealing to God's will. They take the fact that God permits disbelief as proof that their worship of others is approved by Him, thereby confusing divine will with divine command. The Qur'an rebukes this by stating that such claims rest on no knowledge, only on conjecture. Divine permission of an act does not make it lawful or true, and the verse calls the reader to rely on revealed knowledge rather than on speculation about what God wills.

translation: Or have We given them a Book before this (Qur'an), so that they are holding fast to it?
interpretation: The verse challenges the disbelievers of Makkah with a pointed question: their rejection of the Prophet's message has no basis in any prior scripture granted to them, so they cannot appeal to an earlier revelation as proof of their claims. Since they hold no written authority from before the Qur'an that they cling to, their stubborn refusal to accept the message must rest on something other than divine warrant, namely their own inherited habits and assumptions. The rhetorical force lies in exposing the emptiness of their position: they are attached to a source that cannot support them, and they are invited to reconsider on the basis of reason and truth rather than blind adherence.

translation: Nay, they say: "We found our fathers following a certain community, and we are indeed guided by their footsteps."
interpretation: The verse exposes the reflex of blind imitation, in which people justify their beliefs and conduct merely by appeal to the inherited practices of their forebears rather than by reasoned examination of truth. The word "Bal" (Nay) signals a rejection of this argument as no proof at all. Its deeper lesson is that ancestry and tradition carry no intrinsic authority; what matters is whether a path is sound, and therefore the believer is called to test inherited customs against revelation and reason, while the claim of being "guided" by mere footsteps reveals how easily a crowd's habit can be mistaken for divine guidance.

translation: And likewise, We did not send a warner before you to any town except that its affluent people said, "Indeed, we found our fathers following a certain path, and we are, in their footsteps, following."
interpretation: The verse shows a recurring pattern in the history of prophethood: those who enjoyed luxury and worldly comfort in each community were the first to resist the warnings of the messengers, not because of any evidence but because of their attachment to inherited customs. Their wealth made them feel self-sufficient and unaccountable, so they equated the faith of their ancestors with truth and treated blind imitation as sufficient justification. The verse thus warns that tradition and social privilege are not proofs of correctness, and that the comfortable elite often become the strongest obstacle to a message that calls for change, requiring each person to examine what they inherit rather than following it merely because it is familiar.

translation: He said: "Even if I brought you something better guiding than what you found your forefathers following?" They said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in what you have been sent with."
interpretation: This verse captures the recurring stance of the disbelievers facing the prophets: they measure truth by inherited custom rather than by its own merit. The messenger's question, "even if I brought you better guidance," shows that the prophet does not ask them to abandon their heritage blindly but invites them to judge the message by its guidance. Their reply reveals that they had already closed the door to reasoning; they reject the message outright because it departs from what their fathers held, so that loyalty to ancestral practice becomes a barrier that prevents them from recognizing the clearer path set before them.

translation: So We took retribution against them. Then observe how was the end of those who denied.
interpretation: The verse presents divine justice as the consequence of persistent denial of the messengers: after warning and rejection, God's retribution fell upon the wrongdoers. The call to 'look' at their fate turns history into a lesson, inviting the listener to reflect that falsehood and arrogance toward truth lead to ruin, while those who heed the message are spared. It affirms that God's promise of reckoning is certain and that the final outcome belongs to the righteous.

translation: And [mention] when Abraham said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am free from what you worship."
interpretation: This verse presents Abraham's declaration of disassociation from idolatry, spoken even to his own father and kin, which reveals that true faith requires a clear and courageous break from inherited practices when they contradict monotheism. Abraham's words make tawhid the decisive criterion of loyalty, placing belief in God above family ties and social custom. The verse also teaches that the prophetic call begins with a principled stance of rejection toward false worship before it affirms devotion to the One God, so that clarity of disavowal is itself a foundation of sincere worship.

translation: Except He who created me, for indeed He will guide me.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) in Surah Az-Zukhruf (43:27) and echoing his declaration of devotion to the One God, reveals the foundation of his monotheistic conviction: he disassociates himself from the idols his people worshipped and affirms that his Lord, the Creator who brought him into being, is the only one worthy of worship. The phrase 'fatarani' (He who originated and shaped me) ties guidance directly to creation, suggesting that the same Power that gave a human being existence also provides the innate disposition and the continuing direction toward truth. Ibrahim's trust that 'He will guide me' expresses a reliance on divine guidance that is not merely a past gift but a continuous assurance, teaching that the believer should look to the Creator alone for direction, especially when surrounded by false traditions and inherited practices.

translation: And He made it a word that remains among his descendants, so that they might return (to the truth).
interpretation: The verse refers to Abraham (Ibrahim) and the tawhid he declared when he disavowed what his people worshipped, saying that he is free from them except the One who originated him. God made this declaration of pure monotheism a lasting word, a principle of faith that would endure in his progeny, so that generations after him would be guided back to the worship of the One God. The pronoun 'it' points to this word of sincere monotheism, and the hope expressed in 'so that they might return' indicates that the enduring legacy of Abraham's testimony is a continual call for his descendants to turn back to God whenever they stray, making the prophetic line that came from him a living source of guidance.

translation: Nay, I gave enjoyment to these people and their fathers until the truth came to them and a clear messenger.
interpretation: The verse points to a divine pattern of patience: God allowed the Quraysh and those before them to enjoy worldly comforts and a long respite, not as a sign of approval, but as a test that delayed their reckoning until the truth was made plain to them through a manifest messenger. Their heedlessness is thus shown to stem not from a lack of clarity but from the attachment to inherited ways that prevented them from recognizing what had already arrived. The 'nay' rejects their claim that prosperity or the ways of their forefathers justify their disbelief, and it implicitly warns that the continuation of blessings should never be mistaken for being right, since the clear message has now reached them and they are answerable for it.

translation: And when the truth came to them, they said, "This is pure magic, and we reject it."
interpretation: The verse exposes the reflexive response of those who are confronted with a truth they have not sought and do not wish to accept: rather than examining its claim on its own merits, they dismiss it by labeling it sorcery, a convenient category that spares them from reflection and from the discomfort of change. Their denial is not born of ignorance of the message but of a settled refusal, so that the very clarity of the truth becomes the occasion of their rejection. The verse thus warns that disbelief often arises less from a lack of evidence than from a prior unwillingness to submit, and it invites the reader to look at the substance of what is brought rather than at the labels with which it is hastily covered.

translation: And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two cities?"
interpretation: The verse records the objection of the disbelievers who rejected the revelation not on its content but on the social criteria of their own status-driven values. They judged that prophethood should belong to a man of wealth, rank, and worldly eminence in one of the two great towns, Makkah and Ta'if, rather than to Muhammad, whom they regarded as an ordinary orphan of no prominence. The Qur'an elsewhere answers this reasoning by stating that God alone chooses His messenger and distributes His mercy, and that worldly distinctions are not the measure of divine favor. The verse thus exposes the error of equating social standing with spiritual worth, a theme that runs throughout the revelation and reminds the reader that truth is recognized by its substance rather than by the prestige of its bearer.

translation: Is it they who would apportion the mercy of your Lord? It is We who have apportioned among them their livelihood in the life of this world, and We have raised some of them above others in ranks, so that some may take others in service. But the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the distribution of worldly provision and social rank is entirely God's decree, not the choice of people, and that such differences are a means of mutual need and service within society, so no one should presume to govern God's mercy. Since true mercy, namely guidance, the hereafter, and divine favor, surpasses all worldly accumulation, the believer is directed to measure success by that mercy rather than by wealth and status, and to view one's own station with gratitude and humility.

translation: And were it not that mankind would become one community (of disbelief), We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver ceilings for their houses, and staircases upon which they would ascend.
interpretation: The verse discloses the measure by which worldly abundance is withheld from those who reject God: wealth and luxury are not, in themselves, marks of divine favor, and their distribution is governed by a wisdom that prevents attachment to this world from becoming a universal temptation to disbelief. Had material prosperity been bestowed on the disbelievers without restraint, the entire human community might have gathered around the pursuit of worldly splendor, so God ties the extent of such gifts to the condition of faith. The imagery of silver roofs and ascending stairways portrays the fleeting, external grandeur of the unbelievers' homes, contrasted with the enduring reward reserved for the righteous in the Hereafter. The verse thus directs the believer to measure success not by the elevation of buildings but by the elevation of the soul toward God.

translation: And for their houses, doors and couches upon which they recline.
interpretation: The verse, spoken in the context of the adornments of the people of the Garden or of the worldly luxury of the wealthy, points to the comfort and ease that the believers enjoy in the hereafter, where their dwellings are furnished with doors and raised couches on which they recline at rest. Read against the preceding verses about silver vessels and golden cups, it shows that the ultimate pleasures are not hidden from the believers but are shaped so that they can be seen and enjoyed, while also warning that such worldly splendor, when it is the sole object of a person's attachment, becomes a snare of ostentation and heedlessness rather than a sign of God's favor. The reclining posture in particular suggests a state of tranquility, security and honor, the opposite of the anxious striving of those absorbed in the transient world.

translation: And ornaments of gold. Yet all of that is but the enjoyment of the worldly life; and the Hereafter, with your Lord, is for the righteous.
interpretation: The verse sets the fleeting adornments of this world, gold and luxury, against the enduring reward of the Hereafter. Worldly possessions are real but temporary comforts, and their pull can mislead the heart into mistaking the display of wealth for true worth. The lasting station with God belongs only to those who guard themselves through piety, so a believer is directed to measure success by God's standard rather than by what the world admires.

translation: And whoever turns blind to the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil, and he becomes his constant companion.
interpretation: The verse describes a moral and spiritual consequence: when a person deliberately turns away from or neglects the remembrance of Allah (dhikr al-Rahman, which includes both the Qur'an and the constant awareness of God), he becomes spiritually blinded, and his heart is left open to the influence of Satan. The word "yaʿshu" suggests a dimming of perception, as one who has lost sight of the truth; the consequence is not arbitrary but follows from his own turning away. The devil then becomes an inseparable companion (qarin) who misguides him, makes evil appear attractive, and keeps him from the path, so that the person is bound to his own chosen neglect. The verse thus teaches that constant remembrance of God is a shield, and that heedlessness invites a companionship that leads one further astray.

translation: And indeed, they turn them away from the way, while they think that they are guided.
interpretation: The verse exposes a deceptive self-image: those who lead others astray are not aware of their own error. Their misguidance is doubled, since they both obstruct others from the path of truth and remain confident that they themselves are rightly guided. The verse thus warns that the most dangerous state is not simply being lost, but being lost while believing oneself to be on the right course, which calls believers to examine their intentions and sources of guidance with humility and self-scrutiny rather than relying on self-assurance.

translation: Until, when he comes to Us, he says: "Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts! For wretched is the companion."
interpretation: The verse depicts the regret of one who turned away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful (as described in the preceding verses), and who was given a devil as a companion. On the Day of Reckoning, when he stands before God, he wishes that the separation between himself and that misguiding companion were as vast as the distance between the two easts, since the bond of misguidance has become a source of torment rather than support. The phrase "the two easts" may denote the extreme distance between the rising points of the sun in winter and summer, or the east and the west together, conveying an absolute separation. The closing judgment, "wretched is the companion," reveals that the very friendship which once seemed pleasant in worldly life has become the cause of his ruin, teaching that the company one keeps in this world will either accompany one to salvation or to loss.

translation: And it will not benefit you today, since you have wronged yourselves, that you will be sharing in the punishment.
interpretation: The verse exposes the futility of shared suffering as a consolation on the Day of Judgment. The wrongdoers may imagine that being one among many in punishment lightens their own burden, yet the verse declares that such companionship in torment brings them no relief, because their injustice was personal and each soul bears the consequence of its own choices. It turns the worldly comfort of collective guilt into a bitter realization: the crowd that once shielded them from accountability now only multiplies the anguish, and the bond of shared wrongdoing is severed by the reality of the Day, where every person stands answerable for what they themselves did.

translation: Can you then make the deaf hear, or guide the blind, or one who is in clear error?
interpretation: The verse poses a rhetorical question to the Prophet Muhammad, affirming that guidance belongs to God alone. Just as no one can make the deaf hear or lead the blind to their path, the Prophet cannot compel those who have closed their hearts and senses to the truth to accept it. The comparison underlines that a person who has deliberately turned away from clear signs remains in manifest error, and that the responsibility of the messenger is only to convey the message, while the granting of true hearing and sight is in the hands of God.

translation: So whether We take you away, indeed We will take vengeance upon them.
interpretation: The verse comforts the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) amid the opposition of his people: whether God allows him to die or removes him from among them before the punishment falls, the retribution against those who persistently rejected the message is certain. It teaches that the prophet's responsibility is to convey the message, while the matter of requital rests entirely with God, who will not leave the wrongdoers unaccountable.

translation: Whether We show you part of what We have promised them, or We take you before that, indeed they are, over them, omnipotent.
interpretation: The verse assures the Prophet that the outcome of his mission does not depend on his witnessing the punishment or the victory promised to his opponents. Whether God allows him to see its fulfillment in his lifetime or takes him before it, the matter rests entirely with God, who holds absolute power over those who denied the message. The divine promise is certain, and its timing is God's alone, which calls the believer to patience and trust in the wisdom behind divine timing.

translation: So hold firmly to that which has been revealed to you. Indeed, you are on a straight path.
interpretation: The verse directs the Prophet Muhammad to cling steadfastly to the revelation sent down to him, rather than to any human desires or the misguided demands of his opponents. Its ordering is significant: the command to hold fast comes first, and the reassurance that he stands on a straight path follows, so that firmness in the revealed guidance is itself the proof of his rectitude. The phrase 'that which has been revealed' points to the whole of the message as a trust to be guarded and lived by, and by extension it addresses every believer, who is called to hold to the divine guidance with the same steadfastness amid pressures to compromise or waver.

translation: And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people, and you are going to be questioned.
interpretation: The verse establishes the Qur'an as a source of honor and remembrance for the Prophet Muhammad and his community, the people to whom it was first addressed, so that its guidance is a standing reminder of their identity, duties, and purpose. The closing warning, "and you are going to be questioned," links this privilege to accountability: the one who receives a reminder bears the responsibility of heeding it, and will be held to account before God for how they received and lived by it. Thus the honor of possessing revelation is inseparable from the obligation to act upon it.

translation: And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers: Did We appoint gods besides the Most Merciful to be worshipped?
interpretation: The verse points to the unbroken unity of the message carried by all the prophets: from Noah and Abraham down to Muhammad, every messenger called to the worship of the One God alone. By directing the Prophet to ask those before him, it invites reflection on the prior revelations and makes the question itself a proof, since no earlier messenger ever sanctioned worship of other deities beside the All-Merciful. The phrase 'the Most Merciful' highlights that divine mercy is the very reason worship belongs to God alone, and that setting up rivals to Him contradicts the nature of the One who has shown mercy to creation.

translation: And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, and he said, "Indeed, I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: The verse presents the mission of Moses as rooted in divine authority: he is sent with clear signs, not merely with his own claims, and he opens his message by identifying himself as a messenger of the Lord of all creation. Addressing Pharaoh and his elite signals that the call to truth is directed first at those who hold power and shape public opinion, and that no earthly authority stands above the sovereignty of the Lord of the worlds. The emphasis on his title as a messenger underscores that his role is to convey, not to rule by his own will, which sets the standard for prophetic humility against tyranny.

translation: But when he brought them Our signs, behold, they laughed at them.
interpretation: The verse portrays the disposition of those who, confronted with clear divine signs, respond not with reflection or humility but with mockery. Their laughter is a defense against the truth: rather than examining the evidence that has come to them, they treat it as a joke, revealing a heart that has closed itself to guidance. It warns that ridicule of revelation is a symptom of spiritual heedlessness, and that the signs of God are not diminished by the scorn of those who refuse them, but their scorn returns as a sign of their own blindness.

translation: And We did not show them any sign except that it was greater than its sister, and We seized them with punishment so that they might return.
interpretation: The verse describes how each sign sent to Pharaoh's people was greater than the one before it, a progression designed to awaken them, yet they persisted in denial. Their seizure by punishment was a final mercy meant to humble them and turn them back toward God, and the verse reveals that the purpose of affliction is repentance, while the hardness of heart that resists even escalating proofs shows that guidance depends on the willingness of the one who receives it.

translation: And they said, "O you sorcerer, invoke your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you; indeed, we will be guided."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Pharaoh's people to Moses (Surah Az-Zukhruf 43:49), reveals a mixture of respect forced by crisis and a hollow, conditional faith. They address Moses as a 'sorcerer,' a label they use to dismiss his miracles, yet they ask him to invoke his Lord, acknowledging that the plagues come from a power beyond their own magicians. Their phrase 'by what He has covenanted with you' appeals to the special bond Moses claimed with God, and their promise 'we will be guided' is made only in exchange for the removal of the punishment. The verse thus exposes a recurring human pattern: turning to God in distress while withholding true submission once relief arrives, treating faith as a bargain rather than as a sincere response to divine truth.

translation: But when We removed the punishment from them, behold, they broke their word at once.
interpretation: The verse portrays a recurring pattern of human nature: under the pressure of calamity, people turn to God in humility and make promises of faithfulness, but as soon as the hardship is lifted, they revert to their former heedlessness and break their covenant. The sudden shift captured by the word 'idhā' (behold, at once) underlines how quickly relief dissolves sincere resolve. The lesson is that true gratitude and steadfastness must be sustained beyond moments of fear, and that God's mercy in relieving suffering is meant to lead to lasting faithfulness rather than renewed rebellion.

translation: And Pharaoh called out among his people, saying: "O my people, does not the dominion of Egypt belong to me, and these rivers flowing beneath me? Do you not then see?"
interpretation: Pharaoh's appeal rests on worldly possession: he equates his control over Egypt and its life-giving Nile with divine standing, so that power and wealth become the measure of truth. His question "Do you not see?" is a call to judge by appearances alone, a mirror of the human tendency to take material abundance as proof of worth. The verse exposes how arrogance blinds a person to the Source of all dominion, and it warns that those who trust in what flows beneath them, rather than in the One who granted it, have lost the true sight that the question ironically demands.

translation: Or am I not better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly make himself clear?
interpretation: Pharaoh's words expose a worldview that measures human worth by outward signs of power, wealth, and eloquence rather than by truth and sincerity. Having seized on Moses's modest bearing and his lack of polished speech, he treats these as proof of Moses's inferiority and his own superiority, while the very prophetic message he dismisses carries the weight that his worldly status cannot give him. The verse thus reveals how arrogance blinds a person to the value of the truth itself, judging the messenger by appearances and missing the substance of the message.

translation: So why have bracelets of gold not been cast upon him, or why have the angels not come with him in procession?
interpretation: The verse is spoken by Pharaoh, who mocks Moses by pointing to the outward signs of authority that he believes a true messenger should bear: gold bracelets as a mark of rank and an escort of angels accompanying him. Pharaoh measures prophethood by worldly markers of status and wealth, which reveals his own values and his contempt for the humble appearance of Moses. The verse thus exposes a recurring pattern in which those who hold worldly power judge truth by display and dignity of station, while God's messengers are sent with clear proofs rather than material splendor.

translation: So he made his people feeble-minded, and they obeyed him. Indeed, they were a defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: The verse shows how a leader who exploits the weakness of others' judgment can lead a people astray: Pharaoh did not overpower their reason by argument but belittled and unsettled them, so that they surrendered their discernment and followed him. The verse then reveals the root of the disaster: their obedience was not innocent submission but the fruit of a corrupted disposition, a habitual turning away from truth (fisq). A people who have already chosen to depart from right guidance become easy prey for a tyrant, and their following him is itself the proof of their moral deviance. It is a warning that political and spiritual misguidance is sustained not only by the ambition of the misleader but by the complicity of those who abandon their own judgment.

translation: So when they angered Us, We took retribution from them, and We drowned them all together.
interpretation: The verse presents a pattern in divine justice: the people's persistence in transgression reached a point where they provoked God's anger, and their defiance was met not with immediate mercy but with decisive requital. The phrase 'āsafūnā' conveys that their conduct grieved and angered God, signaling that they had exhausted the space for reform. The drowning that follows, 'ajma'īn' (all of them), emphasizes the completeness of the punishment, leaving none of the wrongdoers spared. Read reflectively, the verse warns that persistent rejection of guidance brings a reckoning that is both certain and total, and it invites the listener to heed the signs before the limit of patience is reached.

translation: So We made them a precedent and an example for those who came after.
interpretation: The verse points to the principle that the fate of earlier peoples who rejected their messengers serves as a lasting lesson. By making them a 'salaf' (a forerunner that stands as a warning) and a 'mathal' (a parable or exemplary case), God turns their destruction into a visible admonition for later generations, calling people to reflect on the consequences of denying the truth and to take heed before facing the same end.

translation: And when the son of Mary was cited as an example, behold, your people turn away from it in derision.
interpretation: The verse points to the way some people react to divine truth when it is presented to them through a striking example. Here the example of Jesus, son of Mary, is used by the disbelievers as a pretext for mockery rather than reflection: they seize upon it to argue that their own gods are no different, while ignoring the actual point that Jesus was a servant upon whom Allah bestowed favor. The verse thus exposes a habit of heart in which argument is pursued not to seek guidance but to win, and it warns the believers against adopting the same disposition when confronted with signs and parables that challenge their assumptions.

translation: And they said, "Are our gods better, or is he? They did not strike this comparison for you except to dispute. Rather, they are a quarrelsome people."
interpretation: The verse exposes the disputatious mindset of those who rejected the Prophet: when they are presented with the example of the one God set against their idols, they do not weigh the matter in good faith but raise it as a contentious debate, deliberately pitting their false deities against the truth to win an argument rather than to seek guidance. The Qur'an thus diagnoses their problem not as a lack of evidence but as an inclination toward obstinate contention, and it warns the believer that such argumentativeness, when it is pursued for its own sake, is itself a sign of spiritual error and a barrier to receiving the truth.

translation: He was nothing but a servant upon whom We bestowed favor, and We made him an example for the Children of Israel.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that the one spoken of is purely a human servant of God, not divine, and that the favor bestowed upon him was a sign of God's grace. By making him a model (mathal) for the Children of Israel, God presented him as a clear proof and lesson, so that his case would show them the truth of God's power and the reality of human servanthood, countering the exaggerated claims that had been made about him.

translation: And if We willed, We would have made from among you angels upon the earth, succeeding one another.
interpretation: The verse (Az-Zukhruf 43:60) shows that the arrangement of human existence on earth is a matter of divine wisdom rather than of limitation. God was fully capable of making angels the successors on earth in place of humans, yet He chose to make humanity His vicegerents (khalifa), so that human beings, endowed with free will, bear the trust of building and maintaining the earth. The phrase 'yakhlifun' points to a chain of succession, in which each generation takes over from the one before it. The verse therefore invites reflection on the honor given to humankind and on the responsibility that comes with it: humans are not made to succeed by necessity, as angels obey by nature, but by choice, which makes their obedience and their stewardship of the earth a matter of merit.

translation: And indeed, it (Jesus) is a sign of the Hour, so do not doubt it, and follow me. This is a straight path.
interpretation: The verse points to the return of Jesus before the Day of Judgment as a sign of the Hour, so the believers are commanded not to be skeptical about the Hour. The call to follow the Prophet, or the one sent with the message, is presented as the straight path that leads away from doubt and error. Its emphasis is that certainty about the Hour is inseparable from obedience and guidance: the one who truly believes in the Hour must follow the clear way laid out for him.

translation: And let not Satan avert you (from the path); indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.
interpretation: The verse warns believers against allowing Satan to turn them away from the truth and the straight path. By calling him a 'clear enemy,' it emphasizes that his hostility is not hidden but evident, so the believer should recognize his whispers and temptations for what they are and guard against being led astray by them, since his purpose is to divert humanity from its own good and from God's guidance.

translation: And when Jesus came with clear proofs, he said, "I have certainly come to you with wisdom, and to make clear to you some of that about which you differ. So fear Allah and obey me."
interpretation: The verse presents Jesus as a messenger who arrived with unmistakable signs and with wisdom, not with new disputes of his own making. His mission was to clarify the matters on which his people had fallen into disagreement, so that religious differences would be resolved through clear guidance rather than rivalry. The call to taqwa and obedience reveals that the remedy for division is God-consciousness joined with submission to the messenger who conveys God's command. The verse thus implies that sincere devotion to God and faithful adherence to revealed guidance is the path out of confusion and sectarian conflict.

translation: Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path.
interpretation: The verse places the call to exclusive worship at the center of the prophetic message: the one God is the shared Lord of the prophet and of his people, so the bond between them is not one of rival lordships but of common servitude to a single Creator and Sustainer. The command "so worship Him" follows directly from the fact of His lordship, showing that acknowledging God as Lord (tawhid al-rububiyya) necessarily leads to devoting worship to Him alone (tawhid al-uluhiyya). By calling this "a straight path" (sirat mustaqim), the verse presents monotheistic worship not as an arbitrary demand but as the direct, unswerving route that corresponds to the reality of who God is, in contrast to the crooked paths of associating partners with Him.

translation: So the factions differed among themselves, but woe to those who did wrong from the punishment of a painful day.
interpretation: The verse points to a recurring pattern in which communities that received revelation split into rival factions over its meaning, each group claiming a partial truth for itself. Such division is not merely a difference of opinion but a departure from the unity of the message, and the Qur'an places the responsibility for it on those who wronged themselves and others by distorting or rejecting the truth. Their division will not save them: the verse warns that a day of reckoning will come, and the painful punishment awaiting the wrongdoers on that day will expose the emptiness of their sectarian claims. The passage thus joins a critique of communal discord with a call to moral accountability before God.

translation: Do they await anything but the Hour, that it may come upon them suddenly while they are unaware?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who deny the Hereafter by pointing to the certainty and suddenness of the Last Hour. Their stance is one of waiting for nothing more than the inevitable Day of Judgment, which will overtake them unexpectedly while they are heedless and unprepared. The point is a call to awareness: since the Hour's arrival cannot be foreseen, one should not postpone righteous action and reflection on one's accountability before God, lest the reckoning find a person negligent and without recourse.

translation: Close friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous.
interpretation: The verse points to the fragility of friendships that are built on worldly interests, shared sin, or mutual desires, since on the Day of Judgment those bonds will turn into mutual hostility and blame, as each friend bears the consequences of what they encouraged in the other. Only friendships grounded in piety and the fear of God endure beyond the grave, because they are rooted in the love of what pleases God. The verse thus calls the believer to choose companions carefully, and to see true friendship as a bond that serves one's salvation rather than leading one astray.

translation: O My servants, no fear shall be upon you today, nor shall you grieve.
interpretation: The address "O My servants" is spoken by God directly to the believers on the Day of Judgment, and it carries a tone of tender intimacy, reminding the faithful that their relationship with their Lord is one of loving servanthood rather than mere obligation. The double negation, "no fear" and "nor grief," covers both the anxiety about what lies ahead and the sorrow over what has been lost in the world, so that the believer is freed from both the future and the past. The word "today" anchors this assurance in the present moment of the reckoning, suggesting that the security granted is not a distant promise but a reality that takes effect immediately for those who have lived in devotion. The verse thus presents the ultimate fulfilment of faith: a state in which the fears that burdened the soul in this life are lifted by the nearness and mercy of God.

translation: Those who believed in Our signs and were submitting (to Allah).
interpretation: The verse defines the true believers by two inseparable marks: inner faith (iman) in Allah's signs, whether the revealed verses or the signs manifest in creation, and outward submission (islam) expressed in surrender of the will to the Creator. Belief that never translates into submission remains hollow, and submission without sincere belief lacks its root; the verse thus joins the heart's conviction with the body's obedience as one unified path of devotion.

translation: Enter Paradise, you and your spouses, rejoicing.
interpretation: The verse portrays the believers being welcomed into Paradise together with their righteous spouses, and the word "tuhbarun" points to a joy that is radiant, honoured and refined, a delight that reflects the dignity of those admitted. It suggests that the bliss of the hereafter is not solitary but shared within the bonds of family and companionship that were cherished in this world, so that the reunion of loved ones becomes part of the completeness of the reward. The command "enter" conveys the honour of admission, as though the believers are being received as guests whose faith and good deeds have earned them a place of ease and happiness.

translation: There will be circulated among them platters of gold and cups, and therein is whatever the souls desire and whatever delights the eyes, and you will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: The verse portrays the bliss of Paradise as a complete fulfillment of human longing, addressing both the soul's desires and the senses' delight. By describing gold vessels served by attendants, it presents honor and abundance, while the closing phrase "and you will abide therein eternally" frames this joy as permanent, free from the loss, decay, and anxiety that shadow worldly pleasures. The verse thus teaches that the ultimate reward is a state where every legitimate desire is satisfied and the believer's happiness is secure forever.

translation: And that is the Paradise which you have been given as an inheritance for what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse presents Paradise as an inheritance rather than a mere reward earned in exchange for deeds, since inheritance passes to heirs by right of their connection to the one who left it. Yet the verse ties this inheritance to "what you used to do," showing that human action is the means by which one becomes worthy of it: God's mercy grants the inheritance, while faithful striving in this world is the cause that makes its people its rightful heirs. It thus holds together divine grace and human responsibility, reminding the believer that the eternal abode is the fruit of a life lived in obedience and good works.

translation: You will have therein abundant fruits, from which you will eat.
interpretation: The verse presents the abundance of provision awaiting the righteous in the Gardens, where fruit is not scarce or restricted but plentiful and freely available, so that the believers may partake of it at will. This abundance reflects the generosity of the Creator toward those who have striven in faith and good deeds, and it stands in contrast to the worldly life, where sustenance is often gained through toil and limited by need. The verse thus invites the reader to contemplate a state in which every longing for nourishment and delight is fulfilled, and to orient their conduct toward attaining that enduring ease.

translation: Indeed, the criminals will abide eternally in the punishment of Hell.
interpretation: The verse establishes that those who persist in sin and wrongdoing, the 'mujrimun', will not merely face punishment but will remain in it forever. The emphasis on their being 'khalidun' (abiding eternally) and on the punishment being that of Hell underscores the seriousness of persistent criminality before God, and it stands as a warning that the consequences of deliberate rebellion against divine guidance are final and inescapable in the hereafter, which in turn highlights the mercy and opportunity of repentance available in this life.

translation: Their punishment will not be lightened for them, and they will be in it despairing, utterly hopeless.
interpretation: The verse describes the state of the disbelievers in the Fire: their torment will never be eased or interrupted, and they will remain within it in utter despair, having lost all hope of relief or mercy. This is a warning that the lack of any respite is itself a dimension of their punishment, since the complete absence of hope intensifies their anguish and shows the finality of their condition as a consequence of their rejection of faith.

translation: And We did not wrong them, but they were the ones who were wrongdoing themselves.
interpretation: The verse affirms that divine justice is perfect: God does not oppress anyone, and the ruin that befalls a people comes from their own choices. Wrongdoing is a self-inflicted harm, since by persisting in disbelief, defiance and injustice, people close the doors of guidance upon themselves, so that the punishment they receive is the consequence of their own conduct rather than an act of divine cruelty.

translation: And they will call out, "O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us." He will say, "Indeed, you will remain (here forever)."
interpretation: The verse portrays the despair of the people of the Fire, who, after their suffering has become unbearable, cry out to the keeper of Hell, Malik, asking him to request that their Lord bring their punishment to a close through death or annihilation. Their request is answered with a stark refusal that they will abide in the Fire permanently. The verse thus reveals that the punishment of the disbelievers is not temporary, and that the hope of release is cut off, which serves as a warning to humanity to turn to God in faith and righteousness while there is still opportunity.

translation: We have certainly brought you the truth, but most of you are averse to the truth.
interpretation: The verse expresses a disappointing reality: the message was delivered clearly and its truth is evident, yet the majority of the people did not accept it, not because of any lack of proof but because of their inner aversion. It shows that rejection of the truth often stems from the heart's dislike of what it requires, such as giving up desires, habits, or pride, rather than from intellectual uncertainty. It also consoles the messenger, reminding him that his duty is only to convey the truth clearly, while the responsibility for refusing it lies with those who turn away from it.

translation: Or have they devised a plot? Then it is We who are the devisers of plots.
interpretation: The verse confronts those who conspired against the Messenger and the believers with a decisive warning: their scheming is laid bare before God, who has already determined the outcome. Whatever stratagem they have settled upon in secret, it is God's counter-plan that will prevail, as their own designs rebound upon them. It reassures the believers that the final judgment over hidden plots rests with the One who knows what is concealed in hearts and who defeats all deception.

translation: Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private conversations? Yes indeed, and Our messengers are with them, recording.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who believe their hidden plots and whispered counsel escape divine knowledge. God's hearing encompasses what is concealed, and the affirmation "Yes indeed" stresses the certainty of this knowledge. The reference to recording messengers, who are with them, conveys that every word and deed is preserved and will be reckoned with. The verse thus calls the heedless to sincerity, since no secret is hidden from the One who records all.

translation: Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers.
interpretation: The verse places the Prophet in a conditional hypothetical to expose the absurdity of attributing a son to God. The phrase 'If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers' is not an affirmation that God has offspring but a rhetorical reductio: if such a thing were true, the one most obligated to honour and submit to it would be the Prophet himself, yet he affirms the opposite by his very existence as a servant. Its force lies in rejecting the claim through its own logic, since true sonship would demand worship, and the Prophet's servanthood ('abd) is the proof that no divine son exists. The verse thus stresses God's absolute oneness and transcendence above any begetting, a theme that runs through the surah of Maryam and the surah of al-Ikhlas.

translation: Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.
interpretation: The verse declares God's absolute transcendence over every false attribution. By naming Him as Lord of the heavens, the earth, and the Throne, it places the whole of creation and sovereignty under His dominion, and so the claims made about Him by those who associate partners with Him or ascribe to Him falsehoods are shown to be empty and unworthy of Him. Tasbih, glorifying Him by declaring Him free of every defect, is thus the proper response of the believer, who recognizes that the One who governs the highest and the lowest is far exalted above any description that falls short of His majesty.

translation: So leave them to plunge in vain talk and play until they meet their Day which they are promised.
interpretation: The verse is a divine instruction to the Prophet to disengage from those who mock and dismiss the message, turning away from their frivolous disputing and amusement. It conveys that such persons are left to their own course for a time, not in approval but as a measure of their own choice, until the Day of Judgment arrives, the day they have been warned of and have denied. Its force lies in a sober detachment: the believer is not required to win over the unwilling, and the consequences of heedlessness will become unavoidably evident on that appointed day.

translation: And it is He who is God in the heavens and God on the earth. And He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse affirms that divine sovereignty and worship belong to one God alone, who is recognized as the sole deity both in the heavens and on the earth, so that no realm of existence stands outside His lordship. The naming of Him as the All-Wise and the All-Knowing grounds this affirmation of tawhid in His perfect wisdom and comprehensive knowledge: the one who is worshipped is also the one who governs all things with wisdom and is aware of every hidden and manifest matter. Thus the verse invites the believer to direct devotion to Him alone, trusting that the one whose knowledge encompasses heaven and earth is the only fitting object of worship.

translation: And blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, and with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: The verse opens by declaring the blessedness of God, whose sovereignty is total and encompasses both the vast heavens and the earth and everything in the space between them, so that nothing in creation stands outside His ownership and authority. It then singles out a matter that lies beyond all human reach: knowledge of the Hour belongs to Him alone, meaning that the precise moment of the end of worldly existence is hidden from every creature, a reminder of the limits of human knowledge and the absolute nature of divine knowledge. The closing phrase brings the believer back to the central reality of accountability, that all people will ultimately be returned to their Lord, so that the awareness of His dominion and of the hidden timing of the Hour should guide a person to live with humility, vigilance, and readiness for the meeting with God.

translation: And those whom they invoke besides Him do not possess intercession, except one who testifies to the truth while they have knowledge.
interpretation: The verse denies that those worshipped besides God have any power to intercede, since intercession belongs to God alone and is granted only by His permission.
