translation: When those who disbelieved had placed in their hearts zealotry, the zealotry of the time of ignorance, then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and made them adhere to the word of piety, and they were most deserving of it and worthy of it. And Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing.
interpretation: The verse points to the moment at Hudaybiyyah, when the pagans of Makkah, moved by a proud and reflexive clannish arrogance inherited from the age of ignorance, refused to allow the Muslims to perform the pilgrimage and to write the treaty in the terms the Prophet proposed. Their zealotry was not rooted in any true principle but in wounded pride and the reflex of tribal honor, which the Qur'an calls hamiyyat al-jahiliyyah. In contrast, Allah sent down sakinah, a settled composure of heart, upon the Prophet and the believers, so that they remained steady, restrained their anger, and accepted terms that outwardly appeared humiliating. This tranquility then bound them to kalimat al-taqwa, the word of God-consciousness, which in this context is the reaffirmation of their faith and its discipline, and the believers proved themselves its rightful owners and most worthy of it. The lesson is that true honor lies in piety and inner peace, not in the blind pride of tribe and tradition, and that Allah's knowledge encompasses the sincere intentions behind such decisions.

translation: Allah has certainly fulfilled for His Messenger the vision in truth: you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security, with your heads shaved and [your hair] shortened, fearing no one. He knew what you did not know, and He arranged before that a near victory.
interpretation: The verse presents the dream of the Prophet as a divine promise that was fulfilled in its proper time and manner, teaching believers that Allah's decree unfolds according to a wisdom that surpasses human foresight. The Muslims, who expected immediate entry into Makkah, were given instead the treaty of Hudaybiyyah, which seemed a setback but was in fact the 'near victory' that opened the way to peace, the spread of Islam, and eventually the entry into the Sacred Mosque. The conditional phrase 'if Allah wills' reminds the believer to attach every plan to the will of God, and the verse thus instructs patience and trust in divine knowledge when outcomes appear contrary to what one hopes.

translation: It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, that He may make it prevail over all religion. And sufficient is Allah as a witness.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the mission of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ rests on two inseparable components: guidance, meaning clear knowledge and divine direction, and the religion of truth, meaning right conduct and belief grounded in reality. The promise that this religion will prevail over all others is best understood as a divine assurance of its ultimate intellectual, moral, and social superiority, realized through its evidence and its spread, not merely through force. The closing statement that Allah suffices as a witness reassures the believers that their cause is known to God, who attests to the truth of the Messenger's mission and to the sincerity of those who follow it, so they need not fear opposition or seek validation from others.

translation: Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are forceful against the disbelievers and merciful among themselves. You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and His approval. The mark of their prostration is on their faces. That is their description in the Torah, and their description in the Gospel is like a seed that sends out its shoot, strengthens it, so it grows thick and stands firm on its stalk, pleasing the sowers, so that Allah may enrage the disbelievers by them. Allah has promised those among them who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: The verse's closing image of a seed that sends out its shoot, is strengthened, thickens, and stands firm on its stalk points to the community's gradual, organic growth, shown as a process of nurturing rather than a sudden achievement. The believers' strength is thus presented as the fruit of patient cultivation, and the final image of the sowers being pleased suggests that such steady, visible flourishing is itself a source of divine satisfaction and a warning to those who oppose them.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O you who have believed, do not put yourselves forward before Allah and His Messenger, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing.
interpretation: The verse opens by addressing the believers directly, calling them to a discipline of conduct toward the Prophet and toward God. To 'put forward' before Allah and His Messenger is to act or speak ahead of divine and prophetic guidance, making one's own opinion or desire the measure of matters that belong to God's command and the Messenger's direction. Such presumption is a failure of reverence, and the believer's proper stance is to wait upon revelation and the Prophet's judgment. The command to fear Allah binds this etiquette to inward consciousness rather than mere outward form, so that the restraint arises from awareness that God is constantly present. The closing names of God, the All-Hearing and All-Knowing, remind the believer that nothing said or intended escapes divine knowledge, so that even the lowering of one's voice and the timing of one's words are weighed before Him.

translation: O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, and do not speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another, lest your deeds become worthless while you do not perceive.
interpretation: The verse establishes a principle of reverence and decorum toward the Prophet that carries over into how believers treat the authority and teachings he brought. Raising one's voice above his, or addressing him with the casual loudness used among peers, reveals a heart that has not fully weighed his station, and the warning is that such heedlessness can silently erode the value of one's good works, since a person may be unaware of the damage being done. The phrase "while you do not perceive" points to the danger of inner negligence that goes unnoticed, urging the believer toward constant self-scrutiny in matters of respect, humility, and attentiveness to what is sacred. The lesson extends beyond the immediate context to any relationship where honor is due, reminding that outward manners are inseparable from the sincerity of faith.

translation: Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah - those are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for piety. For them is forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: The verse ties outward courtesy to inward condition: lowering one's voice before the Prophet is not merely a matter of etiquette but a sign that the heart has been tested and found to be receptive to God-consciousness. Reverence expressed in conduct reveals where piety truly resides, and the reward promised is both the pardon of shortcomings and a great recompense for those whose hearts have been shaped by taqwa. The lesson extends beyond the Prophet's own lifetime, reminding believers that sincere respect for the sacred, expressed through restraint and humility, is itself a fruit of a God-fearing heart.

translation: Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the private chambers—most of them do not use their reason.
interpretation: The verse rebukes a group of people who came to the Prophet's private quarters and called out to him loudly from outside, disturbing him, rather than waiting patiently for him to come out. Its meaning reaches beyond that single incident: it teaches that respect, decorum, and patience are owed to the Messenger and to those in positions of trust, and that lack of courtesy toward them is a sign of diminished understanding. By noting that most of them do not reason, the verse suggests that true intelligence is shown in restraint, humility, and the careful consideration of how one addresses others, especially in matters of honor and sacred relationship.

translation: And if they had been patient until you came out to them, it would have been better for them. But Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who called out to the Prophet from outside his private quarters, disturbing him without regard for his dignity. Restraint and patient waiting for him to emerge would have been better for them, since it reflects respect, good manners, and consideration for the Messenger's time and rest. The closing reminder that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful signals that past lapses in courtesy are pardoned for those who repent and reform, so the lesson is both moral correction and an open door to returning to proper conduct.

translation: O you who have believed, if a deviator brings you a report, verify it, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and then become regretful over what you have done.
interpretation: The verse establishes a principle of responsible information-handling within the community of believers: news carried by a person of questionable character must not be accepted at face value but must be investigated before any action is taken. Its concern is that hasty reliance on unverified reports, especially when they come from unreliable sources, can lead to real injustice against innocent people, born of ignorance rather than knowledge, and the resulting remorse is the natural consequence of acting without due diligence. Read in its wider context, the verse also teaches that social harmony depends on careful verification and restraint, since rumor and slander can ignite conflict between people who should be united.

translation: And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah. If he were to obey you in much of the matter, you would surely be in difficulty. But Allah has endeared to you faith and made it beautiful in your hearts, and has made disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience hateful to you. Those are the rightly guided.
interpretation: The verse reveals that the Prophet's presence was a mercy that the believers should not take for granted. Had the Messenger followed the opinions and desires of the majority, the community would have fallen into hardship and error, since people's preferences often serve their immediate impulses rather than what is good for them. The true safeguard lies in Allah's grace, which turned the believers' hearts toward faith and made it dear to them while making rejection, deviance, and defiance repugnant. Guidance, then, is not measured by agreement with one's own wishes but by the inner love of faith that Allah plants in the heart, and those who possess this love and this aversion are the ones who have truly found the right path.

translation: As a bounty and favor from Allah. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse presents the preceding command or ruling as something flowing from Allah's own grace rather than from any necessity on His part. The words 'fadlan' (bounty) and 'ni'mah' (favor) point to a divine generosity that bestows benefit beyond what is strictly deserved, so that the believer's obedience and its rewards are understood as gifts rather than wages owed. The closing pair of divine names, 'Al-'Alim' (the All-Knowing) and 'Al-Hakim' (the All-Wise), anchors this generosity in perfect knowledge and wisdom: Allah knows precisely what benefits His servants and orders affairs according to that knowledge, so the grace is never arbitrary but always fitting and purposeful. The verse thus invites the reader to gratitude and to trust in the justice and wisdom behind every divine provision.

translation: And if two groups of the believers fight each other, then make peace between them. But if one of them oppresses the other, then fight against the one that oppresses until it returns to the command of Allah. And if it returns, then make peace between them with justice and be equitable. Indeed, Allah loves those who are equitable.
interpretation: This verse establishes that when believers fall into armed conflict, the community's first obligation is reconciliation, reminding them that they remain brothers and sisters in faith. It also shows that peacemaking must not be passive: when one side persists in aggression after mediation, the rest of the community must act to restrain it, with the aim not of destruction but of bringing the transgressor back to obedience to God's command. Once the aggressor desists, the verse insists that reconciliation be carried out with strict fairness, so that the settlement does not favor one party out of resentment or partisanship. The closing affirmation that God loves the equitable makes justice, even toward a former enemy, the measure of a truly righteous society.

translation: The believers are but brothers, so make peace between your two brothers, and fear Allah that you may receive mercy.
interpretation: The verse grounds the bond among believers in faith itself, describing it as a kinship that is as binding as blood ties. Because this brotherhood is established by God rather than by human choice, it carries a duty: when discord arises between two believers, the community must not remain indifferent or take sides out of partisanship, but must actively work to reconcile them. The closing call to taking God as a protector and being mindful of Him is the foundation that makes this reconciliation sincere, since fear of God restrains pride and self-interest. The promise of mercy at the end links social harmony with divine grace, showing that preserving unity among the faithful is itself an act of worship that brings God's compassion upon the community.

translation: O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people, perhaps they may be better than them; nor let women ridicule [other] women, perhaps they may be better than them. And do not defame one another, nor insult each other by [offensive] nicknames. Wretched is the name of defiance after belief. And whoever does not repent, then it is those who are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse establishes that dignity and honor are not measured by lineage, gender, appearance, or social standing, since the one mocked may be better in the sight of God, and so mockery, defamation, and derisive nicknames strike at the bonds of faith that the believers share. By naming such conduct 'defiance' after having believed, it shows that these social sins are not minor lapses but a corruption of one's new identity as a believer, and the call to repentance at its close makes clear that a community of faith is preserved only when its members guard one another's honor, recognizing that the inner worth of a person is known to God alone and that the believer's own self is included in the warning against the harm done to others.

translation: O you who have believed, avoid much suspicion; indeed, some suspicion is sin. And do not spy on one another, and do not backbite one another. Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would detest it. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Accepting of repentance and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse builds a moral framework for protecting the dignity and trust within the believing community by targeting the inner and outer sources of harm to others. It begins with the heart, warning against excessive suspicion, since assumptions about others' hidden motives can lead a person into injustice and sin. It then moves to action, forbidding the probing into others' private affairs and the speaking ill of them in their absence. The striking image of eating the flesh of a dead brother shows that backbiting is not merely a social offense but a violation of a person who cannot defend himself, and the natural revulsion people feel at that image is meant to awaken the same revulsion toward slandering others. The verse closes by returning the believer to taqwa and the hope of divine mercy, implying that a person who has wronged others through such conduct should turn back to God in repentance, for Allah accepts repentance and is merciful.

translation: O mankind, indeed We have created you from a male and a female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware.
interpretation: The verse establishes that all human beings share a single origin, so lineage, nation, and tribe are not grounds for pride or superiority; they exist so that people may come to know and cooperate with one another. The only true measure of honor before God is taqwa, conscious awareness of God expressed through righteous conduct, and since God knows the inner reality of every person, worth is judged by sincerity and piety rather than by outward distinctions.

translation: The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; rather say, 'We have submitted,' for faith has not yet entered your hearts. But if you obey Allah and His Messenger, He will not deprive you [of the reward] of your deeds at all. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."
interpretation: The verse draws a distinction between outward submission (islam), which is the public acceptance of the religion through speech and conformity to its practices, and inner faith (iman), which is the settled conviction that dwells in the heart. The Bedouins claimed the full station of belief before it had taken root within them, and the Prophet is instructed to correct the claim by reserving the word iman for what has truly entered the heart, while allowing them the more modest name of submission. The verse thus teaches that outward acceptance is a real starting point that the Qur'an does not reject, yet it must not be mistaken for the completed reality of faith. The closing promise shows that sincere obedience to Allah and His Messenger is what allows faith to mature and secures the reward of one's deeds, and the mention of Allah's forgiveness and mercy offers hope to those who are still on the path toward inward belief.

translation: The believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger and then have not doubted and have striven with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah. It is those who are the truthful.
interpretation: The verse defines true faith not as a mere verbal profession but as a complete commitment that combines firm conviction free from any lingering doubt with active sacrifice of one's property and self for the sake of God. By tying the title of 'the truthful' (al-sadiqun) to this combination, it shows that sincerity of belief is verified through its costly enactment: a person's claim to faith is tested by whether they are willing to give up what they own and what they are in the path of God. Doubt and reluctance to sacrifice are thus presented as signs that the claim of belief is incomplete, while steadfast certainty joined with readiness to give is the mark of genuine faithfulness.

translation: Say: "Will you inform Allah about your religion, when Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth? And Allah is Knowing of everything."
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who sought to present their faith to God as though He needed to be informed of it, as in the context of Surah Al-Hujurat 49:16 where Bedouins claimed to have submitted. Its point is that sincerity cannot be displayed or announced to the All-Knowing, since God's knowledge encompasses everything hidden in the heavens and the earth. Religion is therefore not a matter of claims or outward proclamation, but of genuine inner conviction that is already fully known to God.

translation: They consider it a favor to you that they have embraced Islam. Say: Do not consider your Islam a favor to me. Rather, it is God who has conferred a favor upon you, that He guided you to faith, if you are truthful.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the Bedouin Arabs who claimed that their acceptance of Islam was a kindness done to the Prophet. Their conversion is not a benefit they bestow upon him or upon the community; the true benefactor is God, who guided their hearts to belief. Their claim to have done a favor is thus exposed: if their faith is genuine, they should recognize that gratitude is owed to God for guidance, not to the Prophet for accepting their submission. The phrase 'if you are truthful' challenges the sincerity of their profession, implying that outward submission without inner conviction is no real achievement and no cause for boasting.

translation: Indeed, Allah knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse establishes that divine knowledge is complete and unbounded: nothing hidden from human perception, whether in the farthest reaches of the heavens or the depths of the earth, escapes Allah. The shift from His knowledge of the unseen to His seeing of human deeds brings this cosmic certainty down to the personal level, reminding the believer that their outward actions and inner intentions alike are fully witnessed. This awareness is meant to ground moral responsibility, since no concealment before people can conceal anything from the One who knows what is hidden.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an.
interpretation: The verse opens with the disjointed letter Qaf, one of the enigmatic letters that begin several surahs, whose precise meaning is known only to Allah; its placement before the oath signals a challenge to attention and a call to reflect on the Qur'an itself. By swearing by the glorious Qur'an, Allah elevates the revelation to the highest standing, affirming its dignity, its grandeur, and its truth, and inviting the listener to recognize that the message which follows, concerning resurrection and accountability, is anchored in this noble and authoritative Book.

translation: Nay, they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves, and the disbelievers say, "This is a strange thing."
interpretation: The verse exposes the root of the disbelievers' rejection: it is not a lack of evidence but astonishment that a messenger should arise from among ordinary people rather than from some extraordinary source. Their wonder at the familiar becoming a bearer of warning reveals a heart that finds it hard to accept that guidance can come through a human being they already know. By calling the message "strange," they turn away from its content and judge it by the novelty of its messenger, which is a reminder that prejudice about the form of truth can blind a person to the truth itself.

translation: "When we have died and become dust, [will we be returned]? That is a return far-fetched."
interpretation: The verse voices the disbelievers' incredulity at bodily resurrection: they find it inconceivable that scattered dust and decayed remains could ever be reassembled into living persons. Their words reveal a reasoning that measures divine power by human limitation, placing the act of raising the dead beyond possibility. The surrounding context of Surah Qaf answers this denial by pointing to God's perfect knowledge of what the earth consumes of human bodies, and to His creation of the heavens and earth without weariness, so that the return the disbelievers deem remote is in fact easy for the One who originated creation.

translation: We certainly know what the earth diminishes of them, and with Us is a preserved record (kitab hafiz).
interpretation: The verse affirms God's complete and precise knowledge of every human being, including what the earth takes from them after death, such as their bodies, their decay and their scattering. Nothing about a person is lost to God, even when it seems to have vanished into the ground. This knowledge is not left to chance but is recorded in a guarded book that preserves every detail. The verse thus offers assurance to the believer that the Resurrection is not beyond God's power to reassemble what has been dispersed, and it warns that no deed or trace of a person escapes the divine record.

translation: Nay, but they have denied the truth when it came to them, so they are in a confused and disordered state.
interpretation: The verse describes the condition of those who reject the truth not out of lack of evidence but after it has clearly reached them. Their rejection is not the product of honest uncertainty; it is a deliberate turning away that leaves them in a state of confusion and disarray, with no stable ground to stand on. Their inner chaos is thus portrayed as the consequence of their own refusal, for a heart that closes against clear guidance is left wandering among contradictory opinions, unable to settle on a sound conviction.

translation: Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We constructed it and adorned it, and it has no rifts?
interpretation: The verse calls the human being to reflective observation of the heavens, the most immediate and majestic sign above every head. The phrase 'how We built it' points to the sky's firm, deliberate construction, held together without fault, while 'and adorned it' points to the beauty of its stars and lights that delight the beholder. The statement 'it has no rifts' (la furud) affirms its perfect integrity and flawless order, so that the one who contemplates it is led from the visible harmony of creation to recognition of the Creator's power, wisdom, and care, and to the conviction that the One who ordered the heavens with such precision is able to bring about the resurrection and accountability the surrounding passages affirm.

translation: And the earth—We spread it out, and cast into it firm mountains, and caused to grow therein every beautiful pair of plants.
interpretation: The verse invites the reader to contemplate the earth as a deliberate act of divine design. Its being 'spread out' (madadnaha) evokes a habitable, expansive ground, while the 'firm mountains' (rawasi) cast into it serve as anchors that steady it and keep it from shaking, so that life can settle upon it. The phrase 'every beautiful pair' (min kulli zawjin bahij) points to the abundance and diversity of vegetation, where each kind comes in complementary pairs that delight the eye. Taken together, the verse moves from the physical stability of the earth to its fertility, presenting the natural world as a sign of God's power, generosity, and care for the living, and asking the believer to recognize in the beauty of growing things a reminder of the Creator who sustains them.

translation: A insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back in repentance (to God).
interpretation: The verse presents the signs and reminders of God's creation as a means of insight for those who are truly devoted to Him. The phrase 'every servant who turns back' (munib) singles out the one whose heart is humble and receptive: such a person repeatedly returns to God, and therefore the reminders awaken his understanding, while the heedless remain blind to what is plainly before them. Thus, the capacity to benefit from divine guidance depends less on the abundance of evidence than on the inner disposition of the heart that turns toward its Lord.

translation: And We sent down from the sky blessed water, and with it We caused to grow gardens and the grain of harvest.
interpretation: The verse presents rain as a blessing descending from the heavens, the source of all life on earth. Water is called mubarak because from it flows abundance: gardens rise, fruit trees flourish, and grain ripens for harvest. The sequence moves from the gift of water to the living growth it produces, inviting the reader to reflect on the divine care that sustains human livelihood, and to see in the cycle of rain and harvest a sign of the same power that brings the dead earth back to life and will one day bring the dead to life again.

translation: And the date palms with their spathes laden (with fruit) in rows, one above another
interpretation: The verse draws the believer's attention to the date palm, standing tall and heavy with clusters of blossom packed in orderly layers within their sheaths. Its ordered, gradually unfolding growth points to a deliberate design and a Creator who arranges life with precision, so that the sight of a single tree becomes a reminder of divine power and the abundance that sustains people. Placed among the verses about rain, the earth's revival and the resurrection, it suggests that the same power which brings forth fruit from dry ground can bring the dead back to life.

translation: As a provision for the servants; and We give life thereby to a dead land. Thus will be the resurrection.
interpretation: The verse draws an analogy between the rain sent down from the sky and the resurrection of the dead. Just as rain is a provision (rizq) for God's servants, bringing forth sustenance from the earth, so too the revival of barren, lifeless land by water is a visible sign of God's power to bring the dead back to life. The earth that lay withered and dry is stirred to life and yields growth, and the same creative power will bring humans forth from their graves on the Day of Resurrection (al-khurūj). The verse thus invites the believer to reflect on the cycle of death and renewal in nature as evidence that the return to life after death is within God's ability, and that the One who provides for His creation in this world will equally raise them up for judgment.

translation: Before them, the people of Noah denied (the truth), and the companions of the Rass, and Thamud.
interpretation: The verse opens a series of examples from earlier nations to show that rejection of the messengers is an old and recurring pattern in human history. By naming Noah's people, the companions of the Rass, and Thamud, it places the Quraysh and the listeners of the Prophet within a long chain of communities that received guidance and turned away from it. The repetition of the act of denial (kadhdhaba) in each case highlights that the cause of destruction was not a lack of signs but a stubborn refusal to accept them. The implicit lesson is a warning: the same disbelief brings the same consequence, and the story of these peoples is meant to awaken the heart to reflection before the fate of earlier nations befalls the present one.

translation: And [the people of] 'Ad, and Pharaoh, and the brothers of Lot [i.e., the people of Lot].
interpretation: The verse places the nations of 'Ad, Pharaoh, and the people of Lot side by side as examples of communities that denied their messengers and were destroyed for their arrogance and corruption. Their grouping is a warning to the listener that divine punishment is not reserved for any one people: power in the case of Pharaoh, wealth and strength in the case of 'Ad, and moral deviance in the case of Lot's people each led to the same end. The phrase "brothers of Lot" emphasizes that they were of the same kinship and stock as the prophet who called them, yet their rejection of his guidance did not spare them. The lesson is that closeness of relation or previous prosperity offers no protection against accountability before God, and that the people of the present are summoned to reflect on these earlier examples.

translation: And the companions of the thicket and the people of Tubba'. Each of them denied the messengers, so My warning was justly fulfilled against them.
interpretation: The verse closes a series of past nations by showing that their denial of the messengers was not a mere disagreement but a rejection that brought its own consequence. The phrase "fa-haqqa wa'id" (the warning came due) indicates that the threat made through the prophets is not empty: it is bound to the truth of what was announced, so that when a people persists in rejecting guidance, the promised reckoning arrives in its appointed time. The mention of the companions of the thicket and the people of Tubba' serves as a reminder to the listeners that the pattern of denial and divine retribution is consistent across history, and that the same warning stands for those who follow their example.

translation: Did We then tire of the first creation? Rather, they are in confusion about a new creation.
interpretation: The verse answers those who denied resurrection and doubted being brought back to life. Its reasoning is that the One who originated creation without weariness is not incapable of recreating it. The question is rhetorical: since they accept the first creation, which they witnessed in its origin, they have no rational ground to deny a second one. The phrase 'in confusion' (fi labs) signals that their denial arises not from evidence but from a muddled, unsettled state of mind that refuses clear reasoning. The verse thus calls the heedless to reflect on their own beginning as proof that God's power extends to bringing forth creation again on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And We have already created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than his jugular vein.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God's knowledge encompasses the innermost thoughts and inclinations of the human being, the subtle promptings that arise within the self before they are ever spoken or acted upon. By describing God as nearer to a person than the jugular vein, which is the most intimate and vital part of the body, it conveys that divine presence and awareness are not distant but constantly accompanying the human soul. The point is twofold: it reminds the believer that nothing hidden within them escapes God's knowledge, and it offers reassurance that the Creator who knows the self so intimately is also the One who is always near, responsive, and capable of guiding it.

translation: When the two receivers receive (their records), one sitting on the right and one on the left.
interpretation: This verse (Qaf 50:17) refers to the two angels assigned to every person, who are constantly present with him and record his deeds. The one on the right records good deeds and the one on the left records evil ones, so that nothing a person does, says, or thinks escapes record. The verse conveys that human conduct is continuously observed and documented, which should move the believer toward accountability and sincerity, knowing that a complete account will be presented on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Man does not utter a single word except that there is with him a watchful observer ready to record it.
interpretation: The verse affirms that every word a person speaks is known and recorded, since an attentive angelic witness is always present beside him. It calls the speaker to moral accountability: because nothing said is lost or ignored, a believer should weigh his speech carefully, knowing that his words will be presented before him on the Day of Judgment as part of his own record.

translation: And the intoxication of death will come with the truth. That is what you used to flee from.
interpretation: The verse presents death not as an accident but as a reality that arrives in its true and appointed form, the "truth" that the heedless have long tried to evade. The word sakrat (intoxication or overwhelming stupor) depicts the state of the dying person, whose senses and composure are overcome as the reality of the Hereafter is unveiled to him. The address "that is what you used to flee from" turns the reproach inward: the person's lifelong avoidance of contemplating mortality and accountability is exposed at the very moment it can no longer be avoided, so that the verse calls the listener to face now what will inevitably confront him then.

translation: And the Trumpet will be blown. That is the Day of the Warning (the promised Day of threat and fulfillment).
interpretation: The verse points to the decisive moment that closes the present world and opens the reckoning. The blowing of the trumpet is presented as a signal that the hidden order of things is about to be unveiled, and that no one can delay or escape what has been promised. By calling it the Day of al-Wa'id, the verse ties the event to the warnings that were given throughout revelation, so that the listener is reminded that the threat was not an empty word. The imagery of the trumpet conveys both the suddenness of the summons and the total authority of the One who calls humanity to account, leaving the heedless with no excuse and urging the believer to prepare for that appointed hour.

translation: And every soul will come, accompanied by a driver and a witness.
interpretation: The verse depicts the Day of Judgment, when each soul is brought forward to account for its deeds. The 'driver' is an angel who escorts the soul to the place of reckoning, while the 'witness' is one who testifies to what the soul did, so that no one can deny or escape the record of their actions. It conveys that accountability is complete and inescapable: a person is both led to judgment and confronted by a witness to their conduct, emphasizing that every deed, however hidden in this world, will be exposed before God.

translation: You were certainly heedless of this, so We have removed from you your covering, and your sight today is sharp.
interpretation: The verse depicts the moment after death, when the veil of worldly distraction and denial that blinded a person in life is lifted, and the reality of the Hereafter becomes plainly visible. What was dismissed as unseen or unlikely is now directly witnessed, and the sharpened sight signifies that the soul perceives the truth without any remaining doubt, making the lesson of heedlessness painfully clear and inescapable.

translation: And his companion will say: This is what is with me, ready and present.
interpretation: This verse belongs to the scene of the Day of Judgment, where the accompanying angel (the 'qarin' assigned to each person, who recorded deeds) presents the record of the person's conduct before the Lord. The phrase 'ready and present' ('atid') conveys that the account is complete and prepared, with nothing omitted or lost: every deed is set forth exactly as it was done. It reminds the listener that human actions are recorded and will be brought forward without any possibility of denial or escape, so that accountability becomes immediate and unavoidable.

translation: Cast into Hell every stubborn, obstinate disbeliever.
interpretation: The dual command is addressed to the two angels who accompanied the soul on the Day of Judgment, one driving and one bearing witness, so the verse portrays the final execution of divine justice carried out by those assigned to the reckoning. The word 'anid' describes not mere ignorance but a persistent, deliberate refusal to accept truth after it has been made clear, so the punishment falls on those who hardened themselves against the signs of God. The verse thus teaches that disbelief rooted in stubborn rejection, rather than honest uncertainty, is what brings a person to the fire.

translation: Forbidder of good, transgressor beyond bounds, one in doubt and suspicion.
interpretation: The three attributes form a chain of cause and effect. Stinginess, which keeps good from others and withholds the rights of the needy, is rooted in transgression, a stepping beyond the limits God has set, and that transgression grows from a doubt about the Hereafter and divine accountability. The verse thus diagnoses the inner disease behind miserliness: it is not merely a financial habit but a spiritual condition in which unbelief in the reckoning to come drives a person to hoard and to overstep.

translation: "Who set up another god with God, so cast him both into the severe punishment."
interpretation: The verse, spoken in the context of the command to cast into Hell (Qaf 50:24-26 style address, here addressed to the angelic guards), describes the person who associated a rival deity with God as deserving the harshest punishment. The repetition of the command to cast him into the severe torment underscores that shirk is the gravest of offenses, for it denies the unique oneness of the Creator and misdirects the worship owed to Him alone. The verse thus warns that polytheism is not merely an intellectual error but a rebellion that brings its own dreadful consequence, while also implicitly calling the listener to tawhid, the sincere affirmation that there is no god but God.

translation: His companion [the devil assigned to him] will say: Our Lord, I did not make him transgress, but he was already in far-reaching error.
interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Judgment dialogue in which the disbeliever's constant companion, the devil, disclaims responsibility for his ruin, so that the sinner's own chosen straying is shown to be the real cause of his fate, since the companion could only invite and never compel. It teaches that misguidance is ultimately rooted in the human soul's own persistence in error, and that accountability cannot be shifted onto Satan once the truth has been made clear.

translation: He said, "Do not dispute before Me, for I had already sent forth to you the warning."
interpretation: This verse presents the moment of divine judgment in which God forbids the people from contending with one another in His presence, since the matter has already been settled by His decree. Having sent His messengers and warnings to them in the world, God makes clear that they cannot now escape accountability by argument or blame-shifting. The verse thus underscores that the opportunity for guidance was given beforehand, so the futility of disputing on the Day of Reckoning lies in the fact that the truth was already conveyed and rejected through their own choice.

translation: The word is not changed with Me, and I am not ever unjust to the servants.
interpretation: The verse is spoken in the context of the Day of Judgment, where a rebellious soul is confronted with its deeds and tries to shift blame onto others. God answers that His decree is fixed and cannot be altered, so the promise of reward and the warning of punishment stand as He declared them. This immutability is not harshness but the guarantee of justice: since God does not wrong anyone, each person meets exactly what their own choices have earned. The believer is thus invited to find certainty in God's word and security in His fairness, while recognizing that no one can escape accountability by denial, excuse, or pointing at others.

translation: On the Day We will say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it will say, "Is there any more?"
interpretation: The verse presents Hell as a vast, responsive reality on the Day of Judgment, addressed directly by God and answering Him. Its question, "Is there any more?", pictures the immensity of the punishment prepared for the disobedient, and the fullness of Hell stands as a sign of the justice of the Divine reckoning: none who deserve it escape, and none are punished beyond what they have earned. The image also reminds the believer of the seriousness of accountability and of the mercy of avoiding what fills that abyss.

translation: And Paradise will be brought near to the God-conscious, not far away.
interpretation: The verse portrays the nearness of Paradise as a reward for those who guard themselves with taqwa. Its placement close to them, rather than distant, signifies that the believers will not have to strive across a great distance to reach it; the bliss that was promised is made immediately accessible at the moment of reckoning. This conveys both honor and comfort: the righteous see the fruit of their conduct drawn to them, and the nearness itself becomes a sign of God's favor, dissolving the anxiety of the Day of Judgment into the assurance of a reward that is already within reach.

translation: "This is what you are promised, for every one who turns back in repentance and carefully guards (his covenant with Allah)." (Qur'an 50:32)
interpretation: The verse directs the believer's attention to the reward already promised, and ties it to two qualities of the one who earns it. The "awwab" is one who returns to Allah again and again, not only once, turning from heedlessness and sin toward Him in sincere and continual repentance. The "hafiz" is the guardian who preserves what was entrusted to him: his duties toward Allah, his limits set by the law, his own heart and senses, and his trust toward others. The promise is therefore not for a single good deed but for a settled character, one that keeps returning to its Lord and keeps watch over what is owed to Him. Read in its context, which describes the Garden brought near to the God-conscious, the verse teaches that nearness to Allah is reached through a repentant heart joined with vigilant, faithful conduct.

translation: Whoever feared the Most Merciful unseen, and came to Him with a repentant (turning-back) heart.
interpretation: The verse describes the true believer by two inward qualities. The first is khashyah, a reverent fear of the Most Merciful that is rooted in awareness of Him even when He is unseen, so that the person's conduct is guided by God's presence rather than by the gaze of others. The second is inābah, a heart that continually turns back to God in repentance, humility and devotion. Fear without turning to God would be mere dread, and turning without reverence would be shallow; the verse joins them, showing that the one who is mindful of God in private and returns to Him sincerely is the one who will be welcomed with peace and the garden, as the following verses indicate.

translation: Enter it in peace. That is the Day of Eternity.
interpretation: The call to enter Paradise "in peace" signals that the believers are received into a state of complete security, tranquility, and freedom from every fear, grief, and harm, with the angels or the Lord greeting them with peace. The phrase "the Day of Eternity" (yawm al-khulud) points to the endlessness of this blessed condition: unlike the transient world, where every joy is followed by loss, the reward here is everlasting, so the day of their entry becomes the beginning of an unending life of peace. The verse thus joins the promise of bliss with the assurance that it will never end, inviting the reader to see the final reward as both a homecoming and a permanence beyond any earthly comfort.

translation: They will have therein whatever they wish, and with Us is more.
interpretation: The verse speaks of the complete fulfillment of the believers' desires in Paradise: whatever the soul longs for is granted without lack or limit. The closing phrase "and with Us is more" points to the boundless generosity of God, whose gifts exceed even what human desire can imagine. It conveys that the reward of the righteous is not merely a fixed portion but an ever-increasing bounty, reflecting God's infinite grace and the honor bestowed upon those who gave themselves in obedience to Him.

translation: And how many generations did We destroy before them, who were far greater than them in strength, so that they roamed through the lands. Is there any escape?
interpretation: The verse turns the listener's gaze to history as a warning: the Meccan disbelievers who dismissed the messengers were not the first to be tested, and earlier peoples who surpassed them in power and reach, who dug through and traversed the lands seeking advantage, were nonetheless seized by God for their denial. Their fate poses the rhetorical question 'Is there any escape?' as a final reproach, implying that no might, wealth, or cunning can shield anyone from divine accountability, and that the only true refuge lies in heeding the message before the reckoning comes.

translation: Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while being present and attentive.
interpretation: The verse points to the fact that the lessons of past peoples and the signs of God are not received by everyone equally; only one who brings a living, open heart to them, or who listens with full presence of mind and attention, truly benefits. Its wording suggests that understanding depends less on mere possession of faculties than on the willingness to engage them, so that heedlessness, not the absence of evidence, is what keeps a person from being admonished.

translation: And We have certainly created the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us.
interpretation: The verse affirms the absolute power of God, who creates the vast cosmos in six days without any weariness, since His creative act is by His command alone, and it rejects the anthropomorphic notion that the Creator becomes tired. It also reminds the reader that the divine power that brought the universe into being is the same power that can bring about resurrection, which the disbelievers denied in the preceding verses. The mention of 'six days' points to the stages of creation, which are not to be measured by human days, and the verse thus invites reflection on the perfection of divine making and on the Creator's independence from all need.

translation: So be patient over what they say, and glorify your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting.
interpretation: The verse teaches that patience in the face of opponents' hostile words is sustained not by retaliation but by turning to God in constant remembrance and praise. The prophet is commanded to anchor his steadfastness in regular worship at the beginning and end of the day, when the soul is most attentive, so that consolation and strength come from the Lord rather than from the approval or rebuke of people. The dawn and dusk glorification thus becomes a daily discipline that renews inner calm amid opposition.

translation: And during the night, glorify Him, and (also) after the prostrations.
interpretation: The verse directs the believer to remember God in the night through glorification (tasbih), and to extend that remembrance to the moments immediately following the prostrations of prayer. Night is singled out as a time of stillness and solitude, when the heart is most free to turn to God, while the phrase 'after the prostrations' ties continuous praise to the ritual act of worship, suggesting that devotion should not end with the formal prayer but carry on into the rest of one's conduct and nightly hours.

translation: And listen, on the Day the Caller calls out from a nearby place.
interpretation: The verse directs the listener to attend closely to the summons of the Day of Resurrection, when a caller will proclaim from a place near to all. The nearness of the call suggests that it will reach every person without any distance or obstruction, so that no one can claim they were out of earshot. It conveys the inescapability of the Final Reckoning: the call that gathers humanity cannot be ignored, and the imagery of hearing what is close at hand invites the believer to heed the reminder of accountability now, before that summons arrives.

translation: The Day they hear the Shout in truth. That is the Day of Coming Forth.
interpretation: The verse points to the Resurrection as a moment when the dead are called back to life by a single, real and decisive sound, the blast of the trumpet, which is nothing like the false or empty noises of this world. The phrase "the Day of Coming Forth" (yawm al-khurooj) emphasizes that the dead will emerge from their graves, leaving behind the confines of the earth, to stand before their Lord. Its wording suggests that the reality of that call is what gives the whole Hereafter its truth, so that people are reminded to prepare for an event they cannot escape or deny.

translation: Indeed, it is We who give life and cause death, and to Us is the final return.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's absolute sovereignty over the beginning and end of every living being: He alone grants life and decrees death, and so human beings have no real control over their own existence. By stressing that all return is to Him, it reminds the believer that every deed, intention, and worldly attachment will ultimately be presented before Him for judgment. The awareness of this certain return is meant to turn the heart away from heedlessness toward humility, gratitude, and preparation for the Hereafter, since life is a trust on loan and death is not an ending but a passage to the One who will call all creatures to account.

translation: On the Day the earth splits open over them, rushing forth swiftly. That gathering is easy for Us.
interpretation: The verse portrays the Resurrection as a sudden, effortless event: the earth itself is split open and the dead come out hurrying toward their Lord. The image of rapid emergence signals that the gathering of all creatures for judgment requires no preparation or difficulty for God, whose power is absolute. It is a call to recognize that the Hour which seems distant to the heedless is, for God, a simple matter, so one should prepare for the reckoning now.

translation: We know best what they say, and you are not a compeller over them. So remind, by the Qur'an, those who fear My warning.
interpretation: The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad in the face of his people's rejection and mockery. God assures him that He knows fully what they say, so the Prophet need not be anxious or grieved by their words. His role is not to force belief upon them, since he is not a tyrant or compeller over them. His duty is simply to deliver the reminder of the Qur'an, and its real benefit reaches only those whose hearts are open to fear God and to be mindful of His warning. The passage thus establishes that guidance is a matter of conveyance and of the receptive heart, not of coercion, and that the responsibility of the messenger ends with clear reminder.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By the scatterers (winnowing winds) that scatter far and wide,
interpretation: The oath is sworn by the winds, which are called 'adh-dhariyat' because they scatter and disperse what they carry, such as dust, seeds, and clouds. By calling attention to these mighty natural forces, the verse directs the listener to reflect on the signs of Allah's power in creation and on the certainty of what is promised in the surah that follows.

translation: And [by] those that carry heavy loads,
interpretation: The 'carriers of heavy loads' are most commonly understood as the clouds, laden with water, or the winds that bear them, so the verse points to the signs of God's power in the natural order that bring rain and life to the earth, inviting the reader to reflect on the Creator who makes this provision possible.

translation: And by those that glide along with ease.
interpretation: The verse swears by things that move smoothly and effortlessly, most often understood as ships gliding across the water by the grace of God, so that people may travel, trade, and seek His bounty. The ease of their motion is itself a sign of divine favor, reminding the listener that the means of livelihood and movement are subject to God's will.

translation: And by those who apportion affairs by command,
interpretation: The oath is sworn by the angels entrusted with dividing and executing God's decrees: they apportion sustenance, rain, life, and death, and every matter assigned to them, acting only by the command of their Lord. The verse thus points to the orderly, divinely appointed administration of the created world, reminding the listener that the distribution of what they receive is never random but is governed by God's will and wisdom.

translation: Indeed, what you are promised is surely true.
interpretation: The verse (Surah Adh-Dhariyat 51:5) is a solemn affirmation that the promise made to humankind—the reckoning, the resurrection, and the reward and punishment that follow—is undeniably true and will certainly come to pass. Its emphatic phrasing, introduced with the particle inna and the emphatic lam, is meant to dispel doubt and to call the listener to reflect on the reality of the Hereafter, which the preceding verses present through oaths by natural phenomena that scatter, bear, and distribute, pointing to a God whose promise cannot fail.

translation: And indeed, the Judgment (or recompense) is surely going to occur.
interpretation: The verse affirms with emphasis (through the particles inna and the lam of certainty) that the Day of Reckoning is an unavoidable reality. Its certainty is presented as a firm truth that no one can escape, meaning that every person will be held accountable for their deeds, and this should move the listener to live with awareness of that coming accountability.

translation: By the sky with its intricate, well-woven paths.
interpretation: The oath by 'the sky full of paths' (al-hubuk) directs the mind to the orderly, meticulously structured cosmos. The word hubuk evokes the fine weaving or the ripples on sand and water, suggesting that the heavens are not chaotic but arranged with precise design and beauty. By swearing upon this carefully crafted sky, the verse invites the reader to contemplate the artistry and purposeful harmony of creation as evidence of the Creator's wisdom, and it prepares the listener to consider the truth of what follows in the surah, which concerns the divergence of people in their beliefs.

translation: Indeed, you are in a contradictory (divergent) opinion.
interpretation: This verse (Surah Adh-Dhariyat 51:8) is addressed to the Quraysh who disputed the Prophet's message, describing them as being in conflicting and inconsistent views: some called him a poet, others a sorcerer, others a madman, so their accusations contradicted one another. The verse exposes the instability of their rejection, since a denial that shifts between incompatible claims reveals that it lacks a sound basis and is driven by opposition rather than by evidence.

translation: Turned away from it is whoever is turned away.
interpretation: The phrase "yu'fak 'anhu man ufik" (Adh-Dhariyat 51:9) describes the one who is averted from the Prophet's message and the truth it carries. The verb "ufika" denotes being turned away or perverted from the right course, and the passive construction suggests that such aversion is the result of a person's own choices, which in turn caused them to be deprived of guidance. The verse thus points to a moral reality: those who persistently reject the truth are the ones who, by their own inclination and stubbornness, end up turned away from it.

translation: Destroyed are the fabricators of falsehood, the conjecturers.
interpretation: The verse condemns those who build certainties on mere conjecture about the unseen, especially the Hour and the Day of Recompense, and who ask mockingly about its timing while neglecting the reality it announces. It warns that speculation detached from knowledge and revelation leads a person into heedlessness and confusion, and that the one who invents claims about God's affairs and then presents them as truth stands under a curse of ruin, so faith must rest on sound knowledge and humble reflection rather than on guesses and fabricated assumptions.

translation: Those who are in their heedlessness, forgetful (or unmindful).
interpretation: The verse describes those who are immersed in a deep flood of worldly distraction and preoccupation, so that they lose awareness of their accountability before God. Their 'ghamra' is a state of being submerged and overwhelmed by desires and pleasures, and their 'sahw' is a neglectful forgetfulness that causes them to ignore the purpose of their creation and the reality of the Hereafter. The verse thus points to the spiritual danger of allowing material concerns to drown out remembrance of God, and it implicitly calls the believer to vigilance, reflection, and regular turning back to God.

translation: They ask: When is the Day of Recompense?
interpretation: The verse captures the question posed by those who deny the Resurrection, mocking or doubting when the Day of Judgment will arrive. The word "ayyana" expresses a demand for a specific date, implying disbelief and impatience rather than sincere inquiry. The Qur'an elsewhere answers such questions by affirming that the Hour's timing is known only to God, and that the Day of Recompense will certainly come, so the heedless are reminded to prepare for it through faith and righteous action rather than to dispute its occurrence.

translation: On the Day they will be tormented over the Fire.
interpretation: The phrase "يوم هم على النار يفتنون" (Adh-Dhariyat 51:13) belongs to a sequence of verses that describe the fate of those who denied the truth, and it sets the scene of their judgment by placing their trial on the Day of Reckoning. The word "يفتنون" derives from the root f-t-n, which carries the sense of being tested, put under pressure, or burned in a smelting furnace, where gold is heated to separate the pure from the impure. The verse thus presents the punishment of the Fire as a kind of ordeal that exposes what the deniers truly were, just as the test of this world exposed their hearts. Their being "upon the Fire" conveys that they are not merely near it but are being subjected to it, and the mention of their own "tormenting" emphasizes that the torment is the consequence of their own choices, mirroring the mockery they directed at the truth in the preceding verses. The verse therefore invites the listener to reflect that the trials of this life are a preparation for a final reckoning in which every hidden inclination is laid bare.

translation: "Taste your trial; this is what you used to seek to hasten." (Qur'an 51:14)
interpretation: The verse addresses those who mocked the promise of Resurrection and Judgment and demanded that it be brought about quickly. Their scornful challenge is turned back on them: the very punishment they wished to hasten is now made to be experienced, as a trial that they will taste in full. The phrase "taste" conveys that the torment is not merely witnessed but personally felt, and the word "fitnatakum" signals that the chastisement is itself a test that exposes the true state of their hearts. The verse thus teaches that heedlessness toward the reality of accountability, when it is ridiculed rather than respected, ends in the very reality that was denied, and that hastening what one mocks does not spare one from it.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and springs.
interpretation: The verse presents the reward of the God-conscious (al-muttaqun) as a state of settled, abundant blessing: gardens lush with life and springs flowing freely. Its brevity places the emphasis on the nature of the reward itself, which stands in contrast to the restlessness and scarcity of worldly life. Read alongside its context, it invites the believer to see piety (taqwa) not as a burden but as the path toward a place of security, beauty, and abundance, where the very things a person longs for in this world are granted in their fullness.

translation: Receiving what their Lord has given them. Indeed, they were before that doers of good.
interpretation: The verse describes the state of the righteous in the Garden, who joyfully accept the bounties their Lord bestows upon them, and it grounds this reward in their earlier conduct: they were people of ihsan in the world, doing good with sincerity and excellence. Their present acceptance of divine favor is thus the fruit of a life lived in devotion and beneficence, showing that the recompense of God corresponds to the good deeds a person has truly performed.

translation: They used to sleep but little of the night.
interpretation: The verse describes the righteous believers (the muttaqun of the preceding verses in Surah adh-Dhariyat) who kept vigil in worship during the night, sleeping only a small portion of it. Their sparing sleep reflects the depth of their devotion, their eagerness to remain close to their Lord in the stillness of the night, and their readiness to stand before Him in prayer rather than yield fully to rest. It is an image of a heart that longs for its Lord, so that the night, which others give wholly to sleep, becomes for them a time of standing, supplication, and nearness to God.

translation: And at the hours before dawn they would ask forgiveness of Allah.
interpretation: The verse praises the righteous believers, described in the surrounding passage as those who were few in sleep at night, by portraying their devotion in the last hours of the night, when they rose from rest to seek forgiveness. Choosing the pre-dawn time, a moment of stillness and sincerity when most people are asleep, suggests that their repentance was humble, private, and wholehearted. It teaches that true faith shows itself not only in worship performed in public but in the quiet turning to God in the hours when no one else is watching, and that seeking forgiveness is a constant habit of the believer, marked by awareness of one's shortcomings before the Creator.

translation: And in their wealth there is a right for the beggar and the deprived.
interpretation: The verse describes the righteous believers, who recognize that their wealth is not solely their own but carries a binding right owed to others. The 'right' (haqq) is not presented as mere charity or a voluntary favor, but as a due obligation owed to those who ask openly, the sa'il, and to those who refrain from asking out of dignity and poverty, the mahrum, who are often overlooked. This teaches that social responsibility is woven into faith itself: wealth is a trust from God, and its purification lies in extending its benefit to the needy, so that the bond between the wealthy and the poor becomes a matter of justice and spiritual accountability rather than condescension.

translation: And on the earth are signs for those who have certainty (of faith).
interpretation: The verse directs the reader's attention beyond scripture to the created world itself: the earth, with its varied terrains, living creatures, seasons, and the intricate balance that sustains life, is presented as a book of signs pointing to the reality of God's power, wisdom, and design. Yet the verse specifies that these signs are fully legible only to those who have certainty (yaqin). This implies that the natural world does not compel belief in a mechanical way; rather, a heart that is sincerely open and inwardly settled in conviction perceives in creation a continuous testimony to the Creator, while one who is heedless sees only phenomena. Thus reflection on the earth is itself an act of worship and a path that deepens and confirms faith.

translation: And [also] in yourselves. Will you not then see?
interpretation: The verse directs the reader's attention inward, to the human self as a sign (ayah) pointing to the Creator. The intricate formation of the human body, the faculties of hearing, sight, reason and speech, and the capacity for growth from a single drop into a conscious being are all presented as evidence of divine wisdom and power. By asking "will you not see?", the verse rebukes heedlessness: the signs are not distant or hidden but lie within each person, so the failure to perceive God is not a failure of evidence but of attentive reflection. The verse thus invites the believer to turn contemplation toward his own existence as a path to recognizing the Creator's oneness and to deepening gratitude and faith.

translation: And in the heaven is your provision, and that which you are promised.
interpretation: The verse directs the human mind upward to recognize that the true source of sustenance and the fulfillment of divine promises lies beyond the visible, earthly means on which people depend. Provision is ultimately decreed from above, so the believer's trust should rest on the One who controls the heavens rather than on the apparent causes of livelihood alone. The mention of 'what you are promised' extends this to the reward and the consequences announced by God, reminding humanity that these matters are certain, since they are fixed in the heavens and not subject to human control.

translation: So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth, just as it is true that you speak.
interpretation: The verse is an oath by the Lord of heaven and earth affirming the absolute certainty of the promise of resurrection and reckoning mentioned in the surrounding verses, which the disbelievers were doubting. By likening this truth to the undeniable fact of human speech, it points to a certainty that is as self-evident as one's own ability to speak; the reality of what is promised does not depend on human doubt or acceptance. The oath by the Lord of heaven and earth reminds the listener that the One who governs the whole cosmos is the one who guarantees this promise, so its fulfillment is beyond question.

translation: Has there reached you the story of the honored guests of Abraham?
interpretation: The verse opens with a question that draws the listener's attention to a story already known to the Prophet, and it places the account of Abraham's guests within a narrative of honor and hospitality. The word 'mukramīn' (honored) signals that these visitors were noble angelic messengers, and the question prepares the reader to see Abraham's generous welcome as a model of faithful hospitality, which then leads into the announcement of the good news of a son and the divine mission entrusted to them.

translation: When they entered upon him and said, "Peace." He said, "Peace, you are a people unknown (to me)."
interpretation: The verse presents Abraham's hospitality toward unexpected guests who arrive without introduction. Their greeting of peace is answered in kind, yet Abraham's words, "a people unknown," reveal his cautious reserve and his uncertainty about who they are, a moment that sets up his prompt and generous provision of a meal. It teaches that a gracious response to strangers combines courtesy with discernment, offering welcome first while remaining attentive to who has come and why.

translation: Then he turned quietly to his family and brought a fattened calf.
interpretation: The verse depicts Abraham's hospitality toward his unexpected guests, who were angels. He secretly withdrew to his household and quickly returned with a choice, well-fed calf, which he prepared to serve them. The swiftness and discretion of his act reflect the generosity of a host who honors his guests with the best he has, offering a model of hospitality that the believer is called to emulate. The verse also shows that the guests did not eat, which in the narrative prompts Abraham's unease, highlighting how the moral excellence of giving is measured by its sincerity and promptness.

translation: Then he brought it near to them, [and] said: Will you not eat?
interpretation: This verse, from the account of Abraham's guests (Surah adh-Dhariyat 51:27), shows the grace and discreet hospitality of the prophet toward strangers whom he did not yet recognize. He brings the food to them without announcing it or making a display, and his question, 'Will you not eat?', is a gentle invitation that also prepares the reader for the subsequent revelation that these guests were angels, and that the host's unhesitating generosity was itself a model of righteous conduct.

translation: So he felt a fear of them. They said, "Do not fear." And they gave him good tidings of a boy endowed with knowledge.
interpretation: The verse shows Abraham's natural human reaction when unknown visitors arrive without being recognized as messengers of God; his inward apprehension is met with reassurance, and the angels' tidings of a knowledgeable son point to the divine grace that follows patient trust. The fear is not a failure of faith but a moment of human unease that God's messengers dissolve with peace, as the good news of a son who will be wise becomes a sign that God's promise often arrives precisely where human expectation has grown weary or uncertain.

translation: Then his wife came forward crying out, and she struck her face and said, "An old woman, barren!"
interpretation: The verse captures the moment of astonishment at the announcement of a child to an elderly and long-barren couple. Her loud cry and the gesture of striking her face reveal a mixture of surprise, disbelief, and perhaps embarrassment at the thought of bearing a child in her advanced age. Her words, "an old woman, barren," describe her own condition as she understood it by human reckoning, showing that the wonder lies not only in the good news but in the contrast between ordinary causes and the power of God, who brings life where nature has closed the door. The passage thus teaches that divine promise can exceed what human expectation and natural circumstance allow.

translation: They said: "So it is; your Lord has said, indeed He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing."
interpretation: The verse conveys a reply to a question posed in the preceding context, where the answer is affirmed by appeal to divine decree: the matter is as God has determined, not because of human reasoning or wishes. The phrase "Thus says your Lord" establishes that the word of the Lord is final and beyond dispute, and the closing attributes of wisdom and knowledge assure the hearer that the decree proceeds from perfect understanding, which encompasses every detail and purpose. The lesson is that a believer should rest in the judgment of One whose wisdom is complete and whose knowledge leaves nothing hidden, accepting what He decrees even when its reasons are not immediately apparent to human minds.

translation: He said, "What is your business, O messengers?"
interpretation: This verse comes from the account of Abraham, where angels arrive as messengers, first bringing him news of a son and then being sent to the people of Lot. Abraham, who had first been unsettled by their visit and offered them food, now asks them directly about the purpose of their mission, as one who wants to know the reason behind a commission that has come to his household and his community. The question shows his composure and readiness to hear the matter plainly, and it prepares the ground for the divine decree concerning the guilty people that the messengers are about to reveal.

translation: They said: Indeed, we have been sent to a people who are criminals (guilty of sin).
interpretation: The verse, spoken by the angels sent to Lot's people (Surah Al-Hijr 15:58 and Adh-Dhariyat 51:32 narrate the same scene), reveals the nature of the divine decree that had already been determined against a community steeped in grave transgression. Their words are not an accusation born of anger but a calm, factual announcement, showing that God's punishment follows only after a people's persistent crimes have become fully manifest. The word 'mujrimin' conveys people who have deliberately cut themselves off from what is right, and the verse thereby underlines that divine justice is precise: the messengers are dispatched to a specific, morally defined condition rather than striking at random.

translation: لِنُرْسِلَ عَلَيْهِمْ حِجَارَةً مِنْ طِينٍ — "That We may send down upon them stones of clay."
interpretation: The verse describes the punishment prepared against those who transgress beyond limits, here evoking the people of Lot and the calamity that befell them. The stones of baked clay signify a destruction that is both precisely targeted and marked as coming from God, showing that no transgressor escapes divine decree. The image of clay, a humble and ordinary material, underscores that the instruments of divine justice need not be extraordinary: what appears common becomes a force of annihilation, reminding the reader that worldly pride and power offer no shelter from the consequences of persistent wrongdoing.

translation: Marked with distinct signs in the presence of your Lord, for those who transgress the limits.
interpretation: The phrase 'marked in the presence of your Lord' shows that the stones of clay were not random. Each was distinguished and recorded by God's decree and knowledge, so the punishment was precisely assigned. 'For the transgressors' ties that exact assignment to the people's excess in disbelief and wrongdoing, showing that divine retribution is measured, deliberate, and aimed at those who exceed the bounds God set.

translation: So We brought out whoever was in it of the believers.
interpretation: The verse refers to the deliverance of Lot's household from the doomed town, where Allah separated the faithful from the wicked before the punishment descended. It shows that divine justice is precise: those who submitted to faith are rescued from the destruction that engulfs the rest, and the believers in such a community are never lost in the collective ruin, since Allah knows exactly who belongs to Him.

translation: So We found in it no house other than one of the submitters (Muslims).
interpretation: This verse, from the story of Lot's people in Surah Adh-Dhariyat, points to the rarity of righteousness even in a town marked for destruction. Only one household was found among its people who had submitted to God, and God singled them out for deliverance. The phrase underscores that faith and submission are a matter of individual commitment, and that divine mercy preserves those who stand apart from a corrupt majority. It also shows that the messengers' call was not ignored entirely, since a small righteous household responded, which is why it is preserved as a lasting sign for those who fear the painful punishment.

translation: And We left therein a sign for those who fear the painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse points to the story of Lot's people and the town destroyed for their wickedness, which was left as a lasting sign. Its ruins and the traces of its destruction are meant to lead the heedful to reflect and draw the lesson that disobedience brings a severe reckoning. Only those whose hearts are open to fear of God's painful chastisement truly benefit from this sign, for it stirs them toward repentance and awe, while the heedless pass over it without reflection. The verse thus teaches that God's signs are preserved in history and in the land itself as a warning and a guide for those who are conscious of their accountability before Him.

translation: And in Moses (is also a sign), when We sent him to Pharaoh with a clear authority.
interpretation: The verse places the story of Moses within the same pattern of signs found in the preceding accounts, pointing to the divine commission as the source of his mission. The phrase 'with a clear authority' (bi-sultanin mubin) indicates that Moses did not come to Pharaoh on his own initiative or by worldly power, but bearing manifest proof and undeniable evidence from God, namely the clear signs and the miracles given to him. The emphasis falls on the clarity of the divine credential, which leaves the one who rejects it without excuse, and it implicitly contrasts the vast worldly authority of Pharaoh with the humble but unassailable authority of the prophet who speaks in God's name.

translation: So he turned away with his supporters and said, "A magician or a madman!"
