interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet to glorify (tasbih) God by the mention of His name, the Great. Glorification here is an act of humble acknowledgment that God is far exalted above every deficiency and every likeness to creation, and that all true greatness belongs to Him alone. By directing the believer to venerate God's name, the verse ties the remembrance of God in speech and heart to a sincere recognition of His supreme majesty, so that the one who professes it orients his whole life toward the Lord whose greatness surpasses all things.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Whatever is in the heavens and the earth exalts Allah, and He is the Almighty, the Most Wise.
interpretation: The verse presents the whole of creation as engaged in a continuous act of glorification of God, so that the act of praise is not confined to human beings but is the natural state of everything in the heavens and the earth. The sequence that follows the glorification, naming God as al-Aziz and al-Hakim, ties this universal praise to the two qualities that govern it: a power that nothing can resist and a wisdom that orders all things in their proper place. The created order therefore testifies, by its very existence and its harmony, to the majesty and wisdom of its Creator, and the human being is invited to recognize this and to join in the praise that creation already offers.

translation: To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death, and He is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse establishes absolute sovereignty as the foundation of divine power: possession of the heavens and the earth is not borrowed or shared but belongs to God alone, so every created thing stands under His authority. The pairing of giving life and causing death shows that the most fundamental boundary of human existence, the beginning and the end of a life, lies entirely within His will, which should humble the believer and free him from fear of any other power. The closing affirmation that He is capable of all things points to the completeness of His ability, so that the one who controls birth and death is also the one who can bring about resurrection and fulfil every promise made to His servants.

translation: He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden, and He is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: The four divine names paired here, al-Awwal and al-Akhir, al-Zahir and al-Batin, describe God's absolute encompassing of time and space: He precedes all existence without beginning and outlasts it without end, and He is both evident through His signs in creation and beyond the reach of perception in His essence. The verse closes by tying these attributes to knowledge, so that the believer understands that the One who surrounds all things in being also surrounds them in knowledge, and therefore nothing hidden from the self or the world escapes Him. Such recognition should turn the heart toward reflection on the visible signs of God while humbly acknowledging that His true reality lies beyond human grasp.

translation: It is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself above the Throne. He knows what enters into the earth and what emerges from it, what descends from the sky and what ascends into it. And He is with you wherever you are. And Allah is Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse presents God's complete knowledge and nearness as a source of awareness for the believer: the One who created the cosmos and governs it from above the Throne is not distant from human affairs but encompasses them in knowledge, tracing every movement between earth and sky. His being 'with you' wherever you are is understood by the scholars as a knowledge and encompassing presence, not a spatial mixing with creation, which calls the human being to constant mindfulness, sincerity, and accountability, since nothing done in secret or openly escapes His sight.

translation: To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned.
interpretation: The verse affirms that absolute sovereignty over everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah alone, so no created being truly possesses authority independent of Him. It follows that human power, however extensive, is borrowed and temporary. By stating that all affairs ultimately return to Him, it reminds the believer that the outcome of every matter, whether worldly or spiritual, rests with the One who owns and governs all things. This calls for trust in Him in times of hardship, humility in success, and accountability in the knowledge that all actions will be judged by the Sovereign to whom they ultimately belong.

translation: He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and He is All-Knowing of what is within the breasts.
interpretation: The verse points to the continuous, orderly alternation of night and day, where one gradually merges into the other as the length of each shifts across the seasons, a sign that the universe is governed by a single, precise divine design. Having drawn the reader's attention to this outward, observable order, it closes by turning inward: the One who orchestrates the cosmos also knows the hidden thoughts, intentions, and secrets of hearts. The movement from the visible sky to the concealed interior suggests that the same knowledge and power that regulate the external world encompass the innermost self, inviting the believer to be mindful that nothing within the heart escapes God's awareness.

translation: Believe in Allah and His Messenger, and spend from that which He has made you inheritors of. So those of you who believe and spend – for them is a great reward.
interpretation: The verse roots faith and generosity in a single relationship: wealth is not owned outright but entrusted, since the believer is only a steward (mustakhlaf) over what Allah has placed in their hands. Belief in God and His Messenger is therefore the foundation, and charity is the practical proof that this belief has become sincere. The reference to 'those of you who believe' sets the reward of great recompense on the one who unites faith with giving, implying that possessions spent in obedience turn from a burden into a source of lasting reward, while hoarding treats the trust as if it were one's own.

translation: And why do you not believe in God, while the Messenger calls you to believe in your Lord, and He has already taken your covenant, if you are [truly] believers?
interpretation: The verse rebukes the hearers for failing to respond to faith when every reason for it is present: the Messenger is summoning them, their Lord is the one to whom they owe belief, and they have already bound themselves to God through a covenant, the primordial pledge of acknowledging Him. The conditional closing, 'if you are believers,' turns the rebuke inward, suggesting that genuine faith is measured by responsiveness to a call that the heart has already accepted in principle. Faith, on this reading, is not merely an inherited identity but an ongoing answer to a summons that the believer's own prior commitment should make irresistible.

translation: He it is who sends down to His servant clear verses, that He may bring you out from darknesses into light. Indeed, Allah is Kind and Merciful toward you.
interpretation: The verse presents revelation as the means by which God lifts humanity out of spiritual and moral darkness into light. The 'clear verses' sent to His servant the Prophet Muhammad are not merely words to be recited but a guiding illumination that dispels ignorance, misguidance and the confusion of the heart, so that a person can see the truth and walk toward it. The phrase 'darknesses' in the plural suggests the many forms of error, desire and disbelief that cloud human life, while 'light' points to the singular, unified path of guidance that leads back to God. The closing reminder that God is Ra'uf and Rahim shows that this guidance flows from mercy rather than from need: the very act of bringing people out of darkness is an expression of divine compassion, inviting the believer to respond with gratitude and trust.

translation: And what is [wrong] with you that you do not spend in the cause of Allah, while to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth? Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest. Those are greater in rank than those who spent and fought after it. But to each Allah has promised the best, and Allah is Acquainted with what you do.
interpretation: The verse calls believers to generous spending and striving for God's cause by reminding them that all that is in the heavens and earth ultimately belongs to God, so wealth held in one's hands is only a trust. It establishes a principle of graded merit based on timing and sacrifice: those who gave and fought at the critical moment of need, before the victory that opened Mecca, hold a higher station than those who came afterward, yet God's promise of goodness extends to all who sincerely serve, and His awareness of every deed ensures no sacrifice is lost.

translation: Who is it that would lend Allah a goodly loan, so He will multiply it for him manifold, and he will have a noble reward?
interpretation: The verse frames charity given in the path of Allah as a loan made to Him, an image of generosity that honors the giver by treating his spending as something entrusted to the Divine rather than merely lost. The word "goodly" (hasan) points to sincerity and purity of intention, and the promise of multiplication shows that what is given with a pure heart returns far greater than its outward measure. The closing phrase about a noble reward suggests that the recompense is not only abundant in quantity but dignified in quality, reaching the believer in the hereafter as an honor. The interpretation draws the believer toward a relationship of trust with God, in which the act of giving becomes an act of faith rather than a transaction of loss.

translation: On the Day you will see the believing men and the believing women, their light running before them and on their right sides: "Good tidings for you today: gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the supreme triumph."
interpretation: The verse portrays the light of the believers on the Day of Judgment as a sign of their faith and deeds, shining before them and on their right hands, the side of honor and of receiving one's record. Their light marks their passage toward Paradise, and the angelic or divine address of glad tidings confirms that their striving in this world has reached its fulfillment. The phrase "the supreme triumph" points to the true success of the believer, which is not worldly gain but eternal nearness to God in lasting gardens, so that the scene calls the listener to persevere in faith now, so that the same light may guide them then.

translation: On the Day when the hypocrite men and hypocrite women will say to those who believed, "Wait for us, that we may acquire some of your light." It will be said, "Turn back behind you and seek light." So a wall will be put up between them with a gate; inside it is mercy, and outside it, facing it, is punishment.
interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Judgment, when the light that the believers carried in this life through their faith and righteous deeds becomes visible to them, while the hypocrites, who displayed faith outwardly but lacked it inwardly, are left in darkness. Their request to share the believers' light is met with rejection, for the light was earned through sincere conviction and action in the world, not borrowed at the last moment. The dividing wall with its gate symbolizes the complete separation between the two groups: the inner side, where the believers dwell in mercy, and the outer side, where the hypocrites face the torment that their concealed disbelief and deception have brought upon them.

translation: They will call out to them, "Were we not with you?" They will say, "Yes, but you led yourselves into temptation, waited (for our ruin), doubted, and were deceived by wishful hopes until the command of Allah came; and the deceiver deceived you concerning Allah."
interpretation: This verse depicts the scene of the hypocrites on the Day of Resurrection, when the believers are separated from them at the boundary between Paradise and Hell (Surah al-Hadid 57:13). The hypocrites, who in the world outwardly shared the believers' company, ask them to recall their former association. The believers reply that they were indeed together outwardly, but that the hypocrites brought ruin upon themselves through inner corruption: they tempted their own souls into hypocrisy, awaited the misfortune of the believers, harbored doubt about the truth of the message, and were deluded by vain desires and false hopes of escaping accountability until death, the decree of Allah, arrived. The verse then points to the root of their destruction: the chief deceiver, Satan or worldly delusion, misled them about Allah, so that they felt secure in His forbearance while neglecting His truth. The lesson is that hypocrisy is a self-inflicted sickness of the heart, and that false hopes which lead a person to postpone repentance are the very means by which they are lost.

translation: So today no ransom will be taken from you, nor from those who disbelieved. Your refuge is the Fire; it is your protector, and what an evil destination it is.
interpretation: The verse speaks to the moment of reckoning, when the usual means of escape the disbelievers relied upon, such as ransom, wealth, and worldly bargaining, are shown to be worthless. Nothing can be exchanged for deliverance on that Day, because the account is settled by deeds alone. The phrase 'your protector' is spoken with bitter irony: the Fire becomes the only companion they have chosen for themselves, the very thing they denied and mocked in life. The closing words, 'what an evil destination,' turn the warning into a stark sense of finality, urging the listener to recognize now that the true refuge lies in faith and righteous action before that Day arrives.

translation: Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should become humbly submissive at the remembrance of God and at what has been revealed of the truth, and that they should not be like those who were given the Scripture before, and a long time passed over them so their hearts hardened? And many of them are defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse addresses the believers with a gentle rebuke, asking whether the time has not yet arrived for their hearts to soften and submit in awe when God is remembered and when the revealed truth is recited to them. It warns against repeating the pattern of the earlier People of the Book, who let long stretches of time pass after their revelation, grew heedless, and whose hearts became hard as a result, leading to widespread moral deviance. The lesson is that spiritual vitality depends on continual renewal of remembrance and attentiveness to scripture, since neglect and prolonged distance from the message gradually harden the heart.

translation: Know that Allah gives life to the earth after its death. We have certainly made the signs clear to you, so that you may understand.
interpretation: The verse invites the reader to reflect on the revival of barren land after rain as a visible sign of God's power to bring the dead back to life, including on the Day of Resurrection. By linking this natural renewal to the clarity of God's revealed signs, it teaches that the same reasoning which perceives the earth's revival should lead the mind to understand the truth of the message and to act upon it.

translation: Indeed, those who give charity, men and women, and who lend to Allah a goodly loan, it will be multiplied for them, and they will have a generous reward.
interpretation: The verse links sincere almsgiving with lending to God, presenting charity not as a loss but as a loan that God repays many times over. The phrase 'a goodly loan' suggests that the giver's wealth returns to them as increase, while the mention of men and women together affirms that both are equally called to generosity and equally rewarded. The word 'karim' (generous) signals that the reward is not merely proportionate but noble and abundant, reflecting God's own generosity toward those who give freely.

translation: And those who believe in Allah and His messengers - it is they who are the steadfast in truthfulness (al-siddiqun) and the martyrs (al-shuhada') in the sight of their Lord. For them is their reward and their light. But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs - those are the companions of Hellfire.
interpretation: The verse presents faith in Allah and His messengers as the root from which true sincerity and witness flow: the siddiqun are those whose inner truthfulness matches their outward profession, and the shuhada' are those who bear witness to the truth through their lives and sacrifice, both standing in a station of honor before their Lord. Their reward is joined with a light that accompanies them, an image of guidance that is both inward and visible on the Day of Reckoning. Set against them is the contrasting fate of those who reject the truth and deny the signs of God, showing that the verse defines human destiny by one's response to divine revelation, with belief illuminating the path and denial leading to the fire.

translation: Know that the life of this world is but play and amusement, adornment and boasting among yourselves, and competition in wealth and children. It is like a rain whose vegetation pleases the disbelievers; then it dries up and you see it turning yellow, then it becomes debris. And in the Hereafter there is severe punishment, and forgiveness from Allah and approval. And the life of this world is not but the enjoyment of delusion.
interpretation: The verse portrays worldly life through the image of rain-grown crops: they dazzle the eye for a moment, then wither into straw, revealing that everything prized in this world (pleasure, display, rivalry over wealth and offspring) is transient. The contrast with the Hereafter directs the believer's heart away from illusory attachments toward what endures, namely Allah's forgiveness and approval, and warns that heedlessness toward the Hereafter leads to severe loss.

translation: Race one another toward forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden as wide as the heaven and the earth, prepared for those who believe in Allah and His messengers. That is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills, and Allah is the possessor of great bounty.
interpretation: The verse calls believers to a competitive eagerness for the means of salvation, namely divine forgiveness and Paradise, treating worldly rivalry as misplaced and redirecting the human drive to excel toward what is eternal. Its vastness, 'as wide as the heaven and the earth,' conveys that the reward exceeds any measure the human mind can grasp, while the condition of faith in Allah and His messengers shows that true success is bound to belief in God and obedience to His prophets. By stating that this grace is Allah's bounty granted to whomever He wills, the verse reminds the believer that such merit cannot be earned by mere effort or claimed as a right, so that humility and gratitude accompany striving.

translation: No calamity strikes upon the earth or within yourselves except that it is in a Record before We bring it into being. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.
interpretation: The verse establishes that every affliction, whether it touches the land or the soul, is not a random accident but is already written in a divine Record before it comes to pass, so that the believer's heart is anchored in the knowledge that nothing escapes the decree of Allah. This foreknowledge is meant to free a person from the grief that follows what is lost and from the pride that follows what is gained, as the Qur'an itself states in the verses that follow, that one should not despair over what has passed nor exult over what has been given. The phrase that this is easy for Allah reminds the reader that the vast order of creation, with all its events, requires no effort from its Creator, so that trust in Him becomes the natural response to hardship. The verse thus turns the experience of misfortune into an occasion for submission, patience, and a deeper reliance on the One who has written all things with perfect wisdom.

translation: So that you do not despair over what has escaped you, and do not exult over what He has given you. And Allah does not love every arrogant boaster.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Hadid 57:23) teaches a balanced inner attitude toward worldly fortune. Its purpose is stated at the outset: Allah informs the believers of the transience of worldly gain and loss so that the heart is not crushed by grief over what slips away nor inflated with pride over what is granted. Loss and gain are both within the decree of Allah, so the believer meets hardship with patient acceptance and blessings with gratitude and humility rather than vanity. The closing line makes the stakes clear: the one who becomes exultant and boastful over possessions, forgetting their Giver, is one whom Allah does not love, since such pride cuts a person off from the humility that opens the heart to guidance and to generosity toward others.

translation: Those who are stingy and enjoin stinginess upon people. And whoever turns away, indeed Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse exposes a double fault: the miser not only hoards his own wealth but also commands others to do the same, turning his stinginess into a social doctrine that corrodes generosity and solidarity among people. By pairing this with the warning about turning away, it shows that withholding from God's path is a rejection of the divine command, and that such a person harms no one but himself, since Allah is in no need of anyone's wealth or obedience, and He is worthy of praise regardless of whether people give thanks or not.

translation: We had already sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Scripture and the balance, so that people might uphold justice. And We sent down iron, in which there is great might and benefits for mankind, and so that Allah may know who supports Him and His messengers unseen. Indeed, Allah is Strong and Mighty.
interpretation: The verse presents the purpose of prophethood and revelation as the establishment of justice in human society, supported by both scripture and the balance, meaning a moral and legal measure by which people weigh their actions and dealings. The mention of iron immediately after shows that divine guidance must be backed by material strength and organized power, since iron represents both the force needed to restrain oppression and the tools that serve human welfare. The phrase about knowing who supports God and His messengers unseen indicates that true support is a sincere commitment made without public display or worldly witness, and that the believer's readiness to defend truth is a test of faith. The closing names of God, Strong and Mighty, remind that the ultimate victory belongs to Him, while humans are responsible for carrying out justice with the means He has provided.

translation: And We had certainly sent Noah and Abraham, and We placed in their descendants prophethood and the Scripture. Among them is one who is guided, but many of them are defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse shows that divine guidance was entrusted to the lineage of Noah and Abraham, whose descendants received prophethood and revealed books, yet this great inheritance did not guarantee faith for all of them. Its lesson is that noble ancestry and prophetic heritage cannot substitute for personal guidance; each person must accept the path of God through their own choice, and the majority who turn away from it bear the responsibility for their own deviation.

translation: Then We followed up after them with Our messengers, and We followed up with Jesus, son of Mary, and gave him the Gospel, and We placed in the hearts of those who followed him kindness and mercy, and monasticism which they invented—We did not prescribe it for them; they sought only the pleasure of Allah, but they did not observe it with its proper observance. So We gave those of them who believed their reward, but many of them are defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse shows that the followers of Jesus, who had been given kindness and mercy in their hearts, adopted a monastic practice that God had not prescribed for them, sincerely intending to seek His pleasure, yet they failed to maintain it as it should have been kept. This teaches that human innovation in worship, even when motivated by piety, can become a burden that is not upheld faithfully, and that God's favor is reserved for those who believe, while many who deviate from His commands remain in rebellion.

translation: O you who have believed, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger; He will give you a double portion of His mercy, and will make for you a light by which you will walk, and will forgive you. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse addresses the believers directly and joins two duties: taqwa of Allah and faith in His Messenger. It presents these not as a burden but as the path to a twofold reward of divine mercy, the 'double portion' (kiflayn) that may be read as the reward for faith in the earlier messengers together with faith in Muhammad, or as the reward for both outward submission and inward sincerity. The 'light' by which they walk points to the guidance and clarity that accompany piety, so that the believer moves through life with discernment, as in the Qur'anic image of light upon light. Finally, the verse closes with forgiveness and mercy, showing that God's relationship with the believer rests on His pardon and compassion as much as on the command itself.

translation: So that the People of the Scripture may know that they have no power over anything of the bounty of Allah, and that bounty is in the hand of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills, and Allah is the Owner of great bounty.
interpretation: The verse points to a reversal of the assumed privilege of the People of the Scripture: they had come to regard divine favor as a monopoly of their own community, so the verse affirms that grace is wholly in God's hand and not bound to any lineage, group, or claim of election. By stating that they have no control over it, the verse breaks their sense of entitlement and places the believers' standing under God's free and sovereign choice. The closing phrase, Allah is the Owner of great bounty, teaches that God's generosity is boundless and therefore calls the heart away from envy and rivalry toward a trust in God's wide and unrestricted giving.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Allah has already heard the statement of the woman who pleads with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah, and Allah hears your mutual dialogue. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Seeing.
interpretation: The verse opens with the assurance that God has heard the plea of a woman who came to the Prophet disputing over her husband's pronouncement of zihar, the pre-Islamic practice of likening a wife to one's mother, which made her unlawful to him. Her turning to God rather than only to the Prophet shows that a grievance brought before Him is never lost, even when human authority seems unable to answer it. The verse thus establishes that divine attention reaches the most personal and humble of complaints, and that God's hearing and sight encompass every word spoken between people in private distress. The rulings that follow in the chapter then give legal remedy to the injustice, so the verse joins comfort for the oppressed with the principle that justice is accomplished through God's law.

translation: Those of you who divorce their wives by zihar (saying 'you are to me like the back of my mother') — they are not their mothers. Their mothers are only those who bore them. And indeed, they utter an objectionable word and a falsehood. But indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse dismantles the pre-Islamic practice of zihar, in which a husband likened his wife to his mother's back, thereby treating her as forbidden to him as a mother while keeping her as a wife. God establishes that a wife cannot become a mother through such words, since maternity is defined by biological birth alone, so the utterance is revealed as a baseless and deceitful speech that has no power to transform the marital bond. By calling it 'an objectionable word and a falsehood,' the verse exposes the moral wrong of using a spouse as a tool for harm and sets the stage for the expiation that follows. The closing reassurance of God's pardon and forgiveness signals that divine mercy remains open to the one who has spoken rashly and who turns back to make amends.

translation: And those who divorce by zihar from their wives and then retract what they said - then the freeing of a slave before they touch each other. That is what you are admonished with, and Allah is Acquainted with what you do.
interpretation: The verse establishes that zihar, the pre-Islamic practice of a husband likening his wife to his mother's back to declare her forbidden to himself, carries real legal weight and cannot be dismissed as idle speech. Its expiation is obligatory only when the husband seeks to return to the marital relationship he had renounced; the requirement to free a slave before any renewed intimacy places a meaningful cost on the act, so that a rash utterance is not treated lightly and the wife is protected from being left in suspended limbo. The closing reminder that Allah knows all deeds signals that this ruling is a moral admonition as well as a legal one, calling the believer to guard the sanctity of marriage and to weigh his words before he speaks them.

translation: So whoever does not find [a slave to free], then [he must fast two consecutive months before they touch each other. And whoever is not able, then [he must feed sixty needy people. That is so that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger. These are the limits of Allah, and for the disbelievers there is a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah al-Mujadilah, lays down the graded expiation (kaffarah) for a man who has pronounced zihar, likening his wife to his mother's back, and then wishes to resume marital relations. He must first free a slave; if he cannot find one, he must fast two consecutive months before any further intimacy; and if he is unable even to fast, he must feed sixty needy persons. The order of these obligations reflects the gravity of the offense and the mercy of allowing graduated relief according to one's means. The closing words frame these rulings as limits set by God that a believer must respect, so that obedience to them is an expression of faith in God and His Messenger, while rejection of these bounds brings a painful punishment.

translation: Indeed, those who oppose Allah and His Messenger will be humiliated just as those before them were humiliated, and We have certainly sent down clear signs, and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse establishes a divine principle of consequence: opposition to Allah and His Messenger is not a matter that goes unanswered, for those who set themselves against the revealed order are brought low in the same manner as the earlier nations who rejected their prophets. The phrase 'kubitu' (humiliated, disgraced) points to a defeat that is both worldly and spiritual, a loss of honour and standing. The mention of the clear signs that have already been sent down signifies that the proof has been made manifest, so the rejection that follows is not born of ignorance but of wilful denial, which is why the punishment is described as humiliating. The verse thus combines a warning to the contemporaries of the Prophet with a reassurance that the truth, once made plain, will prevail over those who oppose it.

translation: On the Day when Allah will resurrect them all, He will inform them of what they did. Allah has enumerated it, while they had forgotten it, and Allah is Witness over everything.
interpretation: The verse points to a complete and unforgettable divine accountability: while people may forget their deeds, nothing escapes the knowledge of Allah, Who records and preserves every action. The resurrection is thus not merely a gathering but a disclosure, in which the hidden reality of each person's conduct is made plain. The sense of being watched over by an all-witnessing God should lead a believer toward sincerity and mindfulness in every deed, since forgetfulness on the human side never implies neglect on the divine side.

translation: Do you not see that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth? There is no secret conversation among three except that He is their fourth, nor among five except that He is their sixth, nor less than that nor more, except that He is with them wherever they are. Then He will inform them of what they did on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: The verse affirms that Allah's knowledge encompasses every hidden whisper and private exchange, however small the gathering, so that no secret is beyond His awareness. His being 'with them' is a knowledge and watchfulness that accompanies people everywhere, not a physical mingling, and it should awaken a sense of accountability: the deeds and words that people think are concealed will be laid bare on the Day of Resurrection, when Allah will inform them of all they did.

translation: Have you not seen those who were forbidden from secret consultation, yet they return to what they were forbidden and confer together in sin, enmity, and disobedience to the Messenger? And when they come to you, they greet you with a greeting that God has not greeted you with, and they say to themselves, "Why does God not punish us for what we say?" Hell is sufficient for them; they will burn in it, and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: The verse exposes a hypocritical group who, despite being warned against secret whispering that breeds sin and hostility, persist in it, showing that open defiance of divine and prophetic guidance is compounded by deceit. Their distorted greeting, which mocks the Prophet by using words God did not prescribe, reveals contempt disguised as courtesy. Their inner conviction that they are safe from accountability because they are not immediately punished exposes a dangerous misreading of divine patience as indifference. The verse teaches that God's delay of punishment is not impunity, and that the truest protection against such corruption is sincere obedience and transparency in one's dealings.

translation: O you who have believed, when you confer privately, do not confer over sin and aggression and disobedience of the Messenger, but confer over righteousness and piety. And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered.
interpretation: The verse addresses the believers and regulates the ethics of private conversation: secret counsel is not forbidden in itself, but it must not become a vehicle for planning wrongdoing, transgression against others, or defiance of the Prophet's guidance. Instead, the believers' whispered exchanges should be directed toward what is good and God-conscious. The closing reminder of God-consciousness and of the Return to Him ties the social conduct of the community to accountability before God, so that the inner intention behind every private conversation is itself subject to divine judgment.

translation: Secret counsel is only from Satan, that he may grieve those who believe, but he cannot harm them at all, except by the permission of Allah. And upon Allah let the believers rely.
interpretation: The verse exposes the whispered conspiracies of the hypocrites and the mischief-makers as a tool of Satan, whose sole aim is to sow sorrow and anxiety in the hearts of the believers. Yet it teaches that his power over them is bounded entirely by the will of God, so that whatever grief he stirs cannot become real harm without God's leave. The remedy is therefore not fear of whispers but trust: the believer is directed to place reliance on Allah alone, for the one who entrusts his affairs to God finds in Him the sufficiency that defeats every scheme of the devil.

translation: O you who have believed, when you are told to make room in the assemblies, then make room; Allah will make room for you. And when you are told to rise, then rise. Allah will raise those who have believed among you and those who were given knowledge by degrees. And Allah is Acutely Aware of what you do.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true honor before God is earned through faith and knowledge, not through seating position or social status in gatherings. By readily complying with the courteous and communal etiquette of making room for others and rising when asked for the sake of the common good, believers show the humility and good character that faith demands, and God responds by granting them spaciousness and elevation. The mention of those given knowledge being raised in rank signals that learning and its faithful application are among the highest marks of distinction, and the closing reminder that God is fully aware of every action directs the believer toward sincerity, since ranks in the sight of God are measured by inward intention and deed rather than outward display.

translation: O you who have believed, when you consult the Messenger privately, spend something in charity before your private consultation. That is better for you and purer. But if you cannot find [anything to give], then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse establishes a discipline of honoring the Prophet's presence: a believer who wishes to speak with him privately is asked to first give in charity, so that the burden of the request is matched by a sincere act of giving, which filters out frivolous or idle consultations and purifies the heart. The concession that follows, that Allah forgives the one who finds nothing to give, shows that the obligation is measured by ability and that God's mercy accompanies the rule. Its deeper lesson is that reverence for the Messenger and generosity toward the needy are linked, and that intimacy with the sacred is best approached with purity of intention and readiness to sacrifice.

translation: Are you afraid that you will have to offer charity before your private consultations? So when you did not do so and God forgave you, then establish prayer, give zakat, and obey God and His Messenger. And God is Aware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse comes in the context of the rule of paying charity before private consultation with the Messenger. It reveals God's mercy in lifting an burdensome obligation that was imposed to separate the sincere from those who burden the Prophet with frivolous whispering. Having relieved the believers of that duty, God redirects them to the core obligations of worship and obedience: steadfast prayer, zakat, and wholehearted submission to God and His Messenger. The closing reminder that God is fully aware of their deeds calls the believer to inner sincerity, since no action, public or private, is hidden from Him.

translation: Have you not considered those who have taken as allies a people with whom God is angry? They are neither of you nor of them, and they swear falsely while they know.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites of Medina who secretly bound themselves in alliance with the Jews, a people under divine displeasure, while outwardly claiming to belong to the believers. Their allegiance is not rooted in conviction or community but in self-interest and fear, so they stand belonging to neither side. Their oaths of loyalty are knowing lies, showing that the core of hypocrisy is a deliberate divorce between the tongue and the heart. The passage warns that befriending those whom God has cursed or rejected draws a person into their condition, and that false swearing made with full awareness of its falsehood is a grave moral corruption that severs one from both the believing community and the truth.

translation: Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment. Indeed, evil is what they used to do.
interpretation: The verse closes a warning by joining two ideas: the severity of the punishment prepared by Allah and the moral reason behind it. The phrase "ساء ما كانوا يعملون" (evil is what they were doing) shifts the focus from the outcome to the nature of their conduct, indicating that the punishment is not arbitrary but the fitting consequence of deeds that were themselves corrupt. The repetition of the past-continuous form "كانوا يعملون" conveys that this wrongdoing was habitual and persistent, a settled pattern of life rather than a single lapse. The verse thus teaches that divine justice is measured against the character of one's actions, and that persisting in evil brings its own grave reckoning.

translation: They have taken their oaths as a shield, and so they have barred others from the way of God; for them there is a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: The verse exposes a pattern of hypocrisy in which people use oaths as a protective cover, invoking God's name and swearing allegiance to hide their true intentions and shield themselves from suspicion or accountability. Their oaths are not sincere commitments but a barrier that both conceals their own disbelief and obstructs others from following the path of God, so their double offense of deceit and obstruction is met with a punishment that matches it in humiliation: just as they sought to protect their standing through false display, they will be disgraced in the end.

translation: Neither their wealth nor their children will avail them anything against Allah. They are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever.
interpretation: The verse establishes that worldly assets and family ties, which people often treat as their sources of security and honor, carry no weight before God on the Day of Judgment. Their value lies only in this life, and when they are relied upon in place of faith and obedience, they become a snare rather than a shield. By naming the disbelievers as companions of the Fire who abide in it forever, the verse makes clear that the criterion of salvation is the state of the heart and its submission to God, not the abundance of possessions or the number of offspring. It is a warning against misplaced trust in material wealth and lineage, and a call to measure one's standing by one's relationship with the Creator.

translation: On the Day when Allah raises them all up, they will swear to Him just as they swear to you, and they will think that they are standing on something. Verily, it is they who are the liars.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah al-Mujadila (58:18), depicts the hypocrites who, on the Day of Resurrection, will swear false oaths before Allah just as they had sworn falsely before the believers in this world, presuming that such deceit will avail them as it did before men. Their vain hope that their claims rest on some firm ground is exposed: their own oaths on that Day testify against them, for the veil of worldly pretense is lifted and the truth of their hypocrisy becomes evident. The verse thus warns that deception practiced upon people cannot deceive the Omniscient Lord, and that the sincere believer's standing rests on truth, not on the mere display of oaths.

translation: Satan has overcome them and caused them to forget the remembrance of God. Those are the party of Satan. Verily, the party of Satan are the losers.
interpretation: The verse portrays the gradual capture of the heart: when a person yields to Satan's whisperings, Satan gains dominion over them (istahwadha, a word implying he has taken full possession, as a master over a herd), and the immediate consequence is heedlessness of God's remembrance, which is the very source of the heart's life and guidance. Forgetting God is therefore both the sign and the mechanism of satanic control, and it is why the verse defines those so afflicted as belonging to Satan's party. Their loss is not merely worldly but a loss of their own selves and their true purpose, since they have traded the eternal for the fleeting. The verse thus warns that the greatest danger is not an external enemy but the inner slackening of dhikr, and that vigilance in remembrance is the believer's shield against being absorbed into the camp of Satan.

translation: Indeed, those who oppose Allah and His Messenger will be among the most humiliated.
interpretation: The verse declares that opposition to Allah and His Messenger is not merely a matter of disbelief but a form of hostility that brings about the deepest abasement. Those who set themselves against the divine command and the guidance of the Prophet place themselves on the side of weakness and disgrace, for true honor belongs only to Allah, His Messenger, and the believers. The humiliation mentioned is both a consequence in this world, as such people are cast down and defeated by the truth, and a reality in the Hereafter, where their rejection of submission to the Creator is fully exposed. The phrase among the most humiliated emphasizes that they are placed in the lowest ranks of disgrace, showing that what appears to them as strength through defiance is in fact the greatest weakness.

translation: God has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail." Indeed, God is Powerful, Mighty.
interpretation: The verse affirms that victory belongs ultimately to God and to His messengers, for it is a decree written by God Himself that cannot be reversed. The prophets may face opposition, rejection and hardship, yet the triumph of truth is guaranteed, not by the strength of the messengers alone, but by the power and might of God, who is able to accomplish what He wills. The believer is thus reassured that the outcome of the struggle between truth and falsehood is settled in favor of God's cause, and that patience and steadfastness in carrying the message are the appropriate response while awaiting that promised victory.

translation: You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their kindred. Those are the ones in whose hearts He has written faith and whom He has strengthened with a spirit from Himself. And He will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. Those are the party of Allah. Unquestionably, the party of Allah are the successful.
interpretation: The verse establishes that true faith is measured by loyalty: genuine belief in God and the Last Day cannot coexist with friendship toward those who oppose God and His Messenger, however close the blood tie may be. Such loyalty is not a matter of mere kinship but of the heart, which God has inscribed with faith and sustained with a divine spirit. The reward is a mutual pleasure between God and the believers, and their identity becomes that of the 'party of Allah,' whose success is affirmed as certain. The lesson is that allegiance in the religious sense ranks above natural family bonds when the two conflict.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: The verse opens by placing all of creation in a single act of worship: everything in the heavens and on the earth declares Allah free from every deficiency, not in words alone but through the very existence and order of each thing, which follows the nature Allah has given it. Human beings, who alone can choose to glorify Him, are thus invited to recognize that their own praise is joining a cosmic chorus rather than originating it. The closing names, al-'Aziz (the Mighty, whose power none can resist) and al-Hakim (the Wise, whose every decree is purposeful), show that the glorification is owed because His might and His wisdom are perfect; the universe's harmony is itself evidence of that wisdom, and the believer's reflection on it becomes a path to humility and gratitude.

translation: It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture from their homes at the first gathering. You did not expect that they would leave, and they thought their fortresses would protect them from Allah, but Allah came to them from where they did not expect and cast terror into their hearts. They destroyed their own homes with their hands and the hands of the believers. So take warning, O people of insight.
interpretation: The verse shows that worldly strength, wealth, and fortifications offer no real refuge against the decree of God, since security that depends on material means alone collapses when Allah's command arrives from an unexpected direction. The Banu al-Nadir believed their walls and their confidence in their own position would keep them safe, yet their downfall came from within as much as from without, as their own treachery and fear ruined their homes by their own hands. The deeper lesson is that the true cause of a people's ruin is often the hollowing out of their hearts through arrogance and betrayal, so the insightful believer should learn from such events to examine his own reliance and conduct rather than trusting in the apparent solidity of his defenses.

translation: And had Allah not decreed for them the exile, He would have punished them in this world; and for them in the Hereafter is the punishment of the Fire.
interpretation: The verse, revealed concerning the Banu Nadir's expulsion from Medina, shows that God's mercy toward a people can take the form of a lesser, worldly punishment rather than total destruction. Exile, though painful, was a milder judgment than the annihilation or harsher torment that had befallen earlier rebellious communities. The verse also draws a clear distinction between the temporal consequences of wrongdoing, which may be softened, and the eternal reckoning of the Hereafter, where the fire awaits those who persist in opposing God and His messenger. Its lesson is that worldly hardship can itself be a form of divine dealing that warns and restrains, and that the believer should read historical calamities as moral signs rather than mere accidents of fortune.

translation: That is because they opposed Allah and His Messenger. And whoever opposes Allah - indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.
interpretation: The verse establishes a direct causal link between the punishment and the act of opposition (mushaqqah): the chastisement described is not arbitrary but the consequence of deliberately setting oneself against God and His messenger. The word shaqq, meaning to split or to take a side that cuts one off from the other, conveys a defiant separation from the path of obedience, as though the rebel places himself on the far side of a divide. By pairing Allah with His Messenger, the verse shows that opposing the Prophet is equivalent to opposing God, so obedience to the messenger is inseparable from obedience to God. The closing phrase, that Allah is severe in retribution, serves as a warning that divine justice is firm and that no one can escape its consequences through worldly strength or cunning.

translation: Whatever palm trees you cut down or left standing on their roots, it was by the permission of Allah, and so that He might disgrace the defiantly wicked.
interpretation: The verse addresses the Muslims' conduct during the siege of the Banu Nadir, when some palm trees were cut down and others spared. Its point is that both acts, though they appear to be opposite choices, were equally sanctioned by God, so the believers need not fear that their military actions were wrongful. The divine permission ensures that the outcome, including the humbling of the transgressors, is achieved through a justice that is not reducible to the judgment of the fighters themselves. The verse thus teaches that the purposes of war are ultimately under God's command, and that what humans perceive as destruction or preservation is woven into a wider plan that exposes and shames those who have rebelled against truth.

translation: And whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from them - you did not spur toward it horse or camel, but Allah gives His messengers power over whom He wills, and Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the spoils taken from the Banu al-Nadir came to the Prophet through divine grace rather than through the fierce military exertion of the Muslims, for they had not ridden hard to reach them with horses or camels. This teaches that victory and wealth ultimately belong to God, who empowers His messengers over whomever He chooses, so that the community should recognize that its success rests on Divine will rather than on its own strength alone, and that such gains are distributed by the guidance revealed to the Prophet for the benefit of those in need.

translation: Whatever Allah has returned to His Messenger from the people of the towns belongs to Allah and to the Messenger and to the near of kin and the orphans and the needy and the wayfarer, so that it does not circulate only among the rich among you. And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.
interpretation: The verse establishes that wealth gained without battle from the settled communities (fay') is not distributed like war spoils but is placed under the authority of Allah and His Messenger for the benefit of the most vulnerable and the public good, so that wealth does not become a closed circuit held by the affluent. Its principle is a social economic justice that prevents concentration of riches. The verse then extends the obligation of obedience to the Prophet's rulings in general, binding the believers to accept what he gives and abstain from what he forbids, grounding this obedience in taqwa and the warning of Allah's severe retribution.

translation: (This wealth belongs) to the poor emigrants who were driven out of their homes and their possessions, seeking bounty from Allah and His pleasure, and supporting Allah and His Messenger. Those are the truthful.
interpretation: The verse defines true faith through action rather than mere claim: the emigrants' sincerity is proven by their willingness to abandon homeland and property, seeking God's grace and approval rather than worldly gain, and by their active support of God's cause and His Messenger. The word 'truthful' (al-sadiqun) suggests that the honesty of one's faith is measured by the sacrifice it demands, so that the bond between belief and costly deed is inseparable. It also implies that material loss, when borne for the sake of God, becomes the very evidence of a sincere heart.

translation: And those who had already settled in the abode and in faith before them love those who emigrate to them, and do not find in their breasts any need for what the emigrants were given, and they prefer them over themselves, even though they themselves were in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, it is those who are the successful.
interpretation: The verse portrays the ideal of the Ansar of Madinah toward the Muhajirun, but it also sets out a universal ethic: true faith is measured by generosity that overcomes envy and self-interest. The absence of resentment in the hearts of the believers shows that a community is bound together not by shared territory alone but by a purified heart that rejoices in others' good. Preferring others over oneself, even in need, reveals that the soul's natural greed (shuhh) is the greatest obstacle to success, and that being freed from it is the real path to prosperity in this life and the next.

translation: And those who came after them say: "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and do not put in our hearts any resentment toward those who have believed. Our Lord, You are indeed Kind and Merciful."
interpretation: This verse describes the believers of later generations, who are defined by a prayer that binds them to the earlier community of faith rather than by lineage or place. Their supplication begins with forgiveness, first for themselves and then for their predecessors, showing that the bond of faith extends across time and that a believer's honor for the early Muslims is expressed through prayer for them. The request to be spared any rancor (ghill) toward fellow believers reveals that the true measure of the faithful community is a heart purified of envy and enmity, so that the unity of the ummah rests on sincere love and mutual goodwill. The closing names of Allah as Raʾūf and Raḥīm point the heart toward the mercy it seeks, teaching that a person who longs for purity of heart is ultimately turning to the boundless compassion of God.

translation: Have you not considered those who practiced hypocrisy, saying to their brothers who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture: "If you are expelled, we will surely leave with you, and we will never obey anyone concerning you; and if you are fought, we will surely support you." And Allah testifies that indeed they are liars.
interpretation: The verse exposes the inner duplicity of the hypocrites, whose words of loyalty to their allies among the People of the Scripture are empty promises spoken to win favor and hedge against loss. Their pledges to depart with the expelled or to fight alongside the besieged are shown to be unreliable, since their true allegiance lies in self-preservation and in the pursuit of advantage. By declaring them liars through God's own testimony, the verse teaches that the believer should look beyond eloquent assurances to the reality of conduct, and that alliances founded on opportunism and fear rather than sincere faith and principle will fail when tested.

translation: Even if they are expelled, they will not go forth with them; and even if they are fought against, they will not support them; and even if they support them, they will surely turn their backs, and then they will not be helped.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hollowness of the alliance between the hypocrites and the People of the Book who had broken faith with the Prophet. It shows that their promises of solidarity are empty: when the moment of trial comes, they will neither leave their homes to stand with their allies, nor fight alongside them, nor truly lend aid. Even in the unlikely case they do intervene, they will flee at the first sign of battle, and the support they were counted upon to give will never materialize. The verse thus teaches that alliances built on fear, hypocrisy, and worldly calculation collapse under pressure, and that true strength lies in sincere faith and God's support rather than in the pledges of those who do not truly stand by their word.

translation: Indeed, you are more fearsome in their breasts than Allah. That is because they are a people who do not understand.
interpretation: The verse exposes the root of the hypocrites' and unbelievers' fear: they dread the believers more than they dread God, which reveals a deficiency in their understanding rather than any real strength in the Muslims. Their hearts are filled with worldly fear because they fail to grasp the true majesty and power of God, who alone deserves awe. Their lack of fiqh, or deep comprehension, means they cannot perceive that all power belongs to God, so their misplaced dread is a sign of their spiritual blindness. The verse thus contrasts the proper reverence owed to God with the distorted priorities of those who do not reflect.

translation: They will not fight you all together, except within fortified towns or from behind walls. Their violence among themselves is severe; you think them united, but their hearts are divided. That is because they are a people who do not reason.
interpretation: The verse describes the internal weakness of a hostile group whose outward appearance of unity conceals deep division. Their fighting is limited to defensive positions, since they cannot face the believers in open combat, and their strife among themselves is fierce. The contrast between apparent collective strength and divided hearts shows that unity grounded in shared conviction and reason is lacking in them. The closing statement attributes this condition to their failure to use their intellect, suggesting that abandoning reflection leads to disunity, fear, and dependence on fortifications rather than on sound judgment and truth.

translation: Like those before them, shortly before them, who tasted the evil consequence of their conduct, and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse places the hypocrites who abandoned their allies and the deceiver Satan who promised them support and then disowned them within a recurring pattern of history. Those who came shortly before them, who chose betrayal and defiance, already tasted in this world the bitter fruit of their own choices, and a painful punishment awaits them in the Hereafter. The lesson is that worldly consequences of wrongdoing are a warning that the same outcome, and a greater reckoning, will come to those who follow the same path of deception and broken commitments.

translation: Like the Shaytan when he says to the human, "Disbelieve!" and when he disbelieves, he says, "Indeed, I am free of you; indeed, I fear Allah, the Lord of the worlds."
interpretation: The verse uses the image of Satan's abandonment of his followers to expose the hollowness of the promises that lure people into disbelief. Satan first beguiles the human being into rejecting faith, but once the person has fallen into it, he disowns him and claims a fear of God he never had, leaving the deceived alone with the consequences of his choice. The lesson is that whoever follows an enticer's counsel toward disbelief will find that the enticer offers no real protection at the moment of reckoning, so the believer should look to the true source of refuge, the Lord of all the worlds, rather than to the one who beckons toward ruin.

translation: So the outcome for both of them was that they would be in the Fire, abiding therein forever. And that is the recompense of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse closes a narrative of two figures who chose the path of wrongdoing, and it expresses the justice of the outcome: the consequence of their deeds was not merely temporary punishment but an eternal state of dwelling in the Fire. By stating that this is the recompense of the zalimin, the verse makes clear that wrongdoing (zulm), whether it is injustice toward others or transgression against one's own soul and against God, carries its own inescapable consequence. The phrase emphasizes that the punishment is not arbitrary but a fitting reflection of the choices made, teaching that the destiny of a person is shaped by the direction of their actions and that the gravest loss is the failure to keep to what is right.

translation: O you who have believed, fear Allah. And let every soul look to what it has put forward for tomorrow. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do.
interpretation: The verse calls the believers to taqwa, the conscious awareness of God that guards the heart and limbs, and then ties that awareness to accountability by directing each soul to examine its own deeds as an investment for the Hereafter, the "tomorrow" that is the Day of Judgment. The repetition of the command to fear Allah at its beginning and end frames self-examination within constant God-consciousness, and the closing reminder that Allah is fully aware of every action removes any hope of concealment, so that a person's reckoning before the Hereafter becomes a motivation to purify intention and deed now.

translation: And do not be like those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves. Those are the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse warns believers against imitating those who abandoned remembrance of God. Forgetting Allah is not merely a lapse of memory but a neglect of the heart's orientation toward its Creator, and its consequence is a loss of self-knowledge: a person who does not remember his Lord ends up unaware of his true purpose, his accountability, and his real worth, so he is left to pursue his desires and become estranged from his own soul. The phrase 'He made them forget themselves' presents this self-forgetfulness as the just outcome of their own choice, since God leaves to themselves those who turn away. The closing description of them as al-fasiqun identifies such people as having stepped outside the bounds of obedience, and it implies that remembrance of God is the foundation of both moral clarity and genuine selfhood.

translation: The companions of the Fire and the companions of Paradise are not equal. The companions of Paradise are the ones who are triumphant.
interpretation: The verse draws a clear moral distinction between two destinies that no one should confuse or regard as equivalent. Equality is denied not merely in outcome but in worth: those who lived in a way that leads to the Fire and those who lived in faith and righteousness are placed in fundamentally different states. By calling the people of Paradise 'the triumphant' (al-fa'izun), the verse frames true success not as worldly gain, power, or status, which can be fleeting, but as salvation from the Fire and admission to eternal bliss. The brief, unadorned sentence invites the listener to examine which path they are walking and to recognize that the choices made in this life determine which of these two companionships one will ultimately belong to.

translation: Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split asunder out of fear of God. And these parables We set forth for people, that perhaps they may reflect.
interpretation: The verse uses a striking contrast to expose the hardness of the human heart. A mountain, though inanimate and massive, would tremble, humble itself, and crack apart if it grasped the weight of divine speech, while human beings often hear the Qur'an and remain unmoved. The awe the mountain feels is a call to the listener to recognize the majesty of the revelation and to let it soften the heart. The closing reference to parables indicates that God presents these images deliberately, so that people will turn their thoughts inward, contemplate the meanings behind them, and respond with reverence rather than heedlessness.

translation: He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity; the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed. He is the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: The verse opens by affirming the absolute oneness of God: the one whose divinity is exclusive, so that worship belongs to Him alone and no other being shares in it. It then grounds this exclusivity in His complete knowledge, encompassing both what lies hidden from human perception and what is manifest and observed, so that nothing escapes Him. The closing names, al-Rahman and al-Rahim, reveal that this all-knowing sovereign is also the source of boundless mercy: the knowledge that might inspire awe is joined to a compassion that embraces creation and guides believers to draw near to Him with hope.

translation: He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the Sovereign, the Most Holy, the Source of Peace, the Bestower of Security, the Guardian, the Almighty, the Compeller, the Majestic. Glory be to Allah above what they associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse closes the list of divine names in Surah al-Hashr by moving from description to declaration: the names of sovereignty, holiness, peace, security, watchfulness, might, and greatness are not an abstract catalogue but a demonstration that the One who alone is worthy of worship is the only one who truly possesses these attributes. The final exclamation of tanzih (declaring Allah far above) follows naturally, because every association of partners with Him collapses before the completeness of these names. The believer thus learns that true tawhid is both intellectual, in recognizing who God is, and practical, in refusing to attribute to any creature a share of what belongs only to Him.

translation: He is Allah, the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner. To Him belong the most beautiful names. Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Him, and He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: The verse opens by gathering three acts of divine creation, khalq (bringing into being according to a measure), bari' (originating and producing things free of mutual discord or imperfection), and musawwir (giving each thing its distinct form and shape), to show that the One who creates is also the One who differentiates and perfects every existing thing. Having established this, it places the beautiful names as the fitting expression of such perfection, since each name reveals a real attribute of the Creator that the created order reflects. The statement that all that is in the heavens and earth glorifies Him points to a universal witness: creation itself, in its order, variety and harmony, proclaims the absence of any deficiency in its Maker, even where human beings fail to perceive it. The closing pair, al-'Aziz and al-Hakim, joins power to wisdom, teaching that the One who is able to do all things does not act without purpose, so that the glorification of creation and the diversity of forms both rest on a mighty and wise governance.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies, extending to them affection, while they have disbelieved in what has come to you of the truth, expelling the Messenger and yourselves [from your homeland] because you believe in Allah, your Lord. If you have gone out for jihad in My cause and seeking My approval, [then do not] confide to them with affection, for I am most knowing of what you conceal and what you declare. And whoever of you does that has certainly strayed from the sound way.
interpretation: The verse addresses believers at a moment of tension with the Quraysh, warning that loyalty and private affection toward those who oppress the faithful contradicts the purpose of their sincere striving. Its deeper lesson is that the heart's inclinations must be aligned with God's cause alone, since divine knowledge reaches what is hidden within a person as surely as what is openly displayed, and a believer's allegiance is tested not only in action but in the secret tenderness of the heart.

translation: If they gain the upper hand over you, they will be your enemies and will stretch out their hands and their tongues against you with evil, and they wish that you would disbelieve.
interpretation: The verse exposes the enduring hostility of those who reject faith toward the believers: its opening condition, "if they overcome you," shows that their enmity is not a passing mood but a settled disposition that would be unleashed the moment they gained power. The phrase "stretch out their hands and tongues" names both physical aggression and verbal harm, indicating that persecution takes the form of violence, slander, and mockery alike. Yet the final clause reveals the deepest aim behind this hostility: it is not merely to defeat the believers but to pull them back from their faith, so that their wish for the believers' disbelief becomes the true measure of their enmity. The verse thus teaches the faithful to recognize that opposition rooted in a desire to see them abandon their religion calls for vigilance, steadfastness, and clarity about where their loyalty must lie, rather than naive trust in those who have shown themselves hostile.

translation: Your relatives and your children will never benefit you on the Day of Resurrection; He will separate you. And Allah is Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse dismantles the illusion that kinship and descent can substitute for personal faith and deeds before God. Blood ties, which people instinctively rely on for protection and honor, carry no weight of their own on the Day of Judgment, when every soul stands alone and the bonds of this world are severed by God's decree. The final phrase, 'Allah is Seeing of what you do,' shifts the focus from the external refuge people trust in to the inner reality that God observes. The lesson is that salvation is earned through one's own conduct and sincerity, so a person should not presume upon the piety of parents or children, but should instead take responsibility for his or her own actions while knowing that God sees them fully.

translation: There has already been for you an excellent example in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people, "Indeed, we are disassociated from you and from whatever you worship besides Allah. We have rejected you, and there has appeared between us and you enmity and hatred forever until you believe in Allah alone" — except for the saying of Abraham to his father, "I will surely ask forgiveness for you, though I have no power to obtain for you anything from Allah. Our Lord, upon You we have relied, and to You we have turned in repentance, and to You is the final return."
interpretation: The passage presents Abraham and his companions as a model of uncompromising loyalty to monotheism: a clear public break with idolatry, which must not be softened into false friendship, is required of the believers, while their dependence on God and their return to Him remain the foundation of that stance. The exception concerning Abraham's promise to pray for his father shows that this promise was a personal gesture made before the truth of his father's enmity to God was clear, and that it was not a model to be imitated in seeking forgiveness for unbelievers; once Abraham recognized that his father was an enemy of God, he disassociated himself from him, so the believers are taught that love and loyalty must be governed by faith in God alone.

translation: Our Lord, do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve, and forgive us, our Lord. Indeed, You are the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse expresses a believer's humble supplication to God at a moment of seeking refuge from the very trials that can arise from the people of disbelief. The request "do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve" can be understood in two complementary ways: that believers should not be placed in circumstances where their faith is corrupted, their resolve weakened, or their conduct made a pretext for ridicule of the truth, and that they should not be made the occasion through which disbelievers wrongly judge God's religion. The supplicants then ask for forgiveness, acknowledging that their own shortcomings may be what exposes them to such tests. The closing attributes, al-'Aziz (the Mighty, who is able to do all things) and al-Hakim (the Wise, who orders all things with perfect purpose), indicate that the believers place their hope in God's power to protect them and in His wisdom in governing the trials He sends. Thus the verse teaches that sincere faith combines dependence on God's might, trust in His wisdom, and continual repentance.

translation: There has certainly been for you an excellent example in them for whoever hopes in Allah and the Last Day. But whoever turns away - indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse presents the believers of Abraham and those with him as a model worth imitating, but it ties the benefit of that model to sincere hope in Allah and the Last Day, meaning that true imitation is a matter of inner faith and conviction rather than mere outward resemblance. It then warns that turning away from this path harms no one but the one who turns away, since Allah has no need of His creatures and is worthy of praise in Himself, so the call to follow the righteous is an act of mercy toward human beings rather than a benefit to God.

translation: It may be that Allah will place affection between you and those among them with whom you have been at enmity. And Allah is Competent (over all things), and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse opens with a word of hope ("It may be"), reminding believers that hostility is not permanent and that Allah, who controls hearts, can transform enmity into affection. Its meaning is tied to its context in Surah al-Mumtahanah, where the believers are warned against taking the enemies of Allah as allies while those enemies were actively opposing them. Yet the verse keeps the door open: sincere reconciliation is always possible when Allah wills it. The closing names of Allah, the All-Powerful, the Forgiving and the Merciful, reassure the believers that the One who can change hearts also pardons past wrongs and shows mercy, so they should hold to faith and justice without despair over their enemies.

translation: God does not forbid you from those who do not fight you because of your religion and do not expel you from your homes, from being kind to them and dealing with them justly. Indeed, God loves those who act justly.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the basis of relations between Muslims and non-Muslims is not hostility but righteousness and equity. The permission to show kindness and justice is conditioned on the absence of aggression against the believers in their faith or their homeland, which shows that the ethical obligation to deal fairly is grounded in the principle of reciprocal peace rather than in the nature of the other party's creed. By tying the command to God's love for those who act justly, the verse elevates fairness itself into a form of worship and reveals that justice is owed even to those outside the community of faith, so long as they do not oppress it.

translation: Allah only forbids you from those who fight you over religion, expel you from your homes, and aid in your expulsion, that you make allies of them. And whoever makes allies of them, then it is those who are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse (60:9) draws a clear line between enmity born of hostility to the faith and its people and the ordinary human relations that Islam otherwise encourages, including kindness and justice toward non-Muslims who live peacefully. The prohibition targets those who actively wage war against believers, drive them out of their homes, and conspire to support that expulsion; aligning with such people in their hostility, by entrusting them with loyalty, support, and confidantes' secrets, is what is forbidden. The verse frames such alliance as a form of wrongdoing (zulm) because it places loyalty where it betrays one's own community and the cause of justice.
