Its scope is tied to the specific circumstances of hostility and aggression described, so it should be read together with other verses that command fairness and goodness toward those who do not fight the believers.

translation: O you who have believed, when believing women come to you as emigrants, test them. Allah is most knowing of their faith. And if you know them to be believers, then do not return them to the disbelievers. They are not lawful [wives] for the disbelievers, nor are the disbelievers lawful [husbands] for them. But give the disbelievers what they had spent. And there is no blame upon you in marrying them once you have given them their due compensation. And do not hold on to marriage bonds with disbelieving women; ask for what you have spent and let them ask for what they have spent. That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you. And Allah is Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: The verse establishes a principle of moral and legal discernment in the early Muslim community: faith is ultimately known only to God, so believers must test the sincerity of women who migrate to them, yet the outward evidence of belief becomes the basis for their protection. It reveals that the bond of faith overrides tribal and marital ties to unbelievers, and that the dissolution of such bonds is to be carried out through fair settlement of what was spent, not through coercion or injustice. The verse thus teaches that religious identity, justice in financial dealings, and reciprocal fairness between the two communities must be balanced, with the final authority resting on God's knowledge and wisdom.

translation: And if any of your wives have gone over to the disbelievers, and you then have a turn of fortune (victory and spoils), then give to those whose wives have gone the equivalent of what they had spent; and fear Allah, in whom you are believers.
interpretation: This verse belongs to the settlement of the treaty of Hudaybiyyah, when women who embraced Islam fled to the Muslims from Makkah and some believing men's wives went back to the disbelievers. It establishes a principle of justice even toward enemies: a believer whose spouse was lost to the enemy is compensated from what the community gains in its own dealings, so that no one bears the loss alone. The closing command to fear Allah reminds believers that their faith must govern how they treat others, even in matters of property and rights, and that obedience to God is the measure of their sincerity.

translation: O Prophet, when believing women come to you pledging to you that they will not associate anything with Allah, will not steal, will not commit adultery, will not kill their children, will not bring forth a slander they have invented between their hands and their feet, and will not disobey you in what is right, then accept their pledge and ask Allah's forgiveness for them. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse presents the allegiance (bay'ah) of believing women to the Prophet as a formal covenant built on the core moral and social commitments of faith: monotheism, the protection of life, lineage, and property, and truthfulness in speech. The phrase about children is widely understood to refer to infanticide, a practice of the pre-Islamic era, and the 'slander between their hands and feet' points to false claims about paternity or fabricated accusations, since the hands and feet are the means by which a person acts and the place where such deceit is carried out. The final clause, 'and will not disobey you in what is right,' ties the pledge to obedience to the Prophet only within what is good, showing that submission to legitimate authority is bounded by righteousness. The instruction to accept their pledge and seek forgiveness for them reflects the mercy that accompanies the ethical framework, and the closing names of Allah affirm that divine forgiveness is open to those who sincerely turn to Him.

translation: O you who believe, do not take as allies a people upon whom Allah has been angry, who have despaired of the Hereafter just as the disbelievers have despaired of those in the graves.
interpretation: The verse warns believers against forming close loyalty and alliance with those who have incurred divine wrath and who have lost hope in the Hereafter, since such a disposition of despair in the unseen reward reflects a spiritual condition that the believer must not adopt or be drawn into. The comparison to disbelievers who despair of those in the graves, that is, of the dead being restored or of them ever being reunited, shows that denial of resurrection leads to a hopelessness that corrupts the heart. Thus the believer's loyalty should rest with those whose faith and hope align with his own, so that his own hope in the Hereafter is protected from being weakened by association with those who have abandoned it.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: The verse opens by declaring that all of creation, in the heavens and on the earth, is in a state of constant glorification of God, which means that every created thing bears witness to its Creator's perfection, freedom from every deficiency, and worthiness of worship, whether or not humans take notice. The closing names point to the source of this universal praise: God is 'al-Aziz', the One whose power is unassailable and whose dominion cannot be overturned, and 'al-Hakim', whose every act and decree is governed by perfect wisdom. The juxtaposition invites the reader to see the orderly, purposeful motion of the cosmos as a continual testimony that the One who holds ultimate might also acts with flawless wisdom, so that human beings should respond to this reality with humility, gratitude, and their own glorification of God.

translation: O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?
interpretation: The verse rebukes believers who make verbal claims or promises that their conduct does not match. Faith is not proven by words alone; a sincere believer's speech must be backed by action, and the gap between what one professes and what one practices is strongly condemned. The principle extends beyond any single occasion to every form of hypocritical speech, teaching that integrity requires consistency between tongue and deed, since God is displeased by such emptiness.

translation: Great is the hatred in the sight of God that you say what you do not do.
interpretation: The verse condemns the gap between speech and action, showing that God regards it as an extremely grave matter to make promises or claims one does not fulfill. Its wording, 'great is hatred' (kabura maqtan), signals how deeply displeasing such hypocrisy is to God, since words that are not backed by deeds corrupt trust, undermine sincerity, and turn faith into mere formality. The verse calls believers to integrity: that what they profess with the tongue be matched by their conduct, so that their words carry truth and their lives bear witness to what they claim to believe.

translation: Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in ranks, as if they were a solid structure joined together firmly.
interpretation: The verse presents the believers' collective strength as rooted in unity and cohesion: when they stand together in close, organized ranks with a shared purpose, they become like a well-built wall that no force can easily breach. The image teaches that Allah's love is directed at those whose devotion to the cause is expressed through discipline, solidarity, and mutual reinforcement, so that each member supports the others. Its meaning extends beyond the battlefield to every community striving for a righteous goal, reminding believers that individual strength gains its real effect only when it is bonded to the whole, and that division weakens what unity would protect.

translation: And [remember] when Moses said to his people, "O my people, why do you harm me while you know that I am the messenger of Allah to you?" So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: The verse exposes a paradox at the heart of persistent disobedience: the people harmed their own prophet despite knowing his truthfulness, which shows that their injury was directed not merely at Moses but at the clear signs of God's message. Their deliberate turning away was the initial act of choice, and God's turning of their hearts is presented as the consequence of that choice, a divine confirmation of what they had chosen for themselves. The verse thus teaches that knowledge without sincere submission hardens the heart, and that continued deviation can close the heart to guidance altogether, so that persistent defiance becomes its own punishment.

translation: And [mention] when Jesus, the son of Mary, said: "O Children of Israel, indeed I am the messenger of Allah to you, confirming what came before me of the Torah and giving good tidings of a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad." But when he came to them with clear evidences, they said, "This is obvious magic."
interpretation: The verse shows Jesus affirming his role within the continuity of revelation: he confirms the Torah that preceded him, and he announces a future messenger whose name is Ahmad, a name related to praise and often understood as a reference to Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. The rejection of the clear signs as mere sorcery reveals a recurring pattern of stubbornness among those who are presented with undeniable proof, while the prophetic chain is shown as unified in its message and its succession of guidance.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah while he is being invited to Islam? And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: The verse identifies the gravest form of injustice as deliberately inventing falsehood about God at the very moment when the truth is being offered to him. Such a person is not merely mistaken but has chosen to close his heart against a clear invitation, so the guidance he refuses is withheld from him as a consequence of his own persistent wrongdoing. The verse thus links the moral act of lying against God with the spiritual outcome of being deprived of divine guidance, warning that willful rejection of the call to submission hardens a person until he cannot recognize the path.

translation: They want to extinguish the light of God with their mouths, but God will perfect His light, even though the disbelievers dislike it.
interpretation: The verse portrays the opponents of the message as men trying to blow out a flame with their breath: their opposition is futile, because the divine light is not something a human voice or scheme can extinguish. The image of "mouths" suggests that their hostility is mere empty speech, slander and propaganda, lacking any real power. God's declaration that He will complete His light affirms that the truth He sends will reach its full realization regardless of the resentment of those who reject it, so the believer is reassured that ultimate victory belongs to God's purpose rather than to the arrogance of the disbelievers.

translation: He it is who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, that He may make it prevail over all religion, even though the polytheists dislike it.
interpretation: The verse presents the mission of the Messenger as a divinely willed combination of guidance ('huda', the knowledge that illuminates the path) and the religion of truth ('din al-haqq', the practice that embodies it in action). Its promise that this religion will prevail over all other systems is best understood as a prophecy of the triumph of truth through argument, moral supremacy, and the eventual dominance of its principles, not merely as a claim of political conquest. The closing clause, 'even though the polytheists dislike it,' reminds the believers that opposition is a natural response to truth, and that their confidence should rest on God's decree rather than on the approval of those who reject it.

translation: O you who have believed, shall I direct you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?
interpretation: The verse presents faith and striving in God's cause as a profitable exchange, framing the believer's life as a commerce with God in which the true gain is deliverance from the painful torment of the Hereafter. It invites the believer to see worldly sacrifice, such as wealth and effort, not as loss but as the price of salvation, and it reminds that the most valuable trade is the one that secures the soul's safety on the Day of Reckoning.

translation: You believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives. That is better for you, if you only knew.
interpretation: The verse presents faith and striving as a single, inseparable commitment: true belief in Allah and His Messenger is proven through active sacrifice of one's property and self in the path of Allah. It teaches that the believer's wealth and life are not ends in themselves but trusts to be spent for the sake of the faith, and that this exchange is genuinely the best course for the one who has knowledge of its worth. The conditional closing, 'if you only knew,' turns the reader inward, suggesting that the reluctance to give is rooted in ignorance of what is truly gained through sacrifice in God's way.

translation: He will forgive you your sins and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence. That is the great achievement.
interpretation: The verse presents a sequence of divine reward that begins with forgiveness and only then arrives at entry into paradise, suggesting that the removal of sin is the foundation upon which every blessing rests. The pleasant dwellings in Eden are not merely a physical reward but a state of settled security and peace that stands in contrast to the restlessness of worldly life. By calling this success 'the great achievement' (al-fawz al-azim), the verse redefines true victory: not worldly gain or dominance, but nearness to God and lasting reward. The verse invites the believer to measure their striving against this final goal, and to see that repentance and righteous deeds are the path toward it.

translation: And another [favor] that you love: victory from Allah and an imminent conquest. So give good tidings to the believers.
interpretation: The verse points to a twofold promise: beyond the immediate blessings the believers desire, there is a further gift they cherish, namely divine help that brings decisive success and a near opening. Its placement at the close of Surah As-Saff, after the call to be steadfast like the supporters of Jesus, shows that such victory is not merely a worldly achievement but the fruit of sincere faith and struggle in God's cause. The command to give glad tidings reminds the believer that hope rests on Allah's support, and that the reward of perseverance is both certain and near at hand.

translation: O you who have believed, be helpers of Allah, as when Jesus, the son of Mary, said to the disciples, "Who will be my helpers for Allah?" The disciples said, "We will be helpers of Allah." So a group of the Children of Israel believed, and a group disbelieved. Then We supported those who believed against their enemy, and they became dominant.
interpretation: The verse calls believers to actively take up the cause of God, not merely to profess faith, by drawing a direct parallel with the disciples of Jesus who answered his call to help God's cause. Their willingness to respond exposed a division between belief and disbelief even among the same community, showing that faith is proven by readiness to stand with the truth when it is challenged. The promise that God strengthened the believers against their enemy and granted them victory is tied to this readiness: divine support follows sincere commitment, and the believers' ascendancy is the outcome of their standing firm in the face of opposition rather than a matter of mere numbers or worldly power.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, the Sovereign, the Pure, the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse opens by ordering all creation under one truth: everything in the heavens and the earth, conscious or not in the manner we know, turns toward its Creator in praise and declares Him free of every deficiency. The four names that follow each carry a distinct meaning that explains why this glorification is due. He is the Sovereign (al-Malik), so dominion belongs to Him alone and no created thing rules independently; He is the Pure (al-Quddus), exalted above every imperfection, need, and resemblance to His creation; He is the Almighty (al-Aziz), whose power cannot be overcome; and He is the All-Wise (al-Hakim), whose acts and decrees are always grounded in purpose. The cosmos, by its very existence and order, testifies to these attributes, and the believer is invited to recognize in the orderly motion of the heavens and the earth a continual tasbih that should awaken a corresponding humility, purity of heart, and praise in human beings.

translation: It is He who sent among the unlettered people a messenger from among themselves, reciting to them His verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom, though they were before in clear error.
interpretation: The verse presents the prophetic mission as a divine favor granted to a people who lacked a prior scripture and were in manifest misguidance. Its significance lies in the messenger's origin: he is one of them, so his guidance is intelligible and near to them, and his role is threefold: conveying God's revelation, cleansing the hearts and conduct of his community, and imparting the Book and wisdom. The verse thus binds revelation, moral transformation, and knowledge together, and shows that the transition from ignorance to guidance is itself a blessing that should be recognized with gratitude.

translation: And [He will raise] others among them who have not yet joined them. And He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: The verse, revealed in the context of the Prophet's mission to the unlettered people, points to the universality of the message: the Messenger's mission is not confined to the first generation of his companions but extends to later generations of believers who will join them in faith and in following his guidance, even though they have not yet come into existence at the time of revelation. It reassures the believers that God's plan of guidance is complete and sure, since His might ensures that His purpose is accomplished and His wisdom ensures that every people is brought into the fold in its proper time and manner. Thus the verse binds the community across time into a single body united under one Messenger and one divine guidance.

translation: That is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills, and Allah is the Owner of great bounty.
interpretation: The verse establishes that divine favor is entirely in God's hands and not earned or owed by human effort alone. Its distribution follows His wisdom and will rather than human calculation, so the believer should neither envy others nor presume upon what is given. By tying this bounty to God's boundless greatness, the verse directs the heart away from comparing one's lot with others and toward gratitude and reliance on the One whose generosity has no limit.

translation: The likeness of those who were entrusted with the Torah but did not carry it is like that of a donkey carrying books. Wretched is the example of the people who deny the signs of Allah. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: The verse portrays those who were given the Torah yet failed to act upon it as a donkey burdened with volumes it cannot comprehend: the animal bears the weight of knowledge without gaining any of its benefit. The image targets the gap between possessing scripture and living by its meaning, as the donkey's load is physical while its understanding is absent. The concluding lines make the point sharper, condemning those who reject God's signs as having the worst of examples, and declaring that persistent wrongdoing closes the heart to guidance.

translation: Say, "O you who have become Jews, if you claim that you are allies of God to the exclusion of the rest of mankind, then wish for death, if you are truthful."
interpretation: The verse confronts the Jewish community with the falsity of their claim to a unique closeness to God. If they are sure that the hereafter is theirs alone, then the natural consequence of that certainty should be a longing for death, since whoever is truly confident of reaching God's favor would welcome passing into it. Their reluctance to wish for death exposes the hollowness of their boast, for it reveals an inner awareness of their own deeds and of the accountability that awaits them. The challenge thus works as a test of sincerity: a claim of privileged standing before God must be backed by conviction strong enough to override the ordinary human dread of death, and their failure to meet that test unmasks the claim as mere assertion rather than genuine faith.

translation: And they will never wish for it (death), because of what their hands have sent forward. And Allah is All-Knowing of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Baqarah (2:95), refers to the Jews who claimed that they alone were the friends of Allah in the Hereafter, and who were challenged to wish for death if their claim were true. The verse reveals that their own deeds, the evil they had committed and sent ahead, would prevent them from ever longing for death, because they knew what awaited them. The phrase "what their hands have sent forward" points to the consequences of one's actions being stored up for the Hereafter, a common Qur'anic image of deeds preceding a person. The closing statement that Allah knows the wrongdoers reminds the listener that nothing of their injustice, whether in belief or conduct, is hidden from God, and that their false claims will be exposed.

translation: Say: Indeed, the death from which you flee will surely meet you. Then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the seen, and He will inform you of what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse confronts the human instinct to flee from death, showing that flight is futile because death is an appointed encounter that cannot be escaped, wherever a person seeks refuge. It shifts the focus from the fear of the moment to the ultimate accountability that follows: the return to God, who knows both the hidden and the witnessed realms, and who will reveal the true account of every deed. The message thus calls the believer to live with awareness that life's purpose is measured not by the length of its years but by the righteousness of its actions, since the final disclosure of all deeds is certain.

translation: O you who have believed, when the call is made for prayer on the day of Jumu'ah, hasten to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trade. That is better for you, if you only knew.
interpretation: The verse calls believers to give priority to the remembrance of God over worldly business when the Friday congregational prayer is called. Hastening (sa'y) here is not running but a sincere, purposeful movement of the heart and body toward worship, signaling that the prayer takes precedence over commerce. By singling out trade, the verse reveals that what preoccupies a person's livelihood can become a barrier to their spiritual life, so the believer is taught to measure gain by what it brings in the hereafter. The closing phrase, 'if you only knew,' points to the limits of human judgment: a person may think that continuing to trade is more profitable, yet true benefit lies in obeying God's command and in the blessing that comes from putting Him first.

translation: And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse within the land and seek of Allah's bounty, and remember Allah much so that you may prosper.
interpretation: The verse shows that Islam does not confine a believer's devotion to the mosque alone. Once the sacred obligation is fulfilled, the believer returns to the ordinary affairs of life, pursuing lawful livelihood and earning God's provision through honest work, and in doing so should not let worldly activity draw them away from God. The command to remember Allah abundantly is the thread that ties the two together: the believer's worship in the prayer and the believer's labour in the marketplace and the land are meant to be one continuous state of consciousness of God. Success (falah) is thus presented as the fruit of balancing economic striving with constant dhikr, so that the rhythm of prayer structures the day and the heart remains anchored in remembrance even while engaged in the pursuit of sustenance.

translation: And when they see a trade or a diversion, they rush toward it and leave you standing. Say: What is with Allah is better than diversion and than trade, and Allah is the best of providers.
interpretation: The verse, revealed concerning the people who abandoned the Prophet during the Friday sermon when a caravan arrived with merchandise and they scattered to it, exposes a grave disorder of the heart in which worldly gain and passing amusement pull the believer away from the remembrance and presence of God at the very moment of His worship. The image of being left standing is a sharp rebuke: the one who speaks the truth is left alone while the crowd chases what glitters and vanishes. The divine reply reorients the scale of value, teaching that whatever is with God, in reward, nearness, and lasting good, far outweighs every profit and pleasure of this world, and that true sustenance is from Allah, so seeking provision must never be placed above obedience to Him. It is a call to order one's priorities so that livelihood serves faith rather than replacing it.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. When the hypocrites come to you, they say, "We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah." Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger, and Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars.
interpretation: The verse exposes the gap between outward profession and inward reality. The hypocrites' oath of testimony is a performance meant to secure safety and acceptance among the believers, yet their words are contradicted by their hearts, which is why the verse immediately sets divine knowledge against their claim: God knows the truth of the Prophet's mission, and God Himself testifies to the hypocrites' lying. The lesson is that a faith confirmed only by the tongue carries no weight before God, and that the believer should look beyond eloquent declarations to the sincerity behind them. It also consoles the Prophet, showing that his mission rests on God's own witness rather than on the approval of those who merely pretend to accept it.

translation: They have taken their oaths as a shield, and so they have averted [people] from the way of Allah. Indeed, evil is what they have been doing.
interpretation: The verse exposes a hypocritical strategy in which people repeatedly swear oaths to protect themselves from accountability and suspicion, using their false sincerity as a shield behind which they can obstruct others from the path of God. The oaths serve both as concealment of their true inner state and as a tool for deflecting scrutiny, so that their outward claims of faith become the very means by which they lead others astray. The closing statement judges their conduct as evil, indicating that the gap between their professed words and their actual deeds is itself a grave moral failing, and that the true measure of a person is found in what they do rather than in the oaths they swear.

translation: That is because they believed, then disbelieved, so their hearts were sealed, and so they do not understand.
interpretation: The verse identifies a cause-and-effect sequence in the spiritual condition of a certain group: their initial faith followed by deliberate rejection was not merely a passing lapse but a turning away that hardened their hearts. Each successive act of disbelief closes the heart further, so that the capacity to grasp truth, which is the very purpose of understanding, is gradually lost. The sealing of the heart is thus presented not as an arbitrary decree that precedes their choice, but as the consequence of their own repeated refusal, and it serves as a warning that persistent rejection of guidance can progressively deprive a person of the faculty needed to recognize it.

translation: When you see them, their physical forms impress you, and when they speak you listen to their words. They are like propped-up pieces of timber. They think every cry is aimed against them. They are the enemy, so beware of them. May Allah destroy them; how are they deluded away from the truth?
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites by contrast between outward appearance and inner reality. Their bodies and eloquence attract admiration, yet their hearts are empty of faith, so they resemble hollow timber that stands upright but gives no benefit. Their fear is constant because a guilty conscience sees danger in every sound, which shows that their allegiance is not with the believers. The believers are therefore warned not to be deceived by impressive looks or persuasive speech, and to judge people by their sincerity and actions. The closing curse shows how far they have turned away from the truth despite its clarity.

translation: And when it is said to them, "Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you," they turn their heads away, and you see them turning away while they are arrogant.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrites' refusal of the Prophet's call even when it offers them the very thing they need: his prayer for their forgiveness. Their turning of the head is not merely physical but a sign of inner pride (istikbar) that makes them reject submission to the Messenger, regarding seeking his intercession as beneath them. Their outward posture of self-sufficiency conceals a spiritual disease, and the verse teaches that arrogance is the great barrier between a person and guidance, since it shuts the door to the mercy that is freely offered.

translation: It is the same for them whether you seek forgiveness for them or do not seek forgiveness for them; Allah will never forgive them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: The verse (9:80) teaches that the forgiveness of God is not a matter of the Prophet's intercession but of the inner state of the one who seeks it. Those who have persistently rejected the truth and deliberately chosen hypocrisy and rebellion have closed their own hearts to guidance, so that even the most earnest prayer of the Messenger cannot benefit them. The statement is thus less a decree of arbitrary rejection than a declaration that persistent defiance removes a person from the path by which forgiveness is reached, and it warns believers not to place their hope in the mere intercession of others while neglecting repentance and sincere turning to God.

translation: They are the ones who say, "Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse." But to Allah belong the treasuries of the heavens and the earth, but the hypocrites do not understand.
interpretation: The verse exposes the arrogance and worldly calculation of the hypocrites, who believed that the wealth of the believers was what sustained the Prophet's companions and that withholding it would force them to abandon him. Their words reveal a heart that measures divine provision by human means, forgetting that sustenance rests entirely with Allah, Who alone owns all that is in the heavens and the earth. Their failure lies not in lack of resources but in lack of understanding, for they cannot grasp that true strength and provision belong to God, not to those who hold the purse. The verse thus teaches that spiritual blindness, rooted in hypocrisy, makes a person see power where there is none and see none where God's power is supreme.

translation: They say, "If we return to Medina, the more honorable will surely expel the more humble from it." But honor belongs to Allah, His Messenger, and the believers, but the hypocrites do not know.
interpretation: The verse exposes the arrogance of the hypocrites led by Abdullah ibn Ubayy, who, speaking after the Battle of al-Muraysi' (al-Mustaliq), used the language of rank and lineage to claim that they, the 'honorable,' would drive out the Prophet's emigrant companions, whom they labeled 'humble.' The Qur'an reverses their measure of worth: true honor (al-'izza) is not derived from tribe, wealth, or worldly power but is rooted in God, and it is shared by His Messenger and by those believers who stand with them. The closing remark that the hypocrites do not know points to the core defect of hypocrisy, which is a failure of true understanding, since they mistake worldly prestige for real dignity and thus cannot perceive where honor truly lies.

translation: O you who have believed, let not your wealth or your children divert you from the remembrance of Allah. And whoever does that, then those are the losers.
interpretation: The verse warns believers that attachment to wealth and children, which are among the most natural and beloved things to the human heart, can quietly become a distraction that pulls the heart away from the remembrance of God. The danger lies not in possessing them but in allowing them to occupy the place that belongs to God alone, so that worldly concerns crowd out worship, mindfulness, and obedience. The verse presents such diversion as a real loss, since a person who lets these attachments displace the remembrance of God has exchanged what is lasting for what is fleeting, and so stands among those who have truly lost. It calls for a constant inner vigilance in which family and property are enjoyed as trusts from God rather than treated as ultimate ends.

translation: And spend from what We have provided you, before death comes to one of you and he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me for a brief term so I could give charity and be among the righteous."
interpretation: The verse calls believers to spend in charity from the provision God has granted them while there is still time, before death arrives and closes the opportunity for good deeds. At that moment the person regrets his neglect and begs for a little more time, longing to give in charity and become righteous, but the chance has passed. It is a warning that wealth and life are trusts on loan, and that delaying generosity and righteousness until the last moment leaves a person with only regret.

translation: And Allah will never delay a soul when its term has come. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.
interpretation: The verse affirms that every soul's appointed term (ajal) is fixed with absolute precision by Allah, and when that moment arrives no delay or postponement is possible, whether of death or of the consequences decreed for it. This reminder of the inescapability of the appointed time is paired with the assurance that Allah is fully aware of all deeds, so human beings should be mindful that both their life's limit and their actions are known and recorded by Him. The juxtaposition invites the listener to live with awareness that time is finite and every action will be accounted for.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and to Him belongs the dominion, and to Him belongs all praise, and He is over all things Competent.
interpretation: The verse opens by presenting all of creation as in a state of constant glorification of God, so that existence itself, beyond human speech, testifies to His transcendence and perfection. The movement from the heavens and the earth to the twofold attribution of sovereignty and praise suggests that God's rightful ownership of the cosmos and His being the sole object of praise are inseparable: the one who truly rules is the one who alone deserves to be praised. The closing affirmation of His power over all things anchors this cosmic praise in a reality of absolute capability, inviting the believer to recognize that the order of the universe, which proclaims Him, is grounded in a power that nothing can limit, and to align his own worship with the praise already sounding throughout creation.

translation: It is He who created you, and among you is the disbeliever and among you is the believer. And Allah is Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: The verse establishes that God is the sole Creator of human beings, yet He did not create them all with one fixed disposition: creation is the origin, while belief or disbelief is the outcome of each person's free choice, which is exercised within the framework of that creation. By placing the disbeliever and the believer side by side as both coming from the same Creator, the verse shows that the difference between them is not a difference of origin but of response and conduct. The closing phrase, 'Allah is Seeing of what you do,' ties this freedom to accountability: God perceives every action and intention, so human choice carries moral weight and is to be recognized as a trust for which one will answer.

translation: He created the heavens and the earth in truth, and shaped you and perfected your forms, and to Him is the final return.
interpretation: The verse binds together three great facts about the relationship between the Creator and the human being. The creation of the heavens and the earth 'in truth' indicates that the cosmos is not a idle or meaningless game but an ordered work carrying a purpose, so that the grandeur of the universe itself testifies to a wise and purposeful Maker. Immediately after this cosmic horizon, the verse turns to the human form: God did not merely bring us into existence but gave us shape and made that shape excellent, which invites the believer to recognize that the body and its faculties are a trust and a gift to be used in obedience rather than in corruption. The verse closes with 'to Him is the final return,' so that the beauty of creation and the truth of the universe both find their meaning only in the return to the One who originated them. Thus the reflection on one's own form becomes a reminder of accountability: the one who was shaped in the best form is also the one who will stand before the Lord of that form.

translation: He knows what is in the heavens and the earth, and He knows what you conceal and what you reveal. And Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts.
interpretation: The verse affirms the all-encompassing knowledge of God, which reaches beyond the visible and the hidden alike: nothing in the cosmos escapes Him, and even a person's private intentions and secret inclinations, the deepest contents of the heart, are laid bare before Him. This should lead the believer to sincerity and inward integrity, since human beings may deceive one another, but no concealment can shield anything from the One who knows the innermost thoughts.

translation: Has there not come to you the news of those who disbelieved before you? So they tasted the consequence of their affair, and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse addresses the listeners as a warning drawn from history: the fate of earlier peoples who rejected their messengers is presented as a known report, so that the present audience may reflect and avoid the same denial. The 'taste' of the consequence of their deeds signals that the worldly ruin they suffered was an immediate foretaste of their deeds' outcome, while the painful punishment awaiting them points to a greater and lasting requital in the Hereafter. The rhetorical question draws attention to a truth that is already plainly established, turning history itself into a lesson in the consequences of disbelief.

translation: That is because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs, but they said, 'Shall mere humans guide us?' So they disbelieved and turned away, and Allah was without need, and Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse traces the rejection of prophecy to a specific cause: people refused to accept guidance because it came through a human being like themselves, even though the messengers brought manifest signs. Their objection was not based on evidence but on a sense of pride and a misplaced notion that divine guidance must come in a form that flatters their expectations. The consequence of this stubbornness was disbelief and withdrawal, yet this harms none but themselves, since God is entirely independent of His creatures' faith and worship, and He alone is worthy of all praise. The passage thus teaches that the humanity of the messenger is no obstacle to the truth of his message, and that rejecting clear proof out of arrogance is the root of spiritual loss.

translation: The disbelievers claim that they will never be resurrected. Say, "Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected; then you will surely be informed of what you did. And that is easy for Allah."
interpretation: The verse answers the denial of resurrection with a threefold emphatic affirmation: the Prophet is commanded to swear by his Lord that the dead will be raised, then called to account, so that the reckoning is not separated from the resurrection but follows it directly. The phrase "that is easy for Allah" reframes the matter: what the disbelievers judge impossible is, for the One who originated creation, a trivial act, so their doubt rests on a mistaken measure of divine power rather than on any real difficulty. The verse thus ties together the certainty of the afterlife, the accountability of human deeds, and the absolute power of God.

translation: So believe in Allah and His Messenger, and in the light which We have sent down. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.
interpretation: The verse calls the people directly to faith that unites belief in Allah with belief in His Messenger and in the divine light revealed through him, namely the Qur'an that guides out of darkness into clarity. It joins the command to believe with a reminder of divine knowledge, since Allah sees and knows every deed, so that faith is not merely a claim on the tongue but a sincere commitment that will be measured by what people actually do.

translation: The Day He gathers you for the Day of Gathering - that is the Day of Mutual Loss and Gain. And whoever believes in God and does righteous deeds, He will remove from him his misdeeds and admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great triumph.
interpretation: The verse frames the Day of Judgment as a day named for mutual gathering and for the reckoning of gain and loss, so that human beings are made to see their lives as a trade whose results become manifest only when all are assembled before God. The believer who joins faith to righteous action is shown to be the one who truly profits, for the removal of misdeeds and the gift of everlasting gardens reveal that the real measure of success lies not in worldly accumulation but in the state of the soul at the moment of gathering. The word "al-fawz" pointing to a triumph that is both complete and lasting suggests that the ultimate victory is an enduring nearness and mercy that no loss can ever reverse.

translation: But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs—those are the companions of the Fire, abiding eternally therein. And wretched is the destination.
interpretation: The verse draws a clear line between faith and denial: rejecting God's signs, whether the revealed verses or the signs woven into creation, is not merely an intellectual error but a moral and spiritual choice with consequences. Its concluding phrase, 'wretched is the destination,' emphasizes that the final outcome is not a matter of chance but the natural result of one's chosen path. The eternal abiding in the Fire signals the gravity of persistent denial, while also inviting the listener to reflect on their own response to the signs of God before that destination is reached.

translation: No calamity strikes except by the permission of Allah. And whoever believes in Allah - He guides his heart. And Allah is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: This verse teaches that every misfortune that befalls a person occurs only by the leave and decree of Allah, so nothing in the created order escapes His will and knowledge. Yet this truth is not meant to produce despair but steadfast faith: the one who believes in Allah and accepts that what reaches him was destined is granted inner guidance, so that his heart is settled, patient, and at peace amid hardship. Thus belief in divine decree becomes a source of tranquility, since the believer recognizes that the trial is known to a Lord who is All-Knowing and who guides the heart of the sincere believer.

translation: And obey Allah and obey the Messenger. But if you turn away, then the duty of Our Messenger is only to convey clearly.
interpretation: The verse binds faith to obedience: submission to Allah is inseparable from obedience to His Messenger, since the Messenger's guidance is the channel through which Allah's command reaches people. It then clarifies the limits of the Messenger's role. If people turn away, the responsibility does not fall on the Messenger to compel belief; his duty is only to deliver the message in a plain and unmistakable way. Accountability for rejection rests with the one who refuses, while the prophetic mission is fulfilled by clear communication alone.

translation: Allah — there is no deity except Him. So upon Allah let the believers rely.
interpretation: The verse grounds tawakkul, complete reliance upon God, in the foundation of tawhid: since there is no true deity beside Him, trust cannot rightly be placed in any created power, means, or person as though they held independent authority. Because all affairs belong to the One God alone, the believer's inner security comes from entrusting outcomes to Him after doing what is within one's own power. Reliance is thus not passivity but a heart oriented toward the sole Lord, whose sovereignty makes trust in Him both reasonable and complete.

translation: O you who have believed, indeed among your spouses and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them. But if you pardon and overlook and forgive, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse warns believers that family ties, though dear, can sometimes pull a person away from obedience to Allah, from his duties, or from good conduct, so they must be wary of letting spouses and children become obstacles to faith. Yet it immediately opens the door to mercy: when a believer responds to such family failings with pardon, forbearance, and forgiveness rather than anger or retaliation, he imitates Allah's own attributes, and he is assured of Allah's forgiveness and mercy. The lesson is a balance between vigilance over one's loved ones and the generous, merciful heart that family life requires.

translation: Your wealth and your children are only a trial, and with Allah is a great reward.
interpretation: The verse reminds the believer that wealth and children, though dear and sources of joy, are a test that reveals the heart's true priorities. Because they can divert a person from obedience to Allah and from generosity and remembrance, one should hold them as entrusted gifts rather than ultimate goals. The true and lasting recompense lies with Allah, so the wise believer measures success by what is pleasing to Him, not by accumulation of possessions or progeny.

translation: So fear Allah as much as you are able, and listen and obey, and spend in charity; it is better for yourselves. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful.
interpretation: The verse binds piety to human capacity: God does not demand the impossible, but asks for sincere, sustained effort within one's limits. Hearing and obeying are presented as the inner posture of taqwa, and generosity is shown to be a benefit returning to the giver's own soul rather than a loss. The deepest obstacle is the soul's own avarice (shuh), and freedom from it, not wealth itself, is what marks true success.

translation: If you lend Allah a goodly loan, He will multiply it for you and forgive you. And Allah is Appreciative and Forbearing.
interpretation: The verse presents charity given in the path of God as a loan made to Him, an image that honors the believer's giving and assures that nothing spent sincerely is lost. Its reward is not merely returned but multiplied, and it is joined to forgiveness of sins, showing that generosity both increases one's gain and cleanses the heart. The closing names, Appreciative (Shakur) and Forbearing (Halim), reveal that God rewards even small sacrifices generously and is patient with human shortcomings, inviting the believer to give with sincerity and trust in His mercy.

translation: Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse presents God's knowledge as encompassing both what lies hidden from human perception (al-ghayb), such as the realities of the unseen world, the future, and the inner thoughts of hearts, and what is manifest and observable (al-shahada). Placing these two domains together affirms that nothing escapes divine knowledge, so the believer is to live with constant awareness that the Lord sees both outward conduct and inward intention. The pairing of 'al-Aziz' (the Mighty, whose power is irresistible) with 'al-Hakim' (the All-Wise, who acts with perfect purpose) then links this comprehensive knowledge to sovereign power and wise governance: the One who knows all also has the ability to enforce His will, and His decisions are never arbitrary but rooted in wisdom. The interpretive lesson is that human humility should follow from this, since knowledge of the limits of our own perception should lead to trust in the perfect knowledge and justice of God.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them at their prescribed waiting period, and count the waiting period carefully, and be mindful of God, your Lord. Do not expel them from their homes, nor should they leave, unless they commit a clear immorality. These are the limits set by God, and whoever transgresses the limits of God has wronged himself. You do not know; perhaps God will bring about after that some new circumstance.
interpretation: The verse addresses the Prophet as a representative of the community, establishing that divorce must be carried out in a manner that respects the prescribed waiting period (iddah), so that the couple has a genuine opportunity for reconsideration and reconciliation, and so that the rights of the woman are protected. The command to count the waiting period precisely and to fear God reflects the seriousness of marriage dissolution as more than a personal impulse, requiring discipline and accountability before God. The prohibition against expelling divorced women from their homes during this period safeguards their dignity, security, and the possibility of reunion, with the exception of a clear grave misconduct. The closing reflection that one does not know what God may bring about afterward points to the hope that a separation may be followed by reconciliation, so that hasty decisions are discouraged and patience and trust in God's providence are encouraged.

translation: So when they have reached their prescribed term, either retain them in kindness or part from them in kindness, and call to witness two just men from among you, and establish the testimony for the sake of Allah. That is what is admonished to whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day. And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out.
interpretation: The verse addresses the conclusion of the waiting period of a divorced woman and sets the ethical standard for what follows: she must be either taken back with honorable intent, not for harm, or released with dignity and generosity, never left suspended or wronged. The command to call two upright witnesses and to give testimony sincerely for Allah's sake establishes that the divorce or reconciliation be transparent and protected from dispute, injustice, or concealment. The closing reminder ties this legal guidance to faith, indicating that only one who truly believes in God and the Last Day will heed it, and promises that piety itself becomes the means by which God opens a path out of hardship and confusion for the believer.

translation: And He provides for him from where he does not expect. And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him. Indeed, Allah will accomplish His purpose. Certainly, Allah has set a decree for everything.
interpretation: The verse teaches that true reliance upon Allah (tawakkul) brings a sufficiency that surpasses human calculation, since provision and relief often come through channels the believer never anticipated. Allah's sufficiency is not merely material but encompasses protection and guidance for the one who entrusts his affairs to Him. The closing affirmations that Allah fulfills His command and has measured every thing in precise proportion call the believer to balance firm trust with confidence that outcomes are governed by a perfect divine measure, freeing the heart from anxiety about what lies beyond its control while still encouraging faithful effort.

translation: And those of your women who have despaired of menstruation - if you are in doubt, then their waiting period is three months, and [likewise for] those who have not menstruated. And for those who are pregnant, their term is until they give birth. And whoever fears Allah - He will make for him of his matter ease.
interpretation: The verse sets out the waiting period ('iddah) for women whose menstrual cycle has ceased or never began, fixing it at three months when doubt arises about their status, and for pregnant women it extends until delivery, showing that the wisdom of the divine law lies in determining lineage and allowing reflection on the marriage bond. It closes by linking obedience to God's commands with the granting of facility in one's affairs, indicating that adherence to divine limits brings ease rather than hardship.

translation: That is the command of Allah which He has sent down to you. And whoever fears Allah, He will remove from him his misdeeds and enlarge for him his reward.
interpretation: The verse, which follows the discussion of divorce and the waiting period in Surah At-Talaq, presents the divine legislation as a mercy sent down from Allah, not a burden imposed arbitrarily. It links obedience to these commands with taqwa, a conscious awareness of God that guides a believer to act rightly. The promise is twofold: a person who lives in this God-consciousness has his shortcomings covered and his sins erased, and he receives a great reward that exceeds what his deeds alone would seem to merit. The lesson is that adherence to Allah's law is itself the path to forgiveness and abundant grace, so that the rules of life become a means of nearness to God rather than mere restriction.

translation: Lodge them where you dwell, according to your means, and do not harm them so as to constrict them. And if they are pregnant, then spend on them until they deliver their burden. And if they nurse for you, then give them their payment, and confer among yourselves in a reasonable manner. But if you disagree, then another woman may nurse for him.
interpretation: The verse establishes that a divorced woman's right to lodging and maintenance continues during her waiting period and, if pregnant, until she gives birth, so that the husband's responsibility is not abandoned at separation. It forbids using housing as a means of pressure or harassment to force her to give up her rights or to leave. It then extends the principle of fair dealing to the nursing of the child: the mother who nurses is to be compensated fairly, and the parents should consult together with kindness and good sense. Where they cannot agree, the child's welfare is not to be sacrificed, and another nurse may be engaged, showing that the child's need takes precedence over rigid disputes between the parents.

translation: Let the one of wide means spend from his wealth, and whoever has his provision restricted, let him spend from what Allah has given him. Allah does not burden a soul beyond what He has given it. Allah will bring about ease after hardship.
interpretation: The verse establishes a principle of proportionate charity: each person is called to spend according to what God has granted him, so that the wealthy give generously from their abundance and the less affluent are not pressed beyond their capacity. Divine justice is manifest in that obligation is measured by ability, and the believer is assured that hardship is not permanent, for God will open a way of relief after difficulty. Thus the verse unites generosity, contentment with one's lot, and trust in God's providence.

translation: And how many a town rebelled against the command of its Lord and His messengers, so We called it to a severe account and punished it with a terrible punishment.
interpretation: The verse warns that nations which arrogantly defied God's command and rejected His messengers were not left unaccountable. Their rebellion was met with a stern reckoning in this life, so that their fate becomes a lesson that divine justice is exact and inescapable, and that persistent arrogance against revelation brings its own consequences, drawing the listener to humility and obedience.

translation: So she tasted the evil consequence of her affair, and the outcome of her affair was loss and ruin.
interpretation: The verse describes the fate of one who chooses a path of defiance and disobedience: the act that seemed to promise gain ends in the bitter result of its own making. The word 'wabal' (evil consequence) points to a burden that the person herself carries, and 'khusran' (loss) signals that what was sought as advantage became total ruin. The verse teaches that every deed carries its own outcome, and that turning away from what is right, however attractive it appears at first, leads inevitably to a loss that no worldly gain can compensate for.

translation: Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment. So fear Allah, O people of understanding who have believed. Allah has indeed sent down to you a reminder.
interpretation: The verse links divine warning with a call to conscientiousness: after announcing a severe punishment prepared for those who oppose the truth, it addresses the people of sound intellect and faith, urging them to guard themselves through taqwa. The sending down of a 'reminder' (dhikr) shows that the reason for this obligation is not left unexplained; the revelation itself is the means by which the believer's intellect is awakened and their heart kept mindful of God. Thus true understanding is shown to be inseparable from faith and from heeding the reminder God has given, since it is the reminder that turns reason toward reverence and action.

translation: A Messenger reciting to you the clear revelations of Allah, that he may bring out those who believe and do righteous deeds from darknesses into light. And whoever believes in Allah and does righteous work - He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. Allah has certainly perfected for him a provision.
interpretation: The verse presents the Prophet's mission as a movement of rescue from spiritual darkness into light: faith joined with righteous action is the means by which a person is brought out of ignorance, confusion and moral blindness into guidance and knowledge of God. The reward promised to the believers, eternal gardens and a generous provision, is therefore not merely a future recompense but the fulfilment of a life already lived in the light of revelation, where belief in God and good conduct are inseparable.

translation: God is the One who created seven heavens and of the earth the like of them; His command descends among them, that you may know that God is capable of everything, and that God has encompassed all things in knowledge.
interpretation: The verse points to the vast, layered order of creation, where the heavens and the earth are bound together by a single divine command that continually descends through them. By naming God's power over all things and His encompassing knowledge, it invites the believer to reflect on the cosmos as a sign pointing to the Creator's sovereignty and omniscience, so that recognition of these attributes leads to awe, trust, and a deeper understanding of one's dependence on Him.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O Prophet, why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you, seeking the pleasure of your wives? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The verse opens with a gentle address to the Prophet, and its question carries a reproach that is tempered by mercy. The Prophet had made unlawful for himself something God had permitted, apparently out of a desire to please his wives. The verse teaches that even a righteous leader must not place his personal inclinations or the approval of those close to him above what God has made lawful, and that a sincere sense of accountability should guide his choices. Yet the closing words, 'And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful,' show that God's pardon follows a sincere lapse. The passage thus balances the seriousness of God's limits with the reassurance that repentance and divine compassion remain open, especially for those closest to God's guidance.

translation: Allah has already prescribed for you the dissolution of your oaths. And Allah is your Protector, and He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.
interpretation: The verse reveals that Allah, out of mercy and wisdom, has provided a way for believers to release themselves from oaths they have sworn, particularly oaths that prove burdensome or that were made hastily, by means of expiation (kaffarah) as detailed in the preceding verses of Surah At-Tahrim and Surah Al-Ma'idah. Its placement after the account of the Prophet's private matter with his wives highlights that the rules governing human vows are not meant to create hardship, and that the believer should turn to Allah, who is their Mawla, the one who protects, guides, and takes responsibility for them. The closing names, Al-Alim and Al-Hakim, remind the reader that this relief is no arbitrary concession but flows from perfect knowledge of human weakness and perfect wisdom in legislation.

translation: And when the Prophet confided a matter to one of his wives, and when she divulged it, and Allah informed him of it, he made known part of it and ignored part. So when he informed her of that, she said, "Who told you this?" He said, "I was informed by the All-Knowing, All-Aware."
interpretation: The verse recalls a domestic incident within the Prophet's household in which a confidence entrusted to one wife was disclosed to another, and it teaches that Allah makes known to His Messenger what is hidden from others, so that concealed betrayals cannot escape divine knowledge. The Prophet's partial disclosure and partial silence show a gentle, measured dignity that avoids humiliating those involved, while the wife's question underscores how the believers should be mindful that their secrets and words are never fully hidden from the One who knows all. The closing reply, attributing the knowledge to the All-Knowing, All-Aware, directs the reader's attention from the household quarrel to the reality of God's comprehensive knowledge.

translation: If you two repent to Allah, then your hearts have indeed inclined (toward that). But if you back each other up against him, then indeed Allah is his protector, and Gabriel and the righteous among the believers, and the angels after that are supporters.
interpretation: The verse addresses the wives of the Prophet (peace be upon him) who had conspired together and caused him distress. It opens with a gentle call to repentance, reminding them that their hearts had deviated from what is right, and that turning back to God is the proper course. It then warns that if they persist in colluding against the Prophet, they should know that he has a powerful array of protectors: God Himself, the angel Gabriel, the righteous believers, and the angels who stand behind him as supporters. The verse thus combines mercy and a clear warning, showing that the Prophet's honor is guarded by God and that opposing him through collusion is ultimately futile.

translation: It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you: submissive, faithful, devoutly obedient, repentant, worshipful, traveling (in devotion), previously married and virgins.
interpretation: The verse is spoken within the context of the Prophet's household, warning his wives that if they cause him to separate from them, God can replace them with better spouses. It establishes that the worth of a believing woman lies in her faith, submission to God, repentance, and devotion, rather than in her position or lineage. By listing both previously married women and virgins, it shows that God's favor is not limited to a single category, and it serves as a reminder to the wives of the Prophet to hold fast to righteousness and obedience so they do not lose their honored station.

translation: O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones; over it are angels, harsh and strong, who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded.
interpretation: The verse directs believers first to a personal and familial responsibility: faith is not merely a private profession but a duty to shield oneself and those under one's care from the consequences of disobedience. By describing the Fire's fuel as people and stones, it conveys the gravity of that end and the seriousness of the matter, while the angels set over it, unbending and mighty yet perfectly obedient, present an image of absolute submission to God's command that the believer is called to emulate. The household is thus made the first sphere of moral and spiritual accountability, where guidance, instruction, and example become acts of mercy as well as obligations.

translation: O you who have disbelieved, do not make excuses today. You are only being repaid for what you used to do.
interpretation: The verse speaks to the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, when excuses will no longer benefit them because the account is final and transparent. Its force lies in closing the door on pleading: a person's deeds are the sole basis of recompense, so the moment to act was in the world, and the reckoning now simply reflects what they chose and practiced. It is a call to self-accountability in this life, since in the Hereafter the truth of one's conduct will be laid bare beyond any possibility of denial or justification.

translation: O you who have believed, repent to God with sincere repentance. Perhaps your Lord will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow, on the Day God will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believed with him. Their light will run before them and on their right hands; they will say, "Our Lord, perfect for us our light and forgive us. Indeed, You are over all things Competent."
interpretation: The verse presents sincere repentance (tawbah nasuh) as a turning back to God that is genuine, complete, and leaves no inclination to return to sin, and it links this inner turning to the hope of forgiveness and entry into paradise. By placing the Prophet and his companions as those whom God will not disgrace, it shows that faithful believers who follow the Prophet will be honored on the Day of Judgment, their light guiding them across the Sirat. Their prayer for their light to be perfected reveals that the believer's need is ongoing: even those granted light must continually seek God's completion of it and His forgiveness, acknowledging their dependence on His power over all things.

translation: O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be stern with them. Their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet to confront both open disbelievers and hidden hypocrites with firmness, but the firmness it asks for is principled resolve rather than cruelty. The distinction is significant: the hypocrites are named alongside the disbelievers because their danger lies in concealment, since they wear the outward appearance of the community while undermining it from within, so the verse calls for steadfastness toward those who corrupt trust from the inside. The phrase 'be stern with them' (wa-ghluz 'alayhim) is best understood as a refusal to flatter, compromise, or grant false legitimacy to those who reject the truth or betray it, while the Prophet's own mercy toward believers and his gentleness in his personal dealings remain intact, as other verses describe. The closing reference to their refuge in Hell and the wretchedness of their final destination serves to make clear that the consequences of persistent rejection and hypocrisy are real, which gives the community a sober perspective on where such inner and outer opposition leads.

translation: God presents an example to those who disbelieve: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot. They were under two of Our righteous servants, but they betrayed them, so the two men could not avail them at all against God. And it was said, "Enter the Fire with those who enter."
interpretation: The verse shows that closeness to a prophet by family ties or social bond does not save a person; salvation depends on one's own faith and righteousness. Noah and Lot were righteous messengers, yet their wives, by their disbelief and betrayal (understood by classical commentators as opposing their husbands' message and aiding its opponents), were not protected. Thus God sets before the disbelievers the lesson that each soul bears responsibility for its own deeds, and that the mere relationship to the righteous, even to the best of men, cannot shield one from the consequences of rejecting faith.

translation: And Allah presents an example for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh, when she said, "My Lord, build for me a house with You in Paradise, and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds, and save me from the wrongdoing people."
interpretation: The verse sets the wife of Pharaoh before the believers as a model of faith that rises above circumstance. Though she lived under the most tyrannical ruler of her time, in a household of oppression and disbelief, her faith remained her own and was not determined by the people around her. Her supplication shows that true belief turns the heart toward its Lord and seeks refuge in Him alone, and that a believer's nearness to Allah is measured by sincerity and righteousness rather than by worldly status or family ties. By placing her among the examples offered to the believers, the verse teaches that no environment, however corrupt or powerful, can prevent a sincere soul from turning to God and seeking His protection and reward.

translation: And Mary, daughter of 'Imran, who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our spirit, and she believed in the words of her Lord and His scriptures, and she was among the devoutly obedient.
interpretation: The verse presents Mary as a model of purity and faith. Her guarding of her chastity is joined to her full acceptance of God's words and scriptures and her steadfast devotion, showing that true piety unites inner purity, sincere belief, and obedience. The breathing of the spirit into her marks the honor God bestowed upon her, and her name is placed in a sequence of virtues that elevates her as an exemplar for believers, especially for the women of the community. Her story thus teaches that closeness to God rests on integrity of heart and action, not on lineage or circumstance alone.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion, and He is over all things competent.
interpretation: The verse opens by declaring the blessedness (tabarak) of Allah, a word that signals an exalted, abundant and unceasing goodness that belongs to Him alone. The phrase 'in whose hand is the dominion' places all sovereignty, both visible and unseen, under His direct control, so that no authority in the heavens or on earth stands independent of Him. The closing words 'and He is over all things competent' link this sovereignty to absolute power: whatever He wills to create, sustain, change or end is within His capacity. The believer is thereby led to recognize that true kingship belongs to God, that human rulers hold only what He grants, and that turning to Him in worship and reliance is the fitting response to such unlimited power and majesty.

translation: He who created death and life that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed. And He is the Exalted in Might, the Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse places the entire arc of human existence, from death to life, within a purposeful divine design whose aim is moral testing rather than mere existence. By naming death as a created thing alongside life, it reframes mortality not as a meaningless end but as a deliberate boundary that gives every moment its weight, since the measure set is excellence of deed rather than quantity of days or worldly possession. The closing names pair God's might with His forgiveness, suggesting that the one who sets the test is both able to hold humanity accountable and merciful toward those who stumble, so that the call to act well is joined with the hope of pardon for shortcomings along the way.

translation: He who created seven heavens in layers. You see no discrepancy in the creation of the Most Merciful. So return your gaze; do you see any flaw?
interpretation: The verse invites the reader to contemplate the cosmos as a perfectly ordered whole. The heavens are arranged in stacked, harmonious layers, and the repeated call to look again shows that careful, repeated observation only confirms the absence of any disorder or gap. The perfection of creation is thus presented as evidence of its divine origin, and the attentive observer is led from the visible order of the sky to recognition of the Merciful Creator behind it.

translation: Then return your gaze twice; your gaze will come back to you humbled and weary.
interpretation: The verse invites the reader to look again and again at the created order of the heavens, and to find in that repeated scrutiny no flaw, no crack, no disorder. Each return of the gaze meets only a failing sight, which comes back defeated and exhausted, unable to find any imperfection in the perfect harmony of God's creation. The image turns the act of observation itself into a witness: the more honestly human reason examines the cosmos, the more it is brought back to humility before its flawless design and its Maker.

translation: And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps, and made them as missiles against the devils, and We have prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze.
interpretation: The verse presents the lower heaven as beautified by celestial lights, a sign of divine order and majesty that is visible to all who look up. Yet these same lights serve a second function: they guard the heavens against the rebellious devils who try to eavesdrop on the higher realm, so that beauty and protection are joined in one creation. The closing phrase turns from the cosmic scene to the fate of those who persist in rebellion, reminding the reader that the ordered universe is also a witness to accountability, and that the Blaze awaits those who reject the truth.

translation: And for those who disbelieve in their Lord is the punishment of Hell, and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: The verse closes the portion that contrasts the fate of the disbelievers with the reward of the believers by fixing the consequence of rejecting one's Lord: a punishment of Hellfire that is not merely a place but a final outcome. The phrase 'wretched is the destination' (wa-bi'sa al-masir) is a deliberate judgment on the end they have chosen for themselves, since disbelief in the Lord who created and sustains them severs a person from the only source of true refuge. The verse thus teaches that belief in the Lord is not a neutral matter of opinion but the axis on which a person's eternal destiny turns, and it calls the listener to reflect on where their own choices are leading.

translation: When they are cast into it, they will hear from it a roaring inhalation, while it boils up and surges.
interpretation: The verse portrays Hell as a living, perceptible force: its groaning intake of breath and its violent seething show that the fire is not inert but actively responsive to the damned, so that the terror of the scene is conveyed through sound and motion before the torment itself is described. The imagery of a boiling, surging fire is meant to awaken the listener's awareness that the consequences of denial are vivid and inescapable, urging reflection on one's own conduct in this world.

translation: It nearly bursts apart from rage. Every time a group is thrown into it, its keepers will ask them, "Did no warner come to you?"
interpretation: The verse portrays Hell as a living, enraged entity, so intense is its fury against the disbelievers that it seems ready to burst open, and this image conveys the terrifying reality of divine justice. The questioning by its keepers is not a request for information but a rhetorical rebuke that exposes the disbelievers' own admission: the messengers had come and they had been warned. Thus the verse underscores that no one will be able to claim ignorance on the Day of Judgment, since the warning was delivered and rejected by their own choice.

translation: They said, "Yes indeed! A warner had come to us, but we denied him and said, 'Allah has not sent down anything. You are only in great error.'"
interpretation: This verse depicts the people of the Fire confessing, when questioned about whether warners were sent to them, that the warning did indeed reach them, yet their confession comes too late to help them. Their rejection was not born of a lack of evidence but of an arrogant refusal to accept the message, which led them to deny revelation altogether and to dismiss the messengers as men in manifest error. The verse reveals a recurring pattern in human response to prophetic guidance: the warning is heard, its bearer is discredited, and the denial of divine revelation becomes a self-chosen blindness.
