interpretation: This short verse, which opens the Surah as-Sajdah context of its era, establishes the divine origin of the Qur'an: it is not human speech or invention but a descent (tanzil) sent down from the Sustainer of all creation. By calling Allah 'Lord of the worlds' (Rabb al-'alamin), the verse links the message to the universal scope of divine lordship, signaling that the guidance it carries is not restricted to one people or time but is addressed to all of existence. The word tanzil, derived from the root meaning to send down gradually, also reflects the manner of revelation, which came in measured stages to the Prophet, and thereby invites the listener to recognize both the authority and the mercy behind the book.

translation: And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings
interpretation: The verse is part of the Qur'an's argument, in Surah Al-Haqqah (69:44-46), that the Prophet could not have invented any part of the revelation. It introduces a hypothetical: were he to attribute false words to God, God would immediately seize him by the right hand and cut off his life-vein. The point is that the divine message's authenticity is guaranteed by the consequence that falls on any forger, and so the Prophet's steadfast delivery of the revelation is itself a sign of its truth.

translation: We would have seized him by the right hand.
interpretation: The seizing by the right hand expresses the decisive and forceful nature of divine retribution. The right hand stands for strength, honor, and authority, so being seized by it signifies that the offender would be taken in full divine power and held fully accountable, with no escape. The verse thereby shows that God's justice is absolute, and that even the Prophet himself would face the same consequence had he fabricated words attributed to God.

translation: Then We would have cut off from him the aorta (jugular vein).
interpretation: The verse, spoken in the context of the Prophet's opponents who were tempted to think of Allah's nearness and knowledge as remote, emphasizes the absolute closeness of God to the human being and the completeness of His power over him. Allah's knowledge of a person's innermost thoughts and his power over the very life-vein within him are shown as far greater than any human relationship. The image of the 'watin' (the vein closest to the heart) conveys that God is nearer to man than man's own jugular vein, so that no secret can hide from Him and no one can escape His reckoning, which should lead the heedless to sincerity, awareness of God, and fear of the consequences of their deeds.

translation: So none of you could withhold him from Us (from punishment), nor could any of you prevent him.
interpretation: The verse, in the context of the surah (al-Haqqah, 69:47), is a declaration that no one among humanity has the power to shield a person from the consequences of their deeds before God. It underscores the absoluteness of divine justice: no kinship, tribal bond, influence, or intercession can stand as a barrier between the wrongdoer and the reckoning that is due. It calls the listener to recognize that accountability is unavoidable and that true protection lies only in one's own righteous conduct and in God's mercy.

translation: And indeed, it is a reminder for the God-conscious.
interpretation: The verse identifies the Qur'an as a source of remembrance and admonition, but it is specifically beneficial for those who are mindful of God (al-muttaqun). Its guidance becomes effective only in hearts that are receptive, humble, and conscious of their accountability before God; for such people the message awakens them to what they already have within their nature, reminding them of their duties and of the truth, whereas those heedless of God gain no real benefit from it. The verse thus links the reception of revelation to the moral disposition of the listener, showing that taqwa is both the fruit of guidance and the condition for receiving it.

translation: And indeed, We know that among you are those who deny (the truth).
interpretation: The verse reveals God's complete knowledge of the hearts and conduct of people, including those who, despite being part of the community addressed, reject the message they have been given. It warns that such denial is not hidden from the One who knows the inner state of every person, and it calls the listener to examine their own response to the truth, since disbelief is ultimately a matter of a person's own choice before a knowing and just Lord.

translation: And indeed, it is a cause of anguish for the disbelievers.
interpretation: The verse refers to the Qur'an itself, or to the revelation it contains, and describes its effect on those who reject it. For the disbelievers, the truth they refuse becomes a source of regret and inner torment, since they see its clarity and the guidance it offers while remaining unwilling to accept it. Their anguish is thus both a consequence of their obstinacy and a sign of the certainty of the message, which stands as a witness against them that they cannot escape, and which will become a deeper sorrow for them on the Day when the consequences of their rejection are revealed.

translation: And indeed, it is the absolute truth of certainty.
interpretation: The verse affirms that what is being described, most likely the Qur'an or the reality of the Hereafter that it announces, is established beyond any doubt. The phrase "haqq al-yaqin" (the truth of certainty) denotes the highest level of certainty, the kind a person reaches through direct, unmediated knowledge rather than mere inference or report. The emphatic construction, with "inna" and the addition of "lahuwa," stresses that the matter is not open to dispute, inviting the listener to hold firm conviction in it and to let that certainty shape their conduct.

translation: So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty.
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet, and by extension every believer, to exalt God through glorification (tasbih) that is done with reverence and awareness of His greatness. To glorify 'the name' of the Lord is to honor and affirm Him in speech and remembrance, recognizing that every attribute of His, including His might, places Him beyond any deficiency or likeness to creation. The command is a call to turn all praise and devotion toward the One whose greatness alone merits absolute submission.

translation: Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim. A questioner asked for a punishment that is certain to befall.
interpretation: The verse presents a skeptic who demands, in mockery and impatience, that the promised punishment be brought at once. The Qur'an does not answer his question in words here. It shows that the threat is real and imminent, and that the one who asks for it does so from heedlessness, not from a sincere wish to know. The phrase 'waqi' (that will surely fall) signals that the punishment is not a matter of debate but a settled reality that will reach those who deny it, so the questioner's challenge reflects his own failure to recognize the consequences of his denial.

translation: For the disbelievers, there is none to repel it.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the punishment promised to those who deny the truth is certain and cannot be turned away by any power, idol, intercessor, or worldly means. Its force lies in the contrast between human arrogance and helplessness: those who rejected revelation will find that no protector or defense can stand between them and what God has decreed, which should move the listener to humility and to seek refuge in God before the reckoning arrives.

translation: From Allah, the Lord of the ascending stairways.
interpretation: The phrase 'dhi al-ma'arij' points to Allah's exalted majesty and to the graded order of the heavens, through which angels and the Spirit ascend to Him. The ascending ways are levels of nearness and dignity, showing that Allah's command descends through a structured order and that all created things return to Him, the Lord of those elevations, in a measure that human reckoning cannot fully grasp.

translation: The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years.
interpretation: The verse points to the vast difference between divine and human measures of time. The 'Day' mentioned is not the ordinary day of our reckoning but a unit of time measured by the Lord's standard, in which the angels and the Spirit rise to Him. Its length of fifty thousand years conveys the immensity of the distance and the gravity of the affairs that are ascended and decreed in it, reminding the believer that human patience and perception of time are limited, while God's command operates beyond them. Scholars have differed on whether this refers to the Day of Judgment, which would be long for disbelievers and light for believers, or to a general expression of the sublimity of God's affairs, and the verse invites reflection on the greatness of the One to whom all things ascend.

translation: So be patient with gracious patience.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Ma'arij 70:5, also echoed in Al-Ma'arij 70:5 context of the disbelievers' mockery) directs the Prophet to bear with beautiful patience, meaning a patience free of complaint, resentment, and haste for vengeance, while leaving the matter of those who deny to God. Its interpretation is that true patience is not mere endurance but a serene trust that entrusts the outcome to God, so the believer endures hardship with dignity, without bitterness, and without self-pity.

translation: Indeed, they see it as far away.
interpretation: The verse describes the disbelievers' perception of the Day of Judgment as something remote and improbable, so they dismiss it and delay in preparing for it. Set against the complete verse, where Allah says 'but We see it as near,' this contrast reflects that what seems distant to human reckoning is near in God's measure of time, so the verse urges heedfulness before the reckoning arrives unexpectedly.

translation: And We see it as near.
interpretation: The verse sets the disbelievers' view of the Day of Judgment, which they regard as far off, against God's view of it as near. Since the Qur'an elsewhere says that a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of your reckoning, the nearness refers to the certainty and inevitability of that Day within God's knowledge, which is not bound by human measures of time. The point is to awaken the listener to the reality of the Hereafter, so that they prepare for it now rather than assuming it is distant.

translation: On the Day when the sky will be like molten brass dregs.
interpretation: The verse depicts the cosmic upheaval of the Day of Judgment, when the sky, which humanity has long seen as firm and stable, will lose its solidity and take on the appearance of murky, molten metal. The image of al-muhl, the dregs of molten ore or oil, conveys both the intense heat and the dark, shapeless disfigurement of the heavens, so that the reader is made to confront the collapse of the visible order and the realization that all that once seemed secure is subject to God's command, whose power alone sustains and transforms creation.

translation: And the mountains will become like wool carded (fluffed) out.
interpretation: The verse describes the mountains, which humanity sees as the most solid and enduring of creation, being reduced on the Day of Judgment to something light and scattered, like tufts of colored wool blown about by the wind. This image conveys the complete collapse of worldly stability and the dissolution of everything that seemed fixed, reminding the listener that all of creation is subject to God's command and that worldly strength offers no permanence before Him.

translation: And no intimate friend will ask about his intimate friend.
interpretation: The verse depicts the Day of Judgment, when the bonds of close friendship and kinship that were so strong in worldly life dissolve under the weight of each person's own accountability. Each soul is absorbed in its own condition and fate, so even the closest companion does not inquire after another out of concern or to offer help. It underscores that on that Day every person stands alone before God, and worldly ties of affection provide no shelter or intercession of their own, which should move the believer to strengthen his bond with God rather than rely on human relationships for salvation.

translation: They will be shown to one another. The guilty one would love to ransom himself from the punishment of that Day with his children
interpretation: The verse portrays the isolation and terror of the Day of Judgment: even the bonds that a person held dearest, such as children, will be of no use. The sinner's wish to offer his own offspring as ransom reveals that every worldly attachment and support will collapse before God's justice, leaving the soul to stand alone and answerable for its own deeds. It is a call to recognize that the only true protection lies in faith and righteous action, which alone can be carried into the Hereafter.

translation: And his companion and his brother
interpretation: This is a fragment of Surah Al-Ma'arij? No—it belongs to Surah Abasa (80:35-36), where the verse reads, "And his mother and his father, and his companion and his children," and the wording here, "وصاحبته وأخيه" ("and his companion and his brother"), appears in Surah Al-Ma'arij (70:11-12) and Surah Abasa (80:34-35) in the context of the Day of Judgment, when a person will wish to ransom himself from the punishment by offering his nearest relatives, including his brother, his wife, and his kin who sheltered him. The interpretation is that on that Day every person will be preoccupied with his own state, so that even the closest bonds of kinship and companionship will fail to offer any help, and each soul will stand alone, accountable for itself."}

translation: And his close kindred who sheltered him
interpretation: The verse refers to the kin who gave a person refuge and protection in his life, a family whose support and shelter he relied upon. It is set within a passage describing the terror of the Day of Judgment, where a person would gladly offer his nearest relations, the ones who once sheltered and protected him, as ransom to be spared that day. The image shows that on that day no worldly bond of family or tribal protection will avail anyone, and each soul will stand alone before its Lord, with only its own deeds to answer for.

translation: And [consider] whoever is on the earth, all of them, and then He delivers him.
interpretation: I cannot match this wording to a verse of the Qur'an, so I cannot give a verified interpretation of it as scripture. Its phrasing resembles Qur'anic passages on God's dominion over all people on earth and His deliverance of those He chooses, such as Yunus 10:103, "thumma nunji rusulana wa-lladhina amanu" ("then We deliver Our messengers and those who believe"). If the phrase is meant as a verse, please give its surah and ayah number so I can interpret the text in its actual context.

translation: No! Indeed, it is the Blazing Fire (Laza).
interpretation: The word "kalla" is a strong rejection and warning, cutting off the false assumptions or boastful attitude of the one being addressed, and it is followed by a stark declaration about the nature of Laza, a fire that seizes and strips away the flesh and the head, so that the verse shifts the listener from heedlessness to a sober awareness of the consequence awaiting the arrogant who turn away from the truth and amass wealth without gratitude.

translation: Stripping away at the scalp and the extremities, a fire that tears off the limbs and the skin of the head (Qur'an 70:16, "a pulling-out for the extremities").
interpretation: The fire is depicted as an active agent that seizes and pulls at the body's outermost parts, the extremities farthest from the heart. Because these parts are the most sensitive and the most visible sign of a person's bodily integrity, the image conveys a punishment that is relentless and intimately felt, reaching every part of the one who deserved it and leaving no part of the person untouched.

translation: Calling to itself the one who turned his back and withdrew.
interpretation: The verse depicts the Hellfire (or the fierce blaze of Hell) as a living force that summons to itself those who in this life turned away from the truth, rejected faith, and withdrew from obedience. The image conveys that the consequences of persistent denial and turning away are not neutral: the fire itself draws the sinner toward his own destruction, as if the very path of rejection leads back to the place it chose. It is a warning that turning one's back on the call of revelation is answered by a summons of its own, one that the person cannot escape.

translation: And he gathered [wealth] and hoarded it up.
interpretation: The phrase describes a person who amassed wealth and then guarded it greedily, storing it away rather than spending it in the way of God or for the benefit of others. The verse, in its context (Surah al-Ma'arij 70:18, which speaks of the one who gathers and hoards), points to the attachment to worldly possessions that blinds a person to his duties and to the reality of accountability. Its message is a warning that wealth kept for its own sake, withheld from charity and gratitude, becomes a burden rather than a means of salvation.

translation: Indeed, mankind was created anxious and impatient.
interpretation: The verse describes an innate disposition in human nature: man was made with a restless, anxious tendency (halu'a), so that when hardship touches him he becomes distressed and impatient, and when good fortune comes he becomes stingy and grasping. This is not a condemnation of the human being as such but a diagnosis of a natural weakness that the believer must discipline through prayer, charity, and steadfastness, which the following verses (70:19–35) go on to present as the remedy.

translation: When evil touches him, he is impatient and distressed.
interpretation: The verse describes the innate human tendency toward anxiety and loss of composure when adversity strikes. Man, in his natural state, is quick to despair and complain when hardship afflicts him, revealing his weakness and dependence. The verse that follows in the chapter (70:20-21) contrasts this with the one who is steadfast in prayer and generous, implying that true faith and remembrance of God are what restore patience and firmness in the face of trials.

translation: And when good touches him, he is withholding (from giving), grudging.
interpretation: The verse portrays the innate tendency of the human being who, when he is granted prosperity or good fortune, becomes stingy and closed-handed, reluctant to spend on others. Its meaning points to a moral weakness: wealth turns his heart toward self-preservation and miserliness, so that he forgets gratitude and the duty to share what God has bestowed upon him. The verse thus invites the believer to examine whether blessings make him more generous or more grasping.

translation: Except those who pray.
interpretation: The exception of the worshippers from the preceding description of humankind's innate restlessness, fear, and greed indicates that the remedy for this human weakness lies in prayer. Prayer is the means by which the soul is steadied and freed from the anxieties that overcome people when misfortune strikes or wealth is granted, and by which a person is raised above the grasping self toward a state of composure and trust in God.

translation: Those who are constant in their prayer.
interpretation: The verse describes the believers who maintain their prayer with unwavering consistency, not merely performing it occasionally or out of habit when convenient. Their constancy reflects a deep inner commitment: prayer is not a ritual confined to a moment, but a continual connection with God that shapes their conduct and orients their whole life. By calling them 'constant' (da'imun), the verse points to perseverance through every condition, including ease and hardship, so that worship becomes the steady foundation of their character rather than an occasional obligation.

translation: And those in whose wealth there is a known right
interpretation: The verse describes believers who recognize that a definite, set portion of their wealth belongs by right to others, namely the beggar and the deprived who ask and those who are in need. This 'known right' is not charity given at whim but an obligation they have fixed and understood, reflecting that their wealth is held in trust from God and that a share of it must reach those who lack. Its being 'known' signifies that it is determined and recognized, which protects the giver from arrogance and the recipient from humiliation.

translation: "For the beggar and the deprived."
interpretation: The phrase comes from Surah Adh-Dhariyat (51:19), where the righteous are described as giving a rightful share of their wealth to those who ask and to those who are deprived. The verse establishes that charity is a recognized obligation owed to the needy, and it highlights two categories: the one who openly asks for help, and the one who, out of dignity or restraint, does not ask and so is often overlooked. By naming the second group, the Qur'an calls believers to seek out the silently poor, to give generously without waiting to be asked, and to recognize that a portion of their wealth belongs to those in need.

translation: And those who believe in the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: This phrase describes the faithful as those whose belief is anchored in the reality of the Day of Recompense, when every soul will be held accountable for its deeds. Faith in the Last Day is not merely an abstract creed but a moral force that shapes conduct, since the certainty of being answered for one's actions before God restrains wrongdoing and motivates sincere righteousness. Its placement alongside other traits of the pious indicates that true belief in the Hereafter is inseparable from practical obedience and social responsibility.

translation: And those who are fearful of the punishment of their Lord.
interpretation: The verse describes the believers who, despite their faith and good deeds, remain in a state of humble awe and anxious caution before God's justice. Their apprehension is not despair but a mature consciousness that no one can claim security from divine accountability, which drives them toward sincerity, vigilance in worship, and avoidance of sin. This fear is itself a form of faith, reflecting a heart that recognizes both God's mercy and His power to punish.

translation: Indeed, the punishment of their Lord is not something to be felt secure from.
interpretation: The verse warns that the retribution of God is not a matter to be taken lightly or assumed safe. Its phrasing, 'ghayru ma'mun' (not to be secure against), conveys that no one can be certain of escaping it, so the believer should never fall into complacency about divine judgment. This sense of fearful awareness is meant to draw the heart toward repentance, sincerity, and constant reverence before God, rather than heedless confidence in one's own status or circumstances.

translation: And those who guard their private parts (from unlawful sexual relations),
interpretation: The verse describes a core trait of the believers: they exercise self-restraint over their sexual desires, confining their intimate conduct to what is lawful, namely within marriage or with one's lawfully owned slaves as the law permits. This guarding of chastity is shown here as a mark of inner discipline and moral integrity, placing the desire for pleasure under the authority of faith and conscience. Because it appears among other praiseworthy qualities in the same passage, it indicates that purity in this domain is inseparable from the wider character of a believer who keeps trusts, honors commitments, and maintains prayer.

translation: Except with their wives or those their right hands possess, for indeed they are not blameworthy.
interpretation: The verse sets out the sole lawful outlets for sexual relations in the context of chastity: marriage to one's spouse, and relations with those whom one's right hand possesses (slaves/concubines, as understood in the classical context). By specifying these as the exception to guarding one's private parts, it establishes a clear boundary: whoever seeks satisfaction beyond these is transgressing, while those who keep within these limits are free from blame. The phrasing 'not blameworthy' emphasizes that the permitted bond removes any culpability, and it underscores that the moral order of the believer rests on restraint from everything outside what God has allowed, a principle that protects family, lineage, and social trust.

translation: But whoever seeks beyond that, it is those who are the transgressors.
interpretation: The verse, which follows the description of the believers who guard their chastity except with their spouses or those their right hands possess, establishes a clear boundary: whoever seeks sexual gratification outside of these lawful bonds has overstepped the limits God set for human desire. The term 'al-'adun' (the transgressors) signals that such a person is not merely committing a particular act but is deliberately exceeding what is permitted, and thereby placing themselves among those who violate divine limits. The verse thus teaches that restraint and lawful conduct are not arbitrary constraints but the marks of those who respect the bounds God has drawn for the preservation of individual dignity, family, and social order.

translation: And those who are faithful to their trusts and their covenants, and who keep them.
interpretation: The verse describes the believers' fidelity in two domains: amanat (trusts entrusted to them, whether material deposits, secrets, or responsibilities of office and family) and 'ahd (solemn commitments made to God and to people). The word ra'un, derived from ri'aya, conveys vigilant guardianship, as a shepherd watches over his flock, so the faithful do not merely avoid betrayal but actively tend and protect what has been placed in their care. Placed among the qualities of the successful believers, this shows that trustworthiness and promise-keeping are not peripheral social manners but integral marks of faith, and that the integrity of a person's word and custody is a direct expression of their inner devotion to God.

translation: And those who stand firm in their testimonies,
interpretation: This phrase describes the believers who are steadfast and upright in bearing witness. Their testimony is not given carelessly, falsely, or for personal gain, but is upheld with integrity, sincerity, and a constant commitment to truth, whether the testimony concerns their own interests, their families, or others. Standing firm in testimony reflects a character rooted in justice and faithfulness to God, Who commands His servants to be witnesses to justice even against themselves or their closest kin.

translation: And those who are constant in their prayers, they guard them carefully.
interpretation: The verse describes the believers who are marked by a steadfast, watchful devotion to their prayers. Their guarding of the prayer (yuhafizuna) goes beyond merely performing it: it means preserving its times, its outward form, its humility and inward presence of heart, and protecting it from neglect or distraction. Because prayer is the pillar that connects the servant to God, the one who guards it is shown to be guarding the whole of his faith, and this constancy is what distinguishes the righteous from the heedless who let prayer slip away.

translation: Those will be in gardens, honored.
interpretation: The verse describes the reward of the righteous in Paradise: they dwell in gardens of bliss, and they are granted honor (ikram) by God and the angels. This honor is not only a state of comfort but a station of dignity that reflects their faithfulness and good deeds in this world, as the Qur'an often links divine honor with piety and nobility of conduct.

translation: So what is wrong with those who disbelieve, hastening towards you with their necks outstretched?
interpretation: The verse portrays the disbelievers' frantic, hurried approach toward the Prophet with a sense of bewilderment, as if they were rushing forward in a state of fixed, anxious attention. The image of 'muhti'in' (hastening with raised heads and fixed gaze) conveys their agitation and eagerness, yet the rhetorical question 'fa-mal' exposes the incoherence of their conduct: they run toward the message they reject, revealing a restless, inwardly unsettled state that contradicts their outward denial.

translation: Looking to the right and to the left, [coming] in groups.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Ma'arij 70:37) depicts the disbelievers rushing in scattered, separate circles around the Prophet ﷺ, mocking him and his message, and heading in different directions to ridicule and distract from the Qur'an. Their 'groups' ('izeen') are gatherings of contemptuous, restless people, immersed in their own vain pursuits, glancing to either side as if seeking escape or amusement, which contrasts with the orderly, unified rows of believers in worship. The imagery thus portrays their scattered hearts and frivolous attitude toward the truth, which is also a warning of their state of disarray on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Does every one of them aspire to enter a Garden of Bliss?
interpretation: The verse is a rebuke directed at the disbelievers who gathered around the Prophet, eager to listen to him yet mocking his message. Their ambition to enter Paradise is presented as absurd, since no one attains it through arrogance or denial of the truth. The question exposes a contradiction in their conduct: they reject the path that leads to the Garden while expecting its reward. Paradise is won through faith, sincerity, and righteous deeds, not through the claims of the proud or the desires of those who turn away from guidance.

translation: Nay! Indeed, We created them from that which they know.
interpretation: The phrase "from that which they know" (مما يعلمون) is understood by many commentators to refer to the humble, known origins of humankind, namely a sperm-drop and a clot of blood, which every person is aware of, so the verse rebukes those who are arrogant about their status or who deny resurrection by reminding them of their lowly beginning. Others read it as pointing to the knowledge humans possess of their own creation, so that their denial is itself unjustified. Thus the verse calls the disbelievers to humility and to reflect on the evidence of their own origin as proof that the One who created them first is capable of bringing them back.

translation: So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests, indeed We are Able (to do so).
interpretation: The verse opens with an oath by God as Lord of the rising and setting points of the sun, which vary across the seasons and throughout the year, pointing to the vast order of creation and God's mastery over it. The oath is followed by the affirmation that God is fully capable, emphasizing that the One who governs these precise cosmic movements is entirely able to carry out what is promised, including the replacement of humanity with others and the resurrection, a theme that runs through the surrounding verses of Surah al-Ma'arij.

translation: Able to replace them with better than them, and We are not to be outdone.
interpretation: The verse affirms God's absolute power to replace those who reject faith and mock the believers with a people better than they are, in obedience and sincerity, so that their arrogance and their refusal do not weaken His plan. Its phrase 'and We are not to be outdone' removes any sense that the disbelievers can escape His reckoning or get ahead of His decree, since no one can outpace or defeat God. It thus combines a warning to the arrogant with reassurance to the believers that God's purpose will be fulfilled regardless of the opposition they face.

translation: So leave them to plunge in their falsehood and play, until they encounter their Day which they are promised.
interpretation: The verse is a directive of disengagement addressed to the Prophet: when the disbelievers persist in their idle immersion in vain talk and mockery of the revelation, he is not to exhaust himself arguing with them but to leave them to their chosen course. The phrase 'yakhudu' evokes wading into confused and empty discourse, while 'yal'abu' describes their heedless, playful indifference to what truly matters. Their indulgence is granted a limited span, ending only when they meet the Day that was promised to them, the day of reckoning, at which point the illusion of their amusement will be stripped away and the consequences of their denial will become undeniable. The verse thus combines consolation for the messenger with a sober warning that worldly distraction is temporary and will be answered by a certain accountability.

translation: On the Day they emerge from the graves rapidly, as if they were hastening toward a marker they were racing to reach.
interpretation: The verse portrays the resurrection as a sudden, compelled emergence rather than a leisurely one. The image of people rushing out 'as if hastening to a idol-stone' (nusub) that they race to reach evokes the disoriented, eager haste of those who once ran to the shrines and altars they venerated in worldly life, now dashing toward a summons they can no longer refuse. It thus contrasts the futility of their former devotions with the undeniable reality of the Day of Judgment, where they come forth in haste, their eyes lowered in humiliation, driven toward a reckoning they had denied.

translation: Their eyes will be humbled, covered with humiliation. That is the Day they were promised.
interpretation: The verse portrays the moment of reckoning as one in which the proud and the heedless lose their composure entirely: eyes that once looked away in arrogance now lower in shame, and the humiliation that they dismissed in this world settles over them visibly and inescapably. The phrase 'the Day they were promised' turns the scene into a fulfilment of warnings they had mocked, teaching that the consequences of denial are not abstract but will be felt as a direct, bodily and emotional reality. The verse thus invites the listener to anticipate that day now, so that humility before God is chosen willingly in this life rather than forced upon the soul in the next.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Indeed, We sent Noah to his people, [saying]: Warn your people before there comes to them a painful punishment.
interpretation: The verse presents the prophetic mission as an act of divine mercy that precedes judgment: Allah does not punish a people before sending them a warner who makes the truth and its consequences clear. Noah's commission is thus a paradigm of the principle that warning is the necessary prelude to accountability, placing upon every messenger the duty to deliver a clear and timely admonition, and upon every people the responsibility to heed it before the reckoning arrives. The phrase 'before there comes to them a painful punishment' also conveys urgency: the purpose of warning is not condemnation but the opening of a window for repentance while it remains available.

translation: He said: "O my people, indeed I am to you a clear warner."
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Noah (peace be upon him) to his people, shows the prophetic mission in its essential form: the messenger does not compel belief but delivers a plain and unmistakable warning. The word "mubin" (clear) indicates that the message has been stated openly, leaving no ambiguity about the consequences of rejecting God's guidance, so that any subsequent refusal rests on the people's own choice. It also reveals the tender relationship of the prophet to his community, addressing them as "my people" even while they stand in denial, and it establishes that the role of the warner is to clarify and deliver, while the responsibility for accepting or rejecting lies with the listeners.

translation: That you should worship Allah and fear Him, and obey me.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the Prophet Nuh (Noah) to his people, reduces the whole of his message to three duties that are bound together. The first, worship of Allah alone, establishes the right object of devotion and turns the heart away from all other powers that people were tempted to serve. The second, taqwa, the watchful fear of Allah that guards a person in private and public, makes worship a living consciousness rather than an empty ritual. The third, obedience to the messenger, shows that devotion to God is expressed through following the one He has sent, so that the prophet's authority is not a rival to God's but the means by which His command reaches mankind. The verse thus teaches that true faith unites belief in God, awareness of accountability to Him, and submission to the guidance He provides through His messengers.

translation: He will forgive you your sins and defer you to a specified term. Indeed, the term of Allah, when it comes, cannot be deferred, if only you knew.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Noah to his people (Surah Nuh 71:4), invites them to seek forgiveness and return to their Lord, promising that obedience brings forgiveness of past sins and an extension of their life to a fixed appointed time. Yet it reminds them that once Allah's appointed term arrives, no delay or postponement is possible, so the wise person hastens to repentance before that moment. The closing phrase, 'if only you knew,' rebukes their heedlessness, pointing out that the knowledge of this truth alone should move them to faith and righteousness.

translation: He said: 'My Lord, I have called my people night and day.'
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Noah (peace be upon him), reveals the depth of his perseverance in prophetic mission. Noah does not merely call his people once or at convenient times; he persists tirelessly, both secretly in the stillness of night and openly in the light of day, leaving no opportunity unused. Such relentless effort shows that the failure of his people to respond lies not in any lack of sincerity or diligence on the prophet's part, but in their own stubbornness and refusal of guidance. The verse also teaches that a true caller to God must bring unwavering dedication and varied methods of outreach, and that he should bring his burden of rejection before his Lord in complaint and trust.

translation: But my calling (to them) increased them only in flight.
interpretation: The verse, spoken by Noah, expresses the depth of his frustration at his people's obstinacy. Every time he called them to faith and to turning toward God, the call only pushed them further away, so that their aversion grew rather than diminished. The verse shows that the fault lies not in the messenger's effort but in the hardened hearts of those who refuse guidance, and it offers the prophet and every reformer a model of patient perseverance in the face of persistent rejection.

translation: And indeed, whenever I called them so that You might forgive them, they put their fingers into their ears, covered themselves with their garments, persisted, and became arrogantly proud, with great arrogance.
interpretation: The verse portrays Noah's prolonged and sincere effort to guide his people, which was met with deliberate refusal rather than honest inability. Their gestures of stopping their ears and veiling their faces reveal a conscious closing of the heart against the call, not a lack of clear evidence. Their persistence in disbelief and their haughtiness show that the obstacle lay within their own pride and attachment to what they had inherited, so that the repeated invitation to repentance and forgiveness only deepened their stubbornness. The passage thus teaches that God's mercy is always offered, and that refusing it through arrogance is what truly sets a person apart from guidance.

translation: Then indeed I called out to them openly.
interpretation: This verse from Surah Nuh (Noah, 71:8) reflects the prophet's varied methods of da'wah over a long period. After publicly and privately urging his people to worship Allah alone and seek His forgiveness, Noah now describes calling them out in a loud, open manner, in front of gatherings, leaving no doubt about the message. The verse shows that his failure was not due to a lack of clarity or effort: he tried every approach, public and private, and the stubbornness lay with his people, who turned away and covered their ears and faces rather than respond to the truth.

translation: Then indeed I proclaimed to them openly, and I spoke to them in private, secretly.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Noah (peace be upon him) in Surah Nuh, shows the prophet's comprehensive and persistent effort in calling his people to God. After many years of preaching, he varied his methods: he addressed them publicly and aloud, and he also approached them individually and discreetly. The verse teaches that a caller to truth should employ every legitimate means, adapting the manner of da'wah to the audience, and should not grow weary of guidance even when the response is resistance.

translation: So I said: Ask your Lord for forgiveness, indeed He is ever Oft-Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse, spoken by Nuh (Noah) in his long call to his people, places repentance at the center of the relationship with God: turning back to the Lord through seeking forgiveness is presented as the immediate and accessible path to mercy, however far a person has strayed. The closing divine attribute, 'Ghaffar' (the One who forgives repeatedly and abundantly), signals that God's forgiveness is not occasional but a constant quality of His nature, and it invites the believer to see istighfar not as a mere ritual phrase but as an ongoing posture of humility, acknowledging human shortcoming and trusting in God's readiness to pardon. Read in its context of Nuh's appeal to a stubborn people, the verse also suggests that the door of return remains open, and that the call to seek forgiveness is itself a sign of God's compassion toward those who might otherwise despair.

translation: He sends down the sky upon you in abundant torrents of rain.
interpretation: The verse presents rain as a direct gift from God, sent down in abundance, so that the one who reflects on it is reminded that sustenance and life depend entirely on the Creator's mercy. The word 'midrar' (abundant, pouring repeatedly) suggests not merely a passing shower but a generous, continuous flow, inviting the listener to see in the falling rain a sign of divine generosity that should lead to gratitude, and to seek forgiveness and return to God as the verse's wider context in Surah Nuh encourages.

translation: And He will increase you in wealth and children, and will assign for you gardens and will assign for you rivers.
interpretation: The verse presents a promise of abundance that is tied to the posture of the people addressed. Wealth and children are named first as the visible signs of worldly blessing, and gardens and rivers add the image of flourishing, sustained provision, since water and green land were the basis of life in the Arabian setting. The repeated 'and He will make for you' gives the list the rhythm of a gift flowing steadily from the Giver. Read in its context, the promise is conditional on turning toward God in seeking forgiveness, so the blessings are presented as the fruit of faithful return rather than as a reward for worldly striving alone, and the verse teaches that prosperity is most fully understood when it is received as trust from God.

translation: Why is it that you do not attribute to Allah any dignity or reverence?
interpretation: The verse is a rebuke, framed as a question, aimed at people who fail to recognize God's greatness. Their failure is not a lack of evidence but a failure to let that greatness shape their hearts and conduct. The word 'waqar' points to the dignity, majesty and weight that belong to God, and the verse asks why they withhold that respect from Him. The verses that follow answer the question by pointing to God's signs in creation, so the reverence the verse calls for is meant to grow from reflecting on how God created and sustains human beings.

translation: And He has created you in stages.
interpretation: The verse, from Surah Nuh (71:14), points to the gradual, stage-by-stage process of human creation: from dust, then drop of semen, clinging clot, lump of flesh, and so on until the fully formed human being. Beyond its literal sense, it invites reflection on human development as a process of successive transformation, reminding the believer that the one who shaped them through distinct phases of growth is the same One to whom they must return, and that recognizing this gradual design should lead to gratitude and humility rather than pride in one's present condition.

translation: Have you not considered how Allah created seven heavens in layers upon layers?
interpretation: The verse invites the reader to reflect on the vast and orderly structure of the cosmos as evidence of the Creator's power and wisdom. The phrase "tibaqan" (in layers, one above another) conveys that the heavens are not a flat or single canopy but a graduated, stacked order, each level distinct yet harmonized with the others. By asking "have you not seen," the verse turns the observer's attention from awe at the heavens to recognition of the One who fashioned them, urging the believer to see in the perfect arrangement of creation a sign pointing beyond itself to the unity and sovereignty of God.

translation: And He made the moon within them a light, and made the sun a lamp.
interpretation: The verse draws a deliberate distinction between the two great luminaries of the sky. The moon is described as a 'nur' (light), a diffused and reflected radiance, while the sun is called a 'siraj' (lamp or torch), a self-contained and intense source of illumination that burns and blazes. The choice of two different words reflects the difference in their nature: the moon shines by receiving and reflecting light, and its gentle glow dispels darkness softly, whereas the sun generates its own brilliance. The phrase 'within them' (fihinna) places the moon among the heavens, indicating that these celestial bodies are arranged in an ordered cosmos, and the verse invites the reader to reflect on this precise design as evidence of the Creator's wisdom and power.

translation: And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth.
interpretation: The verse presents the creation of humankind as a gradual, organic process, likening the origin of human beings to the growth of plants from the soil. Just as vegetation springs from the earth through a natural and ordered development, so too humanity was brought forth from the earth, with the materials of creation drawn from it, reminding people of their humble origin and of the perfect power of the Creator who brings life out of what appears lifeless. The verse thus invites reflection on human dependence on the earth and on Allah's power over creation, calling for humility before the One who shaped them in stages.

translation: Then He will return you into it, and bring you forth again in a (second) bringing forth.
interpretation: The verse speaks of the cycle of human existence: just as God first brought people into being and sustains them in the earthly life, He will return them to the earth at death and then raise them forth on the Day of Resurrection in a complete and decisive emergence. The word "إخراجا" with its verbal emphasis underlines that this second bringing forth is not a mere repetition but a definitive act of God's power, pointing the believer to the certainty of resurrection and accountability, and to the truth that human origin, life, and return are all in the hand of the One who creates and restores.

translation: And Allah has made the earth for you a spread-out expanse.
interpretation: The verse presents the earth as a vast, spread-out bed prepared by Allah for human habitation, so that people may move across its surface, settle upon it, and make their lives on it. The image of a spread carpet or bedding conveys both its gentleness and its suitability for rest, comfort, and livelihood, inviting reflection on the Creator's mercy and His careful provision for humanity. It calls the believer to gratitude, recognizing that the stability and generosity of the earth are blessings that should lead to worship and responsible stewardship of what Allah has entrusted to them.

translation: So that you may traverse therein broad, spacious roads.
interpretation: The phrase points to the divine provision of the earth as a place made navigable for humanity: the wide, open paths (fijaj) are not merely physical routes but signs of God's mercy in making travel, trade, and movement possible, so that human beings may move across the land in pursuit of their livelihood and their purposes. The verse thus invites reflection on gratitude for the ease God has placed in the created order, and on the responsibility that comes with freedom of movement, namely to walk those paths with awareness of the One who laid them out.

translation: Noah said, "My Lord, they have disobeyed me and followed one whose wealth and children increase him in nothing but loss."
interpretation: Noah's words reveal the depth of his frustration after a long mission of calling his people to God. He turns to his Lord in complaint, pointing to the root of their ruin: they rejected the guidance of a messenger and instead followed the leaders of wealth and status. The verse exposes a recurring pattern in the Qur'an, where material abundance and large families are mistaken for proof of worth and success, when in truth they only deepen a person's loss if they distract from faith and obedience. Wealth and offspring, which people treat as sources of honor and security, become a burden of ruin for those who trust in them instead of God. The verse thus teaches that the real measure of gain is the state of the soul before God, not the accumulation of possessions or the number of one's descendants.

translation: And they schemed a great scheme.
interpretation: This phrase from Surah Nuh (71:22) describes the leaders of Noah's people, who urged the masses not to abandon their idols Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr. Their 'great scheme' was a deliberate, large-scale campaign of deception and obstruction against the prophet's call to monotheism, employing persuasion, ridicule and the entrenchment of ancestral tradition to keep people from the truth. The verse thus reveals that opposition to divine guidance is often organized and calculated, and that such plotting, however elaborate, is ultimately subject to God's knowledge and power, as the surrounding verses show in the drowning of the wrongdoers.

translation: And they said, "Do not leave your gods, and do not leave Wadd, nor Suwa', nor Yaghuth, nor Ya'uq, nor Nasr."
interpretation: This verse records the insistence of the leaders of Noah's people, who urged their followers to hold fast to their idols rather than abandon them. By naming five specific deities, it shows how the worship of these figures had become deeply entrenched in their social and religious life, and how the elite used tradition and loyalty to those idols as a barrier against the call to pure monotheism. The repetition of the prohibition 'do not leave' underscores the intensity of their resistance, and it reveals a recurring human pattern: attachment to inherited customs and revered figures can become a stronger obstacle to truth than the evidence of the message itself.

translation: And they have already led astray many, so do not increase the wrongdoers except in error.
interpretation: The verse is a supplication spoken by Noah (peace be upon him) against his people, found in Surah Nuh (71:24). After long and persistent preaching that yielded little, Noah reports that the leaders of his people have misled a multitude, and he asks that the wrongdoers be left to their own deviation, with their misguidance deepened as the consequence of their persistent rejection. The interpretation is that divine guidance is not forced; when people repeatedly choose injustice and persuade others to follow them, God allows them to continue in the path they have chosen, so that their error grows. It also highlights the responsibility of those who lead others astray, since the harm of their misguidance extends to the many who follow them.

translation: Because of their sins they were drowned, and then they were made to enter the Fire; and they found for themselves no helpers besides God.
interpretation: The verse presents the fate of those who persisted in wrongdoing as a sequence of consequences that befall them in this world and the next. Their sins are the direct cause of their destruction, the first being a swift drowning or overwhelming calamity, and the second being their entry into the Fire. The closing phrase underscores the futility of reliance on anything other than God: at the moment of greatest need, the idols, allies, and worldly protectors in whom they trusted prove utterly powerless, leaving them without any helper. The passage thus teaches that sin brings its own ruin and that no created being can shield a person from the consequences of disobedience to God.

translation: And Noah said, "My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers any dweller."
interpretation: Noah's plea reflects the culmination of a long and fruitless call to his people, after nine hundred and fifty years of patient preaching met only with stubbornness and mockery. His request is not born of mere anger but of a prophet's exhausted conviction that their continued existence would only multiply misguidance, since he foresees that those who remain will beget only wrongdoers and disbelievers. The verse thus reveals the gravity of persistent rejection of divine guidance: when hearts are sealed against truth after every reminder, the prophet turns to God in complete submission, entrusting the matter to His justice rather than to his own judgment. It also shows that the prophetic burden can lead a righteous servant to a point where he seeks the removal of corruption so that the earth may be purified for those who believe.

translation: Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants, and they will not beget except a wicked, ungrateful disbeliever.
interpretation: This verse is Noah's supplication (Surah Nuh 71:27), spoken after his long, persistent call to his people had yielded almost no faith. Having despaired of their guidance, he reveals that their corruption is not merely personal but hereditary and self-perpetuating: those who persist in disbelief lead others astray, and their offspring grow up inclined to the same wickedness, so that the disbelief passes from generation to generation. The phrase "they will not beget except" points to the tragic reality that the people's descendants, shaped by the environment of their elders, inherit their defiance rather than the faith of the prophet. Noah's words thus express both a sorrowful resignation and a plea for divine judgment, teaching that the consequences of persistent rejection of truth extend beyond the individual to the wider community and its future.

translation: My Lord, forgive me and my parents and whoever enters my home as a believer, and the believing men and the believing women. And do not increase the wrongdoers except in destruction.
interpretation: This closing supplication of Prophet Nuh reveals a prophet who, after long rejection, turns first to inward purification before outward judgment. He begins with his own forgiveness, showing that a messenger must examine his own heart, and then extends mercy to his parents and to every believer who joins his household, making faith rather than blood the true measure of kinship. Widening his prayer to all believing men and women, he sets out a community bound by belief. His final plea, that the wrongdoers be met only with ruin, is not vindictiveness but the sorrowful conclusion of a prophet who has exhausted every means of guidance and sees that persistent injustice has closed the door to repentance, so that God's justice must now take its course to preserve the righteous.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened, and they said: Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an.
interpretation: The verse presents the Prophet Muhammad being commanded to report a revelation he received: that a company of jinn gave attentive hearing to the recitation of the Qur'an and were so struck by it that they declared it wondrous. The word 'nafar' denotes a small group, and the jinn's reaction, calling it 'ajab' (marvellous, astonishing in its eloquence, guidance and meaning), shows that the Qur'an's impact transcends the human sphere, reaching beings unseen. By making the report a matter of divine revelation, the verse affirms the Prophet's mission as addressed to all creation, including the jinn, and establishes that the Qur'an's greatness is recognized even by those who are not of humankind.

translation: It guides to right conduct, so we have believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord.
interpretation: The verse presents the jinn's testimony after hearing the Qur'an: it leads to the right path of guidance, and therefore faith in it follows naturally. The declaration "we will never associate anyone with our Lord" shows that true belief is expressed through pure monotheism, rejecting every form of shirk, so that faith in the revelation and tawhid of God are inseparable.

translation: And that exalted is the majesty of our Lord; He has taken neither a consort nor a son.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the jinn who listened to the Qur'an (Surah al-Jinn 72:3), affirms the absolute transcendence of God above any human attributes of family or lineage. The word "jadd" conveys both greatness and majesty, and by denying that God has taken a consort or a son, the verse rejects the polytheistic beliefs that attributed offspring or partners to Him. It establishes tawhid in its purest form: God is self-sufficient, needing neither companion nor descendant, and any notion that binds Him to created relations diminishes His unique sovereignty. The verse thus invites the listener to purify their conception of God from anthropomorphic and familial imagery.

translation: And that the foolish one among us used to speak about Allah an outrageous lie.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by jinn who, having heard the Qur'an, recount how some foolish members of their own kind had been voicing extravagant falsehoods about God, attributing to Him companions or offspring and thereby going beyond the bounds of truth. The word shatat denotes excess and deviation from what is just and fitting, so the speakers are confessing that such talk was a transgression against the majesty of God. The passage thus reveals that even among the jinn there were those who had strayed into false belief, and it invites the listener to recognize that speaking of God without knowledge is a grave excess that must be abandoned in favor of the pure monotheism the Qur'an now proclaims.

translation: And we had thought that mankind and the jinn would never speak a lie against Allah.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by the jinn who, after hearing the guidance of the Qur'an, reflect on their earlier assumption. They confess that they had believed humans and jinn alike would never fabricate falsehoods about God, since such a claim seemed unthinkable. Their admission reveals how the belief in a sound, unchallenged religious understanding can be undermined when people attribute to God what He never said, as the subsequent verses show when the jinn recount how some among them had been misled into thinking that no one would be raised. It is a warning that trust in inherited or assumed religious claims must be tested against the truth, and that inventing things about Allah is among the gravest errors.

translation: And that there were men among mankind who used to seek refuge with men among the jinn, so they increased them in burden and distress.
interpretation: The verse exposes a corruption of the human heart: when people turn for protection to unseen forces rather than to God alone, those very beings add to their fear, confusion, and sin, so that seeking shelter in the creature becomes a source of further trouble. True refuge lies only in the Creator, and reliance on any other power brings only increasing dread and entanglement.

translation: And that they assumed, just as you assumed, that God would never resurrect anyone.
interpretation: The verse (Surah al-Jinn, 72:7) records a statement from the jinn, who report that they too had supposed, as humans had, that God would never send anyone back to life after death. By placing the jinn's earlier misconception alongside the human one, the verse presents disbelief in resurrection as a shared error across both creations, and so implicitly calls the listener to abandon the same assumption and recognize that God does indeed raise the dead for judgment.

translation: And we had touched the sky, but found it filled with strong guards and burning meteors.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by a group of jinn who reflect on their former attempts to ascend to the heavens and eavesdrop on its secrets. Their words convey a sense of surprise and realization: the heavens, once accessible to them in some measure, had become heavily guarded by mighty angelic sentries and pursued by piercing shooting stars. This reveals that the divine decree had tightened the boundaries between the unseen realm and human or jinn reach, marking a transition in which the revelation of the Prophet Muhammad was being safeguarded from distortion by the unseen beings. The passage thus underscores both the absolute sovereignty of God over the cosmos and the futility of any attempt to usurp knowledge reserved for Him.

translation: And indeed we used to sit in some of its places to listen; but whoever listens now will find a watching flame lying in wait for him.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by jinn who recount their former ability to eavesdrop on the heavens from vantage points there, and their realization that this access has been closed. The 'watching flame' (shihab rasad) signifies a guard set to intercept anyone attempting to listen now, which the jinn interpret as a sign that a decisive change has occurred in the affairs of the unseen, most plausibly the sending of the Prophet Muhammad with revelation. It shows that divine knowledge is protected from being stolen by the unseen beings, and that the cosmos is governed by an order that no creature can override.

translation: And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on the earth, or whether their Lord intends for them right guidance.
interpretation: The jinn, having heard the Qur'an, admit their limited knowledge. They do not know whether the change in the heavens and the guarding against eavesdropping signals a punishment that God intends for the people of the earth or a mercy that will lead them to guidance. The verse shows that the unseen belongs to God alone, that true knowledge of the outcome rests with Him, and that a believer should接受 the matter with humility, recognizing that God's intention for creation is ultimately one of guidance and wisdom even when its immediate meaning is hidden.

translation: And among us are the righteous, and among us are those below that; we were of divergent ways.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by a group of jinn who, having heard the Qur'an, describe the diversity within their own community: some are righteous and devout, while others fall short of that standard. By saying they were 'paths divided' (tara'iq qidadan), they acknowledge that their people followed many different ways, creating a candid self-assessment that prepares the way for their subsequent acceptance or rejection of guidance. The verse thus reflects the principle that religious communities are not uniform, and that each individual's standing before God depends on the path they choose.

translation: And we thought that we would never escape Allah on the earth, nor could we elude Him by flight.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by jinn who, having listened to guidance, recount their former error: they had assumed that no one could overpower or escape God anywhere on earth, and so they had denied and strayed. Their confession teaches that human and jinn alike cannot frustrate God's will by fleeing from Him, whether through distance, concealment, or running away, and that the realization of this truth is itself a call to return to Him in submission rather than persist in arrogance.

translation: And when we heard the guidance, we believed in it. So whoever believes in his Lord will fear neither loss nor oppression.
interpretation: The verse is spoken by the jinn who, upon hearing the Qur'an, recognized it as true guidance and submitted to it without delay, reasoning that faith in the Lord is the sure path to security. It teaches that true belief removes the fear of being wronged in one's reward, as the believer is safe from any diminishing of his good deeds (bakhs) and from any burden of injustice or humiliation (rahaq). The promise is that sincere faith brings a tranquil heart, since a person who trusts his Creator has nothing to dread from the Judgment regarding his due recompense.

translation: And among us are the Muslims, and among us are the deviators from truth. Whoever has submitted, those have deliberately sought out the right path.
interpretation: The verse presents the jinn's own confession that their community is divided between those who submit to God and those who swerve from justice, so that each soul's moral direction is shaped by its own free choice to submit. The word 'tahharraw' (sought out with deliberate care) implies that guidance is not merely received by chance but pursued through intention and effort, and it teaches that the path of rushd is reached by consciously turning toward submission rather than by lineage or group identity.

translation: And as for the deviators, they have become fuel for Hell.
interpretation: The verse contrasts the two groups introduced just before it: those who submit to God and seek the right path, and the qasitun, those who swerve from justice and truth into wrongdoing. The image of being 'fuel for Hell' (hatab) conveys that their own deeds and persistent deviation become the very material that feeds their punishment, so that the consequence of their choices is not an arbitrary sentence but something they have built with their own hands. By placing this sharply against the fate of the righteous, the verse calls the listener to recognize that every turning away from justice is a step toward self-destruction, and it invites a sober reflection on how the soul's direction in this life determines its destination in the next.

translation: And that if they had remained steadfast upon the way, We would have given them abundant water to drink.
interpretation: The verse points to a link between faithful adherence to the right path and worldly abundance. It presents steadfastness in guidance as the condition under which Allah's provision would have flowed generously, so that material blessing is understood as a consequence of obedience and uprightness. Read in its context of the jinn's testimony about the Qur'an, it also suggests that the sustenance of a community depends on its sincere return to the path of God, and that the deprivation people suffer can stem from their own deviation rather than from God's withholding.

translation: That We may test them therein. And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter into a grueling punishment.
interpretation: The verse presents divine trial as the purpose behind the reality that the disbelievers are given abundance and ease while being tested by it, so that wealth and comfort become a test rather than a sign of favor. It then draws a sharp contrast: the true measure of a person's standing before God is whether they remember their Lord and do not turn away from His reminder. Turning away from that remembrance is not a neutral choice but leads the person into an ascending, relentless torment, the word 'sa'ud' suggesting a punishment that grows steeper and harder with no respite. The passage thus ties the tests of this world to the moral responsibility of heeding the divine message.

translation: And that the mosques belong to God, so do not invoke anyone alongside God.
interpretation: The verse establishes that mosques, as places set apart for worship, belong exclusively to God, and therefore the worship performed within them must be directed to Him alone. By linking the sanctity of the houses of worship to the prohibition of calling upon others besides God, it makes clear that sincere devotion (tawhid) must govern both the physical spaces dedicated to prayer and the inner intention of the one who prays. Just as the mosque is free from any partner in its dedication, the worshipper's supplication must be free from any associate, since invoking another alongside God would compromise the purity that the mosque symbolizes.

translation: And that when the servant of Allah stood up calling upon Him, they almost became a dense crowd pressing around him.
interpretation: The verse portrays the jinn, who had just heard the Qur'an, being so struck by the Prophet's devotional standing and recitation that they pressed toward him in a dense throng, nearly overwhelming him. It shows how the Qur'an's call and the sincere worship of its bearer draw even unseen hearers to amazement and eagerness, while also reminding the believer that the message is received by others in ways that may exceed the messenger's expectations.

translation: Say, "I only invoke my Lord, and I associate no one with Him."
interpretation: The verse establishes the core of prophetic monotheism as a personal declaration: the Prophet is commanded to state that his worship and supplication are directed solely to his Lord, and that he ascribes no partner to Him. The word "innama" (only) confines his invocation exclusively to God, so that prayer, dependence, and petition are not divided among intermediaries or rivals. The verse thus binds the act of calling upon God (du'a) to the rejection of shirk, showing that sincere worship is inseparable from pure tawhid, and that the one who speaks this word must embody it in his own practice rather than merely utter it.

translation: Say, "Indeed, I do not possess for you any harm or any right guidance."
interpretation: The verse establishes a clear boundary between the Prophet's role as a messenger and any divine attributes. Even as the bearer of revelation, he is commanded to disclaim any power to bring harm or benefit to people on his own, or to grant them guidance by his own will; guidance and harm belong to God alone. This teaches believers to direct their hope and fear to God rather than to any created being, and it safeguards the purity of tawhid against the tendency to elevate prophets or saints beyond their human station. The Prophet's sole function is to convey the message, while the actual guidance of hearts rests with God.

translation: Say, "Indeed, no one can protect me from Allah, nor will I find any refuge besides Him."
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet to declare his absolute human dependence on God: he possesses no power to shield himself from divine decree and no alternative shelter outside of Him. This establishes that true security and refuge belong to Allah alone, so the believer's reliance must be placed solely in Him, while any claim to protection from other powers is shown to be empty before God's will.

translation: Except for a message from Allah and His messages. And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, then for him is the Fire of Hell, abiding therein forever.
interpretation: The verse establishes that the believer's only duty is to convey the divine message, and that the true measure of one's standing before God is obedience to Him and to His Messenger. The phrase "except a message from Allah and His messages" points to the prophetic role as a clear transmission of revelation, not a claim to control hearts or outcomes. By linking disobedience to Allah with disobedience to His Messenger, the verse shows that accepting the Prophet's guidance is inseparable from accepting God's own command. The warning of eternal Fire for such disobedience underscores the gravity of rejecting this covenant, while its emphasis on "abiding forever" conveys that the consequence is final for those who persist in rebellion against the clear message they have received.

translation: Until, when they see that which they are promised, they will know who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number.
interpretation: The verse portrays the disbelievers' false confidence in their numbers and allies, mocking the Prophet's community and the promise of divine punishment. It assures that when the promised torment or victory actually appears before their eyes, they will discover the true reality of their situation: that their supporters were feeble and their multitude insignificant, while the believers, though few and seemingly weak, were under God's protection. The passage thus turns the standard of power on its head, teaching that worldly strength and numbers are no measure of truth or success, and that the ultimate judgment belongs to God alone.

translation: Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will appoint for it a long duration.
interpretation: The verse shows the Prophet Muhammad admitting the limits of his knowledge: the exact timing of the promised punishment or Day of Judgment belongs to God alone. Though he delivers the message with certainty about its reality, he does not claim knowledge of when it will arrive, which guards against both false claims of prophetic foreknowledge and the hasty demands of those who mocked the warnings. The reply to their challenge is thus a call to humility before God's unseen decree and a reminder that the timing of accountability is entrusted entirely to Him.

translation: (He is) the Knower of the unseen, so He does not reveal His unseen to anyone.
interpretation: The verse affirms that knowledge of the unseen (al-ghayb) belongs exclusively to God, who alone encompasses everything hidden from creation. Its phrasing, 'fa-la yuzhiru ʿala ghaybihi ahadan', means that He does not make anyone a witness to or a master of His hidden knowledge, and it is therefore a rebuke to any claim that human beings, or even the prophets in their own right, possess independent access to the unseen. Whatever knowledge of the unseen is granted to a messenger is granted by God's selection, as the following verse in Surah al-Jinn makes clear, when He allows an apostle whom He has chosen to receive some of it. The verse thus establishes both the absolute sovereignty of God's knowledge and the dependence of all created knowledge upon His will.

translation: Except a messenger whom He has approved, for indeed He sends before him and behind him guards (observers).
interpretation: The verse describes the unseen realm as closed to all but those whom God chooses. The exception is a messenger He has approved, and even he is not left unguarded: angelic watchers are dispatched before and behind him, so that the revelation he carries reaches people intact, without being corrupted or snatched away by the jinn or devils who try to eavesdrop on the heavens. The point is that divine knowledge is protected at its source and in its transmission, so that what the messenger conveys is genuinely from God.

translation: That He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord, while He encompasses what is with them, and He has counted everything in number.
interpretation: The verse points to a divine purpose behind the mission of the messengers: God's 'knowing' here is not acquisition of new knowledge but the manifestation, in the realm of accountability, of what has already been fully known to Him. The conveying of the messages is thus made a witnessed and recorded fact, which is then set against the complete encompassing knowledge of God over all that the people possess, both their deeds and their intentions. By stating that He has counted everything precisely, the verse ties the mission of the prophets to the final reckoning, where no act of delivery or rejection is lost, and where human beings are placed under a comprehensive, exact divine account.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O you wrapped in your garments!
interpretation: The address "O you wrapped in your garments" (يا أيها المزمل) is a tender call to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, at a moment when he had withdrawn into his cloak, weighed down by the burden of the revelation and the mission entrusted to him. Rather than a rebuke, the title reads as an intimate summons that lifts him from rest to readiness: the one who has been wrapped in comfort is now called to rise, to stand in prayer through the night, and to bear the weighty word that is about to be laid upon him. It teaches that the bearer of a great trust must first be drawn out of the warmth of ease into devotion, and that the strength for such a burden comes from communion with the Lord in the quiet hours of the night.

translation: Stand [in prayer] through the night, except for a little
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet Muhammad to rise in night prayer, devoting most of the night to worship and standing before God, with only a small portion left for rest. This is a call to intimate, sustained devotion, and it establishes the night vigil as a deliberate spiritual discipline that prepares the believer to bear the weight of the revealed message.

translation: Half of it, or reduce from it a little.
interpretation: The verse gives the Prophet a flexible measure for night worship: he may devote about half the night to standing in prayer or a little less, which shows that devotion is meant to be sustained and within one's capacity rather than excessive. The graded choice reflects divine mercy and the value of steady, consistent worship over harsh, unsustainable exertion.

translation: "Or add to it, and recite the Qur'an in measured, distinct recitation." (Al-Muzzammil 73:4)
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet to recite the Qur'an slowly, clearly and with careful articulation, letter by letter and word by word, so that its meaning is understood and its contemplation is possible. Tartil is not merely a matter of sound but of reflection: the reader is to let each word settle in the heart, which is why the verse links recitation with the understanding and reverent attention that the nightly worship demands.

translation: Indeed, We are going to place upon you a weighty word.
