interpretation: The verse announces to the Prophet Muhammad that he is about to receive a heavy burden, namely the revelation of the Qur'an, which is weighty in its message, its responsibility, and the demands it places on the one who carries it. The phrase conveys that prophethood is not an honor without cost: the Messenger must bear the trust, deliver it faithfully, and endure the difficulty of its reception and of the opposition it provokes. Classical commentators such as al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi note that the 'weight' refers both to the content of the revelation and to the strain of receiving it, which the Prophet experienced physically when inspiration came upon him. It thus prepares him, and the believers after him, for the seriousness of the divine word and the steadfastness required to uphold it.

translation: Indeed, the rising at night is stronger in impact and more upright in speech.
interpretation: The verse praises the night vigil as a discipline of the soul that is more forceful and effective than daytime worship, because in the stillness of the night the heart is free from distraction and the tongue and body are most aligned with what is recited. Its 'trampling' or firm impact suggests that the worship made in that hour sinks deeply into the self and takes hold of the will, while 'more upright in speech' indicates that the words uttered are more sincere, more correct, and more composed, as the worshipper is wholly present with his Lord. The verse thus teaches that the quality of devotion is measured not only by its quantity but by the inward presence and steadfastness it produces in the believer.

translation: Indeed, for you by day there is extensive occupation (and much movement and busyness).
interpretation: The verse, from Surah Al-Muzzammil (73:7), sets the believer's daytime life against the night of worship. Although the Prophet was commanded to rise at night for prayer and recitation, the day is not an empty space for him; it is filled with a long stretch of activity, preaching, dealing with people, and the affairs of the community. The verse teaches that the one who carries a mission must divide his time: the night is for closeness and inner strengthening through remembrance and the Qur'an, so that the strength gained there can carry him through the demanding obligations of the day.

translation: And mention the name of your Lord and devote yourself to Him with complete devotion.
interpretation: The verse calls the believer to a life centered on remembrance of God and wholehearted dedication to Him. 'Dhikr' of the Lord's name is not limited to uttering it with the tongue but includes keeping Him present in the heart throughout the day, so that every act becomes an orientation toward Him. The command to 'devote yourself' (tabattul) uses an intensive verbal form that implies cutting oneself off from distractions and rivals of the heart in order to turn fully toward God alone. This is a call to sincere, exclusive devotion that resonates with the verse's context in Surah al-Muzzammil, where the Prophet is instructed to rise in the night for prayer and to bear the burdens of his mission with steadfastness, and it teaches that true strength for any mission is drawn from constant turning to the Lord.

translation: Lord of the East and the West; there is no god but Him, so take Him as a Guardian (disposer of affairs).
interpretation: The verse presents God as the sovereign Lord over all of creation, the One who governs every horizon where the sun rises and sets, which signifies His dominion over all of space and time. Because His oneness is affirmed in the declaration that there is no god but Him, reliance on any other power is shown to be misplaced. The command to take Him as a trustee (wakil) is therefore an invitation to entrust one's affairs fully to Him, placing tawakkul at the heart of faith: a believer who truly grasps that the Lord of all directions is the sole Master of all matters will find in Him sufficient protection and direction, free from anxiety over the plots or power of others.

translation: And be patient over what they say, and part from them with gracious parting.
interpretation: The verse instructs the Prophet to meet the hostility, mockery, and false accusations of his opponents with steadfast patience rather than retaliation or anger, and to withdraw from them in a dignified manner, without bitterness, quarrel, or reproach. The beautiful parting (hajran jamilan) is a separation that keeps the believer's composure and moral integrity intact: he leaves the arena of futile disputation while entrusting the matter to God, who knows best how to deal with those who deny. Thus patience and graceful disengagement become the believer's response to persecution, preserving the dignity of the message and of the one who carries it.

translation: And leave Me with those who deny the truth, the possessors of ease and luxury, and give them respite a little while.
interpretation: The verse is a divine address to the Prophet Muhammad, assuring him that the matter of those who reject the message is entrusted entirely to God. The phrase "leave Me with" (wadhharni) signals that God Himself will take account of them, so the Prophet need not exhaust himself in dealing with their stubbornness. Describing them as "possessors of ease and luxury" points to the way prosperity often breeds arrogance and heedlessness toward the truth, as the worldly comforts they enjoy become a veil over their hearts. The word "a little" (qalilan) emphasizes that their respite is brief and temporary, a limited span of time that will end in a reckoning. The verse thus combines consolation for the believer with a warning to the complacent: the apparent security of the wealthy deniers is only a short reprieve before their accountability.

translation: Indeed, with Us are shackles and a blazing Fire.
interpretation: The verse, from Surah Al-Muzzammil (73:12), speaks of the punishment awaiting those who deny the message and turn away from the remembrance of their Lord. The 'ankal' (heavy shackles) signify the restraint and humiliation of the wrongdoers, binding them so they cannot escape or act freely, which contrasts with the freedom they enjoyed in worldly life. The mention of the 'jahim' (blazing fire) completes the image of suffering, indicating that the consequence of arrogance and heedlessness is not only a loss of liberty but a severe and enduring torment. Placed within a surah that calls the Prophet to patience and night prayer, the verse reminds the believer that divine justice is certain, and that God's measure of accountability reserves for the rebellious a punishment matched to their defiance, while the righteous are assured of recompense.

translation: And food that chokes in the throat, and a painful torment.
interpretation: This verse, describing the provisions of the Hellfire's inhabitants, presents a food that cannot be swallowed easily, lodging in the throat and choking the one who tries to eat it, as a fitting counterpart to the worldly comforts they once enjoyed without gratitude. The phrase 'a painful torment' joins this bodily distress to a broader punishment, so that the very sustenance meant to nourish becomes a source of suffering, reminding the listener that what is taken in heedlessness can turn into affliction in the Hereafter.

translation: On the Day when the earth and the mountains will quake violently, and the mountains will become heaps of sand, crumbling and flowing.
interpretation: The verse depicts the Day of Resurrection as a cosmic upheaval in which the firm, stable order of the world collapses. The earth trembles and the mountains, which in the familiar world stand as symbols of permanence and immovability, are reduced to loose, shifting heaps of sand that pour down and scatter. The imagery teaches that nothing in creation, however solid it appears to human eyes, is beyond God's power to dissolve, and it calls the listener to reflect on the transience of this world and to prepare for the reckoning that follows it.

translation: Indeed, We have sent to you a messenger as a witness over you, just as We sent a messenger to Pharaoh.
interpretation: The verse draws a deliberate parallel between the Prophet Muhammad and Moses, sent to Pharaoh, to show that a pattern of divine dispatch recurs throughout history. The difference lies in the outcome for each community: Pharaoh rejected his messenger and was destroyed, so the verse implicitly warns the addressees that the same consequence awaits those who reject the messenger now sent to them. The phrase "a witness over you" adds that the messenger will testify to their conduct, making them accountable for how they respond to his call.

translation: But Pharaoh disobeyed the Messenger, so We seized him with a severe seizing.
interpretation: The verse points to the pattern of the Pharaoh's story as a warning: rejecting a messenger sent by God is not a neutral act but a defiance that carries consequences. By describing the seizing as 'wabilan' (heavy, severe, grievous), the verse emphasizes that divine retribution is proportionate to the arrogance of the one who refuses guidance, and it reminds the listener that the same principle applies to any people who turn away from the messengers of their own time.

translation: How then will you guard yourselves, if you disbelieve, against a Day that will turn children grey-haired?
interpretation: The verse uses the image of children turning grey-haired to convey the overwhelming terror of the Day of Judgment, when the horror of that day will be so severe that even the young will be aged by it. It is a rhetorical challenge to the disbelievers: if they reject faith, what shield could they possibly have against such a day? The verse thus calls the listener to taqwa, awareness and guarding of oneself before God, by recognizing that disbelief leaves a person defenseless before the reckoning that is coming.

translation: The sky will be split asunder by it; His promise has always been fulfilled.
interpretation: The pronoun "به" points back to the Day mentioned in the previous verse, the Day that turns children grey-headed. The splitting of the sky conveys the overwhelming cosmic upheaval and terror of that Day, when the familiar order of creation breaks apart. The closing phrase, "كان وعده مفعولا", affirms that God's promise of the Resurrection and Judgment is certain and will be fulfilled, so the listener is called to take heed and prepare while there is still time.

translation: Indeed, this is a reminder, so whoever wills may take a path to his Lord.
interpretation: The verse presents the Qur'an as a reminder that calls the human being back to his innate awareness of his Creator, and it places the choice of guidance in the hand of the individual: the path to the Lord is open, but it is entered only through one's own will and striving. Divine reminder does not compel; it makes the road visible and leaves the decision to the heart. The phrase 'whoever wills' reflects the moral dignity of human freedom, which makes a person accountable for the direction he chooses, while the word 'sabil' (path) suggests that nearness to God is reached through a deliberate, ongoing journey rather than a single act. The verse thus joins divine mercy in providing guidance with human responsibility in responding to it.

translation: Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand in prayer almost two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it, and so do a group of those with you. And Allah measures the night and the day. He knows that you will not be able to keep count of it, so He has turned to you in mercy. So recite what is easy of the Qur'an. He knows that there will be among you those who are ill, and others who travel through the land seeking of Allah's bounty, and others who fight in the cause of Allah. So recite what is easy of it, establish the prayer, give the zakat, and loan Allah a goodly loan. Whatever good you send forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah, better and greater in reward. And seek Allah's forgiveness. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: The opening of this surah establishes that the Prophet's night vigil and that of the believers with him was a demanding discipline, and God, who alone measures night and day, lightened it out of mercy once exact reckoning proved impossible. The command to recite 'what is easy' shows that devotion is to be sustained within human capacity, so that worship does not become a burden that breaks the one who carries it. By placing illness, travel for livelihood, and fighting for God's cause side by side, the verse teaches that every legitimate form of struggle in life is itself a form of service, and that the obligations of prayer, zakat, and generous spending remain the constant foundation beneath all of them. Good deeds stored up for the hereafter are presented as a loan to God, returned multiplied, and the verse closes by joining the duty of seeking forgiveness to the assurance of God's forgiving mercy.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O you who are wrapped up (in your garment)!
interpretation: The address "O you who are wrapped up" (ya ayyuha al-muddaththir) opens the surah with a tender, intimate call to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, at a moment when he was wrapped in his cloak, likely after the trying experience of the first revelation and its overwhelming weight. The verse thus combines comfort with a summons: the Messenger is gently roused from his rest and his withdrawal to take up the immense duty of warning mankind. The image of the one wrapped up suggests both the exhaustion of a burdened soul and the readiness that is now being called forth, so that the rest of the surah unfolds as a command to rise, to warn, and to glorify the Lord.

translation: Arise and warn!
interpretation: The verse is the opening command of Surah Al-Muddaththir (74:2), addressed to the Prophet Muhammad as he is wrapped in his garment after the initial revelation. It marks the shift from private reflection and quiet retreat to a public mission. The command "qum" (arise) signals resolve and readiness to act, not merely physical standing, while "fa-andhir" (then warn) defines the core task: to alert people to the consequences of their choices and to the reality of accountability before God. The verse thus establishes that the prophetic role involves active responsibility, moving from receiving the message to delivering it, and it sets a lasting pattern for those who carry the message forward: to rise with conviction and to warn with sincerity and care.

translation: And your Lord, glorify [Him] with greatness.
interpretation: The verse commands the Prophet to magnify his Lord, declaring God's greatness above all things. Having been given the mission of warning, he is to make his Lord's supremacy the central reality of his life and speech, proclaiming takbir (Allahu Akbar) and acknowledging that no power, idol, or worldly authority can rival Him. The command to exalt God is thus both an act of devotion and the foundation of the believer's stance against the arrogance of those who deny the message.

translation: And your garments, purify them.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Muddaththir (74:4), is a command to the Prophet to keep his clothing clean. Classical scholars understood it both literally, as a call to physical cleanliness and avoiding impurities in dress, and figuratively, as a call to purify one's conduct, character and inner self, since garments in Arabic idiom often signify a person's behavior and reputation. The verse thus joins outer purity with moral integrity, placing ethical and spiritual cleanliness at the heart of the call to prophethood that opens the surah.

translation: And the filth, avoid it.
interpretation: This short verse, from Surah Al-Muddaththir (74:5), is a command to abandon whatever is ritually and morally impure. The word "ar-rujz" denotes filth, idols, and sin in their many forms, and the command to "forsake" it calls for a complete and deliberate turning away from them, not merely avoiding them in passing. Its placement right after the call to rise and warn shows that the one who carries a message must first purify his own conduct and beliefs before he can guide others.

translation: And do not give (or bestow favors) seeking to receive more in return.
interpretation: The verse forbids the believer from bestowing favors or kindness with the expectation of gaining more in return, whether through reminding others of one's benevolence or through seeking to gain back more than one gave. Such conduct is a form of self-interest that undermines the sincerity and purity of giving. Giving should be done for the sake of God, with a generous heart that does not calculate or expect reward from the recipient, and it is in the same spirit that the verse counsels against the reproach and self-regard that can spoil charity.

translation: And for your Lord, then be patient.
interpretation: This short verse, from Surah Al-Muddaththir (74:7), is a command to the Prophet Muhammad to bear patiently whatever he faces in the course of his mission. The word 'ولربك' places the patience entirely in service of the Lord: it is not patience for personal gain or to be seen enduring, but a sincere, devoted steadfastness undertaken for the sake of God. Coming right after the call to rise and warn, it teaches that the one who carries a divine message must expect opposition and must meet it with constancy, anchoring that endurance in devotion to the One who commissioned him.

translation: And when the Trumpet is blown with a single blast.
interpretation: The verse introduces the Day of Resurrection through the sound of the Trumpet (al-Naqur), the blast that marks the end of the present world and the beginning of the Hereafter. Its phrasing, "fa-idha naqara fi al-naqur," conveys the suddenness and decisiveness of the event: no gradual transition, but a single summons that gathers all creation for reckoning. The verse thus calls the listener to awareness of the imminence of accountability, and it sets up the sequence of the surah's subsequent verses describing how severe that Day will be for the disbelievers and how it will be unlike any ordinary day.

translation: So that Day, it will be a difficult day.
interpretation: The verse describes the Day of Judgment (referenced in the preceding verses as a day of disbelievers' distress) as one of severe hardship for those who denied the truth. Its difficulty is not merely physical but a moral and existential weight, sharply contrasting with the ease granted to the believers. It serves as a warning that the consequences of one's choices will be heavy on that day, prompting the listener to reflect on how they prepare for it.

translation: Upon the disbelievers, it will be anything but easy.
interpretation: The phrase "ghayru yasir" (not easy) is a deliberate understatement that intensifies the meaning. For the disbelievers that Day is not merely difficult but severe and heavy, and the ease that the believers may find on it is withheld from them entirely. The verse places the hardship of the Day on those who rejected the message, implying that their denial brings a reckoning that offers them no relief, while the wording also leaves room for the awful weight of that Day to be felt in its full, unspoken magnitude.

translation: Leave me with the one whom I created alone.
interpretation: The verse is God's address to the Prophet, telling him to entrust to God alone the affair of a man who opposed the message. The phrase 'whom I created alone' emphasizes that this person came into existence through God's sole act of creation, without any partner, and so his ultimate reckoning rests with his Creator. The Prophet is thereby relieved of the burden of dealing with him, as God will deal with him directly. The verse also implies that the man, despite having been created in such a singular way, was given wealth, children, and standing, yet remained ungrateful, so God leaves him to be held accountable for his arrogance and denial.

translation: And I made for him wealth extended (abundant and lasting), spread out without limit.
interpretation: The verse, spoken in the context of the arrogant man who rejected the signs of God (Surah al-Muddaththir), points to the trap of worldly provision: God granted him a broad, flowing wealth, yet this abundance was not a sign of favor that drew him toward gratitude but a test that fed his pride and his denial. It teaches that material expansion given without thankfulness becomes a snare, as the heart grows attached to what it possesses and forgets its Giver, so that the very means of ease turn into the cause of ruin.

translation: And sons who are present (as witnesses) beside him.
interpretation: This phrase from Surah Al-Muddaththir (74:13), describing the wealth and provision granted to a man, refers to the sons who are constantly present with him, never far from him. Their presence is taken as a sign of worldly favor and status, as they live in his company, share in his prosperity, and are a source of pride and support, so that he feels secure and honored among his household and community.

translation: And I spread out for him abundant provision, spreading it out extensively and making his affairs smooth and easy.
interpretation: The word tamhid points to a wide, smooth, and comfortable provision granted to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, including wealth, status, and ease in his affairs. Yet this very abundance became a test, since he met God's favor with ingratitude and greed for more. The verse teaches that worldly ease given without gratitude is not a sign of divine approval but a respite that can lead a person to ruin.

translation: Then he desires that I should increase him further.
interpretation: The verse describes a man who, despite having been given abundant wealth and sons, remains insatiably greedy and still hopes for more, as though his blessings earned him a claim on God's further favor. Classical commentators link it to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who rejected the Qur'an while craving more worldly gain. Its point is that greed for increase, combined with ingratitude and denial of the revealed signs, is a spiritual disease that blinds a person to the true source and purpose of his blessings, and that such hope is misplaced because God's favor is not owed to the arrogant.

translation: Nay! Indeed, he was stubbornly opposed to Our signs.
interpretation: The verse rebukes a man who, having been shown Our clear signs, chose obstinate rejection over humble acceptance. The word 'ʿanīd' describes one who sets himself against the truth deliberately and refuses to yield even when the evidence is plain, so his denial springs not from a lack of proof but from arrogance and an unwillingness to submit. The opening 'Kallā' (Nay!) cuts off his excuses and his claims of entitlement, showing that stubbornness before revelation is itself the root of his fate, and that a heart which hardens against God's signs has closed the door to guidance.

translation: I will overwhelm him with a grueling ascent.
interpretation: The verse uses the image of a steep, relentless climb to depict the suffering awaiting the one who rejected the message: just as a person struggling uphill is pressed down by each step, he will be burdened by a punishment that grows ever heavier and more exhausting, with no relief in sight. The ascent becomes a metaphor for the escalating hardship of his arrogance, which had raised him up in pride and is now reversed into a painful, unending struggle upward.

translation: Indeed, he reflected and calculated.
interpretation: The verse exposes how intellect can be turned against truth. The man in question did think and plan, but his reflection was driven by a prior decision to reject the Qur'an, so his calculation served his pride and bias rather than a sincere search for guidance. Human reasoning is a gift, yet when it is bent to justify a conclusion already chosen, it becomes a means of self-deception, and the verse warns that such ingenuity, however sophisticated, is judged by the intention and direction behind it.

translation: So he was destroyed; how he calculated!
interpretation: The verse mocks a person who reflected on the Qur'an and calculated how to disparage it, a reference traditionally linked to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who weighed the Qur'an's words and then dismissed them as sorcery. Its point is that deliberate, calculated rejection of the truth, however clever it appears, leads to ruin, and that a mind which uses its reasoning to serve arrogance and denial brings about its own destruction.

translation: Then he was destroyed; how he calculated and plotted.
interpretation: The verse mocks the deliberate calculation of a man who weighed the Qur'an and then rejected it, as the surrounding verses describe. Through the repeated exclamation "how he calculated," God shows that his scheming was futile and self-destructive, since human planning against divine truth can only bring ruin on its planner.

translation: Then he looked (and reflected).
interpretation: The word "ثم" (then) marks a deliberate sequence: after gathering his thoughts, the man in this passage directs his gaze and reflection toward the Qur'an, yet his looking is not the open search for guidance that a seeker would undertake. It is the calculating scrutiny of one who has already decided to reject the message and is searching for some flaw or insinuation with which to discredit it. The verse thus exposes how the faculty of reason and observation can be turned away from truth when pride and hostility govern the heart, and it warns that sincere reflection is the one that opens the way to understanding.

translation: Then he frowned and scowled.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Muddaththir (74:22), describes the disposition of a man who, having considered the Qur'an and sought to dismiss it, turned his face away in displeasure and contempt. The frowning and scowling reflect an inner state of arrogance and rejection of the truth after it has been clearly presented. The verse conveys that the obstinate refusal of guidance is not merely intellectual but manifests visibly in the countenance, revealing a heart closed to reflection, and it warns that such hardened denial is a choice that invites the consequences described immediately after it.

translation: Then he turned his back, striving (against the truth), and was arrogant.
interpretation: This verse describes the response of Pharaoh to the clear signs shown by Moses. Having been shown the truth, he did not accept it with humility but turned away from it deliberately, refusing to heed the call. His turning away was accompanied by arrogance, meaning he placed his own status and pride above the recognition of the truth, which is the root of disbelief: the heart that is unwilling to submit to what is evident and to the One who sent it.

translation: Then he said, "This is nothing but magic that is transmitted (from others)."
interpretation: The verse (Al-Muddaththir 74:24) records the reasoning of a hardened opponent who, having considered the Qur'an, dismissed it as mere sorcery passed down from earlier practitioners rather than a genuine revelation from God. The phrase "yu'thar" conveys that this magic is inherited and narrated, implying the claim is borrowed and lacks any original, divine source. The verse thus exposes the rhetorical strategy of those who, unable to deny the Qur'an's power, sought to undermine its authority by attributing it to human trickery, a pattern that reflects the stubborn refusal to accept the truth despite recognizing its force.

translation: This is not but the word of a human being.
interpretation: The verse records the disbelievers' dismissal of the Qur'an as merely human speech, a claim the Qur'an answers elsewhere by challenging them to produce a single chapter like it. Its significance lies in the way it denies the Prophet's message any divine origin while exposing the weakness of that denial: the speech they reject is of the same kind they themselves use, yet they cannot match its eloquence, its order, and its power over hearts. The verse thus turns a rhetorical accusation into an unintended confirmation of the Qur'an's inimitability.

translation: Soon I will expose him to Saqar (Hell).
interpretation: The phrase "سأصليه سقر" (74:26) is a warning of severe punishment in the Hereafter. The verb "أصليه" means to cause him to burn or to be roasted in the fire, and "سقر" is one of the names of Hell, whose scorching is described as intense and relentless. The verse, spoken in the context of a person who arrogantly rejected the revelation and claimed it was mere human speech, conveys that such denial and pride will be met with a direct and certain consequence: the one who rejects the truth will face the fire that burns without mercy.

translation: And what will make you know what Saqar is?
interpretation: The verse uses the rhetorical question "And what will make you know what Saqar is?" to convey that the true nature of Saqar lies beyond ordinary human comprehension and imagination. By repeating the form "And what will make you know" (wa ma adraka), the Qur'an signals that its horror is of a magnitude that cannot be grasped through familiar experience, so that the listener is startled into awe and into taking seriously the warning of the punishment that follows in the verses after it.

translation: "It leaves nothing behind and spares nothing" (Qur'an 74:28, Al-Muddaththir: "لَا تُبْقِي وَلَا تَذَرُ")
interpretation: The phrase describes the fire of Hell (Saqar) in its totality: it consumes everything cast into it, leaving no remnant of the body or the soul's flesh, and then it restores and burns again, sparing no one who has earned it. The verse conveys the absolute, relentless nature of divine punishment, where no mercy interrupts its severity, and it serves as a warning to the heedless that the consequences of denial and arrogance are complete and inescapable, which is why the surah's speaker is urged to reflect on that terrifying reality.

translation: (From Surah Al-Muddaththir 74:29) "Scorching and blackening the human being."
interpretation: The phrase describes the fire of Saqar, which the preceding verse says leaves nothing and spares nothing. Its distinctive trait is that it strips away the human form by blackening and burning the skin, so the verse presents the punishment as total and unsparing, reaching the body that the one who denied and turned away once took pride in. Read alongside the verses that precede it, the image ties the physical severity of the Fire to the moral stance of those who rejected the message, suggesting that their bodily suffering answers their refusal to accept the truth.

translation: Over it are nineteen.
interpretation: This phrase, from Surah Al-Muddaththir (74:30), refers to the guardians of Hell, described as nineteen in number, who are set over the fire. The number is presented as a trial for those who disbelieve: it strengthens the certainty of the People of the Book and deepens the faith of the believers, while those with sickness in their hearts and the disbelievers are left in doubt. The verse thus teaches that the unseen realm is governed by a precise divine order, and that the reality of the Hereafter is tested through what people accept or reject of the revealed word.

translation: And We have not made the keepers of the Fire except angels, and We have not made their number except as a trial for those who disbelieve, so that those who were given the Scripture may be certain, those who believe may increase in faith, those who were given the Scripture and the believers may not doubt, and those in whose hearts is disease and the disbelievers may say, 'What did Allah intend by this as an example?' Thus does Allah leave astray whom He wills and guide whom He wills. And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him. And it is not but a reminder to mankind.
interpretation: The verse shows that the number placed over the Fire is a test that sorts hearts rather than a mere numerical fact. For the People of the Scripture it confirms what their books already contain, which steadies their certainty, and for the believers it deepens faith as they accept what they cannot fully measure. For those with sickness in their hearts and for the disbelievers, the same figure becomes a pretext for mockery and a question asked from doubt. The closing lines teach that the full reckoning of God's hosts lies beyond human knowledge, so the proper response to such signs is humble submission and reflection, and the Qur'an itself is a reminder that the sincere seeker can receive.

translation: Nay, by the moon,
interpretation: The verse opens with the emphatic particle "kallā" (nay/indeed not), which negates a preceding claim or denial, and is followed by a solemn oath sworn by the moon. In the Qur'an, God swears by His creations such as the moon to draw attention to the matter that follows, which in the surrounding context (surah al-Muddaththir) is a rebuke of those who reject the message and a firm affirmation of the truth of the warning. The moon, with its regular waxing and waning that marks time and reckoning, serves as a sign of God's power and order, inviting the reflective believer to contemplate the signs of creation and the certainty of what is being announced.

translation: And by the night when it turns its back and withdraws.
interpretation: God swears by the night as it retreats and departs, its darkness receding before the coming light of dawn. The oath draws attention to the orderly alternation of day and night as a sign of divine power and wisdom, and the image of the night turning away invites the reader to reflect on the passing of times and the certainty of the new day that follows.

translation: And by the morning when it brightens (unfolds its light).
interpretation: God swears by the dawn as it breaks and spreads its light across the sky. The brightening of morning after the darkness of night is presented as a sign of God's power to bring forth light from darkness, and a reminder that just as the night gives way to day, hardship gives way to ease. The oath draws the believer's attention to the regularity and beauty of creation as evidence of the Creator's wisdom and mercy.

translation: Indeed, it is one of the greatest (calamities).
interpretation: The pronoun "it" points back to Saqar, the Fire described in the preceding verses, and the phrase "one of the greatest" stresses that its severity surpasses ordinary tribulations. By placing it among the supreme matters, the verse confronts the listener with the seriousness of the Hereafter, so that the warning that follows in the next verse is received as a grave summons to reflection and to heeding the message before the consequence arrives.

translation: A warner to mankind.
interpretation: The phrase نذيرا للبشر (a warner to mankind) describes the Prophet Muhammad's mission as universal rather than limited to one people or region. The word نذيرا, meaning one who gives warning, points to his role in alerting humanity to the consequences of rejecting God and to the reality of accountability before Him. Its address to all of البشر, mankind, emphasizes that the message is meant for every human being across time and place, calling each person to reflect, prepare for the Hereafter, and choose the path of faith and righteousness.

translation: For whoever among you wills to go forward or to lag behind.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that the choice of striving toward righteousness rests with each person's own will. Human beings are granted the freedom to advance on the path of guidance or to hold back from it, and each bears the responsibility for the direction they select. It is a reminder that moral accountability begins with intention and resolve, since God has made the path available to all who choose to walk it.

translation: Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned.
interpretation: The verse (Al-Muddaththir 74:38, and similar wording in Al-Tur 52:21) affirms that each person is individually accountable for their own deeds, and that a soul remains bound or mortgaged by its works until it is judged. Just as a pledged item is held as security until its debt is discharged, a person's actions hold them answerable, and they cannot escape the consequences of what they have done or be freed except through the mercy and judgment of God. It underscores personal responsibility, the impossibility of shifting one's burden onto another, and the call to accumulate good deeds that will serve as one's release on the Day of Judgment.

translation: except the companions of the right
interpretation: The phrase 'companions of the right' (aṣḥāb al-yamīn) refers to those who receive their record in their right hand, the sign of acceptance. Placed as an exception to the principle that every soul is held in pledge for what it earned, it shows that these people are the ones whose righteous deeds secure their release from that pledge. Their rank is a reward for faith and good conduct, and it stands in contrast to the guilty who are left in the Fire.

translation: In gardens, they will ask one another (about the guilty ones; this is the continuation of Qur'an 74:40-41, "In gardens they will ask one another about the criminals").
interpretation: The image is of the righteous enjoying their reward in gardens of bliss, where their happiness is deepened by a conversation in which they look on the fate of those who once denied and mocked the truth. Their questioning is not born of cruelty but of a settled tranquility that allows them to reflect on how they were spared and how the wrongdoers were left in their own ruin. The verse thus teaches that the ultimate reward of faith includes a serene clarity about the consequences of one's choices, so that the blessed look back upon the worldly life with gratitude and understanding.

translation: (Within the gardens they will ask one another) about the criminals. [Al-Muddaththir 74:41, the verse begins at 74:40 with the gardens and the questioning]
interpretation: The verse presents the scene of the righteous in Paradise, who are secure and at ease, questioning one another about the guilty who are now in the Fire. Their inquiry is not born of cruelty but serves to show the justice of God, the consequence of the choices each soul made in the world, and the gratitude of the believers for their salvation. It reminds the listener that every person will be held to account for what they did, and that the separation between the righteous and the criminals will be made clear on the Day of Judgment.

translation: "What has brought you into Saqar?"
interpretation: The question is less a request for information than a reproach that forces the dwellers of the Fire to confront the cause of their own ruin. Saqar is not presented as an arbitrary fate but as the outcome of their own conduct: their neglect of prayer, their refusal to feed the needy, their immersion in idle talk, and their denial of the Day of Judgment. Asked in the presence of those who were saved, the question makes the reasons for their punishment plain and shows that each person's destination is the consequence of the path they chose in life.

translation: They will say: "We were not among those who used to pray."
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Muddaththir (74:43), is part of the dialogue of the people of the Fire, who are asked what brought them into Hellfire. Their answer identifies the first cause of their fate: they neglected the prayer, which was the foundation of their relationship with God. Their admission shows that abandoning worship was not a minor lapse but the root of their wider wrongdoing, since one who does not stand before God in prayer is typically led away from feeding the needy, from speaking the truth, and from the other duties that follow. The verse thus teaches that the salah is the pillar that holds up the rest of the religious life, and that its neglect carries grave consequences in the hereafter.

translation: "And we did not used to feed the needy."
interpretation: Spoken by the dwellers of the Fire when asked what led them into Saqar, this confession shows that neglecting the duty to feed the poor is treated as a grave moral failing, placed alongside neglect of prayer. Feeding the needy is therefore not a mere optional kindness but a sign of genuine faith, and withholding it reveals a heart closed to God's mercy and to the suffering of others. The verse teaches that religious life is judged by its social expression, so worship that does not produce compassion for the poor remains incomplete.

translation: And we used to plunge into vain talk along with those who plunge into it.
interpretation: This verse is spoken by the people of the Fire, who confess their past conduct on the Day of Judgment. Their confession reveals that their downfall was rooted in their habit of joining in idle, frivolous, and mocking discourse against the truth and its people, immersing themselves in what was vain alongside those who did the same. The verse teaches that companionship in heedlessness and participation in falsehood, even passively through the willingness to engage in such talk, is itself a serious moral failing that leads to ruin, and that believers must guard their tongues and their gatherings from vain and derisive speech.

translation: And we used to deny the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: This verse is spoken by the people of the left hand (the companions of the left) who describe the reason for their fate. Their punishment is not arbitrary; it follows from their persistent denial of the Day of Recompense. Denying the Day of Judgment is not merely an intellectual error but a moral disorder, for whoever believes that they will be held accountable for their deeds acts with restraint and responsibility, while whoever rejects accountability is freed to indulge in wrongdoing. Thus the verse shows that belief in the Last Day is the foundation of moral conduct, and that the root of their ruin was this heedlessness toward the reckoning that awaits every soul.

translation: Until there came to us the certainty.
interpretation: The 'certainty' (al-yaqin) refers to death, the one reality no denier can dispute once it arrives. The verse, spoken by the people of the Fire in Surah al-Muddaththir, shows that their denial of the Day of Judgment persisted until death removed all doubt, at which point the truth they had rejected became undeniable and their excuses were of no use.

translation: So the intercession of those who intercede will not benefit them.
interpretation: The verse, spoken in the context of those who turn away from the reminder (Surah al-Muddaththir 74:48), teaches that on the Day of Judgment no intercession will avail the disbelievers and the heedless, because intercession is not a means of escaping accountability for one's own refusal of guidance. Its benefit is conditioned on the permission of God and on the sincere faith of the one for whom it is sought, so those who have rejected the truth in this life find that no one's advocacy can replace their own faith and righteous deeds. The verse thus turns the reader back to personal responsibility: salvation is sought by turning to God in this world, not by relying on others to speak for us in the next.

translation: Then what is wrong with them that they turn away from the reminder?
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who, despite the clear and plain reminder set before them, deliberately turn their backs on it. Their aversion is not a result of a lack of evidence but of stubborn heedlessness, so the question 'what is wrong with them' expresses astonishment at the irrationality of rejecting guidance that is so evidently beneficial. It implies that the reminder itself is sufficient, and the fault lies in the hearts that refuse to be admonished.

translation: As if they were startled, frightened donkeys (asses) in flight.
interpretation: The image portrays those who turn away from the Qur'anic reminder as fleeing in blind panic, much like wild donkeys bolting in terror. Their aversion is not the product of reasoned rejection but of a heedless, instinctive fear that drives them away from guidance. The simile exposes the emptiness of their stance: they run from the truth without understanding what they flee, and the animal's frantic flight stands as a stark mirror of a soul that has surrendered its judgment to dread.

translation: (As if they were startled donkeys) fleeing from a lion.
interpretation: The verse portrays those who turn away from the Qur'anic reminder as frightened wild donkeys that bolt in panic at the mere sound of a lion, mocking the baseless terror that makes them recoil from guidance they should embrace. Their flight is absurd because the true danger lies in their own heedlessness, not in the reminder that calls them back to God.

translation: Nay, but every one of them desires that he be given scrolls spread open.
interpretation: The verse exposes the arrogance of those who rejected the Prophet's message: they were not content with the clear signs already present, and each one demanded a personal, open revelation addressed to himself, as though he alone deserved direct divine communication. The word 'bal' (nay, rather) rebukes this presumption, and the image of scrolls 'spread open' (munashsharah) mocks the demand for a tangible, publicly displayed book, in contrast with the Qur'an's own recognition that the true cause of their disbelief lies not in lack of evidence but in their refusal to accept accountability and humility before God.

translation: Nay, indeed! Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter.
interpretation: The verse rebukes those who deny or dismiss the Hereafter by pointing to the root of their denial: it is not a lack of evidence but a lack of fear and accountability in their hearts. Because they do not dread the consequences of their deeds before God, they feel free to reject the message and to live without restraint. The word "kallā" (nay, indeed not) rejects their false claims or pretexts, and "bal" (rather) reveals the true cause, which is heedlessness of the Last Day. In this light, genuine faith is shown to be tied to a living awareness of accountability, since fear of the Hereafter is what restrains the soul from wrongdoing and opens it to guidance.

translation: Nay, indeed it is a reminder.
interpretation: The verse refers to the Qur'an, which is declared to be a reminder (tadhkira) for those who seek guidance. The word "kalla" (nay/no) is a firm rebuttal of what precedes it, rejecting the false claims or indifference of those who turn away from the message. By affirming that the revelation is itself a reminder, the verse establishes that its purpose is to awaken the heart to what is forgotten: the truth of the Creator, accountability, and the moral duties of the human being. Its authority lies not in the eloquence of the messenger but in its inherent capacity to recall the soul to its original disposition toward God.

translation: So whoever wills, let him remember it.
interpretation: The phrase places the choice of remembrance squarely in the hands of the individual: the reminder is clear and available, but whether a person takes heed of it depends on his own will and sincere inclination. Remembrance is thus presented as a matter of personal responsibility, where the divine message is offered freely and each soul must decide whether to accept it and keep it in mind.

translation: And they do not remember (or accept admonition) except that Allah wills it. He is the One deserving of piety, and the One deserving of forgiveness.
interpretation: The verse reminds the believer that human remembrance and receptiveness to guidance are not self-generated but depend entirely on Allah's will; no one can take hold of the reminder unless He grants the capacity to do so. This humbles the heart, turning it away from self-reliance and toward constant dependence on God. The closing phrase, 'He is the One deserving of piety and the One deserving of forgiveness,' points to the fitting response to this reality: since God alone is worthy of being feared and obeyed, and since He is also the source of pardon, the servant should both revere Him with consciousness of duty and turn to Him in hope of mercy, asking Him for the guidance that only He can bestow.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Nay, I swear by the Day of Resurrection.
interpretation: The opening oath of Surah Al-Qiyamah is a solemn affirmation that the Day of Resurrection is real and certain. The particle 'La' before the verb 'uqsimu' is understood by many classical exegetes as an emphatic device that negates a presumed denial, as if to say that the matter needs no doubt, and the oath then draws the listener's attention to the reckoning that awaits every soul. By swearing by the Day itself, the verse elevates the promise of accountability to the highest level of seriousness, inviting the reader to reflect on how life would be lived if the certainty of standing before God were kept constantly in mind.

translation: And I swear by the reproaching soul (an-nafs al-lawwamah).
interpretation: God swears by the self that blames itself: the conscience that, even when it falls into wrongdoing, turns back in regret and reproaches itself for its failings. This verse elevates that inner self-accountability to the level of an oath, showing that the capacity to feel remorse and to measure one's own conduct against the standard of God is a sign of a living faith. Such a soul is not complacent; it is the inner witness that keeps a person from settling into heedlessness, and it stands in contrast to the soul that is wholly inclined toward evil or the soul that has come to rest in peace with its Lord. The verse thus reminds the believer that the struggle for righteousness begins within, in the honest self-examination that refuses to excuse one's own shortcomings.

translation: Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?
interpretation: The verse confronts the denier of resurrection with a rhetorical question that exposes the folly of his assumption: the same Creator who formed man from nothing and fashioned his bones with precision is fully capable of gathering them again after they have scattered in the grave. The word 'yahsab' points to a heedless, presumptuous supposition, as if man imagined that his scattered remains would be beyond divine power to reassemble. Its deeper message is that disbelief in the Resurrection rests not on evidence but on a careless assumption, and that a person who reflects on his own origin and the intricate structure of his body will recognize that bringing him back is far easier for the One who created him in the first place.

translation: Yes, [We are] able to reconstruct even his fingertips.
interpretation: The verse, revealed in response to those who deny resurrection, emphasizes the precision of God's power: the fingertips are singled out as a sign of how minutely God can restore the human body on the Day of Judgment. Far from being a minor detail, the fingerprint-like arrangement of the tips reflects the exactness of divine creation, so that the One who shaped each human being with such fine distinction is certainly able to bring every person back in complete and unique form.

translation: Nay, but man wishes to continue in sin ahead of him (that he may indulge in wickedness without restraint, denying the Day of Reckoning).
interpretation: The verse exposes the inner motive behind human denial of accountability: rather than seeking the truth, the human being desires to keep sinning freely into the future, so he resists the idea of a Day of Judgment that would restrain him. The word yafjur, from fujur, denotes transgression and the breaking of moral bounds, and the phrase 'amamahu' (before him) points to his determination to press forward in wrongdoing without looking back at consequences. The verse thus shows that disbelief in the Hereafter is often not born of intellectual doubt alone but of a desire to be free from moral responsibility.

translation: He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?" (Surah Al-Qiyamah 75:6)
interpretation: The question is not asked in sincere seeking of guidance but in denial, mockery, and dismissal of accountability. The one who asks wants to postpone or disregard the reckoning, as if the Day were a matter to be scheduled by him. The verses that follow answer him in a way that rebukes this attitude: the Day will come at a time known only to God, and the one who doubts will be confronted with the reality of his own deeds, even as he tries to deny them. The verse thus exposes the heedlessness of a person who treats the Hereafter as a distant or absurd topic, rather than preparing for it with conscious awareness.

translation: So when the sight is dazzled.
interpretation: This verse is from Surah Al-Qiyamah (75:7), describing the signs of the Day of Resurrection. It speaks of the moment when the eye is struck with dazzling terror and amazement at the unveiling of what was previously unseen, as the reality of the Hereafter becomes manifest. The dazzling of sight points to the bewilderment of the disbelievers, who will be startled by the approach of the Day, when their vision, formerly averted from the truth, is overwhelmed by the clear and undeniable reality before them.

translation: And the moon will be eclipsed.
interpretation: This phrase, drawn from Surah Al-Qiyamah (75:8), describes one of the signs accompanying the Day of Resurrection, when the moon loses its light and is darkened. Its placement alongside the bewildering of the sight and the joining of the sun and moon conveys the collapse of the cosmic order that the familiar world depends upon. The verse reminds the human being that the regularity of the heavens, which is so often taken for granted, is entirely subject to God's command and will end when He wills. Its force lies in provoking reflection on the transience of all created things and the certainty of accountability before the Creator.

translation: And the sun and the moon are joined together.
interpretation: This phrase, from Surah al-Qiyamah (75:9), describes one of the signs of the Day of Resurrection. The sun and the moon, which in ordinary life rise and set on fixed courses and never meet, will be brought together in a state of collapse and confusion, as their regular order is overturned. It conveys the complete dissolution of the cosmic system that humans have always taken for granted, and so underscores the seriousness of the Hereafter and the certainty that the present order is not eternal.

translation: On that Day will man say, "Where is the escape?" (Qur'an 75:10)
interpretation: The verse depicts the moment of the Day of Resurrection when the human being, confronted with the reality of accountability, finds that every avenue of refuge has closed. Having relied in worldly life on wealth, power, kinship, and deceptive hopes, he now realizes that none of these can shield him, and his question "where is the escape?" expresses the helplessness of a soul that has nowhere to flee from God's judgment. It is a reminder to act in this world with the awareness that true refuge lies only in God and in righteous deeds performed before that Day arrives.

translation: Nay, there is no refuge.
interpretation: The verse is a rebuke spoken in the context of the Day of Judgment (Surah Al-Qiyamah, 75:11), where a person who wishes to flee from accountability is told that there is no place of refuge or shelter. The word "wazar" refers to a mountain or fortress one might take shelter in, and the verse conveys that on the Day of Reckoning no stronger ground, wealth, or allied protection will save the wrongdoer. It directs the listener toward sincere preparation for their ultimate return to God, since escape from His judgment is impossible and refuge is found only in Him.

translation: To your Lord, that Day, will be the place of rest.
interpretation: The verse points to the ultimate destination of all created beings: on the Day of Judgment, the final place of settlement and return is with God alone. Just as the journey of life begins and proceeds under His command, it concludes in His presence, where each soul's fate is determined by Him. The word 'mustaqarr' conveys a settled, fixed abode, suggesting that the human being's ultimate state is not left to chance or to any other authority, but rests entirely with the Lord who governs the beginning and the end. This calls the reader to keep in mind that every action is moving toward that final reckoning and that true security and stability belong only to the One to whom all matters return.

translation: On that Day, man will be informed of what he sent forward and what he left behind.
interpretation: The verse points to the moment of reckoning, when a person's full record is laid open before him, so that nothing of his deeds, whether those he performed earlier in life and those whose effects continued after him, remains hidden. The phrase "what he sent forward" refers to the deeds he advanced toward his Lord, while "what he left behind" refers to the traces he left in the world, such as the good or harm that outlived him and the consequences that followed his actions. The verse thus calls the listener to examine his conduct now, since on that Day he will know completely the account of his life.

translation: Nay, but man, against himself, will be a witness with insight.
interpretation: The verse tells us that a person is, in the end, the most accurate witness against his own soul. Though he may offer excuses and make claims before others, his inner awareness and conscience know the truth of his deeds, so on the Day of Reckoning his own self will testify to what he did, and no one can deny what he knows within himself. The verse thus calls the believer to self-examination, to hold his soul to account now, before his own inner insight becomes the evidence that condemns him.

translation: Even if he presents his excuses.
interpretation: The verse means that on the Day of Judgment, a person's excuses will not save him, because his own soul will be a witness against him and the truth of his deeds will be fully exposed. Its deeper point is that self-justification fails before the inner reckoning: a person who knows himself best cannot escape accountability by offering pretexts, and the self-deception that made those excuses seem convincing in this life will collapse before the reality of what he did.

translation: Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it (the revelation).
interpretation: The verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad during the early moments of receiving revelation, when he would move his lips and tongue quickly while the angel Gabriel was reciting, eager to memorize it before it was complete. God instructs him to refrain from this haste, teaching that the preservation and recitation of the Qur'an rests with God alone. It models a larger spiritual lesson: the believer should approach divine guidance with patient attentiveness and trust in God's timing rather than anxious urgency, relying on God's assurance that He will gather and make the words clear.

translation: Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation.
interpretation: The verse assures the Prophet that God Himself takes responsibility for gathering the revelation in his heart and for enabling its recitation, so he need not hasten to memorize it out of anxiety about losing any of it. It reflects divine guardianship over the Qur'an from its descent to its preservation, and it is a reassurance that the message will be perfectly secured and made accessible.

translation: So when We have recited it, follow its recitation.
interpretation: The verse instructs the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to listen attentively to the revelation as it is recited to him by the angel Gabriel and to follow its recitation closely, without rushing ahead of it. It reflects the careful, receptive manner in which divine revelation was to be received and memorized, and it implies that the Prophet should submit his attention and tongue to the recitation that God has arranged for him.

translation: Then indeed, upon Us is its explanation.
interpretation: This verse (Al-Qiyamah 75:19) comes in the context of the revelation to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who would move his tongue quickly to memorize the Qur'an as it was revealed, out of eagerness to retain it. God reassures him that the task of collecting and preserving the revealed words is entrusted to Him, and that their clarification and explanation (bayan) is likewise His responsibility. The verse thus affirms divine guarantee over both the preservation of the scripture and the making clear of its meanings, relieving the Prophet of anxiety over forgetting or misunderstanding what was revealed.

translation: No! Rather, you love the hastening (fleeting) world.
interpretation: The verse rebukes the human tendency to prefer what is immediate and transient over what is lasting. Its opening word "kalla" is a sharp refusal of a false claim or attitude, and "bal" turns the reader from it to the real condition of the heart: a love of the present life that is quick to come and quick to pass. The emphasis lies on the inclination of the heart itself, so the verse calls the believer to examine where his affection truly rests, and to weigh the fleeting pleasures of this world against the enduring reward that the Hereafter offers.

translation: But you prefer the present life, [and neglect the Hereafter].
interpretation: The verse rebukes people for choosing the fleeting comforts of this world over the everlasting reward of the Hereafter. It points to a common human tendency to prioritize immediate, visible gains and pleasures while leaving aside what is lasting and of greater worth, calling the believer toorient their choices, efforts, and priorities toward the eternal life to come.

translation: Faces that Day will be radiant,
interpretation: The verse describes the faces of the righteous on the Day of Judgment as luminous and fresh with joy, a visible sign of the bliss they have earned. Their radiance reflects the inner state of contentment and the nearness to their Lord, in contrast to the darkened faces of those who will be overcome with sorrow and humiliation, as mentioned in the verses that follow. The image teaches that true inner reward eventually shows outwardly, and that the believer's hope is to be recognized on that Day by the light of faith and good deeds.

translation: Looking toward their Lord.
interpretation: The verse, from Surah Al-Qiyamah (75:23), describes the faces of the righteous on the Day of Resurrection as radiant and gazing upon their Lord. Scholars of the Sunni tradition, such as Al-Ash'ari and most of the major commentators, understand 'nazirah' literally as seeing with the eyes, taking the verse as affirmation of the believers' vision of God in the Hereafter, a bliss that surpasses all other delights. The Mu'tazilah, by contrast, interpreted 'nazirah' as waiting or expecting the reward of God, rejecting a literal beholding. The interpretation that this verse affirms a real, literal seeing of God by the faithful in Paradise, while acknowledging the transcendence of God beyond all comparison, is the view I hold.

translation: And faces, that Day, will be scowling, frowning.
interpretation: The verse describes the faces of the wrongdoers on the Day of Judgment as gloomy and contorted with dread and despair. The face, which normally reflects a person's inner state of ease and hope, becomes a visible sign of the anguish they carry within, as they anticipate the consequences of their deeds. This imagery teaches that the reckoning is not only a matter of outward punishment but also of the inner condition a person has cultivated, which becomes manifest on that Day.

translation: Thinking that a calamity that breaks the back is about to be inflicted upon them.
interpretation: The verse depicts the moment when the one who denied the Hereafter is confronted with the reality of what awaits. Expecting a catastrophe that will shatter the spine, they are gripped by dread, and the awareness of their fate arrives only when it can no longer be undone. The image of 'faqirah', a calamity that breaks the back, conveys both the severity of the punishment and the crushing helplessness of the one who once dismissed it.

translation: Nay! When the soul reaches the collarbones (throat).
interpretation: The verse depicts the moment of death as a decisive turning point that no one can escape or postpone. The word "kalla" is a sharp rebuke, rejecting a heedless attitude toward the truth and the Hereafter. When the dying soul rises up to the collarbones, the struggle of departure has reached its final stage, reminding the human being that life is brief and that the reckoning he has long ignored is about to arrive. The image urges the listener to prepare for that moment now, while there is still time to act, rather than being overtaken by it unprepared.

translation: And it will be said: "Who is a healer (who can save him)?"
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Qiyamah (75:27), depicts the moment of death, when the soul reaches the collarbones and the dying person is surrounded by the anxious question of those present, who look for someone to give a charm or cure. The question underscores the helplessness of human beings before the decree of God: no physician, enchanter, or remedy can avert the approaching end. It turns the reader's attention from worldly hopes of healing to the reality that only God holds ultimate power over life and death, and it calls the heedless to prepare for that final departure before it arrives.

translation: And he will be certain that it is the parting (from the world).
interpretation: The verse depicts the moment of death, when the dying person, in the anguish of his final breath, realizes that the time of separation has arrived. The word "ظن" here carries the sense of certainty rather than mere supposition, so the separation is one he cannot doubt. It is the parting of the soul from the body, and of the person from family, wealth, and all the worldly attachments he once held. The verse reminds the listener that this departure is inevitable and near, so one should prepare for it in this life.

translation: And leg will be wrapped around leg.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Qiyamah (75:29), depicts the moment of death, when the dying person's legs become entangled or stiffened, signalling that life is departing the body. Read alongside the preceding verses, it presents the final stage of the soul's departure, in which the physical body's failing is shown as a sign that the individual is being drawn toward the reckoning that awaits them.

translation: To your Lord, that Day, will be the driving (of all creatures).
interpretation: This verse, from Surah al-Qiyamah (75:30), speaks of the final gathering on the Day of Judgment, when all of creation is driven back to its Lord for reckoning. The word al-masaq denotes the act of being driven or led forcefully, evoking the image of humanity compelled toward its Creator, with no escape or refuge except in Him. It affirms that the ultimate destination of every soul is the presence of God, where every deed is weighed and every person returns to the One who originated them.

translation: So he neither affirmed the truth nor prayed.
interpretation: The verse pairs two negations, first of inward belief (tasdiq, confirming the truth in the heart) and then of outward worship (salah, prayer), to show that real faith is both conviction within and devotion expressed in action. The rejection of the message is shown first in the heart and then in the neglect of prayer, which suggests that abandoning the prayer is a visible sign of the inner denial, and that the one who turns away from the truth also turns away from submission to God.

translation: But he denied and turned away.
interpretation: This phrase, from Surah An-Nazi'at (79:22) in the context of the story of Pharaoh and Moses, describes the response of the arrogant rejecter of truth: after being shown the signs, he did not merely fail to believe but actively called the message a lie and turned his back on it. The verse highlights a two-fold sin, intellectual denial (takdhib) joined with practical refusal and withdrawal (tawalli), and shows that rejection of guidance is rooted not in lack of evidence but in pride and unwillingness to submit.

translation: Then he went back to his family, swaggering with conceit.
interpretation: The verse depicts the arrogant disposition of a man who, after rejecting the truth and turning away from it, returns to his household with self-importance and pride, stretching himself out in vanity as if he had achieved something great. His outward display of satisfaction contrasts with the emptiness of his rejection, showing how pride and heedlessness can make a person swagger in his own eyes while standing condemned before God. It is a warning against the posture of haughtiness that blinds one to the truth and to the consequences that follow.

translation: Woe to you, and woe once more; woe to you, and woe once more.
interpretation: The phrase is a stern warning of repeated ruin and misfortune directed at the one who turns away from the truth and persists in denial. Its doubling intensifies the threat, conveying that the punishment is certain and that each step toward destruction brings a further and greater calamity, as the wrongdoer is reminded that his arrogance and heedlessness will lead him to his own undoing.

translation: Then nearer to ruin for you, and nearer again. Then nearer to ruin for you, and nearer still. (That is, woe upon you, and woe again; then woe upon you, and woe again.)
interpretation: The repetition of the phrase, which means that ruin is drawing ever closer to the one addressed, conveys both the certainty and the escalation of the threat. Having turned away in arrogance from the truth, the disbeliever is told that each step of his denial and pride brings him nearer to his destruction, and that the doom awaiting him is not a single blow but a sequence of consequences that closes in on him inevitably.

translation: Does the human being think that he will be left neglected, without purpose or accountability?
interpretation: The verse poses a rhetorical question that challenges the human tendency to assume that life is without meaning and that one will escape any reckoning. The word 'sudan' conveys being left aimless, unattended, and unaccountable, like an animal let loose without a herder. By asking whether man supposes this, the verse affirms that human existence is purposeful: God created him with intention, will raise him after death, and will hold him responsible for his deeds. The question thus calls the heedless to reflect on their creation and to recognize that disbelief in accountability is a form of arrogant self-deception.

translation: Was he not a drop of semen emitted (in ejaculation)?
interpretation: The verse poses a rhetorical question to humankind, reminding them of their humble origin: a mere drop of fluid that is discharged. By recalling this lowly beginning, it confronts human arrogance and denial of resurrection, pointing to the same Creator who shaped a complete human being from something so insignificant, and who is therefore able to bring the dead back to life and hold them accountable.

translation: Then He made him a clinging clot, then fashioned [him] and proportioned him properly.
interpretation: The verse describes the stages of human formation in the womb as a process of gradual creation under God's direction. The 'clinging clot' (alaqah) points to the early embryonic stage, when the developing form attaches itself to the uterine wall and draws sustenance from it, reflecting both the fragility of the human origin and the dependence of human life on a Creator at every stage. The movement from clot to shaped form ('fashioned' and 'proportioned') emphasizes that creation is not random or instantaneous but ordered, purposeful and balanced, with each part of the body given its measure and function. The verse thus invites reflection on the humility of human beginnings and on the precision of divine craftsmanship, which calls the human being to gratitude and awareness of his own Maker.

translation: So He made from it two mates, the male and the female.
interpretation: The verse points to the origin of human life in a single source from which He then brought into being two complementary sexes, male and female. This pairing is presented as a deliberate divine design: the distinction between male and female is not accidental but purposeful, establishing the basis on which human beings multiply, find companionship, and sustain the continuity of life. It invites reflection on the order and wisdom woven into creation, in which difference becomes the means of mutual completion rather than mere division.

translation: Is not He who does that able to give life to the dead?
interpretation: The verse poses a rhetorical question that draws the listener to a self-evident conclusion: the One who has created the heavens and the earth, and who brought about the original creation, is certainly able to restore life to the dead. The question is meant to dissolve doubt about resurrection by directing the mind from the greater act of creation to the lesser act of revival. Since the initial origination of existence required no prior model or effort beyond His command, bringing the dead back to life is within the same power, and denying it amounts to denying the evidence of one's own creation and the world around them.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?
interpretation: The verse poses a rhetorical question that directs the human being to reflect on his own origin. Before he existed, he was nothing that could be named or remembered, so the verse invites him to recognize that his existence, with all its faculties, is a gift granted by the Creator. This recollection of a state of non-existence humbles the one who forgets his beginning, and it prepares the reader for the subsequent verses that describe his creation from a drop of mingled fluid and his being endowed with hearing and sight, thereby calling him to gratitude and to recognition of his dependence on God.

translation: Indeed, We created man from a drop of mingled fluid, [so that] We may test him; and We made him hearing and seeing.
interpretation: The verse places the human being's origin in a humble, mingled fluid, which points to his dependence and weakness from the start, yet it honors him with the faculties of hearing and seeing. These faculties are the instruments of trial: God endows man with the means to perceive truth and falsehood, and his subsequent choices in response to what he hears and sees become the arena of the test. Thus humility about his beginning and responsibility for his conduct are joined in one picture of the human condition.

translation: Indeed, We guided him to the way; he is either grateful or ungrateful.
interpretation: The verse presents divine guidance as a gift offered to every human being: God has made the path of truth clear through reason, revelation, and signs. Because the choice of walking it is left to the human will, the verse places each person before a decisive fork, where gratitude for guidance leads to belief and righteous conduct, while ingratitude leads to rejection. Thus human moral responsibility is affirmed, since the guidance is given but its acceptance or refusal rests with the individual.

translation: Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers chains, and shackles, and a blazing Fire.
interpretation: The verse presents the punishment of those who reject faith as a deliberate, prepared reality rather than a chance occurrence, emphasizing divine justice and the completeness of their confinement. The chains and shackles evoke total loss of freedom and humiliation, binding both body and will, which reflects how persistent disbelief enslaves the soul to its own choices. The blazing Fire marks the culmination of this bondage, suggesting that the consequences of rejecting guidance are both inescapable and immediate in their severity, and inviting the listener to reflect on the freedom that faith offers in contrast.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is of camphor.
interpretation: The verse portrays the reward of the righteous (al-abrar) in the Hereafter as a pure and refreshing drink, its blend being camphor, a substance known for its coolness and fragrance. Since the Arabic word mizaj denotes what is mixed into a drink, the imagery conveys a beverage that is cooling, delightful, and free of the impurities of worldly drink. The image points to the honor and bliss prepared for those who have lived in devotion and uprightness, with the sensory delight of the garden serving as a sign of their elevated station before God.

translation: A spring from which the servants of Allah drink; they make it gush forth in abundance.
interpretation: The verse portrays the reward of the righteous (al-abrar) in Paradise: a spring of pure drink reserved for the servants of Allah, who do not merely receive it passively but direct its flow to wherever they wish, as a sign of honor and ease. The image of them causing it to gush forth abundantly suggests that the blessings of the Hereafter are granted with generosity and under the believers' own control, a contrast to the scarcity and dependence of worldly life, and it invites the reader to aspire to be among those whose devotion and good deeds earn such nearness to God.

translation: They fulfill their vows and fear a Day whose evil will be widespread.
interpretation: The verse describes the righteous (al-abrar) by two qualities that flow from one root: their faithfulness to what they bind themselves to, even when it is voluntary as in a vow, and their constant awareness of the Day of Judgment. Fulfilling a vow reflects a conscience that treats every promise made before God as a trust, so that the inner commitment of the heart is matched by outward action. Fear of a Day whose harm is 'far-spreading' (mustatir) reflects a recognition that the consequences of wrongdoing will not remain contained but will reach everyone and everything, which in turn motivates a life of caution, discipline, and responsibility. Together these qualities show that true piety is not merely ritual but a sustained integrity of word, deed, and accountability before God.

translation: And they give food, despite their love for it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive.
interpretation: The verse portrays the righteous (al-abrar, as described in the surrounding verses of Surah al-Insan) as people whose charity is sincere and costly: they give food while still loving it, which shows that their generosity comes from attachment to God rather than from surplus or self-interest.
